Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Awakened One.

17. Cattālīsanipāto

17. The Book of Forty

[521] 1. Tesakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[521] 1. The Commentary on the Tesakuṇa Jātaka

Vessantaraṃ [V 5.0104][P 5.0109][M 5.0114] taṃ pucchāmīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño ovādavasena kathesi. Tañhi rājānaṃ dhammassavanatthāya āgataṃ satthā āmantetvā “mahārāja, raññā nāma dhammena rajjaṃ kāretabbaṃ, yasmiñhi samaye rājāno adhammikā honti, rājayuttāpi tasmiṃ samaye adhammikā hontī”ti catukkanipāte (a. ni. 4.70) āgatasuttanayena ovaditvā agatigamane agatiagamane ca ādīnavañca ānisaṃsañca kathetvā “supinakūpamā kāmā”tiādinā nayena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ vitthāretvā, “mahārāja, imesañhi sattānaṃ –

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story beginning with the words, 'Vessantaraṃ taṃ pucchāmi,' by way of advice to the King of Kosala. For when that king came to hear the Dhamma, the Teacher addressed him and said: 'O great king, a king should indeed rule the kingdom with righteousness. For when kings are unrighteous, their officials also become unrighteous.' Then, having advised him according to the method of the sutta found in the Book of Fours (A.N. 4.70), and having spoken of the dangers of falling into prejudice and the benefits of not falling into prejudice, he elaborated on the dangers of sensual pleasures by the method beginning with 'Sensual pleasures are like a dream,' saying: 'O great king, for these beings—'

‘Maccunā saṅgaro natthi, lañjaggāho na vijjati;

Yuddhaṃ natthi jayo natthi, sabbe maccuparāyaṇā’.

'There is no truce with Death, no bribe can be given; there is no battle, there is no victory—all are bound for death.'

Tesaṃ paralokaṃ gacchantānaṃ ṭhapetvā attanā kataṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ aññā patiṭṭhā nāma natthi. Evaṃ ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ avassaṃ pahātabbaṃ, na yasaṃ nissāya pamādaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, appamatteneva hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Porāṇakarājāno anuppannepi buddhe paṇḍitānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā devanagaraṃ pūrayamānā gamiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

For those going to the next world, apart from the wholesome deeds they have done themselves, there is no other support. Thus, this transient existence must certainly be abandoned. It is not fitting to be heedless by relying on fame; rather, one should rule the kingdom righteously, being ever diligent. Ancient kings, even when Buddhas had not arisen, abiding by the advice of the wise, ruled righteously and went on to fill the city of the gods.' Having said this, being requested by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rajjaṃ kārento aputtako ahosi, patthentopi puttaṃ vā dhītaraṃ vā na labhi. So ekadivasaṃ mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā divasabhāgaṃ uyyāne kīḷitvā maṅgalasālarukkhamūle [P 5.0110] sayanaṃ attharāpetvā thokaṃ niddāyitvā pabuddho sālarukkhaṃ oloketvā tattha sakuṇakulāvakaṃ passi, saha dassanenevassa sineho uppajji. So ekaṃ purisaṃ pakkosāpetvā “imaṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā etasmiṃ kulāvake kassaci atthitaṃ vā natthitaṃ vā jānāhī”ti āha. So “sādhu, devā”ti vatvā abhiruhitvā tattha [M 5.0115] tīṇi aṇḍakāni [V 5.0105] disvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “tena hi etesaṃ upari nāsavātaṃ mā vissajjesī”ti vatvā “caṅkoṭake kappāsapicuṃ attharitvā tattheva tāni aṇḍakāni ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ otarāhī”ti otārāpetvā caṅkoṭakaṃ hatthena gahetvā “katarasakuṇaṇḍakāni nāmetānī”ti amacce pucchi. Te “mayaṃ na jānāma, nesādā jānissantī”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā nesāde pakkosāpetvā pucchi. Nesādā, “mahārāja, tesu ekaṃ ulūkaaṇḍaṃ, ekaṃ sālikāaṇḍaṃ, ekaṃ suvakaaṇḍa”nti kathayiṃsu. Kiṃ pana ekasmiṃ kulāvake tiṇṇaṃ sakuṇikānaṃ aṇḍāni hontīti. Āma, deva, paripanthe asati sunikkhittāni na nassantīti. Rājā tussitvā “ime mama puttā bhavissantī”ti tāni tīṇi aṇḍāni tayo amacce paṭicchāpetvā “ime mayhaṃ puttā bhavissanti, tumhe sādhukaṃ paṭijaggitvā aṇḍakosato nikkhantakāle mamāroceyyāthā”ti āha. Te tāni sādhukaṃ rakkhiṃsu.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom but was childless; though he longed for a son or a daughter, he did not obtain one. One day, he went to the park with a large retinue, spent part of the day playing in the park, and had a bed prepared at the foot of an auspicious sāla tree. After sleeping for a short while and waking up, he looked at the sāla tree and saw a bird's nest there. As soon as he saw it, affection arose in him. He summoned a man and said, 'Climb this tree and find out whether there is anything in this nest or not.' The man replied, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' climbed up, and upon seeing three eggs there, reported it to the king. The king said, 'Then, do not let your breath fall upon them,' and instructed, 'Spread a wad of cotton in a basket, place the eggs there, and come down carefully.' After having them brought down, he held the basket in his hand and asked his ministers, 'What kind of bird's eggs are these?' They replied, 'We do not know, but the fowlers will know.' The king summoned the fowlers and asked them. The fowlers said, 'Great king, of these, one is an owl's egg, one is a myna's egg, and one is a parrot's egg.' 'But can there be eggs of three different birds in one nest?' 'Yes, Your Majesty, when there is no danger, well-placed eggs do not perish.' Pleased, the king said, 'These will be my sons,' and entrusted the three eggs to three ministers, saying, 'These will become my sons. Take good care of them and inform me when they emerge from the eggshells.' They carefully guarded them.

Tesu paṭhamaṃ ulūkaaṇḍaṃ bhijji. Amacco ekaṃ nesādaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tvaṃ itthibhāvaṃ vā purisabhāvaṃ vā jānāhī”ti vatvā tena taṃ vīmaṃsitvā “puriso”ti vutte rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “putto te, deva, jāto”ti āha. Rājā tuṭṭho tassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā “puttakaṃ me sādhukaṃ paṭijagga, ‘vessantaro’ti cassa nāmaṃ karohī”ti vatvā uyyojesi. So tathā akāsi. Tato katipāhaccayena sālikāaṇḍaṃ bhijji. Sopi amacco taṃ nesādena vīmaṃsāpetvā “itthī”ti sutvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “dhītā te, deva, jātā”ti āha. Rājā tuṭṭho tassapi bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā “dhītaraṃ [P 5.0111] me sādhukaṃ paṭijagga, ‘kuṇḍalinī’ti cassā nāmaṃ karohī”ti vatvā uyyojesi. Sopi tathā akāsi. Puna katipāhaccayena suvakaaṇḍaṃ bhijji. Sopi amacco nesādena taṃ vīmaṃsitvā “puriso”ti vutte rañño santikaṃ gantvā “putto te, deva, jāto”ti āha. Rājā tuṭṭho tassapi bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā “puttassa me mahantena parivārena maṅgalaṃ katvā ‘jambuko’tissa nāmaṃ karohī”ti vatvā uyyojesi. Sopi tathā akāsi. Te tayopi sakuṇā tiṇṇaṃ amaccānaṃ gehesu rājakumāraparihāreneva vaḍḍhanti. Rājā “mama putto, mama dhītā”ti voharati. Athassa amaccā aññamaññaṃ avahasanti “passatha, bho, rañño [M 5.0116] kiriyaṃ, tiracchānagatepi ‘putto me, dhītā me’ti vadanto vicaratī”ti.

Among them, first the owl egg hatched. The minister summoned a fowler and said, 'You must determine whether it is female or male.' After the fowler examined it and said, 'It is male,' the minister approached the king and announced, 'Your Majesty, a son has been born to you.' The king, delighted, gave him much wealth and said, 'Take good care of my little son, and name him "Vessantara",' then dismissed him. He did so. Then, after a few days, the myna egg hatched. That minister also had it examined by the fowler, and upon hearing 'It is female,' he went to the king and said, 'Your Majesty, a daughter has been born to you.' The king, delighted, gave him much wealth as well and said, 'Take good care of my daughter, and name her "Kuṇḍalinī",' then dismissed him. He also did so. Again, after a few days, the parrot egg hatched. That minister also had it examined by the fowler, and upon being told 'It is male,' he went to the king and said, 'Your Majesty, a son has been born to you.' The king, delighted, gave him much wealth as well and said, 'Perform a grand ceremony for my son with a great retinue and name him "Jambuka",' then dismissed him. He also did so. Those three birds grew up in the homes of the three ministers with the care befitting royal princes. The king would refer to them as, 'My son, my daughter.' Then his ministers mocked the king among themselves, saying, 'Behold, sirs, the king’s actions—he goes around calling even animals "my son" and "my daughter".'

Taṃ sutvā rājā cintesi – “ime amaccā etesaṃ mama puttānaṃ paññāsampadaṃ na jānanti, pākaṭaṃ nesaṃ karissāmī”ti. Athekaṃ amaccaṃ vessantarassa santikaṃ pesesi – “tumhākaṃ pitā pañhaṃ pucchitukāmo, kadā kira āgantvā pucchatū”ti. So amacco gantvā vessantaraṃ [V 5.0106] vanditvā taṃ sāsanaṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā vessantaro attano paṭijaggakaṃ amaccaṃ pakkositvā “mayhaṃ kira pitā maṃ pañhaṃ pucchitukāmo, tassa idhāgatassa sakkāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kadā āgacchatū”ti pucchi. Amacco “ito sattame divase tava pitā āgacchatū”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā vessantaro “pitā me ito sattame divase āgacchatū”ti vatvā uyyojesi. So āgantvā rañño ācikkhi. Rājā sattame divase nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā puttassa nivesanaṃ agamāsi. Vessantaro rañño mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ kāresi, antamaso dāsakammakārānampi sakkāraṃ kāresi. Rājā vessantarasakuṇassa gehe bhuñjitvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavitvā sakaṃ nivesanaṃ āgantvā rājaṅgaṇe mahantaṃ maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā alaṅkatamaṇḍapamajjhe mahājanaparivāro nisīditvā “vessantaraṃ [P 5.0112] ānetū”ti amaccassa santikaṃ pesesi. Amacco vessantaraṃ suvaṇṇapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā ānesi. Vessantarasakuṇo pitu aṅke nisīditvā pitarā saha kīḷitvā gantvā tattheva suvaṇṇapīṭhe nisīdi. Atha naṃ rājā mahājanamajjhe rājadhammaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king thought: “These ministers do not know the wisdom of my sons; I will make it manifest to them.” Then he sent a minister to Vessantara with the message: “Your father wishes to ask a question; when, pray, should he come to ask it?” The minister went, paid homage to Vessantara, and delivered the message. Hearing this, Vessantara summoned his attendant minister and asked, “My father, it seems, wishes to ask me a question; it is proper to show hospitality to him when he comes here. When should he come?” The minister replied, “Let your father come on the seventh day from now.” Hearing this, Vessantara said, “Let my father come on the seventh day from now,” and sent the messenger away. He went back and informed the king. On the seventh day, the king had a drum beaten throughout the city and went to his son’s residence. Vessantara showed great honor to the king; he even had honor shown to the servants and workers. The king dined in the house of the bird Vessantara, enjoyed great glory, and returned to his own residence. He had a grand pavilion built in the royal courtyard, had a drum beaten throughout the city, and sat surrounded by a great crowd in the middle of the adorned pavilion. Then he sent a message to a minister, saying, “Bring Vessantara.” The minister had Vessantara seated on a golden throne and brought him. The bird Vessantara sat on his father’s lap, played with his father, and then went and sat on that same golden throne. Then the king, questioning him about the duty of a king in the midst of the great crowd, spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Vessantaraṃ taṃ pucchāmi, sakuṇa bhaddamatthu te;

Rajjaṃ kāretukāmena, kiṃ su kiccaṃ kataṃ vara”nti.

“Vessantara, I ask you, O bird, may blessings be upon you. For one who wishes to rule a kingdom, what is the best duty to be done?”

Tattha sakuṇāti taṃ ālapati. Kiṃ sūti kataraṃ kiccaṃ kataṃ varaṃ uttamaṃ hoti, kathehi me, tāta, sakalaṃ rājadhammanti evaṃ kira taṃ so pucchi.

Here, he addresses him as 'sakuṇa'. 'Kiṃ su' means: 'Which duty, when done, is excellent and supreme? Explain to me, dear one, the entire royal duty.' Thus, it is said, he asked him.

Taṃ sutvā vessantaro pañhaṃ akathetvāva rājānaṃ tāva pamādena codento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Vessantara, without yet answering the question, first reproached the king for his negligence, uttering the second verse:

2.

2.

“Cirassaṃ vata maṃ tāto, kaṃso bārāṇasiggaho;

Pamatto appamattaṃ maṃ, pitā puttaṃ acodayī”ti.

“Indeed, after a long time, my father, Kaṃsa, the ruler of Bārāṇasī, has questioned me, his diligent son, while he himself was negligent.”

Tattha [M 5.0117] tātoti pitā. Kaṃsoti idaṃ tassa nāmaṃ. Bārāṇasiggahoti catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi bārāṇasiṃ saṅgahetvā vattanto. Pamattoti evarūpānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ santike vasanto pañhassa apucchanena pamatto. Appamattaṃ manti sīlādiguṇayogena maṃ appamattaṃ. Pitāti posakapitā. Acodayīti amaccehi “tiracchānagate putte katvā voharatī”ti avahasiyamāno pamādaṃ āpajjitvā cirassaṃ ajja codesi, pañhaṃ pucchīti vadati.

Therein, 'tāto' means father. 'Kaṃso' is his name. 'Bārāṇasiggaho' means one who rules, having supported the people of Bārāṇasī with the four bases of sympathy. 'Pamatto' means being negligent by not asking questions even while living near such wise ones. 'Appamattaṃ maṃ' means me, who am diligent through the practice of virtues like morality. 'Pitā' means the foster father. 'Acodayī' means that, having become negligent after being ridiculed by the ministers who said, “He treats his sons as if they were animals,” today, after a long time, he questioned me, that is, he asked a question.

Evaṃ [V 5.0107] so imāya gāthāya codetvā “mahārāja, raññā nāma tīsu dhammesu ṭhatvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretabba”nti vatvā rājadhammaṃ kathento imā gāthāyo āha –

Having thus censured him with this verse, he said, “Great king, a king should govern righteously, abiding in three principles,” and while explaining the royal duty, he spoke these verses:

3.

3.

“Paṭhameneva vitathaṃ, kodhaṃ hāsaṃ nivāraye;

Tato kiccāni kāreyya, taṃ vataṃ āhu khattiya.

“First of all, one should restrain falsehood, anger, and frivolous laughter. Then, one should perform duties—this, O warrior, they call the kingly observance.”

4.

4.

“Yaṃ tvaṃ tāta tapokammaṃ, pubbe katamasaṃsayaṃ;

Ratto duṭṭho ca yaṃ kayirā, na taṃ kayirā tato puna.

“Dear one, whatever austerity you have formerly performed was without doubt. But whatever one might do out of lust or hatred, one should not do that again thereafter.”

5.

5.

“Khattiyassa pamattassa, raṭṭhasmiṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Sabbe bhogā vinassanti, rañño taṃ vuccate aghaṃ.

“For a king negligent in the realm, O promoter of the realm, all possessions perish; this is called the king’s misfortune.”

6.

6.

“Sirī tāta alakkhī ca, pucchitā etadabravuṃ;

Uṭṭhānavīriye pose, ramāhaṃ anusūyake.

“Fortune, dear one, and Misfortune, when asked, replied thus: ‘I delight in the person who is energetic, persevering, and unjealous.’”

7.

7.

“Usūyake [P 5.0113] duhadaye, purise kammadussake;

Kāḷakaṇṇī mahārāja, ramati cakkabhañjanī.

“Misfortune, O great king, the wheel-breaker, delights in the envious, hardhearted person, and the one who spoils work.”

8.

8.

“So tvaṃ sabbe suhadayo, sabbesaṃ rakkhito bhava;

Alakkhiṃ nuda mahārāja, lakkhyā bhava nivesanaṃ.

“Therefore, be good-hearted towards all and protected by all. O great king, dispel misfortune and be an abode of fortune.”

9.

9.

“Sa lakkhīdhitisampanno, puriso hi mahaggato;

Amittānaṃ kāsipati, mūlaṃ aggañca chindati.

“For that person endowed with fortune and steadfastness is truly of great worth; O Lord of the Kāsis, he destroys the root and the branch of his enemies.”

10.

10.

“Sakkopi hi bhūtapati, uṭṭhāne nappamajjati;

Sa kalyāṇe dhitiṃ katvā, uṭṭhāne kurute mano.

“Even Sakka, lord of beings, does not neglect diligence. Having fixed his resolve on what is good, he sets his mind on exertion.”

11.

11.

“Gandhabbā [M 5.0118] pitaro devā, sājīvā honti tādino;

Uṭṭhāhato appamajjato, anutiṭṭhanti devatā.

“The celestial musicians, the ancestors, and the gods—such ones have well-lived lives; deities attend to one who is energetic and unremitting.”

12.

12.

“So [V 5.0108] appamatto akkuddho, tāta kiccāni kāraya;

Vāyamassu ca kiccesu, nālaso vindate sukhaṃ.

“Therefore be diligent and without anger, dear one, and have your duties performed. Strive in your tasks, for the lazy do not find happiness.”

13.

13.

“Tattheva te vattapadā, esāva anusāsanī;

Alaṃ mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amittānaṃ dukhāya cā”ti.

“Therein indeed are your principles of conduct; this indeed is the instruction. It is sufficient to gladden friends and to cause suffering to enemies.”

Tattha paṭhameneva vitathanti, tāta, rājā nāma āditova musāvādaṃ nivāraye. Musāvādino hi rañño raṭṭhaṃ nirojaṃ hoti, pathaviyā ojā kammakaraṇaṭṭhānato sattaratanamattaṃ heṭṭhā bhassati, tato āhāre vā telamadhuphāṇitādīsu vā osadhesu ojā na hoti. Nirojāhārabhojanā manussā bahvābādhā honti, raṭṭhe thalajalapathesu āyo nuppajjati, tasmiṃ anuppajjante rājāno duggatā honti. Te sevake saṅgaṇhituṃ na sakkonti, asaṅgahitā sevakā rājānaṃ garucittena na olokenti. Evaṃ, tāta, musāvādo nāmesa nirojo, na so jīvitahetupi kātabbo, saccaṃ pana sādutaraṃ rasānanti tadeva paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Apica musāvādo nāma guṇaparidhaṃsako vipattipariyosāno, dutiyacittavāre avīciparāyaṇaṃ karoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe “dhammo have hato hantī”ti cetiyajātakaṃ (jā. 1.8.45 ādayo) kathetabbaṃ.

Therein, 'first of all, falsehood' means: dear one, a king should restrain false speech from the very beginning. For in the case of a king who speaks falsely, the kingdom becomes devoid of vitality. The vitality of the earth, from the place of labor, sinks downwards by the measure of seven cubits. Then, in food, oil, honey, molasses, and medicines, there is no vitality. People who eat food lacking vitality become afflicted with many illnesses. In the kingdom, prosperity does not arise on land or water routes. When this does not arise, kings fall into misfortune. They cannot support their servants, and unsupported servants do not regard the king with respect. Thus, dear one, falsehood is indeed devoid of vitality—it should not be done even for the sake of life. Truth, however, is sweeter than any taste, and so it should be embraced. Moreover, falsehood destroys virtues and ends in ruin, leading to Avīci hell at the time of the second consciousness. On this point, the Cetiya Jātaka ('For the Dhamma, indeed, when destroyed, destroys') should be told.

Kodhanti, tāta, rājā nāma paṭhamameva kujjhanalakkhaṇaṃ kodhampi nivāreyya. Tāta, aññesañhi kodho khippaṃ matthakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, rājūnaṃ pāpuṇāti. Rājāno nāma vācāvudhā kujjhitvā olokitamattenāpi paraṃ vināsenti, tasmā raññā aññehi manussehi atirekataraṃ nikkodhena bhavitabbaṃ, khantimettānuddayāsampannena attano piyaputtaṃ viya lokaṃ volokentena bhavitabbaṃ. Tāta, atikodhano nāma rājā uppannaṃ yasaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkoti. Imassa panatthassa dīpanatthaṃ khantivādijātaka- (jā. 1.4.49 ādayo) cūḷadhammapālajātakāni (jā. 1.5.44 ādayo) kathetabbāni. Cūḷadhammapālajātakasmiñhi mahāpatāpano nāma rājā puttaṃ ghātetvā [P 5.0114] puttasokena hadayena phalitena matāya deviyā sayampi deviṃ anusocanto [M 5.0119] hadayena phaliteneva mari. Atha te tayopi ekaāḷāhaneva jhāpesuṃ. Tasmā raññā paṭhamameva musāvādaṃ vajjetvā dutiyaṃ kodho vajjetabbo.

‘Anger’ means: dear one, a king should first restrain anger, which has the characteristic of rage. Dear one, in others, anger does not quickly reach its peak, but in kings, it does. Kings, armed with words, can destroy others with just a glance when angered. Therefore, a king must be even more free from anger than other men, endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, surveying the world as if it were his own beloved son. Dear one, an excessively angry king cannot protect the glory he has attained. To illustrate this point, the Khantivādi Jātaka and the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka should be told. In the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, King Mahāpatāpana, having had his son executed, saw the queen die with a broken heart from grief over their son; he himself, lamenting the queen, also died with a broken heart. Then, the three of them were cremated on a single pyre. Therefore, a king must first abandon falsehood and secondly abandon anger.

Hāsanti hassaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tesu tesu kiccesu uppilāvitacittatāya keḷisīlataṃ parihāsaṃ nivāreyya. Tāta, raññā nāma keḷisīlena na bhavitabbaṃ, aparapattiyena hutvā sabbāni kiccāni attapaccakkheneva kātabbāni. Uppilāvitacitto hi rājā atuletvā [V 5.0109] kammāni karonto laddhaṃ yasaṃ vināseti. Imasmiṃ panatthe sarabhaṅgajātake (jā. 2.17.50 ādayo) purohitassa vacanaṃ gahetvā daṇḍakirañño kisavacche aparajjhitvā saha raṭṭhena ucchijjitvā kukkuḷaniraye nibbattabhāvo ca mātaṅgajātake (jā. 1.15.1 ādayo) majjharañño brāhmaṇānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā mātaṅgatāpase aparajjhitvā saha raṭṭhena ucchijjitvā niraye nibbattabhāvo ca ghaṭapaṇḍitajātake (jā. 1.10.165 ādayo) dasabhātikarājadārakānaṃ mohamūḷhānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā kaṇhadīpāyane aparajjhitvā vāsudevakulassa nāsitabhāvo ca kathetabbo.

‘Hāsaṃ’ means amusement; or this is simply the reading. In various duties, one should restrain jesting and mockery, which are due to a frivolous mind and a tendency to amusement. Dear one, a king should not be given to jesting. Being one who is not dependent on others, all duties should be done by his own direct experience. For a king with a frivolous mind, performing actions without due consideration, destroys the glory he has gained. Regarding this matter, it should be told how in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, heeding the words of the chaplain, King Daṇḍaki wronged the young ascetic Kisavaccha and, along with his kingdom, was destroyed and reborn in the Kukkuḷa hell; and how in the Mātaṅga Jātaka, King Majjha, heeding the words of the brahmins, wronged the ascetic Mātaṅga and, along with his kingdom, was destroyed and reborn in hell; and how in the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka, the ten brother princes, deluded by folly, heeding their own counsel, wronged Kaṇhadīpāyana, and brought about the destruction of the Vāsudeva clan.

Tato kiccāni kāreyyāti evaṃ, tāta, paṭhamaṃ musāvādaṃ dutiyaṃ kodhaṃ tatiyaṃ adhammahāsaṃ vajjetvā tato pacchā rājā raṭṭhavāsīnaṃ kattabbakiccāni kāreyya. Taṃ vataṃ āhu khattiyāti, khattiyamahārāja, yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, etaṃ rañño vatasamādānanti porāṇakapaṇḍitā kathayiṃsu.

‘Then, one should perform duties’ means thus: dear one, having first avoided false speech, secondly anger, and thirdly improper laughter, the king should thereafter carry out the duties to be done for the inhabitants of the kingdom. ‘This, O warrior, they call the practice’ means: O great warrior king, what I have said is the king's undertaking of his duties—so the ancient wise ones have said.

Na taṃ kayirāti yaṃ tayā rāgādivasena pacchā tāpakaraṃ kammaṃ kataṃ hoti, tato pubbe katato puna tādisaṃ kammaṃ na kayirā, mā kareyyāsi, tātāti. Vuccateti taṃ rañño aghanti vuccati, evaṃ porāṇakapaṇḍitā kathayiṃsu. Sirīti idaṃ vessantarasakuṇo pubbe bārāṇasiyaṃ pavattitakāraṇaṃ āharitvā dassento āha. Tattha abravunti suciparivāraseṭṭhinā pucchitā kathayiṃsu. Uṭṭhānavīriyeti yo poso uṭṭhāne vīriye ca patiṭṭhito, na ca paresaṃ sampattiṃ disvā usūyati, tasmiṃ ahaṃ abhiramāmīti āha. Evaṃ tāva tāta sirī kathesi. Usūyaketi alakkhī pana, tāta, pucchitā ahaṃ parasampattiusūyake duhadaye ducitte kalyāṇakammadūsake yo kalyāṇakammaṃ dussanto [M 5.0120] appiyāyanto aṭṭīyanto na karoti, tasmiṃ abhiramāmīti āha. Evaṃ sā kāḷakaṇṇī, mahārāja, ramati patirūpadesavāsādino kusalacakkassa bhañjanī.

Do not do that deed which, done by you out of passion and the like, would later bring torment. Having done such a deed before, do not do it again; do not do it, dear one. Thus it is said, 'That is called the king's affliction,' so spoke the ancient wise ones. Regarding 'Sirī', the Vessantara bird, presenting the account of what previously took place in Bārāṇasī, spoke thus. There, questioned by the merchant Suciparivāra, they spoke. 'One who is established in effort and energy, and does not envy the success of others—in him I delight,' she said. Thus far, dear one, Sirī spoke. 'As for the envious one,' Alakkhī, dear one, being questioned, said: 'I delight in one who envies the success of others, in the ill-hearted, in the ill-minded, in the corrupter of good deeds—one who, defiling, disliking, and loathing good deeds, does not perform them.' Thus, O great king, does she, Kāḷakaṇṇī, delight; she is the breaker of the wheel of the wholesome, which begins with dwelling in a suitable place and so on.

Suhadayoti sundaracitto hitacittako. Nudāti nīhara. Nivesananti lakkhiyā pana nivesanaṃ bhava patiṭṭhā hohi. Sa lakkhīdhitisampannoti, mahārāja, kāsipati so puriso paññāya ceva vīriyena ca sampanno. Mahaggatoti mahajjhāsayo corānaṃ paccayabhūte gaṇhanto amittānaṃ mūlaṃ core gaṇhanto amittānaṃ aggaṃ chindatīti vadati. Sakkoti [P 5.0115] indo. Bhūtapatīti rājānaṃ ālapati. Uṭṭhāneti uṭṭhānavīriye. Nappamajjatīti na pamajjati, sabbakiccāni karoti. Sa kalyāṇeti so devarājā uṭṭhānavīriye manaṃ karonto pāpakammaṃ akatvā [V 5.0110] kalyāṇe puññakammasmiññeva dhitiṃ katvā appamatto uṭṭhāne manaṃ karoti, tassa pana kalyāṇakamme vīriyakaraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ sarabhaṅgajātake dvīsu devalokesu devatāhi saddhiṃ kapiṭṭhārāmaṃ āgantvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā dhammassa sutabhāvo, mahākaṇhajātake (jā. 1.12.61 ādayo) attano ānubhāvena janaṃ tāsetvā osakkantassa sāsanassa pavattitabhāvo cāti evamādīni vatthūni kathetabbāni.

'Suhadayo' means beautiful-hearted and benevolent-hearted. 'Nuda' means to drive away. 'Nivesana' means to be a dwelling place or a foundation for fortune. 'Sa lakkhīdhitisampanno' (he who is endowed with fortune and resolution) means, O great king, that man, the lord of Kāsi, is endowed with wisdom and energy. 'Mahaggato' means having a noble disposition; by apprehending those who are the cause of thieves and capturing the thieves who are the root of enemies, he cuts off the chief of the enemies, so it is said. 'Sakka' means Indra. 'Bhūtapati' is an address to the king. 'Uṭṭhāne' means in energetic effort. 'Nappamajjati' means he does not neglect; he performs all duties. 'Sa kalyāṇe' means that king of gods, applying his mind to energetic effort, not doing evil, having resolution only in virtuous deeds of merit, is diligent and applies his mind to effort. To show his energetic activity in virtuous deeds, stories such as these should be told: in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, having come to the Kapiṭṭha park with deities from two heavenly realms and asked a question, there was the hearing of the Dhamma; in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka, by his own power terrifying the people, there was the re-establishment of the declining dispensation.

Gandhabbāti cātumahārājikānaṃ heṭṭhā catuyonikā devā, catuyonikattāyeva kira te gandhabbā nāma jātā. Pitaroti brahmāno. Devāti upapattidevavasena cha kāmāvacaradevā. Tādinoti tathāvidhassa kusalābhiratassa rañño. Sājīvā hontīti samānajīvikā upajīvitabbā. Tādisā hi rājāno dānādīni puññāni karontā devatānaṃ pattiṃ denti, tā taṃ pattiṃ anumoditvā sampaṭicchitvā dibbayasena vaḍḍhanti. Anutiṭṭhantīti tādisassa rañño vīriyaṃ karontassa appamādaṃ āpajjantassa devatā anutiṭṭhanti anugacchanti, dhammikaṃ rakkhaṃ saṃvidahantīti attho.

'Gandhabbas' means the deities below the Four Great Kings, of four kinds of birth; indeed, they are called Gandhabbas because they are of four kinds of birth. 'Fathers' means the Brahmās. 'Deities' means the six sense-sphere deities by way of divine birth. 'Of such a one' means of such a king who delights in the wholesome. 'They live with him' means they have the same means of livelihood, being dependent on him. For such kings, performing meritorious deeds like giving, share the merit with the deities. Those deities, rejoicing in and accepting that share of merit, increase in divine glory. 'They attend upon' means the deities attend upon and follow such a king who exerts effort and practices diligence, establishing righteous protection—this is the meaning.

Soti so tvaṃ. Vāyamassūti tāni raṭṭhakiccāni karonto tulanavasena tīraṇavasena paccakkhakammavasena tesu tesu kiccesu vīriyaṃ karassu. Tattheva te vattapadāti, tāta, yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ kiṃsu kiccaṃ kataṃ varanti [M 5.0121] pucchi, tattha tava pañheyeva ete mayā “paṭhameneva vitatha”ntiādayo vuttā, ete vattapadā vattakoṭṭhāsā, evaṃ tattha vattassu. Esāti yā te mayā kathitā, esāva tava anusāsanī. Alanti evaṃ vattamāno hi rājā attano mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amittānañca dukkhāya alaṃ pariyatto samatthoti.

'So' means 'that you.' 'Vāyamassū' means: performing those state duties, you should exert energy in those various duties by way of weighing, examining, and direct action. 'Tattheva te vattapadā' means: dear one, regarding the question you asked me, 'What duty is best to be done?', in that very question these things beginning with 'Firstly, falsehood' were spoken by me. These are the courses of action, the sections of conduct; thus should you conduct yourself therein. 'Esā' means: what has been spoken by me to you, this indeed is your instruction. 'Alaṃ' means: a king conducting himself thus is indeed capable, sufficient, and competent to make his friends happy and to bring suffering to his enemies.

Evaṃ vessantarasakuṇena ekāya gāthāya rañño pamādaṃ codetvā ekādasahi gāthāhi dhamme kathite “buddhalīḷāya pañho kathito”ti mahājano acchariyabbhutacittajāto sādhukārasatāni pavattesi. Rājā somanassappatto amacce āmantetvā pucchi – “bhonto! Amaccā mama puttena vessantarena evaṃ kathentena kena kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ kata”nti. Mahāsenaguttena, devāti. “Tena hissa mahāsenaguttaṭṭhānaṃ dammī”ti vessantaraṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapesi. So tato paṭṭhāya mahāsenaguttaṭṭhāne ṭhito pitu kammaṃ akāsīti.

Thus, when the Vessantara bird, with a single verse, had rebuked the king's negligence and had expounded the Dhamma in eleven verses, the great assembly, their hearts filled with wonder and amazement, thinking, 'The question has been answered with the grace of a Buddha,' raised hundreds of cries of approval. The king, filled with joy, addressed his ministers and asked, 'Sirs! Ministers! My son Vessantara having spoken thus, by whom has the duty that ought to be done been performed?' 'By the commander-in-chief, Your Majesty.' 'Then I shall give him the position of commander-in-chief (Mahāsenagutta),' he said, and appointed Vessantara to that high office. From that time onwards, established in the position of commander-in-chief, he performed his father's duties.

Vessantarapañho niṭṭhito.

The Question of Vessantara is concluded.

Puna [V 5.0111][P 5.0116] rājā katipāhaccayena purimanayeneva kuṇḍaliniyā santikaṃ dūtaṃ pesetvā sattame divase tattha gantvā paccāgantvā tattheva maṇḍapamajjhe nisīditvā kuṇḍaliniṃ āharāpetvā suvaṇṇapīṭhe nisinnaṃ rājadhammaṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

Again, after some days had passed, the king, in the same manner as before, sent a messenger to Kuṇḍalinī. On the seventh day, having gone there and returned, he sat down in the very middle of the pavilion. Having had Kuṇḍalinī brought and seated on a golden stool, he inquired about the duties of a king, speaking this verse:

14.

14.

“Sakkhisi tvaṃ kuṇḍalini, maññasi khattabandhuni;

Rajjaṃ kāretukāmena, kiṃ su kiccaṃ kataṃ vara”nti.

Are you able, Kuṇḍalinī, do you know, O kinswoman of warriors, what excellent deed should be done by one who desires to rule a kingdom?

Tattha sakkhisīti mayā puṭṭhapañhaṃ kathetuṃ sakkhissasīti pucchati. Kuṇḍalinīti tassā saliṅgato āgatanāmenālapati. Tassā kira dvīsu kaṇṇapiṭṭhesu kuṇḍalasaṇṭhānā dve lekhā ahesuṃ, tenassā “kuṇḍalinī”ti nāmaṃ kāresi. Maññasīti jānissasi mayā puṭṭhapañhassa atthanti. Khattabandhunīti khattassa mahāsenaguttassa bhaginibhāvena naṃ evaṃ ālapati. Kasmā panesa vessantarasakuṇaṃ evaṃ apucchitvā imameva pucchatīti? Itthibhāvena. Itthiyo hi parittapaññā, tasmā “sace sakkoti, pucchissāmi, no ce, na pucchissāmī”ti vīmaṃsanavasena evaṃ pucchitvā taññeva pañhaṃ pucchi.

Herein, 'sakkhisi' (are you able?) means he asks, 'Will you be able to explain the question I have asked?' 'Kuṇḍalinī' is how he addresses her, by the name derived from her physical mark. It is said that on both her earlobes there were two lines shaped like earrings, for which reason the name 'Kuṇḍalinī' was given to her. 'Maññasi' (do you know?) means, 'Will you know the meaning of the question I ask?' 'Khattabandhunī' (kinswoman of a warrior) is how he addresses her on account of her being the sister of Mahāsenagutta, the Khattiya. But why does he ask her in this way, when he did not ask the Vessantara bird thus? Because she is a woman. For women are indeed of limited wisdom; therefore, by way of testing, thinking, 'If she is able, I will ask; if not, I will not ask,' he asked that same question in this manner.

Sā [M 5.0122] evaṃ raññā rājadhamme pucchite, “tāta, tvaṃ maṃ ‘itthikā nāma kiṃ kathessatī’ti vīmaṃsasi maññe, sakalaṃ te rājadhammaṃ dvīsuyeva padesu pakkhipitvā kathessāmī”ti vatvā āha –

When she was thus questioned by the king about the duties of a king, she said, 'Dear father, I believe you are testing me, thinking, "What can a mere woman say?" I will explain to you the entire duty of a king, having placed it into just two points.' Having said this, she spoke:

15.

15.

“Dveva tāta padakāni, yattha sabbaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ;

Aladdhassa ca yo lābho, laddhassa cānurakkhaṇā.

Dear father, there are just two points, wherein all is established: the acquisition of what has not been acquired, and the preservation of what has been acquired.

16.

16.

“Amacce tāta jānāhi, dhīre atthassa kovide;

Anakkhākitave tāta, asoṇḍe avināsake.

Know, dear father, your ministers to be wise and skilled in purpose; not addicted to dice, dear father, not given to drink, and not destructive.

17.

17.

“Yo ca taṃ tāta rakkheyya, dhanaṃ yañceva te siyā;

Sūtova rathaṃ saṅgaṇhe, so te kiccāni kāraye.

Whoever, dear father, would protect you and whatever wealth may be yours, let him carry out your duties, as a charioteer controls a chariot.

18.

18.

“Susaṅgahitantajano, sayaṃ vittaṃ avekkhiya;

Nidhiñca iṇadānañca, na kare parapattiyā.

He whose retinue is well-gathered, having personally assessed his wealth, should not make deposits or give loans on the word of another.

19.

19.

“Sayaṃ [V 5.0112] āyaṃ vayaṃ jaññā, sayaṃ jaññā katākataṃ;

Niggaṇhe niggahārahaṃ, paggaṇhe paggahārahaṃ.

He himself should know his income and expenditure; he himself should know what has been done and what has not. He should censure those worthy of censure, and support those worthy of support.

20.

20.

“Sayaṃ [P 5.0117] jānapadaṃ atthaṃ, anusāsa rathesabha;

Mā te adhammikā yuttā, dhanaṃ raṭṭhañca nāsayuṃ.

O bull among charioteers, personally instruct the affairs of the country. Let not your unrighteous officials destroy your wealth and your kingdom.

21.

21.

“Mā ca vegena kiccāni, karosi kārayesi vā;

Vegasā hi kataṃ kammaṃ, mando pacchānutappati.

Do not perform duties with haste, nor cause them to be performed; for a deed done with haste, the fool afterwards regrets.

22.

22.

“Mā te adhisare muñca, subāḷhamadhikopitaṃ;

Kodhasā hi bahū phītā, kulā akulataṃ gatā.

Do not unleash your authority when it is excessively provoked and agitated; for due to anger, many prosperous families have gone to ruin.

23.

23.

“‘Mā tāta issaromhī’ti, anatthāya patārayi;

Itthīnaṃ purisānañca, mā te āsi dukhudrayo.

“Do not, dear one, by thinking ‘I am a lord,’ bring yourself to ruin; may you not be a source of sorrow for women and men.”

24.

24.

“Apetalomahaṃsassa, rañño kāmānusārino;

Sabbe bhogā vinassanti, rañño taṃ vuccate aghaṃ.

For a king devoid of compunction, who indulges in desires, all his possessions vanish; that, it is said, is the king's ruin.

25.

25.

“Tattheva te vattapadā, esāva anusāsanī;

Dakkhassudāni puññakaro, asoṇḍo avināsako;

Sīlavāssu mahārāja, dussīlo vinipātiko”ti.

“These are the customary duties for you, this is the instruction; now then, be diligent, a doer of merit, unwasteful and non-destructive; be virtuous, O great king, for the unvirtuous one falls into ruin.”

Tattha [M 5.0123] padakānīti kāraṇapadāni. Yatthāti yesu dvīsu padesu sabbaṃ atthajātaṃ hitasukhaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ. Aladdhassāti yo ca pubbe aladdhassa lābhassa lābho, yā ca laddhassa anurakkhaṇā. Tāta, anuppannassa hi lābhassa uppādanaṃ nāma na bhāro, uppannassa pana anurakkhaṇameva bhāro. Ekacco hi yasaṃ uppādetvāpi yase pamatto pamādaṃ uppādetvā pāṇātipātādīni karoti, mahācoro hutvā raṭṭhaṃ vilumpamāno carati. Atha naṃ rājāno gāhāpetvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpenti. Atha vā uppannarūpādīsu kāmaguṇesu pamatto ayoniso dhanaṃ nāsento sabbasāpateyye khīṇe kapaṇo hutvā cīrakavasano kapālamādāya carati. Pabbajito vā pana ganthadhurādivasena lābhasakkāraṃ nibbattetvā pamatto hīnāyāvattati. Aparo paṭhamajhānādīni [V 5.0113] nibbattetvāpi muṭṭhassatitāya tathārūpe ārammaṇe bajjhitvā jhānā parihāyati. Evaṃ uppannassa yasassa vā jhānādilābhassa vā rakkhaṇameva dukkaraṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthaṃ pana devadattassa vatthu ca, mudulakkhaṇa- (jā. 1.1.66) lomasakassapa- (jā. 1.9.60 ādayo) haritacajātaka- (jā. 1.9.40 ādayo) saṅkappajātakādīni (jā. 1.3.1 ādayo) ca kathetabbāni. Eko pana lābhasakkāraṃ uppādetvā appamāde ṭhatvā kalyāṇakammaṃ karoti, tassa so yaso sukkapakkhe cando viya vaḍḍhati, tasmā tvaṃ, mahārāja, appamatto payogasampattiyā ṭhatvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento tava uppannaṃ yasaṃ anurakkhāhīti.

Therein, 'bases' (padakāni) are causal conditions. 'Where' refers to the two bases in which all benefits and happiness are established. ‘Of what has not been obtained’ refers to the acquisition of gain not previously acquired, and the preservation of what has been acquired. Dear one, generating gain that has not yet arisen is indeed no burden, but the preservation of what has arisen is truly a burden. For one person, even after generating fame, being heedless with regard to that fame and developing negligence, commits acts such as killing living beings, and becoming a great thief, wanders about plundering the kingdom. Then kings have him arrested and bring him to great ruin. Or else, being heedless regarding arisen sense pleasures such as forms, unwisely dissipating wealth, when all his possessions are exhausted, he becomes wretched, wearing rags and carrying a bowl. Or a renunciate, having generated gain and honor by means of the burden of study and so forth, being heedless, reverts to a lower state. Another, even having developed the first jhāna and so forth, through loss of mindfulness becomes attached to such an object and falls away from jhāna. Thus, indeed, the maintenance of arisen fame or gain such as jhāna is difficult. To illustrate this meaning, the story of Devadatta, and the Mudulakkhaṇa Jātaka (jā. 1.1.66), the Lomasakassapa Jātaka (jā. 1.9.60 ādayo), the Haritaca Jātaka (jā. 1.9.40 ādayo), the Saṅkappa Jātaka (jā. 1.3.1 ādayo), and others should be related. But one person, having produced gain and honor, standing in diligence performs meritorious deeds; his fame grows like the moon in the bright fortnight. Therefore, great king, remaining diligent and established in the accomplishment of effort, ruling the kingdom righteously, maintain the fame that you have gained.

Jānāhīti bhaṇḍāgārikakammādīnaṃ karaṇatthaṃ upadhārehi. Anakkhākitaveti anakkhe akitave ajutakare ceva akerāṭike ca[P 5.0118]. Asoṇḍeti pūvasurāgandhamālāsoṇḍabhāvarahite. Avināsaketi tava santakānaṃ dhanadhaññādīnaṃ avināsake. Yoti yo amacco. Yañcevāti yañca te ghare dhanaṃ siyā, taṃ rakkheyya. Sūtovāti rathasārathi viya. Yathā sārathi visamamagganivāraṇatthaṃ asse saṅgaṇhanto rathaṃ saṅgaṇheyya, evaṃ yo saha bhogehi taṃ rakkhituṃ sakkoti, so te amacco nāma tādisaṃ saṅgahetvā bhaṇḍāgārikādikiccāni kāraye.

By 'Jānāhi' (Know this) is meant, 'You should investigate them for the purpose of performing duties such as that of a treasurer.' By 'Anakkhākitavo' is meant one who is not given to dice-play, not a cheat, not one who gambles, and not a trickster. By 'Asoṇḍo' is meant one free from the state of being addicted to cakes, liquor, perfumes, and garlands. By 'Avināsako' is meant one who does not destroy your wealth, grain, and other possessions. By 'Yo' is meant the minister who is such a one. By 'Yañca eva' (whatever indeed) is meant, 'Whatever wealth there may be in your house, that he should protect.' By 'Sūtova' is meant 'like a charioteer'. Just as a charioteer, restraining the horses for the purpose of preventing them from going on a rough path, should control the chariot, so too whoever is capable of protecting you together with your possessions—that one is indeed your minister; having appointed such a one, you should have him carry out duties such as that of a treasurer.

Susaṅgahitantajanoti, tāta, yassa hi rañño attano antojano attano valañjanakaparijano ca dānādīhi asaṅgahito hoti, tassa antonivesane suvaṇṇahiraññādīni tesaṃ asaṅgahitamanussānaṃ vasena [M 5.0124] nassanti, antojanā bahi gacchanti, tasmā tvaṃ suṭṭhusaṅgahitaantojano hutvā “ettakaṃ nāma me vitta”nti sayaṃ attano dhanaṃ avekkhitvā “asukaṭṭhāne nāma nidhiṃ nidhema, asukassa iṇaṃ demā”ti idaṃ ubhayampi na kare parapattiyā, parapattiyāpi tvaṃ mā kari, sabbaṃ attapaccakkhameva kareyyāsīti vadati.

Regarding 'Susaṅgahitantajano,' dear one, for a king whose own inner folk and personal attendants are not well-treated through gifts and such, the gold, silver, and other valuables in his inner chambers are lost because of those neglected people, and the inner folk depart. Therefore, you should be one who treats his inner folk very well. Having personally inspected your own wealth, thinking, 'This is the extent of my wealth,' you should not perform either the burying of treasure in a certain place or the giving of a loan to a certain person by relying on others. Do not act even by relying on others; you should do everything by personal observation—so he says.

Āyaṃ vayanti tato uppajjanakaṃ āyañca tesaṃ tesaṃ dātabbaṃ vayañca sayameva jāneyyāsīti. Katākatanti saṅgāme vā navakamme vā aññesu vā kiccesu “iminā idaṃ nāma mayhaṃ kataṃ, iminā na kata”nti etampi sayameva jāneyyāsi, mā parapattiyo hohi. Niggaṇheti, tāta, rājā nāma sandhicchedādikārakaṃ niggahārahaṃ ānetvā dassitaṃ upaparikkhitvā sodhetvā porāṇakarājūhi ṭhapitadaṇḍaṃ oloketvā dosānurūpaṃ niggaṇheyya. Paggaṇheti yo pana paggahāraho hoti, abhinnassa vā parabalassa bhedetā, bhinnassa vā sakabalassa ārādhako, aladdhassa vā rajjassa āharako, laddhassa vā thāvarakārako, yena vā [V 5.0114] pana jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ hoti, evarūpaṃ paggahārahaṃ paggahetvā mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ kareyya. Evaṃ hissa kiccesu aññepi uraṃ datvā kattabbaṃ karissanti.

Regarding 'Āyaṃ vayaṃ,' you should yourself know the income arising from that and the expenditure to be given for various purposes. Regarding 'Katākataṃ,' in battle, or in new constructions, or in other duties, you should yourself know, 'This has been done for me by this person; this has not been done by that person,' and do not rely on the reports of others. Regarding 'Niggaṇheyya,' dear one, a king should bring those deserving of punishment—such as housebreakers and the like—and having examined and verified what is presented, and having looked at the punishments established by ancient kings, he should punish them according to their offense. Regarding 'Paggaṇheyya,' whoever is worthy of favor—whether a divider of an undivided enemy force, a reconciler of his own divided force, a bringer of a kingdom not yet attained, or a stabilizer of one already attained, or one by whom life has been given—having favored such a one worthy of reward, he should bestow great honor and respect. For in this way, others too will devote themselves to performing what needs to be done in his affairs.

Jānapadanti janapadavāsīnaṃ atthaṃ sayaṃ attapaccakkheneva anusāsa. Adhammikā yuttāti adhammikā tattha tattha niyuttā āyuttakā lañjaṃ gahetvā vinicchayaṃ bhindantā tava dhanañca raṭṭhañca mā nāsayuṃ. Iminā kāraṇena appamatto hutvā sayameva anusāsa. Vegenāti sahasā atuletvā atīretvā. Vegasāti atuletvā atīretvā chandādivasena sahasā kataṃ kammañhi na sādhu na sundaraṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tādisañhi katvā mando pacchā vippaṭisāravasena idha loke apāyadukkhaṃ anubhavanto paraloke ca anutappati. Ayaṃ panettha attho “isīnamantaraṃ katvā, bharurājāti me suta”nti bharujātakena (jā. 1.2.125-126) dīpetabbo[P 5.0119].

Regarding 'Jānapadaṃ': Personally govern the affairs of the country dwellers through your own direct observation. Regarding 'Adhammikā yuttā': Let not unrighteous officials appointed here and there, who take bribes and pervert justice, destroy your wealth and your kingdom. For this reason, being heedful, govern them yourself. Regarding 'Vegena': Hastily, without weighing or deliberating. Regarding 'Vegasā': An action done hastily, without weighing or deliberating, through the influence of desire and such, is neither good nor excellent. Why is that? For having done such an act, the fool later experiences the misery of ruin in this world and grieves in the next world due to remorse. This meaning here is to be illustrated by the Bharu Jātaka (Ja. 1.2.125–126) with the verse: 'Having created a rift among the sages, King Bharu, so I have heard.'

Mā te adhisare muñca, subāḷhamadhikopitanti, tāta, tava hadayaṃ kusalaṃ adhisaritvā atikkamitvā pavatte paresaṃ akusalakamme suṭṭhu bāḷhaṃ adhikopitaṃ kujjhāpitaṃ hutvā mā muñca, mā patiṭṭhāyatūti attho. Idaṃ [M 5.0125] vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, yadā te vinicchaye ṭhitassa iminā puriso vā hato sandhi vā chinnoti coraṃ dassenti, tadā te paresaṃ vacanehi suṭṭhu kopitampi hadayaṃ kodhavasena mā muñca, apariggahetvā mā daṇḍaṃ paṇehi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Acorampi hi “coro”ti gahetvā ānenti, tasmā akujjhitvā ubhinnaṃ attapaccatthikānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā suṭṭhu sodhetvā attapaccakkhena tassa corabhāvaṃ ñatvā paveṇiyā ṭhapitadaṇḍavasena kattabbaṃ karohi. Raññā hi uppannepi kodhe hadayaṃ sītalaṃ akatvā kammaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Yadā panassa hadayaṃ nibbutaṃ hoti mudukaṃ, tadā vinicchayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Pharuse hi citte pakkuthite udake mukhanimittaṃ viya kāraṇaṃ na paññāyati. Kodhasā hīti, tāta, kodhena hi bahūni phītāni rājakulāni akulabhāvaṃ gatāni mahāvināsameva pattānīti. Imassa panatthassa dīpanatthaṃ khantivādijātaka- (jā. 1.4.49 ādayo) nāḷikerarājavatthusahassabāhuajjunavatthuādīni kathetabbāni.

Regarding ‘Mā te adhisare muñca, subāḷhamadhikopitaṃ’: Dear father, do not let your heart, having become intensely provoked and angered by the unwholesome deeds of others which have overstepped and exceeded what is wholesome, be set loose [into anger]; that is, do not let it remain established there. This is what is said: Dear father, when you are presiding over judgment and they bring a thief before you, saying, ‘This man killed someone’ or ‘This man broke into a house,’ then do not let your heart, even if greatly provoked by the words of others, be set loose through the power of anger. Do not inflict punishment without having fully grasped the facts. Why? For even the innocent are apprehended and brought in as ‘thieves.’ Therefore, without becoming angry, after hearing the accounts of both parties—the claimant and the accused—and having thoroughly investigated and personally ascertained his status as a thief, do what must be done according to the punishment established by tradition. Indeed, when anger has arisen in a king, he should not take action without first cooling his heart. Only when his heart is calm and softened should the work of judgment be done. For when the mind is harsh, like boiling water, the truth of the matter is not seen, just as a reflection of a face is not seen in boiling water. Regarding ‘Kodhasā hi’: Dear father, indeed, through anger many prosperous royal families have met with ruin and come to great destruction. To illustrate this point, the Khantivādi Jātaka, the story of King Nāḷikera, the story of King Sahassabāhu Ajjuna, and others should be recounted.

Mā, tāta, issaromhīti, anatthāya patārayīti, tāta, “ahaṃ pathavissaro”ti mā mahājanaṃ kāyaduccaritādianatthāya patārayi mā otārayi, yathā taṃ anatthaṃ samādāya vattati, mā evamakāsīti attho. Mā te āsīti, tāta, tava vijite manussajātikānaṃ vā tiracchānajātikānaṃ vā itthipurisānaṃ dukhudrayo dukkhuppatti mā āsi. Yathā hi adhammikarājūnaṃ [V 5.0115] vijite manussā kāyaduccaritādīni katvā niraye uppajjanti, tava raṭṭhavāsīnaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ yathā na hoti, tathā karohīti attho.

‘Mā, tāta, issaromhīti, anatthāya patārayi’: Dear father, do not, thinking ‘I am the lord of the earth,’ lead the multitude to harm, such as bodily misconduct, nor cause them to enter into it, so that they engage in such harm. Do not act thus—this is the meaning. ‘Mā te āsi’: Dear father, in your territory, let there be no arising of suffering for men and women, whether of human or animal kind. For just as in the realms of unrighteous kings, people commit bodily misconduct and the like and are reborn in hell, you should act in such a way that this suffering does not befall the inhabitants of your kingdom—this is the meaning.

Apetalomahaṃsassāti attānuvādādibhayehi nibbhayassa. Iminā imaṃ dasseti – tāta, yo rājā kismiñci āsaṅkaṃ akatvā attano kāmameva anussarati, chandavasena yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ karoti, vissaṭṭhayaṭṭhi viya andho niraṅkuso viya ca caṇḍahatthī hoti, tassa sabbe bhogā vinassanti, tassa taṃ bhogabyasanaṃ aghaṃ dukkhanti vuccati.

‘Apetalomahaṃsassā’ means: of one who is fearless regarding the fears of self-reproach and so on. By this, he shows this: Dear father, the king who, without any apprehension, merely follows his own desires and, according to his impulses, does whatever he wishes—like a blind man who has dropped his staff or a fierce elephant without a goad—all his possessions are destroyed. That ruin of his possessions is called the king's suffering.

Tattheva te vattapadāti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Dakkhassudānīti, tāta, tvaṃ imaṃ anusāsaniṃ sutvā idāni dakkho analaso puññānaṃ karaṇena [M 5.0126] puññakaro surādipariharaṇena. Asoṇḍo diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikassa atthassa avināsanena avināsako bhaveyyāsīti. Sīlavāssūti sīlavā ācārasampanno bhava, dasasu rājadhammesu patiṭṭhāya rajjaṃ kārehi. Dussīlo vinipātikoti dussīlo hi, mahārāja, attānaṃ niraye vinipātento vinipātiko nāma hotīti.

‘Tattheva te vattapadā’ should be connected in the same way as before. ‘Dakkhassudānīti’ means: My dear, having heard this instruction, you should now be skilled and diligent, a doer of merit by performing meritorious deeds. ‘Asoṇḍo’ means not a drunkard by abstaining from liquor and the like. ‘Avināsako’ means may you be one who does not destroy the welfare pertaining to this life and the next. ‘Sīlavāssūti’ means: be virtuous, be endowed with good conduct, establish yourself in the ten royal virtues, and rule. ‘Dussīlo vinipātikoti’ means: for indeed, great king, an immoral person, by casting himself into hell, is called one who falls.

Evaṃ [P 5.0120] kuṇḍalinīpi ekādasahi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desesi. Rājā tuṭṭho amacce āmantetvā pucchi – “bhonto! Amaccā mama dhītāya kuṇḍaliniyā evaṃ kathayamānāya kena kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ kata”nti. Bhaṇḍāgārikena, devāti. “Tena hissā bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānaṃ dammī”ti kuṇḍaliniṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapesi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā pitu kammaṃ akāsīti.

Thus, Kuṇḍalinī taught the Dhamma in eleven verses. The king, pleased, addressed his ministers and asked, “Sirs, ministers! While my daughter Kuṇḍalinī was speaking thus, whose task has been performed?” “By the treasurer, Your Majesty,” they replied. “In that case, I shall bestow the treasurer’s office upon her,” he said, and installed Kuṇḍalinī in that position. From that time on, holding the treasurer’s position, she carried out her father’s duties.

Kuṇḍalinipañho niṭṭhito.

The Question of Kuṇḍalinī is concluded.

Puna rājā katipāhaccayena purimanayeneva jambukapaṇḍitassa santikaṃ dūtaṃ pesetvā sattame divase tattha gantvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā paccāgato tattheva maṇḍapamajjhe nisīdi. Amacco jambukapaṇḍitaṃ kañcanabhaddapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā pīṭhaṃ sīsenādāya āgacchi. Paṇḍito pitu aṅke nisīditvā kīḷitvā gantvā kañcanapīṭheyeva nisīdi. Atha naṃ rājā pañhaṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

Again, after a few days, the king sent a messenger to Jambuka the Wise as before. On the seventh day, the king went there, experienced hospitality, and returned to sit in the middle of the pavilion. The minister, having seated Jambuka the Wise on a splendid golden seat, then came carrying the seat on his head. The wise one, after sitting on his father’s lap and playing, went and sat upon the golden seat. Then the king, wishing to ask him a question, spoke this verse:

26.

26.

“Apucchimha kosiyagottaṃ, kuṇḍaliniṃ tatheva ca;

Tvaṃ dāni vadehi jambuka, balānaṃ balamuttama”nti.

“We asked Kosiyagotta, and likewise Kuṇḍalinī; now you speak, Jambuka, of the supreme strength among strengths.”

Tassattho [V 5.0116] – tāta, jambuka, ahaṃ tava bhātaraṃ kosiyagottaṃ vessantaraṃ bhaginiñca te kuṇḍaliniṃ rājadhammaṃ apucchiṃ, te attano balena kathesuṃ, yathā pana te pucchiṃ, tatheva idāni, putta jambuka, taṃ pucchāmi, tvaṃ me rājadhammañca balānaṃ uttamaṃ balañca kathehīti.

The meaning is: My dear Jambuka, I asked your brother Vessantara of the Kosiyagotta clan, and your sister Kuṇḍalinī, about the royal duties. They spoke according to their own capacity. Just as I asked them, so now, my son Jambuka, I ask you: Tell me of the royal duties and the supreme strength among strengths.

Evaṃ rājā mahāsattaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto aññesaṃ pucchitaniyāmena apucchitvā visesetvā pucchi. Athassa paṇḍito “tena hi, mahārāja, ohitasoto suṇāhi, sabbaṃ te kathessāmī”ti pasāritahatthe sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapento viya dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi –

Thus, the king, questioning the Great Being, did not ask in the same manner as he had asked the others, but asked him specifically. Then the wise one said, “Well then, great king, listen with attentive ears. I will explain everything to you,” and, as if placing a purse of a thousand coins into an outstretched hand, he began the teaching of the Dhamma:

27.

27.

“Balaṃ [M 5.0127] pañcavidhaṃ loke, purisasmiṃ mahaggate;

Tattha bāhubalaṃ nāma, carimaṃ vuccate balaṃ.

“In the world, strength is fivefold in a person of great resolve; among them, strength of arms is said to be the lowest strength.

28.

28.

“Bhogabalañca dīghāvu, dutiyaṃ vuccate balaṃ;

Amaccabalañca dīghāvu, tatiyaṃ vuccate balaṃ.

“And the strength of possessions, O long-lived one, is called the second strength; and the strength of ministers, O long-lived one, is called the third strength.

29.

29.

“Abhijaccabalañceva, taṃ catutthaṃ asaṃsayaṃ;

Yāni cetāni sabbāni, adhigaṇhāti paṇḍito.

“And the strength of noble birth, that is certainly the fourth. A wise person masters all these strengths.

30.

30.

“Taṃ [P 5.0121] balānaṃ balaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, aggaṃ paññābalaṃ balaṃ;

Paññābalenupatthaddho, atthaṃ vindati paṇḍito.

“That strength of wisdom is the best of strengths, the supreme strength. Supported by the strength of wisdom, the wise person attains the goal.

31.

31.

“Api ce labhati mando, phītaṃ dharaṇimuttamaṃ;

Akāmassa pasayhaṃ vā, añño taṃ paṭipajjati.

“Even if a fool obtains the most excellent and fertile land, another seizes it from him by force, against his will.

32.

32.

“Abhijātopi ce hoti, rajjaṃ laddhāna khattiyo;

Duppañño hi kāsipati, sabbenapi na jīvati.

“Even if a warrior of noble birth obtains a kingdom, if he is a foolish king of Kasi, he does not survive with all of that.

33.

33.

“Paññāva sutaṃ vinicchinī, paññā kittisilokavaḍḍhanī;

Paññāsahito naro idha, api dukkhe sukhāni vindati.

“Wisdom indeed discerns what is heard; wisdom increases fame and renown; a person endowed with wisdom here, even in suffering, finds happiness.

34.

34.

“Paññañca [V 5.0117] kho asussūsaṃ, na koci adhigacchati;

Bahussutaṃ anāgamma, dhammaṭṭhaṃ avinibbhujaṃ.

“Indeed, no one attains wisdom without the desire to listen, without approaching one who is greatly learned, established in the Dhamma, and discerning.

35.

35.

“Yo ca dhammavibhaṅgaññū, kāluṭṭhāyī atandito;

Anuṭṭhahati kālena, kammaphalaṃ tassijjhati.

“He who knows the analysis of the Dhamma, rises at the proper time and is tireless, and strives at the right time—the fruit of his action succeeds.

36.

36.

“Anāyatanasīlassa, anāyatanasevino;

Na nibbindiyakārissa, sammadattho vipaccati.

“For one of unrestrained conduct, who consorts with the unsuitable, and who acts with weariness, the right goal does not mature.

37.

37.

“Ajjhattañca payuttassa, tathāyatanasevino;

Anibbindiyakārissa, sammadattho vipaccati.

“For one who is internally diligent, who consorts with the suitable, and who acts without growing weary, the right goal matures.

38.

38.

“Yogappayogasaṅkhātaṃ, sambhatassānurakkhaṇaṃ;

Tāni tvaṃ tāta sevassu, mā akammāya randhayi;

Akammunā hi dummedho, naḷāgāraṃva sīdatī”ti.

“Exertion and application, and the protection of what has been gathered—these, my dear, you should cultivate. Do not be vulnerable to inaction; for through inaction a fool collapses like a house of reeds.”

Tattha [M 5.0128] mahaggateti, mahārāja, imasmiṃ sattaloke mahajjhāsaye purise pañcavidhaṃ balaṃ hoti. Bāhubalanti kāyabalaṃ. Carimanti taṃ atimahantampi samānaṃ lāmakameva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Andhabālabhāvena. Sace hi kāyabalaṃ mahantaṃ nāma bhaveyya, vāraṇabalato laṭukikāya balaṃ khuddakaṃ bhaveyya, vāraṇabalaṃ pana andhabālabhāvena maraṇassa paccayaṃ jātaṃ, laṭukikā attano ñāṇakusalatāya vāraṇaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Imasmiṃ panatthe “na heva sabbattha balena kiccaṃ, balañhi bālassa vadhāya hotī”ti suttaṃ (jā. 1.5.42) āharitabbaṃ.

Therein, ‘mahaggate’ means: Great king, in this world of beings, in a person of great resolve, there are five kinds of strength. ‘Bāhubalaṃ’ is bodily strength. ‘Carimaṃ’ means that even though it may be very great, it is still inferior. Why? Due to blind foolishness. For if bodily strength were truly superior, then the strength of a quail would be small compared to the strength of an elephant; but the elephant's strength, due to its blind foolishness, became a cause of its death, while the quail, through its own wisdom and skill, brought the elephant to the destruction of its life. In this regard, the verse should be cited: ‘Strength is not needed in every case; indeed, strength is for the destruction of the fool.’

Bhogabalanti upatthambhanavasena sabbaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādi upabhogajātaṃ bhogabalaṃ nāma, taṃ kāyabalato mahantataraṃ. Amaccabalanti abhejjamantassa sūrassa suhadayassa amaccamaṇḍalassa atthitā, taṃ balaṃ saṅgāmasūratāya purimehi balehi mahantataraṃ. Abhijaccabalanti tīṇi kulāni atikkamitvā khattiyakulavasena jātisampatti[P 5.0122], taṃ itarehi balehi mahantataraṃ. Jātisampannā eva hi sujjhanti, na itareti. Yāni cetānīti yāni ca etāni cattāripi balāni paṇḍito paññānubhāvena adhigaṇhāti abhibhavati, taṃ sabbabalānaṃ paññābalaṃ seṭṭhanti ca agganti ca vuccati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tena hi balena upatthaddho paṇḍito atthaṃ vindati, vuḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇāti[V 5.0118]. Tadatthajotanatthaṃ “puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ yena ca peyyamāhū”ti puṇṇanadījātakañca (jā. 1.2.127 ādayo) sirīkāḷakaṇṇipañhaṃ pañcapaṇḍitapañhañca sattubhastajātaka- (jā. 1.7.46 ādayo) sambhavajātaka- (jā. 1.16.138 ādayo) sarabhaṅgajātakādīni (jā. 2.17.50 ādayo) ca kathetabbāni.

By 'the power of wealth' (bhogabala) is meant all things for enjoyment such as gold and silver, by way of support; this is called the second power, greater than bodily strength but less than the power of ministers. By 'the power of ministers' (amaccabala) is meant the existence of a council of ministers with unbreakable counsel, who are valiant and kind-hearted; this is called the third power, greater than bodily strength and the power of wealth, but less than the power of high birth. By 'the power of high birth' (abhijaccabala) is meant excellence of birth by way of the warrior caste, surpassing three other castes; this is called the fourth power, greater than bodily strength, wealth, and the power of ministers, but less than the power of wisdom. For those endowed with noble birth are indeed pure, not others. By 'and these powers' (yāni cetāni) is meant that a wise person, through the power of wisdom, undoubtedly masters and overcomes all these four powers. Therefore, the power of wisdom is called the best and supreme among all powers. For what reason? Because, supported by the power of wisdom, a wise person finds success and attains growth. To elucidate this meaning, the following should be narrated: the Puṇṇa Nadī Jātaka, the Sirikāḷakaṇṇi question, the five wise men's question, the Sattubhasta Jātaka, the Sambhava Jātaka, the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, and others.

Mandoti mandapañño bālo. Phītanti, tāta, mandapañño puggalo sattaratanapuṇṇaṃ cepi uttamaṃ dharaṇiṃ labhati, tassa anicchamānasseva pasayhakāraṃ vā pana katvā añño paññāsampanno taṃ paṭipajjati. Mando hi laddhaṃ yasaṃ rakkhituṃ kulasantakaṃ vā pana paveṇiāgatampi rajjaṃ adhigantuṃ na sakkoti. Tadatthajotanatthaṃ “addhā pādañjalī sabbe, paññāya atirocatī”ti pādañjalījātakaṃ (jā. 1.2.194-195) kathetabbaṃ. Laddhānāti jātisampattiṃ nissāya kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ labhitvāpi. Sabbenapīti tena sakalenapi rajjena na jīvati, anupāyakusalatāya duggatova hotīti.

By 'a fool' (mando) is meant a person of weak wisdom, a simpleton. By 'flourishing' (phītaṃ), O Great King, even if a person of weak wisdom obtains the supreme earth filled with the seven treasures, another person endowed with wisdom would govern that earth, even by force and against his will. Indeed, a fool is unable to protect the glory he has gained, or even a kingdom inherited by family succession. To illustrate this meaning, the Pādañjalī Jātaka should be told: 'Surely, Pādañjalī outshines all through wisdom.' By 'having obtained' (laddhāna) is meant even after obtaining the family kingdom by virtue of high birth. By 'by all' (sabbena) is meant he does not live even with that entire kingdom; due to lack of skill in means, he remains wretched.

Evaṃ [M 5.0129] mahāsatto ettakena ṭhānena apaṇḍitassa aguṇaṃ kathetvā idāni paññaṃ pasaṃsanto “paññā”tiādimāha. Tattha sutanti sutapariyatti. Tañhi paññāva vinicchinati. Kittisilokavaḍḍhanīti kittighosassa ca lābhasakkārassa ca vaḍḍhanī. Dukkhe sukhāni vindatīti dukkhe uppannepi nibbhayo hutvā upāyakusalatāya sukhaṃ paṭilabhati. Tadatthadīpanatthaṃ –

Thus the Great Being, having spoken of the faults of the unwise to this extent, now praising wisdom, said 'wisdom' and so on. Here, 'learning' (suta) means the accomplishment of learning and knowledge, which wisdom itself discerns. By 'increasing fame and renown' (kittisilokavaḍḍhanī) is meant that which increases the sound of fame as well as gain and honor. By 'finds happiness in suffering' (dukkhe sukhāni vindati) is meant that even when suffering arises, one becomes fearless and obtains happiness through skill in means. To illustrate this meaning—

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava”. (jā. 1.1.57);

“He who has these four qualities, O king of monkeys, as you do;”

Alametehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi cā”ti. (jā. 1.2.115) –

“Enough with these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits.”

Ādīni jātakāni kathetabbāni.

These and other Jātaka stories should be narrated.

Asussūsanti paṇḍitapuggale apayirupāsanto assuṇanto. Dhammaṭṭhanti sabhāvakāraṇe ṭhitaṃ bahussutaṃ anāgamma taṃ asaddahanto. Avinibbhujanti atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ anogāhanto atīrento na koci paññaṃ adhigacchati, tātāti.

By 'not listening' (asussūsaṃ) is meant not attending to and not hearing from wise people. By 'one established in the Dhamma' (dhammaṭṭhaṃ) is meant not approaching a learned person who is established in the cause of reality, and not listening to him. By 'not distinguishing' (avinibbhujaṃ) is meant not discerning or reflecting upon benefit and harm, cause and non-cause. Thus, O Great King, no one attains wisdom.

Dhammavibhaṅgaññūti dasakusalakammapathavibhaṅgakusalo. Kāluṭṭhāyīti vīriyaṃ kātuṃ yuttakāle vīriyassa kārako. Anuṭṭhahatīti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ karoti. Tassāti tassa puggalassa [V 5.0119] kammaphalaṃ samijjhati nipphajjati. Anāyatanasīlassāti anāyatanaṃ vuccati lābhayasasukhānaṃ anākaro dussīlyakammaṃ, taṃsīlassa tena dussīlyakammena samannāgatassa, anāyatanabhūtameva dussīlapuggalaṃ sevantassa, kusalassa kammassa karaṇakāle nibbindiyakārissa nibbinditvā ukkaṇṭhitvā karontassa evarūpassa, tāta, puggalassa kammānaṃ attho sammā na vipaccati na sampajjati, tīṇi kulaggāni ca cha kāmasaggāni ca na upanetīti attho. Ajjhattañcāti [P 5.0123] attano niyakajjhattaṃ aniccabhāvanādivasena payuttassa. Tathāyatanasevinoti tatheva sīlavante puggale sevamānassa. Vipaccatīti sampajjati mahantaṃ yasaṃ deti.

By 'one who knows the analysis of the Dhamma' (dhammavibhaṅgaññū) is meant one skilled in the analysis of the ten wholesome courses of action. By 'one who rises at the proper time' (kāluṭṭhāyī) is meant one who exerts effort at the appropriate time for effort. By 'strives' (anuṭṭhahati) is meant performing each task at the proper time. By 'his' (tassa) is meant that the fruit of action for that wise person succeeds and is fulfilled. By 'of one whose conduct is not a proper basis' (anāyatanasīlassa) is meant that 'anāyatana' refers to immoral action, which is a source that does not yield gain, fame, or happiness; for one endowed with such immoral conduct, who associates with immoral persons who are not a proper basis, and who, when performing wholesome actions, does so with reluctance and aversion—for such a person, O Great King, the noble goal of his actions does not properly ripen or succeed, meaning it does not lead him to the three foremost families or the six heavenly realms. By 'and internally' (ajjhattañca) is meant one who exerts effort in wholesome qualities within his own continuity by way of developing insight into impermanence and so forth. By 'associating with such a basis' (tathāyatanasevino) is meant associating with virtuous persons of such character. By 'it ripens' (vipaccati) is meant the noble goal succeeds and is fulfilled.

Yogappayogasaṅkhātanti yoge yuñjitabbayuttake kāraṇe payogakoṭṭhāsabhūtaṃ paññaṃ. Sambhatassāti rāsikatassa dhanassa anurakkhaṇaṃ. Tāni tvanti etāni ca dve purimāni ca mayā vuttakāraṇāni sabbāni, tāta, tvaṃ sevassu, mayā vuttaṃ ovādaṃ hadaye katvā attano ghare [M 5.0130] dhanaṃ rakkha. Mā akammāya randhayīti ayuttena akāraṇena mā randhayi, taṃ dhanaṃ mā jhāpayi mā nāsayi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Akammunā hīti ayuttakammakaraṇena dummedho puggalo sakaṃ dhanaṃ nāsetvā pacchā duggato. Naḷāgāraṃva sīdatīti yathā naḷāgāraṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya jīramānaṃ appatiṭṭhaṃ patati, evaṃ akāraṇena dhanaṃ nāsetvā apāyesu nibbattatīti.

By 'reckoned as effort and application' (yogappayogasaṅkhātaṃ) is meant wisdom which is the portion of application in a cause that is fit for effort. By 'of accumulated' (sambhatassa) is meant the protection of accumulated wealth. By 'those things you...' (tāni tvaṃ) is meant: all these reasons spoken by me, including these two and the previous ones, O Great King, you should practice. Having taken my advice to heart, guard the wealth in your own home. By 'do not destroy through an unsuitable action' (mā akammāya randhayī) is meant do not exert effort to exhaust wealth through an unsuitable, wrong cause; do not destroy that wealth. For what reason? By 'for by an unsuitable action' (akammunā hi) is meant that by doing an unsuitable action, a foolish person destroys their own wealth and later suffers ruin. By 'sinks like a reed hut' (naḷāgāraṃva sīdati) is meant: just as a rotting reed hut, without support from its foundation, sinks and falls, so too, by destroying wealth through a wrong cause, one is ruined. Therefore, do not strive to exhaust your wealth through unsuitable means.

Evampi bodhisatto ettakena ṭhānena pañca balāni vaṇṇetvā paññābalaṃ ukkhipitvā candamaṇḍalaṃ nīharanto viya kathetvā idāni dasahi gāthāhi rañño ovādaṃ dento āha –

Thus the Bodhisatta, having praised the five powers to this extent and extolled the power of wisdom as if bringing forth the full moon, and now wishing to give further advice to the king, said:

39.

39.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, mātāpitūsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, towards your mother and father, O warrior. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

40.

40.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, puttadāresu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, towards your children and wives, O warrior. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

41.

41.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, mittāmaccesu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, among your friends and ministers, O warrior. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

42.

42.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, vāhanesu balesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, concerning your conveyances and forces. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

43.

43.

“Dhammaṃ [V 5.0120] cara mahārāja, gāmesu nigamesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king, in the villages and market towns. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.”

44.

44.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, raṭṭhe janapadesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king, in the realm and the provinces. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.”

45.

45.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, samaṇe brāhmaṇesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king, toward ascetics and brahmins. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.”

46.

46.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, migapakkhīsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king, toward beasts and birds, O khattiya. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.”

47.

47.

“Dhammaṃ [M 5.0131] cara mahārāja, dhammo ciṇṇo sukhāvaho;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king; the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.”

48.

48.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, saindā devā sabrahmakā;

Suciṇṇena divaṃ pattā, mā dhammaṃ rāja pāmado”ti.

“Practice the Dhamma, O great king. The devas with Indra, along with the Brahmās, reached heaven through the well-practiced Dhamma. Do not be heedless of the Dhamma, O king.”

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva idha dhammanti mātāpitupaṭṭhānadhammaṃ. Taṃ kālasseva vuṭṭhāya mātāpitūnaṃ mukhodakadantakaṭṭhadānamādiṃ katvā sabbasarīrakiccapariharaṇaṃ karontova pūrehīti vadati. Puttadāresūti puttadhītaro tāva pāpā nivāretvā kalyāṇe nivesento sippaṃ uggaṇhāpento [P 5.0124] vayappattakāle patirūpakulavaṃsena āvāhavivāhaṃ karonto samaye dhanaṃ dento puttesu dhammaṃ carati nāma, bhariyaṃ sammānento anavamānento anaticaranto issariyaṃ vossajjento alaṅkāraṃ anuppadento dāresu dhammaṃ carati nāma. Mittāmaccesūti mittāmacce catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgaṇhanto avisaṃvādento etesu dhammaṃ carati nāma. Vāhanesu balesu cāti hatthiassādīnaṃ vāhanānaṃ balakāyassa ca dātabbayuttakaṃ dento sakkāraṃ karonto hatthiassādayo mahallakakāle kammesu ayojento tesu dhammaṃ carati nāma.

Here, in the first verse, 'the Dhamma here' refers to the duty of attending to one's parents. It is said that one fulfills it by rising early and performing all necessary bodily services for one's parents, beginning with offering water for the face and tooth-sticks. Regarding 'children and spouses,' one practices the Dhamma toward children by first restraining sons and daughters from evil, establishing them in goodness, having them learn skills, and when they come of age, arranging suitable marriages with families of good lineage, and giving them wealth at the proper time. One practices the Dhamma toward one's wife by honoring her, not disparaging her, not being unfaithful, entrusting authority to her, and providing adornments. Regarding 'friends and companions,' one practices the Dhamma toward them by winning them over through the four bases of social harmony and not deceiving them. As for 'vehicles and forces,' one practices the Dhamma toward vehicles such as elephants and horses, and toward the military forces, by giving them what is suitable, showing respect, and not employing elephants, horses, and the like in tasks when they are old.

Gāmesu nigamesu cāti gāmanigamavāsino daṇḍabalīhi apīḷentova tesu dhammaṃ carati nāma. Raṭṭhe janapadesu cāti raṭṭhañca janapadañca akāraṇena kilamento hitacittaṃ apaccupaṭṭhapento [V 5.0121] tattha adhammaṃ carati nāma, apīḷento pana hitacittena pharanto tattha dhammaṃ carati nāma. Samaṇe brāhmaṇesu cāti tesaṃ cattāro paccaye dentova tesu dhammaṃ carati nāma. Migapakkhīsūti sabbacatuppadasakuṇānaṃ abhayaṃ dento tesu dhammaṃ carati nāma. Dhammo ciṇṇoti sucaritadhammo ciṇṇo. Sukhāvahoti tīsu kulasampadāsu chasu kāmasaggesu sukhaṃ āvahati. Suciṇṇenāti idha ciṇṇena kāyasucaritādinā suciṇṇena. Divaṃ pattāti devalokabrahmalokasaṅkhātaṃ divaṃ gatā, tattha dibbasampattilābhino jātā. Mā dhammaṃ rāja pāmadoti tasmā tvaṃ, mahārāja, jīvitaṃ jahantopi dhammaṃ mā pamajjīti.

Regarding 'villages and market towns,' one practices the Dhamma toward the villagers and town dwellers by not oppressing them with punishments or taxes. Regarding 'the realm and the provinces,' one practices unrighteousness there by tormenting the realm and the countryside without cause and not establishing a benevolent mind. But one practices the Dhamma there by not oppressing them and pervading them with a benevolent mind. Regarding 'ascetics and brahmins,' one practices the Dhamma toward them by providing them with the four requisites. Regarding 'beasts and birds,' one practices the Dhamma toward them by granting fearlessness to all quadrupeds and birds. 'The Dhamma is practiced' means the Dhamma of good conduct is practiced. 'Brings happiness' means it brings happiness in the three kinds of prosperity and in the six heavens of the sense sphere. 'Well-practiced' means here it is well-practiced by means of good conduct of body and so on. 'They reached heaven' means they have gone to heaven, known as the realms of the devas and Brahmās, and there they have attained divine prosperity. 'O king, do not be heedless of the Dhamma' means therefore, O great king, even at the cost of your life, do not neglect the Dhamma.

Evaṃ [M 5.0132] dasa dhammacariyagāthāyo vatvā uttaripi ovadanto osānagāthamāha –

Having thus spoken the ten verses on the practice of the Dhamma, and exhorting him further, he spoke the concluding verse:

49.

49.

“Tattheva te vattapadā, esāva anusāsanī;

Sappaññasevī kalyāṇī, samattaṃ sāma taṃ vidū”ti.

“In those very answers are your principles of conduct; this alone is the instruction. Associating with the wise, being virtuous, understand that fully for yourself.”

Tattha tattheva te vattapadāti idaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Sappaññasevī kalyāṇī, samattaṃ sāma taṃ vidūti, mahārāja, taṃ mayā vuttaṃ ovādaṃ tvaṃ niccakālaṃ sappaññapuggalasevī kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato hutvā samattaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ sāmaṃ vidū attapaccakkhatova jānitvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjāti.

Here, 'In those very answers are your principles of conduct' should be applied according to the previous method. 'Associating with the wise, being virtuous, understand that fully for yourself' means: O great king, always associating with wise persons and being endowed with virtuous qualities, you should realize that advice I have spoken, fully and completely, through your own direct knowledge, and practice as instructed.

Evaṃ mahāsatto ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājano mahāsakkāraṃ akāsi, sādhukārasahassāni adāsi. Rājā tuṭṭho amacce āmantetvā pucchi – “bhonto! Amaccā mama puttena [P 5.0125] taruṇajambuphalasamānatuṇḍena jambukapaṇḍitena evaṃ kathentena kena kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ kata”nti. Senāpatinā, devāti. “Tena hissa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ dammī”ti jambukaṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapesi. So tato paṭṭhāya senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhatvā pitu kammāni akāsi. Tiṇṇaṃ sakuṇānaṃ mahanto sakkāro ahosi. Tayopi janā rañño atthañca dhammañca anusāsiṃsu. Mahāsattassovāde ṭhatvā rājā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi. Amaccā rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā sakuṇānaṃ ārocetvā “sāmi, jambukasakuṇa rājā tumhākaṃ chattaṃ ussāpetabbaṃ akāsī”ti vadiṃsu. Mahāsatto “na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, tumhe appamattā rajjaṃ kārethā”ti mahājanaṃ sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “evaṃ vinicchayaṃ pavatteyyāthā”ti vinicchayadhammaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Tassovādo cattālīsa vassasahassāni pavattati.

Thus, the Great Being taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges. The multitude made a great offering and gave thousands of acclamations of 'Sādhu!'. The king, pleased, addressed his ministers: 'Sirs! By speaking thus, my son Jambuka the wise, whose beak is like a tender rose-apple, has performed the duty of whom?' 'The commander-in-chief, Your Majesty,' they replied. 'Then I shall give him the post of commander-in-chief,' and he appointed Jambuka to that position. From then on, serving as commander-in-chief, he carried out his father's duties. There was great honor for the three birds. All three of them advised the king on his welfare and the Dhamma. Abiding by the Great Being's advice, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving and was destined for heaven. The ministers, having performed the king's funeral rites, informed the birds, saying: 'Lord Jambuka bird, the king has arranged for the royal umbrella to be raised for you.' The Great Being said, 'I have no need for kingship; you should govern the kingdom diligently.' Having established the multitude in the precepts, he had the principles of judgment written on a golden plate, saying: 'In this way you should conduct judgment,' and then entered the forest. His advice remained in force for forty thousand years.

Satthā [V 5.0122] rañño ovādavasena imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ desetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, kuṇḍalinī uppalavaṇṇā, vessantaro sāriputto, jambukasakuṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having given this Dhamma teaching by way of advice to the king, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, Kuṇḍalinī was Uppalavaṇṇā, Vessantara was Sāriputta, and the Jambuka bird was indeed myself.'

Tesakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Tesakuṇa Jātaka, the First.

[522] 2. Sarabhaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā

[522] 2. The Commentary on the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka

Alaṅkatā [M 5.0133] kuṇḍalino suvatthāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto mahāmoggallānattherassa parinibbānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāriputtatthero tathāgataṃ jetavane viharantaṃ attano parinibbānaṃ anujānāpetvā gantvā nāḷakagāmake jātovarake parinibbāyi. Tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ sutvā satthā rājagahaṃ gantvā veḷuvane vihāsi. Tadā mahāmoggallānatthero isigilipasse kāḷasilāyaṃ viharati. So pana iddhibalena koṭippattabhāvena devalokacārikañca ussadanirayacārikañca gacchati. Devaloke buddhasāvakānaṃ mahantaṃ issariyaṃ disvā ussadanirayesu ca titthiyasāvakānaṃ mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ disvā manussalokaṃ āgantvā “asuko upāsako asukā ca upāsikā asukasmiṃ nāma devaloke nibbattitvā mahāsampattiṃ anubhavanti, titthiyasāvakesu asuko ca asukā ca nirayādīsu asukaapāye [P 5.0126] nāma nibbattā”ti manussānaṃ kathesi. Manussā sāsane pasīdanti, titthiye parivajjenti. Buddhasāvakānaṃ sakkāro mahanto ahosi, titthiyānaṃ parihāyati.

‘Adorned with earrings and well-dressed’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s final Nibbāna. The Elder Sāriputta, having obtained the Tathāgata’s permission for his own final Nibbāna while the Tathāgata was dwelling in Jetavana, went and attained final Nibbāna in his birth-chamber at Nālaka village. Hearing of his final Nibbāna, the Teacher went to Rājagaha and stayed in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling on the Black Rock near Isigili. By the power of his psychic abilities, having reached the highest peak of power, he traveled to the deva realms and the Ussada hells. In the deva realms, he saw the great majesty of the Buddha’s disciples, and in the Ussada hells, he saw the immense suffering of the sectarians’ followers.
