Returning to the human world, he told people, ‘Such-and-such a lay follower and such-and-such a laywoman have been reborn in such-and-such a deva realm, enjoying great prosperity, while among the sectarians’ followers, such-and-such have been reborn in such-and-such a hell or other miserable state.’ People gained faith in the Dispensation and avoided the sectarians. The honor shown to the Buddha’s disciples grew greatly, while that of the sectarians declined.

Te there āghātaṃ bandhitvā “imasmiṃ jīvante amhākaṃ upaṭṭhākā bhijjanti, sakkāro ca parihāyati, mārāpessāma na”nti therassa māraṇatthaṃ samaṇaguttakassa nāma corassa sahassaṃ adaṃsu. So “theraṃ māressāmī”ti mahantena parivārena saddhiṃ kāḷasilaṃ agamāsi. Thero taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva iddhiyā uppatitvā pakkāmi. Coro taṃ divasaṃ theraṃ adisvā nivattitvā punadivasepīti cha divase agamāsi. Theropi tatheva iddhiyā pakkāmi. Sattame pana divase therassa pubbe kataṃ aparāpariyavedanīyakammaṃ okāsaṃ labhi. So kira pubbe bhariyāya vacanaṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro māretukāmo yānakena araññaṃ netvā corānaṃ uṭṭhitākāraṃ katvā mātāpitaro pothesi pahari. Te cakkhudubbalatāya rūpadassanarahitā taṃ attano puttaṃ asañjānantā “corā eva ete”ti saññāya, “tāta, asukā nāma corā no ghātenti, tvaṃ paṭikkamāhī”ti tassevatthāya parideviṃsu. So cintesi – “ime mayā pothiyamānāpi mayhaṃ yevatthāya paridevanti, ayuttaṃ kammaṃ karomī”ti. Atha ne assāsetvā corānaṃ palāyanākāraṃ [V 5.0123] dassetvā tesaṃ hatthapāde sambāhitvā “amma[M 5.0134], tātā, mā bhāyittha, corā palātā”ti vatvā puna attano gehameva ānesi. Taṃ kammaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ okāsaṃ alabhitvā bhasmapaṭicchanno aṅgārarāsi viya ṭhatvā imaṃ antimasarīraṃ upadhāvitvā gaṇhi. Yathā hi pana sunakhaluddakena migaṃ disvā sunakho vissajjito migaṃ anubandhitvā yasmiṃ ṭhāne pāpuṇāti, tasmiṃyeva gaṇhāti, evaṃ idaṃ kammaṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne okāsaṃ labhati, tasmiṃ vipākaṃ deti, tena mutto nāma natthi.

Conceiving a grudge, they thought, ‘While this Moggallāna lives, our supporters will be lost and our honor will decline; let us have him killed.’ So they gave a thousand coins to a bandit named Samaṇaguttaka to kill the elder. The bandit, with a large retinue, went to the Black Rock, intending to kill him. The elder, seeing him approach, flew into the air by his psychic power and departed. The bandit, not seeing the elder that day, returned, and did so for six consecutive days. The elder similarly departed each time. On the seventh day, however, the elder’s previously committed kamma, to be experienced in a future life, found its opportunity. It is said that in a past life, acting on his wife’s words and wishing to kill his parents, he took them in a carriage to the forest, and feigning the arrival of bandits, he struck and beat his parents. Because of their weak eyes, they were unable to see and, not recognizing their own son, thought, ‘These are indeed bandits.’ Lamenting for his sake, they said, ‘Dear son, such-and-such bandits are beating us; you must flee!’ He thought, ‘Even as I beat them, they lament for my sake. I am doing an unworthy deed.’ Then he reassured them, feigned that the bandits had fled, massaged their hands and feet, and saying, ‘Mother, father, do not fear—the bandits have fled,’ he brought them back home. That kamma, having found no opportunity for so long, remained like a heap of embers covered in ashes, and now in this final existence, it rushed upon him and seized him. Just as a dog released by a hunter, upon seeing a deer, chases and catches it wherever it reaches, so too does kamma yield its result wherever it finds an opening. There is no escape from it.

Thero attanā katakammassa ākaḍḍhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā na apagacchi. Thero tassa nissandena ākāse uppatituṃ nāsakkhi. Nandopanandadamanasamatthavejayantakampanasamatthāpissa iddhi kammabalena dubbalataṃ pattā. Coro theraṃ gahetvā therassa aṭṭhīni taṇḍulakaṇamattāni karonto bhinditvā sañcuṇṇetvā palālapiṭṭhikakaraṇaṃ nāma katvā “mato”ti saññāya ekasmiṃ gumbapiṭṭhe khipitvā saparivāro pakkāmi. Thero satiṃ paṭilabhitvā “satthāraṃ passitvā parinibbāyissāmī”ti cintetvā sarīraṃ jhānaveṭhanena veṭhetvā thiraṃ katvā ākāsaṃ uppatitvā ākāsena satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “bhante, āyusaṅkhāro me ossaṭṭho, parinibbāyissāmī”ti āha. “Parinibbāyissasi, moggallāna”āti. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kattha gantvā parinibbāyissasī”ti. “Kāḷasilāpaṭṭe, bhante”ti. Tena hi, moggallāna, dhammaṃ mayhaṃ kathetvā yāhi, tādisassa sāvakassa idāni dassanaṃ natthīti. So “evaṃ karissāmi, bhante”ti satthāraṃ vanditvā tālappamāṇaṃ ākāse uppatitvā parinibbānadivase sāriputtatthero viya nānappakārā iddhiyo katvā dhammaṃ kathetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā kāḷasilāyaṃ aṭaviyaṃ parinibbāyi.

The elder, knowing that his past kamma was drawing its result, did not retreat. Due to that consequence, he was unable to fly into the air. Even his psychic power, capable of subduing the nāga-king Nandopananda and shaking the Vejayanta palace, became weak due to the force of kamma. The bandit seized the elder and pounded his bones until they were the size of broken rice grains, crushing them into powder and reducing them to a state like straw-chaff. Thinking ‘he is dead,’ he threw him onto a thicket and left with his followers. The elder regained mindfulness and, thinking ‘I will attain final Nibbāna after seeing the Teacher,’ bound his body with the band of jhāna to make it firm, rose into the air, and went to the presence of the Teacher. Paying homage, he said, ‘Venerable sir, my life-formation is released; I will attain final Nibbāna.’ ‘Will you attain final Nibbāna, Moggallāna?’ ‘Yes, Venerable sir.’ ‘Where will you go to do so?’ ‘On the Black Rock slab, Venerable sir.’ ‘Then, Moggallāna, teach me the Dhamma before you go, for there will be no seeing such a disciple hereafter.’ He said, ‘I will do so, Venerable sir,’ and having paid homage, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree. Like the elder Sāriputta on his final day, he performed various miracles and taught the Dhamma. Then, paying homage to the Teacher, he attained final Nibbāna on the Black Rock slab in the forest.

Taṅkhaṇaññeva cha devalokā ekakolāhalā ahesuṃ, “amhākaṃ kira ācariyo parinibbuto”ti dibbagandhamālāvāsadhūmacandanacuṇṇāni ceva nānādārūni ca gahetvā āgamiṃsu, ekūnasataratanacandanacitakā [P 5.0127] ahosi. Satthā therassa santike ṭhatvā sarīranikkhepaṃ kāresi. Āḷāhanassa samantato yojanamatte padese pupphavassaṃ vassi. Devānaṃ antare manussā, manussānaṃ antare devā ahesuṃ. Yathākkamena devānaṃ antare yakkhā tiṭṭhanti, yakkhānaṃ antare gandhabbā tiṭṭhanti, gandhabbānaṃ antare nāgā tiṭṭhanti, nāgānaṃ antare venateyyā tiṭṭhanti, venateyyānaṃ antare kinnarā tiṭṭhanti, kinnarānaṃ antare chattā tiṭṭhanti, chattānaṃ antare suvaṇṇacāmarā [M 5.0135] tiṭṭhanti, tesaṃ antare dhajā tiṭṭhanti, tesaṃ antare paṭākā tiṭṭhanti. Satta divasāni sādhukīḷaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Satthā therassa dhātuṃ gāhāpetvā veḷuvanadvārakoṭṭhake cetiyaṃ kārāpesi. Tadā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, sāriputtatthero tathāgatassa santike [V 5.0124] aparinibbutattā buddhānaṃ santikā mahantaṃ sammānaṃ na labhi, moggallānatthero pana buddhānaṃ samīpe parinibbutattā mahāsammānaṃ labhī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva moggallāno mama santikā sammānaṃ labhati, pubbepi labhiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

At that very moment, the six heavenly realms of the sense sphere were in an uproar, saying, "It is said that our teacher has attained parinibbāna." Bringing divine perfumes, garlands, incense, sandalwood powder, and various kinds of wood, they came; and there was a sandalwood pyre ninety-nine cubits high. The Teacher, standing near the elder, had the body laid upon the pyre. For a distance of a yojana around the cremation site, a rain of flowers fell. Humans were among the devas, and devas were among the humans. In order, yakkhas stood among the devas, gandhabbas stood among the yakkhas, nāgas stood among the gandhabbas, garuḷas stood among the nāgas, kinnaras stood among the garuḷas, parasols stood among the kinnaras, golden yak-tail fans stood among the parasols, banners stood among them, and flags stood among them. For seven days they celebrated the festival of merit-making. The Teacher had the elder’s relics collected and caused a cetiya to be built at the gate-tower of the Veḷuvana monastery. Then, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, because the Venerable Sāriputta did not attain parinibbāna in the presence of the Tathāgata, he did not receive great honor from the Buddha; but because the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained parinibbāna near the Buddha, he received great honor." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?" When they said, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Moggallāna receives honor from me; he received it in the past as well." Having said this, he recounted a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto purohitassa brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā dasamāsaccayena paccūsasamaye mātukucchito nikkhami. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare sabbāvudhāni pajjaliṃsu. Purohito puttassa jātakkhaṇe bahi nikkhamitvā ākāsaṃ olokento nakkhattayogaṃ disvā “iminā nakkhattena jātattā eso kumāro sakalajambudīpe dhanuggahānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti ñatvā kālasseva rājakulaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ sukhasayitabhāvaṃ pucchi. “Kuto me, ācariya, sukhaṃ, ajja sakalanivesane āvudhāni pajjalitānī”ti vutte “mā bhāyi, deva, na tumhākaṃ nivesaneyeva, sakalanagarepi pajjaliṃsuyeva, ajja amhākaṃ gehe kumārassa jātattā evaṃ ahosī”ti. “Ācariya, evaṃ jātakumārassa pana kiṃ bhavissatī”ti? “Na kiñci, mahārāja, so pana sakalajambudīpe dhanuggahānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti. “Sādhu, ācariya, tena hi naṃ paṭijaggitvā vayappattakāle amhākaṃ dasseyyāsī”ti vatvā khīramūlaṃ tāva sahassaṃ dāpesi. Purohito taṃ gahetvā nivesanaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇiyā datvā puttassa nāmaggahaṇadivase jātakkhaṇe āvudhānaṃ pajjalitattā “jotipālo”tissa nāmaṃ akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the purohita's wife. After ten months, he came forth from his mother's womb at dawn. At that moment, in the city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent, all the weapons blazed. At the moment of his son's birth, the purohita went outside, looked at the sky, and seeing the conjunction of the stars, he knew, "Because he was born under this star, this boy will be the foremost of archers in all Jambudīpa." Knowing this, he went to the palace early in the morning and asked the king if he had slept well. When the king replied, "How could I be at ease, teacher? Today, in the whole palace, the weapons blazed!" the purohita said, "Do not fear, O King. It was not only in your palace; they blazed throughout the whole city. This happened because a boy was born in our house today." "Teacher, what will happen to the boy born like this?" "Nothing harmful, Great King; rather, he will become the foremost of archers in all Jambudīpa." "Good, teacher; then look after him and show him to us when he comes of age," the king said, and gave a thousand coins as a nursing fee. The purohita took it, went home, and gave it to his wife; on the naming day, he named him "Jotipāla" because the weapons had blazed at the moment of his birth.

So mahantena parivārena vaḍḍhamāno soḷasavassakāle uttamarūpadharo ahosi. Athassa pitā sarīrasampattiṃ oloketvā sahassaṃ datvā, “tāta, takkasilaṃ gantvā [P 5.0128] disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sippaṃ uppaṇhāhī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ācariyabhāgaṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā tattha gantvā sahassaṃ datvā [M 5.0136] sippaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sattāheneva nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa ācariyo tussitvā attano santakaṃ khaggaratanaṃ sandhiyuttaṃ meṇḍakasiṅgadhanuṃ sandhiyuttaṃ tūṇīraṃ attano sannāhakañcukaṃ uṇhīsañca datvā “tāta jotipola, ahaṃ mahallako, idāni tvaṃ ime māṇavake sikkhāpehī”ti pañcasatamāṇavakepi tasseva niyyādesi. Bodhisatto sabbaṃ upakaraṇaṃ gahetvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasimeva āgantvā mātāpitaro vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ vanditvā ṭhitaṃ pitā avoca “uggahitaṃ te, tāta, sippa”nti. “Āma, tātā”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā rājakulaṃ gantvā “putto me[V 5.0125], deva, sippaṃ sikkhitvā āgato, kiṃ karotū”ti āha. “Ācariya, amhe upaṭṭhahatū”ti. “Paribbayamassa jānātha, devā”ti. “So devasikaṃ sahassaṃ labhatū”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā gehaṃ gantvā kumāraṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahā”ti āha. So tato paṭṭhāya devasikaṃ sahassaṃ labhitvā rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahi.

He grew up with a great retinue and became exceptionally beautiful by the age of sixteen. Then his father, seeing his physical perfection, gave him a thousand coins and said, "Son, go to Takkasilā and learn the arts from a world-renowned teacher." He agreed, saying, "Very well," took the teacher's fee, paid respects to his parents, went there, gave the thousand, began his studies, and reached mastery in just seven days. Then his teacher, being pleased, gave him his own precious sword, a composite bow made of ram's horn, a composite quiver, and his own suit of armor and turban, and saying, "Son Jotipāla, I am old; now you teach these students," he handed over the five hundred students to him. The Bodhisatta took all the equipment, paid respects to the teacher, returned to Bārāṇasī, and stood after paying respects to his parents. Then his father said to him as he stood there, "Son, have you learned the arts?" "Yes, father." Hearing his words, the father went to the palace and said, "Great King, my son has returned after learning the arts; what should he do?" "Teacher, let him serve us." "Know his allowance, O King." "Let him receive a thousand coins daily." He agreed, saying, "Very well," went home, summoned the young man, and said, "Son, serve the king." From then on, he received a thousand coins daily and served the king.

Rājapādamūlikā ujjhāyiṃsu – “mayaṃ jotipālena katakammaṃ na passāma, devasikaṃ sahassaṃ gaṇhāti, mayamassa sippaṃ passitukāmā”ti. Rājā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā purohitassa kathesi. Purohito “sādhu, devā”ti puttassārocesi. So “sādhu, tāta, ito sattame divase dassessāmi sippaṃ, apica rājā attano vijite dhanuggahe sannipātāpetū”ti āha. Purohito gantvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā dhanuggahe sannipātāpesi. Saṭṭhisahassā dhanuggahā sannipatiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ sannipatitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “nagaravāsino jotipālassa sippaṃ passantū”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ sajjāpetvā mahājanaparivuto pallaṅkavare [P 5.0129] nisīditvā dhanuggahe pakkosāpetvā “jotipālo āgacchatū”ti pesesi. So ācariyena dinnāni dhanutūṇīrasannāhakañcukauṇhīsāni nivāsanantare ṭhapetvā khaggaṃ gāhāpetvā pakativesena rañño santikaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

The king's retainers complained, saying, 'We do not see any work done by the youth Jotipāla. He receives a thousand daily, yet we wish to see his skill.' Hearing their words, the king spoke to the chaplain. The chaplain said, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' and informed his son. He replied, 'Very well, father. On the seventh day from now, I will show my skill. Moreover, let the king assemble the archers within his own kingdom.' The chaplain went and reported this matter to the king. The king had a drum beaten throughout the city and assembled the archers. Sixty thousand archers gathered. Knowing they had assembled, the king had a drum beaten in the city, announcing, 'Let the citizens see the skill of the youth Jotipāla.' He had the royal courtyard prepared and, surrounded by a great crowd, sat on a splendid throne. He then summoned the archers and sent a message, saying, 'Let Jotipāla come.' Having placed the bow, quiver, armored tunic, and turban given by his teacher within the folds of his lower garment, and having someone carry his sword, Jotipāla went to the king’s presence in his ordinary appearance and stood to one side.

Dhanuggahā “jotipālo kira dhanusippaṃ dassetuṃ āgato, dhanuṃ aggahetvā pana āgatattā amhākaṃ hatthato dhanuṃ gahetukāmo bhavissati[M 5.0137], nāssa dassāmā”ti katikaṃ kariṃsu. Rājā jotipālaṃ āmantetvā “sippaṃ dassehī”ti āha. So sāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā antosāṇiyaṃ ṭhito sāṭakaṃ apanetvā sannāhakañcukaṃ pavesetvā uṇhīsaṃ sīse paṭimuñcitvā meṇḍakasiṅgadhanumhi pavālavaṇṇaṃ jiyaṃ āropetvā tūṇīraṃ piṭṭhe bandhitvā khaggaṃ vāmato katvā vajiraggaṃ nārācaṃ nakhapiṭṭhena parivattetvā sāṇiṃ vivaritvā pathaviṃ bhinditvā alaṅkatanāgakumāro viya nikkhamitvā gantvā rañño apacitiṃ dassetvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā mahājanā vagganti nadanti apphoṭenti seḷenti. Rājā “dassehi, jotipāla, sippa”nti āha. Deva, tumhākaṃ dhanuggahesu akkhaṇavedhivālavedhisaravedhisaddavedhino cattāro dhanuggahe pakkosāpehīti. Atha rājā pakkosāpesi.

The archers made an agreement: 'It is said that the youth Jotipāla has come to demonstrate his skill in archery. However, since he has come without a bow, he must intend to take a bow from our hands. Let us not give him one.' The king addressed Jotipāla and said, 'Show your skill.' Jotipāla had a curtain enclosure set up and, standing inside the curtain, he removed his outer garments, put on his armored tunic, fastened the turban on his head, and strung the ram's horn bow with a coral-colored string. He fastened the quiver on his back, girded his sword on his left side, and rubbed an adamantine-tipped iron arrow with the surface of his fingernail. Then, opening the curtain, he emerged like an adorned young Nāga splitting the earth. He went and paid respect to the king and stood there. Seeing him, the great crowd cheered, shouted, clapped their hands, and roared. The king said, 'Jotipāla, show your skill.' Jotipāla replied, 'Your Majesty, from among your archers, please summon four who are experts: a lightning-shot, a hair-piercer, an arrow-piercer, and a sound-piercer.' Then the king had them summoned.

Mahāsatto rājaṅgaṇe caturassaparicchedabbhantare maṇḍalaṃ katvā catūsu kaṇṇesu cattāro dhanuggahe ṭhapetvā ekekassa tiṃsa tiṃsa kaṇḍasahassāni dāpetvā ekekassa santike ekekaṃ kaṇḍadāyakaṃ ṭhapetvā sayaṃ vajiraggaṃ nārācaṃ gahetvā maṇḍalamajjhe ṭhatvā “mahārāja, ime cattāro [V 5.0126] dhanuggahā ekappahāreneva sare khipitvā maṃ vijjhantu, ahaṃ etehi khittakaṇḍāni nivāressāmī”ti āha. Rājā “evaṃ karothā”ti āṇāpesi. Dhanuggahā āhaṃsu, “mahārāja, mayaṃ akkhaṇavedhivālavedhisaravedhisaddavedhino, jotipālo taruṇadārako, na mayaṃ vijjhissāmā”ti. Mahāsatto “sace sakkotha, vijjhatha ma”nti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ekappahāreneva kaṇḍāni khipiṃsu. Mahāsatto tāni nārācena paharitvā yathā vā tathā [P 5.0130] vā na pātesi, bodhikoṭṭhakaṃ pana parikkhipanto viya tālena tālaṃ, vālena vālaṃ, daṇḍakena daṇḍakaṃ, vājena vājaṃ anatikkamanto khipitvā saragabbhaṃ akāsi. Dhanuggahānaṃ kaṇḍāni khīṇāni. So tesaṃ kaṇḍakhīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā saragabbhaṃ avināsentova uppatitvā gantvā rañño santike aṭṭhāsi. Mahājano unnādento vagganto apphoṭento seḷento accharaṃ paharanto mahākolāhalaṃ katvā vatthābharaṇādīni khipi. Evaṃ ekarāsibhūtaṃ aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ ahosi.

The Great Being made a pavilion within a square enclosure in the royal courtyard and placed the four archers at the four corners. He had thirty thousand arrows given to each of them and stationed an arrow-giver near each one. Taking an adamantine-tipped iron arrow himself, he stood in the middle of the pavilion and said, 'Great King, let these four archers shoot their arrows at me all at once, and I will ward off the arrows they shoot with a single arrow.' The king commanded, 'Do as he says.' The archers said, 'Great King, we are experts: a lightning-shot, a hair-piercer, an arrow-piercer, and a sound-piercer. Jotipāla is but a young lad; we will not shoot him.' The Great Being replied, 'If you are able, shoot at me.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and shot their arrows all at once. The Great Being struck those arrows with his iron arrow, not letting them fall here or there; instead, as if surrounding a Bodhi shrine with a railing, he shot them point to point, notch to notch, shaft to shaft, and feather to feather, without overshooting, and created an arrow-chamber. The archers' arrows were exhausted. Knowing their arrows were spent, he leapt up without destroying the arrow-chamber and went to stand in the king's presence. The great crowd, roaring, cheering, clapping, shouting, and snapping their fingers, created a great uproar and threw their garments and ornaments. In this way, the wealth gathered in one heap amounted to eighteen crores.

Atha [M 5.0138] naṃ rājā pucchi – “kiṃ sippaṃ nāmetaṃ jotipālā”ti? Sarapaṭibāhanaṃ nāma, devāti. Aññe etaṃ jānantā atthīti. Sakalajambudīpe maṃ ṭhapetvā añño natthi, devāti. Aparaṃ dassehi, tātāti. Deva, ete tāva catūsu kaṇṇesu ṭhatvā cattāropi janā maṃ vijjhituṃ na sakkhiṃsu, ahaṃ panete catūsu kaṇṇesu ṭhite ekeneva sarena vijjhissāmīti. Dhanuggahā ṭhātuṃ na ussahiṃsu. Mahāsatto catūsu kaṇṇesu catasso kadaliyo ṭhapāpetvā nārācapuṅkhe rattasuttakaṃ bandhitvā ekaṃ kadaliṃ sandhāya khipi. Nārāco taṃ kadaliṃ vijjhitvā tato dutiyaṃ, tato tatiyaṃ, tato catutthaṃ, tato paṭhamaṃ viddhameva vijjhitvā puna tassa hattheyeva patiṭṭhahi. Kadaliyo suttaparikkhittā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahājano unnādasahassāni pavattesi. Rājā “kiṃ sippaṃ nāmetaṃ, tātā”ti? Cakkaviddhaṃ nāma, devāti. Aparampi dassehi, tātāti. Mahāsatto saralaṭṭhiṃ nāma, sararajjuṃ nāma, saravedhiṃ nāma dassesi, sarapāsādaṃ nāma, sarasopānaṃ nāma, saramaṇḍapaṃ nāma, sarapākāraṃ nāma, sarapokkharaṇiṃ nāma akāsi, sarapadumaṃ nāma pupphāpesi, saravassaṃ nāma vassāpesi. Iti aññehi asādhāraṇāni [P 5.0131] imāni dvādasa sippāni dassetvā puna aññehi asādhāraṇeyeva satta mahākāye padālesi, aṭṭhaṅgulabahalaṃ udumbarapadaraṃ vijjhi, caturaṅgulabahalaṃ asanapadaraṃ, dvaṅgulabahalaṃ tambapaṭṭaṃ, ekaṅgulabahalaṃ ayapaṭṭaṃ, ekābaddhaṃ phalakasataṃ vinivijjhitvā palālasakaṭavālukasakaṭapadarasakaṭānaṃ purimabhāgena saraṃ khipitvā pacchābhāgena nikkhamāpesi, pacchābhāgena saraṃ khipitvā purimabhāgena nikkhamāpesi, udake catuusabhaṃ, thale aṭṭhausabhaṭṭhānaṃ kaṇḍaṃ pesesi. Vātiṅgaṇasaññāya usabhamattake vālaṃ vijjhi. Bodhisatto sare khipitvā ākāse sarapāsādādīni katvā puna ekena sarena te sare [V 5.0127] pātento bhaṅgavibhaṅge akāsīti “sarabhaṅgo”ti nāma paññāto. Tassa ettakāni sippāni dassentasseva sūriyo atthaṅgato.

Then the king asked him, 'What is this skill called, Jotipāla?' 'It is called Arrow-Warding, O king.' 'Are there others who know this?' 'Except for me, there is no other in all of Jambudīpa, O king.' 'Show another skill, dear one.' 'O king, while those four archers stationed at the four corners were unable to hit me, I shall hit those four archers stationed at the four corners with a single arrow.' The archers did not dare to take their positions. The Great Being had four banana trees placed at the four corners, tied a red thread to the nock of an iron arrow, and aiming at one banana tree, he shot. The iron arrow pierced that banana tree, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, and then, piercing the first one again that was already hit, it returned and came to rest in his hand. The banana trees stood encircled by the thread. The great crowd raised thousands of cheers. The king asked, 'What is this skill called, dear one?' 'It is called Wheel-Piercing, O king.' 'Show yet another skill, dear one.' The Great Being demonstrated the arrow-staff, the arrow-rope, and arrow-on-arrow piercing; he made an arrow-palace, an arrow-staircase, an arrow-pavilion, an arrow-wall, and an arrow-pond; he made an arrow-lotus bloom, and he made an arrow-rain fall. Thus, having displayed these twelve skills not shared by other archers, he then, with other skills also not shared by others, shattered seven great objects: he pierced an udumbara plank eight fingers thick, an asana plank four fingers thick, a copper plate two fingers thick, and an iron plate one finger thick. He pierced through a hundred planks bound together. He shot an arrow into the front of a cartload of straw, a cartload of sand, and a cartload of planks, and made it exit from the back; he shot an arrow into the back and made it exit from the front. He sent an arrow four usabhas over water and to a distance of eight usabhas on land. By the sign of an eggplant, he pierced a hair-tip at a distance of one usabha. The Bodhisatta, shooting arrows into the sky to create arrow-palaces and such, then brought those arrows down with a single arrow, breaking and shattering them. Thus he became known as "Sarabhaṅga," the Arrow-Breaker. While he was displaying these many skills, the sun set.

Athassa rājā senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ paṭijānitvā “jotipāla, ajja vikālo, sve tvaṃ senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ sakkāraṃ gaṇhissasi, kesamassuṃ kāretvā nhatvā ehī”ti taṃ divasaṃ paribbayatthāya satasahassaṃ adāsi. Mahāsatto [M 5.0139] “iminā mayhaṃ attho natthī”ti aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ sāmikānaññeva datvā mahantena parivārena nhāyituṃ nadiṃ gantvā kesamassuṃ kāretvā nhatvā sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍito anopamāya siriyā nivesanaṃ pavisitvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā sirisayanaṃ abhiruyha nipanno dve yāme sayitvā pacchimayāme pabuddho uṭṭhāya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā sayanapiṭṭhe nisinnova attano sippassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ olokento “mama sippassa āditova paramāraṇaṃ paññāyati, majjhe kilesaparibhogo, pariyosāne nirayamhi paṭisandhi, pāṇātipāto kilesaparibhogesu ca adhimattappamādo niraye paṭisandhiṃ deti, raññā mayhaṃ mahantaṃ senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ dinnaṃ, mahantaṃ me issariyaṃ bhavissati, bhariyā ca puttadhītaro ca bahū bhavissanti. Kilesavatthu kho pana vepullagataṃ duccajaṃ hoti, idāneva nikkhamitvā ekakova araññaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ [P 5.0132] pabbajituṃ yuttaṃ mayha”nti mahāsayanato uṭṭhāya kañci ajānāpento pāsādā oruyha aggadvārena nikkhamitvā ekakova araññaṃ pavisitvā godhāvarinadītīre tiyojanikaṃ kapiṭṭhavanaṃ sandhāya pāyāsi.

Then the king, intending to bestow the position of commander-in-chief upon him, said, 'Jotipāla, it is not yet the time today. Tomorrow you shall receive the honor of the position of commander-in-chief. Have your hair and beard trimmed, bathe, and come.' For that day's provisions, he gave him a hundred thousand. The Great Being, thinking, 'I have no use for this,' gave the wealth amounting to eighteen crores back to its owners. With a great retinue, he went to the river to bathe. Having had his hair and beard trimmed and having bathed, adorned with all his ornaments, he entered his residence with incomparable splendor. He ate a meal of various excellent flavors, ascended his splendid couch, and lay down. Having slept for two watches, he awoke in the last watch, arose, and sitting cross-legged upon the couch, he contemplated the beginning, middle, and end of his craft: 'From the very beginning of my craft, the killing of others is apparent; in the middle, the enjoyment of sensual defilements; at the end, rebirth in hell. The taking of life and the extreme heedlessness in the enjoyment of defilements lead to rebirth in hell. The king has offered me the great position of commander-in-chief. My power will be great; I will have many wives, sons, and daughters. But the objects of defilement, once they have grown great, are difficult to abandon. It is right for me to go forth now, to enter the forest all alone and undertake the ascetic life of a seer.' Rising from his great couch without letting anyone know, he descended from the palace, left by the main gate, and entered the forest all alone, setting out for the wood-apple forest that was three yojanas in extent on the bank of the Godhāvarī river.

Tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā sakko vissakammaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, jātipālo abhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, mahāsamāgamo bhavissati, godhāvarinadītīre kapiṭṭhavane assamaṃ māpetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādehī”ti āha. So tathā akāsi. Mahāsatto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā ekapadikamaggaṃ disvā “pabbajitānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānena bhavitabba”nti tena maggena tattha gantvā kañci apassanto paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitaparikkhāre disvā “sakko devarājā mama nikkhantabhāvaṃ aññāsi maññe”ti cintetvā sāṭakaṃ apanetvā rattavākaciraṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca ajinacammaṃ ekaṃsagataṃ akāsi, jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ bandhitvā khārikājaṃ aṃse katvā kattaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā caṅkamaṃ āruyha katipayavāre aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā pabbajjāsiriyā vanaṃ upasobhayamāno kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā pabbajitato sattame divase aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca abhiññāyo ca nibbattetvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāhāro ekakova vihāsi. Mātāpitaro mittasuhajjādayo ñātivaggāpissa taṃ apassantā rodantā paridevantā vicaranti.

Knowing that he had gone forth, Sakka summoned Vissakamma and said, 'Dear one, Jotipāla has gone forth in the great renunciation. There will be a great assembly of ascetics. Create a hermitage in the wood-apple forest on the bank of the Godhāvarī river and prepare the requisites of an ascetic.' He did so. The Great Being, reaching that place and seeing a single-foot path, thought, 'This must be the dwelling place of ascetics.' Following that path, he went there, and seeing no one, he entered a leaf-hut and saw the requisites of an ascetic. He thought, 'Sakka, king of the gods, must have known of my renunciation.' Taking off his layman's clothes, he dressed himself in a red bark-cloth garment, placed a black antelope skin over one shoulder, tied his hair in a matted topknot, placed a carrying-pole filled with requisites on his shoulder, took up a walking staff, and went out from the leaf-hut. Ascending the walking-path, he paced back and forth a few times, adorning the forest with the splendor of his renunciation. Having performed the preliminary meditation on the kasiṇas, on the seventh day after his renunciation, he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five direct knowledges, and lived there alone, seeking his food from the roots and fruits of the forest. His mother and father, friends, companions, and kinsfolk, not seeing him, wandered about, weeping and lamenting.

Atheko [V 5.0128][M 5.0140] vanacarako araññaṃ pavisitvā kapiṭṭhakaassamapade nisinnaṃ mahāsattaṃ disvā sañjānitvā gantvā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā nagaraṃ gantvā tassa mātāpitūnaṃ ārocesi. Te rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā “etha naṃ passissāmā”ti tassa mātāpitaro gahetvā mahājanaparivuto vanacarakena desitena maggena godhāvarinadītīraṃ pāpuṇi. Bodhisatto nadītīraṃ āgantvā ākāse nisinno dhammaṃ desetvā te sabbe assamapadaṃ [P 5.0133] pavesetvā tatrapi tesaṃ ākāse nisinnova kāmesu ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Rājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbeva pabbajiṃsu. Bodhisatto isigaṇaparivuto tattheva vasi. Athassa tattha vasanabhāvo sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi. Aññepi rājāno raṭṭhavāsīhi saddhiṃ āgantvā tassa santike pabbajiṃsu, samāgamo mahā ahosi. Anupubbena anekasatasahassaparisā ahesuṃ. Yo kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā vitakketi, mahāsatto gantvā tassa purato ākāse nisīditvā dhammaṃ deseti, kasiṇaparikammaṃ ācikkhati. Tassovāde ṭhatvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo uppādetvā jhānanipphattiṃ pattā sālissaro meṇḍissaro pabbato kāḷadevilo kisavaccho anusisso nāradoti satta jeṭṭhantevāsino ahesuṃ. Aparabhāge kapiṭṭhakaassamo paripūri. Isigaṇassa vasanokāso nappahoti.

Then a certain forest dweller entered the forest and, seeing the Great Being seated at the Kapiᅩᅩhaka hermitage, recognized him. He approached, exchanged greetings, and then went to the city to inform the Great Being's parents. They, in turn, informed the king. The king said, "Come, let us see him," and taking the parents, surrounded by a great multitude, reached the bank of the Godhāvarĩ River by the path shown by the forest dweller. The Bodhisatta, having come to the riverbank, sat in the air and taught the Dhamma, then led them all to the hermitage. There too, while seated in the air, he revealed the dangers of sensual pleasures and taught the Dhamma. Starting with the king, they all went forth. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by a company of ascetics, remained there. His dwelling there became well-known throughout all of Jambudĩpa. Other kings, along with their subjects, came and went forth in his presence, and a great gathering took place. Gradually, the assembly grew to many hundreds of thousands. Whenever anyone entertained thoughts of sensuality, ill will, or harm, the Great Being would go and sit before them in the air, teach the Dhamma, and instruct them in the preliminary meditation on the kasiᅆas. Established in his teaching, Sālissara, Meᅆᅆissara, Pabbata, Kāᄷadevila, Kisavaccha, Anusissa, and Nārada became his seven chief disciples, having attained the eight meditative absorptions and reached the perfection of jhāna. In time, the Kapiᅩᅩhaka hermitage became full; the dwelling place was no longer sufficient for the company of ascetics.

Atha mahāsatto sālissaraṃ āmantetvā “sālissara, ayaṃ assamo isigaṇassa nappahoti, tvaṃ imaṃ isigaṇaṃ gahetvā majjharañño vijite kalappacullakanigamaṃ upanissāya vasāhī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā anekasahassaṃ isigaṇaṃ gahetvā gantvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. Manussesu āgantvā pabbajantesu puna assamo paripūri. Bodhisatto meṇḍissaraṃ āmantetvā, “meṇḍissara, tvaṃ imaṃ isigaṇaṃ ādāya suraṭṭhajanapadassa sīmantare sātodikā nāma nadī atthi, tassā tīre vasāhī”ti uyyojesi, puna kapiṭṭhakaassamo paripūri. Etenupāyena tatiyavāre pabbataṃ āmantetvā “pabbata, tvaṃ mahāaṭaviyaṃ añjanapabbato nāma atthi, taṃ upanissāya vasāhī”ti pesesi. Catutthavāre kāḷadevilaṃ āmantetvā “kāḷadevila, tvaṃ dakkhiṇapathe avantiraṭṭhe ghanaselapabbato nāma atthi, taṃ upanissāya vasāhī”ti [M 5.0141] pesesi. Puna kapiṭṭhakaassamo paripūri, pañcasu ṭhānesu anekasatasahassaisigaṇo ahosi. Kisavaccho pana mahāsattaṃ āpucchitvā daṇḍakirañño [P 5.0134] vijite kumbhavatinagaraṃ nāma atthi, taṃ upanissāya uyyāne vihāsi. Nārado majjhimadese añjanagirināmake pabbatajālantare vihāsi. Anusisso pana mahāsattassa santikeva ahosi.

Then the Great Being addressed Sālissara: "Sālissara, this hermitage is not sufficient for the company of ascetics. You take this company of ascetics and dwell near the village of Kalappacullaka in the territory of King Majjha." He replied, "Very well," accepted the instruction, and taking many thousands of ascetics, went and settled there. As people came and went forth, the hermitage became full again. The Bodhisatta then addressed Meᅆᅆissara: "Meᅆᅆissara, you take this company of ascetics and dwell on the banks of the river named Sātodikā, at the border of the Suraᅩᅩha country." He sent him away, and once more the Kapiᅩᅩhaka hermitage became full. In the same way, on the third occasion, he addressed Pabbata: "Pabbata, in the great forest there is a mountain named Ajanapabbata. Dwell near it," and sent him away. On the fourth occasion, he addressed Kāᄷadevila: "Kāᄷadevila, in the country of Avantĩ in the southern region, there is a mountain named Ghanaselapabbata. Dwell near it," and sent him away. Again, the Kapiᅩᅩhaka hermitage became full. In these five places, there were many hundreds of thousands of ascetics. Kisavaccha, however, having taken leave of the Great Being, dwelt in a garden near the city of Kumbhavatĩ in the territory of King Daᅆᅆaki. Nārada lived in the Middle Country, amidst a range of mountains named Ajanagiri. Anusissa, for his part, remained close to the Great Being.

Tasmiṃ kāle daṇḍakirājā ekaṃ laddhasakkāraṃ gaṇikaṃ ṭhānā cāvesi. Sā attano dhammatāya [V 5.0129] vicarantī uyyānaṃ gantvā kisavacchatāpasaṃ disvā “ayaṃ kāḷakaṇṇī bhavissati, imassa sarīre kaliṃ pavāhetvā nhatvā gamissāmī”ti dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ tassūpari bahalakheḷaṃ niṭṭhubhantī kisavacchatāpasassa jaṭantare niṭṭhubhitvā dantakaṭṭhampissa sīseyeva khipitvā sayaṃ sīsaṃ nhāyitvā gatā. Rājāpi taṃ saritvā puna pākatikameva akāsi. Sā mohamūḷhā hutvā “kāḷakaṇṇisarīre kaliṃ pavāhetvā mampi rājā puna ṭhāne ṭhapeti mayā yaso laddho”ti saññamakāsi. Tato nacirasseva rājā purohitaṃ ṭhānato cāvesi. So tassā santikaṃ gantvā “tvaṃ kena kāraṇena puna ṭhānaṃ labhasī”ti pucchi. Athassa sā “rājuyyāne kāḷakaṇṇisarīre kalissa pavāhitattā”ti ārocesi. Purohito gantvā tatheva tassa sarīre kaliṃ pavāhesi, tampi rājā puna ṭhāne ṭhapesi. Athassa aparabhāge paccanto kuppi. So senaṅgaparivuto yuddhāya nikkhami. Atha naṃ mohamūḷho purohito, “mahārāja, kiṃ tumhe jayaṃ icchatha, udāhu parājaya”nti pucchitvā “jaya”nti vutte – “tena hi rājuyyāne kāḷakaṇṇī vasati, tassa sarīre kaliṃ pavāhetvā yāhī”ti āha. So tassa kathaṃ gahetvā “ye mayā saddhiṃ āgacchanti, te uyyāne kāḷakaṇṇisarīre kaliṃ pavāhentū”ti vatvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ sayameva tassa jaṭantare kheḷaṃ niṭṭhubhitvā dantakaṭṭhañca khipitvā sīsaṃ nhāyi. Balakāyopissa tathā akāsi.

At that time, King Daᅆᅆaki dismissed from her position a courtesan who had received honors. Wandering according to her nature, she went to the park and saw the ascetic Kisavaccha. Thinking, "This must be an unlucky person; after washing away my bad luck onto his body, I will bathe and leave," she chewed a toothstick and, first of all, spat a thick glob of saliva into Kisavaccha's matted hair, threw the toothstick onto his head, then bathed her head and left. The king, remembering her, restored her to her former position. Deluded by folly, she thought, "Because I washed away my bad luck onto the body of that unlucky person, the king has restored me to my position; I have gained glory." Not long after, the king dismissed his chaplain from his position. The chaplain went to her and asked, "For what reason did you regain your position?" She told him, "Because I washed away my bad luck onto the body of the unlucky person in the royal park." The chaplain went and likewise washed away his bad luck onto the ascetic's body, and the king also restored him to his position. Later, a border region revolted. The king, surrounded by his army, set out for battle. Then the deluded chaplain asked him, "Great king, do you desire victory or defeat?" When the king said, "Victory," the chaplain replied, "In that case, there is an unlucky person dwelling in the royal park. Go and wash away your bad luck onto his body." Accepting his words, the king said, "Let those who come with me wash away their bad luck onto the body of the unlucky person in the park," and he entered the park. Chewing a toothstick, he himself first spat saliva into the ascetic's matted hair, threw the toothstick there, and bathed his head. His army also did the same.

Tasmiṃ pakkante senāpati gantvā tāpasaṃ disvā dantakaṭṭhādīni nīharitvā sādhukaṃ nhāpetvā “bhante, rañño kiṃ bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Āvusā [M 5.0142] mayhaṃ manopadoso natthi, devatā pana kupitā [P 5.0135] ito sattame divase sakalaraṭṭhaṃ araṭṭhaṃ karissanti, tvaṃ puttadāraṃ gahetvā sīghaṃ palāyitvā aññattha yāhīti. So bhītatasito gantvā rañño ārocesi, rājā tassa vacanaṃ na gaṇhi. So nivattitvā attano gehaṃ gantvā puttadāraṃ ādāya palāyitvā aññaṃ raṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Sarabhaṅgasatthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā dve taruṇatāpase pesetvā “kisavacchaṃ mañcasivikāya ānethā”ti ākāsena āṇāpesi. Rājā yujjhitvā core gahetvā nagarameva paccāgami. Tasmiṃ āgate devatā paṭhamaṃ devaṃ vassāpesuṃ, vassoghena sabbakuṇapesu avahaṭesu suddhavālukavassaṃ vassi, suddhavālukamatthake dibbapupphavassaṃ vassi, dibbapupphamatthake māsakavassaṃ, māsakamatthake kahāpaṇavassaṃ, kahāpaṇamatthake dibbābharaṇavassaṃ vassi, manussā somanassappattā hiraññasuvaṇṇābharaṇāni gaṇhituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ sarīre sampajjalitaṃ nānappakāraṃ āvudhavassaṃ vassi, manussā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chijjiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ upari mahantamahantā vītaccitaṅgārā patiṃsu[V 5.0130], tesaṃ upari mahantamahantāni pajjalitapabbatakūṭāni patiṃsu, tesaṃ upari saṭṭhihatthaṭṭhānaṃ pūrayantaṃ sukhumavālukavassaṃ vassi. Evaṃ saṭṭhiyojanaṭṭhānaṃ araṭṭhaṃ ahosi, tassa evaṃ araṭṭhabhāvo sakalajambudīpe paññāyi.

When the king had departed, the general went and saw the ascetic. After removing the toothsticks and other refuse, he bathed him thoroughly and asked, “Venerable sir, what will happen to the king?” “Friend, I bear no ill will, but the deities are angered. On the seventh day from now, they will turn this entire kingdom into a wasteland. You should take your wife and children and flee quickly to another land.” Terrified and agitated, he went and reported this to the king, but the king did not heed his words. So he returned to his own home, took his wife and children, and fled to another kingdom. The teacher Sarabhaṅga, knowing the situation, sent two young ascetics through the air, commanding them, “Bring Kisavaccha on a litter-bed.” The king, after fighting and capturing the rebels, returned to the city. Upon his arrival, the deities first caused a great rain to fall. When the flood of rain had washed away all the corpses, they rained pure sand. Upon the pure sand, they rained divine flowers. Upon the divine flowers, they rained māsaka coins. Upon the māsaka coins, they rained kahāpaṇa coins. Upon the kahāpaṇa coins, they rained divine ornaments. The people, overjoyed, began to gather the gold, silver, and ornaments. Then, upon their bodies, a rain of various kinds of blazing weapons fell, and the people were cut to pieces. Next, enormous, glowing embers fell upon them, followed by massive, blazing mountain peaks. Above these, a rain of fine sand fell, filling the area to a depth of sixty cubits. Thus, an area of sixty leagues became a wasteland, and the fact of its devastation became known throughout all of Jambudīpa.

Atha tassa raṭṭhassa anantararaṭṭhādhipatino kāliṅgo, aṭṭhako, bhīmarathoti tayo rājāno cintayiṃsu – “pubbe bārāṇasiyaṃ kalābukāsikarājā khantivāditāpase aparajjhitvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭhoti sūyati, tathā “nāḷikerarājā tāpase sunakhehi khādāpetvā, sahassabāhu ajjuno ca aṅgīrase aparajjhitvā, idāni daṇḍakirājā kisavacche aparajjhitvā saha raṭṭhena vināsaṃ patto”ti sūyati. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ rājūnaṃ nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ mayaṃ na jānāma, taṃ no ṭhapetvā sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ añño kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, taṃ upasaṅkamitvā ime pañhe pucchissāmā”ti[P 5.0136]. Te tayopi mahantena parivārena pañhapucchanatthāya nikkhamiṃsu. Te pana “asukopi nikkhanto”ti na jānanti, ekeko “ahameva gacchāmī”ti maññati, tesaṃ godhāvarinadito avidūre samāgamo [M 5.0143] ahosi. Te rathehi otaritvā tayopi ekameva rathaṃ abhiruyha godhāvarinadītīraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu.

Then, the three kings of the adjacent kingdoms—Kāliṅga, Aṭṭhaka, and Bhīmaratha—thought: 'It is heard that in the past, King Kalābu of Bārāṇasī, having wronged the ascetic Khantivādi, entered the earth. Likewise, it is heard that King Nāḷikera had an ascetic devoured by dogs; that Sahassabāhu Ajjuna wronged Aṅgīrasa; and that now King Daṇḍaki, having wronged Kisavaccha, has perished along with his kingdom. We, however, do not know the place of rebirth of these four kings. Apart from our Teacher Sarabhaṅga, there is no one else capable of explaining this to us. Let us approach him and ask these questions.' Thus, all three set out with a large retinue for the purpose of asking their questions. They did not know that the others had also set out, each thinking, 'I alone am going.' Their meeting occurred not far from the Godāvarī River. Descending from their chariots, all three boarded a single chariot and reached the bank of the Godāvarī River.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko paṇḍukambalasilāsane nisinno satta pañhe cintetvā “ime pañhe ṭhapetvā sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ añño sadevake loke kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, taṃ ime pañhe pucchissāmi, imepi tayo rājāno sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ pañhaṃ pucchituṃ godhāvarinadītīraṃ pattā, etesaṃ pañhepi ahameva pucchissāmī”ti dvīsu devalokesu devatāhi parivuto devalokato otari. Taṃ divasameva kisavaccho kālamakāsi. Tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretuṃ catūsu ṭhānesu anekasahassā isayo tattheva gantvā pañcasu ṭhānesu maṇḍapañca kāretvā anekasahassā isigaṇā kisavacchassa tāpasassa candanacitakaṃ katvā sarīraṃ jhāpesuṃ. Āḷāhanassa samantā aḍḍhayojanamatte ṭhāne dibbakusumavassaṃ vassi. Mahāsatto tassa sarīranikkhepaṃ kārāpetvā assamaṃ pavisitvā tehi isigaṇehi parivuto nisīdi. Tesampi rājūnaṃ nadītīraṃ āgatakāle mahāsenāvāhanatūriyasaddo ahosi. Mahāsatto taṃ sutvā anusissaṃ tāpasaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, tvaṃ gantvā tāva jānāhi, kiṃ saddo nāmeso”ti āha. So pānīyaghaṭaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā te rājāno disvā pucchanavasena paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, Sakka, seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, pondered seven questions and thought, 'Apart from the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, there is no one in the world with its gods capable of explaining these questions. I shall ask him these questions. Moreover, these three kings have arrived at the bank of the Godāvarī River to ask the Teacher Sarabhaṅga questions; I myself shall ask their questions as well.' Surrounded by deities from two celestial realms, he descended from the world of the gods. That very day, the ascetic Kisavaccha passed away. To perform his funeral rites, many thousands of sages from four places went there, and having built pavilions in five places, the many thousands of sages cremated the body of the ascetic Kisavaccha on a sandalwood pyre. Around the cremation ground, in a space of half a yojana, a rain of divine flowers fell. The Great Being, having arranged for the funeral rites, entered the hermitage and sat down, surrounded by those companies of sages. When those kings arrived at the riverbank, there arose the sound of a great army with its vehicles and musical instruments. Hearing this, the Great Being addressed the disciple ascetic Anusissa, saying, 'Dear one, go and find out what this sound is.' Taking a water pot, he went there and, upon seeing the kings, spoke the first verse by way of a question:

50.

50.

“Alaṅkatā kuṇḍalino suvatthā, veḷuriyamuttātharukhaggabandhā;

Rathesabhā tiṭṭhatha ke nu tumhe, kathaṃ vo jānanti manussaloke”ti.

"Adorned, wearing earrings, and well-clothed, with sword-hilts of beryl and pearl, and swords girded on; you stand in a single chariot, foremost of chariot-riders. Who are you? How are you known in the world of humans?"

Tattha veḷuriyamuttātharukhaggabandhāti [V 5.0131] veḷuriyamaṇīhi ceva muttālambakehi ca alaṅkatatharūhi khaggaratanehi samannāgatā. Tiṭṭhathāti ekasmiṃ rathe tiṭṭhatha. Ke nūti ke nāma tumhe, kathaṃ vo sañjānantīti?

Therein, 'veḷuriyamuttātharukhaggabandhā' means endowed with excellent swords whose hilts are adorned with beryl gems and pearl pendants. 'Tiṭṭhatha' means 'you stand in one chariot.' 'Ke nū' means 'Who indeed are you?' and 'kathaṃ vo sañjānantī' means 'How are you known?'

Te [P 5.0137] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā rathā otaritvā vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tesu aṭṭhakarājā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, they descended from the chariot, paid homage, and stood there. Among them, King Aṭṭhaka, conversing with him, spoke the second verse:

51.

51.

“Ahamaṭṭhako [M 5.0144] bhīmaratho panāyaṃ, kāliṅgarājā pana uggatoyaṃ;

Susaññatānaṃ isīnaṃ dassanāya, idhāgatā pucchitāyemha pañhe”ti.

"I am Aṭṭhaka, this is Bhīmaratha, and this is the King of Kāliṅga, Uggata. We have come here to see the well-restrained sages; we have come to ask questions."

Tattha uggatoti cando viya sūriyo viya ca pākaṭo paññāto. Susaññatānaṃ isīnanti, bhante, na mayaṃ vanakīḷādīnaṃ atthāya āgatā, atha kho kāyādīhi susaññatānaṃ sīlasampannānaṃ isīnaṃ dassanatthāya idhāgatā. Pucchitāyemha pañheti sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ pañhe pucchituṃ emha, āgatāmhāti attho. Ya-kāro byañjanasandhikaroti veditabbo.

Therein, 'uggato' means manifest and renowned, like the moon or the sun. 'Susaññatānaṃ isīnaṃ' means: 'Venerable sir, we have not come for the purpose of forest sports and so on, but rather we have come here for the sight of sages who are well-restrained in body and so forth, and endowed with virtue.' 'Pucchitāyemha pañhe' means 'we have come to ask questions of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga'; that is, 'we have come.' The letter 'ya' should be understood as performing a consonant sandhi.

Atha ne tāpaso “sādhu mahārājā, āgantabbaṭṭhānaññeva āgatāttha, tena hi nhatvā vissamitvā assamapadaṃ pavisitvā isigaṇaṃ vanditvā sarabhaṅgasatthārameva pañhaṃ pucchathā”ti tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ ukkhipitvā udakatheve puñchanto ākāsaṃ olokento sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ devagaṇaparivutaṃ erāvaṇakkhandhavaragataṃ otarantaṃ disvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the ascetic said to them, 'Good, great kings, you have come to the very place one ought to come to. Therefore, bathe, rest, enter the hermitage grounds, pay homage to the company of sages, and ask your questions of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga himself.' After exchanging friendly greetings with them, he lifted the water pot, and while wiping off the water drops and looking up at the sky, he saw Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by a host of deities, descending mounted on the excellent elephant Erāvaṇa. Conversing with him, he spoke the third verse:

52.

52.

“Vehāyasaṃ tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe, pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando;

Pucchāmi taṃ yakkha mahānubhāva, kataṃ taṃ jānanti manussaloke”ti.

"You stand poised in the sky, in mid-air, like the moon at its zenith on the fifteenth day. I ask you, O yakkha of great power, how are you known in the world of humans?"

Tattha vehāyasanti abbhuggantvā antalikkhe ākāse tiṭṭhasi. Pathaddhunoti pathaddhagato, addhapathe gaganamajjhe ṭhitoti attho.

Therein, 'vehāyasaṃ' means having risen up, you stand in the atmosphere, in the sky. 'Pathaddhuno' means one who has gone on the path; the meaning is, standing in the middle of the path, in the middle of the sky.

Taṃ sutvā sakko catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka spoke the fourth verse:

53.

53.

“Yamāhu [V 5.0132] devesu ‘sujampatī’ti, ‘maghavā’ti taṃ āhu manussaloke;

Sa devarājā idamajja patto, susaññatānaṃ isīnaṃ dassanāyā”ti.

"He whom they call 'Sujampati' among the gods, him they call 'Maghavā' in the world of humans; that King of the Gods has arrived here today for the sight of the well-restrained sages."

Tattha [P 5.0138] sa devarājāti so ahaṃ sakko devarājā. Idamajja pattoti idaṃ ṭhānaṃ ajja āgato. Dassanāyāti dassanatthāya vandanatthāya sarabhaṅgasatthārañca pañhaṃ pucchanatthāyāti āha.

Therein, 'sa devarājā' means: 'I am Sakka, the king of the gods.' 'Idamajja patto' means: 'I have come to this place today.' 'Dassanāya' means: for the purpose of seeing, for the purpose of paying homage, and for the purpose of asking a question of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga.

Atha [M 5.0145] naṃ anusisso “sādhu, mahārāja, tumhe pacchā āgacchathā”ti vatvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ ādāya assamapadaṃ pavisitvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ paṭisāmetvā tiṇṇaṃ rājūnaṃ devarājassa ca pañhapucchanatthāya āgatabhāvaṃ mahāsattassa ārocesi. So isigaṇaparivuto mahāvisālamāḷake nisīdi. Tayo rājāno āgantvā isigaṇaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Sakkopi otaritvā isigaṇaṃ upasaṅkamitvā añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhito isigaṇaṃ vaṇṇetvā vandamāno pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Anusissa said to him, 'Very well, great king, you may come later.' Taking the water pot, he entered the hermitage grounds, put it away, and informed the Great Being that the three kings and the king of the gods had come to ask questions. Surrounded by a company of sages, the Great Being sat in a great, spacious pavilion. The three kings arrived, paid homage to the company of sages, and sat to one side. Sakka also descended, approached the company of sages, and stood with his palms joined in reverence. Then, while praising and paying homage to the company of sages, he spoke the fifth verse:

54.

54.

“Dūre sutā no isayo samāgatā, mahiddhikā iddhiguṇūpapannā;

Vandāmi te ayire pasannacitto, ye jīvalokettha manussaseṭṭhā”ti.

"From afar we have heard of the sages assembled, of great psychic power, endowed with the qualities of iddhi; I pay homage to you, O noble ones, with a serene mind, you who are the foremost among humans in this living world."

Tattha dūre sutā noti, bhante, amhehi tumhe dūre devaloke ṭhitehiyeva sutāti mamāyanto evamāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime idha samāgatā amhākaṃ isayo dūre sutā yāva brahmalokā vissutā pākaṭāti. Mahiddhikāti mahānubhāvā. Iddhiguṇūpapannāti pañcavidhena iddhiguṇena samannāgatā. Ayireti, ayye. Yeti ye tumhe imasmiṃ jīvaloke manussesu seṭṭhāti.

Therein, 'dūre sutā no' means: 'Venerable sirs, we heard of you while we were far away, residing in the world of the gods'; thus he spoke, regarding them as his own. This is what is meant: 'These our sages, assembled here, are heard of from afar, renowned and manifest as far as the Brahma-world.' 'Mahiddhikā' means 'of great power.' 'Iddhiguṇūpapannā' means 'endowed with the fivefold quality of psychic power.' 'Ayire' means 'O noble ones.' 'Ye... manussaseṭṭhā' means 'you who are the foremost among humans in this living world.'

Evaṃ isigaṇaṃ vaṇṇetvā sakko cha nisajjadose pariharanto ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ isīnaṃ adhovāte nisinnaṃ disvā anusisso chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus praised the company of sages, Sakka, avoiding the six faults of sitting, sat down to one side. Then Anusissa, seeing him sitting downwind from the sages, recited the sixth verse:

55.

55.

“Gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ, kāyā cuto gacchati mālutena;

Ito paṭikkamma sahassanetta, gandho isīnaṃ asuci devarājā”ti.

"The scent of the long-ordained sages, issuing from their bodies, is carried by the wind. Retreat from here, O Thousand-Eyed One; the scent of the sages is impure, O King of the Gods."

Tattha ciradikkhitānanti cirapabbajitānaṃ. Paṭikkammāti paṭikkama apehi. Sahassanettāti ālapanametaṃ. Sakko hi amaccasahassehi cintitaṃ atthaṃ ekakova passati, tasmā “sahassanetto”ti vuccati[P 5.0139]. Atha vā sahassanettānaṃ pana devānaṃ dassanūpacārātikkamanasamatthoti [V 5.0133] sahassanettā[M 5.0146]. Asucīti sedamalādīhi paribhāvitattā duggandho, tumhe ca sucikāmā, tena vo esa gandho bādhatīti.

Here, 'long-ordained' means those who have long gone forth. 'Retreat' means step back, go away. 'Thousand-eyed' is a form of address. For Sakka alone sees the meaning pondered by a thousand ministers, hence he is called 'thousand-eyed.' Alternatively, because he is capable of surpassing the vision and attendance of a thousand devas, he is 'thousand-eyed.' 'Impure' means foul-smelling because it is imbued with sweat, grime, and the like, and since you desire purity, this scent troubles you.

Taṃ sutvā sakko itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka spoke the following verse:

56.

56.

“Gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ, kāyā cuto gacchatu mālutena;

Vicittapupphaṃ surabhiṃva mālaṃ, gandhañca etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhāma bhante;

Na hettha devā paṭikkūlasaññino”ti.

"Let the scent from the bodies of the long-ordained sages be carried by the wind; like a garland of varied and fragrant flowers, we desire this scent, O venerable sirs; for the devas here have no perception of repulsion."

Tattha gacchatūti yathāsukhaṃ pavattatu, nāsapuṭaṃ no paharatūti attho. Pāṭikaṅkhāmāti icchāma patthema. Etthāti etasmiṃ gandhe devā jigucchasaññino na honti. Dussīleyeva hi devā jigucchanti, na sīlavanteti.

Here, 'let it go forth' means let it proceed as it pleases, let it strike our nostrils. 'We desire' means we desire and long for it. 'Here' means in regard to this scent, the devas do not have a perception of disgust. For the devas are disgusted only by the immoral, not by the virtuous.

Evañca pana vatvā “bhante, anusissa ahaṃ mahantena ussāhena pañhaṃ pucchituṃ āgato, okāsaṃ me karohī”ti āha. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā isigaṇaṃ okāsaṃ karonto gāthādvayamāha –

Having said this, he said further: "Venerable sir, I have come with great zeal to ask a question. Please grant me an opportunity." Hearing his words, he rose from his seat and, making an opportunity for the assembly of sages, recited these two verses:

57.

57.

“Purindado bhūtapatī yasassī, devānamindo sakko maghavā sujampati;

Sa devarājā asuragaṇappamaddano, okāsamākaṅkhati pañha pucchituṃ.

"Purindada, lord of beings, glorious, king of devas, Sakka, Maghavā, Sujampati; that king of devas, crusher of the host of asuras, seeks an opportunity to ask a question."

58.

58.

“Ko nevimesaṃ idha paṇḍitānaṃ, pañhe puṭṭho nipuṇe byākarissati;

Tiṇañca raññaṃ manujādhipānaṃ, devānamindassa ca vāsavassā”ti.

"Who among these wise ones here, when asked subtle questions, will explain them for the three kings, the lords of men, and for Vāsava, the king of devas?"

Tattha “purindado”tiādīni sakkasseva guṇanāmāni. So hi pure dānaṃ dinnattā purindado, bhūtesu jeṭṭhakattā bhūtapati, parivārasampadāya yasassī, paramissaratāya devānamindo, sattannaṃ vattapadānaṃ suṭṭhu katattā sakko, purimajātivasena maghavā, sujāya asurakaññāya patibhāvena [M 5.0147] sujampati, devānaṃ rañjanatāya devarājā. Ko nevāti ko nu eva. Nipuṇeti saṇhasukhume pañhe. Raññanti rājūnaṃ. Imesaṃ catunnaṃ rājūnaṃ manaṃ gahetvā ko imesaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ isīnaṃ pañhe kathessati, pañhaṃ nesaṃ kathetuṃ samatthaṃ jānāthāti vadati.

There, 'Purindada' and so on are names of Sakka based on his qualities. Indeed, because he gave gifts in the past, he is called Purindada. Because he is the foremost among beings, he is called Bhūtapati. Due to the prosperity of his retinue, he is Yasassī. Because of his supreme sovereignty, he is Devānaminda, king of devas. Because he has well performed the seven vows, he is Sakka. Due to his past life, he is Maghavā. Because of his being the husband of Sujā, the asura maiden, he is Sujampati. Because he delights the devas, he is Devarājā, king of devas. 'Ko nevā' means 'who indeed.' 'Nipuṇa' means subtle and profound questions. 'Raññaṃ' means of kings. Having grasped the intention of these four kings, he asks, 'Who among these wise sages will answer their questions? Know who is capable of explaining the questions to them.'

Taṃ [V 5.0134][P 5.0140] sutvā isigaṇo, “mārisa, anusissa tvaṃ pathaviyaṃ ṭhatvā pathaviṃ apassanto viya kathesi, ṭhapetvā sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ ko añño etesaṃ pañhaṃ kathetuṃ samattho”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the assembly of sages said, "Friend Anusissa, you speak as if you are standing on the ground yet do not see the ground. Except for the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, who else is capable of answering the questions of these four kings?" So saying, they recited this verse:

59.

59.

“Ayaṃ isi sarabhaṅgo tapassī, yato jāto virato methunasmā;

Āceraputto suvinītarūpo, so nesaṃ pañhāni viyākarissatī”ti.

"This sage Sarabhaṅga, an ascetic, who since birth has abstained from sexual intercourse; the son of a teacher, of well-disciplined character, he will explain their questions."

Tattha sarabhaṅgoti sare khipitvā ākāse sarapāsādādīni katvā puna ekena sarena te sare pātento bhaṅgavibhaṅge akāsīti sarabhaṅgo. Methunasmāti methunadhammato. So kira methunaṃ asevitvā pabbajito. Āceraputtoti rañño ācariyassa purohitassa putto.

There, 'Sarabhaṅga' means he shot arrows into the sky and created arrow-pavilions and so forth, then with a single arrow caused those arrows to fall, breaking and shattering them—thus, Sarabhaṅga. 'Methunasmā' means from the practice of sexual intercourse. It is said that he went forth as an ascetic without having engaged in sexual intercourse. 'Āceraputta' means the son of the king's teacher, the royal chaplain.

Evañca pana vatvā isigaṇo anusissaṃ āha – “mārisa, tvameva satthāraṃ vanditvā isigaṇassa vacanena sakkena pucchitapañhakathanāya okāsaṃ kārehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā okāsaṃ kārento anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the assembly of sages said to Anusissa: "Friend, you should pay homage to the Teacher and, on behalf of the assembly of sages, ask for an opportunity for him to explain the questions asked by Sakka." He assented, saying, "Very well," and after paying homage to the Teacher to request the opportunity, he immediately recited this verse:

60.

60.

“Koṇḍañña pañhāni viyākarohi, yācanti taṃ isayo sādhurūpā;

Koṇḍañña eso manujesu dhammo, yaṃ vuddhamāgacchati esa bhāro”ti.

"Koṇḍañña, explain the questions; the virtuous sages ask this of you. Koṇḍañña, this is the way among humans, that this burden falls upon those mature in wisdom."

Tattha koṇḍaññāti taṃ gottenālapati. Dhammoti sabhāvo. Yaṃ vuddhanti yaṃ paññāya vuddhaṃ purisaṃ esa pañhānaṃ vissajjanabhāro nāma āgacchati, eso manujesu sabhāvo, tasmā candimasūriyasahassaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya pākaṭaṃ katvā devarañño pañhe kathehīti.

There, 'Koṇḍañña' is an address by his clan name. 'Dhamma' means nature or custom. 'Yaṃ vuddhaṃ' means that person who is mature in wisdom. This burden of answering questions comes to him; this is the nature among humans. Therefore, as if making a thousand suns and moons rise and become visible, explain the questions to the king of devas.

Tato [M 5.0148] mahāpuriso okāsaṃ karonto anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, granting the opportunity, immediately recited this verse:

61.

61.

“Katāvakāsā pucchantu bhonto, yaṃ kiñci pañhaṃ manasābhipatthitaṃ;

Ahañhi taṃ taṃ vo viyākarissaṃ, ñatvā sayaṃ lokamimaṃ parañcā”ti.

"Opportunity is granted; ask, venerable sirs, whatever question is desired in your mind. For I shall explain each and every one to you, having realized this world and the next myself."

Tattha [P 5.0141] yaṃ kiñcīti na kevalaṃ tumhākaṃyeva, atha kho sadevakassapi lokassa yaṃ manasābhipatthitaṃ, taṃ maṃ bhavanto pucchantu. Ahañhi vo idhalokanissitaṃ vā paralokanissitaṃ vā sabbaṃ pañhaṃ imañca parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ paññāya sacchikatvā kathessāmīti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ sampavāresi.

Here, 'whatever it may be' means: not only yours, but indeed whatever is desired by the world with its devas—let the venerable sirs ask me. For I will explain every question, whether pertaining to this world or the next, having personally realized both worlds through my own wisdom—thus he made an invitation like one who is omniscient.

Evaṃ [V 5.0135] tena okāse kate sakko attanā abhisaṅkhataṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

When he had granted the opportunity, Sakka asked a question he had formulated himself. Revealing that matter, the Teacher said:

62.

62.

“Tato ca maghavā sakko, atthadassī purindado;

Apucchi paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ, yañcāsi abhipatthitaṃ.

Then Maghavā Sakka, Purindada, the seer of benefit, first asked the question which he had desired.

63.

63.

“Kiṃ sū vadhitvā na kadāci socati, kissappahānaṃ isayo vaṇṇayanti;

Kassīdha vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha, akkhāhi me koṇḍañña etamattha”nti.

"What is it that, having slain, one never grieves? The abandoning of which do the sages praise? Whose harsh words spoken here should one endure? Explain this matter to me, Koṇḍañña."

Tattha yañcāsīti yaṃ tassa manasā abhipatthitaṃ āsi, taṃ pucchīti attho. Etanti etaṃ mayā pucchitamatthaṃ akkhāhi meti ekagāthāya tayo pañhe pucchi.

There, 'yañcāsi' means that which was desired in his mind, that is what he asked. 'Etam' means 'explain to me this matter I have asked'—thus in one verse, he asked three questions.

Tato paraṃ byākaronto āha –

Thereupon, providing the explanation, he said:

64.

64.

“Kodhaṃ vadhitvā na kadāci socati, makkhappahānaṃ isayo vaṇṇayanti;

Sabbesaṃ vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha, etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo”ti.

"Having slain anger, one never grieves; the sages praise the abandonment of ingratitude. One should endure the harsh words of all; the wise call this patience supreme."

Tattha kodhaṃ vadhitvāti kodhaṃ māretvā chaḍḍetvā. Socanto hi paṭighacitteneva socati, kodhābhāvā kuto soko. Tena vuttaṃ [M 5.0149] “na kadāci socatī”ti. Makkhappahānanti parehi attano kataguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇassa akataññubhāvasaṅkhātassa makkhassa pahānaṃ isayo vaṇṇayanti. Sabbesanti hīnamajjhimukkaṭṭhānaṃ sabbesampi pharusaṃ vacanaṃ khametha. Santoti porāṇakā paṇḍitā evaṃ kathenti.

There, 'having slain anger' means having killed and abandoned anger. For one who grieves does so with a mind of aversion; if anger is absent, how can there be grief? Therefore it is said, "he never grieves." 'The abandonment of ingratitude (makkha)' means the sages praise the giving up of ingratitude, which is characterized by the concealing of good done to oneself by others. 'Sabbesaṃ' means one should endure harsh speech from everyone, whether they be inferior, middling, or superior. 'Santo' means the ancient wise ones speak thus.

Sakko āha –

Sakka said:

65.

65.

“Sakkā ubhinnaṃ vacanaṃ titikkhituṃ, sadisassa vā seṭṭhatarassa vāpi;

Kathaṃ nu hīnassa vaco khametha, akkhāhi me koṇḍañña etamattha”nti.

"It is possible to endure the words of both an equal or a superior; but how should one endure the speech of one who is inferior? Explain this matter to me, Koṇḍañña."

Sarabhaṅgo āha –

Sarabhaṅga said:

66.

66.

“Bhayā [V 5.0136] hi seṭṭhassa vaco khametha, sārambhahetū pana sādisassa;

Yo [P 5.0142] cīdha hīnassa vaco khametha, etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo”ti. –

"Out of fear, one should endure the words of a superior; due to avoid rivalry, those of an equal. But whoever here endures the words of an inferior, the wise call that patience supreme."

Evamādīnaṃ gāthānaṃ vacanappaṭivacanavasena sambandho veditabbo.

The connection of these and similar verses should be understood as a dialogue of question and answer.

Tattha akkhāhi meti, bhante koṇḍañña, tumhehi dve pañhā sukathitā, eko me cittaṃ na gaṇhāti, kathaṃ sakkā attano hīnatarassa vacanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ, taṃ mama akkhāhīti pucchanto evamāha. Etaṃ khantinti yadetaṃ jātigottādihīnassa vacanaṃ khamanaṃ, etaṃ khantiṃ uttamanti porāṇakapaṇḍitā vadanti. Yaṃ panetaṃ jātiādīhi seṭṭhassa bhayena, sadisassa karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇe sārambhe ādīnavadassanena khamanaṃ, nesā adhivāsanakhanti nāmāti attho.

Here, 'explain to me' means, "Venerable Koṇḍañña, you have well explained two questions, but one does not satisfy my mind: how can one tolerate the words of an inferior? Explain that to me." 'This patience' (etaṃ khantiṃ) refers to the tolerance of words from one inferior in birth, lineage, and so forth; the ancient wise ones call this patience supreme. However, endurance out of fear of a superior, or from an equal to avoid the faults of rivalry and the desire to surpass, is not considered true patience of endurance. That is the meaning.

Evaṃ vutte sakko mahāsattaṃ āha – “bhante, paṭhamaṃ tumhe ‘sabbesaṃ vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha, etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo’ti vatvā idāni ‘yo cīdha hīnassa vaco khametha, etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo’ti vadatha, na vo purimena pacchimaṃ sametī”ti. Atha naṃ mahāsatto, “sakka, pacchimaṃ mayā ‘ayaṃ hīno’ti ñatvā pharusavacanaṃ adhivāsentassa vasena vuttaṃ, yasmā pana na sakkā rūpadassanamattena sattānaṃ seṭṭhādibhāvo ñātuṃ, tasmā [M 5.0150] purimaṃ vutta”nti vatvā sattānaṃ aññatra saṃvāsā rūpadassanamattena seṭṭhādibhāvassa duviññeyyataṃ pakāsento gāthamāha –

When this was said, Sakka said to the Great Being: "Venerable sir, first you said, 'One should endure the harsh words of all; the virtuous ones of old called such endurance the highest patience.' Now you say, 'One should endure the words of a lowly person; they call such endurance the highest patience.' Your former and latter statements do not agree." Then the Great Being said to him: "Sakka, the latter statement was made in terms of the power of one who, knowing 'this person is lowly,' endures harsh words. But because the superiority or the like of beings cannot be known merely by seeing their appearance, the former statement was made." Thus, setting aside the factor of living together, and wishing to reveal the difficulty of knowing superiority and so on merely by seeing appearance, he spoke this verse:

67.

67.

“Kathaṃ vijaññā catupattharūpaṃ, seṭṭhaṃ sarikkhaṃ athavāpi hīnaṃ;

Virūparūpena caranti santo, tasmā hi sabbesaṃ vaco khamethā”ti.

"How can one know by the physical form as manifested in the four postures whether one is superior, equal, or even inferior? Virtuous ones wander in disguises; therefore, one should endure the words of all."

Tattha catupattharūpanti catūhi iriyāpathehi paṭicchannasabhāvaṃ. Virūparūpenāti virūpānaṃ lāmakapuggalānaṃ rūpena uttamaguṇā santopi vicaranti. Imasmiṃ panatthe majjhantikattherassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ.

Here, 'catupattharūpaṃ' means a nature concealed by the four postures. 'Virūparūpena' means that even those possessing excellent qualities wander about in the guise of unseemly or inferior persons. In this connection, the story of the Elder Majjhantika should be told.

Taṃ sutvā sakko nikkaṅkho hutvā, “bhante, etāya no khantiyā ānisaṃsaṃ kathehī”ti yāci. Athassa mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Having heard the words of the Great Being, Sakka became free from doubt and requested: "Venerable sir, preach to us the benefit of that patience." Then, wishing to preach the benefit of patience to Sakka, the Great Being spoke this verse:

68.

68.

“Na [V 5.0137] hetamatthaṃ mahatīpi senā, sarājikā yujjhamānā labhetha;

Yaṃ [P 5.0143] khantimā sappuriso labhetha, khantībalassūpasamanti verā”ti.

"Not even a great army with its king, while fighting, could obtain that benefit which a patient, virtuous person obtains; for through the power of patience, enmities are stilled."

Tattha etamatthanti etaṃ veravūpasamanippaṭighasabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ.

There, 'etaṃ atthaṃ' refers to that benefit known as the state of stilling enmity and the nature of non-retaliation.

Evaṃ mahāsattena khantiguṇe kathite te rājāno cintayiṃsu – “sakko attanova pañhe pucchati, amhākaṃ pucchanokāsaṃ na dassatī”ti. Atha nesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā sakko attanā abhisaṅkhate cattāro pañhe ṭhapetvāva tesaṃ kaṅkhaṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

When the virtue of patience was thus preached by the Great Being, those three kings thought: "Sakka asks only his own questions; he will not give us an opportunity to ask." Then, knowing the intention of those three kings, Sakka, setting aside the four questions he had himself prepared, wished to ask the question desired by the three kings and spoke this verse:

69.

69.

“Subhāsitaṃ te anumodiyāna, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāmi tadiṅgha brūhi;

Yathā ahuṃ daṇḍakī nāḷikero, athajjuno kalābu cāpi rājā;

Tesaṃ gatiṃ brūhi supāpakamminaṃ, katthūpapannā isīnaṃ viheṭhakā”ti.

"Having rejoiced in your well-spoken words, I ask you another; pray tell me this: What became of Daṇḍakī, Nāḷikera, and also Ajjuna and King Kalābu? Tell me the destination of those of very evil deeds, the tormentors of sages—where are they reborn?"

Tattha [M 5.0151] anumodiyānāti idaṃ mayā puṭṭhānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjanasaṅkhātaṃ tava subhāsitaṃ anumoditvā. Yathā ahunti yathā cattāro janā ahesuṃ. Kalābu cāti kalāburājā ca. Athajjunoti atha ajjunarājā.

There, 'anumodiyāna' means: having rejoiced in your well-spoken words, which are the answers to the three questions I asked. 'Yathā ahuṃ' means: how those four people were. 'Kalābu cā' means: and King Kalābu. 'Athajjuno' means: then King Ajjuna.

Athassa vissajjento mahāsatto pañca gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, wishing to answer Sakka, spoke these five verses:

70.

70.

“Kisañhi vacchaṃ avakiriya daṇḍakī, ucchinnamūlo sajano saraṭṭho;

Kukkuḷanāme nirayamhi paccati, tassa phuliṅgāni patanti kāye.

"Having desecrated Kisa Vaccha, Daṇḍakī was uprooted along with his people and territory; he now roasts in the hell called Kukkuḷa, where sparks fall upon his body."

71.

71.

“Yo saññate pabbajite aheṭhayi, dhammaṃ bhaṇante samaṇe adūsake;

Taṃ nāḷikeraṃ sunakhā parattha, saṅgamma khādanti viphandamānaṃ.

"He who harmed the restrained renunciant, the faultless ascetic who spoke the Dhamma; dogs in the next world gather and devour that Nāḷikera as he writhes."

72.

72.

“Athajjuno niraye sattisūle, avaṃsiro patito uddhaṃpādo;

Aṅgīrasaṃ [P 5.0144] gotamaṃ heṭhayitvā, khantiṃ tapassiṃ cirabrahmacāriṃ.

"Then Ajjuna, for harming Aṅgīrasa Gotama—the patient, austere one who had long practiced the holy life—has fallen into hell, impaled on a spear, head downward and feet upward."

73.

73.

“Yo khaṇḍaso pabbajitaṃ achedayi, khantiṃ vadantaṃ samaṇaṃ adūsakaṃ;

Kalābuvīciṃ upapajja paccati, mahāpatāpaṃ kaṭukaṃ bhayānakaṃ.

"He who cut the renunciant into pieces, the faultless ascetic who spoke of patience; Kalābu, having reached Avīci, roasts there—a hell of great heat, bitter and terrifying."

74.

74.

“Etāni [V 5.0138] sutvā nirayāni paṇḍito, aññāni pāpiṭṭhatarāni cettha;

Dhammaṃ care samaṇabrāhmaṇesu, evaṃkaro saggamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

"Having heard of these hells and others even more evil here, a wise person should practice the Dhamma toward ascetics and brahmins; acting thus, one attains a heavenly state."

Tattha kisanti appamaṃsalohitattā kisasarīraṃ. Avakiriyāti avakiritvā niṭṭhubhanadantakaṭṭhapātanena tassa sarīre kaliṃ pavāhetvā. Ucchinnamūloti [M 5.0152] ucchinnamūlo hutvā. Sajanoti sapariso. Kukkuḷanāme nirayamhīti yojanasatappamāṇe kappasaṇṭhite uṇhachārikaniraye. Phuliṅgānīti vītaccitaṅgārā. Tassa kira tattha uṇhakukkuḷe nimuggassa navahi vaṇamukhehi uṇhā chārikā pavisanti, sīse mahantamahantā aṅgārā patanti. Tesaṃ pana patanakāle sakalasarīraṃ dīparukkho viya jalati, balavavedanā vattanti. So adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto mahāviravaṃ ravati. Sarabhaṅgasatthā pathaviṃ bhinditvā taṃ tattha tathāpaccamānaṃ dassesi, mahājano bhayasantāsamāpajji. Tassa ativiya bhītabhāvaṃ ñatvā mahāsatto taṃ nirayaṃ antaradhāpesi.

There, 'kisaṃ' means having an emaciated body due to the lack of flesh and blood. 'Avakiriya' means having defiled him by spitting and throwing tooth-sticks, causing impurity to flow onto his body. 'Ucchinnamūlo' means having his roots cut off. 'Sajano' means with his retinue. 'In the hell called Kukkuḷa' refers to the hot-ash hell, a hundred leagues in size, which remains for an aeon. 'Phuliṅgāni' means glowing embers. It is said that when he is submerged in that hot ash, the hot ash enters through his nine bodily openings, and very large embers fall on his head. At the time they fall, his entire body burns like a lamp-tree, and intense pains occur. Unable to endure it, he lets out a great cry. The teacher Sarabhaṅga, having split the earth, showed him being tormented there in that way, and the great crowd fell into fear and terror. Knowing his extreme state of fear, the Great Being made that hell disappear."

Dhammaṃ bhaṇanteti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ bhāsante. Samaṇeti samitapāpe. Adūsaketi niraparādhe. Nāḷikeranti evaṃnāmakaṃ rājānaṃ. Paratthāti paraloke niraye nibbattaṃ. Saṅgammāti ito cito ca samāgantvā chinditvā mahantamahantā sunakhā khādanti. Tasmiṃ kira kaliṅgaraṭṭhe dantapuranagare nāḷikere nāma raññe rajjaṃ kārayamāne eko mahātāpaso pañcasatatāpasaparivuto himavantā āgamma rājuyyāne vāsaṃ kappetvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desesi. “Dhammikatāpaso uyyāne vasatī”ti raññopi ārocayiṃsu. Rājā pana adhammiko adhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. So amaccesu tāpasaṃ pasaṃsantesu “ahampi dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Tāpaso raññā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “kiṃ, mahārāja, dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, janaṃ na pīḷesī”ti āha. So tassa kujjhitvā “ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo ettakaṃ kālaṃ nāgarānaṃ santike mamaññeva aguṇaṃ kathesi maññe, hotu jānissāmī”ti cintetvā “sve amhākaṃ gharadvāraṃ āgaccheyyāthā”ti nimantetvā punadivase purāṇagūthassa cāṭiyo paripūrāpetvā tāpasesu āgatesu tesaṃ bhikkhābhājanāni gūthassa pūrāpetvā dvāraṃ pidahāpetvā musalāni ca lohadaṇḍe ca gāhāpetvā [P 5.0145] isīnaṃ sīsāni bhindāpetvā jaṭāsu gāhāpetvā kaḍḍhāpetvā sunakhehi khādāpetvā tattheva bhinnaṃ pathaviṃ pavisitvā sunakhamahāniraye nibbattati, tatrassa tigāvutappamāṇasarīraṃ [M 5.0153] ahosi. Atha naṃ mahantamahantā mahāhatthippamāṇā pañcavaṇṇā sunakhā anubandhitvā ḍaṃsitvā navayojanāya jalitaayapathaviyā pātetvā mukhapūraṃ luñcantā vipphandamānaṃ khādiṃsu. Mahāsatto pathaviṃ dvidhā bhinditvā taṃ nirayaṃ dassetvā mahājanassa bhītabhāvaṃ ñatvā antaradhāpesi.

“‘They speak the Dhamma’ means they speak the doctrine of the ten wholesome courses of action. ‘An ascetic’ (Samaṇa) means one who has quelled evil. ‘The innocent’ (Adūsake) means those without offense. ‘Nāḷikera’ refers to the king of that name. ‘In the next world’ (Parattha) means reborn in hell in the life to come. ‘Coming together’ (Saṅgamma) means having gathered from here and there, enormous dogs tear him apart and devour him. It is said that at that time, in the Kalinga country, in the city of Dantapura, while a king named Nāḷikera was ruling, a great ascetic came from the Himalayas with a retinue of five hundred ascetics and took up residence in the royal park, teaching the Dhamma to the people. They reported to the king, ‘A righteous ascetic is dwelling in the park.’ But the king was unrighteous and ruled unjustly. When his ministers praised the ascetic, the king thought, ‘I too shall listen to the Dhamma,’ and went to the park. After paying respects to the ascetic, he sat down. The ascetic, exchanging greetings with the king, asked, ‘Great king, do you rule justly and not oppress the people?’ Enraged at him, the king thought, ‘This deceitful matted-hair ascetic has, I suppose, been speaking ill of me before the citizens for so long. Very well, I shall find out.’ He then invited the ascetics, saying, ‘Come to our palace gate tomorrow.’ The next day, he had pots filled with old dung. When the ascetics arrived, he had their alms bowls filled with dung, shut the gate, and having had clubs and iron rods seized, he had the seers’ heads split open, their matted hair seized, and had them dragged away and devoured by dogs. Right there, the earth split open, and he was reborn in the Great Dog Hell, where his body was three gāvutas in size. Then, enormous dogs, as big as elephants and of five colors, chased him, bit him, and threw him onto a nine-yojana expanse of burning iron ground. Tearing out mouthfuls, they devoured him as he writhed in agony. The Great Being split the earth in two, revealed that hell, and knowing the people were terrified, made it disappear.”

Athajjunoti [V 5.0139] sahassabāhurājā. Aṅgīrasanti aṅgehi raṃsīnaṃ niccharaṇato evaṃladdhanāmaṃ. Heṭhayitvāti viheṭhetvā visapītakaṇḍena vijjhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā. So kira ajjuno nāma rājā mahisakaraṭṭhe ketakarājadhāniyaṃ rajjaṃ kārento migavaṃ gantvā mige vadhitvā aṅgārapakkamaṃsaṃ khādanto vicari. Athekadivasaṃ migānaṃ āgamanaṭṭhāne koṭṭhakaṃ katvā mige olokayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tadā so tāpaso tassa rañño avidūre ekaṃ kārarukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā phalāni ocinanto ocinitaphalasākhaṃ muñci. Tassā vissaṭṭhāya saddena taṃṭhānaṃ pattā migā palāyiṃsu. Rājā kujjhitvā tāpasaṃ visamissitena sallena vijjhi. So parigalitvā patanto matthakena khadirakhāṇukaṃ āsādetvā sūlaggeyeva kālamakāsi. Rājā taṅkhaṇeyeva dvidhā bhinnaṃ pathaviṃ pavisitvā sattisūlaniraye nibbatti, tigāvutappamāṇaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi. Tatra taṃ nirayapālā jalitehi āvudhehi koṭṭetvā jalitaṃ ayapabbataṃ āropenti. Pabbatamatthake ṭhitakāle vāto paharati, so vātappahārena parigalitvā patati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe heṭṭhā navayojanāya jalitaayapathaviyā mahātālakkhandhappamāṇaṃ jalitaṃ ayasūlaṃ uṭṭhahati. So sūlaggamatthakeyeva āsādetvā sūlāvuto tiṭṭhati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pathavī jalati, sūlaṃ jalati, tassa sarīraṃ jalati. So tattha mahāravaṃ ravanto paccati. Mahāsatto pathaviṃ dvidhā katvā taṃ nirayaṃ dassetvā mahājanassa bhītabhāvaṃ ñatvā antaradhāpesi.

“‘Then Ajjuna’ refers to the thousand-armed king. ‘Aṅgīrasa’ is so named because of the rays issuing from his limbs. ‘Having harmed’ means having afflicted him, having pierced him with a poison-smeared arrow, and having brought him to the end of his life. It is said that King Ajjuna, while ruling in the city of Ketaka in the kingdom of Mahisaka, went hunting, killed deer, and wandered about eating meat roasted over charcoal. One day, having made a blind at a place where deer gathered, he stood watching for them. At that time, an ascetic climbed a nearby kāra tree to pick fruit and released a branch from which he had picked the fruit. Startled by the sound of its release, the deer that had come to that place fled. The king, angered, shot the ascetic with a poisoned arrow. Slipping and falling, he struck the top of his head on a khadira stake and died right on the tip of the stake. At that very moment, the earth split in two, and the king plunged into it, reborn in the Spear-and-Spike Hell, his body being three gāvutas in size. There, the hell-wardens struck him with blazing weapons and made him climb a mountain of burning iron. While he stood at the top of the mountain, the wind struck him, and he fell.
