At that instant, a blazing iron spike, as tall as a great palm trunk, rose from the burning iron ground nine yojanas below. He landed on the very tip of the spike and remained impaled. At that moment, the earth burned, the spike burned, and his body burned. There, he screamed loudly as he was tormented. The Great Being split the earth in two, revealed that hell, and knowing the people were terrified, made it disappear.”

Khaṇḍasoti cattāro hatthapāde kaṇṇanāsañca khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ katvā. Adūsakanti niraparādhaṃ. Tathā chedāpetvā dvīhi kasāhi pahārasahassehi tāḷāpetvā jaṭāsu gahetvā ākaḍḍhāpetvā paṭikujjaṃ nipajjāpetvā [M 5.0154] piṭṭhiyaṃ paṇhiyā paharitvā mahādukkhasamappitaṃ akāsi. Kalābuvīcinti kalābu avīciṃ. Kaṭukanti tikhiṇavedanaṃ, evarūpaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjitvā channaṃ jālānaṃ antare paccati. Vitthārato pana kalāburañño vatthu khantivādijātake (jā. 1.4.49-52) kathitameva. Aññāni pāpiṭṭhatarāni cetthāti etehi nirayehi pāpiṭṭhatarāni ca aññāni nirayāni sutvā. Dhammaṃ careti, sakka devarāja, paṇḍito kulaputto na kevalaṃ eteyeva cattāro nirayā, eteyeva ca rājāno nerayikā, atha kho aññepi nirayā, aññepi ca rājāno nirayesu uppannāti viditvā catupaccayadānadhammikārakkhāvaraṇasaṃvidhānasaṅkhātaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇesu dhammaṃ careyyāti.

“‘Piece by piece’ means having cut his four limbs, and his ears and nose, into pieces. ‘The innocent’ means those without offense. Having had him cut up like that, the king had him beaten with two thousand lashes of the whip, seized by his matted hair, dragged along, made to lie face down, and struck on the back with his heels, inflicting great suffering. ‘Kalābu in Avīci’ means Kalābu in the Avīci hell. ‘Bitter’ means sharp pain; having been reborn in such a hell, he is tormented amidst the six networks of flames. The story of King Kalābu is told in detail in the Khantivādi Jātaka. ‘And having heard of others more evil than these’ means having heard of other hells even more terrible than these. ‘Should practice Dhamma’: Sakka, king of the gods, a wise son of a good family, knowing that not only are there these four hells and these kings who are now hell-beings, but also other hells and other kings reborn in them, should practice the Dhamma toward ascetics and brahmins, which consists of providing the four requisites, righteous protection, and shelter.”

Evaṃ [P 5.0146] mahāsattena catunnaṃ rājūnaṃ nibbattaṭṭhāne dassite tayo rājāno nikkaṅkhā ahesuṃ. Tato sakko avasese cattāro pañhe pucchanto gāthamāha –

Thus, when the Great Being had shown the places of rebirth of the four kings, the other three kings became free from doubt. Then Sakka, wishing to ask the remaining four questions, spoke this verse:

75.

75.

“Subhāsitaṃ [V 5.0140] te anumodiyāna, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāmi tadiṅgha brūhi;

Kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadanti;

Kathaṃvidhaṃ sappurisaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ no siri no jahātī”ti.

“Rejoicing in your well-spoken words, I ask you another; pray, tell me this: What kind of person do they call virtuous? What kind of person do they call wise? What kind of person do they call a good person? And what kind of person does fortune never forsake?”

Tattha kathaṃvidhaṃ no siri no jahātīti kathaṃvidhaṃ nu purisaṃ paṭiladdhasirī na jahātīti.

Therein, the phrase “what kind of person does glory not forsake” means: what kind of person who has attained glory is not forsaken by it?

Athassa vissajjento mahāsatto catasso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, answering him, uttered these four verses:

76.

76.

“Kāyena vācāya ca yodha saññato, manasā ca kiñci na karoti pāpaṃ;

Na attahetū alikaṃ bhaṇeti, tathāvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti.

“One who is restrained in body and speech, and does no evil whatsoever in mind; who does not speak falsely for his own sake—such a one they call virtuous.

77.

77.

“Gambhīrapañhaṃ [M 5.0155] manasābhicintayaṃ, nāccāhitaṃ kamma karoti luddaṃ;

Kālāgataṃ atthapadaṃ na riñcati, tathāvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadanti.

“Pondering a profound question with his mind, he does no cruel and improper deed; he does not forsake a timely, beneficial matter—such a one they call wise.

78.

78.

“Yo ve kataññū katavedi dhīro, kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hoti;

Dukhitassa sakkacca karoti kiccaṃ, tathāvidhaṃ sappurisaṃ vadanti.

“One who is grateful, appreciative of what is done, wise, a good friend, and steadfast in loyalty; who carefully attends to the needs of the afflicted—such a one they call a good person.

79.

79.

“Etehi sabbehi guṇehupeto, saddho mudū saṃvibhāgī vadaññū;

Saṅgāhakaṃ sakhilaṃ saṇhavācaṃ, tathāvidhaṃ no siri no jahātī”ti.

“Endowed with all these qualities—faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous, kind, friendly, and pleasant-spoken—such a one glory never forsakes.”

Tattha [P 5.0147] “kāyenā”tiādīni padāni tividhasucaritadvāravasena vuttāni. Na attahetūti desanāsīsamevetaṃ, attahetu vā parahetu vā yasahetu vā dhanahetu vā lābhahetu vā āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā alikaṃ na kathetīti attho. Kāmañcesa attho “vācāya saññato”ti imināva siddho, musāvādino pana akattabbaṃ pāpaṃ nāma natthīti garubhāvadīpanatthaṃ puna evamāhāti veditabbo. Taṃ puggalaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti.

Here, the words beginning with 'by body' are stated in terms of the doors of threefold good conduct. 'Not for one's own sake'—this is a representative example of the teaching, meaning that one does not speak falsely whether for one's own sake or another's sake, for fame, wealth, gain, or for any trivial material benefit. And although this meaning is already established by the phrase 'restrained in speech,' it should be understood that it is repeated to emphasize the gravity of the matter, for there is no evil that a liar would not do. Such a person they call virtuous.

Gambhīrapañhanti atthato ca pāḷito ca gambhīraṃ guḷhaṃ paṭicchannaṃ sattubhastajātaka- (jā. 1.7.46 ādayo) sambhavajātaka- (jā. 1.16.138 ādayo) mahāumaṅgajātakesu (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āgatasadisaṃ pañhaṃ. Manasābhicintayanti manasā abhicintento atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā candasahassaṃ sūriyasahassaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya pākaṭaṃ katvā yo kathetuṃ sakkotīti [V 5.0141] attho. Nāccāhitanti na atiahitaṃ, hitātikkantaṃ luddaṃ pharusaṃ sāhasikakammañca yo na karotīti attho. Imassa panatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ –

A profound question (gambhīrapañha) is one that is deep, obscure, and concealed in both meaning and wording, like those found in the Sattubhasta Jātaka, the Sambhava Jātaka, and the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka. ‘Pondering with the mind’ (manasābhicintayanti) means one who, having thoroughly reflected with the mind and penetrated the meaning, is able to explain it clearly, as if raising a thousand moons and a thousand suns. ‘Not excessively harmful’ (nāccāhitaṃ) means one who does not commit deeds that are exceedingly harmful, beyond what is beneficial, cruel, harsh, or rash and violent. To clarify this meaning, the following is stated:

“Na [M 5.0156] paṇḍitā attasukhassa hetu, pāpāni kammāni samācaranti;

Dukkhena phuṭṭhā piḷitāpi santā, chandā dosā ca na jahanti dhamma”nti. –

“The wise do not engage in evil deeds for the sake of their own happiness. Though touched by suffering and oppressed, they do not abandon the Dhamma due to desire or hatred.”

Bhūripañho kathetabbo.

The profound question should be told.

Kālāgatanti ettha dānaṃ dātabbakāle, sīlaṃ rakkhaṇakāle, uposathaṃ upavāsakāle, saraṇesu patiṭṭhānakāle, pabbajitakāle, samaṇadhammakaraṇakāle, vipassanācārasmiṃ yuñjanakāle cāti imāni dānādīni sampādento kālāgataṃ atthapadaṃ na riñcati na hāpeti na gaḷāpeti nāma. Tathāvidhanti sakka sabbaññubuddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca bodhisattā ca paññavantaṃ kathentā evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ kathenti.

Here, regarding ‘at the proper time’ (kālāgataṃ): one who fulfills these—namely, giving at the time for giving, observing virtue at the time for guarding it, keeping the Uposatha at the time for fasting, establishing oneself in the refuges at the time for establishing, undertaking the going forth at the time for going forth, performing the duties of an ascetic at the time for performing them, and engaging in the practice of insight meditation at the time for engaging in it—such a one does not abandon, neglect, or let slip the meaningful phrase ‘at the proper time’. Regarding ‘such a one’ (tathāvidhaṃ): Sakka, the All-knowing Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Bodhisattas, when speaking of a wise person, describe such a person.

“Yo ve”ti gāthāya parena attano kataguṇaṃ jānātīti kataññū. Evaṃ ñatvā pana yenassa guṇo kato, tassa guṇaṃ paṭikaronto katavedī nāma. Dukhitassāti attano sahāyassa dukkhappattassa dukkhaṃ attani āropetvā yo tassa uppannakiccaṃ sahatthena sakkaccaṃ karoti, buddhādayo evarūpaṃ sappurisaṃ nāma kathenti. Apica sappurisā nāma kataññū katavedino hontīti satapattajātaka- (jā. 1.3.85-87) cūḷahaṃsajātaka- (jā. 1.15.133 ādayo) mahāhaṃsajātakādīni (jā. 2.21.89 ādayo) kathetabbāni. Etehi sabbehīti sakka yo etehi heṭṭhā vuttehi sīlādīhi sabbehipi guṇehi upeto. Saddhoti okappanasaddhāya samannāgato. Mudūti piyabhāṇī. Saṃvibhāgīti sīlasaṃvibhāgadānasaṃvibhāgābhiratattā saṃvibhāgī. Yācakānaṃ vacanaṃ ñatvā dānavasena vadaññū. Catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi tesaṃ tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanato saṅgāhakaṃ, madhuravacanatāya sakhilaṃ, maṭṭhavacanatāya saṇhavācaṃ tathāvidhaṃ nu puggalaṃ adhigatayasasobhaggasaṅkhātā sirī no jahāti, nāssa sirī vinassatīti.

In the verse beginning ‘Who indeed’ (yo ve): one who knows the good done to them by another is grateful (kataññū). Having known this, one who repays the good done to them is called appreciative (katavedī). Regarding ‘of the distressed’ (dukhitassa): when a friend is afflicted with suffering, one who takes their suffering upon themselves and diligently attends to their needs with their own hands—the Buddhas and others call such a one a true person (sappurisa). Moreover, that true persons are grateful and appreciative should be illustrated through the Satapatta Jātaka, the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, and others. Regarding ‘with all these’ (etehi sabbehi): O Sakka, one who is endowed with all these virtues mentioned above, such as morality. ‘Faithful’ (saddho) means possessing resolute faith. ‘Gentle’ (mudū) means speaking pleasantly. ‘Sharing’ (saṃvibhāgī) means one who delights in sharing virtue and gifts. Knowing the request of petitioners, one is generous by way of giving, thus being bountiful (vadaññū). By the four means of benevolence, one is benevolent (saṅgāhaka); with sweet speech, one is friendly (sakhila); with smooth speech, one is pleasant-spoken (saṇhavāca). Fortune, which is reckoned as attained glory and splendor, does not abandon such a person; their fortune does not perish.

Evaṃ [P 5.0148] mahāsatto gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya cattāro pañhe vissajjesi. Tato paraṃ sesapañhānaṃ pucchā ca vissajjanañca hoti –

Thus the Great Being answered the four questions as if raising the full moon in the sky. Thereafter, the asking and answering of the remaining questions takes place:

80.

80.

“Subhāsitaṃ [V 5.0142][M 5.0157] te anumodiyāna, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāmi tadiṅgha brūhi;

Sīlaṃ siriñcāpi satañca dhammaṃ, paññañca kaṃ seṭṭhataraṃ vadanti.

“Rejoicing in your well-spoken words, I ask you another; please tell me this: Of virtue, fortune, the Dhamma of the good, and wisdom—which do they declare to be the most excellent?”

81.

81.

“Paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti, nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ;

Sīlaṃ sirī cāpi satañca dhammo, anvāyikā paññavato bhavanti.

“Wisdom, indeed, the skilled declare to be the best, like the moon, the king of stars, among the constellations. Virtue, fortune, and the Dhamma of the good—these are followers of one who is wise.”

82.

82.

“Subhāsitaṃ te anumodiyāna, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāmi tadiṅgha brūhi;

Kathaṃkaro kintikaro kimācaraṃ, kiṃ sevamāno labhatīdha paññaṃ;

Paññāya dānippaṭipadaṃ vadehi, kathaṃkaro paññavā hoti macco.

“Rejoicing in your well-spoken words, I ask you another; please tell me this: By doing how, by doing what, by practicing what, by associating with what does one gain wisdom here? Now declare the path to wisdom: how does a mortal become wise?”

83.

83.

“Sevetha vuddhe nipuṇe bahussute, uggāhako ca paripucchako siyā;

Suṇeyya sakkacca subhāsitāni, evaṃkaro paññavā hoti macco.

“One should associate with the mature, the astute, and the learned; one should be one who learns the texts and thoroughly questions their meaning. One should listen respectfully to well-spoken words; by doing so, a mortal becomes wise.”

84.

84.

“Sa paññavā kāmaguṇe avekkhati, aniccato dukkhato rogato ca;

Evaṃ vipassī pajahāti chandaṃ, dukkhesu kāmesu mahabbhayesu.

“That wise one contemplates the strands of sensual pleasure as impermanent, as suffering, and as a disease. Thus seeing with insight, one abandons desire for sensual pleasures, which are full of suffering and great terror.”

85.

85.

“Sa vītarāgo pavineyya dosaṃ, mettaṃ cittaṃ bhāvaye appamāṇaṃ;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ, anindito brahmamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

“He, devoid of lust, having dispelled aversion, should cultivate a boundless mind of loving-kindness. Having laid down the rod toward all beings, blameless, he attains the Brahma realm.”

Tattha [P 5.0149] sīlanti ācārasīlaṃ. Sirinti issariyasiriṃ. Satañca dhammanti sappurisadhammaṃ. Paññanti supaññaṃ. Evaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ dhammānaṃ kataraṃ dhammaṃ seṭṭhataraṃ vadantīti pucchati. Paññā hīti, sakka, etesu catūsu dhammesu yā esā paññā [M 5.0158] nāma, sāva seṭṭhā, iti buddhādayo kusalā vadanti. Yathā hi tārakagaṇā candaṃ parivārenti, candova tesaṃ uttamo. Evaṃ sīlañca sirī cāpi satañca dhammoti ete tayopi anvāyikā paññavato bhavanti paññavantameva anugacchanti, paññāya eva parivārā hontīti attho.

Here, ‘virtue’ (sīla) means moral conduct. ‘Fortune’ (siri) means sovereign fortune. ‘And the Dhamma of the good’ (satañca dhamma) means the quality of a true person (sappurisadhamma). ‘Wisdom’ (paññā) means good wisdom. Thus, he asks: among these four qualities, which quality do they declare to be the most excellent? ‘Wisdom, indeed’ (paññā hi): O Sakka, among these four qualities, that which is called wisdom is the most excellent; so say the Buddhas and other skilled ones. Just as the host of stars surrounds the moon, and the moon is supreme among them, so too virtue, fortune, and the Dhamma of the good—these three are followers of one who is wise; they follow the wise one, they are indeed attendants of wisdom—this is the meaning.

“Kathaṃkaro”tiādīni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Kathaṃkaroti kiṃ nāma kammaṃ karonto kiṃ ācaranto kiṃ sevamāno bhajamāno payirupāsamāno idhaloke paññaṃ labhati, paññāyameva paṭipadaṃ vadehi, jānitukāmomhi, kathaṃkaro macco paññavā nāma hotīti pucchati. Vuddheti paññāvuddhippatte paṇḍite. Nipuṇeti sukhumakāraṇajānanasamatthe. Evaṃkaroti yo puggalo evaṃ vuttappakāre [V 5.0143] puggale sevati bhajati payirupāsati, pāḷiṃ uggaṇhāti, punappunaṃ atthaṃ pucchati, pāsāṇe lekhaṃ khaṇanto viya kañcananāḷiyā sīhavasaṃ sampaṭicchanto viya ohitasoto sakkaccaṃ subhāsitāni suṇāti, ayaṃ evaṃkaro macco paññavā hotīti.

‘How does one act?’ (kathaṃkaro) and so on, are simply synonyms. ‘How does one act?’ means: performing what action, practicing what, associating with, frequenting, or attending upon whom does one gain wisdom in this world? ‘Declare the very path of wisdom; I wish to know: how does a mortal become known as wise?’—thus he asks. ‘The mature’ (vuddhe) means the learned who have attained growth in wisdom. ‘Astute’ (nipuṇe) means those capable of understanding subtle causes. ‘Thus acting’ (evaṃkaro) refers to the person who associates with, frequents, and attends upon individuals described in this way; who learns the scriptures and repeatedly inquires about the meaning; who listens respectfully to well-spoken words with attentive ears—like one carving an inscription in stone or receiving lion's fat in a golden tube. A mortal who acts thus becomes wise.

Evaṃ mahāsatto pācīnalokadhātuto sūriyaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya paññāya paṭipadaṃ kathetvā idāni tassā paññāya guṇaṃ kathento “sa paññavā”tiādimāha. Tattha kāmaguṇeti kāmakoṭṭhāse hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccato, diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvena dukkhato, aṭṭhanavutiyā rogamukhānaṃ kāme nissāya uppattisambhavena rogato ca avekkhati oloketi, so evaṃ vipassī etehi kāraṇehi kāmānaṃ aniccāditaṃ passanto “kāme nissāya uppajjanakadukkhānaṃ anto natthi, kāmānaṃ pahānameva sukha”nti viditvā dukkhesu kāmesu mahabbhayesu chandaṃ pajahāti. Sa vītarāgoti, “sakka, so puggalo evaṃ vītarāgo navāghātavatthuvasena uppajjanakasabhāvadosaṃ vinetvā mettacittaṃ bhāveyya, appamāṇasattārammaṇattā appamāṇaṃ taṃ bhāvetvā aparihīnajjhāno agarahito brahmaloke uppajjatī”ti.

Thus, the great being, having explained the way of wisdom as if raising the sun from the eastern world-sphere, now speaks of the virtues of that wisdom, saying, ‘He is wise’ (sa paññavā), and so on. Herein, ‘strands of sensual pleasure’ (kāmaguṇe) means one contemplates (avekkhati, oloketi) them as impermanent in the sense of non-existence, since they are a portion of sensual pleasure; as suffering in the sense of being the basis for suffering in both this life and the next; and as a disease due to the possibility of the arising and origin of ninety-eight kinds of diseases dependent on sensual pleasures. Seeing thus with insight, perceiving the impermanence and so on of sensual pleasures by these reasons, and realizing, ‘There is no end to the suffering born of dependence on sensual pleasures; abandoning sensual pleasures alone is happiness,’ he abandons desire for sensual pleasures, which are suffering and a great danger. ‘He is devoid of lust’ (sa vītarāgo): O Sakka, that person, being thus devoid of lust, having removed the fault of aversion that arises by way of the nine bases of aggression, should develop a mind of loving-kindness. Having developed it as immeasurable due to its immeasurable beings as object, he is reborn in the Brahma-world, not having fallen away from absorption and unblamed.

Evaṃ mahāsatte kāmānaṃ dosaṃ kathenteyeva tesaṃ tiṇṇampi rājūnaṃ sabalakāyānaṃ tadaṅgappahānena pañcakāmaguṇarāgo pahīno. Taṃ ñatvā mahāsatto tesaṃ pahaṃsanavasena gāthamāha –

Thus, as the Great Being was explaining the danger of sensual pleasures, the passion for the five cords of sensual pleasure was abandoned in those three kings and their entire retinues through momentary abandonment. Knowing this, the Great Being spoke a verse to gladden them:

86.

86.

“Mahatthiyaṃ [M 5.0159] āgamanaṃ ahosi, tavamaṭṭhakā bhīmarathassa cāpi;

Kāliṅgarājassa ca uggatassa, sabbesa vo kāmarāgo pahīno”ti.

“Great was the arrival of you, Aṭṭhaka, and of Bhīmaratha; and also of King Kaliṅga and of Uggata. In all of you, sensual passion has been abandoned.”

Tattha [P 5.0150] mahatthiyanti mahatthaṃ mahāvipphāraṃ mahājutikaṃ. Tavamaṭṭhakāti tava aṭṭhakā. Pahīnoti tadaṅgappahānena pahīno.

Here, “mahatthiyaṃ” means of great import, of great diffusion, of great brilliance. “Tavamaṭṭhakā” means your Aṭṭhaka. “Pahīno” means abandoned by momentary abandonment.

Taṃ sutvā rājāno mahāsattassa thutiṃ karontā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing this, the kings, praising the Great Being, spoke a verse:

87.

87.

“Evametaṃ paracittavedi, sabbesa no kāmarāgo pahīno;

Karohi okāsamanuggahāya, yathā gatiṃ te abhisambhavemā”ti.

“Thus it is, O knower of others’ thoughts, sensual passion is abandoned in all of us. Grant us the opportunity for your favor, so that we may fully attain your destination.”

Tattha anuggahāyāti pabbajjatthāya okāsaṃ no karohi. Yathā mayaṃ pabbajitvā tava gatiṃ nipphattiṃ abhisambhavema pāpuṇeyyāma, tayā paṭividdhaguṇaṃ paṭivijjheyyāmāti vadiṃsu.

Here, “anuggahāya” means “make an opportunity for us to go forth.” They said, “So that by going forth, we may attain your destination and accomplishment, and penetrate the virtues you have penetrated.”

Atha [V 5.0144] nesaṃ okāsaṃ karonto mahāsatto itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, making an opportunity for them, spoke the other verse:

88.

88.

“Karomi okāsamanuggahāya, tathā hi vo kāmarāgo pahīno;

Pharātha kāyaṃ vipulāya pītiyā, yathā gatiṃ me abhisambhavethā”ti.

“I make an opportunity for your favor, for indeed your sensual passion is abandoned. Pervade the body with abundant rapture, so that you might fully attain my destination.”

Tattha pharātha kāyanti jhānapītiyā vipulāya kāyaṃ pharathāti.

Here, “pharātha kāyaṃ” means “pervade the body with the abundant rapture of jhāna.”

Taṃ sutvā te sampaṭicchantā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing this, they agreed and spoke a verse:

89.

89.

“Sabbaṃ karissāma tavānusāsaniṃ, yaṃ yaṃ tuvaṃ vakkhasi bhūripañña;

Pharāma kāyaṃ vipulāya pītiyā, yathā gatiṃ te abhisambhavemā”ti.

“We will do all according to your instruction, O you of vast wisdom, whatever you may say. We will pervade the body with abundant rapture, so that we may attain your destination.”

Atha nesaṃ sabalakāyānaṃ mahāsatto pabbajjaṃ dāpetvā isigaṇaṃ uyyojento gāthamāha –

Then, having had those with their entire retinues ordained, the Great Being sent off the company of sages, speaking a verse:

90.

90.

“Katāya [M 5.0160] vacchassa kisassa pūjā, gacchantu bhonto isayo sādhurūpā;

Jhāne ratā hotha sadā samāhitā, esā ratī pabbajitassa seṭṭhā”ti.

“Honor has been done to Kisavaccha. Go, venerable and virtuous sages; be ever concentrated, delighting in jhāna. This is the foremost delight for one who has gone forth.”

Tattha gacchantūti attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni gacchantu.

Here, “gacchantu” means “let them go to their own dwelling places.”

Isayo [P 5.0151] tassa sarabhaṅgasatthuno vacanaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchitvā vanditvā ākāsaṃ uppatitvā sakāni vasanaṭṭhānāni gamiṃsu. Sakkopi uṭṭhāyāsanā mahāsattassa thutiṃ katvā añjaliṃ paggayha sūriyaṃ namassanto viya mahāsattaṃ namassamāno sapariso pakkāmi. Etamatthaṃ viditvā satthā imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

The sages, having reverently accepted the words of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, having paid homage, rose into the sky, and went to their own dwelling places. Sakka, too, rose from his seat, praised the Great Being, raised his joined hands in reverence, and departed with his retinue, venerating the Great Being as if venerating the sun. Understanding this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:

91.

91.

“Sutvāna gāthā paramatthasaṃhitā, subhāsitā isinā paṇḍitena;

Te vedajātā anumodamānā, pakkāmu devā devapuraṃ yasassino.

“Having heard the verses connected with the ultimate meaning, well-spoken by the wise sage, the gods, filled with joy and rejoicing, departed to the glorious city of the gods.”

92.

92.

“Gāthā imā atthavatī subyañjanā, subhāsitā isinā paṇḍitena;

Yo kocimā aṭṭhikatvā suṇeyya, labhetha pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ;

Laddhāna pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ, adassanaṃ maccurājassa gacche”ti.

“These verses, meaningful and well-phrased, are well-spoken by the wise sage. Whoever listens to them, paying careful attention, would gain a progressive distinction. Having gained that progressive distinction, they would go beyond the sight of the King of Death.”

Tattha [V 5.0145] paramatthasaṃhitāti aniccādidīpanena nibbānanissitā. Gāthā imāti idaṃ satthā sarabhaṅgasatthuno nibbānadāyakaṃ subhāsitaṃ vaṇṇento āha. Tattha atthavatīti nibbānadāyakaṭṭhena paramatthanissitā. Subyañjanāti parisuddhabyañjanā. Subhāsitāti sukathitā. Aṭṭhikatvāti attano atthikabhāvaṃ katvā atthiko hutvā sakkaccaṃ suṇeyya. Pubbāpariyanti paṭhamajjhānaṃ pubbaviseso, dutiyajjhānaṃ aparaviseso. Dutiyajjhānaṃ pubbaviseso, tatiyajjhānaṃ aparavisesoti evaṃ aṭṭhasamāpatticatumaggavasena pubbāparabhāvena ṭhitaṃ visesaṃ. Adassananti pariyosāne aparavisesaṃ [M 5.0161] arahattaṃ labhitvā nibbānaṃ pāpuṇeyya. Nibbānappatto hi puggalo maccurājassa adassanaṃ gato nāma hotīti.

Here, ‘paramatthasaṃhitā’ means connected to Nibbāna by revealing impermanence and so forth. ‘Gāthā imā’—the Teacher spoke this while extolling the well-spoken words of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, which bestow Nibbāna. Herein, ‘atthavatī’ means connected to the ultimate goal by way of bestowing Nibbāna. ‘Subyañjanā’ means having pure syllables. ‘Subhāsitā’ means well-spoken. ‘Aṭṭhikatvā’ means having made oneself interested, being interested, one should listen attentively. ‘Pubbāpariyaṃ’—the first jhāna is the preceding distinction, the second jhāna is the subsequent distinction; the second jhāna is the preceding distinction, the third jhāna is the subsequent distinction—thus, the distinction exists as preceding and subsequent states by way of the eight attainments and the four paths. ‘Adassanaṃ’ means that in the end, having attained the ultimate distinction of Arahantship, one would reach Nibbāna. For a person who has attained Nibbāna is said to have gone beyond the sight of the King of Death.

Evaṃ satthā arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi moggallānassa āḷāhane pupphavassaṃ vassī”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānento āha –

Thus, the Teacher, having brought the teaching to its summit with Arahantship, said, “Not now only, monks, but even in the past, a rain of flowers fell upon Moggallāna’s funeral pyre,” and revealing the Truths, he connected the Jātaka, saying:

93.

93.

“Sālissaro sāriputto, meṇḍissaro ca kassapo;

Pabbato anuruddho ca, kaccāyano ca devalo;

“Sālissara was Sāriputta, and Meṇḍissara was Kassapa; Pabbata was Anuruddha, and Devala was Kaccāyana;

94.

94.

“Anusisso ca ānando, kisavaccho ca kolito;

Nārado udāyitthero, parisā buddhaparisā;

Sarabhaṅgo lokanātho, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti.

“Anusissa was Ānanda, and Kisavaccha was Kolita; Nārada was the elder Udāyi; the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; Sarabhaṅga was the Lord of the World—thus remember the Jātaka.”

Sarabhaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka is the second.

[523] 3. Alambusājātakavaṇṇanā

[523] 3. The Commentary on the Alambusā Jātaka

Athabravīti [P 5.0152] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu indriyajātake (jā. 1.8.60 ādayo) vitthāritameva. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti vatvā “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti vutte “bhikkhu esā itthī tuyhaṃ anatthakārikā, tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya jhānaṃ nāsetvā tīṇi saṃvaccharāni mūḷho visaññī nipajjitvā uppannāya saññāya mahāparidevaṃ paridevī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Athabravī” (Then he spoke)—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the enticement by a former wife. The story is detailed in the Indriya Jātaka. The Teacher, however, asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” and was asked, “By whom have you been made discontented?” and answered, “By a former wife,” the Teacher said, “Monk, this woman is one who brings you harm. Relying on her, you destroyed your jhāna and lay for three years, deluded and unconscious. When perception arose, you lamented with a great lamentation.” And he related the past.

Atīte [V 5.0146] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpesi. Athekā migī tassa passāvaṭṭhāne sambhavamissakaṃ tiṇaṃ khāditvā udakaṃ pivi. Ettakeneva ca tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā tato paṭṭhāya katthaci agantvā tattheva tiṇaṃ khāditvā assamassa sāmanteyeva vicarati[M 5.0162]. Mahāsatto pariggaṇhanto taṃ kāraṇaṃ aññāsi. Sā aparabhāge manussadārakaṃ vijāyi. Mahāsatto taṃ puttasinehena paṭijaggi, “isisiṅgo”tissa nāmaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto viññutappattaṃ pabbājetvā attano mahallakakāle taṃ ādāya nārivanaṃ nāma gantvā, “tāta, imasmiṃ himavante imehi pupphehi sadisā itthiyo nāma honti, tā attano vasaṃ gate mahāvināsaṃ pāpenti, na tāsaṃ vasaṃ nāma gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ovaditvā aparabhāge brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. Having reached maturity and attained mastery in all arts, he went forth as a sage and, dwelling in the forest, sustained himself on forest roots and fruits. Once, a doe ate grass mixed with semen in the place where the sage had urinated and drank the water. Through this alone, she conceived with her mind bound to him; from then on, she went nowhere else but grazed on grass right there and wandered near the hermitage. The Great Being, upon investigating, understood the cause. Later, she gave birth to a human child. The Great Being cared for the child with paternal love and named him Isisiṅga. When the boy reached the age of understanding, the Great Being ordained him. In his old age, taking Isisiṅga with him, he went to a forest of woman-vines called Nārivana and advised him: 'Dear son, in this Himālaya region, there are women who resemble these flowers. They bring great ruin to those who come under their sway; one should not come under their sway.' Afterward, the Great Being was destined for the Brahma world.

Isisiṅgopi jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto himavantappadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Ghoratapo paramadhitindriyo ahosi. Athassa sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi, sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ maṃ sakkattā cāveyya, ekaṃ accharaṃ pesetvā sīlamassa bhindāpessāmī”ti sakaladevalokaṃ upaparikkhanto attano aḍḍhateyyakoṭisaṅkhānaṃ paricārikānaṃ majjhe ekaṃ alambusaṃ nāma accharaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ tassa sīlaṃ bhindituṃ samatthaṃ adisvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa sīlabhedaṃ kātuṃ āṇāpesi. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0153] āvikaronto satthā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Isisiṅga also dwelt in the Himālaya region, delighting in the sport of jhāna. He practiced severe austerities and possessed supreme steadfastness of the faculties. Then, through the power of his virtue, the abode of Sakka trembled. Sakka, reflecting on the cause, understood it and thought, 'This sage might dislodge me from my position as Sakka; I shall send a celestial nymph to destroy his virtue.' Searching through the entire world of devas among his twenty-five million attendants, he found a celestial nymph named Alambusā. Seeing no other capable of breaking the sage's virtue, he summoned her and commanded her to break his virtue. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the first verse:

95.

95.

“Athabravi brahā indo, vatrabhū jayataṃ pitā;

Devakaññaṃ parābhetvā, sudhammāyaṃ alambusa”nti.

95. Then spoke the great Indra, the slayer of Vatra, the father of the victors, having selected the celestial maiden Alambusā in the Sudhammā hall.

Tattha brahāti mahā. Vatrabhūti vatrassa nāma asurassa abhibhavitā. Jayataṃ pitāti jayantānaṃ jayappattānaṃ sesānaṃ tettiṃsāya devaputtānaṃ pitukiccasādhanena pitā. Parābhetvāti hadayaṃ bhinditvā olokento viya taṃ “paṭibalā aya”nti ñatvāti attho. Sudhammāyanti sudhammāyaṃ devasabhāyaṃ.

95. In that verse, ‘brahā’ means great. ‘Vatrabhū’ means the conqueror of the Asura named Vatra. ‘Jayataṃ pitā’ means the father of the victors, as he performs the duties of a father for the other thirty-three gods who have attained victory. ‘Parābhetvā’ means as if looking after having pierced her heart, that is, knowing, ‘She is capable.’ ‘Sudhammāyaṃ’ means in the Sudhammā hall of the gods.

Paṇḍukambalasilāsane nisinno taṃ alambusaṃ pakkosāpetvā idamāha –

Seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, he summoned Alambusā and said this:

96.

96.

“Misse [V 5.0147] devā taṃ yācanti, tāvatiṃsā saindakā;

Isippalobhane gaccha, isisiṅgaṃ alambuse”ti.

96. O lady, the gods entreat you—the Tāvatiṃsa with their Indra: Go, Alambusā, to entice the sage Isisiṅga.

Tattha [M 5.0163] misseti taṃ ālapati, idañca tassā nāmaṃ, sabbā panitthiyo purise kilesamissanena missanato “missā”ti vuccanti, tena sādhāraṇena guṇanāmenālapanto evamāha. Isippalobhaneti isīnaṃ palobhanasamatthe. Isisiṅganti tassa kira matthake migasiṅgākārena dve cūḷā uṭṭhahiṃsu, tasmā evaṃ vuccati.

In this context, 'misse' is how he addresses her, and this is also her name. However, all women are called 'missā' because they mingle with men through the mingling of defilements. Thus, addressing her by this common attribute-name, he speaks in this way. 'Isippalobhane' means 'O you who are capable of enticing sages.' 'Isisiṅga' is so called, it is said, because two top-knots in the shape of a deer's horn arose on his head; therefore he is called thus.

Iti sakko “gaccha isisiṅgaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano vasaṃ ānetvā sīlamassa bhindā”ti alambusaṃ āṇāpesi.

Thus Sakka commanded Alambusā: "Go, approach Isisiṅga, bring him under your power, and break his virtue."

97.

97.

“Purāyaṃ amhe acceti, vattavā brahmacariyavā;

Nibbānābhirato vuddho, tassa maggāni āvarā”ti. – vacanaṃ āha;

He spoke this verse: 'Before this one surpasses us, accomplished in observances and the holy life, mature, delighting in Nibbāna—block his paths.'

Tattha purāyanti ayaṃ tāpaso vattasampanno ca brahmacariyavā ca, so panesa dīghāyukatāya nibbānasaṅkhāte magge abhirato guṇavuddhiyā ca vuddho. Tasmā yāva esa amhe nātikkamati, na abhibhavitvā imamhā ṭhānā cāveti, tāvadeva tvaṃ gantvā tassa devalokagamanāni maggāni āvara, yathā idha nāgacchati, evaṃ karohīti attho.

In this context, 'purāyaṃ' means: this ascetic is accomplished in observances and the holy life. Moreover, because of his long life, he delights in the path to the celestial realm called Nibbāna and is mature through the increase of his virtues. Therefore, 'before he surpasses us, before he overcomes us and dislodges us from this position, you must go at once and block his paths to the deva world, so that he does not come here'—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā alambusā gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, Alambusā spoke two verses:

98.

98.

“Devarāja kimeva tvaṃ, mameva tuvaṃ sikkhasi;

Isippalobhane gaccha, santi aññāpi accharā.

"O King of Devas, why do you single me out? You say, 'Go to entice the sage,' yet there are other celestial nymphs."

99.

99.

“Mādisiyo pavarā ceva, asoke nandane vane;

Tāsampi hotu pariyāyo, tāpi yantu palobhanā”ti.

"There are those like me and even superior ones in the sorrowless Nandana grove; let it be their turn also, let them also go to entice him."

Tattha [P 5.0154] kimeva tvanti kiṃ nāmetaṃ tvaṃ karosīti dīpeti. Mameva tuvaṃ sikkhasīti imasmiṃ sakaladevaloke mameva tuvaṃ ikkhasi, aññaṃ na passasīti adhippāyena vadati. Sa-kāro panettha byañjanasandhikaro. Isippalobhane gacchāti kiṃkāraṇā maññeva evaṃ vadesīti adhippāyo[V 5.0148]. Pavarā cevāti mayā uttaritarā ceva. Asoketi sokarahite. Nandaneti nandijanake. Pariyāyoti gamanavāro.

In this context, 'kimeva tvaṃ' indicates: 'What is this you are doing?' 'Mameva tuvaṃ sikkhasī' means she speaks with the intention: 'In this entire deva world, you see only me and do not see another.' The 's-' here is a euphonic consonant for conjunction. 'Isippalobhane gaccha' has the intention: 'For what reason do you speak thus to me alone?' 'Pavarā cevāti' means 'those even more excellent than me.' 'Asoke' means 'in the sorrow-free.' 'Nandane' means 'in the joy-producing.' 'Pariyāyo' means 'a turn to go.'

Tato [M 5.0164] sakko tisso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then Sakka spoke three verses:

100.

100.

“Addhā hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, santi aññāpi accharā;

Tādisiyo pavarā ceva, asoke nandane vane.

"Indeed, you speak the truth; there are other celestial nymphs, those like you and even superior ones, in the sorrowless Nandana grove."

101.

101.

“Na tā evaṃ pajānanti, pāricariyaṃ pumaṃ gatā;

Yādisaṃ tvaṃ pajānāsi, nāri sabbaṅgasobhane.

"But they do not understand the art of serving a man, having approached him, as you do, O woman, beautiful in every limb."

102.

102.

“Tvameva gaccha kalyāṇi, itthīnaṃ pavarā casi;

Taveva vaṇṇarūpena, savasamānayissasī”ti.

"Go yourself, O lovely one, you are the best of women; with your beauty and form, you will bring him completely under your power."

Tattha pumaṃ gatāti purisaṃ upasaṅkamantā samānā purisapalobhinipāricariyaṃ na jānanti. Vaṇṇarūpenāti sarīravaṇṇena ceva rūpasampattiyā ca. Savasamānayissasīti taṃ tāpasaṃ attano vasaṃ ānessasīti.

In this context, 'pumaṃ gatā' means: approaching a man, they do not know the service that entices a man. 'Vaṇṇarūpena' means with bodily complexion and with perfection of form. 'Savasamānayissasī' means you will bring that ascetic under your power.

Taṃ sutvā alambusā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, Alambusā spoke two verses:

103.

103.

“Na vāhaṃ na gamissāmi, devarājena pesitā;

Vibhemi cetaṃ āsāduṃ, uggatejo hi brāhmaṇo.

"It is not that I will not go, being sent by the King of Devas; but I fear to approach him, for the brahmin is of fierce energy."

104.

104.

“Aneke nirayaṃ pattā, isimāsādiyā janā;

Āpannā mohasaṃsāraṃ, tasmā lomāni haṃsaye”ti.

"Many people, having offended a sage, have fallen into hell; they have entered the cycle of delusion; therefore my hair stands on end."

Tattha na vāhanti na ve ahaṃ. Vibhemīti bhāyāmi. Āsādunti āsādituṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nāhaṃ, deva, tayā pesitā na gamissāmi, apicāhaṃ taṃ isiṃ sīlabhedanatthāya allīyituṃ bhāyāmi, uggatejo hi soti. Āsādiyāti āsādetvā. Mohasaṃsāranti mohena saṃsāraṃ, mohena isiṃ palobhetvā saṃsāraṃ āpannā vaṭṭadukkhe patiṭṭhitā sattā gaṇanapathaṃ atikkantā[V 5.0149]. Tasmāti tena kāraṇena. Lomāni haṃsayeti ahaṃ lomāni uṭṭhapemi, “tassa kirāhaṃ sīlaṃ bhindissāmī”ti cintayamānāya me lomāni pahaṃsantīti vadati.

Herein, 'na vāhaṃ' means 'na ve ahaṃ' (it is not that I). 'Vibhemi' means 'I am afraid.' 'Āsāduṃ' means 'to seduce' or 'to approach.' This is what is said: 'It is not, O deva, that I will not go, having been sent by you; but I fear to approach that sage for the purpose of breaking his virtue, for he is of fierce energy.' 'Āsādiyā' means 'having seduced.' 'Mohasaṃsāraṃ' means transmigration due to delusion; beings who, having seduced a sage through delusion, have entered transmigration and are established in the suffering of the cycle, are beyond reckoning. 'Tasmā' means 'for that reason.' 'Lomāni haṃsaye' means 'I cause my hairs to stand on end'; she says: 'As I think, "Am I really to break his virtue?" my hairs bristle.'

105.

105.

“Idaṃ vatvāna pakkāmi, accharā kāmavaṇṇinī;

Missā missitumicchantī, isisiṅgaṃ alambusā.

Having said this, the nymph of desirable beauty departed; Alambusā, called Missā, desiring to mingle, went towards Isisiṅga.

106.

106.

“Sā [P 5.0155][M 5.0165] ca taṃ vanamogayha, isisiṅgena rakkhitaṃ;

Bimbijālakasañchannaṃ, samantā addhayojanaṃ.

And she, having entered that forest protected by Isisiṅga, which was covered with a thicket of red sprouts and extended for half a yojana all around,

107.

107.

“Pātova pātarāsamhi, udaṇhasamayaṃ pati;

Aggiṭṭhaṃ parimajjantaṃ, isisiṅgaṃ upāgamī”ti. – imā abhisambuddhagāthā;

Early in the morning, at the time of the morning meal, around sunrise, she approached Isisiṅga as he was sweeping the fire-hall. — These are verses of perfect enlightenment.

Tattha pakkāmīti tena hi, devarāja, āvajjeyyāsi manti attano sayanagabbhaṃ pavisitvā alaṅkaritvā isisiṅgaṃ kilesena missituṃ icchantī pakkāmi, bhikkhave, sā accharā tassa assamaṃ gatāti. Bimbijālakasañchannanti rattaṅkuravanena sañchannaṃ. Pātova pātarāsamhīti, bhikkhave, pātarāsavelāya pātova pageyeva atipageva. Udaṇhasamayaṃ patīti sūriyuggamanavelāyameva. Aggiṭṭhanti aggisālaṃ. Rattiṃ padhānamanuyuñjitvā pātova nhatvā udakakiccaṃ katvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ thokaṃ jhānasukhena vītināmetvā nikkhamitvā aggisālaṃ sammajjantaṃ taṃ isisiṅgaṃ sā upāgami, itthivilāsaṃ dassentī tassa purato aṭṭhāsi.

Here, 'pakkāmī' means: 'Then, O king of devas, you should consider me.' Having entered her own bedchamber and adorned herself, desiring to mingle with Isisiṅga through defilement, she departed. 'She departed, bhikkhus,' means that nymph went to his hermitage. 'Bimbijālakasañchannanti' means 'covered with a forest of red sprouts.' 'Pātova pātarāsamhi' means, 'bhikkhus, at breakfast time, very early, exceedingly early.' 'Udaṇhasamayaṃ pati' means 'at the very time of sunrise.' 'Aggiṭṭhaṃ' means 'the fire hall.' Having spent the night devoted to exertion, having bathed early in the morning and performed her water duties, and having spent a little time in the joy of meditation in the leaf hut, she came out and approached Isisiṅga as he was sweeping the fire hall; displaying her feminine charms, she stood before him.

Atha naṃ tāpaso pucchanto āha –

Then the ascetic, questioning her, said:

108.

108.

“Kā nu vijjurivābhāsi, osadhī viya tārakā;

Vicittahatthābharaṇā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā.

“Who are you, shining like lightning, like the morning star? Adorned with various hand ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings.

109.

109.

“Ādiccavaṇṇasaṅkāsā, hemacandanagandhinī;

Saññatūrū mahāmāyā, kumārī cārudassanā.

“Radiant as the sun, fragrant with gold and sandalwood, with shapely thighs, full of guile, a maiden fair to behold.

110.

110.

“Vilaggā mudukā suddhā, pādā te suppatiṭṭhitā;

Gamanā kāmanīyā te, harantiyeva me mano.

“Slender-waisted, soft, and pure, your feet are well-set; your gait is desirable, it truly steals away my mind.

111.

111.

“Anupubbā [V 5.0150] ca te ūrū, nāganāsasamūpamā;

Vimaṭṭhā tuyhaṃ sussoṇī, akkhassa phalakaṃ yathā.

“Your thighs are tapering, resembling an elephant's trunk; your lovely hips are smooth, like a gaming board.

112.

112.

“Uppalasseva kiñjakkhā, nābhi te sādhusaṇṭhitā;

Purā kaṇhañjanasseva, dūrato patidissati.

“Like the filaments of a blue lotus, your navel is perfectly formed; from afar, it appears deep and dark like black collyrium.

113.

113.

“Duvidhā [M 5.0166] jātā urajā, avaṇṭā sādhupaccudā;

Payodharā apatitā, aḍḍhalābusamā thanā.

“Born in two parts on the chest, stalkless and well-prominent are your breasts; firm and not fallen, your breasts are like half a golden gourd.

114.

114.

“Dīghā kambutalābhāsā, gīvā eṇeyyakā yathā;

Paṇḍarāvaraṇā vaggu, catutthamanasannibhā.

“Long and lustrous like a golden conch shell, your neck is like a gazelle’s; lovely are your lips, red like the tongue.

115.

115.

“Uddhaggā [P 5.0156] ca adhaggā ca, dumaggaparimajjitā;

Duvijā nelasambhūtā, dantā tava sudassanā.

“Your upper and lower teeth, polished with a tooth-stick, are twice-born, sprung from a faultless place, and beautiful to see.

116.

116.

“Apaṇḍarā lohitantā, jiñjūkaphalasannibhā;

Āyatā ca visālā ca, nettā tava sudassanā.

“Not pale, with reddish corners, like crab’s eye seeds; long and wide, your eyes are very beautiful to see.

117.

117.

“Nātidīghā susammaṭṭhā, kanakabyāsamocitā;

Uttamaṅgaruhā tuyhaṃ, kesā candanagandhikā.

“Not too long and well-combed, anointed with scented oil from a golden bowl, the hair on your head is fragrant with sandalwood.

118.

118.

“Yāvatā kasigorakkhā, vāṇijānañca yā gati;

Isīnañca parakkantaṃ, saññatānaṃ tapassinaṃ.

“Whatever the pursuits of farmers and herdsmen, or whatever is the way of merchants, or the striving of sages, of the restrained ascetics—

119.

119.

“Na te samasamaṃ passe, asmiṃ pathavimaṇḍale;

Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“I see no one equal to you in all this earthly realm. Who are you? Whose son? How may we know you?”

Tattha vicittahatthābharaṇāti vicittehi hatthābharaṇehi samannāgatā. Hemacandanagandhinīti suvaṇṇavaṇṇacandanagandhavilepanā. Saññatūrūti suvaṭṭitaghanaūru sampannaūrulakkhaṇā. Vilaggāti saṃkhittamajjhā. Mudukāti mudu sukhumālā. Suddhāti nimmalā. Suppatiṭṭhitāti samaṃ pathaviṃ phusantā [V 5.0151] suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitā. Gamanāti gacchamānā. Kāmanīyāti kantā kāmitabbayuttakā. Harantiyeva me manoti ete evarūpena paramena itthivilāsena caṅkamantiyā tava pādā mama cittaṃ harantiyeva. Vimaṭṭhāti visālā. Sussoṇīti sundarasoṇī. Akkhassāti sundaravaṇṇassa akkhassa suvaṇṇaphalakaṃ viya visālā te soṇīti vadati. Uppalasseva kiñjakkhāti nīluppalakaṇṇikā viya. Kaṇhañjanassevāti sukhumakaṇhalomacittattā evamāha.

Here, 'vicittahatthābharaṇā' (adorned with various hand ornaments) means 'she is endowed with diverse hand ornaments.' 'Hemacandanagandhinī' (fragrant with gold and sandalwood) means 'she has the color of gold and uses sandalwood-scented ointments.' 'Saññatūrū' (with shapely thighs) means 'her thighs are well-shaped, thick, and possess the auspicious marks of good thighs.' 'Vilaggā' (slender-waisted) means 'having a constricted waist.' 'Mudukā' (soft) means 'soft, delicate, and refined.' 'Suddhā' (pure) means 'immaculate.' 'Suppatiṭṭhitā' (well-set) means 'her feet touch the ground evenly and are firmly set.' 'Gamanā' (as she walks) means 'while walking.' 'Kāmanīyā' (desirable) means 'beautiful and worthy of being desired.' 'Harantiyeva me mano' (it truly steals away my mind) means 'as you walk with such supreme feminine charm, your feet indeed steal my mind.' 'Vimaṭṭhā' (smooth) means 'spacious.' 'Sussoṇī' (lovely hips) means 'beautiful hips.' 'Akkhassa' (of the axle) means 'he says: your hips are broad like a golden plate of a beautiful-colored axle.' 'Uppalasseva kiñjakkhā' (like the filaments of a blue lotus) means 'like the pericarp of a blue lotus.' 'Kaṇhañjanasseva' (like dark eye-ointment) means 'he speaks thus because of the fine black body hair that adorns her.'

“Duvidhā”tigāthaṃ thane vaṇṇayanto āha. Te hi dve hutvā ure jātā vaṇṭassa abhāvā avaṇṭā, ure laggā eva hutvā suṭṭhu nikkhantattā [M 5.0167] sādhupaccudā, payassa dhāraṇato payodharā, apatitāti na patitā, amilātatāya vā alambanatāya vā na anto paviṭṭhāti apatitā, suvaṇṇaphalake ṭhapitasuvaṇṇamayavaṭṭaalābuno aḍḍhena sadisatāya aḍḍhalābusamā thanā. Eṇeyyakā yathāti eṇīmigassa hi dīghā ca vaṭṭā ca gīvā sobhati yathā, evaṃ tava gīvā thokaṃ dīghā. Kambutalābhāsāti suvaṇṇāliṅgatalasannibhā gīvāti attho. Paṇḍarāvaraṇāti dantāvaraṇā. Catutthamanasannibhāti catutthamano vuccati catutthamanavatthubhūtā jivhā. Abhirattabhāvena jivhāsadisaṃ te oṭṭhapariyosānanti vadati. Uddhaggāti heṭṭhimadantā. Adhaggāti uparimadantā. Dumaggaparimajjitāti [P 5.0157] dantakaṭṭhaparimajjitā parisuddhā. Duvijāti dvijā. Nelasambhūtāti niddosesu hanumaṃsapariyosānesu sambhūtā.

Regarding the verse beginning 'Duvidhā,' he spoke, describing the breasts. Being born on the chest as two, they are 'avaṇṭā' (stemless) due to the absence of stems. Being well-protruding as if attached to the chest, they are 'sādhupaccudā' (well-prominent). They are 'payodharā' (milk-bearers) because they hold milk. 'Apatitā' (not fallen) means they do not fall; either because they are not withered or because they do not hang down, they have not sunk inward. The breasts are 'aḍḍhalābusamā' (like half a gourd) because they resemble half of a round golden gourd placed on a golden plate. 'Eṇeyyakā yathā' (like a doe’s) means: just as the neck of a female deer is long, round, and beautiful, so too is your neck slightly long. 'Kambutalābhāsā' means the neck resembles the surface of a golden conch. 'Paṇḍarāvaraṇā' means 'covering for the teeth,' that is, the lips. 'Catutthamanasannibhā' means resembling the fourth mind-object; the fourth mind-object is said to be the tongue, which is the basis for the fourth mind-object. He says that the ends of your lips resemble the tongue due to their deep redness. 'Uddhaggā' means the lower teeth. 'Adhaggā' means the upper teeth. 'Dumaggaparimajjitā' means cleaned with a tooth-stick, perfectly pure. 'Duvijā' means twice-born. 'Nelasambhūtā' means born from the flawless ends of the jaw-flesh.

Apaṇḍarāti kaṇhā. Lohitantāti rattapariyantā. Jiñjūkaphalasannibhāti rattaṭṭhāne jiñjukaphalasadisā. Sudassanāti passantānaṃ atittikarā pañcapasādasamannāgatā. Nātidīghāti pamāṇayuttā. Susammaṭṭhāti suṭṭhu sammaṭṭhā. Kanakabyāsamocitāti kanakabyā vuccati suvaṇṇaphaṇikā, tāya gandhatelaṃ ādāya paharitā suracitā. Kasigorakkhāti iminā kasiñca gorakkhañca nissāya jīvanakasatte dasseti. Yā gatīti yattakā nipphatti. Parakkantanti yattakaṃ isīnaṃ parakkantaṃ, vitthārīkatā imasmiṃ himavante yattakā isayo vasantīti attho. Na te samasamanti tesu sabbesu ekampi rūpalīḷāvilāsādisamatāya tayā samānaṃ na passāmi. Ko vā tvanti idaṃ tassā itthibhāvaṃ jānanto purisavohāravasena pucchati.

'Apaṇḍarā' means dark, not pale. 'Lohitantā' means red at the edges. 'Jiñjūkaphalasannibhā' means resembling the jiñjuka fruit in the red parts. 'Sudassanā' means insatiably pleasing to those who see, endowed with the five kinds of grace. 'Nātidīghā' means of proper measure, not too long. 'Susammaṭṭhā' means very well smoothed. 'Kanakabyāsamocitā' means adorned with a golden comb; 'kanakabyā' is a golden comb; having taken fragrant oil with it, the hair is stroked and well-arranged. 'Kasigorakkhā' means by this, he indicates beings who live dependent on farming and cattle-herding. 'Yā gati' means whatever accomplishment. 'Parakkantaṃ' means as much as the sages have striven; the meaning is, as many sages as dwell spread throughout this Himalaya. 'Na te samasamaṃ' means among all of them, I do not see even one equal to you in beauty, grace, charm, and so forth. 'Ko vā tvaṃ' means knowing her female nature, he asks this using masculine terms.

Evaṃ pādato paṭṭhāya yāva kesā attano vaṇṇaṃ bhāsante tāpase alambusā tuṇhī hutvā tassā kathāya yathānusandhiṃ gatāya tassa sammūḷhabhāvaṃ ñatvā gāthamāha –

While the ascetic was thus describing her beauty from her feet to her hair, Alambusā remained silent. When his speech had reached its conclusion, knowing his bewildered state, she spoke this verse:

120.

120.

“Na [V 5.0152] pañhakālo bhaddante, kassapevaṃ gate sati;

Ehi samma ramissāma, ubho asmākamassame;

Ehi taṃ upagūhissaṃ, ratīnaṃ kusalo bhavā”ti.

“This is not the time for questions, good sir, when Kassapa's mind has gone thus. Come, friend, let us enjoy ourselves, both of us, in our hermitage. Come, I will embrace you; be skilled in sensual delights.”

Tattha [M 5.0168] kassapevaṃ gate satīti kassapagotta evaṃ tava citte pavatte sati pañhakālo na hoti. Sammāti vayassa, piyavacanālapanametaṃ. Ratīnanti pañcakāmaguṇaratīnaṃ.

Here, 'kassapevaṃ gate sati' means: “O Kassapa of the Kassapa clan, when your mind is thus engaged, it is not the time for questions.” 'Samma' means “friend;” it is an affectionate address. 'Ratīnaṃ' refers to the delights of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Evaṃ vatvā alambusā cintesi – “nāyaṃ mayi ṭhitāya hatthapāsaṃ āgamissati, gacchantī viya bhavissāmī”ti. Sā itthimāyākusalatāya tāpasaṃ anupasaṅkamitvā āgatamaggābhimukhī pāyāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, Alambusā thought: “He will not come within arm’s reach if I remain standing; I must appear as if I am leaving.” Skilled in feminine wiles, she did not approach the ascetic but walked away, facing the path by which she had come. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

121.

121.

“Idaṃ vatvāna pakkāmi, accharā kāmavaṇṇinī;

Missā missitumicchantī, isisiṅgaṃ alambusā”ti.

“Having said this, the celestial nymph of lovely form, Alambusā, departed, wishing to unite with Isisiṅga.”

Atha [P 5.0158] naṃ tāpaso gacchantiṃ disvā “ayaṃ gacchatī”ti attano dandhaparakkamaṃ mandagamanaṃ chinditvā vegena dhāvitvā kesesu hatthena parāmasi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then, seeing her walking away, the ascetic, thinking, “She is leaving!”, abandoning his slow exertion and slow gait, ran swiftly and grasped her hair with his hand. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

122.

122.

“So ca vegena nikkhamma, chetvā dandhaparakkamaṃ;

Tamuttamāsu veṇīsu, ajjhappatto parāmasi.

“He rushed out swiftly, abandoning his slow exertion; reaching her excellent braids, he grasped them.

123.

123.

“Tamudāvatta kalyāṇī, palissaji susobhanā;

Cavitamhi brahmacariyā, yathā taṃ atha tositā.

“That beautiful woman, fair to look upon, turned back and embraced him. When he had fallen from the holy life, the King of Devas was then satisfied.”

124.

124.

“Manasā agamā indaṃ, vasantaṃ nandane vane;

Tassā saṅkappamaññāya, maghavā devakuñjaro.

“With her mind she called to Indra, dwelling in the Nandana Grove. Knowing her intention, Maghavā, the chief of gods,”

125.

125.

“Pallaṅkaṃ pahiṇī khippaṃ, sovaṇṇaṃ sopavāhanaṃ;

Sauttaracchadapaññāsaṃ, sahassapaṭiyatthataṃ.

“Quickly he sent a golden couch, with its attendants, overspread with fifty canopies, covered with a thousand cloths.”

126.

126.

“Tamenaṃ [V 5.0153] tattha dhāresi, ure katvāna sobhanā;

Yathā ekamuhuttaṃva, tīṇi vassāni dhārayi.

“There she held him, the beautiful one, placing him on her breast; as if for a single moment, she supported him for three years.”

127.

127.

“Vimado tīhi vassehi, pabujjhitvāna brāhmaṇo;

Addasāsi haritarukkhe, samantā aggiyāyanaṃ.

“Sobered from intoxication after three years, the brahmin awoke and saw green trees all around the fire-hall.”

128.

128.

“Navapattavanaṃ phullaṃ, kokilaggaṇaghositaṃ;

Samantā paviloketvā, rudaṃ assūni vattayi.

“Beholding the newly leaved forest in bloom all around, resounding with the cries of flocks of cuckoos, he wept and let flow his tears.”

129.

129.

“Na [M 5.0169] juhe na jape mante, aggihuttaṃ pahāpitaṃ;

Ko nu me pāricariyāya, pubbe cittaṃ palobhayi.

“I did not offer sacrifices, nor did I recite the mantras; the fire sacrifice was abandoned. Who was it that formerly enticed my mind with service?”

130.

130.

“Araññe me viharato, yo me tejā ha sambhutaṃ;

Nānāratanaparipūraṃ, nāvaṃva gaṇhi aṇṇave”ti.

“While I lived in the forest, who has brought to ruin the power born of my asceticism, like a ship filled with various jewels in the midst of the ocean?”

Tattha ajjhappattoti sampatto. Tamudāvatta kalyāṇīti taṃ kese parāmasitvā ṭhitaṃ isiṃ udāvattitvā nivattitvā kalyāṇadassanā sā suṭṭhu sobhanā. Palissajīti āliṅgi. Cavitamhi brahmacariyā, yathā taṃ atha tositāti, bhikkhave, tassa isino tāvadeva jhānaṃ antaradhāyi. Tasmiṃ tamhā jhānā brahmacariyā cavite yathā taṃ sakkena patthitaṃ, tatheva ahosi. Atha sakkassa patthanāya samiddhabhāvaṃ viditvā sā devakaññā tositā, tassa tena brahmacariyavināsena sañjanitapītipāmojjāti attho.

Here, “ajjhappatto” means reached. “Tamudāvatta kalyāṇī” means that after the seer had grasped her hair and stood there, she of beautiful appearance, having turned back and returned, was very beautiful. “Palissaji” means she embraced him. “Cavitamhi brahmacariyā, yathā taṃ atha tositā” means, monks, at that very moment, that ascetic’s meditation disappeared. When he had fallen from that meditation, from the holy life, it happened just as Sakka had wished. Then, knowing the success of Sakka’s wish, that heavenly maiden was delighted; the meaning is that she felt joy and delight generated by the destruction of his holy life.

Manasā agamāti sā taṃ āliṅgitvā ṭhitā “aho vata sakko pallaṅkaṃ me peseyyā”ti evaṃ pavattena manasā indaṃ agamā. Nandane vaneti nandijananasamatthatāya nandanavanasaṅkhāte tāvatiṃsabhavane vasantaṃ. Devakuñjaroti devaseṭṭho[P 5.0159]. Pahiṇīti pesesi. “Pāhiṇī”tipi pāṭho. Sopavāhananti saparivāraṃ. Sauttaracchadapaññāsanti paññāsāya uttaracchadehi paṭicchāditaṃ. Sahassapaṭiyatthatanti sahassadibbakojavatthataṃ. Tamenaṃ tatthāti taṃ isisiṅgaṃ tattha dibbapallaṅke nisinnā sā ure katvā dhāresi. Tīṇi vassānīti ekamuhuttaṃ viya manussagaṇanāya tīṇi vassāni taṃ ure nipajjāpetvā tattha nisinnā dhāresi.

“Manasā agamā” means she, having embraced him and stood there, went to Indra with a thought that arose thus: “Oh, if only Sakka would send me a couch!” “In the Nandana grove” means dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa abode, known as the Nandanavana because it is capable of generating joy. “Devakuñjaro” means the chief of gods. “Pahiṇī” means sent. “Pāhiṇī” is also a reading. “Sopavāhanaṃ” means with its paraphernalia. “Sauttaracchadapaññāsaṃ” means covered by fifty upper coverings. “Sahassapaṭiyatthatanti” means covered with a thousand divine cloths. “Tamenaṃ tattha” means she, seated on that divine couch, held that Isisiṅga on her breast. “Tīṇi vassāni” means she held him there, having made him lie on her breast, for three years by human reckoning, as if for a single moment.

Vimadoti [V 5.0154] nimmado vigatasaññabhāvo. So hi tīṇi saṃvaccharāni visañño sayitvā pacchā paṭiladdhasañño pabujjhi. Tasmiṃ pabujjhamāne hatthādiphandanaṃ disvāva alambusā tassa pabujjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā pallaṅkaṃ antaradhāpetvā sayampi antarahitā aṭṭhāsi. Addasāsīti so assamapadaṃ olokento “kena nu khomhi sīlavināsaṃ pāpito”ti cintetvā mahantena saddena paridevamāno addasāsi. Haritarukkheti aggiyāyanasaṅkhātaṃ aggisālaṃ samantā parivāretvā ṭhite haritapattarukkhe. Navapattavananti taruṇehi navapattehi sañchannaṃ vanaṃ. Rudanti paridevanto.

“Vimado” means free from intoxication, devoid of consciousness. For he, having slept without consciousness for three years, later regained consciousness and awoke. At the moment of his awakening, seeing the movement of his hands and so forth, Alambusā, recognizing his awakened state, made the couch disappear and herself stood there, having vanished. “Addasāsi” means he, looking around the hermitage, thought, “By whom have I been led to the destruction of virtue?” and, lamenting with a loud cry, he saw. “Haritarukkhe” refers to the green-leaved trees standing all around, encircling the fire-hall known as Aggiyāyana. “Navapattavanaṃ” means a forest covered with young, fresh leaves. “Rudaṃ” means lamenting.

Na [M 5.0170] juhe na jape manteti ayamassa paridevanagāthā. Pahāpitanti hāpitaṃ, pa-kāro upasaggamattaṃ. Pāricariyāyāti ko nu kilesapāricariyāya ito pubbe mama cittaṃ palobhayīti paridevati. Yo me tejā ha sambhutanti ha-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Yo mama samaṇatejena sambhūtaṃ jhānaguṇaṃ nānāratanaparipuṇṇaṃ mahantaṃ mahaṇṇave nāvaṃ viya gaṇhi, vināsaṃ pāpesi, ko nāmesoti paridevatīti.

“Na juhe na jape mante”—this is his verse of lamentation. “Pahāpitaṃ” means “hāpitaṃ”; the syllable “pa-” is merely a prefix. “Pāricariyāya” means he laments thus: “Who indeed enticed my mind before for the service of defilements?” “Yo me tejā ha sambhutaṃ”—the particle “ha” is merely an expletive. He laments thus: “Who is it that seized and brought to ruin the quality of jhāna that arose from my ascetic power—a quality filled with various jewels, like a great ship on the vast ocean? Who could it be?”

Taṃ sutvā alambusā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ na kathessāmi, ayaṃ me abhisapissati, handassa kathessāmī”ti. Sā dissamānena kāyena ṭhatvā gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Alambusā thought: ‘If I do not speak, this seer will curse me. Very well, I shall speak to him.’ Standing there in visible form, she spoke this verse:

131.

131.

“Ahaṃ te pāricariyāya, devarājena pesitā;

Avadhiṃ cittaṃ cittena, pamādo tvaṃ na bujjhasī”ti.

“I was sent by the king of the gods to serve you. I subdued your mind with my mind; in your heedlessness, you did not realize it.”

So tassā kathaṃ sutvā pitarā dinnaovādaṃ saritvā “pitu vacanaṃ akatvā mahāvināsaṃ pattomhī”ti paridevanto catasso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Hearing her words, and recalling the advice given by his father, he lamented, ‘By not following my father's words, I have met with great ruin,’ and spoke these four verses:

132.

132.

“Imāni kira maṃ tāto, kassapo anusāsati;

Kamalāsadisitthiyo, tāyo bujjhesi māṇava.

“Indeed, my father Kassapa once instructed me with these words: ‘There are women like flower-creepers; be wary of them, young man!’”

133.

133.

“Uregaṇḍāyo bujjhesi, tāyo bujjhesi māṇava;

Iccānusāsi maṃ tāto, yathā maṃ anukampako.

“‘Be wary of those with protuberances on the chest; be wary of them, young man!’ Thus did my compassionate father instruct me.”

134.

134.

“Tassāhaṃ [P 5.0160] vacanaṃ nākaṃ, pitu vuddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Araññe nimmanussamhi, svajja jhāyāmi ekako.

“I did not follow his words, the instruction of my wise and aged father. Today, in the wilderness devoid of people, I lament alone.”

135.

135.

“Sohaṃ [V 5.0155] tathā karissāmi, dhiratthu jīvitena me;

Puna vā tādiso hessaṃ, maraṇaṃ me bhavissatī”ti.

“I shall act accordingly—shame on this life of mine! Either I shall become like that again, or death will be mine.”

Tattha imānīti imāni vacanāni. Kamalāsadisitthiyoti kamalā vuccati nāripupphalatā, tāsaṃ pupphasadisā itthiyo. Tāyo bujjhesi māṇavāti māṇava tvaṃ tāyo jāneyyāsi, ñatvā dassanapathaṃ agantvā palāpeyyāsīti yāni evarūpāni vacanāni tadā maṃ tāto anusāsati, imāni kira tānīti. Uregaṇḍāyoti uramhi dvīhi gaṇḍehi samannāgatā. Tāyo bujjhesi, māṇavāti, māṇava, tāyo attano [M 5.0171] vasaṃ gate vināsaṃ pāpentīti tvaṃ jāneyyāsi. Nākanti nākariṃ. Jhāyāmīti pajjhāyāmi paridevāmi. Dhiratthu jīvitena meti dhiratthu garahitaṃ mama jīvitaṃ, jīvitena me ko attho. Puna vāti tathā karissāmi, yathā puna vā tādiso bhavissāmi, naṭṭhaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā vītarāgo bhavissāmi, maraṇaṃ vā me bhavissatīti.

In this context, ‘these’ refers to these words. Regarding ‘women like lotuses’: ‘Kamalā’ refers to a flower-creeper, and the women are like its flowers. Regarding ‘be wary of them, young man’: ‘Young man, you should recognize them, and having known them, you should flee without coming into their sight.’ Such were the words with which my father then instructed me, saying, ‘Indeed, these are they.’ Regarding ‘with protuberances on the chest’: it means endowed with two protuberances on the chest. Regarding ‘be wary of them, young man’: ‘Young man, you should know that these lead to ruin those who fall under their power.’ Regarding ‘I did not do’: I did not follow. Regarding ‘I lament’: I pine and lament. Regarding ‘Shame on this life of mine!’: my life is contemptible; what is the use of my life? Regarding ‘Or again’: I shall act in such a way that either I shall become like that again—having regained the lost jhāna, I shall be free from lust—or death will be mine.

So kāmarāgaṃ pahāya puna jhānaṃ uppādesi. Athassa samaṇatejaṃ disvā jhānassa ca uppāditabhāvaṃ ñatvā alambusā bhītā khamāpesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dve gāthāyo abhāsi –

Having abandoned sensual desire, he again generated jhāna. Then, seeing his ascetic power and knowing that jhāna had been produced, Alambusā, being afraid, asked for his forgiveness. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:

136.

136.

“Tassa tejaṃ vīriyañca, dhitiṃ ñatvā avaṭṭhitaṃ;

Sirasā aggahī pāde, isisiṅgaṃ alambusā.

“Knowing his power, energy, and unwavering resolve, Alambusā touched the feet of Isisiṅga with her head.”

137.

137.

“Mā me kujjha mahāvīra, mā me kujjha mahāise;

Mahā attho mayā ciṇṇo, tidasānaṃ yasassinaṃ;

Tayā pakampitaṃ āsi, sabbaṃ devapuraṃ tadā”ti.

“Do not be angry with me, O great hero; do not be angry with me, O great seer. A great purpose was served by me for the glorious Thirty gods; the entire city of the gods then trembled because of you.”

Atha naṃ so “khamāmi te, bhadde, yathāsukhaṃ gacchā”ti vissajjento gāthamāha –

Then, dismissing her by saying, ‘I forgive you, good lady, go as you please,’ he spoke this verse:

138.

138.

“Tāvatiṃsā ca ye devā, tidasānañca vāsavo;

Tvañca bhadde sukhī hohi, gaccha kaññe yathāsukha”nti.

“May the gods of Tāvatiṃsa and Vāsava, the lord of the Thirty, be happy. And may you too, good lady, be happy. Go, maiden, as you please.”

Sā taṃ vanditvā teneva suvaṇṇapallaṅkena devapuraṃ gatā. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0161] pakāsento satthā tisso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Having paid homage to him, she went to the city of the gods on that very golden couch. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke three verses:

139.

139.

“Tassa [V 5.0156] pāde gahetvāna, katvā ca naṃ padakkhiṇaṃ;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, tamhā ṭhānā apakkami.

“Having grasped his feet and circumambulated him, and having raised her hands in reverence, she departed from that place.”

140.

140.

“Yo ca tassāsi pallaṅko, sovaṇṇo sopavāhano;

Sauttaracchadapaññāso, sahassapaṭiyatthato;

Tameva pallaṅkamāruyha, agā devāna santike.

“That very couch of hers, golden and with a support, with fifty upper coverings and spread with a thousand rugs; mounting that very couch, she went into the presence of the gods.”

141.

141.

“Tamokkamiva āyantiṃ, jalantiṃ vijjutaṃ yathā;

Patīto sumano vitto, devindo adadā vara”nti.

“As she approached like a lamp, or like flashing lightning, the lord of gods, pleased, happy, and satisfied, granted her a boon.”

Tattha [M 5.0172] okkamivāti dīpakaṃ viya. “Patīto”tiādīhi tuṭṭhākārova dassito adadā varanti āgantvā vanditvā ṭhitāya tuṭṭho varaṃ adāsi.

In this context, ‘okkamiva’ means like a lamp. By ‘pleased’ and so forth, the appearance of satisfaction is shown. ‘He granted a boon’ means that, being pleased with her as she came, paid homage, and stood there, he granted her a boon.

Sā tassa santike varaṃ gaṇhantī osānagāthamāha –

As she received the boon in his presence, she spoke this concluding verse:

142.

142.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Nisippalobhikā gacche, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare”ti.

“If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, sovereign lord of all beings: may I never go to entice an ascetic again—this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.”

Tassattho – “sakka devarāja, sace me tvaṃ varaṃ ado, puna isipalobhikāya na gaccheyyaṃ, mā maṃ etadatthāya pahiṇeyyāsi, etaṃ varaṃ vare yācāmī”ti.

The meaning is: ‘Sakka, king of gods, if you grant me a boon, may I not go again to entice ascetics. Do not send me for this purpose—this is the boon I ask for.’

Satthā tassa bhikkhuno imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā alambusā purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, isisiṅgo ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, pitā mahāisi pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma teaching to that monk, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, Alambusā was the former wife, Isisiṅga was the discontented monk, and the great seer, his father, was I myself.

Alambusājātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Alambusā Jātaka is finished.

[524] 4. Saṅkhapālajātakavaṇṇanā

[524] 4. 4. The Saṅkhapāla Jātaka

Ariyāvakāsosīti [V 5.0157] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathakammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā uposathike upāsake sampahaṃsetvā “porāṇakapaṇḍitā mahatiṃ nāgasampattiṃ pahāya uposathavāsaṃ upavasiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Ariyāvakāsosi...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Uposatha observance. At that time, having greatly gladdened the lay devotees observing the Uposatha, the Teacher said, “The wise of old, having abandoned great nāga prosperity, indeed undertook the Uposatha observance,” and at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte rājagahe magadharājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, “duyyodhano”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā āgantvā pitu sippaṃ dassesi. Atha naṃ pitā rajje abhisiñcitvā isipabbajjaṃ [P 5.0162] pabbajitvā uyyāne vasi. Bodhisatto divasassa tikkhattuṃ pitu santikaṃ agamāsi. Tassa mahālābhasakkāro udapādi. So teneva palibodhena kasiṇaparikammamattampi kātuṃ asakkonto cintesi – “mahā me [M 5.0173] lābhasakkāro, na sakkā mayā idha vasantena imaṃ jaṭaṃ chindituṃ, puttassa me anārocetvāva aññattha gamissāmī”ti. So kañci ajānāpetvā uyyānā nikkhamitvā magadharaṭṭhaṃ atikkamitvā mahisakaraṭṭhe saṅkhapāladahato nāma nikkhantāya kaṇṇaveṇṇāya nadiyā nivattane candakapabbataṃ upanissāya paṇṇasālaṃ katvā tattha vasanto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā uñchācariyāya yāpesi. Tamenaṃ saṅkhapālo nāma nāgarājā mahantena parivārena kaṇṇaveṇṇanadito nikkhamitvā antarantarā upasaṅkamati. So tassa dhammaṃ desesi. Athassa putto pitaraṃ daṭṭhukāmo gataṭṭhānaṃ ajānanto anuvicārāpetvā “asukaṭṭhāne nāma vasatī”ti ñatvā tassa dassanatthāya mahantena parivārena tattha gantvā ekamante khandhavāraṃ nivāsetvā katipayehi amaccehi saddhiṃ assamapadābhimukho pāyāsi.

In the past, in Rājagaha, a king of Magadha ruled. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen, and they named him Duyyodhana. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and, upon returning, demonstrated his skills to his father. Then, his father anointed him as king and, having gone forth into the ascetic’s life, dwelled in a park. The Bodhisatta visited his father three times a day. Great gain and honor arose for him. Burdened by this very impediment, he found himself unable to perform even the preliminary work for kasiṇa meditation. He thought, “Great is my gain and honor. It is not possible for me, while living here, to sever this entanglement. Without informing my son, I will go elsewhere.” Without letting anyone know, he left the park, passed through the Magadha kingdom, and in the Mahisaka kingdom, near Mount Candaka, at a bend of the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River which flows from Lake Saṅkhapāla, he built a leaf-hut. Dwelling there, he performed the preliminary work for kasiṇa meditation, developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and sustained himself by gleaning. A nāga king named Saṅkhapāla, emerging from the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River with a large retinue, would visit him from time to time. He taught him the Dhamma. Then his son, wishing to see his father but not knowing where he had gone, had inquiries made and learned, “He dwells in such-and-such a place.” Desiring to see him, he went there with a large retinue, established his camp at a distance, and proceeded toward the hermitage accompanied by a few ministers.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe saṅkhapālo mahantena parivārena dhammaṃ suṇanto nisīdi. So taṃ rājānaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā isiṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Rājā pitaraṃ vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā nisīditvā pucchi – “bhante, katararājā nāmesa tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgato”ti. Tāta, saṅkhapālanāgarājā nāmesoti. So tassa sampattiṃ nissāya nāgabhavane lobhaṃ katvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā pitu bhikkhāhāraṃ nibaddhaṃ dāpetvā attano nagarameva gantvā catūsu dvāresu dānasālāyo kāretvā sakalajambudīpaṃ saṅkhobhento dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā nāgabhavanaṃ patthetvā āyupariyosāne nāgabhavane nibbattitvā saṅkhapālanāgarājā ahosi[P 5.0163]. So gacchante kāle tāya sampattiyā vippaṭisārī hutvā tato paṭṭhāya manussayoniṃ patthento [V 5.0158] uposathavāsaṃ vasi. Athassa nāgabhavane vasantassa uposathavāso na sampajjati, sīlavināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. So tato paṭṭhāya nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā kaṇṇaveṇṇāya nadiyā avidūre mahāmaggassa ca ekapadikamaggassa ca antare ekaṃ vammikaṃ parikkhipitvā uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya samādinnasīlo “mama cammamaṃsādīhi atthikā cammamaṃsādīni harantū”ti attānaṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā vammikamatthake nipanno samaṇadhammaṃ karonto cātuddase pannarase vasitvā pāṭipade nāgabhavanaṃ gacchati.

At that moment, Saṅkhapāla, with a large retinue, sat listening to the Dhamma. Seeing the king approaching, he paid homage to the sage, rose from his seat, and departed. The king, having paid respects to his father and exchanged greetings, sat down and asked, “Venerable sir, what king was it that came to you?” “My son, it was the Nāga king named Saṅkhapāla.” Inspired by that one's prosperity, the king conceived a desire for the nāga realm. After staying for a few days and arranging for his father’s alms-food to be regularly given, he returned to his own city. There, he established alms halls at the four gates and, stirring up the whole of Jambudīpa, gave alms, maintained his virtue, observed the Uposatha, and aspired for the nāga realm. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the nāga realm and became the Nāga king Saṅkhapāla. As time went on, he felt remorse over that prosperity and from then on, aspiring for a human birth, he observed the Uposatha. But while dwelling in the nāga realm, his Uposatha observance was not successful, and his virtue would be broken. Therefore, leaving the nāga realm, he went to a place near the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River, between a great highway and a footpath, and coiled himself around an anthill. Having undertaken the Uposatha precepts, he offered himself as a gift, declaring, “Let those who need my skin, flesh, and so on, take them.” Lying atop the anthill and practicing the ascetic’s duty, he would dwell there on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the fortnight, and on the first day of the next, he would return to the nāga realm.

Tasmiṃ [M 5.0174] ekadivasaṃ evaṃ sīlaṃ samādiyitvā nipanne paccantagāmavāsino soḷasa janā “maṃsaṃ āharissāmā”ti āvudhahatthā araññe vicarantā kiñci alabhitvā nikkhantā taṃ vammikamatthake nipannaṃ disvā “mayaṃ ajja godhāpotakampi na labhimhā, imaṃ nāgarājānaṃ vadhitvā khādissāmā”ti cintetvā “mahā kho panesa gayhamāno palāyeyya, yathānipannameva taṃ bhogesu sūlehi vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā gaṇhissāmā”ti sūlāni ādāya upasaṅkamiṃsu. Bodhisattassa sarīraṃ mahantaṃ ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitasumanapupphadāmaṃ viya jiñjukaphalasannibhehi akkhīhi jayasumanapupphasadisena ca sīsena samannāgataṃ ativiya sobhati. So tesaṃ soḷasannaṃ janānaṃ padasaddena bhogantarato sīsaṃ nīharitvā rattakkhīni ummīletvā te sūlahatthe āgacchante disvā cintesi – “ajja mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissati, ahaṃ attānaṃ dānamukhe niyyādetvā vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nipanno, ime mama sarīraṃ sattīhi koṭṭetvā chiddāvachiddaṃ karonte kodhavasena akkhīni ummīletvā na olokessāmī”ti attano sīlabhedabhayena daḷhaṃ adhiṭṭhāya [P 5.0164] sīsaṃ bhogantareyeva pavesetvā nipajji. Atha naṃ te upagantvā naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā kaḍḍhantā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā tikhiṇasūlehi aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vijjhitvā sakaṇṭakakāḷavettayaṭṭhiyo pahāramukhehi pavesetvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kājenādāya mahāmaggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu, mahāsatto sūlehi vijjhanato paṭṭhāya ekaṭṭhānepi kodhavasena akkhīni ummīletvā te na olokesi. Tassa aṭṭhahi kājehi ādāya nīyamānassa sīsaṃ olambetvā bhūmiyaṃ pahari. Atha naṃ “sīsamassa olambatī”ti mahāmagge nipajjāpetvā taruṇasūlena nāsāpuṭaṃ vijjhitvā rajjukaṃ pavesetvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā kājakoṭiyaṃ laggitvā punapi ukkhipitvā maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu.

On that day, while he was lying down, having undertaken such a precept, sixteen villagers from the border region, armed with weapons, wandered through the forest, thinking, 'We will bring back meat.' Finding nothing, they were about to leave when they spotted him lying on top of the anthill. They thought, 'Today, we could not even get a young monitor lizard. Let us kill this naga king and eat him.' Then they thought, 'But if this great one is seized, he might escape. Therefore, while he is lying exactly as he is, we will pierce him with stakes in his coils, weaken him, and then take him.' So, taking their stakes, they approached. The Bodhisatta's body was massive, the size of a single-log boat, and was exceedingly beautiful, like a garland of jasmine flowers laid out in a coil. With eyes resembling jiñjuka fruits and a head like a red hibiscus flower, he was extremely radiant. Hearing the footsteps of those sixteen men, he drew his head out from within his coils and opened his red eyes. Seeing them approaching with stakes in hand, he thought, 'Today, my heart's desire will reach its goal. I have surrendered myself at the door of generosity and am lying here, having made a firm resolve. Even if they pierce my body with spears and make it full of holes, I will not open my eyes in anger to look at them.' Fearing that his virtue might be broken, he made a firm resolve, tucked his head back into his coils, and lay still. Then they approached him, seized him by the tail, dragged him, and struck him against the ground. They pierced him in eight places with sharp stakes and inserted thorny black rattan sticks through the wounds. Carrying him at eight places with poles, they set out along the high road. From the moment the stakes pierced him, the Great Being did not open his eyes in anger to look at them even once. As he was being carried by eight poles, his head hung down and struck the ground. Then, saying, 'The naga's head is hanging,' they laid him down on the high road, pierced his nostril with a fresh stake, threaded a small rope through, and lifting his head, tied it to the end of the pole. Then, lifting him up again, they proceeded along the high road.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe videharaṭṭhe mithilanagaravāsī āḷāro nāma kuṭumbiko pañca sakaṭasatāni ādāya sukhayānake nisīditvā gacchanto te bhojaputte bodhisattaṃ tathā gaṇhitvā gacchante disvā tesaṃ soḷasannampi soḷasahi vāhagoṇehi saddhiṃ pasataṃ pasataṃ suvaṇṇamāsake sabbesaṃ nivāsanapārupanāni [V 5.0159] bhariyānampi nesaṃ vatthābharaṇāni datvā vissajjāpesi. Atha so nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā tattha papañcaṃ akatvā mahantena [M 5.0175] parivārena nikkhamitvā āḷāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nāgabhavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā taṃ ādāya nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā tīhi nāgakaññāsatehi saddhiṃ mahantamassa yasaṃ datvā dibbehi kāmehi santappesi. Āḷāro nāgabhavane ekavassaṃ vasitvā dibbakāme paribhuñjitvā “icchāmahaṃ, samma, pabbajitu”nti nāgarājassa kathetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre gahetvā nāgabhavanato himavantappadesaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā tattha ciraṃ vasitvā aparabhāge cārikaṃ caranto bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bhikkhāya nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ bārāṇasirājā disvā iriyāpathe pasīditvā pakkosāpetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhojetvā [P 5.0165] aññatarasmiṃ nīce āsane nisinno vanditvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, a householder named Alara from the city of Mithila in the Videha country, taking five hundred carts and seated in a comfortable carriage, was traveling along. Seeing those hunters carrying the Bodhisatta in such a manner, he gave each of those sixteen hunters a handful of gold coins along with sixteen draft oxen. He also gave all the hunters garments for themselves and ornaments and clothes for their wives, and thus had him released. The Sankhapala Naga King went to the naga realm, but without staying long, he came out with a large retinue and approached the merchant Alara. After speaking of the virtues of the naga realm, he took the merchant Alara there. In the naga realm, he gave the merchant great wealth along with three hundred naga maidens and satisfied him with divine sensual pleasures. Alara lived in the naga realm for a year, enjoying divine pleasures. He said to the naga king, 'Friend naga king, I wish to go forth as a monk.' Taking the requisites of an ascetic, he left the naga realm for the Himalayan region and went forth as an ascetic. After living there for a long time, while wandering later on tour, he arrived at the city of Varanasi and stayed in the royal park. In the morning, he entered the city for alms and went to the gate of the king's palace. Then the King of Varanasi, seeing the ascetic Alara and being pleased with his deportment, had him summoned, seated on a prepared seat, and served him food of various excellent flavors. Sitting on a lower seat and paying homage, the king, wishing to converse with and question the ascetic Alara, spoke the first verse:

143.

143.

“Ariyāvakāsosi pasannanetto, maññe bhavaṃ pabbajito kulamhā;

Kathaṃ nu vittāni pahāya bhoge, pabbaji nikkhamma gharā sapaññā”ti.

“You have a noble appearance and serene eyes; I think, sir, you have gone forth from a high family. How is it that you, a wise man, have abandoned wealth and enjoyments and gone forth from home?”

Tattha ariyāvakāsosīti niddosasundarasarīrāvakāsosi, abhirūposīti attho. Pasannanettoti pañcahi pasādehi yuttanetto. Kulamhāti khattiyakulā vā brāhmaṇakulā vā seṭṭhikulā vā pabbajitosīti maññāmi. Kathaṃ nūti kena kāraṇena kiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā dhanañca upabhoge ca pahāya gharā nikkhamitvā pabbajitosi sapañña paṇḍitapurisāti pucchati.

In this verse, 'ariyāvakāsosi' means you have a faultless and beautiful bodily appearance, meaning you are handsome. 'Pasannanetto' means having eyes endowed with the five kinds of clarity. 'Kulamhā' means I think you have gone forth from a noble family, whether a kshatriya family, a brahmin family, or a treasurer's family. 'Kathaṃ nu'—for what reason or basis did you leave home and go forth, O wise and learned man?—thus he asks.

Tato paraṃ tāpasassa ca rañño ca vacanappaṭivacanavasena gāthānaṃ sambandho veditabbo –

Thereafter, the connection of the verses should be understood by way of the dialogue between the ascetic and the king:

144.

144.

“Sayaṃ vimānaṃ naradeva disvā, mahānubhāvassa mahoragassa;

Disvāna puññāna mahāvipākaṃ, saddhāyahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja.
