“Having myself seen the palace, O king of men, of the great and powerful serpent, and having seen the great result of merit, I have gone forth with faith, O king.”

145.

145.

“Na [M 5.0176] kāmakāmā na bhayā na dosā, vācaṃ musā pabbajitā bhaṇanti;

Akkhāhi me pucchito etamatthaṃ, sutvāna me jāyihitippasādo.

“Not out of desire for sensual pleasures, nor out of fear or hatred, do renunciates speak falsehood. Explain this matter to me when asked; upon hearing it, confidence will arise in me.”

146.

146.

“Vāṇijja raṭṭhādhipa gacchamāno, pathe addasāsimhi bhojaputte;

Pavaḍḍhakāyaṃ uragaṃ mahantaṃ, ādāya gacchante pamodamāne.

“O lord of the realm, while I was traveling for trade, I saw hunters on the road; they were carrying a great serpent of mighty body, rejoicing as they went.”

147.

147.

“Sohaṃ [V 5.0160] samāgamma janinda tehi, pahaṭṭhalomo avacamhi bhīto;

Kuhiṃ ayaṃ nīyati bhīmakāyo, nāgena kiṃ kāhatha bhojaputtā.

“Approaching them, O lord of men, with hair standing on end and filled with fear, I asked: ‘Where is this one of fearsome body being taken? O hunters, what will you do with this naga?’”

148.

148.

“Nāgo [P 5.0166] ayaṃ nīyati bhojanatthā, pavaḍḍhakāyo urago mahanto;

Sāduñca thūlañca muduñca maṃsaṃ, na tvaṃ rasaññāsi videhaputta.

“‘This naga is being taken for food, a great serpent of mighty body; its flesh is sweet, fat, and tender—you, son of Videha, do not know its taste.’”

149.

149.

“Ito mayaṃ gantvā sakaṃ niketaṃ, ādāya satthāni vikopayitvā;

Maṃsāni bhokkhāma pamodamānā, mayañhi ve sattavo pannagānaṃ.

“Having gone from here to our own home, taking weapons and cutting it up, we will eat the flesh, rejoicing; for indeed, we are enemies of serpents.”

150.

150.

“Sace ayaṃ nīyati bhojanatthā, pavaḍḍhakāyo urago mahanto;

Dadāmi vo balibaddāni soḷasa, nāgaṃ imaṃ muñcatha bandhanasmā.

“If this great serpent with a fully grown body is being taken for food, I will give you sixteen oxen—release this serpent from its bonds!”

151.

151.

“Addhā hi no bhakkho ayaṃ manāpo, bahū ca no uragā bhuttapubbā;

Karoma te taṃ vacanaṃ aḷāra, mittañca no hohi videhaputta.

“Truly, this is a pleasing meal for us, and many serpents have we eaten before; we will do as you say, O Āḷāra, and be a friend to us, son of Videha.”

152.

152.

“Tadāssu [M 5.0177] te bandhanā mocayiṃsu, yaṃ natthuto paṭimokkassa pāse;

Mutto ca so bandhanā nāgarājā, pakkāmi pācīnamukho muhuttaṃ.

“Then they released him from the bonds, and from the noose that was fastened through his nostrils. Freed from his bonds, the Nāga king went facing eastward for a moment.”

153.

153.

“Gantvāna pācīnamukho muhuttaṃ, puṇṇehi nettehi palokayī maṃ;

Tadāssahaṃ piṭṭhito anvagacchiṃ, dasaṅguliṃ añjaliṃ paggahetvā.

“Having gone eastward for a moment, he looked back at me with eyes full of tears. Then I followed behind, holding up my clasped hands in reverence.”

154.

154.

“Gaccheva kho tvaṃ taramānarūpo, mā taṃ amittā punaraggahesuṃ;

Dukkho hi luddehi punā samāgamo, adassanaṃ bhojaputtāna gaccha.

“Go quickly, in a hurrying manner; let not enemies seize you again. Reunion with the cruel is surely painful; go where you are unseen by the hunters.”

155.

155.

“Agamāsi so rahadaṃ vippasannaṃ, nīlobhāsaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ sutitthaṃ;

Samotataṃ [P 5.0167] jambuhi vetasāhi, pāvekkhi nittiṇṇabhayo patīto.

“He went to the lake with clear water, blue-shining, delightful, and with good fords; covered with rose-apple and rattan trees, he entered, free from fear and delighted.”

156.

156.

“So taṃ pavissa nacirassa nāgo, dibbena me pāturahū janinda;

Upaṭṭhahī maṃ pitaraṃva putto, hadayaṅgamaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhaṇanto.

“Not long after entering there, that Nāga appeared before me in divine form, O lord of men; he attended me like a son attending his father, speaking words pleasing to the heart and delightful to the ear.”

157.

157.

“Tvaṃ [V 5.0161] mesi mātā ca pitā aḷāra, abbhantaro pāṇadado sahāyo;

Sakañca iddhiṃ paṭilābhakosmi, aḷāra passa me nivesanāni;

Pahūtabhakkhaṃ bahuannapānaṃ, masakkasāraṃ viya vāsavassā”ti.

“You are my mother and father, O Āḷāra, my intimate life-giving friend and companion. I have regained my power; O Āḷāra, behold my dwellings! Abundant in food and drink, like Masakkasāra for Vāsava.”

Tattha vimānanti saṅkhapālanāgarañño anekasatanāṭakasampattisampannaṃ kañcanamaṇivimānaṃ. Puññānanti tena katapuññānaṃ mahantaṃ vipākaṃ disvā kammañca [M 5.0178] phalañca paralokañca saddahitvā pavattāya saddhāya ahaṃ pabbajito. Na kāmakāmāti na vatthukāmenapi bhayenapi dosenapi musā bhaṇanti. Jāyihitīti, bhante, tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā mayhampi pasādo somanassaṃ jāyissati. Vāṇijjanti vāṇijjakammaṃ karissāmīti gacchanto. Pathe addasāsimhīti pañcannaṃ sakaṭasatānaṃ purato sukhayānake nisīditvā gacchanto mahāmagge janapadamanusse addasaṃ. Pavaḍḍhakāyanti vaḍḍhitakāyaṃ. Ādāyāti aṭṭhahi kājehi gahetvā. Avacamhīti abhāsiṃ. Bhīmakāyoti bhayajanakakāyo. Bhojaputtāti luddaputtake piyasamudācārenālapati. Videhaputtāti videharaṭṭhavāsitāya āḷāraṃ ālapiṃsu. Vikopayitvāti chinditvā. Mayañhi vo sattavoti mayaṃ pana nāgānaṃ verino nāma. Bhojanatthāti bhojanatthāya. Mittañca no hohīti tvaṃ amhākaṃ mitto hohi, kataguṇaṃ jāna.

Herein, 'vimāna' refers to the golden and jeweled palace of King Saṅkhapāla, endowed with the riches of many hundreds of theatrical performances. 'Puññāni' means: having seen the great result of the wholesome deeds he had done, and having faith in kamma, its fruit, and the other world, I went forth inspired by that faith. 'Na kāmakāmā' means they do not speak falsely out of desire for sensual pleasures, nor out of fear, nor out of hatred. 'Jāyihiti' means: 'Venerable sir, upon hearing your words, confidence and joy will arise in me as well.' 'Vāṇijja' means: going with the thought, 'I will engage in trade.' 'Pathe addasāsimhi' means: while traveling ahead of five hundred carts, seated in a comfortable vehicle, I saw people of the countryside on the great road. 'Pavaḍḍhakāya' means a body grown large. 'Ādāya' means taking with eight carrying poles. 'Avacamhi' means I spoke. 'Bhīmakāya' means a body that inspires terror. 'Bhojaputtā' means he addresses the sons of the hunter with an affectionate term. 'Videhaputtā' means they addressed Āḷāra thus because he was a resident of the Videha country. 'Vikopayitvā' means having cut. 'Mayañhi vo sattavo' means we are indeed enemies of the nāgas. 'Bhojanatthā' means for the sake of food. 'Mittañca no hohi' means: 'Be our friend, and recognize the good that has been done.'

Tadāssu teti, mahārāja, tehi bhojaputtehi evaṃ vutte ahaṃ tesaṃ soḷasa vāhagoṇe nivāsanapārupanāni pasataṃ pasataṃ suvaṇṇamāsake bhariyānañca nesaṃ vatthālaṅkāraṃ adāsiṃ, atha te saṅkhapālanāgarājānaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā attano kakkhaḷatāya sakaṇṭakakāḷavettalatāya koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Athāhaṃ nāgarājānaṃ kilamantaṃ disvā akilamentova asinā tā latā chinditvā dārakānaṃ kaṇṇavedhato vaṭṭinīharaṇaniyāmena adukkhāpento saṇikaṃ nīhariṃ, tasmiṃ kāle te bhojaputtā yaṃ bandhanaṃ assa natthuto pavesetvā pāse paṭimokkaṃ, tasmā bandhanā taṃ [P 5.0168] uragaṃ mocayiṃsu. Tassa nāsato saha pāsena taṃ rajjukaṃ nīhariṃsūti dīpeti. Iti te uragaṃ vissajjetvā thokaṃ gantvā “ayaṃ urago dubbalo, matakāle naṃ gahetvā gamissāmā”ti nilīyiṃsu.

Then, O great king, when those sons of hunters spoke thus, I gave them sixteen draft oxen, inner and outer robes, a handful of gold coins each, and clothes and ornaments for their wives. Then, having made King Saṅkhapāla lie down on the ground, they began to drag him, holding him by the tip of a rough, thorny, black rattan creeper. Seeing the nāga king distressed, I, without tiring, cut those creepers with a sword and gently pulled him out, as one removes a thread from a pierced ear without causing pain. At that time, the sons of the hunters had inserted a cord through his nostril and fastened a noose, and from that bond they released the serpent. It is explained that they pulled out the rope along with the noose from his nose. Thus, having released the serpent, they went a short distance and hid, thinking, 'This serpent is weak; we will take him when he is about to die.'

Puṇṇehīti sopi muhuttaṃ pācīnābhimukho gantvā assupuṇṇehi nettehi maṃ palokayi. Tadāssahanti tadā assa ahaṃ. Gacchevāti evaṃ taṃ avacanti vadati. Rahadanti kaṇṇaveṇṇadahaṃ. Samotatanti ubhayatīresu jamburukkhavetasarukkhehi otataṃ vitataṃ. Nittiṇṇabhayo patītoti so [M 5.0179] kira taṃ dahaṃ pavisanto āḷārassa nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā yāva naṅguṭṭhā otari, udake [V 5.0162] paviṭṭhaṭṭhānamevassa nibbhayaṃ ahosi, tasmā nittiṇṇabhayo patīto haṭṭhatuṭṭho pāvekkhīti. Pavissāti pavisitvā. Dibbena meti nāgabhavane pamādaṃ anāpajjitvā mayi kaṇṇaveṇṇatīraṃ anatikkanteyeva dibbena parivārena mama purato pāturahosi. Upaṭṭhahīti upāgami. Abbhantaroti hadayamaṃsasadiso. Tvaṃ mama bahupakāro, sakkāraṃ te karissāmi. Passa me nivesanānīti mama nāgabhavanaṃ passa. Masakkasāraṃ viyāti masakkasāro vuccati osakkanaparisakkanābhāvena ghanasāratāya ca sinerupabbatarājā. Ayaṃ tattha māpitaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ sandhāyevamāha.

Herein, 'Puṇṇehi' means: having gone a short distance facing east, he looked back at me with tear-filled eyes. 'Tadāssahaṃ' means 'then I to him.' 'Gaccheva' means he is saying, 'thus I spoke to him.' 'Rahada' refers to the Kaṇṇaveṇṇa lake. 'Samotata' means covered and spread on both shores by rose-apple and vetasa trees. 'Nittiṇṇabhayo patīto' means: it is said that as he entered that lake, having shown his respect to Āḷāra, he descended until his tail was submerged, and the very place where he entered the water became safe for him; therefore, 'his fear crossed, delighted,' he entered, joyful and glad. 'Pavissa' means having entered. 'Dibbena me' refers to his appearing before me with a divine retinue, without having become negligent in the nāga world, while I had not yet gone beyond the shore of the Kaṇṇaveṇṇa. 'Upaṭṭhahi' means he approached. 'Abbhantaro' means like the flesh of the heart. The quote 'You have been of great help to me; I will honor you. Behold my dwellings' means 'behold my nāga palace'. 'Masakkasāraṃ viya' means: Masakkasāra is said to be Sineru, the king of mountains, due to its solidity and immovability. He spoke thus referring to the Tāvatiṃsa palace built there.

Mahārāja! Evaṃ vatvā so nāgarājā uttari attano nāgabhavanaṃ vaṇṇento gāthādvayamāha –

“Great king! Having said this, that Nāga king further described his own Nāga palace in two verses:”

158.

158.

“Taṃ bhūmibhāgehi upetarūpaṃ, asakkharā ceva mudū subhā ca;

Nīcattiṇā apparajā ca bhūmi, pāsādikā yattha jahanti sokaṃ.

“That ground, endowed with pleasing features, is without gravel, soft, and beautiful; with short grass and little dust, delightful, where beings relinquish their sorrow.”

159.

159.

“Anāvakulā veḷuriyūpanīlā, catuddisaṃ ambavanaṃ surammaṃ;

Pakkā ca pesī ca phalā suphullā, niccotukā dhārayantī phalānī”ti.

“Undisturbed, with beryl-like dark blue water, a mango grove charming in all four directions; with fruits ripe, ripening, and young, fully blossomed, it constantly bears fruit in every season.”

Tattha asakkharāti yā tattha bhūmi pāsāṇasakkhararahitā mudu subhā kañcanarajatamaṇimayā sattaratanavālukākiṇṇā. Nīcattiṇāti indagopakapiṭṭhisadisavaṇṇehi nīcatiṇehi samannāgatā. Apparajāti paṃsurahitā. Yattha jahanti sokanti yattha paviṭṭhamattāva nissokā honti. Anāvakulāti [P 5.0169] na avakulā akhāṇumā upari ukkulavikulabhāvarahitā vā samasaṇṭhitā. Veḷuriyūpanīlāti veḷuriyena upanīlā, tasmiṃ nāgabhavane veḷuriyamayā pasannasalilā nīlobhāsā anekavaṇṇakamaluppalasañchannā pokkharaṇīti attho. Catuddisanti tassā pokkharaṇiyā catūsu disāsu. Pakkā cāti tasmiṃ ambavane ambarukkhā pakkaphalā ca [M 5.0180] aḍḍhapakkaphalā ca taruṇaphalā ca phullitāyevāti attho. Niccotukāti channampi utūnaṃ anurūpehi pupphaphalehi samannāgatāti.

Herein, 'asakkharā' means the ground there is free from stones and gravel, soft, beautiful, made of gold, silver, and jewels, strewn with the sand of the seven precious substances. 'Nīcattiṇā' means abounding with low grass the color of an indagopaka insect's back. 'Apparajā' means without dust. 'Yattha jahanti sokaṃ' means just by entering there, they become free from sorrow. 'Anāvakulā' means not uneven, without stumps, or free from being rough and irregular; it is evenly laid out. 'Veḷuriyūpanīlā' means dark blue like beryl; this refers to the ponds in that Nāga palace, which are made of beryl, have clear water, a blue glow, and are covered with lotuses and water lilies of many colors. 'Catuddisaṃ' means on all four sides of that pond. 'Pakkā ca' means in that mango grove, the mango trees have ripe fruits, half-ripe fruits, and young fruits, and are in blossom. 'Niccotukā' means endowed with flowers and fruits suitable for all six seasons.

160.

160.

Tesaṃ vanānaṃ naradeva majjhe, nivesanaṃ bhassarasannikāsaṃ;

Rajataggaḷaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ uḷāraṃ, obhāsatī vijjurivantalikkhe.

“Amidst those forests, O king of men, is a magnificent and golden dwelling of radiant appearance, with silver door-bolts, shining like lightning in the sky.”

161.

161.

“Maṇīmayā [V 5.0163] soṇṇamayā uḷārā, anekacittā satataṃ sunimmitā;

Paripūrā kaññāhi alaṅkatāhi, suvaṇṇakāyūradharāhi rāja.

“Made of gems and gold, magnificent, with varied designs, ever well-crafted; they are filled with adorned maidens wearing golden armlets, O king.”

162.

162.

“So saṅkhapālo taramānarūpo, pāsādamāruyha anomavaṇṇo;

Sahassathambhaṃ atulānubhāvaṃ, yatthassa bhariyā mahesī ahosi.

“Then Saṅkhapāla, moving swiftly and of noble complexion, ascended the palace of a thousand pillars and unparalleled grandeur, where his wife and chief queen dwelt.”

163.

163.

“Ekā ca nārī taramānarūpā, ādāya veḷuriyamayaṃ mahagghaṃ;

Subhaṃ maṇiṃ jātimantūpapannaṃ, acoditā āsanamabbhihāsi.

“And one woman, moving swiftly, unbidden brought a beautiful seat made of costly beryl and noble gems.”

164.

164.

“Tato maṃ urago hatthe gahetvā, nisīdayī pāmukhaāsanasmiṃ;

Idamāsanaṃ atra bhavaṃ nisīdatu, bhavañhi me aññataro garūnaṃ.

“Then the serpent took me by the hand and seated me on the principal seat, saying: ‘May the venerable one sit here on this seat, for you are one of those I revere.’”

165.

165.

“Aññā ca nārī taramānarūpā, ādāya vāriṃ upasaṅkamitvā;

Pādāni pakkhālayī me janinda, bhariyāva bhattū patino piyassa.

“Another woman, moving swiftly, approached with water and washed my feet, O lord of men, like a wife for her dear, beloved husband.”

166.

166.

“Aparā [P 5.0170][M 5.0181] ca nārī taramānarūpā, paggayha sovaṇṇamayāya pātiyā;

Anekasūpaṃ vividhaṃ viyañjanaṃ, upanāmayī bhatta manuññarūpaṃ.

“And yet another woman, moving swiftly, holding up a golden bowl, offered a pleasing meal with many soups and various dishes.”

167.

167.

“Turiyehi maṃ bhārata bhuttavantaṃ, upaṭṭhahuṃ bhattu mano viditvā;

Tatuttariṃ maṃ nipatī mahantaṃ, dibbehi kāmehi anappakehī”ti.

“After I had eaten, O Bhārata, they attended upon me with musical instruments, knowing their master's mind. And beyond that, I was served with a great abundance of divine pleasures.”

Tattha nivesananti pāsādo. Bhassarasannikāsanti pabhassaradassanaṃ. Rajataggaḷanti rajatadvārakavāṭaṃ. Maṇīmayāti evarūpā tattha kūṭāgārā ca gabbhā ca. Paripūrāti sampuṇṇā. So saṅkhapāloti, mahārāja, ahaṃ evaṃ tasmiṃ nāgabhavanaṃ vaṇṇente taṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosiṃ, atha maṃ tattha netvā so saṅkhapālo hatthe gahetvā taramāno veḷuriyathambhehi sahassathambhaṃ pāsādaṃ āruyha yasmiṃ ṭhāne assa mahesī ahosi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ netīti dīpeti. Ekā cāti mayi pāsādaṃ abhiruḷhe ekā itthī aññehi maṇīhi jātimahantehi upetaṃ subhaṃ veḷuriyāsanaṃ tena nāgarājena avuttāva. Abbhihāsīti abhihari, attharīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, 'nivesana' means the palace. 'Bhassarasannikāsa' means having a radiant appearance. 'Rajataggaḷa' means the silver door panels. 'Maṇīmayā' means the gabled chambers and inner chambers there were of such a kind. 'Paripūrā' means complete. 'So Saṅkhapālo' means: O great king, as he was describing that Nāga dwelling, I became desirous of seeing it. Then, taking me there, that Saṅkhapāla led me by the hand and, ascending swiftly, brought me to the thousand-pillared palace with its beryl pillars, to the place where his chief queen was—this he explains. 'Ekā ca' means: as I ascended the palace, one woman, unbidden by the Nāga king, brought forth a splendid beryl seat adorned with other precious gems of noble kind. 'Abbhāsi' means she brought it forth; that is to say, she laid it out.

Pāmukhaāsanasminti pamukhāsanasmiṃ, uttamāsane nisīdāpesīti attho. Garūnanti mātāpitūnaṃ [V 5.0164] me tvaṃ aññataroti evaṃ vatvā nisīdāpesi. Vividhaṃ viyañjananti vividhaṃ byañjanaṃ. Bhatta manuññarūpanti bhattaṃ manuññarūpaṃ. Bhāratāti rājānaṃ ālapati. Bhuttavantanti bhuttāviṃ katabhattakiccaṃ. Upaṭṭhahunti anekasatehi turiyehi gandhabbaṃ kurumānā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Bhattu mano viditvāti attano patino cittaṃ jānitvā. Tatuttarinti tato gandhabbakaraṇato uttariṃ. Maṃ nipatīti so nāgarājā maṃ upasaṅkami. Mahantaṃ dibbehīti mahantehi uḷārehi dibbehi kāmehi tehi ca anappakehi.

'Pāmukhaāsanasminti' means 'in the foremost seat,' that is, he had me seated in the highest seat. 'Garūnaṃ' means he had me sit, saying, 'You are like one of my parents.' 'Vividhaṃ viyañjanaṃ' means 'various side dishes.' 'Bhatta manuññarūpaṃ' means 'pleasing food.' 'Bhārata' means he addressed the king. 'Bhuttavantaṃ' means 'having eaten,' that is, having completed the meal duties. 'Upaṭṭhahuṃ' means they attended, performing music with hundreds of musical instruments. 'Bhattu mano viditvā' means 'knowing her husband's mind,' that is, understanding her own husband's thought. 'Tatuttariṃ' means 'beyond that,' that is, beyond that performance of music. 'Maṃ nipatī' means 'he approached me,' that is, that Nāga king approached me. 'Mahantaṃ dibbehi' means 'with great divine,' that is, with great, splendid, divine pleasures, and with not a few of them.

Evaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ca pana gāthamāha –

“And having thus approached, he then spoke this verse:”

168.

168.

“Bhariyā mametā tisatā aḷāra, sabbattamajjhā padumuttarābhā;

Aḷāra etāssu te kāmakārā, dadāmi te tā paricārayassū”ti.

“These three hundred wives of mine, O Āḷāra, with slender waists and radiant like the finest lotuses; O Āḷāra, they are yours to command. I give them to you; let them attend upon you.”

Tattha [M 5.0182] sabbattamajjhāti sabbā attamajjhā, pāṇinā gahitappamāṇamajjhāti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sumajjhā”ti pāṭho. Padumuttarābhāti [P 5.0171] padumavaṇṇauttarābhā, padumavaṇṇauttaracchaviyoti attho. Paricārayassūti tā attano pādaparicārikā karohīti vatvā tīhi itthisatehi saddhiṃ mahāsampattiṃ mayhaṃ adāsi.

“In this context, 'sabbattamajjhā' means 'all with waists that can be grasped by the hand.' In the commentary, however, the reading is 'sumajjhā' (well-waisted). 'Padumuttarābhā' means 'having a radiance like the finest lotuses.' 'Paricārayassu' means: having said, 'Make them your attendants,' he gave me great fortune along with three hundred women.”

So āha –

He said:

169.

169.

“Saṃvaccharaṃ dibbarasānubhutvā, tadāssuhaṃ uttarimajjhabhāsiṃ;

Nāgassidaṃ kinti kathañca laddhaṃ, kathajjhagamāsi vimānaseṭṭhaṃ.

“Having enjoyed divine pleasures for a year, I then spoke further: ‘How was this fortune of the Nāga gained? How did you attain this most excellent mansion?’”

170.

170.

“Adhiccaladdhaṃ pariṇāmajaṃ te, sayaṃkataṃ udāhu devehi dinnaṃ;

Pucchāmi taṃ nāgarājetamatthaṃ, kathajjhagamāsi vimānaseṭṭha”nti.

“‘Was this obtained by chance, or born of transformation, or self-made, or given by the gods? I ask you this, O Nāga king, how did you attain this most excellent mansion?’”

Tattha dibbarasānubhutvāti dibbe kāmaguṇarase anubhavitvā. Tadāssuhanti tadā assu ahaṃ. Nāgassidanti bhadramukhassa saṅkhapālanāgarājassa idaṃ sampattijātaṃ kinti kiṃ nāma kammaṃ katvā kathañca katvā laddhaṃ, kathametaṃ vimānaseṭṭhaṃ tvaṃ ajjhagamāsi, iti naṃ ahaṃ pucchiṃ. Adhiccaladdhanti ahetunā laddhaṃ. Pariṇāmajaṃ teti kenaci tava atthāya pariṇāmitattā pariṇāmato jātaṃ. Sayaṃkatanti kārake pakkosāpetvā ratanāni datvā kāritanti.

“In this context, 'dibbarasānubhutvā' means having experienced the divine pleasures of the senses. 'Tadāssuhaṃ' means 'then indeed I.' 'Nāgassidaṃ' means: 'This fortune of Saṅkhapāla, the king of Nāgas—by doing what deed and how was it obtained? How did you attain this excellent mansion?' Thus I asked him. 'Adhiccaladdhaṃ' means 'obtained without cause.' 'Pariṇāmajaṃ' means 'born of transformation' for your sake. 'Sayaṃkataṃ' means 'self-made,' having summoned workers and had it built.”

Tato [V 5.0165] parā dvinnampi vacanappaṭivacanagāthāva –

“Then followed these verses of speech and counter-speech between them:”

171.

171.

“Nādhiccaladdhaṃ na pariṇāmajaṃ me, na sayaṃkataṃ nāpi devehi dinnaṃ;

Sakehi kammehi apāpakehi, puññehi me laddhamidaṃ vimānaṃ.

“‘It was not obtained by chance, nor was it born of transformation for me, nor self-made, nor given by the gods. By my own blameless deeds and meritorious acts, this mansion was obtained by me.’”

172.

172.

“Kiṃ [M 5.0183] te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ, kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Akkhāhi me nāgarājetamatthaṃ, kathaṃ nu te laddhamidaṃ vimānaṃ.

“‘What was your observance, what was your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the fruit? Explain this matter to me, O Nāga king. How was this mansion obtained by you?’”

173.

173.

“Rājā ahosiṃ magadhānamissaro, duyyodhano nāma mahānubhāvo;

So [P 5.0172] ittaraṃ jīvitaṃ saṃviditvā, asassataṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ.

“I was once a king, lord of the Magadhans, Duyyodhana by name, of great power. Having well understood life to be brief, impermanent, and subject to change—”

174.

174.

“Annañca pānañca pasannacitto, sakkacca dānaṃ vipulaṃ adāsiṃ;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi, santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

“With a clear and confident mind, I respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink. My home was then like a public well; ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.”

175.

175.

“Mālañca gandhañca vilepanañca, padīpiyaṃ yānamupassayañca;

Acchādanaṃ sayanamathannapānaṃ, sakkacca dānāni adamha tattha.

“Garlands, perfumes, and ointments; lamps, vehicles, and lodgings; clothing, bedding, and also food and drink—we respectfully gave these gifts there.”

176.

176.

“Taṃ me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ, tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Teneva me laddhamidaṃ vimānaṃ, pahūtabhakkhaṃ bahuannapānaṃ;

Naccehi gītehi cupetarūpaṃ, ciraṭṭhitikaṃ na ca sassatāyaṃ.

“That was my religious observance, that my holy life; this is the fruit of that well-practiced virtue. By that I have obtained this celestial mansion, with abundant food and much to eat and drink, endowed with dance and song—long-lasting, yet not eternal.”

177.

177.

“Appānubhāvā taṃ mahānubhāvaṃ, tejassinaṃ hanti atejavanto;

Kimeva dāṭhāvudha kiṃ paṭicca, hatthattamāgacchi vanibbakānaṃ.

“Those of little power harm one of great power; the powerless strike one full of majesty. Why indeed, O you armed with fangs, on what account did you fall into the hands of hunters?”

178.

178.

“Bhayaṃ nu te anvagataṃ mahantaṃ, tejo nu te nānvagaṃ dantamūlaṃ;

Kimeva dāṭhāvudha kiṃ paṭicca, kilesamāpajji vanibbakānaṃ.

“Did a great fear come upon you, or did your venom not reach the root of your fangs? Why indeed, O you with fangs for weapons, on what account did you come to such affliction from those hunters?”

179.

179.

“Na [M 5.0184] me bhayaṃ anvagataṃ mahantaṃ, tejo na sakkā mama tehi hantuṃ;

Satañca dhammāni sukittitāni, samuddavelāva duraccayāni.

“No great fear came upon me, nor could they overcome my power. But the well-proclaimed laws of the virtuous are, like the ocean’s shore, not to be transgressed.”

180.

180.

“Cātuddasiṃ [V 5.0166] pañcadasiṃ aḷāra, uposathaṃ niccamupāvasāmi;

Athāgamuṃ soḷasa bhojaputtā, rajjuṃ gahetvāna daḷhañca pāsaṃ.

“On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, O Aḷāra, I always observe the Uposatha. Then there came sixteen hunters, taking a rope and a strong snare.”

181.

181.

“Bhetvāna [P 5.0173] nāsaṃ atikassa rajjuṃ, nayiṃsu maṃ samparigayha luddā;

Etādisaṃ dukkhamahaṃ titikkhaṃ, uposathaṃ appaṭikopayanto.

“Having pierced my nose and passed a rope through it, the hunters seized and led me away. Such suffering I endured, not letting my Uposatha observance be violated.”

182.

182.

“Ekāyane taṃ pathe addasaṃsu, balena vaṇṇena cupetarūpaṃ;

Siriyā paññāya ca bhāvitosi, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

“They saw you on that narrow path, endowed with strength and beauty, developed in glory and wisdom. What do you desire, O Nāga, that you practice such austerity?”

183.

183.

“Na puttahetū na dhanassa hetū, na āyuno cāpi aḷāra hetu;

Manussayoniṃ abhipatthayāno, tasmā parakkama tapo karomi.

“Not for the sake of sons, nor for the sake of wealth, nor even for the sake of long life, O Aḷāra; but desiring birth in the human realm, therefore I strive and practice austerity.”

184.

184.

“Tvaṃ lohitakkho vihatantaraṃso, alaṅkato kappitakesamassu;

Surosito lohitacandanena, gandhabbarājāva disā pabhāsasi.

“You, with red eyes and well-formed shoulders, adorned with trimmed hair and beard, well-anointed with red sandalwood, illuminate the directions like a king of the Gandharvas.”

185.

185.

“Deviddhipattosi mahānubhāvo, sabbehi kāmehi samaṅgibhūto;

Pucchāmi taṃ nāgarājetamatthaṃ, seyyo ito kena manussaloko.

“You have attained divine power, you are of great might, and you are endowed with all sensual pleasures. I ask you this matter, O king of Nāgas: In what way is the human world better than this?”

186.

186.

“Aḷāra [M 5.0185] nāññatra manussalokā, suddhīva saṃvijjati saṃyamo vā;

Ahañca laddhāna manussayoniṃ, kāhāmi jātimaraṇassa antaṃ.

“O Aḷāra, except in the human world, there is no purity of mind or self-restraint. If I obtain a human birth, I will make an end of birth and death.”

187.

187.

“Saṃvaccharo me vasato tavantike, annena pānena upaṭṭhitosmi;

Āmantayitvāna palemi nāga, cirappavuṭṭhosmi ahaṃ janinda.

“For a year I have lived in your presence and have been served with food and drink. Having taken my leave, I now depart, O Nāga, for I have been long away from the world of men, O lord of people.”

188.

188.

“Puttā ca dārā anujīvino ca, niccānusiṭṭhā upatiṭṭhathetaṃ;

Kaccinnu [P 5.0174] taṃ nābhisapittha koci, piyañhi me dassanaṃ tuyhaṃ aḷāra.

“May your sons, wife, and dependents, being constantly instructed, attend upon you. I hope no one has spoken ill of you. For seeing you is dear to me, O Aḷāra.”

189.

189.

“Yathāpi mātū ca pitū agāre, putto piyo paṭivihito vaseyya;

Tatopi mayhaṃ idhameva seyyo, cittañhi te nāga mayī pasannaṃ.

“Just as a beloved son, well cared for, might dwell in the house of his mother and father, even better than that is my stay here, for your heart, O Nāga, is kindly disposed towards me.”

190.

190.

“Maṇī [V 5.0167] mamaṃ vijjati lohitaṅko, dhanāharo maṇiratanaṃ uḷāraṃ;

Ādāya tvaṃ gaccha sakaṃ niketaṃ, laddhā dhanaṃ taṃ maṇimossajassū”ti.

“I have a gem, a ruby, a wealth-bringing and splendid jewel-treasure. Take it and go to your own home; having obtained wealth, you should then let the gem go.”

Tattha kiṃ te vatanti kiṃ tava vatasamādānaṃ. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Opānabhūtanti catumahāpathe khatapokkharaṇī viya dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjitabbavibhavaṃ. Na ca sassatāyanti ciraṭṭhitikaṃ samānampi ce taṃ mayhaṃ sassataṃ na hotīti me katheti.

Here, 'kiṃ te vataṃ' means 'what is your vow and commitment?' 'Brahmacariyaṃ' means 'the holy life,' that is, the best conduct. 'Opānabhūtaṃ' means 'like a drinking well,' that is, like a pond dug at a crossroads, a resource to be enjoyed at will by righteous ascetics and brahmins. 'Na ca sassatāyaṃ' means 'and it is not eternal,' that is, 'even if it lasts a long time, it is not eternal for me,' he tells me.

Appānubhāvāti bhojaputte sandhāyāha. Hantīti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu sūlehi vijjhantā kiṃkāraṇā haniṃsu. Kiṃ paṭiccāti kiṃ sandhāya tvaṃ tadā tesaṃ hatthattaṃ āgacchi vasaṃ upagato. Vanibbakānanti bhojaputtā idha “vanibbakā”ti vuttā. Tejo nu te nānvagaṃ dantamūlanti kiṃ nu tava tejo [M 5.0186] bhojaputte disvā tadā bhayaṃ mahantaṃ anvagataṃ, udāhu visaṃ dantamūlaṃ na anvagataṃ. Kilesanti dukkhaṃ. Vanibbakānanti bhojaputtānaṃ santike, bhojaputte nissāyāti attho.

'Appānubhāvā' he says, referring to the Bhoja princes. 'Hanti' means 'they harm,' that is, piercing with stakes in eight places—for what reason did they kill? 'Kiṃ paṭicca' means 'on what account,' that is, on what account did you then come into their hands, becoming subject to them? 'Vanibbakānaṃ' here refers to the Bhoja princes, who are called 'wanderers.' 'Tejo nu te nānvagaṃ dantamūlaṃ' means 'did your fiery power not reach the root of your fang?'; that is, seeing the Bhoja princes, were you then overcome by great fear, or did the poison not reach the root of your fang? 'Kilesaṃ' means 'suffering.' 'Vanibbakānaṃ' means 'in the presence of the Bhoja princes,' that is, on account of the Bhoja princes—that is the meaning.

Tejo na sakkā mama tehi hantunti mama visatejo aññassa tejena abhihantumpi na sakkā. Satanti buddhādīnaṃ. Dhammānīti sīlasamādhipaññākhantianuddayamettābhāvanāsaṅkhātāni dhammāni. Sukittitānīti suvaṇṇitāni sukathitāni. Kinti katvā? Samuddavelāva duraccayānīti tehi samuddavelā viya sappurisehi jīvitatthampi duraccayānīti vaṇṇitāni, tasmā ahaṃ sīlabhedabhayena khantimettādisamannāgato hutvā mama kopassa sīlavelantaṃ atikkamituṃ na adāsinti āha.

'Tejo na sakkā mama tehi hantuṃ' means 'my fiery power cannot be harmed by another's power.' 'Sataṃ' refers to the Buddhas and the like. 'Dhammāni' refers to the qualities known as morality, concentration, wisdom, patience, compassion, and the cultivation of loving-kindness. 'Sukittitāni' means 'well-described, well-spoken of.' How so? 'Samuddavelāva duraccayāni' means 'like the ocean's shore, insurmountable,' that is, they are described by good people as difficult to overcome even for the sake of life, like the ocean's shore. Therefore, endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and the like, fearing the breach of my virtue, I did not allow my anger to cross the boundary of my virtue—thus he spoke.

“Imissā pana saṅkhapāladhammadesanāya dasapi pāramiyo labbhanti. Tadā hi mahāsattena sarīrassa pariccattabhāvo dānapāramī nāma hoti, tathārūpenāpi visatejena sīlassa abhinnatā sīlapāramī, nāgabhavanato nikkhamitvā samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ nekkhammapāramī, ‘idañcidañca kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti saṃvidahanaṃ paññāpāramī, adhivāsanavīriyaṃ vīriyapāramī, adhivāsanakhanti khantipāramī, saccasamādānaṃ saccapāramī, ‘mama sīlaṃ na bhindissāmī’ti adhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramī, anuddayabhāvo [P 5.0175] mettāpāramī, vedanāya majjhattabhāvo upekkhāpāramī”ti.

Moreover, in this discourse on the Dhamma by Saṅkhapāla, the ten perfections are found. For at that time, the Great Being's relinquishing of his body is the perfection of generosity; the unbroken nature of his virtue even in the face of such fiery power is the perfection of virtue; his going forth from the nāga realm and undertaking the ascetic practice is the perfection of renunciation; his arranging, 'This and this is fit to be done,' is the perfection of wisdom; the energy of endurance is the perfection of energy; the patience of endurance is the perfection of patience; the undertaking of truth is the perfection of truth; the resolution, 'I will not break my virtue,' is the perfection of resolution; his state of compassion is the perfection of loving-kindness; his state of equanimity regarding feeling is the perfection of equanimity.

Athāgamunti athekadivasaṃ vammikamatthake nipannaṃ disvā soḷasa bhojaputtā khararajjuñca daḷhapāsañca [V 5.0168] sūlāni ca gahetvā mama santikaṃ āgatā. Bhetvānāti mama sarīraṃ aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu bhinditvā sakaṇṭakakāḷavettalatā pavesetvā. Nāsaṃ atikassa rajjunti thokaṃ gantvā sīsaṃ me olambantaṃ disvā mahāmagge nipajjāpetvā puna nāsampi me bhinditvā vaṭṭarajjuṃ atikassa āvunitvā kājakoṭiyaṃ laggetvā samantato pariggahetvā maṃ nayiṃsu.

‘Athāgamuṃ’ means: then, one day, seeing me lying on the top of an anthill, sixteen Bhoja princes came to me carrying a rough rope, a strong noose, and stakes. ‘Bhetvāna’ means: having split my body in eight places, they inserted thorny black rattan creepers. ‘Nāsaṃ atikassa rajjuṃ’ means: having gone a short distance and seeing my head hanging down, they made me lie down on the highway. Then, breaking my nose again, they passed a round rope through it, fastened it to the tip of a yoke, and surrounding me on all sides, they led me away.

Addasaṃsūti, samma saṅkhapāla, te bhojaputtā ekāyane ekagamane jaṅghapadikamagge taṃ balena ca vaṇṇena ca upetarūpaṃ passiṃsu, tvaṃ pana issariyasobhaggasiriyā ca paññāya ca bhāvito vaḍḍhito, so tvaṃ evarūpo samānopi [M 5.0187] kimatthaṃ tapaṃ karosi, kimicchanto uposathavāsaṃ vasasi, sīlaṃ rakkhasi. “Addasāsi”ntipi pāṭho, ahaṃ ekāyane mahāmagge taṃ addasinti attho. Abhipatthayānoti patthento. Tasmāti yasmā manussayoniṃ patthemi, tasmā vīriyena parakkamitvā tapokammaṃ karomi.

‘Addasaṃsu’ means: Dear Saṅkhapāla, those Bhoja princes saw you on a solitary path, a footpath, endowed with strength and beauty. But you, though such as you are, developed and grown in sovereignty, good fortune, glory, and wisdom—why do you practice austerity? What do you seek by observing the Uposatha, by guarding virtue? There is also the reading ‘Addasāsi’ (You saw), meaning, ‘I saw you on that solitary highway.’ ‘Abhipatthayāno’ means longing. ‘Tasmā’ means: ‘Because I long for the human state, therefore I strive with energy and practice austerity.’

Surositoti suṭṭhu manulitto. Itoti imamhā nāgabhavanā manussaloko kena uttaritaro. Suddhīti maggaphalanibbānasaṅkhātā visuddhi. Saṃyamoti sīlaṃ. Idaṃ so manussalokeyeva buddhapaccekabuddhānaṃ uppattiṃ sandhāyāha. Kāhāmīti attano appaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ karonto jātijarāmaraṇassantaṃ karissāmīti. Evaṃ, mahārāja, so saṅkhapālo manussalokaṃ vaṇṇesi. Saṃvaccharo meti evaṃ, mahārāja, tasmiṃ manussalokaṃ vaṇṇente ahaṃ pabbajjāya sinehaṃ katvā etadavocaṃ. Tattha upaṭṭhitosmīti annapānena ceva dibbehi ca kāmaguṇehi pariciṇṇo mānito asmi. Palemīti paremi gacchāmi. Cirappavuṭṭhosmīti ahaṃ manussalokato cirappavuṭṭho asmi.

‘Surosito’ means well-anointed. ‘Ito’ means: ‘By what is the human world superior to this nāga realm?’ ‘Suddhi’ means the purity consisting of the path, fruition, and Nibbāna. ‘Saṃyamo’ means virtue. This he said with reference to the arising of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas in the human world itself. ‘Kāhāmi’ means: making his state without rebirth, he will make an end to birth, aging, and death. Thus, great king, Saṅkhapāla praised the human world. ‘Saṃvaccharo me’—thus, great king, while he was praising the human world, having developed affection for renunciation, I spoke thus: ‘Tattha upaṭṭhitosmi’ means: ‘I am honored and respected, attended to with food and drink and divine sensual pleasures.’ ‘Palemi’ means: ‘I will go.’ ‘Cirappavuṭṭhosmi’ means: ‘I have been long separated from the human world.’

Nābhisapitthāti kacci nu kho mama puttādīsu koci taṃ na akkosi na paribhāsīti pucchati. “Nābhisajjethā”tipi pāṭho, na kopesīti attho. Paṭivihitoti paṭijaggito. Maṇī mamanti sace, samma āḷāra, gacchasiyeva, evaṃ sante mama lohitaṅko dhanahārako sabbakāmadado maṇi saṃvijjati, taṃ uḷāraṃ maṇiratanaṃ ādāya tava gehaṃ gaccha, tattha imassānubhāvena yāvadicchakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhā puna imaṃ maṇiṃ ossajassu, ossajanto ca aññattha anossajitvā attano udakacāṭiyaṃ ossajeyyāsīti vatvā mayhaṃ maṇiratanaṃ upanesīti vadati.

‘Nābhisapittha’—he asks, wondering, ‘Surely no one among my sons and others has abused or reviled you?’ There is also the reading ‘Nābhisajjetha,’ meaning, ‘you were not angered.’ ‘Paṭivihito’ means well-attended. ‘Maṇī mama’—he says: ‘If, dear Āḷāra, you really must go, then in that case, I have a gem, the Lohitaṅka, that brings wealth and grants all desires. Take that magnificent jewel and go to your home. There, by its power, obtain as much wealth as you desire, and then return the gem. When returning it, do not leave it elsewhere, but leave it in your own water pot.’ Having said this, he presented the jewel to me.

Evaṃ vatvā āḷāro “athāhaṃ, mahārāja, nāgarājānaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘samma, nāhaṃ dhanenatthiko, pabbajituṃ pana icchāmī’ti [P 5.0176] pabbajitaparikkhāraṃ yācitvā teneva saddhiṃ nāgabhavanā [V 5.0169] nikkhamitvā taṃ nivattetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitomhī”ti vatvā rañño dhammakathaṃ kathento gāthādvayamāha –

Having said this, Āḷāra continued: ‘Then, great king, I addressed the Nāga king thus: “Friend, I have no need for wealth, but I wish to go forth as an ascetic.” Having requested the requisites of an ascetic, and having left the Nāga realm with him, after sending him back, I entered the Himalayas and went forth.’ Having said this, while giving a Dhamma discourse to the king, he spoke these two verses:

191.

191.

“Diṭṭhā mayā mānusakāpi kāmā, asassatā vipariṇāmadhammā;

Ādīnavaṃ kāmaguṇesu disvā, saddhāyahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja.

‘I have seen human sensual pleasures, impermanent and subject to change. Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, I have gone forth in faith, O king.’

192.

192.

“Dumapphalānīva [M 5.0188] patanti māṇavā, daharā ca vuddhā ca sarīrabhedā;

Etampi disvā pabbajitomhi rāja, apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo”ti.

‘Like fruits from trees, human beings fall at the breaking up of the body, both the young and the old. Seeing this also, O king, I have gone forth; the certain path of the ascetic life is indeed better.’

Tattha saddhāyāti kammañca phalañca nibbānañca saddahitvā. Dumapphalānīva patantīti yathā rukkhaphalāni pakkānipi apakkānipi patanti, tathā māṇavā daharā ca vuddhā ca patanti. Apaṇṇakanti aviraddhaṃ niyyānikaṃ. Sāmaññameva seyyoti pabbajjāva uttamāti pabbajjāya guṇaṃ disvā pabbajitomhi, mahārājāti.

Here, ‘saddhāya’ means having faith in kamma and its results, and in Nibbāna. ‘Dumapphalānīva patanti’ means that just as fruits from a tree fall, whether they be ripe or unripe, so too do human beings fall, both the young and the old. ‘Apaṇṇakaṃ’ means unerring and leading to liberation. ‘Sāmaññameva seyyo’ means: ‘The ascetic life is indeed the best.’ Seeing the virtue of the ascetic life, I have gone forth, O great king.

Taṃ sutvā rājā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king then spoke the next verse:

193.

193.

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāgañca sutvāna tavañcaḷāra, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

‘Indeed, the wise should be associated with—the learned who consider many things. Having heard both the Nāga and you, O Āḷāra, I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.’

Tattha ye bahuṭhānacintinoti ye bahūni kāraṇāni jānanti. Nāgañcāti tathā appamādavihārinaṃ nāgarājānañca tava ca vacanaṃ sutvā.

Here, ‘ye bahuṭhānacintino’ means those who know many reasons. ‘Nāgañca’ means: having heard the words of both the Nāga king, who dwells in diligence, and your words.

Athassa ussāhaṃ janento tāpaso osānagāthamāha –

Then, to inspire him, the ascetic spoke the concluding verse:

194.

194.

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāgañca sutvāna mamañca rāja, karohi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

‘Indeed, the wise should be associated with—the learned who consider many things. Having heard both the Nāga and me, O king, perform abundant meritorious deeds.’

Evaṃ [P 5.0177] so rañño dhammaṃ desetvā tattheva cattāro vassānamāse vasitvā puna himavantaṃ gantvā yāvajīvaṃ cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi. Saṅkhapālopi yāvajīvaṃ uposathavāsaṃ vasitvā rājā ca dānādīni puññāni karitvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king, he stayed there for the four months of the rainy season and then returned to the Himalayas. There, he developed the four divine abidings for the rest of his life and was reborn in the Brahma world. Saṅkhapāla also observed the Uposatha for the rest of his life, and the king, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 5.0170] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pitā tāpaso kassapo ahosi, bārāṇasirājā ānando, āḷāro sāriputto, saṅkhapālanāgarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: ‘At that time, the ascetic father was Kassapa, the king of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, Āḷāra was Sāriputta, but the Nāga king Saṅkhapāla was I myself.’

Saṅkhapālajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The commentary on the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka, the fourth.

[525] 5. Cūḷasutasomajātakavaṇṇanā

[525] 5. The Commentary on the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka

Āmantayāmi [M 5.0189] nigamanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto nekkhammapāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu mahānāradakassapajātakasadisameva (jā. 2.22.1153 ādayo). Atīte pana bārāṇasī sudassanaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, tattha brahmadatto nāma rājā ajjhāvasi. Bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, dasamāsaccayena mātukucchito nikkhami. Tassa pana puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ mukhaṃ ahosi, tenassa “somakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So viññutaṃ patto sutavittako savanasīlo ahosi, tena naṃ “sutasomo”ti sañjāniṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggahetvā āgato pitu santakaṃ setacchattaṃ labhitvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, mahantaṃ issariyaṃ ahosi. Tassa candādevippamukhāni soḷasa itthisahassāni ahesuṃ. So aparabhāge puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhanto gharāvāse anabhirato araññaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitukāmo ahosi.

‘Āmantayāmi nigamaṃ’ (I address the town)—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of renunciation. The present story is just like that of the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka. In the past, the city of Bārāṇasī was named Sudassana, where a king named Brahmadatta reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen and emerged from his mother’s womb after ten months. His face was radiant like the full moon, so they named him ‘Somakumāra.’ When he reached the age of discretion, he became learned and fond of hearing the teachings, thus they knew him as ‘Sutasoma.’ Having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he returned and, receiving the white parasol from his father, ruled righteously and possessed great sovereignty. He had sixteen thousand wives, headed by Candādevī. Later, as he prospered with sons and daughters, he became discontent with household life and wished to enter the forest and go forth.

So ekadivasaṃ kappakaṃ āmantetvā “yadā me, samma, sirasmiṃ palitaṃ passeyyāsi, tadā me āroceyyāsī”ti āha. Kappako tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā aparabhāge palitaṃ disvā ārocetvā “tena hi naṃ, samma kappaka, uddharitvā mama hatthe patiṭṭhapehī”ti vutte suvaṇṇasaṇḍāsena uddharitvā rañño hatthe ṭhapesi. Taṃ disvā mahāsatto “jarāya me sarīraṃ abhibhūta”nti bhīto taṃ palitaṃ gahetvāva pāsādā otaritvā mahājanassa [P 5.0178] dassanaṭṭhāne paññatte rājapallaṅke nisīditvā senāpatippamukhāni asītiamaccasahassāni purohitappamukhāni saṭṭhibrāhmaṇasahassāni aññe ca raṭṭhikajānapadanegamādayo bahū jane pakkosāpetvā “sirasmiṃ me palitaṃ jātaṃ, ahaṃ mahallakosmi, mama pabbajitabhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, he summoned his barber and said, ‘Friend, when you see a gray hair on my head, you must inform me.’ The barber agreed to his request. Later, seeing a gray hair, he informed him. The king then said, ‘Well then, friend barber, pluck it out and place it in my hand.’ When this was said, the barber removed it with golden tweezers and placed it in the king's hand. Seeing it, the Great Being was frightened, thinking, ‘My body has been overcome by old age.’ Holding that gray hair, he descended from the palace and sat on the royal throne prepared in a place where the people could see him. He summoned many people, including the eighty thousand ministers headed by the commander-in-chief, the sixty thousand brahmins led by the royal priest, and other country-dwellers and town-dwellers. Then he declared, ‘A gray hair has appeared on my head; I have grown old. Know that I shall go forth.’ And he spoke the first verse:

195.

195.

“Āmantayāmi nigamaṃ, mittāmacce parissaje;

Sirasmiṃ palitaṃ jātaṃ, pabbajjaṃ dāni rocaha”nti.

‘I address the townspeople, friends, ministers, and attendants; a gray hair has appeared on my head, now renunciation pleases me.’

Tattha [V 5.0171] āmantayāmīti jānāpemi. Rocahanti “rocemi ahaṃ, tassa me, bhonto! Pabbajitabhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti.

Herein, ‘āmantayāmi’ means ‘I make known.’ ‘Rocahaṃ’ means: ‘I like it, sirs! Therefore, know my state of having gone forth.’

Taṃ [M 5.0190] sutvā tesu eko visāradappatto hutvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, one among them, having attained confidence, spoke this verse:

196.

196.

“Abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, sallaṃ me deva urasi kappesi;

Sattasatā te bhariyā, kathaṃ nu te tā bhavissantī”ti.

‘Why do you speak of misfortune to me, O king? You have fixed a dart in my breast. You have seven hundred wives; how then will they fare?’

Tattha abhunti avaḍḍhiṃ. Urasi kappesīti urasmiṃ sunisitadhotasattiṃ cāresi. Sattasatāti samajātikā khattiyakaññā sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ nu te tā bhavissantīti tā tava bhariyā tayi pabbajite anāthā nippaccayā kathaṃ bhavissanti, etā anāthā katvā tumhākaṃ pabbajjā nāma na yuttāti.

Herein, ‘abhuṃ’ means misfortune. ‘Urasi kappesi’ means he drove a well-sharpened and polished spear into the chest. ‘Sattasatā’—this was said referring to khattiya maidens of the same caste. ‘Kathaṃ nu te tā bhavissantī’ means: when you have gone forth, how will those wives of yours be, helpless and without support? To go forth after making them helpless is not proper for you.

Tato mahāsatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being spoke the third verse:

197.

197.

“Paññāyihinti etā, daharā aññampi tā gamissanti;

Saggañca patthayāno, tena ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti.

‘They will be manifest; being young, they will go to another. And desiring heaven, for that reason I will go forth.’

Tattha paññāyihintīti attano kammena paññāyissanti. Ahaṃ etāsaṃ kiṃ homi, sabbāpetā daharā, yo añño rājā bhavissati, taṃ etā gamissantīti.

Herein, ‘paññāyihinti’ means they will be known by their own kamma. What am I to them? They are all young. Whoever will be the next king, they will go to him.

Amaccādayo bodhisattassa paṭivacanaṃ dātuṃ asakkontā tassa mātu santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Sā turitaturitā āgantvā [P 5.0179] “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, tāta, pabbajitukāmosī”ti vatvā dve gāthāyo abhāsi –

The ministers and others, unable to give a reply to the Bodhisatta, went to his mother and informed her of the matter. She came in great haste and said, ‘Is it true, dear son, that you desire to go forth?’ Then, blaming the king, she spoke these two verses to lament:

198.

198.

“Dulladdhaṃ me āsi sutasoma, yassa te homahaṃ mātā;

Yaṃ me vilapantiyā, anapekkho pabbajasi deva.

‘It was a misfortune for me, Sutasoma, that I am your mother; since while I lament, you go forth without regard, O king.’

199.

199.

“Dulladdhaṃ me āsi sutasoma, yaṃ taṃ ahaṃ vijāyissaṃ;

Yaṃ me vilapantiyā, anapekkho pabbajasi devā”ti.

‘It was a misfortune for me, Sutasoma, that I gave birth to you; since while I lament, you go forth without regard, O king.’

Tattha [V 5.0172][M 5.0191] dulladdhanti yaṃ etaṃ mayā labhantiyā puttaṃ jammaṃ laddhaṃ dulladdhaṃ. Yaṃ meti yena kāraṇena mayi nānappakārakaṃ vipalantiyā tvaṃ pabbajituṃ icchasi, tena kāraṇena tādisassa puttassa labhanaṃ mama dulladdhaṃ nāmāti.

Herein, ‘dulladdhaṃ’ means: the son that was obtained by me was a wretched birth. ‘Yaṃ me’ means: for the reason that you wish to go forth while I am lamenting in various ways, for that reason the obtaining of such a son is a misfortune for me.

Bodhisatto evaṃ paridevamānāyapi mātarā saddhiṃ kiñci na kathesi. Sā roditvā kanditvā sayameva ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Athassa pitu ārocesuṃ. So āgantvā ekaṃ tāva gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta said nothing to his mother, even while she was lamenting thus. After weeping and wailing, she stood aside in a suitable place. Then they informed his father. He came and first spoke one verse to ask the king:

200.

200.

“Ko nāmeso dhammo, sutasoma kā ca nāma pabbajjā;

Yaṃ no amhe jiṇṇe, anapekkho pabbajasi devā”ti.

‘What is this Dhamma, Sutasoma, and what is this going forth? That you go forth without regard for us in our old age, O king!’

Tattha yaṃ no amheti yaṃ tvaṃ amhākaṃ putto samāno amhe jiṇṇe paṭijaggitabbakāle appaṭijaggitvā papāte silaṃ pavaṭṭento viya chaḍḍetvā anapekkho pabbajasi, tena taṃ vadāmi ko nāmeso tava dhammoti adhippāyo.

Herein, ‘yaṃ no amhe’ means: that you, being our son, at a time when we are old and should be cared for, do not care for us, but abandon us as if rolling a stone down a precipice and go forth without regard—for that reason I say to you, ‘What is this Dhamma of yours?’ This is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto tuṇhī ahosi. Atha naṃ pitā, “tāta sutasoma, sacepi te mātāpitūsu sineho natthi, puttadhītaro te bahū taruṇā, tayā vinā vattituṃ na sakkhissanti, tesaṃ vuḍḍhippattakāle pabbajissasī”ti vatvā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Great Being remained silent. Then his father said to him, ‘Dear Sutasoma, even if you have no affection for your mother and father, you have many young sons and daughters who will not be able to live without you. You shall go forth when they have reached maturity.’ Then, wishing to state the reason, he spoke the seventh verse:

201.

201.

“Puttāpi [P 5.0180] tuyhaṃ bahavo, daharā appattayobbanā;

Mañjū tepitaṃ apassantā, maññe dukkhaṃ nigacchantī”ti.

‘Many are your children, young, not having reached adulthood; charming as they are, not seeing you, they will, I think, come to suffering.’

Tattha mañjūti madhuravacanā. Nigacchantīti nigacchissanti kāyikacetasikadukkhaṃ paṭilabhissantīti maññāmi.

Herein, ‘mañjū’ means sweet-voiced. ‘Nigacchanti’ means they will undergo, that is, they will obtain physical and mental suffering—so I think.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke a verse:

202.

202.

“Puttehi ca me etehi, daharehi appattayobbanehi;

Mañjūhi sabbehipi tumhehi, cirampi ṭhatvā vināsabhāvo”ti.

‘Even if I remain for a long time with these children of mine, who are young and have not yet reached adulthood, and with all of you who are so charming, there is bound to be a state of separation.’

Tattha [V 5.0173][M 5.0192] sabbehipi tumhehīti, tāta, na kevalaṃ putteheva, atha kho tumhehipi aññehipi sabbasaṅkhārehi ciraṃ ṭhatvāpi dīghamaddhānaṃ ṭhatvāpi vināsabhāvova niyato. Sakalasmimpi hi lokasannivāse ekasaṅkhāropi nicco nāma natthīti.

Herein, ‘sabbehipi tumhehi’ means, dear father, not only with the children, but also with you and with all other conditioned things—even after remaining for a long time, even for a long period—the state of destruction is certain. For in this entire world, not even a single conditioned thing is permanent.

Evaṃ mahāsatto pitu dhammakathaṃ kathesi. So tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā tuṇhī ahosi. Athassa sattasatānaṃ bhariyānaṃ ārocayiṃsu. Tā ca pāsādā oruyha tassa santikaṃ gantvā gopphakesu gahetvā paridevamānā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Thus the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to his father. Having heard his Dhamma talk, the father remained silent. Then they informed his seven hundred wives. They, descending from the palace, approached the Bodhisatta, seized his ankles, and lamenting, spoke this verse:

203.

203.

“Chinnaṃ nu tuyhaṃ hadayaṃ, adu te karuṇā ca natthi amhesu;

Yaṃ no vikandantiyo, anapekkho pabbajasi devā”ti.

"Has your heart been severed from us? Or is there no compassion for us in you, that you go forth regardless, while we wail, O King?"

Tassattho – sāmi sutasoma, amhe vidhavā katvā gacchantassa appamattakassapi sinehassa abhāvena tava hadayaṃ amhesu chinnaṃ nu, udāhu karuṇāya abhāvena kāruññaṃ vā natthi, yaṃ no evaṃ vikandantiyo pahāya pabbajasīti.

The meaning is: ‘Lord Sutasoma, as you go away having made us widows, is your heart severed from us due to the absence of even the slightest affection? Or is it that there is no compassion or pity in you, that you abandon us while we are thus wailing and go forth?’

Mahāsatto tāsaṃ pādamūle parivattitvā paridevamānānaṃ paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of them lamenting as they rolled about at his feet, immediately spoke this verse:

204.

204.

“Na [P 5.0181] ca mayhaṃ chinnaṃ hadayaṃ, atthi karuṇāpi mayhaṃ tumhesu;

Saggañca patthayāno, tena ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti.

"My heart has not been severed, and I do have compassion for you; but aspiring to heaven, I shall go forth."

Tattha saggañcāti ahaṃ saggañca patthayanto yasmā ayaṃ pabbajjā nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇitā, tasmā pabbajissāmi, tumhe mā cintayitthāti tā assāsesi.

Here, ‘and heaven’ (saggañca) means: ‘Since I aspire to heaven, and because this going forth is praised by the Buddhas and others, I shall go forth; do not worry’—thus he consoled them.

Athassa aggamahesiyā ārocesuṃ. Sā garubhārā paripuṇṇagabbhāpi samānā āgantvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā tisso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then they informed his chief queen. Although she was heavy with child and her womb was full-term, she came, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and standing to one side, spoke these three verses:

205.

205.

“Dulladdhaṃ [M 5.0193] me āsi sutasoma, yassa te ahaṃ bhariyā;

Yaṃ me vilapantiyā, anapekkho pabbajasi deva.

"To my misfortune was it attained, Sutasoma, that I became your wife, since you go forth regardless while I lament, O King.

206.

206.

“Dulladdhaṃ [V 5.0174] me āsi sutasoma, yassa te ahaṃ bhariyā;

Yaṃ me kucchipaṭisandhiṃ, anapekkho pabbajasi deva.

To my misfortune was it attained, Sutasoma, that I became your wife, since you go forth regardless of the child in my womb, O King.

207.

207.

“Paripakko me gabbho, kucchigato yāva naṃ vijāyāmi;

Māhaṃ ekā vidhavā, pacchā dukkhāni addakkhi”nti.

My womb is full-term; wait until I give birth to the child within. May I not see suffering alone and widowed afterwards."

Tattha yaṃ meti yasmā mama vilapantiyā tvaṃ anapekkho pabbajasi, tasmā yaṃ mayā tava santikā aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ dulladdhameva āsi. Dutiyagāthāya yasmā maṃ tvaṃ kucchipaṭisandhiṃ pahāya anapekkho pabbajasi, tasmā yaṃ mayā tava bhariyattaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ dulladdhaṃ meti attho. Yāva nanti yāvāhaṃ taṃ gabbhaṃ vijāyāmi, tāva adhivāsehīti.

Here, ‘since you’ (yaṃ me) means: ‘Since you go forth regardless while I lament, the status of chief queen that I attained from you was indeed ill-attained.’ In the second verse, the meaning is: ‘Since you go forth regardless, abandoning me with a child in the womb, my having become your wife was ill-attained for me.’ ‘Until I give birth to him’ (yāva naṃ) means: ‘Please wait until I give birth to that child.’

Tato mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke a verse:

208.

208.

“Paripakko te gabbho, kucchigato iṅgha tvaṃ vijāyassu;

Puttaṃ [P 5.0182] anomavaṇṇaṃ, taṃ hitvā pabbajissāmī”ti.

"Your womb is full-term; go now and give birth to the child within. I shall go forth after leaving behind that son of supreme beauty."

Tattha puttanti, bhadde, tava gabbho paripakkoti jānāmi, tvaṃ pana vijāyamānā puttaṃ vijāyissasi, na dhītaraṃ, sā tvaṃ sotthinā vijāyassu puttaṃ, ahaṃ pana saddhiṃ tayā taṃ puttaṃ hitvā pabbajissāmiyevāti.

Here, regarding ‘son’ (puttaṃ): ‘Dear lady, I know your womb is full-term. When you give birth, you will bear a son, not a daughter. May you safely give birth to the son. But I shall indeed go forth, leaving that son with you.’

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontī “ito dāni paṭṭhāya, deva, amhākaṃ sirī nāma natthī”ti ubhohi hatthehi hadayaṃ dhārayamānā assūni muñcantī mahāsaddena paridevi. Atha naṃ samassāsento mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, unable to contain her grief, she said, "O King, from this day forth, there is no glory left for us." Clutching her heart with both hands and shedding tears, she lamented loudly. Then, comforting her, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

209.

209.

“Mā [M 5.0194] tvaṃ cande rudi, mā soci vanatimiramattakkhi;

Āroha varapāsādaṃ, anapekkho ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti.

"Do not weep, O Candā; do not grieve, O you with eyes dark and lovely as the forest. Ascend the excellent palace; I shall go forth without looking back."

Tattha mā tvaṃ cande rudīti, bhadde candādevi, tvaṃ mā rodi mā soci. Vanatimiramattakkhīti girikaṇṇikapupphasamānanette. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “koviḷāratambakkhī”ti likhitaṃ, tassā koviḷārapupphaṃ viya tambanetteti attho.

Therein, ‘do not weep, O Candā’ means, ‘Dear lady, Queen Candā, do not weep, do not grieve.’ ‘O you with eyes dark and lovely as the forest’ (vanatimiramattakkhi) means eyes like the blossoms of the girikaṇṇikā flower. In the Pāli text, however, it is written as ‘kovilāratambakkhī,’ which means her eyes are reddish like the kovilāra flower.

Sā [V 5.0175] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā ṭhātuṃ asakkontī pāsādaṃ āruyha rodamānā nisīdi. Atha naṃ bodhisattassa jeṭṭhaputto disvā “kiṃ nu kho me mātā rodantī nisinnā”ti taṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, unable to remain standing, she ascended the palace and sat weeping. Then the Bodhisatta's eldest son, seeing her, asked, "Why is my mother sitting and weeping?" and spoke this verse:

210.

210.

“Ko taṃ amma kopesi, kiṃ rodasi pekkhasi ca maṃ bāḷhaṃ;

Kaṃ avajjhaṃ ghātemi, ñātīnaṃ udikkhamānāna”nti.

"Who, mother, has angered you? Why do you weep and look at me so intensely? Whom, even one who should not be killed, shall I slay while our kinsmen look on?"

Tattha kopesīti, amma! Ko nāma taṃ kopesi, ko te appiyaṃ akāsi. Pekkhasi cāti maṃ bāḷhaṃ pekkhantī kiṃkāraṇā rodasīti adhippāyo. Kaṃ avajjhaṃ ghātemīti aghātetabbampi kaṃ ghātemi attano ñātīnaṃ udikkhamānānaññeva, akkhāhi meti pucchati.

Here, ‘has angered you’ (kopesi) means, ‘Mother, who has angered you, who has done what is unpleasant to you?’ ‘And look’ (pekkhasi ca) means, ‘For what reason do you weep while looking at me so intensely?’—this is the intended meaning. ‘Whom, even one who should not be killed, shall I slay’ means, ‘Whom shall I kill, even one who is not to be killed, while my own kinsmen are watching? Tell me!’—thus he asks.

Tato devī gāthamāha –

Then the queen spoke a verse:

211.

211.

“Na hi so sakkā hantuṃ, vijitāvī yo maṃ tāta kopesi;

Pitā [P 5.0183] te maṃ tāta avaca, anapekkho ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti.

"He cannot be killed, dear child—that conqueror who has angered me. Your father, dear child, said to me: ‘I shall go forth without looking back.’"

Tattha vijitāvīti, tāta, yo maṃ imissā pathaviyā vijitāvī kopesi, appiyasamudācārena me hadaye kopañca sokañca pavesesi, so tayā hantuṃ na sakkā, mañhi, tāta, tava pitā “ahaṃ rajjasiriñca tañca pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā pabbajissāmī”ti avaca, idaṃ me rodanakāraṇanti.

There, ‘conqueror’ (vijitāvī) means, ‘Dear child, the one who, as a conqueror of this earth, has angered me and caused anger and sorrow to enter my heart by his disagreeable conduct. He cannot be killed by you. For, dear child, your father said to me: "I will abandon royal glory and you, and having entered the forest, I will go forth." This is the reason for my weeping.’

So [M 5.0195] tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “amma! Kiṃ nāma tvaṃ kathesi, nanu evaṃ sante mayaṃ anāthā nāma bhavissāmā”ti paridevanto gāthamāha –

Hearing her words, he lamented, saying, "Mother, what is it that you are saying? If this be so, shall we not become protectorless?"—and he spoke this verse:

212.

212.

“Yohaṃ pubbe niyyāmi, uyyānaṃ mattakuñjare ca yodhemi;

Sutasome pabbajite, kathaṃ nu dāni karissāmī”ti.

"I who previously went out to the park and caused intoxicated elephants to fight; now that Sutasoma has gone forth, what shall I do now?"

Tassattho – yo ahaṃ pubbe catuājaññayuttaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rathaṃ abhiruyha uyyānaṃ gacchāmi, mattakuñjare ca yodhemi, aññehi ca assakīḷādīhi kīḷāmi, svāhaṃ idāni sutasome pabbajite kathaṃ karissāmīti?

The meaning is this: 'I who previously would mount a chariot yoked with four thoroughbreds, adorned with all ornaments, and go to the park, and would cause intoxicated elephants to fight and play other games such as horse-sports—what shall I do now that Sutasoma has gone forth?'

Athassa [V 5.0176] kaniṭṭhabhātā sattavassiko te ubhopi rodante disvā mātaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “amma! Kiṃkāraṇā tumhe rodathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “tena hi mā rodatha, ahaṃ tātassa pabbajituṃ na dassāmī”ti ubhopi te assāsetvā dhātiyā saddhiṃ pāsādā oruyha pitu santikaṃ gantvā, “tāta, tvaṃ kira amhe akāmake pahāya ‘pabbajāmī’ti vadasi, ahaṃ te pabbajituṃ na dassāmī”ti pitaraṃ gīvāya daḷhaṃ gahetvā gāthamāha –

Then his youngest brother, who was seven years old, seeing both of them weeping, approached his mother and asked, "Mother, why are you weeping?" Upon hearing the reason, he said, "Well then, do not weep. I will not let father go forth." Comforting both of them, he descended from the palace with his nurse and went to his father. "Father," he said, "I hear you are saying, 'I will go forth,' abandoning us against our will. I will not allow you to go forth!" Then, firmly grasping his father by the neck, he spoke this verse:

213.

213.

“Mātucca me rudantyā, jeṭṭhassa ca bhātuno akāmassa;

Hatthepi te gahessaṃ, na hi gacchasi no akāmāna”nti.

"With my mother weeping and my elder brother unwilling, I will seize you even by the hand; for you shall not go against our will."

Mahāsatto cintesi – “ayaṃ me paripanthaṃ karoti, kena nu kho naṃ upāyena paṭikkamāpeyya”nti. Tato dhātiṃ oloketvā, “amma! Dhāti handimaṃ maṇikkhandhapiḷandhanaṃ, taveso hotu [P 5.0184] hatthe, puttaṃ apanehi, mā me antarāyaṃ karī”ti sayaṃ puttaṃ hatthe gahetvā apanetuṃ asakkonto tassā lañjaṃ paṭijānetvā gāthamāha –

The Great Being thought: "This child is creating an obstacle for me; by what means can I make him retreat?" Then, looking at the nurse, he said, "Nurse, here, take this jeweled ornament; let it be yours. Take my son away; do not cause me any hindrance." Unable to remove the child himself, he promised her a bribe and spoke this verse:

214.

214.

“Uṭṭhehi tvaṃ dhāti, imaṃ kumāraṃ ramehi aññattha;

Mā me paripanthamakāsi, saggaṃ mama patthayānassā”ti.

"Arise, nurse, take this child and amuse him elsewhere; do not be a hindrance to me as I aspire to heaven."

Tattha [M 5.0196] imaṃ kumāranti, amma! Dhāti tvaṃ uṭṭhehi, imaṃ kumāraṃ apanetvā āgantvā imaṃ maṇiṃ gahetvā aññattha naṃ abhiramehīti.

Here, 'this child' means: 'Nurse! Arise, take this child away, and having come, take this gem and amuse him elsewhere.'

Sā lañjaṃ labhitvā kumāraṃ saññāpetvā ādāya aññattha gantvā paridevamānā gāthamāha –

Having obtained the bribe, she persuaded the boy and taking him elsewhere, lamenting, she spoke this verse:

215.

215.

“Yaṃ nūnimaṃ dadeyyaṃ pabhaṅkaraṃ, ko nu me imināttho;

Sutasome pabbajite, kiṃ nu menaṃ karissāmī”ti.

"What if I take this radiant jewel? What use is it to me? Since Sutasoma has gone forth, what shall I do with it?"

Tassattho – yaṃ nūna ahaṃ imaṃ lañjatthāya gahitaṃ pabhaṅkaraṃ suppabhāsaṃ maṇiṃ dadeyyaṃ, ko nu mayhaṃ sutasomanarinde pabbajite iminā attho, kiṃ nu menaṃ karissāmi, ahaṃ tasmiṃ pabbajite imaṃ labhissāmi, labhantīpi ca kiṃ nu kho etaṃ karissāmi, passatha me kammanti.

The meaning is this: 'What if I take this bright, radiant jewel, received as a bribe? What purpose would this serve me now that King Sutasoma has gone forth? What shall I do with it? Even if I were to receive this from him who has gone forth, what then would I do with it? Behold my situation!'

Tato [V 5.0177] mahāsenagutto cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā “gehe me dhanaṃ manda’nti saññaṃ karoti maññe, bahubhāvamassa kathessāmī”ti. So uṭṭhāya vanditvā gāthamāha –

Then the great general Senagutta thought: "This king, it seems, imagines 'my wealth at home is scant.' I will speak of his great abundance." Rising and paying homage, he spoke this verse:

216.

216.

“Koso ca tuyhaṃ vipulo, koṭṭhāgārañca tuyhaṃ paripūraṃ;

Pathavī ca tuyhaṃ vijitā, ramassu mā pabbaji devā”ti.

"Your treasury is vast, and your storehouse is full; the earth is your conquest. Enjoy yourself, do not go forth, O king!"

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being spoke a verse:

217.

217.

“Koso ca mayhaṃ vipulo, koṭṭhāgārañca mayhaṃ paripūraṃ;

Pathavī ca mayhaṃ vijitā, taṃ hitvā pabbajissāmī”ti.

"My treasury is vast, and my storehouses are full. I have conquered the earth, yet I will abandon it and go forth."

Taṃ [P 5.0185] sutvā tasmiṃ apagate kulavaḍḍhanaseṭṭhi nāma uṭṭhāya vanditvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, when he had departed, a wealthy merchant named Kulavaḍḍhana rose, paid homage, and spoke this verse:

218.

218.

“Mayhampi [M 5.0197] dhanaṃ pahūtaṃ, saṅkhyātuṃ nopi deva sakkomi;

Taṃ te dadāmi sabbampi, ramassu mā pabbaji devā”ti.

"I too have abundant wealth, O king, more than I am able to count. I give you all of it; enjoy yourself, do not go forth, O king!"

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being spoke a verse:

219.

219.

“Jānāmi dhanaṃ pahūtaṃ, kulavaḍḍhana pūjito tayā casmi;

Saggañca patthayāno, tena ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti.

"I know your wealth is abundant, Kulavaḍḍhana, and I am honored by you. But aspiring to heaven, for that reason I will go forth."

Taṃ sutvā kulavaḍḍhane apagate mahāsatto somadattaṃ kaniṭṭhabhātaraṃ āmantetvā, “tāta, ahaṃ pañjarapakkhitto vanakukkuṭo viya ukkaṇṭhito, maṃ gharāvāse anabhirati abhibhavati, ajjeva pabbajissāmi, tvaṃ imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajjā”ti rajjaṃ niyyādento gāthamāha –

Hearing this, when Kulavaḍḍhana had departed, the Great Being summoned Somadatta, his younger brother, and said, "Dear brother, like a jungle fowl kept in a cage, I am deeply weary. Discontent with household life overwhelms me. Today I shall go forth; you must take up this kingdom." Handing over the kingdom, he spoke this verse:

220.

220.

“Ukkaṇṭhitosmi bāḷhaṃ, arati maṃ somadatta āvisati;

Bahukāpi me antarāyā, ajjevāhaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti.

"I am intensely weary, Somadatta, discontent invades me; there are many obstacles for me, today I will go forth."

Taṃ sutvā sopi pabbajitukāmo taṃ dīpento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, he, also desiring to go forth, revealed this by speaking another verse:

221.

221.

“Idañca [V 5.0178] tuyhaṃ rucitaṃ, sutasoma ajjeva dāni tvaṃ pabbaja;

Ahampi pabbajissāmi, na ussahe tayā vinā ahaṃ ṭhātu”nti.

"If this is your wish, Sutasoma, then go forth today; I too shall go forth, for I am not able to remain without you."

Atha naṃ so paṭikkhipitvā upaḍḍhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having refused him, he spoke half a verse:

222.

222.

“Na hi sakkā pabbajituṃ, nagare na hi paccati janapade cā”ti.

"It is not possible to go forth, for food is not cooked in the city or the country."

Tattha [P 5.0186] na hi paccatīti idāneva tāva mama pabbajjādhippāyaṃ sutvāva imasmiṃ dvādasayojanike sudassananagare ca sakalajanapade ca na paccati, koci uddhane aggiṃ na jāleti, amhesu pana dvīsu pabbajitesu anāthāva raṭṭhavāsino bhavissanti, tasmā na hi sakkā tayā pabbajituṃ, ahameva pabbajissāmīti.

Here, 'food is not cooked' means that as soon as my intention to go forth is heard, in this twelve-yojana city of Sudassana and throughout the entire land, no one cooks, no one lights a fire in the hearth. If both of us were to go forth, the inhabitants of the kingdom would be without a protector. Therefore, it is not possible for you to go forth—only I shall go forth.

Taṃ sutvā mahājano mahāsattassa pādamūle parivattitvā paridevanto upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

Hearing this, the great crowd, rolling about at the Great Being's feet and lamenting, spoke half a verse:

“Sutasome pabbajite, kathaṃ nu dāni karissāmā”ti.

"Now that Sutasoma has gone forth, what shall we do now?"

Tato mahāsatto “alaṃ mā socayittha, ahaṃ cirampi ṭhatvā tumhehi vinā bhavissāmi, uppannasaṅkhāro hi nicco nāma natthī”ti mahājanassa dhammaṃ kathento āha –

Then the Great Being, teaching the Dhamma to the great crowd, said: "Enough, do not grieve. Even if I stayed for a long time, I would be separated from you. For no conditioned thing that has arisen is permanent." He said:

223.

223.

“Upanīyatidaṃ [M 5.0198] maññe, parittaṃ udakaṃva caṅkavāramhi;

Evaṃ suparittake jīvite, na ca pamajjituṃ kālo.

"I consider this life to be led onward, like a little water in a dyer's trough; in a life so very brief, there is no time for heedlessness."

224.

224.

“Upanīyatidaṃ maññe, parittaṃ udakaṃva caṅkavāramhi;

Evaṃ suparittake jīvite, andhabālā pamajjanti.

"I consider this life to be led onward, like a little water in a dyer's trough; in a life so very brief, blind fools are heedless."

225.

225.

“Te vaḍḍhayanti nirayaṃ, tiracchānayoniñca pettivisayañca;

Taṇhāya bandhanabaddhā, vaḍḍhenti asurakāya”nti.

"They increase hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; bound by the bonds of craving, they increase the host of asuras."

Tattha upanīyatidaṃ maññeti, tāta, “idaṃ jīvitaṃ upanīyatī”ti ahaṃ maññāmi. Aññesu suttesu upasaṃharaṇattho upaniyyanattho, idha pana pariyādānattho. Tasmā yathā parittaṃ udakaṃ [V 5.0179] rajakānaṃ khāracaṅkavāre pakkhittaṃ sīghaṃ pariyādiyati, tathā jīvitampi. Evaṃ suparittake jīvite taṃ parittakaṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ gahetvā vicarantānaṃ sattānaṃ na puññakiriyāya pamajjituṃ kālo, appamādova kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti ayamettha attho. Andhabālā pamajjantīti ajarāmarā viya hutvā gūthakalale sūkarā viya hutvā kāmapaṅke nimujjantā [P 5.0187] pamajjanti. Asurakāyanti kāḷakañjikaasurayoniñca vaḍḍhentīti attho.

In this context, 'upanīyatidaṃ maññe' means: 'O friends, I think "this life is being exhausted."' In other discourses, 'upanīyati' has the meaning of being led onward, but here it means exhaustion. Therefore, just as a small amount of water put into a dyer’s lye-pot is quickly exhausted, so too is life. Thus, in such a very brief life, for beings wandering about having grasped this limited life-formation, there is no time to be heedless in performing meritorious deeds; only heedfulness should be practiced. This is the meaning here. 'Andhabālā pamajjanti' means: acting as if they were ageless and deathless, like pigs in a pit of filth, they are heedless while sinking into the mire of sensual pleasures. 'Asurakāya' means they increase the Kāḷakañjika asura realm. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ mahāsatto mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā pubbakaṃ nāma pāsādaṃ āruyha sattamāya bhūmiyā ṭhito khaggena cūḷaṃ chinditvā “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ kiñci na homi, attano rājānaṃ gaṇhathā”ti saveṭhanaṃ cūḷaṃ mahājanassa antare khipi. Taṃ gahetvā mahājano bhūmiyaṃ parivaṭṭento parivaṭṭento paridevi. Tasmiṃ ṭhāne mahantaṃ rajaggaṃ uṭṭhahi. Paṭikkamitvā ṭhitajano taṃ oloketvā “raññā cūḷaṃ chinditvā saveṭhanā cūḷā mahājanassa antare khittā bhavissati, tenāyaṃ pāsādassa avidūre rajavaṭṭi uggatā”ti paridevanto gāthamāha –

Thus, the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to the multitude, ascended the palace named Pubbaka and, standing on the seventh floor, cut off his topknot with a sword and declared, "I am nothing to you; take your own king," then threw the topknot together with the turban into the midst of the crowd. Taking it, the people rolled on the ground, lamenting. At that spot, a great mass of dust arose. The people standing at a distance looked at it and said, "The king must have cut off his topknot and thrown it with the turban into the midst of the crowd. That is why this mass of dust has risen near the palace." Lamenting, they spoke this verse:

226.

226.

“Ūhaññate rajaggaṃ avidūre, pubbakamhi ca pāsāde;

Maññe no kesā chinnā, yasassino dhammarājassā”ti.

"A mass of dust is raised up not far away, at the Pubbaka palace; I think the hair of our glorious Dhamma King has been cut."

Tattha ūhaññateti uṭṭhahati. Rajagganti rajakkhandho. Avidūreti ito amhākaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānato avidūre. Pubbakamhīti pubbakapāsādassa samīpe. Maññe noti amhākaṃ dhammarājassa kesā chinnā bhavissantīti maññāma.

There, 'ūhaññate' means it rises up. 'Rajaggaṃ' means a mass of dust. 'Avidūre' means not far from here, from our standing place. 'Pubbakamhi' means near the Pubbaka palace. 'Maññe no' means 'we think that the hair of our Dhamma King has been cut'.

Mahāsatto [M 5.0199] paricārikaṃ pesetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre āharāpetvā kappakena kesamassuṃ ohārāpetvā alaṅkāraṃ sayanapiṭṭhe pātetvā rattapaṭānaṃ dasāni chinditvā tāni kāsāyāni nivāsetvā mattikāpattaṃ vāmaaṃsakūṭe laggetvā kattaradaṇḍaṃ ādāya mahātale aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā pāsādā otaritvā antaravīthiṃ paṭipajji. Gacchantaṃ pana naṃ na koci sañjāni. Athassa sattasatā khattiyakaññā pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā taṃ adisvā ābharaṇabhaṇḍameva disvā otaritvā avasesānaṃ soḷasasahassānaṃ itthīnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ piyasāmiko sutasomamahissaro pabbajito”ti mahāsaddena paridevamānāva bahi nikkhamiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahājano [P 5.0188] tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ aññāsi, sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhitvā “rājā kira no pabbajito”ti rājadvāre sannipati, mahājano “idha rājā bhavissati, ettha bhavissatī”ti pāsādādīni rañño paribhogaṭṭhānāni gantvā rājānaṃ adisvā –

The Great Being sent for an attendant, had him bring the requisites of a renunciate, and had a barber shave off his hair and beard. He cast off his ornaments onto the bed, cut the fringes of the red-dyed cloths and donned those dyed robes, fastened an earthen bowl to his left shoulder, took a walking staff, paced back and forth on the great terrace, descended from the palace, and proceeded along the main street. As he walked, no one recognized him. Then, seven hundred noble maidens ascended to the palace, and not seeing him but only seeing his ornaments, they descended and went to the remaining sixteen thousand women. Wailing loudly, they cried, "Our beloved lord, the renowned King Sutasoma, has gone forth!" and rushed outside. At that moment, the multitude realized he had renounced. The whole city was in turmoil as they exclaimed, "Our king has gone forth!" and gathered at the palace gates. The crowd, thinking, "The king will be here, he will be there," went to the palace and other places the king frequented, but not finding him, they wandered about lamenting:

227.

227.

“Ayamassa [V 5.0180] pāsādo, sovaṇṇapupphamālyavītikiṇṇo;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his palace, strewn with golden flowers and garlands; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

228.

228.

“Ayamassa pāsādo, sovaṇṇapupphamālyavītikiṇṇo;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his palace, strewn with golden flowers and garlands; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

229.

229.

“Idamassa kūṭāgāraṃ, sovaṇṇapupphamālyavītikiṇṇaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his gabled hall, strewn with golden flowers and garlands; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

230.

230.

“Idamassa kūṭāgāraṃ, sovaṇṇapupphamālyavītikiṇṇaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his gabled hall, strewn with golden flowers and garlands; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

231.

231.

“Ayamassa asokavanikā, supupphitā sabbakālikā rammā;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his Asoka grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

232.

232.

“Ayamassa asokavanikā, supupphitā sabbakālikā rammā;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his Asoka grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

233.

233.

“Idamassa uyyānaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari [P 5.0189] rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his garden, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

234.

234.

“Idamassa [M 5.0200] uyyānaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his garden, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

235.

235.

“Idamassa kaṇikāravanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his Kaṇikāra grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

236.

236.

“Idamassa kaṇikāravanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his Kaṇikāra grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

237.

237.

“Idamassa [V 5.0181] pāṭalivanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his Pāṭali grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

238.

238.

“Idamassa pāṭalivanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his Pāṭali grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

239.

239.

“Idamassa ambavanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his mango grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

240.

240.

“Idamassa ambavanaṃ, supupphitaṃ sabbakālikaṃ rammaṃ;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghena.

"This is his mango grove, beautiful and in bloom at all seasons; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

241.

241.

“Ayamassa pokkharaṇī, sañchannā aṇḍajehi vītikiṇṇā;

Yahimanuvicari [P 5.0190] rājā, parikiṇṇo itthāgārehi.

"This is his lotus pond, covered with flowers and teeming with birds; where the king, surrounded by the women of his court, used to wander."

242.

242.

“Ayamassa pokkharaṇī, sañchannā aṇḍajehi vītikiṇṇā;

Yahimanuvicari rājā, parikiṇṇo ñātisaṅghenā”ti. –

"This is his lotus pond, covered with flowers and teeming with birds; where the king, surrounded by the assembly of kinsmen, used to wander."

Imāhi gāthāhi paridevanto vicari.

With these verses, the great crowd wandered, lamenting.

Tattha vītikiṇṇoti sovaṇṇapupphehi ca nānāmālyehi ca samokiṇṇo. Parikiṇṇoti parivārito. Itthāgārehīti dāsiyo upādāya itthiyo itthāgārā nāma. Ñātisaṅghenāti amaccāpi idha ñātayo eva. Kūṭāgāranti sattaratanavicitto sayanakūṭāgāragabbho. Asokavanikāti asokavanabhūmi. Sabbakālikāti sabbakālaparibhogakkhamā niccapupphitā vā. Uyyānanti nandanavanacittalatāvanasadisaṃ uyyānaṃ[M 5.0201]. Sabbakālikanti chasupi utūsu uppajjanakapupphaphalasañchannaṃ. Kaṇikāravanādīsu sabbakālikanti sabbakāle supupphitaphalitameva. Sañchannāti nānāvidhehi jalajathalajakusumehi suṭṭhu sañchannā. Aṇḍajehi vītikiṇṇāti sakuṇasaṅghehi okiṇṇā.

There, `vītikiṇṇa` (strewn) means strewn with golden flowers and various garlands. `Parikiṇṇa` (surrounded) means encircled. `Itthāgārehi` (by his women) refers to the women, including the female attendants, who are called the `itthāgāra` (women's quarters). `Ñātisaṅghena` (by his kinsmen) here includes the ministers as well. `Kūṭāgāra` (gabled hall) refers to the bedchamber in the seven-jeweled gabled hall. `Asokavanikā` means the Asoka woodland. `Sabbakālika` (of all seasons) means always capable of being enjoyed, or always flowering. `Uyyāna` (garden) is a garden like the Nandana grove or the Cittalatā grove. `Sabbakālika` also means covered with flowers and fruits that arise in all six seasons. In the Kaṇikāra grove and others, `sabbakālika` means always fully blossoming and bearing fruit. `Sañchannā` (covered) means well covered with various aquatic and terrestrial flowers. `Aṇḍajehi vītikiṇṇā` (strewn with egg-born creatures) means crowded with flocks of birds.

Evaṃ tesu tesu ṭhānesu paridevitvā mahājano puna rājaṅgaṇaṃ āgantvā –

Thus, having lamented in all those various places, the multitude returned to the royal courtyard and—

243.

243.

“Rājā [V 5.0182] vo kho pabbajito, sutasomo rajjaṃ imaṃ pahatvāna;
