Kāsāyavatthavasano, nāgova ekako caratī”ti. –

"Indeed, your King Sutasoma has gone forth, abandoning this kingdom; clad in ochre robes, he wanders alone like a great elephant."

Gāthaṃ vatvā attano ghare vibhavaṃ pahāya puttadhītaro hatthesu gahetvā nikkhamitvā bodhisattasseva santikaṃ agamāsi, tathā mātāpitaro puttadārā soḷasasahassā ca nāṭakitthiyo. Sakalanagaraṃ tucchaṃ viya ahosi, janapadavāsinopi tesaṃ pacchato pacchato gamiṃsu. Bodhisatto dvādasayojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā himavantābhimukho pāyāsi. Athassa abhinikkhamanaṃ ñatvā sakko vissakammaṃ āmantetvā, “tāta vissakamma, sutasomamahārājā abhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [P 5.0191] laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, samāgamo ca mahā bhavissati, gaccha himavantapadese gaṅgātīre tiṃsayojanāyāmaṃ pañcadasayojanavitthataṃ assamapadaṃ māpehī”ti pesesi. So tathā katvā tasmiṃ assamapade pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādetvā ekapadikamaggaṃ māpetvā devalokameva gato.

Having spoken this verse, the multitude, leaving their wealth in their own houses and taking their sons and daughters by the hand, departed and went into the presence of the Bodhisatta; likewise his parents, his wives and children, and sixteen thousand dancing women followed. The entire city seemed as if empty, and the country-dwellers followed close behind them. The Bodhisatta, taking the company of twelve yojanas, set out toward the Himalayas. Then, knowing of his renunciation, Sakka summoned Vissakamma and said, 'Friend Vissakamma, the Great King Sutasoma has gone forth in renunciation. It is fitting to have a dwelling place, and there will be a large gathering. Go to the Himalayan region on the banks of the Ganges and construct a hermitage ground thirty yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width.' He sent him forth. Vissakamma did as he was told, and having prepared the requisites for renunciants in that hermitage and laid out a single-file path, he returned to the world of the gods.

Mahāsatto tena maggena gantvā taṃ assamapadaṃ pavisitvā paṭhamaṃ sayaṃ pabbajitvā pacchā sese pabbājesi, aparabhāge bahū pabbajiṃsu. Tiṃsayojanikaṃ ṭhānaṃ paripūri. Vissakammena pana assamamāpitaniyāmo ca bahūnaṃ pabbajitaniyāmo ca bodhisattassa assamapadasaṃvidahitaniyāmo ca hatthipālajātake (jā. 1.15.337 ādayo) āgatanayeneva veditabbo. Tattha mahāsatto yassa yasseva kāmavitakkādi micchāvitakko uppajjati, taṃ taṃ ākāsena upasaṅkamitvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā ovadanto gāthādvayamāha –

The Great Being, having gone by that path and entered the hermitage, first ordained himself and afterwards ordained the rest. Later, many others were ordained. The area of thirty yojanas was filled. The manner in which Vissakamma created the hermitage, the manner in which many were ordained, and the manner in which the Bodhisatta arranged the hermitage should be understood according to the method given in the Hatthipāla Jātaka. There, whenever a wrong thought such as a sensual thought arose in any of the ascetics, the Great Being would approach them through the air, and sitting cross-legged in the sky, he would give advice, reciting these two verses:

244.

244.

“Māssu [M 5.0202] pubbe ratikīḷitāni, hasitāni ca anussarittha;

Mā vo kāmā haniṃsu, rammañhi sudassanaṃ nagaraṃ.

"Do not recall past delights and amusements, nor the laughter; let not sensual desires destroy you, for the city of Sudassana is truly delightful."

245.

245.

“Mettacittañca bhāvetha, appamāṇaṃ divā ca ratto ca;

Agacchittha devapuraṃ, āvāsaṃ puññakammina”nti.

"And develop a heart of loving-kindness, immeasurable, by day and by night. You shall go to the city of the gods, the abode of those of meritorious deeds."

Tattha ratikīḷitānīti kāmaratiyo ca kāyavācākhiḍḍāvasena pavattakīḷitāni ca. Mā vo kāmā haniṃsūti mā tumhe vatthukāmakilesakāmā haniṃsu. Rammaṃ hīti sudassananagaraṃ nāma ramaṇīyaṃ, taṃ mā anussarittha. Mettacittanti idaṃ desanāmattameva, so pana cattāropi brahmavihāre [V 5.0183] ācikkhi. Appamāṇanti appamāṇasattārammaṇaṃ. Agacchitthāti gamissatha. Devapuranti brahmalokaṃ.

There, 'ratikīḷitāni' means sensual delights and amusements occurring through the play of body and speech. 'Mā vo kāmā haniṃsu' means let not the sensual objects or the sensual defilements destroy you. 'Rammaṃ hi' refers to the charming city named Sudassana; do not recall it. 'Mettacitta' is mentioned by way of a mere illustration, for he also taught all four divine abidings. 'Appamāṇaṃ' means having immeasurable beings as its object. 'Agacchittha' is equivalent to 'gamissatha' (you shall go). 'Devapura' means the Brahma-world.

Sopi [P 5.0192] isigaṇo tassovāde ṭhatvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosīti sabbaṃ hatthipālajātake āgatanayeneva kathetabbaṃ.

That group of sages, too, established in his advice, became destined for the Brahma-world. All this should be related in the manner given in the Hatthipāla Jātaka.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, candādevī rāhulamātā, jeṭṭhaputto sāriputto, kaniṭṭhaputto rāhulo, dhāti khujjuttarā, kulavaḍḍhanaseṭṭhi kassapo, mahāsenagutto moggallāno, somadattakumāro ānando, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, sutasomarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse, said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too the Tathāgata went forth in the great renunciation." Having said this, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the parents were of the great royal family; Queen Candā was Rāhula's mother; the eldest son was Sāriputta; the younger son was Rāhula; the nurse was Khujjuttarā; the merchant Kulavaḍḍhana was Kassapa; the commander-in-chief Mahāsenagutta was Moggallāna; Prince Somadatta was Ānanda; the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's assembly; and King Sutasoma was I myself."

Cūḷasutasomajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka is the fifth.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Suvapaṇḍitajambukakuṇḍalino, varakaññamalambusajātakañca;

Pavaruttamasaṅkhasirīvhayako, sutasomaarindamarājavaro.

Suva, Paṇḍita, Jambuka, Kuṇḍalī, and the Jātaka of the excellent maiden Alambusā; the supreme and excellent Saṅkha, called Sirī; and the noble King Sutasoma, tamer of foes.

Cattālīsanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of Forties is concluded.

18. Paṇṇāsanipāto

18. The Book of Fifties

[526] 1. Niḷinikājātakavaṇṇanā

[526] 1. The Commentary on the Niḷinikā Jātaka

Uddayhate [V 5.0184][P 5.0193][M 5.0203] janapadoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabba kathesi. Kathento ca taṃ bhikkhuṃ “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti pucchitvā “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti vutte “na esā kho, bhikkhu, idāneva tava anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya jhānā parihāyitvā mahāvināsaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"The country is burning up"—this the Teacher told while staying at Jetavana, concerning the allurement by a former wife. In the course of his talk, he asked that monk, "Monk, by whom have you been made dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "By my former wife," the Teacher said, "Monk, she is not causing you harm only now; in the past too, because of her, you fell away from meditation and met with great ruin." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto uggahitasippo isipabbajjaṃ pabbijitvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Alambusājātake vuttanayeneva taṃ paṭicca ekā migī gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā puttaṃ vijāyi, “isisiṅgo”tvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi. Atha naṃ pitā vayappattaṃ pabbājetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. So nacirasseva jhānābhiññā uppādetvā jhānasukhena kīḷi, ghoratapo paramadhitindriyo ahosi. Tassa sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “upāyenassa sīlaṃ bhindissāmī”ti tīṇi saṃvaccharāni sakalakāsiraṭṭhe vuṭṭhiṃ nivāresi, raṭṭhaṃ aggidaḍḍhaṃ viya ahosi. Sasse asampajjamāne dubbhikkhapīḷitā manussā sannipatitvā rājaṅgaṇe upakkosiṃsu. Atha ne rājā vātapāne ṭhito “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi. “Mahārāja, tīṇi [P 5.0194] saṃvaccharāni devassa avassantattā sakalaraṭṭhaṃ uddayhati, manussā dukkhitā, devaṃ vassāpehi, devā”ti. Rājā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathaṃ upavasantopi vassaṃ vassāpetuṃ nāsakkhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a wealthy northern brahmin family. Having come of age and mastered the arts, he went forth into the life of a sage, developed meditative attainments and higher knowledges, and took up residence in the Himalayan region. In the manner described in the Alambusā Jātaka, a doe conceived because of him and gave birth to a son, whose name was Isisiṅga. Then, when he reached maturity, his father ordained him and had him learn the preliminary exercises for kasina meditation. Before long, he produced meditative attainments and higher knowledges, delighted in the bliss of meditation, and became a severe ascetic with supreme control over his senses. Through the power of his virtue, Sakka’s abode shook. Sakka, reflecting and knowing the reason, thought, "I will break his virtue by an artifice." For three years, he withheld rain from the entire kingdom of Kāsi, and the land became as if scorched by fire. When the crops failed, the people, oppressed by famine, gathered and cried out in the palace courtyard. Then the king, standing at the window, asked, "What is this?" They replied, "Great King, because the deva has not sent rain for three years, the entire kingdom is burning; the people are suffering; make the deva rain, O King!" Although the king undertook the precepts and observed the Uposatha, he was unable to make it rain.

Tasmiṃ kāle sakko aḍḍharattasamaye tassa sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā ekobhāsaṃ katvā vehāse aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā “kosi tva”nti pucchi. “Sakkohamasmī”ti. “Kenatthenāgatosī”ti? “Vassati te, mahārāja[M 5.0204], raṭṭhe devo”ti? “Na vassatī”ti. “Jānāsi panassa avassanakāraṇa”nti? “Na jānāmi, sakkā”ti. “Mahārāja, himavantapadese [V 5.0185] isisiṅgo nāma tāpaso paṭivasati ghoratapo paramadhitindriyo. So nibaddhaṃ deve vassante kujjhitvā ākāsaṃ olokesi, tasmā devo na vassatī”ti. “Idāni panettha kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Tassa tape bhinne devo vassissatī”ti. “Ko panassa tapaṃ bhindituṃ samattho”ti? “Dhītā te, mahārāja, niḷinikā samatthā, taṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gantvā tāpasassa tapaṃ bhindāhī’ti pesehī”ti. Evaṃ so rājānaṃ anusāsitvā sakaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Rājā punadivase amaccehi saddhiṃ mantetvā dhītaraṃ pakkosāpetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, Sakka, at midnight, entered the king's royal chamber, made it bright with a single radiance, and stood in the air. The king, seeing him, asked, 'Who are you?' 'I am Sakka.' 'For what purpose have you come?' 'Great king, does the rain fall in your realm?' 'It does not rain.' 'Do you know the reason it does not rain?' 'I do not know, Sakka.' 'Great king, in the Himalayan region there lives an ascetic named Isisiṅga, of severe austerity and supreme control over his faculties. He constantly, whenever it rains, gets angry and glares at the sky; that is why the rain does not fall.' 'What, then, should be done about this?' 'When his austerity is broken, the rain will fall.' 'But who is capable of breaking his austerity?' 'Your daughter, great king, Niḷinikā, is capable. Summon her and send her, saying, "Go to such-and-such a place and break the ascetic’s austerity."' Having thus advised the king, Sakka returned to his own abode. The next day, the king consulted with his ministers, summoned his daughter, and spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Uddayhate janapado, raṭṭhañcāpi vinassati;

Ehi niḷinike gaccha, taṃ me brāhmaṇamānayā”ti.

"The countryside is burning up, the kingdom too is perishing; come, Niḷinikā, go, and bring that brahmin to me."

Tattha taṃ meti taṃ mama anatthakāriṃ brāhmaṇaṃ attano vasaṃ ānehi, kilesarativasenassa sīlaṃ bhindāhīti.

Here, 'bring that brahmin to me' means: 'bring that brahmin, who is causing me harm, under your control; break his virtue by the power of sensual passion.'

Taṃ sutvā sā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, she spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Nāhaṃ dukkhakkhamā rāja, nāhaṃ addhānakovidā;

Kathaṃ ahaṃ gamissāmi, vanaṃ kuñjarasevita”nti.

"I cannot endure hardship, O king, nor am I skilled in long journeys. How shall I go to the forest frequented by elephants?"

Tattha dukkhakkhamāti ahaṃ, mahārāja, dukkhassa khamā na homi, addhānampi na jānāmi, sāhaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmīti.

Here, 'cannot endure hardship' means: 'O great king, I am not one who can endure hardship, nor do I know the way; how then shall I go?'

Tato rājā dve gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then the king spoke two verses:

3.

3.

“Phītaṃ janapadaṃ gantvā, hatthinā ca rathena ca;

Dārusaṅghāṭayānena, evaṃ gaccha niḷinike.

"Go through the prosperous countryside by elephant and by chariot; and by a vehicle of joined wood, thus you must go, Niḷinikā."

4.

4.

“Hatthiassarathe [P 5.0195] pattī, gacchevādāya khattiye;

Taveva vaṇṇarūpena, vasaṃ tamānayissasī”ti.

"Go, O princess, taking with you elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers; by your very beauty and form, you will bring him under your control."

Tattha [V 5.0186] dārusaṅghāṭayānenāti, amma, niḷinike na tvaṃ padasā gamissasi, phītaṃ pana subhikkhaṃ khemaṃ attano janapadaṃ hatthivāhanehi ca rathavāhanehi ca [M 5.0205] gantvā tato parampi ajjhokāse paṭicchannena vayhādinā udakaṭṭhāne nāvāsaṅkhātena dārusaṅghāṭayānena gaccha. Vaṇṇarūpenāti evaṃ akilamamānā gantvā tava vaṇṇena ceva rūpasampadāya ca taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ attano vasaṃ ānayissasīti.

Here, 'by a vehicle of joined wood' means: 'My dear Niḷinikā, you will not go on foot. Rather, having gone to your own prosperous, well-provisioned, and secure territory by means of elephants and chariots, go further through the open country in a covered palanquin or the like, and at the water, go by a vehicle of joined wood, which is known as a boat.' 'By beauty and form' means: 'thus going without fatigue, by your beauty and the perfection of your form you will bring that brahmin under your control.'

Evaṃ so dhītarā saddhiṃ akathetabbampi raṭṭhaparipālanaṃ nissāya kathesi. Sāpi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Athassā sabbaṃ dātabbayuttakaṃ datvā amaccehi saddhiṃ uyyojesi. Amaccā taṃ ādāya paccantaṃ patvā tattha khandhāvāraṃ nivāsāpetvā rājadhītaraṃ ukkhipāpetvā vanacarakena desitena maggena himavantaṃ pavisitvā pubbaṇhasamaye tassa assamapadassa samīpaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisatto puttaṃ assamapade nivāsāpetvā sayaṃ phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ paviṭṭho hoti. Vanacarako sayaṃ assamaṃ agantvā tassa pana dassanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā niḷinikāya taṃ dassento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, for the sake of protecting the kingdom, he spoke with his daughter even of matters that should not be spoken of. She too agreed, saying, "Very well." Then, having given her everything that was fitting to be given, he sent her off with his ministers. The ministers, taking her, reached the border region, set up a camp there, and had the princess carried in a litter. Entering the Himalayas by the path shown by a forest-dweller, they arrived near the hermitage in the morning. At that moment, the Bodhisatta, having settled his son in the hermitage, had himself entered the forest for the sake of gathering fruits. The forest-dweller, not going to the hermitage himself but standing in a place from which it could be seen, showed it to Niḷinikā and spoke two verses:

5.

5.

“Kadalīdhajapaññāṇo, ābhujīparivārito;

Eso padissati rammo, isisiṅgassa assamo.

"Marked by banners of plantain trees, surrounded by birch trees, there appears the delightful hermitage of Isisiṅga."

6.

6.

“Eso aggissa saṅkhāto, eso dhūmo padissati;

Maññe no aggiṃ hāpeti, isisiṅgo mahiddhiko”ti.

"There is the well-kindled fire, and there the smoke is visible; I think the powerful Isisiṅga is tending his fire."

Tattha kadalīsaṅkhātā dhajā paññāṇaṃ assāti kadalīdhajapaññāṇo. Ābhujīparivāritoti bhujapattavanaparikkhitto. Saṅkhātoti eso aggi assa isisiṅgassa jhānena saṅkhāto paccakkhagato jalati. Maññe no agginti aggiṃ no hāpeti juhati paricaratīti maññāmi.

Here, 'kadalīdhajapaññāṇo' means its sign is banners known as plantain trees. 'Ābhujīparivārito' means surrounded by a forest of birch trees. 'Saṅkhāto' means this fire of Isisiṅga's, well-kindled by his meditative absorption and directly perceived, is burning. 'Maññe no aggiṃ hāpeti' means 'I think he does not let the fire go out, but offers oblations and attends to it.'

Amaccāpi bodhisattassa araññaṃ paviṭṭhavelāya assamaṃ parivāretvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā rājadhītaraṃ isivesaṃ gāhāpetvā [P 5.0196] suvaṇṇacīrakena nivāsanapārupanaṃ katvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā tantubaddhaṃ cittageṇḍukaṃ gāhāpetvā assamapadaṃ pesetvā sayaṃ bahi rakkhantā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sā tena geṇḍukena kīḷantī caṅkamakoṭiyaṃ otari. Tasmiṃ khaṇe isisiṅgo paṇṇasāladvāre pāsāṇaphalake nisinno hoti. So taṃ āgacchantiṃ disvā bhītatasito uṭṭhāya paṇṇasālaṃ [V 5.0187] pavisitvā aṭṭhāsi[M 5.0206]. Sāpissa paṇṇasāladvāraṃ gantvā kīḷiyeva. Satthā tañca tato uttari ca atthaṃ pakāsento tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The ministers, when the Bodhisatta had entered the forest, surrounded the hermitage and set up guards. They had the princess take the guise of an ascetic, dressed her in a golden bark-cloth for her inner and outer robes, adorned her with all her ornaments, and had her take a variegated ball tied with a string. They sent her into the hermitage while they themselves stood guard outside. Playing with the ball, she went down to the edge of the cloister walk. At that moment, Isisiṅga was seated on a stone slab at the door of the leaf-hut. Seeing her approach, frightened and alarmed, he rose, entered the leaf-hut, and stood there. She, still playing, went to the door of his leaf-hut. The Teacher, revealing the meaning of that and what followed, spoke these three verses:

7.

7.

“Tañca disvāna āyantiṃ, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Isisiṅgo pāvisi bhīto, assamaṃ paṇṇachādanaṃ.

“Seeing her approaching, wearing jeweled earrings, Isisiṅga, terrified, entered the leaf-covered hermitage.”

8.

8.

“Assamassa ca sā dvāre, geṇḍukenassa kīḷati;

Vidaṃsayantī aṅgāni, guyhaṃ pakāsitāni ca.

“At the door of the hermitage, she plays with her ball, displaying her limbs, both the hidden and the revealed.”

9.

9.

“Tañca disvāna kīḷantiṃ, paṇṇasālagato jaṭī;

Assamā nikkhamitvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravī”ti.

“Seeing her playing, the matted-haired ascetic in the leaf-hut came out from the hermitage and spoke these words.”

Tattha geṇḍukenassāti assa isisiṅgassa assamadvāre geṇḍukena kīḷati. Vidaṃsayantīti dassentī. Guyhaṃ pakāsitāni cāti guyhañca rahassaṅgaṃ pakāsitāni ca pākaṭāni mukhahatthādīni. Abravīti so kira paṇṇasālāya ṭhatvā cintesi – “sacāyaṃ yakkho bhaveyya, paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā maṃ murumurāpetvā khādeyya, nāyaṃ yakkho, tāpaso bhavissatī”ti assamā nikkhamitvā pucchanto gāthamāha –

Here, `geṇḍukenassāti` means 'she plays with a ball at the hermitage door of this Isisiṅga.' `Vidaṃsayantīti` means 'showing.' `Guyhaṃ pakāsitāni cāti` means 'both the secret, private parts, and the revealed, visible parts, such as the face and hands.' `Abravīti`—it is said that he stood in the leaf-hut and thought: 'If this were a yaksha, it would enter the leaf-hut, crunch me up and devour me. This is no yaksha; this must be an ascetic.' Then, coming out of the hermitage, he inquired by speaking a verse:

10.

10.

“Ambho ko nāma so rukkho, yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalaṃ;

Dūrepi khittaṃ pacceti, na taṃ ohāya gacchatī”ti.

“Friend, what is the name of that tree whose fruit is of such a nature? Even when thrown far, it returns; it does not leave you and go away.”

Tattha yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalanti yassa tava rukkhassa evaṃgatikaṃ manoramaṃ phalaṃ. Ko nāma so rukkhoti citrageṇḍukassa adiṭṭhapubbattā “rukkhaphalena tena bhavitabba”nti maññamāno evaṃ pucchati.

Here, `yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalanti` means 'of which tree of yours is there such a delightful fruit?' `Ko nāma so rukkhoti`—never having seen a painted ball before, he thinks, 'It must be the fruit of a tree,' and thus he asks.

Athassa sā rukkhaṃ ācikkhantī gāthamāha –

Then, telling him of the tree, she spoke this verse:

11.

11.

“Assamassa mama brahme, samīpe gandhamādane;

Bahavo tādisā rukkhā, yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalaṃ;

Dūrepi khittaṃ pacceti, na maṃ ohāya gacchatī”ti.

“Near my hermitage, O Brahmin, on Gandhamādana, there are many such trees whose fruits are of such a nature; even when thrown far, they return, not leaving me to go elsewhere.”

Tattha [V 5.0188][P 5.0197] samīpe gandhamādaneti gandhamādanapabbate mama assamassa samīpe. Yassa tevaṃgatanti yassa evaṃgataṃ, ta-kāro byañjanasandhikaroti.

Here, `samīpe gandhamādaneti` means 'near my hermitage on Gandhamādana mountain.' `Yassa tevaṃgatanti` is `yassa evaṃgataṃ`; the letter 'ta' creates a consonant sandhi.

Iti [M 5.0207] sā musāvādaṃ abhāsi. Itaropi saddahitvā “tāpaso eso”ti saññāya paṭisanthāraṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Thus she spoke a falsehood. The other, believing her and thinking, “This is an ascetic,” offered a friendly welcome and spoke this verse:

12.

12.

“Etū bhavaṃ assamimaṃ adetu, pajjañca bhakkhañca paṭiccha dammi;

Idamāsanaṃ atra bhavaṃ nisīdatu, ito bhavaṃ mūlaphalāni bhuñjatū”ti.

“Pray, enter this hermitage and partake of what is here. I offer ointment for your feet and food; please accept. Here is a seat, sir; please be seated. From here, sir, eat roots and fruits.”

Tattha assamimanti assamaṃ imaṃ bhavaṃ pavisatu. Adetūti yathāsannihitaṃ āhāraṃ paribhuñjatu. Pajjanti pādabbhañjanaṃ. Bhakkhanti madhuraphalāphalaṃ. Paṭicchāti paṭiggaṇha. Idamāsananti paviṭṭhakāle evamāha.

Here, `assamimanti` means 'may your reverence enter this hermitage.' `Adetūti` means 'may you partake of the food that is available.' `Pajjanti` means 'ointment for the feet.' `Bhakkhanti` means 'sweet fruits and other fruits.' `Paṭicchāti` means 'accept.' `Idamāsananti`: this is said at the time of entering.

Tassā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kaṭṭhattharaṇe nisīdantiyā suvaṇṇacīrake dvidhā gate sarīraṃ appaṭicchannaṃ ahosi. Tāpaso mātugāmasarīrassa adiṭṭhapubbattā taṃ disvā “vaṇṇo eso”ti saññāya evamāha –

When she entered the leaf-hut and sat on a wooden pallet, her golden garment parted, leaving her body partly uncovered. The ascetic, never having seen a woman's body before, upon seeing it, perceived, 'This is a wound!' and spoke thus:

13.

13.

“Kiṃ te idaṃ ūrūnamantarasmiṃ, supicchitaṃ kaṇharivappakāsati;

Akkhāhi me pucchito etamatthaṃ, kose nu te uttamaṅgaṃ paviṭṭha”nti.

“What is this between your thighs, so well-closed and appearing like something black? Tell me, whom I ask, this matter: has your principal organ entered a sheath?”

Tattha supicchitanti dvinnaṃ ūrūnaṃ samāgamakāle suphusitaṃ sippipuṭamukhasaṇṭhānaṃ. Subhalakkhaṇena hi asamannāgatāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvāṭadhātukaṃ hoti, samannāgatāya abbhunnataṃ sippipuṭamukhasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kaṇharivappakāsatīti ubhosu passesu kāḷakaṃ viya khāyati. Kose nu te uttamaṅgaṃ paviṭṭhanti tava uttamaṅgaṃ liṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ na paññāyati, kiṃ nu taṃ tava sarīrasaṅkhāte kose paviṭṭhanti pucchati.

Here, `supicchitanti` means 'well-closed,' referring to the shape of an oyster shell's mouth when the two thighs come together. For one not endowed with excellent characteristics, that place is like a pit; for one so endowed, it is raised like the mouth of an oyster shell. `Kaṇharivappakāsatīti` means 'it appears as if blackish on both sides.' `Kose nu te uttamaṅgaṃ paviṭṭhanti` means he asks: 'Your principal organ, the shape of the male member, is not apparent; has it entered the sheath that is your body?'

Atha naṃ sā vañcayantī gāthādvayamāha –

Then, deceiving him, she spoke two verses:

14.

14.

“Ahaṃ vane mūlaphalesanaṃ caraṃ, āsādayiṃ acchaṃ sughorarūpaṃ;

So [P 5.0198] maṃ patitvā sahasājjhapatto, panujja maṃ abbahi uttamaṅgaṃ.

“While wandering in the forest seeking roots and fruits, I encountered a bear of most terrifying form. It attacked me, suddenly seized me, and having thrown me down, tore out my principal organ.

15.

15.

“Svāyaṃ [V 5.0189][M 5.0208] vaṇo khajjati kaṇḍuvāyati, sabbañca kālaṃ na labhāmi sātaṃ;

Paho bhavaṃ kaṇḍumimaṃ vinetuṃ, kurutaṃ bhavaṃ yācito brāhmaṇattha”nti.

“This wound aches and itches; I find no comfort at any time. Your reverence is able to remove this itch; being asked, please act for a brahmin's benefit.”

Tattha āsādayinti ghaṭṭesiṃ, āgacchantaṃ disvā leḍḍunā paharinti attho. Patitvāti upadhāvitvā. Sahasājjhappattoti mamaṃ sahasā ajjhappatto sampatto. Panujjāti atha maṃ potetvā. Abbahīti mukhena mama uttamaṅgaṃ luñcitvā pakkāmi, tato paṭṭhāya imasmiṃ ṭhāne vaṇo jāto. Svāyanti so ayaṃ tato paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ vaṇo khajjati ceva kaṇḍuvañca karoti, tappaccayā sāhaṃ sabbakālaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ na labhāmi. Pahoti pahu samattho. Brāhmaṇatthanti bhavaṃ mayā yācito imaṃ brāhmaṇassa atthaṃ karotu, idaṃ me dukkhaṃ harāhīti vadati.

Here, `āsādayinti` means 'I provoked,' that is, 'seeing it coming, I struck it with a clod of earth.' `Patitvāti` means 'having run towards.' `Sahasājjhappattoti` means 'it suddenly reached me, came upon me.' `Panujjāti` means 'then, having thrown me down.' `Abbahīti` means 'it pulled out my principal organ with its mouth and departed, and from then on a wound appeared in this place.' `Svāyanti` means 'this wound of mine, from that time on, both aches and itches, and on account of that I do not obtain physical or mental happiness at any time.' `Pahoti` means 'able, capable.' `Brāhmaṇatthanti` means she says: 'Your reverence, being asked by me, please do this for a brahmin's benefit; remove this suffering of mine.'

So tassā musāvādaṃ “sabhāvo”ti saddahitvā “sace te evaṃ sukhaṃ hoti, karissāmī”ti taṃ padesaṃ oloketvā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Believing her lie to be the truth, he thought, “If this brings you relief, I will do it.” Then, looking at that place, he immediately spoke this verse:

16.

16.

“Gambhīrarūpo te vaṇo salohito, apūtiko vaṇagandho mahā ca;

Karomi te kiñci kasāyayogaṃ, yathā bhavaṃ paramasukhī bhaveyyā”ti.

“Your wound is deep and bloody, not putrid, and its smell is strong. I will prepare an astringent remedy for you, so that your reverence may become supremely comfortable.”

Tattha salohitoti rattobhāso. Apūtikoti pūtimaṃsarahito. Vaṇagandhoti thokaṃ duggandho. Kasāyayoganti ahaṃ keci rukkhakasāye gahetvā tava ekaṃ kasāyayogaṃ karomīti.

Here, `salohitoti` means 'reddish in appearance.' `Apūtikoti` means 'free from putrid flesh.' `Vaṇagandhoti` means 'a slightly unpleasant smell.' `Kasāyayoganti` means, 'I will take some tree-astringents and prepare an astringent remedy for you.'

Tato niḷinikā gāthamāha

Then Niḷinikā spoke this verse:

17.

17.

“Na mantayogā na kasāyayogā, na osadhā brahmacāri kamanti;

Yaṃ te mudu tena vinehi kaṇḍuṃ, yathā ahaṃ paramasukhī bhaveyya”nti.

“O holy one, neither applications of spells, nor applications of astringents, nor medicines are effective. With that soft part of yours, remove the itch, so that I may become supremely happy.”

Tattha [P 5.0199][M 5.0209] kamantīti, bho brahmacāri, imasmiṃ mama vaṇe neva mantayogā, na kasāyayogā, na pupphaphalādīni osadhāni kamanti, anekavāraṃ katehipi tehi etassa phāsukabhāvo na bhūtapubbo. Yaṃ pana te etaṃ mudu aṅgajātaṃ, tena ghaṭṭiyamānasseva tassa kaṇḍu na hoti, tasmā tena vinehi kaṇḍunti.

Here, `kamantīti` means: 'O holy one, on this wound of mine, neither applications of spells, nor applications of astringents, nor medicines such as flowers and fruits are effective. Though they have been applied many times, a state of comfort has never before arisen from them. But when that soft organ of yours is rubbed against it, the itch ceases. Therefore, with that, remove the itch.'

So [V 5.0190] “saccaṃ eso bhaṇatī”ti sallakkhetvā “methunasaṃsaggena sīlaṃ bhijjati, jhānaṃ antaradhāyatī”ti ajānanto mātugāmassa adiṭṭhapubbattā methunadhammassa ca ajānanabhāvena “bhesajja”nti vadantiyā tāya methunaṃ paṭisevi. Tāvadevassa sīlaṃ bhijji, jhānaṃ parihāyi. So dve tayo vāre saṃsaggaṃ katvā kilanto hutvā nikkhamitvā saraṃ oruyha nhatvā paṭippassaddhadaratho āgantvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ nisīditvā punapi taṃ “tāpaso”ti maññamāno vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

Reflecting, 'He speaks the truth,' and being unaware that 'virtue is broken and meditation vanishes through sexual contact,' due to never having seen a woman before and not knowing the nature of sexual activity, he engaged in intercourse with her as she spoke of it as 'medicine.' Immediately, his virtue was broken and his meditation was lost. Having engaged in such contact two or three times, he became exhausted; he went out, descended into the lake, bathed, and with his distress calmed, he returned and sat in the leaf hut. Still thinking her to be an ascetic, he asked about her dwelling place, reciting this verse:

18.

18.

“Ito nu bhoto katamena assamo, kacci bhavaṃ abhiramasi araññe;

Kacci nu te mūlaphalaṃ pahūtaṃ, kacci bhavantaṃ na vihiṃsanti vāḷā”ti.

From here, venerable sir, in which direction is your hermitage? Do you delight in the forest? Are roots and fruits abundant for you? Do wild beasts not harm you?

Tattha katamenāti ito katamena disābhāgena bhoto assamo. Bhavanti ālapanametaṃ.

In this context, 'katamena' means: 'By which direction from here is your hermitage, sir?' 'Bhoto' is a term of address.

Tato niḷinikā catasso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then Niḷinikā recited these four verses:

19.

19.

“Ito ujuṃ uttarāyaṃ disāyaṃ, khemā nadī himavatā pabhāvī;

Tassā tīre assamo mayha rammo, aho bhavaṃ assamaṃ mayhaṃ passe.

Straight from here, in the northern direction, is the Khemā river, which flows from the Himalayas. On its bank is my delightful hermitage. Oh, venerable sir, may you see my hermitage!

20.

20.

“Ambā ca sālā tilakā ca jambuyo, uddālakā pāṭaliyo ca phullā;

Samantato kimpurisābhigītaṃ, aho bhavaṃ assamaṃ mayhaṃ passe.

Mangoes, sal trees, tilakas and rose-apples, uddālakas and pāṭalis are in full bloom. All around, it is filled with the songs of kimpurisas. Oh, venerable sir, may you see my hermitage!

21.

21.

“Tālā [M 5.0210] ca mūlā ca phalā ca mettha, vaṇṇena gandhena upetarūpaṃ;

Taṃ [P 5.0200] bhūmibhāgehi upetarūpaṃ, aho bhavaṃ assamaṃ mayhaṃ passe.

Palmyra palms, roots, and fruits are here, endowed with color, fragrance, and beauty. That place is endowed with delightful regions. Oh, venerable sir, may you see my hermitage!

22.

22.

“Phalā ca mūlā ca pahūtamettha, vaṇṇena gandhena rasenupetā;

Āyanti ca luddakā taṃ padesaṃ, mā me tato mūlaphalaṃ ahāsu”nti.

Abundant fruits and roots are there, endowed with color, fragrance, and taste. Hunters come to that place—may they not take my roots and fruits from there!

Tattha uttarāyanti uttarāya. Khemāti evaṃnāmikā nadī. Himavatā pabhāvīti himavantato pavattati. Ahoti patthanatthe nipāto. Uddālakāti vātaghātakā. Kimpurisābhigītanti samantato parivāretvā madhurasaddena gāyantehi kimpurisehi abhigītaṃ. Tālā ca mūlā ca phalā ca metthāti ettha mama assame pāsādikā tālarukkhā ca tesaññeva vaṇṇagandhādisampannā kandasaṅkhātā [V 5.0191] mūlā ca phalā ca. Pahūtametthāti nānārukkhaphalā ca rukkhavallimūlā ca pahūtā ettha. Mā me tatoti taṃ mama assamapadaṃ sambahulā luddakā āgacchanti, mayā cettha āharitvā ṭhapitaṃ bahu madhurasamūlaphalāphalaṃ atthi, te mayi cirāyante mūlaphalāphalaṃ hareyyuṃ. Te tato mama mūlaphalāphalaṃ mā hariṃsu, tasmā sacepi mayā saddhiṃ āgantukāmo, ehi, no ce, ahaṃ gamissāmīti āha.

Herein, 'uttarāyanti' means in the north. 'Khemā' is a river of that name. 'Himavatā pabhāvīti' means it flows from the Himalayas. 'Ahoti' is a particle in the sense of a wish. 'Uddālakāti' refers to vātaghātaka trees. 'Kimpurisābhigītanti' means celebrated by kimpurisas, who surround the area and sing with sweet voices. 'Tālā ca mūlā ca phalā ca metthāti' means: here in my hermitage there are pleasing palmyra trees, and their roots (known as tubers) and fruits, endowed with color, fragrance, and so on. 'Pahūtametthāti' means: here there are abundant fruits of various trees and roots of trees and vines. 'Mā me tatoti' means: 'Many hunters come to that hermitage of mine, and I have brought and stored many sweet roots and fruits of all kinds there; if I delay, they might take the roots and fruits. May they not take my roots and fruits from there! Therefore, if you wish to come with me, come; if not, I shall go,' she said.

Taṃ sutvā tāpaso yāva pitu āgamanā adhivāsāpetuṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the ascetic, wishing her to wait until his father's return, spoke this verse:

23.

23.

“Pitā mamaṃ mūlaphalesanaṃ gato, idāni āgacchati sāyakāle;

Ubhova gacchāmase assamaṃ taṃ, yāva pitā mūlaphalato etū”ti.

My father has gone to seek roots and fruits; he will return now in the evening. We shall both go to that hermitage; let us wait until my father returns from the forest with roots and fruits.

Tattha ubhova gacchāmaseti mama pitu ārocetvā ubhova gamissāma.

Herein, 'ubhova gacchāmaseti' means: 'We will both go, having informed my father.'

Tato [M 5.0211] sā cintesi – “ayaṃ tāva araññeva vaḍḍhitabhāvena mama itthibhāvaṃ na jānāti, pitā panassa maṃ disvāva jānitvā ‘tvaṃ idha kiṃ karosī’ti kājakoṭiyā paharitvā sīsampi me bhindeyya, tasmiṃ anāgateyeva mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭati, āgamanakammampi me niṭṭhita”nti. Sā tassa āgamanūpāyaṃ ācikkhantī itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then she thought: 'This one, having grown up only in the forest, does not know my female nature. But his father, upon seeing me, will recognize me as a woman and, striking me with the end of his carrying pole, might even break my head, saying, "What are you doing here in my hermitage?" It is better for me to leave before he returns; the purpose of my coming from Bārāṇasī is also accomplished.' Devising a means for him to come, she spoke the next verse:

24.

24.

“Aññe [P 5.0201] bahū isayo sādhurūpā, rājīsayo anumagge vasanti;

Teyeva pucchesi mamassamaṃ taṃ, te taṃ nayissanti mamaṃ sakāse”ti.

Many other ascetics of virtuous appearance, royal sages, dwell along the path. Ask them about my hermitage, and they will lead you to my presence.

Tattha rājīsayoti, samma, mayā na sakkā cirāyituṃ, aññe pana sādhusabhāvā rājisayo ca brāhmaṇisayo ca anumagge mama assamamaggapasse vasanti, ahaṃ tesaṃ ācikkhitvā gamissāmi, tvaṃ te puccheyyāsi, te taṃ mama santikaṃ nayissantīti.

Herein, 'rājīsayoti' means: 'Friend, I cannot stay long. But other virtuous royal sages and brahmin sages dwell along the path, beside the way to my hermitage. I will inform them and go; you may ask them, and they will bring you to my presence.'

Evaṃ sā attano palāyanūpāyaṃ katvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā taṃ olokentameva “tvaṃ nivattā”ti vatvā āgamanamaggeneva amaccānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Te taṃ gahetvā khandhāvāraṃ gantvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sakkopi taṃ divasameva tussitvā sakalaraṭṭhe devaṃ vassāpesi, tato subhikkhaṃ janapadaṃ ahosi. Isisiṅgatāpasassapi tāya pakkantamattāya eva kāye ḍāho uppajji. So kampanto paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā vākacīraṃ pārupitvā [V 5.0192] socanto nipajji. Bodhisatto sāyaṃ āgantvā puttaṃ apassanto “kahaṃ nu kho gato”ti kājaṃ otāretvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā taṃ nipannakaṃ disvā “tāta, kiṃ karosī”ti piṭṭhiṃ parimajjanto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, having devised a means for her departure, she left the leaf-hut and, while he was still looking, said, 'Friend, follow after me,' and went by the same path back to the ministers. They took her and went to the camp, gradually reaching Bārāṇasī. Sakka, being highly pleased, caused rain to fall throughout the entire kingdom on that very day, and thus the land became prosperous. As soon as she had departed, a burning sensation arose in the body of the ascetic Isisiṅga. Trembling, he entered the leaf-hut, wrapped himself in a bark garment, and lay down in sorrow. In the evening, the Bodhisatta returned and, not seeing his son, wondered, 'Where could he have gone?' He put down his carrying pole, entered the leaf-hut, and seeing him lying there, stroking his back, he asked, 'Dear son, what is the matter?' and spoke these three verses:

25.

25.

“Na te kaṭṭhāni bhinnāni, na te udakamābhataṃ;

Aggīpi te na hāpito, kiṃ nu mandova jhāyasi.

Your firewood is not split, your water is not brought, and your fire has not been kindled—why do you brood so listlessly?

26.

26.

“Bhinnāni kaṭṭhāni huto ca aggi, tapanīpi te samitā brahmacārī;

Pīṭhañca mayhaṃ udakañca hoti, ramasi tuvaṃ brahmabhūto puratthā.

The firewood was split, the fire was offered, and your weariness was calmed, O practitioner of the holy life. My seat and water were prepared, and you, being like a Brahmā, took delight here formerly.

27.

27.

“Abhinnakaṭṭhosi [M 5.0212] anābhatodako, ahāpitaggīsi asiddhabhojano;

Na me tuvaṃ ālapasī mamajja, naṭṭhaṃ nu kiṃ cetasikañca dukkha”nti.

Your firewood is not split, your water is not fetched, your fire is not lit, and your meal is uncooked; you do not speak to me today. What has been lost? What is this mental suffering?

Tattha [P 5.0202] bhinnānīti araññato uddhaṭāni. Na hāpitoti na jalito. Bhinnānīti pubbe tayā mamāgamanavelāya kaṭṭhāni uddhaṭāneva honti. Huto ca aggīti aggi ca huto hoti. Tapanīti visibbanaaggisaṅkhātā tapanīpi te samitāva sayameva saṃvidahitāva hoti. Pīṭhanti mama āsanatthāya pīṭhañca paññattameva hoti. Udakañcāti pādadhovanaudakampi upaṭṭhāpitameva hoti. Brahmabhūtoti tuvampi ito puratthā seṭṭhabhūto imasmiṃ assame abhiramasi. Abhinnakaṭṭhosīti so dāni ajja anuddhaṭakaṭṭhosi. Asiddhabhojanoti na te kiñci amhākaṃ kandamūlaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā seditaṃ. Mamajjāti, mama putta, ajja na me tvaṃ ālapasi. Naṭṭhaṃ nu kinti kiṃ nu te naṭṭhaṃ vā, kiṃ cetasikaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, akkhāhi me nipannakāraṇanti pucchati.

Herein, 'bhinnāni' means: gathered from the forest. 'Na hāpito' means: not kindled. 'Bhinnāni' (in the second instance) means: 'previously, by the time of my arrival, the firewood was already gathered by you.' 'Huto ca aggi' means: 'and the fire was kindled.' 'Tapanī' refers to the fire for warming oneself; even that was prepared and arranged by you. 'Pīṭhaṃ' means: 'a seat was also already prepared for my sitting.' 'Udakaṃ' means: 'and water for washing the feet was also set out.' 'Brahmabhūto' means: 'formerly, you also, having become excellent, delighted in this hermitage.' 'Abhinnakaṭṭhosi' means: 'now, today, you are one who has not gathered firewood.' 'Asiddhabhojanoti' means: 'none of our roots or leaves have been boiled.' 'Mamajja' means: 'My son, today you do not speak to me.' 'Naṭṭhaṃ nu kinti' means he asks: 'What has been lost to you, or what mental suffering is there? Tell me the reason for your lying down.'

So pitu vacanaṃ sutvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathento āha –

Hearing his father's words, explaining the reason, he said:

28.

28.

“Idhāgamā jaṭilo brahmacārī, sudassaneyyo sutanū vineti;

Nevātidīgho na panātirasso, sukaṇhakaṇhacchadanehi bhoto.

A matted-haired young ascetic came here, beautiful to behold, with a lovely body, who illuminates this place with his radiance; neither too tall nor too short, with beautiful black locks of hair.

29.

29.

“Amassujāto apurāṇavaṇṇī, ādhārarūpañca panassa kaṇṭhe;

Dve yamā gaṇḍā ure sujātā, suvaṇṇatindukanibhā pabhassarā.

He was beardless, of a fresh complexion, and on his neck was an ornament like a ring. Two twin swellings were well-formed on his chest, radiant, like golden tinduka fruits.

30.

30.

“Mukhañca [V 5.0193] tassa bhusadassaneyyaṃ, kaṇṇesu lambanti ca kuñcitaggā;

Te jotare carato māṇavassa, suttañca yaṃ saṃyamanaṃ jaṭānaṃ.

His face was exceedingly beautiful to see, and from his ears hung ornaments with curled tips. These shone as the young man walked, as did the string that bound his matted hair.

31.

31.

“Aññā [M 5.0213] ca tassa saṃyamāni catasso, nīlā pītā lohitikā ca setā;

Tā piṃsare carato māṇavassa, tiriṭisaṅghāriva pāvusamhi.

Moreover, he has four other ornaments, blue, yellow, red, and white. They jingle as the young man walks, like a swarm of dragonflies in the rainy season.

32.

32.

“Na mikhalaṃ muñjamayaṃ dhāreti, na santhare no pana pabbajassa;

Tā [P 5.0203] jotare jaghanantare vilaggā, sateratā vijjurivantalikkhe.

He does not wear a girdle made of muñja grass, nor a bark garment, nor one made of grass. Those girdles fastened about his hips shine like a hundred flashes of lightning in the sky.

33.

33.

“Akhīlakāni ca avaṇṭakāni, heṭṭhā nabhyā kaṭisamohitāni;

Aghaṭṭitā niccakīḷaṃ karonti, haṃ tāta kiṃrukkhaphalāni tāni.

Without skin and without stalks, fastened to the waist below the navel; without touching each other, they play constantly. Oh, dear father, what tree-fruits are those?

34.

34.

“Jaṭā ca tassa bhusadassaneyyā, parosataṃ vellitaggā sugandhā;

Dvedhā siro sādhu vibhattarūpo, aho nu kho mayha tathā jaṭāssu.

His matted hair is exceedingly beautiful, with more than a hundred locks, fragrant, with curled ends. His head is well-divided by the arrangement of his locks. Oh, that my matted hair were like that!

35.

35.

“Yadā ca so pakirati tā jaṭāyo, vaṇṇena gandhena upetarūpā;

Nīluppalaṃ vātasameritaṃva, tatheva saṃvāti panassamo ayaṃ.

And when he loosens those matted locks, endowed with beauty and fragrance, this hermitage becomes fragrant, just like a blue lotus stirred by the wind.

36.

36.

“Paṅko ca tassa bhusadassaneyyo, netādiso yādiso mayhaṃ kāye;

So vāyati erito mālutena, vanaṃ yathā aggagimhe suphullaṃ.

The paste on his body is exceedingly beautiful, not like that on my body. It smells fragrant when stirred by the breeze, like a forest in full bloom at the peak of summer.

37.

37.

“Nihanti so rukkhaphalaṃ pathabyā, sucittarūpaṃ ruciraṃ dassaneyyaṃ;

Khittañca tassa punarehi hatthaṃ, haṃ tāta kiṃrukkhaphalaṃ nu kho taṃ.

He strikes a tree-fruit on the ground, of varied beauty, lovely to see; and when thrown, it returns to his hand. Oh, dear father, what kind of tree-fruit is that?

38.

38.

“Dantā [M 5.0214] ca tassa bhusadassaneyyā, suddhā samā saṅkhavarūpapannā;

Mano pasādenti vivariyamānā, na hi nūna so sākamakhādi tehi.

His teeth are exceedingly beautiful, pure, even, and like the finest conch shell; they gladden the mind when revealed. Surely he did not eat greens with them.

39.

39.

“Akakkasaṃ aggaḷitaṃ muhuṃ muduṃ, ujuṃ anuddhataṃ acapalamassa bhāsitaṃ;

Rudaṃ [P 5.0204] manuññaṃ karavīkasussaraṃ, hadayaṅgamaṃ rañjayateva me mano.

His speech is not harsh, not faltering, fluent, soft, direct, not arrogant, and not fickle; his voice is pleasing, with the sweet tone of a karavīka bird, heart-captivating, it truly delights my mind.

40.

40.

“Bindussaro [V 5.0194] nātivisaṭṭhavākyo, na nūna sajjhāyamatippayutto;

With a resonant voice, his speech not too diffuse; surely he is not excessively devoted to recitation.

Icchāmi bho taṃ punadeva daṭṭhuṃ, mitto hi me māṇavohu puratthā.

I wish, sir, to see him once again, for that young man was my friend in the past.

41.

41.

“Susandhi sabbattha vimaṭṭhimaṃ vaṇaṃ, puthū sujātaṃ kharapattasannibhaṃ;

Teneva maṃ uttariyāna māṇavo, vivaritaṃ ūruṃ jaghanena piḷayi.

A wound, well-joined and smooth all over, was broad and well-formed, like a lotus bud. Having come over me, the young man pressed my exposed thigh with his hip.

42.

42.

“Tapanti ābhanti virocare ca, sateratā vijjurivantalikkhe;

Bāhā mudū añjanalomasādisā, vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa sobhare.

They glow, they shine, and they radiate like a hundred flashes of lightning in the sky. His arms are soft, with hair dark as collyrium, and his fingers, beautifully rounded, are splendid.

43.

43.

“Akakkasaṅgo na ca dīghalomo, nakhāssa dīghā api lohitaggā;

Mudūhi bāhāhi palissajanto, kalyāṇarūpo ramayaṃ upaṭṭhahi.

His body is not rough, nor is his hair long; his nails are long and red-tipped. Embracing me with soft arms, the beautiful one delighted and attended to me.

44.

44.

“Dumassa tūlūpanibhā pabhassarā, suvaṇṇakambutalavaṭṭasucchavi;

Hatthā mudū tehi maṃ samphusitvā, ito gato tena maṃ dahanti tāta.

His hands are soft like cotton and radiant, with beautiful skin like the round surface of a golden mirror. Having touched me with them, he has gone from here; for that reason, they consume me, dear father.

45.

45.

“Na [M 5.0215] nūna so khārividhaṃ ahāsi, na nūna so kaṭṭhāni sayaṃ abhañji;

Na nūna so hanti dume kuṭhāriyā, na hissa hatthesu khilāni atthi.

Surely he did not carry a shoulder-yoke, surely he did not split firewood himself; surely he does not chop trees with an axe, for there are no calluses on his hands.

46.

46.

“Accho ca kho tassa vaṇaṃ akāsi, so maṃbravi ‘sukhitaṃ maṃ karohi’;

Tāhaṃ [P 5.0205] kariṃ tena mamāsi sokhyaṃ, so cabravi ‘sukhitosmī’ti brahme.

Indeed, a bear made a wound in his thigh, and he said to me, 'Make me happy.' I did so, and through that I had pleasure, and he said, 'I am happy,' O Brahmin.

47.

47.

“Ayañca te māluvapaṇṇasanthatā, vikiṇṇarūpāva mayā ca tena ca;

Kilantarūpā udake ramitvā, punappunaṃ paṇṇakuṭiṃ vajāma.

And this, your spread of māluvā leaves, is in a state of disorder because of me and him; exhausted after playing in the water, we returned again and again to the leaf-hut.

48.

48.

“Na majja mantā paṭibhanti tāta, na aggihuttaṃ napi yaññatantaṃ;

Na cāpi te mūlaphalāni bhuñje, yāva na passāmi taṃ brahmacāriṃ.

Today, the mantras do not occur to me, dear father, nor the fire sacrifice, nor the ritual; nor will I eat your roots and fruits as long as I do not see that young ascetic.

49.

49.

“Addhā pajānāsi tuvampi tāta, yassaṃ disaṃ vasate brahmacārī;

Taṃ maṃ disaṃ pāpaya tāta khippaṃ, mā te ahaṃ amarimassamamhi.

Surely you also know, dear father, in which direction that young ascetic dwells; lead me to that direction quickly, dear father, before I die in your hermitage.

50.

50.

“Vicitraphullañhi [V 5.0195] vanaṃ sutaṃ mayā, dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ dijasaṅghasevitaṃ;

Taṃ maṃ vanaṃ pāpaya tāta khippaṃ, purā te pāṇaṃ vijahāmi assame”ti.

For I have heard of a forest with variegated flowers, resounding with birds and frequented by flocks of birds; lead me quickly to that forest, dear father, before I give up my life in your hermitage.

Tattha idhāgamāti, tāta, imaṃ assamapadaṃ āgato. Sudassaneyyoti suṭṭhu dassaneyyo. Sutanūti suṭṭhu tanuko nātikiso nātithūlo[M 5.0216]. Vinetīti attano sarīrappabhāya assamapadaṃ ekobhāsaṃ viya vineti pūreti. Sukaṇhakaṇhacchadanehi bhototi, tāta, tassa bhoto sukaṇhehi kaṇhacchadanehi bhamaravaṇṇehi kesehi sukaṇhasīsaṃ sumajjitamaṇimayaṃ viya khāyati. Amassūjātoti na tāvassa massu jāyati, taruṇoyeva. Apurāṇavaṇṇīti acirapabbajito. Ādhārarūpañca panassa kaṇṭheti kaṇṭhe ca panassa amhākaṃ bhikkhābhājanaṭṭhapanaṃ pattādhārasadisaṃ piḷandhanaṃ atthīti muttāhāraṃ sandhāya vadati. Gaṇḍāti thane sandhāyāha. Ure sujātāti uramhi sujātā. “Urato”tipi pāṭho. Pabhassarāti pabhāsampannā. “Pabhāsare”tipi pāṭho, obhāsantīti attho.

Here, ‘has come’ means, dear father, he has come to this hermitage site. ‘Very beautiful to see’ means exceedingly lovely to see. ‘Of slender body’ means very slim, not too thin nor too stout. ‘Illuminates’ means he fills the hermitage site with his own bodily radiance, making it like a single expanse of light. ‘With very dark, dark coverings,’ dear father, means his head, with very dark, dark coverings—that is, hair the color of bees—appears like a well-polished gem. ‘Beardless’ means a beard has not yet grown on him, for he is young. ‘Of fresh appearance’ means he has not long been gone forth. ‘And a support-like form on his throat’ means that on his throat there is an ornament like a stand for our alms-bowl, referring to a pearl necklace. ‘Cheeks’ refers to the breasts. ‘Well-formed on the chest’ means well-formed on the chest. ‘From the chest’ is also a reading. ‘Radiant’ means possessed of radiance. ‘They radiate’ is also a reading, meaning they shine.

Bhusadassaneyyanti ativiya dassanīyaṃ. Kuñcitaggāti sīhakuṇḍalaṃ sandhāya vadati. Suttañcāti yaṃ tassa jaṭābandhanasuttaṃ, tampi jotati pabhaṃ muñcati. “Saṃyamāni catasso”ti iminā maṇisuvaṇṇapavāḷarajatamayāni cattāri piḷandhanāni dasseti[P 5.0206]. Tā piṃsareti tāni piḷandhanāni pāvusamhi pavuṭṭhe deve tiriṭisaṅghā viya viravanti. Mikhalanti mekhalaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ nivatthakañcanacīrakaṃ sandhāyāha. Na santhareti na vāke. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, yathā mayaṃ tiṇamayaṃ vā vākamayaṃ vā cīrakaṃ dhārema, na tathā so, so pana suvaṇṇacīrakaṃ dhāretīti. Akhīlakānīti atacāni nippaṇṇāni. Kaṭisamohitānīti kaṭiyaṃ baddhāni. Niccakīḷaṃ karontīti aghaṭṭitānipi niccakālaṃ kīḷāyanti. Haṃ, tātāti hambho, tāta. Kiṃ rukkhaphalāni tānīti tāni tassa māṇavassa suttāruḷhāni kaṭiyaṃ baddhāni katararukkhaphalāni nāmāti maṇisaṅghāṭiṃ sandhāyāha.

‘Very beautiful to see’ means exceedingly lovely to see. ‘With curled ends’ refers to lion-earrings. ‘And the thread’ refers to the cord binding his matted hair, which also shines and emits radiance. ‘Four restraints’ indicates the four ornaments made of gems, gold, coral, and silver. ‘They jingle’ means those ornaments resound like a flock of tiriṭa birds when it has rained in the rainy season. ‘Girdle’ means mekhala, or this is the reading itself. This refers to the golden bark-cloth that he wears. ‘Not a covering’ means not of bark. This is what is meant: dear father, just as we wear a garment made of grass or bark, he does not; instead, he wears a golden garment. ‘Without blemishes’ means without skin, smooth. ‘Concealed at the waist’ means bound at the waist. ‘They constantly play’ means even when unstruck, they are always playing. ‘Alas, dear father’ means ‘Indeed, dear father.’ ‘What tree-fruits are those?’ refers to a cluster of gems, as if asking: what tree's fruits are those, strung on a thread and bound to that young man's waist?

Jaṭāti jaṭāmaṇḍalākārena baddharatanamissakakesavaṭṭiyo sandhāyāha. Vellitaggāti kuñcitaggā. Dvedhāsiroti tassa sīsaṃ dvedhā katvā baddhānaṃ jaṭānaṃ vasena suṭṭhu vibhattarūpaṃ. Tathāti yathā tassa māṇavassa jaṭā, tathā tumhehi mama na baddhā, aho vata mamapi tathā assūti patthento āha. Upetarūpāti upetasabhāvā. Vātasameritaṃvāti [M 5.0217] yathā nāma nīluppalaṃ vātena samīritaṃ, tatheva ayaṃ imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe assamo saṃvāti. Netādisoti, tāta, yādiso [V 5.0196] mama kāye paṅko, netādiso tassa sarīre. So hi dassanīyo ceva sugandho ca. Aggagimheti vasantasamaye.

‘Matted hair’ refers to the tresses of hair mixed with jewels, bound in the shape of a circular crest. ‘With twisted ends’ means with curled ends. ‘Head in two parts’ means his head is beautifully formed by means of the matted locks being bound in two parts. ‘Thus’ means he expresses a longing: just as that young man’s matted hair is, so mine has not been bound by you; oh, would that mine were also thus! ‘Possessed of form’ means possessed of such a nature. ‘Stirred by the wind’ means just as a blue lotus is stirred by the wind, so this hermitage in this forest grove becomes fragrant. ‘Not like that’ means, dear father, the paste on his body is not like the mud on my body. For his is both lovely to see and fragrant. ‘At the height of summer’ means in the spring season.

Nihantīti paharati. Kiṃ rukkhaphalaṃ nu kho tanti katararukkhassa nu kho taṃ phalaṃ. Saṅkhavarūpapannāti sudhotasaṅkhapaṭibhāgā. Na hi nūna so sākamakhādi tehīti na nūna so māṇavo mayaṃ viya tehi dantehi rukkhapaṇṇāni ceva mūlaphalāphalāni ca khādi. Amhākañhi tāni khādantānaṃ sabalā paṇṇavaṇṇā dantāti dīpeti.

‘Strikes’ means hits. ‘What tree-fruit indeed is that?’ means of which tree indeed is that fruit. ‘Possessed of the form of a fine conch’ means resembling a well-washed conch. ‘Surely he did not eat greens with them’ means surely that young man did not, like us, eat tree leaves and various roots and fruits with those teeth. For it is shown that for us who eat those things, our teeth become mottled and leaf-colored.

Akakkasanti, tāta, tassa bhāsitaṃ apharusaṃ agaḷitaṃ, punappunaṃ vadantassāpi madhuratāya muhuṃ muduṃ, apamussatāya ujuṃ, avikkhittatāya anuddhaṭaṃ, patiṭṭhitatāya acapalaṃ. Rudanti bhāsamānassa sarasaṅkhātaṃ rudampi manoharaṃ karavīkassa viya sussaraṃ sumadhuraṃ. Rañjayatevāti mama mano rañjatiyeva. Bindussaroti piṇḍitassaro. Māṇavohūti so hi māṇavo puratthā mama mitto ahu.

‘Not harsh,’ dear one, is his speech—neither rough nor grating. Even when speaking repeatedly, due to its sweetness, it is exceedingly soft. It does not slip away, but is direct; it is not scattered, but composed; it is established, not unsteady. When he speaks, his voice, known as sound, is also delightful, melodious and very sweet like that of the karavīka bird. ‘It truly delights’ means my mind is truly delighted. ‘Bindussara’ means having a compact voice. ‘He was a young man’ means that young man was formerly my friend.

Susandhi sabbattha vimaṭṭhimaṃ vaṇanti tāta tassa māṇavassa ūrūnaṃ antare ekaṃ vaṇaṃ atthi, taṃ susandhi suphusitaṃ sippipuṭamukhasadisaṃ, sabbattha vimaṭṭhaṃ samantato maṭṭhaṃ. Puthūti mahantaṃ. Sujātanti susaṇṭhitaṃ. Kharapattasannibhanti [P 5.0207] supupphitapadumamakuḷasannibhaṃ. Uttariyānāti uttaritvā avattharitvā. Piḷayīti pīḷesi. Tapantīti tassa māṇavassa sarīrato niccharantā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaraṃsiyo jalanti obhāsanti virocanti ca. Bāhāti bāhāpissa mudū. Añjanalomasādisāti añjanasadisehi lomehi samannāgatā. Vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa sobhareti hatthāpissa varalakkhaṇavicitrāhi pavālaṅkurasadisāhi vaṭṭaṅgulīhi samannāgatā sobhanti.

‘A mark well-joined and smooth all over’: Dear one, between that young man's thighs there is a mark; it is well-joined, well-fitting, like the opening of an oyster shell, smooth all over, polished all around. ‘Broad’ means large. ‘Well-formed’ means well-proportioned. ‘Like a kharapattā’ means like a fully blossomed lotus bud. ‘Having covered’ means having come over and covered. ‘He pressed’ means he pressed. ‘They glow’ means the golden-colored rays issuing from that young man's body burn, shine, and radiate. ‘Arms’ means his arms are also soft. ‘Like collyrium-dark hair’ means endowed with hairs like collyrium. ‘His fingers, beautifully rounded, are splendid’ means his hands, too, are splendid, being endowed with beautifully rounded fingers, adorned with excellent marks and like coral sprouts.

Akakkasaṅgoti kacchupīḷakādirahitaaṅgapaccaṅgo. Ramayaṃ upaṭṭhahīti maṃ ramayanto upaṭṭhahi paricari. Tūlūpanibhāti mudubhāvassa upamā. Suvaṇṇakambutalavaṭṭasucchavīti suvaṇṇamayaṃ ādāsatalaṃ viya vaṭṭā ca succhavi ca, parimaṇḍalatalā ceva sundaracchavi cāti attho. Samphusitvāti suṭṭhu phusitvā attano hatthasamphassaṃ mama sarīre pharāpetvā. Ito gatoti mama [M 5.0218] olokentasseva ito gato. Tena maṃ dahantīti tena tassa hatthasamphassena idāni maṃ dahanti. Tathā hi tassa gatakālato paṭṭhāya mama sarīre ḍāho uṭṭhito, tenamhi domanassappatto nipannoti.

‘With limbs not rough’ means his major and minor limbs were free from scabies, boils, and so on. ‘He attended, delighting me’ means delighting me, he attended upon and served me. ‘Like cotton down’ is a simile for softness. ‘Like a golden mirror-surface, round and of beautiful skin’ means it was round and of beautiful skin like the surface of a golden mirror; the meaning is that its surface is perfectly round and its complexion is beautiful. ‘Having touched me thoroughly’ means having touched me well, causing the touch of his hand to pervade my body. ‘He departed from here’ means he departed from here even as I was looking on. ‘By that, they burn me’ means now, by that touch of his hand, they burn me. Indeed, from the time he departed, a burning sensation has arisen in my body; because of that, afflicted with grief, I am lying down.

Na [V 5.0197] nūna so khārividhanti, tāta, nūna so māṇavo na khāribhāraṃ ukkhipitvā vicari. Khilānīti kilāni, “ayameva vā pāṭho. Sokhyanti sukhaṃ. Māluvapaṇṇasanthatā vikiṇṇarūpāvāti, tāta, ayaṃ tava māluvapaṇṇasanthatā ajja mayā ca tena ca aññamaññaṃ parāmasanāliṅganavasena parivattantehi vikiṇṇā viya ākulabyākulā jātā. Punappunaṃ paṇṇakuṭiṃ vajāmāti, tāta, ahañca so ca abhiramitvā kilantarūpā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā udakaṃ pavisitvā ramitvā vigatadarathā punappunaṃ imameva kuṭiṃ pavisāmāti vadati.

‘Surely he is not a carrier of a shoulder-pole’ means, dear one, surely that young man did not wander about carrying a load on a shoulder-pole. ‘Khilāni’ means weary; or this is indeed the reading. ‘Sokhya’ means happiness. ‘This spread of māluvā leaves is as if scattered’ means, dear one, this spread of your māluvā leaves today, by me and him turning over through mutual touching and embracing, has become as if scattered and disarranged. ‘Again and again we go to the leaf hut’ means he says: ‘Dear one, I and he, having delighted ourselves and become weary, having emerged from the leaf-hall, entered the water and delighted therein, our fatigue dispelled, again and again we enter this very hut.’

Na majja mantāti ajja mama tassa gatakālato paṭṭhāya neva mantā paṭibhanti na upaṭṭhahanti na ruccanti. Na aggihuttaṃ napi yaññatantanti mahābrahmuno ārādhanatthāya kattabbahomavidhūpanādiyaññakiriyāpi me na paṭibhāti na upaṭṭhāti na ruccati. Na cāpi teti tayā ābhatamūlaphalāphalānipi na bhuñjāmi. Yassaṃ disanti yassaṃ disāyaṃ. Vananti tassa māṇavassa assamaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitavananti.

‘Not for me today are spells’ means: today, from the time of his departure, spells neither occur to me, nor come to mind, nor do they please me. ‘Neither the fire-oblation nor the sacrificial ritual’ means: even the sacrificial rites, such as oblations and fumigations to be performed for the propitiation of Mahābrahmā, neither occur to me, nor come to mind, nor do they please me. ‘Nor yours’ means: I do not even eat the roots and various fruits brought by you. ‘In which direction’ means in whichever direction. ‘The forest’ means the forest standing around that young man’s hermitage.

Tassevaṃ vilapantassa taṃ vilāpaṃ sutvā mahāsatto “ekāya itthiyā imassa sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā taṃ ovadanto cha gāthāyo abhāsi –

Hearing the lamentation of his son who was thus wailing, the Great Being, knowing, 'A woman must have destroyed this one’s virtue,' and wishing to advise him, spoke six verses:

51.

51.

“Imasmāhaṃ jotirase vanamhi, gandhabbadevaccharasaṅghasevite;

Isīnamāvāse [P 5.0208] sanantanamhi, netādisaṃ aratiṃ pāpuṇetha.

“In this forest where the sacrificial fire glows, frequented by throngs of gandhabbas and celestial nymphs, in this ancient abode of seers, you should not give way to such discontent.”

52.

52.

“Bhavanti mittāni atho na honti, ñātīsu mittesu karonti pemaṃ;

Ayañca jammo kissa vā niviṭṭho, yo neva jānāti ‘kutomhi āgato’.

“Friends may exist, and then they may not; people show affection among relatives and friends. But this wretched fellow, on what is he intent, who does not even know, ‘From where have I come?’”

53.

53.

“Saṃvāsena [M 5.0219] hi mittāni, sandhīyanti punappunaṃ;

Sveva mitto asaṃgantu, asaṃvāsena jīrati.

“Indeed, through living together, friendships are joined again and again. But for a person who does not associate, that very friendship decays through lack of association.”

54.

54.

“Sace tuvaṃ dakkhasi brahmacāriṃ, sace tuvaṃ sallape brahmacārinā;

Sampannasassaṃva mahodakena, tapoguṇaṃ khippamimaṃ pahissasi.

“If you see that ascetic, if you converse with that ascetic, then like a field of ripe grain swept away by a great flood, you will quickly lose this ascetic quality.”

55.

55.

“Punapi ce dakkhasi brahmacāriṃ, punapi ce sallape brahmacārinā;

Sampannasassaṃva mahodakena, usmāgataṃ khippamimaṃ pahissasi.

“Again, if you see that ascetic, again if you converse with that ascetic, then like a field of ripe grain swept away by a great flood, you will quickly lose this spiritual glow.”

56.

56.

“Bhūtāni [V 5.0198] hetāni caranti tāta, virūparūpena manussaloke;

Na tāni sevetha naro sapañño, āsajja naṃ nassati brahmacārī”ti.

“Indeed, dear one, these spirits roam about in the human world in varied forms. A wise person should not associate with them; for having encountered them, the celibate perishes.”

Tattha imasmāti imasmiṃ. Hanti nipātamattaṃ. Jotiraseti hūyamānassa jotino raṃsiobhāsite. Sanantanamhīti porāṇake. Pāpuṇethāti pāpuṇeyya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, evarūpe vane vasanto yaṃ aratiṃ tvaṃ patto, etādisaṃ na pāpuṇeyya paṇḍito kulaputto, pattuṃ nārahatīti attho.

Therein, `imasmā` means `imasmiṃ` (in this). `Haṃ` is merely a particle. ‘In the radiant’ (jotirase) means illuminated by the rays of the sacrificial fire. ‘Immemorial’ (sanantanamhi) means ancient. ‘You should attain’ (pāpuṇetha) means ‘one should attain’ (pāpuṇeyya). This is what is said: ‘Dear one, dwelling in such a forest, a wise son of good family should not attain such discontent as you have reached; the meaning is, it is not fitting to attain it.’

“Bhavantī”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ mahāsatto antogatameva bhāsati. Ayamettha adhippāyo – loke sattānaṃ mittāni nāma hontipi na hontipi tattha yesaṃ honti, te attano ñātīsu ca mittesu ca pemaṃ karonti. Ayañca jammoti migasiṅgo lāmako. Kissa vā niviṭṭhoti kena nāma kāraṇena tasmiṃ mātugāme mittasaññāya niviṭṭho, so migiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattitvā araññe vaḍḍhitattā “kutomhi āgato”ti attano āgataṭṭhānamattampi [P 5.0209] na jānāti, pageva ñātimitteti.

The Great Being spoke this verse beginning with ‘Friends may be’ (Bhavanti) only to himself. This is the meaning here: in the world, beings may or may not have friends; among those who do, they show affection to their own relatives and friends. ‘And this base person’ (Ayañca jammo) refers to the wretched Migasiṅga. ‘On what is he intent?’ (Kissa vā niviṭṭho) means for what reason is he intent on that woman with the perception of friendship? Having been conceived in a doe’s womb and raised in the forest, he does not even know the place from which he came, let alone relatives and friends.

Punappunanti, tāta, mittāni nāma punappunaṃ saṃvāsena saṃsevanena sandhīyanti ghaṭīyanti. Sveva mittoti so eva mitto asaṃgantu asamāgacchantassa purisassa tena asamāgamasaṅkhātena asaṃvāsena jīrati vinassati[M 5.0220]. Saceti tasmā, tāta, sace tvaṃ punapi taṃ dakkhasi, tena vā sallapissasi, atha yathā nāma nipphannasassaṃ mahoghena harīyati, evaṃ imaṃ attano tapoguṇaṃ pahissasi hāressasīti attho. Usmāgatanti samaṇatejaṃ.

‘Again and again’ means, dear one, friendships are indeed bound and joined together again and again through living together and association. ‘That very friend’ means: for a person who does not associate or meet, that very friendship decays and perishes through that lack of association, which is called non-meeting. ‘If’ means: therefore, dear one, if you see her again or converse with her, then just as a ripened crop is swept away by a great flood, so too will you abandon and lose your own ascetic quality; this is the meaning. ‘Feverish heat’ means the ascetic’s spiritual power.

Virūparūpenāti vividharūpena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, manussalokasmiñhi etāni yakkhinisaṅkhātāni bhūtāni vividharūpapaṭicchannena attano rūpena attano vasaṃ gate khādituṃ caranti, tāni sapañño naro na sevetha. Tādisañhi bhūtaṃ āsajja naṃ patvā nassati brahmacārī, diṭṭhosi tāya yakkhiniyā na khāditoti puttaṃ ovadi.

‘With varied form’ means with various forms. This is what is said: ‘Dear one, in the human world, these beings known as yakkhiṇīs roam about, their own forms concealed by various forms, in order to devour those who have come under their power. A wise person should not associate with them. For having encountered such a being, the celibate perishes. You were seen by that yakkhiṇī, but you were not devoured’—thus he admonished his son.

So pitu kathaṃ sutvā “yakkhinī kira sā”ti bhīto cittaṃ nivattetvā “tāta, etto na gamissāmi, khamatha me”ti khamāpesi. Sopi naṃ samassāsetvā “ehi tvaṃ, māṇava, mettaṃ bhāvehi, karuṇaṃ, muditaṃ, upekkha”nti brahmavihārabhāvanaṃ ācikkhi. So tathā paṭipajjitvā puna jhānābhiññā nibbattesi.

Hearing his father’s words and thinking, ‘It seems she is a yakkhiṇī,’ he became frightened and turned his mind away. Saying, ‘Father, I will not go from here; forgive me,’ he asked for forgiveness. His father consoled him and instructed him, teaching the cultivation of the divine abodes: ‘Come, young man, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.’ Practicing accordingly, he again attained the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges.

Satthā [V 5.0199] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā niḷinikā purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, isisiṅgo ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, pitā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Niḷinikā was the former wife, Isisiṅga was the discontented monk, and the father was none other than myself.

Niḷinikājātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Niḷinikā Jātaka, the First.

[527] 2. Ummādantījātakavaṇṇanā

[527] 2. The Commentary on the Ummādantī Jātaka

Nivesanaṃ kassanudaṃ sunandāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ itthiṃ oloketvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā cittaṃ nivattetuṃ asakkonto vihārameva āgantvā tato paṭṭhāya sallaviddho viya rāgāturo bhantamigapaṭibhāgo kiso dhamanīsanthatagatto uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto anabhirato ekiriyāpathepi [M 5.0221] cittassādaṃ alabhanto ācariyavattādīni pahāya uddesaparipucchākammaṭṭhānānuyogarahito vihāsi. So sahāyabhikkhūhi “pubbe tvaṃ, āvuso, santindriyo vippasannamukhavaṇṇo, idāni no tathā, kiṃ [P 5.0210] nu kho kāraṇa”nti puṭṭho, “āvuso, anabhiratomhī”ti āha. Atha naṃ te “abhiramāvuso, sāsane, buddhuppādo nāma dullabho, tathā saddhammassavanaṃ manussapaṭilābho ca, so tvaṃ manussapaṭilābhaṃ paṭilabhitvā dukkhassantakiriyaṃ patthayamāno assumukhaṃ ñātijanaṃ pahāya saddhāya pabbajitvā kiṃkāraṇā kilesavasaṃ yāsi, kilesā nāmete gaṇḍuppādakapāṇakaṃ upādāya sabbabālajanasādhāraṇā, ye tesaṃ vatthubhūtā, tepi appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā, maṃsapesūpamā kāmā, tiṇukkūpamā kāmā, aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā, supinakūpamā kāmā, yācitakūpamā kāmā, rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā, asisūnūpamā kāmā, sattisūlūpamā kāmā, sappasirūpamā kāmā, aggikkhandhūpamā kāmā, tvaṃ nāma evarūpe buddhasāsane pabbajitvā evaṃ anatthakārakānaṃ kilesānaṃ vasaṃ gatosī”ti ovaditvā attano kathaṃ gāhāpetuṃ asakkontā satthu santikaṃ dhammasabhaṃ netvā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, anicchamānakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ānayitthā”ti vutte, “bhante, ayaṃ kira bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhito”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā “saccaṃ kirā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitā rajjaṃ anusāsantāpi kilese uppanne tassa vasaṃ agantvā cittaṃ nivāretvā na ayuttakaṃ kariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Whose beautiful dwelling is this?” The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a discontented monk. It is said that one day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a beautifully adorned woman of supreme beauty. His mind became attached, and unable to turn it away, he returned to the monastery. From then on, like one struck by an arrow, tormented by lust, resembling a frantic deer, emaciated, his body covered with veins, pale and wan, he took no delight. Unable to find any pleasure even in a single posture, he abandoned his duties towards his teacher and others, and lived neglectful of recitation, questioning, and the practice of meditation subjects. When his fellow monks asked him, “Friend, formerly your faculties were calm and your countenance serene, but now it is not so. What is the reason?” he replied, “Friends, I am discontented.” Then they advised him, “Friend, take delight in the Dispensation. The arising of a Buddha is rare, as is hearing the true Dhamma and obtaining a human birth. Having obtained a human birth, striving for the end of suffering, having left behind your weeping relatives and gone forth out of faith, for what reason do you fall under the sway of the defilements? These defilements, beginning even with earthworms, are common to all foolish people. The things that are their basis—sensual pleasures—are of little satisfaction, full of suffering and distress; the danger in them is even greater. Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, like a piece of flesh, like a grass torch, like a pit of coals, like a dream, like borrowed goods, like the fruit of a tree, like a butcher’s block, like a spear and stake, like a snake’s head, like a blazing fire. You, having gone forth in such a Dispensation of the Buddha, have come under the sway of such destructive defilements!” Unable to make him accept their words, they brought him to the Dhamma assembly in the presence of the Teacher. When the Teacher asked, “Monks, why have you brought this unwilling monk?” they replied, “Venerable sir, this monk is discontented.” The Teacher asked, “Is it true?” and when it was said, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” he said, “Monks, the wise men of old, even while ruling a kingdom, when defilements arose, did not fall under their sway but restrained their minds and did nothing improper.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 5.0200] siviraṭṭhe ariṭṭhapuranagare sivi nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti, “sivikumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Senāpatissapi putto jāyi, “abhipārako”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te ubhopi sahāyā hutvā abhivaḍḍhantā soḷasavassikā hutvā takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgamiṃsu. Rājā puttassa rajjaṃ adāsi. Sopi abhipārakaṃ senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tasmiṃyeva nagare tiriṭivacchassa nāma asītikoṭivibhavassa seṭṭhino dhītā nibbatti uttamarūpadharā sobhaggappattā subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatā, tassā nāmaggahaṇadivase “ummādantī”ti [M 5.0222] nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Sā soḷasavassikakāle atikkantamānusavaṇṇā devaccharā viya abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā ahosi. Ye ye puthujjanā taṃ passanti, te te sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā [P 5.0211] surāpānamadamattā viya kilesamadena mattā hutvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ samatthā nāma nāhesuṃ.

In the past, in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the Sivi kingdom, a king named Sivi reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, and they named him “Prince Sivi.” A son was also born to the general, and they named him “Abhipāraka.” The two grew up as companions, and at the age of sixteen, they went to Takkasilā, learned the arts, and returned. The king gave the kingdom to his son. He, having established Abhipāraka in the position of general, ruled righteously. In that very city, a daughter was born to a merchant named Tiriṭivaccha, who possessed eighty crores of wealth. She was of supreme beauty, had attained good fortune, and was endowed with auspicious marks. On her naming day, they named her “Ummādantī.” At the age of sixteen, her beauty surpassed that of humans—she was as lovely as a celestial nymph, beautiful, charming, pleasing, and endowed with the highest perfection of complexion. Whatever ordinary men saw her, they were unable to maintain their composure; like those intoxicated by drinking liquor, they became drunk with the intoxication of the defilements and were not at all capable of establishing mindfulness.

Athassā pitā tiriṭivaccho rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, mama gehe itthiratanaṃ uppannaṃ, raññova anucchavikaṃ, lakkhaṇapāṭhake brāhmaṇe pesetvā taṃ vīmaṃsāpetvā yathāruci karohī”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti vatvā brāhmaṇe pesesi. Te seṭṭhigehaṃ gantvā katasakkārasammānā pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe ummādantī sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā tesaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Te taṃ disvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontā kilesamadamattā hutvā attano vippakatabhojanabhāvaṃ na jāniṃsu. Ekacce ālopaṃ gahetvā “bhuñjissāmā”ti saññāya sīse ṭhapesuṃ, ekacce upakacchantare khipiṃsu, ekacce bhittiṃ pahariṃsu, sabbeva ummattakā ahesuṃ. Sā te disvā “ime kira mama lakkhaṇaṃ vīmaṃsissanti, gīvāyaṃ ne gahetvā nīharathā”ti nīharāpesi. Te maṅkubhūtā rājanivesanaṃ gantvā ummādantiyā kuddhā “deva, sā itthī kāḷakaṇṇī, na tumhākaṃ anucchavikā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā “kāḷakaṇṇī kirā”ti na taṃ āṇāpesi. Sā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “ahaṃ kira kāḷakaṇṇīti raññā na gahitā, kāḷakaṇṇiyo nāma na evarūpā hontī”ti vatvā “hotu, sace pana taṃ rājānaṃ passissāmi, jānissāmī”ti tasmiṃ āghātaṃ bandhi. Atha naṃ pitā abhipārakassa adāsi, sā tassa piyā ahosi manāpā.

Then her father, Tiriṭivaccha, approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, a jewel of a woman has arisen in my house, one who is suitable for the king. Please send brahmins who are readers of bodily marks to have her examined, and then do as you please.” The king said, “Very well,” and sent the brahmins. They went to the merchant’s house, received hospitality and honor, and ate rice-porridge. At that moment, Ummādantī, adorned with all her ornaments, approached them. Seeing her, they were unable to maintain mindfulness, and becoming intoxicated with the madness of the defilements, they were unaware of the fact that their meal was unfinished. Some, taking a morsel with the intention of eating, placed it on their heads; some threw it into their armpits; some struck the wall. All of them became like madmen. Seeing them, she thought, “These, it seems, are to examine my marks!” and saying, “Seize them by the neck and throw them out,” she had them expelled. Disgraced, they went to the royal palace and, being angry with Ummādantī, said, “Your Majesty, that woman is a bringer of misfortune; she is not suitable for you.” The king, thinking, “She is, it seems, a bringer of misfortune,” did not send for her. When she heard this news, she thought, “It seems the king did not take me because I was called a bringer of misfortune. Those who are truly bringers of misfortune are not like this! So be it. If I ever see that king, I will make him know,” and she bore a grudge against him. Then her father gave her to the commander Abhipāraka, and she became his dear and beloved wife.

Kassa pana kammassa nissandena sā evaṃ abhirūpā ahosīti? Rattavatthadānassa nissandenāti. Sā kira atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ daliddakule nibbattitvā ussavadivase puññasampannā itthiyo kusumbharattavatthaṃ nivāsetvā alaṅkatā kīḷantiyo disvā tādisaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā [V 5.0201] kīḷitukāmā hutvā mātāpitūnaṃ ārocetvā tehi, “amma, mayaṃ daliddā, kuto no evarūpaṃ vattha”nti vutte “tena hi maṃ ekasmiṃ aḍḍhakule bhatiṃ kātuṃ anujānātha[M 5.0223], te mama guṇaṃ ñatvā dassantī”ti vatvā tehi [P 5.0212] anuññātā ekaṃ kulaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kusumbharattavatthena bhatiṃ karomī”ti āha. Atha naṃ te “tīṇi saṃvaccharāni kamme kate tava guṇaṃ ñatvā dassāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Sā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā kammaṃ paṭipajji. Te tassā guṇaṃ ñatvā aparipuṇṇesuyeva tīsu saṃvaccharesu tassā ghanakusumbharattavatthena saddhiṃ aññampi vatthaṃ datvā “tava sahāyikāhi saddhiṃ gantvā nhatvā nivāsehī”ti taṃ pesayiṃsu. Sā sahāyikā ādāya gantvā rattavatthaṃ nadītīre ṭhapetvā nhāyi.

By the result of what deed did she become so beautiful? By the result of the gift of safflower-dyed cloth. It is said that in the past, having been born into a poor family in Benares, on a festival day, seeing merit-endowed women adorned and celebrating while dressed in safflower-dyed cloth, she desired to celebrate dressed in such cloth. She informed her parents, who replied, “Dear, we are poor—where would we get such cloth for you?” She then said, “Then allow me to work for hire in a wealthy household. When they recognize my service, they will give it to me.” Having obtained their permission, she approached a household and said, “I will work for hire for safflower-dyed cloth.” They replied, “After working for three years, having recognized your service, we will give it to you.” She agreed and took up the work. Recognizing her service even before the three years were complete, they gave her thick safflower-dyed cloth along with another garment, saying, “Go bathe with your friends and then dress in this.” Taking her friends, she went to the riverbank, set the safflower-dyed cloth on the bank, and bathed.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko kassapadasabalassa sāvako acchinnacīvaro sākhābhaṅgaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca taṃ padesaṃ pāpuṇi. Sā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ bhadanto acchinnacīvaro bhavissati, pubbepi adinnabhāvena me nivāsanaṃ dullabhaṃ jāta”nti taṃ vatthaṃ dvidhā phāletvā “ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ ayyassa dassāmī”ti cintetvā uttaritvā attano nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā “tiṭṭhatha, bhante”ti vatvā theraṃ vanditvā rattavatthaṃ majjhe phāletvā tassekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ adāsi. So ekamante paṭicchanne ṭhatvā sākhābhaṅgaṃ chaḍḍetvā tassekaṃ kaṇṇaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā nikkhami. Athassa vatthobhāsena sakalasarīraṃ taruṇasūriyo viya ekobhāsaṃ ahosi. Sā taṃ disvā “mayhaṃ ayyo paṭhamaṃ na sobhati, idāni taruṇasūriyo viya virocati, idampi etasseva dassāmī”ti dutiyampi koṭṭhāsaṃ datvā “bhante, ahaṃ bhave bhave vicarantī uttamarūpadharā bhaveyyaṃ, maṃ disvā koci puriso sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ mā asakkhi, mayā abhirūpatarā nāma aññā mā hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Theropi anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

At that moment, a disciple of Kassapa of the Ten Powers, whose robes had been snatched away, arrived at that place, wearing and wrapped in foliage. Seeing him, she thought, “This venerable one must have been robbed of his robes. Even in the past, due to my not having given, a garment has been hard for me to obtain.” She then planned to tear the cloth in two, thinking, “I will give one portion to the venerable one.” Having come out of the water and put on her own garment, she said, “Wait, venerable sir,” paid respects to the elder, tore the safflower-dyed cloth in the middle, and gave him one portion. Standing aside in a secluded spot, he discarded the foliage, put on one corner of the cloth as a lower garment, wrapped the other around himself, and emerged. Then, his whole body shone with the radiance of the cloth, like the morning sun. Seeing this, she thought, “At first, my lord was not resplendent, but now he glows like the morning sun. I will give him this other part as well.” She gave him the second portion and made this aspiration: “Venerable sir, may I, wandering in existence after existence, be one possessing supreme beauty, so that no man seeing me may be able to maintain his self-control, and may no other woman be more beautiful than I.” The elder gave his blessing and departed.

Sā devaloke saṃsarantī tasmiṃ kāle ariṭṭhapure nibbattitvā tathā abhirūpā ahosi. Atha tasmiṃ nagare kattikachaṇaṃ ghosayiṃsu, kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ nagaraṃ sajjayiṃsu. Abhipārako attano ārakkhaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto taṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, ummādanti [P 5.0213] ajja kattikarattivāro chaṇo, rājā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ imaṃ gehadvāraṃ āgamissati, mā kho tassa attānaṃ dassesi, sopi taṃ disvā satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti āha. Sā “gaccha tvaṃ, sāmi, ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti sampaṭicchitvā [M 5.0224] tasmiṃ gate dāsiṃ āṇāpesi “rañño imaṃ gehadvāraṃ āgatakāle mayhaṃ āroceyyāsī”ti. Atha sūriye atthaṅgate uggahe puṇṇacande devanagare viya nagare alaṅkate sabbadisāsu dīpesu jalitesu rājā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito ājaññarathavaragato [V 5.0202] amaccagaṇaparivuto mahantena yasena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto paṭhamameva abhipārakassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Taṃ pana gehaṃ manosilāvaṇṇapākāraparikkhittaṃ alaṅkatadvāraṭṭālakaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ pāsādikaṃ. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dāsī ummādantiyā ārocesi. Sā pupphasamuggaṃ gāhāpetvā kinnarilīḷāya vātapānaṃ nissāya ṭhitā rañño pupphāni khipi. So taṃ ulloketvā kilesamadamatto satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto “abhipārakassetaṃ geha”nti sañjānitumpi nāsakkhi, atha sārathiṃ āmantetvā pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

She, wandering through the celestial realms, was reborn at that time in the city of Ariṭṭhapura and was of such a nature. Then, in that city, the Kattika festival was proclaimed; on the full-moon day of Kattika, they decorated the city of Ariṭṭhapura. Abhipāraka, the commander-in-chief, going to his residence, which was said to be well-guarded, called Ummādantī and said: 'Lady Ummādantī, today is the turn for the festival on the full-moon night of Kattika. When the king makes a rightwise circumambulation of the city, he will first arrive at the street of this house door.
