Do not show yourself to the king, for if he sees you, he will not be able to maintain his mindfulness.' She said: 'My lord, you may go; I shall know what to do.' When the commander-in-chief Abhipāraka had gone, she called her servant girl and instructed her: 'Lady, when King Sivi arrives at this house door, come and inform me.' Then, as the sun set and the full moon rose, the whole city of Ariṭṭhapura was adorned like a celestial city, with lamps burning brightly in all directions. King Sivi, adorned with all ornaments, mounted on a noble chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses, and surrounded by a host of ministers, made a rightwise circumambulation of Ariṭṭhapura with great glory. He first arrived at the door of the commander-in-chief Abhipāraka’s house. That house was surrounded by a wall with the color of realgar. It had decorated gate-towers and was a site of great beauty and pleasant to behold. At that moment, the instructed servant girl informed Ummādantī. Having someone carry a basket of flowers, she stood leaning against the window with the grace of a kinnarī and threw flowers at King Sivi. When King Sivi saw her, he looked up and, intoxicated by the madness of passion, was unable to maintain mindfulness; he could not even recognize that 'this is the house of the commander-in-chief Abhipāraka.' Then, wishing to ask, he addressed the charioteer and spoke these two verses:

57.

57.

“Nivesanaṃ kassa nudaṃ sunanda, pākārena paṇḍumayena guttaṃ;

Kā dissati aggisikhāva dūre, vehāyasaṃ pabbataggeva acci.

“Whose dwelling is this, Sunanda, protected by a wall of pale-red hue? Who is seen from afar like a crest of fire, like a blaze on a mountain peak in the sky?”

58.

58.

“Dhītā nvayaṃ kassa sunanda hoti, suṇisā nvayaṃ kassa athopi bhariyā;

Akkhāhi me khippamidheva puṭṭho, avāvaṭā yadi vā atthi bhattā”ti.

“Whose daughter is she, Sunanda? Whose daughter-in-law is she, or whose wife? Tell me quickly as I ask you here—is she unclaimed, or does she have a husband?”

Tattha kassa nudanti kassa nu idaṃ. Paṇḍumayenāti rattiṭṭhakamayena. Dissatīti vātapāne ṭhitā paññāyati. Accīti analajālakkhandho. Dhītā [P 5.0214] nvayanti dhītā nu ayaṃ. Avāvaṭāti apetāvaraṇā apariggahā. Bhattāti yadi vā assā sāmiko atthi, etaṃ me akkhāhīti.

In this context, 'kassa nudaṃ' means 'whose is this?' 'Paṇḍumayena' means 'made of red bricks.' 'Dissatī' means she is discerned while standing at the window. 'Acci' means a mass of fire-flames. 'Dhītā nvayaṃ' means 'is this woman the daughter?' 'Avāvaṭā' means 'unobstructed' or 'unclaimed.' 'Bhattā' means 'if she has a husband,' as in 'tell me this'.

Athassa so ācikkhanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then, explaining to him, he spoke these two verses:

59.

59.

“Ahañhi jānāmi janinda etaṃ, matyā ca petyā ca athopi assā;

Taveva so puriso bhūmipāla, rattindivaṃ appamatto tavatthe.

“Indeed, O lord of men, I know her by her mother and father, and also her husband. That man is your very own, O protector of the earth, who is vigilant day and night in your service.”

60.

60.

“Iddho [M 5.0225] ca phīto ca suvaḍḍhito ca, amacco ca te aññataro janinda;

Tassesā bhariyābhipārakassa, ummādantī nāmadheyyena rājā”ti.

“He is prosperous, wealthy, and well-advanced—one of your ministers, O lord of men. This is the wife of that Abhipāraka, O king, Ummādantī by name.”

Tattha matyā ca petyā cāti mātito ca pitito cetaṃ jānāmi. Athopi assāti atha sāmikampi assā jānāmīti vadati. Iddhoti samiddho. Phītoti vatthālaṅkārehi supupphito. Suvaḍḍhitoti suṭṭhu vuddho. Nāmadheyyenāti nāmena. Ayañhi yo naṃ passati, taṃ ummādeti, satimassa paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ na deti, tasmā ummādantīti vuccati.

In this context, 'matyā ca petyā ca' means 'I know her through both mother and father.' 'Athopi assā' means 'I also know her husband.' 'Iddho' means 'successful.' 'Phīto' means 'fully flourished with clothes and ornaments.' 'Suvaḍḍhito' means 'well-grown' or 'promoted.' 'Nāmadheyyena' means 'by name.' For whoever sees her, she maddens them; she does not allow them to maintain mindfulness. Thus she is called Ummādantī.

Taṃ [V 5.0203] sutvā rājā nāmamassā thomento anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to praise her name, spoke this subsequent verse:

61.

61.

“Ambho ambho nāmamidaṃ imissā, matyā ca petyā ca kataṃ susādhu;

Tadā hi mayhaṃ avalokayantī, ummattakaṃ ummadantī akāsī”ti.

“O friends, O friends, this name of hers, given by her mother and father, is most appropriate. For when she looked upon me, Ummādantī truly made me mad.”

Tattha matyā ca petyā cāti mātarā ca pitarā ca. Mayhanti upayogatthe sampadānavacanaṃ. Avalokayantīti mayā avalokitā sayampi maṃ avalokayantī maṃ ummattakaṃ akāsīti attho.

In this context, 'matyā ca petyā ca' means 'by mother and father.' 'Mayhaṃ' is a dative used in the sense of the accusative. 'Avalokayantī' means: 'while being looked at by me, she too looking at me, made me a madman'—this is the meaning.

Sā tassa kampitabhāvaṃ ñatvā vātapānaṃ thaketvā sirigabbhameva agamāsi. Raññopi tassā diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya nagaraṃ padakkhiṇakaraṇe cittameva nāhosi. So sārathiṃ āmantetvā, “samma sunanda, rathaṃ nivattehi, ayaṃ chaṇo [P 5.0215] amhākaṃ nānucchaviko, abhipārakassa senāpatissevānucchaviko, rajjampi tassevānucchavika”nti rathaṃ nivattāpetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha sirisayane nipajjitvā vippalapanto āha –

Recognizing his agitation, she closed the window and went to her magnificent bedchamber. From the time the king saw her, he no longer had any desire to circumambulate the city. He addressed the charioteer: 'Friend Sunanda, turn the chariot back. This festival is not suitable for us; it is only suitable for the commander-in-chief named Abhipāraka. This kingship also is only suitable for that Abhipāraka.' Having caused the chariot to turn back, he ascended the palace, lay on his royal bed, and, wishing to lament, said:

62.

62.

“Yā puṇṇamāse migamandalocanā, upāvisi puṇḍarīkattacaṅgī;

Dve puṇṇamāyo tadahū amaññahaṃ, disvāna pārāvatarattavāsiniṃ.

“On the full-moon night, she with eyes like a deer’s and limbs beautiful like a white lotus, sat there. Seeing her clad in the crimson color of pigeons, I thought there were two full moons that day.”

63.

63.

“Aḷārapamhehi [M 5.0226] subhehi vaggubhi, palobhayantī maṃ yadā udikkhati;

Vijambhamānā harateva me mano, jātā vane kimpurisīva pabbate.

“When she looks at me, enticing me with her beautiful, long, and charming eyelashes, and stretching herself, she steals my mind like a kinnarī born in a mountain forest.”

64.

64.

“Tadā hi brahatī sāmā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Ekaccavasanā nārī, migī bhantāvudikkhati.

“Then indeed, the magnificent, dark-complexioned one, adorned with jeweled earrings, a woman clad in a single garment, gazes like a bewildered doe.”

65.

65.

“Kadāssu maṃ tambanakhā sulomā, bāhā mudū candanasāralittā;

Vaṭṭaṅgulī sannatadhīrakuttiyā, nārī upaññissati sīsato subhā.

“When will that beautiful woman with copper-colored nails and fine hair, her arms soft and anointed with sandalwood paste, with rounded fingers and skillful, steady movements, attend upon me, beginning from my head?”

66.

66.

“Kadāssu maṃ kañcanajāluracchadā, dhītā tirīṭissa vilaggamajjhā;

Mudūhi bāhāhi palissajissati, brahāvane jātadumaṃva māluvā.

“When will she, with a golden net covering her breast, the slender-waisted daughter of Tirīṭa, embrace me with her soft arms, like a Māluvā creeper a tree grown in a great forest?”

67.

67.

“Kadāssu [V 5.0204] lākhārasarattasucchavī, bindutthanī puṇḍarīkattacaṅgī;

Mukhaṃ mukhena upanāmayissati, soṇḍova soṇḍassa surāya thālaṃ.

“When will she, with skin beautifully colored like lac dye, with breasts like rounded drops, and a body like a white lotus, bring her face to my face, as a drunkard brings a bowl of liquor to his mouth?”

68.

68.

“Yadāddasaṃ taṃ tiṭṭhantiṃ, sabbabhaddaṃ manoramaṃ;

Tato sakassa cittassa, nāvabodhāmi kañcinaṃ.

“When I saw her standing there, all-auspicious and delightful to the mind, then I was no longer master of my own mind and comprehended nothing at all.”

69.

69.

“Ummādantimahaṃ daṭṭhā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Na supāmi divārattiṃ, sahassaṃva parājito.

“Having seen Ummādantī, wearing jeweled earrings, I cannot sleep day or night, as if defeated a thousand times.”

70.

70.

“Sakko [P 5.0216] ce me varaṃ dajjā, so ca labbhetha me varo;

Ekarattaṃ dirattaṃ vā, bhaveyyaṃ abhipārako;

Ummādantyā ramitvāna, sivirājā tato siya”nti.

“If Sakka would grant me a boon, and if that boon were granted to me, I would become Abhipāraka for one night or two. After delighting with Ummādantī, I would then return to being the Sivi king.”

Tattha puṇṇamāseti puṇṇacandāya rattiyā. Migamandalocanāti kaṇḍasantāsena palāyitvā vanantare ṭhatvā luddaṃ olokentiyā migiyā viya mandāni [M 5.0227] locanāni assāti migamandalocanā. Upāvisīti padumavaṇṇena karatalena pupphāni khipitvā maṃ olokentī vātapāne nisīdi. Puṇḍarīkattacaṅgīti rattapadumavaṇṇasarīrā. Dve puṇṇamāyoti ahaṃ tadahu tasmiṃ chaṇadivase taṃ pārāvatapādasamānavaṇṇarattavatthanivatthaṃ disvā tassā mukhasobhaṃ olokento ekassa pācīnalokadhātuto ekassa abhipārakassa senāpatino nivesaneti dvinnaṃ puṇṇacandānaṃ uggatattā dve puṇṇamāyo amaññiṃ. Aḷārapamhehīti visālapakhumehi. Subhehīti parisuddhehi. Vaggubhīti madhurākārehi. Udikkhatīti evarūpehi nettehi yasmiṃ khaṇe oloketi. Pabbateti yathā himavantapabbate supupphitavane vīṇaṃ ādāya tantissarena attano saraṃ saṃsandantī kimpurisī kimpurisassa manaṃ harati, evaṃ harateva me manoti vippalapati.

Here, ‘puṇṇamāse’ means ‘on the full-moon night.’ ‘Migamandalocanā’ means ‘her eyes are timid like those of a doe who, frightened by an arrow, has fled and stood in the forest, looking back at the hunter.’ ‘Upāvisīti’ means ‘having thrown flowers with her lotus-colored hand, she sat by the window, looking at me.’ ‘Puṇḍarīkattacaṅgī’ means ‘her body was the color of a red lotus.’ ‘Dve puṇṇamāyo’ means ‘on that festive day, seeing her dressed in red garments the color of a pigeon’s feet, and gazing at the beauty of her face, I thought there were two full moons—one risen from the eastern world-element and the other from the mansion of Abhipāraka, the commander-in-chief.’ ‘Aḷārapamhehīti’ means ‘with wide eyelashes.’ ‘Subhehīti’ means ‘pure.’ ‘Vaggubhīti’ means ‘sweet in appearance.’ ‘Udikkhatīti’ means ‘at the moment she looks with such eyes.’ ‘Pabbateti’ means ‘just as on Mount Himavat, in a richly blossomed forest, a kimpurisī takes up a lute and, blending her voice with the sound of the strings, captivates the mind of a kimpurisa, so too she captivates my mind’—thus he laments.

Brahatīti uḷārā. Sāmāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇasāmā. Ekaccavasanāti ekaccikavasanā, ekavatthanivatthāti attho. Bhantāvudikkhatīti saṇhakesā puthunalāṭā āyatabhamū visālakkhī tuṅganāsā rattoṭṭhā setadantā tikhiṇadāṭhā suvaṭṭitagīvā sutanubāhu susaṇṭhitapayodharā karamitamajjhā visālasoṇī suvaṇṇakadalisamānoru sā uttamitthī tasmiṃ khaṇe maṃ udikkhantī bhayena vanaṃ pavisitvā puna nivattitvā luddaṃ udikkhantī bhantā migīva maṃ udikkhatīti vadati. Bāhāmudūti mudubāhā. Sannatadhīrakuttiyāti suphusitachekakaraṇā. Upaññissati [V 5.0205] manti sā subhā nārī kadā nu maṃ tehi tambanakhehi sīsato paṭṭhāya sannatena dhīrena karaṇena paritosessatīti patthento vilapati.

‘Brahatīti’ means ‘magnificent.’ ‘Sāmā’ means ‘golden-complexioned.’ ‘Ekaccavasanā’ means ‘wearing a single garment,’ that is, ‘dressed in one cloth.’ ‘Bhantāvudikkhatīti’ means ‘that supreme woman—with fine hair, a broad forehead, arched eyebrows, wide eyes, a high nose, red lips, white teeth, sharp eye-teeth, a well-rounded neck, slender arms, firm breasts, a slender waist, broad hips, and thighs like golden plantain stems—at that moment looking at me, is like a bewildered doe that, having entered the forest out of fear, turns back and looks at the hunter,’ thus he says. ‘Bāhāmudūti’ means ‘with soft arms.’ ‘Sannatadhīrakuttiyāti’ means ‘with gentle and skillful conduct.’ ‘Upaññissati manti’: longing, he laments: ‘When will that beautiful woman please me with those copper-colored nails, beginning from the head, with her gentle and skillful behavior?’

Kañcanajāluracchadāti kañcanamayauracchadālaṅkārā. Vilaggamajjhāti vilaggasarīrā tanumajjhimā. Brahāvaneti mahāvane. Lākhārasarattasucchavīti hatthapādatalaagganakhaoṭṭhamaṃsesu lākhārasarattamaṇipavālavaṇṇā. Bindutthanīti udakapupphuḷaparimaṇḍalatthanī. Tatoti yadā taṃ tiṭṭhantiṃ addasaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya. Sakassa cittassāti attano cittassa anissaro jātomhīti adhippāyo. Kañcinanti kañci “ayaṃ asuko nāmā”ti na jānāmi, ummattako jātomhīti vadati. Daṭṭhāti disvā. Na supāmīti neva rattiṃ, na divā niddaṃ labhāmi. So ca labbhethāti yaṃ me sakko varaṃ dadeyya, so ca me varo labbhetha, labheyyāhaṃ taṃ varanti attho.

‘Kañcanajāluracchadā’ means adorned with golden ornaments for the chest. ‘Vilaggamajjhā’ means having a slender body and a slender waist. ‘Brahāvane’ means in a great forest. ‘Lākhārasarattasucchavī’ means having the color of red lacquer, ruby, or coral on the flesh of the palms, the soles, the fingernails, and the lips. ‘Bindutthanī’ means having breasts round like water-bubbles. ‘Tato’ means from the time when I saw her standing. ‘Sakassa cittassā’ means the sense is, ‘I have become no longer master of my own mind.’ ‘Kañcinanti’ means, ‘I do not know anyone, thinking “this is so-and-so”; I have become mad,’ so he says. ‘Daṭṭhā’ means having seen. ‘Na supāmi’ means I obtain no sleep, neither at night nor during the day. ‘So ca labbhetha’ means, ‘If Sakka were to grant me a boon, and if that boon were obtainable by me, may I obtain that boon’—this is the meaning.

Atha [M 5.0228] te amaccā abhipārakassapi ārocayiṃsu – “sāmi rājā, nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto tumhākaṃ gharadvāraṃ patvā nivattitvā [P 5.0217] pāsādaṃ abhiruhī”ti. So attano gehaṃ gantvā ummādantiṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, kacci rañño attānaṃ dassesī”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, eko mahodaro mahādāṭhiko rathe ṭhatvā āgato puriso atthi, ahaṃ taṃ rājā vā arājā vāti na jānāmi, eko issaroti pana vutte vātapāne ṭhatvā pupphāni khipiṃ, so tāvadeva nivattitvā gato”ti. So taṃ sutvā “nāsitomhi tayā”ti punadivase pātova rājanivesanaṃ āruyha sirigabbhadvāre ṭhatvā rañño ummādantiṃ nissāya vippalāpaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ ummādantiyā paṭibaddhacitto jāto, taṃ alabhanto marissati, rañño ca mama ca aguṇaṃ mocetvā imassa mayā jīvitaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti attano nivesanaṃ gantvā ekaṃ daḷhamantaṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “tāta, asukaṭṭhāne susiracetiyarukkho atthi, tvaṃ kañci ajānāpetvā atthaṅgate sūriye tattha gantvā antorukkhe nisīda, ahaṃ tattha balikammaṃ karonto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā devatā namassanto, ‘sāmi devarāja, amhākaṃ rājā nagaramhi chaṇe vattamāne akīḷitvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā vippalapantova nipanno, mayaṃ tattha kāraṇaṃ na jānāma, rājā devatānaṃ bahūpakāro, anusaṃvaccharaṃ sahassaṃ vissajjetvā balikammaṃ karoti, idaṃ nāma nissāya rājā vippalapatīti ācikkhatha, rañño no jīvitadānaṃ dethā’ti yācissāmi, tvaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe saddaṃ parivattitvā, ‘senāpati, tumhākaṃ rañño byādhi nāma natthi, so pana tava bhariyāya ummādantiyā paṭibaddhacitto. Sace naṃ labhissati, jīvissati, no ce, marissati. Sace [V 5.0206] tassa jīvitaṃ icchasi, ummādantimassa dehī’ti vadeyyāsī”ti evaṃ taṃ uggaṇhāpetvā uyyojesi.

Then the ministers informed Abhipāraka: “Lord, the king, while circumambulating the city, upon reaching the door of your house, turned back and ascended his palace.” He went to his own house, called Ummādantī, and asked, “Madam, did you show yourself to the king?” “Lord, there was a man with a large belly and large fangs standing on a chariot who came. I do not know whether he was the king or not, but when it was said, ‘He is a ruler,’ I stood by the window and threw flowers. He immediately turned back and left.” Hearing this, he exclaimed, “You have ruined me!” The next day, early in the morning, he went to the king’s residence and stood at the door of the royal chamber. Hearing the king’s ramblings about Ummādantī, he thought, “The king has become infatuated with Ummādantī. If he does not obtain her, he will die. To prevent misfortune for both the king and myself, it is proper for me to give him his life.” He returned to his own residence, summoned a trusted attendant, and instructed him: “Dear one, in a certain place, there is a hollow shrine tree. Without letting anyone know, go there after sunset and sit inside the tree. I will come there to perform a ritual offering. While paying homage to the deities, I will say, ‘Lord divine king, our king, while a festival is underway in the city, has not taken part in the play, but has entered the royal chamber and lies there rambling. We do not know the reason. The king has been a great benefactor to the deities, offering thousands annually and performing rituals. Please tell us why the king rambles. Grant us the gift of the king’s life.’ At that moment, you must disguise your voice and say, ‘General, your king has no illness. He is infatuated with your wife, Ummādantī. If he obtains her, he will live; if not, he will die. If you wish for his life, give Ummādantī to him.’” Having thus instructed him, he sent him forth.

So gantvā tasmiṃ rukkhe nisīditvā punadivase senāpatinā amaccagaṇaparivutena taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā yācito tathā abhāsi. Senāpati “sādhū”ti vatvā devataṃ vanditvā amacce jānāpetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājanivesanaṃ āruyha sirigabbhadvāraṃ ākoṭesi. Rājā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā [P 5.0218] “ko eso”ti pucchi. Ahaṃ, deva, abhipārakoti. Athassa rājā dvāraṃ vivari. So pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā gāthamāha –

Having gone there, he sat down in that tree. The next day, the commander-in-chief, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, went to that place and, being requested, the deity spoke thus. The commander-in-chief, saying, "Very well," paid homage to the deity, informed the ministers, entered the city, ascended to the palace, and knocked on the door of the royal chamber. The king, regaining his composure, asked, "Who is this?" "It is I, O king, Abhipāraka." Then the king opened the door for him. Having entered and paid homage to the king, he spoke this verse to explain the situation:

71.

71.

“Bhūtāni [M 5.0229] me bhūtapatī namassato, āgamma yakkho idametadabravi;

Rañño mano ummadantyā niviṭṭho, dadāmi te taṃ paricārayassū”ti.

“As I was paying homage to the deities, a yakkha, the lord of beings, approached and spoke this to me: ‘The king’s mind is fixed on Ummādantī. I give her to you; let him enjoy her.’”

Tattha namassatoti tumhākaṃ vippalāpakāraṇajānanatthaṃ balikammaṃ katvā namassantassa. Tanti ahaṃ taṃ ummādantiṃ tumhākaṃ paricārikaṃ katvā dadāmīti.

In that context, “namassato” means “while I was paying homage, having performed a ritual offering to know the reason for your rambling.” “Taṃ” means “I give that Ummādantī to you [the King], having made her your attendant.”

Atha naṃ rājā, “samma abhipāraka, mama ummādantiyā paṭibaddhacittatāya vippalapitabhāvaṃ yakkhāpi jānantī”ti pucchi. Āma, devāti. So “sabbalokena kira me lāmakabhāvo ñāto”ti lajjidhamme patiṭṭhāya anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king asked him, “Friend Abhipāraka, do even the deities know that I have been rambling because my mind is infatuated with Ummādantī?” “Yes, O king,” he replied. Then, thinking, “The whole world surely knows of my wretched state,” and being established in the quality of a virtuous person, he spoke the following verse to the commander-in-chief:

72.

72.

“Puññā ca dhaṃse amaro na camhi, jano ca me pāpamidañca jaññā;

Bhuso ca tyassa manaso vighāto, datvā piyaṃ ummadantiṃ adaṭṭhā”ti.

“I would fall from merit, nor am I immortal; and the people would know of this evil of mine. And surely there would be great torment of mind for you, having given away your beloved Ummādantī and then not seeing her.”

Tattha dhaṃseti, samma abhipāraka, ahaṃ tāya saddhiṃ kilesavasena paricārento puññato ca dhaṃseyyaṃ, tāya saddhiṃ paricāritamattena amaro ca na homi, mahājano ca me imaṃ lāmakabhāvaṃ jāneyya, tato “ayuttaṃ raññā kata”nti garaheyya, tañca mama datvā pacchā piyabhariyaṃ adaṭṭhā tava manaso vighāto cassāti attho.

Here, “dhaṃse” means, “Friend Abhipāraka, if I were to enjoy her by way of defilements, I would fall from merit; I do not become immortal merely by enjoying her; and the great multitude would know of this wretched state of mine, and would then blame me, saying, ‘The king has done what is improper.’ Furthermore, having given your beloved wife to me, you would suffer great mental distress because you would no longer see her.”

Sesā ubhinnampi vacanapaṭivacanagāthā honti –

The following verses constitute the dialogue between the two:

73.

73.

“Janinda [V 5.0207] nāññatra tayā mayā vā, sabbāpi kammassa katassa jaññā;

Yaṃ te mayā ummadantī padinnā, bhusehi rājā vanathaṃ sajāhi.

“O lord of men, none other than you or I would know of this deed performed. Since Ummādantī has been given to you by me, O king, fulfill your desire and be free from your longing.”

74.

74.

“Yo pāpakaṃ kammakaraṃ manusso, so maññati māyida maññiṃsu aññe;

Passanti [P 5.0219] bhūtāni karontametaṃ, yuttā ca ye honti narā pathabyā.

“The man who performs an evil deed thinks, ‘May others not know this of me!’ But deities see him doing it, as do those people on earth who are endowed with psychic power.”

75.

75.

“Añño [M 5.0230] nu te koci naro pathabyā, saddheyya lokasmi na me piyāti;

Bhuso ca tyassa manuso vighāto, datvā piyaṃ ummadantiṃ adaṭṭhā.

“Is there any other man on earth who would believe that your dear wife is my legitimate queen? And there would be great torment of mind for you, having given away your beloved Ummādantī and then not seeing her.”

76.

76.

“Addhā piyā mayha janinda esā, na sā mamaṃ appiyā bhūmipāla;

“Indeed, O lord of men, she is dear to me; she is not unloved by me, O protector of the earth.”

Gaccheva tvaṃ ummadantiṃ bhadante, sīhova selassa guhaṃ upeti.

“Go then to Ummādantī, my lord; may you be blessed, like a lion approaching a cave in the mountain.”

77.

77.

“Na pīḷitā attadukhena dhīrā, sukhapphalaṃ kamma pariccajanti;

Sammohitā vāpi sukhena mattā, na pāpakammañca samācaranti.

“The wise, even when oppressed by their own suffering, do not renounce wholesome actions that bear pleasant fruit; nor, when deluded or intoxicated by pleasure, do they commit evil deeds.”

78.

78.

“Tuvañhi mātā ca pitā ca mayhaṃ, bhattā patī posako devatā ca;

Dāso ahaṃ tuyha saputtadāro, yathāsukhaṃ sāmi karohi kāmaṃ.

“For you are like a mother and father to me, my lord, my provider, my sustainer, and my deity. I am your servant, along with my wife and son. O master, fulfill your desire as you please.”

79.

79.

“Yo ‘issaromhī’ti karoti pāpaṃ, katvā ca so nuttasate paresaṃ;

Na tena so jīvati dīghamāyu, devāpi pāpena samekkhare naṃ.

“He who, thinking ‘I am the ruler,’ does evil, and having done it, has no fear of others, does not live a long life because of that deed; even the deities look upon him with an eye of blame for his evil.”

80.

80.

“Aññātakaṃ sāmikehī padinnaṃ, dhamme ṭhitā ye paṭicchanti dānaṃ;

Paṭicchakā dāyakā cāpi tattha, sukhapphalaññeva karonti kammaṃ.

“When those established in the Dhamma receive a gift of another's property given by its owners, then both the receivers and the givers perform an action that yields only pleasant fruit.”

81.

81.

“Añño nu te koci naro pathabyā, saddheyya lokasmi na me piyāti;

Bhuso [P 5.0220] ca tyassa manaso vighāto, datvā piyaṃ ummadantiṃ adaṭṭhā.

“Is there any other man on earth who would believe that your dear wife is my queen? And there would be great torment of mind for you, having given away your beloved Ummādantī and then not seeing her.”

82.

82.

“Addhā [M 5.0231] piyā mayha janinda esā, na sā mamaṃ appiyā bhūmipāla;

Yaṃ te mayā ummadantī padinnā, bhusehi rājā vanathaṃ sajāhi.

“Indeed, O lord of men, she is dear to me; she is not unloved by me, O protector of the earth. Since I have given Ummādantī to you, O king, fulfill your desire and let your passion be calmed.”

83.

83.

“Yo [V 5.0208] attadukkhena parassa dukkhaṃ, sukhena vā attasukhaṃ dahāti;

Yathevidaṃ mayha tathā paresaṃ, yo evaṃ jānāti sa vedi dhammaṃ.

“He who attributes another’s suffering to himself by his own suffering, or his own happiness to others; whoever knows thus, ‘As this is for me, so it is for others’—he truly knows the Dhamma.”

84.

84.

“Añño nu te koci naro pathabyā, saddheyya lokasmi na me piyāti;

Bhuso ca tyassa manaso vighāto, datvā piyaṃ ummadantiṃ adaṭṭhā.

“Is there any other man on earth who would believe that your dear wife is my queen? And there would be great torment of mind for you, having given away your beloved Ummādantī and then not seeing her.”

85.

85.

“Janinda jānāsi piyā mamesā, na sā mamaṃ appiyā bhūmipāla;

Piyena te dammi piyaṃ janinda, piyadāyino deva piyaṃ labhanti.

“O lord of men, you know that she is dear to me; she is not unloved by me, O protector of the earth. Out of love for your welfare, I give you a loved one; those who give what is dear, O king, obtain what is dear.”

86.

86.

“So nūnāhaṃ vadhissāmi, attānaṃ kāmahetukaṃ;

Na hi dhammaṃ adhammena, ahaṃ vadhitumussahe.

“Surely, I would be destroying myself on account of desire. I do not dare to destroy the Dhamma with unrighteousness.”

87.

87.

“Sace tuvaṃ mayha satiṃ janinda, na kāmayāsi naravīra seṭṭha;

Cajāmi naṃ sabbajanassa sibyā, mayā pamuttaṃ tato avhayesi naṃ.

“If, O lord of men, O noblest of heroes, you do not desire her because of your regard for me, I shall divorce her in the midst of all the people; when she has been released by me, then you may call for her.”

88.

88.

“Adūsiyaṃ ce abhipāraka tvaṃ, cajāsi katte ahitāya tyassa;

Mahā ca te upavādopi assa, na cāpi tyassa nagaramhi pakkho.

“If you, O Abhipāraka, should abandon one who is innocent, it would be to your own detriment, even though you are a good minister who carries out all royal duties; and there would be great reproach against you, nor would you have any allies in the city.”

89.

89.

“Ahaṃ [M 5.0232] sahissaṃ upavādametaṃ, nindaṃ pasaṃsaṃ garahañca sabbaṃ;

Mametamāgacchatu bhūmipāla, yathāsukhaṃ sivi karohi kāmaṃ.

“I will endure this reproach, and all blame, praise, and censure; let it all come upon me, O protector of the earth. O Sivi king, fulfill your desire as you please.”

90.

90.

“Yo [P 5.0221] neva nindaṃ na panappasaṃsaṃ, ādiyati garahaṃ nopi pūjaṃ;

Sirī ca lakkhī ca apeti tamhā, āpo suvuṭṭhīva yathā thalamhā.

“He who cares neither for blame nor praise, nor for censure nor honor—glory and prosperity depart from him, like heavy rain running off high ground.”

91.

91.

“Yaṃ kiñci dukkhañca sukhañca etto, dhammātisārañca manovighātaṃ;

Urasā ahaṃ paccuttarissāmi sabbaṃ, pathavī yathā thāvarānaṃ tasānaṃ.

“Whatever suffering or happiness arises from this, and whatever transgression of Dhamma or mental distress, I will bear it all with my own breast, just as the earth bears all things, both stationary and moving.”

92.

92.

“Dhammātisārañca manovighātaṃ, dukkhañca nicchāmi ahaṃ paresaṃ;

Ekovimaṃ hārayissāmi bhāraṃ, dhamme ṭhito kiñci ahāpayanto.

“I do not wish for transgression of the Dhamma, mental distress, or suffering for others. Standing firm in the Dhamma and causing no one to suffer, I alone will bear this burden.”

93.

93.

“Saggūpagaṃ [V 5.0209] puññakammaṃ janinda, mā me tuvaṃ antarāyaṃ akāsi;

Dadāmi te ummadantiṃ pasanno, rājāva yaññe dhanaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ.

“O lord of men, do not obstruct my meritorious deed that leads to heaven. With a clear mind, I give you Ummādantī, just as a king gives wealth to Brahmins at a sacrifice.”

94.

94.

“Addhā tuvaṃ katte hitesi mayhaṃ, sakhā mamaṃ ummadantī tuvañca;

Nindeyyu devā pitaro ca sabbe, pāpañca passaṃ abhisamparāyaṃ.

“Truly, you work for my welfare, my friend. You and Ummādantī are my companions. All the gods and ancestors would censure me, seeing the evil in the life to come.”

95.

95.

“Na hetadhammaṃ sivirāja vajjuṃ, sanegamā jānapadā ca sabbe;

Yaṃ te mayā ummadantī padinnā, bhusehi rājā vanathaṃ sajāhi.

O King of Sivi, all the townsfolk and countryfolk would say this is not the Dhamma. Since Ummadantī was given to you by me, enjoy her greatly, O king, and thus abandon your craving.

96.

96.

“Addhā [M 5.0233] tuvaṃ katte hitesi mayhaṃ, sakhā mamaṃ ummadantī tuvañca;

Satañca dhammāni sukittitāni, samuddavelāva duraccayāni.

Truly, you act for my welfare, O creator; you are my friend, and so is Ummadantī. And the principles of the good, well-proclaimed, are like the ocean's shore, hard to transgress.

97.

97.

“Āhuneyyo mesi hitānukampī, dhātā vidhātā casi kāmapālo;

Tayī [P 5.0222] hutā rāja mahapphalā hi, kāmena me ummadantiṃ paṭiccha.

You are worthy of offerings to me, compassionate for my welfare; you are a supporter, a provider, and a guardian of desires. Indeed, O king, offerings made to you bear great fruit. Out of my desire, accept Ummadantī from me.

98.

98.

“Addhā hi sabbaṃ abhipāraka tvaṃ, dhammaṃ acārī mama kattuputta;

Añño nu te ko idha sotthikattā, dvipado naro aruṇe jīvaloke.

Truly, O Abhipāraka, you have practiced all righteousness for me, my dutiful son. Who else here, what other two-legged man in this world of the living at the rising of the sun, could be a bringer of well-being for you?

99.

99.

“Tuvaṃ nu seṭṭho tvamanuttarosi, tvaṃ dhammagutto dhammavidū sumedho;

So dhammagutto cirameva jīva, dhammañca me desaya dhammapāla.

You are indeed the best; you are unsurpassed; you are a guardian of the Dhamma, a knower of the Dhamma, highly wise. As such, a guardian of the Dhamma, may you live long, and teach me the Dhamma, O protector of the Dhamma.

100.

100.

“Tadiṅgha abhipāraka, suṇohi vacanaṃ mama;

Dhammaṃ te desayissāmi, sataṃ āsevitaṃ ahaṃ.

Come now, Abhipāraka, listen to my words; I will teach you the Dhamma that is followed by the good.

101.

101.

“Sādhu dhammarucī rājā, sādhu paññāṇavā naro;

Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassākaraṇaṃ sukhaṃ.

A king who delights in the Dhamma is good; a wise man is good; non-betrayal of friends is good; and the non-doing of evil is happiness.

102.

102.

“Akkodhanassa vijite, ṭhitadhammassa rājino;

Sukhaṃ manussā āsetha, sītacchāyāya saṅghare.

In the realm of a king who is without anger and established in the Dhamma, people dwell happily in their homes, as if in cool shade.

103.

103.

“Na [V 5.0210] cāhametaṃ abhirocayāmi, kammaṃ asamekkhakataṃ asādhu;

Ye vāpi ñatvāna sayaṃ karonti, upamā imā mayhaṃ tuvaṃ suṇohi.

And I do not approve of this unwholesome deed done without consideration, nor of those who, knowingly, do it themselves. Listen now to these similes of mine.

104.

104.

“Gavaṃ [M 5.0234] ce taramānānaṃ, jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti, nette jimhaṃ gate sati.

If, among cattle crossing a ford, the lead bull goes crookedly, all the others go crookedly when their leader has gone crookedly.

105.

105.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So ce adhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko.

Even so among humans, he who is considered the best, if he practices unrighteousness, how much more so the other people. The whole kingdom dwells in suffering if the king is unrighteous.

106.

106.

“Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, ujuṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā gāvī ujuṃ yanti, nette ujuṃ gate sati.

If, among cattle crossing a ford, the lead bull goes straight, all the cows go straight when their leader has gone straight.

107.

107.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So sace dhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti dhammiko.

Even so among humans, he who is considered the best, if he practices the Dhamma, how much more so the other people. The whole kingdom dwells in happiness if the king is righteous.

108.

108.

“Na [P 5.0223] cāpāhaṃ adhammena, amarattamabhipatthaye;

Imaṃ vā pathaviṃ sabbaṃ, vijetuṃ abhipāraka.

Nor do I wish for immortality through unrighteousness, O Abhipāraka, nor to conquer all this earth.

109.

109.

“Yañhi kiñci manussesu, ratanaṃ idha vijjati;

Gāvo dāso hiraññañca, vatthiyaṃ haricandanaṃ.

For whatever treasures exist here among humans—cows, slaves, and gold, garments and yellow sandalwood,

110.

110.

“Assitthiyo ratanaṃ maṇikañca, yañcāpi me candimasūriyā abhipālayanti;

Na tassa hetu visamaṃ careyyaṃ, majjhe sivīnaṃ usabhomhi jāto.

horses, women, treasures and gems, and all that the moon and sun watch over—for the sake of these I would not act unjustly, for I am born as a leader among the Sivis.

111.

111.

“Netā hitā uggato raṭṭhapālo, dhammaṃ sivīnaṃ apacāyamāno;

So dhammamevānuvicintayanto, tasmā sake cittavase na vatto.

A leader, beneficial, exalted, and protector of the kingdom, revering the tradition of the Sivis; reflecting only upon the Dhamma, I am therefore not under the sway of my own mind.

112.

112.

“Addhā [V 5.0211] tuvaṃ mahārāja, niccaṃ abyasanaṃ sivaṃ;

Karissasi ciraṃ rajjaṃ, paññā hi tava tādisī.

Truly, O great king, you will rule the kingdom for a long time, always without misfortune and peacefully, for such is your wisdom.

113.

113.

“Etaṃ te anumodāma, yaṃ dhammaṃ nappamajjasi;

Dhammaṃ pamajja khattiyo, raṭṭhā cavati issaro.

We rejoice in this of yours, that you are not heedless of the Dhamma. A khattiya, a ruler who is heedless of the Dhamma, falls from his kingdom.

114.

114.

“Dhammaṃ [M 5.0235] cara mahārāja, mātāpitūsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards your mother and father, O khattiya. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

115.

115.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, puttadāresu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards your children and wives, O khattiya. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

116.

116.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, mittāmaccesu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards your friends and ministers, O khattiya. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

117.

117.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, vāhanesu balesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards your mounts and troops. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

118.

118.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, gāmesu nigamesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, in your villages and towns. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

119.

119.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, raṭṭhesu janapadesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, in your kingdoms and countrysides. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

120.

120.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards ascetics and brahmins. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

121.

121.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, migapakkhīsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king, towards beasts and birds, O khattiya. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

122.

122.

“Dhammaṃ [V 5.0212] cara mahārāja, dhammo ciṇṇo sukhāvaho;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king; the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to a heavenly world.

123.

123.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, saindā devā sabrahmakā;

Suciṇṇena divaṃ pattā, mā dhammaṃ rāja pāmado”ti.

Practice the Dhamma, O great king. The gods with Indra, and those with Brahmā, reached heaven through good practice. O king, do not be heedless of the Dhamma.

Tattha [P 5.0224] sabbāpīti, janinda, ahametaṃ ekakova paṭicchādetvā ānessāmi, tasmā ṭhapetvā mamañca tuvañca aññā sabbāpi pajā imassa katassa ākāramattampi na jaññā na jānissanti. Bhusehīti tāya saddhiṃ abhiramanto attano taṇhāvanathaṃ bhusaṃ karohi vaḍḍhehi manorathaṃ pūrehi. Sajāhīti manorathaṃ pana pūretvā sace te na ruccati, atha naṃ sajāhi mayhameva paṭidehi. Kammakaranti, samma abhipāraka, yo manusso pāpakaṃ kammaṃ [M 5.0236] karonto, so pacchā mā idha aññe idaṃ pāpakammaṃ maññiṃsu mā jānantūti maññati cinteti, ducintitametaṃ tassa. Kiṃkāraṇā? Passanti bhūtāni karontametanti ye ca buddhā paccekabuddhā buddhaputtā iddhiyā yuttā, te ca naṃ passantiyeva. Na me piyāti, samma abhipāraka, añño nu te koci “idha lokasmiṃ sakalāyapi pathaviyā na me ummādantī piyā”ti evaṃ saddaheyya.

Herein, 'all' means: O lord of men, I alone will conceal this and bring her; therefore, apart from me and you, no other people will know or get to know even the slightest detail of this deed. 'Bhusehi' means: delighting with her, make your forest of craving exceedingly strong, increase it, fulfill your heart's desire. 'Sajāhi' means: but having fulfilled your heart's desire, if she does not please you, then abandon her, give her back to me. Regarding 'the doer of a deed': friend Abhipāraka, a person who commits an evil deed afterwards thinks, 'Let others here not think of this evil deed, let them not know'—this is a wrong thought of his. For what reason? 'Beings see him doing it' means: those who are Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and sons of the Buddha endowed with psychic power, they indeed see him. 'Not dear to me' means: friend Abhipāraka, would anyone else believe you saying, 'Here in the world, on the entire earth, Ummadantī is not dear to me'?

Sīhova selassa guhanti, mahārāja, sace tvaṃ taṃ idha na ānesi, atha yathā sīho kilesapariḷāhe uppanne sīhapotikāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ maṇiguhaṃ upeti, evaṃ tassā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gaccha, tattha attano patthanaṃ pūrehīti. Sukhapphalanti, samma abhipāraka, paṇḍitā attano dukkhena phuṭṭhā samānā na sukhavipākadāyakakammaṃ pariccajanti, sammohitā vāpi hutvā mohena mūḷhā sukhena mattā pāpakammaṃ nāma na samācaranti. Yathāsukhaṃ, sāmi, karohi kāmanti, sāmi sivirāja, attano dāsiṃ paricārentassa garahā nāma natthi, tvaṃ yathāsukhaṃ yathājjhāsayaṃ kāmaṃ karohi, attano icchaṃ pūrehīti. Na tena so jīvatīti, samma abhipāraka, yo “issaromhī”ti pāpaṃ karoti, katvā ca kiṃ maṃ devamanussā vakkhantīti na uttasati na ottappati, so tena kammena na ca dīghakālaṃ jīvati, khippameva marati, devatāpi pana “kiṃ imassa pāparañño rajjena, varamassa vāḷukaghaṭaṃ gale bandhitvā maraṇa”nti lāmakena cakkhunā olokenti.

'Like a lion in a mountain cave' means, O great king, if you do not bring her here, then just as a lion, when the burning of defilements arises, goes to his jeweled cave, the dwelling place of the lioness, so too go to her dwelling place and fulfill your longing there. 'Sukhapphala' means, dear Abhipāraka, the wise, even when afflicted by suffering, do not abandon actions that yield a pleasant result; nor do the deluded, blinded by ignorance and intoxicated by pleasure, commit evil deeds. 'Yathāsukhaṃ, sāmi, karohi kāmaṃ' means, O lord King Sivirāja, there is no blame for one who enjoys his own female slave; do as you wish, as you please, fulfill your desires. 'Na tena so jīvati' means, dear Abhipāraka, one who, thinking, 'I am powerful,' commits evil, and having done so, does not fear or have moral dread of what gods and humans will say of him—such a person does not live long by that deed, but dies quickly. Even the deities look upon him with a contemptuous eye, thinking, 'What use is a kingdom to this wicked king? It would be better for him to die with a pot of sand tied around his neck.'

Aññātakanti, mahārāja, aññesaṃ santakaṃ tehi sāmikehi padinnaṃ dānaṃ ye attano dhamme [V 5.0213] ṭhitā paṭicchanti, te tattha paṭicchakā ca dāyakā ca sabbepi sukhapphalameva kammaṃ karonti. Paṭiggāhake hi paṭiggaṇhante taṃ dānaṃ dāyakassa mahantaṃ vipākaṃ detīti. Yo attadukkhenāti, samma abhipāraka, yo attano dukkhena pīḷito taṃ parassa dahati, attano sarīrato apanetvā parassa sarīre khipati, parassa vā sukhena attano sukhaṃ dahati, parassa sukhaṃ gahetvā attani pakkhipati, “attano dukkhaṃ harissāmī”ti paraṃ dukkhitaṃ karoti, “attānaṃ sukhessāmī”ti paraṃ dukkhitaṃ karoti, “attānaṃ sukhessāmī”ti parassa sukhaṃ nāseti, na so dhammaṃ jānāti. Yo pana evaṃ jānāti “yathevidaṃ mayhaṃ [M 5.0237] sukhadukkhaṃ, tathā paresa”nti, sa vedi dhammaṃ jānāti nāmāti ayametissā gāthāya attho.

'Aññātakaṃ' means, O great king, a gift belonging to others, given by its owners, which those who are established in their own Dhamma accept. In that case, both the receivers and the givers all perform an action that bears the fruit of happiness. For when the recipients accept the gift, it yields a great result for the giver. 'Yo attadukkhena' means, dear Abhipāraka, one who, oppressed by his own suffering, inflicts it upon another—taking it from his own body and casting it upon another's body; or who establishes his own happiness by means of another's happiness—seizing another's happiness and placing it upon himself; who, thinking, 'I will remove my own suffering,' makes another suffer; or thinking, 'I will make myself happy,' makes another suffer; or thinking, 'I will make myself happy,' destroys another's happiness—such a one does not know the Dhamma. But one who understands thus: 'Just as this happiness and suffering is mine, so it is for others'—that one, it is said, truly knows the Dhamma. This is the meaning of this verse.

Piyena te dammīti piyena kāraṇabhūtena piyaṃ phalaṃ patthento dammīti attho. Piyaṃ labhantīti saṃsāre saṃsarantā piyameva labhanti. Kāmahetukanti, samma abhipāraka[P 5.0225], kāmahetukaṃ ayuttaṃ katvā “attānaṃ vadhissāmī”ti me parivitakko uppajjati. Mayha satinti mama santakaṃ. “Mayha satī”tipi pāṭho, mama santakāti evaṃ maññamāno sace tvaṃ taṃ na kāmesīti attho. Sabbajanassāti sabbā seniyo sannipātāpetvā tassa sabbajanassa ayaṃ mayhaṃ ahitāti pariccajissāmi. Tato avhayesīti tato taṃ apariggahitattā āneyyāsi. Adūsiyanti anaparādhaṃ. Katteti tameva aparena nāmena ālapati. So hi rañño hitaṃ karoti, tasmā “kattā”ti vuccati. Na cāpi tyassāti evaṃ akiccakārīti nagare tava koci pakkhopi na bhaveyya.

'Piyena te dammi' means: I give, desiring a dear result, with what is dear as the cause. 'Piyaṃ labhanti' means: wandering in saṃsāra, they obtain only what is dear. 'Kāmahetukaṃ' means, dear Abhipāraka, having done what is unsuitable due to desire, the thought arises in me: 'I will destroy myself.' 'Mayha sati' means my possession. There is also the reading 'Mayha satī,' which means: thinking 'she is my possession,' if you do not desire her. 'Sabbajanassa' means: having assembled all the armies, I will renounce her before all those people, saying, 'This one is harmful to me.' 'Tato avhayesi' means: then, because she is unaccepted, you would bring her. 'Adūsiyaṃ' means without offense. 'Katte' means he addresses him by another name. For he does what is beneficial for the king; therefore, he is called 'doer.' 'Na cāpi tyassa' means: thus, being a doer of what should not be done, there would be no supporter for you in the city.

Nindanti na kevalaṃ upavādameva, sacepi maṃ koci sammukhā nindissati vā pasaṃsissati vā, dosaṃ vā pana āropento garahissati, tampāhaṃ nindaṃ pasaṃsaṃ garahañca sabbaṃ sahissāmi, sabbametaṃ mama āgacchatūti vadati. Tamhāti yo ete nindādayo na gaṇhāti, tamhā purisā issariyasaṅkhātā sirī ca paññāsaṅkhātā lakkhī ca thalaṭṭhānato suvuṭṭhisaṅkhāto āpo viya apeti na patiṭṭhātīti. Ettoti ito mama tassā pariccattakāraṇā. Dhammātisārañcāti dhammaṃ atikkamitvā pavattaṃ akusalaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci hoti. Paccuttarissāmīti sampaṭicchissāmi dhārayissāmi. Thāvarānaṃ tasānanti yathā mahāpathavī khīṇāsavānañca puthujjanānañca kiñci sampaṭicchati sabbaṃ adhivāseti, tathevāhampi sabbametaṃ sampaṭicchissāmi adhivāsessāmīti dīpeti. Ekovimanti ahaṃ ekova imampi attano dukkhabhāraṃ hārayissāmi dhārayissāmi vahissāmi. Dhamme ṭhitoti vinicchayadhamme paveṇidhamme tividhasucaritadhamme ca ṭhito hutvā.

'Nindanti' means not only reproach; for even if someone were to blame or praise me to my face, or accuse me of faults and criticize, I would endure all that blame, praise, and criticism, saying, 'Let all that come to me.' 'Tamhā' means that from a person who does not take up these things—blame and the like—glory, which is sovereignty, and prosperity, which is wisdom, depart like water from a well-rained high ground, and do not remain. 'Etto' means from this, because of my renunciation of her. 'Dhammātisārañca' means whatever unwholesome thing arises by transgressing the Dhamma. 'Paccuttarissāmi' means I will accept it, I will bear it. 'Thāvarānaṃ tasānaṃ' means: just as the great earth accepts and endures all things, whether from those with defilements destroyed or from ordinary people, so too, he shows, will I accept and endure all this. 'Eko'vim' means I alone will carry, bear, and endure even this burden of my own suffering. 'Dhamme ṭhito' means having stood firm in the Dhamma of judgment, customary Dhamma, and the threefold good conduct.

Saggūpaganti[V 5.0214], deva, puññakammaṃ nāmetaṃ saggūpagaṃ hoti. Yaññe dhananti yaññadhanaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sakhāti ummādantīpi mama sahāyikā, tvampi [M 5.0238] sahāyako. Pitaroti brahmāno. Sabbeti na kevalaṃ devabrahmānova, sabbe raṭṭhavāsinopi maṃ passatha, “bho, sahāyakassa bhariyā sahāyikā iminā gehe katā”ti nindeyyuṃ. Na hetadhammanti na hi etaṃ adhammikaṃ. Yaṃ te mayāti yasmā mayā sā tuyhaṃ dinnā, tasmā etaṃ adhammoti na vadissanti. Satanti santānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ khantimettābhāvanāsīlācārasaṅkhātāni dhammāni suvaṇṇitāni samuddavelāva duraccayāni, tasmā yathā samuddo velaṃ nātikkamati, evamahampi sīlavelaṃ nātikkamissāmīti vadati.

'Saggūpagaṃ' means, O deva, a meritorious action is what is called 'leading to heaven.' 'Yaññe dhanaṃ' means sacrificial wealth; or this is the reading. 'Sakhā' means: Ummādantī is my female friend, and you too are a friend. 'Pitaro' means the Brahmās. 'Sabbe' means: not only the devas and Brahmās, but all the inhabitants of the kingdom will see me and would criticize me, saying, 'Look, the wife of a friend has been made a female friend in this house by him.' 'Na hetadhammam' means: for this is not unrighteous. 'Yaṃ te mayā' means: since she was given to you by me, therefore they will not say this is unrighteous. 'Sataṃ' means: the well-praised qualities of good people such as the Buddhas—namely patience, loving-kindness, meditation, morality, and conduct—are difficult to transgress, like the ocean's shore. Therefore, he says, 'Just as the ocean does not cross its shore, so I too will not cross the shore of virtue.'

Āhuneyyo mesīti, mahārāja, tvaṃ mama āhunapāhunasakkārassānucchaviko. Dhātā vidhātā casi kāmapāloti tvaṃ mama, deva, dhāraṇato dhātā issariyasukhassa vidahanato vidhātā icchitapatthitānaṃ [P 5.0226] kāmānaṃ pālanato kāmapālo. Tayī hutāti tuyhaṃ dinnā. Kāmena meti mama kāmena mama patthanāya ummādantiṃ paṭicchāti evaṃ abhipārako rañño deti. Rājā “na mayhaṃ attho”ti paṭikkhipati. Bhūmiyaṃ patitaṃ sākuṇikapacchiṃ piṭṭhipādena paharitvā aṭaviyaṃ khipantā viya ubhopi naṃ jahanteva. Idāni rājā puna akathanatthāya taṃ santajjento “addhā hī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha kattuputtāti pitāpissa kattāva, tena naṃ evaṃ ālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – addhā tvaṃ ito pubbe mayhaṃ sabbadhammaṃ acari, hitameva vuḍḍhimeva akāsi, idāni pana paṭipakkho hutvā bahuṃ kathesi, “mā evaṃ vippalapasi, añño nu te dvipado naro, ko idha jīvaloke aruṇeyeva sotthikattā, sace hi ahaṃ viya añño rājā tava bhariyāya paṭibaddhacitto abhavissa, antoaruṇeyeva tava sīsaṃ chindāpetvā taṃ attano ghare kareyya, ahaṃ pana akusalabhayeneva na karomi, tuṇhī hohi, na me etāya attho”ti taṃ santajjesi.

'Āhuneyyo me si' means, O great king, you are suitable for my offerings, hospitality, and honor. 'Dhātā vidhātā casi kāmapālo' means: you, O lord, are to me the establisher by maintaining, the provider by bestowing the joy of sovereignty, and the protector of desires by fulfilling wished-for desires. 'Tayī hutā' means given to you. 'Kāmena me' means: Abhipāraka gives Ummādantī to the king, saying, 'By my desire, by my longing, accept her.' The king refuses, saying, 'I have no need of her.' Like fowlers kicking a fowler's basket that has fallen on the ground with the back of their foot and throwing it into the forest, both abandon her. Now the king, to prevent him from speaking further, threatens him, speaking the verse beginning 'Addhā hi.' Therein, 'kattuputta' means: his father was also a doer; therefore, he addresses him thus. This is what was said: 'Indeed, previously you performed every duty for me, doing only what was beneficial and for my growth. But now, having become an opponent, you speak much. Do not babble thus! Is there another man for you? Who in this living world is a source of safety even before dawn? For if another king like me were infatuated with your wife, he would have your head cut off before dawn and take her into his own house. But I do not do so out of fear of what is unwholesome. Be silent! I have no need of her.' Thus he threatened him.

So taṃ sutvā puna kiñci vattuṃ asakkonto rañño thutivasena “tuvaṃ nū”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – mahārāja, tvaññeva sakalajambudīpe sabbesaṃ narindānaṃ seṭṭho, tvaṃ anuttaro, tvaṃ vinicchayadhammapaveṇidhammasucaritadhammānaṃ gopāyanena dhammagutto, tesaṃ viditattā dhammavidū tvaṃ sumedho, so tvaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ gopesi, teneva gutto cīraṃ jīva, dhammañca me desehi dhammapālaka, dhammagopaka, rājavarāti.

Hearing this, unable to say anything further, he praised the king with the verse, "You indeed!" The meaning is: O great king, you alone are the foremost among all kings in the entire Jambudīpa; you are unsurpassed; you are the guardian of the Dhamma through protecting the Dhamma of judgment, the customary Dhamma, and the Dhamma of good conduct; you are a knower of Dhamma because of knowing them; you are intelligent. Therefore, may you, who protect the Dhamma, live long, guarded by that very Dhamma. O protector of the Dhamma, O guardian of the Dhamma, O excellent king, teach me the Dhamma!

Atha [M 5.0239] rājā dhammaṃ desento “tadiṅghā”tiādimāha. Tattha iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto, yasmā [V 5.0215] maṃ tvaṃ codesi, tasmāti attho. Satanti buddhādīhi sappurisehi āsevitaṃ. Sādhūti sundaro pasattho. Vinicchayapaveṇisucaritadhamme rocetīti dhammaruci. Tādiso hi jīvitaṃ jahantopi akiccaṃ na karoti, tasmā sādhu. Paññāṇavāti ñāṇasampanno. Mittānamaddubbhoti mittassa adussanabhāvo. Ṭhitadhammassāti patiṭṭhitatividhadhammassa. Āsethāti āseyyuṃ nisīdeyyuṃ. Desanāsīsameva cetaṃ, cattāropi iriyāpathe sukhaṃ kappeyyunti ayaṃ panettha attho. Sītacchāyāyāti puttadārañātimittānaṃ sītalāya chāyāya. Saṅghareti sakaghare, attano geheti attho. Adhammabalidaṇḍādīhi anupaddutā sukhaṃ vaseyyunti dasseti. Na cāhametanti, samma abhipāraka, yametaṃ asamekkhitvā kataṃ asādhukammaṃ, etaṃ ahaṃ na rocayāmi. Ye vāpi ñatvānāti ye vā pana rājāno ñatvā tuletvā tīretvā sayaṃ karonti, tesāhaṃ kammaṃ rocemīti adhippāyo. Upamā imāti imasmiṃ panatthe tvaṃ mayhaṃ imā dve upamā suṇohi.

Then the king, teaching the Dhamma, said, 'Tadiṅghā' and so on. Here, 'iṅgha' is a particle in the sense of urging; it means, 'Because you urge me, therefore...' 'Sataṃ' refers to what is cultivated by good people such as the Buddhas. 'Sādhu' means excellent, praiseworthy. 'Dhammaruci' means one who delights in the Dhamma of judgment, customary Dhamma, and Dhamma of good conduct. Such a person, even at the cost of life, does not do what is unseemly—hence, 'sādhu.' 'Paññāṇavā' means endowed with wisdom. 'Mittānamaddubbho' means the state of not being hostile to friends. 'Ṭhitadhammassa' means one established in the threefold Dhamma. 'Āsetha' means they should sit or settle. This is indeed the main point of the teaching; the four postures should be comfortable—this is the meaning here. 'Sītacchāyāya' means in the cool shade of children, wife, relatives, and friends. 'Saṅghare' means in one’s own home, one’s own house. It shows that one should live happily, unoppressed by unjust taxes, punishments, and so on. 'Na cāhametaṃ' means, 'Dear Abhipāraka, I do not approve of this unconsidered, unwholesome deed.' 'Ye vāpi ñatvā' means, 'But those kings who, after knowing, weighing, scrutinizing, and acting themselves—I approve of their deeds.' This is the intent. 'Upamā imā' means, 'Now, in this matter, listen to these two similes of mine.'

Jimhanti vaṅkaṃ. Netteti yo gāviyo neti, tasmiṃ jeṭṭhakausabhe. Pagevāti tasmiṃ adhammaṃ carante itarā pajā pageva carati, ativiya karotīti attho. Dhammikoti cattāri agatigamanāni pahāya dhammena rajjaṃ kārento. Amarattanti devattaṃ. Ratananti saviññāṇakāviññāṇakaratanaṃ. Vatthiyanti kāsikavatthameva. Assitthiyoti vātasamagatiassepi uttamarūpadharā itthiyopi. Ratanaṃ maṇikañcāti sattavidharatanañca mahagghabhaṇḍakañca. Abhipālayantīti [P 5.0227] ālokaṃ karontā rakkhanti. Na tassāti tassa cakkavattirajjassapi hetu na visamaṃ careyyaṃ. Usabhomhīti yasmā ahaṃ sivīnaṃ majjhe jeṭṭhakarājā hutvā jāto, tasmā cakkavattirajjakāraṇampi na visamaṃ carāmīti attho. Netāti mahājanaṃ kusale patiṭṭhāpetvā devanagaraṃ netā, hitakaraṇena tassa hitā, “sivirājā kira dhammacārī”ti sakalajambudīpe ñātattā uggato, samena raṭṭhapālanato raṭṭhapālo. Apacāyamānoti sivīnaṃ porāṇakarājūnaṃ paveṇidhammaṃ apacāyamāno. Soti so ahaṃ tameva dhammaṃ anuvicintayanto tasmā tena kāraṇena attano cittassa vase na vattāmi.

'Jimhaṃ' means crooked. 'Nette' means in the leader, that is, in the chief bull who leads the cows. 'Pageva' means, 'When he acts unrighteously, the rest of the people act even more so, doing excessively.' This is the meaning. 'Dhammiko' means one who rules righteously, having abandoned the four wrong courses. 'Amarattaṃ' means the divine state. 'Ratanaṃ' means the jewel with consciousness and the jewel without consciousness. 'Vatthiyaṃ' means Kāsi cloth. 'Assitthiyo' means horses with the speed of the wind and women of the finest beauty. 'Ratanaṃ maṇikañca' means the seven kinds of jewels and the most precious goods. 'Abhipālayanti' means they protect by illuminating and guarding. 'Na tassa' means, 'Not even for the sake of that universal sovereignty would I act unjustly.' 'Usabhomhi' means, 'Because I was born as the chief king among the Sivis, therefore, even for the sake of universal sovereignty, I do not act unjustly.' This is the meaning. 'Netā' means a leader, one who leads the great populace to the divine city by establishing them in what is wholesome; one who is beneficial to them by doing what is helpful; renowned because of being known throughout all Jambudīpa as 'the Sivi king is indeed a righteous practitioner'; a protector of the realm because of protecting the realm with justice. 'Apacāyamāno' means revering the traditional law of the ancient Sivi kings. 'So' means, 'I, reflecting on that very Dhamma, for that reason do not act under the sway of my own mind.'

Evaṃ [M 5.0240] mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā abhipārako thutiṃ karonto “addhā”tiādimāha. Nappamajjasīti attanā kathitadhammaṃ nappamajjasi tattheva vattesi. Dhammaṃ pamajjāti dhammaṃ pamussitvā agativasena gantvā. Evaṃ so tassa thutiṃ katvā “dhammaṃ carā”ti dhammacariyāya niyyojento uttaripi dasa ovādagāthā abhāsi. Tāsamattho heṭṭhā tesakuṇajātake (jā. 2.17.1 ādayo) vaṇṇitova.

Having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Great Being, Abhipāraka, praising him, said, 'Indeed!' and so on. 'You do not neglect,' means you do not neglect the Dhamma you yourself have taught, but abide in that very thing. 'Neglecting the Dhamma' means forgetting the Dhamma and going by way of the wrong courses. Thus, having praised him, and exhorting him with 'Practice the Dhamma,' he further spoke ten verses of advice. Their meaning has already been described below in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka (Jā. 2.17.1, etc.).

Evaṃ [V 5.0216] abhipārakasenāpatinā rañño dhamme desite rājā ummādantiyā paṭibaddhacittaṃ vinodesi.

Thus, when the Dhamma was taught to the king by the general Abhipāraka, the king dispelled the attachment of his mind to Ummādantī.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Tadā sunandasārathi ānando ahosi, abhipārako sāriputto, ummādantī uppalavaṇṇā, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, sivirājā ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Sunanda the charioteer was Ānanda, Abhipāraka was Sāriputta, Ummādantī was Uppalavaṇṇā, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Sivi was myself.

Ummādantījātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Ummādantī Jātaka, the Second.

[528] 3. Mahābodhijātakavaṇṇanā

[528] 3. The Commentary on the Mahābodhi Jātaka

Kiṃ nu daṇḍaṃ kimajinanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahāumaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavā parappavādappamaddanoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'What indeed is the staff, what is the deerskin?'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom. The story will become clear in the Mahā-Umaṅga Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.590, etc.). Then the Teacher said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, the Tathāgata was wise and a crusher of the doctrines of others,' and he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe asītikoṭivibhavassa udiccabrāhmaṇamahāsālassa kule nibbatti, “bodhikumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo paccāgantvā agāramajjhe vasanto aparabhāge kāme pahāya himavantapadesaṃ pavisitvā paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā [P 5.0228] tattheva vanamūlaphalāhāro ciraṃ vasitvā vassārattasamaye himavantā oruyha cārikaṃ caranto anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase paribbājakasāruppena nagare bhikkhāya caranto rājadvāraṃ pāpuṇi [M 5.0241] tamenaṃ sīhapañjare ṭhito rājā disvā tassa upasame pasīditvā taṃ attano bhavanaṃ pavesetvā rājapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā katapaṭisanthāro thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ dāpesi. Mahāsatto bhattaṃ gahetvā cintesi – “idaṃ rājakulaṃ nāma bahudosaṃ bahupaccāmittaṃ hoti, ko nu kho mama uppannaṃ bhayaṃ nittharissatī”ti. So avidūre ṭhitaṃ rājavallabhaṃ ekaṃ piṅgalasunakhaṃ disvā mahantaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā tassa dātukāmatākāraṃ dassesi. Rājā ñatvā sunakhassa bhājanaṃ āharāpetvā bhattaṃ gāhāpetvā dāpesi. Mahāsattopi tassa datvā bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Rājāpissa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā antonagare rājuyyāne paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā pabbajitaparikkhāre [V 5.0217] datvā taṃ tattha vāsāpesi, devasikañcassa dve tayo vāre upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Bhojanakāle pana mahāsatto niccaṃ rājapallaṅkeyeva nisīditvā rājabhojanameva bhuñjati. Evaṃ dvādasa saṃvaccharāni atītāni.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in the Kasi country into the family of a great brahmin from the northern country, possessing eighty crores of wealth. They named him 'Bodhi Kumara.' Having come of age and mastered the arts in Takkasila, he returned. While living in the household, he later renounced sensual pleasures and entered the Himalayan region, where he took up the wandering ascetic life. Living there for a long time, sustaining himself on wild fruits and roots, he descended from the Himalayas during the rainy season and wandered on alms-round. Gradually, he arrived in Benares and stayed in the royal park. The next day, dressed as a wandering ascetic, he entered the city for alms and reached the royal gate. Standing in the lion window, the king saw him and, pleased by his serene demeanor, invited him into his palace. Seating him on the royal throne, the king offered him hospitality. After listening briefly to a Dhamma talk, he served him various delicious dishes. The Great Being, having received the meal, thought: 'This royal household is full of faults and many adversaries. Who will save me if danger arises?' Noticing a favorite tawny dog of the king nearby, he gestured as if wishing to give it a large portion of food. Understanding his intention, the king had a bowl brought and had food given to the dog. The Great Being, having given to the dog, finished his meal. The king, having taken his promise, built a leaf-hut for him in the royal park within the inner city and provided him with the requisites of an ascetic, allowing him to stay there. Daily, the king attended to him two or three times. At mealtime, the Bodhisatta always sat on the royal throne and ate the king's food. Thus, twelve years passed.

Tassa pana rañño pañca amaccā atthañca dhammañca anusāsanti. Tesu eko ahetukavādī, eko issarakatavādī, eko pubbekatavādī, eko ucchedavādī, eko khattavijjavādī. Tesu ahetukavādī “ime sattā saṃsārasuddhikā”ti mahājanaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Issarakatavādī “ayaṃ loko issaranimmito”ti mahājanaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Pubbekatavādī “imesaṃ sattānaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā uppajjamānaṃ pubbekateneva uppajjatī”ti mahājanaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Ucchedavādī “ito paralokaṃ gato nāma natthi, ayaṃ loko ucchijjatī”ti mahājanaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Khattavijjavādī “mātāpitaropi māretvā attanova attho kātabbo”ti mahājanaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Te rañño vinicchaye niyuttā lañjakhādakā [P 5.0229] hutvā assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ, sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ karonti.

Now, that king had five ministers who advised him on matters of worldly advantage and righteousness. Among them, one was a proponent of non-causality, one of a supreme creator, one of past actions, one of annihilationism, and one of the warrior's science. The proponent of non-causality taught the people, saying, 'These beings are purified through the cycle of rebirth.' The proponent of a supreme creator taught the people, saying, 'This world is created by a supreme being.' The proponent of past actions taught the people, saying, 'Whatever happiness or suffering arises for these beings arises solely due to past actions.' The proponent of annihilationism taught the people, saying, 'There is no such thing as going to another world from this one; this world is annihilated.' The proponent of the warrior's science taught the people, saying, 'For one’s own benefit, one should kill even one’s mother and father.' Appointed to the king's court of justice, they became takers of bribes, making the non-owner an owner, and the owner a non-owner.

Athekadivasaṃ eko puriso kūṭaṭṭaparājito mahāsattaṃ bhikkhāya carantaṃ rājagehaṃ pavisantaṃ disvā vanditvā, “bhante, tumhe rājagehe bhuñjamānā vinicchayāmacce lañjaṃ gahetvā lokaṃ vināsente kasmā ajjhupekkhatha, idāni pañcahi amaccehi kūṭaṭṭakārakassa hatthato lañjaṃ gahetvā sāmikova samāno assāmiko kato”ti paridevi. So [M 5.0242] tasmiṃ kāruññavasena vinicchayaṃ gantvā dhammena vinicchinitvā sāmikaññeva sāmikaṃ akāsi. Mahājano ekappahāreneva mahāsaddena sādhukāraṃ adāsi. Rājā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃsaddo nāmāya”nti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā katabhattakiccaṃ mahāsattaṃ upanisīditvā pucchi – “bhante, ajja kira vo aṭṭo vinicchito”ti. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Bhante, tumhesu vinicchinantesu mahājanassa vuḍḍhi bhavissati, ito paṭṭhāya tumheva vinicchinathā”ti. “Mahārāja, mayaṃ pabbajitā nāma, netaṃ kammaṃ amhākaṃ kamma”nti. “Bhante, mahājane kāruññena kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tumhe sakaladivasaṃ mā vinicchinatha, uyyānato pana idhāgacchantā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā pātova cattāro aṭṭe vinicchinatha, bhutvā uyyānaṃ gacchantā cattāro, evaṃ mahājanassa vuḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti. So tena punappunaṃ yāciyamāno “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya tathā akāsi.

Then one day, a man who had been defeated by a fraudulent lawsuit saw the Great Being wandering for alms and entering the royal palace. He paid homage and lamented, 'Venerable sir, while you dine in the royal palace, why do you remain indifferent to the ministers who, taking bribes, are destroying the world? Just now, the five ministers, having taken a bribe from the perpetrator of the fraudulent case, have made the rightful owner into a non-owner.' Moved by compassion for him, the Great Being went to the court of justice, judged the case righteously, and made the rightful owner the owner once more. The great crowd, with a single voice, gave a great cry of approval. Hearing the sound, the king asked, 'What is this sound?' Upon learning the matter, he finished his meal, sat down near the Great Being, and asked, 'Venerable sir, it is said that you judged a case today.' 'Yes, great king.' 'Venerable sir, when you are the one judging, the people will prosper. From now on, you alone should judge.' 'Great king, we are renunciants; this is not our work.' 'Venerable sir, it is fitting to act out of compassion for the people. Do not judge all day long. Rather, on your way here from the park, go to the judgment hall and judge four cases in the morning; then, after eating, judge four more on your way to the park. Thus, the people will prosper.' Being repeatedly requested by him, the Great Being consented, saying, 'Very well,' and from then on, he did so.

Kūṭaṭṭakārakā okāsaṃ na labhiṃsu. Tepi amaccā lañjaṃ alabhantā duggatā hutvā cintayiṃsu [V 5.0218] – “bodhiparibbājakassa vinicchinanakālato paṭṭhāya mayaṃ kiñci na labhāma, handa naṃ ‘rājaveriko’ti vatvā rañño antare paribhinditvā mārāpessāmā”ti. Te rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “mahārāja, bodhiparibbājako tumhākaṃ anatthakāmo”ti vatvā asaddahantena raññā “sīlavā esa ñāṇasampanno, na evaṃ karissatī”ti vutte, “mahārāja, tena sakalanagaravāsino attano hatthe katvā kevalaṃ amheyeva pañca [P 5.0230] jane kātuṃ na sakkā, sace amhākaṃ vacanaṃ na saddahatha, tassa idhāgamanakāle parisaṃ olokethā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “sādhū”ti sīhapañjare ṭhito taṃ āgacchantaṃ olokento parivāraṃ disvā attano aññāṇena aṭṭakārakamanusse “tassa parivārā”ti maññamāno bhijjitvā te amacce pakkosāpetvā “kinti karomā”ti pucchi. “Gaṇhāpetha naṃ, devā”ti. “Oḷārikaṃ aparādhaṃ apassantā kathaṃ gaṇhāmā”ti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, pakatiparihāramassa hāpetha, taṃ parihāyantaṃ disvā paṇḍito paribbājako kassaci anārocetvā sayameva palāyissatī”ti.

The perpetrators of fraudulent cases found no opportunity. Those ministers too, unable to obtain bribes, became impoverished and thought, 'Since the time the Bodhi wanderer began judging cases, we have gained nothing. Come, let us call him an enemy of the king and, by creating a rift between him and the king, have him killed.' They approached the king and said, 'Great king, the Bodhi wanderer wishes you harm.' The king, not believing them, replied, 'He is virtuous and endowed with wisdom; he would not do such a thing.' They then said, 'Great king, he has brought all the city-dwellers under his control; it is only we five people whom he has been unable to win over. If you do not believe our words, observe his retinue when he comes here.' The king said, 'Very well,' and standing at the lion-window, he watched him arrive. Seeing the retinue and, due to his own lack of wisdom, thinking the litigants were the wanderer's followers, his mind was alienated. He summoned those ministers and asked, 'What should we do?' 'Have him seized, Your Majesty,' they said. 'Without seeing a gross offense, how can we seize him?' 'In that case, great king, reduce his customary honors. Seeing his support dwindling, the wise wanderer will flee by himself without telling anyone.'"

Rājā “sādhū”ti vatvā anupubbena tassa parihāraṃ parihāpesi. Paṭhamadivasaṃ tāva naṃ tucchapallaṅkeyeva nisīdāpesuṃ. So tucchapallaṅkaṃ disvāva [M 5.0243] rañño paribhinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā sayameva uyyānaṃ gantvā taṃ divasameva pakkamitukāmo hutvāpi “ekantena ñatvā pakkamissāmī”ti na pakkāmi. Athassa punadivase tucchapallaṅke nisinnassa raññopakatibhattañca aññañca gahetvā missakabhattaṃ adaṃsu. Tatiyadivase mahātalaṃ pavisituṃ adatvā sopānasīseyeva ṭhapetvā missakabhattaṃ adaṃsu. So tampi ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā bhattakiccaṃ akāsi. Catutthadivase heṭṭhāpāsāde ṭhapetvā kaṇājakabhattaṃ adaṃsu. So tampi gahetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā bhattakiccaṃ akāsi. Rājā amacce pucchi – “bodhiparibbājako sakkāre parihāpitepi na pakkamati, kinti naṃ karomā”ti? “Deva, na so bhattatthāya carati, chattatthāya pana carati. Sace bhattatthāya careyya, paṭhamadivasaṃyeva palāyeyyā”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karomā”ti? “Sve ghātāpetha naṃ, mahārājā”ti. So “sādhū”ti tesaññeva hatthe khagge ṭhapetvā “sve antaradvāre ṭhatvā pavisantassevassa sīsaṃ chinditvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā kañci ajānāpetvā vaccakuṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā nhatvā āgaccheyyāthā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “sve āgantvā evaṃ karissāmā”ti aññamaññaṃ [P 5.0231] vicāretvā evaṃ attano nivesanaṃ agamaṃsu.

The king said, "Very well," and gradually reduced his honors. On the first day, they made him sit on a mere empty couch. Seeing the empty couch and realizing the king’s estrangement, he went to the park by himself. Though he wished to leave that very day, he did not depart, thinking, "I will leave only after knowing for certain." The next day, as he sat on the empty couch, they took the king's customary food and other food and gave him mixed food. On the third day, not allowing him to enter the upper floor, they kept him at the head of the stairs and gave him mixed food. He took that too, went to the park, and ate his meal. On the fourth day, keeping him below the palace, they gave him a meal of broken rice. He took that too, went to the park, and ate his meal. The king asked his ministers, "Even though his honors have been reduced, the Bodhi wanderer does not depart; what shall we do with him?" They replied, "Your Majesty, he does not go about for the sake of food, but for the sake of the royal parasol. If he went about for food, he would have fled on the very first day." "What shall we do now?" "Have him killed tomorrow, Great King." The king said, "Very well," and placing swords in their hands, he said, "Tomorrow, stand between the gates, and as soon as he enters, cut off his head, chop him into pieces, and without letting anyone know, throw him into the latrine, then bathe and return." They accepted, saying, "Very well," and after discussing among themselves, "Tomorrow we will come and do this," they went to their own homes.

Rājāpi sāyaṃ bhuttabhojano sirisayane nipajjitvā mahāsattassa guṇe anussari. Athassa tāvadeva soko uppajji, sarīrato sedā mucciṃsu, sayane assāsaṃ alabhanto aparāparaṃ [V 5.0219] parivatti. Athassa aggamahesī upanipajji, so tāya saddhiṃ sallāpamattampi na kari. Atha naṃ sā “kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, sallāpamattampi na karotha, api nu kho me koci aparādho atthī”ti pucchi. “Natthi devi, apica kho bodhiparibbājako kira amhākaṃ paccatthiko jātoti tassa sve ghātanatthāya pañca amacce āṇāpesiṃ, te pana naṃ māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā vaccakūpe pakkhipissanti, so pana amhākaṃ dvādasa saṃvaccharāni bahuṃ dhammaṃ desesi, ekāparādhopissa mayā paccakkhato na diṭṭhapubbo, parapattiyena hutvā tassa mayā vadho āṇatto, tena kāraṇena socāmī”ti. Atha naṃ sā “sace te deva so paccatthiko jāto, taṃ ghātento kiṃ socasi, paccatthikaṃ nāma puttampi ghātetvā attano sotthibhāvo kātabbova, mā socitthā”ti assāsesi. So tassā vacanena paṭiladdhassāso niddaṃ okkami.

The king, having eaten his evening meal, lay down on his royal bed and reflected on the virtues of the Great Being. Then sorrow arose in him at once; sweat poured from his body, and unable to find comfort in his bed, he tossed and turned repeatedly. Then his chief queen lay down beside him, but he did not exchange even a word with her. So she asked him, "Why, great king, do you not speak even a word to me? Have I perhaps done some wrong?" "No, queen. But the ascetic Bodhisatta, they say, has become our enemy. Tomorrow, for his execution, I have ordered five ministers. They will kill him, cut him into pieces, and throw him into a cesspool. Yet for twelve years he has taught us much of the Dhamma, and never before have I seen any fault in him directly. But because of others' persuasion, I have ordered his death. That is why I grieve." Then she consoled him, saying, "If, lord, he has become your enemy, why grieve over killing him? An enemy must indeed be slain, even if it be one’s own son, for the sake of one’s own safety. Do not grieve." Comforted by her words, he fell asleep.

Tasmiṃ [M 5.0244] khaṇe koleyyako piṅgalasunakho taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “sve mayā attano balenassa jīvitaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā punadivase pātova pāsādā oruyha mahādvāraṃ āgantvā ummāre sīsaṃ katvā mahāsattassa āgamanamaggaṃ olokentova nipajji. Tepi amaccā pātova khaggahatthā āgantvā dvārantare aṭṭhaṃsu. Bodhisattopi velaṃ sallakkhetvā uyyānā nikkhamma rājadvāraṃ āgañchi. Atha naṃ sunakho disvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā catasso dāṭhā dassetvā “kiṃ tvaṃ, bhante, jambudīpatale aññattha bhikkhaṃ na labhasi, amhākaṃ rājā tava māraṇatthāya pañca amacce khaggahatthe dvārantare ṭhapesi, mā tvaṃ nalāṭena maccuṃ gahetvā āgami, sīghaṃ pakkamā”ti mahāsaddena viravi. So sabbarutaññutāya tamatthaṃ ñatvā tatova nivattitvā uyyānaṃ gantvā [P 5.0232] pakkamanatthāya parikkhāre ādiyi. Rājā sīhapañjare ṭhito taṃ āgacchantaṃ gacchantañca disvā “sace ayaṃ mama paccatthiko bhaveyya, uyyānaṃ gantvā balaṃ sannipātāpetvā kammasajjo bhavissati. No ce, attano parikkhāre gahetvā gamanasajjo bhavissati, jānissāmi tāvassa kiriya”nti uyyānaṃ gantvā mahāsattaṃ attano parikkhāre ādāya “gamissāmī”ti paṇṇasālato nikkhantaṃ caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ disvāva vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the palace-bred tawny dog named Piᅅgala, having heard that conversation, thought, 'Tomorrow, I must save the life of that Bodhi wanderer by my own strength.' The next morning, he descended from the palace early, went to the great gate, and lay down with his head on the threshold, watching the path by which the Great Being would come. The ministers, too, arrived early with swords in hand and stood between the outer and inner gates. The Bodhisatta, observing the time, left the garden and approached the royal gate. Then the dog Piᅅgala, seeing him, opened its mouth, bared its four fangs, and barked with a loud voice, 'Venerable sir, do you not find alms elsewhere in Jambudĩpa? Our king has stationed five sword-wielding ministers between the two gates to kill you. Do not come, carrying death upon your forehead—leave quickly!' Knowing the sounds of all creatures, he understood the meaning and, turning back from there, went to the garden to take up his requisites for departure. The king, standing at the lion-window, saw him coming and going and thought, 'If this Bodhi wanderer were my enemy, he would go to the garden, gather his forces, and prepare for battle. If not, he would take his belongings and prepare to flee. I shall know his intentions.' Going to the garden, he saw the Great Being, who had taken his requisites and come out of his leaf-hut, at the end of the walking path. The king paid his respects, stood to one side, and wishing to ask him, spoke the first verse:

124.

124.

“Kiṃ nu daṇḍaṃ kimajinaṃ, kiṃ chattaṃ kimupāhanaṃ;

Kimaṅkusañca pattañca, saṅghāṭiñcāpi brāhmaṇa;

Taramānarūpohāsi, kiṃ nu patthayase disa”nti.

"What is the staff, what the antelope hide, what the sunshade, what the sandals? What is the hook and the bowl, and the outer robe too, Brahmin? You appear hurried; to what direction do you aspire?"

Tassattho [V 5.0220] – bhante, pubbe tvaṃ amhākaṃ gharaṃ āgacchanto daṇḍādīni na gaṇhāsi, ajja pana kena kāraṇena daṇḍañca ajinañca chattūpāhanañca mattikapasibbakolambanaaṅkusañca mattikapattañca saṅghāṭiñcāti sabbepime parikkhāre taramānarūpo gaṇhāsi, kataraṃ nu disaṃ patthesi, kattha gantukāmosīti pucchi.

The meaning is: Venerable sir, previously when you came to our house, you did not carry a staff and other such things. But today, for what reason do you hastily take all these requisites—the staff, the antelope hide, the sunshade, the sandals, the hook for hanging the bowl-bag, the bowl, and the outer robe? To which direction do you aspire? Where do you wish to go? Thus he asked.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ attanā katakammaṃ na jānātīti maññati, jānāpessāmi na”nti dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the Great Being thought, 'This king thinks I do not know the deed he has done. I will let him know.' Desiring to inform him, he spoke these two verses:

125.

125.

“Dvādasetāni vassāni, vusitāni tavantike;

Nābhijānāmi soṇena, piṅgalenābhikūjitaṃ.

"For twelve years I have lived in your presence; I do not recall ever being barked at by the tawny dog Piᅅgala."

126.

126.

“Svāyaṃ [M 5.0245] dittova nadati, sukkadāṭhaṃ vidaṃsayaṃ;

Tava sutvā sabhariyassa, vītasaddhassa maṃ patī”ti.

"Now it barks as if bold, displaying its white fangs, having heard the words you spoke with your wife, when you lost faith in me."

Tattha abhikūjitanti etena tava sunakhena evaṃ mahāviravena viravitaṃ na jānāmi. Ditto vāti dappito viya. Sabhariyassāti tava sabhariyassa mama māraṇatthāya pañcannaṃ amaccānaṃ āṇattabhāvaṃ kathentassa sutvā “kiṃ tvaṃ aññattha bhikkhaṃ na labhasi, raññā te vadho āṇatto, idha māgacchī”ti dittova nadati. Vītasaddhassa maṃ patīti mamantare vigatasaddhassa tava vacanaṃ sutvā eva nadatīti āha.

Therein, 'abhikũjitaᅃ' means: I do not recall being barked at by your dog with such a loud roar. 'Ditto vā' means: as if bold or aggressive. 'Sabhariyassa' means: having heard you, together with your wife, giving the order to the five ministers for my execution, it barks as if bold, saying, 'Do you not find alms elsewhere? Your death has been ordered by the king; do not come here!' 'Vĩtasaddhassa maᅃ patĩ' means: it barks thus having heard your words, you who have lost faith in me.

Tato rājā attano dosaṃ sampaṭicchitvā taṃ khamāpento catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king, acknowledging his own fault and wishing to ask for forgiveness, spoke the fourth verse:

127.

127.

“Ahu [P 5.0233] esa kato doso, yathā bhāsasi brāhmaṇa;

Esa bhiyyo pasīdāmi, vasa brāhmaṇa māgamā”ti.

"This fault was indeed committed, just as you say, Brahmin; now I have even greater faith. Stay, Brahmin, do not go."

Tattha bhiyyoti saccaṃ mayā evaṃ āṇattaṃ, ayaṃ me doso, esa panāhaṃ idāni adhikataraṃ tayi pasīdāmi, idheva vasa, mā aññattha gamīti.

Herein, 'bhiyyo' means: It is true that such an order was given by me; this is my fault. But now I have even greater faith in you. Stay right here; do not go elsewhere.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto, “mahārāja, paṇḍitā nāma tādisena parapattiyena apaccakkhakārinā saddhiṃ na vasantī”ti vatvā tassa anācāraṃ pakāsento āha –

Hearing that, the Great Being said, 'Great king, the wise do not dwell with those who trust the words of others and do not see things for themselves.' Then, to show the king's disrespectful conduct, he spoke these nine verses:

128.

128.

“Sabbaseto [V 5.0221] pure āsi, tatopi sabalo ahu;

Sabbalohitako dāni, kālo pakkamituṃ mama.

"Formerly the rice was all white, then it became variegated; now it is all red. It is time for me to depart."

129.

129.

“Abbhantaraṃ pure āsi, tato majjhe tato bahi;

Purā niddhamanā hoti, sayameva vajāmahaṃ.

"Formerly, it was inside, then in the middle, then outside; before there is expulsion, I go forth of my own accord."

130.

130.

“Vītasaddhaṃ na seveyya, upadānaṃvanodakaṃ;

Sacepi naṃ anukhaṇe, vāri kaddamagandhikaṃ.

"One should not serve the faithless, like a waterless well; even if one digs around it, the water is muddy and foul-smelling."

131.

131.

“Pasannameva seveyya, appasannaṃ vivajjaye;

Pasannaṃ payirupāseyya, rahadaṃvudakatthiko.

"One should serve only the faithful, and avoid the faithless; one should attend upon the faithful, like a thirsty man at a lake."

132.

132.

“Bhaje bhajantaṃ purisaṃ, abhajantaṃ na bhajjaye;

Asappurisadhammo so, yo bhajantaṃ na bhajjati.

"One should associate with a person who associates with oneself; one should not associate with one who does not. It is the way of an ignoble person not to associate with one who associates with him."

133.

133.

“Yo [M 5.0246] bhajantaṃ na bhajati, sevamānaṃ na sevati;

Sa ve manussapāpiṭṭho, migo sākhassito yathā.
