"He who does not associate with one who associates with him, nor serve one who serves him, is truly the most wretched of men, like a monkey on its branch."

134.

134.

“Accābhikkhaṇasaṃsaggā, asamosaraṇena ca;

Etena mittā jīranti, akāle yācanāya ca.

"Through excessively frequent association, and through not meeting; by these, and by untimely requests, friendships decay."

135.

135.

“Tasmā nābhikkhaṇaṃ gacche, na ca gacche cirāciraṃ;

Kālena yācaṃ yāceyya, evaṃ mittā na jīyare.

"Therefore, one should not go too often, nor stay away for too long; one should make requests at the proper time; thus, friendships do not decay."

136.

136.

“Aticiraṃ nivāsena, piyo bhavati appiyo;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma, purā te homa appiyā”ti.

"By staying too long, one who is dear becomes undear. We take our leave of you; let us go, before we become undear to you."

Tattha sabbasetoti, mahārāja, paṭhamameva tava nivesane mama odano sabbaseto ahosi, yaṃ tvaṃ bhuñjasi, tameva dāpesīti attho. Tatoti tato pacchā paribhedakānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā tava mayi virattakāle sabalo missakodano jāto. Dānīti idāni sabbalohitako jāto. Kāloti aguṇaññussa [V 5.0222] tava santikā idāni mama pakkamituṃ kālo. Abbhantaranti paṭhamaṃ mama abbhantaraṃ [P 5.0234] āsanaṃ āsi, alaṅkatamahātalamhi ussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅkeyeva maṃ nisīdāpesuṃ. Majjheti sopānamatthake. Purā niddhamanā hotīti yāva gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nikkaḍḍhanā na hoti.

Therein, 'all white' means: 'Great king, at first, the rice given to me in your palace was all white; you had the same rice given to me that you yourself ate.' 'Then' means: 'After that, when you listened to slanderers and became disaffected with me, it became mixed rice.' 'Now' means: 'Now it has become all red.' 'Time' means: 'Now is the time for me to depart from you, who are ungrateful.' 'Inside' means: 'At first, my seat was in the inner chamber; they had me sit on the royal couch itself, under the white parasol.' 'Middle' means: 'At the head of the stairs.' 'Before there is expulsion' means: 'Before they seize me by the neck and drag me out.'

Anukhaṇeti sacepi anudakaṃ udapānaṃ patto puriso udakaṃ apassanto kalalaṃ viyūhitvā anukhaṇeyya, tathāpi taṃ vāri kaddamagandhikaṃ bhaveyya, amanuññatāya na piveyya, tatheva vītasaddhaṃ payirupāsantena laddhapaccayāpi parittā ceva lūkhā ca, amanuññā aparibhogārahāti attho. Pasannanti patiṭṭhitasaddhaṃ. Rahadanti gambhīraṃ mahārahadaṃ. Bhajantanti attānaṃ bhajantameva bhajeyya. Abhajantanti paccatthikaṃ. Na bhajjayeti na bhajeyya. Na bhajjatīti yo puriso attānaṃ bhajantaṃ hitacittaṃ puggalaṃ na bhajati, so asappurisadhammo nāmāti. Manussapāpiṭṭhoti manussalāmako patikuṭṭho sabbapacchimako. Sākhassitoti makkaṭo.

'Even if one were to dig' means that if a man, having reached a waterless well and not seeing water, were to clear away the mud and dig into it, even then that water would be foul-smelling from the mud and he would not drink it because it is unpleasant. Similarly, even if one associating with a faithless person were to receive requisites, they would be meager and coarse, unpleasant and unfit for use. 'Faithful' means one with established faith. 'Lake' means a deep, great lake. 'Associate' means one should associate only with one who is devoted to one. 'One who does not associate' means an adversary. 'He should not associate' means one should not associate with him. 'He does not associate' means: the person who does not associate with a friend who is devoted to him and wishes him well is called one of ignoble conduct. 'Worst of men' means a person who is very base and contemptible. 'Sākhassito' (clinging to a branch) refers to a monkey.

Accābhikkhaṇasaṃsaggāti [M 5.0247] ativiya abhiṇhasaṃsaggena. Akāleti ayuttappattakāle parassa piyabhaṇḍaṃ yācanāya mittā jīranti nāma, tvampi aticiraṃ nivāsena mayi mittiṃ bhindi. Tasmāti yasmā accābhikkhaṇasaṃsaggena asamosaraṇena ca mittā jīranti, tasmā. Cirāciranti cirakālaṃ vītināmetvā ciraṃ na gacche na upasaṅkameyya. Yācanti yācitabbaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ yuttakāle yāceyya. Na jīyareti evaṃ mittā na jīranti. Purā te homa appiyāti yāva tava appiyā na homa, tāva āmantetvāva taṃ gacchāmāti.

'Excessive association' means through excessively frequent interaction. 'Untimely' means at an inappropriate time; begging for another’s beloved possessions causes friendships to wither. You too, by staying too long, have broken friendship with me. 'Therefore' means because friendships decay through excessively frequent association and not meeting, therefore. 'Cirāciraṃ' means that after letting a long time pass, one should not go and visit for a long time. 'Yācaṃ' means one should ask for the item that needs to be asked for at the proper time. 'Do not wither' means thus, friendships do not decay. 'Before we become displeasing to you' means: before we become displeasing to you, we will take leave of you and depart.

Rājā āha –

The king said:

137.

137.

“Evaṃ ce yācamānānaṃ, añjaliṃ nāvabujjhasi;

Paricārakānaṃ sataṃ, vacanaṃ na karosi no;

Evaṃ taṃ abhiyācāma, puna kayirāsi pariyāya”nti.

If, when we beg like this, you do not recognize our joined palms; if you do not heed the word of us, your hundred attendants; thus we beseech you, that you might make another visit.

Tattha nāvabujjhasīti sace, bhante, evaṃ yācantena mayā kataṃ añjaliṃ na jānāsi, na paṭiggaṇhasīti attho. Pariyāyanti puna idhāgamanāya ekavāraṃ kareyyāsīti yācati.

Here, 'do not recognize' means, "Venerable sir, if you do not recognize the joined palms I make while begging thus, if you do not accept it"—this is the meaning. 'Another visit' means he begs, "May you make one occasion to return here."

Bodhisatto āha –

The Bodhisatta said:

138.

138.

“Evaṃ [V 5.0223] ce no viharataṃ, antarāyo na hessati;

Tuyhaṃ vāpi mahārāja, mayhaṃ vā raṭṭhavaddhana;

Appeva nāma passema, ahorattānamaccaye”ti.

If, as we dwell thus, no harm befalls us, O great king, neither you nor me, O prosperer of the kingdom, perhaps we may see each other at the passing of days and nights.

Tattha evaṃ ce noti sace, mahārāja, evaṃ nānā hutvā viharantānaṃ amhākaṃ antarāyo na hessati, tuyhaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā jīvitaṃ pavattissatīti dīpeti. Passemāti api nāma passeyyāma.

Therein, 'If thus for us' indicates: if, great king, no harm will befall us who are dwelling thus separately, and your life or mine will continue. 'We may see' means perhaps we may see.

Evaṃ [P 5.0235] vatvā mahāsatto rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti vatvā uyyānā nikkhamitvā ekasmiṃ sabhāgaṭṭhāne bhikkhāya caritvā bārāṇasito nikkhamma anupubbena himavantokāsameva gantvā kiñci kālaṃ vasitvā puna otaritvā ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya araññe vasi. Tassa pana gatakālato paṭṭhāya te amaccā puna vinicchaye nisīditvā vilopaṃ karontā cintayiṃsu – “sace mahābodhiparibbājako punāgamissati, jīvitaṃ no natthi, kiṃ nu khvassa anāgamanakāraṇaṃ kareyyāmā”ti. Atha [M 5.0248] nesaṃ etadahosi – “ime sattā paṭibaddhaṭṭhānaṃ nāma jahituṃ na sakkonti, kiṃ nu khvassa idha paṭibaddhaṭṭhāna”nti. Tato “rañño aggamahesī”ti ñatvā “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ so imaṃ nissāya āgaccheyya, paṭikacceva naṃ mārāpessāmā”ti te rājānaṃ etadavocuṃ – “deva, imasmiṃ divase nagare ekā kathā sūyatī”ti. “Kiṃ kathā nāmā”ti? “Mahābodhiparibbājako ca kira devī ca aññamaññaṃ sāsanapaṭisāsanaṃ pesentī”ti. “Kinti katvā”ti? Tena kira deviyā pesitaṃ “sakkā nu kho attano balena rājānaṃ mārāpetvā mama setacchattaṃ dātu”nti. Tāyapissa pesitaṃ “rañño māraṇaṃ nāma mama bhāro, mahābodhiparibbājako khippaṃ āgacchatū”ti rājā tesaṃ punappunaṃ kathentānaṃ saddahitvā “idāni kiṃ kattabba”nti pucchitvā “deviṃ māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte anupaparikkhitvāva “tena hi naṃ tumheva māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā vaccakūpe khipathā”ti āha. Te tathā kariṃsu. Tassā māritabhāvo sakalanagare pākaṭo ahosi.

Having spoken thus, the Great Being taught the king the Dhamma and said, "Be vigilant, great king." Then he left the park, wandered for alms in a suitable place, departed from Bārāṇasī, and gradually went to the Himalayan region itself. After dwelling there for some time, he descended again and lived in the forest relying on a border village. From the time he left, those ministers, sitting in judgment again, engaged in corruption and thought, "If the great Bodhisatta ascetic returns, our lives are forfeited. What can we do to prevent his return?" Then it occurred to them, "These beings cannot abandon a place to which they are attached. What is his place of attachment here?" Knowing that it was "the king’s chief queen," they thought, "There is a chance he might return relying on her. Let us have her killed beforehand." So they told the king, "Sire, a rumor is being heard in the city today." "What rumor?" "They say the great Bodhisatta ascetic and the queen are exchanging messages." "How so?" "It is said that he sent a message to the queen: ‘Is it possible, by your own power, to have the king killed and give me the white parasol?’ And a message was also sent by her: ‘The killing of the king is my responsibility; let the great Bodhisatta ascetic come quickly.’" The king, believing what they repeatedly told him, asked, "What should be done now?" When they said, "The queen should be executed," without any investigation, he ordered, "Then you yourselves kill her, cut her into pieces, and throw her into a latrine pit." They did so. The news of her execution became known throughout the entire city.

Athassā cattāro puttā “iminā no niraparādhā mātā māritā”ti rañño paccatthikā ahesuṃ. Rājā mahābhayappatto ahosi. Mahāsatto paramparāya taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā cintesi – “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño te kumāre saññāpetvā pitaraṃ khamāpetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, rañño ca jīvitaṃ dassāmi, kumāre ca pāpato mocessāmī”ti. So punadivase paccantagāmaṃ pavisitvā [V 5.0224] manussehi dinnaṃ makkaṭamaṃsaṃ khāditvā tassa [P 5.0236] cammaṃ yācitvā gahetvā assamapade sukkhāpetvā niggandhaṃ katvā nivāsesipi pārupesipi aṃsepi ṭhapesi. Kiṃkāraṇā? “Bahūpakāro me”ti vacanatthāya. So taṃ cammaṃ ādāya anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā kumāre upasaṅkamitvā “pitughātakakammaṃ nāma dāruṇaṃ, taṃ vo na kātabbaṃ, ajarāmaro satto nāma natthi, ahaṃ tumhe aññamaññaṃ samagge karissāmicceva āgato, tumhe mayā pahite sāsane āgaccheyyāthā”ti kumāre ovaditvā antonagare uyyānaṃ pavisitvā makkaṭacammaṃ attharitvā silāpaṭṭe nisīdi.

Then her four sons became enemies of the king, thinking, "Our innocent mother was killed by him." The king was struck with great fear. The Great Being, having heard the sequence of events in succession, reflected: "Except for me, there is no one else capable of convincing these princes and persuading them to ask forgiveness of their father. I will give the king his life and free the princes from evil." The next day, he entered a border village, ate monkey meat given by the people, requested and took its skin, dried it in his hermitage, made it odorless, and wore it as a lower garment, an upper garment, and also on his shoulder. For what reason? To express the meaning, "It has been very helpful to me." Taking that skin, he gradually went to Bārāṇasī, approached the princes, and advised them: "The act of killing one's father is indeed dreadful; you must not do it. There is no being that is ageless and deathless. I have come for the very purpose of reconciling you with each other. You should come when you receive the message I send." Having advised the princes, he entered the garden in the inner city, spread the monkey skin, and sat on a stone slab.

Atha naṃ uyyānapālako disvā vegena gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā sutvāva sañjātasomanasso hutvā te amacce ādāya [M 5.0249] tattha gantvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā paṭisanthāraṃ kātuṃ ārabhi. Mahāsatto tena saddhiṃ asammoditvā makkaṭacammameva parimajji. Atha naṃ evamāha – “bhante, tumhe maṃ akathetvā makkaṭacammameva parimajjatha, kiṃ vo idaṃ mayā bahūpakāratara”nti? “Āma mahārāja, bahūpakāro me esa vānaro, ahamassa piṭṭhe nisīditvā vicariṃ, ayaṃ me pānīyaghaṭaṃ āhari, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sammajji, ābhisamācārikavattapaṭivattaṃ mama akāsi, ahaṃ pana attano dubbalacittatāya assa maṃsaṃ khāditvā cammaṃ sukkhāpetvā attharitvā nisīdāmi ceva nipajjāmi ca, evaṃ bahūpakāro esa mayha”nti. Iti so tesaṃ vāde bhindanatthāya vānaracamme vānaravohāraṃ āropetvā taṃ taṃ pariyāyaṃ sandhāya imaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. So hi tassa nivutthapubbattā “piṭṭhe nisīditvā vicari”nti āha; taṃ aṃse katvā pānīyaghaṭassa āhaṭapubbattā “pānīyaghaṭaṃ āharī”ti āha; tena cammena bhūmiyaṃ sammaṭṭhapubbattā “vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjī”ti āha; nipannakāle tena cammena piṭṭhiyā, akkantakāle pādānaṃ phuṭṭhapubbattā “vattapaṭivattaṃ me akāsī”ti āha. Chātakāle pana tassa maṃsaṃ labhitvā khāditattā “ahaṃ pana [P 5.0237] attano dubbalacittatāya tassa maṃsaṃ khādi”nti āha.

Then the park-keeper saw him and quickly went to inform the king. Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and, taking his ministers, went there. He paid homage to the Great Being, sat down to one side, and began to exchange courtesies. The Great Being did not exchange courtesies with him but merely stroked the monkey-hide. Then the king said, “Venerable sir, without speaking to me, you merely stroke the monkey-hide. Is this of greater service to you than I am?” “Indeed, great king, this monkey has been of great service to me. I traveled about seated on its back; it brought me a water-pot; it swept my dwelling-place; it performed for me the duties of proper conduct. But I, due to my own weak-mindedness, ate its flesh, dried its hide, spread it out, and now sit and lie upon it. Thus, it has been of great service to me.” Thus, in order to refute their arguments, he attributed the behavior of a monkey to the monkey-hide and spoke these words with various implications, alluding to the relevant circumstances. Because he had previously sat upon it, he said, “I traveled about seated on its back.” Because he had previously brought a water-pot by placing the hide on his shoulder, he said, “It brought me a water-pot.” Because he had previously swept the ground with the hide, he said, “It swept my dwelling-place.” Because the hide had touched his back when lying down and his feet when walking, he said, “It performed the duties for me.” And because, when hungry, he had obtained and eaten its flesh, he said, “But I, due to my own weak-mindedness, ate its flesh.”

Taṃ sutvā te amaccā “pāṇātipāto tena kato”ti saññāya “passatha, bho, pabbajitassa kammaṃ, makkaṭaṃ kira māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā cammaṃ gahetvā vicaratī”ti pāṇiṃ paharitvā parihāsamakaṃsu. Mahāsatto te tathā karonte disvā “ime attano vādabhedanatthāya mama cammaṃ ādāya āgatabhāvaṃ na jānanti, jānāpessāmi ne”ti ahetukavādiṃ tāva āmantetvā pucchi – “āvuso, tvaṃ kasmā maṃ parihasasī”ti? “Mittadubbhikammassa ceva pāṇātipātassa [V 5.0225] ca katattā”ti. Tato mahāsatto “yo pana gatiyā ceva diṭṭhiyā ca te saddahitvā evaṃ kareyya, tena kiṃ dukkaṭa”nti tassa vādaṃ bhindanto āha –

Hearing this, the ministers, thinking, “He has committed the destruction of life,” mocked him, clapping their hands and saying, “Look, sirs, at the deed of this ascetic! They say he killed a monkey, ate its flesh, took its hide, and now wanders about with it.” Seeing them act thus, the Great Being thought, “These men do not know that I have come here with this hide to break down their arguments; I will make them understand.” First, he addressed the proponent of causelessness and asked, “Friend, why do you mock me?” “Because you have acted disloyally toward a friend and have committed the destruction of life.” Then the Great Being, refuting his argument, said, “But if someone, trusting in your way and your view, were to act thus, what fault would there be?”

139.

139.

“Udīraṇā ce saṃgatyā, bhāvāyamanuvattati;

Akāmā akaraṇīyaṃ vā, karaṇīyaṃ vāpi kubbati;

Akāmakaraṇīyamhi, kvidha pāpena lippati.

“If the assertion is that existence proceeds from association and follows its nature; if one, unwillingly, does what should not be done or what should be done; when an act is done unwillingly, who here is tainted by evil?”

140.

140.

“So [M 5.0250] ce attho ca dhammo ca, kalyāṇo na ca pāpako;

Bhoto ce vacanaṃ saccaṃ, suhato vānaro mayā.

“If that meaning and the doctrine are good and not evil, and if your words are true, then the monkey was well slain by me.”

141.

141.

“Attano ce hi vādassa, aparādhaṃ vijāniyā;

Na maṃ tvaṃ garaheyyāsi, bhoto vādo hi tādiso”ti.

“If you would recognize the fault in your own assertion, you would not blame me, for your assertion is just like that.”

Tattha udīraṇāti kathā. Saṃgatyāti saṃgatiyā channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ taṃ taṃ abhijātiṃ upagamanena. Bhāvāyamanuvattatīti bhāvena anuvattati, karaṇatthe sampadānaṃ. Akāmāti akāmena anicchāya. Akaraṇīyaṃ vā karaṇīyaṃ vāpīti akattabbaṃ pāpaṃ vā kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ vā. Kubbatīti karoti. Kvidhāti ko idha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tvaṃ ahetukavādī “natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”tiādidiṭṭhiko, ayaṃ loko saṃgatiyā ceva sabhāvena ca anuvattati pariṇamati, tattha tattha sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Akāmakova pāpaṃ vā puññaṃ vā karotīti vadasi, ayaṃ tava udīraṇā sace tathā, evaṃ sante akāmakaraṇīyasmiṃ attano dhammatāya pavattamāne pāpe ko idha satto pāpena lippati, sace hi attanā akatena pāpena lippati, na koci na lippeyyāti.

Here, ‘assertion’ (udīraṇā) means speech. ‘Through association’ (saṃgatyā) means by entering any of the six classes of birth. ‘Follows nature’ (bhāvāyamanuvattati) means it follows by way of nature; the dative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. ‘Unwilling’ (akāmā) means without desire or intention. ‘What should not be done or what should be done’ (akaraṇīyaṃ vā karaṇīyaṃ vāpi) means either evil that should not be done or good that should be done. ‘Does’ (kubbati) means performs. ‘Who here’ (kvidha) means who in this world. This is what is meant: You, a proponent of causelessness, hold the view, “There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings,” and so on. You claim this world proceeds and evolves through association and nature, and experiences pleasure and pain here and there. You say that one does evil or merit quite unwillingly. If this assertion of yours is true, then in that case, when evil is done unintentionally through its own nature, what being in this world is tainted by evil? For if one were tainted by evil not done by oneself, then no one could remain untainted.

So ceti so ahetukavādasaṅkhāto tava bhāsitattho ca atthajotako dhammo ca kalyāṇo na ca pāpako. “Ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti, sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyantī”ti idaṃ bhoto vacanaṃ [P 5.0238] saccaṃ ce, suhato vānaro mayā, ko ettha mama dosoti attho. Vijāniyāti, samma, sace hi tvaṃ attano vādassa aparādhaṃ jāneyyāsi, na maṃ garaheyyāsi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Bhoto vādo hi tādiso, tasmā ayaṃ mama vādaṃ karotīti maṃ pasaṃseyyāsi, attano pana vādaṃ ajānanto maṃ garahasīti.

‘If that’ (so ce) means if that meaning of your doctrine of causelessness and the doctrine that illustrates the meaning are good and not evil. If your statement, “Beings are defiled without cause or condition, experiencing pleasure and pain,” is true, then the monkey was well slain by me; the meaning is, what fault is there of mine in this? ‘If you would recognize’ (vijāniyā) means: friend, if you would recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me. Why? Because your doctrine is of such a nature; therefore, you should praise me, thinking, ‘He is acting according to my doctrine.’ But instead, not understanding your own doctrine, you blame me.

Evaṃ [V 5.0226] mahāsatto taṃ niggaṇhitvā appaṭibhāṇaṃ akāsi. Sopi rājaparisati maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho nisīdi. Mahāsattopi tassa vādaṃ bhinditvā issarakatavādiṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, āvuso, maṃ kasmā parihasasi, yadi issaranimmitavādaṃ sārato paccesī”ti vatvā āha –

Thus, the Great Being rebuked him and rendered him speechless. And he, humiliated in the royal assembly, sat down with drooping shoulders. The Great Being, having refuted his doctrine, then addressed the proponent of divine creation, saying, “Friend, why do you mock me, if you truly believe in the doctrine of divine creation?” and then said:

142.

142.

“Issaro sabbalokassa, sace kappeti jīvitaṃ;

Iddhiṃ byasanabhāvañca, kammaṃ kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Niddesakārī puriso, issaro tena lippati.

“If a lord of the entire world determines life, success, and misfortune, as well as good and evil deeds; then a person is merely one who carries out instructions, and the lord is tainted by that evil.”

143.

143.

“So [M 5.0251] ce attho ca dhammo ca, kalyāṇo na ca pāpako;

Bhoto ce vacanaṃ saccaṃ, suhato vānaro mayā.

“If that meaning and the doctrine are good and not evil, and if your words are true, then the monkey was well slain by me.”

144.

144.

“Attano ce hi vādassa, aparādhaṃ vijāniyā;

Na maṃ tvaṃ garaheyyāsi, bhoto vādo hi tādiso”ti.

“If you would recognize the fault in your own assertion, you would not blame me, for your assertion is just like that.”

Tattha kappeti jīvitanti sace brahmā vā añño vā koci issaro “tvaṃ kasiyā jīva, tvaṃ gorakkhenā”ti evaṃ sabbalokassa jīvitaṃ saṃvidahati vicāreti. Iddhiṃ byasanabhāvañcāti issariyādibhedā iddhiyo ca ñātivināsādikaṃ byasanabhāvañca sesañca kalyāṇapāpakaṃ kammaṃ sabbaṃ yadi issarova kappeti karoti. Niddesakārīti yadi tassa niddesaṃ āṇattimeva seso yo koci puriso karoti, evaṃ sante yo koci puriso pāpaṃ karoti, tassa issarena katattā issarova tena pāpena lippati. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha.

Here, ‘determines life’ (kappeti jīvitaṃ) means if Brahmā or any other lord were to say, ‘You live by farming, you by cattle-rearing,’ thus arranging and directing the lives of the entire world. ‘Power and misfortune’ (iddhiṃ byasanabhāvañca) refers to various kinds of lordship and powers, as well as misfortunes like the destruction of relatives, and all other good and evil deeds—if the lord alone determines and does them. ‘One who carries out instructions’ (niddesakārī) means if any other person merely carries out the lord’s command, then whoever does evil, since it was done by the lord, the lord alone is tainted by that evil. The rest should be understood in the same way as before. As it is here, so it is everywhere.

Iti so ambatova muggaraṃ gahetvā ambaṃ pātento viya issarakaraṇeneva issarakatavādaṃ bhinditvā pubbekatavādiṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, āvuso, maṃ kiṃ parihasasi, yadi pubbekatavādaṃ saccaṃ maññasī”ti vatvā āha –

Thus, as if taking a club from a mango tree itself to fell the mango, he shattered the doctrine of divine creation by means of the very notion of a lord’s doing. Then, addressing the proponent of past actions, he said: “Friend, why do you mock me if you consider the doctrine of past actions to be true?” He then said:

145.

145.

“Sace pubbekatahetu, sukhadukkhaṃ nigacchati;

Porāṇakaṃ kataṃ pāpaṃ, tameso muccate iṇaṃ;

Porāṇaka iṇamokkho, kvidha pāpena lippati.

“If one meets with pleasure and pain due to past action, one is freed from that old evil deed as from a debt; in the release from an old debt, how is one here tainted by evil?”

146.

146.

“So [V 5.0227][P 5.0239] ce attho ca dhammo ca, kalyāṇo na ca pāpako;

Bhoto ce vacanaṃ saccaṃ, suhato vānaro mayā.

“If that meaning and doctrine are good and not evil, and if your words are true, then the monkey was well slain by me.”

147.

147.

“Attano ce hi vādassa, aparādhaṃ vijāniyā;

Na maṃ tvaṃ garaheyyāsi, bhoto vādo hi tādiso”ti.

“If you would recognize a fault in your own assertion, you would not blame me, for your assertion is just like that.”

Tattha pubbekatahetūti pubbakatahetu purimabhave katakammakāraṇeneva. Tameso muccate iṇanti yo vadhabandhādīhi dukkhaṃ pāpuṇāti, yadi so yaṃ tena porāṇakaṃ kataṃ pāpaṃ, taṃ idāni iṇaṃ muccati, evaṃ sante mamapi esa porāṇakaiṇato mokkho, anena hi makkaṭena pubbe [M 5.0252] paribbājakena hutvā ahaṃ makkaṭo samāno māretvā khādito bhavissāmi, svāyaṃ idha makkaṭattaṃ patto mayā paribbājakattaṃ pattena māretvā khādito bhavissati, ko idha pāpena lippatīti.

Here, ‘due to a past deed’ means for the reason of a deed done in a former existence. ‘One is freed from that debt’ means: whoever attains suffering through execution, imprisonment, or the like, if that ancient evil deed done by him is now discharged as a debt, then in that case, this is my release from an ancient debt as well. For in a past life, this monkey must have been a wandering ascetic, and I, being a monkey, must have been killed and eaten by him. Now he, having attained the state of a monkey, will be killed and eaten by me, who has attained the state of a wandering ascetic. Who here is tainted by evil?

Iti so tassapi vādaṃ bhinditvā ucchedavādiṃ abhimukhaṃ katvā “tvaṃ, āvuso, ‘itthi dinna’ntiādīni vatvā ‘idheva sattā ucchijjanti, paralokaṃ gatā nāma natthī’ti maññamāno kasmā maṃ parihasasī”ti santajjetvā āha –

Thus, having refuted his doctrine as well, and turning to face the proponent of annihilationism, he rebuked him, saying: “Friend, you who say such things as ‘alms are given,’ and who think that beings are annihilated right here and that there is no one who has gone to another world—why do you mock me?”

148.

148.

“Catunnaṃyevupādāya, rūpaṃ sambhoti pāṇinaṃ;

Yato ca rūpaṃ sambhoti, tatthevānupagacchati;

Idheva jīvati jīvo, pecca pecca vinassati.

“Dependent on the four elements, form arises for living beings; and from where form arises, right there it returns. Right here the living being lives; having passed away, it utterly perishes.”

149.

149.

“Ucchijjati ayaṃ loko, ye bālā ye ca paṇḍitā;

Ucchijjamāne lokamhi, kvidha pāpena lippati.

“This world is annihilated, both the foolish and the wise. When the world is being annihilated, who here is tainted by evil?”

150.

150.

“So ce attho ca dhammo ca, kalyāṇo na ca pāpako;

Bhoto ce vacanaṃ saccaṃ, suhato vānaro mayā.

“If that principle and doctrine are good and not evil, and if your word is true, then the monkey was well slain by me.”

151.

151.

“Attano ce hi vādassa, aparādhaṃ vijāniyā;

Na maṃ tvaṃ garaheyyāsi, bhoto vādo hi tādiso”ti.

“If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me, for your doctrine is indeed of such a kind.”

Tattha [V 5.0228] catunnanti pathavīādīnaṃ bhūtānaṃ. Rūpanti rūpakkhandho. Tatthevāti yato taṃ rūpaṃ sambhoti, nirujjhanakālepi tattheva anupagacchati. Iminā tassa “cātumahābhūtiko ayaṃ puriso yadā kālaṃ karoti, tadā pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, āpo… tejo… vāyo vāyokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, ākāsaṃ indriyāni saṅkamanti, āsandhipañcamā purisā mataṃ ādāya gacchanti, yāva āḷāhanā padāni paññāyanti, kāpotakāni aṭṭhīni bhavanti, bhasmantā āhutiyo[P 5.0240], dattupaññattaṃ yadidaṃ dānaṃ, tesaṃ tucchā musā vilāpo, ye keci atthikavādaṃ vadanti, bāle ca paṇḍite ca kāyassa bhedā ucchijjanti vinassanti, na honti paraṃ maraṇā”ti imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Idhevāti imasmiṃyeva loke jīvo jīvati. Pecca pecca vinassatīti paraloke nibbatto satto gativasena idha anāgantvā tattheva paraloke vinassati [M 5.0253] ucchijjati. Evaṃ ucchijjamāne lokasmiṃ ko idha pāpena lippatīti.

Here, ‘of the four’ refers to the elements beginning with earth. ‘Form’ is the form aggregate. ‘Right there’ means that from where that form arises, at the time of its cessation, it also returns right there. By this, he established this view: ‘This person is composed of the four great elements. When he dies, the earth element returns to the body of earth, water… fire… air returns to the body of air, and the faculties pass into space. Four men, with the bier as fifth, carry the dead body away. Their footsteps are seen as far as the charnel ground; the bones become dove-colored, and offerings end in ashes. This giving is a doctrine of fools. The talk of those who profess a doctrine of existence is empty, false chatter. Both the foolish and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are annihilated and destroyed—they do not exist after death.’ ‘Right here’ means that the living being lives in this very world. ‘Having passed away, it utterly perishes’ means that a being who is reborn in the next world, not returning here by way of his destiny, perishes and is annihilated right there in the next world. Thus, when the world is being annihilated, who here is tainted by evil?

Iti so tassapi vādaṃ bhinditvā khattavijjavādiṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, āvuso, ‘mātāpitaropi māretvā attano attho kātabbo’ti imaṃ laddhiṃ ukkhipitvā vicaranto kasmā maṃ parihasasī”ti vatvā āha –

Having thus refuted his doctrine as well, he addressed the exponent of the science of ruling, saying, ‘Friend, you who wander about propagating the doctrine that “one should kill even one’s parents to achieve one’s own benefit,” why do you ridicule me?’ He then said:

152.

152.

“Āhu khattavidā loke, bālā paṇḍitamānino;

Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ haññe, atho jeṭṭhampi bhātaraṃ;

Haneyya puttadāre ca, attho ce tādiso siyā”ti.

“Those skilled in the science of ruling say in the world, fools who think themselves wise: ‘One should slay mother and father, and even an elder brother; one should slay children and wife, if the purpose were such.’”

Tattha khattavidāti khattavijjā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Khattavijjācariyānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Bālā paṇḍitamāninoti bālā samānāpi “paṇḍitā mayaṃ attano paṇḍitabhāvaṃ pakāsemā”ti maññamānā paṇḍitamānino hutvā evamāhu. Attho ceti sace attano yathārūpo koci attho siyā, na kiñci parivajjeyya, sabbaṃ haneyyevāti vadanti, tvampi nesaṃ aññataroti.

Here, ‘khattavidā’ refers to the science of ruling, or this is the reading itself. This is the name for teachers of the science of statecraft. ‘Fools who think themselves wise’ means: though they are fools, thinking, ‘We are wise; let us display our wisdom,’ they become conceited as if wise and speak thus. ‘If the purpose were such’ means: ‘If there were any purpose for oneself of whatever kind, one should not avoid anything, one would slay everything’—thus they say. You too are one of them.

Evaṃ tassa laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapetvā attano laddhiṃ pakāsento āha –

Having thus established his doctrine, proclaiming his own doctrine, he said:

153.

153.

“Yassa rukkhassa chāyāya, nisīdeyya sayeyya vā;

Na tassa sākhaṃ bhañjeyya, mittadubbho hi pāpako.

“In the shade of whatever tree one might sit or lie down, one should not break its branch, for a betrayer of a friend is evil.”

154.

154.

“Atha [V 5.0229] atthe samuppanne, samūlamapi abbahe;

Attho me sambalenāpi, suhato vānaro mayā.

“But when a need arises, one might uproot it completely. My purpose was for provisions; the monkey was well slain by me.”

155.

155.

“So ce attho ca dhammo ca, kalyāṇo na ca pāpako;

Bhoto ce vacanaṃ saccaṃ, suhato vānaro mayā.

“If that principle and doctrine are good and not evil, and if your word is true, then the monkey was well slain by me.”

156.

156.

“Attano ce hi vādassa, aparādhaṃ vijāniyā;

Na maṃ tvaṃ garaheyyāsi, bhoto vādo hi tādiso”ti.

If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me, for your doctrine is indeed of such a kind.

Tattha ambho khattavida amhākaṃ pana ācariyā evaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Attanā paribhuttacchāyassa rukkhassapi sākhaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā na bhañjeyya. Kiṃkāraṇā[P 5.0241]? Mittadubbho hi pāpako. Tvaṃ pana evaṃ vadesi – “atha atthe samuppanne samūlamapi [M 5.0254] abbahe”ti, mama ca pātheyyena attho ahosi, tasmā sacepesa mayā hato, tathāpi attho me sambalenāpi, suhato vānaro mayā.

Here, O expert in the science of ruling, our teachers explain thus: One should not break even a branch or a leaf of a tree whose shade one has enjoyed. Why? For betraying a friend is indeed evil. But you say thus: ‘But when a need arises, one might uproot it completely.’ And I had a need for provisions; therefore, even if he was killed by me, still my need was for provisions; the monkey was well slain by me.

Evaṃ so tassapi vādaṃ bhinditvā pañcasu tesu apaṭibhānesu nisinnesu rājānaṃ āmantetvā, “mahārāja, tvaṃ ime pañca raṭṭhavilopake mahācore gahetvā vicarasi, aho bālo, evarūpānañhi saṃsaggena puriso diṭṭhadhammikampi samparāyikampi mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇeyyā”ti vatvā rañño dhammaṃ desento āha –

Having thus refuted his doctrine as well, and with those five sitting there without a ready answer, he addressed the king: 'Great king, you go about with these five great thieves, plunderers of the kingdom. Oh, you fool! For by associating with such people, a person may encounter great suffering both in this very life and in the next.' Teaching the Dhamma to the king, he then said:

157.

157.

“Ahetuvādo puriso, yo ca issarakuttiko;

Pubbekatī ca ucchedī, yo ca khattavido naro.

The person who is a proponent of causelessness, and one who is a proponent of creation by a supreme being; one who holds that all is due to past deeds, and an annihilationist, and the man who is skilled in the science of ruling—

158.

158.

“Ete asappurisā loke, bālā paṇḍitamānino;

Kareyya tādiso pāpaṃ, atho aññampi kāraye;

Asappurisasaṃsaggo, dukkhanto kaṭukudrayo”ti.

These are ignoble persons in the world, fools who think themselves wise. Such a one would do evil, and would cause others to do it too. Association with ignoble persons ends in suffering and has a bitter outcome.

Tattha tādisoti, mahārāja, yādisā ete pañca diṭṭhigatikā, tādiso puriso sayampi pāpaṃ kareyya. Yvāssa vacanaṃ suṇāti, taṃ aññampi kāraye. Dukkhantoti evarūpehi asappurisehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggo idhalokepi paralokepi dukkhanto kaṭukudrayova hoti. Imassa panatthassa [V 5.0230] pakāsanatthaṃ “yāni kānici, bhikkhave, bhayāni uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato”ti suttaṃ (a. ni. 3.1) āharitabbaṃ. Godhajātaka- (jā. 1.1.138) sañjīvajātaka- (jā. 1.1.150) akittijātakādīhi (jā. 1.13.83 ādayo) cāyamattho dīpetabbo.

Here, 'such a one' means, great king, a person like these five who hold wrong views—he himself would do evil, and would cause another who listens to his word to do it too. 'Ends in suffering' means that association with such ignoble persons results in suffering both in this life and the next, and has a bitter outcome. To clarify this meaning, the sutta should be cited: 'Whatever fears arise, monks, all arise from the fool.' And this meaning should be illustrated with the Godha Jātaka, the Sañjīva Jātaka, the Akitti Jātaka, and others.

Idānī opammadassanavasena dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhento āha –

Now, expanding the Dhamma teaching by way of an illustration, he said:

159.

159.

“Urabbharūpena vakassu pubbe, asaṃkito ajayūthaṃ upeti;

Hantvā uraṇiṃ ajikaṃ ajañca, utrāsayitvā yenakāmaṃ paleti.

Formerly, a wolf in the form of a ram, unhesitatingly, approached a flock of goats. Having slain a ewe, a she-goat, and a he-goat, and having terrified the flock, it fled wherever it pleased.

160.

160.

“Tathāvidheke [M 5.0255] samaṇabrāhmaṇāse, chadanaṃ katvā vañcayanti manusse;

Anāsakā thaṇḍilaseyyakā ca, rajojallaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ;

Pariyāyabhattañca [P 5.0242] apānakattā, pāpācārā arahanto vadānā.

Just so, some ascetics and brahmins, having put on a disguise, deceive people. They practice fasting, sleep on the bare ground, are covered in dust and dirt, are devoted to the squatting posture, eat food by turns, and abstain from drinking—yet they are of wicked conduct, though they declare themselves to be arahants. Thus they maintain their disguise.

161.

161.

“Ete asappurisā loke, bālā paṇḍitamānino;

Kareyya tādiso pāpaṃ, atho aññampi kāraye;

Asappurisasaṃsaggo, dukkhanto kaṭukudrayo.

These are ignoble persons in the world, fools who think themselves wise. Such a person would do evil himself, and would also cause others to do it. Association with ignoble persons leads to an end in suffering and has a bitter outcome.

162.

162.

“Yamāhu natthi vīriyanti, ahetuñca pavadanti ye;

Parakāraṃ attakārañca, ye tucchaṃ samavaṇṇayuṃ.

Those who say that there is no result of effort, and those who speak of causelessness; those who describe the deeds of others and their own deeds as empty—

163.

163.

“Ete asappurisā loke, bālā paṇḍitamānino;

Kareyya tādiso pāpaṃ, atho aññampi kāraye;

Asappurisasaṃsaggo, dukkhanto kaṭukudrayo.

These are ignoble persons in the world, fools who think themselves wise. Such a person would do evil himself, and would also cause others to do it. Association with ignoble persons leads to an end in suffering and has a bitter outcome.

164.

164.

“Sace hi vīriyaṃ nāssa, kammaṃ kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Na bhare vaḍḍhakiṃ rājā, napi yantāni kāraye.

If indeed there were no result of effort, and no wholesome or unwholesome kamma, the king would not support a carpenter, nor would he have palaces and mechanical works constructed.

165.

165.

“Yasmā ca vīriyaṃ atthi, kammaṃ kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Tasmā yantāni kāreti, rājā bharati vaḍḍhakiṃ.

But because there is a result of effort, and there is wholesome and unwholesome kamma, therefore the king has palaces constructed and supports the carpenter.

166.

166.

“Yadi [V 5.0231] vassasataṃ devo, na vasse na himaṃ pate;

Ucchijjeyya ayaṃ loko, vinasseyya ayaṃ pajā.

If for a hundred years the sky did not rain, and if frost did not fall, this world would be annihilated, and these beings would perish.

167.

167.

“Yasmā ca vassatī devo, himañcānuphusāyati;

Tasmā sassāni paccanti, raṭṭhañca pālite ciraṃ.

But because the sky rains and the frost falls in drops, therefore the crops ripen, and the kingdom is protected for a long time.

168.

168.

“Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti, nette jimhaṃ gate sati.

Among cattle that are crossing a stream, if the lead bull goes crookedly, then all of them go crookedly, when the leader has gone astray.

169.

169.

“Evameva [M 5.0256] manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So ce adhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko.

Just so among men, if he who is considered the best behaves unrighteously, how much more so will the rest of the people. The whole realm dwells in suffering if the king is unrighteous.

170.

170.

“Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, ujuṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā gāvī ujuṃ yanti, nette ujuṃ gate sati.

Among cattle that are crossing a stream, if the lead bull goes straight, then all the cows go straight, when the leader has gone straight.

171.

171.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So sace dhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti dhammiko.

Even so among men, if he who is considered the best practices the Dhamma, how much more so will the other people. The whole realm dwells in happiness if the king is righteous.

172.

172.

“Mahārukkhassa phalino, āmaṃ chindati yo phalaṃ;

Rasañcassa na jānāti, bījañcassa vinassati.

A person who picks the unripe fruit of a great fruit-bearing tree does not know its true taste, and the seed of that fruit is also destroyed.

173.

173.

“Mahārukkhūpamaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, adhammena pasāsati;

Rasañcassa na jānāti, raṭṭhañcassa vinassati.

The king who governs the realm, which is like a great tree, unrighteously, does not enjoy its true flavor, and his realm is destroyed.

174.

174.

“Mahārukkhassa phalino, pakkaṃ chindati yo phalaṃ;

Rasañcassa vijānāti, bījañcassa na nassati.

A person who picks the ripe fruit of a great fruit-bearing tree knows its true taste, and the seed of that fruit is not destroyed.

175.

175.

“Mahārukkhūpamaṃ [V 5.0232][P 5.0243] raṭṭhaṃ, dhammena yo pasāsati;

Rasañcassa vijānāti, raṭṭhañjassa na nassati.

The king who governs the realm, which is like a great tree, righteously, knows its true flavor, and his realm is not destroyed.

176.

176.

“Yo ca rājā janapadaṃ, adhammena pasāsati;

Sabbosadhīhi so rājā, viruddho hoti khattiyo.

When a king governs the country unrighteously, that khattiya ruler becomes hostile to all medicinal herbs and plants.

177.

177.

“Tatheva negame hiṃsaṃ, ye yuttā kayavikkaye;

Ojadānabalīkāre, sa kosena virujjhati.

Likewise, by harming the townspeople engaged in buying and selling, and those who render wealth and tribute, he comes into conflict with the treasury.

178.

178.

“Pahāravarakhettaññū, saṅgāme katanissame;

Ussite hiṃsayaṃ rājā, sa balena virujjhati.

The king, by harming those skilled in the field of combat, those who have exerted themselves in battle, and those who are prominent, comes into conflict with his army.

179.

179.

“Tatheva isayo hiṃsaṃ, saññate brahmacārino;

Adhammacārī khattiyo, so saggena virujjhati.

Likewise, the unrighteous ruler, by harming ascetics who are restrained and leading the holy life, comes into conflict with heaven.

180.

180.

“Yo [M 5.0257] ca rājā adhammaṭṭho, bhariyaṃ hanti adūsikaṃ;

Luddhaṃ pasavate ṭhānaṃ, puttehi ca virujjhati.

And the king who is unrighteous, who slays his innocent wife, engenders a cruel destiny and comes into conflict with his sons.

181.

181.

“Dhammaṃ care jānapade, negamesu balesu ca;

Isayo ca na hiṃseyya, puttadāre samaṃ care.

He should practice Dhamma in the countryside, in towns, and among the armed forces. He should not harm ascetics, and he should treat his children and wife justly.

182.

182.

“Sa tādiso bhūmipati, raṭṭhapālo akodhano;

Sapatte sampakampeti, indova asurādhipo”ti.

Such a ruler of the earth, a protector of the realm, without anger, makes his adversaries tremble, like Indra over the lord of the asuras.

Tattha vakassūti vako assu, assūti nipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, pubbe eko urabbharūpo vako ahosi, tassa naṅguṭṭhamattameva dīghaṃ, taṃ pana so antarasattimhi pakkhipitvā urabbharūpena asaṃkito ajayūthaṃ upeti. Tattha uraṇikañca ajikañca ajañca hantvā yenakāmaṃ paleti. Tathāvidheketi tathāvidhā eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pabbajjāliṅgena chadanaṃ katvā attānaṃ chādetvā madhuravacanādīhi hitakāmā viya hutvā lokaṃ vañcenti. “Anāsakā”tiādi tesaṃ chadanassa dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekacce hi “mayaṃ anāsakā na kiñci [V 5.0233] āhāremā”ti manusse vañcenti, apare “mayaṃ thaṇḍilaseyyakā”ti. Aññesaṃ pana rajojallaṃ chadanaṃ, aññesaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ, te gacchantāpi uppatitvā ukkuṭikāva gacchanti. Aññesaṃ sattāhadasāhādivārabhojanasaṅkhātaṃ [P 5.0244] pariyāyabhattachadanaṃ, apare apānakattā honti, “mayaṃ pānīyaṃ na pivāmā”ti vadanti. Arahanto vadānāti pāpācārā hutvāpi “mayaṃ arahanto”ti vadantā vicaranti. Eteti, mahārāja, ime vā pañca janā hontu aññe vā, yāvanto diṭṭhigatikā nāma, sabbepi ete asappurisā. Yamāhūti ye āhu, ye vadanti.

Here, 'vakassūti' means 'may there be a wolf'; 'assūti' is merely a particle. This is said: Great king, in the past there was a wolf shaped like a ram, whose tail was only as long as a thumb. Yet, hiding it between his thighs, and appearing as a ram, he approached the goat herd without suspicion. There, he would kill a ram, a she-goat, or a he-goat and then leave as he pleased. Similarly, some ascetics and brahmins, using the outward signs of renunciation as a cover, conceal themselves, and pretending to be well-wishers with sweet words and such, they deceive the world. The phrase 'Anāsakā' and so on is said to reveal their deception. For instance, some deceive people by saying, 'We are abstainers, we do not consume any food.' Others say, 'We sleep on bare ground.' For some, dust and dirt serve as their disguise, while for others, it is the practice of squatting—they even walk by jumping while squatting. For others, periodic meals, such as eating every seven or ten days, serve as a disguise; some are non-drinkers, declaring, 'We do not drink water.' Though they behave wickedly, they wander about claiming, 'We are Arahants.' These, great king, whether these five kinds of people or others—as many as there are who hold wrong views—all of them are ignoble persons. 'Yamāhu' means 'those who say,' 'those who declare.'

Sace hi vīriyaṃ nāssāti, mahārāja, sace ñāṇasampayuttaṃ kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ na bhaveyya. Kammanti kalyāṇapāpakaṃ kammampi yadi na bhaveyya. Na bhareti evaṃ sante vaḍḍhakiṃ vā aññe vā kārake rājā na poseyya, napi yantānīti napi tehi sattabhūmikapāsādādīni yantāni kāreyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Vīriyassa ceva kammassa ca abhāvā. Ucchijjeyyāti, mahārāja, yadi ettakaṃ kālaṃ neva devo vasseyya, na himaṃ pateyya[M 5.0258], atha kappuṭṭhānakālo viya ayaṃ loko ucchijjeyya. Ucchedavādinā kathitaniyāmena pana ucchedo nāma natthi. Pāliteti pālayati.

Here, 'if there were no effort' means, great king, if there were no bodily and mental effort accompanied by wisdom. 'Action' means if there were no action, whether wholesome or unwholesome. 'He would not support' means, if this were so, the king would not support carpenters or other workers, nor would he have contrivances such as seven-storied palaces and the like made by them. Why is that? Because of the absence of effort and action. 'It would be destroyed' means, great king, if for such a long time no rain fell, no snow descended, then this world would be destroyed like at the time of cosmic dissolution. But annihilation, in the way described by the annihilationists, does not exist. 'Is preserved' means he protects.

“Gavaṃ ce”ti catasso gāthā rañño dhammadesanāyameva vuttā, tathā “mahārukkhassā”tiādikā. Tattha mahārukkhassāti madhuraambarukkhassa. Adhammenāti agatigamanena. Rasañcassa na jānātīti adhammiko rājā raṭṭhassa rasaṃ ojaṃ na jānāti, āyasampattiṃ na labhati. Vinassatīti suññaṃ hoti, manussā gāmanigame chaḍḍetvā paccantaṃ pabbatavisamaṃ bhajanti, sabbāni āyamukhāni pacchijjanti. Sabbosadhīhīti sabbehi mūlatacapattapupphaphalādīhi ceva sappinavanītādīhi ca osadhehi virujjhati, tāni na sampajjanti. Adhammikarañño hi pathavī nirojā hoti, tassā nirojatāya osadhānaṃ ojā na hoti, tāni rogañca vūpasametuṃ na sakkonti. Iti so tehi viruddho nāma hoti.

'If cattle'—these four verses were spoken by the king as a teaching on Dhamma, just like 'of the great tree' and so on. Here, 'of the great tree' refers to the sweet mango tree. 'Unrighteously' means by going the wrong way. 'He does not know its essence' means an unrighteous king does not understand the essence or nourishment of the kingdom and does not gain prosperity. 'It perishes' means it becomes empty; people abandon villages and towns and flee to remote, uneven mountains; all sources of revenue are cut off. 'With all medicinal herbs' means he comes into conflict with all medicinal herbs—all roots, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, as well as ghee, fresh butter, and other medicinal substances; they do not thrive. For under an unrighteous king, the earth becomes infertile, and due to its infertility, the nourishment of medicinal herbs is lost, and they cannot even alleviate diseases. Thus, he is said to be in conflict with them.

Negameti nigamavāsikuṭumbike. Hiṃsanti hiṃsanto pīḷento. Ye yuttāti ye kayavikkaye yuttā āyānaṃ mukhā thalajalapathavāṇijā, te ca hiṃsanto. Ojadānabalīkāreti tato tato bhaṇḍāharaṇasuṅkadānavasena ojadānañceva chabhāgadasabhāgādibhedaṃ baliñca karonte. Sa kosenāti so ete hiṃsanto adhammikarājā dhanadhaññehi parihāyanto kosena virujjhati nāma. Pahāravarakhettaññūti “imasmiṃ ṭhāne vijjhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti evaṃ pahāravarānaṃ khettaṃ jānante dhanuggahe. Saṅgāme katanissameti yuddhe sukatakamme mahāyodhe. Ussiteti uggate paññāte mahāmatte[V 5.0234]. Hi sayanti evarūpe sayaṃ vā hiṃsanto parehi vā hiṃsāpento. Balenāti balakāyena. Tathāvidhañhi rājānaṃ “ayaṃ bahukāre attano rajjadāyakepi hiṃsati, kimaṅgaṃ pana amhe”ti avasesāpi yodhā vijahantiyeva. Iti so balena viruddho nāma hoti.

'In the town' means the households dwelling in the town. 'Harming' means harming, oppressing. 'Those engaged' means those engaged in buying and selling, merchants of land and sea routes who are sources of income, harming them too. 'Providing wealth, gifts, and tribute' means (harming) those who provide wealth-gifts (by way of bringing goods from here and there and through duties and taxes) and tribute, such as the sixth or tenth share. 'He is opposed by his treasury' means that unrighteous king, harming these, declining in wealth and grain, is said to be in conflict with his treasury. 'Knowers of the field of excellent blows' means archers who know the field of excellent blows, thinking, 'It is fitting to shoot here.' 'Skilled in battle' means great warriors who have done good deeds in battle. 'Prominent ones' means prominent, well-known great ministers. 'Harming' (hiṃsayaṃ) means harming such people either by oneself or by causing others to harm. 'By force' means by the army. For such a king, thinking, 'This one harms even his own benefactors, who even give him his kingdom, what more of us?'—the remaining warriors too abandon him. Thus, he is said to be in conflict with his army.

Tatheva isayo hiṃsanti yathā ca negamādayo, tatheva esitaguṇe pabbajite akkosanapaharaṇādīhi [P 5.0245] hiṃsanto adhammacārī rājā kāyassa bhedā apāyameva upeti, sagge nibbattituṃ na sakkotīti [M 5.0259] saggena viruddho nāma hoti. Bhariyaṃ hanti adūsikanti attano bāhucchāyāya vaḍḍhitaṃ puttadhītāhi saṃvaḍḍhaṃ sīlavatiṃ bhariyaṃ mittapatirūpakānaṃ corānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā māreti. Luddhaṃ pasavate ṭhānanti so attano nirayūpapattiṃ pasavati nipphādeti. Puttehi cāti imasmiññeva attabhāve attano puttehi saddhiṃ virujjhatīti.

'Similarly, they harm sages' means: just as townsfolk and others do, so too does an unrighteous king, harming renunciants who possess sought-after virtues with abuse, assault, and the like. After the breakup of the body, he goes only to the lower realms, unable to be reborn in heaven—thus, he is said to be in conflict with heaven. 'He kills his innocent wife' means, having accepted the words of thieves who resemble friends, he kills his virtuous wife, who grew up under the protection of his own arms and has raised his sons and daughters. 'He generates a cruel place' means he generates, he produces his own rebirth in hell. 'And with his children' means even in this very existence, he is in conflict with his own children.

Evamassa so tesaṃ pañcannaṃ janānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā deviyā māritabhāvañca puttānaṃ viruddhabhāvañca sandhimukhe coraṃ cūḷāyaṃ gaṇhanto viya kathesi. Mahāsatto hi tesaṃ amaccānaṃ niggaṇhanañca dhammadesanañca deviyā tehi māritabhāvassa āvikaraṇatthañca tattha anupubbena kathaṃ āharitvā okāsaṃ katvā etamatthaṃ kathesi. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā attano aparādhaṃ jāni. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “ito paṭṭhāya, mahārāja, evarūpānaṃ pāpānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā mā puna evamakāsī”ti vatvā ovadanto “dhammaṃ care”tiādimāha.

Thus, taking up the story of those five people—how the queen was killed and how the sons became hostile—he narrated it like one catching a thief by the top-knot at a breach in the wall. Indeed, the Great Being, in order to rebuke those ministers, teach the Dhamma, and reveal that the queen had been killed by them, gradually brought up the story, created an opportunity, and explained this matter. Hearing his words, the king recognized his own fault. Then the Great Being, advising him, said, “From now on, great king, do not act thus again after accepting the words of such evil people,” and spoke the verses beginning: “One should practice the Dhamma.”

Tattha dhammaṃ careti, mahārāja, rājā nāma janapadaṃ adhammikena balinā apīḷento janapade dhammaṃ careyya, sāmike asāmike akaronto negamesu dhammaṃ careyya, aṭṭhāne akilamento balesu dhammaṃ careyya. Vadhabandhaakkosaparibhāse pariharanto paccaye ca nesaṃ dadanto isayo na vihiṃseyya, dhītaro yuttaṭṭhāne patiṭṭhāpento putte ca sippāni sikkhāpetvā sammā pariharanto bhariyaṃ issariyavossaggaalaṅkāradānasammānanādīhi anuggaṇhanto puttadāre samaṃ careyya. Sa tādisoti so tādiso rājā paveṇiṃ abhinditvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kārento rājāṇāya rājatejena sapatte sampakampeti tāseti cāleti. “Indovā”ti idaṃ upamatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā asure jetvā abhibhavitvā ṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya asurādhipoti saṅkhyaṃ gato indo attano sapattabhūte asure kampesi, tathā kampetīti.

Here, 'one should practice the Dhamma' means, great king, a king should practice the Dhamma in the countryside by not oppressing the people with unjust taxes. He should practice the Dhamma in the towns by not making owners into non-owners. He should practice the Dhamma in the army by not causing them to toil improperly. He should not harm ascetics, avoiding executions, imprisonment, abuse, and insult, and providing for their requisites. He should establish his daughters in suitable positions, train his sons in skills and care for them properly, and support his wife with the bestowal of authority, ornaments, gifts, and respect, treating his children and wife equally. 'Such a one' means such a king, not breaking with tradition, ruling the kingdom with righteousness and fairness, makes his enemies tremble, be terrified, and shake with his royal command and royal majesty. 'Like Indra'—this is said by way of simile. Just as Indra, having conquered and subdued the asuras, from that time onward was reckoned as the lord of asuras, and made his enemies, the asuras, tremble, so he makes them tremble.

Evaṃ mahāsatto rañño dhammaṃ desetvā cattāropi kumāre pakkosāpetvā ovaditvā rañño katakammaṃ pakāsetvā rājānaṃ khamāpetvā “mahārāja, ito paṭṭhāya atuletvā paribhedakānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā [V 5.0235] mā evarūpaṃ sāhasikakammaṃ akāsi, tumhepi kumārā mā rañño [M 5.0260] dubbhitthā”ti sabbesaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi. Atha naṃ rājā āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhesu ca deviyā ca aparajjhanto ime nissāya etesaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā etaṃ pāpakammaṃ kariṃ, ime pañcapi māremī”ti[P 5.0246]. Na labbhā, mahārāja, evaṃ kātunti. Tena hi tesaṃ hatthapāde chedāpemīti. Idampi na labbhā kātunti. Rājā “sādhu, bhante”ti sampaṭicchitvā te sabbasaṃharaṇe katvā pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñcanehi avamānetvā raṭṭhā pabbājesi. Bodhisatto tattha katipāhaṃ vasitvā “appamatto hohī”ti rājānaṃ ovaditvā himavantaṃyeva gantvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā yāvajīvaṃ brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to the king, summoned the four princes as well, advised them, made known the king's deed, and had them ask the king for forgiveness. He gave advice to them all, saying: “Great king, from now on, do not act so rashly, without reflecting or accepting the words of those who cause division. And you, princes, do not be hostile toward the king.” Then the king said to him, “Venerable sir, it was by relying on these villains and accepting their words that I committed this evil deed, offending against you and the queen. I shall kill these five.” “That is not proper, great king.” “Then I shall have their hands and feet cut off.” “This too is not proper.” The king, saying, “Very well, venerable sir,” accepted. He had all their property confiscated, and having humiliated them by shaving their heads into five tufts, binding them with leather thongs, and sprinkling them with cow dung, he banished them from the kingdom. The Great Being, having stayed there in Bārāṇasī for a few days, advised the king, “Be diligent,” and then went to the Himalayas. There, he developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal knowledges, cultivated the divine abidings throughout his life, and was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ desanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavāyeva parappavādappamaddanoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā pañca diṭṭhigatikā pūraṇakassapamakkhaligosālapakudhakaccānaajitakesakambalanigaṇṭhanāṭaputtā ahesuṃ, piṅgalasunakho ānando, mahābodhiparibbājako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, the Tathāgata was wise and a crusher of the doctrines of others.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time, the five who held wrong views were Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Ajita Kesakambala, and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta. The dog Piṅgala was Ānanda, and the wandering ascetic Mahābodhi was none other than myself.”

Mahābodhijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The commentary on the Mahābodhi Jātaka, the third.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Summary of the Jātakas:

Saniḷīnikamavhayano paṭhamo, dutiyo pana saummadantivaro;

Tatiyo pana bodhisirīvhayano, kathitā pana tīṇi jinena subhāti.

The first is called Saniḷīnika, the second is the excellent Ummadantī; the third is called Bodhisirī. Thus, three were well spoken by the Victor.

Paṇṇāsanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of Fifty is concluded.

19. Saṭṭhinipāto

19. The Book of Sixty

[529] 1. Soṇakajātakavaṇṇanā

[529] 1. 1. Soṇaka Jātaka. The importance of listening to the words of the virtuous.

Kassa [V 5.0236][P 5.0247][M 5.0261] sutvā sataṃ dammīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto nekkhammapāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi bhagavā dhammasabhāyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ vaṇṇayantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe nisīditvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Having heard whose words shall I give a hundred?”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of renunciation. At that time, the Blessed One, sitting in the midst of monks extolling the perfection of renunciation in the Dhamma hall, said, “Monks, it is not only now, but in the past too, that the Tathāgata made the great renunciation.” Then he recounted the past.

Atīte rājagahe magadharājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti, nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa “arindamakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa jātadivaseyeva purohitassapi putto jāyi, “soṇakakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te ubhopi ekatova vaḍḍhitvā vayappattā uttamarūpadharā rūpena nibbisesā hutvā takkasilaṃ gantvā uggahitasippā tato nikkhamitvā “sabbasamayasippañca desacārittañca jānissāmā”ti anupubbena cārikaṃ carantā bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. Taṃ divasañca ekacce manussā “brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ karissāmā”ti pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādetvā āsanāni paññāpetvā āgacchante te kumāre disvā gharaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpesuṃ. Tattha bodhisattassa paññattāsane suddhavatthaṃ atthataṃ ahosi, soṇakassa rattakambalaṃ. So taṃ nimittaṃ disvāva “ajja me piyasahāyo arindamakumāro [P 5.0248] bārāṇasirājā bhavissati, mayhaṃ pana senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ dassatī”ti aññāsi. Te ubhopi katabhattakiccā uyyānameva agamaṃsu.

In the past, a king of Magadha ruled in Rājagaha. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, and on the naming day, they named him “Prince Arindama.” On the very day of his birth, the royal chaplain also had a son, and they named him “Prince Soṇaka.” Both grew up together and, when they came of age, being of the most excellent beauty and indistinguishable in appearance, they went to Takkasilā to learn the arts. After mastering them, they left and thought, “We shall learn the doctrines of all sects and the arts, and the customs of the lands,” and gradually traveling, they arrived at Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park. The next day, they entered the city. On that day, some people, intending to have a recitation of the Vedas for brahmins, prepared milk-rice and set out seats. Seeing the princes approaching, they invited them into the house and seated them on the prepared seats. There, the seat prepared for the Bodhisatta was spread with white cloth, while Soṇaka’s was spread with a red blanket. Seeing this sign, Soṇaka understood, “Today, my dear friend Prince Arindama will become the king of Bārāṇasī, and he will give me the position of commander-in-chief.” Both of them, having finished their meal, returned to the park.

Tadā bārāṇasirañño kālakatassa sattamo divaso hoti, aputtakaṃ rājakulaṃ. Amaccādayo pātova sasīsaṃ nhātā sannipatitvā “rajjārahassa santikaṃ gamissatī”ti phussarathaṃ yojetvā vissajjesuṃ. So nagarā nikkhamitvā anupubbena rājuyyānaṃ gantvā uyyānadvāre nivattitvā ārohaṇasajjo hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto maṅgalasilāpaṭṭesasīsaṃ pārupitvā [V 5.0237] nipajji, soṇakakumāro tassa santike nisīdi. So tūriyasaddaṃ sutvā “arindamassa phussaratho āgacchati, ajjesa rājā [M 5.0262] hutvā mama senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ dassati, na kho pana mayhaṃ issariyenattho, etasmiṃ gate nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā ekamante paṭicchanne aṭṭhāsi. Purohito uyyānaṃ pavisitvā mahāsattaṃ nipannakaṃ disvā tūriyāni paggaṇhāpesi. Mahāsatto pabujjhitvā parivattitvā thokaṃ nipajjitvā uṭṭhāya silāpaṭṭe pallaṅkena nisīdi. Atha naṃ purohito añjaliṃ paggaṇhitvā āha – “rajjaṃ te, deva, pāpuṇātī”ti. “Kiṃ aputtakaṃ rājakula”nti? “Evaṃ, devā”ti. “Tena hi sādhū”ti. Atha naṃ te tattheva abhisiñcitvā rathaṃ āropetvā mahantena parivārena nagaraṃ pavesesuṃ. So nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pāsādaṃ abhirūhi. So yasamahantatāya soṇakakumāraṃ na sari.

At that time, it was the seventh day since the king of Bārāṇasī had passed away, and the royal family was without an heir. The ministers and others, having bathed from head to toe, gathered together. Thinking, “It will go to one worthy of kingship,” they prepared the festal chariot and sent it forth. Leaving the city, it gradually proceeded to the royal park. At the park gate, it turned back and stood ready for someone to mount. The Bodhisatta, having wrapped himself head and all, lay down on the auspicious stone slab. Prince Soṇaka sat near him. Hearing the sound of musical instruments, Soṇaka thought, “Arindama’s festal chariot is coming. Today he will become king and will give me the position of commander-in-chief. But I have no need for power. Once he has gone, I will go forth and renounce the world.” Thinking thus, he stood aside in a secluded place. The royal priest entered the park and, seeing the Great Being lying there, had the musical instruments played. The Great Being awoke, turned over, lay for a short while, then arose and sat cross-legged on the stone slab. Then the priest, raising his hands in reverence, said, “Sire, the kingdom has come to you.” “Is the royal family without an heir?” he asked. “Indeed, sire,” they replied. “Very well, then,” he said. Then and there, they anointed him, had him ascend the chariot, and entered the city with a great retinue. After circumambulating the city, he ascended to the palace. Due to the greatness of his prosperity, he did not remember Prince Soṇaka.

Sopi tasmiṃ nagaraṃ paviṭṭhe pacchā āgantvā silāpaṭṭe nisīdi. Athassa purato bandhanā pavuttaṃ sālarukkhato paṇḍupalāsaṃ pati. So taṃ disvāva “yathevetaṃ, tathā mamapi sarīraṃ jaraṃ patvā patissatī”ti aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā paccekabodhiṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃkhaṇaññevassa gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, pabbajitaliṅgaṃ pāturahosi. So “natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti udānaṃ udānento nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Mahāsattopi cattālīsamattānaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena saritvā “kahaṃ nu kho me sahāyo soṇako”ti soṇakaṃ punappunaṃ sarantopi “mayā suto [P 5.0249] vā diṭṭho vā”ti vattāraṃ alabhitvā alaṅkatamahātale rājapallaṅke nisinno gandhabbanāṭakanaccagītādīhi parivuto sampattimanubhavanto “yo me kassaci santike sutvā ‘asukaṭṭhāne nāma soṇako vasatī’ti ācikkhissati, tassa sataṃ dassāmi, yo me sāmaṃ disvā ārocessati, tassa sahassa”nti ekaṃ udānaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā gītavasena udānento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

After the king had entered the city, Soṇaka arrived later and sat on the stone slab. Then, a withered leaf, released from its stalk, fell from a sāl tree before him. Seeing it, he established insight by way of impermanence and other such reflections, thinking, 'Just as this leaf, so too will my body, having reached old age, fall away.' He then attained the enlightenment of a Private Buddha. At that very moment, his layman's appearance vanished, and the appearance of a monk became manifest. Uttering the inspired exclamation, 'Now there is no further becoming,' he went to the Nandamūlaka cave. The Great Being, after some forty years had passed, remembered his friend, 'Where now is my friend Soṇaka?' Though he repeatedly thought of Soṇaka, he could find no one to say, 'I have heard of him,' or 'I have seen him.' Seated on the royal couch on the great decorated terrace, surrounded by musicians, dancers, and singers, he enjoyed his royal prosperity. He then composed an inspired utterance and, delivering it as a song, spoke the first verse:

“Kassa sutvā sataṃ dammi, sahassaṃ diṭṭha soṇakaṃ;

Ko me soṇakamakkhāti, sahāyaṃ paṃsukīḷita”nti.

“To one who has heard, I give a hundred; to one who has seen Soṇaka, a thousand. Who will tell me of Soṇaka, my companion who played in the dust?”

Athassa mukhato luñcantī viya gahetvā ekā nāṭakītthī taṃ gāyi. Athaññā athaññāti “amhākaṃ rañño piyagīta”nti sabbā orodhā gāyiṃsu. Anukkamena nagaravāsinopi jānapadāpi tameva gītaṃ gāyiṃsu. Rājāpi [M 5.0263] punappunaṃ tameva gītaṃ gāyati. Paṇṇāsamattānaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena panassa bahū puttadhītaro ahesuṃ, jeṭṭhaputto dīghāvukumāro nāma ahosi. Tadā [V 5.0238] soṇakapaccekabuddho “arindamarājā maṃ daṭṭhukāmo, ahaṃ tattha gantvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme cānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā pabbajjanākāraṃ karomī”ti cintetvā iddhiyā ākāsenāgantvā uyyāne nisīdi. Tadā eko sattavassiko pañcacūḷakakumārako mātarā pahito gantvā uyyānavane dārūni uddharanto punappunaṃ tameva gītaṃ gāyi. Atha naṃ so pakkositvā “kumāraka, tvaṃ aññaṃ agāyitvā ekameva gītaṃ gāyasi, kiṃ aññaṃ na jānāsī”ti pucchi. “Jānāmi, bhante, amhākaṃ pana rañño idameva piyaṃ, tena naṃ punnappunaṃ gāyāmī”ti. “Etassa pana te gītassa paṭigītaṃ gāyanto koci diṭṭhapubbo”ti. “Na diṭṭhapubbo, bhante”ti. “Ahaṃ taṃ sikkhāpessāmi, sakkhissasi rañño santikaṃ gantvā paṭigītaṃ gāyitu”nti. “Āma, bhante”ti. Athassa so paṭigītaṃ ācikkhanto “mayhaṃ sutvā”tiādimāha. Uggaṇhāpetvā ca pana [P 5.0250] taṃ uyyojesi – “gaccha, kumāraka, imaṃ paṭigītaṃ raññā saddhiṃ gāyāhi, rājā te mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dassati, kiṃ te dārūhi, vegena yāhī”ti.

Then, as if plucking it from his very mouth, a certain dancing girl took up the song and sang it. Then others followed, until all the women of the harem sang it, saying, 'This is our king’s favorite song.' In due course, the city-dwellers and the country-folk also sang that same song. The king, too, sang that same song again and again. After some fifty years had passed, he had many sons and daughters; his eldest son was named Prince Dīghāvu. At that time, the Private Buddha Soṇaka thought, 'King Arindama wishes to see me. I will go there, speak on the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit of renunciation, and show him the way to go forth.' By means of his psychic power, he traveled through the air and sat down in the royal park. At that time, a seven-year-old boy named Pañcacūḷaka, sent by his mother, was gathering firewood in the woods near the park, repeatedly singing that same song. The Private Buddha called to him and asked, 'Young boy, you sing only one song and not another. Do you not know any others?' 'I know others, venerable sir, but this is our king’s favorite, so I sing it again and again.' 'Have you ever seen anyone who knows the counter-song to this song?' 'I have not, venerable sir.' 'I will teach it to you. Will you be able to go to the king and sing the counter-song?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' Then, wanting him to hear the counter-song, he recited the verse beginning with 'For hearing from me...' After teaching it to him, he sent him on his way, saying, 'Go, young boy, sing this counter-song with King Arindama. The king will give you great prosperity. What need have you for firewood? Go quickly!'

So “sādhū”ti taṃ paṭigītaṃ uggaṇhitvā vanditvā, “bhante, yāvāhaṃ rājānaṃ ānemi, tāva idheva hothā”ti vatvā vegena mātu santikaṃ gantvā, “amma, khippaṃ maṃ nhāpetvā alaṅkarotha, ajja taṃ daliddabhāvato mocessāmī”ti vatvā nhātamaṇḍito rājadvāraṃ gantvā “ayya dovārika, ‘eko dārako tumhehi saddhiṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyissāmīti āgantvā dvāre ṭhito’ti rañño arocehī”ti āha. So vegena gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “āgacchatū”ti pakkosāpetvā, “tāta, tvaṃ mayā saddhiṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyissasī”ti āha. “Āma, devā”ti. “Tena hi gāyassū”ti. “Deva, imasmiṃ ṭhāne na gāyāmi, nagare pana bheriṃ carāpetvā mahājanaṃ sannipātāpetha, mahājanamajjhe gāyissāmī”ti. Rājā tathā kāretvā alaṅkatamaṇḍape pallaṅkamajjhe nisīditvā tassānurūpaṃ āsanaṃ dāpetvā “idāni tava gītaṃ gāyassū”ti āha. “Deva, tumhe tāva gāyatha, athāhaṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyissāmī”ti. Tato rājā paṭhamaṃ gāyanto gāthamāha –

The boy said, 'Very well,' and having learned the counter-song, he paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, please stay here until I bring the king.' He went quickly to his mother and said, 'Mother, quickly bathe and adorn me. Today I will free you from poverty.' Having been bathed and adorned, he went to the palace gate and said, 'Master Gatekeeper, please inform the king that a boy has come to the gate saying, "I will sing a counter-song with the king."' The gatekeeper went quickly and informed the king. The king had him summoned and asked, 'My dear boy, will you sing a counter-song with me?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'Then sing.' 'Your Majesty, I will not sing here. Rather, have a drum beaten throughout the city and assemble the people. I will sing in the midst of the crowd.' The king did as the boy asked. Seated on a throne in the center of a decorated pavilion, he had a suitable seat provided for the boy and said, 'Now, sing your song.' 'Your Majesty, you sing first, and then I will sing the counter-song.' Then the king, singing first, spoke this verse:

1.

1.

“Kassa [M 5.0264] sutvā sataṃ dammi, sahassaṃ diṭṭha soṇakaṃ;

So me soṇakamakkhāti, sahāyaṃ paṃsukīḷita”nti.

“To one who has heard, I give a hundred; to one who has seen Soṇaka, a thousand. Who will tell me of Soṇaka, my companion who played in the dust?”

Tattha sutvāti “asukaṭṭhāne nāma te piyasahāyo soṇako vasatī”ti tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sutvā ārocentassa kassa sataṃ dammi. Diṭṭhāti “asukaṭṭhāne nāma mayā diṭṭho”ti disvā ārocentassa kassa sahassaṃ dammīti.

In that verse, 'having heard' means: to whom shall I give a hundred, who reports after having heard the place where he lives, saying, 'Your dear friend Soṇaka lives in such-and-such a place'? 'Having seen' means: to whom shall I give a thousand, who reports after having seen him, saying, 'I saw him in such-and-such a place'?

Evaṃ [V 5.0239] raññā paṭhamaṃ udānagāthāya gītāya pañcacūḷakadārakena paṭigītabhāvaṃ pakāsento satthā abhisambuddho hutvā dīyaḍḍhagāthā abhāsi –

Thus, after the king had first sung the song with the verse of inspired utterance, the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke a verse and a half to reveal that the boy Pañcacūḷaka sang the counter-song:

2.

2.

“Athabravī māṇavako, daharo pañcacūḷako;

Mayhaṃ sutvā sataṃ dehi, sahassaṃ diṭṭha soṇakaṃ;

Ahaṃ te soṇakakkhissaṃ, sahāyaṃ paṃsukīḷita”nti.

Then spoke the young boy, the youth Pañcacūḷaka: 'For hearing from me, give a hundred; for my having seen Soṇaka, a thousand. I will tell you of Soṇaka, your companion who played in the dust.'

Tena vuttagāthāya pana ayamattho – mahārāja, yaṃ tvaṃ “sutvā ārocentassa sataṃ dammī”ti vadasi, tampi mameva dehi, yaṃ “disvā ārocentassa sahassaṃ [P 5.0251] dammī”ti vadasi, tampi mayhameva dehi, ahaṃ te piyasahāyaṃ idāneva paccakkhatova “ayaṃ soṇako”ti ācikkhissanti.

The meaning of the verse he spoke is: 'Great king, what you say—"I give a hundred to one who tells me upon hearing"—give that to me. What you say—"I give a thousand to one who tells me upon seeing"—give that to me too. I will point out your dear friend to you right now, directly, saying, "This is Soṇaka."'

Ito paraṃ suviññeyyā sambuddhagāthā pāḷinayeneva veditabbā –

From here onward, the verses of the Sambuddha are easily understood and should be known according to the Pāli method.

3.

3.

“Katamasmiṃ so janapade, raṭṭhesu nigamesu ca;

Kattha soṇakamaddakkhi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

"In which district, in which kingdoms and market towns did you see Soṇaka? Tell me, as you have been asked."

4.

4.

“Taveva deva vijite, tavevuyyānabhūmiyaṃ;

Ujuvaṃsā mahāsālā, nīlobhāsā manoramā.

"In your own realm, O king, in your own parkland, are great sāl trees, straight-trunked, of dark lustre, and delightful."

5.

5.

“Tiṭṭhanti meghasamānā, rammā aññoññanissitā;

Tesaṃ mūlamhi soṇako, jhāyatī anupādano;

Upādānesu lokesu, ḍayhamānesu nibbuto.

"They stand like clouds, delightful, leaning on one another; at their roots Soṇaka meditates, without clinging. In worlds burning with clinging, he is extinguished."

6.

6.

“Tato [M 5.0265] ca rājā pāyāsi, senāya caturaṅgiyā;

Kārāpetvā samaṃ maggaṃ, agamā yena soṇako.

"Then the king set out with his fourfold army; having had a level road prepared, he went to where Soṇaka was."

7.

7.

“Uyyānabhūmiṃ gantvāna, vicaranto brahāvane;

Āsīnaṃ soṇakaṃ dakkhi, ḍayhamānesu nibbuta”nti.

"Having gone to the parkland, wandering in the great forest, he saw Soṇaka seated, extinguished amidst the burning."

Tattha [V 5.0240] ujuvaṃsāti ujukkhandhā. Mahāsālāti mahārukkhā. Meghasamānāti nīlameghasadisā. Rammāti ramaṇīyā. Aññoññanissitāti sākhāhi sākhaṃ, mūlena mūlaṃ saṃsibbitvā ṭhitā. Tesanti tesaṃ evarūpānaṃ tava uyyānavane sālānaṃ heṭṭhā. Jhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaārammaṇūpanijjhānasaṅkhātehi jhānehi jhāyati. Anupādanoti kāmupādānādivirahito. Ḍayhamānesūti ekādasahi aggīhi ḍayhamānesu sattesu. Nibbutoti te aggī nibbāpetvā sītalena hadayena jhāyamāno tava uyyāne maṅgalasālarukkhamūle silāpaṭṭe nisinno esa te sahāyo kañcanapaṭimā viya sobhamāno paṭimānetīti. Tato cāti, bhikkhave, tato so arindamo rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvāva “soṇakapaccekabuddhaṃ passissāmī”ti caturaṅginiyā senāya pāyāsi nikkhami. Vicarantoti ujukameva agantvā tasmiṃ mahante vanasaṇḍe vicaranto tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ āsīnaṃ addakkhi.

Therein, 'ujuvaṃsā' means straight-trunked. 'Mahāsālā' means great trees. 'Meghasamānā' means like dark clouds. 'Rammā' means delightful. 'Aññoññanissitā' means standing intertwined, branches with branches, roots with roots. 'Tesaṃ' means beneath such sāl trees in your park-forest. 'Jhāyati' means he meditates with the meditations known as close contemplation of characteristics and close contemplation of the object. 'Anupādano' means free from clinging to sensual pleasures and so forth. 'Ḍayhamānesu' means among beings burning with the eleven fires. 'Nibbuto' means, having extinguished those fires, with a cool heart, he meditates in your park, seated on a stone slab at the foot of the auspicious sāl tree, shining like a golden image; thus he awaits you. 'Tato ca' means, monks, then King Arindama, having heard those words and thinking, \"I will see the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka,\" set out with his fourfold army. 'Vicaranto' means instead of going directly, he wandered in that great grove and, approaching him, saw him seated.

So taṃ avanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā attano kilesābhiratattā taṃ “kapaṇo”ti maññamāno imaṃ gāthamāha –

Without paying homage to him, he sat down to one side and, due to his own delight in defilements, thinking him a wretch, spoke this verse:

8.

8.

“Kapaṇo vatayaṃ bhikkhu, muṇḍo saṅghāṭipāruto;

Amātiko apitiko, rukkhamūlasmi jhāyatī”ti.

"Wretched indeed is this monk, shaven-headed, cloaked in his outer robe; without mother, without father, he meditates at the root of a tree."

Tattha jhāyatīti nimmātiko nippitiko kāruññappatto jhāyati.

Therein, 'jhāyati' means: being without mother and without father, having reached a pitiable state, he meditates.

9.

9.

“Imaṃ vākyaṃ nisāmetvā, soṇako etadabravi;

Na rāja kapaṇo hoti, dhammaṃ kāyena phassayaṃ.

"Hearing these words, Soṇaka said this: 'One who experiences the Dhamma with the body, O king, is not wretched.'"

10.

10.

“Yo [P 5.0252] ca dhammaṃ niraṃkatvā, adhammamanuvattati;

Sa rāja kapaṇo hoti, pāpo pāpaparāyaṇo”ti.

"But one who, having rejected the Dhamma, pursues what is not the Dhamma, that one, O king, is wretched, evil, and bound for an evil destination."

Tattha [M 5.0266] imanti tassa kilesābhiratassa pabbajjaṃ arocentassa imaṃ pabbajjāgarahavacanaṃ sutvā. Etadabravīti pabbajjāya guṇaṃ pakāsento etaṃ abravi. Phassayanti phassayanto yena ariyamaggadhammo nāmakāyena phassito, so kapaṇo nāma na hotīti dassento evamāha. Niraṃkatvāti attabhāvato nīharitvā. Pāpo pāpaparāyaṇoti sayaṃ pāpānaṃ karaṇena pāpo, aññesampi karontānaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvena pāpaparāyaṇoti.

Herein, 'imaṃ' refers to hearing this speech disparaging the going forth, spoken by one who delights in defilements and finds no delight in the going forth. 'Etadabravi' means, declaring the qualities of the going forth, he said this. 'Phassayan' means contacting; showing that one by whom the Dhamma of the noble path has been contacted with the mental-body is not called a wretch, he spoke thus. 'Niraṃkatvā' means having discarded it from one's own being. 'Pāpo pāpaparāyaṇo' means evil by doing evil oneself, and having an evil destination by being a support for others who do evil.

Evaṃ [V 5.0241] so bodhisattaṃ garahi. So attano garahitabhāvaṃ ajānanto viya hutvā nāmagottaṃ kathetvā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Thus he (Soṇaka) rebuked the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, acting as if unaware that he had been rebuked, stated his name and clan, and making friendly conversation with him, spoke this verse:

11.

11.

“Arindamoti me nāmaṃ, kāsirājāti maṃ vidū;

Kacci bhoto sukhasseyyā, idha pattassa soṇakā”ti.

"My name is Arindama; they know me as the king of Kāsī. I trust your rest is pleasant, O Soṇaka, you who have arrived here."

Tattha kaccīti amhākaṃ tāva na kiñci aphāsukaṃ, bhoto pana kacci idha pattassa imasmiṃ uyyāne vasato sukhavihāroti pucchati.

Therein, 'kacci' is a question. He asks: 'For our part, there is no discomfort at all; but for you, venerable sir, who have arrived here and dwell in this park, is your abiding a pleasant one?'

Atha naṃ paccekabuddho, “mahārāja, na kevalaṃ idha, aññatrāpi vasantassa me asukhaṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā tassa samaṇabhadragāthāyo nāma ārabhi –

Then the Paccekabuddha said to him, "Great king, not only here, but wherever I dwell, there is no such thing as discomfort for me." Having said this, he began to recite the verses known as the Samaṇabhadra Gāthā:

12.

12.

“Sadāpi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Na tesaṃ koṭṭhe openti, na kumbhiṃ na kaḷopiyaṃ;

Paraniṭṭhitamesānā, tena yāpenti subbatā.

"Always it is well for the penniless, homeless monk. They fill no storehouse, no pot, nor food basket; seeking what is prepared by others, the well-disciplined thus maintain their lives."

13.

13.

“Dutiyampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Anavajjapiṇḍo bhottabbo, na ca kocūparodhati.

"Secondly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: blameless almsfood is to be eaten, and no one causes obstruction."

14.

14.

“Tatiyampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Nibbuto piṇḍo bhottabbo, na ca kocūparodhati.

"Thirdly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: cooled almsfood is to be eaten, and no one causes obstruction."

15.

15.

“Catutthampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Muttassa raṭṭhe carato, saṅgo yassa na vijjati.

"Fourthly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk, who wanders liberated in the land, for whom no attachment is found."

16.

16.

“Pañcamampi [M 5.0267] bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Nagaramhi ḍayhamānamhi, nāssa kiñci aḍayhatha.

"Fifthly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: when a city is burning, nothing of his is burned."

17.

17.

“Chaṭṭhampi [P 5.0253] bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Raṭṭhe vilumpamānamhi, nāssa kiñci ahīratha.

"Sixthly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: when the country is being plundered, nothing of his is carried away."

18.

18.

“Sattamampi [V 5.0242] bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Corehi rakkhitaṃ maggaṃ, ye caññe paripanthikā;

Pattacīvaramādāya, sotthiṃ gacchati subbato.

"Seventhly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: the well-conducted one, taking his bowl and robe, travels in safety along a road guarded by thieves and other highwaymen."

19.

19.

“Aṭṭhamampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno;

Yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ pakkamati, anapekkhova gacchatī”ti.

"Eighthly, it is well for the penniless, homeless monk: whatever direction he sets out for, he goes without any longing."

Tattha anāgārassāti, mahārāja, gharāvāsaṃ pahāya anāgāriyabhāvaṃ pattassa adhanassa akiñcanassa bhikkhuno sabbakālaṃ bhadrameva. Na tesanti, mahārāja, tesaṃ adhanānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na koṭṭhāgāre dhanadhaññāni openti, na kumbhiyaṃ, na pacchiyaṃ, te pana subbatā paraniṭṭhitaṃ paresaṃ ghare pakkaṃ āhāraṃ saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā kapālamādāya gharapaṭipāṭiyā esānā pariyesantā tena tato laddhena piṇḍena taṃ āhāraṃ navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasena paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjitvā jīvitavuttiṃ yāpenti.
