Therein, 'anāgārassa' means this: O great king, for a monk who is without wealth, without possessions, who has abandoned household life and attained the state of homelessness, it is always auspicious. 'Na tesaṃ' means this: O great king, those monks without wealth do not put wealth and grain in a storehouse, nor in a pot, nor in a basket. But those of good conduct, seeking what is prepared by others, food cooked in the houses of others, covering themselves with the outer robe, taking the alms-bowl, and going from house to house in order, maintain their livelihood by that almsfood obtained from there, consuming it after reflecting on that food according to the ninefold repulsiveness.

Anavajjapiṇḍo bhottabboti vejjakammādikāya anesanāya vā kuhanā lapanā nemittikatā nippesikatā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāti evarūpena micchājīvena vā uppāditā cattāro paccayā, dhammena uppāditāpi apaccavekkhitvā paribhuttā sāvajjapiṇḍo nāma. Anesanaṃ pana pahāya micchājīvaṃ vajjetvā dhammena samena uppāditā “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevāmī”ti vuttanayeneva paccavekkhitvā paribhuttā anavajjapiṇḍo nāma. Yena evarūpo anavajjapiṇḍo bhottabbo paribhuñjitabbo, yañca evarūpaṃ anavajjaṃ piṇḍaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ paccaye nissāya koci appamattakopi kileso na uparodhati na pīḷeti, tassa dutiyampi bhadraṃ adhanassa anāgārassa bhikkhuno.

'Blameless almsfood is to be eaten' means this: The four requisites produced by improper seeking, such as practicing medicine, or by wrong livelihood such as deceit, boasting, divination, importuning, or pursuing gain with gain—or even those produced righteously but consumed without reflection—are called 'blameworthy almsfood'. But that which is produced righteously and justly, having abandoned improper seeking and avoided wrong livelihood, and is consumed after reflecting in the manner stated, 'Wisely reflecting, I use the robe...', is called 'blameless almsfood'. Because such blameless almsfood is to be eaten and enjoyed, and because for one consuming such blameless almsfood no defilement, not even the slightest, arises on account of the requisites to obstruct or afflict him, this is the second good thing for the penniless, homeless monk.

Nibbutoti puthujjanabhikkhuno dhammena uppannapiṇḍopi paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjiyamāno nibbutapiṇḍo nāma, ekantato pana khīṇāsavassa piṇḍova nibbutapiṇḍo nāma. Kiṃkāraṇā? So hi theyyaparibhogo, iṇaparibhogo[M 5.0268], dāyajjaparibhogo, sāmiparibhogoti imesu catūsu paribhogesu sāmiparibhogavasena taṃ bhuñjati, taṇhādāsabyaṃ atīto sāmī hutvā paribhuñjati, na taṃ tappaccayā koci appamattakopi kileso uparodhati.

"Extinguished" means that even the almsfood of an ordinary monk, acquired righteously and consumed after reflection, is called extinguished almsfood. However, only the almsfood of one with destroyed outflows is truly called extinguished almsfood. Why? Because he consumes it as a master's use among these four kinds of uses: use as stolen goods, use as a debt, use as an inheritance, and use as a master. Having gone beyond the slavery of craving, he consumes it as a master; not even the slightest defilement obstructs him because of it.

Muttassa raṭṭhe caratoti upaṭṭhākakulādīsu alaggamānasassa chinnavalāhakassa viya rāhumukhā [V 5.0243] pamuttassa vimalacandamaṇḍalassa viya ca yassa gāmanigamādīsu carantassa rāgasaṅgādīsu ekopi saṅgo natthi. Ekacco hi kulehi saṃsaṭṭho viharati sahasokī sahanandī, ekacco mātāpitūsupi alaggamānaso vicarati korunagaragāmavāsī daharo viya, evarūpassa puthujjanassapi bhadrameva[P 5.0254].

Wandering in a country as one who is free means for one whose mind does not cling to families of supporters and the like, like a detached cloud, and like the spotless moon freed from the mouth of Rahu—for such a one, wandering in villages and towns, there is not even a single clinging to lust and the like. For some, indeed, dwell mingling with families, sharing sorrow and joy. Some wander without clinging even to their parents, like a young man dwelling in the town of Korunagara. Even for such an ordinary person, it is indeed auspicious.

Nāssa kiñcīti yo hi bahuparikkhāro hoti, so “mā me corā parikkhāre hariṃsū”ti atirekāni ca cīvarādīni antonagare upaṭṭhākakule nikkhipati, atha nagaramhi ḍayhamāne “asukakule nāma aggi uṭṭhito”ti sutvā socati kilamati, evarūpassa bhadraṃ nāma natthi. Yo pana, mahārāja, sakuṇavattaṃ pūreti, kāyapaṭibaddhaparikkhārova hoti, tassa tādisassa na kiñci aḍayhatha, tenassa pañcamampi bhadrameva.

'He has nothing' means that he who has many possessions, thinking, "May thieves not steal my belongings," stores extra robes and other requisites in the homes of supporters within the city. Then, when he hears that a fire has broken out in such-and-such a family's house in the city, he grieves and is distressed. For such a one, there is no auspicious quality. But, O great king, he who fulfills the practice of a bird, possessing only the requisites that are bound to the body—for such a one, nothing is burned; thus, for him, even the fifth is an auspicious quality.

Vilumpamānamhīti viluppamānamhi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Ahīrathāti yathā pabbatagahanādīhi nikkhamitvā raṭṭhaṃ vilumpamānesu coresu bahuparikkhārassa antogāme ṭhapitaṃ vilumpati harati, tathā yassa adhanassa kāyapaṭibaddhaparikkhārassa na kiñci ahīratha tassa chaṭṭhampi bhadrameva.

'Vilumpamānamhi' means 'while being plundered'; or this may also be the reading. 'Was carried away' means that just as when robbers emerge from mountain thickets and the like and plunder a country, they plunder and carry away the many requisites that have been placed inside a village, so too, for one who is without wealth and has only requisites bound to the body, nothing is carried away; thus, for him, even the sixth is an auspicious quality.

Ye caññe paripanthikāti ye ca aññepi tesu tesu ṭhānesu suṅkagahaṇatthāya ṭhapitā paripanthikā, tehi ca rakkhitaṃ. Pattacīvaranti corānaṃ anupakāraṃ suṅkikānaṃ asuṅkārahaṃ mattikāpattañceva katadaḷhīkammaparibhaṇḍaṃ paṃsukūlacīvarañca appagghāni kāyabandhanaparissāvanasūcivāsipattatthavikāni cāti sabbepi aṭṭha parikkhāre kāyapaṭibaddhe katvā maggappaṭipanno kenaci aviheṭhiyamāno sotthiṃ gacchati. Subbatoti lobhanīyāni hi cīvarādīni disvā corā haranti, suṅkikāpi “kiṃ nu kho etassa hatthe”ti [M 5.0269] pattatthavikādīni sodhenti, subbato pana sallahukavutti tesaṃ passantānaññeva sotthiṃ gacchati, tenassa sattamampi bhadrameva.

'And others who obstruct the path'—those others who are stationed in various places to collect tolls—and he is protected from them. 'The bowl and robes'—these are of no use to thieves, nor are they items for which toll collectors demand payment: a clay bowl, a well-strengthened requisite, a rag-robe of little value, along with the waistband, the water strainer, the needle, the razor, and the bowl-bag—all eight requisites tied to the body. Thus, one who travels the path, unharmed by anyone, goes safely. 'One of good conduct'—for when thieves see desirable robes and such, they steal them, and toll collectors inspect bowl-bags and the like, thinking, 'What does this one have in hand?' But one of good conduct, living lightly, goes safely even as they watch. Thus, for such a one, even the seventh is auspicious.

Anapekkhova gacchatīti kāyapaṭibaddhato atirekassa vihāre paṭisāmitassa kassaci parikkhārassa abhāvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ nivattitvāpi na oloketi. Yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ gantukāmo hoti, taṃ taṃ gacchanto anapekkhova gacchati anurādhapurā nikkhamitvā thūpārāme pabbajitānaṃ dvinnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ vuḍḍhataro viya.

'He goes without attachment' means that, owing to the absence of any extra requisite beyond what is bound to the body stored away in the monastery, he does not look back even when leaving his dwelling place. Whichever direction he wishes to go, he goes in that direction without attachment, like the elder of the two sons of good family who, having left Anurādhapura, went forth at the Thūpārāma.

Iti soṇakapaccekabuddho aṭṭha samaṇabhadrakāni kathesi. Tato uttariṃ pana satampi sahassampi [V 5.0244] aparimāṇāni samaṇabhadrakāni esa kathetuṃ samatthoyeva. Rājā pana kāmābhiratattā tassa kathaṃ pacchinditvā “mayhaṃ samaṇabhadrakehi attho natthī”ti attano kāmādhimuttataṃ pakāsento āha –

Thus the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka spoke these eight auspicious qualities of an ascetic. Furthermore, he was indeed capable of speaking hundreds, thousands, even countless auspicious qualities of an ascetic beyond that. But the king, being engrossed in sensual pleasures, interrupted his discourse and, revealing his own inclination toward desires, said: \"I have no need for these auspicious qualities of an ascetic.\"

20.

20.

“Bahūni samaṇabhadrāni, ye tvaṃ bhikkhu pasaṃsasi;

Ahañca giddho kāmesu, kathaṃ kāhāmi soṇaka.

"Many are the auspicious qualities of an ascetic, which you, monk, praise; but I am greedy for sensual pleasures, how can I, Soṇaka, do it?

21.

21.

“Piyā me mānusā kāmā, atho dibyāpi me piyā;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, ubho loke labhāmase”ti.

"Dear to me are human sensual pleasures, and dear also are divine ones; yet by what means can we obtain both worlds?"

Tattha [P 5.0255] vaṇṇenāti kāraṇena.

Herein, 'by means' means 'by reason'.

Atha naṃ paccekabuddho āha –

Then the Paccekabuddha said to him:

22.

22.

“Kāme giddhā kāmaratā, kāmesu adhimuccitā;

Narā pāpāni katvāna, upapajjanti duggatiṃ.

"Greedy for sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, and infatuated with them—people, having done evil deeds, are reborn in a state of misery.

23.

23.

“Ye ca kāme pahantvāna, nikkhantā akutobhayā;

Ekodibhāvādhigatā, na te gacchanti duggatiṃ.

"But those who have abandoned sensual pleasures, having gone forth free from fear, have attained singleness of mind; they do not go to a state of misery.

24.

24.

“Upamaṃ te karissāmi, taṃ suṇohi arindama;

Upamāya midhekacce, atthaṃ jānanti paṇḍitā.

"I will make a comparison for you; listen, O Arindama. By means of a comparison, some wise people in this world understand the meaning.

25.

25.

“Gaṅgāya kuṇapaṃ disvā, vuyhamānaṃ mahaṇṇave;

Vāyaso samacintesi, appapañño acetaso.

"Seeing an elephant's corpse in the Ganges, being carried along in the wide waters, a crow of little wisdom and witless thought to himself:

26.

26.

“Yānañca [M 5.0270] vatidaṃ laddhaṃ, bhakkho cāyaṃ anappako;

Tattha rattiṃ tattha divā, tattheva nirato mano.

"'Indeed, this vehicle has been found, and this food is plentiful'; there by night and there by day, his mind was constantly delighted.

27.

27.

“Khādaṃ [V 5.0245] nāgassa maṃsāni, pivaṃ bhāgīrathodakaṃ;

Sampassaṃ vanacetyāni, na palettha vihaṅgamo.

"Eating the elephant's flesh, drinking the water of the Ganges, and seeing the forest haunts, the bird did not fly away to the forest.

28.

28.

“Tañca otaraṇī gaṅgā, pamattaṃ kuṇape rataṃ;

Samuddaṃ ajjhagāhāsi, agatī yattha pakkhinaṃ.

"And the Ganges, flowing down to the ocean, carried that corpse along with the heedless bird that delighted in it, to the ocean where there is no landing place for birds.

29.

29.

“So ca bhakkhaparikkhīṇo, udapatvā vihaṅgamo;

Na pacchato na purato, nuttaraṃ nopi dakkhiṇaṃ.

"When its food was exhausted, the bird flew up; but it found no landing place to the west or to the east, nor to the north nor to the south.

30.

30.

“Dīpaṃ so najjhagāgañchi, agatī yattha pakkhinaṃ;

So ca tattheva pāpattha, yathā dubbalako tathā.

"It did not reach an island where birds might land; and there it fell, just as a weakling does.

31.

31.

“Tañca sāmuddikā macchā, kumbhīlā makarā susū;

Pasayhakārā khādiṃsu, phandamānaṃ vipakkhakaṃ.

"Then the ocean fish, crocodiles, makaras, and porpoises violently devoured it as it fluttered with broken wings.

32.

32.

“Evameva tuvaṃ rāja, ye caññe kāmabhogino;

Giddhā ce na vamissanti, kākapaññāva te vidū.

"Even so, O king, you and others who enjoy sensual pleasures—if, being greedy, you do not relinquish them, the wise know that you have wisdom like that of a crow."

33.

33.

“Esā te upamā rāja, atthasandassanī katā;

Tvañca paññāyase tena, yadi kāhasi vā na vā”ti.

"This simile, O king, has been made for you to show the meaning. And by it you will be known, whether you will act upon it or not."

Tattha [P 5.0256] pāpānīti, mahārāja, tvaṃ kāmagiddho, narā ca kāme nissāya kāyaduccaritādīni pāpāni katvā yattha supinantepi dibbā ca mānusikā ca kāmā na labbhanti, taṃ duggatiṃ upapajjantīti attho. Pahantvānāti kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pahāya. Akutobhayāti rāgādīsu kutoci anāgatabhayā. Ekodibhāvādhigatāti ekodibhāvaṃ ekavihārikataṃ adhigatā. Na teti te evarūpā pabbajitā duggatiṃ na gacchanti.

Herein, 'evil deeds' means: O great king, you are greedy for sensual pleasures, and people, relying on sensual pleasures and having committed evil deeds such as bodily misconduct, are reborn in a woeful destination where divine and human sensual pleasures are not obtained even in a dream. 'Having abandoned' means having abandoned it like a lump of spittle. 'Fearless from any quarter' means having no fear from any quarter concerning lust and other defilements. 'Having attained a unified state' means having attained a unified state, a state of dwelling alone. 'They do not go' means that such renunciants do not go to a woeful destination.

Upamaṃ teti, mahārāja, dibbamānusake kāme patthentassa hatthikuṇape paṭibaddhakākasadisassa tava ekaṃ upamaṃ karissāmi, taṃ suṇohīti attho. Kuṇapanti hatthikaḷevaraṃ. Mahaṇṇaveti gambhīraputhule udake[M 5.0271]. Eko kira mahāvāraṇo gaṅgātīre caranto gaṅgāyaṃ [V 5.0246] patitvā uttarituṃ asakkento tattheva mato gaṅgāya vuyhi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vāyasoti ākāsena gacchanto eko kāko. Yānañca vatidanti so evaṃ cintetvā tattha nilīyitvā “idaṃ mayā hatthiyānaṃ laddhaṃ, ettha nilīno sukhaṃ carissāmi, ayameva ca me anappako bhakkho bhavissati, idāni mayā aññattha gantuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti sanniṭṭhānamakāsi. Tattha rattinti tattha rattiñca divā ca tattheva mano abhirato ahosi. Na paletthāti na uppatitvā pakkāmi.

“I will give you a simile,” O great king, means: I will give a simile for you, who longs for divine and human sensual pleasures and is like a crow attached to an elephant's carcass. Listen to it. “Carcass” means an elephant's corpse. “In the great ocean” means in deep and vast waters. It is said that a great elephant, wandering on the bank of the Ganges, fell into the river and, being unable to get out, died right there and was carried away by the Ganges. This was said in reference to that. “A crow” means a crow flying through the sky. “And a vehicle indeed” means that it thought, “I have now obtained this elephant-vehicle. Settling here, I will live happily, and this will be no small food for me. Now it is not proper for me to go elsewhere,” and having alighted there, it made a firm resolve. “There by night” means that both by night and by day its mind delighted in that very place. “It did not flee” means it did not fly up and depart.

Otaraṇīti samuddābhimukhī otaramānā. “Ohāriṇī”tipi pāṭho, sā samuddābhimukhī avahāriṇīti attho. Agatī yatthāti samuddamajjhaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhakkhaparikkhīṇoti parikkhīṇabhakkho. Udapatvāti khīṇe camme ca maṃse ca aṭṭhisaṅghāto ūmivegena bhinno udake nimujji. Atha so kāko udake patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto uppati, evaṃ uppatitvāti attho. Agatī yattha pakkhinanti yasmiṃ samuddamajjhe pakkhīnaṃ agati, tattha so evaṃ uppatito pacchimaṃ disaṃ gantvā tattha patiṭṭhaṃ alabhitvā puratthimaṃ, tato uttaraṃ, tato dakkhiṇanti catassopi disā gantvā attano patiṭṭhānaṃ na ajjhagā nāgañchīti attho. Atha vā vāyaso evaṃ uppatitvā pacchimādīsu ekekaṃ disaṃ āgañchi, dīpaṃ pana najjhāgamāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Pāpatthāti papatito. Yathā dubbalakoti yathā dubbalako pateyya, tatheva patito. Susūti susunāmakā caṇḍamacchā. Pasayhakārāti anicchamānakaṃyeva balakkārena. Vipakkhakanti viddhastapakkhakaṃ.

“Descending” means descending towards the ocean. There is also the reading “Ohāriṇī,” which means carrying away towards the ocean. “Where there is no resort” refers to the middle of the ocean. “With its food exhausted” means its food was exhausted. “Sank in the water” means that when the skin and flesh were gone, the mass of bones, broken by the force of the waves, sank in the water. Then that crow, unable to find a footing in the water, flew up; this is the meaning of “thus it flew up.” “Where for birds there is no resort” means that in the middle of the ocean, where there is no resort for birds, it flew up. Having gone to the western direction and not finding a perch, it went to the eastern, then the northern, then the southern. Having gone to all four directions, it did not find a perch for itself, it did not arrive—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning here should be seen thus: the crow, having flown up, went to each of the directions, west and so on, but it did not reach an island. “It fell” means it fell down. “Like a weak one” means it fell just as a weak one would fall. “By the Susus” means by the fierce fish named Susu. “Forcibly” means by force, even when it was unwilling. “With wings destroyed” means its wings were torn apart.

Giddhā ce na vamissantīti yadi giddhā hutvā kāme na vamissanti, na chaḍḍessanti. Kākapaññāva teti kākassa samānapaññā iti te buddhādayo paṇḍitā vidū vidanti, jānantīti attho. Atthasandassanīti atthappakāsikā. Tvañca paññāyaseti tvañca paññāyissasi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, mayā hitakāmena tava ovādo dinno, taṃ pana tvaṃ yadi kāhasi, devaloke nibbattissasi, yadi na kāhasi, kāmapaṅke nimuggo jīvitapariyosāne niraye nibbattissasīti evaṃ tvameva tena [M 5.0272] kāraṇena vā akāraṇena [P 5.0257] vā sagge vā niraye vā paññāyissasi. Ahaṃ pana sabbabhavehi mutto appaṭisandhikoti.

“If, being greedy, they do not vomit” means: if, being greedy, they do not vomit up sensual pleasures, they will not discard them. “Of crow-like wisdom” means: those wise ones, the Buddhas and others, know them as having wisdom similar to a crow's; the wise know, they understand—this is the meaning. “That shows the meaning” means it illuminates the meaning. “And you will be known” means you yourself will be known. This is what is said: O great king, desiring your welfare, I have given you advice. If you follow it, you will be reborn in the world of the devas. If you do not follow it, having sunk into the mire of sensual pleasures, at the end of your life you will be reborn in hell. Thus you yourself will be known, for that reason or for no reason, in heaven or in hell. But I am freed from all kinds of existence, with no future rebirth.

Imaṃ pana ovādaṃ dentena paccekabuddhena nadī dassitā, tāya vuyhamānaṃ hatthikuṇapaṃ dassitaṃ, kuṇapakhādako kāko dassito, tassa kuṇapaṃ khāditvā pānīyapivanakālo dassito, ramaṇīyavanasaṇḍadassanakālo dassito, kuṇapassa nadiyā vuyhamānassa samuddapaveso dassito, samuddamajjhe [V 5.0247] kākassa hatthikuṇape patiṭṭhaṃ alabhitvā vināsaṃ pattakālo dassito. Tattha nadī viya anamataggo saṃsāro daṭṭhabbo, nadiyā vuyhamānaṃ hatthikuṇapaṃ viya saṃsāre pañca kāmaguṇā, kāko viya bālaputhujjano, kākassa kuṇapaṃ khāditvā pānīyapivanakālo viya puthujjanassa kāmaguṇe paribhuñjitvā somanassikakālo, kākassa kuṇape laggasseva ramaṇīyavanasaṇḍadassanaṃ viya puthujjanassa kāmaguṇesu laggasseva savanavasena aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇadassanaṃ, kuṇape samuddaṃ paviṭṭhe kākassa patiṭṭhaṃ labhituṃ asakkontassa vināsaṃ pattakālo viya bālaputhujjanassa kāmaguṇagiddhassa pāpaparāyaṇassa kusaladhamme patiṭṭhaṃ labhituṃ asakkontassa mahāniraye mahāvināsapatti daṭṭhabbāti.

Now, in giving this advice, the Paccekabuddha showed a river. He showed an elephant's carcass being carried along by it. He showed a crow eating the carcass. He showed the time when, after eating the carcass, it drank water. He showed the time when it saw a delightful forest grove. He showed the carcass's entry into the ocean as it was carried by the river. He showed the time when the crow, unable to find a footing on the elephant carcass in the middle of the ocean, met with destruction. Herein, the river should be seen as saṃsāra, which is without a discoverable beginning. The elephant carcass carried by the river is like the five cords of sensual pleasure in saṃsāra. The crow is like a foolish worldling. The time when the crow drank water after eating the carcass is like the time of gladness for a worldling after enjoying sensual pleasures. The crow's seeing a delightful forest grove while attached to the carcass is like a worldling's seeing the thirty-eight objects by way of hearing while attached to sensual pleasures. The time when the crow met with destruction, unable to find a footing when the carcass entered the ocean, should be seen as being like the great destruction in the great hell attained by a foolish worldling who is greedy for sensual pleasures, intent on evil, and unable to find a footing in wholesome states.

Evamassa so imāya upamāya ovādaṃ datvā idāni tameva ovādaṃ thiraṃ katvā patiṭṭhapetuṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus given him advice with this simile, he now spoke a verse to make that same advice firm and established:

34.

34.

“Ekavācampi dvivācaṃ, bhaṇeyya anukampako;

Tatuttariṃ na bhāseyya, dāsovayyassa santike”ti.

"A compassionate person should speak once or twice; he should not speak more than that, like a servant in the presence of his master."

Tattha na bhāseyyāti vacanaṃ aggaṇhantassa hi tato uttariṃ bhāsamāno sāmikassa santike dāso viya hoti. Dāso hi sāmike kathaṃ gaṇhantepi aggaṇhantepi kathetiyeva. Tena vuttaṃ “tatuttariṃ na bhāseyyā”ti.

In that passage, 'he should not speak' means that if one speaks further to someone who does not accept the words, one becomes like a servant in the presence of a master. For a servant continues to speak whether the master accepts the words or not. Therefore it was said, 'he should not speak more than that.'

35.

35.

“Idaṃ vatvāna pakkāmi, soṇako amitabuddhimā;

Vehāse antalikkhasmiṃ, anusāsitvāna khattiya”nti. –

"Having said this, Sonaka departed, he of immeasurable wisdom; having instructed the khattiya, he went through the sky, through the air."

Ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā.

This is a verse by one who is Fully Enlightened.

Tattha [M 5.0273] idaṃ vatvānāti, bhikkhave, so paccekabuddho amitāya lokuttarabuddhiyā amitabuddhimā idaṃ vatvā iddhiyā uppatitvā “sace pabbajissasi, taveva, no ce pabbajissasi, taveva, dinno te mayā ovādo, appamatto hohī”ti evaṃ anusāsitvāna khattiyaṃ pakkāmi.

Herein, 'Having said this' means: Bhikkhus, that Paccekabuddha, of immeasurable wisdom due to his immeasurable supramundane knowledge, having said this and risen up by psychic power, departed after instructing the khattiya thus: 'If you go forth, it is for your own sake; if you do not go forth, it is for your own sake. My advice has been given to you. Be heedful!'

Bodhisattopi taṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ yāva dassanapathā olokento ṭhatvā tasmiṃ cakkhupathe [V 5.0248] atikkante saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhitvā cintesi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo hīnajacco samāno asambhinne khattiyavaṃse jātassa mama matthake attano pādarajaṃ [P 5.0258] okiranto ākāsaṃ uppatitvā gato, mayāpi ajjeva nikkhamitvā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So rajjaṃ niyyādetvā pabbajitukāmo gāthādvayamāha –

The Bodhisatta, too, stood watching him as he went through the sky as far as the range of vision. When he had passed beyond the range of sight, the Bodhisatta was overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency and reflected: 'This ascetic, though of lower birth, has gone, flying up into the sky and showering the dust from his feet upon my head, though I was born into an unbroken warrior lineage. It is fitting that I myself should go forth this very day.' Desiring to go forth after handing over the kingdom, he spoke two verses:

36.

36.

“Ko nume rājakattāro, suddā veyyattamāgatā;

Rajjaṃ niyyādayissāmi, nāhaṃ rajjena matthiko.

"Where now are my king-makers, the attendants who have attained proficiency? I will hand over the kingdom; I have no need for kingship.

37.

37.

“Ajjeva pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvaga”nti.

"Today itself I will go forth; who knows if death will come tomorrow? Let me not, like that foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures."

Tattha ko numeti kuhiṃ nu ime. Rājakattāroti ye rājārahaṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ karonti. Suddā veyyattamāgatāti suddā ca ye ca aññe byattabhāvaṃ āgatā mukhamaṅgalikā. Rajjena matthikoti rajjena atthiko. Ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suveti maraṇaṃ ajja vā suve vāti idaṃ ko jānituṃ samattho.

In that passage, 'Where now' means 'Where are they?' 'King-makers' means those who anoint one worthy of royalty and make him king. 'Those who have attained proficiency' means the attendants and others who have become skilled and auspicious of speech. 'In need of kingship' means one who desires a kingdom. 'Who knows if death will come tomorrow' means who is able to know if death will come today or tomorrow?

Evaṃ rajjaṃ niyyādentassa sutvā amaccā āhaṃsu –

Hearing him thus handing over the kingdom, the ministers said:

38.

38.

“Atthi te daharo putto, dīghāvu raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Taṃ rajje abhisiñcassu, so no rājā bhavissatī”ti.

"You have a young son named Dīghāvu, who increases the prosperity of the realm; anoint him in the kingdom, and he will be our king."

Tato paraṃ raññā vuttagāthamādiṃ katvā udānasambandhagāthā pāḷinayeneva veditabbā –

After that, the verses connected with the inspired utterance, beginning with the verse spoken by the king, should be understood in accordance with the method of the Pāli text.

39.

39.

“Khippaṃ kumāramānetha, dīghāvuṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhanaṃ;

Taṃ rajje abhisiñcissaṃ, so vo rājā bhavissati.

"Quickly bring the prince, Dīghāvu, who increases the prosperity of the realm. I will anoint him in the kingdom; he will be your king."

40.

40.

“Tato [M 5.0274] kumāramānesuṃ, dīghāvuṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhanaṃ;

Taṃ disvā ālapī rājā, ekaputtaṃ manoramaṃ.

"Then they brought the prince, Dīghāvu, who increases the prosperity of the realm. Seeing him, his only delightful son, the king addressed him:

41.

41.

“Saṭṭhi [V 5.0249] gāmasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Te putta paṭipajjasu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

"Sixty thousand villages, completely full in every way—take charge of them, my son; I hand the kingdom over to you.

42.

42.

“Ajjeva pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kāko va dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

"Today itself I will go forth; who knows if death will come tomorrow? Let me not, like that foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures."

43.

43.

“Saṭṭhi nāgasahassāni, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā;

Suvaṇṇakacchā mātaṅgā, hemakappanavāsasā.

"Sixty thousand elephants, adorned with all their ornaments, of the Matanga breed, with golden girths and golden trappings and covers."

44.

44.

“Ārūḷhā gāmaṇīyebhi, tomaraṅkusapāṇibhi;

Te putta paṭipajjassu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

“Mounted by elephant riders with lances and goads in hand; take charge of them, my son, I hand the kingdom over to you.

45.

45.

“Ajjeva [P 5.0259] pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

“Today itself I will go forth; who knows? Death may come tomorrow. Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures.”

46.

46.

“Saṭṭhi assasahassāni, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā;

Ājānīyāva jātiyā, sindhavā sīghavāhino.

“Sixty thousand horses, adorned with all their ornaments, thoroughbreds by birth, Sindhu steeds, swift runners.

47.

47.

“Ārūḷhā gāmaṇīyebhi, illiyācāpadhāribhi;

Te putta paṭipajjassu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

“Mounted by horse riders, bearing short swords and bows; take charge of them, my son, I hand the kingdom over to you.

48.

48.

“Ajjeva pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

“Today itself I will go forth; who knows? Death may come tomorrow. Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures.

49.

49.

“Saṭṭhi rathasahassāni, sannaddhā ussitaddhajā;

Dīpā athopi veyyagghā, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā.

“Sixty thousand chariots, harnessed, with banners raised high, covered with leopard and tiger skins, embellished with all ornaments.

50.

50.

“Ārūḷhā gāmaṇīyebhi, cāpahatthehi vammibhi;

Te putta paṭipajjassu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

“Mounted by chariot-warriors with bows in hand and clad in armor; take charge of them, my son, I hand over the kingdom to you.

51.

51.

“Ajjeva [V 5.0250] pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

“Today itself I will go forth; who knows? Death may come tomorrow. Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures.

52.

52.

“Saṭṭhi dhenusahassāni, rohaññā puṅgavūsabhā;

Tā putta paṭipajjassu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

“Sixty thousand milch cows, reddish ones with excellent bulls among them; take charge of them, my son, I hand over the kingdom to you.

53.

53.

“Ajjeva [M 5.0275] pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

“Today itself I will go forth; who knows? Death may come tomorrow. Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures.

54.

54.

“Soḷasitthisahassāni, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā;

Vicitravatthābharaṇā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Tā putta paṭipajjassu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.

“Sixteen thousand women, adorned with all ornaments, with colorful garments and finery, wearing pearl and jeweled earrings; take charge of them, my son, I hand over the kingdom to you.

55.

55.

“Ajjeva pabbajissāmi, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ.

“Today itself I will go forth; who knows? Death may come tomorrow. Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual pleasures.

56.

56.

“Daharasseva me tāta, mātā matāti me sutaṃ;

Tayā vinā ahaṃ tāta, jīvitumpi na ussahe.

“Father, I have heard that my mother died when I was just a child; without you, father, I am not able even to live.

57.

57.

“Yathā āraññakaṃ nāgaṃ, poto anveti pacchato;

Jessantaṃ giriduggesu, samesu visamesu ca.

“Just as a young elephant follows from behind a forest elephant, as it wanders through mountain passes, on level and uneven ground,

58.

58.

“Evaṃ taṃ anugacchāmi, pattamādāya pacchato;

Subharo te bhavissāmi, na te hessāmi dubbharo.

“So I will follow you from behind, carrying your bowl; I will be easy for you to support, I will not be a burden to you.

59.

59.

“Yathā sāmuddikaṃ nāvaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Vohāro tattha gaṇheyya, vāṇijā byasanī siyā.

“Just as with a sea-going ship of merchants seeking wealth, if disaster should seize it there, the merchants would meet with ruin.

60.

60.

“Evamevāyaṃ puttakali, antarāyakaro mama;

Imaṃ kumāraṃ pāpetha, pāsādaṃ rativaḍḍhanaṃ.

“Even so, this wretched son is an obstacle for me. Take this prince to the Rativaḍḍhana palace, the palace that increases delight.

61.

61.

“Tattha [V 5.0251][P 5.0260] kambusahatthāyo, yathā sakkaṃva accharā;

Tā naṃ tattha ramessanti, tāhi ceso ramissati.

“There, women with hands adorned with gold, like celestial nymphs around Sakka, will delight him, and he will delight in them.

62.

62.

“Tato kumāraṃ pāpesuṃ, pāsādaṃ rativaḍḍhanaṃ;

Taṃ disvā avacuṃ kaññā, dīghāvuṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhanaṃ.

Then they brought the prince to the Rativaḍḍhana palace. Seeing Dīghāvu, the prosperer of the realm, the maidens said:

63.

63.

“Devatānusi gandhabbo, adu sakko purindado;

Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

“Are you a deva, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada? Who are you? Whose son are you? How may we know you?

64.

64.

“Namhi [M 5.0276] devo na gandhabbo, nāpi sakko purindado;

Kāsirañño ahaṃ putto, dīghāvu raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Mamaṃ bharatha bhaddaṃ vo, ahaṃ bhattā bhavāmi vo.

“I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka Purindada. I am Dīghāvu, son of the king of Kāsi, the prosperer of the realm. Support me, and may it be well with you; I will be your husband.

65.

65.

“Taṃ tattha avacuṃ kaññā, dīghāvuṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhanaṃ;

Kuhiṃ rājā anuppatto, ito rājā kuhiṃ gato.

The maidens there said to him, to Dīghāvu, the prosperer of the realm: ‘Where has the king reached? From here, where has the king gone?’

66.

66.

“Paṅkaṃ rājā atikkanto, thale rājā patiṭṭhito;

Akaṇḍakaṃ agahanaṃ, paṭipanno mahāpathaṃ.

“The king has crossed over the mud; the king is established on dry land. He has set out upon the great path, which is without thorns and without thickets.

67.

67.

“Ahañca paṭipannosmi, maggaṃ duggatigāminaṃ;

Sakaṇṭakaṃ sagahanaṃ, yena gacchanti duggatiṃ.

“But I have entered upon the path that leads to a state of woe, a path with thorns and thickets, by which one goes to a bad destination.

68.

68.

“Tassa te svāgataṃ rāja, sīhasseva giribbajaṃ;

Anusāsa mahārāja, tvaṃ no sabbāsamissaro”ti.

“Welcome to you, O king, as to a lion its mountain cave. Rule over us, great king; you are the lord of us all.”

Tattha khippanti tena hi naṃ sīghaṃ ānetha. Ālapīti “saṭṭhi gāmasahassānī”tiādīni vadanto ālapi. Sabbālaṅkārabhūsitāti te nāgā sabbehi sīsūpagādīhi alaṅkārehi bhūsitā. Hemakappanavāsasāti suvaṇṇakhacitena kappanena paṭicchannasarīrā. Gāmaṇīyebhīti hatthācariyehi. Ājānīyāvāti kāraṇākāraṇavijānanakā va. Jātiyāti sindhavajātiyā sindhuraṭṭhe sindhunadītīre jātā. Gāmaṇīyebhīti assācariyehi. Illiyā cāpadhāribhīti illiyāvudhañca cāpāvudhañca [V 5.0252] dhārentehi. Dīpā athopi veyyagghāti dīpicammabyagghacammaparivārā. Gāmaṇīyebhīti rathikehi. Vammibhīti sannaddhavammehi. Rohaññāti rattavaṇṇā. Puṅgavūsabhāti usabhasaṅkhātena jeṭṭhakapuṅgavena samannāgatā.

Therein, `khippan` ti means: 'Well then, bring him quickly.' `Ālapī`ti means he spoke, saying, 'Sixty thousand villages,' etc. `Sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā`ti means those elephants were adorned with all ornaments such as head-gear. `Hemakappanavāsasā`ti means their bodies were covered with a housing inlaid with gold. `Gāmaṇīyebhī`ti means by elephant trainers. `Ājānīyāvā`ti means they are able to discern what is proper and improper. `Jātiyā`ti means of the Sindh breed, born in the Sindh country on the bank of the river Sindhu. `Gāmaṇīyebhī`ti means by horse trainers. `Illiyā cāpadhāribhī`ti means by those bearing the `illi` weapon and the bow weapon. `Dīpā athopi veyyagghā`ti means furnished with leopard skins and tiger skins. `Gāmaṇīyebhī`ti means by charioteers. `Vammibhī`ti means with armor fastened on. `Rohaññā`ti means reddish in color. `Puṅgavūsabhā`ti means endowed with a chief bull, designated as a leader.

Daharasseva me, tātāti atha naṃ kumāro, tāta, mama daharasseva sato mātā matā iti mayā sutaṃ, sohaṃ tayā vinā jīvituṃ na sakkhissāmīti āha. Pototi taruṇapotako. Jessantanti vicarantaṃ. Sāmuddikanti samudde vicarantaṃ. Dhanesinanti dhanaṃ pariyesantānaṃ. Vohāroti vicitravohāro heṭṭhākaḍḍhanako vāḷamaccho vā [P 5.0261] udakarakkhaso vā āvaṭṭo vā. Tatthāti tasmiṃ samudde. Vāṇijā byasanī siyāti atha te vāṇijā byasanappattā bhaveyyuṃ. “Siyyunti”pi pāṭho[M 5.0277]. Puttakalīti puttalāmako puttakāḷakaṇṇī. Kumāro puna kiñci vattuṃ na visahi. Atha rājā amacce āṇāpento “ima”ntiādimāha. Tattha kambusahatthāyoti kambusaṃ vuccati suvaṇṇaṃ, suvaṇṇābharaṇabhūsitahatthāyoti attho. Yathāti yathā icchanti, tathā karonti.

`Daharasseva me, tātā`ti: Then the prince said, 'Father, I have heard that my mother died when I was just a child; therefore I will not be able to live without you.' `Poto`ti: a young one. `Jessantan`ti: wandering. `Sāmuddikan`ti: faring on the sea. `Dhanesinan`ti: of those seeking wealth. `Vohāro`ti: a strange creature, or something that drags one down, or a sea monster, or a water demon, or a whirlpool. `Tatthā`ti: in that sea. `Vāṇijā byasanī siyā`ti: then those merchants would meet with disaster. `Siyyun`ti is also a reading. `Puttakalī`ti: a wretched son, an inauspicious son. The prince could not say anything more. Then the king, commanding his ministers, said the verse beginning `imam`. Therein, `kambusahatthāyo`ti: `kambu` is said to be gold; the meaning is 'with hands adorned with gold ornaments.' `Yathā`ti: as they wish, so they do.

Evaṃ vatvā mahāsatto tattheva taṃ abhisiñcāpetvā nagaraṃ pāhesi. Sayaṃ pana ekakova uyyānā nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpesi. Mahājanopi kumāraṃ bārāṇasiṃ pavesesi. So nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā “tato”tiādimāha. Taṃ disvā avacuṃ kaññāti taṃ mahantena parivārena sirisobhaggena āgataṃ disvā “asuko nāmeso”ti ajānantiyova tā nāṭakitthiyo gantvā avocuṃ. Mamaṃ bharathāti mamaṃ icchatha. Paṅkanti rāgādikilesapaṅkaṃ. Thaleti pabbajjāya. Akaṇṭakanti rāgakaṇṭakādivirahitaṃ. Teheva gahanehi agahanaṃ. Mahāpathanti saggamokkhagāminaṃ mahāmaggaṃ paṭipanno. Yenāti yena micchāmaggena duggatiṃ gacchanti, taṃ ahaṃ paṭipannoti vadati. Tato tā cintesuṃ – “rājā tāva amhe pahāya pabbajito, ayampi kāmesu virattacittarūpo, sace naṃ nābhiramessāma, nikkhamitvā pabbajeyya, abhiramanākāramassa karissāmā”ti. Atha naṃ abhinandantiyo osānagāthamāhaṃsu. Tattha giribbajanti sīhapotakānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kañcanaguhaṃ kesarasīhassa āgataṃ viya tassa tava āgataṃ suāgataṃ. Tvaṃ noti tvaṃ sabbāsampi amhākaṃ issaro, sāmīti.

Having said this, the Great Being had him consecrated right there and then sent him to the city. He himself, all alone, departed from the park, entered the Himalayas, built a leaf-hut in a delightful spot, went forth as a wandering ascetic, and sustained himself on forest roots and fruits. The people escorted the prince into Bārāṇasī. He circumambulated the city and ascended the palace. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the verse beginning with 'Tato'. 'Taṃ disvā avacuṃ kaññā' means: seeing him approaching with a great retinue and in great splendor, those dancing girls, not knowing who he was, went and spoke to him. 'Mamaṃ bharathā' means 'desire me'. 'Paṅkaṃ' refers to the mud of defilements like lust. 'Thale' refers to the state of renunciation. 'Akaṇṭakaṃ' means free from the thorns of lust and so on. 'Agahanaṃ' means free from those very thickets of defilements. 'Mahāpathaṃ' refers to the great road leading to heaven and liberation. 'Yena' means he is saying, 'I have entered upon that wrong path by which people go to a state of woe.' Then the women thought: 'The king has already abandoned us and gone forth. This prince too seems to have a mind detached from sensual pleasures. If we do not make him enjoy himself, he might also depart and go forth. We must act in a way to make him take delight.' Then, showing their delight in him, they spoke the concluding verse. Therein, 'giribbajaṃ' refers to the golden cave where lion cubs dwell; just as the arrival of a maned lion is welcome there, so is your arrival welcome. 'Tvaṃ no' means: you are the lord and master of us all.

Evañca pana vatvā sabbā tūriyāni paggaṇhiṃsu, nānappakārāni naccagītāni pavattiṃsu[V 5.0253]. Yaso mahā ahosi, so yasamadamatto pitaraṃ na sari, dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā yathākammaṃ gato. Bodhisattopi jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokūpago ahosi.

And having spoken thus, they all took up their musical instruments, and various kinds of dances and songs commenced. His fame was great; intoxicated by fame, he did not remember his father. Having ruled the kingdom righteously, he passed away according to his kamma. The Bodhisatta, having developed the meditative attainments and the supernormal powers, at the end of his life arose in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccekabuddho parinibbāyi, putto rāhulakumāro ahosi[M 5.0278], sesaparisā buddhaparisā, arindamarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: 'Bhikkhus, not only now but also in the past the Tathāgata went forth on the Great Renunciation.' Then he made the connection in the Jātaka: 'At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna, the son was Prince Rāhula, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Arindama was I myself.'

Soṇakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Soṇaka Jātaka, the First.

[530] 2. Saṃkiccajātakavaṇṇanā

[530] 2. The Commentary on the Saṃkicca Jātaka

Disvā nisinnaṃ rājānanti idaṃ satthā jīvakambavane viharanto ajātasattussa pitughātakammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi devadattaṃ nissāya tassa [P 5.0262] vacanena pitaraṃ ghātāpetvā devadattassa saṅghabhedāvasāne bhinnaparisassa roge uppanne “tathāgataṃ khamāpessāmī”ti mañcasivikāya sāvatthiṃ gacchantassa jetavanadvāre pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ sutvā “devadatto sammāsambuddhassa paṭipakkho hutvā pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīciparāyaṇo jāto, mayāpi taṃ nissāya pitā dhammiko dhammarājā ghātito, ahampi nu kho pathaviṃ pavisissāmī”ti bhīto rajjasiriyā cittassādaṃ na labhi, “thokaṃ niddāyissāmī”ti niddaṃ upagatamattova navayojanabahalāyaṃ ayamahāpathaviyaṃ pātetvā ayasūlehi koṭṭiyamāno viya sunakhehi luñjitvā khajjamāno viya bheravaravena viravanto uṭṭhāti.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, told this Saṅkicca Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning ‘Disvā nisinnaṃ rājānaṃ,’ concerning King Ajātasattu’s act of patricide. For he, relying on Devadatta and at his word, had his father, King Bimbisāra, killed. When, at the conclusion of Devadatta’s schism in the Saṅgha, an illness arose in Devadatta whose following had been broken, Devadatta was being carried on a palanquin to Sāvatthī, thinking, ‘I will ask the Tathāgata for forgiveness.’ But when Ajātasattu heard that Devadatta had sunk into the earth at the gate of the Jetavana monastery, he became terrified, thinking: ‘Devadatta, having become an opponent of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, has sunk into the earth and is destined for Avīci. I too, relying on him, killed my father, a righteous king who ruled by the Dhamma. Will I too sink into the earth?’ Thus terrified, he found no delight in the splendor of kingship. Even when he lay down to sleep a little, as soon as he fell into sleep, he would start up, screaming with a dreadful sound, as if he had been cast into the great iron earth nine yojanas thick, being pierced with iron stakes, and being torn and devoured by dogs.

Athekadivasaṃ komudiyā cātumāsiniyā amaccagaṇaparivuto attano yasaṃ oloketvā “mama pitu yaso ito mahantataro, tathārūpaṃ nāma ahaṃ dhammarājānaṃ devadattaṃ nissāya ghātesi”nti cintesi. Tassevaṃ cintentasseva kāye ḍāho uppajji, sakalasarīraṃ sedatintaṃ ahosi. Tato “ko nu kho me imaṃ bhayaṃ vinodetuṃ sakkhissatī”ti cintetvā “ṭhapetvā dasabalaṃ añño natthī”ti ñatvā “ahaṃ tathāgatassa mahāparādho, ko nu kho maṃ netvā dassessatī”ti cintento “na añño koci aññatra jīvakā”ti sallakkhetvā tassa gahetvā gamanūpāyaṃ karonto “ramaṇīyā vata, bho, dosinā rattī”ti udānaṃ udānetvā “kaṃ nu [V 5.0254] khvajja samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā payirupāseyyāmī”ti vatvā pūraṇasāvakādīhi pūraṇādīnaṃ guṇe kathite tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyitvā jīvakaṃ paṭipucchitvā tena tathāgatassa guṇaṃ kathetvā “taṃ devo bhagavantaṃ payirupāsatū”ti vutto hatthiyānāni [M 5.0279] kappāpetvā jīvakambavanaṃ gantvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tathāgatena katapaṭisanthāro sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ pucchitvā tathāgatassa madhuraṃ sāmaññaphaladhammadesanaṃ (dī. ni. 1.150 ādayo) sutvā suttapariyosāne upāsakattaṃ paṭiveditvā tathāgataṃ khamāpetvā pakkāmi. So tato paṭṭhāya dānaṃ dento sīlaṃ rakkhanto tathāgatena saddhiṃ saṃsaggaṃ katvā madhuradhammakathaṃ suṇanto kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggena pahīnabhayo vigatalomahaṃso hutvā cittassādaṃ paṭilabhitvā sukhena cattāro iriyāpathe kappesi.

Then one day, on the Komudī full moon at the end of the four months of the rainy season, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, Ajātasattu reflected on his own glory and thought: ‘My father’s glory was greater than this. Yet, relying on Devadatta, I killed such a righteous king.’ As he was thinking this, a fever arose in his body, and his whole frame was drenched in sweat. Then he thought: ‘Who can dispel this fear for me?’ Knowing that ‘except for the Ten-Powered One, there is no other,’ he reflected: ‘I have committed a great offense against the Tathāgata. Who will take me to see him?’ Realizing that ‘there is no one but Jīvaka,’ he looked for a way to go with him and uttered this inspired exclamation: ‘How delightful, sirs, is this moonlit night!’ Then he asked: ‘What ascetic or brahmin should we visit today?’ When the ministers who were followers of Pūraṇa Kassapa and others spoke of their teachers’ virtues, he paid no heed to their words. He then questioned Jīvaka. When Jīvaka spoke of the Tathāgata’s virtues and said, ‘Your Majesty, visit the Blessed One,’ he had the elephant mounts prepared and went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Having approached and paid homage to the Tathāgata, and after the Tathāgata had greeted him courteously, he asked about the visible fruit of the contemplative life. Having heard the Tathāgata’s sweet discourse on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, at the end of the sutta, he declared himself a lay follower who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem. Having asked the Tathāgata for forgiveness, he departed. From then on, by giving alms, observing the precepts, associating with the Tathāgata, and listening to the sweet Dhamma, through the association with a good friend, his fear was allayed and his hair no longer stood on end. He regained peace of mind and lived at ease in all four postures.

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, ajātasattu pitughātakammaṃ katvā bhayappatto ahosi, rajjasiriṃ nissāya cittassādaṃ alabhanto sabbairiyāpathesu dukkhaṃ anubhoti, so dāni tathāgataṃ āgamma kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggena vigatabhayo issariyasukhaṃ anubhotī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya [P 5.0263] nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa pitughātakammaṃ katvā maṃ nissāya sukhaṃ sayī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: ‘Friends, after committing patricide, King Ajātasattu was overcome with fear. Unable to find peace of mind despite his royal splendor, he experienced only suffering in all his postures. But now, having come to the Tathāgata and through the association with a good friend, his fear has vanished and he enjoys the bliss of sovereignty.’ The Teacher arrived and asked: ‘Monks, for what discussion are you gathered together here now?’ When they told him, he said: ‘Monks, not only now, but in the past too, after killing his father, he reached a state of misery and then slept soundly by relying on me.’ Having said this, he brought up a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rajjaṃ kārento brahmadattakumāraṃ nāma puttaṃ paṭilabhi. Tadā bodhisatto purohitassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, jātassevassa “saṃkiccakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te ubhopi rājanivesane ekatova vaḍḍhiṃsu. Aññamaññaṃ sahāyakā hutvā vayappattā takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgamiṃsu. Atha rājā puttassa uparajjaṃ adāsi. Bodhisattopi uparājasseva santike ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ uparājā pitu uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchantassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ disvā tasmiṃ lobhaṃ uppādetvā “mayhaṃ pitā mama bhātikasadiso, sace etassa maraṇaṃ olokessāmi, mahallakakāle rajjaṃ labhissāmi, tadā laddhenapi rajjena ko attho, pitaraṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā bodhisattassa tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bodhisatto, “samma, pitughātakammaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, nirayamaggo, na sakkā etaṃ kātuṃ, mā karī”ti paṭibāhi. So punappunampi kathetvā yāvatatiyaṃ tena paṭibāhito pādamūlikehi saddhiṃ mantesi. Tepi sampaṭicchitvā rañño [M 5.0280] māraṇūpāyaṃ vīmaṃsiṃsu. Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “nāhaṃ etehi saddhiṃ ekato bhavissāmī”ti mātāpitaro anāpucchitvāva aggadvārena nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro vihāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, he had a son named Prince Brahmadatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the house of the royal chaplain. When he was born, they named him Prince Saṅkicca. Both of them grew up together in the royal palace and became dear friends. On coming of age, they went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned. Then the king appointed his son as viceroy. The Bodhisatta also stayed with the viceroy. One day, while the viceroy was going to the park for recreation, he saw his father’s great splendor and conceived a greed for it. He thought: ‘My father is like a brother to me. If I wait for his death, I will only get the kingdom when I am old. What is the use of a kingdom gained at such an age? I will kill my father and seize the kingdom.’ He told this to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta dissuaded him, saying: ‘Friend, the act of patricide is very grave; it is a path to hell. One should not do such a thing. Do not do it.’ Although the prince spoke of it again and again, even when dissuaded for the third time, he consulted with his attendants. They agreed and looked for a way to kill the king. The Bodhisatta, knowing of this, thought, ‘I will not be one of them.’ Without even asking his parents' permission, he left by the main gate, entered the Himalayas, went forth as a wandering ascetic, and having developed the jhānas and higher knowledges, he lived there subsisting on roots and fruits of the forest.

Rājakumāropi [V 5.0255] tasmiṃ gate pitaraṃ mārāpetvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavi. “Saṃkiccakumāro kira isipabbajjaṃ pabbajito”ti sutvā bahū kulaputtā nikkhamitvā tassa santike pabbajiṃsu. So mahatā isigaṇena parivuto tattha vasi. Sabbepi samāpattilābhinoyeva. Rājāpi pitaraṃ māretvā appamattakaṃyeva kālaṃ rajjasukhaṃ anubhavitvā tato paṭṭhāya bhīto cittassādaṃ alabhanto niraye kammakaraṇappatto viya ahosi. So bodhisattaṃ anussaritvā “sahāyo me ‘pitughātakammaṃ bhāriyaṃ, mā karī’ti paṭisedhetvā maṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpetuṃ asakkonto attānaṃ niddosaṃ katvā palāyi. Sace so idha abhavissa[P 5.0264], na me pitughātakammaṃ kātuṃ adassa, idampi me bhayaṃ hareyya, kahaṃ nu kho so etarahi viharati. Sace tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ jāneyyaṃ, pakkosāpeyyaṃ, ko nu kho me tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āroceyyā”ti cintesi. So tato paṭṭhāya antepure ca rājasabhāyañca bodhisattasseva vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

After the Bodhisatta departed, the prince had his father killed and enjoyed great royal majesty. Hearing that "Prince Saᅅkicca has gone forth as an ascetic," many young men of good family left their homes and took ordination under him. He lived there surrounded by a great company of ascetics in the Himalayas. All of them attained the meditative attainments. The king, having killed his father, enjoyed the bliss of kingship for only a short time. From then on, terrified and finding no joy of mind, he felt as if he were suffering the torments of hell. Remembering the Bodhisatta, he thought: "My friend, Saᅅkicca, tried to dissuade me, saying, 'Patricide is a very grave deed; do not do it.' Unable to make me follow his advice, he left, keeping himself blameless. If he were here, he would not have let me commit patricide and would have dispelled this fear of mine. Where could he be living now? If I knew his dwelling place, I would summon him. Who can tell me where he is?" Having thought thus, from that time onward, King Brahmadatta spoke only of the Bodhisatta's virtues in the inner palace and in the royal court.

Evaṃ addhāne gate bodhisatto “rājā maṃ sarati, mayā tattha gantvā tassa dhammaṃ desetvā taṃ nibbhayaṃ katvā āgantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti paṇṇāsa vassāni himavante vasitvā pañcasatatāpasaparivuto ākāsenāgantvā dāyapasse nāma uyyāne otaritvā isigaṇaparivuto silāpaṭṭe nisīdi. Uyyānapālo taṃ disvā “bhante, gaṇasatthā konāmo”ti pucchitvā “saṃkiccapaṇḍito nāmā”ti ca sutvā sayampi sañjānitvā “bhante, yāvāhaṃ rājānaṃ ānemi, tāva idheva hotha, amhākaṃ rājā tumhe daṭṭhukāmo”ti vatvā vegena rājakulaṃ gantvā tassa āgatabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā tassa santikaṃ gantvā kattabbayuttakaṃ upahāraṃ katvā pañhaṃ pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

After a long time had passed, the Bodhisatta thought: "King Brahmadatta is thinking of me. I should go to his palace, teach him the Dhamma, and make him fearless before returning." Having lived in the Himalayas for fifty years, surrounded by five hundred ascetics, he traveled through the air and descended in the park named Dāyapassa. Surrounded by the company of seers, he sat down on the auspicious stone slab. The park keeper saw the Bodhisatta and asked: "Venerable teacher, what is your name?" Hearing it was "Saᅅkicca the Wise," the park keeper recognized him and said: "Venerable sir, please stay here while I go to inform the king. Our king wishes to see you." Having paid respects, he went quickly to the royal palace and informed the king of Saᅅkicca's arrival. The king went to him, paid his respects, and asked a question. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

69.

69.

“Disvā nisinnaṃ rājānaṃ, brahmadattaṃ rathesabhaṃ;

Athassa paṭivedesi, yassāsi anukampako.

Seeing [the sage] seated, the park keeper then reported to King Brahmadatta, the lord of chariots, for whom the king had great regard.

70.

70.

“Saṃkiccāyaṃ [M 5.0281] anuppatto, isīnaṃ sādhusammato;

Taramānarūpo niyyāhi, khippaṃ passa mahesinaṃ.

"Great king, Saᅅkicca has arrived, he who is highly esteemed among seers. Depart in haste; quickly go and see the great seer."

71.

71.

“Tato ca rājā taramāno, yuttamāruyha sandanaṃ;

Mittāmaccaparibyūḷho, agamāsi rathesabho.

Then King Brahmadatta, the lord of chariots, hastening, mounted his yoked chariot; surrounded by his circle of friends and ministers, he departed.

72.

72.

“Nikkhippa [V 5.0256] pañca kakudhāni, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Vālabījanimuṇhīsaṃ, khaggaṃ chattañcupāhanaṃ.

Setting aside the five royal insignia, that prosperer of the Kāsĩ realm: the yak-tail whisk, the turban, the sword, the white parasol, and the golden footwear.

73.

73.

“Oruyha rājā yānamhā, ṭhapayitvā paṭicchadaṃ;

Āsīnaṃ dāyapassasmiṃ, saṃkiccamupasaṅkami.

Descending from his chariot, the king left the five royal insignia in the care of his treasurer and approached Saᅅkicca, who was seated in the Dāyapassa park.

74.

74.

“Upasaṅkamitvā so rājā, sammodi isinā saha;

Taṃ kathaṃ vītisāretvā, ekamantaṃ upāvisi.

Having approached, the king exchanged friendly greetings with the seer. After concluding their conversation, he sat down to one side.

75.

75.

“Ekamantaṃ nisinnova, atha kālaṃ amaññatha;

Tato pāpāni kammāni, pucchituṃ paṭipajjatha.

While seated to one side, he realized the proper time to ask his questions; then he proceeded to ask about the consequences of evil deeds.

76.

76.

“Isiṃ pucchāma saṃkiccaṃ, isīnaṃ sādhusammataṃ;

Āsīnaṃ dāyapassasmiṃ, isisaṅghapurakkhataṃ.

"We ask the seer Saᅅkicca, who is highly esteemed among seers, who sits in the Dāyapassa park surrounded by an assembly of seers."

77.

77.

“Kaṃ [P 5.0265] gatiṃ pecca gacchanti, narā dhammāticārino;

Aticiṇṇo mayā dhammo, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

"Venerable sir, to what destination do people go after death who transgress the ten wholesome courses of action? Venerable sir, I have transgressed against the Dhamma; please answer me regarding this matter as I ask."

Tattha disvāti, bhikkhave, so uyyānapālo rājānaṃ rājasabhāyaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā athassa paṭivedesi, “yassāsī”ti vadanto ārocesīti attho. Yassāsīti, mahārāja, yassa tvaṃ anukampako muducitto ahosi, yassa abhiṇhaṃ vaṇṇaṃ payirudāhāsi, so ayaṃ saṃkicco isīnaṃ antare sādhu laddhakoti sammato anuppatto tava uyyāne silāpaṭṭe isigaṇaparivuto kañcanapaṭimā viya nisinno. Taramānarūpoti, mahārāja, pabbajitā nāma kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā tumhākaṃ gacchantānaññeva pakkameyyuṃ, tasmā taramānarūpo khippaṃ niyyāhi, mahantānaṃ sīlādiguṇānaṃ esitattā passa mahesinaṃ.

Herein, monks, ‘Having seen’: the park keeper, seeing the king seated in the royal court, reported to him. ‘He then reported to him about the one for whom you have compassion’: this is the meaning. ‘For whom you have compassion’ means: ‘O great king, the one for whom you were compassionate and tender-hearted, whose praises you often proclaimed—that Saṅkicca, esteemed among seers as one who has attained the good, has arrived. He is seated in your park on a stone slab, surrounded by a company of seers, like a golden statue.’ ‘Depart in haste’ means: ‘O great king, those who have gone forth are not attached to family or retinue; they might depart even while you are on your way. Therefore depart in haste, go quickly.’ ‘Behold the great seer’ means: ‘See him, for he is a great seer because he is sought for his great qualities such as virtue.’”

Tatoti, bhikkhave, so rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tato tassa vacanato anantarameva. Nikkhippāti nikkhipitvā tassa kira uyyānadvāraṃ [M 5.0282] patvāva etadahosi – “pabbajitā nāma garuṭṭhāniyā, saṃkiccatāpasassa santikaṃ uddhatavesena gantuṃ ayutta”nti. So maṇicittasuvaṇṇadaṇḍaṃ vālabījaniṃ, kañcanamayaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ, suparikkhittaṃ maṅgalakhaggaṃ, setacchattaṃ[V 5.0257], sovaṇṇapādukāti imāni pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni apanesi. Tena vuttaṃ “nikkhippā”ti. Paṭicchadanti tameva rājakakudhabhaṇḍaṃ ṭhapayitvā bhaṇḍāgārikassa hatthe datvā. Dāyapassasminti evaṃnāmake uyyāne. Atha kālaṃ amaññathāti atha so idāni me pañhaṃ pucchituṃ kāloti jāni. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “yathākāla”nti āgataṃ, tassa kālānurūpena pañhapucchanaṃ amaññathāti attho. Paṭipajjathāti paṭipajji. Peccāti paṭigantvā, paralokassa vā nāmetaṃ, tasmā paraloketi attho. Mayāti, bhante, mayā sucaritadhammo aticiṇṇo pitughātakammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi, kaṃ gatiṃ pitughātakā gacchanti, katarasmiṃ niraye paccantīti pucchati.

Then, monks, the king, having heard his words, immediately after that speech, set aside: it is said that upon reaching the garden gate, this occurred to him: ‘Ascetics are worthy of respect; it is not proper to approach the ascetic Saṅkicca with an ostentatious appearance.’ He removed the five royal insignia: the chowrie with a jewel-inlaid golden handle, the golden diadem, the well-girt sword of state, the white parasol, and the golden slippers. Hence it is said, ‘set aside.’ ‘Set aside his outer garment’: having set aside those same royal insignia, he gave them into the hand of the treasurer. ‘In Dāyapassa’: in the park so named. ‘Then he thought it was the time’: then he knew, ‘Now is the time for me to ask my question.’ In the Pāli text, however, it is given as ‘at the proper time,’ the meaning of which is that he considered it the appropriate time for questioning. ‘He proceeded’: he went forward. ‘After death’: having departed; or this is a name for the next world, thus the meaning is ‘in the next world.’ ‘By me’: he asks, ‘Venerable sir, by me the law of good conduct has been transgressed, the act of killing my father has been committed. Tell me, what destiny do patricides go to? In which hell are they boiled?’”

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “tena hi, mahārāja, suṇohī”ti vatvā ovādaṃ tāva adāsi. Satthā tamatthaṃ pakāsento āha –

Hearing his question, the Bodhisatta said, "Well then, great king, listen," and first gave him advice. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

78.

78.

“Isī avaca saṃkicco, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhanaṃ;

Āsīnaṃ dāyapassasmiṃ, mahārāja suṇohi me.

The sage Saᅅkicca, seated in Dāyapassa, spoke to the increaser of the Kāsĩ realm: "Great king, listen to my words."

79.

79.

“Uppathena vajantassa, yo maggamanusāsati;

Tassa ce vacanaṃ kayirā, nāssa maggeyya kaṇṭako.

"If one follows the advice of one who points out the right path to someone traveling on a wrong path beset by thieves, no thorn of danger would find him."

80.

80.

“Adhammaṃ paṭipannassa, yo dhammamanusāsati;

Tassa ce vacanaṃ kayirā, na so gaccheyya duggati”nti.

"If someone instructs in the Dhamma one who is practicing unrighteously, and if one follows his word, he would not go to a bad destination."

Tattha uppathenāti corehi pariyuṭṭhitamaggena. Maggamanusāsatīti khemamaggaṃ akkhāti. Nāssa maggeyya kaṇṭakoti tassa ovādakarassa purisassa [P 5.0266] mukhaṃ corakaṇṭako na passeyya. Yo dhammanti yo sucaritadhammaṃ. Na soti so puriso nirayādibhedaṃ duggatiṃ na gaccheyya. Uppathasadiso hi, mahārāja, adhammo, khemamaggasadiso sucaritadhammo, tvaṃ pana pubbe “pitaraṃ ghātetvā rājā homī”ti mayhaṃ kathetvā mayā paṭibāhito mama vacanaṃ akatvā pitaraṃ ghātetvā idāni [M 5.0283] socasi, paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ akaronto nāma coramaggapaṭipanno viya mahābyasanaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Herein, 'on a wrong path' means on a road beset by thieves. 'Instructs on the path' means pointing out the safe path. 'No thorn would find him' means the robber would not see the face of the person who follows the advice. 'The Dhamma' refers to the law of good conduct. 'He would not go' means that person would not go to a bad destination such as hell. For, great king, unrighteousness is like a wrong path, and good conduct is like a safe path. But you, having previously told me, 'I will become king by killing my father,' were forbidden by me, yet you did not follow my word. You killed your father and now you grieve. One who does not follow the advice of the wise, like one who has taken a path of thieves, meets with great disaster.

Evamassa ovādaṃ datvā upari dhammaṃ desento āha –

Thus, having given him this advice, the Bodhisatta opened up and described the eight great hells and other realms, wishing to teach him further, saying:

81.

81.

“Dhammo [V 5.0258] patho mahārāja, adhammo pana uppatho;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggatiṃ.

"Dhamma is the path, great king, but unrighteousness is the wrong path. Unrighteousness leads to hell; Dhamma leads to a good destination."

82.

82.

“Adhammacārino rāja, narā visamajīvino;

Yaṃ gatiṃ pecca gacchanti, niraye te suṇohi me.

"O king, listen to me about the destination reached in hell after death by those people who practice unrighteousness and live crooked lives."

83.

83.

“Sañjīvo kāḷasutto ca, saṅghāto dve ca roruvā;

Athāparo mahāvīci, tāpano ca patāpano.

"Great king, there is Saᅅjĩva, Kāጷasutta, Saᅅghāta, and the two Roruvas, Jāla-Roruva and Dhšma-Roruva; then there is Mahāvĩci, Tāpana, and Mahātāpana."

84.

84.

“Iccete aṭṭha nirayā, akkhātā duratikkamā;

Ākiṇṇā luddakammehi, paccekā soḷasussadā.

"These are the eight great hells, declared to be hard to transcend. They are filled with hell-wardens who perform cruel deeds. Each of these great hells is surrounded by sixteen subsidiary hells."

85.

85.

“Kadariyatāpanā ghorā, accimanto mahabbhayā;

Lomahaṃsanarūpā ca, bhesmā paṭibhayā dukhā.

"For those who are stingy and deceitful, these are places of torment—gruesome, blazing, greatly dreadful, hair-raising in appearance, terrible, frightful, and painful."

86.

86.

“Catukkaṇṇā catudvārā, vibhattā bhāgaso mitā;

Ayopākārapariyantā, ayasā paṭikujjitā.

"They are four-cornered and have four gates, divided into equal parts and measured out. They are enclosed by an iron wall and covered over with an iron lid."

87.

87.

“Tesaṃ ayomayā bhūmi, jalitā tejasā yutā;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, phuṭā tiṭṭhanti sabbadā.

"Great king, the ground of those hells is made of iron, blazing and endowed with fire. The flames extend for a hundred yojanas all around and stand there at all times."

88.

88.

“Ete patanti niraye, uddhaṃpādā avaṃsirā;

Isīnaṃ ativattāro, saññatānaṃ tapassinaṃ.

"Great king, those who transgress with harsh words against sages, against the restrained and the ascetics, fall into these hells, feet up and head down."

89.

89.

“Te bhūnahuno paccanti, macchā bilakatā yathā;

Saṃvacchare asaṅkheyye, narā kibbisakārino.

Those destroyers of their own prosperity, the men who do evil, are cooked for innumerable years, like fish cut into pieces and cooked.

90.

90.

“Ḍayhamānena gattena, niccaṃ santarabāhiraṃ;

Nirayā nādhigacchanti, dvāraṃ nikkhamanesino.

With their bodies constantly burning, inside and out, though seeking a way out, they do not find the door of escape from hell.

91.

91.

“Puratthimena [V 5.0259] dhāvanti, tato dhāvanti pacchato;

Uttarenapi dhāvanti, tato dhāvanti dakkhiṇaṃ;

Yaṃ yañhi dvāraṃ gacchanti, taṃ tadeva pidhīyare.

They run to the east, then they run to the west; they run to the north, then they run to the south. Whatever door they run towards, that very door is shut against them.

92.

92.

“Bahūni [P 5.0267][M 5.0284] vassasahassāni, janā nirayagāmino;

Bāhā paggayha kandanti, patvā dukkhaṃ anappakaṃ.

For many thousands of years, those people gone to hell, having reached no small suffering, weep with their arms upraised.

93.

93.

“Āsīvisaṃva kupitaṃ, tejassiṃ duratikkamaṃ;

Na sādhurūpe āsīde, saññatānaṃ tapassinaṃ.

One should not assail the virtuous, the restrained ascetics, who are like an enraged viper, powerful and hard to overcome.

94.

94.

“Atikāyo mahissāso, ajjuno kekakādhipo;

Sahassabāhu ucchinno, isimāsajja gotamaṃ.

Ajjuna, the lord of the Kekas, of massive body and a great archer, the thousand-armed one, was destroyed for having assailed the sage Gotama.

95.

95.

“Arajaṃ rajasā vacchaṃ, kisaṃ avakiriya daṇḍakī;

Tālova mūlato chinno, sa rājā vibhavaṅgato.

Having sprinkled dust on the dustless, lean sage Vaccha, King Daṇḍakī was destroyed like a palm tree cut from the root, and went to ruin.

96.

96.

“Upahacca manaṃ majjho, mātaṅgasmiṃ yasassine;

Sapārisajjo ucchinno, majjhāraññaṃ tadā ahu.

King Mejjha, having harbored a corrupt mind towards the glorious Mātaṅga, was destroyed along with his retinue; the Mejjha kingdom then became a wilderness.

97.

97.

“Kaṇhadīpāyanāsajja, isiṃ andhakaveṇḍayo;

Aññoññaṃ musalā hantvā, sampattā yamasādhanaṃ.

Having assailed the sage Kaṇhadīpāyana, the Andhakaveṇḍus struck one another with clubs and reached the abode of Yama.

98.

98.

“Athāyaṃ isinā satto, antalikkhacaro pure;

Pāvekkhi pathaviṃ cecco, hīnatto pattapariyāyaṃ.

Then King Cetiya, cursed by the sage, who formerly traveled through the sky, entered into the earth with a degraded body as he reached his end.

99.

99.

“Tasmā hi chandāgamanaṃ, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā;

Aduṭṭhacitto bhāseyya, giraṃ saccūpasaṃhitaṃ.

Therefore, the wise do not praise going astray through desire and the like; with a mind free from malice, one should speak words connected with truth.

100.

100.

“Manasā ce paduṭṭhena, yo naro pekkhate muniṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, gantā so nirayaṃ adho.

If a man with a corrupted mind looks upon a sage accomplished in knowledge and conduct, he will go to the hell below.

101.

101.

“Ye [V 5.0260] vuḍḍhe paribhāsanti, pharusūpakkamā janā;

Anapaccā adāyādā, tālavatthu bhavanti te.

Those people who use harsh means and revile the elderly become like palm-stumps, without offspring and without heirs.

102.

102.

“Yo ca pabbajitaṃ hanti, katakiccaṃ mahesinaṃ;

Sa kāḷasutte niraye, cirarattāya paccati.

Whoever kills one who has gone forth, a great sage who has done what was to be done, is cooked in the Kāḷasutta hell for a very long time.

103.

103.

“Yo ca rājā adhammaṭṭho, raṭṭhaviddhaṃsano mago;

Tāpayitvā janapadaṃ, tāpane pecca paccati.

And a king who is unrighteous, a beast who destroys the realm, having tormented the people of the country, is cooked after death in the Tāpana hell.

104.

104.

“So ca vassasahassāni, sataṃ dibbāni paccati;

Accisaṅghapareto so, dukkhaṃ vedeti vedanaṃ.

He is cooked for a hundred thousand divine years. Enveloped in a mass of flames, he experiences painful suffering.

105.

105.

“Tassa [P 5.0268][M 5.0285] aggisikhā kāyā, niccharanti pabhassarā;

Tejobhakkhassa gattāni, lomehi ca nakhehi ca.

Luminous flames of fire issue from his body; from the limbs, hairs, and nails of that one who is consumed by fire.

106.

106.

“Ḍayhamānena gattena, niccaṃ santarabāhiraṃ;

Dukkhābhitunno nadati, nāgo tuttaṭṭito yathā.

With his body constantly burning, inside and out, overwhelmed by suffering, he roars like an elephant struck by a goad.

107.

107.

“Yo lobhā pitaraṃ hanti, dosā vā purisādhamo;

Sa kāḷasutte niraye, cirarattāya paccati.

Whoever, a base man, kills his father out of greed or hatred, is cooked in the Kāḷasutta hell for a long time.

108.

108.

“Sa tādiso paccati lohakumbhiyaṃ, pakkañca sattīhi hananti nittacaṃ;

Andhaṃ karitvā muttakarīsabhakkhaṃ, khāre nimujjanti tathāvidhaṃ naraṃ.

Such a one is cooked in an iron cauldron; when cooked and flayed, they strike him with spears. Having blinded him and made him eat urine and excrement, they plunge such a man into caustic liquid.

109.

109.

“Tattaṃ pakkuthitamayoguḷañca, dīghe ca phāle cirarattatāpite;

Vikkhambhamādāya vibandharajjubhi, vivaṭe mukhe sampavisanti rakkhasā.

The hell-wardens take glowing, boiling iron balls and long iron stakes heated for a long time, and having pried open his mouth and bound him with ropes, they thrust them into his open mouth.

110.

110.

“Sāmā ca soṇā sabalā ca gijjhā, kākolasaṅghā ca dijā ayomukhā;

Saṅgamma khādanti vipphandamānaṃ, jivhaṃ vibhajja vighāsaṃ salohitaṃ.

Black and spotted dogs, vultures, flocks of crows, and iron-beaked birds gather together and devour him as he writhes, tearing out his tongue for a bloody meal.

111.

111.

“Taṃ [V 5.0261] daḍḍhatālaṃ paribhinnagattaṃ, nippothayantā anuvicaranti rakkhasā;

Ratī hi tesaṃ dukhino panītare, etādisasmiṃ niraye vasanti;

Ye keci loke idha pettighātino.

The hell-wardens roam about beating him whose body is like a burnt palm tree and whose limbs are shattered. To them, there is delight, while the others are in pain. In such a hell dwell whoever in this world are patricides.

112.

112.

“Putto ca mātaraṃ hantvā, ito gantvā yamakkhayaṃ;

Bhusamāpajjate dukkhaṃ, attakammaphalūpago.

And a son who kills his mother, having gone from here to the realm of Yama, encounters extreme suffering, undergoing the fruit of his own actions.

113.

113.

“Amanussā atibalā, hantāraṃ janayantiyā;

Ayomayehi vālehi, pīḷayanti punappunaṃ.

Non-humans of exceeding strength crush the killer of his mother again and again with iron fibers.

114.

114.

“Tamassavaṃ [P 5.0269][M 5.0286] sakā gattā, rudhiraṃ attasambhavaṃ;

Tambalohavilīnaṃva, tattaṃ pāyenti mattighaṃ.

They make the matricide drink the hot blood flowing from his own limbs, which is like molten copper.

115.

115.

“Jigucchaṃ kuṇapaṃ pūtiṃ, duggandhaṃ gūthakaddamaṃ;

Pubbalohitasaṅkāsaṃ, rahadamogayha tiṭṭhati.

He stands plunged in a lake of disgusting, putrid corpses and foul-smelling mire of excrement, resembling pus and blood.

116.

116.

“Tamenaṃ kimayo tattha, atikāyā ayomukhā;

Chaviṃ bhetvāna khādanti, saṃgiddhā maṃsalohite.

There, worms of massive bodies and iron mouths, having pierced his skin, devour him, being greedy for his flesh and blood.

117.

117.

“So ca taṃ nirayaṃ patto, nimuggo sataporisaṃ;

Pūtikaṃ kuṇapaṃ vāti, samantā satayojanaṃ.

Having reached that hell, he is submerged a hundred man-lengths deep; the stench of putrid corpses emanates from him for a hundred yojanas all around.

118.

118.

“Cakkhumāpi hi cakkhūhi, tena gandhena jīyati;

Etādisaṃ brahmadatta, mātugho labhate dukhaṃ.

Indeed, even the eyes of those who have sight are destroyed by that stench. Such suffering, O Brahmadatta, does a matricide obtain.

119.

119.

“Khuradhāramanukkamma, tikkhaṃ durabhisambhavaṃ;

Patanti gabbhapātiyo, duggaṃ vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ.

Having trod upon the edge of sharp razor blades, hard to endure, abortionists fall into the Vetaraṇī, a river difficult to cross.

120.

120.

“Ayomayā simbaliyo, soḷasaṅgulakaṇṭakā;

Ubhato abhilambanti, duggaṃ vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ.

Iron silk-cotton trees with sixteen-finger-long thorns hang down on both sides over the Vetaraṇī, a river difficult to cross.

121.

121.

“Te [V 5.0262] accimanto tiṭṭhanti, aggikkhandhāva ārakā;

Ādittā jātavedena, uddhaṃ yojanamuggatā.

They stand there blazing, like masses of fire from afar, set alight by fire, rising a yojana high.

122.

122.

“Ete vajanti niraye, tatte tikhiṇakaṇṭake;

Nāriyo ca aticārā, narā ca paradāragū.

Into this hell with its hot, sharp thorns go adulterous women and men who go to the wives of others.

123.

123.

“Te patanti adhokkhandhā, vivattā vihatā puthū;

Sayanti vinividdhaṅgā, dīghaṃ jagganti sabbadā.

They fall headlong, mangled, struck down, and scattered; with their limbs pierced through, they lie; they are always awake for a long time.

124.

124.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, mahatiṃ pabbatūpamaṃ;

Lohakumbhiṃ pavajjanti, tattaṃ aggisamūdakaṃ.

Then, at the end of many nights, they enter a great, mountain-like iron cauldron, blazing hot with fire-like water.

125.

125.

“Evaṃ divā ca ratto ca, dussīlā mohapārutā;

Anubhonti sakaṃ kammaṃ, pubbe dukkaṭamattano.

Thus, day and night, the immoral, shrouded in delusion, experience the fruit of their own kamma, the evil they previously committed.

126.

126.

“Yā ca bhariyā dhanakkītā, sāmikaṃ atimaññati;

Sassuṃ vā sasuraṃ vāpi, jeṭṭhaṃ vāpi nanandaraṃ.

And a wife bought with wealth who despises her husband, or her mother-in-law, or her father-in-law, or her husband's elder brother or his sister—

127.

127.

“Tassā [M 5.0287] vaṅkena jivhaggaṃ, nibbahanti sabandhanaṃ;

Sa [P 5.0270] byāmamattaṃ kiminaṃ, jivhaṃ passati attani;

Viññāpetuṃ na sakkoti, tāpane pecca paccati.

With a hook they draw out the tip of her tongue along with its roots; she sees her own tongue, a fathom long and teeming with worms; she is unable to plead. Having passed away, she is cooked in the Tāpana hell.

128.

128.

“Orabbhikā sūkarikā, macchikā migabandhakā;

Corā goghātakā luddā, avaṇṇe vaṇṇakārakā.

Butchers of sheep, butchers of swine, fishermen, and hunters of beasts; thieves, cattle-slayers, the cruel, and those who praise the blameworthy.

129.

129.

“Sattīhi lohakūṭehi, nettiṃsehi usūhi ca;

Haññamānā khāranadiṃ, papatanti avaṃsirā.

Being struck with spears, iron hammers, swords, and arrows, they fall headlong into the Caustic River.

130.

130.

“Sāyaṃ pāto kūṭakārī, ayokūṭehi haññati;

Tato vantaṃ durattānaṃ, paresaṃ bhuñjare sadā.

Evening and morning, the fraudulent one is struck with iron hammers; then they always feed on the vomit of others.

131.

131.

“Dhaṅkā [V 5.0263] bheraṇḍakā gijjhā, kākolā ca ayomukhā;

Vipphandamānaṃ khādanti, naraṃ kibbisakārakaṃ.

Crows, jackals, vultures, and ravens with iron beaks devour the writhing man who has done evil deeds.

132.

132.

“Ye migena migaṃ hanti, pakkhiṃ vā pana pakkhinā;

Asanto rajasā channā, gantā te nirayussada”nti.

Those who kill a beast with a decoy beast, or a bird with a decoy bird—those wicked ones, covered by passion, go to the Ussada hell.

Tattha dhammo pathoti dasakusalakammapathadhammo khemo appaṭibhayo sugatimaggo. Visamajīvinoti adhammena kappitajīvikā. Niraye teti te etesaṃ nibbattaniraye kathemi. Suṇohi meti mahāsatto raññā pitughātakānaṃ nibbattanirayaṃ pucchitopi pathamaṃ taṃ adassetvā aṭṭha mahāniraye soḷasa ca ussadaniraye dassetuṃ evamāha. Kiṃkāraṇā? Paṭhamañhi tasmiṃ dassiyamāne rājā phalitena hadayena tattheva mareyya, imesu pana nirayesu paccamānasatte disvā diṭṭhānugatiko hutvā “ahaṃ viya aññepi bahū pāpakammino atthi, ahaṃ etesaṃ antare paccissāmī”ti sañjātupatthambho arogo bhavissatīti te pana niraye dassento mahāsatto paṭhamaṃ iddhibalena pathaviṃ dvidhā katvā pacchā dassesi.

Here, “the Dhamma is the path” means the Dhamma of the tenfold path of wholesome actions, the safe, fearless path to a good destination. “Living unrighteously” means those who have arranged their livelihood unrighteously. “They in hell” means: I will tell of the hell where they are reborn. “Listen to me” means: although the Great Being was asked by the king about the hell where patricides are reborn, without showing that one first, he spoke thus to show the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells. For what reason? If that hell were shown first, the king, with a heart split open, might die on the spot. But by seeing beings tormented in these other hells, he would follow what he saw and think, “Like me, there are many other evildoers; I shall be tormented among them.” Thus, with his composure restored, he would become well. Therefore, the Great Being, in showing these hells, first split the earth in two by his psychic power and then displayed them.

Tesaṃ vacanattho – nirayapālehi pajjalitāni nānāvudhāni gahetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinnā hīraṃ hīraṃ katā nerayikasattā punappunaṃ sañjīvanti etthāti sañjīvo. Nirayapālā punappunaṃ nadantā vaggantā pajjalitāni nānāvudhāni gahetvā jalitāya lohapathaviyaṃ nerayike satte aparāparaṃ anubandhitvā paharitvā jalitapathaviyaṃ patite jalitakāḷasuttaṃ pātetvā jalitapharasuṃ [M 5.0288] gahetvā sayaṃ unnadantā mahantena aṭṭassarena viravante aṭṭhaṃse soḷasaṃse karontā ettha tacchantīti kāḷasutto. Mahantā jalitaayapabbatā ghātenti etthāti saṅghāto. Tattha kira satte navayojanāya jalitāya ayapathaviyā yāva kaṭito [P 5.0271] pavesetvā niccale karonti. Atha puratthimato jalito ayapabbato samuṭṭhāya asani viya viravanto āgantvā te satte saṇhakaraṇiyaṃ tile pisanto viya gantvā pacchimadisāya tiṭṭhati, pacchimadisato samuṭṭhitopi tatheva gantvā puratthimadisāya tiṭṭhati. Dve pana ekato samāgantvā ucchuyante ucchukhaṇḍāni viya pīḷenti. Evaṃ tattha bahūni vassasatasahassāni dukkhaṃ anubhonti.

The meaning of their names is this: Because the hell-beings—who have been cut into splinters again and again by the hell-wardens wielding various blazing weapons—revive repeatedly, it is called Sañjīva (Reviving). The hell-wardens, shouting and screaming repeatedly, take up various blazing weapons and chase the hellish beings back and forth across the burning iron ground. They strike them, make them fall onto the burning ground, stretch a blazing black thread over them, and seize blazing axes. Roaring loudly with great cries, they hew them into eight or sixteen pieces—hence it is called Kāḷasutta (Black Thread). Great blazing iron mountains crush them there—hence it is called Saṅghāta (Crushing). There, it is said, beings are made motionless, pressed down on a nine-league-wide burning iron ground up to their waists. Then, from the east, a blazing iron mountain rises up, roaring like a thunderbolt as it approaches. It grinds the beings as finely as sesame seeds, then comes to rest in the western direction. Similarly, another mountain rises from the west and does the same before settling in the eastern direction. When the two collide, they press the beings like sugar cane stalks being squeezed. Thus, for many hundreds of thousands of years, they endure suffering there.

Dve ca roruvāti jālaroruvo, dhūmaroruvo cāti dve. Tattha jālaroruvo kappena saṇṭhitāhi rattalohajālāhi puṇṇo, dhūmaroruvo khāradhūmena puṇṇo. Tesu jālaroruve paccantānaṃ navahi vaṇṇamukhehi jālā pavisitvā sarīraṃ dahanti, dhūmaroruve paccantānaṃ navahi vaṇamukhehi khāradhūmo [V 5.0264] pavisitvā piṭṭhaṃ viya sarīraṃ sedeti. Ubhayatthapi paccantā sattā mahāviravaṃ viravantīti dvepi “roruvā”ti vuttā. Jālānaṃ vā paccanasattānaṃ vā tesaṃ dukkhassa vā vīci antaraṃ natthi etthāti avīci, mahanto avīci mahāvīci. Tattha hi puratthimādīhi bhittīhi jālā uṭṭhahitvā pacchimādīsu paṭihaññati, tā ca bhittiyo vinivijjhitvā purato yojanasataṃ gaṇhāti. Heṭṭhā uṭṭhitā jālā upari paṭihaññati, upari uṭṭhitā heṭṭhā paṭihaññati. Evaṃ tāvettha jālānaṃ vīci nāma natthi. Tassa pana anto yojanasataṃ ṭhānaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhassa pūritanāḷi viya sattehi nirantaraṃ pūritaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi paccantānaṃ sattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, na ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti, sakaṭṭhāneyeva paccanti. Evamettha sattānaṃ vīci nāma natthi. Yathā pana jivhagge cha madhubindūni sattamassa tambalohabinduno anudahanabalavatāya abbohārikāni honti, tathā tattha anudahanabalavatāya sesā cha akusalavipākupekkhā abbohārikā honti, dukkhameva nirantaraṃ paññāyati. Evamettha dukkhassa vīci nāma natthi. Svāyaṃ saha bhittīhi vikkhambhato aṭṭhārasādhikatiyojanasato, āvaṭṭato pana catupaṇṇāsādhikanavayojanasato, saha ussadehi dasa yojanasahassāni. Evamassa mahantatā veditabbā.

And there are two Roruva hells: the Jālaroruva (Flame-Roruva) and the Dhūmaroruva (Smoke-Roruva). Here, the Jālaroruva is filled with red-hot iron flames that remain fixed for an eon, while the Dhūmaroruva is filled with caustic smoke. In the Jālaroruva, flames enter through the nine orifices of the beings and burn their bodies. In the Dhūmaroruva, caustic smoke enters through the nine orifices and cooks the body like a cake.
