In both, the tormented beings scream with great cries, hence both are called Roruva (Screaming). There is no interval (vīci) between the flames, or the beings being tormented, or their suffering, hence it is called Avīci (the Uninterrupted)—the great Avīci. There, flames rise from the eastern wall and strike the western wall, piercing through it and extending a hundred leagues beyond. Flames rising from below strike above, and those rising from above strike below. Thus, there is no interval between the flames. Inside, the space of a hundred leagues is packed with beings without any gap, like a tube filled with rice-gruel. The number of beings being tormented there in the four postures is immeasurable, yet they do not obstruct each other but are cooked in their own places. Thus, there is no interval between the beings. Just as six drops of honey on the tip of the tongue would be overwhelmed by a seventh drop of molten copper due to its intense burning power, so too the other six kinds of equanimity that are the result of unwholesome kamma become inoperative there due to the overwhelming power of the burning, and only suffering is continuously perceived. Thus, there is no interval in their suffering. This hell, including its walls, measures three hundred and eighteen leagues in width, nine hundred and fifty-four leagues in circumference, and with its subsidiary hells, extends ten thousand leagues. Such is its vastness to be understood.

Niccale [M 5.0289] satte tapatīti tāpano. Ativiya tāpetīti patāpano. Tattha tāpanasmiṃ tāva satte tālakkhandhappamāṇe jalitaayasūle nisīdāpenti. Tato heṭṭhā pathavī jalati, sūlāni jalanti, sattā jalanti. Evaṃ so nirayo niccale satte tapati. Itarasmiṃ pana nibbattasatte jalantehi āvudhehi paharitvā jalitaṃ ayapabbataṃ āropenti. Tesaṃ pabbatamatthake ṭhitakāle kammapaccayo vāto paharati. Te tattha saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā uddhaṃpādā adhosirā patanti. Atha heṭṭhā ayapathavito jalitāni ayasūlāni uṭṭhahanti. Te tāni matthakeneva paharitvā tesu vinividdhasarīrā [P 5.0272] jalantā paccanti. Evamesa ativiya tāpetīti.

The one that scorches motionless beings is called Tāpana (the Scorcher). The one that scorches exceedingly is called Patāpana (the Great Scorcher). In the Scorcher hell, beings are made to sit on a blazing iron stake the size of a palm trunk. Then the ground below burns, the stakes burn, and the beings burn. Thus, that hell scorches motionless beings. In the other hell, beings reborn there are struck with blazing weapons and made to climb a blazing iron mountain. When they stand at the mountain's peak, a wind produced by their kamma strikes them. Unable to remain there, they fall with feet up and head down. Then, from the iron ground below, blazing iron stakes rise up. They are pierced on them through the head and, with their bodies impaled, they burn and are cooked. Thus, this one scorches exceedingly.

Bodhisatto pana ete niraye dassento paṭhamaṃ sañjīvaṃ dassetvā tattha paccante nerayikasatte disvā mahājanassa mahābhaye uppanne taṃ antaradhāpetvā puna pathaviṃ dvidhā katvā kāḷasuttaṃ dassesi, tatthapi paccamāne satte disvā mahājanassa mahābhaye uppanne tampi antaradhāpesīti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā dassesi. Tato rājānaṃ āmantetvā, “mahārāja, tayā imesu aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu paccamāne satte disvā appamādaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā puna tesaññeva mahānirayānaṃ kiccaṃ kathetuṃ “iccete”tiādimāha. Tattha akkhātāti mayā ca tuyhaṃ kathitā, porāṇakehi ca kathitāyeva. Ākiṇṇāti paripuṇṇā. Paccekā soḷasussadāti etesaṃ [V 5.0265] nirayānaṃ ekekassa catūsu dvāresu ekekasmiṃ cattāro cattāro katvā soḷasa soḷasa ussadanirayāti sabbepi sataṃ aṭṭhavīsati ca ussadanirayā aṭṭha ca mahānirayāti chattiṃsanirayasataṃ. Kadariyatāpanāti sabbete kadariyānaṃ tāpanā. Balavadukkhatāya ghorā. Kammanibbattānaṃ accīnaṃ atthitāya accimanto. Bhayassa mahantatāya mahabbhayā. Diṭṭhamattā vā sutamattā vā lomāni haṃsantīti lomahaṃsanarūpā ca. Bhīsanatāya bhesmā. Bhayajananatāya paṭibhayā. Sukhābhāvena dukhā. Catukkaṇṇāti sabbepi caturassamañjūsasadisā. Vibhattāti catudvāravasena vibhattā. Bhāgaso mitāti dvāravīthīnaṃ vasena koṭṭhāse ṭhapetvā mitā. Ayasā paṭikujjitāti sabbepi [M 5.0290] navayojanikena ayakapālena paṭicchannā. Phuṭā tiṭṭhantīti sabbepi ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ anupharitvā tiṭṭhanti.

The Bodhisatta, while showing these hells, first displayed the Sañjīva hell. Seeing the hell-beings being tormented there, great fear arose in the great assembly. Then he made that hell disappear and, splitting the earth in two again, revealed the Kāḷasutta hell. Seeing the beings being tormented there as well, great fear arose in the great assembly, and he made that hell vanish too. In this manner, he revealed them in sequence. Then, addressing the king, he said, “Great king, having seen beings being tormented in these eight great hells, it is fitting for you to practice heedfulness.” Having said this, he proceeded to explain the function of those very great hells, beginning with, “Thus these…” There, “explained” means explained by me to you and also recounted by the ancients. “Filled” means completely full. “Sixteen subsidiary hells each” means that for each of these hells, at each of the four gates, there are four subsidiary hells, making sixteen subsidiary hells per great hell. Thus, all together, there are one hundred and twenty-eight subsidiary hells and eight great hells, totaling one hundred and thirty-six hells. “Torment of the miserly” means all these are torments for the miserly. They are terrible due to the intense suffering. They are fiery because of the flames produced by kamma. They are greatly fearsome due to the enormity of the danger. They are hair-raising in nature, for just seeing or hearing of them makes one's hair stand on end. They are dreadful because of their terrifying nature. They are horrifying because they generate fear. They are painful, being devoid of happiness. “Four-cornered” means all are like square boxes. “Divided” means partitioned by way of the four gates. “Measured in parts” means measured by establishing compartments according to the gate-streets. “Encased in iron” means all are covered by an iron shell nine leagues thick. “Pervading and standing” means all stand pervading that much space.

Uddhaṃpādā avaṃsirāti evaṃ tesu tesu nirayesu samparivattitvā punappunaṃ patamāne sandhāyāha. Ativattāroti pharusavācāhi atikkamitvā vattāro. Mahānirayesu kira yebhuyyena dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇesu katāparādhāva paccanti, tasmā evamāha. Te bhūnahunoti te isīnaṃ ativattāro attano vuḍḍhiyā hatattā bhūnahuno koṭṭhāsakatā macchā viya paccanti. Asaṅkheyyeti gaṇetuṃ asakkuṇeyye. Kibbisakārinoti dāruṇakammakārino. Nikkhamanesinoti nirayā nikkhamanaṃ esantāpi gavesantāpi nikkhamanadvāraṃ nādhigacchanti. Puratthimenāti yadā taṃ dvāraṃ apārutaṃ hoti, atha tadabhimukhā dhāvanti, tesaṃ tattha chaviādīni jhāyanti. Dvārasamīpaṃ pattānañca tesaṃ taṃ pidhīyati, pacchimadvāraṃ apārutaṃ viya khāyati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Na sādhurūpeti vuttappakāraṃ sappaṃ viya sādhurūpe isayo na āsīde, na pharusavacanena kāyakammena vā ghaṭṭento upagaccheyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Saññatānaṃ tapassīnaṃ āsāditattā aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu mahādukkhassa anubhavitabbattā.

‘Feet up, head down’ refers to those who, revolving in those various hells, fall again and again. ‘Transgressors’ means those who transgress by speaking harshly. It is said that in the great hells, for the most part, those who have wronged righteous ascetics and brahmins are tormented; therefore, it is stated thus. ‘They destroy their own growth’—those transgressors of the seers, having destroyed their own progress, are tormented like fish cut into pieces. ‘Incalculable’ means what cannot be counted. ‘Doers of evil’ refers to those who commit cruel deeds. ‘Seeking an exit’—though seeking and searching for an exit from hell, they do not find an escape door. ‘By the eastern’—when that door is open, they run toward it, but their skin and so on are burned there. Upon reaching the vicinity of the door, it closes, and the western door appears to be open. This is the pattern everywhere. ‘Not of good form’—one should not assail seers of good form, just as one would not a snake, nor should one approach them, striking them with harsh speech or bodily action. Why? Because having assailed restrained ascetics, one is destined to endure great suffering in the eight great hells.

Idāni ye rājāno tathārūpe āsādetvā taṃ dukkhaṃ pattā, te dassetuṃ “atikāyo”tiādimāha. Tattha atikāyoti balasampanno mahākāyo. Mahissāsoti [P 5.0273] mahādhanuggaho. Kekakādhipoti kekakaraṭṭhādhipati. Sahassabāhūti pañcahi dhanuggahasatehi bāhusahassena āropetabbaṃ dhanuṃ āropanasamatthatāya sahassabāhu. Vibhavaṅgatoti vināsaṃ patto. Vatthūni pana sarabhaṅgajātake (jā. 2.17.50 ādayo) vitthāritāni. Upahacca mananti attano cittaṃ padūsetvā. Mātaṅgasminti mātaṅgapaṇḍite. Vatthu mātaṅgajātake (jā. 1.15.1 ādayo) vaṇṇitaṃ. Kaṇhadīpāyanāsajjāti kaṇhadīpāyanaṃ āsajja. Yamasādhananti nirayapālakarañño āṇāpavattaṭṭhānaṃ. Vatthu ghaṭapaṇḍitajātake (jā. 1.10.165 ādayo) vitthāritaṃ[V 5.0266]. Isināti kapilatāpasena. Pāvekkhīti paviṭṭho. Ceccoti cetiyarājā. Hīnattoti parihīnattabhāvo antarahitaiddhi. Pattapariyāyanti pariyāyaṃ maraṇakālaṃ patvā. Vatthu cetiyajātake (jā. 1.8.45 ādayo) kathitaṃ.

Now, to show those kings who, having assailed such a one, met with that suffering, it is said: ‘Of immense body,’ and so on. Herein, ‘of immense body’ means endowed with strength and a great body. ‘Great archer’ means possessing a great bow. ‘Lord of Kekaka’ means the ruler of the Kekaka country. ‘Thousand-armed’: so called because of his ability to string a bow that had to be strung by five hundred archers with a thousand arms. ‘Gone to ruin’ means having attained destruction. The stories, however, are elaborated in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka. ‘Having corrupted the mind’ means having defiled his own mind. ‘Toward Mātaṅga’: toward Mātaṅga the wise. The story is described in the Mātaṅga Jātaka. ‘Having assailed Kaṇhadīpāyana’: having attacked Kaṇhadīpāyana. ‘Yama’s domain’: the place where the command of the king, the guardian of hell, is exercised. The story is elaborated in the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka. ‘By the seer’: by Kapila the ascetic. ‘He entered’: he went in. ‘Cecca’: King Cetiya. ‘To a low state’: the state of decline, with his psychic power vanished. ‘Having reached his turn’: having reached his time, the time of death. The story is told in the Cetiya Jātaka.

Tasmā [M 5.0291] hīti yasmā cittavasiko hutvā isīsu aparajjhitvā aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu paccati, tasmā hi. Chandāgamananti chandādicatubbidhampi agatigamanaṃ. Paduṭṭhenāti kuddhena. Gantā so nirayaṃ adhoti so tena adhogamaniyena kammena adhonirayameva gacchati. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “nirayussada”nti likhitaṃ, tassa ussadanirayaṃ gacchatīti attho. Vuḍḍheti vayovuḍḍhe ca guṇavuḍḍhe ca. Anapaccāti bhavantarepi apaccaṃ vā dāyādaṃ vā na labhantīti attho. Tālavatthūti diṭṭhadhammepi chinnamūlatālo viya mahāvināsaṃ patvā niraye nibbattanti. Yo ca pabbajitaṃ hantīti yo bālajano samaṇaṃ hanati. Cirarattāyāti ciraṃ kālaṃ.

Therefore: because, being under the sway of his mind, he offends against the seers and is tormented in the eight great hells, therefore it is said. ‘Going the wrong way’ means going by way of the four kinds of wrong paths beginning with desire. ‘With a corrupt mind’ means by one who is angry. ‘He goes down to hell’ means that by that kamma that leads downward, he goes right down to hell. In the Pāli text, however, it is written as ‘to a subsidiary hell,’ the meaning of which is that he goes to a subsidiary hell. ‘The elders’ means those who are old both in age and in virtue. ‘Childless’ means that even in future existences, they obtain neither offspring nor heirs. ‘Made like a palm-stump’ means that even in this life, like a palm tree severed at the root, they meet with great destruction and are reborn in hell. ‘And whoever should slay one gone forth’ means whatever foolish person slays an ascetic. ‘For a long time’ means for a long time.

Evaṃ mahāsatto isiviheṭhakānaṃ paccananiraye dassetvā upari adhammikarājūnaṃ paccananiraye dassento “yo cā”tiādimāha. Tattha raṭṭhaviddhaṃsanoti chandādivasena gantvā raṭṭhassa viddhaṃsano. Accisaṅghaparetoti accisamūhaparikkhitto. Tejobhakkhassāti aggimeva khādantassa. Gattānīti tigāvute sarīre sabbaṅgapaccaṅgāni. Lomehi ca nakhehi cāti etehi saddhiṃ sabbāni ekajālāni honti. Tuttaṭṭītoti āneñjakāraṇaṃ kāriyamāno tuttehi viddho nāgo yathā nadati.

Thus the Great Being, having shown the hells where those who harass seers are tormented, then, showing the hells where unrighteous kings are tormented, spoke the verse beginning ‘And whoever….’ Herein, ‘destroyer of the kingdom’ means one who destroys the kingdom by acting according to desire and so on. ‘Engulfed in a mass of flames’ means surrounded by a mass of flames. ‘Of one who eats fire’ refers to one who eats only fire. ‘The limbs’: all the major and minor limbs in a body three gāvutas in extent. ‘With hairs and nails’: together with these, they all become a single blaze. ‘Afflicted by goads’: he roars like an elephant pierced by goads when being tortured.

Evaṃ mahāsatto adhammikarājūnaṃ paccananiraye dassetvā idāni pitughātakādīnaṃ paccananiraye dassetuṃ “yo lobhā”tiādimāha. Tattha lobhāti yasadhanalobhena. Dosā vāti duṭṭhacittatāya vā. Nittacanti lohakumbhiyaṃ bahūni vasasahassāni pakkaṃ nīharitvā tigāvutamassa sarīraṃ nittacaṃ katvā jalitāya lohapathaviyaṃ pātetvā tiṇhehi ayasūlehi koṭṭetvā cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ karonti. Andhaṃ karitvāti, mahārāja, taṃ pitughātakaṃ nirayapālā jalitalohapathaviyaṃ uttānaṃ pātetvā jalitehi ayasūlehi akkhīni bhinditvā andhaṃ karitvā mukhe uṇhaṃ muttakarīsaṃ pakkhipitvā palālapīṭhaṃ viya naṃ parivattetvā kappena saṇṭhite khāre lohaudake nimujjāpenti. Tattaṃ pakkuthitamayoguḷañcāti puna pakkuthitaṃ gūthakalalañceva jalitaayoguḷañca khādāpenti. So pana taṃ āhariyamānaṃ disvā mukhaṃ pidheti. Athassa dīghe ciratāpite jalamāne phāle ādāya mukhaṃ vikkhambhetvā vivaritvā rajjubaddhaṃ ayabalisaṃ [M 5.0292] khipitvā [V 5.0267] jivhaṃ nīharitvā [P 5.0274] tasmiṃ vivaṭe mukhe taṃ ayoguḷaṃ sampavisanti pakkhipanti. Rakkhasāti nirayapālā.

Thus the Great Being, having shown the hells where unrighteous kings are tormented, now, to show the hells where patricides and others are tormented, spoke the verse beginning ‘Whoever out of greed….’ Herein, ‘out of greed’ means due to greed for fame and wealth. ‘Or out of hatred’ means due to a wicked mind. ‘Skinless’: having taken him out of an iron cauldron where he was cooked for many thousands of years, they make his three-gāvuta-long body skinless, throw him onto a blazing iron ground, and, having pounded him with sharp iron stakes, they reduce him to powder. ‘Having been blinded’: O great king, the hell-guardians throw that patricide face-up onto the blazing iron ground, and having pierced his eyes with blazing iron stakes and blinded him, they put hot urine and excrement in his mouth, roll him around like a bundle of straw, and submerge him in caustic molten metal that has been standing for an eon. ‘And a hot, boiling iron ball’: again they make him eat boiling filth and mud and a blazing iron ball. But seeing it being brought, he shuts his mouth. Then, taking a long, perpetually heated, blazing ploughshare, they pry his mouth open, throw in an iron hook tied to a rope, pull out his tongue, and into that open mouth they insert and place that iron ball. ‘Ogres’: the hell-guardians.

Sāmā cāti, mahārāja, tassa pitughātakassa jivhaṃ balisena nikkaḍḍhitvā ayasaṅkūhi pathaviyaṃ nīhataṃ jivhaṃ sāmā soṇā sabalavaṇṇā sunakhā ca lohatuṇḍā gijjhā ca kākolasaṅghā ca aññe ca nānappakārā sakuṇā samāgantvā āvudhehi chindantā viya vibhajja kākapadākārena koṭṭhāse katvā vipphandamānaṃ salohitaṃ vighāsaṃ khādantā viya satte bhakkhayantīti attho. Taṃ daḍḍhatālanti taṃ pitughātakaṃ jhāyamānatālaṃ viya jalitasarīraṃ. Paribhinnagattanti tattha tattha paribhinnagattaṃ. Nippothayantāti jalitehi ayamuggarehi paharantā. Ratī hi tesanti tesaṃ nirayapālānaṃ sā rati kīḷā hoti. Dukhino panītareti itare pana nerayikasattā dukkhitā honti. Pettighātinoti pitughātakā. Iti imaṃ pitughātakānaṃ paccananirayaṃ disvā rājā bhītatasito ahosi.

‘And black dogs’: O great king, having pulled out the tongue of that patricide with a hook and fixed it to the ground with iron spikes, black dogs, dappled dogs, vultures with iron beaks, flocks of crows, and other birds of various kinds gather together and, as if cutting it with weapons, they divide it, making portions in the shape of a crow’s foot, and devour that throbbing, bloody tongue; the meaning is that they devour the beings as if eating leftover scraps. ‘That burnt palm tree’: that patricide with a body blazing like a burning palm tree. ‘With shattered limbs’: with his limbs shattered here and there. ‘They crush him’: striking him with blazing iron hammers. ‘For that is their delight’: for those hell-guardians, that is their delight and sport. ‘But the others are in pain’: the other hell-beings are afflicted with suffering. ‘Patricides’: those who kill their fathers. Having seen this hell where patricides are tormented, the king became frightened and terrified.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto samassāsetvā mātughātakānaṃ paccananirayaṃ dassesi. Yamakkhayanti yamanivesanaṃ, nirayanti attho. Attakammaphalūpagoti attano kammaphalena upagato. Amanussāti nirayapālā. Hantāraṃ janayantiyāti mātughātakaṃ. Vālehīti ayamakacivālehi veṭhetvā ayayantena pīḷayanti. Tanti taṃ mātughātakaṃ. Pāyentīti tassa pīḷiyamānassa ruhiraṃ gaḷitvā ayakapallaṃ pūreti. Atha naṃ yantato nīharanti, tāvadevassa sarīraṃ pākatikaṃ hoti. Taṃ pathaviyaṃ uttānaṃ nipajjāpetvā vilīnaṃ tambalohaṃ viya pakkuthitaṃ lohitaṃ pāyenti. Ogayha tiṭṭhatīti taṃ bahūni vassasahassāni ayayantehi pīḷetvā jegucche duggandhe paṭikūle mahante gūthakalalaāvāṭe khipanti, so taṃ rahadaṃ ogayha ogāhitvā tiṭṭhati. Atikāyāti ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇasarīrā. Ayomukhāti ayasūcimukhā. Chaviṃ bhetvānāti chavimādiṃ katvā yāva aṭṭhimpi bhetvā aṭṭhimiñjampi khādanti. Saṃgiddhāti gadhitā mucchitā. Na kevalañca khādanteva, adhomaggādīhi pana pavisitvā mukhādīhi [M 5.0293] nikkhamanti, vāmapassādīhi pavisitvā dakkhiṇapassādīhi nikkhamanti, sakalampi sarīraṃ chiddāvachiddaṃ karonti, so tattha atidukkhapareto viravanto paccati. So cāti so mātughātako ca taṃ sataporisaṃ nirayaṃ patto sasīsako nimuggova hoti, tañca kuṇapaṃ samantā yojanasataṃ pūtikaṃ hutvā vāyati. Mātughoti mātughātako.

Then the Great Being, having consoled him, showed him the hell where matricides are tormented. ‘Yama’s wasting’: Yama’s abode, meaning hell. ‘Gone by the fruit of his own kamma’: gone there by the fruit of his own kamma. ‘Non-humans’: the hell-guardians. ‘The slayer of his mother’: the matricide. ‘With bristles’: they wrap him with iron bristles and crush him with an iron machine. ‘That one’: that matricide. ‘They make him drink’: as he is being crushed, his blood flows out and fills an iron bowl. Then they take him out of the machine, and at that very moment his body becomes normal. They lay him face-up on the ground and make him drink his own boiling blood, which is like molten copper. ‘He stands submerged’: after crushing him with iron machines for many thousands of years, they throw him into a vast, disgusting, foul, repulsive pit of filth and mud; he enters that lake and stands submerged in it. ‘Of immense body’: their bodies are the size of a one-doṇa boat. ‘With iron mouths’: with mouths like iron needles. ‘Having pierced the skin’: starting with the skin, they pierce right through to the bone and eat the bone marrow. ‘Greedy’: they are greedy and infatuated. And not only do they eat, but they enter through the lower passages and exit through the mouth, and they enter through the left side and exit through the right side, making his entire body riddled with holes. There, overcome by extreme suffering, he is tormented, wailing. ‘And he’: and that matricide, having fallen into that hell a hundred persons deep, is submerged head-and-all, and that putrid corpse of his stinks for a hundred yojanas all around. ‘Matricide’: one who kills his mother.

Evaṃ mahāsatto mātughātakānaṃ paccananirayaṃ dassetvā puna gabbhapātakānaṃ paccananirayaṃ dassento [V 5.0268] gāthamāha. Khuradhāramanukkammāti khuradhāranirayaṃ atikkamitvā. Tattha kira nirayapālā mahantamahante khure upari dhāre katvā santharanti, tato yāhi gabbhapātanakharabhesajjāni [P 5.0275] pivitvā gabbhā pātitā, tā gabbhapātiniyo itthiyo jalitehi āvudhehi pothentā anubandhanti, tā tikhiṇakhuradhārāsu khaṇḍākhaṇḍikā hutvā punappunaṃ uṭṭhāya taṃ durabhisambhavaṃ khuradhāranirayaṃ akkamantiyo atikkamitvā nirayapālehi anubaddhā duggaṃ duratikkamaṃ visamaṃ vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ patanti. Tattha kammakāraṇaṃ nimijātake (jā. 2.22.421 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

Thus the Great Being, having shown the hell of torment for matricides, then, revealing the hell of torment for those who procure abortions, spoke this verse. 'Having traversed the razor-edge' means having passed beyond the razor-edge hell. There, it is said, the hell-wardens lay out enormous razors with their edges facing upward. Then they pursue those women who have procured abortions by drinking harsh abortifacient potions, striking them with blazing weapons. These women are cut to pieces on the sharp razor edges, but rise up again and again. Treading upon and passing beyond that razor-edge hell, which is so difficult to endure, they are pursued by the hell-wardens and fall into the Vetaraṇi River—treacherous, difficult to traverse, and hard to cross. The karmic cause for this will become clear in the Nimi Jātaka (Jā 541).

Evaṃ gabbhapātinīnaṃ nirayaṃ dassetvā mahāsatto yattha paradārikā ca aticāriniyo ca patantā paccanti, taṃ kaṇṭakasimbalinirayaṃ dassento “ayomayā”tiādimāha. Tattha ubhato abhilambantīti vetaraṇiyā ubhosu tīresu tāsaṃ simbalīnaṃ sākhā olambanti. Te accimantoti te pajjalitasarīrā sattā accimanto hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Yojananti tigāvutaṃ tesaṃ sarīraṃ, tato uṭṭhitajālāya pana saddhiṃ yojanaubbedhā honti. Ete vajantīti te paradārikā sattā nānāvidhehi āvudhehi koṭṭiyamānā ete simbaliniraye abhiruhanti. Te patantīti te bahūni vassasahassāni rukkhaviṭapesu laggā jhāyitvā puna nirayapālehi āvudhehi vihatā vivattā hutvā parivattitvā adhosīsakā patanti. Puthūti bahū. Vinividdhaṅgāti tesaṃ tato patanakāle heṭṭhā ayapathavito sūlāni uṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ matthakaṃ paṭicchanti, tāni tesaṃ adhomaggena nikkhamanti, te evaṃ sūlesu viddhasarīrā cirarattā sayanti. Dīghanti supinepi niddaṃ alabhantā dīgharattaṃ jaggantīti attho. Ratyā vivasāneti rattīnaṃ accayena, cirakālātikkamenāti attho[M 5.0294]. Pavajjantīti saṭṭhiyojanikaṃ jalitaṃ lohakumbhiṃ kappena saṇṭhitaṃ jalitatambaloharasapuṇṇaṃ lohakumbhiṃ nirayapālehi khittā paccanti. Dussīlāti paradārikā.

Having shown the hell for those who procure abortions, the Great Being pointed out the Thorny Silk-Cotton Tree Hell, where adulterous men and unfaithful wives fall and are tormented, saying: 'Made of iron,' and so on. There, 'hanging from both sides' means that the branches of those silk-cotton trees hang down on both banks of the Vetaraṇī River. 'They are fiery' means those beings stand there with blazing bodies. 'A yojana': their bodies are three gāvutas in size, but with the flames that rise up, they become a yojana in height. 'These go': those adulterous beings, being struck with various weapons, climb these silk-cotton trees in hell. 'They fall': after being attached to the tree branches and burning for many thousands of years, they are again struck by the hell-wardens with weapons, turned around, and fall headfirst. 'Many' means numerous. 'With pierced bodies': when they fall from there, spikes rise up from the iron ground below and receive them on their heads; these exit through their lower parts. Thus, with their bodies impaled on the spikes, they lie for a long time. 'Long': this means that, unable to get sleep even in a dream, they remain awake for a long, long time. 'At the end of the nights': this means with the passing of the nights, that is, with the passing of a long time. 'They are cooked': thrown by the hell-wardens, they are cooked in a sixty-yojana burning iron cauldron, which lasts for an aeon and is full of the molten essence of copper and iron. 'The immoral' refers to adulterers.

Evaṃ mahāsatto paradārikaaticārikānaṃ paccanasimbalinirayaṃ dassetvā ito paraṃ sāmikavattasassusasuravattādīni apūrentīnaṃ paccanaṭṭhānaṃ pakāsento “yā cā”tiādimāha. Tattha atimaññatīti bhisajātake (jā. 1.14.78 ādayo) vuttaṃ sāmikavattaṃ akarontī atikkamitvā maññati. Jeṭṭhaṃ vāti sāmikassa jeṭṭhabhātaraṃ. Nanandaranti sāmikassa bhaginiṃ. Etesampi hi aññatarassa hatthapādapiṭṭhiparikammanhāpanabhojanādibhedaṃ vattaṃ apūrentī tesu hirottappaṃ anupaṭṭhapentī te atimaññati nāma, sāpi niraye nibbatti. Vaṅkenāti tassā sāmikavattādīnaṃ aparipūrikāya sāmikādayo akkositvā paribhāsitvā niraye nibbattāya lohapathaviyaṃ [V 5.0269] nipajjāpetvā ayasaṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā balisena jivhaggaṃ nibbahanti, rajjubandhanena sabandhanaṃ kaḍḍhanti. Kiminanti kimibharitaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, so nerayikasatto evaṃ nikkaḍḍhitaṃ attano byāmena byāmamattaṃ jivhaṃ āvudhehi koṭṭitakoṭṭitaṭṭhāne sañjātehi mahādoṇippamāṇehi kimīhi bharitaṃ passati. Viññāpetuṃ na sakkotīti nirayapāle yācitukāmopi kiñci vattuṃ na sakkoti. Tāpaneti evaṃ sā tattha bahūni vassasahassāni paccitvā puna tāpanamahāniraye paccati.

Thus the Great Being, having shown the Thorny Silk-Cotton Tree Hell, the place of torment for adulterous men and unfaithful wives, then, illuminating the place of torment for those women who do not fulfill their duties towards their husbands, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and so on, said: 'And she who…,' and so on. Here, 'despises': she does not perform the duties to her husband mentioned in the Bhisa Jātaka (Jā 488), and through this transgression, she scorns him. 'Or an elder brother': her husband’s elder brother. 'Or a sister-in-law': her husband’s sister. By not fulfilling for any of these the various duties such as massaging their hands, feet, and back, bathing and feeding them, and by not maintaining moral shame and moral dread towards them, she is said to 'despise' them. She, too, is reborn in hell. 'With a hook': because she did not fulfill her duties to her husband and others, and because she scolded and reviled them, she is reborn in hell. There, she is made to lie down on an iron ground, her mouth is pried open with an iron spike, and the tip of her tongue is pulled out with a hook. They pull it out, bound with a rope. 'Full of worms': this is what is said: 'Great king, that hell-being sees her own tongue, stretched out to a fathom’s length, become full of worms the size of large troughs that arise in the places where it is struck again and again with weapons.' 'She is unable to make it known': even though she wants to beg the hell-wardens, she is unable to say anything. 'In the Tāpana': after being cooked there for many thousands of years, she is cooked again in the Tāpana Mahāniraya.

Evaṃ mahāsatto sāmikavattasassusasuravattādīni apūrentīnaṃ paccananirayaṃ dassetvā idāni sūkarikādīnaṃ paccananiraye dassento “orabbhikā”tiādimāha[P 5.0276]. Tattha avaṇṇe vaṇṇakārakāti pesuññakārakā. Khāranadinti ete orabbhikādayo etehi sattiādīhi haññamānā vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ patantīti attho. Sesāni orabbhikādīnaṃ paccanaṭṭhānāni nimijātake āvi bhavissanti. Kuṭakārīti kūṭavinicchayassa ceva tulākūṭādīnañca kārake sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha kūṭavinicchayakūṭaṭṭakārakakūṭaagghāpanikānaṃ paccananirayā nimijātake āvi bhavissanti. Vantanti vamitakaṃ. Durattānanti duggatattabhāvānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, te durattabhāvā sattā ayakūṭehi matthake bhijjamāne vamanti, tato taṃ vantaṃ jalitaayakapallehi tesu ekaccānaṃ mukhe khipanti[M 5.0295], iti te paresaṃ vantaṃ bhuñjanti nāma. Bheraṇḍakāti siṅgālā. Vipphandamānanti adhomukhaṃ nipajjāpitaṃ nikkaḍḍhitajivhaṃ ito cito ca vipphandamānaṃ. Migenāti okacārakamigena. Pakkhināti tathārūpeneva. Gantā teti gantāro te. Nirayussadanti ussadanirayaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “nirayaṃ adho”ti likhitaṃ. Ayaṃ pana nirayo nimijātake āvi bhavissatīti.

Thus the Great Being, having shown the hell of torment for those who do not fulfill their duties to their husbands, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and so on, now, showing the hells of torment for pork-butchers and the like, said: 'Sheep-butchers…,' and so on. Here, 'those who praise the blameworthy' refers to slanderers. 'Into the caustic river': this means that these sheep-butchers and others, being struck with spears and other weapons, fall into the Vetaraṇi River. The other places of torment for sheep-butchers and the like will become clear in the Nimi Jātaka. 'Deceivers': this is said with reference to those who make false judgments and use false weights and measures. The hells of torment for those who make false judgments, use false weights, and set false prices will become clear in the Nimi Jātaka. 'Vomit': what has been vomited. 'Of those in a miserable state': of those who have a miserable existence. This is what is said: 'Great king, those beings in a miserable state vomit as their heads are being smashed with iron hammers. Then that vomit is thrown into the mouths of some of them from blazing iron bowls. Thus they are said to eat the vomit of others.' 'Jackals' means jackals. 'Writhing': lying face down with tongue pulled out, writhing this way and that. 'By a beast': by a lurking beast. 'By a bird': by a bird of a similar kind. 'They who go': those who are goers. 'To a subsidiary hell': to an Ussada hell. In the Pāli text, however, it is written 'to the hell below.' This hell, too, will become clear in the Nimi Jātaka.

Iti mahāsatto ettake niraye dassetvā idāni devalokavivaraṇaṃ katvā rañño devaloke dassento āha –

Thus the Great Being, having shown so many hells, now unveiled the heavenly worlds. Showing the heavenly worlds to the king, he said:

133.

133.

“Santo ca uddhaṃ gacchanti, suciṇṇenidha kammunā;

Suciṇṇassa phalaṃ passa, saindā devā sabrahmakā.

The good go upward through deeds well done here; behold the fruit of good deeds: the gods with their Indras and their Brahmās.

134.

134.

“Taṃ taṃ brūmi mahārāja, dhammaṃ raṭṭhapatī cara;

Tathā rāja carāhi dhammaṃ, yathā taṃ suciṇṇaṃ nānutappeyya pacchā”ti.

Therefore I say to you, great king, lord of the kingdom, practice the Dhamma. Practice the Dhamma, O king, in such a way that your good conduct does not cause you remorse later.

Tattha [V 5.0270] santoti kāyādīhi upasantā. Uddhanti devalokaṃ. Saindāti tattha tattha indehi saddhiṃ. Mahāsatto hissa cātumahārājādike deve dassento, “mahārāja, cātumahārājike deve passa, cattāro mahārājāno passa, tāvatiṃse passa, sakkaṃ passā”ti evaṃ sabbepi saindake sabrahmake ca deve dassento “idampi suciṇṇassa phalaṃ idampi phala”nti dassesi. Taṃ taṃ brūmīti tasmā taṃ bhaṇāmi. Dhammanti ito paṭṭhāya pāṇātipātādīni pañca verāni pahāya dānādīni puññāni karohīti. Yathā taṃ suciṇṇaṃ nānutappeyyāti yathā taṃ dānādipuññakammaṃ suciṇṇaṃ pitughātakammapaccayaṃ vippaṭisāraṃ paṭicchādetuṃ samatthatāya taṃ nānutappeyya, tathā taṃ suciṇṇaṃ cara, bahuṃ puññaṃ karohīti attho.

Here, 'the good' means those who are peaceful in body and so on. 'Upward' means to the heavenly world. 'With their Indras' means together with the Indras in their various realms. The Great Being showed him the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings and others, saying: 'Great king, behold the gods of the Four Great Kings! Behold the Four Great Kings! Behold the Tāvatiṃsa gods! Behold Sakka!' Thus, showing all the gods with their Indras and their Brahmās, he pointed out: 'This is a fruit of good conduct, and this is a fruit.' 'Therefore I say to you' means 'For that reason I tell you.' 'The Dhamma': this means, 'From now on, abandon the five dangerous actions beginning with the destruction of life and perform meritorious deeds such as giving.' 'That your good conduct does not cause you remorse': this means, 'Practice that good conduct—that is, perform much merit—in such a way that this well-practiced meritorious kamma of giving and so on, by its ability to conceal the remorse conditioned by the kamma of patricide, will not cause you remorse.' This is the meaning.

So [P 5.0277] mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya assāsaṃ paṭilabhi. Bodhisatto pana kiñci kālaṃ tattha vasitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaññeva gato.

Hearing the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, from that time on he found consolation. The Bodhisatta, having dwelt there for some time, returned to his own dwelling place.

Satthā [M 5.0296] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mayā assāsitoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā rājā ajātasattu ahosi, isigaṇo buddhaparisā, saṃkiccapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma discourse, said: "Bhikkhus, not only now but in the past, too, he was consoled by me." He then made the connection for the Jātaka: "At that time the king was Ajātasattu, the company of seers was the Buddha’s assembly, and Saṃkicca the Wise was myself."

Saṃkiccajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Saṃkicca Jātaka, the Second.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary Verse for the Jātakas:

Atha saṭṭhinipātamhi, suṇātha mama bhāsitaṃ;

Jātakasavhayano pavaro, soṇakaarindamasavhayano;

Tathā vuttarathesabhakiccavaroti.

Now in the Book of Sixty, listen to what I say: The excellent Jātaka named Soṇaka-Arindama, and likewise the noble Saṃkicca Jātaka.

Saṭṭhinipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Sixty is concluded.

20. Sattatinipāto

20. The Book of the Seventies

[531] 1. Kusajātakavaṇṇanā

[531] 1. The Explanation of the Kusa Jātaka

Idaṃ [V 5.0271][P 5.0278] te raṭṭhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ alaṅkataitthiṃ disvā subhanimittaggāhavasena oloketvā kilesābhibhūto anabhirato vihāsi dīghakesanakho kiliṭṭhacīvaro uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanīsanthatagatto. Yathā hi devalokā cavanadhammānaṃ devaputtānaṃ pañca pubbanimittāni paññāyanti, mālā milāyanti, vatthāni kilissanti, sarīre dubbaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, ubhohi kacchehi sedā muccanti, devo devāsane nābhiramati, evameva sāsanā cavanadhammānaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhūnaṃ pañca pubbanimittāni paññāyanti, saddhāpupphāni milāyanti, sīlavatthāni kilissanti, sarīre maṅkutāya ceva ayasavasena ca dubbaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, kilesasedā muccanti, araññarukkhamūlasuññāgāresu nābhiramanti. Tassapi tāni paññāyiṃsu. Atha naṃ bhikkhū satthu santikaṃ netvā “ayaṃ, bhante, ukkaṇṭhito”ti dassesuṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti taṃ pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “mā, bhikkhu, kilesavasiko hohi, mātugāmo nāmesa pāpo, tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittataṃ vinodehi, sāsane abhirama, mātugāme paṭibaddhacittatāya hi tejavantopi porāṇakapaṇḍitā nittejā hutvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This is your kingdom.” This the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a discontented bhikkhu. It is said that a certain man of good family from Sāvatthī, having dedicated himself to the Dispensation, went forth. One day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a beautifully adorned woman. By grasping the sign of beauty, he was overcome by defilements and lived without delight, with long hair and nails, soiled robes, pale and sallow, his body covered with a network of veins. For just as five premonitory signs appear to devaputtas who are due to pass away from the deva world—their garlands wither, their garments become soiled, a bad complexion comes over their bodies, sweat is released from their armpits, and the deva no longer delights in his deva-seat—even so five premonitory signs appear to bhikkhus who are due to fall away from the Dispensation: the flowers of faith wither, the garments of moral virtue become soiled, a bad complexion comes over their bodies on account of dejection and disgrace, the sweat of defilements is released, and they no longer delight in the forest, at the foot of trees, or in empty dwellings. These signs appeared in him as well. Then the bhikkhus brought him before the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is discontented.” The Teacher asked him, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Bhikkhu, do not be ruled by defilements. A woman, it is said, is a wicked thing; dispel your attachment to her. Delight in the Dispensation. For by being attached to a woman, even powerful ancient sages became powerless and met with calamity and ruin.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte mallaraṭṭhe kusāvatīrājadhāniyaṃ okkāko nāma rājā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhikā [P 5.0279][M 5.0297] sīlavatī nāma aggamahesī ahosi, sā neva puttaṃ, na dhītaraṃ labhi. Athassa nāgarā ceva raṭṭhavāsino ca rājanivesanadvāre sannipatitvā “raṭṭhaṃ nassissati, raṭṭhaṃ nassissatī”ti upakkosiṃsu. Rājā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā “mayi rajjaṃ kārente adhammakāro nāma natthi, kasmā upakkosathā”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, deva, adhammakāro nāma natthi, apica vaṃsānurakkhako [M 5.0298] pana vo putto natthi, añño [V 5.0272] rajjaṃ gahetvā raṭṭhaṃ nāsessati, tasmā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretuṃ samatthaṃ puttaṃ patthethā”ti. “Puttaṃ patthento kiṃ karomī”ti? “Paṭhamaṃ tāva ekaṃ sattāhaṃ cullanāṭakaṃ dhammanāṭakaṃ katvā vissajjetha, sace sā puttaṃ labhissati, sādhu, no ce, atha majjhimanāṭakaṃ vissajjetha, tato jeṭṭhanāṭakaṃ, avassaṃ ettakāsu itthīsu ekā puññavatī puttaṃ labhissatī”ti. Rājā tesaṃ vacanena tathā katvā satta divase yathāsukhaṃ abhiramitvā āgatāgataṃ pucchi – “kacci vo putto laddho”ti? Sabbā “na labhāma, devā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “na me putto uppajjissatī”ti anattamano ahosi. Nāgarā puna tatheva upakkosiṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ upakkosatha, mayā tumhākaṃ vacanena nāṭakāni vissaṭṭhāni, ekāpi puttaṃ na labhati, idāni kiṃ karomā”ti āha. “Deva, etā dussīlā bhavissanti nippuññā, natthi etāsaṃ puttalābhāya puññaṃ, tumhe etāsu puttaṃ alabhantīsupi mā appossukkataṃ āpajjatha, aggamahesī vo sīlavatī devī sīlasampannā, taṃ vissajjetha, tassā putto uppajjissatī”ti.

In the past, in the Malla country, in the royal city of Kusāvatī, a king named Okkāka ruled the kingdom righteously and with equity. His chief queen, the eldest of his sixteen thousand women, was named Sīlavatī; she bore neither a son nor a daughter. Then the townspeople and the country-dwellers gathered at the palace gate and cried out, “The kingdom will perish! The kingdom will perish!” The king opened the lion-window and asked, “While I am ruling, there is no unrighteous conduct. Why do you cry out?” “It is true, Your Majesty, there is no unrighteous conduct, but you have no son to preserve the lineage. Another king will seize the kingdom and destroy it. Therefore, you should wish for a son capable of ruling the kingdom righteously.” “Wishing for a son, what should I do?” “First, for one week, designate the minor harem as 'virtuous dancers' and send them out. If one of them obtains a son, good. If not, then send out the middle harem, and after that the principal harem. Surely, among so many women, one who is meritorious will obtain a son.” The king did according to their word. After they had enjoyed themselves as they pleased for seven days, he asked each one as she returned, “Have you obtained a son?” All replied, “We have not, Your Majesty.” The king became displeased, thinking, “No son will be born to me.” The townspeople again cried out in the same way. The king said, “Why do you cry out? At your word I have sent out the harems, but not one has obtained a son. What should I do now?” “Your Majesty, these women must be immoral and without merit; they have no merit for obtaining a son. Even though you have not obtained a son from them, do not remain unconcerned. Your chief queen, Queen Sīlavatī, is accomplished in moral virtue. Send her out; a son will be born to her.”

So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “ito kira sattame divase rājā sīlavatiṃ deviṃ dhammanāṭakaṃ katvā vissajjessati, purisā sannipatantū”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā sattame divase deviṃ alaṅkārāpetvā rājanivesanā otāretvā vissajjesi. Tassā sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko “kiṃ nu kho”ti āvajjento deviyā puttapatthanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “etissā mayā puttaṃ [P 5.0280] dātuṃ vaṭṭati, atthi nu kho devaloke etissā anucchaviko putto”ti upadhārento bodhisattaṃ addasa. So kira tadā tāvatiṃsabhavane āyuṃ khepetvā uparidevaloke nibbattitukāmo ahosi. Sakko tassa vimānadvāraṃ gantvā taṃ pakkositvā, “mārisa, tayā manussalokaṃ gantvā okkākarañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sampaṭicchāpetvā aparampi devaputtaṃ “tvampi etissā eva putto bhavissasī”ti vatvā “mā kho panassā koci sīlaṃ bhindatū”ti mahallakabrāhmaṇavesena rañño nivesanadvāraṃ agamāsi.

Accepting with, “Good,” he had a drum beaten, announcing: “On the seventh day from today, the king will designate Queen Sīlavatī as a 'virtuous dancer' and send her out. Let the men assemble!” On the seventh day, he had the queen adorned, brought down from the royal palace, and sent her out. Due to the power of her virtue, Sakka’s abode showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting, “What can this be?” understood the queen’s wish for a son and thought: “It is proper for me to give her a son. Is there a suitable son for her in the deva world?” While considering this, he saw the Bodhisatta. It seems the Bodhisatta at that time had exhausted his lifespan in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and wished to be reborn in a higher deva world. Sakka went to the door of his celestial mansion, called to him, and got him to accept, saying: “Friend, you should go to the human world and take conception in the womb of King Okkāka’s chief queen.” He also told another devaputta: “You too will be her son.” Then, thinking, “Let no one violate her virtue,” he went to the king’s palace gate in the guise of an old brahmin.

Mahājanopi nhāto alaṅkato “ahaṃ deviṃ gaṇhissāmi, ahaṃ deviṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti rājadvāre sannipatitvā sakkañca disvā “tvaṃ kasmā āgatosī”ti [M 5.0299] parihāsamakāsi. Sakko “kiṃ maṃ tumhe garahatha, sacepi me sarīraṃ jiṇṇaṃ, rāgo pana na jīrati, sace sīlavatiṃ labhissāmi, ādāya naṃ gamissāmīti āgatomhī”ti vatvā attano ānubhāvena sabbesaṃ puratova aṭṭhāsi. Añño koci tassa tejena purato bhavituṃ nāsakkhi. So taṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nivesanā nikkhamantiññeva hatthe gahetvā pakkāmi. Atha naṃ tattha tattha ṭhitā [V 5.0273] garahiṃsu “passatha, bho, mahallakabrāhmaṇo evaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ deviṃ ādāya gacchati, attano yuttaṃ na jānātī”ti. Devīpi “mahallako maṃ gahetvā gacchatī”ti na aṭṭīyati na harāyati. Rājāpi vātapāne ṭhatvā “ko nu kho deviṃ gahetvā gacchatī”ti olokento taṃ disvā anattamano ahosi.

The great crowd, having bathed and adorned themselves, gathered at the king’s gate, each saying, “I will take the queen! I will take the queen!” Seeing Sakka, they mocked him, saying, “Why have you come?” Sakka replied, “Why do you scorn me? Even if my body is aged, my passion does not age. If I obtain Sīlavatī, I will take her and go—that is why I have come.” By his power, he stood right before them all. No one else could stand before him due to his majesty. As the queen, adorned with all ornaments, was coming out of her dwelling, he took her by the hand and departed. Those standing here and there reproached him, saying, “See, sirs, this old brahmin is taking away the queen of such supreme beauty! He does not know what is fitting for himself.” The queen, too, was neither troubled nor ashamed, thinking, “An old man is taking me away.” The king, standing at the window and watching, wondered, “Who is taking the queen away?” Seeing the old brahmin, he became displeased.

Sakko taṃ ādāya nagaradvārato nikkhamitvā dvārasamīpe ekaṃ gharaṃ māpesi vivaṭadvāraṃ paññattakaṭṭhattharikaṃ. Atha naṃ sā “idaṃ te nivesana”nti pucchi. So “āma, bhadde, pubbe panāhaṃ eko, idānimhā mayaṃ dve janā, ahaṃ bhikkhāya caritvā taṇḍulādīni āharissāmi, tvaṃ imissā kaṭṭhattharikāya nipajjāhī”ti vatvā taṃ mudunā hatthena parāmasanto [P 5.0281] dibbasamphassaṃ pharāpetvā tattha nipajjāpesi. Sā dibbasamphassapharaṇena saññaṃ vissajjesi. Atha naṃ attano ānubhāvena tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ netvā alaṅkatavimāne dibbasayane nipajjāpesi. Sā sattame divase pabujjhitvā taṃ sampattiṃ disvā “na so brāhmaṇo manusso, sakko bhavissatī”ti aññāsi. Sakkopi tasmiṃ samaye pāricchattakamūle dibbanāṭakaparivuto nisinno ahosi. Sā sayanā uṭṭhāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ sakko “varaṃ te, devi, dadāmi, gaṇhāhī”ti āha. “Tena hi, deva, ekaṃ puttaṃ me dehī”ti. “Devi, tiṭṭhatu eko putto, ahaṃ te dve putte dassāmi. Tesu pana eko paññavā bhavissati virūpavā, eko rūpavā na paññavā. Tesu kataraṃ paṭhamaṃ icchasī”ti? “Paññavantaṃ, devā”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā tassā kusatiṇaṃ dibbavatthaṃ dibbacandanaṃ pāricchattakapupphaṃ kokanudañca nāma vīṇaṃ datvā taṃ ādāya rañño sayanagharaṃ pavisitvā raññā saddhiṃ ekasayane nipajjāpetvā aṅguṭṭhakena tassā nābhiṃ parāmasi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe [M 5.0300] bodhisatto tassā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sakkopi sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Paṇḍitā devī gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ jāni.

Sakka took her, went out from the city gate, and near the gate created a house with an open door and a prepared wooden bed. Then she asked him, “Is this your dwelling?” He replied, “Yes, good lady. Before, I was alone, but now we are two. I will go on an alms round and bring back rice and other provisions; you lie down on this wooden bed.” Saying this, he stroked her with his soft hand, suffusing her with divine contact, and laid her down there. With the touch of divine contact, she lost consciousness. Then by his power he took her to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and laid her on a divine couch in an adorned celestial mansion. On the seventh day, she awoke, and seeing that splendor, she knew: “That brahmin was no human; he must be Sakka.” At that time, Sakka was seated at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, surrounded by a troupe of celestial dancers. She rose from her couch, went to him, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then Sakka said to her, “Queen, I give you a boon. Choose one.” “In that case, Your Majesty, give me one son.” “Queen, let us not speak of only one son; I will give you two. But of them, one will be wise but ugly, and the other handsome but not wise. Which of them do you want first?” “The wise one, Your Majesty.” Saying, “Good,” he gave her kusa grass, a divine robe, divine sandalwood, a Pāricchattaka flower, and a lute named Kokanuda. Then, taking her, he entered the king’s bedchamber and laid her on the same bed with the king. With his thumb, he touched her navel. At that moment, the Bodhisatta took conception in her womb. Sakka then returned to his own place. The wise queen knew that conception had been established.

Atha naṃ pabuddho rājā disvā, “devi, kena nītāsī”ti pucchi. “Sakkena, devā”ti. “Ahaṃ paccakkhato ekaṃ mahallakabrāhmaṇaṃ taṃ ādāya gacchantaṃ addasaṃ, kasmā maṃ vañcesī”ti? “Saddahatha, deva, sakko maṃ gahetvā devalokaṃ nesī”ti. “Na saddahāmi, devī”ti. Athassa sā sakkadattiyaṃ kusatiṇaṃ dassetvā “saddahathā”ti āha. Rājā “kusatiṇaṃ nāma yato kutoci labbhatī”ti na saddahi. Athassa sā dibbavatthādīni dassesi. Rājā tāni disvā saddahitvā, “bhadde, sakko tāva taṃ netu, putto pana te laddho”ti pucchi. “Laddho mahārāja, gabbho me patiṭṭhito”ti. So tuṭṭho tassā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi[V 5.0274]. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi, tassa aññaṃ nāmaṃ akatvā kusatiṇanāmameva [P 5.0282] akaṃsu. Kusakumārassa padasā gamanakāle itaro devaputto tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā dasamāse paripuṇṇe puttaṃ vijāyi, tassa “jayampatī”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Te mahantena yasena vaḍḍhiṃsu. Bodhisatto paññavā ācariyassa santike kiñci sippaṃ anuggahetvā attanova paññāya sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi.

Then the king, having awakened, saw her and asked: “Queen, by whom were you taken?” “By Sakka, Your Majesty.” “With my own eyes I saw an old brahmin taking you away. Why do you deceive me?” “Believe me, Your Majesty, Sakka took me to the world of the devas.” “I do not believe you, queen.” Then she showed him the kusa grass given by Sakka and said, “Believe me.” The king said, “Kusa grass can be obtained from anywhere,” and did not believe her. Then she showed him the divine garments and other items. Seeing these, the king believed her and asked: “Good lady, Sakka may have taken you, but have you obtained a son?” “I have, great king; I have conceived.” Delighted, he provided for the protection of her pregnancy. At the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son. Giving him no other name, they named him Kusa. When Prince Kusa was able to walk, the other son of a deva took conception in her womb. When ten months were complete, she gave birth to a son, and they named him Jayampati. They grew up with great renown. The wise Bodhisatta, without learning any craft from a teacher, attained perfection in all the arts by his own wisdom.

Athassa soḷasavassakāle rājā rajjaṃ dātukāmo deviṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, puttassa te rajjaṃ datvā nāṭakāni upaṭṭhapessāma, mayaṃ jīvantāyeva naṃ rajje patiṭṭhitaṃ passissāma, sakalajambudīpe kho pana yassa rañño dhītaraṃ icchati, tamassa ānetvā aggamahesiṃ karissāma, cittamassa jānāhi, kataraṃ rājadhītaraṃ rocesī”ti āha. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “kumārassa imaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā cittaṃ jānāhī”ti ekaṃ paricārikaṃ pesesi. Sā gantvā tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto cintesi – “ahaṃ na rūpavā, rūpasampannā rājadhītā ānītāpi maṃ disvā ‘kiṃ me iminā virūpenā’ti palāyissati iti no lajjitabbakaṃ bhavissati, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, dharamāne mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ accayena nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. So “mayhaṃ neva rajjenattho, na nāṭakehi, ahaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ accayena pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Sā gantvā tassa kathaṃ deviyā ārocesi, devīpi rañño ārocesi. Rājā anattamano hutvā puna katipāhaccayena sāsanaṃ pesesi. Sopi [M 5.0301] paṭibāhatiyeva. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ paṭibāhitvā catutthavāre cintesi – “mātāpitūhi saddhiṃ ekantena paṭipakkhabhāvo nāma na yutto, ekaṃ upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti.

When he was sixteen years old, the king, wishing to give him the kingdom, summoned the queen and said: “Good lady, we will give the kingdom to our son and provide him with dancers. While we are still alive, we wish to see him established in the kingdom. We will bring for him whichever princess in all of Jambudīpa he desires and make her his chief queen. Find out his mind, which princess he fancies.” She agreed, saying, “Very well,” and sent a female attendant, saying: “Go inform the prince of this matter and find out his mind.” She went and told him the matter. On hearing it, the Great Being thought: “I am not handsome. If a princess endowed with beauty is brought here, upon seeing me she will run away, thinking, ‘What do I want with this ugly man?’ This will be a cause for shame. What need have I of the household life? I will look after my parents while they live, and on their passing away, I will go forth.” So he said: “I have no need for the kingdom or for dancers. On my parents’ passing away, I will go forth.” She went and reported his words to the queen, and the queen reported them to the king. The king was displeased and sent a message again after a few days, but he still refused. Having refused up to the third time, on the fourth occasion he thought: “It is not right to be in complete opposition to my parents. I will devise a stratagem.”

So kammārajeṭṭhakaṃ pakkosāpetvā bahuṃ suvaṇṇaṃ datvā “ekaṃ itthirūpakaṃ karohī”ti uyyojetvā tasmiṃ pakkante aññaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā sayampi itthirūpakaṃ akāsi. Bodhisattānañhi adhippāyo nāma samijjhati. Taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ jivhāya avaṇṇanīyasobhaṃ ahosi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto khomaṃ nivāsāpetvā sirigabbhe ṭhapāpesi. So kammārajeṭṭhakena ābhatarūpakaṃ disvā taṃ garahitvā “gaccha amhākaṃ sirigabbhe ṭhapitarūpakaṃ āharā”ti āha. So sirigabbhaṃ paviṭṭho [P 5.0283] taṃ disvā “kumārena saddhiṃ abhiramituṃ ekā devaccharā, āgatā bhavissatī”ti hatthaṃ pasāretuṃ avisahanto nikkhamitvā “deva, sirigabbhe ayyā ekikāva ṭhitā, upagantuṃ na sakkomī”ti āha. “Tāta, gaccha, suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ etaṃ, āharā”ti puna pesito āhari. Kumāro kammārena kataṃ rūpakaṃ suvaṇṇagabbhe nikkhipāpetvā attanā [V 5.0275] kataṃ alaṅkārāpetvā rathe ṭhapāpetvā “evarūpaṃ labhanto gaṇhāmī”ti mātu santikaṃ pahiṇi.

He had the master smith summoned, gave him much gold, and sent him away, saying, 'Make a female image.' When the smith had gone, the prince himself took other gold and made a female image. For the wishes of Bodhisattas are always fulfilled. That golden image was of an indescribable beauty. The Great Being then had it dressed in a robe of fine linen and placed in the auspicious chamber of state. When the master smith brought the image he had made, the prince saw it, and disparaging it, said, 'Go, bring the image that has been placed in our auspicious chamber.' The smith entered the chamber of state, and when he saw the image, he thought, 'A celestial nymph must have come to enjoy herself with the prince.' Not daring to stretch out his hand, he came out and said, 'Lord, a lady is standing alone in the auspicious chamber; I do not dare to approach her.' 'My good man, go! It is a golden image. Bring it.' Sent again, he brought it. The prince had the image made by the smith deposited in the gold treasury, and had the one he himself had made adorned and placed on a chariot. He then sent it to his mother with the message, 'If I can get a princess of such beauty, I will take her.'

Sā amacce pakkosāpetvā, “tātā, mayhaṃ putto mahāpuñño sakkadattiyo anucchavikaṃ kumārikaṃ labhissati, tumhe evarūpaṃ labhantā gaṇhissatha, imaṃ rūpakaṃ paṭicchannayāne ṭhapetvā sakalajambudīpaṃ carantā yassa rañño evarūpaṃ dhītaraṃ passatha, tassetaṃ datvā ‘okkākarājā tumhehi saddhiṃ āvāhaṃ karissatī’ti divasaṃ vavatthapetvā āgacchathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti taṃ ādāya mahantena parivārena nikkhamitvā vicarantā yaṃ rājadhāniṃ pāpuṇanti, tattha sāyanhasamaye mahājanassa samosaraṇaṭṭhāne taṃ rūpakaṃ vatthapupphālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā suvaṇṇasivikaṃ āropetvā titthamagge ṭhapetvā amaccā sayaṃ paṭikkamitvā āgatāgatānaṃ kathāsavanatthaṃ ekamante tiṭṭhanti. Mahājano taṃ oloketvā “suvaṇṇarūpaka”nti saññaṃ akatvā “ayaṃ manussitthī samānāpi devaccharapaṭibhāgā ativiya sobhati, kiṃ nu kho ettha ṭhitā, kuto vā āgatā, amhākaṃ nagare evarūpā natthī”ti vaṇṇento pakkamati. Taṃ sutvā amaccā “sace idha evarūpā dārikā bhaveyya, ‘asukā rājadhītā viya [M 5.0302] asukā amaccadhītā viyā’ti vadeyyuṃ, addhā idha evarūpā natthī”ti taṃ ādāya aññaṃ nagaraṃ gacchanti.

She had the ministers summoned and said, 'My dears, my son is of great merit and a gift from Sakka; he will surely find a suitable princess. If you find one like this, take her. Place this image in a covered carriage and travel through the whole of Jambudīpa. Wherever you see a king’s daughter who resembles this image, give this image to him and say, "King Okkāka will form a marriage alliance with you," and after fixing a day, return.' Saying 'Very well,' they took the image and set out with a large retinue. As they wandered, whenever they reached a royal city, in the evening at the gathering place of the people, they adorned the image with garments, flowers, and ornaments, placed it in a golden palanquin, and set it on the path to the landing place. The ministers themselves would then withdraw and stand to one side to listen to the talk of the people as they came and went. The people would look at it and, not realizing it was a golden image, would praise it and depart, saying, 'Though she is a human woman, she is like a celestial nymph and is exceedingly beautiful. Why is she standing here? Where has she come from? In our city, there is no one like this.' Hearing this, the ministers thought, 'If there were such a girl here, they would say, "She is like such-and-such a king's daughter," or "like such-and-such a minister's daughter." Surely there is no one like her here.' So they took the image and went to another city.

Te evaṃ vicarantā anupubbena maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagaraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Tattha maddarañño aṭṭha dhītaro uttamarūpadharā devaccharapaṭibhāgā, tāsaṃ sabbajeṭṭhikā pabhāvatī nāma. Tassā sarīrato [P 5.0284] bālasūriyassa pabhā viya pabhā niccharanti, andhakārepi catuhatthe antogabbhe padīpakiccaṃ natthi, sabbo gabbho ekobhāsova hoti. Dhātī panassā khujjā, sā pabhāvatiṃ bhojetvā tassā sīsanhāpanatthaṃ aṭṭhahi vaṇṇadāsīhi aṭṭha ghaṭe gāhāpetvā sāyanhasamaye udakatthāya gacchantī titthamagge ṭhitaṃ taṃ rūpakaṃ disvā “pabhāvatī”ti saññāya “ayaṃ dubbinītā ‘sīsaṃ nhāyissāmī’ti amhe udakatthāya pesetvā paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā titthamagge ṭhitā”ti kujjhitvā “are kulalajjāpanike amhehi purimataraṃ āgantvā kasmā idha ṭhitāsi, sace rājā jānissati, nāsessati no”ti vatvā hatthena gaṇḍapasse pahari, hatthatalaṃ bhijjamānaṃ viya jātaṃ. Tato “suvaṇṇarūpaka”nti ñatvā hasamānā tāsaṃ vaṇṇadāsīnaṃ santikaṃ gacchantī “passathetaṃ me kammaṃ, mama dhītātisaññāya pahāraṃ adāsiṃ, ayaṃ mama dhītu santike kimagghati, kevalaṃ me hattho dukkhāpito”ti āha.

Wandering thus, they gradually arrived at the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. There, the king of Madda had eight daughters of supreme beauty, like celestial nymphs. The eldest of them was named Pabhāvatī. From her body, a radiance issued forth like the radiance of the morning sun; even in the dark, in an inner chamber of four cubits, there was no need for a lamp; the whole chamber was filled with a single mass of light. Now her nurse was a hunchback named Khujjā. Having fed Pabhāvatī, she had eight beautiful slave-girls take eight water-pots and was going for water in the evening to wash Pabhāvatī’s head. Seeing the image standing on the path to the landing place, she mistook it for Pabhāvatī and became angry, thinking, 'This ill-behaved girl, saying "I will wash my head," sent us for water, but she has come before us and is standing on the path to the landing place.' She said, 'Hey, you disgrace to your family! Why have you come before us and stood here? If the king finds out, he will ruin us!' With these words, she struck the image on the cheek with her hand. Her palm felt as if it were splitting. Then, realizing it was a golden image, she laughed and went to the beautiful slave-girls, saying, 'Look at what I have done! Thinking it was my daughter, I struck it. What is this worth compared to my daughter? I have only caused pain to my hand.'

Atha naṃ rājadūtā gahetvā “tvaṃ ‘mama dhītā ito abhirūpatarā’ti vadantī kaṃ nāma kathesī”ti [V 5.0276] āhaṃsu. “Maddarañño dhītaraṃ pabhāvatiṃ, idaṃ rūpakaṃ tassā soḷasimpi kalaṃ na agghatī”ti. Te tuṭṭhamānasā rājadvāraṃ gantvā “okkākarañño dūtā dvāre ṭhitā”ti paṭihāresuṃ. Rājā āsanā vuṭṭhāya ṭhitakova “pakkosathā”ti āha. Te pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “mahārāja, amhākaṃ rājā tumhākaṃ ārogyaṃ pucchatī”ti vatvā katasakkārasammānā “kimatthaṃ āgatatthā”ti puṭṭhā “amhākaṃ rañño sīhassaro putto kusakumāro nāma, rājā tassa rajjaṃ dātukāmo amhe tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pahiṇi, tumhākaṃ kira dhītā pabhāvatī, taṃ tassa detha, imañca suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ deyyadhammaṃ gaṇhathā”ti taṃ rūpakaṃ tassa adaṃsu. Sopi “evarūpena mahārājena saddhiṃ vivāhamaṅgalaṃ bhavissatī”ti tuṭṭhacitto sampaṭicchi[P 5.0285]. Atha naṃ dūtā āhaṃsu – “mahārāja, amhehi [M 5.0303] na sakkā papañcaṃ kātuṃ, kumārikāya laddhabhāvaṃ rañño ārocessāma, atha naṃ so āgantvā ādāya gamissatī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā tesaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā vissajjesi. Te gantvā rañño ca deviyā ca ārocesuṃ. Rājā mahantena parivārena kusāvatito nikkhamitvā anupubbena sāgalanagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Maddarājā paccuggantvā taṃ nagaraṃ pavesetvā mahantaṃ sakkāramakāsi.

Then the royal messengers seized the nurse and said, 'You who say, “My daughter is more beautiful than this one,” of whom do you speak?' 'Of Pabhāvatī, the daughter of King Madda. This golden image is not worth even a sixteenth part of her,' she replied. Delighted at heart, they went to the palace gate and had it announced, 'The messengers of King Okkāka are standing at the gate.' The king rose from his seat and, while still standing, said, 'Have them enter.' They entered, paid homage to the king, and said, 'Great king, our king inquires after your health.' After being received with honor and hospitality, they were asked, 'For what purpose have you come?' They replied, 'Our king has a son named Prince Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar. The king wishes to hand over the kingdom to him and has sent us to you. We hear you have a daughter named Pabhāvatī. Please give her to Prince Kusa, and accept this golden image as a gift.' They then presented the image to King Madda. He, with a gladdened mind, accepted, thinking, 'Such a marriage alliance with a great king will be excellent.' Then the messengers said to him, 'Great king, we cannot delay. We will return and inform King Okkāka that the princess has been obtained; he will then come to take her away.' He said, 'Very well,' gave them gifts, and dismissed them. They went and informed the king and Queen Sīlavatī. King Okkāka set out from Kusāvatī with a large retinue and in due course arrived at the city of Sāgala. King Madda went out to meet him, led him into the city, and showed him great honor.

Sīlavatī devī paṇḍitattā “ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissatī”ti ekāhadvīhaccayena maddarājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, suṇisaṃ daṭṭhukāmāmhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ pakkosāpesi. Pabhāvatī sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā dhātigaṇaparivutā āgantvā sassuṃ vandi. Sā taṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ kumārikā abhirūpā, mayhaṃ putto virūpo. Sace esā taṃ passissati, ekāhampi avasitvā palāyissati, upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā maddarājānaṃ āmantetvā, “mahārāja, suṇisā me puttassa anucchavikā, apica kho pana amhākaṃ kulapaveṇiyā āgataṃ cārittaṃ atthi, sace ayaṃ tasmiṃ cāritte vattissati, nessāmi na”nti āha. “Kiṃ pana vo cāritta”nti. “Amhākaṃ vaṃse yāva ekassa gabbhassa patiṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tāva divā sāmikaṃ passituṃ na labhati. Sace esā tathā karissati, nessāmi na”nti. Rājā “kiṃ, amma, sakkhissasi evaṃ vattitu”nti dhītaraṃ pucchi. Sā “āma tātā”ti āha. Tato okkākarājā maddarañño bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā taṃ ādāya pakkāmi. Maddarājāpi mahantena parivārena dhītaraṃ uyyojesi.

Queen Sīlavatī, being wise, thought, 'Who knows what will happen?' After a day or two, she said to King Madda, 'Great king, I wish to see my daughter-in-law.' He agreed and had her summoned. Pabhāvatī, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by a retinue of nurses, came and paid homage to her mother-in-law. Seeing her, the queen thought, 'This princess is extremely beautiful, but my son is ugly. If she sees him, she will not stay even for a single day but will run away. I must devise a plan.' She then addressed King Madda, saying, 'Great king, my daughter-in-law is a perfect match for my son. However, there is a custom that has come down through our lineage. If she will observe that custom, I will take her.' 'And what is your custom?' he asked. 'In our family, until a first pregnancy is established, she is not allowed to see her husband by day. If she agrees to this, I will take her.' The king asked his daughter, 'Dear, will you be able to live according to this custom as Queen Sīlavatī says?' She answered, 'Yes, father.' After Pabhāvatī agreed, King Okkāka gave much wealth to King Madda and departed for the city of Kusāvatī with her. King Madda also sent his daughter off with a great retinue.

Okkāko kusāvatiṃ gantvā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā sabbabandhanāni mocetvā puttassa abhisekaṃ katvā rajjaṃ datvā pabhāvatiṃ aggamahesiṃ kāretvā nagare “kusarājassa āṇā”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Sakalajambudīpatale rājāno yesaṃ dhītaro atthi, te kusarañño dhītaro pahiṇiṃsu[V 5.0277]. Yesaṃ puttā [P 5.0286] atthi, te tena saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ ākaṅkhantā putte upaṭṭhāke katvā pahiṇiṃsu. Bodhisattassa nāṭakaparivāro mahā ahosi, mahantena yasena rajjaṃ kāresi. So pabhāvatiṃ divā passituṃ na labhati, sāpi taṃ divā passituṃ na labhati, ubhinnaṃ rattidassanameva hoti. Tattha pabhāvatiyā sarīrappabhāpi abbohārikā ahosi. Bodhisatto sirigabbhato rattiṃyeva nikkhamati.

King Okkāka went to Kusāvatī, had the city decorated, released all prisoners, consecrated his son as king, handed over the kingdom, and made Pabhāvatī the chief queen. He had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'This is the authority of King Kusa!' All the kings throughout Jambudīpa who had daughters sent them to King Kusa. Those who had sons, desiring friendship with him, sent their sons to serve as his attendants. The Bodhisatta's harem was vast, and he ruled the kingdom with great glory. He was not able to see Pabhāvatī by day, nor was she able to see him; they met only at night. In that place, even Pabhāvatī’s bodily radiance was not apparent. The Bodhisatta would leave the royal chamber only at night.

So [M 5.0304] katipāhaccayena pabhāvatiṃ divā daṭṭhukāmo mātuyā ārocesi. Sā “mā te tāta, rucci, yāva ekaṃ puttaṃ labhasi, tāva āgamehī”ti, paṭikkhipi. So punappunaṃ yāciyeva. Atha naṃ sā āha – “tena hi hatthisālaṃ gantvā hatthimeṇḍavesena tiṭṭha, ahaṃ taṃ tattha ānessāmi, atha naṃ akkhīni pūretvā olokeyyāsi, mā ca attānaṃ jānāpehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā hatthisālaṃ agamāsi. Athassa mātā hatthisālaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā pabhāvatiṃ “ehi sāmikassa hatthino passāmā”ti tattha netvā “ayaṃ hatthī asuko nāma, ayaṃ hatthī asuko nāmā”ti tassā dassesi. Tattha taṃ rājā mātu pacchato gacchantiṃ disvā hatthigopakavesena hatthichakaṇapiṇḍena piṭṭhiyaṃ pahari. Sā kuddhā “rañño kathetvā te hatthaṃ chindāpessāmī”ti vatvā deviṃ ujjhāpesi. Rājamātā “mā amma kujjhī”ti suṇisaṃ saññāpetvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajji. Punapi rājā taṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā assasālāya assagopakavesena taṃ disvā tatheva assachakaṇapiṇḍena pahari. Tadāpi taṃ kuddhaṃ sassu saññāpesi.

After some days, wishing to see Pabhāvatī by day, the king informed his mother. She refused him, saying, 'Do not desire this, my son. Wait until you have a son.' But he pleaded again and again. Then she said to him, 'If you wish to see her so much, go to the elephant stable and stay there in the guise of an elephant groom. I will bring Pabhāvatī there, and then you can look at her to your heart's content. But do not let her know you are her husband.' He agreed and went to the elephant stable. His mother had the stable decorated and, leading Pabhāvatī there, said, 'Come, dear, let us look at your husband's elephants.' She showed her the elephants, saying, 'This elephant is named so-and-so, and this one is so-and-so.' There, the king saw Pabhāvatī walking behind his mother and, in the guise of an elephant groom, struck her on the back with a lump of elephant dung. Angry, she said, 'I will tell the king and have your hand cut off!' and she complained to Queen Sīlavatī. The queen mother calmed her, saying, 'Do not be angry, dear,' and rubbed her back. Later, the king, wishing to see her again, went to the horse stable in the guise of a horse groom. Seeing her, he struck her in the same way with a lump of horse dung. Then, too, the mother-in-law had to soothe her and ask her to be patient.

Punekadivase pabhāvatī mahāsattaṃ passitukāmā hutvā sassuyā ārocetvā “alaṃ mā te ruccī”ti paṭikkhittāpi punappunaṃ yāci. Atha naṃ sā āha – “tena hi sve mama putto nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karissati, tvaṃ sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā taṃ passeyyāsī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā punadivase nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā jayampatikumāraṃ rājavesaṃ gāhāpetvā hatthipiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā bodhisattaṃ pacchimāsane nisīdāpetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kārāpesi. Sā pabhāvatiṃ ādāya sīhapañjare ṭhatvā “passa tava sāmikassa sirisobhagga”nti āha. Sā “anucchaviko [P 5.0287] me sāmiko laddho”ti attamanā ahosi. Taṃ divasaṃ pana mahāsatto hatthimeṇḍavesena jayampatissa pacchimāsane nisīditvā yathādhippāyena pabhāvatiṃ olokento hatthavikārādivasena cittaruciyā keḷiṃ dassesi. Hatthimhi atikkante rājamātā pabhāvatiṃ pucchi – “diṭṭho te, amma, sāmiko”ti. “Āma ayye, pacchimāsane panassa nisinno hatthimeṇḍo ativiya dubbinīto, mayhaṃ hatthavikārādīni dassesi, kasmā evarūpaṃ [M 5.0305] alakkhikaṃ [V 5.0278] rañño pacchimāsane nisīdāpesuṃ, nīharāpehi na”nti? “Amma, rañño pacchimāsane rakkhā nāma icchitabbā”ti.

One day, Pabhāvatī, desiring to see the Great Being, informed her mother-in-law. Although she was refused with the words, 'Enough, do not let it be your wish,' she asked again and again. Then her mother-in-law said to her: 'In that case, tomorrow my son will circumambulate the city. You may open the lion-window and see him.' Having said this, the next day she had the city decorated, had Prince Jayampati take the guise of the king and seated him on an elephant’s back, while seating the Bodhisatta on the rear seat, and had them circumambulate the city. Taking Pabhāvatī with her, she stood at the lion-window and said, 'Behold the splendor and majesty of your husband!' Pabhāvatī was delighted, thinking, 'I have obtained a husband worthy of me.' That day, however, the Great Being, in the guise of an elephant groom, seated in the rear seat behind Jayampati, looked at Pabhāvatī as he pleased and, according to his heart's desire, displayed playful antics with hand gestures and such. When the elephant had passed, the Queen Mother asked Pabhāvatī, 'Did you see your husband, dear?' 'Yes, noble lady. But the elephant groom seated on the rear seat was extremely ill-mannered; he made hand gestures and such at me. Why did they seat such an ill-omened person on the king’s rear seat? Have him removed!' 'Dear,' she replied, 'on the king’s rear seat, what is called a guard is required.'

Sā cintesi – “ayaṃ hatthimeṇḍo ativiya nibbhayo, rājānaṃ ‘rājā’tipi na maññati, kiṃ nu kho esova kusarājā, addhā hi eso ativiya virūpo eva bhavissati, teneva maṃ na dassentī”ti. Sā khujjaṃ kaṇṇamūle āha – “amma, gaccha tāva jānāhi, kiṃ purimāsane nisinnako rājā, udāhu pacchimāsane”ti? “Kathaṃ panāhaṃ jānissāmī”ti. “Sace hi so rājā bhavissati, paṭhamataraṃ hatthipiṭṭhito otarissati, imāya saññāya jānāhī”ti. Sā gantvā ekamante ṭhitā paṭhamaṃ mahāsattaṃ otarantaṃ addasa, pacchā jayampatikumāraṃ. Mahāsattopi ito cito ca olokento khujjaṃ disvā “iminā nāma kāraṇena esā āgatā bhavissatī”ti ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “imaṃ antaraṃ pabhāvatiyā mā kathehī”ti daḷhaṃ vatvā uyyojesi. Sā gantvā “purimāsane nisinno paṭhamaṃ otarī”ti āha. Pabhāvatī tassā vacanaṃ saddahi.

She thought: 'This elephant groom is extremely fearless; he does not even regard the king as “the king.” Could it be that this is King Kusa? Indeed, he must be extremely ugly; for that very reason they do not show him to me.' She whispered in the ear of her hunchbacked attendant: 'Mother, go and find out: is the king the one seated in the front seat, or the one in the back seat?' 'But how shall I know?' 'If he is the king, he will be the first to dismount from the elephant’s back. Know by this sign.' The attendant went and, standing to one side, saw the Great Being dismount first, and then Prince Jayampati. The Great Being, glancing here and there, saw the hunchbacked attendant and, realizing 'She must have come for this reason,' had her summoned. He strictly told her, 'Do not tell Pabhāvatī about this matter,' and sent her away. She went back and said, 'The one seated in the front seat dismounted first.' Pabhāvatī believed her words.

Mahāsattopi puna daṭṭhukāmo hutvā mātaraṃ yāci. Sā paṭikkhipituṃ asakkontī “tena hi aññātakavesena uyyānaṃ gacchāhī”ti āha. So uyyānaṃ gantvā pokkharaṇiyaṃ galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ pavisitvā paduminipattena sīsaṃ chādetvā pupphitapadumena mukhaṃ āvaritvā aṭṭhāsi. Mātāpissa pabhāvatiṃ uyyānaṃ netvā sāyanhasamaye “ime rukkhe passa, sakuṇe passa, mige passā”ti palobhayamānā pokkharaṇītīraṃ pāyāsi. Sā pañcavidhapadumasañchannaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ [P 5.0288] disvā nhāyitukāmā paricārikāhi saddhiṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā kīḷantī taṃ padumaṃ disvā vicinitukāmā hatthaṃ pasāresi. Atha naṃ rājā paduminipattaṃ apanetvā “ahaṃ kusarājā”ti vatvā hatthe gaṇhi. Sā tassa mukhaṃ disvā “yakkho maṃ gaṇhī”ti viravitvā tattheva visaññitaṃ pattā. Athassā rājā hatthaṃ muñci. Sā saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā “kusarājā kira maṃ hatthe gaṇhi, imināvāhaṃ hatthisālāya hatthichakaṇapiṇḍena, assasālāya assachakaṇapiṇḍena pahaṭā, ayameva maṃ hatthissa pacchimāsane nisīditvā uppaṇḍesi, kiṃ me evarūpena dummukhena patinā, imaṃ jahitvā ahaṃ jīvantī aññaṃ patiṃ labhissāmī”ti cintetvā attanā saddhiṃ āgate amacce pakkosāpetvā “mama yānavāhanaṃ sajjaṃ karotha, ajjeva gamissāmī”ti āhaṃ[M 5.0306]. Te rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā cintesi – “sace gantuṃ na labhissati, hadayamassā phalissati, gacchatu puna taṃ attano balena ānessāmī”ti cintetvā athassā gamanaṃ anujāni. Sā pitunagarameva agamāsi.

The Great Being, desiring to see her again, entreated his mother. Unable to refuse, she said: 'In that case, go to the park in disguise.' He went to the park, entered the pond up to his neck in water, covered his head with a lotus leaf, and stood concealing his face with a blooming lotus. His mother, taking Pabhāvatī to the park in the evening and enticing her by saying, 'Look at these trees, look at these birds, look at these deer,' led her to the edge of the pond. Seeing the pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, Pabhāvatī wished to bathe and descended into the pond with her attendants. While playing, she saw that lotus and, wishing to pick it, stretched out her hand. Then the king removed the lotus leaf, said, 'I am King Kusa,' and took her hand. Seeing his face, she cried out, 'A yakkha has seized me!' and fainted on the spot. Then the king released her hand. Regaining consciousness, she thought: 'So King Kusa has taken my hand! It was by him that I was struck with a lump of elephant dung in the elephant stable, and with a lump of horse dung in the horse stable. It was he who mocked me while seated on the rear seat of the elephant. What use have I for a husband with such an ugly face? I will leave him and, while I am alive, I will find another husband.' Having thought this, she summoned the ministers who had come with her and said: 'Prepare my vehicles and mounts; I will leave this very day.' They informed the king. The king thought: 'If she is not allowed to go, her heart will break. Let her go; I will bring her back again by my own power.' Thinking thus, he permitted her departure. She went back to her father’s city.

Mahāsattopi [V 5.0279] uyyānato nagaraṃ pavisitvā alaṅkatapāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Bodhisattañhi sā pubbapatthanāvasena na icchi, sopi pubbakammavaseneva virūpo ahosi. Atīte kira bārāṇasiyaṃ dvāragāme uparimavīthiyā ca heṭṭhimavīthiyā ca dve kulāni vasiṃsu. Ekassa kulassa dve puttā ahesuṃ. Ekassa ekāva dhītā ahosi. Dvīsu puttesu bodhisatto kaniṭṭho. Taṃ kumārikaṃ jeṭṭhakassa adaṃsu. Kaniṭṭho adārabharaṇo bhātu santikeyeva vasi. Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ ghare atirasakapūve paciṃsu. Bodhisatto araññaṃ gato hoti. Tassa pūvaṃ ṭhapetvā avasese bhājetvā khādiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe paccekabuddho bhikkhāya gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. Bodhisattassa bhātujāyā “cūḷapatino aññaṃ pūvaṃ pacissāmī”ti taṃ gahetvā paccekabuddhassa adāsi. Sopi taṃ khaṇaññeva araññato āgacchi. Atha naṃ sā āha – “sāmi, cittaṃ pasādehi, tava koṭṭhāso paccekabuddhassa dinno”ti. So [P 5.0289] “tava koṭṭhāsaṃ khāditvā mama koṭṭhāsaṃ desi, ahaṃ kiṃ khādissāmī”ti kuddho paccekabuddhaṃ anugantvā pattato pūvaṃ gaṇhi. Sā mātu gharaṃ gantvā navavilīnaṃ campakapupphavaṇṇaṃ sappiṃ āharitvā paccekabuddhassa pattaṃ pūresi, taṃ obhāsaṃ muñci. Sā taṃ disvā patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi – “bhante, iminā dānabalena nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne me sarīraṃ obhāsajātaṃ hotu, uttamarūpadharā ca bhaveyyaṃ, iminā ca me asappurisena saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne vāso mā ahosī”ti. Iti sā imissā pubbapatthanāya vasena taṃ na icchi. Bodhisattopi taṃ pūva tasmiṃ sappipatte osīdāpetvā patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi – “bhante, imaṃ yojanasate vasantimpi ānetvā mama pādaparicārikaṃ kātuṃ samattho bhaveyya”nti. Tattha yaṃ so kuddho gantvā pūvaṃ gaṇhi, tassa pubbakammassa vasena virūpo ahosi, pubbapatthanāya sā ca taṃ na icchīti.

The Bodhisatta entered the city from the park and ascended his adorned palace. Indeed, she did not desire the Bodhisatta because of that past aspiration, and he was ugly because of the power of his past kamma. In the past, it is said, two families lived in a village at the gate of Bārāṇasī, one on the upper street and one on the lower street. One family had two sons, while the other had only one daughter. Of the two sons, the Bodhisatta was the younger. They gave that girl to the elder brother. The younger brother, not supporting a wife of his own, lived with his brother. Then one day, in that house, they baked exceedingly delicious cakes. The Bodhisatta had gone to the forest. Setting aside his portion of the cake, they divided and ate the rest. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha came to the door of the house for alms. The Bodhisatta’s sister-in-law, thinking, 'I will bake another cake for my younger brother-in-law,' took his portion and gave it to the Paccekabuddha. He arrived from the forest at that very moment. Then she said to him, 'Lord, be pleased; your portion has been given to the Paccekabuddha.' Angry, he said, 'Having eaten your own portion, you give mine away; what shall I eat?' and following the Paccekabuddha, he snatched the cake from his bowl. She went to her mother’s house, brought freshly melted ghee the color of a campaka flower, and filled the Paccekabuddha’s bowl; it emitted a radiance. Seeing that, she made an aspiration: 'Venerable sir, by the power of this gift, in every place I am reborn, may my body be radiant and may I possess supreme beauty, and may I never have to live in the same place as this ignoble man.' Thus, because of this past aspiration, she did not desire him. The Bodhisatta also, having dipped that cake into the bowl of ghee, made an aspiration: 'Venerable sir, may I be able to bring her, even if she lives a hundred yojanas away, and make her my foot-servant.' In that matter, because he angrily went and took the cake, he became ugly by the power of that past kamma, and she did not desire him because of her past aspiration.

So pabhāvatiyā gatāya sokappatto ahosi, nānākārehi paricārayamānāpi naṃ sesitthiyo olokāpetumpi nāsakkhiṃsu,[M 5.0307], pabhāvatirahitamassa sakalampi nivesanaṃ tucchaṃ viya khāyi. So “idāni sāgalanagaraṃ pattā bhavissatī”ti paccūsasamaye mātu santikaṃ gantvā, “amma, ahaṃ pabhāvatiṃ ānessāmi, tumhe rajjaṃ anusāsathā”ti vadanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

When Pabhāvatī had gone, he was overcome with sorrow. Though the other women attended to him in various ways, they could not even get him to look at them. Bereft of Pabhāvatī, the entire palace seemed empty to him. Thinking, 'By now she must have reached the city of Sāgala,' he went to his mother at dawn and, saying, 'Mother, I will bring Pabhāvatī back; you rule the kingdom,' he spoke the first verse as he wished to entrust the kingdom to her:

1.

1.

“Idaṃ te raṭṭhaṃ sadhanaṃ sayoggaṃ, sakāyuraṃ sabbakāmūpapannaṃ;

Idaṃ te rajjaṃ anusāsa amma, gacchāmahaṃ yattha piyā pabhāvatī”ti.

'This kingdom is yours, with its wealth, its transport, and its regalia, replete with all desires. Rule this kingdom, mother; I am going to where my beloved Pabhāvatī is.'

Tattha sayogganti hatthiyoggādisahitaṃ. Sakāyuranti sapañcarājakakudhabhaṇḍaṃ. Anusāsa, ammāti [V 5.0280] so kira purisassa rajjaṃ datvā puna gaṇhanaṃ nāma na yuttanti pitu vā bhātu vā aniyyādetvā mātu niyyādento evamāha.

Therein, 'sayoggaṃ' means together with its elephant-vehicles and so on. 'Sakāyuraṃ' means with the five articles of royal regalia. 'Rule, mother'—it is said he spoke thus, not entrusting it to his father or brother but to his mother, because he thought it was not proper for a man to be given the kingdom and then have it taken back.

Sā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “tena hi, tāta, appamatto bhaveyyāsi, mātugāmo nāma aparisuddhahadayo”ti vatvā nānaggarasabhojanassa suvaṇṇakaroṭiṃ pūretvā “idaṃ antarāmagge bhuñjeyyāsī”ti [P 5.0290] vatvā uyyojesi.
