So taṃ ādāya mātaraṃ vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā “jīvanto puna tumhe passissāmī”ti vatvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā pañcāvudhaṃ sannayhitvā bhattakaroṭiyā saddhiṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ pasibbake katvā kokanudañca vīṇaṃ ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā mahabbalo mahāthāmo yāva majjhanhikā paṇṇāsa yojanāni gantvā bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā sesadivasabhāgena puna paṇṇāsa yojanāni gantvā ekāheneva yojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ khepetvā sāyanhasamaye nhatvā sāgalanagaraṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ paviṭṭhamatteyeva tassa tejena pabhāvatī sayanapiṭṭhe saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ nipajji. Bodhisattaṃ kilantindriyaṃ vīthiyā gacchantaṃ aññatarā itthī disvā pakkosāpetvā nisīdāpetvā pāde dhovāpetvā sayanaṃ dāpesi. So kilantakāyo nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami.

Hearing his words, she said, 'In that case, dear, be heedful; womankind is indeed impure of heart.' Then, filling a golden vessel with various choice foods, she sent him off, saying, 'Eat this on the way.' Taking it, he paid respects to his mother, circumambulated her three times, and saying, 'If I live, I shall see you again,' he entered his royal chamber, armed himself with the five weapons, put a thousand coins into a bag along with the food vessel, took his lute named Kokanuda, and left the city. Setting out on the journey, being of great strength and power, he traveled fifty yojanas by midday, ate his meal, and in the remaining part of the day traveled another fifty yojanas, thus completing a journey of a hundred yojanas in a single day. Arriving in the evening, he bathed and entered the city of Sāgala. The moment he entered, by his power, Pabhāvatī was unable to remain on her couch and got down to lie on the floor. A certain woman, seeing the Bodhisatta with his faculties weary as he walked along the street, called him over, had him sit down, washed his feet, and gave him a bed. His body being weary, he lay down and fell asleep.

Atha sā tasmiṃ niddamupagate bhattaṃ sampādetvā taṃ pabodhetvā bhattaṃ bhojesi. So tuṭṭho tassā saddhiṃ bhattakaroṭiyā kahāpaṇasahassaṃ [M 5.0308] adāsi. So pañcāvudhaṃ tattheva ṭhapetvā “gantabbaṭṭhānaṃ me atthī”ti vatvā vīṇaṃ ādāya hatthisālaṃ gantvā “ajja me idha vasituṃ detha, gandhabbaṃ vo karissāmī”ti vatvā hatthigopakehi anuññāto ekamante nipajjitvā thokaṃ niddāyitvā paṭippassaddhadaratho uṭṭhāya vīṇaṃ muñcitvā “sāgalanagaravāsino imaṃ saddaṃ suṇantū”ti vīṇaṃ vādento gāyi. Pabhāvatī bhūmiyaṃ nipannā taṃ saddaṃ sutvāva “ayaṃ na aññassa vīṇāsaddo, nissaṃsayaṃ kusarājā mamatthāya āgato”ti aññāsi. Maddarājāpi taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “ativiya madhuraṃ vādeti, sve etaṃ pakkosāpetvā mama gandhabbaṃ kāressāmī”ti cintesi.

Then, when he had fallen asleep, she prepared food and, waking him, fed him. Pleased, he gave her the thousand coins along with the food vessel. Leaving the five weapons there, he said, 'I have a place to go,' and taking his lute, he went to the elephant stable. He said, 'Allow me to stay here for today, and I will perform music for you.' Having received permission from the elephant keepers, he lay down in a corner and slept a little. When his fatigue was allayed, he rose, tuned his lute, and thinking, 'May all the inhabitants of Sāgala hear this sound,' he played the lute and sang. Pabhāvatī, lying on the floor, heard that sound and knew, 'This is the sound of no other lute; without doubt, King Kusa has come for my sake.' King Madda also heard the sound and thought, 'He plays exceedingly sweetly; tomorrow I will summon him and have him perform music for me.'

Bodhisatto “na sakkā idha vasamānena pabhāvatī daṭṭhuṃ, aṭṭhānameta”nti pātova nikkhamitvā sāyaṃ bhuttageheyeva pātarāsaṃ bhuñjitvā vīṇaṃ ṭhapetvā rājakumbhakārassa santikaṃ gantvā tassa antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagantvā ekadivaseneva gharaṃ mattikāya pūretvā [P 5.0291] “bhājanāni karomi ācariyā”ti vatvā, “āma, kārohī”ti vutte ekaṃ mattikāpiṇḍaṃ cakke ṭhapetvā cakkaṃ [V 5.0281] āviñchi, sakiṃ āviddhameva yāva majjhanhikātikkamā bhamiyeva. So nānāvaṇṇāni khuddakamahantāni bhājanāni katvā pabhāvatiyā atthāya bhājanaṃ karonto nānārūpāni samuṭṭhāpesi. Bodhisattānañhi adhippāyo nāma samijjhati, “tāni rūpāni pabhāvatīyeva passatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. So sabbabhājanāni sukkhāpetvā pacitvā gehaṃ pūresi. Kumbhakāro nānābhājanāni gahetvā rājakulaṃ agamāsi. Rājā disvā “kenimāni katānī”ti pucchi. “Mayā, devā”ti. “Ahaṃ tayā katāni jānāmi, kathehi, kena katānī”ti? “Antevāsikena me devā”ti. “Na te so antevāsī, ācariyo te so, tvaṃ tassa santike sippaṃ sikkha, ito paṭṭhāya ca so mama dhītānaṃ bhājanāni karotu, imañcassa sahassaṃ dehī”ti sahassaṃ dāpetvā “nānāvaṇṇāni imāni khuddakabhājanāni mama dhītānaṃ dehī”ti āha.

The Bodhisatta thought: ‐It is not possible to see Pabhāvatġ while living here; this is not the proper place.‑ So he left early in the morning, and after eating his morning meal at the house where he had eaten the previous evening, he set aside his lute and went to the royal potter. He became his apprentice and in a single day filled the house with clay. Saying, ‐I will make pots, teacher,‑ and being told, ‐Yes, make them,‑ he placed a lump of clay on the wheel and turned it. With a single spin, it kept turning until after midday. He made various small and large pots of different colors, and while making a pot for Pabhāvatġ, he created many figures on it. For the intentions of Bodhisattas are always fulfilled. He made a determination: ‐May Pabhāvatġ alone see these figures.‑ After drying and firing all the pots, he filled the house. The potter took the various pots and went to the royal court. The king saw them and asked, ‐Who made these?‑ ‐I did, Your Majesty.‑ ‐I know the ones you make. Tell me, who made these?‑ ‐My apprentice, Your Majesty.‑ ‐He is not your apprentice; he is your teacher. You should learn the craft from him. From now on, let him make pots for my daughters. And give him this thousand.‑ Having had a thousand given, he said, ‐Give these small pots of various colors to my daughters.‑

So tāni tāsaṃ santikaṃ netvā “imāni vo kīḷanatthāya khuddakabhājanānī”ti āha. Tā sabbā āgamiṃsu. Kumbhakāro mahāsattena pabhāvatiyā atthāya katabhājanameva tassā adāsi. Sā ca bhājanaṃ gahetvā [M 5.0309] tattha attano ca mahāsattassa ca khujjāya ca rūpaṃ passitvā “idaṃ na aññena kataṃ, kusarājeneva kata”nti ñatvā kujjhitvā bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā “iminā mayhaṃ attho natthi, icchantānaṃ dehī”ti āha. Athassā bhaginiyo kuddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “khuddakabhājanaṃ kusaraññā katanti maññasi, idaṃ tena na kataṃ, kumbhakāreneva kataṃ, gaṇhāhi na”nti avahasiṃsu. Sā tena katabhāvaṃ tassa ca āgatabhāvaṃ tāsaṃ na kathesi. Kumbhakāro sahassaṃ bodhisattassa datvā “tāta, rājā te tuṭṭho, ito kira paṭṭhāya rājadhītānaṃ bhājanāni kareyyāsi, ahaṃ tāsaṃ harissāmī”ti āha.

He took them to the princesses and said: ‐Here are some small pots for you to play with.‑ They all came. The potter gave to Pabhāvatġ the very pot that had been made for her by the Great Being. Taking the pot and seeing on it the figures of herself, the Great Being, and the hunchbacked woman, she recognized: ‐This was not made by another; it was made by King Kusa himself!‑ Angered, she threw it on the ground and said: ‐This is of no use to me. Give it to those who want it.‑ Then her sisters, noticing she was angry, mocked her, saying: ‐Do you think this little pot was made by King Kusa? It was not made by him; it was made by the potter. Take it!‑ But she did not tell them that it had been made by him and that he had come. The potter gave the thousand to the Bodhisatta and said: ‐My dear, the king is pleased with you. From now on, it seems, you are to make the pots for the princesses, and I will deliver them.‑

So “idhāpi vasantena na sakkā pabhāvatī daṭṭhu”nti taṃ sahassaṃ tasseva datvā rājupaṭṭhākassa naḷakārassa santikaṃ gantvā tassa antevāsiko hutvā pabhāvatiyā atthāya tālavaṇṭaṃ katvā tattheva setacchattañca āpānabhūmiñca [P 5.0292] vatthaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaṃ pabhāvatiñcāti nānārūpāni dassesi. Naḷakāro tañca aññañca tena katabhaṇḍakaṃ ādāya rājakulaṃ agamāsi. Rājā disvā “kenimāni katānī”ti pucchitvā purimanayeneva sahassaṃ datvā “imāni naḷakārabhaṇḍāni mama dhītānaṃ dehī”ti āha. Sopi bodhisattena pabhāvatiyā atthāya kataṃ tālavaṇṭaṃ tassāyeva adāsi. Tatrapi rūpāni añño jano na passati, pabhāvatī pana disvā kusaraññā katabhāvaṃ ñatvā “gaṇhitukāmā gaṇhantū”ti kuddhā bhūmiyaṃ khipi[V 5.0282]. Atha naṃ sesā avahasiṃsu. Naḷakāro sahassaṃ āharitvā bodhisattassa datvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi.

Thinking, ‐Even while living here, it is not possible to see Pabhāvatġ,‑ he gave that thousand to the potter and went to the king’s attendant, a reed-worker. He became his apprentice and, for Pabhāvatġ’s sake, made a palm-leaf fan. On it he depicted various figures: a white parasol, a drinking pavilion, and Pabhāvatġ standing holding a cloth. The reed-worker took that fan and other items made by him and went to the royal court. The king saw them, asked, ‐Who made these?‑ and, in the same way as before, gave a thousand, saying: ‐Give these reed-wares to my daughters.‑ He too gave to Pabhāvatġ the very palm-leaf fan made by the Bodhisatta for her. Here too, other people did not see the figures, but Pabhāvatġ saw them and, recognizing that it had been made by King Kusa, she angrily threw it on the ground, saying: ‐Let those who want to take it, take it!‑ Then the others mocked her. The reed-worker brought the thousand, gave it to the Bodhisatta, and reported the matter to him.

So “idampi mayhaṃ avasanaṭṭhāna”nti sahassaṃ tasseva datvā rājamālākārassa santikaṃ gantvā antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagantvā nānāvidhaṃ mālāvikatiṃ ganthitvā pabhāvatiyā atthāya nānārūpavicitraṃ ekaṃ cumbaṭakaṃ akāsi. Mālākāro taṃ sabbaṃ ādāya rājakulaṃ agamāsi. Rājā disvā “kenimāni ganthitānī”ti pucchi. “Mayā, devā”ti. “Ahaṃ tayā ganthitāni jānāmi, kathehi, kena ganthitānī”ti? “Antevāsikena me[M 5.0310], devā”ti. “Na so antevāsī, ācariyo te so, tvaṃ tassa santike sippaṃ sikkha, ito paṭṭhāya ca so mama dhītānaṃ pupphāni ganthatu, imañcassa sahassaṃ dehī”ti sahassaṃ datvā “imāni pupphāni mama dhītānaṃ dehī”ti āha. Sopi bodhisattena pabhāvatiyā atthāya kataṃ cumbaṭakaṃ tassāyeva adāsi. Sā tattha attano ca rañño ca rūpehi saddhiṃ nānārūpāni disvā tena katabhāvaṃ ñatvā kujjhitvā bhūmiyaṃ khipi. Sesā bhaginiyo taṃ tatheva avahasiṃsu. Mālākāropi sahassaṃ āharitvā bodhisattassa datvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi.

Thinking, ‐This too is not a place for me to live,‑ he gave the thousand to the reed-worker and went to the royal garland-maker, becoming his apprentice. He strung various kinds of garlands and for Pabhāvatġ’s sake made a head-wreath adorned with various figures. The garland-maker took all this and went to the royal court. The king saw it and asked, ‐Who strung these?‑ ‐I did, Your Majesty.‑ ‐I know the ones you string. Tell me, who strung these?‑ ‐My apprentice, Your Majesty.‑ ‐He is not your apprentice; he is your teacher. You should learn the craft from him. From now on, let him string the flowers for my daughters. And give him this thousand.‑ Having had a thousand given, he said, ‐Give these flowers to my daughters.‑ The garland-maker too gave to Pabhāvatġ the very head-wreath made by the Bodhisatta for her. Seeing on it various figures along with those of herself and the king, she recognized that he had made it and, enraged, threw it to the ground. Her other sisters mocked her in the same way. The garland-maker also brought the thousand, gave it to the Bodhisatta, and reported the matter to him.

So “idampi mayhaṃ avasanaṭṭhāna”nti sahassaṃ tasseva datvā rañño sūdassa santikaṃ gantvā antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagacchi. Athekadivasaṃ sūdo rañño bhojanavikatiṃ haranto attano atthāya pacituṃ bodhisattassa aṭṭhimaṃsaṃ adāsi. So taṃ tathā sampādesi, yathāssa gandho sakalanagaraṃ avatthari. Rājā [P 5.0293] taṃ ghāyitvā “kiṃ te mahānase aññampi maṃsaṃ pacasī”ti pucchi. “Natthi, deva, apica kho pana me antevāsikassa aṭṭhimaṃsaṃ pacanatthāya dinnaṃ, tasseva so gandho bhavissatī”ti. Rājā āharāpetvā tato thokaṃ jivhagge ṭhapesi, tāvadeva satta rasaharaṇisahassāni khobhentaṃ phari. Rājā rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā sahassaṃ datvā “ito paṭṭhāya tava antevāsinā mama ca dhītānañca me bhattaṃ pacāpetvā tvaṃ mayhaṃ āhara, so me dhītānaṃ haratū”ti āha. Sūdo gantvā tassa ārocesi. So taṃ sutvā “idāni me manoratho matthakaṃ patto, idāni panāhaṃ pabhāvatiṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhissāmī”ti tuṭṭho taṃ sahassaṃ tasseva datvā punadivase bhattaṃ sampādetvā rañño bhattabhājanāni pesetvā rājadhītānaṃ bhattakājaṃ sayaṃ gahetvā pabhāvatiyā vasanapāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Sā taṃ bhattakājaṃ ādāya pāsādaṃ abhiruhantaṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ attano ananucchavikaṃ dāsakammakarehi kattabbaṃ karoti. Sace panāhaṃ katipāhaṃ tuṇhī bhavissāmi, ‘idāni maṃ esā rocatī’ti saññī hutvā katthaci agantvā maṃ olokento idheva vasissati, idāneva taṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā muhuttampi idha vasituṃ [V 5.0283] adatvā palāpessāmī”ti. Sā dvāraṃ aḍḍhavivaṭaṃ katvā ekaṃ hatthaṃ kavāṭe laggetvā ekena hatthena aggaḷaṃ uppīḷetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thinking, “This too is not a place for me to stay,” he gave the thousand to that same man and went to the king’s cook, becoming his apprentice. One day, while the cook was taking the king’s various dishes, he gave the Bodhisatta some meat on the bone to cook for himself. He prepared it in such a way that its fragrance pervaded the whole city. The king smelled it and asked, “Are you cooking some other meat in the kitchen?” “No, Your Majesty, but I gave my apprentice some meat on the bone to cook; that must be its fragrance.” The king had some brought and placed a little on the tip of his tongue; immediately it spread, stimulating the seven thousand taste nerves. Ensnared by craving for the flavor, the king gave a thousand and said, “From now on, have your apprentice cook the food for me and for my daughters; you bring mine, and let him bring theirs.” The cook went and told him. Hearing this, he was delighted, thinking, “Now my desire has reached its peak; now I shall see Pabhāvatī.” He gave that thousand to the cook and on the next day, after preparing the meal, he sent the king’s food dishes and, taking the carrying-pole of food for the princesses himself, he went up to the palace where Pabhāvatī lived. Seeing him ascending to the palace carrying the food-pole, she thought, “This man is performing an unsuitable task that should be done by slaves and servants. If I remain silent for a few days, he will think, ‘Now she likes me,’ and he will stay right here watching me without going anywhere. I will revile and abuse him right now and drive him away, not letting him stay here even for a moment.” She opened the door halfway, placed one hand on the door leaf, pressed the bolt with the other, and spoke the second stanza:

2.

2.

“Anujjubhūtena [M 5.0311] haraṃ mahantaṃ, divā ca ratto ca nisīthakāle;

Paṭigaccha tvaṃ khippaṃ kusāvatiṃ kusa, nicchāmi dubbaṇṇamahaṃ vasanta”nti.

“Carrying a great load with a crooked heart, by day and by night, and at the time of midnight; go back quickly to Kusāvatī, Kusa! I do not want an ugly one living here.”

Tassattho – mahārāja, tvaṃ bhattakārako hutvā ujukena cittena yopi te sīsaṃ bhindeyya, tassapetaṃ kammaṃ na karosi, anujubhūtena pana cittena mamatthāya etaṃ mahantaṃ kājaṃ haranto divā ca ratto ca nisīthakāle ca mahantaṃ [P 5.0294] dukkhaṃ anubhavissasi, kiṃ te tena anubhūtena dukkhena, tvaṃ attano nagaraṃ kusāvatimeva paṭigaccha, aññaṃ attanā sadisiṃ atirasakapūvasaṇṭhānamukhiṃ yakkhiniṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā rajjaṃ kārehīti. Nicchāmi dubbaṇṇamahaṃ vasantanti ahaṃ pana taṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ dussaṇṭhitaṃ idha vasantaṃ na icchāmīti.

The meaning is: “Great king, having become a cook, you would not do this work even for someone who might break your head if you had an upright heart; but with a crooked heart, for my sake, carrying this great yoke, you will experience great suffering by day, by night, and at midnight. What is the use of that experienced suffering? Go back to your own city, Kusāvatī. Make some other ogress like yourself, with a face shaped like a very tasty cake, your chief queen, and rule your kingdom.” “I do not want an ugly one living here” means: “I do not want you, who are ugly and misshapen, living here.”

So “pabhāvatiyā me santikā kathā laddhā”ti tuṭṭhacitto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Delighted at the thought, “I have received a response from Pabhāvatī,” he recited three stanzas:

3.

3.

“Nāhaṃ gamissāmi ito kusāvatiṃ, pabhāvatī vaṇṇapalobhito tava;

Ramāmi maddassa niketaramme, hitvāna raṭṭhaṃ tava dassane rato.

“I will not go from here to Kusāvatī, Pabhāvatī, for I am captivated by your beauty. Having abandoned my kingdom, I delight in the lovely home of the Madda king, devoted to the sight of you.

4.

4.

“Pabhāvatī vaṇṇapalobhito tava, sammūḷharūpo vicarāmi mediniṃ;

Disaṃ na jānāmi kutomhi āgato, tayamhi matto migamandalocane.

“O Pabhāvatī, captivated by your beauty, I wander the earth completely bewildered. I do not know the direction or whence I have come; I am intoxicated by you, O maiden with eyes like a young deer.”

5.

5.

“Suvaṇṇacīravasane, jātarūpasumekhale;

Sussoṇi tava kāmā hi, nāhaṃ rajjena matthiko”ti.

“O you clad in golden robes, with a beautiful girdle of gold! O you of lovely hips, because of desire for you, I have no need for a kingdom.”

Tattha ramāmīti abhiramāmi na ukkaṇṭhāmi. Sammūḷharūpoti kilesasammūḷho hutvā. Tayamhi mattoti tayi mattomhi, tayā vā mattomhi. Suvaṇṇacīravasaneti suvaṇṇakhacitavatthavasane. Nāhaṃ rajjena matthikoti na ahaṃ rajjena atthiko.

Therein, ‘I delight’ means: I take great pleasure, I am not dissatisfied. ‘Bewildered in form’ means: being bewildered by the defilements. ‘Intoxicated by you’ means: I am intoxicated in you, or I am intoxicated by you. ‘Clad in golden garments’ means: wearing clothes interwoven with gold. ‘I have no need for the kingdom’ means: I am not one who has need of a kingdom.

Evaṃ [M 5.0312] vutte sā cintesi – “ahaṃ etaṃ ‘vippaṭisārī bhavissatī’ti paribhāsāmi, ayaṃ pana rajjitvāva katheti, sace kho pana maṃ ‘ahaṃ kusarājā’ti vatvā hatthe gaṇheyya, ko [V 5.0284] taṃ nivāreyya, koci no imaṃ kathaṃ suṇeyyā”ti dvāraṃ thaketvā sūciṃ datvā anto aṭṭhāsi. Sopi bhattakājaṃ āharitvā bhattaṃ vaḍḍhetvā rājadhītaro bhojesi. Pabhāvatī “gaccha kusarājena pakkabhattaṃ āharā”ti khujjaṃ pesesi. Sā āharitvā “bhuñjāhī”ti āha. Nāhaṃ tena pakkabhattaṃ bhuñjāmi, tvaṃ bhuñjitvā attano laddhanivāpaṃ gahetvā bhattaṃ pacitvā āhara, kusarañño āgatabhāvañca mā kassaci ārocesīti. Khujjā tato paṭṭhāya tassā koṭṭhāsaṃ āharitvā sayaṃ bhuñjati, attano koṭṭhāsaṃ tassā upaneti. Kusarājāpi [P 5.0295] tato paṭṭhāya taṃ passituṃ alabhanto cintesi – “atthi nu kho pabhāvatiyā mayi sineho, udāhu natthi, vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti. So pana rājadhītaro bhojetvā bhattakājaṃ ādāya nikkhanto tassā gabbhadvāre pāsādatalaṃ pādena paharitvā bhājanāni ghaṭṭetvā nitthunitvā visaññī hutvā viya avakujjo pati. Sā tassa nitthunitasaddena dvāraṃ vivaritvā taṃ bhattakājena otthataṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ sakalajambudīpe aggarājā maṃ nissāya rattindivaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhoti, sukhumālatāya bhattakājena avatthato patati, jīvati nu kho, no vā”ti. Sā gabbhato nikkhamitvā tassa nāsavātaṃ upadhāretuṃ gīvaṃ pasāretvā mukhaṃ olokesi. So mukhapūraṃ kheḷaṃ gahetvā tassā sarīre pātesi. Sā taṃ paribhāsitvā gabbhaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ aḍḍhavivaṭaṃ thaketvā ṭhitā gāthamāha –

When this was said, she thought: “I rebuke him thinking, ‘He will feel remorse,’ but he speaks only with infatuation. If he were to say, ‘I am King Kusa,’ and seize me by the hand, who could stop him? And someone might hear this talk.” So she closed the door, shot the bolt, and stayed inside. He too, carrying the food on a pole, served the food and fed the princesses. Pabhāvatī sent the hunchbacked woman, saying, “Go, bring the food cooked by King Kusa.” She brought it and said, “Please eat.” Pabhāvatī said: “I will not eat food cooked by King Kusa. You eat it, and after taking your own allotted portion, cook food and bring it. And do not tell anyone that King Kusa has come.” From then on, the hunchbacked woman would take Pabhāvatī’s portion and eat it herself, and would give her own portion to Pabhāvatī. King Kusa, being unable to see Pabhāvatī from then on, thought: “Does Pabhāvatī have affection for me, or not? I will test her.” Then, after feeding the princesses, he took the food-carrying pole and went out. Near the door of her chamber, on the palace terrace, he struck the floor with his feet, making the vessels rattle and roll, and groaning, he fell face down as if he had become unconscious. Hearing the sound of his groaning, she opened the door and, seeing him fallen, pinned by the carrying-pole, thought: “This is the foremost king in all of Jambudīpa. Because of me, he suffers greatly day and night. Being so delicate, he lies pinned by the food-carrying pole. Is he still alive or not?” She came out of her chamber and, stretching her neck to check the breath from his nose, looked at his face. He took a mouthful of spittle and spat it on her, hitting her body. Rebuking him, she entered her chamber, stood with one door-wing closed, and wishing to lament, she recited this verse:

6.

6.

“Abbhūti tassa bho hoti, yo anicchantamicchati;

Akāmaṃ rāja kāmesi, akantaṃ kantumicchasī”ti.

“Misfortune, sir, befalls him who desires one who does not desire him. O king, you desire one who is unwilling; you wish to make dear one who is not dear.”

Tattha abbhūtīti abhūti, avuḍḍhīti attho.

Herein, ‘abbhūti’ means non-existence, that is, lack of prosperity or gain.

So pana paṭibaddhacittatāya akkosiyamānopi paribhāsiyamānopi vippaṭisāraṃ anuppādetvāva anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

But he, because of his attached heart, did not feel any regret at all even when being reviled and rebuked, and wishing to reply to Pabhāvatī, he spoke the next verse:

7.

7.

“Akāmaṃ vā sakāmaṃ vā, yo naro labhate piyaṃ;

Lābhamettha pasaṃsāma, alābho tattha pāpako”ti.

“Whether she is unwilling or willing, when a man obtains his beloved, we praise this as a gain; in that case, failure to obtain her is a misfortune.”

Sāpi [M 5.0313] tasmiṃ evaṃ kathentepi anosakkitvā thaddhataravacanaṃ vatvā palāpetukāmā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Pabhāvatī, seeing that he did not retreat even while he spoke such unpleasant words, and wishing to make him flee by using even harsher words, spoke this verse:

8.

8.

“Pāsāṇasāraṃ [V 5.0285] khaṇasi, kaṇikārassa dārunā;

Vātaṃ jālena bādhesi, yo anicchantamicchasī”ti.

“You are digging into solid rock with wood from a Kaṇikāra tree; you are trying to trap the wind with a net, you who desire one who does not desire you.”

Tattha kaṇikārassa dārunāti kaṇikārakaṭṭhena. Bādhesīti bandhasīti.

Herein, ‘with a piece of kaṇikāra wood’ means with timber from the Kaṇikāra tree. ‘You trap’ means you bind or snare.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tisso gāthāyo abhāsi –

Hearing that, the king, wishing to reply, spoke these three verses:

9.

9.

“Pāsāṇo nūna te hadaye, ohito mudulakkhaṇe;

Yo te sātaṃ na vindāmi, tirojanapadāgato.

“Surely a stone has been placed in your heart, O lady of gentle features, since I, having come from a distant land, find no pleasure from you.

10.

10.

“Yadā [P 5.0296] maṃ bhakuṭiṃ katvā, rājaputtī udikkhati;

Āḷāriko tadā homi, rañño maddassantepure.

“Whenever the princess looks at me with a frown, then I am but a cook in the inner palace of King Madda.

11.

11.

“Yadā umhayamānā maṃ, rājaputtī udikkhati;

Nāḷāriko tadā homi, rājā homi tadā kuso”ti.

“Whenever the princess looks at me with a smile, then I am no cook; then I am King Kusa.”

Tattha mudulakkhaṇeti mudunā itthilakkhaṇena samannāgate. Yoti yo ahaṃ tiroraṭṭhā āgato tava santike vasanto paṭisanthāramattampi sātaṃ na labhāmi, so evaṃ maññāmi, mayi sinehuppattinivāraṇāya nūna tava hadaye pāsāṇo ṭhapito. Bhakuṭiṃ katvāti kodhavasena valivisamaṃ nalāṭaṃ katvā. Āḷārikoti bhattakārako. Tasmiṃ khaṇe ahaṃ maddarañño antepure bhattakārakadāso viya homīti vadati. Umhayamānāti pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dassetvā hasamānā. Rājā homīti tasmiṃ khaṇe ahaṃ kusāvatīnagare rajjaṃ kārento rājā viya homi, kasmāsi evaṃ pharusā, ito paṭṭhāya mā evarūpaṃ kari, bhaddeti.

Herein, ‘O lady of gentle features’ means endowed with the gentle characteristics of a woman. ‘Since I’: I who, having come from another country and living near you, do not receive even the pleasure of a mere friendly greeting, think thus: ‘Surely a stone has been placed in your heart to prevent the arising of affection for me.’ ‘With a frown’ means having made the forehead wrinkled and uneven through the power of anger. ‘A cook’ means a preparer of meals. At that moment, he says, ‘I become like a slave-cook in the inner palace of King Madda.’ ‘Smiling’ means laughing and showing a delighted appearance. ‘I am King’: at that moment I become like a king exercising sovereignty in the city of Kusāvatī. Why are you so harsh? From now on, do not do such a thing, dear lady.”

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “ayaṃ ativiya allīyitvā katheti, musāvādaṃ katvā upāyena naṃ ito palāpessāmī”ti gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, she thought: “This King Kusa speaks with excessive attachment. I will tell a lie and make him flee from our city by some trick.” Wishing to make him flee, she spoke this verse:

12.

12.

“Sace [M 5.0314] hi vacanaṃ saccaṃ, nemittānaṃ bhavissati;

Neva me tvaṃ patī assa, kāmaṃ chindantu sattadhā”ti.

“If the word of the soothsayers is to be true, you will never be my husband, even if they should cut my body into seven pieces.”

Tassattho [V 5.0286] – mahārāja, mayā “ayaṃ kusarājā mayhaṃ pati bhavissati, na bhavissatī”ti bahū nimittapāṭhakā pucchitā, te “kāmaṃ kira maṃ sattadhā chindantu, neva me tvaṃ pati bhavissasī”ti vadiṃsūti.

Its meaning is: “Great king, I have asked many interpreters of signs whether this King Kusa would be my husband or not. They said: ‘Madam, even if they should certainly cut your body into seven pieces, he shall never be your husband.’”

Taṃ sutvā rājā taṃ paṭibāhanto “bhadde, mayāpi attano raṭṭhe nemittakā pucchitā, te ‘aññatra sīhassarakusarājato tava pati nāma añño natthī’ti byākariṃsu, ahampi attano ñāṇabalanimittena evameva kathesi”nti vatvā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to contradict her, said: “Dear lady, I too have asked the soothsayers in our city of Kusāvatī, and they declared: ‘Apart from King Kusa, who has the voice of a lion, there is no other husband for you.’ I too, by the power of my own knowledge, have interpreted the signs in the same way.” Wishing to convey this, he spoke the next verse:

13.

13.

“Sace hi vacanaṃ saccaṃ, aññesaṃ yadi vā mama;

Neva tuyhaṃ patī atthi, añño sīhassarā kusā”ti.

“If the word is true, whether that of others or my own, there is no other husband for you than Kusa with the voice of a lion.”

Tassattho – yadi hi aññesaṃ nemittānaṃ vacanaṃ saccaṃ, yadi vā mama vacanaṃ saccaṃ, tava añño pati nāma natthīti.

Its meaning is: “Dear Pabhāvatī, if the word of other soothsayers is true, or if my own word is true, and it should be so, then there is indeed no other husband for you except King Kusa, who has the voice of a lion.”

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “na sakkā imaṃ lajjāpetuṃ vā palāpetuṃ vā, kiṃ me iminā”ti dvāraṃ pidhāya attānaṃ na dassesi. Sopi kājaṃ gahetvā otari, tato paṭṭhāya taṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhati, bhattakārakakammaṃ karonto ativiya kilamati[P 5.0297], bhuttapātarāso dārūni phāleti, bhājanāni dhovati, kājena udakaṃ āharati, sayanto ambaṇapiṭṭhe sayati, pāto vuṭṭhāya yāguādīni pacati harati bhojeti, nandirāgaṃ nissāya atidukkhaṃ anubhoti. So ekadivasaṃ bhattagehadvārena gacchantiṃ khujjaṃ disvā pakkosi. Sā pabhāvatiyā bhayena tassa santikaṃ gantuṃ avisahantī turitaturitā viya gacchati. Atha naṃ vegena upagantvā “khujje”ti āha.

Hearing his words, she thought, “It is not possible to shame this man or make him flee. What have I to do with him?” Closing the door, she did not show herself. He too, taking his carrying pole, went down. From then on, he did not get to see her. Doing the work of a cook, he became extremely weary. After his morning meal, he would split firewood, wash the dishes, and carry water with his pole. When he slept, he slept on the rice-trough bench. Rising early, he would cook, carry, and serve gruel and other foods. On account of his lustful passion, he experienced extreme suffering. One day, seeing the hunchbacked woman passing by the kitchen door, he called to her. She, out of fear of Pabhāvatī, was unable to go near him and walked on as if in a great hurry. Then he quickly went up to her and said, “Hunchback!”

Sā nivattitvā ṭhitā “ko eso”ti vatvā “tumhākaṃ saddaṃ na suṇāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ “khujje tvampi sāminīpi te ubhopi ativiya thaddhā, ettakaṃ kālaṃ tumhākaṃ santike vasanto ārogyasāsanamattampi na labhāmi, deyyadhammaṃ pana kiṃ dassatha, tiṭṭhatu tāvetaṃ, api me pabhāvatiṃ mudukaṃ katvā dassetuṃ sakkhissasī”ti āha[M 5.0315]. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Atha naṃ “sace me taṃ dassetuṃ sakkhissasi, khujjabhāvaṃ te ujukaṃ katvā gīveyyakaṃ dassāmī”ti palobhento pañca gāthāyo abhāsi –

She turned and stopped. “Who is that?” she said, and then, “I did not recognize your voice.” Then he said to her: “Hunchback, both you and your mistress are extremely stubborn. Though I have been living near you for so long, I have not received even a simple greeting about her health. What then could I expect as a gift? But let that be. Will you be able to make Pabhāvatī well-disposed and arrange for me to see her?” She agreed, saying, “Very well.” Then, to entice her, he said, “If you can arrange for me to see her, I will straighten your hunchbacked state and give you a necklace,” and he spoke five verses:

14.

14.

“Nekkhaṃ [V 5.0287] gīvaṃ te kāressaṃ, patvā khujje kusāvatiṃ;

Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, olokeyya pabhāvatī.

“O hunchback, when I reach Kusāvatī, I will have a golden necklace made for you, if Pabhāvatī, she of the elephant-trunk thighs, would but look at me.

15.

15.

“Nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te kāressaṃ, patvā khujje kusāvatiṃ;

Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, ālapeyya pabhāvatī.

“O hunchback, when I reach Kusāvatī, I will have a golden necklace made for you, if Pabhāvatī, she of the elephant-trunk thighs, would but speak to me.

16.

16.

“Nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te kāressaṃ, patvā khujje kusāvatiṃ;

Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, umhāyeyya pabhāvatī.

“O hunchback, when I reach Kusāvatī, I will have a golden necklace made for you, if Pabhāvatī, she of the elephant-trunk thighs, would but smile at me.

17.

17.

“Nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te kāressaṃ, patvā khujje kusāvatiṃ;

Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, pamhāyeyya pabhāvatī.

“O hunchback, when I reach Kusāvatī, I will have a golden necklace made for you, if Pabhāvatī, she of the elephant-trunk thighs, would but laugh for me.

18.

18.

“Nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te kāressaṃ, patvā khujje kusāvatiṃ;

Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, pāṇīhi upasamphuse”ti.

“O hunchback, when I reach Kusāvatī, I will have a golden necklace made for you, if Pabhāvatī, she of the elephant-trunk thighs, would but touch me with her hands.”

Tattha nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ teti tava gīveyyaṃ sabbasuvaṇṇamayameva kāressāmīti attho. “Nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te karissāmī”tipi pāṭho, tava gīvāya nekkhamayaṃ piḷandhanaṃ piḷandhessāmīti attho. Olokeyyāti sace tava vacanena maṃ pabhāvatī olokeyya, sace maṃ tāya olokāpetuṃ sakkhissasīti attho. “Ālapeyyā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha pana umhāyeyyāti mandahasitavasena parihāseyya. Pamhāyeyyāti mahāhasitavasena parihāseyya.

There, 'nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te'ti means: 'I will have your neck-ornament made entirely of gold.' There is also the reading 'nekkhaṃ gīvaṃ te karissāmi'ti, which means: 'I will place a golden ornament on your neck.' 'Olokeyyā'ti means: 'if Pabhāvatī would look at me on account of your words; if you will be able to make her look at me.' The same method applies to 'ālapeyyā'ti and so on. Here, 'umhāyeyyā'ti means she would smile a gentle smile; 'pamhāyeyyā'ti means she would laugh a loud laugh.

Sā [P 5.0298] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “gacchatha tumhe, deva, katipāhaccayena naṃ tumhākaṃ vase karissāmi, passatha me parakkama”nti vatvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā pabhāvatiyā santikaṃ gantvā tassā vasanagabbhaṃ sodhentī viya paharaṇayoggaṃ leḍḍukhaṇḍampi asesetvā antamaso pādukāpi nīharitvā sakalagabbhaṃ sammajjitvā gabbhadvāre ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā uccāsanaṃ paññapetvā pabhāvatiyā ekaṃ nīcapīṭhakaṃ attharitvā “ehi, amma, sīse te [M 5.0316] ūkā vicinissāmī”ti taṃ tattha pīṭhake nisīdāpetvā attano ūruantare tassā sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā thokaṃ kaṇḍuyitvā “aho imissā sīse bahū ūkā”ti sakasīsato ūkā gahetvā tassā hatthe ṭhapetvā “passa kittakā te sīse ūkā”ti piyakathaṃ kathetvā mahāsattassa guṇaṃ kathentī gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, she said: “Go, Your Majesty. In a few days I will bring her under your control. Watch my effort!” Having settled that matter, she went to Pabhāvatī. Pretending to clean her living chamber, she removed every clod of earth that could be used as a missile and even took out the sandals, sweeping the entire chamber. At the doorway, she placed the threshold between them, setting up a high seat for herself and spreading a low stool for Pabhāvatī. She said: “Come, dear, I will search for lice on your head.” Having seated her on the stool, she placed Pabhāvatī’s head on her lap. After scratching a little, she said, “Oh, there are many lice on this one’s head!” and taking lice from her own head, she placed them in Pabhāvatī’s hand, saying: “See how many lice are from your head!” Speaking pleasant words and extolling the virtues of the Great Being, she recited a verse:

19.

19.

“Na [V 5.0288] hi nūnāyaṃ rājaputtī, kuse sātampi vindati;

Āḷārike bhate pose, vetanena anatthike”ti.

“Surely this princess finds no pleasure in Kusa, the cook, the servant who has no need of wages.”

Tassattho – ekaṃsena ayaṃ rājaputtī pubbe kusāvatīnagare kusanarindassa santike mālāgandhavilepanavatthālaṅkāravasena appamattakampi sātaṃ na vindati na labhati, tambūlamattampi etena etissā dinnapubbaṃ na bhavissati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Itthiyo nāma ekadivasampi aṅkaṃ avattharitvā nipannasāmikamhi hadayaṃ bhindituṃ na sakkonti, ayaṃ pana āḷārike bhate pose āḷārikattañca bhatakattañca upagate etasmiṃ purise mūlenapi anatthike kevalaṃ taṃyeva nissāya rajjaṃ pahāya āgantvā evaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavante paṭisanthāramattampi na karoti, sacepi te, amma, tasmiṃ sineho natthi, sakalajambudīpe aggarājā maṃ nissāya kilamatīti tassa kiñcideva dātuṃ arahasīti.

Its meaning is this: Assuredly, this princess, previously in the city of Kusāvatī with King Kusa, did not find even the slightest pleasure from garlands, perfumes, ointments, clothes, and ornaments; he probably never gave her so much as a betel leaf. For what reason? Women are unable to be hard-hearted towards a husband who lies down without embracing them even for a single day. But this one does not offer even a mere greeting to this man who has become a cook and a hired servant, who has no need of payment, who has abandoned his kingdom and come here relying only on her, and is now experiencing such hardship. Even if, dear, you have no affection for him, you should give him something, thinking: ‘The foremost king in all Jambudīpa is suffering on account of me.’”

Sā taṃ sutvā khujjāya kujjhi. Atha naṃ khujjā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā antogabbhe khipitvā sayaṃ bahi hutvā dvāraṃ pidhāya āviñchanarajjumhi olambantī aṭṭhāsi. Pabhāvatī taṃ gahetuṃ asakkontī dvāramūle ṭhatvā akkosantī itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Pabhāvatī became angry with the hunchback. Then the hunchback grabbed her by the neck, threw her inside the chamber, and went outside herself. Closing the door, she stood holding onto the pull-rope. Unable to seize her, Pabhāvatī stood at the doorway and reviled her, speaking another verse:

20.

20.

“Na [P 5.0299] hi nūnāyaṃ sā khujjā, labhati jivhāya chedanaṃ;

Sunisitena satthena, evaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇa”nti.

“Surely this hunchback, for speaking such ill words, will have her tongue cut out with a well-sharpened knife!”

Tattha sunisitenāti suṭṭhu nisitena tikhiṇasatthena. Evaṃ dubbhāsitanti evaṃ asotabbayuttakaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇantī.

In that context, ‘sunisitena’ means with a very well-sharpened, sharp weapon. ‘Evaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ’ means speaking such ill-spoken words that are unfit to be heard.

Atha khujjā āviñcanarajjuṃ gahetvā ṭhitāva “nippaññe dubbinīte tava rūpaṃ kiṃ karissati, kiṃ mayaṃ tava rūpaṃ khāditvā yāpessāmā”ti vatvā terasahi [M 5.0317] gāthāhi bodhisattassa guṇaṃ pakāsentī khujjāgajjitaṃ nāma gajji –

Then the hunchback, still standing there holding the pull-rope, said: “O witless, ill-disciplined girl, what will your beauty do for you? Are we going to eat your beauty to survive?” Having said this, proclaiming the Bodhisatta’s virtues in thirteen verses, she roared what is known as the ‘Hunchback’s Roar’:

21.

21.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mahāyasoti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘one of great fame,’ show him affection.

22.

22.

“Mā [V 5.0289] naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mahaddhanoti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘one of great wealth,’ show him affection.

23.

23.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mahabbaloti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘one of great strength,’ show him affection.

24.

24.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mahāraṭṭhoti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘one of a great kingdom,’ show him affection.

25.

25.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mahārājāti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him a ‘Great King,’ show him affection.

26.

26.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Sīhassaroti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘lion-voiced,’ show him affection.

27.

27.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Vaggussaroti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘pleasant-voiced,’ show him affection.

28.

28.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Bindussaroti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘resonant-voiced,’ show him affection.

29.

29.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Mañjussaroti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘sweet-voiced,’ show him affection.

30.

30.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Madhussaroti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘honey-voiced,’ show him affection.

31.

31.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Satasippoti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. O lovely one, considering him ‘skilled in a hundred arts,’ show him affection.”

32.

32.

“Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Khattiyotipi katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or stature; considering that he is a Khattiya, show your love for the delightful one.”

33.

33.

“Mā [V 5.0290][M 5.0318] naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvati;

Kusarājāti katvāna, karassu rucire piya”nti.

“O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or stature; considering him King Kusa, show your love for the delightful one.”

Tattha mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena, pabhāvatīti are pabhāvati, mā tvaṃ etaṃ kusanarindaṃ attano rūpena ārohapariṇāhena pamini, evaṃ pamāṇaṃ gaṇhi. Mahāyasoti mahānubhāvo soti evaṃ hadaye katvāna rucire piyadassane karassu tassa piyaṃ. Ānubhāvoyeva hissa rūpanti vadati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Api ca mahāyasoti mahāparivāro. Mahaddhanoti mahābhogo. Mahabbaloti [P 5.0300] mahāthāmo. Mahāraṭṭhoti vipularaṭṭho. Mahārājāti sakalajambudīpe aggarājā. Sīhassaroti sīhasaddasamānasaddo. Vaggussaroti līlāyuttassaro. Bindussaroti sampiṇḍitaghanassaro. Mañjussaroti sundarassaro. Madhussaroti madhurayuttassaro. Satasippoti paresaṃ santike asikkhitvā attano baleneva nipphannaanekasatasippo. Khattiyoti okkākapaveṇiyaṃ jāto asambhinnakhattiyo. Kusarājāti sakkadattiyakusatiṇasamānanāmo rājā. Evarūpo hi añño rājā nāma natthīti jānitvā etassa piyaṃ karohīti khujjā ettakāhi gāthāhi tassa guṇaṃ kathesi.

Herein, ‘Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena, pabhāvati’ means: O Pabhāvatī, do not measure this King Kusa by his form and stature; do not take these as the measure. ‘Mahāyaso’ means he is of great majesty; thus taking it to heart, ‘O lovely one, pleasant to see, hold him dear.’ She is saying that his majesty itself is his form. This is the method for all the verses. Further: ‘mahāyaso’ means with a great retinue. ‘Mahaddhano’ means of great wealth. ‘Mahabbalo’ means of great strength. ‘Mahāraṭṭho’ means of a vast kingdom. ‘Mahārājā’ means the foremost king in all Jambudīpa. ‘Sīhassaro’ means with a voice like a lion’s. ‘Vaggussaro’ means with a charming voice. ‘Bindussaro’ means with a resonant and full voice. ‘Mañjussaro’ means with a beautiful voice. ‘Madhussaro’ means with a honeyed voice. ‘Satasippo’ means one who has perfected hundreds of skills by his own power without having learned them from others. ‘Khattiyo’ means one born in the Okkāka line, an unmixed Khattiya. ‘Kusarājā’ means a king with a name like the kusa grass given by Sakka. The hunchback extolled his virtues in these many verses, meaning: ‘Knowing that there is no other king like him, hold him dear.’

Pabhāvatī tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “khujje ativiya gajjasi, hatthena pāpuṇantī sasāmikabhāvaṃ te jānāpessāmī”ti khujjaṃ tajjesi. Sāpi taṃ “ahaṃ taṃ rakkhamānā pituno te kusarājassa āgatabhāvaṃ nārocesiṃ, hotu, ajja rañño ārocessāmī”ti mahantena saddena bhāyāpesi. Sāpi “kocideva suṇeyyā”ti khujjaṃ saññāpesi. Bodhisattopi taṃ passituṃ alabhanto satta māse dubbhojanena dukkhaseyyāya kilamanto cintesi – “ko me etāya attho, satta māse vasanto etaṃ passitumpi na labhāmi, ativiya kakkhaḷā sāhasikā, gantvā mātāpitaro passissāmī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko āvajjento tassa ukkaṇṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “rājā satta māse pabhāvatiṃ daṭṭhumpi na labhi, labhanākāramassa karissāmī”ti maddarañño dūte katvā sattannaṃ [M 5.0319] rājūnaṃ dūtaṃ pāhento “pabhāvatī, kusarājaṃ chaḍḍetvā āgatā, āgacchantu pabhāvatiṃ gaṇhantū”ti ekekassa visuṃ visuṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Te mahāparivārena gantvā nagaraṃ patvā aññamaññassa āgatakāraṇaṃ na jānanti. Te “tvaṃ kasmā āgato, tvaṃ kasmā āgatosī”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ ñatvā kujjhitvā “ekaṃ kira dhītaraṃ sattannaṃ dassati, passathassa anācāraṃ, uppaṇḍeti no, gaṇhatha na”nti “sabbesampi amhākaṃ pabhāvatiṃ detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti sāsanāni pahiṇitvā nagaraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Maddarājā sāsanaṃ sutvā bhītatasito amacce āmantetvā “kiṃ karomā”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ amaccā “deva[V 5.0291][P 5.0301], sattapi rājāno pabhāvatiṃ nissāya āgatā, ‘sace na dassati, pākāraṃ bhinditvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā taṃ gaṇhissāmā’ti vadanti, pākāre abhinneyeva tesaṃ pabhāvatiṃ pesessāmā”ti vatvā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Upon hearing her words, Pabhāvatī threatened the hunchback: “Hunchback, you boast excessively! When you are in my hands, I will make you know who your mistress is!” The hunchback, in turn, frightened her by shouting loudly: “While I was looking after you, I did not inform your father of King Kusa’s arrival. So be it! Today I will inform the king!” Pabhāvatī then pacified the hunchback, thinking, “Someone might hear.” The Bodhisatta, unable to see her and exhausted after seven months of poor food and an uncomfortable bed, thought: “What use is she to me? After staying here for seven months, I have not even been able to see her. She is extremely harsh and cruel. I will return to my kingdom and see my parents.” At that moment, Sakka, reflecting on the matter and knowing his dejection, thought: “The king has not even been able to see Pabhāvatī for seven months. I will create the conditions for him to get her.” Acting as a messenger for King Madda, he sent messages to seven kings, each separately: “Pabhāvatī has abandoned King Kusa and returned. Come and take her!” They arrived at the city of Sāgala with great retinues, each unaware of the others' reasons for coming. When they asked one another, “Why have you come?” and learned the reason, they became angry: “It seems he plans to give one daughter to seven kings! See his misconduct! He is insulting us! Let us seize him!” They all sent messages: “Either give Pabhāvatī to us or give us battle,” and they surrounded the city. Hearing this, King Madda was struck with fear and asked his ministers, “What shall we do?” The ministers replied: “Your Majesty, these seven kings have come on account of Pabhāvatī. They say, ‘If he does not give her, we will break down the rampart, enter the city, put him to death, and take her.’ Before they destroy the rampart, let us send Pabhāvatī to them.” Then they spoke this verse:

34.

34.

“Ete nāgā upatthaddhā, sabbe tiṭṭhanti vammitā;

Purā maddanti pākāraṃ, ānentetaṃ pabhāvati”nti.

“These elephants are fierce, all stand armored; before they crush the rampart, let Pabhāvatī be brought out!”

Tattha upatthaddhāti atithaddhā dappitā. Ānentetaṃ pabhāvatinti ānentu etaṃ pabhāvatinti sāsanāni pahiṇiṃsu. Tasmā yāva ete nāgā pākāraṃ na maddanti, tāva nesaṃ pabhāvatiṃ pesehi, mahārājāti.

Herein, ‘fierce’ (upatthaddhā) means very stubborn and proud. ‘Let Pabhāvatī be brought out’ means they sent messages saying, ‘Let this Pabhāvatī be brought.’ Therefore, O great king, before these elephants crush the rampart, send Pabhāvatī to them.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “sacāhaṃ ekassa pabhāvatiṃ pesessāmi, sesā yuddhaṃ karissanti, na sakkā ekassa dātuṃ, sakalajambudīpe aggarājānaṃ ‘virūpo’ti chaḍḍetvā āgatā āgamanassa phalaṃ labhatu, vadhitvāna naṃ satta khaṇḍāni katvā sattannaṃ khattiyānaṃ pesessāmī”ti vadanto anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king thought: “If I send Pabhāvatī to just one, the others will wage war. It is not possible to give her to only one. Since she has come here after rejecting the supreme king in all of Jambudīpa as ‘ugly,’ let her reap the fruit of her coming! I will have her killed, cut into seven pieces, and sent to the seven Khattiyas.” Speaking thus, he then uttered the following verse:

35.

35.

“Satta bile karitvāna, ahametaṃ pabhāvatiṃ;

Khattiyānaṃ padassāmi, ye maṃ hantuṃ idhāgatā”ti.

“Having made seven pieces of this Pabhāvatī, I will give them to the Khattiyas who have come here to kill me.”

Tassa sā kathā sakalanivesane pākaṭā ahosi. Paricārikā gantvā “rājā kira taṃ satta khaṇḍāni katvā sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ pesessatī”ti pabhāvatiyā ārocesuṃ. Sā maraṇabhayabhītā āsanā vuṭṭhāya bhaginīhi parivutā mātu sirigabbhaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

This talk became known throughout the entire palace. The attendants went and reported to Pabhāvatī: “It is said the king will have you cut into seven pieces and sent to the seven kings.” Terrified by the fear of death, she rose from her seat and, surrounded by her sisters, went to her mother's royal chamber. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

36.

36.

“Avuṭṭhahi [M 5.0320] rājaputtī, sāmā koseyyavāsinī;

Assupuṇṇehi nettehi, dāsīgaṇapurakkhatā”ti.

“The princess arose, golden-hued, clad in silk, with eyes full of tears, attended by a retinue of female slaves.”

Tattha sāmāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇā. Koseyyavāsinīti suvaṇṇakhacitakoseyyanivasanā.

Herein, golden-hued means having the color of gold. Clad in silk means wearing a silk garment inlaid with gold.

Sā mātu santikaṃ gantvā mātaraṃ vanditvā paridevamānā āha –

She went to her mother, paid homage to her, and lamenting, said:

37.

37.

“Taṃ [V 5.0292][P 5.0302] nūna kakkūpanisevitaṃ mukhaṃ, ādāsadantātharupaccavekkhitaṃ;

Subhaṃ sunettaṃ virajaṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ, chuddhaṃ vane ṭhassati khattiyehi.

“Surely this face, treated with cosmetic powders, gazed at in a mirror with an ivory handle, beautiful, with fine eyes, spotless and flawless, will be cast aside in the forest by the Khattiyas.”

38.

38.

“Te nūna me asite vellitagge, kese mudū candanasāralitte;

Samākule sīvathikāya majjhe, pādehi gijjhā parikaḍḍhissanti.

“Surely these soft, black, curly-tipped tresses of mine, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, will be dragged by vultures with their feet in the midst of the charnel ground.”

39.

39.

“Tā nūna me tambanakhā sulomā, bāhā mudū candanasāralittā;

Chinnā vane ujjhitā khattiyehi, gayha dhaṅko gacchati yenakāmaṃ.

“Surely these tender arms of mine, with copper-colored nails and fine hair, anointed with the essence of sandalwood—when cut off and cast aside in the forest by the Khattiyas, a crow will seize them and go wherever it wishes.”

40.

40.

“Te nūna tālūpanibhe alambe, nisevite kāsikacandanena;

Thanesu me lambissati siṅgālo, mātūva putto taruṇo tanūjo.

“Surely from these breasts of mine, pendulous like ripe palm fruits and scented with Kāsi sandalwood, a jackal will hang, just like a young son from his mother’s breast.”

41.

41.

“Taṃ nūna soṇiṃ puthulaṃ sukoṭṭitaṃ, nisevitaṃ kañcanamekhalāhi;

Chinnaṃ vane khattiyehī avatthaṃ, siṅgālasaṅghā parikaḍḍhissanti.

“Surely this broad and well-shaped hip of mine, adorned with golden girdles—when cut off by the Khattiyas and left naked in the forest, packs of jackals will drag it away.”

42.

42.

“Soṇā dhaṅkā siṅgālā ca, ye caññe santi dāṭhino;

Ajarā nūna hessanti, bhakkhayitvā pabhāvatiṃ.

“Dogs, crows, and jackals, and whatever other fanged beasts there are, will surely become ageless after devouring Pabhāvatī.”

43.

43.

“Sace [M 5.0321] maṃsāni hariṃsu, khattiyā dūragāmino;

Aṭṭhīni amma yācitvā, anupathe dahātha naṃ.

“Mother, if the far-traveling Khattiyas should carry off my flesh, then beg for my bones and cremate them by the roadside.”

44.

44.

“Khettāni amma kāretvā, kaṇikārettha ropaya;

Yadā te pupphitā assu, hemantānaṃ himaccaye;

Sareyyātha mamaṃ amma, evaṃvaṇṇā pabhāvatī”ti.

“Mother, have flower gardens made and plant Kaṇikāra trees there. When they are in bloom at the end of winter, you should remember me, Mother, thinking: ‘Pabhāvatī was of such a color as these flowers.’”

Tattha kakkūpanisevitantila kakkūpanisevitanti sāsapakakkaloṇakakkamattikakakkatilakakkahaliddikakkamukhacuṇṇakehi imehi pañcahi kakkehi upanisevitaṃ. Ādāsadantātharupaccavekkhitanti [P 5.0303] dantamayatharumhi ādāse paccavekkhitaṃ tattha oloketvā maṇḍitaṃ. Subhanti subhamukhaṃ. Virajanti vigatarajaṃ nimmalaṃ. Anaṅgaṇanti gaṇḍapiḷakādidosarahitaṃ. Chuddhanti amma evarūpaṃ mama mukhaṃ addhā idāni khattiyehi chaḍḍitaṃ vane [V 5.0293] araññe ṭhassatīti paridevati. Asiteti kāḷake. Vellitaggeti unnatagge. Sīvathikāyāti susānamhi. Parikaḍḍhissantīti evarūpe mama kese manussamaṃsakhādakā gijjhā pādehi paharitvā nūna parikaḍḍhissanti. Gayha dhaṅko gacchati yenakāmanti amma mama evarūpaṃ bāhaṃ nūna dhaṅko gahetvā luñjitvā khādanto yenakāmaṃ gacchissati.

Herein, treated with cosmetic paste: treated with these five kinds of cosmetic pastes—mustard paste, salt paste, clay paste, sesame paste, and turmeric paste, and with facial powders. Gazed at in a mirror with an ivory handle: gazed at and adorned in a mirror with an ivory handle. Lovely: a lovely face. Spotless: free from dust, immaculate. Flawless: free from defects such as boils and pimples. Cast aside: she laments, “Mother, this face of mine, so beautiful, will surely now be cast aside by the khattiyas and lie in the forest, the wilderness.” Black: dark-colored. Curly-tipped: with upturned tips. Of the charnel ground: in the cemetery. Will drag: “Surely vultures, eaters of human flesh, will strike such hair of mine with their feet and drag it away.” A crow will seize them and go wherever it wishes: “Mother, surely a crow will seize such an arm of mine, tear at it while eating, and go wherever it wishes.”

Tālūpanibheti suvaṇṇatālaphalasadise. Kāsikacandanenāti sukhumacandanena nisevite. Thanesu meti amma mama susāne patitāya evarūpe thane disvā mukhena ḍaṃsitvā tesu me thanesu attano tanujo mātu taruṇaputto viya nūna siṅgālo lambissati. Soṇinti kaṭiṃ. Sukoṭṭitanti gohanukena paharitvā suvaḍḍhitaṃ. Avatthanti chaḍḍitaṃ. Bhakkhayitvāti amma ete ettakā nūna mama maṃsaṃ khāditvā ajarā bhavissanti.

Herein, like palm fruits means resembling golden palm fruits. With sandalwood from Kāsi means anointed with fine sandalwood. From my breasts: “Mother, when I have fallen in the charnel ground, a jackal, seeing such breasts, will surely seize them with its mouth and hang from them, just like a tender young son from his mother.” Hip: the hip-region. Well-rounded: well-developed, as if shaped by a pestle. Helpless: cast aside. After devouring: “Mother, surely after eating my flesh, all these creatures will become ageless.”

Sace maṃsāni hariṃsūti amma sace te khattiyā mayiṃ paṭibaddhacittā mama maṃsāni hareyyuṃ, atha tumhe aṭṭhīni yācitvā anupathe dahāthanaṃ, jaṅghamaggamahāmaggānaṃ antare daheyyāthāti vadati. Khettānīti amma mama jhāpitaṭṭhāne mālādivatthūni kāretvā ettha etesu khettesu kaṇikārarukkhe ropaya. Himaccayeti himapātātikkame phagguṇamāse. Sareyyāthāti tesaṃ pupphānaṃ suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakaṃ pūretvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā mama dhītā pabhāvatī evaṃvaṇṇāti sareyyātha.

Herein, If... should carry off my flesh: “Mother, if those khattiyas, their hearts attached to me, should carry off my flesh, then you should beg for my bones and cremate them along the path,” that is, between the footpath and the main road. Garden plots: “Mother, at the place where I am cremated, have things like garlands made, and there, in these plots, plant kaṇikāra trees.” When the frost has passed: at the passing of the snowfall, in the month of Phagguṇa. You should remember: “Filling a golden casket with their flowers and placing it on your lap, you should remember me, thinking: ‘My daughter Pabhāvatī was of such beauty.’”

Iti [M 5.0322] sā maraṇabhayatajjitā mātu santike vilapi. Maddarājāpi “pharasuñca gaṇḍikañca gahetvā coraghātako idheva āgacchatū”ti āṇāpesi. Tassa āgamanaṃ sakalarājagehe pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Athassa āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā pabhāvatiyā mātā uṭṭhāyāsanā sokasamappitā rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, tormented by the fear of death, she lamented in her mother’s presence. King Madda also commanded: “Let the executioner come here, bringing an axe and a block.” His arrival became known throughout the entire palace. Then, hearing that he had arrived, Pabhāvatī’s mother, overcome with grief, rose from her seat and went to the king. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

45.

45.

“Tassā mātā udaṭṭhāsi, khattiyā devavaṇṇinī;

Disvā asiñca sūnañca, rañño maddassantepure”ti.

“Her mother arose, a khattiya lady of divine beauty, upon seeing the sword and the chopping block in the inner palace of King Madda.”

Tattha [P 5.0304] udaṭṭhāsīti āsanā uṭṭhāya rañño santikaṃ gantvā aṭṭhāsi. Disvā asiñca sūnañcāti antepuramhi alaṅkatamahātale rañño purato nikkhittaṃ pharasuñca gaṇḍikañca disvā vilapantī gāthamāha –

Herein, ‘arose’ means she rose from her seat, went to the king, and stood there. ‘Upon seeing the sword and the block’ means: having seen the axe and the chopping block placed before the king on the great decorated floor of the inner palace, she lamented and uttered this verse:

46.

46.

“Iminā [V 5.0294] nūna asinā, susaññaṃ tanumajjhimaṃ;

Dhītaraṃ madda hantvāna, khattiyānaṃ padassasī”ti.

“O Madda, surely with this sword, having slain your well-formed, slender-waisted daughter, you will give her to the khattiyas.”

Tattha asināti pharasuṃ sandhāyāha. So hi imasmiṃ ṭhāne asi nāma jāto. Susaññaṃ tanumajjhimanti suṭṭhu saññātaṃ tanumajjhimaṃ.

Herein, with... sword: this is said in reference to the axe, for in this context it is called a “sword.” Well-formed, slender-waisted means well-distinguished and slender-waisted.

Atha naṃ rājā saññāpento āha – “devi, kiṃ kathesi, tava dhītā sakalajambudīpe aggarājānaṃ ‘virūpo’ti chaḍḍetvā gatamagge padavalañje avinaṭṭheyeva maccuṃ nalāṭenādāya āgatā, idāni attano rūpaṃ nissāya īdisaṃ phalaṃ labhatū”ti. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā dhītu santikaṃ gantvā vilapantī āha –

Then the king, explaining to her, said: “Queen, what are you saying? Your daughter rejected the chief king in all of Jambudīpa as ‘ugly’ and came back, bearing death on her forehead, before the footprints on the path she took had even vanished. Let her now reap such a fruit on account of her beauty.” Hearing his words, she went to her daughter and, lamenting, said:

47.

47.

“Na me akāsi vacanaṃ, atthakāmāya puttike;

Sājja lohitasañchannā, gacchasi yamasādhanaṃ.

“You did not heed my words, dear daughter, spoken for your welfare. Today, covered in blood, you go to the abode of Yama.

48.

48.

“Evamāpajjatī poso, pāpiyañca nigacchati;

Yo ve hitānaṃ vacanaṃ, na karoti atthadassinaṃ.

“Thus does a person fall into calamity and come to a bad end, one who does not follow the words of well-wishers who can see what is beneficial.

49.

49.

“Sace ca ajja dhāresi, kumāraṃ cārudassanaṃ;

Kusena jātaṃ khattiyaṃ, suvaṇṇamaṇimekhalaṃ;

Pūjitaṃ ñātisaṅghehi, na gacchasi yamakkhayaṃ.

“If even today you were to bear a prince of lovely appearance, born of Kusa the khattiya, one wearing a golden and jeweled girdle and honored by his assembly of kinsmen, you would not go to destruction in Yama's realm.

50.

50.

“Yatthassu [M 5.0323] bherī nadati, kuñjaro ca nikūjati;

Khattiyānaṃ kule bhadde, kinnu sukhataraṃ tato.

“Where the kettledrum resounds and the elephant trumpets in the noble family of khattiyas, my dear, what could be happier than that?

51.

51.

“Asso ca sisati dvāre, kumāro uparodati;

Khattiyānaṃ kule bhadde, kinnu sukhataraṃ tato.

“Where a horse neighs at the gate and a youth sings to music, in the noble family of khattiyas, my dear, what could be happier than that?

52.

52.

“Mayūrakoñcābhirude, kokilābhinikūjite;

Khattiyānaṃ kule bhadde, kinnu sukhataraṃ tato”ti.

“Filled with the cries of peacocks and herons and the sweet songs of cuckoos, in the noble family of khattiyas, my dear, what could be happier than that?”

Tattha [V 5.0295] puttiketi taṃ ālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – amma, idha kiṃ karissasi, sāmikassa santikaṃ gaccha, mā rūpamadena majjīti evaṃ yācantiyāpi me vacanaṃ na akāsi, sā tvaṃ ajja lohitasañchannā gacchasi yamasādhanaṃ, maccurājassa bhavanaṃ [P 5.0305] gamissasīti. Pāpiyañcāti ito pāpatarañca nigacchati. Sace ca ajja dhāresīti, amma, sace tvaṃ cittassa vasaṃ agantvā kusanarindaṃ paṭicca laddhaṃ attano rūpena sadisaṃ cārudassanaṃ kumāraṃ ajja dhārayissasi. Yamakkhayanti evaṃ sante yamanivesanaṃ na gaccheyyāsi. Tato yamhi khattiyakule ayaṃ vibhūti, tamhā nānābherisaddena ceva mattavāraṇakoñcanādena ca ninnāditā kusāvatīrājakulā kiṃ nu sukhataraṃ disvā idhāgatāsīti attho. Sisatīti hasati. Kumāroti susikkhito gandhabbakumāro. Uparodatīti nānātūriyāni gahetvā upahāraṃ karoti. Kokilābhinikūjiteti kusarājakule sāyaṃ pāto pavattanaccagītavāditūpahāraṃ paṭippharantī viya kokilehi abhinikūjite.

Here, `puttike` is how he addresses her. This is what is meant: 'Mother, what will you do here? Go to your husband. Do not be intoxicated by pride in your beauty.' Even when I pleaded thus, she did not do my bidding. Today you go, covered in blood, to Yama's domain; you will go to the abode of the King of Death. `Pāpiyañca`: and to a worse state. This means she goes to an even more evil state than this. `Sace ca ajja dhāresi`: If you hold on today. This means: Mother, if today, without yielding to your own mind, you would keep the handsome prince, who resembles you in beauty and was obtained on account of King Kusa. `Yamakkhayaṃ`: to the destruction of Yama. In that case, you would not go to Yama's abode. Then, what is the meaning of 'From that khattiya family where there is this splendor, from the royal family of Kusāvatī, which resounds with the sound of various drums and the trumpeting of intoxicated elephants, having seen what greater happiness have you come here?' `Sisati` means he laughs. `Kumāro` means a well-trained gandhabba prince. `Uparodati` means he takes up various musical instruments and makes an offering. `Kokilābhinikūjite`: resounding with cuckoos. This is like the evening and morning performances of dance, song, and music in the royal court of King Kusa being echoed by the cuckoos.

Iti sāpi ettakāhi gāthāhi tāya saddhiṃ sallapitvā “sace ajja kusanarindo idha assa, ime satta rājāno palāpetvā mama dhītaraṃ dukkhā pamocetvā ādāya gaccheyyā”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Thus, having conversed with her with so many verses, she thought, ‘If King Kusa were here today, he would make these seven kings flee, free my daughter from suffering, and take her away.’ Then she spoke this verse:

53.

53.

“Kahaṃ nu kho sattumaddano, pararaṭṭhappamaddano;

Kuso soḷārapaññāṇo, yo no dukkhā pamocaye”ti.

“Where now is the crusher of foes, the subduer of foreign realms? Kusa of eminent wisdom, who could free us from suffering?”

Tattha soḷārapaññāṇoti uḷārapañño.

Here, ‘soḷārapaññāṇo’ means one of eminent wisdom.

Tato [M 5.0324] pabhāvatī “mama mātu kusassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇantiyā mukhaṃ nappahoti, ācikkhissāmi tāvassā tassa idheva āḷārikakammaṃ katvā vasanabhāva”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Then Pabhāvatī thought, ‘My mother’s mouth is not able to speak all the praise of Kusa. I will tell her that he is living right here, doing the work of a cook.’ Thinking thus, she spoke this verse:

54.

54.

“Idheva so sattumaddano, pararaṭṭhappamaddano;

Kuso soḷārapaññāṇo, yo te sabbe vadhissatī”ti.

“Right here is the crusher of foes, the subduer of foreign realms; Kusa of eminent wisdom, who will slay all of them.”

Athassā mātā “ayaṃ maraṇabhayabhītā vippalapatī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Then her mother, thinking, ‘She is babbling, terrified by the fear of death,’ spoke this verse:

55.

55.

“Ummattikā [V 5.0296] nu bhaṇasi, andhabālā pabhāsasi;

Kuso ce āgato assa, kiṃ na jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“Are you speaking as if mad, are you talking like a blind fool? If Kusa had come, why would we not know of him?”

Tattha andhabālāti sammūḷhā aññāṇā hutvā. Kiṃ na jānemūti kena kāraṇena taṃ na jāneyyāma. So hi antarāmagge ṭhitova amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ peseyya, samussitaddhajā caturaṅginīsenā paññāyetha, tvaṃ pana maraṇabhayena kathesīti.

Here, ‘andhabālā’ means being deluded and ignorant. ‘Kiṃ na jānemu’ means: for what reason would we not know of him? For he would stand on the road and send us a message; his fourfold army with banners raised would be seen. But you speak out of fear of death.

Sā [P 5.0306] evaṃ vutte “na me mātā saddahati, tassa idhāgantvā satta māse vasanabhāvaṃ na jānāti, dassessāmi na”nti cintetvā mātaraṃ hatthe gahetvā sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā dassentī gāthamāha –

When this was said, she thought, ‘My mother does not believe me; she does not know that he has been living here for seven months. I will show him to her.’ Taking her mother by the hand, she opened the lion-window, stretched out her hand, and, pointing him out, spoke this verse:

56.

56.

“Eso āḷāriko poso, kumārīpuramantare;

Daḷhaṃ katvāna saṃvelliṃ, kumbhiṃ dhovati oṇato”ti.

“That man, the cook, inside the maidens' quarters, having tucked up his loincloth, is bent over washing a pot.”

Tattha kumārīpuramantareti vātapāne ṭhitā tava dhītānaṃ kumārīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānantare naṃ olokehi. Saṃvellinti kacchaṃ bandhitvā kumbhiṃ dhovati.

Here, ‘kumārīpuramantare’ means: standing at the window, look at him inside the living quarters of your maiden daughters. ‘Saṃvelliṃ’ means: having tucked up his loincloth, he washes the pot.

So kira tadā “ajja me manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissati, addhā maraṇabhayatajjitā, pabhāvatī, mama āgatabhāvaṃ kathessati, bhājanāni dhovitvā paṭisāmessāmī”ti udakaṃ āharitvā bhājanāni dhovituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ mātā paribhāsantī gāthamāha –

It seems that at that time he thought, ‘Today my wish will be fulfilled. Surely Pabhāvatī, threatened by the fear of death, will speak of my arrival. I will wash the vessels and put them away.’ He fetched water and began to wash the vessels. Then her mother, scolding her, spoke this verse:

57.

57.

“Veṇī tvamasi caṇḍālī, adūsi kulagandhinī;

Kathaṃ maddakule jātā, dāsaṃ kayirāsi kāmuka”nti.

“Are you a basket-maker's daughter, or a Candala woman? You are a stain on your clan! How could you, born into the Madda clan, make a slave your lover?”

Tattha [M 5.0325] veṇīti tacchikā. Adūsi kulagandhinīti udāhu tvaṃ kuladūsikā. Kāmukanti kathaṃ nāma tvaṃ evarūpe kule jātā attano sāmikaṃ dāsaṃ kareyyāsīti.

Here, ‘veṇī’ means a carpenter’s daughter. ‘Adūsi kulagandhinī’ means a woman who defiles her clan. ‘Kāmukaṃ’ means: how could you, born into such a family, make your own husband a slave?

Tato pabhāvatī “mama mātā imassa maṃ nissāya evaṃ vasanabhāvaṃ na jānāti maññe”ti cintetvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then Pabhāvatī thought, ‘I think my mother does not know that he is living like this on account of me,’ and she spoke the next verse:

58.

58.

“Namhi [V 5.0297] veṇī na caṇḍālī, na camhi kulagandhinī;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasī”ti.

“I am not a basket-maker's daughter, not a Candala woman, nor am I a stain on the clan. He is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?”

Tattha okkākaputtoti, amma, esa okkākaputto, tvaṃ pana “dāso”ti maññasi, kasmā naṃ ahaṃ “dāso”ti kathessāmīti.

Here, ‘okkākaputto’: Mother, this is a son of Okkāka, but you think he is a ‘slave.’ Why should I call him a ‘slave’?

Idānissa yasaṃ vaṇṇentī āha –

Now, praising his glory, she said:

59.

59.

“Yo brāhmaṇasahassāni, sadā bhojeti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasi.

“He who always feeds twenty thousand brahmins is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?

60.

60.

Yassa [P 5.0307] nāgasahassāni, sadā yojenti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasi.

“He for whom twenty thousand elephants are always harnessed is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?

61.

61.

“Yassa assasahassāni, sadā yojenti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasi.

“He for whom twenty thousand horses are always harnessed is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?”

62.

62.

“Yassa rathasahassāni, sadā yojenti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasi;

Yassa usabhasahassāni, sadā yojenti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasi.

“He for whom twenty thousand chariots are always harnessed is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave? He for whom twenty thousand bulls are always yoked is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?”

63.

63.

“Yassa dhenusahassāni, sadā duhanti vīsatiṃ;

Okkākaputto bhaddante, tvaṃ nu dāsoti maññasī”ti.

“He for whom twenty thousand milch cows are always milked is a son of Okkāka, good lady; do you think he is a slave?”

Evaṃ tāya pañcahi gāthāhi mahāsattassa yaso vaṇṇito. Athassā mātā “ayaṃ asambhitā kathaṃ katheti, addhā evameta”nti saddahitvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. So vegena pabhāvatiyā santikaṃ [M 5.0326] gantvā “saccaṃ kira, amma, kusarājā idhāgato”ti. “Āma tāta, ajjassa satta māsā atikkantā tava dhītānaṃ āḷārikattaṃ karontassā”ti. So tassā asaddahanto khujjaṃ pucchitvā yathābhūtaṃ sutvā dhītaraṃ garahanto gāthamāha –

Thus with five verses she praised the Great Being's glory. Then her mother, thinking, ‘She speaks without fear; it must surely be so,’ believed her and went to the king to report the matter. He went quickly to Pabhāvatī and asked, ‘Is it true, my dear, that King Kusa has come here?’ ‘Yes, father. Seven months have now passed while he has been acting as a cook for your daughters.’ The king, not believing her, questioned the hunchbacked woman and, having heard the truth, rebuked his daughter, speaking this verse:

64.

64.

“Taggha [V 5.0298] te dukkaṭaṃ bāle, yaṃ khattiyaṃ mahabbalaṃ;

Nāgaṃ maṇḍūkavaṇṇena, na taṃ akkhāsidhāgata”nti.

“Truly, you have done wrong, you fool, in that you did not announce that the mighty khattiya, a noble elephant in the appearance of a frog, had come here.”

Tattha tagghāti ekaṃseneva.

Here, ‘taggha’ means certainly.

So dhītaraṃ garahitvā vegena tassa santikaṃ gantvā katapaṭisanthāro añjaliṃ paggayha attano accayaṃ dassento gāthamāha –

Having rebuked his daughter, he went quickly to his presence, exchanged friendly greetings, raised his hands in reverence, and, acknowledging his transgression, spoke this verse:

65.

65.

“Aparādhaṃ mahārāja, tvaṃ no khama rathesabha;

Yaṃ taṃ aññātavesena, nāññāsimhā idhāgata”nti.

“Forgive our offense, great king, bull among charioteers; for we did not recognize you who came here in disguise.”

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ pharusaṃ vakkhāmi, idhevassa hadayaṃ phalissati, assāsessāmi na”nti cintetvā bhājanantare ṭhitova itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being thought, ‘If I speak harshly, his heart will burst right here. I will reassure him.’ And while still standing among the pots, he spoke the next verse:

66.

66.

“Mādisassa na taṃ channaṃ, yohaṃ āḷāriko bhave;

Tvaññeva me pasīdassu, natthi te deva dukkaṭa”nti.

“It is not suitable for one like me to be a cook. You should be gracious to me; there is no wrongdoing on your part, O king.”

Rājā tassa santikā paṭisanthāraṃ labhitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā pabhāvatiṃ pakkosāpetvā khamāpanatthāya pesetuṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having received a friendly greeting from him, ascended the palace, had Pabhāvatī summoned, and spoke this verse to send her to ask for forgiveness:

67.

67.

“Gaccha [P 5.0308] bāle khamāpehi, kusarājaṃ mahabbalaṃ;

Khamāpito kuso rājā, so te dassati jīvita”nti.

“Go, you fool, and ask forgiveness of the mighty King Kusa. When King Kusa has been appeased, he will grant you your life.”

Sā pitu vacanaṃ sutvā bhaginīhi ceva paricārikāhi ca parivutā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Sopi kammakāravesena ṭhitova tassā attano santikaṃ āgamanaṃ ñatvā “ajja pabhāvatiyā mānaṃ bhinditvā pādamūle naṃ kalale nipajjāpessāmī”ti sabbaṃ attanā ābhataṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā khalamaṇḍalamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ madditvā ekakalalaṃ akāsi. Sā tassa santikaṃ gantvā tassa pādesu nipatitvā kalalapiṭṭhe nipannā taṃ khamāpesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Hearing her father’s words, she went to him, surrounded by her sisters and attendants. He, still standing in the guise of a workman, knew she was coming to him and thought, ‘Today I will break Pabhāvatī’s pride and make her lie down in the mud at my feet.’ He poured out all the water he had brought, trampled an area the size of a threshing floor, and made it into one muddy mess. She went to him, fell at his feet, and lying on the mud, asked him for forgiveness. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

68.

68.

“Pitussa [V 5.0299][M 5.0327] vacanaṃ sutvā, devavaṇṇī pabhāvatī;

Sirasā aggahī pāde, kusarājaṃ mahabbala”nti.

“Hearing her father’s word, Pabhāvatī of divine form took with her head the feet of the mighty King Kusa.”

Tattha sirasāti sirasā nipatitvā kusarājānaṃ pāde aggahesīti.

Herein, ‘sirasā’ means: having fallen down with her head, she took hold of King Kusa’s feet.

Gahetvā ca pana naṃ khamāpentī tisso gāthāyo abhāsi –

And having taken hold of his feet, while asking for forgiveness, she spoke three verses:

69.

69.

“Yāmā ratyo atikkantā, tāmā deva tayā vinā;

Vande te sirasā pāde, mā me kujjha rathesabha.

“Whatever nights have passed, O lord, they have passed without you. I venerate your feet with my head; do not be angry with me, bull among charioteers.”

70.

70.

“Sabbaṃ te paṭijānāmi, mahārāja suṇohi me;

Na cāpi appiyaṃ tuyhaṃ, kareyyāmi ahaṃ puna.

“I acknowledge everything to you, great king, listen to me; and I will never again do anything displeasing to you.”

71.

71.

“Evaṃ ce yācamānāya, vacanaṃ me na kāhasi;

Idāni maṃ tāto hantvā, khattiyānaṃ padassatī”ti.

“If, though I beg you thus, you will not do my bidding, my father will now kill me and give me to the khattiyas.”

Tattha ratyoti rattiyo. Tāmāti tā imā sabbāpi tayā vinā atikkantā. Sabbaṃ te paṭijānāmīti, mahārāja, ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayā tava appiyameva kataṃ, idaṃ te ahaṃ sabbaṃ paṭijānāmi, aparampi suṇohi me, ito paṭṭhāyāhaṃ puna tuyhaṃ appiyaṃ na karissāmi. Evaṃ ceti sace evaṃ yācamānāya mama tvaṃ vacanaṃ na karissasīti.

Herein, ‘ratyo’ means nights. ‘Tāmā’ means: all these have passed without you. ‘Sabbaṃ te paṭijānāmi’ means: ‘Great king, for so long I have only done what was displeasing to you; I acknowledge all this to you. And listen further to me: from now on, I will not do anything displeasing to you again.’ ‘Evaṃ ce’ means: ‘If you will not heed my words even when I implore you thus.’

Taṃ sutvā rājā “sacāhaṃ ‘imaṃ tvañceva jānissasī’ti vakkhāmi, hadayamassā phalissati, assāsessāmi na”nti cintetvā āha –

Having heard this, the king thought: “If I say to her, ‘You yourself will know this,’ her heart will break. I will console her,” and he said:

72.

72.

“Evaṃ te yācamānāya, kiṃ na kāhāmi te vaco;

Vikuddho tyasmi kalyāṇi, mā tvaṃ bhāyi pabhāvati.

“When you implore me thus, why should I not do your bidding? I am free from anger towards you, lovely one; do not be afraid, Pabhāvatī.”

73.

73.

“Sabbaṃ [P 5.0309] te paṭijānāmi, rājaputti suṇohi me;

Na cāpi appiyaṃ tuyhaṃ, kareyyāmi ahaṃ puna.

“I promise you everything, princess, listen to me; and I will not do anything displeasing to you again.”

74.

74.

“Tava [V 5.0300] kāmā hi sussoṇi, pahu dukkhaṃ titikkhisaṃ;

Bahuṃ maddakulaṃ hantvā, nayituṃ taṃ pabhāvatī”ti.

“For your sake, O fair-hipped one, I have endured much suffering; though capable of slaying many of the Madda clan to lead you away, Pabhāvatī.”

Tattha kiṃ na kāhāmīti kiṃkāraṇā tava vacanaṃ na karissāmi. Vikuddho tyasmīti vikuddho nikkopo te asmiṃ. Sabbaṃ teti vikuddhabhāvañca idāni appiyakaraṇañca ubhayaṃ te idaṃ sabbameva paṭijānāmi. Tava kāmāti tava [M 5.0328] kāmena taṃ icchamāno. Titikkhisanti adhivāsemi. Bahuṃ maddakulaṃ hantvā nayituṃ tanti bahumaddarājakulaṃ hanitvā balakkārena taṃ netuṃ samatthoti.

Herein, ‘kiṃ na kāhāmi’ means: ‘for what reason should I not do your bidding?’ ‘Vikuddho tyasmi’ means: ‘I am free from anger towards you.’ ‘Sabbaṃ te paṭijānāmi’ means: ‘I acknowledge both this state of being free from anger and my promise not to do anything displeasing to you again.’ ‘Tava kāmā’ means: ‘because of desire for you.’ ‘Titikkhisaṃ’ means: ‘I have endured.’ ‘Bahuṃ maddakulaṃ hantvā nayituṃ taṃ’ means: ‘being capable of slaying many of the Madda royal clan to lead you away by force.’

Atha so sakkassa devarañño paricārikaṃ viya taṃ attano paricārikaṃ disvā khattiyamānaṃ uppādetvā “mayi kira dharamāneyeva mama bhariyaṃ aññe gahetvā gamissantī”ti sīho viya rājaṅgaṇe vijambhamāno “sakalanagaravāsino me āgatabhāvaṃ jānantū”ti vagganto nadanto seḷento apphoṭento “idāni te jīvaggāhaṃ gahessāmi, rathādayo me yojentū”ti anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then, seeing his wife as if she were an attendant of Sakka, king of the devas, he roused his warrior pride, thinking: “While I am still alive, others are taking my wife away!” Like a lion stretching in the royal courtyard, he went about roaring, shouting, boasting, and snapping his fingers, proclaiming: “Let all the city-dwellers know of my arrival! Now I will take them captive alive! Let them yoke my chariots!” He then spoke the following verse:

75.

75.

“Yojayantu rathe asse, nānācitte samāhite;

Atha dakkhatha me vegaṃ, vidhamantassa sattavo”ti.

“Let them yoke the horses to the chariots, those decorated in various ways and well-composed. Then you shall see my speed as I scatter the enemies!”

Tattha nānācitteti nānālaṅkāravicitte. Samāhiteti asse sandhāya vuttaṃ, susikkhite nibbisevaneti attho. Atha dakkhatha me veganti atha me parakkamaṃ passissathāti.

Herein, ‘nānācitte’ means variegated with various ornaments. ‘Samāhite’ is said with reference to the horses; the meaning is well-trained and compliant. ‘Atha dakkhatha me vegaṃ’ means: then you will see my prowess.

Sattūnaṃ gaṇhanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro, gaccha tvaṃ nhatvā alaṅkaritvā pāsādaṃ āruhāti taṃ uyyojesi. Maddarājāpissa parihārakaraṇatthaṃ amacce pahiṇi. Te tassa mahānasadvāreyeva sāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā kappake upaṭṭhapesuṃ. So katamassukammo sīsaṃnhāto sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito amaccādīhi parivuto “pāsādaṃ abhiruhissāmī”ti disā viloketvā apphoṭesi. Olokitaolokitaṭṭhānaṃ vikampi. So “idāni me parakkamaṃ passissathā”ti āha. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

“The capture of the enemies is my responsibility. You go, bathe, adorn yourself, and ascend the palace.” Thus he dismissed her. King Madda also sent ministers to attend to him. They set up a curtain for him right at the entrance to the great kitchen and had barbers attend him. Having had his beard trimmed, having bathed his head, and being adorned with all his ornaments, surrounded by his ministers and others, he looked in the directions and clapped his arms, thinking, “I will ascend the palace.” Every place he looked at trembled. He said, “Now you will see my prowess!” Explaining this matter, the Teacher then spoke the following verse:

76.

76.

“Tañca tattha udikkhiṃsu, rañño maddassantepure;

Vijambhamānaṃ sīhaṃva, phoṭentaṃ diguṇaṃ bhuja”nti.

“And there in King Madda's inner palace they watched him, stretching like a lion, clapping his double arms.”

Tassattho [V 5.0301][P 5.0310] – tañca tattha vijambhantaṃ apphoṭentaṃ rañño antepure vātapānāni vivaritvā itthiyo udikkhiṃsūti.

Its meaning is: The women in the king's inner palace opened the windows and watched him there as he was stretching and clapping his arms.

Athassa maddarājā kataāneñjakāraṇaṃ alaṅkatavaravāraṇaṃ pesesi. So samussitasetacchattaṃ hatthikkhandhaṃ āruyha “pabhāvatiṃ ānethā”ti tampi pacchato nisīdāpetvā caturaṅginiyā senāya parivuto pācīnadvārena [M 5.0329] nikkhamitvā parasenaṃ oloketvā “ahaṃ kusarājā, jīvitatthikā urena nipajjantū”ti tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā sattumaddanaṃ akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then King Madda sent him a splendid, decorated elephant that had been trained to be steadfast. He mounted the elephant's back under a raised white parasol, had Pabhāvatī brought and seated behind him, and, surrounded by the fourfold army, he went out by the eastern gate. Having surveyed the enemy army, he let out a lion's roar three times, saying: “I am King Kusa! Let those who wish to live fall on their chests!” Thus he crushed the enemies. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

77.

77.

“Hatthikkhandhañca āruyha, āropetvā pabhāvatiṃ;

Saṅgāmaṃ otaritvāna, sīhanādaṃ nadī kuso.

“Having mounted the elephant's back, and having seated Pabhāvatī upon it, Kusa entered the battle and roared a lion's roar.

78.

78.

“Tassa taṃ nadato sutvā, sīhassevitare migā;

Khattiyā vipalāyiṃsu, kusasaddabhayaṭṭitā.

“Hearing him roar thus, the khattiyas fled, terrified by the fear of Kusa's voice, just as other beasts flee from a lion.

79.

79.

“Hatthārohā anīkaṭṭhā, rathikā pattikārakā;

Aññamaññassa chindanti, kusasaddabhayaṭṭitā.

“Elephant-riders, cavalry, charioteers, and foot-soldiers, terrified by the fear of Kusa's voice, cut one another down.

80.

80.

“Tasmiṃ saṅgāmasīsasmiṃ, passitvā haṭṭhamānaso;

Kusassa rañño devindo, adā verocanaṃ maṇiṃ.

“At the front of that battle, seeing him, the lord of devas, with a joyful mind, gave King Kusa the Verocana gem.

81.

81.

“So taṃ vijjhitvā saṅgāmaṃ, laddhā verocanaṃ maṇiṃ;

Hatthikkhandhagato rājā, pāvekkhi nagaraṃ puraṃ.

“Having won that battle and obtained the Verocana gem, the king, mounted on the elephant's back, entered the city, his capital.”

82.

82.

“Jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvāna, bandhitvā satta khattiye;

Sasurassūpanāmesi, ime te deva sattavo.

“Having captured the seven khattiyas alive and bound them, he presented them to his father-in-law, saying: ‘Sire, these are your enemies.’

83.

83.

“Sabbeva te vasaṃ gatā, amittā vihatā tava;
