Kāmaṃ karohi te tayā, muñca vā te hanassu vā”ti.

“All have come under your control; your foes have been struck down. Do with them as you wish: either release them or have them slain.”

Tattha [V 5.0302] vipalāyiṃsūti satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontā vipallatthacittā bhijjiṃsu. Kusasaddabhayaṭṭitāti kusarañño saddaṃ nissāya jātena bhayena upaddutā mūḷhacittā. Aññamaññassa chindantīti aññamaññaṃ chindanti maddanti. “Bhindiṃsū”tipi pāṭho. Tasminti evaṃ bodhisattassa saddasavaneneva saṅgāme bhinne tasmiṃ saṅgāmasīse taṃ mahāsattassa parakkamaṃ passitvā tuṭṭhahadayo sakko verocanaṃ nāma maṇikkhandhaṃ tassa adāsi. Nagaraṃ puranti nagarasaṅkhātaṃ puraṃ. Bandhitvāti tesaññeva uttari sāṭakena pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā. Kāmaṃ karohi te tayāti tvaṃ attano kāmaṃ icchaṃ ruciṃ karohi, ete hi tayā dāsā katāyevāti.

Herein, vipalāyiṃsu means: unable to establish mindfulness, with their minds overturned, they were routed. Kusasaddabhayaṭṭitā means: afflicted by the fear that arose on account of King Kusa's sound, with bewildered minds. Aññamaññassa chindanti means: they cut down and crush one another. Bhindiṃsu (they shattered) is also a reading. Tasmiṃ means: thus, when the battle was broken merely by hearing the Bodhisatta's sound, at the head of that battle, having seen the great being's prowess, Sakka, with a delighted heart, gave him a jewel-block named Verocana. Nagaraṃ puraṃ means: the stronghold called a city. Bandhitvā means: having tied their arms behind their backs with their own upper garments. Kāmaṃ karohi te tayā means: you may do according to your own wish, desire, and preference, for they have indeed been made your slaves.

Rājā [P 5.0311][M 5.0330] āha –

The king said:

84.

84.

“Tuyheva sattavo ete, na hi te mayha sattavo;

Tvaññeva no mahārāja, muñca vā te hanassu vā”ti.

“These are your enemies, they are not my enemies. You alone, great king, are our lord; either release them or have them slain.”

Tattha tvaññeva noti, mahārāja, tvaṃyeva amhākaṃ issaroti.

Herein, ‘tvaññeva no’ means: ‘Great king, you alone are our lord.’

Evaṃ [V 5.0303] vutte mahāsatto “kiṃ imehi māritehi, mā tesaṃ āgamanaṃ niratthakaṃ hotu, pabhāvatiyā kaniṭṭhā satta maddarājadhītaro atthi, tā nesaṃ dāpessāmī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

When this was said, the Mahāsatta thought: “What is the use of killing them? Let their coming not be in vain. There are seven younger daughters of the Madda king, younger sisters of Pabhāvatī. I will have them given to these kings.” Then he spoke a verse:

85.

85.

“Imā te dhītaro satta, devakaññūpamā subhā;

Dadāhi nesaṃ ekekaṃ, hontu jāmātaro tavā”ti.

“Here are your seven daughters, lovely, like celestial nymphs. Give one to each of them; let them be your sons-in-law.”

Atha naṃ rājā āha –

Then the king said to him:

86.

86.

“Amhākañceva tāsañca, tvaṃ no sabbesamissaro;

Tvaññeva no mahārāja, dehi nesaṃ yadicchasī”ti.

“You are the lord of us all, both of us and of them. You alone, great king, give them to them as you wish.”

Tattha tvaṃ no sabbesanti, mahārāja kusanarinda, kiṃ vadesi, tvaññeva etesañca sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ mamañca imāsañca sabbesaṃ no issaro. Yadicchasīti yadi icchasi, yassa vā yaṃ dātuṃ icchasi, tassa taṃ dehīti.

Herein, ‘tvaṃ no sabbesaṃ’ means: ‘Great king, lord of men, Kusa, what are you saying? You alone are the lord of all of us—of these seven kings, of me, and of these maidens.’ ‘Yadicchasi’ means: if you wish; or, give whichever one you wish to give to each of them.

Evaṃ vutte so tā sabbāpi alaṅkārāpetvā ekekassa rañño ekekaṃ adāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā pañca gāthāyo abhāsi –

When this was said, he had them all adorned and gave one to each king. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke five verses:

87.

87.

“Ekamekassa ekekaṃ, adā sīhassaro kuso;

Khattiyānaṃ tadā tesaṃ, rañño maddassa dhītaro.

“To each one of those khattiyas, Kusa of the lion-voice then gave one of the daughters of King Madda.

88.

88.

“Pīṇitā tena lābhena, tuṭṭhā sīhassare kuse;

Sakaraṭṭhāni pāyiṃsu, khattiyā satta tāvade.

“Pleased by that gain, delighted with Kusa of the lion-voice, the seven khattiyas then departed for their own kingdoms.

89.

89.

“Pabhāvatiñca ādāya, maṇiṃ verocanaṃ subhaṃ;

Kusāvatiṃ kuso rājā, agamāsi mahabbalo.

“Taking Pabhāvatī and the beautiful Verocana gem, the mighty King Kusa went to Kusāvatī.

90.

90.

“Tyassu ekarathe yantā, pavisantā kusāvatiṃ;

Samānā vaṇṇarūpena, nāññamaññātirocisuṃ.

“Journeying in a single chariot as they entered Kusāvatī, they were equal in beauty and appearance and did not outshine one another.

91.

91.

“Mātā [M 5.0331] puttena saṃgacchi, ubhayo ca jayampatī;

Samaggā te tadā āsuṃ, phītaṃ dharaṇimāvasu”nti.

“The mother was united with her son, and both the husband and wife were then in harmony; they dwelt upon the prosperous earth.”

Tattha pīṇitāti santappitā. Pāyiṃsūti idāni appamattā bhaveyyāthāti kusanarindena ovaditā agamaṃsu. Agamāsīti katipāhaṃ vasitvā “amhākaṃ raṭṭhaṃ [P 5.0312] gamissāmā”ti sasuraṃ āpucchitvā gato. Ekarathe yantāti dvepi ekarathaṃ abhiruyha gacchantā. Samānā vaṇṇarūpenāti vaṇṇena ca rūpena ca samānā hutvā. Nāññamaññātirocisunti eko ekaṃ nātikkami. Maṇiratanānubhāvena kira mahāsatto abhirūpo ahosi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sobhaggappatto, so kira pubbe paccekabuddhassa piṇḍapātanissandena buddhapaṭimākaraṇanissandena ca evaṃ tejavanto ahosi. Saṃgacchīti athassa mātā mahāsattassa āgamanaṃ sutvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā mahāsattassa bahuṃ paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya paccuggamanaṃ katvā samāgacchi. Sopi mātarā saddhiṃyeva nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sattāhaṃ chaṇakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā alaṅkatapāsādatalaṃ abhiruhi. Tepi ubho jayampatikā samaggā ahesuṃ, tato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ samaggā sammodamānā phītaṃ dharaṇiṃ ajjhāvasiṃsūti.

Herein, pīṇitā means satisfied. Pāyiṃsu means: having been advised by King Kusa, “Now you should be heedful,” they departed. Agamāsi means: after staying for a few days, he took leave of his father-in-law, saying, “We will go to our kingdom,” and departed. Ekarathe yantā means: both went, riding in a single chariot. Samānā vaṇṇarūpena means: being equal in complexion and form. Nāññamaññātirocisun means: one did not outshine the other. It is said that by the power of the jewel-gem, the Great Being was handsome, of golden complexion, and had attained beauty. It is said that he became so radiant as a result of having previously offered alms-food to a Paccekabuddha and as a result of having made a Buddha image. Saṃgacchi means: then his mother, having heard of the Great Being’s arrival, had a drum beaten in the city, took many gifts, and went out to meet him. He, together with his mother, circumambulated the city, celebrated a festival for seven days, and ascended to the terrace of the adorned palace. Those two, husband and wife, were harmonious. From then on, for the rest of their lives, they dwelt in harmony and concord, ruling over a prosperous land.

Satthā [V 5.0304] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, kaniṭṭho ānando, khujjā khujjuttarā, pabhāvatī rāhulamātā, parisā buddhaparisā, kusarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, proclaimed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the parents were the members of the Great Royal Family, the younger brother was Ānanda, the hunchbacked woman was Khujjuttarā, Pabhāvatī was Rāhula’s mother, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Kusa was I myself.

Kusajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The explanation of the Kusa Jātaka, the first.

[532] 2. Soṇanandajātakavaṇṇanā

[532] 2. The Commentary on the Soṇananda Jātaka

Devatā nusi gandhabboti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu sāmajātake (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) vatthusadisaṃ. Tadā pana satthā “mā, bhikkhave, imaṃ bhikkhuṃ ujjhāyittha, porāṇakapaṇḍitā sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ labhamānāpi taṃ aggahetvā mātāpitaro posiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Are you a deva or a gandhabba?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who supported his parents. The story is similar to the one in the Sāma Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, do not find fault with this monk. The wise of old, though they obtained sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, did not accept it but supported their parents.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 5.0332] bārāṇasī brahmavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Tattha manojo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tattha aññataro asītikoṭivibhavo brāhmaṇamahāsālo aputtako ahosi. Tassa brāhmaṇī teneva “bhoti puttaṃ patthehī”ti vuttā patthesi. Atha bodhisatto brahmalokā cavitvā tassā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, jātassa cassa “soṇakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle aññopi satto brahmalokā cavitvā tassāyeva kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, tassa jātassa “nandakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tesaṃ uggahitavedānaṃ sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ pattānaṃ vayappattānaṃ rūpasampadaṃ disvā brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiṃ āmantetvā “bhoti puttaṃ soṇakumāraṃ gharabandhanena bandhissāmā”ti āha. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā puttassa tamatthaṃ ācikkhi[P 5.0313]. So “alaṃ, amma, mayhaṃ gharāvāsena, ahaṃ yāvajīvaṃ tumhe paṭijaggitvā tumhākaṃ accayena himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Sā brāhmaṇassa etamatthaṃ ārocesi.

In the past, Benares was the city named Brahmavaḍḍhana. There, a king named Manoja reigned. In that city lived a certain great Brahmin householder with a fortune of eighty crores, but he was childless. When he said to his Brahmin wife, “Lady, pray for a son,” she did so. Then the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Brahma-world, was conceived in her womb. When he was born, they named him Prince Soṇa. When he was old enough to walk, another being passed away from the Brahma-world and was conceived in her womb. When he was born, they named him Prince Nanda. When they had mastered the Vedas, attained perfection in all the arts, and come of age, the Brahmin, seeing their handsome appearance, addressed his wife: “Lady, let us bind our son, Prince Soṇa, with the bond of the household.” She agreed, saying, “Very well,” and told her son about the matter. He replied: “Enough, mother, with the household life! I will look after you both as long as you live, and after your passing, I will enter the Himalayas and go forth.” She then reported this matter to the Brahmin.

Te punappunaṃ kathentāpi tassa cittaṃ alabhitvā nandakumāraṃ āmantetvā “tāta, tena hi tvaṃ kuṭumbaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti vatvā “nāhaṃ bhātarā chaḍḍitakheḷaṃ sīsena ukkhipāmi, ahampi tumhākaṃ accayena bhātarāva saddhiṃ pabbajissāmī”ti vutte tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “ime dve evaṃ taruṇāva kāme pajahanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayaṃ, sabbeyeva pabbajissāmā”ti cintetvā, “tātā[V 5.0305], kiṃ vo amhākaṃ accayena pabbajjāya, idāneva sabbe mayaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti rañño ārocetvā sabbaṃ dhanaṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā dāsajanaṃ bhujissaṃ katvā ñātīnaṃ dātabbayuttakaṃ datvā cattāropi janā brahmavaḍḍhananagarā nikkhamitvā himavantapadese pañcapadumasañchannaṃ saraṃ nissāya ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe assamaṃ māpetvā pabbajitvā tattha vasiṃsu. Ubhopi bhātaro mātāpitaro paṭijaggiṃsu, tesaṃ pātova dantakaṭṭhañca mukhadhovanañca datvā paṇṇasālañca pariveṇañca sammajjitvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā araññato madhuraphalāphalāni āharitvā mātāpitaro khādāpenti, uṇhena vā sītena vā vārinā nhāpenti, jaṭā sodhenti, pādaparikammādīni tesaṃ karonti.

Though they spoke to him again and again, they could not win his consent. Then, addressing Prince Nanda, they said: “Dear son, in that case, you should take over the estate.” When he said, “I will not take upon my head the spittle rejected by my brother. I too will go forth with my brother after your passing,” they heard his words and thought: “These two are renouncing sensual pleasures while so young; what then of us? We should all go forth.” They said to their sons: “Dears, why should you wait for our passing to go forth? We will all go forth right now.” Having informed the king, they gave away all their wealth in alms, freed their servants, gave their relatives what was due to them, and all four departed from the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. They went to the Himalayan region and, near a lake covered with five kinds of lotuses, in a delightful forest grove, they had a hermitage built, went forth, and dwelt there. Both brothers attended to their parents. In the morning, they would give them tooth-sticks and water for washing their faces, sweep the leaf-hut and the precinct, and set out drinking water and water for use. They would bring sweet fruits from the forest and feed their parents, bathe them with hot or cold water, clean their matted hair, and perform services for them such as washing their feet.

Evaṃ [M 5.0333] addhāne gate nandapaṇḍito “mayā ābhataphalāphalāneva paṭhamaṃ mātāpitaro khādāpessāmī”ti purato gantvā hiyyo ca parahiyyo ca gahitaṭṭhānato yāni vā tāni vā pātova āharitvā mātāpitaro khādāpesi. Te tāni khāditvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathikā bhavanti. Soṇapaṇḍito pana dūraṃ gantvā madhuramadhurāni supakkasupakkāni āharitvā upanāmesi. Atha naṃ, “tāta, kaniṭṭhena te ābhatāni mayaṃ pātova khāditvā uposathikā jātā, na idāni no attho”ti vadanti. Iti tassa phalāphalāni paribhogaṃ na labhanti vinassanti, punadivasesupi tathevāti[P 5.0314]. Evaṃ so pañcābhiññatāya dūraṃ gantvāpi āharati, te pana na khādanti.

As time went on in this way, the wise Nanda thought, “I will be the first to have my parents eat the fruits I have brought.” Going ahead, early in the morning he would gather whatever fruits he could find from the same places he had gathered from the day before and the day before that, and he would have his parents eat them. After eating them and rinsing their mouths, they would observe the uposatha. The wise Soṇa, however, would go far away and bring back very sweet and perfectly ripe fruits to offer them. But his parents would say to him: “Dear Soṇa, we have already eaten the fruits brought by your younger brother Nanda early in the morning and are now observing the uposatha. We have no need for them now.” Thus Soṇa’s fruits were not consumed and went to waste; it was the same on the following days. Even though Soṇa, possessing the five higher knowledges, went far away to bring them, they would not eat them.

Atha mahāsatto cintesi – “mātāpitaro me sukhumālā, nando ca yāni vā tāni vā apakkaduppakkāni phalāphalāni āharitvā khādāpeti, evaṃ sante ime na cīraṃ pavattissanti, vāressāmi na”nti. Atha naṃ so āmantetvā “nanda, ito paṭṭhāya phalāphalaṃ āharitvā mamāgamanaṃ paṭimānehi, ubhopi ekatova khādāpessāmā”ti āha. So evaṃ vuttepi attano puññaṃ paccāsīsanto na tassa vacanamakāsi. Mahāsatto “nando mama vacanaṃ akaronto ayuttaṃ karoti, palāpessāmi naṃ, tato ekakova mātāpitaro paṭijaggissāmī”ti cintetvā “nanda, tvaṃ anovādako paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ na karosi, ahaṃ jeṭṭho, mātāpitaro mameva bhāro, ahameva nesaṃ paṭijaggissāmi, tvaṃ idha vasituṃ na lacchasi, aññattha yāhī”ti tassa accharaṃ pahari.

Then the Great Being thought: “My parents are delicate, yet Nanda brings whatever fruits he finds, even those that are unripe or poorly ripened, and has them eat them. If this continues, they will not live long. I must stop him.” Then he addressed him, saying: “Nanda, from now on, after gathering fruits, wait for my return. Both of us together will feed our parents.” Even though his elder brother said this, Nanda, desiring his own merit, did not follow his words. The Great Being thought: “Nanda is doing wrong by not following my words. I will drive him away, and then I alone will look after our parents.” He thought, “Nanda, you do not take advice and do not listen to the words of the wise. I am the elder brother; the parents are my responsibility. I alone will care for them. You shall not stay here. Go elsewhere!” and he snapped his fingers at him in dismissal.

So tena palāpito tassa santike ṭhātuṃ asakkonto taṃ vanditvā mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā attano paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kasiṇaṃ oloketvā taṃ divasameva [V 5.0306] pañca abhiññāyo aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā cintesi – “ahaṃ sīnerupādato ratanavālukā āharitvā mama bhātu paṇṇasālāya pariveṇe okiritvā bhātaraṃ khamāpetuṃ pahomi, evampi na sobhissati, anotattato udakaṃ āharitvā mama bhātu paṇṇasālāya pariveṇe osiñcitvā bhātaraṃ khamāpetuṃ pahomi, evampi na sobhissati, sace me bhātaraṃ devatānaṃ vasena khamāpeyyaṃ, cattāro ca mahārājāno sakkañca ānetvā bhātaraṃ khamāpetuṃ pahomi, evampi na sobhissati[M 5.0334], sakalajambudīpe manojaṃ aggarājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā rājāno ānetvā khamāpessāmi, evaṃ sante mama bhātu guṇo sakalajambudīpe avattharitvā gamissati, candimasūriyo viya paññāyissatī”ti. So tāvadeva iddhiyā gantvā brahmavaḍḍhananagare tassa rañño nivesanadvāre otaritvā ṭhito “eko kira [P 5.0315] vo tāpaso daṭṭhukāmo”ti rañño ārocāpesi. Rājā “kiṃ pabbajitassa mayā diṭṭhena, āhāratthāya āgato bhavissatī”ti bhattaṃ pahiṇi, so bhattaṃ na icchi. Taṇḍulaṃ pahiṇi, taṇḍulaṃ na icchi. Vatthāni pahiṇi, vatthāni na icchi. Tambūlaṃ pahiṇi, tambūlaṃ na icchi. Athassa santike dūtaṃ pesesi, “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti. So dūtena puṭṭho “rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahituṃ āgatomhī”ti āha. Rājā taṃ sutvā “bahū mama upaṭṭhākā, attanova tāpasadhammaṃ karotū”ti pesesi. So taṃ sutvā “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ attano balena sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā dassāmī”ti āha.

Driven away by him and unable to stay near his brother, Nanda paid homage to him, approached his parents to inform them of the matter, and then entered his own leaf hut. He gazed upon the kasiṇa and, on that very day, developed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments. He reflected: “I am able to bring jewel-sand from the foot of Mount Sineru to scatter in my brother’s leaf hut and its surroundings to ask for his forgiveness, but even that would not be grand enough. I could bring water from Lake Anotatta to sprinkle there to ask for his forgiveness, but that too would not be grand enough. If I wished to ask for my brother’s forgiveness through the power of deities, I could bring the Four Great Kings and Sakka to ask for his pardon, but even that would not be grand enough. However, if I bring the kings of all Jambudīpa, starting with the great King Manoja, to ask for his forgiveness, then my brother’s virtue will spread throughout all Jambudīpa and become as well-known as the sun and the moon.” Immediately, by psychic power, he went to the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana and stood at the gate of King Manoja's palace. He had it announced: “An ascetic wishes to see the King.” The king thought, “What use have I for seeing an ascetic? He must have come for food,” and sent food. Nanda did not want it. The king sent rice, cloth, and betel, but Nanda wanted none of it. Then the king sent a messenger to ask, “For what purpose have you come?” Nanda replied, “I have come to serve the king.” Hearing this, the king sent word: “I have many attendants; let him practice his own ascetic duties.” Nanda replied, “By my own power, I will seize and give you kingship over the whole of Jambudīpa.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā cintesi – “pabbajitā nāma paṇḍitā, kiñci upāyaṃ jānissantī”ti taṃ pakkosāpetvā āsane nisīdāpetvā vanditvā “bhante, tumhe kira mayhaṃ sakalajambudīparajjaṃ gahetvā dassathā”ti pucchi. “Āma mahārājā”ti. “Kathaṃ gaṇhissathā”ti? “Mahārāja, antamaso khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ kassaci anuppādetvā tava dhanacchedaṃ akatvā attano iddhiyāva gahetvā dassāmi, apica kevalaṃ papañcaṃ akatvā ajjeva nikkhamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā senaṅgaparivuto nagarā nikkhami. Sace senāya uṇhaṃ hoti, nandapaṇḍito attano iddhiyā chāyaṃ katvā sītaṃ karoti, deve vassante senāya upari vassituṃ na deti, sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā vāreti, magge khāṇukaṇṭakādayo sabbaparissaye antaradhāpeti, maggaṃ kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ viya samaṃ katvā sayaṃ ākāse cammakhaṇḍaṃ pattharitvā pallaṅkena nisinno senāya parivuto gacchati.

Hearing this, the king thought, “Ascetics are indeed wise; they must know some means.” He had Nanda summoned, provided a seat, paid homage, and asked: “Venerable sir, is it true that you will seize and give me kingship over all of Jambudīpa?” “Yes, great king.” “How will you take it?” “Great king, without causing even as much blood as a tiny fly might drink to be shed, and without any loss of your wealth, I will take it and give it to you by my own power. Moreover, without any delay, it is proper to set out this very day.” Trusting his words, the king set out surrounded by his army. If the army felt hot, the wise Nanda used his power to provide shade and coolness. If it rained, he did not let it fall on the army. He warded off cold and heat. He removed all dangers such as stumps and thorns from the path. He made the road as smooth as a kasiṇa circle, and while seated cross-legged on a leather mat spread in the sky, he traveled, surrounded by the army.

Evaṃ senaṃ ādāya paṭhamaṃ kosalaraṭṭhaṃ gantvā nagarassāvidūre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsāpetvā “yuddhaṃ vā no detu setacchattaṃ vā”ti kosalarañño dūtaṃ pāhesi. So kujjhitvā “kiṃ ahaṃ na rājā”ti “yuddhaṃ dammī”ti senāya purakkhato nikkhami. Dve [P 5.0316] senā yujjhituṃ ārabhiṃsu[V 5.0307]. Nandapaṇḍito dvinnampi antare attano nisīdanaṃ ajinacammaṃ mahantaṃ katvā pasāretvā dvīhipi [M 5.0335] senāhi khittasare cammeneva sampaṭicchi. Ekasenāyapi koci kaṇḍena viddho nāma natthi, hatthagatānaṃ pana kaṇḍānaṃ khayena dvepi senā nirussāhā aṭṭhaṃsu. Nandapaṇḍito manojarājassa santikaṃ gantvā “mā bhāyi, mahārājā”ti assāsetvā kosalassa santikaṃ gantvā “mahārāja, mā bhāyi, natthi te paripantho, tava rajjaṃ taveva bhavissati, kevalaṃ manojarañño vasavattī hohī”ti āha. So tassa saddahitvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Atha naṃ manojassa santikaṃ netvā “mahārāja, kosalarājā te vase vattati, imassa rajjaṃ imasseva hotū”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ attano vase vattetvā dve senā ādāya aṅgaraṭṭhaṃ gantvā aṅgaṃ gahetvā tato magadharaṭṭhanti etenupāyena sakalajambudīpe rājāno attano vase vattetvā tato tehi parivuto brahmavaḍḍhananagarameva gato. Rajjaṃ gaṇhanto panesa sattannaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ upari sattadivasādhikehi sattamāsehi gaṇhi. So ekekarājadhānito nānappakāraṃ khajjabhojanaṃ āharāpetvā ekasatarājāno gahetvā tehi saddhiṃ sattāhaṃ mahāpānaṃ pivi.

Having gathered his army, he first went to the Kosala kingdom and set up camp not far from the city. He then sent a messenger to the king of Kosala, saying, 'Either give us battle or the white parasol.' Enraged, the king replied, 'Am I not a king?' and, preceded by his army, marched out. The two armies began to fight. Nanda the Wise made his deerskin seat large and spread it out between the two armies, and with the skin itself he caught the arrows shot by both armies. Not a single person in either army was wounded by an arrow. But as the arrows in their hands were exhausted, both armies lost their enthusiasm and stood still. Nanda the Wise went to King Manoja and reassured him, saying, 'Do not fear, great king.' Then he approached the king of Kosala and said, 'Great king, do not fear. There is no danger to you. Your kingdom will remain yours. Only become a vassal to King Manoja.' The king trusted his words and agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Then Nanda brought him before Manoja and said, 'Great king, the king of Kosala is under your power. Let his kingdom remain his.' He accepted this, saying, 'Very well,' and brought him under his power. Taking both armies, he then went to the Anga kingdom, conquered Anga, and from there to the Magadha kingdom. In this way, he brought all the kings in Jambudīpa under his power and, surrounded by them, returned to the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. The seizing of the kingdom, however, took him seven years, seven months, and seven days. From each royal capital, he had various kinds of food brought, and, taking one hundred and one kings, he held a great drinking festival with them for seven days.

Nandapaṇḍito “yāva rājā sattāhaṃ issariyasukhaṃ anubhoti, tāvassa attānaṃ na dassessāmī”ti uttarakurumhi piṇḍāya caritvā himavante kañcanaguhādvāre sattāhaṃ vasi. Manojopi sattame divase attano mahantaṃ sirivibhavaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ yaso na mayhaṃ mātāpitūhi, na aññehi dinno, nandatāpasaṃ nissāya uppanno, taṃ kho pana me apassantassa ajja sattamo divaso, kahaṃ nu kho me yasadāyako”ti nandapaṇḍitaṃ sari. So tassa anussaraṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgantvā purato ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā cintesi – “ahaṃ imassa tāpasassa devatābhāvaṃ vā manussabhāvaṃ vā na jānāmi, sace esa [P 5.0317] manusso bhaveyya, sakalajambudīparajjaṃ etasseva dassāmi. Atha devo, sakkāramassa karissāmī”ti. So taṃ vīmaṃsanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Nanda the Wise thought, 'Until the king enjoys the bliss of sovereignty for seven days, I will not show myself to him.' After wandering for alms in Uttarakuru, he stayed for seven days at the entrance of a golden cave in the Himalayas. On the seventh day, Manoja, reflecting on his great royal glory and wealth, thought, 'This glory was not given to me by my parents or anyone else; it arose dependent on the ascetic Nanda. Yet, today is the seventh day that I have not seen him. Where is my giver of glory?' He then remembered Nanda the Wise. Knowing he was remembered, Nanda the Wise came and stood in the air before him. Seeing him, the king pondered, 'I do not know whether this ascetic's nature is that of a deity or a human. If he is human, I will give him the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa. If he is a deity, I will pay him homage.' While considering this, the king first spoke this verse:

92.

92.

“Devatā nuti gandhabbo, adu sakko purindado;

Manussabhūto iddhimā, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“Are you a deva or a gandhabba? Or Sakka, Purindada? Or a human being with psychic power? How shall we know you?”

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sabhāvameva kathento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, stating his true nature, he spoke the second verse:

93.

93.

“Nāpi [V 5.0308][M 5.0336] devo na gandhabbo, nāpi sakko purindado;

Manussabhūto iddhimā, evaṃ jānāhi bhāradhā”ti.

“I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka, Purindada; I am a human being with psychic power—thus know, O Bhāradha.”

Tattha bhāradhāti raṭṭhabhāradhāritāya naṃ evaṃ ālapati.

Therein, he addresses him as 'bearer of the burden' because he bears the burden of the kingdom.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “manussabhūto kirāyaṃ mayhaṃ evaṃ bahupakāro, mahantena yasena naṃ santappessāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

Hearing this, the king thought, “This one, being a human, has indeed been of great help to me. I shall satisfy him with great honor,” and said:

94.

94.

“Katarūpamidaṃ bhoto, veyyāvaccaṃ anappakaṃ;

Devamhi vassamānamhi, anovassaṃ bhavaṃ akā.

“What kind of service is this of yours, sir, so vast? While it was raining, you, sir, made it not rain.

95.

95.

“Tato vātātape ghore, sītacchāyaṃ bhavaṃ akā;

Tato amittamajjhesu, saratāṇaṃ bhavaṃ akā.

“Then in the fierce wind and heat, you made cool shade; then amidst enemies, you made a refuge from arrows.

96.

96.

“Tato phītāni raṭṭhāni, vasino te bhavaṃ akā;

Tato ekasataṃ khatye, anuyante bhavaṃ akā.

“Then you made the prosperous kingdoms subject to us; then you made one hundred and one khattiyas follow us.

97.

97.

“Patītāssu mayaṃ bhoto, vada taṃ bhañjamicchasi;

Hatthiyānaṃ assarathaṃ, nāriyo ca alaṅkatā;

Nivesanāni rammāni, mayaṃ bhoto dadāmase.

“We are pleased with you, sir; tell us what treasure you desire. Elephant vehicles, horse chariots, and adorned women, delightful dwellings—we give these to you, sir.

98.

98.

“Atha vaṅge vā magadhe, mayaṃ bhoto dadāmase;

Atha vā assakāvantī, sumanā damma te mayaṃ.

“Or Vanga or Magadha, we will give to you, sir; or Assaka and Avanti, we will give you willingly.

99.

99.

“Upaḍḍhaṃ vāpi rajjassa, mayaṃ bhoto dadāmase;

Sace te attho rajjena, anusāsa yadicchasī”ti.

“Or even half the kingdom, sir, we will give you; if you have need of the kingdom, command as you wish.”

Tattha katarūpamidanti katasabhāvaṃ. Veyyāvaccanti kāyaveyyāvatikakammaṃ. Anovassanti avassaṃ, yathā devo na vassati[P 5.0318], tathā katanti attho. Sītacchāyanti sītalaṃ chāyaṃ. Vasino teti te raṭṭhavāsino amhākaṃ vasavattino. Khatyeti khattiye, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ayameva pāṭho. Patītāssu [V 5.0309] mayanti tuṭṭhā mayaṃ. Vada taṃ bhañjamicchasīti bhañjanti ratanassetaṃ nāmaṃ, varaṃ te dadāmi, yaṃ ratanaṃ icchasi, taṃ vadehīti attho. “Hatthiyāna”ntiādīhi sarūpato taṃ taṃ ratanaṃ dasseti [M 5.0337] . Assakāvantīassakaraṭṭhaṃ vā avantiraṭṭhaṃ vā. Rajjenāti sacepi te sakalajambudīparajjena attho, tampi te datvā ahaṃ phalakāvudhahattho tumhākaṃ rathassa purato gamissāmīti dīpeti. Yadicchasīti etesu mayā vuttappakāresu yaṃ icchasi, taṃ anusāsa āṇāpehīti.

Herein, `katarūpamidaṃ` means 'of what kind is its nature?'. `Veyyāvaccaṃ` means bodily service. `Anovassaṃ` means not raining; the meaning is, 'it was made so that the god would not rain.' `Sītacchāyaṃ` means a cool shade. `Vasino te` means: those country-dwellers are under our power. `Khatye` means `khattiye`; but in the commentary this is the reading. `Patītāssu mayaṃ` means 'we are pleased.' Regarding 'Speak what `bhañja` you desire': `bhañja` is a name for a jewel; the meaning is, 'I give you a boon. Whatever jewel you desire, speak.' By 'elephant vehicle,' etc., he indicates each jewel by its form. `Assakāvantī` means either the kingdom of Assaka or the kingdom of Avanti. By `rajjena` he explains: 'Even if you have need of the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa, having given that to you, I will go before your chariot, with shield and weapon in hand.' `Yadicchasi` means: 'Among these things I have mentioned, whatever you wish, instruct, command it.'

Taṃ sutvā nandapaṇḍito attano adhippāyaṃ āvikaronto āha –

Hearing that, Nanda the Wise, revealing his own intention, said:

100.

100.

“Na me atthopi rajjena, nagarena dhanena vā;

Athopi janapadena, attho mayhaṃ na vijjatī”ti.

“I have no need of a kingdom, nor of a city or of wealth; nor, too, of a country—I find no need for these.”

“Sace te mayi sineho atthi, ekaṃ me vacanaṃ karohī”ti vatvā gāthādvayamāha –

“If you have affection for me, do this one thing for me,” he said, and then spoke two verses:

101.

101.

“Bhotova raṭṭhe vijite, araññe atthi assamo;

Pitā mayhaṃ janettī ca, ubho sammanti assame.

“In your conquered kingdom, sir, there is a hermitage in the forest; my father and my mother both dwell peacefully in that hermitage.

102.

102.

“Tesāhaṃ pubbācariyesu, puññaṃ na labhāmi kātave;

Bhavantaṃ ajjhāvaraṃ katvā, soṇaṃ yācemu saṃvara”nti.

“Towards them, my first teachers, I do not get to make merit. Having made you my leader, sir, let us beg Soṇa for reconciliation.”

Tattha raṭṭheti rajje. Vijiteti āṇāpavattiṭṭhāne. Assamoti himavantāraññe eko assamo atthi. Sammantīti tasmiṃ assame vasanti. Tesāhanti tesu ahaṃ. Kātaveti vattapaṭivattaphalāphalāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ puññaṃ kātuṃ na labhāmi, bhātā me soṇapaṇḍito nāma mamekasmiṃ aparādhe mā idha vasīti maṃ palāpesi. Ajjhāvaranti adhiāvaraṃ te mayaṃ bhavantaṃ saparivāraṃ katvā soṇapaṇḍitaṃ saṃvaraṃ yācemu, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ yācāmāti attho. “Yācemimaṃ vara”ntipi pāṭho, mayaṃ tayā saddhiṃ soṇaṃ yāceyyāma khamāpeyyāma, imaṃ varaṃ tava santikā gaṇhāmīti attho.

Herein, `raṭṭhe` means in the kingdom. `Vijite` means in the place where commands are effective. `Assamo` means: there is a hermitage in the Himalayan forest. `Sammanti` means they live in that hermitage. `Tesāhaṃ` means: towards them, I. `Kātave` means: I do not get to make the merit consisting of performing duties and counter-duties and bringing fruits and non-fruits; my brother, the wise Soṇa, on account of a single offense of mine, drove me away, saying, 'Do not live here.' `Ajjhāvaraṃ` means: having made you and your retinue our protector, we will beg the wise Soṇa for restraint; the meaning is, we ask for restraint in the future. There is also the reading `yācemimaṃ varaṃ` (let us ask for this boon), the meaning of which is: 'Together with you, we would beg Soṇa, we would ask his forgiveness; we take this boon from you.'

Atha naṃ rājā āha –

Then the king said to him:

103.

103.

“Karomi [V 5.0310] te taṃ vacanaṃ, yaṃ maṃ bhaṇasi brāhmaṇa;

Etañca kho no akkhāhi, kīvanto hontu yācakā”ti.

“I will do that word of yours, that you speak to me, brahmin. But please tell us this: how many should the supplicants be?”

Tattha [P 5.0319][M 5.0338] karomīti ahaṃ sakalajambudīparajjaṃ dadamāno ettakaṃ kiṃ na karissāmi, karomīti vadati. Kīvantoti kittakā.

Herein, `karomi` means: 'When I am giving away the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa, why shouldn't I do this much?'—so he says, 'I will do it.' `Kīvanto` means how many.

Nandapaṇḍito āha –

Nanda the Wise said:

104.

104.

“Parosataṃ jānapadā, mahāsālā ca brāhmaṇā;

Ime ca khattiyā sabbe, abhijātā yasassino;

Bhavañca rājā manojo, alaṃ hessanti yācakā”ti.

“Over a hundred country folk, and brahmins of great halls, and all these khattiyas, well-born and renowned, and you, King Manoja—these will be enough supplicants.”

Tattha jānapadāti gahapatī. Mahāsālā ca brāhmaṇāti sārappattā brāhmaṇā ca parosatāyeva. Alaṃ hessantīti pariyattā bhavissanti. Yācakāti mamatthāya soṇapaṇḍitassa khamāpakā.

Herein, ‘country folk’ means householders. ‘And brahmins of great halls’ means brahmins who have attained substance, also over a hundred. ‘Will be enough’ means they will be sufficient. ‘Supplicants’ means those who will ask for the wise Soṇa's forgiveness for my sake.

Atha naṃ rājā āha –

Then the king said to him:

105.

105.

“Hatthī asse ca yojentu, rathaṃ sannayha sārathi;

Ābandhanāni gaṇhātha, pādāsussārayaddhaje;

Assamaṃ taṃ gamissāmi, yattha sammati kosiyo”ti.

“Let them yoke the elephants and horses; O charioteer, harness the chariot. Take the harnesses; raise the banners upon the chariot-fronts. I will go to that hermitage where Kosiya dwells.”

Tattha yojentūti hatthārohā hatthī, assārohā ca asse kappentu. Rathaṃ sannayha sārathīti sammasārathi tvampi rathaṃ sannayha. Ābandhanānīti hatthiassarathesu ābandhitabbāni bhaṇḍāni ca gaṇhatha. Pādāsussārayaddhajeti rathe ṭhapitadhajapādāsu dhaje ussārayantu ussāpentu. Kosiyoti yasmiṃ assame kosiyagotto vasatīti.

In this context, ‘let them yoke’ means let the elephant-riders prepare the elephants and the horse-riders prepare the horses. ‘O charioteer, harness the chariot’ means: you too, O good charioteer, harness the chariot. ‘Harnesses’ means: take the straps and gear to be fastened to the elephants, horses, and chariots. ‘Raise the banners upon the chariot-fronts’ means: let them raise, let them hoist the banners on the banner-stands placed on the chariots. ‘Kosiya’ refers to the hermitage where one of the Kosiya clan dwells.

106.

106.

“Tato ca rājā pāyāsi, senāya caturaṅginī;

Agamā assamaṃ rammaṃ, yattha sammati kosiyo”ti. – ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā;

“Then the king set out with his fourfold army; he went to the lovely hermitage where Kosiya dwells.” — This is a verse spoken after Enlightenment.

Tattha [V 5.0311] tato cāti, bhikkhave, evaṃ vatvā tato so rājā ekasatakhattiye gahetvā mahatiyā senāya parivuto nandapaṇḍitaṃ purato katvā nagarā nikkhami. Caturaṅgīnīti caturaṅginiyā senāya agamāsi, antaramagge vattamānopi avassaṃ gāmitāya evaṃ vutto. Catuvīsatiakkhobhaṇisaṅkhātena balakāyena saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipannassa tassa nandapaṇḍito iddhānubhāvena aṭṭhusabhavitthataṃ maggaṃ samaṃ māpetvā [M 5.0339] ākāse cammakhaṇḍaṃ pattharitvā tattha pallaṅkena nisīditvā senāya parivuto alaṅkatahatthikkhandhe nisīditvā gacchantena raññā saddhiṃ dhammayuttakathaṃ kathento sītauṇhādiparissaye vārento agamāsi.

Herein, ‘then’ means: O monks, after speaking thus, that king took the one hundred and one khattiyas and, surrounded by a great army, placing the wise Nanda in front, departed from the city. ‘With a fourfold army’ means he went with an army of four divisions; although he was still on the journey, it is expressed this way due to the certainty of his arrival. While the king was traveling with a host of forces numbering twenty-four akkhobhiṇīs, the wise Nanda, by his psychic power, created a level path eight usabhas wide. Spreading a piece of leather in the sky and sitting there cross-legged, he traveled along while conversing on matters of the Dhamma with the king—who was seated on the neck of an ornamented elephant—and warding off dangers such as cold and heat.

Athassa assamaṃ pāpuṇanadivase soṇapaṇḍito “mama kaniṭṭhassa atirekasattamāsasattadivasādhikāni satta vassāni [P 5.0320] nikkhantassā”ti āvajjetvā “kahaṃ nu kho so etarahī”ti dibbena cakkhunā olokento “catuvīsatiakkhobhaṇiparivārena saddhiṃ ekasatarājāno gahetvā mamaññeva khamāpetuṃ āgacchatī”ti disvā cintesi – “imehi rājūhi ceva parisāhi ca mama kaniṭṭhassa bahūni pāṭihāriyāni diṭṭhāni, mamānubhāvaṃ ajānitvā ‘ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāti, amhākaṃ ayyena saddhiṃ payojesī’ti maṃ vambhentā kathentā avīciparāyaṇā bhaveyyuṃ, iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ nesaṃ dassessāmī”ti. So caturaṅgulamattena aṃsaṃ aphusantaṃ ākāse kājaṃ ṭhapetvā anotattato udakaṃ āharituṃ rañño avidūre ākāsena pāyāsi. Nandapaṇḍito taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā attānaṃ dassetuṃ avisahanto nisinnaṭṭhāneyeva antaradhāyitvā palāyitvā himavantaṃ pāvisi. Manojarājā pana taṃ ramaṇīyena isivesena tathā āgacchantaṃ disvā gāthamāha –

Then, on the day the king was to arrive at the hermitage, the wise Soṇa reflected: 'Seven years, seven months, and seven days have passed since my younger brother left this place.' He wondered, 'Where is he now?' and looking with the divine eye, he saw: 'He is coming to ask my forgiveness, bringing one hundred and one kings together with a retinue of twenty-four akkhobhiṇīs.' He then thought: 'These kings and their retinues have witnessed many miracles performed by my younger brother. Not knowing my own power, they might disparage me, saying, “This fraudulent ascetic does not know his place; he acts as an equal to our lord,” and by saying such things, they would be destined for Avīci. I shall show them a miracle of psychic power.' Then, placing a carrying-pole in the air so that it was four finger-breadths above his shoulder without touching it, he went through the sky not far from King Manoja to fetch water from Lake Anotatta. The wise Nanda, seeing the wise Soṇa approaching and not daring to show himself, vanished from his seat, fled, and entered the Himalayas. But King Manoja, seeing the wise Soṇa approaching in the beautiful guise of a seer, spoke this verse:

107.

107.

“Kassa kādambayo kājo, vehāsaṃ caturaṅgulaṃ;

Aṃsaṃ asamphusaṃ eti, udahārāya gacchato”ti.

“Whose is this carrying-pole of kadamba wood, four finger-breadths in the air? It moves without touching the shoulder of him who goes to fetch water.”

Tattha kādambayoti kadambarukkhamayo. Aṃsaṃ asamphusaṃ etīti aṃsaṃ asamphusanto sayameva āgacchati. Udahārāyāti udakaṃ āharituṃ gacchantassa kassa esa kājo evaṃ eti, ko nāma tvaṃ, kuto vā āgacchasīti.

Herein, ‘kādambayo’ means made of kadamba wood. ‘It moves without touching the shoulder’ means it moves along without touching the shoulder. ‘Of him who goes to fetch water’ means: whose carrying-pole is this that moves in such a way as he goes to fetch water? Who are you, and where do you come from?

Evaṃ vutte mahāsatto gāthādvayamāha –

When this was said, the Great Being spoke two verses:

108.

108.

“Ahaṃ [V 5.0312] soṇo mahārāja, tāpaso sahitabbato;

Bharāmi mātāpitaro, rattindivamatandito.

“I am Soṇa, O great king, an ascetic endowed with virtue. I support my parents, tirelessly day and night.”

109.

109.

“Vane phalañca mūlañca, āharitvā disampati;

Posemi mātāpitaro, pubbe katamanussara”nti.

“Bringing fruits and roots from the forest, O lord of the land, I nourish my parents, remembering the gratitude for what they did for me in the past.”

Tattha [M 5.0340] sahitabbatoti sahitavato sīlācārasampanno eko tāpaso ahanti vadati. Bharāmīti posemi. Atanditoti analaso hutvā. Pubbe katamanussaranti tehi pubbe kataṃ mayhaṃ guṇaṃ anussarantoti.

Herein, ‘sahitabbato’ means he says, 'I am an ascetic endowed with virtue and good conduct.' ‘Bharāmi’ means I nourish. ‘Atandito’ means being without laziness. ‘Pubbe katamanussaraṃ’ means remembering the kindness they previously showed to me.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ kattukāmo anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to become acquainted with him, spoke this next verse:

110.

110.

“Icchāma [P 5.0321] assamaṃ gantuṃ, yattha sammati kosiyo;

Maggaṃ no soṇa akkhāhi, yena gacchemu assama”nti.

“We wish to go to the hermitage where Kosiya dwells. O Soṇa, tell us the path by which we may reach the hermitage.”

Tattha assamanti tumhākaṃ assamapadaṃ.

Herein, ‘the hermitage’ means your hermitage site.

Atha mahāsatto attano ānubhāvena assamapadagāmimaggaṃ māpetvā gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, by his own power, created a path leading to the hermitage and spoke this verse:

111.

111.

“Ayaṃ ekapadī rāja, yenetaṃ meghasannibhaṃ;

Koviḷārehi sañchannaṃ, ettha sammati kosiyo”ti.

“This is a footpath, O king, leading to that wood which appears like a cloud, covered with koviḷāra flowers. There Kosiya dwells.”

Tassattho – mahārāja, ayaṃ ekapadiko jaṅghamaggo, iminā gacchatha, yena disābhāgena etaṃ meghavaṇṇaṃ supupphitakoviḷārasañchannaṃ vanaṃ dissati, ettha mama pitā kosiyagotto vasati, etassa so assamoti.

Its meaning is: Great king, this is a single-file foot-path. Go by this, in the direction where that cloud-colored forest is seen, covered with well-blossomed koviḷāra trees. Here my father of the Kosiya clan dwells; this is his hermitage.

112.

112.

“Idaṃ vatvāna pakkāmi, taramāno mahāisi;

Vehāse antalikkhasmiṃ, anusāsitvāna khattiye.

“Having said this and instructed the khattiyas while standing in the sky, the great seer departed in haste.”

113.

113.

“Assamaṃ [V 5.0313] parimajjitvā, paññāpetvāna āsanaṃ;

Paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā, pitaraṃ patibodhayi.

“Having swept the hermitage and prepared a seat for his father, he entered the leaf-hut and informed his father.”

114.

114.

“Ime āyanti rājāno, abhijātā yasassino;

Assamā nikkhamitvāna, nisīda tvaṃ mahāise.

“These kings are coming, well-born and famous. Come out from the hermitage, O great seer, and sit down.”

115.

115.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, taramāno mahāisi;

Assamā nikkhamitvāna, sadvāramhi upāvisī”ti. – imā abhisambuddhagāthā;

“Hearing his words, the great seer hurriedly came out of the hermitage and sat down at the door.” — These are verses spoken after Enlightenment.

Tattha [M 5.0341] pakkāmīti anotattaṃ agamāsi. Assamaṃ parimajjitvāti, bhikkhave, so isi vegena anotattaṃ gantvā pānīyaṃ ādāya tesu rājūsu assamaṃ asampattesuyeva āgantvā pānīyaghaṭe pānīyamāḷake ṭhapetvā “mahājano pivissatī”ti vanakusumehi vāsetvā sammajjaniṃ ādāya assamaṃ sammajjitvā paṇṇasāladvāre pitu āsanaṃ paññāpetvā pavisitvā pitaraṃ jānāpesīti attho. Upāvisīti uccāsane nisīdi.

There, ‘departed’ means he went to Lake Anotatta. ‘Having swept the hermitage’ means, monks, that sage quickly went to Anotatta, fetched water, and before those kings arrived at the hermitage, returned. He placed the water pot in the water stand, thinking, “The great crowd will drink,” perfumed it with forest flowers, took a broom, swept the hermitage, prepared a seat for his father at the door of the leaf-hut, entered, and informed his father. ‘Sat’ means he sat on a high seat.

Bodhisattassa mātā pana tassa pacchato nīcaṭṭhāne ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Mahāsatto nīcāsane nisīdi. Nandapaṇḍitopi bodhisattassa anotattato pānīyaṃ ādāya assamaṃ āgatakāle rañño santikaṃ āgantvā assamassa avidūre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsesi. Atha rājā nhatvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito ekasatarājaparivuto nandapaṇḍitaṃ gahetvā mahantena sirisobhaggena bodhisattaṃ khamāpetuṃ assamaṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ tathā āgacchantaṃ bodhisattassa pitā disvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi, sopissa ācikkhi. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0322] pakāsento satthā āha –

The Bodhisatta’s mother sat in a lower place behind the father. The Great Being also sat on a low seat. When the Bodhisatta returned to the hermitage after fetching water from Lake Anotatta, the wise Nanda went to the king and set up camp not far from the hermitage. Then the king, having bathed and adorned himself with all his ornaments, and surrounded by one hundred and one kings, took the wise Nanda with him and entered the hermitage with great splendor to pay respects to the Bodhisatta. When the Bodhisatta’s father saw him approaching in such a manner, he asked the Bodhisatta about it, and the Bodhisatta explained. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

116.

116.

“Tañca disvāna āyantaṃ, jalantaṃriva tejasā;

Khatyasaṅghaparibyūḷhaṃ, kosiyo etadabravi.

Seeing him approaching, blazing as if with splendor, surrounded by a host of kings, Kosiya said this:

117.

117.

“Kassa bherī mudiṅgā ca, saṅkhā paṇavadindimā;

Purato paṭipannāni, hāsayantā rathesabhaṃ.

Whose large drums and tabors, conches, kettledrums, and double-drums proceed in front, delighting the noble lord of the chariot?

118.

118.

“Kassa kañcanapaṭṭena, puthunā vijjuvaṇṇinā;

Yuvā kalāpasannaddho, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Whose is the broad, lightning-colored golden band? Who is this youth, armed with a quiver, coming blazing with splendor?

119.

119.

“Ukkāmukhapahaṭṭhaṃva[V 5.0314], khadiraṅgārasannibhaṃ;

Mukhañca rucirā bhāti, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Like gold from a crucible, like a khadira ember, his beautiful face shines. Who comes blazing with splendor?

120.

120.

“Kassa paggahitaṃ chattaṃ, sasalākaṃ manoramaṃ;

Ādiccaraṃsāvaraṇaṃ, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Whose parasol with its ribs is held up, lovely, a shield from the sun's rays? Who comes blazing with splendor?

121.

121.

“Kassa aṅgaṃ pariggayha, vālabījanimuttamaṃ;

Caranti varapuññassa, hatthikkhandhena āyato.

Surrounding whose entourage do they move the finest yak-tail whisks, as he of excellent merit comes on the shoulder of an elephant?

122.

122.

“Kassa [M 5.0342] setāni chattāni, ājānīyā ca vammitā;

Samantā parikīrenti, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Whose are the white parasols? Whom do the armored warriors on noble steeds surround on all sides? Who comes blazing with splendor?

123.

123.

“Kassa ekasataṃ khatyā, anuyantā yasassino;

Samantānupariyanti, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Whose one hundred renowned kings follow and surround him on all sides? Who comes blazing with splendor?

124.

124.

“Hatthiassarathapatti, senā ca caturaṅginī;

Samantānupariyanti, ko eti siriyā jalaṃ.

Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, a fourfold army, surround him on all sides; who comes blazing with splendor?

125.

125.

“Kassesā mahatī senā, piṭṭhito anuvattati;

Akkhobhaṇī apariyantā, sāgarasseva ūmiyo.

Whose is this vast army that follows behind, an akshauhini, boundless, like the waves of the ocean?

126.

126.

“Rājābhirājā manojo, indova jayataṃ pati;

Nandassajjhāvaraṃ eti, assamaṃ brahmacārinaṃ.

The king of kings, Manoja, like Indra, lord of the victorious, comes with Nanda as his attendant to the hermitage of those living the holy life.

127.

127.

“Tassesā mahatī senā, piṭṭhito anuvattati;

Akkhobhaṇī apariyantā, sāgarasseva ūmiyo”ti.

His is this vast army that follows behind, an akshauhini, boundless, like the waves of the ocean.

Tattha jalantaṃrivāti jalantaṃ viya. Paṭipannānīti etāni tūriyāni kassa purato āgacchantīti attho. Hāsayantāti tosentā. Kañcanapaṭṭenāti, tāta, kassa kañcanamayena vijjuvaṇṇena uṇhīsapaṭṭena nalāṭanto parikkhittoti pucchati. Yuvāti taruṇo. Kalāpasannaddhoti [V 5.0315] sannaddhasaratūṇīro. Ukkāmukhapahaṭṭhaṃ vāti kammārānaṃ uddhane pahaṭṭhaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ viya. Khadiraṅgārasannibhanti vītaccitakhadiraṅgāravaṇṇaṃ. Ādiccaraṃsāvaraṇantiādiccaraṃsīnaṃ āvaraṇaṃ. Aṅgaṃ pariggayhāti aṅgaṃ pariggahetvā, sarīraṃ parikkhipitvāti attho. Vālabījanimuttamanti vālabījaniṃ uttamaṃ[P 5.0323]. Carantīti sañcaranti. Chattānīti ājānīyapiṭṭhe nisinnānaṃ dhāritachattāni. Parikīrentīti tassa samantā sabbadisābhāgesu parikīrayanti. Caturaṅginīti etehi hatthiādīhi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā. Akkhobhaṇīti khobhetuṃ na sakkā. Sāgarassevāti sāgarassa ūmiyo viya apariyantā. Rājābhirājāti ekasatarājūnaṃ pūjito, tesaṃ vā adhiko rājāti rājābhirājā. Jayataṃ patīti jayappattānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ jeṭṭhako. Ajjhāvaranti mamaṃ khamāpanatthāya nandassa parisabhāvaṃ upagantvā eti.

Therein, `jalantaṃriva` means 'as if blazing.' `Paṭipannāni` means: 'Whose musical instruments are these that come before him?' `Hāsayantā` means 'delighting.' `Kañcanapaṭṭena` means he asks: 'Dear sir, whose forehead is encircled with a golden, lightning-colored diadem-band?' `Yuvā` means a youth. `Kalāpasannaddho` means one armed with a quiver for arrows. `Ukkāmukhapahaṭṭhaṃ va` means like gold struck in a smith's furnace. `Khadiraṅgārasannibhaṃ` means the color of a glowing khadira-wood ember. `Ādiccaraṃsāvaraṇaṃ` means a protection from the sun's rays. `Aṅgaṃ pariggayha` means having taken up around the body, that is, having encircled the body. `Vālabījanimuttamaṃ` means the finest yak-tail whisk. `Caranti` means they move about. `Chattāni` means the parasols held for those seated on the backs of noble steeds. `Parikīrenti` means they are scattered around him on all sides, in all directions. `Caturaṅginī` means endowed with these four limbs: elephants, and so on. `Akkhobhaṇī` means it cannot be shaken. `Sāgarasseva` means boundless like the waves of the ocean. `Rājābhirājā` means honored by one hundred and one kings, or the king superior to them is the king of kings. `Jayataṃ pati` means the chief of the victorious Tāvatiṃsa gods. `Ajjhāvaraṃ` means: 'For the purpose of asking my forgiveness, he comes having taken on the status of Nanda's retinue.'

Satthā [M 5.0343] āha –

The Teacher said:

128.

128.

“Anulittā candanena, kāsikuttamadhārino;

Sabbe pañjalikā hutvā, isīnaṃ ajjhupāgamu”nti.

Anointed with sandalwood, wearing the finest Kāsi cloth, all with hands joined in reverence, they approached the seers.

Tattha isīnaṃ ajjhupāgamunti, bhikkhave, sabbepi te rājāno surabhicandanena anulittā uttamakāsikavatthadhārino sirasi patiṭṭhāpitaañjalī hutvā isīnaṃ santikaṃ upagatā.

Therein, 'they approached the seers' means: Monks, all those kings, anointed with fragrant sandalwood and wearing the finest Kāsi garments, with hands raised to their heads in reverence, approached the seers.

Tato manojo rājā taṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno paṭisanthāraṃ karonto gāthādvayamāha –

Then King Manoja, having paid homage to him and sat down to one side, while exchanging friendly greetings, spoke two verses:

129.

129.

“Kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ;

Kacci uñchena yāpetha, kacci mūlaphalā bahū.

Is it well with you, venerable sir? Are you free from illness? Do you sustain yourself by alms-gathering? Are roots and fruits plentiful?

130.

130.

“Kacci ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, kacci hiṃsā na vijjatī”ti.

Are gadflies, mosquitoes, and creeping things few? In the forest teeming with wild beasts, is there no harm?

Tato paraṃ ubhinnaṃ tesaṃ vacanapaṭivacanavasena kathitagāthā honti –

Thereafter, the verses spoken by way of question and answer between the two of them are as follows:

131.

131.

“Kusalañceva [V 5.0316] no rāja, atho rāja anāmayaṃ;

Atho uñchena yāpema, atho mūlaphalā bahū.

It is well with us, O king, and we are free from illness; we sustain ourselves by alms-gathering, and roots and fruits are plentiful.

132.

132.

“Atho ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, hiṃsā mayhaṃ na vijjati.

And there are few gadflies and mosquitoes, and indeed creeping things; in the forest teeming with wild beasts, no harm comes to us.

133.

133.

“Bahūni vassapūgāni, assame sammataṃ idha;

Nābhijānāmi uppannaṃ, ābādhaṃ amanoramaṃ.

For many years that we have lived here in this hermitage, I do not recall any unpleasant illness having arisen.

134.

134.

“Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yaṃ idhatthi pavedaya.

Welcome to you, great king; indeed, your coming is welcome. You are the sovereign who has arrived; declare what you desire of that which is here.

135.

135.

“Tindukāni [P 5.0324] piyālāni, madhuke kāsumāriyo;

Phalāni khuddakappāni, bhuñja rāja varaṃ varaṃ.

Tinduka and piyāla fruits, madhuka and kāsumāri; these fruits are like honey. Enjoy the very best of them, O king.

136.

136.

“Idampi pānīyaṃ sītaṃ, ābhataṃ girigabbharā;

Tato piva mahārāja, sace tvaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

This cool water, too, has been brought from a mountain cavern; drink of it, great king, if you so desire.

137.

137.

“Paṭiggahitaṃ [M 5.0344] yaṃ dinnaṃ, sabbassa agghiyaṃ kataṃ;

Nandassāpi nisāmetha, vacanaṃ so pavakkhati.

What you have offered is accepted; a hospitable reception has been done for us all. Listen also to the words of Nanda, for he will speak.

138.

138.

“Ajjhāvaramhā nandassa, bhoto santikamāgatā;

Suṇātu bhavaṃ vacanaṃ, nandassa parisāya cā”ti.

We have come to your presence as Nanda’s retinue. May your reverence listen to the words of Nanda and of his assembly.

Imā yebhuyyena pākaṭasambandhāyeva, yaṃ panettha apākaṭaṃ, tadeva vakkhāma. Pavedayāti yaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne tava abhirucitaṃ atthi, taṃ no kathehīti vadati. Khuddakappānīti etāni nānārukkhaphalāni khuddakamadhupaṭibhāgāni madhurāni. Varaṃ varanti ito uttamuttamaṃ gahetvā bhuñja. Girigabbharāti anotattato. Sabbassa agghiyanti yena mayaṃ āpucchitā, taṃ amhehi paṭiggahitaṃ nāma tumhehi ca dinnameva nāma, ettāvatā imassa janassa sabbassa agghiyaṃ tumhehi kataṃ. Nandassāpīti amhākaṃ tāva sabbaṃ kataṃ, idāni pana nandapaṇḍito kiñci vattukāmo[V 5.0317], tassapi tāva vacanaṃ suṇātha. Ajjhāvaramhāti mayañhi na aññena kammena āgatā, nandassa pana parisā hutvā tumhākaṃ khamāpanatthāya āgatāti vadati. Bhavanti bhavaṃ soṇapaṇḍito suṇātu.

For the most part, the connection of these verses is clear; we will explain only what is not clear. `Pavedaya` means he says: 'Tell us whatever is pleasing to you in this place.' `Khuddakappāni` means these various tree-fruits, small and sweet, comparable to honey. `Varaṃ varaṃ` means: 'Take the very best of these and enjoy.' `Girigabbharā` means from Anotatta. `Sabbassa agghiyaṃ` means: 'The greeting with which we were addressed has been accepted by us, and what you have offered has indeed been given; thus, you have done what is most valuable for all these people.' `Nandassāpi` means: 'For our part, everything has been done for now; but now Nanda the wise wishes to say something, so first listen to his words.' `Ajjhāvaramhā` means he says: 'We have not come for any other task, but have come as Nanda’s retinue for the purpose of seeking your forgiveness.' `Bhavaṃ` means: 'May the venerable Soṇa the wise listen.'

Evaṃ vutte nandapaṇḍito uṭṭhāyāsanā mātāpitaro ca bhātarañca vanditvā sakaparisāya saddhiṃ sallapanto āha –

When this was said, Nanda the wise rose from his seat, paid homage to his parents and brother, and conversing with his own retinue, said:

139.

139.

“Parosataṃ jānapadā, mahāsālā ca brāhmaṇā;

Ime ca khattiyā sabbe, abhijātā yasassino;

Bhavañca rājā manojo, anumaññantu me vaco.

May the more than one hundred country-folk, the wealthy brahmins, all these noble and renowned kings, and you, King Manoja, approve my words.

140.

140.

“Ye ca santi samītāro, yakkhāni idha massame;

Araññe bhūtabhabyāni, suṇantu vacanaṃ mama.

And whatever gods and spirits are assembled here in this hermitage, and the beings in the forest, existing or to be, let them listen to my words.

141.

141.

“Namo katvāna bhūtānaṃ, isiṃ vakkhāmi subbataṃ;

So tyāhaṃ dakkhiṇā bāhu, tava kosiya sammato.

Having paid homage to the deities, I will speak to you, O sage of good vows. I, O Kosiya, am considered by you to be like your right arm.

142.

142.

“Pitaraṃ me janettiñca, bhattukāmassa me sato;

Vīra puññamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ, mā maṃ kosiya vāraya.

For me who desires to support my father and mother, O hero, this is an occasion for merit; do not hinder me, O Kosiya.

143.

143.

“Sabbhi [P 5.0325][M 5.0345] hetaṃ upaññātaṃ, mametaṃ upanissaja;

Uṭṭhānapāricariyāya, dīgharattaṃ tayā kataṃ;

Dhātāpitūsu puññāni, mama lokadado bhava.

This has indeed been praised by the virtuous; relinquish this merit to me. Through energetic service, this has been performed by you for a long time. Now I wish to perform merits for my father and mother; be one who grants heaven to me.

144.

144.

“Tatheva santi manujā, dhamme dhammapadaṃ vidū;

Maggo saggassa lokassa, yathā jānāsi tvaṃ ise.

Even so, O sage, there are men who understand the path of righteousness within the Dhamma; they know, just as you do, that it is the way to the heavenly world.

145.

145.

“Uṭṭhānapāricariyāya, mātāpitusukhāvahaṃ;

Taṃ maṃ puññā nivāreti, ariyamaggāvaro naro”ti.

The man who prevents me from that merit—which brings happiness to mother and father through energetic service—is an obstructor of the noble path.

Tattha [V 5.0318] anumaññantūti anubujjhantu, sādhukaṃ sutvā paccakkhaṃ karontūti attho. Samītāroti samāgatā. Araññe bhūtabhabyānīti asmiṃ himavantāraññe yāni bhūtāni ceva vuḍḍhimariyādappattāni bhabyāni ca taruṇadevatāni, tānipi sabbāni mama vacanaṃ suṇantūti attho. “Namo katvānā”ti idaṃ so parisāya saññaṃ datvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nibbattadevatānaṃ namakkāraṃ katvā āha. Tassattho – ajja bahūhi devatāhi mama bhātikassa dhammakathāsavanatthaṃ āgatāhi bhavitabbaṃ, ahaṃ vo namakkāro, tumhepi mayhaṃ sahāyā hothāti. So devatānaṃ añjaliṃ paggahetvā parisaṃ jānāpetvā “isiṃ vakkhāmī”tiādimāha. Tattha isinti soṇapaṇḍitaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sammatoti bhātaro nāma aṅgasamā honti, tasmā so te ahaṃ dakkhiṇā bāhūti sammato. Tena me khamituṃ arahathāti dīpeti.

There, 'anumaññantu' means 'let them understand'; the meaning is 'having listened well, let them realize directly.' 'Samītāro' means 'assembled.' 'Araññe bhūtabhabyāni' means: 'in this Himalayan forest, those beings who have reached the limit of growth and the young deities who are to be—let all of them listen to my words.' 'Namo katvānā' means 'having paid homage'; this he said after giving a sign to the assembly and paying respects to the deities born in that grove. Its meaning is: 'Today, many deities must have come to listen to my brother’s Dhamma talk. I pay homage to you; may you also be my companions.' Having raised his hands in añjali to the deities and informed the assembly, he says, 'I will speak of the sage,' and so on. There, 'isi' refers to Soṇa the Wise. 'Sammato' means: 'brothers are like limbs,' therefore, 'I am he who is considered by you as a right arm.' By this he shows, 'therefore, you should forgive me.'

Vīrāti vīriyavanta mahāparakkama. Puññamidaṃ ṭhānanti idaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma puññaṃ saggasaṃvattanikakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontaṃ maṃ mā vārayāti vadati. Sabbhi hetanti etañhi mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma paṇḍitehi upaññātaṃ upagantvā ñātañceva vaṇṇitañca. Mametaṃ upanissajāti idaṃ tvaṃ mayhaṃ nissaja vissajjehi dehi. Uṭṭhānapāricariyāyāti uṭṭhānena ca pāricariyāya ca. Katanti dīgharattaṃ tayā kusalaṃ kataṃ. Puññānīti idāni ahaṃ mātāpitūsu puññāni kattukāmo. Mama lokadadoti tassa mama tvaṃ saggalokadado hoti, ahañhi tesaṃ vattaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ katvā devaloke aparimāṇaṃ yasaṃ labhissāmi, tassa me tvaṃ dāyako hohīti vadati.

'Vīra' means: O energetic one, greatly striving one. 'This is a place of merit' means: this merit called attending to mother and father is a cause leading to heaven; he says, 'Do not hinder me who am doing this.' 'By the good' means: for this attending to mother and father is approached, known, and praised by the wise. 'Relinquish this to me' means: 'You should relinquish, release, and give this to me.' 'By effort and attendance' means: by effort and by attendance. 'Done' means: for a long time, good has been done by you. 'Merits' means: now I wish to make merits for my parents. 'Giver of a world to me' means: 'you become a giver of the heavenly world to me.' For I, having performed my duty and attendance to them, will gain immeasurable fame in the world of the devas. He says: 'Be a giver of that to me.'

Tathevāti [M 5.0346] yathā tvaṃ jānāsi, tatheva aññepi manujā imissaṃ parisāyaṃ santi, te nānappakāre dhamme idaṃ jeṭṭhāpacāyikabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ vadanti. Kinti? Maggo saggassa lokassāti. Sukhāvahanti uṭṭhānena ca pāricariyāya ca mātāpitūnaṃ sukhāvahaṃ. Taṃ manti taṃ maṃ evaṃ sammāpaṭipannampi bhātā soṇapaṇḍito tamhā puññā abhivāreti. Ariyamaggāvaroti so evaṃ vārento ayaṃ naro mama piyadassanatāya ariyasaṅkhātassa vedalokassa maggāvaraṇo nāma hotīti.

'Even so' means: just as you know, so too are there other humans in this assembly; they speak of this section of the Dhamma, known as the state of respecting elders, in various ways. How so? As 'The path to the world of heaven.' 'Bringing happiness' means: bringing happiness to mother and father by effort and attendance. 'That me' means: my brother Soṇa Paṇḍita prevents me, who am thus rightly practicing, from that merit. 'Obstacle to the noble path' means: thus hindering, this man, because of my fondness for seeing him, is called an obstacle to the path of the noble realm.

Evaṃ [P 5.0326] nandapaṇḍitena vutte mahāsatto “imassa tāva tumhehi vacanaṃ sutaṃ, idāni mamapi suṇāthā”ti sāvento āha –

When Nanda the Wise had spoken thus, the Great Being, making them listen, said: 'You have first heard his words; now listen to mine as well.'

146.

146.

“Suṇantu [V 5.0319] bhonto vacanaṃ, bhāturajjhāvarā mama;

Kulavaṃsaṃ mahārāja, porāṇaṃ parihāpayaṃ;

Adhammacārī jeṭṭhesu, nirayaṃ sopapajjati.

Listen, venerable sirs, to my words, you who have come as my brother's assembly. O great king, by neglecting the ancient family lineage, one who behaves unrighteously towards one's elders is reborn in hell.

147.

147.

“Ye ca dhammassa kusalā, porāṇassa disampati;

Cārittena ca sampannā, na te gacchanti duggatiṃ.

But those who are skilled in the ancient Dhamma, O lord of the regions, and are accomplished in conduct, they do not go to a state of suffering.

148.

148.

“Mātā pitā ca bhātā ca, bhaginī ñāti bandhavā;

Sabbe jeṭṭhassa te bhārā, evaṃ jānāhi bhāradha.

Mother and father, brothers and sisters, relatives and kinsmen—all these are the responsibility of the eldest; know this, O bearer of the burden.

149.

149.

“Ādiyitvā garuṃ bhāraṃ, nāviko viya ussahe;

Dhammañca nappamajjāmi, jeṭṭho casmi rathesabhā”ti.

Having taken up the heavy burden, I strive like a boatman; I do not neglect the Dhamma, for I am the eldest, O lord of charioteers.

Tattha bhāturajjhāvarāti mama bhātu parisā hutvā āgatā bhonto sabbepi rājāno mamapi tāva vacanaṃ suṇantu. Parihāpayanti parihāpento. Dhammassāti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammassa paveṇīdhammassa. Kusalāti chekā. Cārittena cāti ācārasīlena sampannā. Bhārāti sabbe ete jeṭṭhena vahitabbā paṭijaggitabbāti tassa bhārā nāma. Nāviko viyāti yathā nāvāya garuṃ bhāraṃ ādiyitvā samuddamajjhe nāvaṃ sotthinā netuṃ nāviko ussaheti vāyamati, saha nāvāya sabbabhaṇḍañca jano ca tasseva bhāro hoti, tathā mameva sabbe ñātakā bhāroti[M 5.0347], ahañca te ussahāmi paṭijaggituṃ sakkomi, tañca jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammaṃ nappamajjāmi, na kevalañca etesaññeva, sakalassapi lokassa jeṭṭho ca asmi, tasmā ahameva saddhiṃ nandena paṭijaggituṃ yuttoti.

There, 'bhāturajjhāvarā' means: 'Venerable sirs, all you kings who have come as my brother's assembly, please listen to my words first.' 'Parihāpayanti' means 'causing to decline' or 'diminish.' 'Of the Dhamma' refers to the Dhamma of respecting elders, the traditional practice. 'Skilled' means 'proficient.' 'And with conduct' means 'endowed with good behavior and virtue.' 'Burden' means all these must be supported and cared for by the eldest; thus, they are called his 'burden.' 'Like a boatman' means just as a boatman, having taken a heavy load in a boat, strives and endeavors to safely guide the boat across the ocean—the boat, its cargo, and the passengers all being his responsibility—in the same way, all my relatives are my burden, and I am able and strive to care for them. I do not neglect this Dhamma of respecting elders, and I am the eldest not only of them but also of the entire world. Therefore, I am the one fit to care for them, together with Nanda.

Taṃ sutvā sabbepi te rājāno attamanā hutvā “jeṭṭhabhātikassa kira avasesā bhārāti ajja amhehi ñāta”nti nandapaṇḍitaṃ pahāya mahāsattaṃ sannissitā hutvā tassa thutiṃ karontā dve gāthā abhāsiṃsu –

Hearing this, all those kings were delighted and said, 'Today we have learned that the rest of the siblings are indeed the responsibility of the eldest brother.' Abandoning Nanda the Wise, they relied upon the Great Being and, offering him praise, spoke these two verses:

150.

150.

“Adhigamā tame ñāṇaṃ, jālaṃva jātavedato;

Evameva no bhavaṃ dhammaṃ, kosiyo pavidaṃsayi.

From darkness we have attained knowledge, like a flame from fire. Even so has the venerable Kosiya revealed the Dhamma to us.

151.

151.

“Yathā [V 5.0320] udayamādicco, vāsudevo pabhaṅkaro;

Pāṇīnaṃ pavidaṃseti, rūpaṃ kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Evameva no bhavaṃ dhammaṃ, kosiyo pavidaṃsayī”ti.

As the rising sun, the light-maker and illuminator, reveals to living beings forms both good and bad, even so has the venerable Kosiya revealed the Dhamma to us.

Tattha [P 5.0327] adhigamāti mayaṃ ito pubbe jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammapaṭicchādake tame vattamānā na jānāma, ajja jātavedato jālaṃva ñāṇaṃ adhigatā. Evameva noti yathā mahandhakāre pabbatamatthake jalito jātavedo samantā ālokaṃ pharanto rūpāni dasseti, tathā no bhavaṃ kosiyagotto dhammaṃ pavidaṃsayīti attho. Vāsudevoti vasudevo vasujotano, dhanapakāsanoti attho.

Therein, 'adhigamā' means: 'Previously, we existed in the darkness of ignorance that concealed the Dhamma of respecting elders and did not know; today we have attained knowledge like a flame from fire.' 'Even so to us' means: just as a fire lit on a mountain peak in great darkness, spreading light all around, reveals forms, so has the venerable one of the Kosiya clan revealed the Dhamma to us. 'Vāsudeva' means 'one who illuminates substances or wealth'; this is the meaning.

Iti mahāsatto ettakaṃ kālaṃ nandapaṇḍitassa pāṭihāriyāni disvā tasmiṃ pasannacitte te rājāno ñāṇabalena tasmiṃ pasādaṃ bhinditvā attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā sabbeva attano mukhaṃ ullokite akāsi. Atha nandapaṇḍito “bhātā me paṇḍito byatto dhammakathiko sabbepime rājāno bhinditvā attano pakkhe kari, ṭhapetvā imaṃ añño mayhaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, imameva yācissāmī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being, who for so long had observed the miracles of Nanda the Wise, saw that the kings were devoted to him. By the power of his own wisdom, he dispelled their devotion to Nanda, made them accept his own words, and caused the entire assembly to look toward him. Then Nanda the Wise thought, 'My brother is wise, experienced, and a preacher of the Dhamma. He has won over all these kings to his side. Aside from him, I have no other refuge. I shall entreat him alone.' Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

152.

152.

“Evaṃ me yācamānassa, añjaliṃ nāvabujjhatha;

Tava baddhacaro hessaṃ, vuṭṭhito paricārako”ti.

Though I entreat you thus, you do not acknowledge my gesture of reverence. I shall be your bound servant, an energetic attendant.

Tassatthā [M 5.0348] – sace tumhe mama evaṃ yācamānassa khamāpanatthāya paggahitaṃ añjaliṃ nāvabujjhatha na paṭiggaṇhatha, tumheva mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahatha, ahaṃ pana tumhākaṃ baddhacaro veyyāvaccakaro hessaṃ, rattindivaṃ analasabhāvena vuṭṭhito paricārako ahaṃ tumhe paṭijaggissāmīti.

Its meaning is: 'If you do not acknowledge or accept the gesture of reverence I offer to seek your forgiveness, then you yourselves care for our parents. I, however, will be your bound servant and helper; day and night, being energetic and diligent, I will attend to you.'

Mahāsattassa pakatiyāpi nandapaṇḍite doso vā veraṃ vā natthi, atithaddhaṃ vacanaṃ kathentassa panassa mānahāpanatthaṃ niggahavasena tathā katvā idānissa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhacitto tasmiṃ pasādaṃ uppādetvā “idāni te khamāmi, mātāpitaro ca paṭijaggituṃ labhissasī”ti tassa guṇaṃ pakāsento āha –

By nature, the Great Being had no anger or enmity toward Nanda the Wise. However, because Nanda had spoken very stubborn words, the Great Being acted thus by way of rebuke to humble his pride. Now, having heard his brother's entreaty, with a pleased mind, he inspired confidence in Nanda and said: 'Now I forgive you, and you shall have the opportunity to care for our parents.' Declaring Nanda’s virtues, he spoke these verses:

153.

153.

“Addhā [V 5.0321] nanda vijānāsi, saddhammaṃ sabbhi desitaṃ;

Ariyo ariyasamācāro, bāḷhaṃ tvaṃ mama ruccasi.

"Surely, Nanda, you understand the true Dhamma taught by the good; noble is your noble conduct, greatly you please me.

154.

154.

“Bhavantaṃ vadāmi bhotiñca, suṇātha vacanaṃ mama;

Nāyaṃ bhāro bhāramato, ahu mayhaṃ kudācanaṃ.

"I address you, Mother and Father, listen to my words; this burden has never been a burden to me.

155.

155.

“Taṃ maṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ santaṃ, mātāpitu sukhāvahaṃ;

Nando ajjhāvaraṃ katvā, upaṭṭhānāya yācati.

"While I was attending to you, bringing happiness to Mother and Father, Nanda, having made a solemn request, asks to perform the service.

156.

156.

“Yo [P 5.0328] ve icchati kāmena, santānaṃ brahmacārinaṃ;

Nandaṃ vo varatha eko, kaṃ nando upatiṭṭhatū”ti.

"Whichever of you desires it, choose Nanda with affection from among your celibate offspring. Which of you shall Nanda attend upon?"

Tattha ariyoti sundaro. Ariyasamācāroti sundarasamācāropi jāto. Bāḷhanti idāni tvaṃ mama ativiya ruccasi. Suṇāthāti amma tātā tumhe mama vacanaṃ suṇātha. Nāyaṃ bhāroti ayaṃ tumhākaṃ paṭijagganabhāro na kadāci mama bhāramato ahu. Taṃ manti taṃ bhāroti amaññitvāva maṃ tumhe upaṭṭhitaṃ samānaṃ. Upaṭṭhānāya yācatīti tumhe upaṭṭhātuṃ maṃ yācati. Yo ve icchatīti mayhañhi tvaṃ me mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā upaṭṭhahāti vattuṃ na yuttaṃ, tumhākaṃ pana santānaṃ brahmacārīnaṃ yo eko icchati, taṃ vadāmi kāmena nandaṃ vo varatha, taṃ mama kaniṭṭhaṃ nandaṃ rocetha, tumhesu kaṃ esa upaṭṭhātu, ubhopi hi mayaṃ tumhākaṃ puttāyevāti.

There, 'ariya' means noble or good. 'Ariyasamācāra' means he has also become of noble conduct. 'Bāḷhaṃ' means 'now you are exceedingly pleasing to me.' 'Suṇātha' means, 'Mother and father, listen to my words.' 'Nāyaṃ bhāro' means this burden of caring for you was never once considered a burden by me. 'Taṃ maṃ' means, 'Without considering it a burden, while I was attending to you.' 'Upaṭṭhānāya yācati' means he asks me for the opportunity to attend to you. 'Yo ve icchati' means, 'It is not proper for me to tell you to attend to my mother or my father; but of you two who are peaceful and celibate, if one desires, I say, choose Nanda with pleasure; approve of my younger brother Nanda. Which of you should he attend to? For both of us are indeed your sons.'

Athassa [M 5.0349] mātā āsanā vuṭṭhāya, “tāta soṇapaṇḍita, cirappavuttho te kaniṭṭho, evaṃ cirāgatampi taṃ yācituṃ na visahāmi, mayañhi taṃ nissitā, idāni pana tayā anuññātā ahaṃ etaṃ brahmacārinaṃ bāhāhi upagūhitvā sīse upasiṅghāyituṃ labheyya”nti imamatthaṃ pakāsentī gāthamāha –

Then his mother rose from her seat and, to clarify this matter to Soṇa the Wise, spoke this verse: 'Dear Soṇa the Wise, your younger brother has been away for a long time. Even though he has returned after such a long time, we do not dare to ask you for him. For we depend on you. But now, with your permission, may I embrace this celibate Nanda with my arms and kiss him on the head?'

157.

157.

“Tayā tāta anuññātā, soṇa taṃ nissitā mayaṃ;

Upaghātuṃ labhe nandaṃ, muddhani brahmacārina”nti.

'Permitted by you, dear Soṇa, we who rely on you; may I embrace Nanda, the celibate, and kiss him on the head.'

Atha mahāsatto “tena hi, amma, anujānāmi, tvaṃ gaccha, puttaṃ nandaṃ āliṅgitvā sīse ghāyitvā cumbitvā tava hadaye sokaṃ nibbāpehī”ti āha. Sā tassa santikaṃ gantvā nandapaṇḍitaṃ [V 5.0322] parisamajjheyeva āliṅgitvā sīsaṃ ghāyitvā cumbitvā hadaye sokaṃ nibbāpetvā mahāsattena saddhiṃ sallapantī āha –

Then the Great Being said, 'In that case, mother, I give my permission. Go, embrace your son Nanda, smell his head, kiss him, and extinguish the sorrow in your heart.' She went to him, and right in the middle of the assembly, she embraced the wise Nanda, smelled his head, kissed him, extinguished the sorrow in her heart, and while conversing with the Great Being, she said:

158.

158.

“Assatthasseva taruṇaṃ, pavāḷaṃ māluteritaṃ;

Cirassaṃ nandaṃ disvāna, hadayaṃ me pavedhati.

'Like a tender, coral-red shoot of the Assattha tree, stirred by the wind, seeing Nanda after so long, my heart trembles.'

159.

159.

“Yadā suttāpi supine, nandaṃ passāmi āgataṃ;

Udaggā sumanā homi, nando no āgato ayaṃ.

'When, even in sleep, in a dream, I see Nanda has come, I am uplifted and joyful, thinking, "This Nanda of ours has come."'

160.

160.

“Yadā ca paṭibujjhitvā, nandaṃ passāmi nāgataṃ;

Bhiyyo āvisatī soko, domanassañcanappakaṃ.

'But when I awaken and see that Nanda has not come, sorrow enters me again, along with no small amount of distress.'

161.

161.

“Sāhaṃ [P 5.0329] ajja cirassampi, nandaṃ passāmi āgataṃ;

Bhattucca mayhañca piyo, nando no pāvisī gharaṃ.

'I, today, after so long, see Nanda has come; dear to both my husband and me, our Nanda has entered the house.'

162.

162.

“Pitupi nando suppiyo, yaṃ nando nappavase gharā;

Labhatū tāta nando taṃ, maṃ nando upatiṭṭhatū”ti.

'Nanda is also very dear to his father, so may Nanda not depart from home; may Nanda, dear one, obtain that service, and may Nanda attend upon me.'

Tattha māluteritanti yathā vātāhataṃ assatthassa pallavaṃ kampati, evaṃ cirassaṃ nandaṃ disvā ajja mama hadayaṃ kampatīti vadati. Suttāti, tāta soṇa, yadāhaṃ suttāpi supine nandaṃ āgataṃ passāmi, tadāpi udaggā homi. Bhattuccāti sāmikassa ca me mayhañca piyo. Nando no pāvisī gharanti, tāta, putto no nando paṇṇasālaṃ pavisatu. Yanti yasmā pitupi suṭṭhu piyo, tasmā puna imamhā gharā na vippavaseyya. Nando [M 5.0350] tanti, tāta, nando yaṃ icchati, taṃ labhatu. Maṃ nandoti, tāta soṇa, tava pitaraṃ tvaṃ upaṭṭhaha, maṃ nando upaṭṭhātu.

There, 'māluteritaṃ' means that just as a sprout of the Assattha tree shaken by the wind trembles, so too, upon seeing Nanda after a long time, my heart trembles today, she says. 'Suttā' means: dear Soṇa, even when I am asleep and see Nanda coming in a dream, then too I am uplifted. 'Bhattucca' means: he is dear both to my husband and to me. 'Nando no pāvisī gharaṃ' means: dear one, let our son Nanda enter the leaf-hut. 'Yaṃ' means: because he is very dear to his father too, therefore he should not depart from this house again. 'Nando taṃ' means: dear one, whatever Nanda desires to serve, let him obtain it. 'Maṃ nando' means: dear Soṇa, you attend to your father, let Nanda attend to me.

Mahāsatto “evaṃ hotū”ti mātu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā “nanda, tayā jeṭṭhakakoṭṭhāso laddho, mātā nāma atiguṇakārikā, appamatto hutvā paṭijaggeyyāsī”ti ovaditvā mātu guṇaṃ pakāsento dve gāthā abhāsi –

The Great Being, accepting his mother's words with 'So be it,' advised his younger brother Nanda, 'Nanda, you have received a great portion. A mother is indeed a great benefactor. Be diligent and care for her.' Then, extolling his mother's virtues, he spoke these two verses:

163.

163.

“Anukampikā [V 5.0323] patiṭṭhā ca, pubbe rasadadī ca no;

Maggo saggassa lokassa, mātā taṃ varate ise.

'She is compassionate, a support, and was formerly the giver of milk to us; a mother is the path to the heavenly world. She desires you, O sage.'

164.

164.

“Pubbe rasadadī gottī, mātā puññūpasaṃhitā;

Maggo saggassa lokassa, mātā taṃ varate ise”ti.

"Formerly the giver of nourishment, a protectress, a mother endowed with merit; a mother is the path to the heavenly world. She desires you, O sage."

Tattha anukampikāti muduhadayā. Pubbe rasadadīti paṭhamameva attano khīrasaṅkhātassa rasassa dāyikā. Mātā tanti mama mātā maṃ na icchati, taṃ varati icchati. Gottīti gopāyikā. Puññūpasaṃhitāti puññūpanissitā puññadāyikā.

Here, 'anukampikā' means tender-hearted. 'Pubbe rasadadī' means the first giver of the essence of her own nourishment, known as milk. 'Mātā taṃ' means: my mother does not desire me, but desires you. 'Gottī' means a protectress. 'Puññūpasaṃhitā' means supported by merit, a giver of merit.

Evaṃ mahāsatto dvīhi gāthāhi mātu guṇaṃ kathetvā punāgantvā tassā āsane nisinnakāle “nanda, tvaṃ dukkarakārikaṃ mātaraṃ labhasi, ubhopi mayaṃ mātarā dukkhena saṃvaḍḍhitā, taṃ idāni tvaṃ appamatto paṭijaggāhi, amadhurāni phalāphalāni mā khādāpehī”ti vatvā parisamajjheyeva mātu dukkarakārikataṃ pakāsento āha –

Thus, the Great Being, having praised the mother's virtues in two verses, returned and, while she was sitting in her seat, said: 'Nanda, you have obtained a mother who is difficult to care for. Both of us were raised by our mother with great difficulty. Therefore, now you must be diligent in caring for her. Do not let her eat unpalatable fruits.' Then, in the midst of the assembly, he revealed the mother's performance of difficult deeds, saying:

165.

165.

“Ākaṅkhamānā [P 5.0330] puttaphalaṃ, devatāya namassati;

Nakkhattāni ca pucchati, utusaṃvaccharāni ca.

'Desiring the fruit of a son, she pays homage to a deity; she inquires about the constellations, the seasons, and the years.'

166.

166.

“Tassā utumhi nhātāya, hoti gabbhassa vokkamo;

Tena dohaḷinī hoti, suhadā tena vuccati.

'When she has bathed in her season, conception occurs; thereby she develops pregnancy cravings, and because of this, she is called "suhadā" (one of a good heart).'

167.

167.

“Saṃvaccharaṃ vā ūnaṃ vā, pariharitvā vijāyati;

Tena sā janayantīti, janetti tena vuccati.

'Carrying the child for a year or for seven months, she gives birth; because she gives birth, she is thereby called "janayantī" and "janetti".'

168.

168.

“Thanakhīrena gītena, aṅgapāvuraṇena ca;

Rodantaṃ puttaṃ toseti, tosentī tena vuccati.

'With milk from her breast, with song, and by holding him close to her body, she soothes her crying son; because she soothes him, she is called "tosentī" (the soother).'

169.

169.

“Tato [M 5.0351] vātātape ghore, mamaṃ katvā udikkhati;

Dārakaṃ appajānantaṃ, posentī tena vuccati.

'Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, she looks after him with great affection; because she nurtures the unknowing child, she is called "posentī" (the nurturer).'

170.

170.

“Yañca [V 5.0324] mātudhanaṃ hoti, yañca hoti pituddhanaṃ;

Ubhayampetassa gopeti, api puttassa no siyā.

'Whatever wealth belongs to the mother, and whatever wealth belongs to the father, she protects both, thinking, "May it be for our son."'

171.

171.

“Evaṃ putta aduṃ putta, iti mātā vihaññati;

Pamattaṃ paradāresu, nisīthe pattayobbane;

Sāyaṃ puttaṃ anāyantaṃ, iti mātā vihaññati.

"'Do this, son! Do that, son!'—thus the mother teaches him. When he is heedless with others' wives, or does not return at night, or when the youth does not return in the evening, the mother is distressed by these things."

172.

172.

“Evaṃ kicchā bhato poso, mātu aparicārako;

Mātari micchā caritvāna, nirayaṃ sopapajjati.

'A man supported with such difficulty who does not attend to his mother, having misconducted himself towards his mother, is reborn in hell.'

173.

173.

“Evaṃ kicchā bhato poso, pitu aparicārako;

Pitari micchā caritvāna, nirayaṃ sopapajjati.

'A man supported with such difficulty who does not attend to his father, having misconducted himself towards his father, is reborn in hell.'

174.

174.

“Dhanāpi dhanakāmānaṃ, nassati iti me sutaṃ;

Mātaraṃ aparicaritvāna, kicchaṃ vā so nigacchati.

'Even for those who desire wealth, their wealth is lost, so I have heard, by not attending to one's mother; and such a man comes to hardship.'

175.

175.

“Dhanāpi dhanakāmānaṃ, nassati iti me sutaṃ;

Pitaraṃ aparicaritvāna, kicchaṃ vā so nigacchati.

'Even for those who desire wealth, their wealth is lost, so I have heard, by not attending to one's father; and such a man comes to hardship.'

176.

176.

“Ānando ca pamodo ca, sadā hasitakīḷitaṃ;

Mātaraṃ paricaritvāna, labbhametaṃ vijānato.
