'Joy and gladness, and constant laughter and play; all this is gained by the wise son who attends to his mother.'

177.

177.

“Ānando ca pamodo ca, sadā hasitakīḷitaṃ;

Pitaraṃ paricaritvāna, labbhametaṃ vijānato.

"Joy and gladness, ever laughter and play; having attended to one's father, this is gained by the wise son."

178.

178.

“Dānañca piyavācā ca, atthacariyā ca yā idha;

Samānattatā ca dhammesu, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Ete kho saṅgahā loke, rathassāṇīva yāyato.

"Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct here, and impartiality in all matters, in each case as is fitting; these indeed are the means of social harmony in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot."

179.

179.

“Ete [V 5.0325] ca saṅgahā nāssu, na mātā puttakāraṇā;

Labhetha [P 5.0331] mānaṃ pūjaṃ vā, pitā vā puttakāraṇā.

"If these means of social harmony did not exist, a mother would not receive respect or honor on account of her child, nor would a father receive them on account of his child."

180.

180.

“Yasmā ca saṅgahā ete, sammapekkhanti paṇḍitā;

Tasmā mahattaṃ papponti, pāsaṃsā ca bhavanti te.

"And because the wise rightly regard these means of social harmony, they therefore attain greatness and become praiseworthy."

181.

181.

“Brahmāti [M 5.0352] mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare;

Āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ, pajāya anukampakā.

"Parents are called 'Brahmā' and 'first teachers'; they are worthy of offerings from their children, being compassionate toward their offspring."

182.

182.

“Tasmā hi ne namasseyya, sakkareyya ca paṇḍito;

Annena atho pānena, vatthena sayanena ca;

Ucchādanena nhāpanena, pādānaṃ dhovanena ca.

"Therefore, a wise person should pay homage to them and honor them with food and drink, with clothing and bedding, with massaging, bathing, and the washing of their feet."

183.

183.

“Tāya naṃ pāricariyāya, mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti.

"On account of that service to parents, the wise praise him right here in this world, and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven."

Tattha puttaphalanti puttasaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ. Devatāya namassatīti “putto me uppajjatū”ti devatāya namakkāraṃ karoti āyācati. Pucchatīti “katarena nakkhattena jāto putto dīghāyuko hoti, katarena appāyuko”ti evaṃ nakkhattāni ca pucchati. Utusaṃvaccharāni cāti “channaṃ utūnaṃ katarasmiṃ utumhi jāto dīghāyuko hoti, katarasmiṃ utumhi appāyuko, kativassāya vā mātuyā jāto putto dīghāyuko hoti, kativassāya appāyuko”ti evaṃ utusaṃvaccharāni ca pucchati. Utumhi nhātāyāti pupphe uppanne utumhi nhātāya. Vokkamoti tiṇṇaṃ sannipātā gabbhāvakkanti hoti, kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāti. Tenāti tena gabbhena sā dohaḷinī hoti. Tenāti tadā tassā kucchimhi nibbattapajāya sineho uppajjati, tena kāraṇena “suhadā”ti vuccati. Tenāti tena kāraṇena sā “janayantī”ti ca “janettī”ti ca vuccati.

Here, 'the fruit of a child' means the fruit reckoned as a child. 'Worships a deity' means one makes obeisance to a deity, requesting, "May a child be born to me." 'Asks' means one inquires, "Under which constellation is a child born long-lived, under which short-lived?" Thus, one asks about the constellations. 'And seasons and years' means one asks, "In which of the six seasons is a child born long-lived, in which short-lived? Or at what age of the mother is a child born long-lived, at what age short-lived?" Thus, one asks about seasons and years. 'Having bathed in season' means having bathed in the season when the flower has appeared. 'Conception' means from the coming together of the three, there is the descent of the embryo, and the embryo is established in the womb. 'Because of that' means because of that embryo, she has cravings. 'Because of that' means at that time, affection arises for the offspring born in her womb; for that reason she is called 'of good heart.' 'Because of that' means for that reason, she is called 'the one who gives birth' and 'the genetrix.'

Aṅgapāvuraṇena cāti thanantare nipajjāpetvā sarīrasamphassaṃ pharāpentī aṅgasaṅkhāteneva pāvuraṇena. Tosentīti saññāpentī hāsentī. Mamaṃ katvā udikkhatīti “puttassa me upari vāto paharati, ātapo pharatī”ti evaṃ mamaṃkāraṃ katvā siniddhena hadayena udikkhati. Ubhayampetassāti [V 5.0326] ubhayampi etaṃ dhanaṃ etassa puttassa atthāya aññesaṃ adassetvā sāragabbhādīsu mātā gopeti. Evaṃ putta, aduṃ puttāti “andhabāla putta, evaṃ rājakulādīsu appamatto hohi, aduñca kammaṃ mā karohī”ti sikkhāpentī iti mātā vihaññati kilamati. Pattayobbaneti [M 5.0353] putte pattayobbane taṃ puttaṃ nisīthe paradāresu pamattaṃ sāyaṃ anāgacchantaṃ ñatvā assupuṇṇehi nettehi maggaṃ olokentī vihaññati kilamati.

'And with the covering of her limbs' means, having laid the child between her breasts and causing the feeling of bodily contact, with the covering reckoned as her own limbs. 'Soothes' means making him understand and making him laugh. 'Having made him 'mine,' she looks upon him' means thinking, "The wind strikes my son, the sun's heat affects him," and thus, having made him 'mine,' she looks upon him with an affectionate heart. 'Both for him' means both this wealth, for the sake of this son, the mother guards in inner chambers and so on, not showing it to others. 'Thus, son, that, son' means instructing, "O blind, foolish son, be heedful in your dealings with royal families and such, and do not do that deed," and thus the mother is vexed and wearied. 'When he has reached youth' means when the son has reached youth, and she knows him to be heedless with others' wives at night, not returning in the evening, she gazes down the road with tear-filled eyes, vexed and wearied.

Kicchā bhatoti kicchena bhato paṭijaggito. Micchā caritvānāti mātaraṃ apaṭijaggitvā. Dhanāpīti dhanampi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – dhanakāmānaṃ [P 5.0332] uppannaṃ dhanampi mātaraṃ apaṭijaggantānaṃ nassatīti me sutanti. Kicchaṃ vā soti iti dhanaṃ vā tassa nassati, dukkhaṃ vāso puriso nigacchati. Labbhametanti etaṃ idhaloke ca paraloke ca ānandādisukhaṃ mātaraṃ paricaritvā vijānato paṇḍitassa labbhaṃ, sakkā laddhuṃ tādisenāti attho.

‘Nourished with difficulty’ (kicchā bhato) means fed and cared for with difficulty. ‘Having behaved wrongly’ (micchā caritvāna) means not having cared for one’s mother. ‘Even wealth’ (dhanāpi) means wealth itself, or this is simply the reading. This is what is said: ‘Even the wealth that has arisen for those desiring wealth, who do not care for their mothers, is lost’—so I have heard. ‘Or he to hardship’ (kicchaṃ vā so) means either his wealth is lost, or that man comes to suffering. ‘This is obtainable’ (labbhametaṃ) means that this happiness, such as joy, in this world and the next, is obtainable for the wise person who knows, having cared for his mother; it is possible for such a one to obtain it—this is the meaning.

Dānañcāti mātāpitūnaṃ dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, piyavacanaṃ bhaṇitabbaṃ, uppannakiccasādhanavasena attho caritabbo. Dhammesūti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammesu tattha tattha parisamajjhe vā rahogatānaṃ vā abhivādanādivasena samānattatā kātabbā, na raho abhivādanādīni katvā parisati na kātabbāni, sabbattha samāneneva bhavitabbaṃ. Ete ca saṅgahā nāssūti sace ete cattāro saṅgahā na bhaveyyuṃ. Sammapekkhantīti sammā nayena kāraṇena pekkhanti. Mahattanti seṭṭhattaṃ. Brahmāti puttānaṃ brahmasamā uttamā seṭṭhā. Pubbācariyāti paṭhamācariyā. Āhuneyyāti āhunapaṭiggāhakā yassa kassaci sakkārassa anucchavikā. Annena athoti annena ceva attho pānena ca. Peccāti kālakiriyāya pariyosāne ito gantvā sagge pamodatīti.

‘And giving’ (dānañca) means a gift should be given to parents, kind words should be spoken, and beneficial action should be performed by way of accomplishing their arisen tasks. ‘In principles’ (dhammesu) means in the principles of honoring elders, one should maintain impartiality by way of showing respect, such as bowing, whether in the midst of a gathering or in private; one should not perform acts of respect in private and then not perform them in public, but should be consistent everywhere. ‘And if these bonds of sympathy were not’ (ete ca saṅgahā nāssu) means if these four bonds of sympathy did not exist. ‘They rightly consider’ (sammapekkhanti) means they consider rightly, with method and reason. ‘Greatness’ (mahattaṃ) means excellence. ‘Brahmā’ (brahmā) means that for their children, parents are like Brahmā, supreme and excellent. ‘First teachers’ (pubbācariyā) means initial teachers. ‘Worthy of offerings’ (āhuneyyā) means worthy of receiving offerings, fit for any honor. ‘With food and also’ (annena atho) means with food and also with drink. ‘Having departed’ (pecca) means at the end of life, having gone from here, one rejoices in heaven.

Evaṃ mahasatto sineruṃ pavaṭṭento viya dhammadesanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ sutvā sabbepi te rājāno balakāyā ca pasīdiṃsu. Atha ne pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “dānādīsu appamattā hothā”ti ovaditvā uyyojesi. Sabbepi dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā āyupariyosāne devanagaraṃ pūrayiṃsu. Soṇapaṇḍitanandapaṇḍitāpi yāvatāyukaṃ mātāpitaro paricaritvā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Thus the Great Being concluded his Dhamma teaching, as if setting Mount Sineru in motion. Hearing this, all those kings and their armies were filled with confidence. Then, establishing them in the five precepts, he advised, ‘Be heedful in generosity and so on,’ and dismissed them. All ruled righteously, and at the end of their lives, they filled the city of the devas. Soṇa the Wise and Nanda the Wise also attended to their parents for as long as they lived and were destined for the Brahmā world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātāpitaro māhārājakulāni [V 5.0327] ahesuṃ, nandapaṇḍito ānando[M 5.0354], manojarājā sāriputto, ekasatarājāno asītimahātherā ceva aññataratherā ca, catuvīsati akkhobhaṇiyo buddhaparisā, soṇapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the parents were the Great King's family; Nanda the Wise was Ānanda; King Manoja was Sāရိပုတ္တရာ; the one hundred and one kings were the eighty great elders and other elders; the twenty-four akkhobhaṇīs were the Buddha’s assembly; and Soṇa the Wise was indeed myself.

Soṇanandajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Second Commentary on the Soṇananda Jātaka.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Summary of the Jātakas:

Atha sattatimamhi nipātavare, sabhāvantu kusāvatirājavaro;

Atha soṇasunandavaro ca puna, abhivāsitasattatimamhi suteti.

Now, in the excellent seventieth section, is the noble King Kusāvati; then again, the excellent Soṇa and Sunanda are in the seventieth tale, so it is heard.

Sattatinipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Seventy is finished.

21. Asītinipāto

21. The Section of Eighty

[533] 1. Cūḷahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[533] 1. The Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka

Sumukhāti [V 5.0328][M 5.0355][P 5.0333] idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto āyasmato ānandassa jīvitapariccāgaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadattena hi tathāgataṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ payojitesu dhanuggahesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ pesitena āgantvā “nāhaṃ, bhante, sakkomi taṃ bhagavantaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ, mahiddhiko so bhagavā mahānubhāvo”ti vutte devadatto “alaṃ, āvuso, mā tvaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitā voropehi, ahameva samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitā voropessāmī”ti vatvā tathāgate gijjhakūṭapabbatassa pacchimachāyāya caṅkamante sayaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā yantavegena mahatiṃ silaṃ pavijjhi, “imāya silāya samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitā voropessāmī”ti. Tadā dve pabbatakūṭā samāgantvā taṃ silaṃ sampaṭicchiṃsu. Tato papaṭikā uppatitvā bhagavato pādaṃ paharitvā ruhiraṃ uppādesi, balavavedanā pavattiṃsu. Jīvako tathāgatassa pādaṃ satthakena phāletvā duṭṭhalohitaṃ vametvā pūtimaṃsaṃ apanetvā dhovitvā bhesajjaṃ ālimpitvā nirogamakāsi. Satthā purimasadisameva bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto mahatiyā buddhalīlāya vicari.

‘Sumukha’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Elder Ānanda’s self-sacrifice. For when Devadatta had hired archers to kill the Tathāgata, the first one sent came and said, ‘Venerable sir, I cannot take the Blessed One’s life. The Blessed One is of great power and might.’ When this was said, Devadatta said, ‘Enough, friend, do not kill the ascetic Gotama. I myself will kill the ascetic Gotama.’ So saying, while the Tathāgata was walking in the western shade of Vulture Peak, Devadatta himself climbed Vulture Peak and hurled a great stone with the force of a machine, thinking, ‘With this stone, I will kill the ascetic Gotama.’ Then two mountain peaks came together and intercepted the stone. A splinter flew off and struck the Blessed One’s foot, drawing blood. Severe pains arose. Jīvaka cut open the Tathāgata’s foot with a scalpel, expelled the bad blood, removed the decayed flesh, washed it, applied medicine, and made him well. The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks as before, continued his great Buddha-activity.

Atha naṃ disvā devadatto cintesi – “samaṇassa gotamassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ sarīraṃ disvā koci manussabhūto upasaṅkamituṃ na sakkoti, rañño kho pana nāḷāgiri nāma hatthī caṇḍo pharuso [P 5.0334] manussaghātako buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇe na jānāti, so taṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessatī”ti. So gantvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā hatthācariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā “samma, sve nāḷāgiriṃ mattaṃ katvā pātova samaṇena gotamena paṭipannavīthiyaṃ vissajjehī”ti āha. Devadattopi naṃ “aññesu divasesu hatthī kittakaṃ suraṃ pivatī”ti pucchitvā “aṭṭha ghaṭe, bhante”ti vutte “tena hi sve tvaṃ taṃ soḷasa ghaṭe [M 5.0356] pāyetvā samaṇena gotamena paṭipannavīthiyaṃ abhimukhaṃ kareyyāsī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Rājā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “sve nāḷāgiriṃ mattaṃ katvā nagare vissajjessati, nāgarā pātova sabbakiccāni katvā antaravīthiṃ mā paṭipajjiṃsū”ti. Devadattopi [V 5.0329] rājanivesanā oruyha hatthisālaṃ gantvā hatthigopake āmantetvā “mayaṃ bhaṇe uccaṭṭhāniyaṃ nīcaṭṭhāne, nīcaṭṭhāniyaṃ vā uccaṭṭhāne kātuṃ samatthā, sace vo yasena attho, sve pātova nāḷāgiriṃ tikhiṇasurāya soḷasa ghaṭe pāyetvā samaṇassa gotamassa āgamanavelāya tuttatomarehi vijjhitvā kujjhāpetvā hatthisālaṃ bhindāpetvā samaṇena gotamena paṭipannavīthiyaṃ abhimukhaṃ katvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpethā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu.

Then, upon seeing him, Devadatta thought: ‘No human being can approach after seeing the beauty and radiance attained by the ascetic Gotama’s body. But the king has an elephant named Nāḷāgiri, fierce, savage, a killer of humans, who knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. He will bring about his death.’ He went and informed the king of this matter. The king, saying ‘Good,’ agreed and summoned the elephant trainer. ‘My good man, tomorrow morning, intoxicate Nāḷāgiri and release him on the street where the ascetic Gotama will be walking,’ he said. Devadatta also asked him, ‘On other days, how much liquor does the elephant drink?’ When told, ‘Eight jars, venerable sir,’ he said, ‘Well then, tomorrow you should make him drink sixteen jars and send him straight towards the street where the ascetic Gotama will be walking.’ He agreed, saying, ‘Good.’ The king had a drum beaten throughout the city: ‘Tomorrow, Nāḷāgiri will be intoxicated and released in the city. Citizens should complete all their business and not go out into the streets early in the morning.’ Devadatta, descending from the royal residence, went to the elephant stable and addressed the elephant keepers: ‘Friends, we are capable of raising those in lowly positions to high positions, and of lowering those in high positions to lowly positions. If you desire honor, tomorrow morning, make Nāḷāgiri drink sixteen jars of strong liquor, and at the time when the ascetic Gotama is coming, provoke him to fury by piercing him with sharp goads and prodding hooks, make him break open the elephant stable, and send him straight towards the street where the ascetic Gotama will be walking, to bring about the ascetic Gotama’s death.’ They agreed, saying, ‘Good.’

Sā pavatti sakalanagare vitthārikā ahosi. Buddhadhammasaṅghamāmakā upāsakā taṃ sutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, devadatto raññā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā sve tumhehi paṭipannavīthiyaṃ nāḷāgiriṃ vissajjāpessati, sve piṇḍāya apavisitvā idheva hotha, mayaṃ vihāreyeva buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Satthāpi “sve piṇḍāya na pavisissāmī”ti avatvāva “ahaṃ sve nāḷāgiriṃ dametvā pāṭihāriyaṃ katvā titthiye madditvā rājagahe piṇḍāya acaritvāva bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto nagarā nikkhamitvā veḷuvanameva āgamissāmi, rājagahavāsinopi bahūni bhattabhājanāni gahetvā veḷuvanameva āgamissanti, sve vihāreyeva bhattaggaṃ bhavissatī”ti iminā kāraṇena tesaṃ adhivāsesi. Te tathāgatassa adhivāsanaṃ viditvā bhattabhājanāni āharitvā “vihāreyeva dānaṃ dassāmā”ti pakkamiṃsu.

This news spread throughout the entire city. Lay followers who were devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, heard this and approached the Teacher, saying, ‘Venerable sir, Devadatta, having joined with the king, will have the elephant Nāဲāgiri released tomorrow on the path you are traveling. Please do not enter for alms tomorrow; stay right here. We will serve alms to the Saဳgha of monks headed by the Buddha right here in the monastery.’ The Teacher, without saying, ‘I will not go for alms tomorrow,’ consented to them by saying, ‘Tomorrow, after taming Nāဲāgiri, performing a miracle, and subduing the heretics, I will leave the city surrounded by the Saဳgha of monks and come to Veဲuvana without even wandering for alms in Rājagaha. The residents of Rājagaha will also bring many vessels of food and come to Veဲuvana. Tomorrow, the meal will take place right here in the monastery.’ Knowing the Tathāgata’s consent, they brought vessels of food and departed, saying, ‘We will give the gift right here in the monastery.’

Satthāpi paṭhamayāme dhammaṃ desetvā majjhimayāme devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetvā pacchimayāmassa paṭhamakoṭṭhāse sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā dutiyakoṭṭhāse phalasamāpattiyā [P 5.0335] vītināmetvā tatiyakoṭṭhāse mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya bodhaneyyabandhave olokento nāḷāgiridamane caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayaṃ disvā vibhātāya rattiyā katasarīrapaṭijaggano hutvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantetvā[M 5.0357], “ānanda, ajja rājagahaparivattakesu aṭṭhārasasu mahāvihāresu sabbesampi bhikkhūnaṃ mayāsaddhiṃ rājagahaṃ pavisituṃ ārocehī”ti āha. Thero tathā akāsi. Sabbepi bhikkhū veḷuvane sannipatiṃsu. Satthā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto rājagahaṃ pāvisi. Atha hatthimeṇḍā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu, mahanto samāgamo ahosi. Saddhāsampannā manussā “ajja kira buddhanāgassa tiracchānanāgena saṅgāmo bhavissati, anūpamāya buddhalīlāya nāḷāgiridamanaṃ passissāmā”ti pāsādahammiyagehacchadanādīni abhiruhitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Asaddhā pana micchādiṭṭhikā “ayaṃ nāḷāgiri caṇḍo pharuso manussaghātako buddhādīnaṃ guṇaṃ na jānāti, so ajja samaṇassa gotamassa [V 5.0330] suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ viddhaṃsetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessati, ajja paccāmittassa piṭṭhiṃ passissāmā”ti pāsādādīsu aṭṭhaṃsu.

The Teacher, having taught the Dhamma in the first watch, answered the questions of the deities in the middle watch, and in the first part of the last watch, having taken the lion’s posture, passed the second part in the attainment of fruition, and in the third part, entered the attainment of great compassion. Upon rising, while surveying those who were ready to be enlightened, he saw that eighty-four thousand beings would realize the Dhamma through the taming of Nāဲāgiri. When the night had turned into dawn, having attended to his bodily needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying, ‘Ānanda, announce today to all the monks in the eighteen great monasteries around Rājagaha that they are to enter Rājagaha with me.’ The elder did so. All the monks assembled at Veဲuvana. The Teacher, surrounded by a great Saဳgha of monks, entered Rājagaha. Then the elephant keepers acted as they had been instructed, and a great gathering took place. Faithful people, thinking, ‘Today, it is said, there will be a battle between the Buddha-nāga and the animal-nāga; we will witness the taming of Nāဲāgiri through the incomparable majesty of a Buddha,’ climbed onto the roofs of palaces, mansions, and houses and stood there. But the faithless and those of wrong view, thinking, ‘This Nāဲāgiri is fierce, savage, and a killer of humans; he knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha and others. Today, he will destroy the golden-hued body of the ascetic Gotama and bring him to the end of his life; today we shall see the defeat of our enemy,’ stood on palaces and other high places.

Hatthīpi bhagavantaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā manusse tāsento gehāni viddhaṃsento sakaṭāni saṃcuṇṇento soṇḍaṃ ussāpetvā pahaṭṭhakaṇṇavālo pabbato viya ajjhottharanto yena bhagavā tenābhidhāvi. Taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “ayaṃ, bhante, nāḷāgiri caṇḍo pharuso manussaghātako imaṃ racchaṃ paṭipanno, na kho panāyaṃ buddhādiguṇaṃ jānāti, paṭikkamatu, bhante, bhagavā, paṭikkamatu sugato”ti. Mā, bhikkhave, bhāyittha, paṭibalo ahaṃ nāḷāgiriṃ dametunti. Athāyasmā sāriputto satthāraṃ yāci – “bhante, pitu uppannakiccaṃ nāma jeṭṭhaputtassa bhāro, ahameva taṃ damemī”ti. Atha naṃ satthā, “sāriputta, buddhabalaṃ nāma aññaṃ, sāvakabalaṃ aññaṃ, tiṭṭha tva”nti paṭibāhi. Evaṃ yebhuyyena asīti mahātherā yāciṃsu. Satthā sabbepi paṭibāhi. Atha āyasmā ānando satthari balavasinehena adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto “ayaṃ hatthī paṭhamaṃ maṃ māretū”ti tathāgatassatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā gantvā satthu purato aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “apehi, ānanda, mā me purato aṭṭhāsī”ti āha. “Bhante, ayaṃ hatthī caṇḍo [P 5.0336] pharuso manussaghātako kappuṭṭhānaggisadiso paṭhamaṃ maṃ māretvā pacchā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchatū”ti thero avaca. Yāvatatiyaṃ vuccamānopi tatheva aṭṭhāsi na paṭikkami. Atha naṃ bhagavā iddhibalena paṭikkamāpetvā bhikkhūnaṃ antare ṭhapesi.

The elephant, seeing the Blessed One approaching, terrifying the people, destroying houses, and crushing carts, raised its trunk and, with its ears and tail erect, charged towards the Blessed One like a mountain bearing down. Seeing it coming, the monks said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, this Nāဲāgiri is fierce, savage, and a killer of humans; he has entered this street. He does not know the virtues of the Buddha and others. May the Blessed One retreat, venerable sir; may the Sugata retreat!’ ‘Monks, do not be afraid; I am capable of taming Nāဲāgiri.’ Then the Venerable Sāriputta requested the Teacher: ‘Venerable sir, what is a matter for the father is the burden of the eldest son; I myself will tame it.’ Then the Teacher restrained him, saying, ‘Sāriputta, the power of a Buddha is one thing, the power of a disciple is another; you stay there.’ In this way, mostly all eighty great elders made the request. The Teacher restrained them all. Then the Venerable Ānanda, being unable to endure because of his strong affection for the Teacher, thinking, ‘Let this elephant kill me first,’ and sacrificing his life for the sake of the Tathāgata, went and stood in front of the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to him, ‘Step aside, Ānanda, do not stand in front of me!’ ‘Venerable sir, this elephant is fierce, savage, and a killer of humans, like the fire at the end of an aeon. Let it kill me first, and then let it come to your presence,’ the elder said. Although told this up to three times, he stood right there and did not retreat. Then the Blessed One, having made him retreat by his psychic power, placed him in the midst of the monks.‒

Tasmiṃ [M 5.0358] khaṇe ekā itthī nāḷāgiriṃ disvā maraṇabhayabhītā palāyamānā aṅkena gahitaṃ dārakaṃ hatthino ca tathāgatassa ca antare chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Hatthī taṃ anubandhitvā nivattitvā dārakassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tadā dārako mahāravaṃ ravi. Satthā nāḷāgiriṃ odissakamettāya pharitvā sumadhuraṃ brahmassaraṃ nicchāretvā “ambho nāḷāgiri taṃ soḷasa surāghaṭe pāyetvā mattaṃ karontā na ‘aññaṃ gaṇhissatī’ti kariṃsu, ‘maṃ gaṇhissatī’ti pana kariṃsu, mā akāraṇena jaṅghāyo kilamento vicari, ito ehī”ti pakkosi. So satthu vacanaṃ sutvā akkhīni ummīletvā bhagavato rūpasiriṃ oloketvā paṭiladdhasaṃvego buddhatejena pacchinnasurāmado soṇḍaṃ olambento kaṇṇe cālento āgantvā tathāgatassa pādesu pati. Atha naṃ satthā, “nāḷāgiri, tvaṃ tiracchānahatthī, ahaṃ buddhavāraṇo, ito paṭṭhāya mā caṇḍo pharuso manussaghātako bhava, sabbasattesu mettacittaṃ paṭilabhā”ti vatvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā kumbhe parāmasitvā –

At that moment, a woman, seeing Nāḷāgiri and terrified by the fear of death, fled, abandoning the child she held on her hip between the elephant and the Tathāgata. The elephant, having pursued her, turned back and approached the child. Then the child cried out loudly. The Teacher, pervading Nāḷāgiri with directed loving-kindness, uttered a supremely sweet voice like that of Brahmā: 'O Nāḷāgiri, those who made you drink sixteen pots of liquor and intoxicated you did not do so thinking, "He will seize another," but rather, "He will seize me." Do not wander about needlessly tiring your legs. Come here!' Hearing the Teacher’s words, he opened his eyes, beheld the splendor of the Blessed One’s form, and, feeling a sense of awe, his intoxication dispelled by the Buddha’s power, he lowered his trunk, let his ears hang down, and approached, falling at the Tathāgata’s feet. Then the Teacher said to him, 'Nāḷāgiri, you are an animal-elephant, but I am the Buddha-elephant. From now on, do not be fierce, violent, or a killer of humans. Develop a mind of loving-kindness towards all beings.' Having spoken thus, he stretched out his right hand, stroked his head, and—

“Mā [V 5.0331] kuñjara nāgamāsado, dukkho hi kuñjara nāgamāsado;

Na hi nāgahatassa kuñjara, sugati hoti ito paraṃ yato.

'O elephant, do not attack the Noble One, for painful indeed, O elephant, is attacking the Noble One; for there is no good destination hereafter for one who has harmed a Noble One, O elephant.'

“Mā ca mado mā ca pamādo, na hi pamattā sugatiṃ vajanti te;

Tvaññeva tathā karissasi, yena tvaṃ sugatiṃ gamissasī”ti. (cūḷava. 342) –

'Be not intoxicated with pride, and be not heedless; for the heedless do not go to a good destination. You yourself should act in such a way that you will go to a good destination.'

Dhammaṃ desesi.

He taught the Dhamma.

Tassa sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi. Sace kira tiracchānagato nābhavissā, sotāpattiphalaṃ adhigamissā. Manussā taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā unnadiṃsu apphoṭiṃsu, sañjātasomanassā nānābharaṇāni khipiṃsu, tāni hatthissa sarīraṃ paṭicchādayiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya [P 5.0337] nāḷāgiri dhanapālako nāma jāto. Tasmiṃ kho pana dhanapālakasamāgame caturāsīti pāṇasahassāni amataṃ piviṃsu. Satthā dhanapālakaṃ pañcasu [M 5.0359] sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. So soṇḍāya bhagavato pāde paṃsūni gahetvā upari muddhani ākiritvā paṭikuṭitova paṭikkamitvā dassanūpacāre ṭhito dasabalaṃ vanditvā nivattitvā hatthisālaṃ pāvisi. Tato paṭṭhāya dantasudanto hutvā na kañci viheṭheti. Satthā nipphannamanoratho “yehi yaṃ dhanaṃ khittaṃ, tesaññeva taṃ hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāya “ajja mayā mahantaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ kataṃ, imasmiṃ nagare piṇḍāya caraṇaṃ appaṭirūpa”nti titthiye madditvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto jayappatto viya khattiyo nagarā nikkhamitvā veḷuvanameva gato. Nagaravāsino bahuṃ annapānakhādanīyaṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃsu.

His entire body was pervaded with continuous joy. If he had not been born as an animal, he would have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Seeing this miracle, the people shouted and clapped their hands. Filled with joy, they threw various ornaments, which covered the elephant’s body. From that time on, Nāḷāgiri became known as Dhanapālaka. At that gathering for Dhanapālaka, eighty-four thousand living beings drank the nectar of the deathless. The Teacher established Dhanapālaka in the five precepts. With his trunk, the elephant took dust from the Blessed One’s feet and sprinkled it over his head. Retiring by backing away respectfully, he stood at a distance within sight, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and then returned to the elephant stable. From then on, being perfectly tamed, he did not harm anyone. The Teacher, having fulfilled his wish, resolved: 'Let the wealth that was thrown belong to the people who threw it.' Thinking, 'Today I have performed a great miracle; it is not fitting for me to wander for alms in this city,' he subdued the sectarians and, surrounded by the community of monks, left the city like a victorious king and went to the Bamboo Grove. The city dwellers brought a great quantity of food, drink, and delicacies to the monastery and offered a great alms-giving.

Taṃ divasaṃ sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhaṃ pūretvā sannisinnā bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, āyasmatā ānandena tathāgatassatthāya attano jīvitaṃ pariccajantena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, nāḷāgiriṃ disvā satthārā tikkhattuṃ paṭibāhiyamānopi nāpagato, aho dukkarakārako, āvuso, āyasmā ānando”ti. Satthā “ānandassa guṇakathā pavattati, gantabbaṃ mayā etthā”ti gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānando tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajiyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

That evening, the monks, having filled the Dhamma hall, sat together and raised a discussion: 'Friends, the Venerable Ānanda has performed a difficult deed, sacrificing his life for the sake of the Tathāgata. Seeing Nāḷāgiri, even though he was forbidden three times by the Teacher, he did not retreat. Ah, friends, the Venerable Ānanda is truly a doer of difficult deeds!' The Teacher, knowing, 'A discussion about Ānanda's virtues is underway; I must go there,' left the Perfumed Chamber and, having arrived, asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?' When they told him, he said, 'Not only now, monks, but even in the past, when reborn in the animal realm, Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake.' At their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 5.0332] mahiṃsakaraṭṭhe sāgalanagare sāgalo nāma rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā nagarato avidūre ekasmiṃ nesādagāmake aññataro nesādo pāsehi sakuṇe bandhitvā nagare vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappesi. Nagarato ca avidūre āvaṭṭato dvādasayojano mānusiyo nāma padumasaro ahosi pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchanno. Tattha nānappakāro sakuṇasaṅgho otari. So nesādo tattha aniyāmena pāse oḍḍesi. Tasmiṃ kāle dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā channavutihaṃsasahassaparivāro cittakūṭapabbate suvaṇṇaguhāyaṃ vasati, sumukho nāmassa senāpati ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ tato haṃsayūthā katipayā [P 5.0338] suvaṇṇahaṃsā mānusiyaṃ saraṃ gantvā pahūtagocare tasmiṃ yathāsukhaṃ vicaritvā suhitā cittakūṭaṃ āgantvā dhataraṭṭhassa ārocesuṃ – “mahārāja, manussapathe [M 5.0360] mānusiyo nāma padumasaro sampannagocaro, tattha gocaraṃ gaṇhituṃ gacchāmā”ti. So “manussapatho nāma sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo, mā vo ruccitthā”ti paṭikkhipitvāpi tehi punappunaṃ vuccamāno “sace tumhākaṃ ruccati, gacchāmā”ti saparivāro taṃ saraṃ agamāsi. So ākāsā otaranto pādaṃ pāse pavesentoyeva otari. Athassa pāso pādaṃ ayapaṭṭakena kaḍḍhanto viya ābandhitvā gaṇhi. Athassa “chindissāmi na”nti ākaḍḍhantassa paṭhamavāre cammaṃ chijji, dutiyavāre maṃsaṃ chijji, tatiyavāre nhāru chijji, pāso aṭṭhiṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi, lohitaṃ pagghari, balavavedanā pavattiṃsu.

In the past, in the land of Mahiṃsaka, in the city of Sāgala, a king named Sāgala ruled righteously. At that time, not far from the city, in a certain fowler's village, a fowler made his living by catching birds with snares and selling them in the city. Not far from the city, there was a lotus pond named Mānusiya, twelve yojanas in circumference, covered with lotuses of five colors. There, flocks of various kinds of birds would descend. That fowler would set his snares there indiscriminately. At that time, the goose king Dhataraṭṭha, surrounded by ninety-six thousand geese, lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa. His general was named Sumukha. Then one day, some golden geese from that flock went to the Mānusiya pond, and having roamed at their ease in its abundant feeding grounds, they returned satisfied to Cittakūṭa and reported to Dhataraṭṭha: 'Great king, in the human world there is a lotus pond called Mānusiya, rich in feeding grounds. Let us go there to feed.' Though he refused them, saying, 'The human world is fraught with danger and fear; do not desire it,' being told again and again by them, he said, 'If you desire it, let us go,' and he went to that pond with his retinue. As he descended from the sky, he placed his foot right into a snare. Then the snare, as if pulling with an iron band, bound and caught his foot. As he pulled at it, thinking, 'I will break it,' first his skin was torn, then his flesh was torn, and then his sinew was torn. The snare struck the bone and held fast; blood flowed, and severe pains arose.

So cintesi – “sacāhaṃ baddharavaṃ ravissāmi, ñātakā me utrastā hutvā gocaraṃ aggaṇhitvā chātajjhattāva palāyantā dubbalatāya mahāsamudde patissantī”ti. So vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā ñātīnaṃ yāvadatthaṃ caritvā haṃsānaṃ kīḷanakāle mahantena saddena baddharavaṃ ravi. Taṃ sutvā te haṃsā maraṇabhayatajjitā vaggavaggā hutvā cittakūṭābhimukhā pakkamiṃsu. Tesu pakkantesu sumukho haṃsasenāpati “kacci nu kho idaṃ bhayaṃ mahārājassa uppannaṃ, jānissāmi na”nti vegena pakkhanditvā purato gacchantassa haṃsagaṇassa antare mahāsattaṃ adisvā majjhimahaṃsagaṇaṃ vicini, tatthapi adisvā pacchimahaṃsagaṇaṃ vicini, tatthapi adisvā “nissaṃsayaṃ tassevedaṃ bhayaṃ uppanna”nti nivattitvā [P 5.0339] āgacchanto mahāsattaṃ pāse baddhaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ dukkhāturaṃ paṅkapiṭṭhe nipannaṃ disvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ahaṃ mama jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā tumhe pāsato mocessāmī”ti vadanto otaritvā mahāsattaṃ assāsentova paṅkapiṭṭhe nisīdi. Atha naṃ vīmaṃsanto mahāsatto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

He thought: 'If I cry out with a captive's cry, my kinsmen, terrified, will not take their food and, afflicted by hunger, will flee in weakness and fall into the great ocean.' Enduring the pain, he waited until his kinsmen had foraged as much as they needed, then at the time when the geese were playing, he let out a loud captive's cry. Hearing it, the geese, terrified by the fear of death, fled in groups toward Mount Cittakūṭa. As they departed, Sumukha, the goose general, thought: 'Could some danger have befallen our great king? I must find out.' Quickly rushing forward, he did not see the Great Being among the flock of geese at the front. He searched among the middle flock of geese, but did not see him there either. Then he searched among the rear flock of geese, and not seeing him there, he thought: 'Without a doubt, this danger has befallen him.' Turning back, as he returned, he saw the Great Being caught in a snare, smeared with blood, afflicted with pain, lying on the surface of the mud. 'Do not fear, great king! I will give up my own life to free you from the snare,' he said, descending. Comforting the Great Being, he sat down on the mud beside him. Then, the Great Being, testing him, spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Sumukha anupacinantā, pakkamanti vihaṅgamā;

Gaccha tuvampi mā kaṅkhi, natthi baddhe sahāyatā”ti.

"Sumukha, the birds depart without looking back with affection; you go too, do not hesitate, for in one who is bound there is no companionship."

Tattha [V 5.0333] anupacinantāti sinehena ālayavasena anolokentā. Pakkamantīti ete channavuti haṃsasahassā ñātivihaṅgamā maṃ chaḍḍetvā gacchanti, tvampi gaccha, mā idha vāsaṃ ākaṅkhi, evañhi pāsena baddhe mayi sahāyatā nāma natthi, na hi te ahaṃ idāni kiñci sahāyakiccaṃ kātuṃ [M 5.0361] sakkhissāmi, kiṃ te mayā nirūpakārena, papañcaṃ akatvā gacchevāti vadati.

Therein, 'anupacinantā' means not looking back with affection or attachment. 'Pakkamanti' means: these ninety-six thousand geese, my kinsmen-birds, are abandoning me and departing. You go too; do not wish to stay here, for in me, bound by this snare, there is no companionship. Indeed, I am now unable to perform any friendly duty for you. What use am I to you, being useless? Without making complications, you should just go—thus he speaks.

Ito paraṃ –

Hereafter:

2.

2.

“Gacche vāhaṃ na vā gacche, na tena amaro siyaṃ;

Sukhitaṃ taṃ upāsitvā, dukkhitaṃ taṃ kathaṃ jahe.

"Whether I go or do not go, I would not thereby become immortal. Having attended upon you in happiness, how could I abandon you in suffering?"

3.

3.

“Maraṇaṃ vā tayā saddhiṃ, jīvitaṃ vā tayā vinā;

Tadeva maraṇaṃ seyyo, yañce jīve tayā vinā.

"Death with you, or life without you; that death is better than a life without you."

4.

4.

“Nesa dhammo mahārāja, yaṃ taṃ evaṃ gataṃ jahe;

Yā gati tuyhaṃ sā mayhaṃ, ruccate vihagādhipa.

"This is not the Dhamma, O great king, that I should abandon you in such a state. Whatever your fate, that is my fate; this is my wish, O lord of birds."

5.

5.

“Kā nu pāsena baddhassa, gati aññā mahānasā;

Sā kathaṃ cetayānassa, muttassa tava ruccati.

"For one bound by a snare, what other destination is there but the cook-house? How can that be pleasing to you, who are conscious and free?"

6.

6.

“Kaṃ vā tvaṃ passase atthaṃ, mama tuyhañca pakkhima;

Ñātīnaṃ vāvasiṭṭhānaṃ, ubhinnaṃ jīvitakkhaye.

"What benefit do you see, O bird, for both me and you, or for our remaining kinsmen, in the destruction of both our lives?"

7.

7.

“Yaṃ na kañcanadepiñcha, andhena tamasā gataṃ;

Tādise sañcajaṃ pāṇaṃ, kamatthamabhijotaye.

"O you with golden wings, what benefit would you show by sacrificing your life in such a case? It is like a lamp for a blind man in the darkness."

8.

8.

“Kathaṃ nu patataṃ seṭṭha, dhamme atthaṃ na bujjhasi;

Dhammo apacito santo, atthaṃ dasseti pāṇinaṃ.

"How is it, O best of fliers, that you do not understand the benefit in the Dhamma? The Dhamma, when practiced, reveals the benefit to living beings."

9.

9.

“Sohaṃ [V 5.0334][P 5.0340] dhammaṃ apekkhāno, dhammā catthaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ;

Bhattiñca tayi sampassaṃ, nāvakaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ.

"I, who am mindful of the Dhamma and of the benefit arising from the Dhamma, and seeing my devotion to you, do not long for my own life."

10. “Addhā eso sataṃ dhammo, yo mitto mittamāpade.

10. "Indeed, this is the Dhamma of the good: that a friend does not desert a friend in misfortune."

Na caje jīvitassāpi, hetudhammamanussaraṃ.

...does not abandon, even for the sake of life, remembering this principle of Dhamma.

11.

11.

“Svāyaṃ dhammo ca te ciṇṇo, bhatti ca viditā mayi;

Kāmaṃ karassu mayhetaṃ, gacchevānumato mayā.

"This Dhamma has been practiced by you, and your devotion is known to me. Fulfill this wish of mine; go, you have my permission."

12.

12.

“Api tvevaṃ gate kāle, yaṃ khaṇḍaṃ ñātinaṃ mayā;

Tayā taṃ buddhisampannaṃ, assa paramasaṃvutaṃ.

"But in such a situation, whatever gap I have left for our kinsmen, may you, endowed with wisdom, be their supreme protector."

13.

13.

“Iccevaṃ [M 5.0362] mantayantānaṃ, ariyānaṃ ariyavuttinaṃ;

Paccadissatha nesādo, āturānamivantako.

"While they were thus conversing, noble ones of noble conduct, the fowler appeared, like Death to the afflicted."

14.

14.

“Te sattumabhisañcikkha, dīgharattaṃ hitā dijā;

Tuṇhīmāsittha ubhayo, na sañcalesumāsanā.

Those two birds, friends for a long time, seeing their enemy, both sat in silence, not stirring from their places.

15.

15.

“Dhataraṭṭhe ca disvāna, samuḍḍente tato tato;

Abhikkhamatha vegena, dijasattu dijādhipe.

Seeing the Dhataraṭṭha geese flying up from here and there, the enemy of birds swiftly approached the lord of birds.

16.

16.

“So ca vegenabhikkamma, āsajja parame dije;

Paccakamittha nesādo, baddhā iti vicintayaṃ.

Then the fowler, having rushed forward with speed and approached those supreme birds, moved forward slowly, thinking, 'Are both caught?'

17.

17.

“Ekaṃva baddhamāsīnaṃ, abaddhañca punāparaṃ;

Āsajja baddhamāsīnaṃ, pekkhamānamadīnavaṃ.

One he saw sitting bound, and another unbound. He approached the one sitting bound, while watching the other who was looking at the danger (of the snare).

18.

18.

“Tato so vimatoyeva, paṇḍare ajjhabhāsatha;

Pavaḍḍhakāye āsīne, dijasaṅghagaṇādhipe.

Then, still in doubt (thinking 'Are both caught?'), he spoke to the pale-colored ones, the leaders of the flock of birds, who were sitting there with large bodies.

19.

19.

“Yaṃ [V 5.0335] nu pāsena mahatā, baddho na kurute disaṃ;

Atha kasmā abaddho tvaṃ, balī pakkhi na gacchasi.

While it is understandable that this bird, bound by a great snare, cannot go to another place; why do you, a strong bird, though unbound and able to go, not depart?

20.

20.

“Kiṃ nu tyāyaṃ dijo hoti, mutto baddhaṃ upāsasi;

Ohāya sakuṇā yanti, kiṃ eko avahīyasi.

What is this bird to you, that you, being free, stay by the bound one? The other birds have abandoned him and flown away; why are you left behind alone?

21.

21.

“Rājā me so dijāmitta, sakhā pāṇasamo ca me;

Neva naṃ vijahissāmi, yāva kālassa pariyāyaṃ.

'He is my king, O enemy of birds, and my friend dear as life itself; I will not abandon him for as long as the turn of death remains.'

22.

22.

“Kathaṃ [P 5.0341] panāyaṃ vihaṅgo, nāddasa pāsamoḍḍitaṃ;

Padañhetaṃ mahantānaṃ, boddhumarahanti āpadaṃ.

But how is it that this bird did not see the snare set for him? For those who are great in wisdom, it is expected that they should recognize impending danger.

23.

23.

“Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhati.

When ruin befalls a person and his life is coming to an end, then even when he encounters a net or a snare, he does not recognize it.

24.

24.

“Api tveva mahāpañña, pāsā bahuvidhā tatā;

Guyhamāsajja bajjhanti, athevaṃ jīvitakkhaye”ti. –

Indeed, O greatly wise one, many kinds of snares are thus spread; encountering the hidden snare when life is at its end, they are bound.'

Imāsaṃ gāthānaṃ sambandho pāḷinayeneva veditabbo.

The connection of these verses should be understood according to the method of the Pāli text itself.

Tattha [M 5.0363] gacche vāti, mahārāja, ahaṃ ito gaccheyyaṃ vā na vā, nāhaṃ tena gamanena vā agamanena vā amaro siyaṃ, ahañhi ito gatopi agatopi maraṇato amuttova, ito pubbe pana sukhitaṃ taṃ upāsitvā idāni dukkhitaṃ taṃ kathaṃ jaheyyanti vadati. Maraṇaṃ vāti mama agacchantassa vā tayā saddhiṃ maraṇaṃ bhaveyya, gacchantassa vā tayā vinā jīvitaṃ. Tesu dvīsu yaṃ tayā saddhiṃ maraṇaṃ, tadeva me varaṃ, yaṃ tayā vinā jīveyyaṃ, na me taṃ varanti attho. Ruccateti yā tava gati nipphatti, sāva mayhaṃ ruccati. Sā kathanti samma sumukha mama tāva daḷhena vālapāsena baddhassa parahatthaṃ gatassa sā gati ruccatu, tava pana cetayānassa sacetanassa paññavato muttassa kathaṃ ruccati.

There, regarding 'Should I go?': 'O great king, whether I go from here or not, I would not become immortal by that going or not going. For whether I have gone from here or not gone, I am not free from death. But having attended upon you when you were happy before this, how can I now abandon you when you are suffering?' Thus he speaks. Regarding 'Or death': 'For me, not going would mean death with you; going would mean life without you. Of these two, death with you is preferable to me; that I should live without you is not preferable to me.' This is the meaning. Regarding 'It pleases me': 'Whatever your destiny or outcome may be, that alone pleases me.' Regarding 'How so?': 'Dear Sumukha, for me, who is bound tightly by a hair-snare and has fallen into another's hands, let that fate be pleasing. But for you, who are thoughtful, conscious, wise, and free, how can it be pleasing?'

Pakkhimāti pakkhasampanna. Ubhinnanti amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ jīvitakkhaye sati tvaṃ mama vā tava [V 5.0336] vā avasiṭṭhañātīnaṃ vā kaṃ atthaṃ passasi. Yaṃ nāti ettha na-kāro upamāne. Kañcanadepiñchāti kañcanadvepiñcha, ayameva vā pāṭho, kañcanasadisaubhayapakkhāti attho. Tamasāti tamasi. Gatanti kataṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Purimassa na-kārassa iminā sambandho, “na kata”nti kataṃ viyāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tayi pāṇaṃ cajantepi acajantepi mama jīvitassa abhāvā yaṃ tava pāṇasañcajanaṃ, taṃ andhena tamasi kataṃ viya kiñcideva rūpakammaṃ apaccakkhaguṇaṃ, tādise tava apaccakkhaguṇe pāṇasañcajane tvaṃ pāṇaṃ sañcajanto kamatthaṃ joteyyāsīti.

'One with wings' means endowed with wings. 'Of both' means: when the lives of us two are destroyed, what benefit do you see for me, or for you, or for any remaining relatives? Here, in 'yaṃ nāti', the particle 'na' is used for comparison. 'Golden-winged' means having two golden wings, or this is the reading; the meaning is 'having both wings like gold.' 'In darkness' means in darkness. 'Done' means made, or this is the reading. The preceding particle 'na' is connected with this, so that 'not done' has the meaning 'as if done.' This is what is said: since my life is forfeit whether you give up your life or not, that giving up of your life is like some form made by a blind man in the dark—a deed whose quality is unseen. In such a giving up of life of unseen quality, by giving up your life, what purpose would you illuminate?

Dhammo apacito santoti dhammo pūjito mānito samāno. Atthaṃ dassetīti vuddhiṃ dasseti. Apekkhānoti apekkhanto. Dhammā catthanti dhammato ca atthaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ passanto[P 5.0342]. Bhattinti sinehaṃ. Sataṃ dhammoti paṇḍitānaṃ sabhāvo. Yo mittoti yo mitto āpadāsu mittaṃ na caje, tassa acajantassa mittassa esa sabhāvo nāma addhā sataṃ dhammo. Viditāti pākaṭā jātā. Kāmaṃ karassūti etaṃ mama kāmaṃ mayā icchitaṃ mama vacanaṃ karassu. Api tvevaṃ gate kāleti api tu evaṃ gate kāle mayi imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāsena baddhe. Paramasaṃvutanti paramaparipuṇṇaṃ.

Regarding 'The Dhamma, being honored...': this means the Dhamma, being honored and respected. 'It reveals the benefit' means it shows growth. 'Expecting' means expecting. 'And benefit from the Dhamma' means seeing the benefit arisen from the Dhamma. 'Devotion' means fondness. 'The nature of the good' means the nature of the wise. 'One who is a friend' means a friend who does not abandon a friend in times of trouble; for such a non-abandoning friend, this nature is indeed the nature of the good. 'Known' means having become manifest. 'Do my will' means 'do this my will, my desired word.' 'But when the time has come to this' means 'but when the time has come to this, with me bound by a snare in this place.' 'Perfectly restrained' means perfectly complete.

Iccevaṃ mantayantānanti “gaccha, na gacchāmī”ti evaṃ kathentānaṃ ariyānanti ācāraariyānaṃ. Paccadissathāti kāsāyāni nivāsetvā rattamālaṃ piḷandhitvā [M 5.0364] muggaraṃ ādāya āgacchanto adissatha. Āturānanti gilānānaṃ maccu viya. Abhisañcikkhāti, bhikkhave, te ubhopi sattuṃ āyantaṃ passitvā. Hitāti dīgharattaṃ aññamaññassa hitā muducittā. Na sañcalesumāsanāti āsanato na caliṃsu, yathānisinnāva ahesuṃ. Sumukho pana “ayaṃ nesādo āgantvā paharanto maṃ paṭhamaṃ paharatū”ti cintetvā mahāsattaṃ pacchato katvā nisīdi.

Regarding 'Thus, while they were conferring': this means while they were speaking thus, 'Go,' 'I will not go.' Regarding 'of the noble ones': this means of those noble in conduct. Regarding 'He appeared': he appeared, having put on ochre robes, wearing a red garland, and, taking up a club, he came forth. Regarding 'for the afflicted': this means like death for the sick. Regarding 'He observed': O monks, both of them, having seen the enemy approaching, observed him. Regarding 'Beneficial': this means for a long time mutually beneficial and gentle-hearted. Regarding 'They did not stir from their seats': they did not move from their seats; they remained just as they were seated. Sumukha, however, thinking, 'Let this hunter, upon coming and striking, strike me first,' placed the Great Being behind him and sat down.

Dhataraṭṭheti haṃse. Samuḍḍenteti maraṇabhayena ito cito ca uppatante disvā. Āsajjāti itare dve jane upagantvā. Paccakamitthāti “baddhā, na baddhā”ti cintento upadhārento akamittha, vegaṃ hāpetvā saṇikaṃ agamāsi. Āsajja baddhamāsīnanti baddhaṃ mahāsattaṃ upagantvā nisinnaṃ sumukhaṃ. Adīnavantiādīnavameva hutvā mahāsattaṃ olokentaṃ disvā. Vimatoti kiṃ nu kho abaddho baddhassa santike nisinno, kāraṇaṃ pucchissāmīti vimatijāto hutvāti attho. Paṇḍareti haṃse, atha vā parisuddhe nimmale, sampahaṭṭhakañcanavaṇṇeti attho. Pavaḍḍhakāyeti vaḍḍhitakāye [V 5.0337] mahāsarīre. Yaṃ nūti yaṃ tāva eso mahāpāsena baddho. Na kurute disanti palāyanatthāya ekaṃ disaṃ na bhajati, taṃ yuttanti adhippāyo. Balīti balasampanno hutvāpi. Pakkhīti taṃ ālapati. Ohāyāti chaḍḍetvā. Yantīti sesasakuṇā gacchanti. Avahīyasīti ohīyasi.

Regarding 'Dhataraṭṭhas': this means the geese. Regarding 'Fluttering about': this means seeing them flying here and there in fear of death. Regarding 'Having approached': this means having gone near the other two. Regarding 'He proceeded cautiously': this means he proceeded, thinking and considering, 'Is he caught or not caught?', and slackening his speed, he went slowly. Regarding 'Approaching the bound one, he sat': this refers to Sumukha, who, having approached the bound Great Being, sat down. Regarding 'Not distressed': this means seeing him, being not distressed, looking at the Great Being. Regarding 'Being perplexed': this means having become perplexed, thinking, 'Why is this unbound one sitting near the bound one? I will ask the reason.' This is the meaning. Regarding 'O white one': this means 'O goose,' or else 'O pure, spotless one'; the meaning is 'O one the color of polished gold.' Regarding 'With a large body': this means with a grown, large body. Regarding 'That now': this means that this one is bound by a great snare. Regarding 'He does not take a direction': this means he does not resort to any direction for the purpose of fleeing; the intention is 'that is proper.' Regarding 'Though strong': this means though endowed with strength. Regarding 'O bird': he addresses him. Regarding 'Having left': this means having abandoned. Regarding 'They go': this means the remaining birds go. Regarding 'You are left behind': this means you are left behind.

Dijāmittāti dijānaṃ amitta. Yāva kālassa pariyāyanti yāva maraṇassa vāro āgacchati. Kathaṃ panāyanti tvaṃ rājā me soti vadasi, rājāno ca nāma paṇḍitā honti, itipi paṇḍito samāno kena kāraṇena oḍḍitaṃ pāsaṃ na addasa. Padaṃ hetanti yasamahattaṃ vā ñāṇamahattaṃ vā pattānaṃ attano āpadabujjhanaṃ nāma padaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tasmā te āpadaṃ boddhumarahanti. Parābhavoti avaḍḍhi. Āsajjāpīti upagantvāpi na bujjhati. Tatāti vitatā oḍḍitā. Guyhamāsajjāti tesu pāsesu yo guḷho paṭicchanno pāso, taṃ āsajja bajjhanti. Athevanti atha evaṃ jīvitakkhaye bajjhantevāti attho.

'Enemy of birds' means the enemy of birds. 'Until the turn of time' means until the turn of death arrives. 'But how is this?' means you say, 'He is my king,' and kings are indeed wise; being wise, for what reason did he not see the spread-out snare? 'A mark of greatness' means for those who have attained great fame or great wisdom, recognizing their own adversity is indeed a mark; therefore, they ought to recognize danger. 'Ruin' means decline. 'Even encountering' means even when approaching, he does not realize. 'Spread' means stretched out or set. 'Encountering the hidden' means encountering the concealed snare among those snares, they are bound. 'And thus' means thus they are indeed bound at the destruction of life.

Iti [M 5.0365] naṃ so kathāsallāpena muduhadayaṃ katvā mahāsattassa jīvitaṃ yācanto gāthamāha –

Thus, having softened the fowler's heart with this conversation and wishing to plead for the Great Being's life, he spoke this verse:

25.

25.

“Api [P 5.0343] nāyaṃ tayā saddhiṃ, saṃvāsassa sukhudrayo;

Api no anumaññāsi, api no jīvitaṃ dade”ti.

“Surely living with you would result in happiness; perhaps you will grant us permission? Perhaps you will grant us our lives?”

Tattha api nāyanti api nu ayaṃ. Sukhudrayoti sukhaphalo. Api no anumaññāsīti cittakūṭaṃ gantvā ñātake passituṃ tvaṃ api no anujāneyyāsi. Api no jīvitaṃ dadeti api no imāya kathāya uppannavissāso na māreyyāsīti.

Here, 'api nāyaṃ' means 'surely this'. 'Sukhudrayo' means having a happy result. 'Perhaps you will permit us' means: would you permit us to go to see our relatives at Cittakūṭa? 'Perhaps you will grant us life' means: with trust arising from this conversation, would you not kill us?

So tassa madhurakathāya bajjhitvā gāthamāha –

The fowler, captivated by his sweet words, spoke this verse:

26.

26.

“Na ceva me tvaṃ baddhosi, napi icchāmi te vadhaṃ;

Kāmaṃ khippamito gantvā, jīva tvaṃ anigho cira”nti.

“You are not bound by me, nor do I desire your death; go quickly from here as you wish, and live long without suffering.”

Tato sumukho catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then Sumukha, wishing to plead for the Bodhisatta's release with reasons, spoke four stanzas:

27.

27.

“Nevāhametamicchāmi[V 5.0338], aññatretassa jīvitā;

Sace ekena tuṭṭhosi, muñcetaṃ mañca bhakkhaya.

“I do not desire my own life apart from his; if you are satisfied with one bird, release him and eat me.

28.

28.

“Ārohapariṇāhena, tulyāsmā vayasā ubho;

Na te lābhena jīvatthi, etena niminā tuvaṃ.

“In height, girth, and age, we both are equal; your gain will not be diminished, so you should make this exchange.

29.

29.

“Tadiṅgha samapekkhassu, hotu giddhi tavamhasu;

Maṃ pubbe bandha pāsena, pacchā muñca dijādhipaṃ.

“Therefore, I urge you, consider us equally; let your greed be for me. First bind me with the snare, then release the lord of birds.

30.

30.

“Tāvadeva ca te lābho, katāssa yācanāya ca;

Mitti ca dhataraṭṭhehi, yāvajīvāya te siyā”ti.

“Your gain will be just the same, and my request will be fulfilled; and you will have friendship with the Dhataraṭṭha geese for as long as you live.”

Tattha etanti yaṃ aññatra etassa jīvitā mama jīvitaṃ, etaṃ ahaṃ neva icchāmi. Tulyāsmāti samānā homa. Niminā tuvanti parivattehi tvaṃ. Tavamhasūti tava amhesu giddhi hotu, kiṃ te etena, mayi lobhaṃ uppādehīti vadati. Tāvadevāti tattakoyeva. Yācanāya cāti yā mama yācanā, sāva katā assāti attho.

Here, 'this' means: my own life apart from his life—that I do not desire. 'We are equal' means we are the same. 'You, by this exchange' means 'you should exchange him for me.' 'In us' means 'let your greed be for me'; he says, 'What is he to you? Arouse greed for me.' 'Just so much' means only that much. 'And of the request' means let my request be fulfilled.

Iti [M 5.0366] so tāya dhammadesanāya tele pakkhittakappāsapicu viya mudugatahadayo mahāsattaṃ tassa dāyaṃ katvā dadanto āha –

Thus, by that Dhamma discourse, his heart became as soft as a tuft of cotton dipped in oil. Wishing to grant the Great Being as a noble gift to Sumukha, he spoke as he gave him:

31.

31.

“Passantu no mahāsaṅghā, tayā muttaṃ ito gataṃ;

Mittāmaccā ca bhaccā ca, puttadārā ca bandhavā.

“May the great assembly of relatives, friends, ministers, servants, wives, children, and kin see him who, having been released by you, has gone from here.

32.

32.

“Na ca te tādisā mittā, bahūnaṃ idha vijjati;

Yathā tvaṃ dhataraṭṭhassa, pāṇasādhāraṇo sakhā.

“Such friends as you are not found for many here, just as you are a life-sharing friend to the Dhataraṭṭha goose.

33.

33.

“So te sahāyaṃ muñcāmi, hotu rājā tavānugo;

Kāmaṃ khippamito gantvā, ñātimajjhe virocathā”ti.

“So I release your companion; may the king follow your wish. Go quickly from here as you wish, and shine among your relatives.”

Tattha [P 5.0344] noti nipātamattaṃ. Tayā muttanti imañhi tvaññeva muñcasi nāma, tasmā imaṃ tayā [V 5.0339] muttaṃ ito cittakūṭapabbataṃ gataṃ mahantā ñātisaṅghā ete ca mittādayo passantu. Ettha ca bandhavāti ekalohitasambandhā. Vijjatīti vijjanti. Pāṇasādhāraṇoti sādhāraṇapāṇo avibhattajīviko, yathā tvaṃ etassa sakhā, etādisā aññesaṃ bahūnaṃ mittā nāma na vijjanti. Tavānugoti etaṃ dukkhitaṃ ādāya purato gacchantassa tava ayaṃ anugo hotūti.

Herein, ‘no’ is a mere particle. ‘Released by you’ means you yourself are the one who releases him; therefore, let the great assembly of relatives, friends, and others see him who was released by you and has gone from here to the Cittakūṭa mountain. And here, ‘relatives’ (bandhavā) means those related by blood. ‘Is found’ (vijjati) is in the sense of plural. ‘Life-sharing’ means sharing the same life, having an undivided existence; just as you are his friend, such friends are not found for many others. ‘Your follower’ means let this one follow you as you lead him away from his suffering.

Evaṃ vatvā pana nesādaputto mettacittena mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā bandhanaṃ chinditvā āliṅgitvā sarato nikkhāmetvā saratīre taruṇadabbatiṇapiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā pāde bandhanapāsaṃ muducittena saṇikaṃ mocetvā dūre khipitvā mahāsatte balavasinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā mettacittena udakaṃ ādāya lohitaṃ dhovitvā punappunaṃ parimajji. Tassa mettacittānubhāvena bodhisattassa pāde sirā sirāhi, maṃsaṃ maṃsena, cammaṃ cammena ghaṭitaṃ, tāvadeva pādo saṃruḷho sañjātachavisañjātalomo ahosi abaddhapādena nibbiseso. Bodhisatto sukhito pakatibhāveneva nisīdi. Atha sumukho attānaṃ nissāya mahāsattassa sukhitabhāvaṃ disvā sañjātasomanasso nesādassa thutimakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, the fowler’s son, with a mind of loving-kindness, approached the Great Being, cut his bonds, embraced him, and led him out of the lake. Seating him on a soft patch of young dabba grass on the lake's edge, with a gentle heart he slowly loosened the snare from his feet and threw it far away. Then, establishing great affection for the Great Being, he brought water with a mind of loving-kindness, washed away the blood, and repeatedly stroked him. By the power of his mind of loving-kindness, on the Bodhisatta’s foot—sinew was joined to sinew, flesh to flesh, skin to skin—and at that very moment the foot was healed, its skin-color and hair regrown, indistinguishable from the unbound foot. The Bodhisatta sat comfortably, restored to his natural state. Then Sumukha, seeing the Great Being’s happiness on account of him, felt joy and praised the fowler. The Teacher, making this matter clear, said:

34.

34.

“So [M 5.0367] patīto pamuttena, bhattunā bhattugāravo;

Ajjhabhāsatha vakkaṅgo, vācaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhaṇaṃ.

“Pleased that his master was freed, and respectful toward his master, the crook-necked one addressed the hunter, speaking words pleasant to the ear:

35.

35.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā dijādhipa”nti.

“Thus rejoice, O hunter, with all your kinsmen, as I rejoice today, seeing the released lord of birds.”

Tattha vakkaṅgoti vaṅkagīvo.

Herein, ‘Vakkaṅga’ means ‘crook-necked.’

Evaṃ luddassa thutiṃ katvā sumukho bodhisattaṃ āha – “mahārāja, iminā amhākaṃ mahāupakāro kato, ayañhi amhākaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā kīḷāhaṃse no katvā issarānaṃ dento bahuṃ dhanaṃ labheyya, māretvā maṃsaṃ vikkiṇanto mūlampi labhetha, attano pana jīvitaṃ anoloketvā amhākaṃ vacanaṃ akari[P 5.0345], imaṃ rañño santikaṃ netvā sukhajīvitaṃ karomā”ti. Mahāsatto sampaṭicchi. Sumukho attano bhāsāya mahāsattena saddhiṃ kathetvā puna manussabhāsāya luddaputtaṃ āmantetvā “samma, tvaṃ kimatthaṃ pāse oḍḍesī”ti pucchitvā “dhanattha”nti vutte “evaṃ sante amhe ādāya nagaraṃ pavisitvā rañño dassehi, bahuṃ te dhanaṃ dāpessāmī”ti vatvā āha –

Having thus praised the fowler, Sumukha said to the Great Being: "Great king, this man has done us a great service. Truly, had he disregarded our words and made us play-geese, he could have gained much wealth by presenting us to the rulers, or even gained a price for our flesh by killing us. However, without regard for his own life, he acted on our words. Let us take him to the king and provide him with a comfortable life." The Great Being agreed. Sumukha, having conversed with the Great Being in his own language, then addressed the fowler's son in human speech: "Friend, why did you set the snare?" When he answered, "For wealth," Sumukha said, "If so, take us to the city and present us to the king. We will have him give you much wealth," and then said:

36.

36.

“Ehi [V 5.0340] taṃ anusikkhāmi, yathā tvamapi lacchase;

Lābhaṃ tavāyaṃ dhataraṭṭho, pāpaṃ kiñci na dakkhati.

“Come, I will instruct you, so that you too may gain. This Dhataraṭṭha is for your gain; he will see no fault in you.

37.

37.

“Khippamantepuraṃ netvā, rañño dassehi no ubho;

Abaddhe pakatibhūte, kāje ubhayato ṭhite.

“Quickly take us both to the inner palace and show us to the king, unbound, in our natural state, standing on both sides of the carrying pole.

38.

38.

“Dhataraṭṭhā mahārāja, haṃsādhipatino ime;

Ayañhi rājā haṃsānaṃ, ayaṃ senāpatītaro.

“‘O great king, these are Dhataraṭṭha geese, lords of their kind. This one is the king of the geese, and this other is his commander.

39. “Asaṃsayaṃ imaṃ disvā, haṃsarājaṃ narādhipo.

39. “Undoubtedly, seeing this king of geese, the king of men…

Patīto sumano vitto, bahuṃ dassati te dhana”nti.

“Pleased, glad, and delighted, he will give you much wealth.”

Tattha anusikkhāmīti anusāsāmi. Pāpanti lāmakaṃ. Rañño dassehi no ubhoti amhe ubhopi rañño dassehi. Ayaṃ bodhisattassa paññāpabhāvadassanatthaṃ, attano mittadhammassa āvibhāvanatthaṃ, luddassa dhanalābhatthaṃ, rañño sīlesu patiṭṭhāpanatthañcāti catūhi kāraṇehi [M 5.0368] evamāha. Dhataraṭṭhāti netvā ca pana rañño evaṃ ācikkheyyāsi, “mahārāja, ime dhataraṭṭhakule jātā dve haṃsādhipatino, etesu ayaṃ rājā, itaro senāpatī”ti. Iti naṃ sikkhāpesi. “Patīto”tiādīni tīṇipi tuṭṭhākāravevacanāneva.

Herein, ‘I will instruct’ means I teach. ‘Evil’ (pāpaṃ) means what is low. ‘Show both of us to the king’ means: show both of us to the king. He said this for four reasons: to demonstrate the power of the Bodhisatta’s wisdom, to reveal his own quality of friendship, for the hunter’s gain of wealth, and to establish the king in virtuous conduct. Regarding ‘Dhataraṭṭha,’ you should take them and inform the king thus: ‘Great king, these two lords of geese were born in the Dhataraṭṭha clan. Among them, this is the king, and the other is the commander.’ Thus he instructed him. ‘Pleased,’ and the following two terms, are synonyms for joy.

Evaṃ vutte luddo, “sāmi, mā vo rājadassanaṃ rucci, rājāno nāma calacittā, kīḷāhaṃse vā vo kareyyuṃ mārāpeyyuṃ vā”ti vatvā, “samma, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ tādisaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ luddaṃ lohitapāṇiṃ dhammakathāya mudukaṃ katvā mama pādesu pātesiṃ, rājāno nāma puññavanto paññavanto ca subhāsitadubbhāsitaññū ca, khippaṃ amhe rañño dassehī”ti vutte “tena hi mā mayhaṃ kujjhittha, ahaṃ avassaṃ tumhākaṃ [P 5.0346] ruciyā nemī”ti vatvā ubhopi kājaṃ āropetvā rājakulaṃ gantvā rañño dassetvā raññā puṭṭho yathābhūtaṃ ārocesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

When this was said, the hunter replied, “Master, may the sight of the king not appeal to you, for kings are fickle-minded. They might make you play-geese or even cause you to be killed.” But the other said, “Friend, do not fear. I have made such a harsh, cruel, and blood-handed hunter gentle with a Dhamma talk and made him fall at my feet. Kings are meritorious, wise, and know what is well-spoken and ill-spoken. Quickly show us to the king.” When this was said, the hunter replied, “If that is so, do not be angry with me. I will surely take you according to your wish.” Having said this, he made them both mount the carrying pole and went to the royal palace. When they were presented to the king and questioned, he related what had happened. To make this matter clear, the Teacher said:

40.

40.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, kammunā upapādayi;

Khippamantepuraṃ gantvā, rañño haṃse adassayi;

Abaddhe pakatibhūte, kāje ubhayato ṭhite.

“Having heard his words, he acted accordingly. Quickly going to the inner palace, he showed the geese to the king: unbound, in their natural state, standing on both sides of the carrying pole.

41.

41.

“Dhataraṭṭhā [V 5.0341] mahārāja, haṃsādhipatino ime;

Ayañhi rājā haṃsānaṃ, ayaṃ senāpatītaro;

“‘O great king, these are Dhataraṭṭha geese, lords of their kind. This one is the king of the geese, and this other is his commander.’

42.

42.

“Kathaṃ panime vihaṅgā, tava hatthattamāgatā;

Kathaṃ luddo mahantānaṃ, issare idha ajjhagā.

“‘How then have these birds come into your hands? How has a hunter here gained mastery over these great ones?’

43.

43.

“Vihitā santime pāsā, pallalesu janādhipa;

Yaṃ yadāyatanaṃ maññe, dijānaṃ pāṇarodhanaṃ.

“‘These snares of mine are set in the marshes, O lord of men, in whatever place I deem a death-trap for birds.’

44.

44.

“Tādisaṃ pāsamāsajja, haṃsarājā abajjhatha;

Taṃ abaddho upāsino, mamāyaṃ ajjhabhāsatha.

“‘Encountering such a snare, the king of geese was caught. While this other sat near him, unbound, he addressed me.

45.

45.

“Sudukkaraṃ anariyebhi, dahate bhāvamuttamaṃ;

Bhatturatthe parakkanto, dhammayutto vihaṅgamo.

“‘He displays the highest nature, a thing very difficult for the ignoble to do; striving for the sake of his master, this bird is endowed with righteousness.

46.

46.

“Attanāyaṃ cajitvāna, jīvitaṃ jīvitāraho;

Anutthunanto āsīno, bhattu yācittha jīvitaṃ.

“‘Though worthy of life, this one gave up his own life. Sitting and extolling his master, he begged for his master’s life.

47.

47.

“Tassa [M 5.0369] taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, pasādamahamajjhagā;

Tato naṃ pāmuciṃ pāsā, anuññāsiṃ sukhena ca.

“‘Having heard his words, I attained serene joy; then I released him from the snare and gladly gave my permission.

48.

48.

“So patīto pamuttena, bhattunā bhattugāravo;

Ajjhabhāsatha vakkaṅgo, vācaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhaṇaṃ.

“‘Pleased that his master was freed, and respectful toward his master, the crook-necked one addressed the hunter, speaking words pleasant to the ear.

49.

49.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā dijādhipaṃ.

“‘Thus rejoice, O hunter, with all your kinsmen, as I rejoice today, seeing the freed lord of birds.’

50.

50.

“Ehi taṃ anusikkhāmi, yathā tvamapi lacchase;

Lābhaṃ tavāyaṃ dhataraṭṭho, pāpaṃ kiñci na dakkhati.

“‘Come, I will instruct you, so that you too may gain. This Dhataraṭṭha is for your gain; he will see no fault in you.

51.

51.

“Khippamantepuraṃ [V 5.0342] netvā, rañño dassehi no ubho;

Abaddhe pakatibhūte, kāje ubhayato ṭhite.

“‘Quickly take us both to the inner palace and show us to the king, unbound, in our natural state, standing on both sides of the carrying pole.

52.

52.

“Dhataraṭṭhā mahārāja, haṃsādhipatino ime;

Ayañhi rājā haṃsānaṃ, ayaṃ senāpatītaro.

“‘O great king, these are Dhataraṭṭha geese, lords of their kind. This one is the king of the geese, and this other is his commander.’”

53.

53.

“Asaṃsayaṃ imaṃ disvā, haṃsarājaṃ narādhipo;

Patīto sumano vitto, bahuṃ dassati te dhanaṃ.

“Undoubtedly, upon seeing this goose king, the king of men, being pleased, glad, and joyful in heart, will give you much wealth.”

54.

54.

“Evametassa [P 5.0347] vacanā, ānītāme ubho mayā;

Ettheva hi ime āsuṃ, ubho anumatā mayā.

“O great king, thus by the words of this Sumukha, these two have been brought by me. Indeed, right here at this Manusiya Lake, they were both permitted by me [to be taken].”

55.

55.

“Soyaṃ evaṃ gato pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Mādisassa hi luddassa, janayeyyātha maddavaṃ.

“O great king, this bird who has come thus, this twice-born one is supremely virtuous. Indeed, he could inspire tenderness even in a hunter like me.”

56.

56.

“Upāyanañca te deva, nāññaṃ passāmi edisaṃ;

Sabbasākuṇikāgāme, taṃ passa manujādhipā”ti.

“O Lord, I see no other such tribute for you; even in the entire village of fowlers, I see no other [like these two]. Behold them, O lord of men.”

Tattha kammunā upapādayīti yaṃ so avaca, taṃ karonto kāyakammena sampādesi. Gantvāti haṃsarājena nisinnakājakoṭiṃ uccataraṃ, senāpatinā nisinnakājakoṭiṃ thokaṃ nīcaṃ katvā ubhopi te ukkhipitvā “haṃsarājā ca senāpati ca rājānaṃ passituṃ gacchanti, ussaratha ussarathā”ti janaṃ ussārento “evarūpā nāma sobhaggappattā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā haṃsarājāno na diṭṭhapubbā”ti muduhadayesu manussesu pasaṃsantesu [M 5.0370] khippamantepuraṃ gantvā. Adassayīti “haṃsarājāno tumhe daṭṭhuṃ āgatā”ti rañño ārocāpetvā tena tuṭṭhacittena “āgacchantū”ti pakkosāpito abhiharitvā dassesi. Hatthattanti hatthesu āgataṃ, pattanti vuttaṃ hoti. Mahantānanti yasamahantappattānaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇānaṃ dhataraṭṭhahaṃsānaṃ issare sāmino kathaṃ tvaṃ luddo hutvā adhigatoti pucchati. “Issaramidhamajjhagā”tipi pāṭho, etesaṃ issariyaṃ tvaṃ kathaṃ ajjhagāti attho.

There, ‘by action he brought about’ means that what he said, he accomplished by bodily action. ‘Having gone’ means: having made the end of the carrying pole where the goose king sat higher, and the end where the general sat slightly lower, and having lifted them both, he cleared the way for the people, saying, ‘The goose king and the general are going to see the king, make way, make way!’ While the gentle-hearted people were praising them, saying, ‘Such splendid, golden-hued goose kings have never been seen before,’ he swiftly went to the inner palace. ‘He showed’ means: having announced to the king, ‘The goose kings have come to see you,’ and having been summoned by him with a pleased mind with the words, ‘Let them come,’ he brought them forth and showed them. ‘Into the hands’ means come into the hands; that is to say, obtained. ‘Of the great ones’ means he asks, ‘How did you, being a hunter, gain mastery over these lords and masters, these great, glorious, golden-hued Dhataraṭṭha geese?’ ‘He attained this lordship’ is also a reading; the meaning is, ‘How did you attain sovereignty over them?’”

Vihitāti yojitā. Yaṃ yadāyatanaṃ maññeti, mahārāja, yaṃ yaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ dijānaṃ pāṇarodhanaṃ [V 5.0343] jīvitakkhayakaraṃ maññāmi, tattha tattha mayā pallalesu pāsā vihitā. Tādisanti mānusiyasare tathāvidhaṃ pāṇarodhanaṃ mayā vihitaṃ pāsaṃ. Tanti taṃ etaṃ tattha baddhaṃ. Upāsinoti attano jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā upagantvā nisinno. Mamāyanti maṃ ayaṃ senāpati ajjhabhāsatha, mayā saddhiṃ kathesi. Sudukkaranti tasmiṃ khaṇe esa amhādisehi anariyehi sudukkaraṃ akāsi. Kiṃ tanti? Dahate bhāvamuttamaṃ, attano uttamaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ dahati vidahati pakāseti. Attanāyanti attano ayaṃ. Anutthunantoti bhattuguṇe vaṇṇento tassa jīvitaṃ muñcāti maṃ yāci.

‘Arranged’ means set up. ‘Whatever location I consider’ means: O great king, wherever I consider a gathering spot for birds, a place for killing creatures that causes the end of life, there in the small ponds I have set snares. ‘Such’ means: in the Mānusiya lake, such a deadly trap, a snare, was set by me. ‘That one’ means that one was bound there. ‘Sitting near’ means approaching and sitting down without regard for his own life. ‘Addressed me’ means this general spoke to me, he conversed with me. ‘Very difficult’ means at that moment he did something very difficult for ignoble ones like us. What is that? ‘He reveals the highest disposition’ means he displays, establishes, and manifests his own highest intention. ‘His own’ means this is his own. ‘Extolling’ means praising the virtues of his master, he begged me, saying, ‘Release his life.’”

Tassāti tassa tathā yācantassa. Sukhena cāti yathāsukhena cittakūṭaṃ gantvā ñātisaṅghaṃ passathāti ca anujāniṃ. Ettheva hīti mayā pana ime dve ettha mānusiyasareyeva cittakūṭagamanāya anumatā ahesuṃ. Evaṃ gatoti evaṃ sattu hatthagato. Janayeyyātha maddavanti attani mettacittaṃ janesi. Upāyananti paṇṇākāraṃ. Sabbasākuṇikāgāmeti [P 5.0348] sabbasmimpi sākuṇikagāme nāhaṃ aññaṃ tava evarūpaṃ kenaci sākuṇikena ābhatapubbaṃ upāyanaṃ passāmi. Taṃ passāti taṃ mayā ābhataṃ upāyanaṃ passa manujādhipāti.

‘Of him’ means of him who was pleading in such a manner. ‘And with ease’ means I permitted them, saying, ‘Go to Cittakūṭa at your leisure and see your assembly of relatives.’ ‘Right here’ means: but by me, these two were permitted to go to Cittakūṭa right here at the Mānusiya lake. ‘Thus gone’ means thus fallen into the enemy’s hand. ‘Could generate gentleness’ means he generated a mind of loving-kindness in me. ‘A gift’ means a present. ‘In all the fowlers’ villages’ means in the entire village of fowlers, I do not see any other such gift previously brought to you by any fowler. ‘See that’ means see that gift brought by me, O lord of men.

Evaṃ so ṭhitakova sumukhassa guṇaṃ kathesi. Tato rājā haṃsarañño mahārahaṃ āsanaṃ, sumukhassa ca suvaṇṇabhaddapīṭhakaṃ dāpetvā tesaṃ tattha nisinnānaṃ suvaṇṇabhājanehi lājamadhuphāṇitādīni dāpetvā niṭṭhite pānabhojanakicce añjaliṃ paggayha mahāsattaṃ dhammakathaṃ yācitvā [M 5.0371] suvaṇṇapīṭhake nisīdi. So tena yācito paṭisanthāraṃ tāva akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, while still standing, he spoke of Sumukha’s virtues to the king. Then the king, having provided a seat worthy of the noble for the goose king and a golden stool for Sumukha, had them served with parched grain, honey, molasses, and such in golden vessels while they were seated there. When the meal was finished, he raised his hands in reverence, requested the Great Being to give a Dhamma talk, and sat down on a golden seat. Being thus requested, the Bodhisatta first offered a courteous greeting. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

57.

57.

“Disvā nisinnaṃ rājānaṃ, pīṭhe sovaṇṇaye subhe;

Ajjhabhāsatha vakkaṅgo, vācaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhaṇaṃ.

“Seeing King Sagala seated on a beautiful golden throne, the golden goose (Vakkaṅga) addressed him, speaking words pleasing to the ear.”

58.

58.

“Kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ;

Kacci raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsasi.

“O noble among men, Lord of the Palace, I hope you are well; I hope you are free from illness. I hope this kingdom of Mahimsaka is prosperous, and that you govern it righteously.”

59.

59.

“Kusalañceva me haṃsa, atho haṃsa anāmayaṃ;

Atho raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsahaṃ.

“I am indeed well, O goose, and also free from illness; and this kingdom of ours is prosperous, and I govern it righteously.”

60.

60.

“Kacci [V 5.0344] bhoto amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Kacci ca te tavatthesu, nāvakaṅkhanti jīvitaṃ.

“O Protector of Beings, O Lord of the Land, I hope no fault is found among your ministers; and do they not disregard their own lives for your sake? [i.e., Do they serve you even at the cost of their lives?]”

61.

61.

“Athopi me amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Athopi te mamatthesu, nāvakaṅkhanti jīvitaṃ.

“Indeed, no fault is found among my ministers; and they do not regard their own lives for my sake. [i.e., They serve me even at the cost of their lives.]”

62.

62.

“Kacci te sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, tava chandavasānugā.

“O Bearer of the Burden of the Realm, O Lord of the Land, I hope you have a queen of equal birth, who is obedient and sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, and attendants, and who follows your will.”

63.

63.

“Atho me sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, mama chandavasānugā”ti.

“And indeed, I have a queen of equal birth, who is obedient and sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, and attendants, and who follows my will.”

Tattha rājānanti sāgalarājānaṃ. Vakkaṅgoti haṃsarājā. Dhammena manusāsasīti dhammena anusāsasi. Dosoti aparādho. Tavatthesūti uppannesu tava yuddhādīsu atthesu. Nāvakaṅkhantīti uraṃ datvā pariccajantā kicci attano jīvitaṃ na patthenti, jīvitañca cajitvā tavevatthaṃ karonti. Sādisīti samānajātikā. Assavāti vacanasampaṭicchikā. Puttarūpayasūpetāti [P 5.0349] puttehi ca rūpena ca yasena ca upetā. Tava chandavasānugāti kacci tava ajjhāsayaṃ tava vasaṃ anuvattati, na attano cittavasena vattatīti pucchati.

Here, ‘the king’ means King Sāgala. ‘The goose’ means the goose-king. ‘You rule righteously’ means you rule by the Dhamma. ‘Fault’ means an offense. ‘For your sake’ means in your affairs that have arisen, such as war. ‘They do not long for’ means that, offering their chests and renouncing their lives, they do not desire their own life at all; and having given up their lives, they do only your work. ‘Your equal’ means of the same caste. ‘Obedient’ means receptive to words. ‘Endowed with sons, beauty, and fame’ means endowed with sons and beauty and fame. ‘Who follows your will’ asks: ‘I hope she conforms to your inclination and your control, not acting according to her own mind?’”

Evaṃ bodhisattena paṭisanthāre kate puna rājā tena saddhiṃ kathento āha –

When the Bodhisatta goose had thus engaged in courteous conversation, King Sagala, wishing to converse further with the Bodhisatta, said:

64.

64.

“Bhavantaṃ [M 5.0372] kacci nu mahā-sattuhatthattataṃ gato;

Dukkhamāpajji vipulaṃ, tasmiṃ paṭhamamāpade.

“O Lord of Birds, O Goose King, I hope that, having fallen into the hands of a great enemy, you did not suffer immense hardship in that first calamity?”

65.

65.

“Kacci yantāpatitvāna, daṇḍena samapothayi;

Evametesaṃ jammānaṃ, pātikaṃ bhavati tāvade.

“I hope that after the trap was sprung, he did not strike you with a stick; for such is the common practice of these wretched hunters at that moment.”

66.

66.

“Khemamāsi mahārāja, evamāpadiyā sati;

Na cāyaṃ kiñci rasmāsu, sattūva samapajjatha.

“It was safe, O great king, even though such a calamity occurred. This man did not inflict any suffering upon us, nor did he act like an enemy.”

67.

67.

“Paccagamittha [V 5.0345] nesādo, pubbeva ajjhabhāsatha;

Tadāyaṃ sumukhoyeva, paṇḍito paccabhāsatha.

“O great king, the hunter approached to investigate; he spoke first with soft words. Then this wise Sumukha replied to him.”

68.

68.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, pasādamayamajjhagā;

Tato maṃ pāmucī pāsā, anuññāsi sukhena ca.

“Hearing those words of his, the hunter was filled with faith. Because of that faith, he released me from the snare and safely gave us permission [to go].”

69.

69.

“Idañca sumukheneva, etadatthāya cintitaṃ;

Bhoto sakāsegamanaṃ, etassa dhanamicchatā.

“O great king, this plan was conceived by Sumukha himself for this purpose: our coming into your presence, as he desired to obtain wealth for this hunter.”

70.

70.

“Svāgatañcevidaṃ bhavataṃ, patīto casmi dassanā;

Eso cāpi bahuṃ vittaṃ, labhataṃ yāvadicchatī”ti.

“O goose king, welcome indeed is your arrival. I am pleased to have seen you. And may this hunter obtain much wealth, as much as he desires.”

Tattha mahāsattuhatthattataṃ gatoti mahantassa sattuno hatthattaṃ gato. Āpatitvānāti upadhāvitvā. Pātikanti pākatikaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – etesañhi jammānaṃ tāvadeva evaṃ pākatikaṃ hoti, sakuṇe daṇḍena pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpento dhanavetanaṃ labhatīti. Kiñci rasmāsūti kiñci amhesu. Sattūvāti sattu viya. Paccagamitthāti, mahārāja, esa amhe disvā baddhāti saññāya thokaṃ osakkittha. Pubbevāti ayameva paṭhamaṃ ajjhabhāsi. Tadāti tasmiṃ kāle. Etadatthāyāti etassa nesādaputtassa atthāya cintitaṃ. Dhanamicchatāti etassa dhanaṃ icchantena [P 5.0350] tava santikaṃ amhākaṃ āgamanaṃ cintitaṃ. Svāgatañcevidanti mā bhonto cintayantu, bhavataṃ idaṃ idhāgamanaṃ svāgatameva. Labhatanti labhatu.

Here, 'mahāsattuhatthattataṃ gato' means he has come under the power of a great enemy. 'Āpatitvāna' means having run up to. 'Pātika' means natural, or this is the reading. This is said—for these wretches, it is immediately natural that by striking a bird with a stick and causing its death, one earns wealth and wages. 'Kiñci rasmāsu' means anything among us. 'Sattūva' means like an enemy. 'Paccagamittha' means, O king, seeing us, he retreated a little with the thought that we were bound. 'Pubbeva' means he himself spoke first. 'Tadā' means at that time. 'Etadatthāya' means for the sake of this hunter's son it was conceived. 'Dhanamicchatā' means by one desiring wealth for this one, our coming to you was conceived. 'Svāgatañcevidaṃ' means do not worry, sirs, your coming here is indeed welcome. 'Labhataṃ' means let him receive.
