Evañca [M 5.0373] pana vatvā rājā aññataraṃ amaccaṃ oloketvā “kiṃ karomi devā”ti vutte “imaṃ nesādaṃ kappitakesamassuṃ nhātānulittaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ kāretvā ānehī”ti vatvā tena tathā katvā ānītassa tassa saṃvacchare saṃvacchare satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gāmaṃ, dve vīthiyo gahetvā ṭhitaṃ mahantaṃ gehaṃ, rathavarañca, aññañca bahuṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ adāsi. Tamatthaṃ āvikaronto satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, King Sagala looked at an official. When asked, 'O lord, what shall I do?', he replied, 'Have this hunter's hair and beard trimmed, have him bathe, anoint him with perfumes, and bring him here adorned with every ornament.' The official did as commanded and brought the hunter. The king then gave him a village yielding an annual revenue of a hundred thousand, a large house situated at a junction of two roads, a noble chariot, and much gold and silver. Revealing this matter, the Teacher said:

71.

71.

“Santappayitvā nesādaṃ, bhogehi manujādhipo;

Ajjhabhāsatha vakkaṅgaṃ, vācaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhaṇa”nti.

“When the lord of men, King Sagala, had satisfied the hunter with riches, he addressed the goose king. And the golden goose (Vakkaṅga), speaking words pleasing to the ear, addressed [the king].”

Atha [V 5.0346] mahāsatto rañño dhammaṃ desesi. So tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhahadayo “dhammakathikassa sakkāraṃ karissāmī”ti setacchattaṃ datvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpento āha –

Then the Bodhisatta goose preached the Dhamma to King Sagala. Having heard the Dhamma talk of the Bodhisatta, the king was greatly delighted and thought, 'I shall pay homage to this Dhamma preacher.' He then offered the white parasol, wishing to bestow the sovereignty upon him, and said:

72.

72.

“Yaṃ khalu dhammamādhīnaṃ, vaso vattati kiñcanaṃ;

Sabbatthissariyaṃ bhavataṃ, pasāsatha yadicchatha.

“O goose king, indeed, in whatever place the ten royal virtues reside and my authority extends—though it be but a little—let all that sovereignty belong to you. Direct it as you wish.”

73.

73.

“Dānatthaṃ upabhottuṃ vā, yaṃ caññaṃ upakappati;

Etaṃ dadāmi vo vittaṃ, issariyaṃ vissajāmi vo”ti.

“O goose king, whether for the purpose of giving or for enjoyment, or for whatever else you find pleasing, I give this wealth to you; I relinquish all sovereignty to you.”

Tattha vaso vattatīti yattha mama vaso vattati. Kiñcananti taṃ appamattakampi. Sabbatthissariyanti sabbaṃ bhavataṃyeva issariyaṃ atthu. Yaṃ caññaṃ upakappatīti puññakāmatāya dānatthaṃ vā chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjameva upabhottuṃ vā yaṃ vā aññaṃ tumhākaṃ ruccati, taṃ karotha, etaṃ dadāmi vo vittaṃ, saddhiṃyeva setacchattena mama santakaṃ issariyaṃ vissajjāmi voti.

Here, 'vaso vattati' means where my power extends. 'Kiñcana' means even that small amount. 'Sabbatthissariyaṃ' means let all sovereignty be yours. 'Yaṃ caññaṃ upakappati' means for the sake of merit-making, whether it be for giving, or raising the parasol to enjoy the kingdom, or whatever else pleases you, do so. 'Etaṃ dadāmi vo vittaṃ, issariyaṃ vissajāmi vo' means this wealth I give to you, and together with the white parasol, I relinquish my sovereignty to you.

Atha mahāsatto raññā dinnaṃ setacchattaṃ puna tasseva adāsi. Rājāpi cintesi – “haṃsarañño tāva me dhammakathā sutā, luddaputtena pana ‘ayaṃ sumukho mudhurakatho’ti ativiya [P 5.0351] vaṇṇito, imassapi dhammakathaṃ sossāmī”ti. So tena saddhiṃ sallapanto anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta gave the white parasol back to the king. King Sagala then thought: 'I have already heard the Dhamma talk of the goose king. But the hunter spoke very highly of Sumukha, saying he is a sweet speaker. I shall listen to Sumukha’s Dhamma too.' Wishing to converse with Sumukha, the king spoke this next verse:

74.

74.

“Yathā ca myāyaṃ sumukho, ajjhabhāseyya paṇḍito;

Kāmasā buddhisampanno, taṃ myāssa paramappiya”nti.

“If this wise Sumukha, who is endowed with wisdom, were to address me of his own accord, that would be most pleasing to me.”

Tattha [M 5.0374] yathāti yadi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi ca me ayaṃ sumukho paṇḍito buddhisampanno kāmasā attano ruciyā ajjhabhāseyya, taṃ me paramappiyaṃ assāti.

Here, 'yathā' means 'if'. This is said: 'If this wise Sumukha, endowed with intelligence, were to address me of his own accord, according to his own liking, that would be most dear to me.'

Tato sumukho āha –

Then Sumukha said:

75.

75.

“Ahaṃ khalu mahārāja, nāgarājārivantaraṃ;

Paṭivattuṃ na sakkomi, na me so vinayo siyā.

“O great king, I am indeed like a serpent king who has entered a basket; I do not dare to speak in reply. If I were to speak back thus, it would not be proper discipline for me.”

76.

76.

“Amhākañceva [V 5.0347] so seṭṭho, tvañca uttamasattavo;

Bhūmipālo manussindo, pūjā bahūhi hetubhi.

“O Bearer of the Burden, Lord of the Land, he (the goose king) is the most excellent among us. And you, O ruler of men, Lord of the Earth, are a supreme being. For many reasons, you are both worthy of honor.”

77.

77.

“Tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ bhaṇataṃ, vattamāne vinicchaye;

Nantaraṃ pativattabbaṃ, pessena manujādhipā”ti.

“When those two are speaking and a decision is being made, a servant should not intervene between them, O lord of men.”

Tattha nāgarājārivantaranti peḷāya abbhantaraṃ paviṭṭho nāgarājā viya. Paṭivattunti tumhākaṃ dvinnaṃ antare vattuṃ na sakkomi. Na me soti sace vadeyyaṃ, na me so vinayo bhaveyya. Amhākañcevāti channavutiyā haṃsasahassānaṃ. Uttamasattavoti uttamasatto. Pūjāti ubho tumhe mayhaṃ bahūhi kāraṇehi pūjārahā ceva pasaṃsārahā ca. Pessenāti veyyāvaccakarena sevakena.

Here, 'nāgarājārivantaraṃ' means like a serpent king who has entered inside a container. 'Paṭivattuṃ' means I am unable to speak between you two. 'Na me so' means if I were to speak, that would not be the discipline for me. 'Amhākañceva' refers to the ninety-six thousand geese. 'Uttamasattavo' means the noblest being. 'Pūjā' means both of you are worthy of honor and worthy of praise by me for many reasons. 'Pessena' means by a serving attendant.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhahadayo “nesādaputto taṃ vaṇṇeti, na aññena tumhādisena madhuradhammakathikena nāma bhavitabba”nti vatvā āha –

Hearing his words, the king, with a delighted heart, said, “The hunter’s son praises you; there could be no other sweet speaker of Dhamma like you,” and then spoke:

78.

78.

“Dhammena kira nesādo, paṇḍito aṇḍajo iti;

Naheva akatattassa, nayo etādiso siyā.

“Rightly, it seems, the hunter says: ‘The bird-born is wise’; for one who has not trained his mind, such wisdom would not exist.”

79.

79.

“Evaṃ aggapakatimā, evaṃ uttamasattavo;

Yāvatatthi mayā diṭṭhā, nāññaṃ passāmi edisaṃ.

“He is of such supreme nature, such a noble being; among all those I have seen, I see no other like him.”

80.

80.

“Tuṭṭhosmi vo pakatiyā, vākyena madhurena ca;

Eso cāpi mamacchando, ciraṃ passeyya vo ubho”ti.

“I am pleased with your natural character and with your sweet speech; and this is also my desire: that I might see both of you for a long time.”

Tattha [M 5.0375][P 5.0352] dhammenāti sabhāvena kāraṇena. Akatattassāti asampāditaattabhāvassa mittadubbhissa. Nayoti paññā. Aggapakatimāti aggasabhāvo. Uttamasattavoti uttamasatto. Yāvatatthīti yāvatā mayā diṭṭhā nāma atthi. Nāññanti tasmiṃ mayā diṭṭhaṭṭhāne aññaṃ evarūpaṃ na passāmi. Tuṭṭhosmi vo pakatiyāti samma haṃsarāja ahaṃ pakatiyā paṭhamameva tumhākaṃ dassanena tuṭṭho. Vākyenāti idāni pana vo madhuravacanena tuṭṭhosmi. Ciraṃ passeyya voti idheva vasāpetvā muhuttampi avippavāsanto ciraṃ tumhe passeyyanti esa me chandoti vadati.

In that context, ‘dhammena’ means by nature or for a reason. ‘Akatattassa’ means for one who has not fulfilled the duty of a self, an ungrateful person. ‘Nayo’ means wisdom. ‘Aggapakatimā’ means having a supreme nature. ‘Uttamasattavo’ means the noblest being. ‘Yāvatatthi’ means among all those who have been seen by me. ‘Nāññaṃ’ means I do not see another like this among those I have seen. ‘Tuṭṭhosmi vo pakatiyā’ means, ‘O friend goose-king, I am pleased with your natural disposition from the very first sight of you.’ ‘Vākyena’ means ‘but now I am pleased by your sweet speech.’ ‘Ciraṃ passeyya vo’ means ‘making you stay right here, not being separated even for a moment, I wish to see you for a long time’—this is my desire, he says.

Tato [V 5.0348] mahāsatto rājānaṃ pasaṃsanto āha –

Then the Great Being, wishing to praise the king, said:

81.

81.

“Yaṃ kiccaṃ parame mitte, katamasmāsu taṃ tayā;

Pattā nissaṃsayaṃ tyāmhā, bhattirasmāsu yā tava.

“Whatever duty should be performed for a supreme friend, that has been done by you for us; we have undoubtedly attained that because of the devotion you have for us.”

82.

82.

“Aduñca nūna sumahā, ñātisaṅghassa mantaraṃ;

Adassanena asmākaṃ, dukkhaṃ bahūsu pakkhisu.

Indeed, great is the separation for the large assembly of relatives; not seeing us brings sorrow to many birds.

83.

83.

“Tesaṃ sokavighātāya, tayā anumatā mayaṃ;

Taṃ padakkhiṇato katvā, ñātiṃ passemurindama.

To dispel their grief, permitted by you, may we, having circumambulated you, O subduer of enemies, see our kinsmen.

84.

84.

“Addhāhaṃ vipulaṃ pītiṃ, bhavataṃ vindāmi dassanā;

Eso cāpi mahā attho, ñātivissāsanā siyā”ti.

Indeed, I find great joy in seeing you. And this is also a great advantage: it would be a reassurance for your kinsmen.

Tattha katamasmāsūti kataṃ amhesu. Pattā nissaṃsayaṃ tyāmhāti mayaṃ nissaṃsayena tayā pattāyeva. Bhattirasmāsu yā tavāti yā tava amhesu bhatti, tāya bhattiyā mayaṃ tayā asaṃsayena pattāyeva, na ca vippayuttā, vippavuṭṭhāpi sahavāsinoyeva nāma mayanti dīpeti. Aduñca nūna sumahāti etañca ekaṃseneva sumahantaṃ. Ñātisaṅghassa mantaranti amhehi dvīhi janehi virahitassa mama ñātisaṅghassa antaraṃ chiddaṃ. Asmākanti amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ adassanena bahūsu pakkhīsu dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ. Passemurindamāti passeyyāma arindama. Bhavatanti bhoto dassanena. Eso cāpi mahā atthoti yā esā ñātisaṅghasaṅkhātā ñātivissāsanā siyā, eso cāpi mahanto atthopi.

In that context, ‘katamasmāsu’ means done for us. ‘Pattā nissaṃsayaṃ tyāmhā’ means we are certainly won by you. ‘Bhattirasmāsu yā tava’ means whatever devotion you have for us; through that devotion, we are certainly won by you without doubt and not separated; it signifies that even if living apart, we are still companions. ‘Aduñca nūna sumahā’ means and this is surely a very great peril. ‘Ñātisaṅghassa mantaraṃ’ means the gap or distress in my assembly of kinsfolk caused by the absence of us two. ‘Asmākaṃ’ means due to the lack of seeing us two, suffering has arisen among many birds. ‘Passemurindama’ means ‘may we see our kin, O subduer of enemies.’ ‘Bhavataṃ’ means ‘by seeing you, sir.’ ‘Eso cāpi mahā attho’ means ‘that which is known as trust among kinsfolk would also be a great benefit.’

Evaṃ vutte rājā tesaṃ gamanaṃ anujāni. Mahāsattopi rañño pañcavidhe dussīlye ādīnavaṃ, sīle ca ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā “imaṃ sīlaṃ rakkha, dhammena [M 5.0376] rajjaṃ kārehi, catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ saṅgaṇhāhī”ti ovaditvā cittakūṭaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0353] pakāsento satthā āha –

When this was said, the king permitted their departure. The Great Being also explained the danger in the fivefold immorality and the benefits of virtue to the king, advising him, “Guard this virtue, rule the kingdom righteously, and support the people with the four bases of sympathy.” Having given this counsel, he departed for Mount Cittakūṭa. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

85.

85.

“Idaṃ vatvā dhataraṭṭho, haṃsarājā narādhipaṃ;

Uttamaṃ javamanvāya, ñātisaṅghaṃ upāgamuṃ.

“Having said this to the lord of men, the two goose-kings of the Dhataraṭṭha lineage, with supreme speed, approached their assembly of kinsfolk.”

86.

86.

“Te [V 5.0349] aroge anuppatte, disvāna parame dije;

Kekāti makaruṃ haṃsā, puthusaddo ajāyatha.

"Seeing them, the supreme birds, arrive unharmed, the geese made the 'kekā' sound; a great noise arose."

87.

87.

“Te patītā pamuttena, bhattunā bhattugāravā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, aṇḍajā laddhapaccayā”ti.

"Pleased by their lord, who was freed, and respectful of their master, the egg-born ones, having gained confidence, surrounded him on all sides."

Tattha upāgamunti aruṇuggamanavelāyameva lājamadhuphāṇitādīni paribhuñjitvā raññā ca deviyā ca dvīhi suvaṇṇatālavaṇṭehi ukkhipitvā gandhamālādīhi katasakkārā tālavaṇṭehi otaritvā rājānaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā raññā añjaliṃ paggayha “gacchatha sāmino”ti vutte sīhapañjarena nikkhantā uttamena javena gantvā ñātigaṇaṃ upāgamiṃsu. Parameti uttame. Kekāti attano sabhāvena “kekā”ti saddamakaṃsu. Bhattugāravāti bhattari sagāravā. Parikiriṃsūti bhattuno muttabhāvena tuṭṭhā taṃ bhattāraṃ samantā parivārayiṃsu. Laddhapaccayāti laddhapatiṭṭhā.

In that context, ‘upāgamuṃ’ means: at the very break of dawn, having consumed parched grain, honey, molasses, and other foods, and having been honored with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, they were lifted up by the king and queen using two golden palm-leaf fans. Descending from the fans, they circumambulated the king to the right and soared into the sky. When the king, with hands joined in reverence, said, ‘Go, my lords,’ they departed through the lion-window and, traveling with supreme speed, reached the assembly of their kin. ‘Parame’ means supreme. ‘Kekā’ means they made the sound ‘kekā’ according to their nature. ‘Bhattugāravā’ means respectful towards their master. ‘Parikiriṃsu’ means, being delighted by their master’s release, those birds surrounded the master on all sides. ‘Laddhapaccayā’ means having obtained a refuge or support.

Evaṃ parivāretvā pana te haṃsā “kathaṃ muttosi, mahārājā”ti pucchiṃsu. Mahāsatto sumukhaṃ nissāya muttabhāvaṃ, sāgalarājaluddaputtehi katakammañca kathesi. Taṃ sutvā tuṭṭho haṃsagaṇo “sumukhasenāpati ca rājā ca luddaputto ca sukhitā niddukkhā ciraṃ jīvantū”ti thutimakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā osānagāthamāha –

Having thus surrounded them, the geese asked, “How were you freed, O great king?” The Great Being explained how they were freed through Sumukha, and recounted the deeds done by King Sāgala and the hunter’s son. Hearing this, the delighted flock of geese rejoiced and made a wish, saying, “May Sumukha the general, the king, and the hunter’s son be happy and live a long life!” To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the final verse:

88.

88.

“Evaṃ mittavataṃ atthā, sabbe honti padakkhiṇā;

Haṃsā yathā dhataraṭṭhā, ñātisaṅghaṃ upāgamu”nti.

“Thus, all the interests of those who have good friends turn out auspiciously, just as the Dhataraṭṭha geese returned to the assembly of their kin.”

Tattha mittavatanti kalyāṇamittasampannānaṃ. Padakkhiṇāti sukhanipphattino vuḍḍhiyuttā. Dhataraṭṭhāti haṃsarājā sumukho raññā ceva luddaputtena cāti dvīhi evaṃ ubhopi te dhataraṭṭhā kalyāṇamittasampannā yathā ñātisaṅghaṃ upāgamuṃ[M 5.0377], ñātisaṅghaupagamanasaṅkhāto nesaṃ attho padakkhiṇo jāto, evaṃ aññesampi mittavataṃ atthā padakkhiṇā hontīti.

In that context, ‘mittavatanti’ means of those endowed with good friends. ‘Padakkhiṇā’ means leading to happiness and success. ‘Dhataraṭṭhā’ refers to the goose-king and Sumukha; both Dhataraṭṭhas, endowed with good friends in the form of the king and the hunter’s son, returned to their kin. Their goal of returning to their kin became successful; similarly, the goals of others who have good friends also become successful.

Satthā [P 5.0354] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na bhikkhave idāneva, pubbepānando mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā nesādo channo ahosi, rājā sāriputto[V 5.0350], sumukho ānando, channavuti haṃsasahassā buddhaparisā, haṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake.” Then he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Channa; King Sāgala was Sāriputta; Sumukha was Ānanda; the ninety-six thousand geese were the Buddha’s assembly; and I myself was the goose-king Dhataraṭṭha, the lord of the ninety-six thousand geese.”

Cūḷahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, the first of the group, is finished.

[534] 2. Mahāhaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[534] 2. The Commentary on the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka

Ete haṃsā pakkamantīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ānandatherassa jīvitapariccāgameva ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva, idha pana satthā atītaṃ āharanto idamāhari.

“These geese are departing”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Veḷuvana Monastery, concerning Elder Ānanda’s sacrifice of his life. The story is just as stated in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka above; however, here the Teacher, in bringing forward the past, related this story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ saṃyamassa nāma bārāṇasirañño khemā nāma aggamahesī ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto navutihaṃsasahassaparivuto cittakūṭe vihāsi. Athekadivasaṃ khemā devī paccūsasamaye supinaṃ addasa. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇā haṃsā āgantvā rājapallaṅke nisīditvā madhurassarena dhammakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Deviyā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇantiyā dhammassavanena atittāya eva ratti vibhāyi. Haṃsā dhammaṃ kathetvā sīhapañjarena nikkhamitvā agamaṃsu. Sā vegenuṭṭhāya “palāyamāne haṃse gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti vatvā hatthaṃ pasārentīyeva pabujjhi. Tassā kathaṃ sutvā paricārikāyo “kuhiṃ haṃsā”ti thokaṃ avahasiṃsu. Sā tasmiṃ khaṇe supinabhāvaṃ ñatvā cintesi – “ahaṃ abhūtaṃ na passāmi, addhā imasmiṃ loke suvaṇṇavaṇṇā haṃsā bhavissanti, sace kho pana ‘suvaṇṇahaṃsānaṃ dhammaṃ sotukāmāmhī’ti rājānaṃ vakkhāmi, ‘amhehi suvaṇṇahaṃsā nāma na diṭṭhapubbā, haṃsānañca kathā nāma abhūtāyevā’ti vatvā nirussukko bhavissati, ‘dohaḷo’ti vutte pana yena kenaci upāyena pariyesissati, evaṃ me manoratho samijjhissatī”ti. Sā gilānālayaṃ dassetvā paricārikānaṃ [P 5.0355] saññaṃ datvā nipajji.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Saṃyama of Bārāṇasī had a chief queen named Khemā. At that time, the Bodhisatta dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety thousand geese. Then one day, Queen Khemā saw a dream at dawn. Golden-hued geese came, sat on the royal couch, and delivered a Dhamma talk in sweet voices. While the queen was applauding and listening to the Dhamma, still unsatisfied with hearing it, the night dawned. The geese, having delivered the Dhamma, left through the lion-window and departed. Rising quickly, she woke up exclaiming, “Catch the fleeing geese, catch them!” as she stretched out her hand. Hearing her words, the attendants asked, “Where are the geese?” and laughed a little. Realizing at that moment that it was a dream, she thought: “I do not see what is unreal. Surely, in this world, there must be golden-hued geese. If I tell the king, ‘I wish to hear the Dhamma from golden geese,’ he might say, ‘We have never seen golden geese before, and the speech of geese is indeed unreal,’ and become indifferent. But if I say it is a pregnancy-craving, he will seek them by any means, and thus my wish will be fulfilled.” Showing the signs of illness, she gave the attendants a signal and lay down.

Rājā [M 5.0378] rājāsane nisinno tassā dassanavelāya taṃ adisvā “kahaṃ, khemā devī”ti pucchitvā “gilānā”ti sutvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā sayanekadese nisīditvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjanto “kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Deva aññaṃ aphāsukaṃ natthi, dohaḷo pana me uppanno”ti. Tena hi “bhaṇa, devi, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ sīghaṃ te upanāmessāmī”ti. “Mahārāja, ahamekassa suvaṇṇahaṃsassa samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinnassa gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ katvā sādhukāraṃ dadamānā dhammakathaṃ sotumicchāmi, sace labhāmi, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce, jīvitaṃ me natthī”ti. Atha naṃ rājā “sace manussaloke atthi, labhissasi[V 5.0351], mā cintayī”ti assāsetvā sirigabbhato nikkhamma amaccehi saddhiṃ mantesi – “ambho, khemā devī, ‘suvaṇṇahaṃsassa dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ labhantī jīvissāmi, alabhantiyā me jīvitaṃ natthī’ti vadati, atthi nu kho suvaṇṇavaṇṇā haṃsā”ti. “Deva amhehi neva diṭṭhapubbā na sutapubbā”ti. “Ke pana jāneyyu”nti? “Brāhmaṇā, devā”ti. Rājā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā sakkāraṃ katvā pucchi – “honti nu kho ācariyā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā haṃsā”ti? “Āma, mahārāja amhākaṃ mantesumacchā, kakkaṭakā, kacchapā, migā, morā, haṃsāti cha ete tiracchānagatā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā hontīti āgatā, tattha dhataraṭṭhakulahaṃsā nāma paṇḍitā ñāṇasampannā, iti manussehi saddhiṃ satta suvaṇṇavaṇṇā hontī”ti.

The king, seated on his royal throne, not seeing her at the time for her audience, asked, “Where is Queen Khemā?” Hearing she was ill, he went to her, sat on the edge of her bed, stroked her back, and asked, “What troubles you?” “My lord, nothing else troubles me, but a pregnancy-craving has arisen in me,” she replied. “Then speak, queen. Whatever you desire, I shall quickly bring to you.” “Great king, I wish to honor a golden goose seated on a royal couch under a raised white parasol, offering him perfumes and garlands, and giving cries of approval while listening to his Dhamma talk. If I obtain this, it will be well; if not, my life will be no more.” Then the king reassured her, saying, “If such exists in the human world, you shall obtain it; do not worry.” Leaving the royal chamber, he consulted his ministers: “Sirs, Queen Khemā says, ‘If I can hear the Dhamma talk of a golden goose, I shall live; if I cannot, my life will be no more.’ Are there indeed golden-colored geese?” “Lord, we have neither seen nor heard of such before.” “Then who might know?” “The brahmins, lord.” The king summoned the brahmins, honored them, and asked, “Teachers, are there indeed golden-colored geese?” “Yes, great king. In our sacred texts it is said that these six kinds of animals—fish, crabs, tortoises, deer, peacocks, and geese—can be golden-colored. Among them, the geese of the Dhataraṭṭha lineage are wise and endowed with knowledge. Thus, including humans, there are seven kinds of golden-colored beings.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā attamano hutvā “kahaṃ nu kho ācariyā dhataraṭṭhahaṃsā vasantī”ti pucchitvā “na jānāma, mahārājā”ti vutte “atha ke pana jānissantī”ti vatvā “luddaputtā”ti vutte sabbe attano vijite luddake sannipātāpetvā pucchi – “tātā, suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dhataraṭṭhakulahaṃsā nāma kahaṃ vasantī”ti? Atheko luddo “himavante kira, deva, cittakūṭapabbateti no kulaparamparāya kathentī”ti āha. “Jānāsi pana nesaṃ gahaṇūpāya”nti? “Na jānāmi, devā”ti. “Ke pana jānissantī”ti? Brāhmaṇāti. So brāhmaṇapaṇḍite pakkosāpetvā [P 5.0356] cittakūṭapabbate suvaṇṇavaṇṇānaṃ haṃsānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ ārocetvā “jānātha nu kho tesaṃ gahaṇūpāya”nti pucchi. “Mahārāja, kiṃ tehi gantvā gahitehi, upāyena te nagarasamīpaṃ ānetvā gahessāmā”ti. “Ko pana upāyo”ti? “Mahārāja, nagarato avidūre uttarena tigāvutamatte tigāvutappamāṇaṃ khemaṃ nāma saraṃ [M 5.0379] kārāpetvā udakassa pūretvā nānādhaññāni ropetvā pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ kārāpetvā ekaṃ paṇḍitaṃ nesādaṃ paṭicchāpetvā manussānaṃ upagantuṃ adatvā catūsu kaṇṇesu ṭhitehi abhayaṃ ghosāpetha, taṃ sutvā nānāsakuṇā dasa disā otarissanti, tepi haṃsā paramparāya tassa sarassa khemabhāvaṃ sutvā āgacchissanti, atha ne vālapāsehi bandhāpetvā gaṇhāpeyyāthā”ti.

Hearing this, the king was delighted and asked, “Teachers, where do the Dhataraṭṭha geese live?” When they said, “We do not know, great king,” he asked, “Then who might know?” When they replied, “The sons of hunters,” he had all the hunters in his kingdom assembled and asked, “My good men, where do the golden-colored geese of the Dhataraṭṭha lineage live?” One hunter said, “Sire, it is said in our family tradition that they live on Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himalayas.” “Do you know a way to capture them?” “I do not know, sire.” “Then who might know?” “The brahmins.” So he summoned the learned brahmins, informed them of the existence of the golden-colored geese on Mount Cittakūṭa, and asked, “Do you know a way to capture them?” “Great king, what is the use of going and capturing them there? By a stratagem, we will bring them near the city and have them captured.” “What is this stratagem?” “Great king, not far from the city, to the north, at a distance of three gāvutas, have a lake named Khema made, three gāvutas in extent. Have it filled with water, have various grains planted, and have it covered with five-colored lotuses. Station a wise fowler there, do not allow people to approach, and from the four corners, have a proclamation of safety made. Hearing this, various birds will descend from the ten directions. Those geese, too, hearing by tradition of the safety of that lake, will come. Then, you may have them bound with hair-snares and captured.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā tehi vuttapadese vuttappakāraṃ saraṃ kārāpetvā chekaṃ nesādaṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa sahassaṃ dāpetvā “tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya attano kammaṃ mā kari, puttadāraṃ te ahaṃ posessāmi, tvaṃ appamatto khemaṃ saraṃ rakkhanto manusse paṭikkamāpetvā catūsu kaṇṇesu abhayaṃ ghosāpetvā āgatāgate sakuṇe mama ācikkheyyāsi, suvaṇṇahaṃsesu āgatesu mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhissasī”ti tamassāsetvā khemaṃ saraṃ paṭicchāpesi. So tato paṭṭhāya raññā vuttanayeneva tattha paṭipajji, “khemaṃ saraṃ rakkhatī”ti cassa “khemanesādo”tveva nāmaṃ udapādi[V 5.0352]. Tato paṭṭhāya ca nānappakārā sakuṇā otariṃsu, “khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ sara”nti paramparāghosena nānāhaṃsā āgamiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ tāva tiṇahaṃsā āgamiṃsu, tesaṃ ghosena paṇḍuhaṃsā, tesaṃ ghosena manosilāvaṇṇā haṃsā, tesaṃ ghosena setahaṃsā, tesaṃ ghosena pākahaṃsā āgamiṃsu. Tesu āgatesu khemako rañño ārocesi – “deva, pañcavaṇṇā haṃsā āgantvā sare gocaraṃ gaṇhanti, pākahaṃsānaṃ āgatattā idāni katipāheneva suvaṇṇahaṃsā āgamissanti, mā [P 5.0357] cintayittha, devā”ti.

Hearing this, the king had a lake constructed in the manner and at the location they described. He summoned a skilled fowler, gave him a thousand coins, and said, 'From now on, do not perform your own work. I will support your wife and children. Vigilantly guarding the Khema Lake, you must turn people away, have immunity proclaimed at the four corners, and report to me the birds that arrive. When the golden swans come, you will receive great honor.' Reassuring him thus, he entrusted him with the Khema Lake. From then on, the fowler acted there exactly as the king had instructed. Because he guarded the Khema Lake, he became known as 'Khemaka the Fowler.' From that time, various kinds of birds descended there. Through the successive proclamations that it was a 'safe and fearless lake,' various types of swans arrived. First, the grass-swans came. At their call, the pale swans; at their call, the realgar-colored swans; at their call, the white swans; and at their call, the Pāka swans arrived. When they had come, Khemaka informed the king: 'Sire, swans of five colors have come and are feeding in the lake. Because the Pāka swans have arrived, the golden swans will now come within a few days. Do not worry, Sire.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā “aññena tattha na gantabbaṃ, yo gacchissati, hatthapādachedanañca gharavilopañca pāpuṇissatī”ti nagara bheriṃ carāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya tattha koci na gacchati. Cittakūṭassa panāvidūre kañcanaguhāyaṃpākahaṃsā vasanti, tepi mahabbalā. Dhataraṭṭhakulena saddhiṃ tesaṃ sarīravaṇṇova viseso. Pākahaṃsarañño pana dhītā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ahosi. So taṃ dhataraṭṭhamahissarassa anurūpāti tassa pādaparicārikaṃ katvā pesesi. Sā tassa piyā ahosi manāpā, teneva ca kāraṇena tāni dve haṃsakulāni aññamaññaṃ vissāsikāni jātāni.

Hearing this, the king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'No one else is to go there. Whoever goes shall suffer the cutting off of hands and feet and the plundering of their house.' From then on, no one dared go there. Not far from Cittakūṭa, in the Golden Cave, lived the Pāka swans, who were also of great strength. The only difference between them and the Dhataraṭṭha lineage was the color of their bodies. Now, the daughter of the king of the Pāka swans was golden-colored. Thinking she was a suitable match for the great lord of the Dhataraṭṭhas, he sent her to be his queen consort. She became dear and pleasing to him, and for that reason, the two swan lineages became mutually trusting.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 5.0380] bodhisattassa parivārahaṃsā pākahaṃse pucchiṃsu – “tumhe imesu divasesu kahaṃ gocaraṃ gaṇhathā”ti? “Mayaṃ bārāṇasito avidūre khemasare gocaraṃ gaṇhāma, tumhe pana kuhiṃ āhiṇḍathā”ti. “Asukaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “kasmā khemasaraṃ na gacchatha, so hi saro ramaṇīyo nānāsakuṇasamākiṇṇo pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchanno nānādhaññaphalasampanno nānappakārabhamaragaṇanikūjito catūsu kaṇṇesu niccaṃ pavattaabhayaghosano, koci naṃ upasaṅkamituṃ samattho nāma natthi, pageva aññaṃ upaddavaṃ kātuṃ, evarūpo so saro”ti khemasaraṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu. Te tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “bārāṇasiyā samīpe kira evarūpo khemo nāma saro atthi, pākahaṃsā tattha gantvā gocaraṃ gaṇhanti, tumhepi dhataraṭṭhamahissarassa ārocetha, sace anujānāti, mayampi tattha gantvā gocaraṃ gaṇheyyāmā”ti sumukhassa kathesuṃ. Sumukho rañño ārocesi. So cintesi – “manussā nāma bahumāyā kharamantā upāyakusalā, bhavitabbamettha kāraṇena, ettakaṃ kālaṃ eso saro natthi, idāni amhākaṃ gahaṇatthāya kato bhavissatī”ti. So sumukhaṃ āha – “mā vo tattha gamanaṃ ruccatha, na so saro tehi sudhammatāya kato, amhākaṃ gahaṇatthāyeva kato, manussā nāma bahumāyā kharamantā upāyakusalā, tumhe sakeyeva gocare carathā”ti[P 5.0358].

Then one day, the attendant swans of the Bodhisatta asked the Pāka swans, 'Where have you been feeding these days?' 'We feed at the Khema Lake not far from Bārāṇasī. But where do you wander?' When they replied, 'In such-and-such a place,' the Pāka swans said, 'Why do you not go to the Khema Lake? For that lake is delightful, teeming with various birds, covered with five-colored lotuses, filled with various grains, and resounds with the humming of many kinds of bees. Immunity is constantly proclaimed at the four corners. No one is able even to approach it, let alone cause any harm. Such is that lake.' Thus they praised the Khema Lake. Hearing their words, the swans said to Sumukha, 'It is said that near Bārāṇasī there is such a lake called Khema. The Pāka swans go there to feed. You should also inform the great lord Dhataraṭṭha. If he permits, we too would like to go there and feed.' Sumukha informed the king. He reflected: 'Humans are full of deceit, harsh in their schemes, and skilled in stratagems. There must be a reason for this. This lake did not exist for all this time; it must have been made now to capture us.' He said to Sumukha: 'Do not let going there be pleasing to you. That lake was not made by them out of righteousness, but only to capture us. Humans are full of deceit, harsh in their schemes, and skilled in stratagems. You should forage only in your own feeding grounds.'

Suvaṇṇahaṃsā “khemaṃ saraṃ gantukāmamhā”ti dutiyampi tatiyampi sumukhassa ārocesuṃ. So [V 5.0353] tesaṃ tattha gantukāmataṃ mahāsattassa ārocesi. Atha mahāsatto “mama ñātakā maṃ nissāya mā kilamantu, tena hi gacchāmā”ti navutihaṃsasahassaparivuto tattha gantvā gocaraṃ gahetvā haṃsakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā cittakūṭameva paccāgami. Khemako tesaṃ gocaraṃ caritvā gatakāle gantvā tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā tuṭṭhacitto hutvā, “samma khemaka, ekaṃ vā dve vā haṃse gaṇhituṃ vāyama, mahantaṃ te yasaṃ dassāmī”ti vatvā paribbayaṃ datvā taṃ uyyojesi. So tattha gantvā cāṭipañjare nisīditvā haṃsānaṃ caraṇaṭṭhānaṃ vīmaṃsi. Bodhisattā nāma nilloluppacārino honti, tasmā mahāsatto otiṇṇaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya sapadānaṃ sāliṃ khādanto agamāsi. Sesā ito cito ca khādantā vicariṃsu.

The golden swans informed Sumukha a second and third time, 'We wish to go to the Khema Lake.' He reported their desire to the Great Being. Then the Great Being thought, 'Let my kinsmen not suffer on my account; therefore, we shall go.' Surrounded by ninety thousand swans, he went there, took food, sported as swans do, and then returned to Cittakūṭa. When they had finished feeding and departed, Khemaka went and reported their arrival to the king. The king, pleased at heart, said, 'Friend Khemaka, strive to capture one or two swans, and I will give you great wealth.' Having provided him with expenses, he sent him off. Khemaka went there, sat in a pot-shaped blind, and observed the swans' feeding place. Bodhisattas are not fickle in their movements. Therefore, the Great Being, starting from the place where he alighted, moved along eating the rice systematically. The other swans wandered about, eating here and there.

Atha [M 5.0381] luddaputto “ayaṃ haṃso nilloluppacārī, imaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā punadivase haṃsesu saraṃ anotiṇṇesuyeva cāṭipañjare nisinno taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā avidūre pañjare attānaṃ paṭicchādetvā chiddena olokento acchi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto navutihaṃsasahassapurakkhato hiyyo otiṇṇaṭṭhāneyeva otaritvā odhiyaṃ nisīditvā sāliṃ khādanto pāyāsi. Nesādo pañjarachiddena olokento tassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ disvā “ayaṃ haṃso sakaṭanābhippamāṇasarīro suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, tīhi rattarājīhi gīvāyaṃ parikkhitto, tisso rājiyo galena otaritvā urantarena gatā, tisso pacchābhāgena nibbijjhitvā gatā, rattakambalasuttasikkāya ṭhapitakañcanakkhandho viya atirocati, iminā etesaṃ raññā bhavitabbaṃ, imameva gaṇhissāmī”ti cintesi. Haṃsarājāpi bahuṃ gocaraṃ caritvā jalakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā haṃsagaṇaparivuto cittakūṭameva agamāsi. Iminā niyāmeneva pañca divase gocaraṃ gaṇhi. Chaṭṭhe divase khemako kāḷaassavālamayaṃ daḷhaṃ mahārajjuṃ vaṭṭitvā yaṭṭhiyā pāsaṃ katvā “sve haṃsarājā imasmiṃ okāse [P 5.0359] otarissatī”ti tathato ñatvā antoudake yaṭṭhipāsaṃ oḍḍi.

Then the fowler's son thought, "This swan is not of fickle conduct; it is fitting to capture him." The next day, before the swans had descended to the lake, he went to that spot and, concealing himself in a vessel-trap not far away, watched through a hole. At that moment, the Great Being, escorted by ninety thousand swans, descended to the same spot as the day before. After settling within the boundary, he began to eat the rice. The fowler, peering through the hole in the trap, saw his magnificent form and thought, "This swan has a body the size of a cart's hub, is golden in color, and is adorned with three red stripes around his neck. Three stripes descend from his throat and pass across his chest, and three go down his back. He shines like a mass of gold placed in a carrier of red woolen cord. He must be the king of these swans. I will capture him alone." The King of Swans, after feeding extensively and frolicking in the water, surrounded by his flock, returned to Cittakūṭa. In this manner, he took food for five days. On the sixth day, Khemaka twisted a strong, thick rope made of black horsehair, fashioned a noose on a stick, and knowing for certain, "Tomorrow the King of Swans will land in this very spot," he set the stick-snare in the water.

Punadivase haṃsarājā otaranto pādaṃ pāse pavesantoyeva otari. Athassa pāso pādaṃ ayapaṭṭakena kaḍḍhanto viya ābandhitvā gaṇhi. So “chindissāmi na”nti vegaṃ janetvā kaḍḍhitvā pātesi. Paṭhamavāre suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ cammaṃ chijji, dutiyavāre kambalavaṇṇaṃ maṃsaṃ chijji, tatiyavāre nhāru chijji, catutthavāre pana “pādā chijjeyyuṃ, rañño pana hīnaṅgatā nāma ananucchavikā”ti na vāyāmaṃ akāsi, balavavedanā ca pavattiṃsu. So cintesi – “sacāhaṃ baddharavaṃ ravissāmi, ñātakā me ñatrastā hutvā gocaraṃ aggahetvā chātajjhattāva palāyantā dubbalattā samudde patissantī”ti. So vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā pāsavase vattetvā sāliṃ khādanto [V 5.0354] viya hutvā tesaṃ yāvadatthaṃ caritvā haṃsakīḷaṃ kīḷanakāle mahantena saddena baddharavaṃ ravi. Taṃ sutvā haṃsā maraṇabhayatajjitā vaggavaggā cittakūṭābhimukhā purimanayeneva pakkamiṃsu.

The next day, as the King of Swans was descending, his foot entered the snare as he alighted. Then the snare, as if pulling his foot with an iron band, bound and seized him. Thinking, "I will break it," he generated force and pulled. On the first attempt, his golden-colored skin was broken; on the second, his crimson-colored flesh was cut; on the third, his sinew was severed. But then, thinking, "My foot might be severed, and it is unbecoming for a king to be maimed," he made no further effort, and intense pain arose. He reflected: "If I cry out a captive's cry, my kinsmen, terrified, will flee without taking food and, weakened by hunger, will fall into the ocean." Enduring the pain, though caught in the snare, he appeared as if eating rice. After they had fed to their satisfaction, at the time of the swans' sport, he let out a loud captive's cry. Hearing this, the swans, terrified by the fear of death, fled in flocks toward Mount Cittakūṭa, just as before.

Sumukhopi [M 5.0382] heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva cintetvā vicinitvā tīsupi koṭṭhāsesu mahāsattaṃ adisvā “addhā tassevedaṃ bhayaṃ uppanna”nti nivattitvā āgato mahāsattaṃ pāsena baddhaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ dukkhāturaṃ paṅkapiṭṭhe nipannaṃ disvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ahaṃ mama jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā tumhe mocessāmī”ti vadanto otaritvā mahāsattaṃ assāsento paṅkapiṭṭhe nisīdi. Mahāsatto “navutihaṃsasahassesu maṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyantesu ayaṃ sumukho ekakova āgato, kiṃ nu kho luddaputtassa āgatakāle maṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyissati, udāhu no”ti vīmaṃsanavasena lohitamakkhito pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ olambantoyeva tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Sumukha also, having considered and investigated in the manner described before, and not seeing the Great Being in any of the three divisions of the flock, thought, 'Surely, this danger has befallen him,' and turned back. Upon returning, he saw the Great Being bound by the snare, smeared with blood, afflicted with pain, and lying on the muddy ground. He said, 'Do not fear, great king. I will give up my own life to free you.' So saying, he descended and, while comforting the Great Being, sat down on the muddy ground. The Great Being thought, 'While ninety thousand swans fled, abandoning me, this Sumukha has returned alone. Now, when the fowler's son arrives, will he abandon me and flee, or not?' For the purpose of testing him, while smeared with blood and hanging from the snare-stick, he spoke three verses:

89.

89.

“Ete haṃsā pakkamanti, vakkaṅgā bhayameritā;

Harittaca hemavaṇṇa, kāmaṃ sumukha pakkama.

“These swans fly away, with bent necks, driven by fear; O golden-skinned, golden-hued Sumukha, depart as you please.”

90.

90.

“Ohāya maṃ ñātigaṇā, ekaṃ pāsavasaṃ gataṃ;

Anapekkhamānā gacchanti, kiṃ eko avahīyasi.

“Having left me, my host of kinsmen, me alone, fallen into the power of a snare, depart without regard. Why do you alone remain behind?”

91.

91.

“Pateva patataṃ seṭṭha, natthi baddhe sahāyatā;

Mā anīghāya hāpesi, kāmaṃ sumukha pakkamā”ti.

“Fly away, O best of fliers! There is no companionship for the bound. Do not forsake the effort for your own freedom from affliction. O Sumukha, depart as you please.”

Tattha [P 5.0360] bhayameritāti bhayena eritā bhayaṭṭitā bhayacalitā. Tatiyapade “harī”tipi “hema”ntipi suvaṇṇasseva nāmaṃ. So ca harittacatāya hemavaṇṇo, tena taṃ evaṃ ālapati. Sumukhāti sundaramukha. Anapekkhamānāti tava ñātakā maṃ anolokentā nirālayā hutvā. Patevāti uppatāhiyeva. Mā anīghāyāti ito gantvā pattabbāya nidukkhabhāvāya vīriyaṃ mā hāpesi.

Therein, 'bhayameritā' means driven by fear, standing in fear, or shaken by fear. In the third line, both 'harī' and 'hema' are names for gold. He is golden-hued due to his golden skin; thus he addresses him so. 'Sumukha' means beautiful-faced. 'Anapekkhamānā' means your kinsmen, not looking back at me, being without concern. 'Pateva' means 'fly up indeed'. 'Mā anīghāya' means 'do not abandon the effort for the state of freedom from suffering which is to be attained by going from here'.

Taṃ sutvā sumukho “ayaṃ haṃsarājā mama piyamittabhāvaṃ na jānāti, anuppiyabhāṇī mittoti maṃ sallakkheti, sinehabhāvamassa dassessāmī”ti cintetvā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, Sumukha thought, 'This King of Swans does not know my dear friendship; he takes me for a friend who speaks only pleasantries. I will show him my affection,' and then spoke four verses:

92.

92.

“Nāhaṃ [V 5.0355] dukkhaparetopi, dhataraṭṭha tuvaṃ jahe;

Jīvitaṃ maraṇaṃ vā me, tayā saddhiṃ bhavissati.

“Even if I were overwhelmed by suffering, O Dhataraṭṭha, I would not abandon you; whether it be life or death for me, it shall be with you.”

93.

93.

“Nāhaṃ [M 5.0383] dukkhaparetopi, dhataraṭṭha tuvaṃ jahe;

Na maṃ anariyasaṃyutte, kamme yojetumarahasi.

“Even if I were overwhelmed by suffering, O Dhataraṭṭha, I would not abandon you. You should not involve me in an action connected with the ignoble.”

94.

94.

“Sakumāro sakhātyasmi, sacitte casmi te ṭhito;

Ñāto senāpatī tyāhaṃ, haṃsānaṃ pavaruttama.

“I am your companion from youth, your friend; I am established in your own mind; I am known to you as the general, most excellent among the geese.”

95.

95.

“Kathaṃ ahaṃ vikattissaṃ, ñātimajjhe ito gato;

Taṃ hitvā patataṃ seṭṭha, kiṃ te vakkhāmito gato;

Idha pāṇaṃ cajissāmi, nānariyaṃ kattumussahe”ti.

“How could I boast of myself, having gone from here among my kin? Having abandoned you, O best of fliers, what shall I tell them? Here I will give up my life; I cannot bring myself to do what is ignoble.”

Tattha nāhanti ahaṃ, mahārāja, kāyikacetasikena dukkhena phuṭṭhopi taṃ na jahāmi. Anariyasaṃyutteti mittadubbhīhi ahirikehi kattabbatāya anariyabhāvena saṃyutte. Kammeti taṃ jahitvā pakkamanakamme. Sakumāroti samānakumāro, ekadivaseneva paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā ekadivase aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā ekato vaḍḍhitakumāroti attho. Sakhātyasmīti ahaṃ te dakkhiṇakkhisamo piyasahāyo. Sacitteti tava sake citte ahaṃ ṭhito tava vase vattāmi, tayi jīvante jīvāmi, na jīvante na jīvāmīti attho. “Saṃcitte”tipi pāṭho, tava citte ahaṃ saṇṭhito suṭṭhu ṭhitoti attho. Ñātoti sabbahaṃsānaṃ antare paññāto. Vikattissanti “kuhiṃ haṃsarājā”ti pucchito ahaṃ kinti kathessāmi. Kiṃ te vakkhāmīti te tava pavattiṃ pucchante haṃsagaṇe kiṃ vakkhāmi.

Therein, ‘nāhaṃ’ means: I, O great king, do not abandon you, even when touched by physical and mental suffering. ‘Anariyasaṃyutte’ means associated with the ignoble, which is to say, connected with the ignoble nature of what should be done by the treacherous and the shameless. ‘Kamme’ refers to the act of abandoning you and departing. ‘Sakumāro’ means a contemporary youth, meaning one who took rebirth on the same day, broke the eggshell on the same day, and grew up together with you. ‘Sakhātyasmi’ means: I am your dear friend, like your right eye. ‘Sacitte’ means: I abide in your own mind, I am under your control; I live while you live, and I do not live when you do not live—this is the meaning. ‘Saṃcitte’ is also a reading, meaning: I am well and firmly established in your mind. ‘Ñāto’ means well-known among all the geese. ‘Vikattissaṃ’ means: if asked, ‘Where is the king of geese?’ what shall I say? ‘Kiṃ te vakkhāmi’ means: when the flock of geese asks about your news, what shall I tell them?

Evaṃ sumukhena catūhi gāthāhi sīhanāde nadite tassa guṇaṃ pakāsento mahāsatto āha –

Thus, when Sumukha had uttered a lion's roar with four verses, the Great Being, wishing to reveal his virtues, said:

96.

96.

“Eso hi dhammo sumukha, yaṃ tvaṃ ariyapathe ṭhito;

Yo bhattāraṃ sakhāraṃ maṃ, na pariccattumussahe.

“This, Sumukha, is indeed the nature of the wise, that you are established on the Noble Path; that you do not venture to abandon me, who am your master and friend.”

97.

97.

“Tañhi [V 5.0356][P 5.0361] me pekkhamānassa, bhayaṃ na tveva jāyati;

Adhigacchasi tvaṃ mayhaṃ, evaṃbhūtassa jīvita”nti.

“Indeed, as I behold you, no fear arises in me; you will secure my life, for me who am in such a state.”

Tattha eso dhammoti esa porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ sabhāvo. Bhattāraṃ sakhāraṃ manti sāmikañca sahāyañca maṃ. Bhayanti cittutrāso mayhaṃ na jāyati, cittakūṭapabbate haṃsagaṇamajjhe ṭhito viya homi. Mayhanti mama jīvitaṃ tvaṃ labhāpessasi.

Therein, ‘eso dhammo’ means: this is the nature of the ancient wise ones. ‘Bhattāraṃ sakhāraṃ maṃ’ means: me, your master and friend. ‘Bhayaṃ’ means: terror of the mind does not arise in me; I am as if standing in the midst of the flock of geese on Mount Cittakūṭa. ‘Mayhaṃ’ means: you will cause me to obtain my life.

Evaṃ [M 5.0384] tesaṃ kathentānaññeva luddaputto sarapariyante ṭhito haṃse tīhi khandhehi palāyante disvā “kiṃ nu kho”ti pāsaṭṭhānaṃ olokento bodhisattaṃ pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ olambantaṃ disvā sañjātasomanasso kacchaṃ daḷhaṃ bandhitvā muggaraṃ gahetvā kappuṭṭhānaggi viya avattharamāno paṇhiyā akkantakalale uparisīsena gantvā purato patante vegena upasaṅkami. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

As they were speaking thus, the hunter's son, standing at the edge of the lake, saw the geese fleeing in three groups. Wondering ‘What is this?’, he looked toward the place of the snare and spotted the Bodhisatta hanging from the snare-stick. Filled with joy, he tightly fastened his loincloth, took up his club, and like the fire at the end of a world-cycle, he swiftly approached, causing the mud he trod upon with his heels to fly up over his head and fall in front of him. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

98.

98.

“Iccevaṃ mantayantānaṃ, ariyānaṃ ariyavuttinaṃ;

Daṇḍamādāya nesādo, āpatī turito bhusaṃ.

“While those noble ones, of noble conduct, were thus consulting, the hunter, taking a club, rushed upon them with great haste.”

99.

99.

“Tamāpatantaṃ disvāna, sumukho atibrūhayi;

Aṭṭhāsi purato rañño, haṃso vissāsayaṃ byathaṃ.

“Seeing him approaching, Sumukha cried out; the goose stood before the king, comforting the distressed one.”

100.

100.

“Mā bhāyi patataṃ seṭṭha, na hi bhāyanti tādisā;

Ahaṃ yogaṃ payuñjissaṃ, yuttaṃ dhammūpasañhitaṃ;

Tena pariyāpadānena, khippaṃ pāsā pamokkhasī”ti.

“Fear not, O best of fliers, for such as you do not fear. I shall apply a suitable endeavor, connected with what is right; by that undertaking, you will quickly be freed from the snare.”

Tattha ariyavuttinanti ariyācāre vattamānānaṃ. Bhusanti daḷhaṃ balavaṃ. Atibrūhayīti anantaragāthāya āgataṃ “mā bhāyī”ti vacanaṃ vadanto atibrūhesi mahāsaddaṃ nicchāresi. Aṭṭhāsīti sace nesādo rājānaṃ paharissati, ahaṃ pahāraṃ sampaṭicchissāmīti jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā purato aṭṭhāsi. Vissāsayanti vissāsento assāsento. Byathanti byathitaṃ bhītaṃ rājānaṃ “mā bhāyī”ti iminā vacanena vissāsento. Tādisāti tumhādisā ñāṇavīriyasampannā. Yoganti ñāṇavīriyayogaṃ. Yuttanti anucchavikaṃ. Dhammūpasañhitanti kāraṇanissitaṃ. Tena pariyāpadānenāti tena mayā payuttena yogena parisuddhena. Pamokkhasīti muccissasi.

Therein, ‘ariyavuttinaṃ’ means ‘of those who abide in noble conduct’. ‘Bhusaṃ’ means ‘firmly, strongly’. ‘Atibrūhayī’ means, uttering the words ‘Do not fear’ which come in the following verse, he cried out loudly and emitted a great sound. ‘Aṭṭhāsi’ means, thinking, ‘If the hunter were to strike the king, I will receive the blow,’ he gave up his life and stood before him. ‘Vissāsayaṃ’ means ‘reassuring, comforting’. ‘Byathaṃ’ means ‘reassuring the distressed, frightened king with the words “Do not fear”’. ‘Tādisā’ means ‘those like you, endowed with wisdom and energy’. ‘Yogaṃ’ means ‘the application of wisdom and energy’. ‘Yuttaṃ’ means ‘appropriate’. ‘Dhammūpasañhitaṃ’ means ‘based on reason’. ‘Tena pariyāpadānena’ means ‘by that pure endeavor applied by me’. ‘Pamokkhasī’ means ‘you will be freed’.

Evaṃ [V 5.0357] sumukho mahāsattaṃ assāsetvā luddaputtassa santikaṃ gantvā madhuraṃ mānusiṃ vācaṃ nicchārento, “samma, tvaṃ konāmosī”ti [P 5.0362] pucchitvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇahaṃsarāja, ahaṃ khemako nāmā”ti vutte, “samma khemaka, ‘tayā oḍḍitavālapāse yo vā so vā haṃso baddho’ti saññaṃ mā kari, navutiyā haṃsasahassānaṃ pavaro dhataraṭṭhahaṃsarājā te pāse [M 5.0385] baddho, ñāṇasīlācārasampanno saṅgāhakapakkhe ṭhito, na taṃ māretuṃ yutto, ahaṃ tava iminā kattabbakiccaṃ karissāmi, ayampi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, ahampi tatheva, ahaṃ etassatthāya attano jīvitaṃ pariccajissāmi, sace tvaṃ etassa pattāni gaṇhitukāmosi, mama pattāni gaṇha, athopi cammamaṃsanhāruaṭṭhīnamaññataraṃ gaṇhitukāmosi, mameva sarīrato gaṇha, atha naṃ kīḷāhaṃsaṃ kātukāmosi, maññeva kara, jīvantameva vikkiṇitvā sace dhanaṃ uppādetukāmosi, maṃ jīvantameva vikkiṇitvā dhanaṃ uppādehi, mā etaṃ ñāṇādiguṇasaṃyuttaṃ haṃsarājānaṃ avadhi, sace hi naṃ vadhissasi, nirayādīhi na muccissasī”ti taṃ nirayādibhayena santajjetvā attano madhurakathaṃ gaṇhāpetvā puna bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ assāsento aṭṭhāsi. Nesādo tassa kathaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ tiracchānagato samāno manussehipi kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ evarūpaṃ mittadhammaṃ karoti, manussāpi evaṃ mittadhamme ṭhātuṃ na sakkonti, aho esa ñāṇasampanno madhurakatho dhammiko”ti sakalasarīraṃ pītisomanassaparipuṇṇaṃ katvā pahaṭṭhalomo daṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā sirasi añjaliṃ patiṭṭhapetvā sūriyaṃ namassanto viya sumukhassa guṇaṃ kittento aṭṭhāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus Sumukha, having comforted the Great Being, went to the hunter’s son and, uttering sweet human speech, asked, ‘Friend, what is your name?’ When the reply came, ‘O golden-colored king of geese, my name is Khemaka,’ Sumukha said, ‘Dear Khemaka, do not think that just any goose has been caught in the hair-snare you set. The one trapped in your snare is Dhataraṭṭha, the supreme king of geese, leader of ninety thousand geese. He is endowed with wisdom, virtue, and good conduct, and stands on the side of the fourfold hospitality. It is not right to kill him. I will perform for you whatever task was to be done with him. He is golden-colored, and so am I. I will give up my life for his sake. If you wish to take his feathers, take mine. Or if you desire his skin, flesh, sinews, or bones, take them from my body. If you wish to make him a pet goose, make me one instead. If you wish to sell him alive to gain wealth, sell me alive and gain your wealth. Do not kill this king of geese, who is endowed with wisdom and other virtues. Truly, if you kill him, you will not escape from hell and other woeful states.’ Having thus frightened him with the fear of hell and other states, and having made him accept his sweet words, Sumukha returned to the Bodhisatta and stood there comforting him. The hunter, hearing his words, thought, ‘This creature, although an animal, performs such an act of friendship as even humans could not do. Even humans are not able to stand so firm in friendship. Oh, how wise, sweet-spoken, and righteous he is!’ His entire body filled with joy and happiness, his hair standing on end, he threw down his club, placed his hands together in reverence on his head, and stood there praising Sumukha’s virtues as if worshiping the sun. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

101.

101.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, sumukhassa subhāsitaṃ;

Pahaṭṭhalomo nesādo, añjalissa paṇāmayi.

“Hearing that well-spoken speech of Sumukha, the hunter, with hair standing on end, raised his joined hands in homage to him.”

102.

102.

“Na me sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā, bhāsanto mānusiṃ dijo;

Ariyaṃ bruvāno vakkaṅgo, cajanto mānusiṃ giraṃ.

“Never have I heard or seen a bird speaking in a human manner, speaking nobly, crooked-necked, uttering human speech.”

103.

103.

“Kiṃ nu tāyaṃ dijo hoti, mutto baddhaṃ upāsasi;

Ohāya sakuṇā yanti, kiṃ eko avahīyasī”ti.

“What is this bird to you, that though free, you attend upon the one who is bound? The other birds have gone, having abandoned him; why are you alone left behind?”

Tattha [P 5.0363] añjalissa paṇāmayīti añjaliṃ assa upanāmayi, “na me”ti gāthāyassa thutiṃ karoti. Tattha mānusinti manussavācaṃ. Ariyanti sundaraṃ niddosaṃ. Cajantoti vissajjento. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma, tvaṃ dijo samāno ajja mayā saddhiṃ mānusiṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto niddosaṃ [V 5.0358] bruvāno mānusiṃ giraṃ cajanto paccakkhato diṭṭho, ito pubbe pana idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayā [M 5.0386] neva sutaṃ na diṭṭhanti. Kiṃ nu tāyanti yaṃ etaṃ tvaṃ upāsasi, kiṃ nu te ayaṃ hoti.

Therein, 'añjalissa paṇāmayīti' means he brought his cupped hands in reverence to him. With the verse beginning 'na me,' he offers praise. Therein, 'mānusinti' means human speech. 'Ariyanti' means beautiful, faultless. 'Cajantoti' means uttering. This is what was said: 'Friend, being a twice-born, today you are seen by me directly, speaking human speech with me, speaking faultlessly, uttering a human voice. Before this, such a wonder was never heard nor seen by me. What is that which you attend upon? What is this one to you?'

Evaṃ tuṭṭhacittena nesādena puṭṭho sumukho “ayaṃ muduko jāto, idānissa bhiyyosomattāya mudubhāvatthaṃ mama guṇaṃ dassesāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

Thus questioned by the fowler, whose mind was delighted, Sumukha thought, 'This fowler has become gentle. Now, for the sake of making him even more gentle, I shall show him my good qualities,' and spoke:

104.

104.

“Rājā me so dijāmitta, senāpaccassa kārayiṃ;

Tamāpade pariccatuṃ, nussahe vihagādhipaṃ.

“He is my king, O hunter friend; he made me his general. I do not venture to abandon that lord of birds in his misfortune.”

105.

105.

“Mahāgaṇāya bhattā me, mā eko byasanaṃ agā;

Tathā taṃ samma nesāda, bhattāyaṃ abhito rame”ti.

“He is my master of a great flock; may he not go to ruin alone. Therefore, friend hunter, I delight in being near this master.”

Tattha nussaheti na samatthomhi. Mahāgaṇāyāti mahato haṃsagaṇassa. Mā ekoti mādise sevake vijjamāne mā ekako byasanaṃ agā. Tathā tanti yathā ahaṃ vadāmi, tatheva taṃ. Sammāti vayassa. Bhattāyaṃ abhito rameti bhattā ayaṃ mama, ahamassa abhito rame santike ramāmi na ukkaṇṭhāmīti.

Herein, 'nussahe' means 'I am not able.' 'Mahāgaṇāya' means 'of a great flock of geese.' 'Mā eko' means 'while a servant such as I exists, may he not go to ruin alone.' 'Tathā taṃ' means 'as I say, so it is for you.' 'Samma' means 'friend.' 'Bhattāyaṃ abhito rame' means 'this is my master; I delight in being near him, I enjoy his presence and do not feel discontent.'

Nesādo taṃ tassa dhammanissitaṃ madhurakathaṃ sutvā somanassappatto pahaṭṭhalomo “sacāhaṃ etaṃ sīlādiguṇasaṃyuttaṃ haṃsarājānaṃ vadhissāmi, catūhi apāyehi na muccissāmi, rājā maṃ yadicchati, taṃ karotu, ahametaṃ sumukhassa dāyaṃ katvā vissajjessāmī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Hearing his sweet words founded on the Dhamma, the fowler, filled with joy and with his hair standing on end, thought: 'If I were to kill this goose-king who is endowed with qualities such as virtue, I would not be freed from the four woeful states. Let the king do with me as he wishes. I shall release this one as a gift to Sumukha.' Thinking thus, he spoke a verse:

106.

106.

“Ariyavattasi vakkaṅga, yo piṇḍamapacāyasi;

Cajāmi te taṃ bhattāraṃ, gacchathūbho yathāsukha”nti.

“You are of noble conduct, O crooked-limbed one, you who honor your master. I release that master to you; may you both go as you please.”

Tattha ariyavattasīti mittadhammarakkhaṇasaṅkhātena ācāraariyānaṃ vattena samannāgatosi. Piṇḍamapacāyasīti bhattu santikā laddhaṃ piṇḍaṃ senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ pūjesi. Gacchathūbhoti dvepi janā assumukhe ñātisaṅghe hāsayamānā yathāsukhaṃ gacchathāti.

Herein, 'ariyavattasi' means 'you are endowed with the conduct of the noble, which is characterized by the protection of the principle of friendship.' 'Piṇḍamapacāyasi' means 'you honored the support received from your master, that is, the position of general.' 'Gacchathūbho' means 'may both of you go as you please, causing your tear-faced kinsfolk to rejoice.'

Evaṃ [V 5.0359][P 5.0364] vatvā nesādo muducittena mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yaṭṭhiṃ onāmetvā paṅkapiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā pāsayaṭṭhiyā mocetvā taṃ ukkhipitvā sarato nīharitvā taruṇadabbatiṇapiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā pāde baddhapāsaṃ [M 5.0387] saṇikaṃ mocetvā mahāsatte balavasinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā mettacittena udakaṃ ādāya lohitaṃ dhovitvā punappunaṃ parimajji, athassa mettānubhāvena sirāya sirā, maṃsena maṃsaṃ, cammena cammaṃ ghaṭitaṃ, pādo pākatiko ahosi, itarena nibbiseso. Bodhisatto sukhappatto hutvā pakatibhāvena nisīdi. Sumukho attānaṃ nissāya rañño sukhitabhāvaṃ disvā sañjātasomanasso cintesi – “iminā amhākaṃ mahāupakāro kato, amhehi etassa kato upakāro nāma natthi, sace esa rājarājamahāmattānaṃ atthāya amhe gaṇhi, tesaṃ santikaṃ netvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissati, sace attano atthāya gaṇhi, amhe vikkiṇitvā dhanaṃ labhissateva, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti. Atha naṃ upakāraṃ kātukāmatāya pucchanto āha –

Having spoken thus, the fowler, with a gentle mind, approached the Great Being, lowered his stick, had him sit on the muddy ground, released him from the snare-stick, lifted him up, and brought him out of the lake. He had him sit on a bed of young dabba grass, slowly untied the snare bound to his foot, and established a strong affection for the Great Being. With a mind of loving-kindness, he took water, washed away the blood, and stroked the wound again and again. Then, through the power of his loving-kindness, vein was joined to vein, flesh to flesh, and skin to skin; the foot became normal, indistinguishable from the other. The Bodhisatta, having become comfortable, sat in his natural manner. Sumukha, seeing that the king was well on his account, was filled with joy and thought: 'This man has done us a great service, but we have done no service for him. If he captured us for the king and the king's great ministers, he could take us to them and receive much wealth. If he captured us for himself, he could sell us and still obtain wealth. I shall ask him first.' Then, wishing to do him a service in return, he asked:

107.

107.

“Sace attappayogena, ohito haṃsapakkhinaṃ;

Paṭiggaṇhāma te samma, etaṃ abhayadakkhiṇaṃ.

“If by your own effort this snare was set for the geese and other birds, we accept from you, friend, this gift of safety.”

108.

108.

“No ce attappayogena, ohito haṃsapakkhinaṃ;

Anissaro muñcamamhe, theyyaṃ kayirāsi luddakā”ti.

“But if not by your own effort the snare was set for the geese and other birds, then in releasing us without authority, you would be committing theft, O hunter.”

Tattha saceti, samma nesāda, sace tayā attano payogena attano atthāya haṃsānañceva sesapakkhīnañca pāso ohito. Anissaroti anissaro hutvā amhe muñcanto yenāsi āṇatto, tassasantakaṃ gaṇhanto theyyaṃ kayirāsi.

Herein, 'sace' means: Friend hunter, if by your own effort and for your own sake you have set this snare for the geese and other birds. 'Anissaro' means: being without authority, in releasing us you would be committing theft, taking what belongs to him by whom you were commanded.

Taṃ sutvā nesādo “nāhaṃ tumhe attano atthāya gaṇhiṃ, bārāṇasiraññā pana saṃyamena gaṇhāpitomhī”ti vatvā deviyā diṭṭhasupinakālato paṭṭhāya yāva raññā tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā, “samma khemaka, ekaṃ vā dve vā haṃse gaṇhituṃ vāyama, mahantaṃ te yasaṃ dassāmī”ti vatvā paribbayaṃ datvā uyyojitabhāvo, tāva sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā sumukho “iminā nesādena attano jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā amhe vissajjentena [P 5.0365] dukkaraṃ kataṃ, sace mayaṃ ito cittakūṭaṃ gamissāma, neva dhataraṭṭharañño paññānubhāvo, na mayhaṃ mittadhammo pākaṭo bhavissati, na luddaputto mahantaṃ yasaṃ lacchati, na rājā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhahissati, na deviyā manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti cintetvā[M 5.0388], “samma, evaṃ sante amhe vissajjetuṃ na [V 5.0360] labhasi, rañño no dassehi, so amhe yathāruciṃ karissatī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the fowler said, 'I did not capture you for my own sake; rather, I was caused to capture you by the command of the King of Bārāṇasī.' Then he recounted the entire story, from the time the queen had her dream up to when the king, having heard of their arrival, said, 'Friend Khemaka, endeavor to catch one or two geese, and I shall grant you great wealth,' and sent him off after giving him provisions. Hearing this, Sumukha thought: 'This fowler has done a difficult thing by releasing us without regard for his own life. If we go from here to Cittakūṭa, then neither will the power of King Dhataraṭṭha’s wisdom become manifest, nor will my own loyalty as a friend become evident, nor will this hunter attain great wealth, nor will the king become established in the five precepts, nor will the queen’s wish be fulfilled.' Thinking thus, he said, 'Friend, that being the case, you are not at liberty to release us. Show us to the king; he will do with us as he pleases.' To make this meaning clear, he spoke a verse:

109.

109.

“Yassa tvaṃ bhatako rañño, kāmaṃ tasseva pāpaya;

Tattha saṃyamano rājā, yathābhiññaṃ karissatī”ti.

“To that very king whose servant you are, by all means lead us. There King Samyama will act according to his pleasure.”

Tattha tassevāti tasseva santikaṃ nehi. Tatthāti tasmiṃ rājanivesane. Yathābhiññanti yathādhippāyaṃ yathāruciṃ.

Herein, 'tasseva' means 'lead us to his very presence.' 'Tattha' means 'in that royal residence.' 'Yathābhiññaṃ' means 'according to his intention, according to his pleasure.'

Taṃ sutvā nesādo “mā vo bhaddante rājadassanaṃ ruccittha, rājāno nāma sappaṭibhayā, kīḷāhaṃse vā vo kareyyuṃ māreyyuṃ vā”ti āha. Atha naṃ sumukho, “samma luddaka mā amhākaṃ cintayi, ahaṃ tādisassa kakkhaḷassa dhammakathāya maddavaṃ janesiṃ, rañño kiṃ na janessāmi, rājāno hi paṇḍitā subhāsitadubbhāsitaññu, khippaṃ no rañño santikaṃ nehi, nayanto ca mā bandhanena nayi, pupphapañjare pana nisīdāpetvā nehi, pupphapañjaraṃ karonto dhataraṭṭhassa mahantaṃ setapadumasañchannaṃ, mama khuddakaṃ rattapadumasañchannaṃ katvā dhataraṭṭhaṃ purato, mamaṃ pacchato nīcataraṃ katvā ādāya khippaṃ netvā rañño dassehī”ti āha. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sumukho rājānaṃ disvā mama mahantaṃ yasaṃ dātukāmo bhavissatī”ti sañjātasomanasso mudūhi latāhi pañjare katvā padumehi chādetvā vuttanayeneva te gahetvā agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Hearing that, the hunter said, 'Good sirs, do not wish for an audience with the king. Kings are indeed fearsome; they might make you into play-geese or even kill you.' Then Sumukha said, 'Friend hunter, do not be concerned about us. I was able to bring about gentleness in such a harsh person as you with a talk on the Dhamma; why should I not be able to do so for the king? For kings are wise; they know what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken. Take us quickly to the king’s presence, but do not lead us bound. Rather, have us sit in flower-cages and carry us. When making the flower-cages, make a large one for Dhataraṭṭha, covered with white lotuses, and a small one for me, covered with red lotuses. Having placed Dhataraṭṭha in front and me behind and lower, take us quickly and show us to the king.' Hearing his words, the hunter, filled with joy, thought, 'Upon seeing the king, Sumukha will wish to have great wealth bestowed upon me.' He made cages from soft vines, covered them with lotuses, and taking the two geese in the manner described, he departed. The Teacher, clarifying this matter, said:

110.

110.

“Iccevaṃ vutto nesādo, hemavaṇṇe harittace;

Ubho hatthehi saṅgayha, pañjare ajjhavodahi.

“Thus addressed, the hunter, seizing with his hands both the golden-hued, golden-skinned geese, placed them inside the cage.”

111.

111.

“Te [P 5.0366] pañjaragate pakkhī, ubho bhassaravaṇṇine;

Sumukhaṃ dhataraṭṭhañca, luddo ādāya pakkamī”ti.

“The hunter, taking Sumukha and Dhataraṭṭha, those two birds of radiant hue who were in the cage, departed.”

Tattha ajjhavodahīti odahi ṭhapesi. Bhassaravaṇṇineti pabhāsampannavaṇṇe.

Therein, 'ajjhavodahi' means he placed or set down. 'Bhassaravaṇṇine' means of an appearance endowed with radiance.

Evaṃ [M 5.0389] luddassa te ādāya pakkamanakāle dhataraṭṭho pākahaṃsarājadhītaraṃ attano bhariyaṃ saritvā sumukhaṃ āmantetvā kilesavasena vilapi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, as that hunter was taking them and departing, Dhataraṭṭha, remembering his queen, the daughter of the Pāka goose-king, addressed Sumukha and lamented due to the power of defilement. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

112.

112.

“Harīyamāno [V 5.0361] dhataraṭṭho, sumukhaṃ etadabravi;

Bāḷhaṃ bhāyāmi sumukha, sāmāya lakkhaṇūruyā;

Asmākaṃ vadhamaññāya, athattānaṃ vadhissati.

Being carried away, Dhataraṭṭha said this to Sumukha: 'I greatly fear, Sumukha, for Sāmā, she with thighs endowed with auspicious marks; thinking we are dead, she will surely slay herself.'

113.

113.

“Pākahaṃsā ca sumukha, suhemā hemasuttacā;

Koñcī samuddatīreva, kapaṇā nūna rucchatī”ti.

'O Sumukha, the queen named Suhemā, daughter of the Pāka goose-king, whose skin is like a golden thread; like a female crane on the seashore, she will surely weep piteously in her loneliness.'

Tattha bhāyāmīti maraṇato bhāyāmi. Sāmāyāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇāya. Lakkhaṇūruyāti lakkhaṇasampannaūruyā. Vacamaññāyāti vadhaṃ jānitvā “mama piyasāmiko mārito”ti saññī hutvā. Vadhissatīti kiṃ me piyasāmike mate jīvitenāti marissati. Pākahaṃsāti pākahaṃsarājadhītā. Suhemāti evaṃnāmikā. Hemasuttacāti hemasadisasundaratacā. Rucchatīti yathā loṇisaṅkhātaṃ samuddaṃ otaritvā mate patimhi koñcī sakuṇikā kapaṇā rodati, evaṃ nūna sā rodissatīti.

Therein, 'I fear' means I fear death. 'Sāmāya' means of golden color. 'Lakkhaṇūruyā' means having thighs endowed with auspicious marks. 'Vadhamaññāya' means, having known of the slaughter, becoming aware, ‘My beloved husband has been slain.’ 'She will slay herself' means, thinking, ‘What use is life to me when my beloved husband is dead?’ she will die. 'Pākahaṃsā' means daughter of the Pāka goose-king. 'Suhemā' means one so-named. 'Hemasuttacā' means having skin as beautiful as gold. 'Rucchatī' means: just as a little curlew bird, having gone down to the sea known as salty, weeps pitifully for her dead mate, so surely will she weep.

Taṃ sutvā sumukho “ayaṃ haṃsarājā aññe ovadituṃ yutto mātugāmaṃ nissāya kilesavasena vilapati, udakassa ādittakālo viya vatiyā uṭṭhāya kedārakhādanakālo viya ca jāto, yaṃnūnāhaṃ attano balena mātugāmassa dosaṃ pakāsetvā etaṃ saññāpeyya”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Having heard the goose-king's lament, Sumukha thought, 'This goose-king, who is fit to advise others, laments on account of a woman due to defilement. It has become like water catching fire, or like the fence rising up to eat the crops it should protect. I shall show him the faults of women by my own power and make him understand.' Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

114.

114.

“Evaṃ mahanto lokassa, appameyyo mahāgaṇī;

Ekitthimanusoceyya, nayidaṃ paññavatāmiva.

“Though so great in the world, immeasurable in virtue, and the leader of a vast following; that you should grieve for a single woman—this does not seem like the way of the wise.”

115.

115.

“Vātova gandhamādeti, ubhayaṃ chekapāpakaṃ;

Bālo āmakapakkaṃva, lolo andhova āmisaṃ.

“Just as the wind carries away both pleasant and foul scents; like a fool who eats both unripe and ripe fruit; or like a greedy blind man who eats any food; so do women resort to any man, whether low or noble.”

116.

116.

“Avinicchayaññu [P 5.0367] atthesu, mandova paṭibhāsi maṃ;

Kiccākiccaṃ na jānāsi, sampatto kālapariyāyaṃ.

“You appear to me as one dull-witted, unable to discern what is right and wrong; having reached the turn of death, you do not know what should and should not be done.”

117.

117.

“Aḍḍhummatto [M 5.0390] udīresi, yo seyyā maññasitthiyo;

Bahusādhāraṇā hetā, soṇḍānaṃva surāgharaṃ.

“You speak like one half-mad with drink, you who consider women superior; for they are common to many, like a tavern for drunkards.”

118.

118.

“Māyā [V 5.0362] cetā marīcī ca, sokā rogā cupaddavā;

Kharā ca bandhanā cetā, maccupāsā guhāsayā;

Tāsu yo vissase poso, so naresu narādhamo”ti.

“They are like an illusion or a mirage, causes of sorrow, disease, and calamity; they are harsh, they are bonds, they are the snares of death lurking in the cave of the body. Whatever man trusts in them, he is the lowest among men.”

Tattha mahantoti mahanto samāno. Lokassāti haṃsalokassa. Appameyyoti guṇehi pametuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Mahāgaṇīti mahantena gaṇena samannāgato gaṇasatthā. Ekitthinti yaṃ evarūpo bhavaṃ ekaṃ itthiṃ anusoceyya, idaṃ anusocanaṃ na paññavataṃ iva, tenāhaṃ ajja taṃ bāloti maññāmīti adhippāyenevamāha.

Therein, 'mahanto' means being great. 'Lokassa' means of the world of geese. 'Appameyyo' means one who cannot be measured by his virtues. 'Mahāgaṇī' means endowed with a great following, a teacher of a group. Regarding 'ekitthiṃ': 'That such a one as your majesty should grieve for a single woman—this grieving is not like that of the wise. For that reason, I consider you a fool today.' He spoke thus with this intention.

Ādetīti gaṇhāti. Chekapāpakanti sundarāsundaraṃ. Āmakapakkati āmakañca pakkañca. Loloti rasalolo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, yathā nāma vāto padumasarādīni paharitvā sugandhampi saṅkāraṭṭhānādīni paharitvā duggandhampīti ubhayaṃ chekapāpakaṃ gandhaṃ ādiyati, yathā ca bālo kumārako ambajambūnaṃ heṭṭhā nisinno hatthaṃ pasāretvā patitapatitaṃ āmakampi pakkampi phalaṃ gahetvā khādati, yathā ca rasalolo andho bhatte upanīte yaṃkiñci samakkhikampi nimmakkhikampi āmisaṃ ādiyati, evaṃ itthiyo nāma kilesavasena aḍḍhampi duggatampi kulīnampi akulīnampi abhirūpampi virūpampi gaṇhanti bhajanti, tādisānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ itthīnaṃ kiṃkāraṇā vippalapasi, mahārājāti.

'Ādeti' means takes. 'Chekapāpakaṃ' means beautiful and unbeautiful. 'Āmakapakkaṃ' means both unripe and ripe. 'Lolo' means greedy for tastes. This is what was said: Great king, just as the wind, blowing over lotus ponds and the like, takes up pleasant smells, and blowing over garbage heaps and the like, takes up foul smells—thus taking both pleasant and foul; and just as a foolish boy, sitting under a mango or rose-apple tree, stretches out his hand and, taking whatever has fallen, whether unripe or ripe, eats it; and just as a blind man greedy for tastes, when food is brought, takes any meat, whether with flies or without; even so, women, due to defilement, take up with and associate with the rich and the poor, the high-born and the low-born, the beautiful and the ugly. For what reason do you lament, great king, for such women of evil nature?

Atthesūti kāraṇākāraṇesu. Mandoti andhabālo. Paṭibhāsi manti mama upaṭṭhāsi. Kālapariyāyanti evarūpaṃ maraṇakālaṃ patto “imasmiṃ kāle idaṃ kattabbaṃ, idaṃ nakattabbaṃ, idaṃ vattabbaṃ, idaṃ na vattabba”nti na jānāsi devāti. Aḍḍhummattoti aḍḍhummattako maññe hutvā. Udīresīti yathā suraṃ pivitvā nātimatto puriso yaṃ vā taṃ vā palapati, evaṃ palapasīti attho. Seyyāti varā uttamā.

'Atthesu' means in causes and non-causes. 'Mando' means a blind fool. 'Paṭibhāsi maṃ' means you appear to me. Regarding 'kālapariyāyaṃ': having reached such a time of death, you do not know, O king, 'At this time this should be done, this should not be done; this should be said, this should not be said.' 'Aḍḍhummatto' means as if having become half-mad. 'Udīresi' means: just as a man who has drunk liquor, not being excessively intoxicated, babbles this or that, so you babble—this is the meaning. 'Seyyā' means excellent, supreme.

“Māyā cā”tiādīsu, deva, itthiyo nāmetā vañcanaṭṭhena māyā, agayhupagaṭṭhena marīcī, sokādīnaṃ paccayattā sokā, rogā, anekappakārā upaddavā, kodhādīhi thaddhabhāveneva kharā. Tā hi nissāya [M 5.0391] andubandhanādīhi bandhanato bandhanā cetā, itthiyo nāma sarīraguhāsayavaseneva maccu nāma etā, devāti. “Kāmahetu, kāmanidānaṃ, kāmādhikaraṇaṃ, kāmānameva hetu rājāno coraṃ gahetvā”ti (ma. ni. 1.168-169) suttenapesa attho dīpetabbo.

In the verses beginning 'Māyā ca': O king, these women are 'māyā' in the sense of deception; 'marīcī' in the sense of being ungraspable; because they are a condition for sorrow and so on, they are 'sorrows', 'diseases', and 'calamities' of many kinds; and 'kharā' because of their stiffness due to anger and so on. On their account, one is bound by fetters and shackles, thus they are 'bonds'. O king, these women are called 'death' because they dwell in the cave of the body. This meaning should also be illustrated by the sutta passage: 'For the sake of sensual desire, because of sensual desire, grounded in sensual desire, for the sake of sensual desire alone, kings... seize a thief.'

Tato [V 5.0363][P 5.0368] dhataraṭṭho mātugāme paṭibaddhacittatāya “tvaṃ mātugāmassa guṇaṃ na jānāsi, paṇḍitā eva etaṃ jānanti, na hetā garahitabbā”ti dīpento āha –

Then Dhataraṭṭha, because his mind was attached to women, said: 'You do not know the virtues of women; only the wise know them. They should not be blamed.' Wishing to show the virtues of women, he said:

119.

119.

“Yaṃ vuddhehi upaññātaṃ, ko taṃ ninditumarahati;

Mahābhūtitthiyo nāma, lokasmiṃ udapajjisuṃ.

“That which is recognized by the elders, who is fit to censure it? Women, indeed, are beings of great importance who arose at the beginning of the world.”

120.

120.

“Khiḍḍā paṇihitā tyāsu, rati tyāsu patiṭṭhitā;

Bījāni tyāsu rūhanti, yadidaṃ sattā pajāyare;

Tāsu ko nibbide poso, pāṇamāsajja pāṇibhi.

“In them is play placed, in them is delight established; in them the seeds of great beings grow, and from them all beings are born. What man, having joined his life with theirs, could feel disgust for them?”

121.

121.

“Tvameva nañño sumukha, thīnaṃ atthesu yuñjasi;

Tassa tyajja bhaye jāte, bhīte na jāyate mati.

“You alone, Sumukha, and no other, occupy yourself with these matters concerning women. For you, now that fear has arisen, being afraid, your wisdom does not manifest.”

122.

122.

“Sabbo hi saṃsayaṃ patto, bhayaṃ bhīrū titikkhati;

Paṇḍitā ca mahantāno, atthe yuñjanti duyyuje.

“Indeed, when all are fallen into uncertainty, the wise man endures the fear of death; only the wise and the great exert themselves in a matter that is difficult to undertake.”

123.

123.

“Etadatthāya rājāno, sūramicchanti mantinaṃ;

Paṭibāhati yaṃ sūro, āpadaṃ attapariyāyaṃ.

“It is for this purpose that kings desire a heroic and wise counselor; so that the hero may ward off calamity and act for one's self-protection.”

124.

124.

“Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase;

Tathā hi vaṇṇo pattānaṃ, phalaṃ veḷuṃva taṃ vadhi.

“May the king’s cooks in the kitchen not carve us up today; let the golden color of our feathers not be our ruin, as its own fruit kills the bamboo.”

125.

125.

“Muttopi na icchi uḍḍetuṃ, sayaṃ bandhaṃ upāgami;

Sopajja saṃsayaṃ patto, atthaṃ gaṇhāhi mā mukha”nti.

“Though freed from the snare, you did not wish to fly away; you yourself entered into bondage. Today, when I have reached uncertainty about my life, you should work for my welfare; do not just open your mouth to blame women.”

Tattha yanti yaṃ mātugāmasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu paññāvuddhehi ñātaṃ, tesameva pākaṭaṃ, na bālānaṃ. Mahābhūtāti mahāguṇā mahānisaṃsā. Udapajjisunti paṭhamakappikakāle [M 5.0392] itthiliṅgasseva paṭhamaṃ pātubhūtattā paṭhamaṃ nibbattāti attho. Tyāsūti sumukha tāsu itthīsu kāyavacīkhiḍḍā ca paṇihitā ohitā ṭhapitā, kāmaguṇarati ca patiṭṭhitā. Bījānīti buddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakacakkavattiādibījāni [V 5.0364] tāsu ruhanti. Yadidanti ye ete sabbepi sattā. Pajāyareti sabbe tāsaññeva kucchimhi saṃvaddhāti dīpeti. Nibbideti nibbindeyya. Pāṇamāsajja pāṇibhīti attano pāṇehipi tāsaṃ pāṇaṃ āsādetvā attano jīvitaṃ cajantopi tā labhitvā ko nibbindeyyāti attho.

Therein, 'yaṃ' means: that subject called 'woman' is known by the wise and mature; it is manifest to them alone, not to fools. 'Mahābhūti' means of great virtue, of great benefit. 'Udapajjisuṃ' means: because in the primordial eon the female gender was the first to appear, she was the first to be born—this is the meaning. 'Tyāsu' means: in those women, bodily and verbal play is applied, set down, and established, and delight in sensual qualities is established. 'Bījāni' means the seeds of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and so on, grow in them. 'Yadidaṃ' means all these beings. 'Pajāyare' shows that all are nurtured in their womb. 'Nibbideti' means one would feel disgust. 'Pāṇamāsajja pāṇibhi' means: even while giving up one's own life for them, having obtained them, who would feel disgust? This is the meaning.

Naññoti na añño, sumukha, mayā cittakūṭatale haṃsagaṇamajjhe nisinnena taṃ adisvā “kahaṃ nu sumukho”ti vutte “esa mātugāmaṃ gahetvā kañcanaguhāyaṃ uttamaratiṃ anubhotī”ti vadanti, evaṃ tvameva thīnaṃ atthesu yuñjasi yuttapayutto hosi, na [P 5.0369] aññoti attho. Tassa tyajjāti tassa te ajja maraṇabhaye jāte iminā bhītena maraṇabhayena bhīto maññe, ayaṃ mātugāmassa dosadassane nipuṇā mati jāyateti adhippāyenevamāha.

‘Nañño’ means ‘not another’, Sumukha. When I was sitting on the pinnacle of Cittakūṭa among the flock of swans and did not see you, and when I asked, ‘Where is Sumukha?’, they said, ‘He has taken a woman and is enjoying supreme pleasure in the golden cave.’ Thus, you alone are engaged in women’s affairs, properly devoted; ‘not another’ is the meaning. ‘Tassa tyajjā’ means: ‘For you today, since the fear of death has arisen, terrified by this fear of death, I think this keen understanding regarding the faults of women arises’—with this intention he spoke thus.

Sabbo hīti yo hi koci. Saṃsayaṃ pattoti jīvitasaṃsayappatto. Bhīrūti bhīrū hutvāpi bhayaṃ adhivāseti. Mahantānoti ye pana paṇḍitā ca honti mahante ca ṭhāne ṭhitā mahantāno, te duyyuje atthe yuñjanti ghaṭenti vāyamanti, tasmā “mā bhāyi, dhīro hohī”ti taṃ ussāhento evamāha. Āpadanti sāmino āgataṃ āpadaṃ esa sūro paṭibāhati, etadatthāya sūraṃ mantinaṃ icchanti. Attapariyāyanti attano parittāṇampi ca kātuṃ sakkotīti adhippāyo.

‘Sabbo hi’ means ‘whoever indeed’. ‘Saṃsayaṃ patto’ means ‘having reached uncertainty of life’. ‘Bhīrū’ means ‘even being fearful, one endures fear’. ‘Mahantāno’ refers to those who are wise and stand in great positions, the great ones; they engage in, arrange, or strive in difficult matters. Therefore, encouraging him, saying, ‘Do not fear, be courageous,’ he spoke thus. ‘Āpadaṃ’ means ‘this hero averts the danger that has come to the lord’; for this purpose, they desire a heroic advisor. ‘Attapariyāyaṃ’ implies the intention that ‘one is capable of even protecting oneself’.

Vikantiṃsūti chindiṃsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma sumukha, tvaṃ mayā attano anantare ṭhāne ṭhapito, tasmā yathā ajja rañño sūdā amhe maṃsatthāya na vikantiṃsu, tathā karohi, tādiso hi amhākaṃ pattavaṇṇo. Taṃ vadhīti svāyaṃ vaṇṇo yathā nāma veḷuṃ nissāya jātaṃ phalaṃ veḷumeva vadhati, tathā mā taṃ vadhi, tañca mañca mā vadhīti adhippāyenevamāha.

‘Vikantiṃsu’ means ‘they cut up’. This was said: ‘Good Sumukha, you have been placed by me in the position immediately after my own. Therefore, act so that the king’s cooks do not cut us up for meat today; such is indeed the color of our feathers.’ ‘Taṃ vadhi’ means: ‘Just as a fruit born dependent on a bamboo destroys the bamboo itself, so may this color not destroy you, and may it not destroy both you and me’—with this intention he spoke thus.

Muttopīti [M 5.0393] yathāsukhaṃ cittakūṭapabbataṃ gacchāti evaṃ luddaputtena mayā saddhiṃ mutto vissajjito samānopi uḍḍituṃ na icchi. Sayanti rājānaṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā sayameva bandhaṃ upagatoti evamidaṃ amhākaṃ bhayaṃ taṃ nissāya āgataṃ. Sopajjāti sopi ajja jīvitasaṃsayaṃ patto. Atthaṃ gaṇhāhi mā mukhanti idāni amhākaṃ muñcanakāraṇaṃ gaṇha, yathā muccāma, tathā vāyama, “vātova gandhamādetī”tiādīni vadanto itthigarahatthāya mukhaṃ mā pasārayi.

‘Muttopi’ means: ‘Go to Mount Cittakūṭa at your pleasure’—thus, even though released by the hunter, he did not wish to fly away. ‘Sayaṃ’ means: ‘Desiring to see the king, he himself entered into bondage’—thus, this fear of ours has come upon us because of him. ‘Sopajja’ means: ‘He too has today reached uncertainty about his life’. ‘Atthaṃ gaṇhāhi mā mukhaṃ’ means: ‘Now seize the means for our release, strive so that we may be freed; do not keep your mouth open for the sake of disparaging women, saying words like, “The wind carries away the fragrance,” and so forth.’

Evaṃ [V 5.0365] mahāsatto mātugāmaṃ vaṇṇetvā sumukhaṃ appaṭibhāṇaṃ katvā tassa anattamanabhāvaṃ viditvā idāni naṃ paggaṇhanto gāthamāha –

Thus, the Great Being, having praised women and rendered Sumukha speechless, and understanding his displeasure, now, wishing to encourage him, spoke this verse:

126.

126.

“So taṃ yogaṃ payuñjassu, yuttaṃ dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ;

Tava pariyāpadānena, mama pāṇesanaṃ carā”ti.

“So apply that effort which is suitable and connected with the truth; by your pure striving, seek my life.”

Tattha soti, samma sumukha, so tvaṃ. Taṃ yoganti yaṃ pubbe “ahaṃ yogaṃ payuñjissaṃ, yuttaṃ dhammūpasaṃhita”nti avacāsi, taṃ idāni payuñjassu. Tava pariyāpadānenāti tava tena yogena parisuddhena. “Pariyodātenā”tipi pāṭho, parittāṇenāti attho, tayā katattā tava santakena parittāṇena mama jīvitapariyesanaṃ carāti adhippāyo.
