Here, ‘so’ means ‘that you’, friend Sumukha. ‘Taṃ yogaṃ’ refers to what you previously said: ‘I will apply myself to the effort, connected with the truth’; now apply yourself to it. ‘Tava pariyāpadānena’ means ‘by your purified effort’. ‘Pariyodātena’ is another reading, meaning ‘by protection’; the meaning is: ‘by the protection that belongs to you because it is performed by you, strive for my survival’.

Atha [P 5.0370] sumukho “ayaṃ ativiya maraṇabhayabhīto mama ñāṇabalaṃ na jānāti, rājānaṃ disvā thokaṃ kathaṃ labhitvā jānissāmi, assāsessāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Then Sumukha thought, “This goose-king is exceedingly afraid of death and does not know the power of my wisdom. Once he sees the King of Bārāṇasī and I have a brief conversation, he will understand; I shall first reassure him.” Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

127.

127.

“Mā bhāyi patataṃ seṭṭha, na hi bhāyanti tādisā;

Ahaṃ yogaṃ payuñjissaṃ, yuttaṃ dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ;

Mama pariyāpadānena, khippaṃ pāsā pamokkhasī”ti.

“Fear not, noblest of birds, for such as you do not fear. I will apply myself to the effort connected with the truth. By my pure striving, you will quickly be freed from the snare.”

Tattha pāsāti dukkhapāsato.

Here, ‘pāsā’ means from the snare of suffering.

Iti tesaṃ sakuṇabhāsāya kathentānaṃ luddaputto na kiñci aññāsi, kevalaṃ pana te kājenādāya bārāṇasiṃ pāvisi. Acchariyabbhutajātena añjalinā mahājanena anuggacchamāno so rājadvāraṃ patvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ rañño ārocāpesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, while they were conversing in the language of birds, the hunter understood nothing. He simply took them on a carrying pole and entered Bārāṇasī. Followed by a great multitude who were struck with wonder and amazement with hands clasped in reverence, he reached the king’s gate and had his arrival announced.

128.

128.

“So [M 5.0394] luddo haṃsakājena, rājadvāraṃ upāgami;

Paṭivedetha maṃ rañño, dhataraṭṭhāyamāgato”ti.

“That hunter, with the geese on a carrying pole, approached the king’s gate: ‘Announce to the king that this Dhataraṭṭha has come!’”

Tattha paṭivedetha manti khemako āgatoti evaṃ maṃ rañño nivedetha. Dhataraṭṭhāyanti ayaṃ dhataraṭṭho āgatoti paṭivedetha.

Here, ‘paṭivedetha maṃ’ means ‘inform the king that Khemaka has arrived.’ ‘Dhataraṭṭhāyam’ means ‘announce: “This Dhataraṭṭha has come.”’

Dovāriko [V 5.0366] gantvā paṭivedesi. Rājā sañjātasomanasso “khippaṃ āgacchatū”ti vatvā amaccagaṇaparivuto samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno khemakaṃ haṃsakājaṃ ādāya mahātalaṃ abhiruḷhaṃ disvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇe haṃse oloketvā “sampuṇṇo me manoratho”ti tassa kattabbakiccaṃ amacce āṇāpesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

The gatekeeper went and reported the matter to the king. The king, filled with joy, said, 'Let him come quickly.' Surrounded by a host of ministers, seated on the royal throne under a raised white umbrella, he saw Khemaka, the hunter, who had ascended to the upper floor carrying the golden geese on a shoulder pole. Gazing at the golden-colored geese, he thought, 'My heart’s desire is fulfilled,' and ordered his ministers to perform the necessary duties for the hunter. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

129.

129.

“Te disvā puññasaṅkāse, ubho lakkhaṇasammate;

Khalu saṃyamano rājā, amacce ajjhabhāsatha.

“Seeing those two, who resembled merit and were esteemed for their auspicious marks, King Saṃyamana indeed addressed his ministers.”

130.

130.

“Detha luddassa vatthāni, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Kāmaṃkaro hiraññassa, yāvanto esa icchatī”ti.

“Give the hunter clothes, food, drink, and provisions; let him have as much gold as he desires.”

Tattha puññasaṅkāseti attano puññasadise. Lakkhaṇasammateti seṭṭhasammate abhiññāte. Khalūti nipāto, tassa “te khalu disvā”ti purimapadena sambandho. “Dethā”tiādīni rājā pasannākāraṃ karonto āha. Tattha kāmaṃkaro hiraññassāti [P 5.0371] hiraññaṃ assa kāmakiriyā atthu. Yāvantoti yattakaṃ esa icchati, tattakaṃ hiraññamassa dethāti attho.

Here, ‘puññasaṅkāse’ means ‘similar to his own merit’. ‘Lakkhaṇasammate’ means ‘esteemed as superior and well-known’. ‘Khalu’ is a particle, connected with the preceding phrase as ‘having indeed seen them’. The king said ‘Give’ and so forth, making a gesture of appreciation. Here, ‘kāmaṃkaro hiraññassa’ means ‘let there be gold for him as he desires’. ‘Yāvanto’ means ‘give him as much gold as he wants’—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ pasannākāraṃ kāretvā pītisomanassāsamussahito “gacchatha naṃ alaṅkaritvā ānethā”ti āha. Atha naṃ amaccā rājanivesanā otāretvā kappitakesamassuṃ nhātānulittaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā rañño dassesuṃ. Athassa rājā saṃvacchare satasahassuṭṭhānake dvādasa gāme ājaññayuttaṃ rathaṃ alaṅkatamahāgehañcāti mahantaṃ yasaṃ dāpesi. So mahantaṃ yasaṃ labhitvā attano kammaṃ pakāsetuṃ “na te, deva, mayā yo vā so vā haṃso ānīto, ayaṃ pana navutiyā haṃsasahassānaṃ rājā dhataraṭṭho nāma, ayaṃ senāpati sumukho nāmā”ti āha[M 5.0395]. Atha naṃ rājā “kathaṃ te, samma, ete gahitā”ti pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having shown such a gesture of appreciation, and being filled with joy and happiness, he said, ‘Go, adorn him and bring him here.’ Then the ministers took him down from the palace, had his hair and beard trimmed, bathed and anointed him, and having adorned him with all ornaments, presented him to the king. The king then granted him great wealth, bestowing twelve villages each yielding a revenue of a hundred thousand a year, a chariot yoked with thoroughbred horses, and an adorned grand mansion. Having received such great wealth, the hunter revealed his deed to the king, saying, ‘O king, it was not just any goose that I brought; this is the golden goose king named Dhataraṭṭha, the ruler of ninety thousand geese, and this is the goose general named Sumukha.’ Then the king asked him, ‘How, my dear man, were these captured by you?’ To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

131.

131.

“Disvā luddaṃ pasannattaṃ, kāsirājā tadabravi;

Yadyāyaṃ samma khemaka, puṇṇā haṃsehi tiṭṭhati.

“Seeing the hunter with a pleased mind, the king of Kāsi then said to him: ‘If, dear Khemaka, this pond of ours remains filled with geese,”

132.

132.

“Kathaṃ rucimajjhagataṃ, pāsahattho upāgami;

Okiṇṇaṃ ñātisaṅghehi, nimmajjhimaṃ kathaṃ gahī”ti.

“How did you, with a snare in hand, approach the beautiful one in the midst of the flock? Surrounded by a throng of relatives, how did you seize the supreme one?”

Tattha [V 5.0367] pasannattanti pasannabhāvaṃ somanassappattaṃ. Yadyāyanti, samma khemaka, yadi ayaṃ amhākaṃ pokkharaṇī navutihaṃsasahassehi puṇṇā tiṭṭhati. Kathaṃ rucimajjhagatanti evaṃ sante tvaṃ tesaṃ rucīnaṃ piyadassanānaṃ haṃsānaṃ majjhagataṃ etaṃ ñātisaṅghehi okiṇṇaṃ. Nimmajjhimanti neva majjhimaṃ neva kaniṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ haṃsarājānaṃ kathaṃ pāsahattho upāgami kathaṃ gaṇhīti.

Here, ‘pasannattaṃ’ means ‘a state of being pleased, having attained joy’. ‘Yadyāyaṃ’ means: ‘Dear Khemaka, if this pond of ours remains filled with ninety thousand geese’. ‘Kathaṃ rucimajjhagataṃ’ means: ‘That being so, how did you approach this one, who was in the midst of those beautiful and lovely geese and surrounded by a throng of relatives?’ ‘Nimmajjhimaṃ’ means ‘neither middle nor young, but the supreme king of geese’—‘how did you approach with a snare in hand and seize him?’

So tassa kathento āha –

Relating the story to him, he said:

133.

133.

“Ajja me sattamā ratti, adanāni upāsato;

Padametassa anvesaṃ, appamatto ghaṭassito.

“Today is the seventh night for me, as I watched the feeding grounds; seeking his footprint, I remained vigilant, hidden in a jar-like pit.”

134.

134.

“Athassa padamaddakkhiṃ, carato adanesanaṃ;

Tatthāhaṃ odahiṃ pāsaṃ, evaṃ taṃ dijamaggahi”nti.

“Then I saw his footprint, as he wandered in search of food; there I set the snare, and thus I captured that bird.”

Tattha [P 5.0372] adanānīti ādānāni, gocaraggahaṇaṭṭhānānīti attho, ayameva vā pāṭho. Upāsatoti upagacchantassa. Padanti gocarabhūmiyaṃ akkantapadaṃ. Ghaṭassitoti cāṭipañjare nissito hutvā. Athassāti atha chaṭṭhe divase etassa adanesanaṃ carantassa padaṃ addakkhiṃ. Evaṃ tanti evaṃ taṃ dijaṃ aggahinti sabbaṃ gahitopāyaṃ ācikkhi.

Here, ‘adanāni’ means ‘takings’, meaning the places where they take their food; or this is simply the reading. ‘Upāsato’ means ‘while approaching’. ‘Padaṃ’ means ‘a footprint trodden on the grazing ground’. ‘Ghaṭassito’ means ‘relying on a large water jar used as a blind’. ‘Athassa’ means: ‘Then on the sixth day, I saw the footprint of this one as he wandered in search of food’. ‘Evaṃ taṃ’ means ‘thus I captured that bird’—he described the entire method of capture.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “ayaṃ dvāre ṭhatvā paṭivedentopi dhataraṭṭhassevāgamanaṃ paṭivedesi, idānipi etaṃ ekameva gaṇhinti vadati, kiṃ nu kho ettha kāraṇa”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king thought, ‘Standing at the gate, he announced only the arrival of Dhataraṭṭha, and even now he says he captured only this one—what could be the reason here?’ Reflecting thus, he spoke a verse:

135.

135.

“Ludda dve ime sakuṇā, atha ekoti bhāsasi;

Cittaṃ nu te vipariyattaṃ, adu kiṃ nu jigīsasī”ti.

“Hunter, here are two birds, yet you speak of only one; has your mind become confused, or what else are you thinking?”

Tattha [M 5.0396] vipariyattanti vipallatthaṃ. Adu kiṃ nu jigīsasīti udāhu kiṃ nu cintesi, kiṃ itaraṃ gahetvā aññassa dātukāmo hutvā cintesīti pucchati.

Here, ‘vipariyattaṃ’ means ‘perverted’ or ‘confused’. ‘Adu kiṃ nu jigīsasī’ means ‘or what are you thinking?’, that is, he asks, ‘Are you thinking of taking the other one and intending to give it to someone else?’

Tato luddo “na me, deva, cittaṃ vipallatthaṃ, nāpi ahaṃ itaraṃ aññassa dātukāmo, apica kho pana mayā ohite pāse ekova baddho”ti āvi karonto āha –

Then the hunter, making the matter clear, said: ‘O king, my mind is not confused, nor do I wish to give the other one to anyone else. But indeed, only one was caught in the snare I laid.’

136.

136.

“Yassa [V 5.0368] lohitakā tālā, tapanīyanibhā subhā;

Uraṃ saṃhacca tiṭṭhanti, so me bandhaṃ upāgami.

“He who has beautiful red streaks, like molten gold, reaching across his breast, he alone has come into my snare.”

137.

137.

“Athāyaṃ bhassaro pakkhī, abaddho baddhamāturaṃ;

Ariyaṃ bruvāno aṭṭhāsi, cajanto mānusiṃ gira”nti.

“Then this radiant bird, though not bound, stood by the one who was bound and distressed, speaking noble words and uttering a human voice.”

Tattha lohitakāti rattavaṇṇā. Lātāti rājiyo. Uraṃ saṃhaccāti uraṃ āhacca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, yassetā rattasuvaṇṇasappaṭibhāgā tisso lohitakā rājiyo gīvaṃ parikkhipitvā uraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti, so ekova mama pāse bandhaṃ upāgatoti. Bhassaroti parisuddho pabhāsampanno. Āturanti gilānaṃ dukkhitaṃ aṭṭhāsīti.

Here, ‘lohitakā’ means red-colored. ‘Lātā’ means streaks. ‘Uraṃ saṃhacca’ means reaching the breast. This is what was said: ‘O great king, he who has these three red streaks resembling red gold, which encircle his neck and reach his breast—he alone came into the bondage of my snare.’ ‘Bhassaro’ means pure and radiant. ‘Āturaṃ’ means the one who was suffering; [the verse says] ‘he stood by him’.

Atha dhataraṭṭhassa baddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā nivattitvā etaṃ samassāsetvā mamāgamanakāle ca paccuggamanaṃ katvā ākāseyeva mayā saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā manussabhāsāya dhataraṭṭhassa guṇaṃ kathento aṭṭhāsi, mama hadayaṃ mudukaṃ [P 5.0373] katvā puna etasseva purato aṭṭhāsi. Athāhaṃ, deva, sumukhassa subhāsitaṃ sutvā pasannacitto dhataraṭṭhaṃ vissajjesiṃ, iti dhataraṭṭhassa pāsato mokkho, ime haṃse ādāya mama idhāgamanañca sumukheneva katanti. Evaṃ so sumukhassa guṇakathaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā sumukhassa dhammakathaṃ sotukāmo ahosi. Luddaputtassa sakkāraṃ karontasseva sūriyo atthaṅgato, dīpā pajjalitā, bahū khattiyādayo sannipatitā, khemā devīpi vividhanāṭakaparivārā rañño dakkhiṇapasse nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā sumukhaṃ kathāpetukāmo gāthamāha –

Then, knowing that Dhataraṭṭha was bound, he turned back and consoled him. At the time of my arrival, he came forward to meet me and, while still in the air, exchanged sweet greetings with me. Speaking in a human voice, he stood there praising the virtues of his master, Dhataraṭṭha, and softening my heart, he stood again before the goose king. Then I, O king, hearing Sumukha’s well-spoken words, with a pleased mind released Dhataraṭṭha. Thus was Dhataraṭṭha freed from the snare, and my coming here to this palace with these two geese was all brought about by Sumukha alone. Thus did the hunter Khema speak of Sumukha’s virtues. Hearing this, the king became eager to listen to Sumukha’s discourse on the Dhamma. While he was honoring the fowler, the sun set, lamps were lit, and many nobles and others gathered. Queen Khemā, surrounded by various performers and attendants, sat on the king’s right side. At that moment, the king, wishing to have Sumukha speak, uttered a verse:

138.

138.

“Atha kiṃ dāni sumukha, hanuṃ saṃhacca tiṭṭhasi;

Adu me parisaṃ patto, bhayā bhīto na bhāsasī”ti.

“Well then, Sumukha, why do you now stand with your jaw set? Or have you come into my assembly and, being terrified out of fear, do not speak?”

Tattha [M 5.0397] hanuṃ saṃhaccāti madhurakatho kira tvaṃ, atha kasmā idāni mukhaṃ pidhāya tiṭṭhasi. Adūti kacci. Bhayā bhītoti parisasārajjabhayena bhīto hutvā.

Here, ‘hanuṃ saṃhacca’ means: although you are said to be of sweet speech, why do you now stand with your mouth closed? ‘Adu’ means ‘is it that?’ ‘Bhayā bhīto’ means having become frightened by the fear of diffidence in the assembly.

Taṃ sutvā sumukho abhītabhāvaṃ dassento gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sumukha, showing his fearlessness to the king, spoke this verse:

139.

139.

“Nāhaṃ [V 5.0369] kāsipati bhīto, ogayha parisaṃ tava;

Nāhaṃ bhayā na bhāsissaṃ, vākyaṃ atthasmiṃ tādise”ti.

“I am not afraid, O lord of Kāsi, having entered your assembly; I do not refrain from speaking out of fear; I shall speak when a matter of such purpose arises.”

Tattha tādiseti apica kho pana tathārūpe atthe uppanne vākyaṃ bhāsissāmīti vacanokāsaṃ olokento nisinnomhīti attho.

Here, ‘tādise’ means: when such a purposeful matter arises, I shall speak; I am sitting looking for an opportunity to speak—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tassa kathaṃ vaḍḍhetukāmatāya parihāsaṃ karonto āha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to encourage his speech and also wishing to speak in jest, said:

140.

140.

“Na te abhisaraṃ passe, na rathe napi pattike;

Nāssa cammaṃva kīṭaṃ vā, vammite ca dhanuggahe.

“I see no reinforcements for you, nor chariots nor infantry; nor a leather shield or a dagger, nor armored archers.

141.

141.

“Na hiraññaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ vā, nagaraṃ vā sumāpitaṃ;

Okiṇṇaparikhaṃ duggaṃ, daḷhamaṭṭālakoṭṭhakaṃ;

Yattha paviṭṭho sumukha, bhāyitabbaṃ na bhāyasī”ti.

“Nor gold or silver, nor a well-built city, a fortress surrounded by moats and hard to cross, with strong watchtowers and gatehouses; wherein having entered, O Sumukha, you do not fear what should be feared.”

Tattha [V 5.0370] abhisaranti rakkhaṇatthāya parivāretvā ṭhitaṃ āvudhahatthaṃ parisaṃ te na passāmi. Nāssāti ettha assāti nipātamattaṃ. Cammanti saraparittāṇacammaṃ. Kīṭanti kīṭaṃ cāṭikapālādi vuccati. Cāṭikapālahatthāpi te santike natthīti dīpeti. Vammiteti cammasannaddhe. Na hiraññanti yaṃ nissāya na bhāyasi, taṃ hiraññampi te na passāmi.

Here, ‘abhisara’ refers to the armed assembly stationed for protection—I see none of yours. In ‘Nāssa’, ‘assa’ is merely a particle. ‘Camma’ means a leather shield for protection against arrows. ‘Kīṭa’ refers to a small shield like a potsherd; it indicates that not even one with such a shield in hand is near you. ‘Vammite’ means clad in leather armor. ‘Na hirañña’ means that gold, relying on which you might not fear, I do not see of yours.

Evaṃ [P 5.0374] raññā “kiṃ te abhāyanakāraṇa”nti vutte taṃ kathento āha –

Thus, when the king asked, “What is the reason for your fearlessness?” he, wishing to explain it to the king, said:

142.

142.

“Na me abhisarenattho, nagarena dhanena vā;

Apathena pathaṃ yāma, antalikkhecarā mayaṃ.

“I have no need of guards, nor of a city, nor of wealth. We travel by the pathless sky; we are wanderers of the air.

143.

143.

“Sutā ca paṇḍitā tyamhā, nipuṇā catthacintakā;

Bhāsematthavatiṃ vācaṃ, sacce cassa patiṭṭhito.

“We have been heard by you to be wise, skilled and discerning of meaning; we would speak meaningful words, if you were established in truth.

144.

144.

“Kiñca [M 5.0398] tuyhaṃ asaccassa, anariyassa karissati;

Musāvādissa luddassa, bhaṇitampi subhāsita”nti.

“But what good will even well-spoken words do for you, an untruthful and ignoble one, a liar and a cruel hunter?”

Tattha abhisarenāti ārakkhaparivārena. Atthoti etena mama kiccaṃ natthi. Kasmā? Yasmā apathena tumhādisānaṃ amaggena pathaṃ māpetvā yāma, ākāsacārino mayanti. Paṇḍitā tyamhāti paṇḍitāti tayā sutāmhā, teneva kāraṇena amhākaṃ santikā dhammaṃ sotukāmo kira no gāhāpesi. Sacce cassāti sace pana tvaṃ sacce patiṭṭhito assa, atthavatiṃ kāraṇanissitaṃ vācaṃ bhāseyyāma. Asaccassāti vacīsaccarahitassa tava subhāsitaṃ muṇḍassa dantasūci viya kiṃ karissati.

Here, ‘abhisarena’ means with a protective entourage. ‘Attho’ means I have no need for this. Why? Because we travel by a path that is not a path for the likes of you; we are sky-wanderers. ‘Paṇḍitā tyamhā’ means we are heard by you to be wise; for that very reason, you had us seized, wishing to hear the Dhamma from us. ‘Sacce cassa’ means if you were established in truth, we would speak meaningful words based on reason. ‘Asaccassa’ refers to you, who are devoid of truth in speech—what good is well-spoken speech to you, like a toothpick to a bald man?

Taṃ sutvā rājā “kasmā maṃ musāvādī anariyoti vadasi, kiṃ mayā kata”nti āha. Atha naṃ sumukho “tena hi, mahārāja, suṇāhī”ti vatvā āha –

Hearing this, the king said, “Why do you call me a liar and ignoble? What have I done?” Then Sumukha, saying “Well then, great king, listen,” wishing to point out the king's falsehood, spoke these verses:

145.

145.

“Taṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vacanā, imaṃ khemamakārayi;

Abhayañca tayā ghuṭṭhaṃ, imāyo dasadhā disā.

“At the word of brahmins, you had this Khema Lake made; and safety was proclaimed by you throughout these ten directions.

146.

146.

“Ogayha te pokkharaṇiṃ, vippasannodakaṃ suciṃ;

Pahūtaṃ cādanaṃ tattha, ahiṃsā cettha pakkhinaṃ.

“One may enter your pond, with its very clear and pure water; abundant food is there, and here there is safety for birds.

147.

147.

“Idaṃ sutvāna nigghosaṃ, āgatamha tavantike;

Te te baddhasma pāsena, etaṃ te bhāsitaṃ musā.

“Having heard this proclamation, we came into your presence; but we were bound by your snare—this that you proclaimed is false.

148.

148.

“Musāvādaṃ purakkhatvā, icchālobhañca pāpakaṃ;

Ubhosandhimatikkamma, asātaṃ upapajjatī”ti.

Having placed false speech foremost, and evil desire and greed, transgressing both rebirths, one is reborn into unpleasantness.

Tattha tanti tvaṃ. Khemanti evaṃnāmikaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ. Ghuṭṭhanti catūsu kaṇṇesu ṭhatvā ghosāpitaṃ. Dasadhāti imāsu dasadhā ṭhitāsu disāsu tayā abhayaṃ ghuṭṭhaṃ. Ogayhāti ogāhetvā āgatānaṃ santikā. Pahūtaṃ cādananti pahūtañca padumapupphasāliādikaṃ adanaṃ. Idaṃ sutvānāti [P 5.0375] tesaṃ taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā āgatānaṃ santikā idaṃ abhayaṃ sutvā tavantike tava samīpe tayā kāritapokkharaṇiṃ āgatāmhāti attho. Te teti te mayaṃ tava pāsena baddhā. Purakkhatvāti purato katvā[M 5.0399]. Icchālobhanti icchāsaṅkhātaṃ pāpakaṃ lobhaṃ. Ubhosandhinti ubhayaṃ devaloke ca manussaloke ca paṭisandhiṃ ime pāpadhamme purato katvā caranto puggalo sugatipaṭisandhiṃ atikkamitvā asātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatīti.

Here, 'taṃ' means you. 'Khemaṃ' refers to the pond named Khema. 'Ghuṭṭhaṃ' means proclaimed, having caused the cry of safety to be made. 'Dasadhā' means in these ten directions. 'Ogayha' means from those who came having entered the pond. 'Pahūtaṃ cādanaṃ' means abundant food such as lotus flowers and rice. 'Idaṃ sutvāna' means: having heard this assurance of safety, we came to the pond made by you—this is the meaning. 'Te te' means: we are bound by your snare. 'Purakkhatvā' means having placed foremost. 'Icchālobhaṃ' refers to the evil greed known as desire. 'Ubhosandhiṃ' means both rebirths—in the divine world and the human world. A person who acts having placed these evil things foremost, transgressing rebirth in a good destination, is reborn into the unpleasant state of hell.

Evaṃ [V 5.0371] parisamajjheyeva rājānaṃ lajjāpesi. Atha naṃ rājā “nāhaṃ, sumukha, tumhe māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo gaṇhāpesiṃ, paṇḍitabhāvaṃ pana vo sutvā subhāsitaṃ sotukāmo gaṇhāpesi”nti pakāsento āha –

In this way, he shamed the king in the midst of the assembly. Then the king, making it clear to him, said, “Sumukha, I did not have you seized because I wanted to kill you and eat your flesh, but because, having heard of your wisdom, I wanted to hear your well-spoken discourse on the Dhamma,” and he spoke these verses:

149.

149.

“Nāparajjhāma sumukha, napi lobhāva maggahiṃ;

Sutā ca paṇḍitātyattha, nipuṇā atthacintakā.

“We did not intend any harm, Sumukha, nor did I have you seized out of greed; for you are heard to be wise, skilled and discerning of meaning.

150.

150.

“Appevatthavatiṃ vācaṃ, byāhareyyuṃ idhāgatā;

Tathā taṃ samma nesādo, vutto sumukha maggahī”ti.

“‘Perhaps those who have come here would speak meaningful words’; for that reason, Sumukha, the fowler, having been instructed by me, seized you.”

Tattha nāparajjhāmāti mārento aparajjhati nāma, mayaṃ na mārema. Lobhāva maggahinti maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo hutvā lobhāva tumhe nāhaṃ aggahiṃ. Paṇḍitātyatthāti paṇḍitāti sutā attha. Atthacintakāti paṭicchannānaṃ atthānaṃ cintakā. Atthavatinti kāraṇanissitaṃ. Tathāti tena kāraṇena. Vuttoti mayā vutto hutvā. Sumukha, maggahīti, sumukhāti ālapati, ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Aggahīti dhammaṃ desetuṃ tumhe gaṇhi.

Here, 'nāparajjhāma' means: to kill is to offend, but we do not kill. 'Lobhāva maggahiṃ' means: I did not seize you out of greed, as one desiring to eat your flesh. 'Paṇḍitātyattha' means: you are heard to be wise. 'Atthacintakā' means: thinkers of hidden and subtle meanings. 'Atthavatiṃ' means: based on reason. 'Tathā' means: for that reason. 'Vutto' means: having been told by me. 'Sumukha, maggahī'—'Sumukha' is an address; the 'm' is a euphonic consonant for joining the words. 'Aggahī' means: he seized you so that you might teach the Dhamma.

Taṃ sutvā sumukho “subhāsitaṃ sotukāmena ayuttaṃ te kataṃ, mahārājā”ti vatvā āha –

Hearing this, Sumukha said, 'Great king, you who desire to hear well-spoken words have acted improperly,' and wishing to explain the reason to the king, he spoke these six verses:

151.

151.

“Neva bhītā kāsipati, upanītasmiṃ jīvite;

Bhāsematthavatiṃ vācaṃ, sampattā kālapariyāyaṃ.

We are not afraid, O lord of Kāsi, even though our lives are brought to an end; having reached the end of our time, we shall speak words full of meaning.

152.

152.

“Yo migena migaṃ hanti, pakkhiṃ vā pana pakkhinā;

Sutena vā sutaṃ kiṇyā, kiṃ anariyataraṃ tato.

He who hunts a deer with a deer, or a bird with a bird, or who ensnares the renowned by means of the renowned—what is more ignoble than that?

153.

153.

“Yo cāriyarudaṃ bhāse, anariyadhammavassito;

Ubho so dhaṃsate lokā, idha ceva parattha ca.

He who speaks noble words with his voice but abides in ignoble conduct, is ruined in both worlds, in this life and the next.

154.

154.

“Na [M 5.0400] majjetha yasaṃ patto, na byādhe pattasaṃsayaṃ;

Vāyametheva kiccesu, saṃvare vivarāni ca.

One who has attained fame should not be intoxicated, nor should one be distressed when facing death; one should strive only in one's duties and close every vulnerability.

155.

155.

[V 5.0372] “Ye [P 5.0376] vuddhā abbhatikkantā, sampattā kālapariyāyaṃ;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, evaṃte tidivaṃ gatā.

Those wise ones who have passed away from this life, having reached the end of their time; having practiced the Dhamma here, they have thus gone to heaven.

156.

156.

“Idaṃ sutvā kāsipati, dhammamattani pālaya;

Dhataraṭṭhañca muñcāhi, haṃsānaṃ pavaruttama”nti.

Having heard this, O lord of Kāsi, protect the Dhamma within yourself; and release Dhataraṭṭha, the most excellent of all swans.

Tattha upanītasminti maraṇasantikaṃ upanīte. Kālapariyāyanti maraṇakālavāraṃ sampattā samānā na bhāsissāma. Na hi dhammakathikaṃ bandhitvā maraṇabhayena tajjetvā dhammaṃ suṇanti, ayuttaṃ te katanti. Migenāti suṭṭhu sikkhāpitena dīpakamigena. Hantīti hanati. Pakkhināti dīpakapakkhinā. Sutenāti khemaṃ nibbhayanti vissutena dīpakamigapakkhisadisena padumasarena. Sutanti “paṇḍito citrakathī”ti evaṃ sutaṃ dhammakathikaṃ. Kiṇyāti “dhammaṃ sossāmī”ti pāsabandhanena yo kiṇeyya hiṃseyya bādheyya. Tatoti tesaṃ kiriyato uttari aññaṃ anariyataraṃ nāma kimatthi.

Here, 'upanītasmiṃ' means: when brought near to death. 'Kālapariyāyaṃ' means: it is not that we will not speak, having reached the turn of the time of death. For one does not listen to the Dhamma by binding a Dhamma teacher and threatening him with the fear of death; what you have done is improper. 'Migena' means: by a well-trained decoy deer. 'Hanti' means: he hunts. 'Pakkhinā' means: by a decoy bird. 'Sutena' means: by that which is renowned as safe and fearless, namely the lotus pond, which is like a decoy deer or bird. 'Sutaṃ' means: a Dhamma teacher renowned as, 'a wise and skilled storyteller.' 'Kiṇyā' means: one who would acquire, harm, or oppress with the binding of a snare, thinking, 'I will listen to the Dhamma.' 'Tato' means: what is more ignoble than that action?

Ariyarudanti mukhena ariyavacanaṃ sundaravacanaṃ bhāsati. Anariyadhammavassitoti kammena anariyadhammaṃ avassito. Ubhoti devalokā ca manussalokā cāti ubhayamhā. Idha cevāti idha uppannopi parattha uppannopi evarūpo dvīhi sugatilokehi dhaṃsitvā nirayameva upapajjati. Pattasaṃsayanti jīvitasaṃsayamāpannampi dukkhaṃ patvā na kilameyya. Saṃvare vivarāni cāti attano chiddāni dvārāni saṃvareyya pidaheyya. Vuddhāti guṇavuddhā paṇḍitā. Abbhatikkantāti imaṃ manussalokaṃ atikkantā. Kālapariyāyanti maraṇakālapariyāyaṃ pattā hutvā. Evaṃteti evaṃ ete. Idanti idaṃ mayā vuttaṃ atthanissitaṃ vacanaṃ. Dhammanti paveṇiyadhammampi sucaritadhammampi.

'Ariyarudaṃ' means: with the mouth one speaks noble words, beautiful words. 'Anariyadhammavassito' means: by one's actions, one resorts to ignoble principles. 'Ubho' means: from both the world of gods and the world of humans. 'Idha ceva' means: such a person, whether born here or born elsewhere, having fallen from the two happy realms, is reborn only in hell. 'Pattasaṃsayaṃ' means: even having reached peril to one's life and experienced suffering, one should not become weary. 'Saṃvare vivarāni ca' means: one should restrain, one should close one's own openings and doors. 'Vuddhā' means: the wise, those who are grown in virtue. 'Abbhatikkantā' means: they have transcended this human world. 'Kālapariyāyaṃ' means: having reached the turn of the time of death. 'Evaṃte' means: thus they. 'Idaṃ' means: this meaningful word spoken by me. 'Dhammaṃ' means: both the traditional Dhamma and the Dhamma of good conduct.

Taṃ sutvā rājā āha –

Hearing that, the king, desiring to release the swan kings and to show the virtues of Sumukha to his ministers, said:

157.

157.

“Āharantudakaṃ pajjaṃ, āsanañca mahārahaṃ;

Pañjarato pamokkhāmi, dhataraṭṭhaṃ yasassinaṃ.

O ministers, bring water for the feet, anointing oil, and a seat worthy of the great; I will release the glorious Dhataraṭṭha from his cage.

158.

158.

“Tañca [M 5.0401] senāpatiṃ dhīraṃ, nipuṇaṃ atthacintakaṃ;

Yo sukhe sukhito rañño, dukkhite hoti dukkhito.

And I will also release that wise commander Sumukha, subtle and discerning of meaning, who is happy when his king is happy, and sorrowful when his king is sorrowful.

159.

159.

“Ediso [V 5.0373] kho arahati, piṇḍamasnātu bhattuno;

Yathāyaṃ sumukho rañño, pāṇasādhāraṇo sakhā”ti.

Such a person is truly worthy to eat the food of his master, just as this Sumukha is the king’s true friend who shares his very life.

Tattha udakanti pādadhovanaṃ. Pajjanti pādabbhañjanaṃ. Sukheti sukhamhi sati.

Here, 'udakaṃ' means water for washing the feet. 'Pajjaṃ' means anointing oil for the feet. 'Sukhe' means when there is happiness.

Rañño vacanaṃ sutvā tesaṃ āsanāni āharitvā tattha nisinnānaṃ gandhodakena pāde dhovitvā satapākena telena abbhañjiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0377] pakāsento satthā āha –

Hearing the king's words, the ministers brought seats for them and, for the two swan kings who sat there, washed their feet with scented water and anointed them with oil cooked a hundred times. To explain this, the Teacher said:

160.

160.

“Pīṭhañca sabbasovaṇṇaṃ, aṭṭhapādaṃ manoramaṃ;

Maṭṭhaṃ kāsikamatthannaṃ, dhataraṭṭho upāvisi.

Dhataraṭṭha sat upon an eight-legged golden seat, delightful and smooth, spread with fine cloth from the kingdom of Kāsi.

161.

161.

“Kocchañca sabbasovaṇṇaṃ, veyyagghaparisibbitaṃ;

Sumukho ajjhupāvekkhi, dhataraṭṭhassanantarā.

And Sumukha sat down next to Dhataraṭṭha on a golden couch covered with tiger skin.

162.

162.

“Tesaṃ kañcanapattahi, puthū ādāya kāsiyo;

Haṃsānaṃ abhihāresu, aggarañño pavāsita”nti.

Taking many golden plates, the people of Kāsi brought and offered to the swans the excellent food sent by the king.

Tattha maṭṭhanti karaṇapariniṭṭhitaṃ. Kāsikamatthannanti kāsikavatthena atthataṃ. Kocchanti majjhe saṃkhittaṃ. Veyyagghaparisibbitanti byagghacammaparisibbitaṃ maṅgaladivase aggamahesiyā nisinnapīṭhaṃ. Kañcanapattehīti suvaṇṇabhājanehi. Puthūti bahū janā. Kāsiyoti kāsiraṭṭhavāsino. Abhihāresunti upanāmesuṃ. Aggarañño pavāsitanti aṭṭhasatapalasuvaṇṇapātiparikkhittaṃ haṃsarañño paṇṇākāratthāya kāsiraññā pesitaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ.

Here, 'maṭṭhaṃ' means well-finished. 'Kāsikamatthannaṃ' means spread with Kāsi cloth. 'Kocchaṃ' means constricted in the middle. 'Veyyagghaparisibbitaṃ' means covered with a tiger skin, the seat upon which the chief queen sits on an auspicious day. 'Kañcanapattehi' means with golden vessels. 'Puthū' means many people. 'Kāsiyo' means the inhabitants of the Kāsi kingdom. 'Abhihāresuṃ' means they brought near. 'Aggarañño pavāsitaṃ' means food of various excellent flavors, served in a golden bowl worth eight hundred palas, sent by the king of Kāsi as a gift for the Swan King.

Evaṃ upanīte pana tasmiṃ kāsirājā tesaṃ sampaggahatthaṃ sayaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ gahetvā upanāmesi. Te tato madhulāje khāditvā madhurodakañca piviṃsu. Atha mahāsatto rañño abhihārañca pasādañca disvā paṭisanthāramakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

When the food was thus presented, the king of Kāsi himself took a golden bowl and offered it to them. They ate roasted grain with honey and drank sweet water. Then, the Great Being, seeing the king's offering and his devotion, made a friendly inquiry. To explain this, the Teacher said:

163.

163.

“Disvā abhihaṭaṃ aggaṃ, kāsirājena pesitaṃ;

Kusalo khattadhammānaṃ, tato pucchi anantarā.

Seeing the excellent offering sent by the king of Kāsi, the swan king, who was skilled in the duties of a king, then asked immediately after:

164.

164.

“Kaccinnu [M 5.0402][V 5.0374] bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ;

Kacci raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsasi.

Is it well with you, sire? Are you free from illness? Is this kingdom prosperous? Do you govern it according to the Dhamma?

165.

165.

“Kusalañceva me haṃsa, atho haṃsa anāmayaṃ;

Atho raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsahaṃ.

I am indeed well, O swan, and also, O swan, free from illness. Furthermore, this kingdom is prosperous, and I govern it according to the Dhamma.

166.

166.

“Kacci bhoto amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Kacci ca te tavatthesu, nāvakaṅkhanti jīvitaṃ.

Is there no fault to be found among your ministers? And do they, for your sake, hold their lives as nothing when your interests are at stake?

167.

167.

“Athopi me amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Athopi te mamatthesu, nāvakaṅkhanti jīvitaṃ.

Indeed, no fault is found among my ministers; and for my sake, they do not cling to their lives when my interests are at stake.

168.

168.

“Kacci te sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, tava chandavasānugā.

Is your wife of equal birth, obedient and sweet-spoken? Is she endowed with children, beauty, and fame, and does she follow your will?

169.

169.

“Atho me sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, mama chandavasānugā.

Indeed, my wife is of equal birth, obedient and sweet-spoken; endowed with children, beauty, and fame, she follows my will.

170.

170.

“Kacci [P 5.0378] raṭṭhaṃ anuppīḷaṃ, akutociupaddavaṃ;

Asāhasena dhammena, samena manusāsasi.

Is the kingdom unoppressed and free from any danger? Do you govern it without violence, according to the Dhamma and with justice?

171.

171.

“Atho raṭṭhaṃ anuppīḷaṃ, akutociupaddavaṃ;

Asāhasena dhammena, samena manusāsahaṃ.

Indeed, the kingdom is unoppressed and free from any danger. I govern it without violence, according to the Dhamma and with justice.

172.

172.

“Kacci santo apacitā, asanto parivajjitā;

No ce dhammaṃ niraṃkatvā, adhammamanuvattasi.

Are the virtuous honored and the unvirtuous avoided? Do you refrain from rejecting the Dhamma and following unrighteousness?

173.

173.

“Santo ca me apacitā, asanto parivajjitā;

Dhammamevānuvattāmi, adhammo me niraṃkato.

The virtuous are indeed honored by me, and the unvirtuous are avoided. I follow only the Dhamma; unrighteousness has been rejected by me.

174.

174.

“Kacci [V 5.0375] nānāgataṃ dīghaṃ, samavekkhasi khattiya;

Kaccimatto madanīye, paralokaṃ na santasi.

Do you look far into the future, O king? Are you intoxicated by things that cause negligence, and do you not fear the next world?

175.

175.

“Nāhaṃ anāgataṃ dīghaṃ, samavekkhāmi pakkhima;

Ṭhito dasasu dhammesu, paralokaṃ na santase.

I do look far into the future, O bird. Established in the ten royal virtues, I do not fear the next world.

176.

176.

“Dānaṃ [M 5.0403] sīlaṃ pariccāgaṃ, ajjavaṃ maddavaṃ tapaṃ;

Akkodhaṃ avihiṃsañca, khantiñca avirodhanaṃ.

Generosity, morality, self-sacrifice, integrity, gentleness, austerity, non-anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition.

177.

177.

“Iccete kusale dhamme, ṭhite passāmi attani;

Tato me jāyate pīti, sāmanassañcanappakaṃ.

‘Thus I see these wholesome states established in myself; because of that, rapture and no small gladness arise in me.’

178.

178.

“Sumukho ca acintetvā, visajji pharusaṃ giraṃ;

Bhāvadosamanaññāya, asmākāyaṃ vihaṅgamo.

‘Sumukha, without reflecting and not knowing our heart’s intent, uttered harsh words; this bird of ours, a flyer through the sky.’

179.

179.

“So kuddho pharusaṃ vācaṃ, nicchāresi ayoniso;

Yānasmesu na vijjanti, nayidaṃ paññavatāmivā”ti.

‘Being angry, he uttered harsh words unwisely; he speaks of faults which do not exist in us. This does not seem like the speech of the wise.’

Tattha disvāti taṃ bahuṃ aggapānabhojanaṃ disvā. Pesitanti āharāpetvā upanītaṃ. Khattadhammānanti paṭhamakāraṇesu paṭisanthāradhammānaṃ. Tato pucchi anantarāti tasmiṃ kāle “kacci nu, bhoto”ti anupaṭipāṭiyā pucchi. Tā panetā cha gāthā heṭṭhā vuttatthāyeva. Anuppīḷanti kacci raṭṭhavāsino yante ucchuṃ viya na pīḷesīti pucchati. Akutociupaddavanti kutoci anupaddavaṃ. Dhammena samena manusāsasīti kacci tava raṭṭhaṃ dhammena samena anusāsasi. Santoti sīlādiguṇasaṃyuttā sappurisā. Niraṃkatvāti chaḍḍetvā. Nānāgataṃ dīghanti anāgataṃ attano jīvitapavattiṃ “kacci dīgha”nti na samavekkhasi, āyusaṅkhārānaṃ parittabhāvaṃ jānāsīti pucchati. Madanīyeti madārahe rūpādiārammaṇe. Na santasīti na bhāyasi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kacci rūpādīsu kāmaguṇesu amatto appamatto hutvā dānādīnaṃ kusalānaṃ katattā paralokaṃ na bhāyasīti.

Here, ‘having seen’ means having seen that abundance of excellent food and drink. ‘Sent’ means having had it brought and presented. ‘The duties of warriors’ means the duties of courteous conduct in the first instance. ‘Then he asked immediately’ means at that time he asked in due order, “I trust, good sir…?” These six verses have the meaning already stated. ‘Unoppressed’ means he asks, “Do you not oppress the inhabitants of your kingdom like sugarcane in a press?” ‘Free from any calamity’ means without calamity from any quarter. ‘Do you rule with righteousness and justice’ means “Do you govern your kingdom righteously and justly?” ‘The virtuous’ means good people endowed with qualities like morality. ‘Having rejected’ means having discarded. ‘The long future’ means he asks, “Do you not consider the future continuation of your own life to be long, knowing the limited nature of life-formations?” ‘In things that intoxicate’ means in sense objects such as forms that are fit to cause intoxication. ‘Do not tremble’ means are not afraid. This is what is meant: “Being moderate and heedful regarding sensual pleasures such as forms, and because you have performed wholesome deeds such as generosity, do you not fear the next world?”

Dasasūti dasasu rājadhammesu. Dānādīsu dasavatthukā cetanā dānaṃ, pañcasīladasasīlāni sīlaṃ[V 5.0376], deyyadhammacāgo [P 5.0379] pariccāgo, ujubhāvo ajjavaṃ, mudubhāvo maddavaṃ, uposathakammaṃ tapo, mettāpubbabhāgo akkodho, karuṇāpubbabhāgo avihiṃsā, adhivāsanā khanti, avirodho avirodhanaṃ. Acintetvāti mama imaṃ guṇasampattiṃ acintetvā. Bhāvadosanti cittadosaṃ. Anaññāyāti ajānitvā. Asmākañhi cittadoso [M 5.0404] nāma natthi, yamesa jāneyya, taṃ ajānitvāva pharusaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ giraṃ vissajjesi. Ayonisoti anupāyena. Yānasmesūti yāni vajjāni amhesu na vijjanti, tāni vadati. Nayidanti tasmāssa idaṃ vacanaṃ paññavataṃ iva na hoti, tenesa mama na paṇḍito viya upaṭṭhāti.

‘In the ten’ means in the ten royal principles. ‘Generosity’ is the volition concerning the ten bases for meritorious action, beginning with giving; ‘virtue’ is the five and ten precepts; ‘liberality’ is the relinquishing of things fit to be given; ‘honesty’ is uprightness; ‘gentleness’ is kindness; ‘austerity’ is the observance of the Uposatha; ‘non-anger’ has loving-kindness as its preliminary part; ‘non-harming’ has compassion as its preliminary part; ‘patience’ is endurance; ‘non-opposition’ is non-contradiction. ‘Without reflecting’ means without considering this accomplishment of virtues of mine. ‘The fault of disposition’ means a fault of mind. ‘Without knowing’ means not understanding. For we indeed have no such thing as a fault of mind; it was without knowing this that he uttered harsh and rough speech. ‘Unreflectively’ means unwisely. ‘Which are not in us’ means he speaks of those faults that are not found in us. ‘This is not’ means therefore his speech is not like that of the wise, and for that reason he does not seem to me to be a wise person.

Taṃ sutvā sumukho “mayā guṇasampannova rājā apasādito, so me kuddho, khamāpessāmi na”nti cintetvā āha –

Hearing this, Sumukha thought, ‘I have disparaged a king who is truly endowed with virtues. He is angry with me; I will ask his forgiveness,’ and said:

180.

180.

“Atthi me taṃ atisāraṃ, vegena manujādhipa;

Dhataraṭṭhe ca baddhasmiṃ, dukkhaṃ me vipulaṃ ahu.

‘That transgression of mine happened through haste, O lord of men; for when Dhatarattha was snared, my suffering was immense.’

181.

181.

“Tvaṃ no pitāva puttānaṃ, bhūtānaṃ dharaṇīriva;

Asmākaṃ adhipannānaṃ, khamassu rājakuñjarā”ti.

‘You are like a father to us, your sons, and like the earth to all living beings; forgive us who have been overcome by anger, O elephant among kings.’

Tattha atisāranti pakkhalitaṃ. Vegenāti ahaṃ etaṃ kathaṃ kathento vegena sahasā kathesiṃ. Dukkhanti cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ mama vipulaṃ ahosi, tasmā kodhavasena yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, taṃ me khamatha, mahārājāti. Puttānanti tvaṃ amhākaṃ puttānaṃ pitā viya. Dharaṇīrivāti pāṇabhūtānaṃ patiṭṭhā pathavī viya tvaṃ amhākaṃ avassayo. Adhipannānanti dosena aparādhena ajjhotthaṭānaṃ khamassūti idaṃ so āsanā oruyha pakkhehi añjaliṃ katvā āha.

Here, ‘transgression’ means a lapse. ‘Through haste’ means, ‘As I was speaking these words, I spoke with speed and rashness.’ ‘Suffering’ means ‘My mental suffering was immense; therefore, great king, forgive what I said through anger.’ ‘To sons’ means you are like a father to us, your sons. ‘Like the earth’ means you are our refuge, just as the earth is the support for living beings. ‘Of those who have been overcome’ means forgive those overwhelmed by fault and offense—this he said, descending from his seat and making a gesture of reverence with his wings.

Atha naṃ rājā āliṅgitvā ādāya suvaṇṇapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā accayadesanaṃ paṭiggaṇhanto āha –

Then the king embraced him, took him and seated him on a golden throne, and, accepting his confession of the offense, said:

182.

182.

“Etaṃ te anumodāma, yaṃ bhāvaṃ na nigūhasi;

Khilaṃ pabhindasi pakkhi, ujukosi vihaṅgamā”ti.

‘We rejoice in this in you, that you do not hide your true disposition; you break through the heart’s obstruction, O bird; you are upright, O flyer through the sky.’

Tattha [V 5.0377] anumodāmāti etaṃ te dosaṃ khamāma. Yanti yasmā tvaṃ attano cittapaṭicchannabhāvaṃ na nigūhasi. Khilanti cittakhilaṃ cittakhāṇukaṃ.

Here, ‘we rejoice’ means we forgive you this fault. ‘That’ means because you do not conceal the hidden state of your mind. ‘Obstruction’ (khila၁) means mental obstruction, a mental stake.

Idañca pana vatvā rājā mahāsattassa dhammakathāya sumukhassa ca ujubhāve pasīditvā “pasannena nāma pasannākāro kātabbo”ti ubhinnampi tesaṃ attano rajjasiriṃ niyyādento āha –

Having said this, the king, being pleased with the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma and with Sumukha’s uprightness, thought, ‘One who is pleased should show a sign of pleasure,’ and handing over the glory of his kingdom to both of them, he said:

183.

183.

“Yaṃ kiñci ratanaṃ atthi, kāsirājanivesane;

Rajataṃ jātarūpañca, muttā veḷuriyā bahū.

‘Whatever treasures there are in the residence of the king of Kasi—silver and gold, and many pearls and beryl gems,’

184.

184.

“Maṇayo [M 5.0405][P 5.0380] saṅkhamuttā ca, vatthakaṃ haricandanaṃ;

Ajinaṃ dantabhaṇḍañca, lohaṃ kāḷāyasaṃ bahuṃ;

Etaṃ dadāmi vo vittaṃ, issaraṃ vissajāmi vo”ti.

‘Jewels and conch-pearls, fine cloth and yellow sandalwood, antelope skins and ivory goods, copper and much iron—this wealth I give to you; I bestow sovereignty upon you.’

Tattha muttāti viddhāviddhamuttā. Maṇayoti maṇibhaṇḍakāni. Saṅkhamuttā cāti dakkhiṇāvaṭṭasaṅkharatanañca āmalakavaṭṭamuttaratanañca. Vatthakanti sukhumakāsikavatthāni. Ajinanti ajinamigacammaṃ. Lohaṃ kāḷāyasanti tambalohañca kāḷalohañca. Issaranti kañcanamālena setacchattena saddhiṃ dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare rajjaṃ.

There, ‘pearls’ means both pierced and unpierced pearls. ‘Jewels’ refers to jewel ornaments. ‘Conch-pearls’ means the right-spiralled conch jewel and the pearl jewel round like an amalaka fruit. ‘Cloth’ refers to fine garments of Kasi. ‘Hides’ means the hide of an ajina antelope. ‘Copper and iron’ refers to both copper and iron. ‘Sovereignty’ means kingship in the city of Bārā၃asģ, twelve yojanas in extent, together with a golden garland and a white parasol.

Evañca pana vatvā ubhopi te setacchattena pūjetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpesi. Atha mahāsatto raññā saddhiṃ sallapanto āha –

Having spoken thus, he honored both of them with a white parasol and handed over the kingdom to them. Then, the Great Being, conversing with the king, said:

185.

185.

“Addhā apacitā tyamhā, sakkatā ca rathesabha;

Dhammesu vattamānānaṃ, tvaṃ no ācariyo bhava.

‘Certainly we have been revered and honored by you, O lord of chariots; to us who abide in the Dhamma, be our teacher.’

186.

186.

“Ācariya manuññātā, tayā anumatā mayaṃ;

Taṃ padakkhiṇato katvā, ñātiṃ passemurindamā”ti.

‘O teacher, being permitted and approved by you, let us circumambulate you and go to see our kinsmen, O tamer of foes.’

Tattha dhammesūti kusalakammapathadhammesu. Ācariyoti tvaṃ amhehi byattataro, tasmā no ācariyo hoti, apica dasannaṃ rājadhammānaṃ kathitattā sumukhassa dosaṃ dassetvā accayapaṭiggahaṇassa [V 5.0378] katattāpi tvaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyova, tasmā idānipi no ācārasikkhāpanena ācariyo bhavāti āha. Passemurindamāti passemu arindama.

Here, ‘in the Dhamma’ means in the principles of the wholesome courses of action. ‘Teacher’ means you are more learned than us; therefore, you are our teacher. Moreover, because you have spoken of the ten royal virtues, pointed out Sumukha’s fault, and accepted our apology, you are indeed our teacher. Therefore, even now, by training us in proper conduct, be our teacher—so he said. ‘Passemurindama’ means: let us see, O tamer of foes.

So tesaṃ gamanaṃ anujāni, bodhisattassapi dhammaṃ kathentasseva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

He permitted their departure. Even as the Bodhisatta was teaching the Dhamma, dawn arose. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said:

187.

187.

“Sabbarattiṃ cintayitvā, mantayitvā yathākathaṃ;

Kāsirājā anuññāsi, haṃsānaṃ pavaruttama”nti.

‘Having thought and consulted throughout the night on every matter, the king of Kasi gave permission to the most noble of geese.’

Tattha yathākathanti yaṃkiñci atthaṃ tehi saddhiṃ cintetabbaṃ mantetabbañca, sabbaṃ taṃ cintetvā ca mantetvā cāti attho. Anuññāsīti gacchathāti anuññāsi.

Here, ‘yathākatha၁’ means having considered and discussed every matter that should be considered and discussed with them—this is the meaning. ‘Anu၃āsi’ means he gave permission, saying, ‘Go.’

Evaṃ [M 5.0406] tena anuññāto bodhisatto rājānaṃ “appamatto dhammena rajjaṃ kārehī”ti ovaditvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Rājā tesaṃ kañcanabhājanehi [P 5.0381] madhulājañca madhurodakañca upanāmetvā niṭṭhitāhārakicce gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā bodhisattaṃ suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakena sayaṃ ukkhipi, khemā devī sumukhaṃ ukkhipi. Atha ne sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā sūriyuggamanavelāya “gacchatha sāmino”ti vissajjesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus permitted by him, the Bodhisatta advised the king, ‘Rule the kingdom righteously and with heedfulness,’ and established him in the five precepts. The king had honeyed parched grain and sweet water served to them in golden vessels, and when their meal was finished, he honored them with perfumes, garlands, and the like. The king himself lifted the Bodhisatta in a golden casket, while Queen Khemā lifted Sumukha. Then, opening the lattice-window at sunrise, they released them, saying, ‘Go, noble sirs.’ Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

188.

188.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Pekkhato kāsirājassa, bhavanā te vigāhisu”nti.

‘Then, as the night ended and the sun rose, while the king of Kasi was watching, they flew forth from the palace into the sky.’

Tattha vigāhisunti ākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu.

Here, ‘they flew forth’ means they leaped into the sky.

Tesu mahāsatto suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakato uppatitvā ākāse ṭhatvā “mā cindayi, mahārāja, appamatto amhākaṃ ovāde vatteyyāsī”ti rājānaṃ samassāsetvā sumukhaṃ ādāya cittakūṭameva gato. Tānipi kho navuti haṃsasahassāni kañcanaguhato nikkhamitvā pabbatatale nisinnāni te āgacchante disvā paccuggantvā parivāresuṃ. Te ñātigaṇaparivutā cittakūṭatalaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Of those two, the Great Being rose from the golden casket, stood in the sky and comforted the king, saying, ‘Do not worry, great king. Be heedful and conduct yourself according to our advice.’ Then, taking Sumukha, he went back to Mount Cittakuta. Those ninety thousand geese also emerged from the golden cave and, while sitting on the mountain slope, saw them coming and went out to meet and surround them. Surrounded by their kinsmen, they entered the plateau of Cittakuta. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

189.

189.

“Te [V 5.0379] aroge anuppatte, disvāna parame dije;

Kekāti makaruṃ haṃsā, puthusaddo ajāyatha.

Seeing those supreme birds arrived unharmed, the geese made a cry of joy; a great sound arose.

190.

190.

“Te patītā pamuttena, bhattunā bhattugāravā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, aṇḍajā laddhapaccayā”ti.

Delighted by their freed master, and out of reverence for their master, the egg-born ones, having regained their support, surrounded him on all sides.

Evaṃ parivāretvā ca pana te haṃsā “kathaṃ muttosi, mahārājā”ti pucchiṃsu. Mahāsatto sumukhaṃ nissāya muttabhāvaṃ saṃyamarājaluddaputtehi katakammañca kathesi. Taṃ sutvā tuṭṭhā haṃsagaṇā “sumukho senāpati ca rājā ca luddaputto ca sukhitā niddukkhā ciraṃ jīvantū”ti āhaṃsu. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0382] pakāsento satthā āha –

Having thus surrounded him, the geese asked, "How were you freed, great king?" The Great Being told of his release because of Sumukha and the deeds of King Saဣyama and the hunter’s son. Hearing this, the flock of geese, pleased, said, "May the commander Sumukha, the king, and the hunter’s son be happy, free from suffering, and live long." Revealing this meaning, the Teacher said:

191.

191.

“Evaṃ mittavataṃ atthā, sabbe honti padakkhiṇā;

Haṃsā yathā dhataraṭṭhā, ñātisaṅghamupāgamu”nti.

"Thus, for those who have friends, all their aims turn out auspiciously, just as the Dhataraဣအha geese returned to their assembly of kinsmen."

Taṃ cūḷahaṃsajātake vuttatthameva.

This has the same meaning as stated in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka.

Satthā [M 5.0407] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānando mamatthāya attano jīvitaṃ pariccajī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā luddaputto channo ahosi, khemā devī, khemā bhikkhunī, rājā sāriputto, sumukho ānando, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, dhataraṭṭhahaṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Ānanda sacrificed his own life for my sake." Connecting the birth story, he said, "At that time, the hunter’s son was Channa, Queen Khemā was the bhikkhunĩ Khemā, the king was Sāriputta, Sumukha was Ānanda, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the goose-king Dhataraဣအha was I myself."

Mahāhaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Mahāhaအsa Jātaka, the Second.

[535] 3. Sudhābhojanajātakavaṇṇanā

[535] 3. The Commentary on the Sudhābhojana Jātaka.

Neva kiṇāmi napi vikkiṇāmīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dānajjhāsayaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ eko kulaputto hutvā satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasannacitto pabbajitvā sīlesu paripūrakārī dhutaṅgaguṇasamannāgato sabrahmacārīsu pavattamettacitto divasassa tikkhattuṃ buddhadhammasaṅghupaṭṭhāne appamatto ācārasampanno dānajjhāsayo ahosi. Sāraṇīyadhammapūrako attanā laddhaṃ paṭiggāhakesu vijjamānesu chinnabhatto hutvāpi detiyeva, tasmā [V 5.0380] tassa dānajjhāsayadānābhiratabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu dānajjhāsayo dānābhirato attanā laddhaṃ pasatamattapānīyampi lobhaṃ chinditvā sabrahmacārīnaṃ deti, bodhisattassevassa ajjhāsayo”ti. Satthā taṃ kathaṃ dibbāya sotadhātuyā sutvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pubbe adānasīlo maccharī tiṇaggena telabindumpi adātā ahosi, atha naṃ ahaṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā dānaphalaṃ vaṇṇetvā dāne patiṭṭhāpesiṃ, so ‘pasatamattaṃ udakampi labhitvā adatvā na pivissāmī’ti mama santike varaṃ aggahesi, tassa phalena dānajjhāsayo dānābhirato jāto”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"I neither buy nor do I sell." This the Teacher said while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a monk with an inclination for giving. It is said that he was a certain clansman in Sāvatthĩ who, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma talk, with a confident mind went forth. He was a fulfiller of the precepts, endowed with the qualities of the ascetic practices, with a mind of active loving-kindness towards his companions in the holy life, heedful in his attendance upon the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha three times a day, accomplished in conduct, and with an inclination for giving. A fulfiller of the principles of cordiality, whatever he received he would give away if recipients were present, even if it meant he went without a meal. Therefore, his inclination for giving and his delight in generosity became well-known in the Sangha of monks. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, the monk so-and-so has an inclination for giving and delights in generosity. Whatever he receives, even a mere handful of water, he cuts off greed and gives it to his companions in the holy life. His inclination is just like that of a Bodhisatta." The Teacher, hearing this conversation with his divine ear-element, came from his fragrant chamber and asked, "For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered?" When he was told, "For such-and-such," he said, "Monks, this monk was formerly of an ungenerous nature, miserly, one who would not give away even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass. Then I tamed him, made him free from that habit, praised the fruit of giving, and established him in generosity. He then took a vow in my presence: 'Having received even a handful of water, I will not drink it without first giving.' As a result of that, he has become one with an inclination for giving, one who delights in generosity." Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko gahapati aḍḍho ahosi asītikoṭivibhavo. Athassa rājā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi[M 5.0408]. So rājapūjito nāgarajānapadapūjito hutvā ekadivasaṃ attano sampattiṃ oloketvā cintesi – “ayaṃ yaso mayā atītabhave neva niddāyantena, na kāyaduccaritādīni karontena laddho, sucaritāni pana [P 5.0383] pūretvā laddho, anāgatepi mayā mama patiṭṭhaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So rañño santikaṃ gantvā “deva, mama ghare asītikoṭidhanaṃ atthi, taṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā “na mayhaṃ tava dhanenattho, bahuṃ me dhanaṃ, itopi yadicchasi, taṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vutte “kiṃ nu, deva, mama dhanaṃ dātuṃ labhāmī”ti āha. Atha raññā “yathāruci karohī”ti vutte catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāre cāti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassapariccāgaṃ karonto mahādānaṃ pavattesi. So yāvajīvaṃ dānaṃ datvā “imaṃ mama dānavaṃsaṃ mā upacchindathā”ti putte anusāsitvā jīvitapariyosāne sakko hutvā nibbatti. Puttopissa tatheva dānaṃ datvā cando hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto sūriyo hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto mātali hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto pañcasikho hutvā nibbatti, tassa pana putto chaṭṭho seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ laddhā macchariyakosiyo nāma ahosi asītikoṭivibhavoyeva. So “mama pitupitāmahā bālā ahesuṃ, dukkhena sambhataṃ dhanaṃ chaḍḍesuṃ, ahaṃ pana dhanaṃ rakkhissāmi, kassaci kiñci na dassāmī”ti cintetvā dānasālā viddhaṃsetvā agginā jhāpetvā thaddhamaccharī ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a wealthy householder with a fortune of eighty crores. The king then granted him the position of treasurer. Honored by the king and by the people of the city and countryside, one day he reflected on his prosperity and thought: 'This glory was gained by me in a past existence not by sleeping, nor by committing bodily misconduct and the like, but by fulfilling good conduct. In the future too, I ought to establish my own foundation.' He went to the king and said, 'Your Majesty, in my house there is wealth of eighty crores—please take it.' When the king replied, 'I have no need of your wealth; I have much wealth. If you wish for anything more, you may take it from here,' the householder asked, 'Then, Your Majesty, may I be permitted to give away my wealth?' The king said, 'Do as you please.' So he had six alms halls built—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at the door of his residence—and, making a daily expenditure of six hundred thousand, he established a great almsgiving. After giving alms for his entire life, he instructed his sons, 'Do not cut off this, my lineage of giving,' and at the end of his life, he was reborn as Sakka. His son likewise gave alms and was reborn as the moon god. His son was reborn as the sun god, his son as Mātali, and his son as Pa#casikha. But the sixth in this lineage, having obtained the position of treasurer, became known as Macchariyakosiya, with a fortune of eighty crores as well. He thought, 'My fathers and grandfathers were fools; they threw away wealth amassed with hardship. I, however, will guard my wealth and give nothing to anyone.' Thinking thus, he destroyed the alms halls, burned them with fire, and became a hardened miser.

Athassa gehadvāre yācakā sannipatitvā bāhā paggayha, “mahāseṭṭhi, mā attano pitupitāmahānaṃ dānavaṃsaṃ nāsayi, dānaṃ dehī”ti mahāsaddena parideviṃsu. Taṃ sutvā mahājano “macchariyakosiyena [V 5.0381] attano dānavaṃso upacchinno”ti taṃ garahi. So lajjito nivesanadvāre yācakānaṃ āgatāgataṭṭhānaṃ nivāretuṃ ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Te nippaccayā hutvā puna tassa gehadvāraṃ na olokesuṃ. So tato paṭṭhāya dhanameva saṃharati, neva attanā paribhuñjati, na puttadārādīnaṃ deti, kañjikabilaṅgadutiyaṃ sakuṇḍakabhattaṃ bhuñjati, mūlaphalamattatantāni thūlavatthāni nivāseti, paṇṇachattaṃ matthake dhāretvā jaraggoṇayuttena jajjararathakena yāti. Iti tassa asappurisassa tattakaṃ [P 5.0384] dhanaṃ sunakhena laddhaṃ nāḷikeraṃ viya ahosi.

Then beggars gathered at the door of his house, and stretching out their arms, they lamented with a great cry, “Great Treasurer, do not destroy the tradition of giving of your fathers and grandfathers! Give alms!” Hearing this, the people reproached him, saying, “Macchariyakosiya has cut off his own tradition of giving.” Ashamed, he placed a guard at the door of his residence to prevent the beggars from approaching. Left without support, they no longer looked toward his house door. From then on, he only hoarded wealth; he neither enjoyed it himself nor gave it to his wife, children, and others. He ate rice with bran accompanied by sour gruel, wore coarse garments made of rough fibers, held a leaf-umbrella over his head, and traveled in a decrepit cart yoked to an old ox. Thus, for that ignoble man, such great wealth was like a coconut obtained by a dog.

So [M 5.0409] ekadivasaṃ rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto “anuseṭṭhiṃ ādāya gamissāmī”ti tassa gehaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe anuseṭṭhi puttadhītādīhi parivuto navasappipakkamadhusakkharacuṇṇehi saṅkhataṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjamāno nisinno hoti. So macchariyakosiyaṃ disvā āsanā vuṭṭhāya “ehi, mahāseṭṭhi, imasmiṃ pallaṅke nisīda, pāyāsaṃ bhuñjissāmā”ti āha. Tassa pāyāsaṃ disvāva mukhe kheḷā uppajji, bhuñjitukāmo ahosi, evaṃ pana cintesi – “sacāhaṃ bhuñjissāmi, anuseṭṭhino mama gehaṃ āgatakāle paṭisakkāro kātabbo bhavissati, evaṃ me dhanaṃ nassissati, na bhuñjissāmī”ti. Atha punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi “idāni me bhuttaṃ, suhitosmī”ti na icchi. Anuseṭṭhimhi bhuñjante pana olokento mukhe sañjāyamānena kheḷena nisīditvā tassa bhattakiccāvasāne tena saddhiṃ rājanivesanaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ passitvā rājanivesanato otaritvā attano gehaṃ anuppatto pāyāsataṇhāya pīḷiyamāno cintesi – “sacāhaṃ ‘pāyāsaṃ bhuñjitukāmomhī’ti vakkhāmi, mahājano bhuñjitukāmo bhavissati, bahū taṇḍulādayo nassissanti, na kassaci kathessāmī”ti. So rattindivaṃ pāyāsameva cintento vītināmetvāpi dhananāsanabhayena kassaci akathetvāva pipāsaṃ adhivāsesi, anukkamena adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto ahosi. Evaṃ santepi dhananāsanabhayena akathento aparabhāge dubbalo hutvā sayanaṃ upagūhitvā nipajji.

One day, while going to wait upon the king, he thought, “I will take the junior treasurer with me,” and went to his house. At that moment, the junior treasurer was seated, surrounded by his sons, daughters, and others, eating milk-rice prepared with fresh ghee, honey, and powdered sugar. Seeing Macchariyakosiya, he rose from his seat and said, “Come, great treasurer, sit on this couch; let us eat milk-rice.” At the mere sight of the milk-rice, saliva arose in his mouth, and he became desirous of eating. But he thought, “If I eat, when the junior treasurer comes to my house, a return courtesy will have to be made, and thus my wealth will be lost; I will not eat.” Though repeatedly urged, he refused, saying, “I have just eaten; I am well-satisfied.” While the junior treasurer ate, he sat watching, with saliva forming in his mouth. When the meal was finished, he went with him to the king's residence. After seeing the king and descending from the royal palace, he arrived back at his own home, tormented by his craving for the milk-rice. He thought, “If I say, ‘I am desirous of eating milk-rice,’ many people will also want to eat, and much rice and other ingredients will be lost; I will not tell anyone.” He spent day and night thinking only of the milk-rice, but out of fear of losing his wealth, he told no one and endured his craving. Gradually becoming unable to endure it, he became extremely pale and jaundiced. Even so, fearing the loss of his wealth, he said nothing. Later, growing weak, he lay down, clutching his bed.

Atha naṃ bhariyā upagantvā hatthena piṭṭhiṃ parimajjamānā “kiṃ te, sāmi, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Taveva sarīre aphāsukaṃ karohi, mama aphāsukaṃ natthī”ti. “Sāmi, uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātosi, kiṃ nu te kāci cintā atthi, udāhu rājā te kupito, adu puttehi avamāno kato, atha vā pana kāci taṇhā uppannā”ti? “Āma, taṇhā me uppannā”ti. “Kathehi, sāmī”ti? “Kathessāmi, sakkhissasi naṃ rakkhitu”nti. “Rakkhitabbayuttakā ce, rakkhissāmī”ti. Evampi [P 5.0385] dhananāsanabhayena kathetuṃ na ussahi. Tāya punappunaṃ pīḷiyamāno kathesi – “bhadde, ahaṃ ekadivasaṃ anuseṭṭhiṃ navasappimadhusakkharacuṇṇehi saṅkhataṃ [V 5.0382] pāyāsaṃ bhuñjantaṃ disvā tato paṭṭhāya tādisaṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjitukāmo jāto”ti. “Asappurisa, kiṃ tvaṃ duggato, sakalamārāṇasivāsīnaṃ pahonakaṃ pāyāsaṃ pacissāmī”ti. Athassa sīse daṇḍena paharaṇakālo [M 5.0410] viya ahosi. So tassā kujjhitvā “jānāmahaṃ tava mahaddhanabhāvaṃ, sace te kulagharā ābhataṃ atthi, pāyāsaṃ pacitvā nāgarānaṃ dehī”ti āha. “Tena hi ekavīthivāsīnaṃ pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Kiṃ te etehi, attano pana santakaṃ khādantū”ti? “Tena hi ito cito ca sattasattagharavāsīnaṃ pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Kiṃ te etehī”ti. “Tena hi imasmiṃ gehe parijanassā”ti. “Kiṃ te etenā”ti? “Tena hi bandhujanasseva pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Kiṃ te etenā”ti? “Tena hi tuyhañca mayhañca pacāmi sāmī”ti. “Kāsi tvaṃ, na tuyhaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Tena hi ekasseva te pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Mayhañca tvaṃ mā paci, gehe pana pacante bahū paccāsīsanti, mayhaṃ pana patthaṃ taṇḍulānaṃ catubhāgaṃ khīrassa accharaṃ sakkharāya karaṇḍakaṃ sappissa karaṇḍakaṃ madhussa ekañca pacanabhājanaṃ dehi, ahaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha pacitvā bhuñjāmī”ti. Sā tathā akāsi. So taṃ sabbaṃ ceṭakena gāhāpetvā “gaccha asukaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhāhī”ti taṃ purato pesetvā ekakova oguṇṭhikaṃ katvā aññātakavesena tattha gantvā nadītīre ekasmiṃ gacchamūle uddhanaṃ kāretvā dārudakaṃ āharāpetvā “tvaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ magge ṭhatvā kañcideva disvā mama saññaṃ dadeyyāsi, mayā pakkositakāleva āgaccheyyāsī”ti taṃ pesetvā aggiṃ katvā pāyāsaṃ paci.

Then his wife approached him and, stroking his back with her hand, asked, “What troubles you, my lord? Are you unwell?” “Keep the discomfort for your own body; I am not unwell.” “My lord, you have become pale and jaundiced. Are you suffering some worry? Has the king become displeased with you, or have your sons shown disrespect, or perhaps has some craving arisen in you?” “Yes, a craving has arisen in me.” “Tell me, my lord.” “I will tell you, but can you keep the secret?” “If it is something that should be kept, I will keep it.” Even so, out of fear of losing his wealth, he hesitated to speak. Pressed repeatedly by her, he finally said, “Dear one, one day I saw the junior treasurer eating milk-rice prepared with fresh ghee, honey, and sugar. Ever since, I have longed to eat such milk-rice.” “You ignoble man! Are you a pauper? I shall prepare milk-rice enough for all the residents of Benares!” At that moment, it was as if he were being struck on the head with a stick. Angered, he said to her, “I know well your great wealth. If you have anything brought from your parental home, cook the milk-rice and give it to the citizens.” “Then I shall prepare enough for the residents of one street.” “What are they to you? Let them eat their own.” “Then I shall prepare enough for the residents of seven houses here and seven houses there.” “What are they to you?” “Then I shall prepare it for the household here.” “What are they to you?” “Then I shall prepare it for our relatives.” “What are they to you?” “Then I shall prepare it for you and me, my lord.” “Who are you? It is not fitting for you.” “Then I shall prepare just enough for you alone.” “And do not cook for me. If you cook in the house, many will expect some. Instead, give me a measure of rice, a small measure of milk, a small vessel of sugar, a small vessel of ghee, a portion of honey, and one cooking pot. I will go into the forest, cook there, and eat.” She did so. He had a servant carry all the items and, sending him ahead, said, “Go and wait at such-and-such a place.” He himself, veiling himself, went there in disguise. By the riverbank, at the foot of a bush, he had a hearth prepared and firewood and water brought. Then he sent the servant away, saying, “Go and stand on the path. If you see anyone, give me a signal. Come back only when I call you.” Then he lit a fire and cooked the milk-rice.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko devarājā dasasahassayojanaṃ alaṅkatadevanagaraṃ, saṭṭhiyojanaṃ [P 5.0386] suvaṇṇavīthiṃ, yojanasahassubbedhaṃ vejayantaṃ, pañcayojanasatikaṃ sudhammasabhaṃ, saṭṭhiyojanaṃ paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ, pañcayojanāvaṭṭaṃ kañcanamālasetacchattaṃ, aḍḍhateyyakoṭisaṅkhā devaccharā, alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ attabhāvanti imaṃ attano siriṃ oloketvā “kiṃ nu kho katvā mayā ayaṃ yaso laddho”ti cintetvā bārāṇasiyaṃ seṭṭhibhūtena pavattitaṃ dānaṃ addasa. Tato “mama puttādayo kuhiṃ nibbattā”ti olokento “putto me cando devaputto hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto sūriyo, tassa putto, mātali, tassa putto, pañcasikho”ti sabbesaṃ nibbattiṃ disvā “pañcasikhassa putto kīdiso”ti olokento attano vaṃsassa upacchinnabhāvaṃ passi. Athassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ asappuriso maccharī hutvā neva attanā paribhuñjati[M 5.0411], na paresaṃ deti, mama vaṃso tena upacchinno, kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbattissati, ovādamassa datvā mama vaṃsaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā etassa imasmiṃ devanagare nibbattanākāraṃ karissāmī”ti. So candādayo pakkosāpetvā “etha manussapathaṃ gamissāma, macchariyakosiyena amhākaṃ vaṃso upacchinno[V 5.0383], dānasālā jhāpitā, neva attanā paribhuñjati, na paresaṃ deti, idāni pana pāyāsaṃ bhuñjitukāmo hutvā ‘ghare paccante aññassapi pāyāso dātabbo bhavissatī’ti araññaṃ pavisitvā ekakova pacati, etaṃ dametvā dānaphalaṃ jānāpetvā āgamissāma, apica kho pana amhehi sabbehi ekato yāciyamāno tattheva mareyya. Mama paṭhamaṃ gantvā pāyāsaṃ yācitvā nisinnakāle tumhe brāhmaṇavaṇṇena paṭipāṭiyā āgantvā yāceyyāthā”ti vatvā sayaṃ tāva brāhmaṇavaṇṇena taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bho, kataro bārāṇasigamanamaggo”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ macchariyakosiyo “kiṃ ummattakosi, bārāṇasimaggampi na jānāsi, kiṃ ito esi, etto yāhī”ti āha.

At that moment, Sakka, the king of the gods, surveyed his own splendor: the decorated celestial city ten thousand leagues in size, the sixty-league golden street, the thousand-league-high Vejayanta palace, the five-hundred-league Sudhamma assembly hall, the sixty-league Paṇḍukambala stone seat, the five-league-round golden garland and white parasol, and the two and a half crores of celestial nymphs, seeing his own person thus beautifully adorned and prepared. Reflecting, 'By what deed have I attained this glory of a king of gods?' he saw the giving that he had practiced when he was a merchant in Bārāṇasī. Then, wondering, 'Where have my descendants been reborn?' he observed: 'My son was reborn as the god Canda, his son as Sūriya, his son as Mātali, and his son as Pañcasikha.' Seeing the rebirth of all of them, he wondered, 'What kind of son does Pañcasikha have?' and saw that his lineage had been cut off. Then he thought, 'This ignoble man, being miserly, neither enjoys his wealth himself nor gives to others. He has cut off my lineage. After death, he will be reborn in hell. I will give him counsel, re-establish my lineage, and arrange for his rebirth in this celestial city.' Summoning Canda and the others, he said, 'Come, let us go to the human world. The miser Kosiya has cut off our lineage. He has destroyed the alms halls and burned them. He neither enjoys his wealth himself nor gives to others. Now, desiring to eat milk-rice, he has entered the forest to cook alone, thinking, "If I cook at home, I will have to give milk-rice to others as well." Let us tame him, make him understand the fruit of giving, and then return. However, if we all beg from him together, he might die on the spot. I will go first and beg for milk-rice, and when I am seated, you come one by one in the guise of brahmins and beg.' Having said this, he himself approached in the guise of a brahmin and asked, 'Sir, which is the road to Bārāṇasī?' Then the miser Kosiya said, 'Are you a madman? You do not even know the road to Bārāṇasī? Why have you come here? Go away from here!'

Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā asuṇanto viya “kiṃ kathesī”ti taṃ upagacchateva. Sopi, “are[P 5.0387], badhira brāhmaṇa, kiṃ ito esi, purato yāhī”ti viravi. Atha naṃ sakko, “bho, kasmā viravasi, dhūmo paññāyati, aggi paññāyati, pāyāso paccati, brāhmaṇānaṃ nimantanaṭṭhānena bhavitabbaṃ, ahampi brāhmaṇānaṃ bhojanakāle thokaṃ labhissāmi, kiṃ maṃ nicchubhasī”ti vatvā “natthettha brāhmaṇānaṃ nimantanaṃ, purato yāhī”ti vutte “tena hi kasmā kujjhasi, tava bhojanakāle thokaṃ labhissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ so “ahaṃ te ekasitthampi na dassāmi, thokaṃ idaṃ mama yāpanamattameva, mayāpi cetaṃ yācitvāva laddhaṃ, tvaṃ aññato āhāraṃ pariyesāhī”ti vatvā bhariyaṃ yācitvā laddhabhāvaṃ sandhāyeva vatvā gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, Sakka, as if he had not heard, said, 'What did you say?' and kept approaching him. Kosiya shouted, 'Hey, you deaf brahmin, why are you coming here? Go on your way!' Then Sakka said, 'Sir, why do you shout? Smoke is visible, fire is visible. Are you cooking milk-rice? This must be a place where brahmins are invited. I too will receive a little at the brahmins' mealtime. Why do you drive me away?' When Kosiya said, 'There is no invitation for brahmins here, go on your way!' Sakka replied, 'If that is so, why are you angry? I will receive a little when you eat.' Then Kosiya said, 'Brahmin, I will not give you even a single mouthful. This milk-rice is only a small amount, just enough for me alone. I too obtained this only by begging. Why not seek food elsewhere?' Saying this, and intending to inform the brahmin that he had obtained it by asking his wife, he spoke this verse:

192.

192.

“Neva kiṇāmi napi vikkiṇāmi, na cāpi me sannicayo ca atthi;

Sukiccharūpaṃ vatidaṃ parittaṃ, patthodano nālamayaṃ duvinna”nti.

“I neither buy nor sell, nor do I have any store of milk-rice; this meager portion was indeed hard-won; this measure of cooked rice is not enough for two.”

Taṃ [M 5.0412] sutvā sakko “ahampi te madhurasaddena ekaṃ silokaṃ kathessāmi, taṃ suṇāhī”ti vatvā “na me tava silokena attho”ti tassa vārentasseva gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing that, Sakka said, “I too will recite a verse for you in a sweet voice; listen to it.” But even as the merchant tried to stop him, saying, “I have no need for your verse,” Sakka spoke these two verses:

193.

193.

“Appamhā appakaṃ dajjā, anumajjhato majjhakaṃ;

Bahumhā bahukaṃ dajjā, adānaṃ nūpapajjati.

“From a little, one should give a little; from a middling amount, a middling amount; from much, one should give much; not giving is not proper.”

194.

194.

“Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samāruha, nekāsī labhate sukha”nti.

“Therefore, I tell you this, Kosiya: give gifts and also enjoy them yourself. Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats alone does not find happiness.”

Tattha [V 5.0384] anumajjhato majjhakanti appamattakampi majjhe chetvā dve koṭṭhāse karitvā ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ datvā tato avasesato anumajjhatopi puna majjhe chetvā eko koṭṭhāso dātabboyeva. Adānaṃ nūpapajjatīti appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā dinnaṃ hotu, adānaṃ nāma na hoti, tampi dānameva mahapphalameva.

There, 'a moderate amount from a small amount' means that having cut even a small quantity in the middle and made two portions, one portion is to be given. Then, from the remainder, having again cut a small portion in the middle, one portion must indeed be given. 'Not giving is not fitting' means that whether little or much is given, it is not called 'not giving'; that too is giving, and it is indeed of great fruit.

So [P 5.0388] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “manāpaṃ te, brāhmaṇa, kathitaṃ, pāyāse pakke thokaṃ labhissasi, nisīdāhī”ti āha. Sakko ekamante nisīdi. Tasmiṃ nisinne cando teneva niyāmena upasaṅkamitvā tatheva kathaṃ pavattetvā tassa vārentasseva gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing his words, the merchant said, “Brahmin, you have spoken pleasing words. When the milk-rice is cooked, you will receive a little. Sit down.” Sakka sat down in a suitable place. After Sakka was seated, the god Canda approached the merchant in the same manner as before, and initiated a conversation in the same way. Even as the merchant was trying to prevent him, Canda spoke these two verses:

195.

195.

“Moghañcassa hutaṃ hoti, moghañcāpi samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, eko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

“His offering is in vain, and his endeavor to accumulate wealth is also in vain, for one who eats a meal alone while a guest is seated.”

196.

196.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samāruha, nekāsī labhate sukha”nti.

“Therefore, I tell you this, Kosiya: give gifts and also enjoy them yourself. Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats alone does not find happiness.”

Tattha samīhitanti dhanuppādanavīriyaṃ.

Therein, 'endeavor' means the effort of acquiring wealth.

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā kicchena kasirena “tena hi nisīda, thokaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. So gantvā sakkassa santike nisīdi. Tato sūriyo teneva nayena upasaṅkamitvā tatheva kathaṃ pavattetvā tassa vārentasseva gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing Canda's words, the merchant, with great difficulty and reluctantly, said, “If that is so, sit down; you will receive a little.” Canda went and sat near Sakka. Then Sūriya approached in the same manner, initiated a conversation in the same way, and spoke these two verses even as the merchant was trying to prevent him:

197.

197.

“Saccañcassa hutaṃ hoti, saccañcāpi samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, neko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

“Fruitful is his offering, and fruitful too is his endeavor to acquire wealth, for one who, when a guest is seated, does not eat his meal alone.”

198.

198.

“Taṃ [M 5.0413] taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samāruha, nekāsī labhate sukha”nti.

“Therefore, I tell you this, Kosiya: give gifts and also enjoy them yourself. Ascend the path of the virtuous; one who does not eat alone finds happiness.”

Tassapi vacanaṃ sutvā kicchena kasirena “tena hi nisīda, thokaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. So gantvā candassa santike nisīdi. Atha naṃ mātali teneva nayena upasaṅkamitvā tatheva kathaṃ pavattetvā tassa vārentasseva imā gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing Sūriya's words also, the merchant reluctantly said, “If that is so, sit down; you will receive a little.” Sūriya went and sat near Canda. Then Mātali approached him in the same manner, initiated a conversation in the same way, and spoke these verses even as the merchant was trying to prevent him:

199.

199.

“Sarañca [V 5.0385] juhati poso, bahukāya gayāya ca;

Doṇe timbarutitthasmiṃ, sīghasote mahāvahe.

“A person approaches and makes offerings at the Sara Lake, and at the Bahukā and Gayā rivers; at the Doṇa and Timbaru fords, in the swift-flowing, great river.”

200.

200.

“Atra cassa hutaṃ hoti, atra cassa samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, neko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

“Here indeed is his offering made, here is his endeavor fulfilled; for one who, when a guest is seated, does not eat his meal alone.”

201.

201.

“Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samāruha, nekāsī labhate sukha”nti.

“This I tell you, Kosiya: give gifts and also enjoy them. Ascend the Noble Path; one who does not eat alone finds happiness.”

Tāsaṃ attho – yo puriso “nāgayakkhādīnaṃ balikammaṃ karomī”ti samuddasoṇḍipokkharaṇīādīsu yaṃ kiñci sarañca upagantvā juhati, tattha balikammaṃ karoti[P 5.0389], tathā bahukāya nadiyā gayāya pokkharaṇiyā doṇanāmake ca timbarunāmake ca titthe sīghasote mahante vārivahe. Atra cassāti yadi atrāpi etesu sarādīsu assa purisassa hutañceva samīhitañca hoti, saphalaṃ sukhudrayaṃ sampajjati. Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ neko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ, ettha vattabbameva natthi, tena taṃ vadāmi – kosiya, dānāni ca dehi, sayañca bhuñja, ariyānaṃ dānābhiratānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ maggaṃ abhiruha. Na hi ekāsī ekova bhuñjamāno sukhaṃ nāma labhatīti.

The meaning of these verses is as follows: A person who intends, “I will perform offering rites to nāgas, yakkhas, and others,” goes to any lake, such as inlets of the sea, ponds, and so on, and makes offerings; there he performs the offering rite. Likewise at the river Gayā with its many streams, at the pond, at the fords named Doṇa and Timbaru, and at the swift-flowing, great watercourse. Regarding ‘Here indeed is his offering made’: if, even here in these lakes and so on, this person’s offering and endeavor occur, it becomes fruitful, resulting in happiness. Regarding ‘one who, when a guest is seated, does not eat his meal alone,’ there is nothing that needs to be said. Therefore, I tell you this, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake yourself; ascend the path of the noble ones, such as the Buddhas, who delight in giving. For indeed, one eating alone does not obtain happiness.

So tassapi vacanaṃ sutvā pabbatakūṭena otthaṭo viya kicchena kasirena “tena hi nisīda, thokaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. Mātali gantvā sūriyassa santike nisīdi. Tato pañcasikho teneva nayena upasaṅkamitvā tatheva kathaṃ pavattetvā tassa vārentasseva gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing his words also, as if crushed by a mountain peak, with difficulty and hardship, he said, “Very well, sit down; you will receive a little.” Mātali went and sat near Sūriya. Then Pañcasikha approached in the same way and, initiating a conversation in the same way, spoke these two verses even as he was being prevented:

202.

202.

“Baḷisañhi [M 5.0414] so nigilati, dīghasuttaṃ sabandhanaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, eko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

“He indeed swallows the hook, the long line with its binding—the one who, when a guest is seated, eats his meal alone.”

203.

203.

“Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samāruha, nekāsī labhate sukha”nti.

“This I tell you, Kosiya: give gifts and also enjoy them. Ascend the Noble Path; one who does not eat alone finds happiness.”

Macchariyakosiyo taṃ sutvā dukkhavedano nitthunanto “tena hi nisīda, thokaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. Pañcasikho gantvā mātalissa santike nisīdi. Iti tesu pañcasu brāhmaṇesu [V 5.0386] nisinnamattesveva pāyāso pacci. Atha naṃ kosiyo uddhanā otāretvā “tumhākaṃ pattāni āharathā”ti āha. Te anuṭṭhāya yathānisinnāva hatthe pasāretvā himavantato māluvapattāni āhariṃsu. Kosiyo tāni disvā “tumhākaṃ etesu pattesu dātabbapāyāso natthi, khadirādīnaṃ pattāni āharathā”ti āha. Te tānipi āhariṃsu. Ekekaṃ pattaṃ yodhaphalakappamāṇaṃ ahosi. So sabbesaṃ dabbiyā pāyāsaṃ adāsi, sabbantimassa dānakālepi ukkhaliyā ūnaṃ na paññāyi, pañcannampi datvā sayaṃ ukkhaliṃ gahetvā nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pañcasikho uṭṭhāya attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā sunakho hutvā tesaṃ purato passāvaṃ karonto agamāsi. Brāhmaṇā attano pāyāsaṃ pattena pidahiṃsu. Kosiyassa hatthapiṭṭhe passāvabindu pati. Brāhmaṇā [P 5.0390] kuṇḍikāhi udakaṃ gahetvā pāyāsaṃ abbhukiritvā bhuñjamānā viya ahesuṃ. Kosiyo “mayhampi udakaṃ detha, hatthaṃ dhovitvā bhuñjissāmī”ti āha. “Tava udakaṃ āharitvā hatthaṃ dhovā”ti. “Mayā tumhākaṃ pāyāso dinno, mayhaṃ thokaṃ udakaṃ dethā”ti. “Mayaṃ piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍakammaṃ nāma na karomā”ti. “Tena hi imaṃ ukkhaliṃ oloketha, hatthaṃ dhovitvā āgamissāmī”ti nadiṃ otari.
