Tasmiṃ khaṇe sunakho ukkhaliṃ passāvassa pūresi. So taṃ passāvaṃ karontaṃ disvā mahantaṃ daṇḍamādāya taṃ tajjento āgacchi. So assājānīyamatto hutvā taṃ anubandhanto nānāvaṇṇo ahosi, kāḷopi hoti setopi suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kabaropi uccopi nīcopi, evaṃ nānāvaṇṇo hutvā macchariyakosiyaṃ anubandhi. So maraṇabhayabhīto brāhmaṇe upasaṅkami. Tepi uppatitvā ākāse ṭhitā. So tesaṃ taṃ iddhiṃ disvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the miserly Kosiya, groaning in distress, said, “Well then, sit down; you will receive a little.” Pañcasikha went and sat near Mātali. As soon as those five brahmins sat down, the milk-rice was cooked. Then Kosiya, taking it off the hearth, said, “Bring your bowls.” Without getting up, just as they were seated, they stretched out their hands and brought māluva leaves from the Himalayas. Seeing these, Kosiya said, “The milk-rice to be given is not for these leaves of yours. Bring leaves of the khadira tree and others.” They brought those as well. Each leaf-bowl was as large as a warrior's shield. He gave milk-rice to all with a ladle, but even when giving to the very last one, the pot did not appear to be diminished. After giving to all five, he himself took the pot and sat down. At that moment, Pañcasikha rose, abandoned his own form, became a dog, and went before them, urinating. The brahmins covered their milk-rice with their leaf-bowls. A drop of urine fell on the back of Kosiya’s hand. The brahmins, taking water from their water pots, sprinkled it over their milk-rice and acted as if they were eating. Kosiya said, “Give me some water too; I will wash my hands and eat.” “Fetch your own water and wash your hands!” “I gave you milk-rice; give me a little water.” “We do not engage in the practice of giving alms in return for alms.” “Then look after this pot; I will wash my hands and return,” and he went down to the river. At that moment, the dog filled the pot with urine. Seeing it urinating, Kosiya took a large stick and came, threatening it. The dog, becoming the size of a thoroughbred horse, pursued him, changing into various colors—it became black, white, golden, dappled, tall, and short—thus appearing in various forms as it pursued the miserly Kosiya. Fearing for his life, he approached the brahmins. They too rose up and stood in the air. Seeing their psychic power, he spoke this verse:

204.

204.

“Uḷāravaṇṇā [M 5.0415] vata brāhmaṇā ime, ayañca vo sunakho kissa hetu;

“Truly, these brahmins are of magnificent appearance, but for what reason is this dog of yours?”

Uccāvacaṃ vaṇṇanibhaṃ vikubbati, akkhātha no brāhmaṇā ke nu tumhe”ti.

“It transforms into various likenesses, high and low. Tell us, O brahmins, who indeed are you?”

Taṃ sutvā sakko devarājā –

Having heard that, Sakka, king of the gods, said:

205.

205.

“Cando ca sūriyo ca ubho idhāgatā, ayaṃ pana mātali devasārathi;

Sakkohamasmi tidasānamindo; Eso ca kho pañcasikhoti vuccatī”ti.

“Canda and Sūriya have both come here, and this is Mātali, the divine charioteer. I am Sakka, lord of the Tidasā gods, and this one is called Pañcasikha.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā tassa yasaṃ vaṇṇento gāthamāha –

Having spoken that verse, extolling his glory, he spoke this verse:

206.

206.

“Pāṇissarā [V 5.0387] mudiṅgā ca, murajālambarāni ca;

Suttamenaṃ pabodhenti, paṭibuddho ca nandatī”ti.

“The sound of hand-clapping music, mudiṅga drums, and muraja and ālambara drums awaken me from sleep; and being awakened, I rejoice.”

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sakka, evarūpaṃ dibbasampattiṃ kinti katvā labhasī”ti pucchi. Sakko “adānasīlā tāva pāpadhammā maccharino devalokaṃ na gacchanti, niraye nibbattantī”ti dassento –

Hearing his words, he asked, “Sakka, by doing what did you attain such divine prosperity?” Sakka, showing that those of an uncharitable nature, of evil ways, and who are miserly do not go to the world of the gods but are reborn in hell, said:

207.

207.

“Ye [P 5.0391] kecime maccharino kadariyā, paribhāsakā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā nirayaṃ vajantī”ti. –

“All those who are stingy, miserly, and revile ascetics and brahmins—having discarded this body right here, at the breakup of the body, they go to hell.”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā dhamme ṭhitānaṃ devalokapaṭilābhaṃ dassetuṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken this verse, to show the attainment of the heavenly world for those established in the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:

208.

208.

“Ye kecime suggatimāsamānā, dhamme ṭhitā saṃyame saṃvibhāge;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ vajantī”ti.

“All those who aspire to a happy destination, established in the Dhamma, in self-restraint, and in sharing—having cast off this body right here, upon the breakup of the body, go to a happy realm.”

Tattha āsamānāti āsīsantā. Ye keci sugatiṃ āsīsanti, sabbe te saṃyamasaṅkhāte dasasīladhamme saṃvibhāgasaṅkhāte dānadhamme ca ṭhitā [M 5.0416] hutvā idha sarīrasaṅkhātaṃ dehaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ vajantīti attho.

Here, ‘āsamānā’ means ‘those who aspire.’ Whoever aspires to a good destination, all of them, being established in the tenfold Dhamma known as restraint and in the Dhamma of giving known as sharing, having cast aside this body here, upon the breakup of that body, go to a good destination—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ vatvā ca pana, “kosiya, na mayaṃ tava santike pāyāsatthāya āgatā, kāruññena pana taṃ anukampamānā āgatāmhā”ti tassa pakāsetuṃ āha –

Having said this, to clarify it to him, he then said to Kosiya: “Kosiya, we have not come to you for milk-rice, but out of compassion, sympathizing with you, we have come.”

209.

209.

“Tvaṃ nosi ñāti purimāsu jātisu, so maccharī rosako pāpadhammo;

Taveva atthāya idhāgatamhā, mā pāpadhammo nirayaṃ gamitthā”ti.

“You were our relative in former lives; now you are miserly, irritable, and of evil character. We have come here for your own benefit, so that you, being of evil character, may not go to hell.”

Tattha soti so tvaṃ. Mā pāpadhammoti ayaṃ amhākaṃ ñāti pāpadhammo mā nirayaṃ agamāti etadatthaṃ āgatamhāti attho.

Here, ‘so’ means ‘that you.’ ‘Mā pāpadhammo’ means ‘may this relative of ours, being of evil character, not go to hell’—we have come for this purpose; this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā kosiyo “atthakāmā kira me, ete maṃ nirayā uddharitvā sagge patiṭṭhāpetukāmā”ti tuṭṭhacitto āha –

Hearing this, Kosiya, with a pleased mind, thought, “Indeed, these beings desire my welfare; they wish to lift me from hell and establish me in heaven,” and said:

210.

210.

“Addhā [V 5.0388] maṃ vo hitakāmā, yaṃ maṃ samanusāsatha;

Sohaṃ tathā karissāmi, sabbaṃ vuttaṃ hitesibhi.

“Indeed, you wish for my welfare, since you instruct me. I will do accordingly, all that is said by those who seek my good.”

211.

211.

“Esāhamajjeva uparamāmi, na cāhaṃ kiñci kareyya pāpaṃ;

Na [P 5.0392] cāpi me kiñci adeyyamatthi, na cāpidatvā udakaṃ pivāmi.

“From this very day, I shall desist, nor shall I do any evil. Nor is there anything of mine that is not to be given, nor will I drink water without having first given.”

212.

212.

“Evañca me dadato sabbakālaṃ, bhogā ime vāsava khīyissanti;

Tato ahaṃ pabbajissāmi sakka, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikānī”ti.

“And as I am giving thus at all times, Vāsava, these possessions of mine will be exhausted. Then, Sakka, I will go forth, having abandoned sensual pleasures according to their limits.”

Tattha manti mama. Voti tumhe. Yaṃ manti yena maṃ samanusāsatha, tena me tumhe hitakāmā. Tathāti yathā vadatha, tatheva karissāmi. Uparamāmīti maccharibhāvato uparamāmi. Adeyyamatthīti ito paṭṭhāya ca mama ālopato upaḍḍhampi adeyyaṃ nāma natthi, na cāpidatvāti udakapasatampi [M 5.0417] cāhaṃ labhitvā adatvā na pivissāmi. Khīyissantīti vikkhīyissanti. Yathodhikānīti vatthukāmakilesakāmavasena yathāṭhitakoṭṭhāsāniyeva.

Here, ‘maṃ’ means ‘of me.’ ‘Vo’ means ‘you.’ The phrase `yaṃ maṃ samanusāsatha` is explained as: ‘Because you instruct me, for that reason you are my well-wishers.’ ‘Tathā’ means ‘as you say, so I shall act accordingly.’ ‘Uparamāmi’ means ‘I desist’ from stinginess. ‘Adeyyamatthi’ means ‘from now on, even half a morsel of food will not be withheld,’ and ‘na cāpidatvā’ means ‘I will not even drink a handful of water that I have received without having given.’ ‘Khīyissanti’ means ‘they will be utterly exhausted.’ ‘Yathodhikāni’ refers to ‘according to the portions as they exist,’ in terms of objective sensual pleasures and defilement sensual pleasures.

Sakko macchariyakosiyaṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā dānaphalaṃ jānāpetvā dhammadesanāya pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā saddhiṃ tehi devanagarameva gato. Macchariyakosiyopi nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājānaṃ anujānāpetvā “gahitagahitabhājanāni pūretvā gaṇhantū”ti yācakānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā tasmiṃ khīṇe nikkhamma himavantato dakkhiṇapasse gaṅgāya ceva ekassa ca jātassarassa antare paṇṇasālaṃ katvā pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhāro tattha ciraṃ vihāsi, jaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā sakkassa āsā saddhā sirī hirīti catasso dhītaro honti. Tā bahuṃ dibbagandhamālaṃ ādāya udakakīḷanatthāya anotattadahaṃ gantvā tattha kīḷitvā manosilātale nisīdiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe nārado nāma brāhmaṇatāpaso tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ divāvihāratthāya gantvā nandanavanacittalatāvanesu divāvihāraṃ katvā pāricchattakapupphaṃ chattaṃ viya chāyatthāya dhārayamāno manosilātalamatthakena attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kañcanaguhaṃ gacchati. Atha tā tassa hatthe taṃ pupphaṃ disvā yāciṃsu. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0393] pakāsento satthā āha –

Sakka, having tamed the miserly Kosiya, made him abandon his miserly ways, taught him the fruit of giving, and established him in the five precepts through a Dhamma discourse, then returned to the city of the gods together with those four deities. The miserly Kosiya, having entered the city and obtained the king's permission, declared, 'Let them fill whatever vessels they bring,' and gave away his wealth to the beggars. When it was exhausted, he departed and, on the southern slope of the Himalayas, between the Ganges and a natural lake, built a leaf hut. Having gone forth and living on forest roots and fruits, he dwelled there for a long time and reached old age. At that time, Sakka had four daughters named Āsā, Saddhā, Sirī, and Hirī. Taking many divine perfumes and garlands, they went to Lake Anotatta to play in the water. After playing, they sat down on the Manosilā stone slab. At that moment, a brahmin ascetic named Nārada, who was traveling to the Tāvatiṃsa realm for his midday rest, after spending the day in the Nandana and Cittalatā groves, was carrying a Pāricchattaka flower like a parasol for shade and was going towards his dwelling, a golden cave, above the Manosilā stone slab. Then, seeing the flower in his hand, they asked him for it. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

213.

213.

“Naguttame girivare gandhamādane, modanti tā devavarābhipālitā;

Athāgamā isivaro sabbalokagū, supupphitaṃ dumavarasākhamādiya.

"On Gandhamādana, the best of mountains, the excellent peak, they rejoice, protected by the best of gods. Then came the lord of sages, who travels through all the worlds, taking a well-blossomed branch of an excellent tree."

214.

214.

“Suciṃ [V 5.0389] sugandhaṃ tidasehi sakkataṃ, pupphuttamaṃ amaravarehi sevitaṃ;

Aladdha maccehiva dānavehi vā, aññatra devehi tadārahaṃ hidaṃ.

"Pure, fragrant, honored by the Thirty, the supreme flower, enjoyed by the best of immortals; it is not obtained by mortals or by dānavas, but except for the gods, it is indeed worthy of them."

215.

215.

“Tato [M 5.0418] catasso kanakattacūpamā, uṭṭhāya nāriyo pamadādhipā muniṃ;

Āsā ca saddhā ca sirī tato hirī, iccabravuṃ nāradadeva brāhmaṇaṃ.

"Then four women with skin like gold, the foremost among women—Āsā, Saddhā, Sirī, and Hirī—stood up and spoke these words to the sage Nārada, the brahmin."

216.

216.

“Sace anuddiṭṭhaṃ tayā mahāmuni, pupphaṃ imaṃ pārichattassa bramhe;

Dadāhi no sabbā gati te ijjhatu, tuvampi no hohi yatheva vāsavo.

"If, O great sage, this flower of the Pāricchattaka tree has not been designated by you, O brahmin, give it to us. May all your wishes be fulfilled; may you be to us just as Vāsava is."

217.

217.

“Taṃ yācamānābhisamekkha nārado, iccabravī saṃkalahaṃ udīrayi;

Na mayhamatthatthi imehi koci naṃ, yāyeva vo seyyasi sā piḷandhathā”ti.

"Nārada, considering the goddesses who were asking, spoke these words, stirring up a quarrel: 'I have no need for these flowers. Whichever among you is the most excellent, let her wear it.'"

Tattha girivareti purimassa vevacanaṃ. Devavarābhipālitāti sakkena rakkhitā. Sabbalokagūti devaloke ca manussaloke ca sabbattha gamanasamattho. Dumavarasākhamādiyāti sākhāya jātattā dumavarasākhanti laddhanāmaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā. Sakkatanti katasakkāraṃ. Amaravarehīti sakkaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Aññatra devehīti ṭhapetvā deve ca iddhimante ca aññehi manussehi vā yakkhādīhi vā aladdhaṃ. Tadārahaṃ hidanti tesaṃyeva hi taṃ arahaṃ anucchavikaṃ. Kanakattacūpamāti kanakūpamā tacā. Uṭṭhāyāti ayyo mālāgandhavilepanādipaṭivirato pupphaṃ na piḷandhissati, ekasmiṃ padese chaḍḍessati, etha taṃ yācitvā pupphaṃ piḷandhissāmāti hatthe pasāretvā yācamānā ekappahāreneva uṭṭhahitvā. Pamadādhipāti pamadānaṃ uttamā. Muninti isiṃ.

There, ‘girivare’ is a synonym for the preceding word. ‘Devavarābhipālitā’ means protected by Sakka. ‘Sabbalokagū’ means capable of going everywhere in both the divine and human worlds. ‘Dumavarasākhamādiyā’ refers to taking a flower that has earned the name ‘branch of an excellent tree’ because it grew on a branch. ‘Sakkataṃ’ means honored. ‘Amaravarehi’ is said in reference to Sakka. ‘Aññatra devehi’ means, apart from gods and those with spiritual power, it was not obtained by other humans or yakkhas, etc. ‘Tadārahaṃ hidaṃ’ means it is indeed worthy and suitable for them. ‘Kanakattacūpamā’ means skin like gold. ‘Uṭṭhāya’ means that the noble one, abstaining from garlands, perfumes, and ointments, will not wear the flower but will discard it in one place. (They thought:) “Come, let us request the flower and wear it.” Stretching out their hands in supplication, they rose up with one movement. ‘Pamadādhipā’ means the foremost of delights. ‘Muni’ means a sage.

Anuddiṭṭhanti “asukassa nāma dassāmī”ti na uddiṭṭhaṃ. Sabbā gati te ijjhatūti sabbā te cittagati ijjhatu, patthitapatthitassa [P 5.0394] lābhī hohīti tassa thulimaṅgalaṃ vadanti. Yatheva vāsavoti yathā amhākaṃ pitā vāsavo icchiticchitaṃ deti, tatheva no tvampi hohīti. Tanti taṃ pupphaṃ. Abhisamekkhāti disvā. Saṃkalahanti nānāgāhaṃ kalahavaḍḍhanaṃ kathaṃ udīrayi. Imehīti imehi pupphehi nāma mayhaṃ attho natthi, paṭivirato ahaṃ [M 5.0419] mālādhāraṇatoti dīpeti. Yāyeva vo seyyasīti yā tumhākaṃ antare jeṭṭhikā. Sā piḷandhathāti sā etaṃ piḷandhatūti attho.

‘Anuddiṭṭhaṃ’ means not designated as “I will give it to such and such.” ‘Sabbā gati te ijjhatū’ means “May all your mental inclinations succeed; may you obtain whatever you desire.” They utter this as a great blessing for him. ‘Yatheva vāsavo’ means “Just as our father Vāsava gives whatever is wished for, so may you be for us.” ‘Taṃ’ refers to that flower. ‘Abhisamekkha’ means having seen. ‘Saṃkalahaṃ’ means he uttered a statement that would increase quarrels due to different views. ‘Imehi’ means “With these flowers I have no need,” showing that “I refrain from wearing garlands.” ‘Yāyeva vo seyyasī’ means whichever among you is the eldest. ‘Sā piḷandhatha’ means “Let her wear this”—this is the meaning.

Tā [V 5.0390] catassopi tassa vacanaṃ sutvā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Having heard his words, all four of those goddesses spoke these verses to the ascetic to inquire about who is superior or inferior:

218.

218.

“Tvaṃ nottamevābhisamekkha nārada, yassicchasi tassā anuppavecchasu;

Yassā hi no nārada tvaṃ padassasi, sāyeva no hehiti seṭṭhasammatā”ti.

"You yourself, O Nārada, should evaluate us to see who is the most excellent, and give it to whomever you wish. For whomever you give it to, Nārada, she alone shall be considered the best among us."

Tattha tvaṃ nottamevāti uttamamahāmuni tvameva no upadhārehi. Tāsaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā nārado tā ālapanto gāthamāha –

There, 'tvaṃ nottameva' means 'you yourself, the supreme great sage, should evaluate us.' Having heard their words, Nārada, calling those goddesses and wishing them to ask Sakka, spoke this verse:

219.

219.

“Akallametaṃ vacanaṃ sugatte, ko brāhmaṇo saṃkalahaṃ udīraye;

Gantvāna bhūtādhipameva pucchatha, sace na jānātha idhuttamādhame”nti.

"This speech of yours is not fitting for me, O fair-bodied ones. What brahmin would stir up a quarrel? Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself; if you do not know the highest and lowest here, go from this place and ask."

Tassattho – bhadde sugatte, idaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ vacanaṃ mama ayuttaṃ, evañhi sati mayā tumhesu ekaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, sesā hīnā karontena kalaho vaḍḍhito bhavissati, ko bāhitapāpo brāhmaṇo kalahaṃ udīraye vaḍḍheyya. Evarūpassa hi kalahavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma ayuttaṃ, tasmā ito gatvā attano pitaraṃ bhūtādhipaṃ sakkameva pucchatha, sace attano uttamaṃ adhamañca na jānāthāti.

The meaning is: “O fair ones, this statement spoken by you is not fitting for me. For if in this way I were to declare one among you the best and the rest inferior, strife would be increased. What brahmin who has banished evil would stir up and increase strife? Indeed, for such a one, increasing strife is improper. Therefore, go from here and ask Sakka, the Lord of Beings, your own father, if you do not know your own superior and inferior.”

Tato satthā gāthamāha –

Thereafter, the goddesses went and asked their father, the Lord of Beings. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:

220.

220.

“Tā nāradena paramappakopitā, udīritā vaṇṇamadena mattā;

Sakāse gantvāna sahassacakkhuno, pucchiṃsu bhūtādhipaṃ kā nu seyyasī”ti.

"They, greatly provoked by Nārada's words and intoxicated with the pride of beauty, went into the presence of the Thousand-eyed One and asked the Lord of Beings, 'Who indeed among us is more excellent?'"

Tattha [M 5.0420] paramappakopitāti pupphaṃ adadantena ativiya kopitā tassa kupitā hutvā. Udīritāti “bhūtādhipameva pucchathā”ti vuttā. Sahassacakkhunoti sakkassa santikaṃ gantvā. Kā nūti amhākaṃ antare katamā uttamāti pucchiṃsu.

Therein, ‘paramappakopitā’ means they were extremely angered, having become angry at him for not giving the flower. ‘Udīritā’ means they were told, “Ask the Lord of Beings.” ‘Sahassacakkhuno’ means having gone into the presence of Sakka. ‘Kā nu’ means they asked, “Which one among us is the best?”

Evaṃ [P 5.0395] pucchitvā ṭhitā –

Sakka, seeing his daughters, asked, 'Who stirred up this quarrel among my dear daughters?' Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:

221.

221.

“Tā disvā āyattamanā purindado, iccabravī devavaro katañjalī;

Sabbāva vo hotha sugatte sādisī, koneva bhadde kalahaṃ udīrayī”ti.

"Seeing them with anxious minds, Purindada, the excellent god to whom other gods offer respect, spoke these words: 'O fair-bodied daughters, may you all be alike. Who indeed, O auspicious ones, stirred up this quarrel here?'"

Tattha [V 5.0391] tā disvāti, bhikkhave, catassopi attano santikaṃ āgatā disvā. Āyattamanāti ussukkamanā byāvaṭacittā. Katañjalīti namassamānāhi devatāhi paggahitañjalī. Sādisīti sabbāva tumhe sādisiyo. Ko nevāti ko nu evaṃ. Kalahaṃ udīrayīti idaṃ nānāgāhaṃ viggahaṃ kathesi vaḍḍhesi.

Therein, ‘tā disvā’ means, O monks, having seen all four who had come into his presence. ‘Āyattamanā’ means eager-minded, with a preoccupied mind. ‘Katañjalī’ means with hands raised in homage by the worshipping deities. ‘Sādisī’ means “All of you are alike.” ‘Ko neva’ means “Who indeed thus?” ‘Kalahaṃ udīrayī’ means “Who spoke of and increased this various grasping and dispute?”

Athassa tā kathayamānā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then, the daughters, wishing to inform their father Sakka clearly, spoke this verse:

222.

222.

“Yo sabbalokaccarito mahāmuni, dhamme ṭhito nārado saccanikkamo;

So nobravi girivare gandhamādane, gantvāna bhūtādhipameva pucchatha;

Sace na jānātha idhuttamādhama”nti.

"The great sage who travels through all worlds, who is established in Dhamma, Nārada of unwavering effort—he spoke to us on the excellent mountain Gandhamādana, saying, 'Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself, if you do not know the highest and lowest here.' Thus did Nārada speak to us."

Tattha saccanikkamoti tathaparakkamo.

There, 'saccanikkamo' means one whose effort is true.

Taṃ sutvā sakko “imā catassopi mayhaṃ dhītarova, sacāhaṃ ‘etāsu ekā guṇasampannā uttamā’ti vakkhāmi, sesā kujjhissanti, na sakkā ayaṃ aḍḍo vinicchinituṃ, imā himavante kosiyatāpasassa santikaṃ pesesāmi, so etāsaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinissatī”ti cintetvā “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ aḍḍaṃ na vinicchinissāmi, himavante kosiyo nāma tāpaso atthi, tassāhaṃ attano sudhābhojanaṃ pesessāmi, so parassa adatvā na bhuñjati, dadanto [M 5.0421] ca vicinitvā guṇavantānaṃ deti, yā tumhesu tassa hatthato bhattaṃ labhissati, sā uttamā bhavissatī”ti ācikkhanto gāthamāha –

Hearing what his daughters said, Sakka thought, 'These four are all my daughters. If I say one of them is virtuous and excellent, the others will be angry. I cannot decide this case. I will send my daughters to the ascetic Kosiya in the Himalayas; he will decide their case.' Thinking, 'I will not decide your dispute. There is an ascetic named Kosiya in the Himalayas. I will send him divine food. He does not eat his food without giving to another, and when giving, he investigates and gives only to the virtuous. Whichever of you receives the divine food from his hand, she will be the best.' Wishing to inform his daughters of this, he spoke a verse:

223.

223.

“Asu brahāraññacaro mahāmuni, nādatvā bhattaṃ varagatte bhuñjati;

Viceyya dānāni dadāti kosiyo,

Yassā hi so dassati sāva seyyasī”ti.

"There is a great sage, a wanderer in the great forest, O fair-bodied ones, who does not eat his meal without giving. Kosiya gives his gifts with discernment; indeed, to whomever he gives, she alone will be the most excellent."

Tattha [P 5.0396] brahāraññadharoti mahāaraññavāsī.

There, 'brahāraññacaro' means a dweller in the great forest.

Iti so tāpasassa santikaṃ pesetvā mātaliṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa santikaṃ pesento anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus sent his daughters to the ascetic's presence, Sakka summoned Mātali and, while sending him to the ascetic's presence, spoke this subsequent verse:

224.

224.

“Asū [V 5.0392] hi yo sammati dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ, gaṅgāya tīre himavantapassani;

Sa kosiyo dullabhapānabhojano, tassa sudhaṃ pāpaya devasārathī”ti.

"Indeed, the one who dwells in the southern direction, on the bank of the Ganges on the slope of the Himalayas—that Kosiya, whose drink and food are difficult to obtain—to him, O divine charioteer Mātali, deliver the nectar."

Tattha sammatīti vasati. Dakkhiṇanti himavantassa dakkhiṇāya disāya. Passanīti passe.

There, 'sammati' means dwells. 'Dakkhiṇaṃ' means in the southern direction of the Himalayas. 'Passani' means on the slope.

Tato satthā āha –

Then the Teacher said:

225.

225.

“Sa mātalī devavarena pesito, sahassayuttaṃ abhiruyha sandanaṃ;

Sukhippameva upagamma assamaṃ, adissamāno munino sudhaṃ adā”ti.

"That Mātali, sent by the excellent god, having mounted the chariot yoked with a thousand horses, very quickly approached the hermitage and, remaining unseen, gave the nectar to the sage."

Tattha adissamānoti, bhikkhave, so mātali devarājassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā taṃ assamaṃ gantvā adissamānakāyo hutvā tassa sudhaṃ adāsi, dadamāno ca rattiṃ padhānamanuyuñjitvā paccūsasamaye aggiṃ paricaritvā vibhātāya rattiyā udentaṃ sūriyaṃ namassamānassa ṭhitassa tassa hatthe sudhābhojanapātiṃ ṭhapesi.

Therein, ‘adissamāno’ means, O monks, that Mātali, having accepted the command of the king of devas, went to that hermitage and, becoming invisible, gave him the nectar. And while giving it, he placed the bowl of nectar-food in the hands of that one who, after striving through the night and tending the fire at dawn, was standing paying homage to the rising sun as the night grew light.

Kosiyo [M 5.0422] taṃ gahetvā ṭhitakova gāthādvayamāha –

Kosiya, taking it, spoke two verses while standing there:

226.

226.

“Udaggihuttaṃ upatiṭṭhato hi me, pabhaṅkaraṃ lokatamonuduttamaṃ;

Sabbāni bhūtāni adhicca vāsavo;

Ko neva me pāṇisu kiṃ sudhodahi.

“Indeed, for me who stands attending to the sacred offering, to the light-maker, the supreme dispeller of the world’s darkness—is it Vāsava, who has surpassed all beings? Who indeed has placed this nectar in my hands?”

227.

227.

“Saṅkhūpamaṃ setamatulyadassanaṃ, suciṃ sugandhaṃ piyarūpamabbhutaṃ;

Adiṭṭhapubbaṃ mama jātu cakkhubhi, kā devatā pāṇisu kiṃ sudhodahī”ti.

“Like a conch shell, white, of incomparable appearance, pure, fragrant, of pleasing form, and wonderful—never before seen by my eyes—what deity has placed what nectar in my hands?”

Tattha udaggihuttanti udakaaggihuttaṃ paricaritvā aggisālato nikkhamma paṇṇasāladvāre ṭhatvā pabhaṅkaraṃ lokatamonudaṃ uttamaṃ ādiccaṃ upatiṭṭhato mama sabbāni bhūtāni adhicca atikkamitvā vattamāno vāsavo nu kho evaṃ mama pāṇīsu kiṃ sudhaṃ kiṃ nāmetaṃ odahi. “Saṅkhūpama”ntiādīhi ṭhitakova sudhaṃ vaṇṇeti.

Therein, ‘udaggihuttaṃ’ refers to me who, having tended the water-and-fire ritual and emerged from the fire-hall, stood at the door of the leaf-hut worshipping the sun—the supreme light-maker, dispeller of the world’s darkness. The meaning is: ‘Is it indeed Vāsava, who exists surpassing and transcending all beings, who has thus placed in my hands what nectar, what is this thing?’ With the words ‘like a conch shell’ and so on, while still standing, he describes the nectar.

Tato [P 5.0397] mātali āha –

Then Mātali said:

228.

228.

“Ahaṃ [V 5.0393] mahindena mahesi pesito, sudhābhihāsiṃ turito mahāmuni;

Jānāsi maṃ mātali devasārathi, bhuñjassu bhattuttama mābhivārayi.

“I, O great sage, was swiftly sent by the great Indra; I have brought nectar. Know me as Mātali, the divine charioteer. Partake of this excellent food; do not refuse it.”

229.

229.

“Bhuttā ca sā dvādasa hanti pāpake, khudaṃ pipāsaṃ aratiṃ daraklamaṃ;

Kodhūpanāhañca vivādapesuṇaṃ, sītuṇha tandiñca rasuttamaṃ ida”nti.

“Once consumed, it destroys twelve evils: hunger, thirst, discontent, distress and fatigue, anger, hostility, strife, slander, cold, heat, and lethargy—this is the supreme essence.”

Tattha sudhābhihāsinti imaṃ sudhābhojanaṃ tuyhaṃ abhihariṃ. Jānāsīti jānāhi maṃ tvaṃ, ahaṃ mātali nāma devasārathīti attho. Mābhivārayīti na bhuñjāmīti appaṭikkhipitvā bhuñja mā papañca kari. Pāpaketi ayañhi [M 5.0423] sudhā bhuttā dvādasa pāpadhamme hanati. Khudanti paṭhamaṃ tāva chātabhāvaṃ hanati, dutiyaṃ pānīyapipāsaṃ, tatiyaṃ ukkaṇṭhitaṃ, catutthaṃ kāyadarathaṃ, pañcamaṃ kilantabhāvaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ kodhaṃ, sattamaṃ upanāhaṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ vivādaṃ, navamaṃ pesuṇaṃ, dasamaṃ sītaṃ, ekādasamaṃ uṇhaṃ, dvādasamaṃ tandiṃ ālasiyabhāvaṃ, idaṃ rasuttamaṃ uttamarasaṃ sudhābhojanaṃ ime dvādasa pāpadhamme hanati.

Therein, ‘sudhābhihāsiṃ’ means ‘I have brought this nectar-food to you.’ ‘Jānāsi’ means ‘Know me; I am Mātali, the divine charioteer.’ ‘Mābhivārayi’ means ‘Eat without rejecting it, saying, “I will not eat”; do not delay.’ ‘Pāpake’ means ‘For this nectar, when eaten, destroys twelve evil qualities.’ It destroys: first, hunger; second, thirst; third, boredom; fourth, bodily distress; fifth, weariness; sixth, anger; seventh, malice; eighth, quarrels; ninth, tale-bearing; tenth, cold; eleventh, heat; twelfth, lethargy and laziness. This supreme essence, this nectar-food of the finest taste, destroys these twelve evil qualities.

Taṃ sutvā kosiyo attano vatasamādānaṃ āvikaronto –

Having heard that, Kosiya, revealing his undertaking of a vow, said:

230.

230.

“Na kappatī mātali mayha bhuñjituṃ, pubbe adatvā iti me vatuttamaṃ;

Na cāpi ekāsnamariyapūjitaṃ, asaṃvibhāgī ca sukhaṃ na vindatī”ti. –

“It is not proper for me, Mātali, to eat without first giving; this is my supreme vow. Eating alone is not praised by the noble ones, and one who does not share does not find happiness.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā, “bhante, tumhehi parassa adatvā bhojane kaṃ dosaṃ disvā idaṃ vataṃ samādinna”nti mātalinā puṭṭho āha –

Having spoken the verse, when asked by Mātali, ‘Venerable sir, what fault did you see in eating without giving to others that you undertook this vow?’ he said:

231.

231.

“Thīghātakā ye cime pāradārikā, mittadduno ye ca sapanti subbate;

Sabbe ca te maccharipañcamādhamā, tasmā adatvā udakampi nāsniye.

“Those who harass women; those who frequent others' wives; those who betray friends; and those who revile the virtuous—all these, with the miserly as the fifth, are the lowest of men. Therefore, without giving, I shall not consume even water.”

232.

232.

“Sohitthiyā [P 5.0398] vā purisassa vā pana, dassāmi dānaṃ vidusampavaṇṇitaṃ;

Saddhā vadaññū idha vītamaccharā, bhavanti hete sucisaccasammatā”ti.

“Whether to a woman or a man, I shall give a gift praised by the wise. Those here who are faithful, generous, and free from stinginess are indeed regarded as pure and true.”

Tattha pubbeti paṭhamaṃ adatvā, atha vā iti me pubbe vatuttamaṃ idaṃ pubbeva mayā vataṃ samādinnanti dasseti. Na cāpi ekāsnamariyapūjitanti ekakassa asanaṃ na ariyehi buddhādīhi [V 5.0394] pūjitaṃ. Sukhanti dibbamānusikaṃ sukhaṃ na labhati. Thīghātakāti itthighātakā. Ye cimeti ye ca ime. Sapantīti akkosanti. Subbateti dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇe. Maccharipañcamāti maccharī pañcamo etesanti maccharipañcamā. Adhamāti ime pañca adhamā nāma. Tasmāti yasmā ahaṃ pañcamaadhamabhāvabhayena adatvā udakampi nāsniye na [M 5.0424] paribhuñjissāmīti imaṃ vataṃ samādiyiṃ. Sohitthiyā vāti so ahaṃ itthiyā vā. Vidusampavaṇṇitanti vidūhi paṇḍitehi buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ. Sucisaccasammatāti ete okappaniyasaddhāya samannāgatā vadaññū vītamaccharā purisā sucī ceva uttamasammatā ca hontīti attho.

There, 'pubbe' means not having given first; or it shows, 'this was my former, supreme vow, undertaken by me before.' 'Na cāpi ekāsnamariyapūjitaṃ' means eating alone is not honored by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas. 'Sukhaṃ' means one does not obtain divine or human happiness. 'Thīghātakā' means killers of women. 'Ye cime' means 'and these.' 'Sapanti' means they revile. 'Subbate' refers to righteous ascetics and brahmins. 'Maccharipañcamā' means the miserly is the fifth among them. 'Adhamā' means these five are called the lowest. 'Tasmā' means 'therefore, out of fear of becoming the fifth lowest, I undertook this vow: I will not consume even water without giving.' 'Sohitthiyā vā' means 'I (so ahaṃ) to a woman or...' 'Vidusampavaṇṇitaṃ' means praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas. 'Sucisaccasammatā' means these men, endowed with unwavering faith, generous, free from stinginess, are both pure and regarded as supreme. That is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā mātali dissamānakāyena aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tā catasso devakaññāyo catuddisaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu, sirī pācīnadisāya aṭṭhāsi, āsā dakkhiṇadisāya, saddhā pacchimadisāya, hirī uttaradisāya. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Hearing that, Mātali stood there with a visible body. At that moment, those four celestial maidens stood in the four directions: Sirī stood in the east, Āsā in the south, Saddhā in the west, and Hirī in the north. To explain that matter, the Teacher said:

233.

233.

“Ato matā devavarena pesitā, kaññā catasso kanakattacūpamā;

Āsā ca saddhā ca sirī tato hirī, taṃ assamaṃ āgamu yattha kosiyo.

“Then, permitted and sent by the king of devas, four maidens with skin like gold came; Āsā and Saddhā and Sirī, then Hirī, they came to the hermitage where Kosiya dwelt.”

234.

234.

“Tā disvā sabbo paramappamodito, subhena vaṇṇena sikhārivaggino;

Kaññā catasso caturo catuddisā, iccabravī mātalino ca sammukhā.

“Seeing them, he was filled with supreme joy; looking at the four beautiful maidens in the four directions who were like the flame of fire, he spoke thus in the presence of Mātali.”

235.

235.

“Purimaṃ disaṃ kā tvaṃ pabhāsi devate, alaṅkatā tāravarāva osadhī;

Pucchāmi taṃ kañcanavelliviggahe, ācikkha me tvaṃ katamāsi devatā.

“Who are you, O deity, shining forth from the eastern direction, adorned like the finest star, the morning star? I ask you, O one with a form like a golden vine, tell me, which deity are you?”

236.

236.

“Sirāha [P 5.0399] devī manujehi pūjitā, apāpasattūpanisevinī sadā;

Sudhāvivādena tavantimāgatā, taṃ maṃ sudhāya varapañña bhājaya.

“I am the goddess Sirī, revered by humans, always attending upon virtuous beings. Having come to your presence on account of a dispute over nectar, O one of excellent wisdom, grant me a portion of the nectar.”

237.

237.

“Yassāhamicchāmi sudhaṃ mahāmuni, so sabbakāmehi naro pamodati;

Sirīti maṃ jānahi jūhatuttama, taṃ maṃ sudhāya varapañña bhājayā”ti.

“For whomever I favor, O great sage, that person rejoices with all desires fulfilled. Know me as Sirī, O supreme worshipper. O one of excellent wisdom, grant me a portion of the nectar.”

Tattha [M 5.0425] atoti tato. Matāti anumatā, atha devavarena anumatā ceva pesitā cāti attho. Sabbo paramappamoditoti anavaseso hutvā atipamodito. “Sāma”ntipi pāṭho, tā devatā [V 5.0395] sāmaṃ disvāti attho. Caturoti caturā. Ayameva vā pāṭho, cāturiyena samannāgatāti attho. Tāravarāti tārakānaṃ varā. Kañcanavelliviggaheti kañcanarūpasadisasarīre. Sirāhāti sirī ahaṃ. Tavantimāgatāti tava santikaṃ āgatā. Bhājayāti yathā maṃ sudhā bhajati, tathā karohi, sudhaṃ me dehīti attho. Jānahīti jāna. Jūhatuttamāti aggiṃ juhantānaṃ uttama.

There, 'ato' means 'from that.' 'Matā' means 'approved,' or the meaning is 'both approved and sent by the king of devas.' 'Sabbo paramappamodito' means being exceedingly delighted without remainder. There is also the reading 'Sāmaṃ,' meaning 'having seen the deities themselves.' 'Caturo' means 'clever.' Or, this very reading means 'endowed with cleverness.' 'Tāravarā' means the best of stars. 'Kañcanavelliviggahe' refers to a body like a golden form. 'Sirāhā' means 'I am Sirī.' 'Tavantimāgatā' means 'having come to your presence.' 'Bhājayā' means 'act so that nectar may be shared with me; give me nectar.' 'Jānahī' means 'know.' 'Jūhatuttama' means 'the best among those who offer to the fire.'

Taṃ sutvā kosiyo āha –

Having heard that, Kosiya said:

238.

238.

“Sippena vijjācaraṇena buddhiyā, narā upetā paguṇā sakammunā;

Tayā vihīnā na labhanti kiñcanaṃ, tayidaṃ na sādhu yadidaṃ tayā kataṃ.

“People endowed with skill, knowledge, conduct, and intelligence, proficient in their own work, gain happiness. Deprived of you, they gain nothing. This that has been done by you is not good.”

239.

239.

“Passāmi posaṃ alasaṃ mahagghasaṃ, sudukkulīnampi arūpimaṃ naraṃ;

Tayānugutto siri jātimāmapi, peseti dāsaṃ viya bhogavā sukhī.

“I see a man who is lazy, a glutton, of very low birth, and of unlovely appearance; yet protected by you, O Sirī, being wealthy and happy, he employs even one of noble birth as if he were a slave.”

240.

240.

“Taṃ taṃ asaccaṃ avibhajjaseviniṃ, jānāmi mūḷhaṃ vidurānupātiniṃ;

Na tādisī arahati āsanūdakaṃ, kuto sudhā gaccha na mayha ruccasī”ti.

“I know you to be false, one who associates indiscriminately, a fool who does not follow the wise. Such a one deserves neither seat nor water; how then nectar? Go, you do not please me.”

Tattha sippenāti hatthiassarathadhanusippādinā. Vijjācaraṇenāti vedattayasaṅkhātāya vijjāya ceva sīlena ca. Paguṇā sakammunāti attano purisakārena padhānaguṇasamannāgatā. Kiñcananti kiñci appamattakampi yasaṃ vā sukhaṃ vā na labhanti. Yadidanti yaṃ etaṃ issariyatthāya sippāni [M 5.0426] uggaṇhitvā carantānaṃ [P 5.0400] tayā vekallaṃ kataṃ, taṃ te na sādhu. Arūpimanti virūpaṃ. Tayānuguttoti tayā anurakkhito. Jātimāmapīti jātisampannampi sippavijjācaraṇabuddhikammehi sampannampi. Pesetīti pesanakārakaṃ karoti. Taṃ tanti tasmā taṃ. Asaccanti sabhāvasaṅkhāte sacce avattanatāya asaccaṃ uttamabhāvarahitaṃ. Avibhajjasevininti avibhajitvā yuttāyuttaṃ ajānitvā sippādisampannepi itarepi sevamānaṃ. Vidurānupātininti paṇḍitānupātiniṃ paṇḍite pātetvā pothetvā viheṭhetvā caramānaṃ. Kuto sudhāti tādisāya nigguṇāya kuto sudhābhojanaṃ, na me ruccasi, gaccha mā idha tiṭṭhāti.

There, 'sippenāti' means by skills such as those involving elephants, horses, chariots, and archery. 'Vijjācaraṇenāti' refers to knowledge, namely the three Vedas, and also to virtue. 'Paguṇā sakkammunāti' means being endowed with the chief quality through one's own effort. 'Kiñcananti' means they do not gain even the slightest bit of fame or happiness. 'Yadidaṃ' (and 'tayidaṃ na sādhu') means: 'That this deficiency was created by you for those who go about having learned skills for the sake of sovereignty—that is not good of you.' 'Arūpimanti' means deformed. 'Tayānuguttoti' means protected by you. 'Jātimāmapīti' means even one who is of noble birth and endowed with skills, knowledge, virtue, and intelligent actions. 'Pesetīti' means one makes him a messenger. 'Taṃ tanti' means therefore that. 'Asaccanti' means untrue, not conforming to truth in its characteristic sense, lacking the highest state. 'Avibhajjasevininti' means associating indiscriminately, not discerning what is suitable or unsuitable, with those who are skilled and with others. 'Vidurānupātiniṃ' means one who causes the wise to fall, one who goes about felling, striking, and harassing them. 'Kuto sudhāti' means 'Whence the partaking of nectar for such a worthless one? I do not like you, go away, do not stay here.'

Sā tena paṭikkhittā tatthevantaradhāyi. Tato so āsāya saddhiṃ sallapanto āha –

She, rejected by him, disappeared right there. Then, conversing with Āsā, he said:

241.

241.

“Kā [V 5.0396] sukkadāṭhā paṭimukkakuṇḍalā, cittaṅgadā kambuvimaṭṭhadhārinī;

Osittavaṇṇaṃ paridayha sobhasi, kusaggirattaṃ apiḷayha mañjariṃ.

“Who are you with white teeth, wearing earrings, adorned with variegated armlets, wearing smooth gold ornaments? Clad in a pure white garment, you shine, having adorned yourself with a crimson cluster of blossoms like the tip of kusa grass.”

242.

242.

“Migīva bhantā saracāpadhārinā, virādhitā mandamiva udikkhasi;

Ko te dutīyo ida mandalocane, na bhāyasi ekikā kānane vane”ti.

“Like a doe, trembling and missed by one bearing a bow and arrow, you look as if smiling. Who is your companion here, O one with gentle eyes? Do you not fear being alone in the great forest?”

Tattha cittaṅgadāti citrehi aṅgadehi samannāgatā. Kambuvimaṭṭhadhārinīti karaṇapariniṭṭhitena vimaṭṭhasuvaṇṇālaṅkāradhārinī. Osittavaṇṇanti avasittaudakadhāravaṇṇaṃ dibbadukūlaṃ. Paridayhāti nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca. Kusaggirattanti kusatiṇaggisikhāvaṇṇaṃ. Apiḷayha mañjarinti sapallavaṃ asokakaṇṇikaṃ kaṇṇe piḷandhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Saracāpadhārināti luddena. Virādhitāti viraddhapahārā. Mandamivāti yathā sā migī bhītā vanantare ṭhatvā taṃ mandaṃ mandaṃ oloketi, evaṃ olokesi.

There, 'cittaṅgadāti' means adorned with variegated armlets. 'Kambuvimaṭṭhadhārinīti' means wearing polished gold ornaments crafted with skill. 'Osittavaṇṇanti' means a divine fine cloth the color of a stream of poured water. 'Paridayhāti' means having worn it as a lower garment and also as an upper garment. 'Kusaggirattanti' means the color of the flame-tip of a kusa grass blade. 'Apiḷayha mañjarinti' means 'having placed in her ear an Asoka ear-ornament with sprouts.' 'Saracāpadhārinā' means by a hunter. 'Virādhitāti' means struck by a blow. 'Mandamivāti' means 'just as that doe, frightened in the forest, stands and gazes at him slowly, slowly, so do you gaze.'

Tato [M 5.0427] āsā āha –

Then Āsā said:

243.

243.

“Na me dutīyo idha matthi kosiya, masakkasārappabhavamhi devatā;

Āsā sudhāsāya tavantimāgatā, taṃ maṃ sudhāya varapañña bhājayā”ti.

“I have no companion here, O Kosiya; I am a deity born in the realm of Masakkasāra. I am Āsā, come to your presence with a desire for nectar. O one of excellent wisdom, grant me a portion of the nectar.”

Tattha masakkasārappabhavāti tāvatiṃsabhavane sambhavā.

There, 'masakkasārappabhavā' means arisen in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

Taṃ [P 5.0401] sutvā kosiyo “tvaṃ kira yo te ruccati, tassa āsāphalanipphādanena āsaṃ desi, yo te na ruccati, tassa na desi, natthi tayā samā patthitatthavināsikā”ti dīpento āha –

Hearing this, Kosiya, revealing his meaning, said: 'It seems you grant hope to whomever you like by fulfilling the fruit of their hope, but you do not grant it to whomever you do not like. There is no one like you for destroying what is desired.'

244.

244.

“Āsāya yanti vāṇijā dhanesino, nāvaṃ samāruyha parenti aṇṇave;

Te tattha sīdanti athopi ekadā, jīnādhanā enti vinaṭṭhapābhatā.

'Out of hope, merchants seeking wealth go forth; having boarded a ship, they cross the ocean. Some sink there, or else, at times, they return with their wealth lost and their capital destroyed.'

245.

245.

“Āsāya khettāni kasanti kassakā, vapanti bījāni karontupāyaso;

Ītīnipātena avuṭṭhitāya vā, na kiñci vindanti tato phalāgamaṃ.

'Out of hope, farmers plow their fields, sowing seeds and doing their work with care; but through calamities or drought, they gain no harvest from that.'

246.

246.

“Athattakārāni [V 5.0397] karonti bhattusu, āsaṃ purakkhatvā narā sukhesino;

Te bhatturatthā atigāḷhitā puna, disā panassanti aladdha kiñcanaṃ.

'Then, men seeking happiness perform personal services for their lords, placing hope before them; yet, being greatly oppressed for their lord's sake, they flee in all directions, having gained nothing.'

247.

247.

“Hitvāna dhaññañca dhanañca ñātake, āsāya saggādhimanā sukhesino;

Tapanti lūkhampi tapaṃ cirantaraṃ, kumaggamāruyha parenti duggatiṃ.

'Having abandoned grain, wealth, and relatives, aspiring for heaven and seeking happiness, they practice even harsh austerities for a very long time; but having taken a wrong path, they fill the states of misery.'

248.

248.

“Āsā [M 5.0428] visaṃvādikasammatā ime, āse sudhāsaṃ vinayassu attani;

Na tādisī arahati āsanūdakaṃ, kuto sudhā gaccha na mayha ruccasī”ti.

'Hope is considered deceptive to these beings. O Hope, banish from yourself the desire for nectar. Such a one as you does not deserve even a seat or water; how much less nectar? Go, you do not please me.'

Tattha parentīti pakkhandanti. Jīnādhanāti jīnadhanā. Iti tava vasena eke sampajjanti eke vipajjanti, natthi tayā sadisā pāpadhammāti vadati. Karontupāyasoti taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ upāyena karonti. Ītīnipātenāti visamavātamūsikasalabhasukapāṇakasetaṭṭhikarogādīnaṃ sassupaddavānaṃ aññataranipātena vā. Tatoti tato sassato te kiñci phalaṃ na vindanti, tesampi āsacchedanakammaṃ tvameva karosīti vadati. Athattakārānīti yuddhabhūmīsu purisakāre. Āsaṃ purakkhatvāti issariyāsaṃ purato katvā. Bhatturatthāti sāmino atthāya. Atigāḷitāti paccatthikehi atipīḷitā viluttasāpateyyā ddhastasenavāhanā hutvā. Panassantīti palāyanti. Aladdha kiñcananti kiñci issariyaṃ alabhitvā[P 5.0402]. Iti etesampi issariyālābhaṃ tvameva karosīti vadati. Saggādhimanāti saggaṃ adhigantumanā. Lūkhanti nirojaṃ pañcatapādikaṃ kāyakilamathaṃ. Cirantaranti cirakālaṃ. Āsā visaṃvādikasammatā imeti evaṃ ime sattā saggāsāya duggatiṃ gacchanti, tasmā tvaṃ āsā nāma visaṃvādikasammatā visaṃvādikāti saṅkhaṃ gatā. Āseti taṃ ālapati.

Here, 'parenti' means 'they rush forward.' 'Jīnādhanā' means 'whose wealth is spent.' Thus he says: 'By your influence some succeed and some perish; there is no evil quality like you.' 'Karontupāyaso' means 'they perform this and that task by some means.' 'Ītīnipātena' means 'by the occurrence of one or another of the crop afflictions, such as unseasonable winds, mice, locusts, parrots, insects, blight, and other diseases.' 'Tato' means 'from that crop they gain no fruit'; he says, 'You alone perform the act of cutting off even their hope.' 'Athattakārāni' means 'manly deeds on battlefields.' 'Āsaṃ purakkhatvā' means 'having put the hope for sovereignty foremost.' 'Bhatturatthā' means 'for the master's sake.' 'Atigāḷitā' means 'being extremely oppressed by enemies, with their property plundered and their army and vehicles destroyed.' 'Panassanti' means 'they flee.' 'Aladdha kiñcanaṃ' means 'having obtained no sovereignty.' Thus he says, 'You alone cause even their failure to gain sovereignty.' 'Saggādhimanā' means 'with a mind to attain heaven.' 'Lūkhaṃ' means 'the dry bodily mortification, such as the five-fire austerity.' 'Cirantaraṃ' means 'for a long time.' 'Āsā visaṃvādikasammatā ime' means 'thus these beings go to a bad destination through hope for heaven; therefore you, O Hope, are considered deceptive, you have acquired the designation "deceptive."' 'Āse' means 'he addresses her.'

Sāpi tena paṭikkhittā antaradhāyi. Tato saddhāya saddhiṃ sallapanto gāthamāha –

Rejected by him, she too disappeared. Then, conversing with Saddhā, he spoke a verse:

249.

249.

“Daddallamānā yasasā yasassinī, jighaññanāmavhayanaṃ disaṃ pati;

Pucchāmi taṃ kañcanavelliviggahe, ācikkha me tvaṃ katamāsi devate”ti.

'Shining with glory, O glorious one, facing the direction called by the name "rear," I ask you, O one with a form like a golden creeper: tell me, what deity are you?'

Tattha daddallamānāti jalamānā. Jighaññanāmavhayananti aparāti ca pacchimāti ca evaṃ jighaññena lāmakena nāmena vuccamānaṃ disaṃ pati daddallamānā tiṭṭhasi.

Here, 'daddallamānā' means 'blazing.' 'Jighaññanāmavhayanaṃ' refers to the western direction. Thus, 'you stand blazing, facing the direction that is called by the low, despicable name "jighañña".'

Tato [M 5.0429][V 5.0398] sā gāthamāha –

Then she spoke a verse:

250.

250.

“Saddhāha devī manujehi pūjitā, apāpasattūpanisevinī sadā;

Sudhāvivādena tavanti māgatā, taṃ maṃ sudhāya varapañña bhājayā”ti.

'I am the goddess Saddhā, honored by humans, always associating with those who are not evil. I have come to your presence because of the dispute about nectar. Therefore, O one of excellent wisdom, grant me a portion of the nectar.'

Tattha saddhāti yassa kassaci vacanapattiyāyanā sāvajjāpi hoti anavajjāpi. Pūjitāti anavajjakoṭṭhāsavasena pūjitā. Apāpasattūpanisevinīti anavajjasaddhāya ca ekantapattiyāyanusabhāvāra paresupi pattiyāyanavidahanasamatthāya devatāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.

Here, 'saddhā' is the acceptance of anyone's words, which can be either blameworthy or blameless. 'Pūjitā' means honored by way of its blameless aspect. 'Apāpasattūpanisevinī' is a name for this deity because of her nature of absolute acceptance with regard to blameless faith, and because she is capable of instilling acceptance in others as well.

Athaṃ naṃ kosiyo “ime sattā yassa kassaci vacanaṃ saddahitvā taṃ taṃ karontā kattabbato akattabbameva bahutaraṃ karonti, taṃ sabbaṃ tayā kāritaṃ nāma hotī”ti vatvā evamāha –

Then Kosiya, saying to her, 'These beings, believing the words of anyone, in doing various deeds, do much more of what should not be done than what should be done; all of that is said to be caused by you,' spoke thus:

251.

251.

“Dānaṃ damaṃ cāgamathopi saṃyamaṃ, ādāya saddhāya karonti hekadā;

Theyyaṃ [P 5.0403] musā kūṭamathopi pesuṇaṃ, karonti heke puna viccutā tayā.

'Out of faith, some sometimes practice generosity, self-control, relinquishment, and also restraint; yet others, led astray by you, again commit theft, lying, fraud, and also slander.'

252.

252.

“Bhariyāsu poso sadisīsu pekkhavā, sīlūpapannāsu patibbatāsupi;

Vinetvāna chandaṃ kulitthirāsupi, karoti saddhaṃ puna kumbhadāsiyā.

'A man with craving for his wives—who are his equals, endowed with virtue, and devoted to their husbands—having given up desire even for women of good family, again places faith in the words of a water-carrier slave.'

253.

253.

“Tvameva saddhe paradārasevinī, pāpaṃ karosi kusalampi riñcasi;

Na tādisī arahati āsanūdakaṃ, kuto sudhā gaccha na mayha ruccasī”ti.

'You yourself, O Saddhā, are the cause for frequenting others' wives; you commit evil and abandon what is wholesome. Such a one as you does not deserve even a seat or water; how much less nectar? Go, you do not please me.'

Tattha dānanti dasavatthukaṃ puññacetanaṃ. Damanti indriyadamanaṃ. Cāganti deyyadhammapariccāgaṃ. Saṃyamanti sīlaṃ. Ādāya saddhāyāti “etāni dānādīni mahānisaṃsāni kattabbānī”ti vadataṃ vacanaṃ saddhāya ādiyitvāpi [M 5.0430] karonti ekadā. Kūṭanti tulākūṭādikaṃ vā gāmakūṭādikaṃ kammaṃ vā. Karonti heketi eke manussā evarūpesu nāma kālesu imesañca atthāya theyyādīni kattabbānīti kesañci vacanaṃ saddahitvā etānipi karonti. Puna viccutā tayāti puna tayā visuttā sāvajjadukkhavipākānetāni na kattabbānīti vadataṃ vacanaṃ apattiyāyitvāpi karonti. Iti tava vasena sāvajjampi anavajjampi kareyyāsi vadati.

Here, 'dāna' refers to the volition for merit based on the ten grounds. 'Dama' is the taming of the sense faculties. 'Cāga' is the relinquishment of things fit to be given. 'Saṃyama' is virtue. 'Ādāya saddhāya' means: 'having accepted with faith the words of those who say, "These acts of generosity and so forth have great results and should be done," they perform them at times.' 'Kūṭa' refers to deceitful acts like cheating with scales or village fraud and such. 'Karonti heke' means: 'some people, believing the words of certain individuals who say, "At such times and for these purposes, theft and the like should be done," perform these acts as well.' 'Puna viccutā tayā' means 'again, being led astray by you'—that is, failing to believe the words of those who say, "These actions, which are blameworthy and have painful results, should not be done," they still perform them. Thus, he says, 'Through your influence, one may do both blameworthy and blameless deeds.'

Sadisīsūti [V 5.0399] jātigottasīlādīhi sadisīsu. Pekkhavāti pekkhā vuccati taṇhā, sataṇhoti attho. Chandanti chandarāgaṃ. Karoti saddhanti kumbhadāsiyāpi vacane saddhaṃ karoti, tassā “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ idaṃ nāma upakāraṃ karissāmī”ti vadantiyā pattiyāyitvā kulitthiyopi chaḍḍetvā tameva paṭisevati, asukā nāma tumhesu paṭibaddhacittāti kumbhadāsiyāpi vacane saddhaṃ katvāva paradāraṃ sevati. Tvameva saddhe paradārasevinīti yasmā taṃ taṃ pattiyāyitvā tava vasena paradāraṃ sevanti pāpaṃ karonti kusalaṃ jahanti, tasmā tvameva paradārasevinī tvaṃ pāpāni karosi, kusalampi riñcasi, natthi tayā samā lokavināsikā pāpadhammā, gaccha na me ruccasīti.

Here, 'sadisīsu' means 'similar in birth, clan, virtue, and so on.' 'Pekkhavā' means 'one with craving,' for 'pekkhā' refers to craving. 'Chandaṃ' means 'lustful desire.' 'Karoti saddhaṃ' means 'he places faith even in the words of a water-carrier slave'; believing her when she says, 'I will do such and such a favor for you,' he abandons even women of good family and consorts with her alone. Or, it is by placing faith in the words of a water-carrier slave who says, 'Such-and-such a woman is devoted to you,' that he consorts with another's wife. 'Tvameva saddhe paradārasevinī' means: 'because, believing this and that, by your influence they consort with others' wives, commit evil, and abandon what is wholesome, therefore you yourself are the cause for frequenting others' wives; you commit evil deeds and abandon what is wholesome. There is no evil quality equal to you, a destroyer of the world. Go, you do not please me.'

Sā tattheva antaradhāyi. Kosiyopi uttarato ṭhitāya hiriyā saddhiṃ sallapanto gāthādvayamāha –

She disappeared right there. Then Kosiya, conversing with Hirī, who was standing to the north, spoke two verses:

254.

254.

“Jighaññarattiṃ aruṇasmimūhate, yā dissati uttamarūpavaṇṇinī;

Tathūpamā [P 5.0404] maṃ paṭibhāsi devate, ācikkha me tvaṃ katamāsi accharā.

'When dawn is rising at the end of the night, as one of excellent form and complexion is seen, so you appear to me, O deity. Tell me, what celestial nymph are you?'

255.

255.

“Kāḷā nidāgheriva aggijāriva, anileritā lohitapattamālinī;

Kā tiṭṭhasi mandamigāvalokayaṃ, bhāsesamānāva giraṃ na muñcasī”ti.

'Dark as a creeper in the summer, or like a flame stirred by the wind, wearing a garland of red flowers; who are you who stands, gazing like a young deer, as if about to speak, yet you do not utter a word?'

Tattha jighaññarattinti pacchimarattiṃ, rattipariyosāneti attho. Ūhateti aruṇe uggate. Yāti yā puratthimā disā rattasuvaṇṇatāya uppamarūpadharā [M 5.0431] hutvā dissati. Kāḷā nidāgherivāti nidāghasamaye kāḷavalli viya. Aggijārivāti aggijālā iva, sāpi nijjhāmakhettesu taruṇauṭṭhitakāḷavalli viyāti attho. Lohitapattamālinīti lohitavaṇṇehi pattehi parivutā. Kā tiṭṭhasīti yathā sā taruṇakāḷavalli vāteritā vilāsamānā sobhamānā tiṭṭhati, evaṃ kā nāma tvaṃ tiṭṭhasi. Bhāsesamānāvāti mayā saddhiṃ bhāsitukāmā viya hosi, na ca giraṃ muñcasi.

Herein, 'jighaññaratti' means the last watch of the night; the meaning is the end of the night. 'Ūhateti' means when the dawn has risen. 'Yā' refers to that eastern direction which appears, having assumed a form comparable to red gold. 'Kāḷā nidāgherivā' means like a black creeper in the hot season. 'Aggijārivā' means like a flame of fire; the meaning is also like a young black creeper newly arisen in scorched fields. 'Lohitapattamālinī' means wreathed with red-colored leaves. 'Kā tiṭṭhasī' means: just as that young black creeper, stirred by the wind, stands gracefully and beautifully, so too, who are you that stands? 'Bhāsesamānāvā' means: you are as if desirous of speaking with me, yet you do not utter a word.

Tato sā gāthamāha –

Then she spoke a verse:

256.

256.

“Hirāha [V 5.0400] devī manujehi pūjitā, apāpasattūpanisevinī sadā;

Sudhāvivādena tavantimāgatā, sāhaṃ na sakkomi sudhampi yācituṃ;

Kopīnarūpā viya yācanitthiyā”ti.

'I am the goddess Hirī, honored by humans, always associating with those who are not evil. I have come to your presence because of the dispute about nectar. I am not able to ask even for nectar; for a woman, begging is like being naked.'

Tattha hirāhanti hirī ahaṃ. Sudhampīti sā ahaṃ sudhābhojanaṃ taṃ yācitumpi na sakkomi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kopīnarūpā viya yācanitthiyā, yasmā itthiyā yācanā nāma kopīnarūpā viya rahassaṅgavivaraṇasadisā hoti, nillajjā viya hotīti attho.

Herein, 'hirāhaṃ' means 'I am Hirī.' 'Sudhampi [yācitum]' means that I, being she, am not able to ask you even for the nectar-food. For what reason? 'Kopīnarūpā viya yācanitthiyā' means that for a woman, asking is like revealing her private parts, similar to exposing a secret limb; the meaning is that it is as if she were shameless.

Taṃ sutvā tāpaso dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard that, the ascetic spoke two verses:

257.

257.

“Dhammena ñāyena sugatte lacchasi, eso hi dhammo na hi yācanā sudhā.

'Rightly and reasonably, O one of beautiful form, you shall obtain it; for this is the rule: nectar is not to be obtained by begging.'

Taṃ taṃ ayācantimahaṃ nimantaye, sudhāya yañcicchasi tampi dammi te.

'Therefore I invite you, who do not ask; whatever nectar you desire, that I give to you.'

258.

258.

“Sā [P 5.0405] tvaṃ mayā ajja sakamhi assame, nimantitā kañcanavelliviggahe;

Tuvañhi me sabbarasehi pūjiyā, taṃ pūjayitvāna sudhampi asniye”ti.

'Today, in my own hermitage, you are invited by me, O one with a body like a golden creeper. For you are indeed to be honored by me with all flavors. Having honored you, I shall partake of the nectar.'

Tattha dhammenāti sabhāvena. Ñāyenāti kāraṇena. Na hi yācanā sudhāti na hi yācanāya sudhā labbhati, teneva kāraṇena itarā tisso [M 5.0432] nalabhiṃsu. Taṃ tanti tasmā taṃ. Yañcicchasīti na kevalaṃ nimantemiyeva, yañca sudhaṃ icchasi, tampi dammi te. Kañcanavelliviggaheti kañcanarāsisassirikasarīre. Pūjiyāti na kevalaṃ sudhāya, aññehipi sabbarasehi tvaṃ mayā pūjetabbayuttakāva. Asniyeti taṃ pūjetvā sace sudhāya avasesaṃ bhavissati, ahampi bhuñjissāmi.

Herein, 'dhammena' means 'by nature.' 'Ñāyena' means 'by reason.' 'Na hi yācanā sudhā' means 'indeed nectar is not obtained by begging'; for that very reason, the other three did not obtain it. 'Taṃ taṃ' means 'therefore you.' 'Yañcicchasi' means 'not only do I invite, but whatever nectar you desire, that too I give to you.' 'Kañcanavelliviggahe' means 'with a body splendid like a heap of gold.' 'Pūjiyā' means 'not only with nectar, but also with all other flavors, you are indeed worthy of being honored by me.' 'Asniye' means 'having honored you, if any nectar remains, I too shall eat it.'

Tato aparā abhisambuddhagāthā –

Then, further, the verses spoken after enlightenment:

259.

259.

“Sā kosiyenānumatā jutīmatā, addhā hiri rammaṃ pāvisi yassamaṃ;

Udakavantaṃ phalamariyapūjitaṃ, apāpasattūpanisevitaṃ sadā.

'Permitted by the radiant Kosiya, Hirī surely entered the delightful hermitage, which was well-watered, abundant in fruit, revered by the Noble Ones, and always frequented by those who are not evil.'

260.

260.

“Rukkhaggahānā bahukettha pupphitā, ambā piyālā panasā ca kiṃsukā;

Sobhañjanā loddamathopi paddhakā, kekā ca bhaṅgā tilakā supupphitā.

Here, many thickets of trees are in bloom: mangoes, piyāla, jackfruits, and kiṃsuka trees; sobhañjana, lodda, and paddhaka; kekā and bhaṅgā, and tilaka trees are in full bloom.

261.

261.

“Sālā [V 5.0401] karerī bahukettha jambuyo, assatthanigrodhamadhukavetasā;

Uddālakā pāṭali sinduvārakā, manuññagandhā mucalindaketakā.

Here are many sal trees, karerī trees, and jambu trees; assattha, nigrodha, madhuka, and vetasa trees; uddālaka, pāṭali, and sinduvāraka trees; and fragrant mucalinda and ketaka trees.

262.

262.

“Hareṇukā veḷukā keṇu tindukā, sāmākanīvāramathopi cīnakā;

Mocā kadalī bahukettha sāliyo, pavīhayo ābhūjino ca taṇḍulā.

Hareṇukā, veḷukā, keṇu, and tinduka; sāmāka, nīvāra, and also cīnaka; mocā and kadalī; here are many sāli and pavīha rices, ābhūjina trees, and taṇḍula grains.

263.

263.

“Tassevuttarapassena, jātā pokkharaṇī sivā;

Akakkasā apabbhārā, sādhu appaṭigandhikā.

On its northern side, a tranquil lotus pond had arisen, smooth, without rugged banks, and delightfully free from unpleasant odors.

264.

264.

“Tattha macchā sanniratā, khemino bahubhojanā;

Siṅgū savaṅkā saṃkulā, satavaṅkā ca rohitā;

Āḷigaggarakākiṇṇā, pāṭhīnā kākamacchakā.

There, fish were well-pleased, safe, and had abundant food: siṅgū, savaṅka, saṃkulā, satavaṅka, and rohitā; it was teeming with āḷigaggara, pāṭhīnā, and kākamacchaka fish.

265.

265.

“Tattha [M 5.0433][P 5.0406] pakkhī sanniratā, khemino bahubhojanā;

Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca, cakkavākā ca kukkuhā;

Kuṇālakā bahū citrā, sikhaṇḍī jīvajīvakā.

There, birds were well-pleased, safe, and had abundant food: swans, herons, peacocks, cakkavākas, and coucals; many colorful kuṇālaka birds, sikhaṇḍī birds, and jīvajīvaka birds.

266.

266.

“Tattha pānāya māyanti, nānā migagaṇā bahū;

Sīhā byagghā varāhā ca, acchakokataracchayo.

There, many diverse herds of animals came to drink: lions, tigers, boars, bears, wolves, and hyenas.

267.

267.

“Palāsādā gavajā ca, mahiṃsā rohitā rurū;

Eṇeyyā ca varāhā ca, gaṇino nīkasūkarā;

Kadalimigā bahukettha, biḷārā sasakaṇṇikā.

Rhinoceroses and gavayas, buffaloes, rohita deer, and ruru deer; eṇeyya deer and boars, gaurs and wild pigs; here are many kadalimiga deer, cats, and long-eared hares.

268.

268.

“Chamāgirī pupphavicitrasanthatā, dijābhighuṭṭhā dijasaṅghasevitā”ti.

The ground-level rocks are strewn with variegated flowers, resound with birds, and are frequented by flocks of birds.

Tattha jutīmatāti ānubhāvasampannena. Pāvisi yassamanti pāvisi assamaṃ, ya-kāro byañjanasandhikaro. Udakavantanti tesu tesu ṭhānesu udakasampannaṃ. Phalanti anekaphalasampannaṃ. Ariyapūjitanti nīvaraṇadosarahitehi jhānalābhīhi ariyehi pūjitaṃ pasatthaṃ. Rukkhaggahānāti pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkhagahanā. Sobhañjanāti siggurukkhā. Loddamathopi paddhakāti loddarukkhā ca padumarukkhā [V 5.0402] ca. Kekā ca bhaṅgāti evaṃnāmakā rukkhā eva. Karerīti karerirukkhā. Uddālakāti vātaghātakā. Mucalindaketakāti mucalindā ca pañcavidhaketakā ca. Hareṇukāti aparaṇṇajāti. Veḷukāti vaṃsabhedakā. Keṇūti araññamāsā. Tindukāti timbarurukkhā. Cīnakāti khuddakarājamāsā. Mocāti aṭṭhikakadaliyo. Sāliyoti nānappakārā jātassaraṃ upanissāya jātā sāliyo. Pavīhayoti nānappakārā vīhayo. Ābhūjinoti bhujapattā. Taṇḍulāti nikkuṇḍakathusāni sayaṃjātataṇḍulasīsāni.

Herein, 'jutīmatā' means 'endowed with splendor.' 'Pāvisi yassamanti' means 'entered the hermitage'; the 'ya' is a euphonic consonant. 'Udakavantanti' means 'abundant with water in various places.' 'Phalanti' means 'endowed with many fruits.' 'Ariyapūjitanti' means 'revered and praised by noble ones who are free from the faults of the hindrances and have attained jhāna.' 'Rukkhaggahānāti' refers to 'thickets of trees laden with flowers and fruits.' 'Sobhañjanāti' means 'siggu trees.' 'Loddamathopi paddhakāti' means 'lodda trees and paduma trees.' 'Kekā ca bhaṅgāti' refers to 'trees known by such names.' 'Karerīti' means 'karerī trees.' 'Uddālakāti' means 'wind-destroying trees.' 'Mucalindaketakāti' means 'mucalinda trees and the five kinds of ketaka trees.' 'Hareṇukāti' means 'a type of pulse.' 'Veḷukāti' means 'different kinds of bamboo.' 'Keṇūti' means 'wild beans.' 'Tindukāti' means 'timbaru trees.' 'Cīnakāti' means 'small royal beans.' 'Mocāti' means 'seeded banana trees.' 'Sāliyoti' means 'various kinds of sāli rice grown relying on the Jātassara lake.' 'Pavīhayoti' means 'various kinds of vīha rice.' 'Ābhūjinoti' means 'bhujapatta trees.' 'Taṇḍulāti' means 'self-grown heads of rice, without husk or chaff.'

Tassevāti, bhikkhave, tasseva assamassa uttaradisābhāge. Pokkharaṇīti pañcavidhapadumasañchannā jātassarapokkharaṇī. Akakkasāti macchasippikasevālādikakkasarahitā. Apabbhārāti acchinnataṭā samatitthā. Appaṭigandhikāti apaṭikkūlagandhena udakena samannāgatā. Tatthāti tassā pokkharaṇiyā. Kheminoti abhayā. “Siṅgū”tiādīni tesaṃ macchānaṃ [M 5.0434] nāmāni. Kuṇālakāti kokilā. Citrāti citrapattā. Sikhaṇḍīti uṭṭhitasikhā morā, aññepi vā matthake jātasikhā pakkhino. Pānāya māyantīti pānāya āyanti. Palāsādāti khaggā. Gavajāti gavayā. Gaṇinoti gokaṇṇā. Kaṇṇikāti kaṇṇikamigā. Chamāgirīti bhūmisamapatthaṭā piṭṭhipāsāṇā. Pupphavicitrasanthatāti vicitrapupphasanthatā. Dijābhighuṭṭhāti madhurassarehi dijehi abhighuṭṭhā. Evarūpā tattha bhūmipabbatāti evaṃ bhagavā kosiyassa assamaṃ vaṇṇeti.

'Of that very,' O monks, refers to the northern part of that very hermitage. 'Pokkharaṇīti' means the Jātassara pond, covered with five kinds of lotuses. 'Akakkasāti' means 'free from harshness,' without the roughness of fish, shells, moss, and so on. 'Apabbhārāti' means 'with unbroken banks and even landing places.' 'Appaṭigandhikāti' means 'endowed with water free from unpleasant odors.' 'Tatthāti' refers to that pond. 'Kheminoti' means 'safe,' 'free from danger.' 'Siṅgū' and so on are the names of those fish. 'Kuṇālakāti' means 'cuckoos.' 'Citrāti' means 'those with variegated wings.' 'Sikhaṇḍīti' means 'peacocks with raised crests,' or other birds with crests on their heads. 'Pānāya māyantīti' means 'come to drink.' 'Palāsādāti' means 'rhinoceroses.' 'Gavajāti' means 'gavayas.' 'Gaṇinoti' means 'gokaṇṇa deer.' 'Chamāgirīti' means 'flat rocks spread out even with the ground.' 'Pupphavicitrasanthatāti' means 'strewn with variegated flowers.' 'Dijābhighuṭṭhāti' means 'resounding with the sweet calls of birds.' 'Such were the lands and mountains there'—thus the Blessed One describes Kosiya’s hermitage.

Idāni hirideviyā tattha pavisanādīni dassetuṃ āha –

Now, to show the goddess Hirī's entering there and so on, he says:

269.

269.

“Sā [P 5.0407] suttacā nīladumābhilambitā, vijjū mahāmegharivānupajjatha;

Tassā susambandhasiraṃ kusāmayaṃ, suciṃ sugandhaṃ ajinūpasevitaṃ;

Atricca kocchaṃ hirimetadabravi, nisīda kalyāṇi sukhayidamāsanaṃ.

She, of fine skin, clinging to the dark trees, appeared like a flash of lightning from a great cloud. Having spread an extraordinary seat for her—made of kusa grass with a well-bound headrest, pure, fragrant, and furnished with a deerskin—he said this to Hirī: 'Sit down, O lovely one, this seat is comfortable.'

270.

270.

“Tassā tadā kocchagatāya kosiyo, yadicchamānāya jaṭājinandharo;

Navehi pattehi sayaṃ sahūdakaṃ, sudhābhihāsī turito mahāmuni.

When she had taken her seat, Kosiya, the great sage wearing matted hair and deerskin, knowing what she desired, swiftly brought nectar with water in fresh leaves by himself.

271.

271.

“Sā taṃ paṭiggayha ubhohi pāṇibhi, iccabravi attamanā jaṭādharaṃ;

Handāhaṃ etarahi pūjitā tayā, gaccheyyaṃ brahme tidivaṃ jitāvinī.

She received it with both hands and joyfully said to the ascetic with matted hair: 'Indeed, now I am honored by you, O Brahmin; may I go to heaven, victorious.'

272.

272.

“Sā [V 5.0403] kosiyenānumatā jutīmatā, udīritā vaṇṇamadena mattā;

Sakāse gantvāna sahassacakkhuno, ayaṃ sudhā vāsava dehi me jayaṃ.

She, permitted by Kosiya, the radiant one, aroused and intoxicated with the pride of beauty, having gone into the presence of the thousand-eyed one, said: 'O Vāsava, this is nectar; grant me victory.'

273.

273.

“Tamena [M 5.0435] sakkopi tadā apūjayi, sahindadevā surakaññamuttamaṃ;

Sā pañjalī devamanussapūjitā, navamhi kocchamhi yadā upāvisī”ti.

Then even Sakka, along with the gods, honored her, the finest of celestial maidens, when she, revered by gods and humans, sat with hands folded in reverence upon the new couch.

Tattha suttacāti succhavī. Nīladumābhilambitāti nīlesu dumesu abhilambitā hutvā, taṃ taṃ nīladumasākhaṃ parāmasantīti attho. Mahāmegharivāti tena nimantitā mahāmeghavijju viya tassa taṃ assamaṃ pāvisi. Tassāti tassā hiriyā. Susambandhasiranti suṭṭhu sambandhasīsaṃ. Kusāmayanti usīrādimissakakusatiṇamayaṃ. Sugandhanti usīrena ceva aññena sugandhatiṇena ca missakattā sugandhaṃ. Ajinūpasevitanti upariatthatena ajinacammena upasevitaṃ. Atricca kocchanti evarūpaṃ kocchāsanaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre attharitvā. Sukhayidamāsananti sukhaṃ nisīda idamāsanaṃ.

Here, 'suttacā' means 'with fine skin'. 'Nīladumābhilambitā' means 'hanging down from blue trees', that is, 'touching the branches of those blue trees'. 'Mahāmegharivā' means: invited by him, she entered that hermitage like lightning from a great rain cloud. 'Tassā' refers to that goddess Hirī. 'Susambandhasiranti' means 'a well-bound headrest'. 'Kusāmayanti' means 'made of kusa grass mixed with usīra root and other fragrant grasses'. 'Sugandhanti' means 'fragrant due to being mixed with usīra root and other sweet-smelling grasses'. 'Ajinūpasevitanti' means 'furnished with a deerskin spread on top'. 'Atricca kocchanti' means 'having spread such a seat at the door of the leaf-hut'. 'Sukhayidamāsananti' means 'sit comfortably; this is a comfortable seat'.

Yanti yāvadatthaṃ. Icchamānāyāti sudhaṃ icchantiyā. Navehi pattehīti taṅkhaṇaññeva pokkharaṇito ābhatehi allapaduminipattehi. Sayanti sahatthena. Sahūdakanti [P 5.0408] dakkhiṇodakasahitaṃ. Sudhābhihāsīti sudhaṃ abhihari. Turitoti somanassavegena turito. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Jitāvinīti vijayappattā hutvā.

'Yanti' means 'as much as is needed'. 'Icchamānāyāti' means 'to her who desired nectar'. 'Navehi pattehīti' means 'with fresh lotus leaves brought immediately from the lotus pond, still moist'. 'Sayaṃ' means 'by himself', that is, 'with his own hands'. 'Sahūdakanti' means 'together with water for a libation'. 'Sudhābhihāsīti' means 'brought nectar'. 'Turitoti' means 'swiftly, with the force of joy'. 'Handā' is a particle indicating encouragement. 'Jitāvinīti' means 'having attained victory'.

Anumatāti idāni yathāruciṃ gacchāti anuññātā. Udīritāti tidasapuraṃ gantvā sakkassa santike ayaṃ sudhāti udīrayi. Surakaññanti devadhītaraṃ. Uttamanti pavaraṃ. Sā pañjalī devamanussapūjitāti pañjalī devehi ca manussehi ca pūjitā. Yadāti yadā nisīdanatthāya sakkena dāpite nave kañcanapīṭhasaṅkhāte kocche sā upāvisi, tadā naṃ tattha nisinnaṃ sakko ca sesadevatā ca pāricchattakapupphādīhi pūjayiṃsu.

'Anumatāti' means 'permitted', that is, 'allowed to go as one wishes'. 'Udīritāti' means 'having gone to the city of the Thirty-three, she proclaimed in the presence of Sakka, “This is nectar!”'. 'Surakaññanti' refers to 'a divine maiden'. 'Uttamanti' means 'the best'. 'Sā pañjalī devamanussapūjitāti' means 'she, with hands folded in reverence, was honored by both gods and humans'. 'Yadāti' means 'when, for the purpose of sitting, Sakka had a new couch known as a golden stool prepared, and she sat upon it, then Sakka and the remaining deities honored her there, seated, with Pāricchattaka flowers and other offerings'.

Evaṃ sakko taṃ pūjetvā cintesi – “kena nu kho kāraṇena kosiyo sesānaṃ adatvā imissāva sudhaṃ adāsī”ti. So tassa kāraṇassa jānanatthāya puna mātaliṃ pesesi. Tamatthaṃ āvi karonto satthā āha –

Thus, having honored her, Sakka thought: 'For what reason did Kosiya give nectar to her alone, and not to the others?' To understand the reason for this, he sent Mātali again. The Teacher, revealing that matter, said:

274.

274.

“Tameva [M 5.0436][V 5.0404] saṃsī punadeva mātaliṃ, sahassanetto tidasānamindo;

Gantvāna vākyaṃ mama brūhi kosiyaṃ, āsāya saddhā siriyā ca kosiya;

Hirī sudhaṃ kena malattha hetunā”ti.

Then again, the thousand-eyed one, lord of the gods, addressed Mātali: 'Go and speak my words to Kosiya: O Kosiya, for what reason did Hirī obtain the nectar, and not Hope, Faith, or Glory?'

Tattha saṃsīti abhāsi. Vākyaṃ mamāti mama vākyaṃ kosiyaṃ brūhi. Āsāya saddhā siriyā cāti āsāto ca saddhāto ca sirito ca hirīyeva kena hetunā sudhamalatthāti.

Here, 'saṃsīti' means 'spoke'. 'Vākyaṃ mamāti' means 'tell Kosiya my words'. 'Āsāya saddhā siriyā cāti' means: for what reason did Hirī alone obtain the nectar, and not Hope, Faith, and Glory?

So tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā vejayantarathamāruyha agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

He, having accepted his words, mounted the Vejayanta chariot and departed. The Teacher, revealing that matter, said:

275.

275.

“Taṃ suplavatthaṃ udatārayī rathaṃ, daddallamānaṃ upakāriyasādisaṃ;

Jambonadīsaṃ tapaneyyasannibhaṃ, alaṅkataṃ kañcanacittasannibhaṃ.

He brought forth that smoothly moving chariot, shining, gleaming like a royal palace, with a pole of Jambu-river gold, resembling refined gold, adorned and like a golden painting.

276.

276.

“Suvaṇṇacandettha bahū nipātitā, hatthī gavāssā kikibyagghadīpiyo;

Eṇeyyakā laṅghamayettha pakkhino, migettha veḷuriyamayā yudhā yutā.

Here, many golden discs were placed, along with elephants, cattle, horses, kinnaras, tigers, and leopards; eṇeyya deer, and here birds in leaping postures; and here deer made of beryl, arrayed for battle.

277.

277.

“Tatthassarājaharayo ayojayuṃ, dasasatāni susunāgasādise;

Alaṅkate [P 5.0409] kañcanajāluracchade, āveḷine saddagame asaṅgite.

There they yoked a thousand tawny, royal horses, resembling young elephants, adorned with golden net chest-coverings, with ear-ornaments, responsive to sound, and unimpeded in their gait.

278.

278.

“Taṃ yānaseṭṭhaṃ abhiruyha mātali, disā imāyo abhinādayittha;

Nabhañca selañca vanappatiniñca, sasāgaraṃ pabyathayittha mediniṃ.

Mounting that excellent chariot, Mātali made these directions resound; and he shook the sky, the mountains, the great forest trees, and the earth together with the ocean.

279.

279.

“Sa [M 5.0437] khippameva upagamma assamaṃ, pāvāramekaṃsakato katañjalī;

Bahussutaṃ vuddhaṃ vinītavantaṃ, iccabravi mātali devabrāhmaṇaṃ.

He, quickly approaching the hermitage, with his upper robe arranged over one shoulder and hands folded in reverence, Mātali spoke thus to the learned, venerable, disciplined, divine brahmin.

280.

280.

“Indassa vākyaṃ nisāmehi kosiya, dūto ahaṃ pucchati taṃ purindado;

Āsāya saddhā siriyā ca kosiya, hirī sudhaṃ kena malattha hetunā”ti.

“Listen to Indra’s words, O Kosiya; I am a messenger, and Purindada asks you: O Kosiya, for what reason did Hirī obtain the nectar, and not Hope, Faith, or Glory?”

Tattha taṃ suplavatthanti taṃ vejayantarathaṃ sukhena plavanatthaṃ. Udatārayīti uttāresi ukkhipitvā gamanasajjamakāsi. Upakāriyasādisanti upakaraṇabhaṇḍehi sadisaṃ, yathā tassa aggisikhāya [V 5.0405] samānavaṇṇāni upakaraṇāni jalanti, tatheva jalitanti attho. Jambonadīsanti jambunadasaṅkhātaṃ rattasuvaṇṇamayaṃ īsaṃ. Kañcanacittasannibhanti, kañcanamayena sattaratanavicittena aṭṭhamaṅgalena samannāgataṃ. Suvaṇṇacandetthāti suvaṇṇamayā candakā ettha rathe. Hatthīti suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimayā hatthī. Gavādīsupi eseva nayo. Laṅghamayettha pakkhinoti ettha rathe laṅghamayā nānāratanamayā pakkhigaṇāpi paṭipāṭiyā ṭhitā. Yudhā yutāti attano attano yudhena saddhiṃ yuttā hutvā dassitā.

Here, 'suplavatthaṃ' means 'for the purpose of moving smoothly'. 'Udatārayīti' means he raised it up; having lifted it, he made it ready for travel. 'Upakāriyasādisanti' means similar to its fittings; just as its fittings, of a color similar to a flame of fire, shine, so too it shines, is the meaning. 'Jambonadīsanti' means the pole, made of red gold known as Jambunada. 'Kañcanacittasannibhanti' means endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, variegated with the seven gems, and made of gold. 'Suvaṇṇacandetthāti' means here, in the chariot, are golden discs. 'Hatthīti' means elephants made of gold, silver, and jewels. The same principle applies to the cattle and other animals. 'Laṅghamayettha pakkhinoti' means here, in the chariot, groups of birds made of various gems are also positioned in order. 'Yudhā yutāti' means shown equipped with their respective weapons.

Assarājaharayoti harivaṇṇamanomayaassarājāno. Susunāgasādiseti balasampattiyā taruṇanāgasadise. Kañcanajāluracchadeti kañcanajālamayena uracchadālaṅkārena samannāgate. Āveḷineti āveḷasaṅkhātehi kaṇṇālaṅkārehi yutte. Saddagameti patodappahāraṃ vinā saddamatteneva gamanasīle. Asaṅgīteti nissaṅge sīghajave evarūpe assarāje tattha yojesunti attho.

'Assarājaharayoti' means mind-made horse-kings of a tawny color. 'Susunāgasādiseti' means like very young nāgas in their abundance of strength. 'Kañcanajāluracchadeti' means endowed with a chest ornament made of golden mesh. 'Āveḷineti' means equipped with ear ornaments known as āveḷa. 'Saddagameti' means accustomed to moving by sound alone, without the strike of a goad. 'Asaṅgīteti' means unhindered and swift-footed; such horse-kings were yoked there, is the meaning.

Abhinādayitthāti yānasaddena ekaninnādaṃ akāsi. Vanappatiniñcāti vanappatinī ca vanasaṇḍe cāti attho. Pabyathayitthāti kampayittha. Tattha ākāsaṭṭhakavimānakampanena nabhakampanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pāvāramekaṃsakatoti ekaṃsakatapāvāradibbavattho. Vuddhanti guṇavuddhaṃ. Vinītavantanti vinītena [M 5.0438] ācāravattena samannāgataṃ. Iccabravīti rathaṃ ākāse ṭhapetvā otaritvā evaṃ abravi. Devabrāhmaṇanti devasamaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ.

'Abhinādayitthāti' means he made a single sound with the sound of the chariot. 'Vanappatiniñcāti' means both the great forest trees and the groves. 'Pabyathayitthāti' means he caused to tremble. There, the trembling of the sky should be understood as the shaking of the celestial mansions situated in the sky. 'Pāvāramekaṃsakatoti' refers to a divine upper garment draped over one shoulder. 'Vuddhanti' means grown in virtue. 'Vinītavantanti' means endowed with disciplined conduct. 'Iccabravīti' means, having placed the chariot in the sky and descended, thus he spoke. 'Devabrāhmaṇanti' means a brahmin equal to a god.

So [P 5.0410] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, he spoke a verse:

281.

281.

“Andhā sirī maṃ paṭibhāti mātali, saddhā aniccā pana devasārathi.

“Glory appears blind to me, Mātali, and faith is impermanent, O divine charioteer.

Āsā visaṃvādikasammatā hi me, hirī ca ariyamhi guṇe patiṭṭhitā”ti.

Hope is considered deceptive by me, and conscience is established in the noble quality.”

Tattha andhāti sippādisampannepi asampannepi bhajanato “andhā”ti maṃ paṭibhāti. Aniccāti saddhā pana taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ pahāya aññasmiṃ aññasmiṃ uppajjanato hutvā abhāvākārena “aniccā”ti maṃ paṭibhāti. Visaṃvādikasammatāti āsā pana yasmā dhanatthikā nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhanditvā vinaṭṭhapābhatā enti, tasmā “visaṃvādikā”ti maṃ paṭibhāti. Ariyamhi guṇeti hirī pana hirottappasabhāvasaṅkhāte parisuddhe ariyaguṇe patiṭṭhitāti.

Here, 'blind' means it appears 'blind' to me because it is partaken of by both those endowed with skills and those not. 'Impermanent' means it appears 'impermanent' to me because faith, abandoning one object, arises in another and another, and by its nature of having been and then ceasing to be. 'Considered deceptive' means it appears 'deceptive' to me because hope is like those desiring wealth who set out on the sea by ship and return with ruined provisions. 'In the noble quality' means that conscience is established in the pure noble quality designated as the nature of conscience and moral dread.

Idāni [V 5.0406] tassā guṇaṃ vaṇṇento āha –

Now, extolling her virtue, he said:

282.

282.

“Kumāriyo yācimā gottarakkhitā, jiṇṇā ca yā yā ca sabhattuitthiyo;

Tā chandarāgaṃ purisesu uggataṃ, hiriyā nivārenti sacittamattano.

“These maidens, protected by their lineage, and those who are old, and those who are wives with husbands—they, out of modesty, restrain their own minds from the desire and lust that has arisen towards men.”

283.

283.

“Saṅgāmasīse sarasattisaṃyute, parājitānaṃ patataṃ palāyinaṃ;

Hiriyā nivattanti jahitva jīvitaṃ, te sampaṭicchanti punā hirīmanā.

“At the head of battle, amidst the clash of arrows and spears, those among the defeated, the falling, and the fleeing, turn back out of shame, forsaking their lives; being mindful of shame, they face the fight once more.”

284.

284.

“Velā yathā sāgaravegavārinī, hirāya hi pāpajanaṃ nivārinī;

Taṃ sabbaloke hirimariyapūjitaṃ, indassa taṃ vedaya devasārathī”ti.

“Just as a shore restrains the ocean’s rushing waters, so does shame restrain people from evil. Honored by the noble ones throughout the world, O charioteer of the gods, inform Indra of that shame.”

Tattha [M 5.0439] jiṇṇāti vidhavā. Sabhattūti sasāmikā taruṇitthiyo. Attanoti tā sabbāpi parapurisesu attano chandarāgaṃ uggataṃ viditvā “ayuttametaṃ amhāka”nti hiriyā sacittaṃ nivārenti, pāpakammaṃ na karonti. Patataṃ palāyinanti patantānañca palāyantānañca antare. Jahitva jīvitanti ye hirimanto honti, te attano jīvitaṃ cajitvā hiriyā nivattanti, evaṃ nivattā ca pana te hirīmanā puna attano sāmikaṃ sampaṭicchanti, amittahatthato mocetvā gaṇhanti. Pāpajanaṃ nivārinīti pāpato janaṃ nivārinī, ayameva vā pāṭho[P 5.0411]. Tanti taṃ hiriṃ. Ariyapūjitanti ariyehi buddhādīhi pūjitaṃ. Indassa taṃ vedayāti yasmā evaṃ mahāguṇā ariyapūjitāvesā, tasmā taṃ evaṃ uttamā nāmesāti indassa kathehīti.

There, ‘jiṇṇā’ means widows. ‘Sabhattū’ refers to young women with husbands. ‘Their own minds’—knowing that their own desire and lust for other men has arisen, all those women, thinking, ‘This is improper for us,’ restrain their own minds out of shame and do not commit evil deeds. ‘Of those who fall and flee’—among those who are falling and those who are fleeing. ‘Having abandoned life’—those who are honorable, having given up their own lives, turn back out of shame; and having turned back in this way, those honorable ones then receive their lord again, rescuing him from the enemy’s grasp and taking him back. ‘Restrainer of evil people’—she restrains people from evil; or this is the reading itself. ‘That’—that shame. ‘Honored by the noble ones’—honored by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas. ‘Inform Indra of that’—because she is thus endowed with such great qualities and honored by the noble ones, therefore, tell Indra that she is thus the most excellent.”

Taṃ sutvā mātali gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Mātali spoke this verse:

285.

285.

“Ko te imaṃ kosiya diṭṭhimodahi, brahmā mahindo atha vā pajāpati;

Hirāya devesu hi seṭṭhasammatā, dhītā mahindassa mahesi jāyathā”ti.

“Who, Kosiya, instilled this view in you—Brahmā, Mahinda, or Pajāpati? For shame is considered best among the gods; the daughter of Mahinda was born as a seeker of great virtue.”

Tattha diṭṭhinti “hirī nāma mahāguṇā ariyapūjitā”ti laddhiṃ. Odahīti hadaye pavesesi. Seṭṭhasammatāti tava santike sudhāya laddhakālato paṭṭhāya indassa santike kañcanāsanaṃ labhitvā sabbadevatāhi pūjiyamānā uttamasammatā jāyatha.
