Here, ‘view’ refers to the belief: “Shame is a great virtue, honored by the noble ones.” ‘Placed’ means it was introduced into the heart. ‘Regarded as supreme’ means: from the time the nectar was obtained in your presence, having received the golden seat in Indra’s presence, you became regarded as the highest, being honored by all the gods.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ kathenteyeva kosiyassa taṅkhaṇaññeva cavanadhammo jāto. Atha naṃ, mātali, “kosiya [V 5.0407] āyusaṅkhāro te ossaṭṭho, cavanadhammopi te sampatto, kiṃ te manussalokena, devalokaṃ gacchāmā”ti tattha netukāmo hutvā gāthamāha –

Even as he was speaking thus, at that very moment the nature of passing away arose for Kosiya. Then Mātali, desiring to lead him there, said to him, “Venerable sir, your life-formation is spent, the state of passing away has come upon you. What is the human world to you? Let us go to the world of the gods,” and spoke this verse:

286.

286.

“Handehi dāni tidivaṃ apakkama, rathaṃ samāruyha mamāyitaṃ imaṃ;

Indo ca taṃ indasagotta kaṅkhati, ajjeva tvaṃ indasahabyataṃ vajā”ti.

“Come now, depart to heaven, ascend this cherished chariot of mine; Indra himself, O Indasagotta, longs for you; go this very day to the companionship of Indra.”

Tattha [M 5.0440] mamāyitanti piyaṃ manāpaṃ. Indasagottāti purimabhave indena samānagotta. Kaṅkhatīti tavāgamanaṃ icchanto kaṅkhati.

There, ‘cherished’ means dear and pleasing. ‘Indasagotta’ means having the same lineage as Indra in a former existence. ‘Longs for’ means he longs for you, desiring your arrival.

Iti tasmiṃ kosiyena saddhiṃ kathenteyeva kosiyo cavitvā opapātiko devaputto hutvā āruyha dibbarathe aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ, mātali, sakkassa santikaṃ nesi. Sakko taṃ disvāva tuṭṭhamānaso attano dhītaraṃ hirideviṃ tassa aggamahesiṃ katvā adāsi, aparimāṇamassa issariyaṃ ahosi. Tamatthaṃ viditvā “anomasattānaṃ kammaṃ nāma evaṃ visujjhatī”ti satthā osānagāthamāha –

Thus, even while he was conversing with Mātali, Kosiya passed away and, having become a spontaneously arisen divine being, mounted the divine chariot and stood there. Then Mātali took him to the presence of Sakka. Upon seeing him, Sakka, with a delighted mind, made his own daughter, the goddess Hiri, his chief queen and gave her to him. His sovereignty became immeasurable. Having understood this matter, and reflecting, “Thus indeed is the kamma of blameless beings purified,” the Teacher spoke this concluding verse:

287.

287.

“Evaṃ visujjhanti apāpakammino, atho suciṇṇassa phalaṃ na nassati;

Ye [P 5.0412] keci maddakkhu sudhāya bhojanaṃ, sabbeva te indasahabyataṃ gatā”ti.

“Thus are those who perform sinless deeds purified, and the fruit of good conduct does not perish; whoever saw the nectar-food, all of them have gone to the companionship of Indra.”

Tattha apāpakamminoti apāpakammā sattā evaṃ visujjhanti ye keci maddakkhūti ye keci sattā tasmiṃ himavantapadese tadā kosiyena hiriyā dīyamānaṃ sudhābhojanaṃ addasaṃsu. Sabbeva teti te sabbepi taṃ dānaṃ anumoditvā cittaṃ pasādetvā indasahabyataṃ gatāti.

Here, ‘performers of sinless deeds’ means beings of sinless kamma are purified in this way. ‘Whoever saw’ refers to whatever beings in that region of the Himalayas who at that time saw the nectar-food being given to Hiri by Kosiya. ‘All of them have gone’ means all of them, having rejoiced in that gift and gladdened their minds, went to the companionship of Indra.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepetaṃ adānābhirataṃ thaddhamacchariyaṃ samānaṃ ahaṃ damesiṃyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā hirī devatā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, kosiyo dānapati bhikkhu, pañcasikho anuruddho, mātali ānando, sūriyo kassapo, cando moggallāno, nārado sāriputto, sakko ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past also, I tamed this monk who was stubborn, miserly, and did not delight in giving.” Then he identified the birth story: “At that time, the deity Hiri was Uppalavaṇṇā, the donor monk was Kosiya, Pañcasikha was Anuruddha, Mātali was Ānanda, Sūriya was Kassapa, Canda was Moggallāna, Nārada was Sāriputta, and Sakka was myself.”

Sudhābhojanajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Sudhābhojana Jātaka is concluded.

[536] 4. Kuṇālajātakavaṇṇanā

[536] 4. 4. Mahākuṇāla Jātaka

Evamakkhāyatīti [V 5.0408] idaṃ satthā kuṇāladahe viharanto anabhiratipīḷite pañcasate bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – sākiyakoliyā [M 5.0441] kira kapilavatthunagarassa ca koliyanagarassa ca antare rohiṇiṃ nāma nadiṃ ekenevāvaraṇena bandhāpetvā sassāni kārenti. Atha jeṭṭhamūlamāse sassesu milāyantesu ubhayanagaravāsīnampi kammakārā sannipatiṃsu. Tattha koliyanagaravāsino vadiṃsu – “idaṃ udakaṃ ubhayato nīhariyamānaṃ neva tumhākaṃ, na amhākaṃ pahossati, amhākaṃ pana sassaṃ ekaudakeneva nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. Kapilavatthuvāsino vadiṃsu – “tumhesu koṭṭhe pūretvā ṭhitesu mayaṃ rattasuvaṇṇanīlamaṇikāḷakahāpaṇe gahetvā na sakkhissāma pacchipasibbakādihatthā tumhākaṃ gharadvāre vicarituṃ, amhākampi sassaṃ ekeneva udakena nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. “Na mayaṃ dassāmā”ti? “Mayampi na dassāmā”ti. Evaṃ kalahaṃ vaḍḍhetvā eko uṭṭhāya ekassa pahāraṃ adāsi, sopi aññassāti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ paharitvā rājakulānaṃ jātiṃ ghaṭṭetvā kalahaṃ pavattesuṃ.

“Thus it is said”—this Mahākuṇāla Jātaka the Teacher related while dwelling at the Kuṇāla Pond, concerning five hundred monks oppressed by discontent. Here is the sequential account: The Sākiyas and Koliyas, it is said, having dammed the Rohiṇī River with a single dam between the cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya, were cultivating their crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops began to wither, the workers from both cities gathered. There, the residents of Koliya said, “This water, if drawn by both sides, will not be enough for either you or us. Our crops, however, can be brought to harvest with a single watering. Give this water to us.” The residents of Kapilavatthu replied, “When your granaries are full, we will not be able to go about at your doors with baskets and bags in hand, taking our red gold, blue gems, and black coins. Our crops too can be brought to harvest with a single watering. Give this water to us.” “We will not give it!” “We will not give it either!” Thus, escalating the quarrel, one rose and struck another, who in turn struck someone else. In this way they came to blows with one another, and, insulting the lineage of the royal families, they started a conflict.

Koliyakammakārā vadanti – “tumhe kapilavatthuvāsike sākiyadārake gahetvā gajjatha[P 5.0413], ye soṇasiṅgālādayo viya attano bhaginīhi saddhiṃ vasiṃsu, etesaṃ hatthiassādayo vā phalakāvudhāni vā amhākaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Sākiyakammakārā vadanti – “tumhe dāni kuṭṭhino dārake gahetvā gajjatha, ye anāthā niggatikā tiracchānā viya kolarukkhe vasiṃsu, etesaṃ hatthiassādayo vā phalakāvudhāni vā amhākaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Te gantvā tasmiṃ kamme niyuttaamaccānaṃ kathesuṃ, amaccā rājakulānaṃ kathesuṃ. Tato sākiyā “bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsikānaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu. Koliyāpi “kolarukkhavāsīnaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu. Apare panācariyā “sākiyakoliyānaṃ dāsīsu udakatthāya nadiṃ gantvā cumbaṭāni bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā sukhakathāya sannisinnāsu ekissā cumbaṭaṃ ekā sakasaññāya gaṇhi, taṃ nissāya ‘mama cumbaṭaṃ, tava cumbaṭa’nti kalahe pavatte kamena ubhayanagaravāsino dāsakammakārā ceva sevakagāmabhojakāmaccauparājāno cāti sabbe yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsū”ti vadanti. Imamhā pana nayā purimanayova bahūsu aṭṭhakathāsu āgato, yuttarūpo cāti sveva gahetabbo.

The Koliya laborers said: 'You boast while taking up the cause of the Sakyan princes residing in Kapilavatthu, who lived with their own sisters like dogs and jackals. What will their elephants and horses, or their shields and weapons, do to us?' The Sakya laborers said: 'Now you boast while taking up the cause of these leprous princes, who were outcasts and helpless, living like animals in the kola trees. What will their elephants and horses, or their shields and weapons, do to us?' They went and reported this matter to the ministers appointed to the work. The ministers reported it to the royal families. Then the Sakyas, thinking, "We will show the strength and power of those who live with their sisters," went out prepared for battle. The Koliyas also, thinking, "We will show the strength and power of those who live in the kola trees," went out prepared for battle. Other teachers, however, say: 'When the Sakya and Koliya slave women went to the river for water, they placed their head-coils on the ground and sat chatting pleasantly. One woman, mistaking it for her own, took another's head-coil. Based on this, a quarrel arose—“This is my head-coil!”, “It is my head-coil!”—and gradually all the inhabitants of both cities, including slave laborers, servants, village headmen, ministers, and viceroys, went out prepared for battle.' However, the former account is found in many commentaries and is more suitable; therefore, it alone should be accepted.

Te [M 5.0442][V 5.0409] pana sāyanhasamaye yuddhasajjā nikkhamissantīti tasmiṃ samaye bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento ime evaṃ yuddhasajje nikkhante addasa, disvā ca “mayi gate esa kalaho vūpasamissati nu kho, no”ti upadhārento “ahamettha gantvā kalahavūpasamatthaṃ tīṇi jātakāni kathessāmi, tato kalaho vūpasamissati, atha sāmaggidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathetvā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ (su. ni. 941 ādayo) desessāmi, desanaṃ sutvā ubhayanagaravāsino aḍḍhateyyāni aḍḍhateyyāni kumārasatāni dassanti, ahaṃ te pabbājessāmi, mahanto samāgamo bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sāyanhasamaye gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā kassaci anārocetvā sayameva pattacīvaramādāya dvinnaṃ senānaṃ antare ākāse pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā tesaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ divā andhakāraṃ kātuṃ kesaraṃsiyo vissajjento nisīdi. Atha nesaṃ saṃviggamānasānaṃ attānaṃ dassento chabbaṇṇā buddharaṃsiyo vissajjesi. Kapilavatthuvāsinopi bhagavantaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭho satthā āgato, diṭṭho nu kho tena amhākaṃ kalahakaraṇabhāvo”ti cintetvā “na kho pana sakkā satthari āgate amhehi parassa sarīre satthaṃ pātetuṃ, koliyanagaravāsino amhe hanantu [P 5.0414] vā bajjhantu vā”ti āvudhāni chaḍḍesuṃ. Koliyanagaravāsinopi tatheva akaṃsu.

Since they were to set out for battle in the evening, the Blessed One, while dwelling in Savatthi at that time, surveyed the world at dawn and saw them setting out thus for battle. Seeing them, he reflected, 'If I go there, will this conflict be pacified or not?' and concluded: 'By going there, I will relate three birth stories to pacify the conflict, and so the conflict will be settled. Then, to illustrate harmony, I will relate two more birth stories and teach the Attadanda Sutta. After hearing the teaching, the inhabitants of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes. I will ordain them, and there will be a great assembly.' Having made this resolution, he attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, walked for alms in Savatthi, and after returning from his alms round, left the Fragrant Cottage in the evening without informing anyone. Taking his bowl and robe, he sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting dark rays from his hair to create darkness during the day to inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in them. Then, revealing himself to those with awed minds, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays. The inhabitants of Kapilavatthu, seeing the Blessed One, thought, 'Our noble kinsman, the Teacher, has arrived. Has he seen our involvement in this conflict?' and concluded, 'Now that the Teacher has arrived, it is impossible for us to strike another's body with a weapon. Let the inhabitants of Koliyanagara kill us or bind us if they will,' and they cast aside their weapons. The inhabitants of Koliyanagara did the same.

Atha bhagavā otaritvā ramaṇīye padese vālukapuline paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi anopamāya buddhasiriyā virocamāno. Tepi rājāno bhagavantaṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Atha ne satthā jānantova “kasmā āgatattha, mahārājā”ti pucchi. “Neva, bhante, nadidassanatthāya, na kīḷanatthāya, apica kho pana imasmiṃ ṭhāne saṅgāmaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā āgatamhā”ti. “Kiṃ nissāya vo kalaho, mahārājā”ti? “Udakaṃ nissāya bhante”ti. “Udakaṃ kiṃ agghati mahārājā”ti? “Appagghaṃ, bhante”ti. “Pathavī nāma kiṃ agghati, mahārājā”ti? “Anagghā, bhante”ti. “Khattiyā kiṃ agghanti, mahārājā”ti? “Khattiyā nāma anagghā, bhante”ti. “Appagghaṃ udakaṃ nissāya kasmā anagghe khattiye nāsetha, mahārāja, kalahasmiñhi assādo [M 5.0443] nāma natthi, kalahavasena hi mahārājā ekāya rukkhadevatāya kāḷasīhena saddhiṃ baddhāghāto sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ anuppattoyevā”ti vatvā phandanajātakaṃ (jā. 1.13.14 ādayo) kathesi. Tato “parapattiyena nāma mahārājā na bhavitabbaṃ, parapattiyā hi hutvā ekassa sasassa kathāya tiyojanasahassavitthate himavante catuppadagaṇā mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandino ahesuṃ, tasmā parapattiyena na bhavitabba”nti vatvā daddarajātakaṃ (jā. 1.243-44; 1.4.13-16; 1.9.105 ādayo) kathesi. Tato “kadāci mahārājā dubbalopi [V 5.0410] mahabbalassa randhaṃ passati, kadāci mahabbalopi dubbalassa randhaṃ passati, laṭukikāpi hi sakuṇikā hatthināgaṃ ghātesī”ti vatvā laṭukikajātakaṃ (jā. 1.5.39 ādayo) kathesi. Evaṃ kalahavūpasamanatthāya tīṇi jātakāni kathetvā sāmaggiparidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathesi. “Samaggānañhi mahārājā koci otāraṃ nāma passituṃ na sakkotī”ti vatvā rukkhadhammajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.74) kathesi. Tato “samaggānaṃ mahārājā koci vivaraṃ passituṃ nāsakkhi, yadā pana aññamaññaṃ vivādamakaṃsu, atha ne eko nesādaputto jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ādāya gato, vivāde assādo nāma natthī”ti vatvā vaṭṭakajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.35, 118; 1.6.128-133) kathesi. Evaṃ imāni pañca jātakāni kathetvā avasāne attadaṇḍasuttaṃ (su. ni. 941 ādayo) kathesi.

Then the Blessed One, having descended, sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat on a beautiful sandy bank, shining with incomparable Buddha-splendor. Those kings too, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down. Then the Teacher, knowing full well, asked them, 'Great kings, why have you come?' 'Venerable sir, we have come neither to see the river nor for sport, but we have come having prepared for battle in this place.' 'On what account is your quarrel, great kings?' 'On account of the water, venerable sir.' 'How much is the water worth, great kings?' 'It is of little value, venerable sir.' 'How much is the earth worth, great kings?' 'It is priceless, venerable sir.' 'How much are the khattiyas worth, great kings?' 'Khattiyas are priceless, venerable sir.' 'Great kings, why do you destroy priceless khattiyas for the sake of water that is of little value? Indeed, there is no satisfaction in a quarrel. On account of a quarrel, great kings, the grudge formed by a tree-deity against a black lion has persisted through this entire aeon.' Having said this, he related the Phandana Jātaka. Then he said, 'Great kings, one should not be led by the words of others. For by being led by others, due to the talk of a single hare, the herds of four-footed animals in the three-thousand-league-wide Himalayas plunged into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not be led by others' words.' Having said this, he related the Daddara Jātaka. Then he said, 'Sometimes, great kings, even the weak see a vulnerability in the strong, and sometimes the strong see a vulnerability in the weak. For even a little quail killed a noble elephant.' Having said this, he related the Laṭukika Jātaka. Thus, for the sake of pacifying the quarrel, he related three Jātakas, and then for the sake of illustrating harmony, he related two Jātakas. 'Great kings, no one is able to find an opening against those who are united.' Having said this, he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. Then he said, 'Great kings, no one was able to find a breach among those who were united. But when they quarreled with one another, then a hunter brought them to their destruction and took them away. There is no satisfaction in a quarrel.' Having said this, he related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Thus, having related these five Jātakas, at the end he recited the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Atha rājāno pasannā “sace satthā nāgamissa, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ vadhitvā lohitanadiṃ pavattayissāma, satthāraṃ nissāya no jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ. Sace pana satthā agāraṃ ajjhāvasissa, dvisahassadīpaparivāraṃ catumahādīparajjaṃ hatthagataṃ abhavissa, atirekasahassaṃ kho panassa puttā abhavissaṃsu, tato khattiyaparivārova avicarissa, taṃ kho panesa sampattiṃ pahāya nikkhamitvā [P 5.0415] sambodhiṃ patto, idānipi khattiyaparivārova vicaratū”ti ubhayanagaravāsino aḍḍhateyyāni aḍḍhateyyāni kumārasatāni adaṃsu. Bhagavā te pabbājetvā mahāvanaṃ agamāsi. Punadivasato paṭṭhāya tehi parivuto ekadā kapilavatthunagare ekadā koliyanagareti dvīsu nagaresu piṇḍāya carati. Ubhayanagaravāsino mahāsakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Tesaṃ garugāravena na attano ruciyā pabbajitānaṃ anabhirati uppajji. Purāṇadutiyikāyopi nesaṃ anabhiratijananatthāya [M 5.0444] taṃ taṃ vatvā sāsanaṃ pesesuṃ. Te atirekataraṃ ukkaṇṭhiṃsu. Bhagavā āvajjento tesaṃ anabhiratabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ime bhikkhū mādisena buddhena saddhiṃ ekato vasantā ukkaṇṭhanti, kathaṃ rūpā nu kho tesaṃ dhammakathā sappāyā”ti upadhārento kuṇāladhammadesanaṃ passi. Athassa etadahosi – “ahaṃ ime bhikkhū himavantaṃ netvā kuṇālakathāya nesaṃ mātugāmadosaṃ pakāsetvā anabhiratiṃ haritvā sotāpattimaggaṃ dassāmī”ti.

Then the kings, being inspired with confidence, thought: 'If the Teacher had not come, we would have killed each other and caused a river of blood to flow. We have gained our lives because of the Teacher. If the Teacher had lived the household life, the sovereignty over the four great continents, surrounded by two thousand islands, would have come into his hand, and he would have had more than a thousand sons. Then he would have moved about with a retinue of khattiyas. But having abandoned that prosperity and gone forth, he attained enlightenment. Even now, let him move about with a retinue of khattiyas.' Thus, the inhabitants of both cities gave two hundred and fifty princes each. The Blessed One ordained them and went to the Mahāvana. From the next day onward, surrounded by them, he wandered for alms sometimes in the city of Kapilavatthu and sometimes in the city of Koliya. The inhabitants of both cities paid great homage. Because they had gone forth out of respect for the Teacher and not of their own choice, dissatisfaction arose in them. Their former wives also sent messages saying this and that to generate discontent in them. They became even more dissatisfied. The Blessed One, reflecting and knowing their state of discontent, considered, 'These monks are dissatisfied while living together with a Buddha like me; what kind of Dhamma talk would be suitable for them?' and he saw the teaching of the Kuṇāla Jātaka. Then it occurred to him: 'I will take these monks to the Himalayas, and by means of the Kuṇāla story, I will reveal to them the faults of women, remove their discontent, and show them the path to stream-entry.'

So pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kapilavatthuṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhattakiccavelāyameva te pañcasate bhikkhū āmantetvā “diṭṭhapubbo vo, bhikkhave, ramaṇīyo himavantapadeso”ti pucchi. “Nohetaṃ, bhante”ti. “Gacchissatha pana himavantacārika”nti? “Bhante, aniddhimanto mayaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmā”ti. “Sace pana vo koci gahetvā gaccheyya, gaccheyyāthā”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. Satthā sabbepi te attano iddhiyā [V 5.0411] gahetvā ākāse uppatitvā himavantaṃ gantvā gaganatale ṭhitova ramaṇīye himavantapadese kañcanapabbataṃ rajatapabbataṃ maṇipabbataṃ hiṅgulikapabbataṃ añjanapabbataṃ sānupabbataṃ phalikapabbatanti nānāvidhe pabbate, pañca mahānadiyo, kaṇṇamuṇḍakaṃ rathakāraṃ sīhapapātaṃ chaddantaṃ tiyaggaḷaṃ anotattaṃ kuṇāladahanti satta dahe dassesi. Himavanto ca nāma mahā pañcayojanasatubbedho tiyojanasahassavitthato, tassa imaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ ekadesaṃ attano ānubhāvena dassesi. Tattha katanivāsāni sīhabyagghahatthikulādīni catuppadānipi ekadesato dassesi. Tattha ārāmarāmaṇeyyakādīni pupphūpagaphalūpage rukkhe nānāvidhe sakuṇasaṅghe jalajathalajapupphāni himavantassa puratthimapasse suvaṇṇatalaṃ, pucchimapasse hiṅgulatalaṃ dassesi. Imesaṃ rāmaṇeyyakānaṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ purāṇadutiyikāsu chandarāgo pahīno.

Then, in the morning, having dressed, taken his bowl and robe, he entered Kapilavatthu for alms. After the meal, having returned from his alms round, at the very time of the meal duties, he addressed those five hundred monks: 'Monks, have you ever seen the delightful region of the Himalayas before?' 'No, Venerable Sir.' 'Would you go on a journey in the Himalayas?' 'Venerable Sir, without psychic power, how could we go?' 'But if someone were to take you, would you go?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' The Teacher, taking all of them by his own psychic power, rose into the air and went to the Himalayas. Standing in the sky, in the delightful region of the Himalayas, he showed them various kinds of mountains: the golden mountain, the silver mountain, the jewel mountain, the cinnabar mountain, the antimony mountain, the mountain with plateaus, and the crystal mountain; the five great rivers; and the seven lakes: Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Rathakāra, Sīhapapāta, Chaddanta, Tiyaggaḷa, Anotatta, and Kuṇālada. The Himalayas, indeed, are vast, five hundred yojanas high and three thousand yojanas wide. Through his own power, he showed them this delightful part of it. He also showed them some of the four-footed animals dwelling there, such as families of lions, tigers, and elephants. There, he showed them the delightful groves and parks, trees laden with flowers and fruits, various flocks of birds, aquatic and terrestrial flowers, the golden plateau on the eastern side of the Himalayas, and the cinnabar plateau on the western side. From the moment they saw these delightful sights, the monks’ lustful desire for their former wives was abandoned.

Atha satthā te bhikkhū gahetvā ākāsato [P 5.0416] otaritvā himavantapacchimapasse saṭṭhiyojanike manosilātale sattayojanikassa kappaṭṭhikasālarukkhassa heṭṭhā tiyojanikāya manosilātalāya tehi bhikkhūhi parivuto chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjento aṇṇavakucchiṃ khobhetvā jalamāno sūriyo viya nisīditvā madhurassaraṃ nicchārento [M 5.0445] te bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ himavante tumhehi adiṭṭhapubbaṃ pucchathā”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dve citrakokilā ubhosu koṭīsu daṇḍakaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā majjhe attano sāmikaṃ nisīdāpetvā aṭṭha citrakokilā purato, aṭṭha pacchato, aṭṭha vāmato, aṭṭha dakkhiṇato, aṭṭha heṭṭhā, aṭṭha upari chāyaṃ katvā evaṃ citrakokilaṃ parivāretvā ākāsenāgacchanti. Atha te bhikkhū taṃ sakuṇasaṅghaṃ disvā satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu – “ke nāmete, bhante sakuṇā”ti? “Bhikkhave, esa mama porāṇako vaṃso, mayā ṭhapitā paveṇī, maṃ tāva pubbe evaṃ paricariṃsu, tadā panesa sakuṇagaṇo mahā ahosi, aḍḍhuḍḍhāni dijakaññāsahassāni maṃ paricariṃsu. Anupubbena parihāyitvā idāni ettako jāto”ti. “Kathaṃ evarūpe pana, bhante, vanasaṇḍe etā dijakaññāyo tumhe paricariṃsū”ti? Atha nesaṃ satthā “tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇāthā”ti satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā atītaṃ āharitvā dassento āha –

Then the Teacher, taking those monks, descended from the sky and sat on a sixty-yojana-wide red arsenic plateau on the western slope of the Himalayas, beneath an eon-lasting sāla tree seven yojanas high, on a three-yojana-wide red arsenic terrace. Surrounded by those monks, radiating six-colored rays, agitating the ocean's depths like the blazing sun, he sat down. Emitting a sweet voice, he addressed those monks: 'Monks, in this Himalaya, ask about what you have not seen before.' At that moment, two variegated cuckoos, holding a stick in their beaks at both ends, seated their master in the middle. Eight variegated cuckoos in front, eight behind, eight to the left, eight to the right, eight below, and eight above, forming a canopy of shade, thus surrounded the variegated cuckoo king and approached through the sky. Seeing that flock of birds, the monks asked the Teacher, 'Venerable Sir, what kind of birds are these?' 'Monks, this is my ancient lineage, a tradition established by me. Long ago, they served me in this way. At that time, this flock of birds was vast—three thousand five hundred female bird attendants served me. Gradually declining, they have now become only this many.' 'But, Venerable Sir, how did such female bird attendants serve you in such a forest grove?' Then the Teacher said to them, 'Well then, monks, listen.' Establishing mindfulness, he recalled the past and revealed it, saying:

“Evamakkhāyati evamanusūyati, sabbosadhadharaṇidhare nekapupphamālyavitate gajagavajamahiṃsarurucamarapasadakhaggagokaṇṇasīhabyagghadīpiacchakokataracchauddārakadali- migabiḷārasasakaṇṇikānucarite ākiṇṇanelamaṇḍalamahāvarāhanāgakulakareṇusaṅghādhivuṭṭhe issamigasākhamigasarabhamigaeṇīmigavātamigapasadamigapurisālukimpurisayakkharakkha- sanisevite amajjavamañjarīdharapahaṭṭhapupphaphusitaggānekapādapagaṇavitake [V 5.0412] kuraracakoravāraṇamayūraparabhatajīvañjīvakacelāvakabhiṅkārakaravīkamattavihaṅgagaṇasatatasampaghuṭṭhe añjanamanosilāharitālahiṅgulakahemarajatakanakānekadhātu- satavinaddhapaṭimaṇḍitapadese evarūpe khalu, bho, ramme vanasaṇḍe kuṇālo nāma sakuṇo paṭivasati ativiya [P 5.0417] citto ativiya cittapattacchadano”.

Thus it is declared, thus it is heard: in a forest grove bearing all kinds of medicinal herbs, spread with diverse flowers and garlands, frequented by elephants, wild oxen, buffaloes, ruru deer, yaks, pasada deer, rhinoceroses, sambar deer, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, wolves, hyenas, otters, kadali-deer, cats, hares, and frequented by kaṇṇikā deer; inhabited by great boars with blue circles and herds of noble elephants and their mates; resorted to by the issamiga, sākhamiga, sarabhamiga, eṇīmiga, vātamiga, and pasadamiga deer, as well as by purasālu-demons, kimpurisas, yakkhas, and rakkhasas; spread with numerous trees bearing non-intoxicating clusters with blossoming tips; constantly resounding with hundreds of flocks of joyful birds such as the kurara, cakora, vāraṇa, peacock, cuckoo, jīvañjīvaka, celāvaka, bhiṅkāra, and karavīka; decorated with regions embellished with antimony, red arsenic, yellow orpiment, cinnabar, gold, silver, and gold, and adorned with hundreds of various minerals—in such a delightful forest grove, friends, dwells a bird named Kuṇāla, exceedingly variegated, with exceedingly variegated wings. Thus it is said, thus it is heard regarding the forest grove where that Kuṇāla king of birds dwells.

“Tasseva khalu, bho, kuṇālassa sakuṇassa aḍḍhuḍḍhāni itthisahassāni paricārikā dijakaññāyo, atha khalu, bho, dve dijakaññāyo kaṭṭhaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā taṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ majjhe nisīdāpetvā uḍḍentimā naṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ addhānapariyāyapathe kilamatho ubbāhetthā”ti.

Indeed, friends, that very bird Kuṇāla had three thousand five hundred female bird attendants. Then, friends, two female bird attendants, holding a stick in their beaks, would seat that bird Kuṇāla in the middle and fly, carrying that Kuṇāla bird, thinking, 'May weariness not overcome him on the long journey.'

“Pañcasatā [M 5.0446] dijakaññāyo heṭṭhato heṭṭhato uḍḍenti ‘sacāyaṃ kuṇālo sakuṇo āsanā paripatissati, mayaṃ taṃ pakkhehi paṭiggahessāmā’ti.

Five hundred female bird attendants flew below him, thinking, 'If this bird Kuṇāla falls from his seat, we will catch him with our wings.'

“Pañcasatā dijakaññāyo uparūpari uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ ātapo paritāpesī’ti.

Five hundred female bird attendants flew directly above him, thinking, 'May the heat not distress the bird Kuṇāla.'

“Pañcasatā dijakaññāyo ubhatopassena uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā tiṇaṃ vā rajo vā vāto vā ussāvo vā upapphusī’ti.

Five hundred female bird attendants flew on both sides, thinking, 'May cold or heat, grass or dust, wind or dew not touch the bird Kuṇāla.'

“Pañcasatā dijakaññāyo purato purato uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ gopālakā vā pasupālakā vā tiṇahārakā vā kaṭṭhahārakā vā vanakammikā vā kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalena vā pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā sakkharāhi vā pahāraṃ adaṃsu, māyaṃ kuṇālo sakuṇo gacchehi vā latāhi vā rukkhehi vā sākhāhi vā thambhehi vā pāsāṇehi vā balavantehi vā pakkhīhi saṅgamesī’ti.

Five hundred young female birds flew in front, thinking, 'May cowherds or shepherds, grass-cutters or wood-gatherers, or forest workers not strike the bird Kuṇāla with a stick, a potsherd, the hand, a clod, a staff, a weapon, or gravel. May the bird Kuṇāla not collide with shrubs, vines, trees, branches, posts, rocks, or powerful birds.'

“Pañcasatā dijakaññāyo pacchato pacchato uḍḍenti saṇhāhi sakhilāhi mañjūhi madhurāhi vācāhi samudācarantiyo ‘māyaṃ kuṇālo sakuṇo āsane pariyukkaṇṭhī’ti.

Five hundred young female birds flew behind, conversing in gentle, friendly, charming, and sweet tones, thinking, 'May the bird Kuṇāla not grow weary of his seat.'

“Pañcasatā [V 5.0413] dijakaññāyo disodisaṃ uḍḍenti anekarukkhavividhavikatiphalamāharantiyo ‘māyaṃ kuṇālo sakuṇo khudāya parikilamitthā’ti.

Five hundred young female birds flew in all directions, bringing various fruits from many trees, thinking, 'May the bird Kuṇāla not be exhausted by hunger.'

“Atha khalu, bho, tā dijakaññāyo taṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ ārāmeneva ārāmaṃ, uyyāneneva uyyānaṃ, nadītittheneva nadītitthaṃ, pabbatasikhareneva pabbatasikharaṃ, ambavaneneva ambavanaṃ, jambuvaneneva jambuvanaṃ, labujavaneneva labujavanaṃ, nāḷikerasañcāriyeneva nāḷikerasañcāriyaṃ khippameva abhisambhonti ratitthāya.

Then, friends, those young female birds swiftly brought the bird Kuṇāla from grove to grove, park to park, river ford to river ford, mountain peak to mountain peak, mango grove to mango grove, rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, and from coconut grove to coconut grove, for the sake of pleasure.

“Atha [M 5.0447] khalu, bho, kuṇālo sakuṇo tāhi dijakaññāhi divasaṃ paribyūḷho evaṃ apasādeti [P 5.0418] ‘nassatha tumhe vasaliyo, vinassatha tumhe vasiliyo coriyo dhuttiyo asatiyo lahucittāyo katassa appaṭikārikāyo anilo viya yenakāmaṃgamāyo’” ti.

Then, friends, the bird Kuṇāla, surrounded by those young female birds all day, would revile them thus: 'Perish, you outcasts! Be destroyed, you outcasts, thieves, deceivers, unmindful ones, fickle-minded ones, ungrateful for favors done, wandering where you wish like the wind!'

Tatrāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – bhikkhave, so vanasaṇḍo evaṃ akkhāyati evañca anusūyati. Kinti? Sabbosadhadharaṇidhareti vitthāro. Tattha sabbosadhadharaṇidhareti mūlatacapattapupphādisabbosadhadharāya dharaṇiyā samannāgateti attho, sabbosadhayutto vā dharaṇidharo. So hi padeso sabbosadhadharaṇidharoti evamakkhāyati evañca anusūyati, tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍeti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesapadayojanāyapi eseva nayo. Nekapupphamālyavitateti anekehi phalatthāya uppannapupphehi ceva piḷandhanamālyehi ca vitate. Rurūti suvaṇṇavaṇṇā migā. Uddārāti uddā. Biḷārāti mahābiḷārā. Nelamaṇḍalaṃ vuccati taruṇabhiṅkacchāpamaṇḍalaṃ. Mahāvarāhāti mahāhatthino, ākiṇṇanelamaṇḍalamahāvarāhena gocariyādibhedena dasavidhena nāgakulena ceva kareṇusaṅghena ca adhivuṭṭheti attho. Issamigāti kāḷasīhā. Vātamigāti mahāvātamigā. Pasadamigāti citramigā. Purisālūti vaḷavāmukhayakkhiniyo. Kimpurisāti devakinnaracandakinnaradumakinnaradaṇḍamāṇavakakonti- sakuṇakaṇṇapāvuraṇādibhedā kinnarā. Amajjavamañjarīdharapahaṭṭhapupphaphusitaggānekapādapagaṇavitateti makuladharehi ceva mañjarīdharehi ca supupphitehi ca aggamattapupphitehi ca anekehi pādapagaṇehi vitate. Vāraṇā nāma hatthiliṅgasakuṇā. Celāvakātipi ete sakuṇāyeva. Hemañca kanakañcāti dve suvaṇṇajātiyo. Etehi añjanādīhi anekadhātusatehi anekehi vaṇṇadhāturāsīhi vinaddhapaṭimaṇḍitapadese. Bhoti dhammālapanamattametaṃ. Cittoti mukhatuṇḍakepi heṭṭhāudarabhāgepi citrova.

Here is the explanation of the meaning: Bhikkhus, that forest grove is thus proclaimed and thus renowned. How so? As 'the bearer of all medicinal herbs'—this is the extent. Therein, 'the bearer of all medicinal herbs' means it is endowed with earth that bears all medicinal herbs—roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and so forth; or it is a bearer of earth connected with all medicinal herbs. For that region is proclaimed and renowned as 'the bearer of all medicinal herbs'; in that forest grove, it is said. This same method applies to the connection of the remaining words. 'Adorned with many flower garlands' means spread with numerous flowers that have bloomed for the sake of fruit and with garlands for adornment. 'Ruru' are golden-colored deer. 'Uddāra' are otters. 'Biḷāra' are large wildcats. 'Nelamaṇḍala' is said to be a flock of young peacocks. 'Mahāvarāha' means great elephants; the meaning is that it is inhabited by a flock of young peacocks and great elephants, that is, by ten kinds of elephant families, distinguished by their grazing grounds and so on, and by a herd of she-elephants. 'Issamiga' are black lions. 'Vātamiga' are great wind-deer. 'Pasadamiga' are spotted deer. 'Purisālū' are female yakkhas with the faces of mares. 'Kimpurisa' are kinnaras of various kinds, such as divine kinnaras, moon kinnaras, tree kinnaras, staff-bearing youths, and those with heron-bird ear-coverings. 'Spread with many groups of trees whose tips are touched with flowers, bearing buds and blossoms' means spread with many groups of trees bearing buds, blossoms, fully bloomed flowers, and flowers only at their tips. 'Vāraṇā' are birds called 'hatthiliṅga'. 'Celāvakā' are also birds. 'Hema and kanaka' are two kinds of gold. 'In a region interwoven and adorned with these and hundreds of other minerals such as antimony, and with many heaps of colored ores.' 'Bho' is merely a term of address. 'Citta' means variegated, both on the beak and also on the lower part of the belly.

Aḍḍhuḍḍhānīti [V 5.0414] aḍḍhacatutthāni, tīṇi sahassāni pañceva satānīti attho. Addhānapariyāyapatheti addhānasaṅkhāte gamanamagge. Ubbāhetthāti [M 5.0448] bādhayittha. Upapphusīti upagantvā phusi. Pahāraṃ adaṃsūti ettha “mā na”nti padassa sāmivasena attho veditabbo. Saṅgamesīti samāgacchi. Saṇhāhīti maṭṭhāhi. Sakhilāhīti piyāhi. Mañjūhīti sakhilāhi. Madhurāhīti madhurassarāhi. Samudācarantiyoti gandhabbakaraṇavasena paricarantiyo. Anekarukkhavividhavikatiphalanti anekehi rukkhehi vividhavikatiphalaṃ. Ārāmeneva ārāmanti pupphārāmādīsu aññatarena ārāmeneva aññataraṃ ārāmaṃ nentīti attho. Uyyānādīsupi eseva nayo. Nāḷikerasañcāriyenevāti nāḷikeravaneneva aññaṃ nāḷikeravanaṃ. Atisambhontīti evaṃ netvā tattha naṃ khippaññeva [P 5.0419] ratitthāya pāpuṇanti.

`Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni` means three and a half (aḍḍhacatutthāni), that is, three thousand five hundred. `Addhānapariyāyapathe` means on the road designated as a journey. `Ubbāhettha` means they might obstruct. `Upapphusī` means having come near, he touched. Regarding `Pahāraṃ adaṃsu` (they gave a blow), the meaning of the prohibitive phrase `mā naṃ` should be understood here in its general application. `Saṅgamesī` means he came together. `Saṇhāhi` means smooth. `Sakhilāhi` means amiable. `Mañjūhi` means amiable. `Madhurāhi` means sweet-voiced. `Samudācarantiyo` means serving by way of the arts of celestial musicians. `Anekarukkhavividhavikatiphala` means various fruits of different kinds from many trees. `Ārāmeneva ārāmaṃ` means leading from one grove, such as a flower grove, to another grove. The same method applies to parks and so on. `Nāḷikerasañcāriyeneva` means from one coconut grove to another coconut grove. `Abhisambhonti` means having led him thus, they quickly bring him there for the sake of pleasure.

Divasaṃ paribyūḷhoti sakaladivasaṃ paribyūḷho. Apasādetīti tā kira taṃ evaṃ divasaṃ paricaritvā nivāsarukkhe otāretvā parivāretvā rukkhasākhāsu nisīditvā “appeva nāma madhuravacanaṃ labheyyāmā”ti patthayantiyo iminā uyyojitakāle attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmāti vasanti. Kuṇālarājā pana tā uyyojento “nassathā”tiādivacanehi apasādeti. Tattha nassathāti gacchatha. Vinassathāti sabbatobhāgena nassatha. Gehe dhanadhaññādīnaṃ nāsanena coriyo, bahumāyatāya dhuttiyo, naṭṭhassatitāya asatiyo, anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lahucittāyo, katavināsanena mittadubbhitāya katassa appaṭikārikāyoti.

`Divasaṃ paribyūḷho` means surrounded the entire day. `Apasādeti` means he rejects—it is said that after attending to him thus the whole day, having led him down to his dwelling tree and surrounded him, they sat on the branches, wishing, 'Perhaps we may receive sweet words.' They wait, intending to go to their own dwelling places at the time of his dismissal. But King Kuṇāla, dismissing them, rejected them with words like 'Vanish!' There, 'Vanish!' means 'Go away!' 'Be utterly destroyed!' means 'Vanish completely!' By the destruction of wealth, grain, and so on in the house, they are thieves; by great deceit, they are deceivers; by lost mindfulness, they are unmindful; by unsteadiness of mind, they are fickle-minded; by destroying what has been done and by treachery to friends, they are ungrateful for what has been done.

Evañca pana vatvā “iti kho, bhikkhave, ahaṃ tiracchānagatopi itthīnaṃ akataññutaṃ bahumāyataṃ anācārataṃ dussīlatañca jānāmi, tadāpāhaṃ tāsaṃ vase avattitvā tā eva attano vase vattemī”ti imāya kathāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anabhiratiṃ haritvā satthā tuṇhī ahosi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dve kāḷakokilā sāmikaṃ daṇḍakena ukkhipitvā heṭṭhābhāgādīsu catasso catasso hutvā taṃ padesaṃ āgamiṃsu. Te bhikkhū tāpi disvā satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthā “pubbe, bhikkhave, mama sahāyo puṇṇamukho nāma phussakokilo ahosi, tassāyaṃ vaṃso”ti vatvā purimanayeneva tehi bhikkhūhi pucchito āha –

Having spoken thus, the Teacher said: 'Thus, monks, even when I was an animal, I knew the ingratitude, great deceitfulness, bad conduct, and immorality of women. Even then, not being under their will, I made them follow my own will.' With this talk, the Teacher dispelled the discontent of those monks and remained silent. At that moment, two black cuckoos, carrying their master with a stick, came to that place, with four female birds each flying below and in other positions. The monks, seeing these birds as well, asked the Teacher. The Teacher said, 'Previously, monks, I had a companion, a spotted cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha. This is his lineage.' Then, being questioned by the monks as before, he said:

“Tasseva [M 5.0449] khalu, bho, himavato pabbatarājassa puratthimadisābhāge susukhumasunipuṇagirippabhavaharitupayantiyo”ti.

Indeed, friends, in the eastern part of that king of mountains, the Himālaya, there are very delicate and exceedingly fine, mountain-born, green streams approaching the lake.

Tattha suṭṭhu sukhumasaṇhasalilatāya susukhumasunipuṇā, giri etāsaṃ pabhavoti girippabhavā[V 5.0415], himavantato sandamānaharitatiṇamissaoghatāya haritā, kuṇāladahaṃ upagamanena upayantiyoti susukhumasunipuṇagirippabhavaharitupayantiyo, evarūpā nadiyo yasmiṃ sandantīti attho.

There, 'susukhumasunipuṇā' means perfectly fine and delicate due to their gentle, soft water. 'Girippabhavā' means the mountain is their source. 'Haritā' means green, due to the stream being mixed with fresh, green grass flowing from the Himālaya. 'Upayantiyo' means approaching the Kuṇāla Lake. The meaning of the compound 'susukhumasunipuṇagirippabhavaharitupayantiyo' is a place where such rivers flow.

Idāni yaṃ kuṇāladahaṃ tā upayanti, tattha pupphāni vaṇṇento āha –

Now, describing the flowers in the Kuṇāla Lake which those rivers approach, he said:

“Uppalapadumakumudanalinasatapattasogandhikamandālakasampativiruḷhasucigandhamanuññamāvakappadese”ti.

In a delightful and purely fragrant place where blue lotuses, red lotuses, water lilies, white lotuses, hundred-petaled lotuses, fragrant water lilies, and mandālaka flowers flourish together.

Tattha uppalanti nīluppalaṃ. Nalinanti setapadumaṃ. Satapattanti paripuṇṇasatapattapadumaṃ. Sampatīti etehi sampativiruḷhehi abhinavajātehi sucigandhena ceva manuññena ca hadayabandhanasamatthatāya māvakena ca padesena samannāgateti attho.

Therein, 'uppala' is the blue lotus. 'Nalina' is the white lotus. 'Satapatta' is the fully-bloomed hundred-petaled lotus. The meaning is that it is endowed with a place which, by these newly arisen flowers flourishing together, is purely fragrant, delightful, and captivating, capable of binding the heart.

Idāni tasmiṃ dahe rukkhādayo vaṇṇento āha –

Now, describing the trees and other things in that lake, he said:

“Kuravakamucalindaketakavedisavañjulapunnāgabakulatilakapiyakahasanasālasaḷala- campakaasokanāgarukkhatirīṭibhujapattaloddacandanoghavane [P 5.0420] kāḷāgarupadmakapiyaṅgudevadārukacocagahane kakudhakuṭajaaṅkolakaccikārakaṇikārakaṇṇikāra- kanaverakoraṇḍakakoviḷārakiṃsukayodhikavanamallikamanaṅgaṇamanavajjabhaṇḍisurucira- bhaginimālāmalyadhare jātisumanamadhugandhikadhanutakkāritālīsatagaramusīrakoṭṭhakacchavitate atimuttakasaṃkusumitalatāvitatapaṭimaṇḍitappadese haṃsapilavakādambakāraṇḍavābhinadite vijjādharasiddhasamaṇatāpasagaṇādhivuṭṭhe varadevayakkharakkhasadānavagandhabbakinnaramahoragānuciṇṇappadese – evarūpe khalu, bho, ramme vanasaṇḍe puṇṇamukho nāma phussakokilo pativasati ativiya madhuragiro vilāsitanayano mattakkho.

In such a delightful grove, friends—a forest with clusters of Kuravaka, Mucalinda, Ketaka, Vedisa, Vañjula, Punnāga, Bakula, Tilaka, Piyaka, Hasana, Sāla, Saḷala, Campaka, Asoka, Nāga-trees, Tirīṭi, Bhujapatta, Lodda, and Sandalwood; a thicket of black aloe wood, Padmaka, Piyaṅgu, Devadāru, and banana; a place with Kakudha, Kuṭaja, Aṅkola, Kaccikāra, Kaṇikāra, Kaṇṇikāra, Kanavera, Koraṇḍaka, Koviḷāra, Kiṃsuka, Yodhika, and Vanamallikā; bearing spotless, blameless, and beautiful Bhaginimālā garlands and flowers like the Bhaṇḍi; a place spread with Jāti, Sumana, Madhugandhika, Dhanutakkāri, Tālīsa, Tagara, Musīra, and Koṭṭhaka; a region adorned and covered with blossoming Atimuttaka vines; resounded with the cries of swans, water-fowl, Kādamba-geese, and Kāraṇḍava-ducks; inhabited by groups of Vidyādharas, Siddhas, ascetics, and hermits; frequented by noble Devas, Yakkhas, Rakkhasas, Dānavas, Gandhabbas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas—in such a charming grove dwells the spotted cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha, whose voice is exceedingly sweet, with playful eyes and a gaze like one intoxicated.

“Tasseva [M 5.0450] khalu, bho, puṇṇamukhassa phussakokilassa aḍḍhuḍḍhāni itthisatāni paricārikā dijakaññāyo. Atha khalu, bho, dve dijakaññāyo kaṭṭhaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ majjhe nisīdāpetvā uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ addhānapariyāyapathe kilamatho ubbāhetthā’ti.

Indeed, friends, that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha had three hundred and fifty female attendants, all young bird-maidens. Then, friends, two young bird-maidens would take a stick in their beaks, seat that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha in the middle, and fly, thinking, 'May the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha not be exhausted or fatigued by the long journey on the path.'

“Paññāsa [V 5.0416] dijakaññāyo heṭṭhato heṭṭhato uḍḍenti ‘sacāyaṃ puṇṇamukho phussakokilo sakuṇo āsanā paripatissati, mayaṃ taṃ pakkhehi paṭiggahessāmā’ti.

Fifty young bird-maidens fly below, thinking, 'If this spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha should fall from his seat, we will catch him with our wings.'

“Paññāsa dijakaññāyo uparūpari uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ ātapo paritāpesī’ti.

Fifty young bird-maidens fly above, thinking, 'May the sun not torment the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha!'

“Paññāsa paññāsa dijakaññāyo ubhatopassena uḍḍenti ‘mānaṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā tiṇaṃ vā rajo vā vāto vā ussāvo vā upapphusī’ti.

Fifty bird-maidens fly on each of the two sides, thinking, 'May the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha not be touched by cold or heat, grass, dust, wind, or dew!'

“Paññāsa dijakaññāyo purato purato uḍḍenti ‘mā naṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ gopālakā vā pasupālakā vā tiṇahārakā vā kaṭṭhahārakā vā vanakammikā vā kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā sakkharāhi vā pahāramadaṃsu, māyaṃ puṇṇamukho phussakokilo gacchehi vā latāhi vā rukkhehi vā sākhāhi vā thambhehi vā pāsāṇehi vā balavantehi vā pakkhīhi saṅgamesī’ti.

Fifty bird-maidens fly ever in front, thinking, ‘Lest the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha be struck by cowherds or shepherds, grass-cutters or wood-gatherers, or forest workers with a stick or a potsherd, with a hand or a clod, with a staff or a weapon, or with gravel; lest this spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha collide with bushes or vines, trees or branches, posts or rocks, or with strong birds.’

“Paññāsa dijakaññāyo pacchato pacchato uḍḍenti saṇhāhi sakhilāhi [P 5.0421] mañjūhi madhurāhi vācāhi samudācarantiyo ‘māyaṃ puṇṇamukho phussakokilo āsane pariyukkaṇṭhī’ti.

Fifty bird-maidens fly ever behind, addressing him with soft, affectionate, lovely, and sweet voices, thinking, ‘Lest this spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha become weary in his seat.’

“Paññāsa dijakaññāyo disodisaṃ uḍḍenti anekarukkhavividhavikatiphalamāharantiyo ‘māyaṃ puṇṇamukho phussakokilo khudāya parikilamitthā’ti.

Fifty bird-maidens fly in all directions, bringing various kinds of fruits from many trees, thinking, ‘Lest this spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha suffer from hunger.’

“Atha khalu, bho, tā dijakaññāyo taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ ārāmeneva ārāmaṃ, uyyāneneva uyyānaṃ, nadītittheneva [M 5.0451] nadītitthaṃ, pabbatasikhareneva pabbatasikharaṃ, ambavaneneva ambavanaṃ, jambuvaneneva jambuvanaṃ, labujavaneneva labujavanaṃ, nāḷikerasañcāriyeneva nāḷikerasañcāriyaṃ khippameva abhisambhonti ratitthāya.

Then, good sir, those bird-maidens swiftly conveyed that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha from grove to grove, from park to park, from river-ford to river-ford, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove, from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, and from coconut grove to coconut grove, for the sake of pleasure.

“Atha khalu, bho, puṇṇamukho phussakokilo tāhi dijakaññāhi divasaṃ paribyūḷho [V 5.0417] evaṃ pasaṃsati ‘sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo, etaṃ kho bhaginiyo tumhākaṃ patirūpaṃ kuladhītānaṃ, yaṃ tumhe bhattāraṃ paricareyyāthā’ti.

Then, good sir, the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha, surrounded by those bird-maidens all day, praised them thus: ‘Well done, well done, sisters! This is indeed fitting for you, daughters of good families, to attend to your husband.’

“Atha khalu, bho, puṇṇamukho phussakokilo yena kuṇālo sakuṇo tenupasaṅkami. Addasaṃsu kho kuṇālassa sakuṇassa paricārikā dijakaññāyo taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ, disvāna yena puṇṇamukho phussakokilo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ayaṃ, samma puṇṇamukha, kuṇālo sakuṇo ativiya pharuso ativiya pharusavāco, appeva nāma tavampi āgamma piyavācaṃ labheyyāmā’ti. ‘Appeva nāma bhaginiyo’ti vatvā yena kuṇālo sakuṇo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā kuṇālena sakuṇena saddhiṃ paṭisammoditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, ekamantaṃ nisinno kho puṇṇamukho phussakokilo taṃ kuṇālaṃ sakuṇaṃ etadavoca – ‘kissa tvaṃ, samma kuṇāla, itthīnaṃ sujātānaṃ kuladhītānaṃ sammāpaṭipannānaṃ micchāpaṭipannosi, amanāpabhāṇīnampi kira, samma kuṇāla, itthīnaṃ manāpabhāṇinā bhavitabbaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana manāpabhāṇīna’nti.

Then, good sir, the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha approached the bird Kuṇāla. The bird-maidens, attendants of the bird Kuṇāla, saw the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha coming from afar. Seeing him, they approached the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha, and having approached, they said to him: ‘Friend Puṇṇamukha, this bird Kuṇāla is exceedingly harsh, exceedingly harsh in speech. Perhaps because of you we might receive pleasing words.’ ‘Perhaps so, sisters,’ he replied, and then approached the bird Kuṇāla. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the bird Kuṇāla and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha said to the bird Kuṇāla: ‘Why, friend Kuṇāla, are you ill-disposed toward well-born women, daughters of good families, who conduct themselves rightly? Indeed, friend Kuṇāla, one should be a speaker of pleasant words even to women who speak unpleasantly; how much more so to those who speak pleasantly?’

“Evaṃ vutte kuṇālo sakuṇo taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ evaṃ apasādesi – ‘nassa tvaṃ, samma jamma vasala, vinassa tvaṃ, samma jamma vasala, ko nu tayā viyatto jāyājinenā’ti. Evaṃ apasādito ca pana puṇṇamukho phussakokilo tatoyeva [P 5.0422] paṭinivatti.

When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha thus: ‘Away with you, you wretched outcast! Be utterly destroyed, you wretched outcast! Who indeed is as clever as you, conquered by a wife?’ Thus rebuked, the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha returned from that very place.

“Atha [M 5.0452] khalu, bho, puṇṇamukhassa phussakokilassa aparena samayena nacirasseva kharo ābādho uppajji, lohitapakkhandikā bāḷhā vedanā vattanti māraṇantikā. Atha khalu, bho, puṇṇamukhassa phussakokilassa paricārikānaṃ dijakaññānaṃ etadahosi – ‘ābādhiko kho ayaṃ puṇṇamukho phussakokilo, appeva nāma imamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyyā’ti ekaṃ adutiyaṃ ohāya yena kuṇālo sakuṇo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Addasā kho kuṇālo sakuṇo tā dijakaññāyo dūratova āgacchantiyo, disvāna tā dijakaññāyo etadavoca – ‘kahaṃ pana tumhaṃ vasaliyo bhattā’ti. ‘Ābādhiko kho, samma kuṇāla, puṇṇamukho phussakokilo appeva nāma tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyyā’ti. Evaṃ vutte kuṇālo sakuṇo tā dijakaññāyo evaṃ apasādesi – ‘nassatha tumhe vasaliyo, vinassatha tumhe vasaliyo coriyo dhuttiyo asatiyo lahucittāyo katassa appaṭikārikāyo [V 5.0418] anilo viya yenakāmaṃgamāyo’ti vatvā yena puṇṇamukho phussakokilo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ etadavoca – ‘haṃ, samma, puṇṇamukhā’ti. ‘Haṃ, samma, kuṇālā’ti.

Then, good sir, not long after, a severe illness arose in the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha: a violent bloody flux, with intense, deadly pains. Then, good sir, it occurred to the bird-maidens, attendants of the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha: ‘This spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha is indeed ill; perhaps he might recover from this illness.’ Abandoning him alone, they approached the bird Kuṇāla. The bird Kuṇāla saw those bird-maidens coming from afar, and upon seeing them, he said to those bird-maidens: ‘Where, you outcasts, is your husband?’ ‘Friend Kuṇāla, the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha is ill; perhaps he might recover from that illness.’ When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked those bird-maidens thus: ‘Away with you, you outcasts! Be utterly destroyed, you outcasts—thieves, deceivers, unfaithful, fickle-minded, ungrateful for what has been done, going wherever you please like the wind!’ Having spoken thus, he approached the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha. Having approached, he said to that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha: ‘Friend Puṇṇamukha, are you alive?’ ‘Friend Kuṇāla, I am alive.’

“Atha khalu, bho, kuṇālo sakuṇo taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ pakkhehi ca mukhatuṇḍakena ca pariggahetvā vuṭṭhāpetvā nānābhesajjāni pāyāpesi. Atha khalu, bho, puṇṇamukhassa phussakokilassa so ābādho paṭippassambhī”ti.

Then, good sir, the bird Kuṇāla, supporting that spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha with his wings and beak, raised him up and made him drink various medicines. Then, good sir, that illness of the spotted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha abated.

Tattha piyakāti setapupphā. Hasanāti ha-kāro sandhikaro, asanāyeva. Tirīṭīti ekā rukkhajāti. Candanāti rattasurabhicandanā. Oghavaneti etesaṃ oghena ghaṭāya samannāgatavane. Devadārukacocagahaneti devadārurukkhehi ceva kadalīhi ca gahane. Kaccikārāti ekā rukkhajāti. Kaṇikārāti mahāpupphā. Kaṇṇikārāti khuddakapupphā. Kiṃsukāti vātaghātakā. Yodhikāti yūthikā. Vanamallikamanaṅgaṇamanavajjabhaṇḍisurucirabhaginimālāmalyadhareti mallikānañca anaṅgaṇānaṃ [M 5.0453] anavajjānañca bhaṇḍīnaṃ surucirānañca bhaginīnaṃ pupphehi mālyadhārayamāne. Dhanutakkārīti dhanupāṭali. Tālīsāti tālīsapattarukkhā. Kacchavitateti etehi jātisumanādīhi vitate nadikacchapabbatakacche. Saṃkusumitalatāti tesu tesu ṭhānesu suṭṭhu kusumitaatimuttakehi ceva nānāvidhalatāhi ca vitatapaṭimaṇḍitapadese. Gaṇādhivuṭṭheti etesaṃ vijjādharādīnaṃ gaṇehi adhivuṭṭhe. Puṇṇamukhoti mukhaparipuṇṇatāya puṇṇamukho. Parehi [P 5.0423] phuṭṭhatāya phussakokilo. Vilāsitanayanoti vilāsitanetto. Mattakkhoti yathā mattānaṃ akkhīni rattāni honti, evaṃ rattakkho, pamāṇayuttanetto vā.

Therein, ‘piyakā’ refers to white flowers. ‘Hasanā’—the syllable ‘ha’ is a euphonic insertion, meaning just ‘asanā’. ‘Tirīṭī’ is a type of tree. ‘Candanā’ refers to red fragrant sandalwood. ‘Oghavana’ means a forest endowed with an abundance of these, like a flood. ‘Devadārukacocagahana’ refers to a thicket of devadāru trees and plantains. ‘Kaccikārā’ is another type of tree. ‘Kaṇikārā’ has large flowers. ‘Kaṇṇikārā’ has small flowers. ‘Kiṃsukā’ are wind-destroyers. ‘Yodhikā’ means ‘yūthikā’ (jasmine). ‘Vanamallikamanaṅgaṇamanavajjabhaṇḍisurucirabhaginimālāmalyadhareti’—wearing garlands made of mallikā flowers, anaṅgaṇa flowers, flawless bhaṇḍī flowers, and the beautiful flowers of the bhaginī. ‘Dhanutakkārī’ is the dhanupāṭali tree. ‘Tālīsā’ refers to the tālīsa-leaf tree. ‘Kacchavitateti’—spread out along riverbanks and mountain slopes with these jasmine and other flowers. ‘Saṃkusumitalatāti’—in those various places, beautifully adorned with well-bloomed atimuttaka and various kinds of creepers spread out. ‘Gaṇādhivuṭṭheti’—inhabited by groups of vidyādharas and others. ‘Puṇṇamukho’—full-faced, because his face is perfectly full. ‘Phussakokilo’—a phussa cuckoo, because he is touched by others. ‘Vilāsitanayano’—with playful eyes. ‘Mattakkho’—his eyes are red like those of intoxicated persons, or his eyes are of appropriate size.

Bhaginiyoti ariyavohārena ālapanaṃ. Paricareyyāthāti sakaladivasaṃ gahetvā vicareyyātha. Iti so piyakathaṃ kathetvā uyyojeti. Kadāci pana kuṇālo saparivāro puṇṇamukhaṃ dassanāya gacchati, kadāci puṇṇamukho kuṇālassa santikaṃ āgacchati. Tenāha “atha khalu, bho”ti. Sammāti vayassa. Āgammāti paṭicca upanissāya. Labheyyāmāti kuṇālassa santikā piyavacanaṃ labheyyāma. Appeva nāmāti api nāma labheyyātha, vakkhāmi nanti. Sujātānanti samajātikānaṃ.

‘Bhaginiyo’: an address by way of noble usage. ‘Paricareyyātha’: you should attend to him, taking him and moving about throughout the day. Thus, having spoken pleasant words, he dismissed them. Sometimes Kuṇāla with his retinue would go to see Puṇṇamukha, and sometimes Puṇṇamukha would come to Kuṇāla. Therefore, it is said, ‘Then, good sir.’ ‘Sammā’: friend. ‘Āgamma’: depending on, based on. ‘Labheyyāma’: we would receive pleasing words from Kuṇāla. ‘Appeva nāma’: perhaps you might obtain. ‘Sujātānaṃ’: of similar birth.

Nassāti palāya. Jammāti lāmaka. Viyattoti ko nu tayā sadiso añño byatto nāma atthi. Jāyājinenāti jāyājitena, ayameva vā pāṭho. Evaṃ itthiparājitena tayā sadiso [V 5.0419] ko nāma byatto atthīti taṃ puna evarūpassa vacanassa abhaṇanatthāya apasādeti. Tatoyevāti “kuddho me kuṇālo”ti cintetvā tatoyeva paṭinivatti, so nivattitvā saparivāro attano nivāsaṭṭhānameva agamāsi.

‘Nassa’: flee. ‘Jamma’: base. ‘Viyatto’: who else is there called ‘distinguished’ who is similar to you? ‘Jāyājinenāti’: by one conquered by a wife, or this is the reading. Thus, who else is there called ‘distinguished’ who is similar to you, conquered by a woman? He disparaged him to prevent him from uttering such words again. ‘Tatoyeva’: thinking, ‘Kuṇāla is angry with me,’ he immediately turned back. Having turned back, he and his retinue went to his own dwelling place.

Appeva nāmāti saṃsayaparivitakko, imamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyya vā no vāti evaṃ cintetvā taṃ ohāya pakkamiṃsu. Tumhanti tumhākaṃ. Appeva nāmāti tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyya vā no vā, amhākaṃ āgatakāle mato bhavissati. Mayañhi idāneva so marissatīti ñatvā tumhākaṃ pādaparicārikā bhavituṃ āgatā. Tenupasaṅkamīti imā itthiyo sāmikassa [M 5.0454] matakāle āgatā paṭikkūlā bhavissāmāti taṃ pahāya āgatā, ahaṃ gantvā mama sahāyakaṃ pupphaphalādīni nānābhesajjāni saṃharitvā arogaṃ karissāmīti cintetvā nāgabalo mahāsatto ākāse uppatitvā yena so tenupasaṅkami. Hanti nipāto, “jīvasi, sammā”ti pucchanto evamāha. Itaropissa “jīvāmī”ti vadanto “haṃ sammā”ti āha. Pāyāpesīti pāyesi. Paṭippassambhīti vūpasamīti.

The phrase “Perhaps” (appeva nāma) indicates doubt and deliberation: “Will he recover from this illness or not?” Thinking thus, they abandoned him and departed. “Yours” (tumhaṃ) means “belonging to you.” The thought “Perhaps he will recover from that illness or not; by the time we return, he will be dead. For, knowing that he would die soon, we came to be your foot-attendants” is what they considered. The phrase “Then he approached” (tenupasaṅkami) refers to the Great Being Nāgabala, who, thinking “These women, having abandoned him and come here, will become repulsive when their husband dies; I will go, gather flowers, fruits, and various medicines, and restore my friend to health,” rose into the sky and approached him. “Hanti” is a particle. Asking “Do you live, friend?” he spoke thus. The other, saying “I live,” replied “Yes, friend.” “He made him drink” (pāyāpesi) means “he caused him to drink” (pāyesi). “It subsided” (paṭippassambhī) means “it became calm” (vūpasami).

Tāpi dijakaññāyo asmiṃ aroge jāte āgatā. Kuṇālopi puṇṇamukhaṃ katipāhaṃ phalāphalāni khādāpetvā tassa balappattakāle, “samma, idāni tvaṃ arogo, attano paricārikāhi saddhiṃ vasa, ahampi attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ so “imā, samma, maṃ bāḷhagilānaṃ pahāya palāyanti, na me etāhi dhuttīhi attho”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “tena hi te, samma, itthīnaṃ pāpabhāvaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti puṇṇamukhaṃ gahetvā himavantapasse manosilātalaṃ netvā sattayojanikasālarukkhamūle manosilāsane nisīdi. Ekasmiṃ passe puṇṇamukho saparivāro nisīdi. Sakalahimavante devaghosanā cari – “ajja kuṇālo sakuṇarājā himavante manosilāsane nisīditvā buddhalīlāya dhammaṃ desessati, taṃ suṇāthā”ti. Paramparaghosena [P 5.0424] cha kāmāvacaradevā sutvā yebhuyyena tattha sannipatiṃsu. Bahunāgasupaṇṇakinnaravijjādharādīnampi devatā tamatthaṃ ugghosesuṃ. Tadā ānando nāma gijjharājā dasasahassagijjhaparivāro gijjhapabbate paṭivasati. Sopi taṃ kolāhalaṃ sutvā “dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti saparivāro āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Nāradopi pañcābhiñño tāpaso dasasahassatāpasaparivuto himavantapadese viharanto taṃ devaghosanaṃ sutvā “sahāyo kira me kuṇālo itthīnaṃ aguṇaṃ kathessati, mahāsamāgamo bhavissati, mayāpi taṃ desanaṃ sotuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tāpasadasasahassena saddhiṃ iddhiyā tattha gantvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Buddhānaṃ desanāsannipātasadiso mahāsamāgamo ahosi. Atha mahāsatto jātissarañāṇena itthidosapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [V 5.0420] atītabhave diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ [M 5.0455] puṇṇamukhaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā kathesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Those young female birds also came when he had recovered from his illness. The bird Kuᅆāla, having fed Puᅆᅆamukha various fruits for a few days, said to him when he had regained his strength: ‘Friend, now you are healthy; stay with your own attendants. I, too, shall return to my own dwelling place.’ Then he replied: ‘Friend, these females abandoned me when I was gravely ill and fled; I have no use for these profligate women.’ Hearing this, the Great Being Kuᅆāla said: ‘In that case, friend, I shall teach you about the evil nature of women.’ Taking Puᅆᅆamukha to the Manosilā plateau on the slopes of the Himalayas, he sat upon the Manosilā seat at the foot of a sal tree seven leagues high. On one side, Puᅆᅆamukha sat with his retinue. A divine proclamation spread throughout the entire Himalayas: ‘Today, Kuᅆāla, the bird king, seated upon the Manosilā seat in the Himalayas, will teach the Dhamma with the majesty of a Buddha. Listen to that Dhamma!’ Through the successive announcements, the devas from the six sense-sphere heavens heard and mostly gathered at that Manosilā plateau. The deities also proclaimed this matter to many nāgas, garuᅁas, kinnaras, vidyādharas, and others. At that time, a vulture king named Ānanda, dwelling on Vulture Peak with a retinue of ten thousand vultures, heard that commotion and came with his retinue to listen to the Dhamma, sitting to one side. The ascetic Nārada, too, possessing the five higher knowledges and dwelling in the Himalayan region with ten thousand ascetics, heard that divine proclamation and thought: ‘Indeed, my friend Kuᅆāla will speak about the faults of women. A great assembly will gather; it is fitting for me too to hear that teaching.’ With his ten thousand ascetics, he traveled there by psychic power and sat to one side. There was a great assembly like those gathered for the teachings of the Buddhas. Then the Great Being Kuᅆāla, by means of his knowledge of past births, narrated matters seen in past existences regarding the faults of women, making Puᅆᅆamukha a personal witness. Expounding this matter, the Teacher said:’

“Atha khalu, bho, kuṇālo sakuṇo taṃ puṇṇamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ gilānavuṭṭhitaṃ aciravuṭṭhitaṃ gelaññā etadavoca –

‘Then indeed, friends, the bird Kuᅆāla said this to Puᅆᅆamukha, the Phussa cuckoo, who had recovered from illness and had not long risen from his sickness:’

“‘Diṭṭhā mayā, samma puṇṇamukha, kaṇhā dvepitikā pañcapatikāya chaṭṭhe purise cittaṃ paṭibandhantiyā, yadidaṃ kabandhe pīṭhasappimhī’”ti. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

‘’I have seen, friend Puᅆᅆamukha, the woman Kaᅆhā, who had two fathers and five husbands, setting her heart on a sixth man—a crippled, trunk-like man.’’ And here, moreover, there is an unsurpassed statement:’

290.

290.

“Athajjuno nakulo bhīmaseno, yudhiṭṭhilo sahadevo ca rājā;

Ete patī pañca maticca nārī, akāsi khujjavāmanakena pāpa’nti.

‘‘Then Arjuna, Nakula, BhĦmasena, Yudhiᅣᅣhila, and King Sahadeva—having transgressed against these five husbands, that woman committed evil with a hunchbacked, crippled dwarf.’’

“Diṭṭhā mayā, samma puṇṇamukha, saccatapāpī nāma samaṇī susānamajjhe vasantī catutthabhattaṃ pariṇāmayamānā surādhuttakena pāpamakāsi.

‘‘I have seen, friend Puᅆᅆamukha, the female ascetic named Saccakā-pāpĦ, living in the middle of a cemetery, who, while observing a four-day fast, committed evil with a drunken rogue.’’

“Diṭṭhā mayā, samma puṇṇamukha, kākavatī nāma devī samuddamajjhe vasantī bhariyā venateyyassa naṭakuverena pāpamakāsi.

‘‘I have seen, friend Puᅆᅆamukha, the queen named KākavatĦ, living in the middle of the ocean, the wife of Venateyya, who committed evil with the dancer Naᅣakuvera.’’

“Diṭṭhā mayā, samma puṇṇamukha, kuruṅgadevī nāma lomasuddarī eḷikakumāraṃ [P 5.0425] kāmayamānā chaḷaṅgakumāradhanantevāsinā pāpamakāsi.

‘‘I have seen, friend Puᅆᅆamukha, the woman named KuruᅅgadevĦ, whose belly was as beautiful as a fine skin, who, while desiring the prince Eᄳika, committed evil with DhanantevāsĦ, the attendant of Prince Chaᄳaᅅga.’’

“Evañhetaṃ mayā ñātaṃ, brahmadattassa mātaraṃ;

Ohāya kosalarājaṃ, pañcālacaṇḍena pāpamakāsi.

‘‘Thus have I known this: the mother of Brahmadatta, abandoning the king of Kosala, committed evil with Pacālacaᅆᅁa.’’

291.

291.

“Etā ca aññā ca akaṃsu pāpaṃ, tasmāhamitthīnaṃ na vissase nappasaṃse;

Mahī yathā jagati samānarattā, vasundharā itarītarāpatiṭṭhā;

Sabbasahā aphandanā akuppā, tathitthiyo tāyo na vissase naro.

‘‘These and others have committed evil; therefore, I neither trust nor praise women. Just as the earth, the ground, which supports all wealth and is the foundation for both the high and the low, is all-enduring, unmoving, and unshakeable—so too are women; a man should not trust them.’’

292.

292.

“Sīho [M 5.0456][V 5.0421] yathā lohitamaṃsabhojano, vāḷamigo pañcāvudho suruddho;

Pasayhakhādī parahiṃsane rato, tathitthiyo tāyo na vissase naro.

‘‘As a lion feeding on blood and flesh, a fierce wild animal with its five weapons, greatly enraged, devouring by force, and delighting in harming others—so too are women; a man should not trust them.’’

“Na khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, vesiyo nāriyo gamaniyo, na hetā bandhakiyo nāma, vadhikāyo nāma etāyo, yadidaṃ vesiyo nāriyo gamaniyo”ti.

‘‘Indeed, friend Puᅆᅆamukha, they are not only called harlots, women, accessible ones, or profligate ones; by their very nature, they are murderers—namely, these harlots, women, and accessible ones.’’

“Coro viya veṇikatā madirāva diddhā vāṇijo viya vācāsanthutiyo issasiṅgamiva viparivattāyo uragamiva dujivhāyo. Sobbhamiva paṭicchannā pātālamiva duppūrā rakkhasī viya duttosā yamovekantahāriyo. Sikhīriva sabbabhakkhā nadīriva sabbavāhī anilo viya yenakāmaṃcarā neru viya avisesakarā visarukkho viya niccaphalitāyoti. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

‘‘Like thieves, they disguise themselves with their braids; like poisoned liquor; like a merchant, they are full of verbal praise; like a bear’s quickness, they are fickle; like a snake, they have double tongues. Like a hidden pit; like an abyss hard to fill; like an ogress hard to satisfy; like Yama, they carry one away inevitably. Like fire, they consume everything; like a river, they sweep everything away; like the wind, they wander wherever they wish; like Mount Neru, they make no distinction; like a poisonous tree, they are always bearing fruit. And here, moreover, there is an unsurpassed statement:’’

293.

293.

“‘Yathā coro yathā diddho, vāṇijova vikatthanī;

Issasiṅgamiva parivattā, dujivhā urago viya.

‘‘’Just like a thief, like poisoned liquor, like a merchant who boasts, like a bear’s quickness, they are fickle; like a snake, they have double tongues.’’’

294.

294.

“‘Sobbhamiva paṭicchannā, pātālamiva duppurā;

Rakkhasī viya duttosā, yamovekantahāriyo.

‘‘’Like a concealed pit, like an abyss hard to fill, like an ogress hard to satisfy, like Yama, they carry one away inevitably.’’’

295.

295.

“Yathā sikhī nadī vāto, nerunāva samāgatā;

Visarukkho viya niccaphalā, nāsayanti ghare bhogaṃ;

Ratanantakaritthiyo’”ti.

‘‘’Just like fire, a river, and the wind, they are like Mount Neru in making no distinction; like a poisonous tree, they are constantly bearing fruit; they destroy wealth in the home; women are the destroyers of treasures.’’’

Tattha gilānavuṭṭhitanti paṭhamaṃ gilānaṃ pacchā vuṭṭhitaṃ. Diṭṭhā mayāti atīte kira brahmadatto kāsirājā sampannabalavāhanatāya kosalarajjaṃ gahetvā kosalarājānaṃ māretvā tassa aggamahesiṃ sagabbhaṃ gahetvā bārāṇasiṃ [P 5.0426] gantvā taṃ attano aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Sā aparabhāge dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Rañño pana pakatiyā dhītā vā putto vā natthi, so tussitvā, “bhadde, varaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. Sā gahitakaṃ katvā [M 5.0457] ṭhapesi. Tassā pana kumārikāya “kaṇhā”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Athassā vayappattāya mātā taṃ āha – “amma, pitarā tava varo dinno, tamahaṃ gahetvā ṭhapesiṃ, tava ruccanakaṃ varaṃ gaṇhā”ti. Sā “amma, mayhaṃ aññaṃ avijjamānaṃ natthi, patiggahaṇatthāya me sayaṃ varaṃ kārehī”ti kilesabahulatāya hirottappaṃ [V 5.0422] bhinditvā mātaraṃ āha. Sā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “yathārucitaṃ patiṃ gaṇhatū”ti vatvā sayaṃ varaṃ ghosāpesi. Rājaṅgaṇe sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā bahū purisā sannipatiṃsu. Kaṇhā pupphasamuggaṃ ādāya uttarasīhapañjare ṭhitā olokentī ekampi na rocesi.

Therein, 'recovered from illness' (gilānavuṭṭhita) means first being ill, and later recovered. 'I have seen' (diṭṭhā mayā): In the past, it is said, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī, possessing a powerful army and vehicles, seized the kingdom of Kosala, killed the king of Kosala, and took his chief queen, who was pregnant, back to Bārāṇasī, where he made her his own chief queen. Later, she gave birth to a daughter. Now, the king had no natural daughter or son of his own, so he was pleased and said, 'Good lady, choose a boon.' She accepted the offer and set it aside. They named the young girl 'Kaṇhā.' When she came of age, her mother said to her: 'Dear, your father granted you a boon, which I accepted and set aside. Now, choose a boon that pleases you.' Due to her abundance of defilements, she cast aside shame and moral dread and said to her mother: 'Mother, there is nothing else I lack. Arrange a self-choice ceremony (sayaṃ vara) for me to take a husband.' The mother informed the king. Saying 'Let her choose a husband as she wishes,' the king had the self-choice ceremony proclaimed. In the royal courtyard, many men, adorned with all their ornaments, gathered. Kaṇhā, taking a flower-basket, stood in the northern lion-window and, looking around, did not approve of a single one.

Tadā paṇḍurājagottato ajjuno nakulo bhīmaseno yudhiṭṭhilo sahadevoti ime pañca paṇḍurājaputtā takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggahetvā “desacārittaṃ jānissāmā”ti vicarantā bārāṇasiṃ patvā antonagare kolāhalaṃ sutvā pucchitvā tamatthaṃ ñatvā “mayampi gamissāmā”ti kañcanarūpasamānarūpā tattha gantvā paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhaṃsu. Kaṇhā te disvā pañcasupi tesu paṭibaddhacittā hutvā pañcannampi sīsesu mālācumbaṭakāni khipitvā, “amma, ime pañca jane varemī”ti āha. Sāpi rañño ārocesi. Rājā varassa dinnattā “na labhissatī”ti avatvā anattamanova “kiṃjātikā kassa puttā”ti pucchitvā paṇḍurājaputtabhāvaṃ ñatvā tesaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā taṃ pādaparicārikaṃ adāsi.

At that time, from the lineage of King Paṇḍu—Ajjuna, Nakula, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṭṭhila, and Sahadeva—these five sons of King Paṇḍu, having mastered the arts under a world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā, were traveling about to learn the customs of various regions. They arrived at Bārāṇasī and, hearing a commotion in the inner city, inquired and learned of the matter. Thinking, 'We too shall go,' they went there, their forms as beautiful as golden statues, and stood in a row. Kaṇhā, seeing them, her heart became captivated by all five, and she threw flower wreaths on the heads of all five, saying, 'Mother, I choose these five men.' The mother informed the king. Because the boon had already been granted, the king did not say, 'She cannot have them,' but, though displeased, asked, 'Of what lineage are they? Whose sons are they?' Learning that they were the sons of King Paṇḍu, he honored them and gave her to them as their wife.

Sā sattabhūmikapāsāde te kilesavasena saṅgaṇhi. Eko panassā paricārako khujjo pīṭhasappī atthi. Sā pañca rājaputte kilesavasena saṅgaṇhitvā tesaṃ bahi nikkhantakāle okāsaṃ labhitvā kilesena anuḍayhamānā khujjena saddhiṃ pāpaṃ karoti, tena ca saddhiṃ kathentī – “mayhaṃ tayā sadiso piyo natthi, rājaputte mārāpetvā tesaṃ galalohitena tava pāde makkhāpessāmī”ti vadati. Itaresupi jeṭṭhabhātikena missībhūtakāle – “imehi catūhi tvameva mayhaṃ piyataro, mayā jīvitampi tavatthāya pariccattaṃ, mama pitu accayena tuyhaññeva rajjaṃ dāpessāmī”ti vadati. Itarehi saddhiṃ missībhūtakālepi eseva [M 5.0458] nayo. Te “ayaṃ amhe piyāyati, issariyañca no etaṃ nissāya jāta”nti tassā ativiya tussanti.

In a seven-storied palace, she won them over by means of her defilements. Now, she had an attendant who was a hunchback and a cripple who moved about on a stool. Having won over the five princes through lust, she would find an opportunity when they went out, and, burning with passion, she would commit misconduct with the hunchback. Speaking with him, she would say: 'There is none dearer to me than you. I will have the princes killed and smear your feet with the blood from their throats.' When she was united with the eldest brother, she would say: 'Of these four others, you alone are the most dear to me. I would even give up my life for your sake. After my father's passing, I will have the kingdom given to you alone.' When she was united with each of the others, she spoke in the same way. Thinking, 'She loves us, and our prosperity is born because of her,' they were all exceedingly pleased with her.

Sā ekadivasaṃ ābādhikā ahosi. Atha naṃ te parivāretvā eko sīsaṃ sambāhanto nisīdi, sesā ekekaṃ hatthañca pādañca. Khujjo pana pādamūle nisīdi. Sā sīsaṃ sambāhamānassa jeṭṭhabhātikassa ajjunakumārassa – “mayhaṃ tayā piyataro natthi, jīvamānā tuyhaṃ jīvissāmi, pitu accayena tuyhaṃ rajjaṃ dāpessāmī”ti sīsena saññaṃ dadamānā taṃ saṅgaṇhi, itaresampi hatthapādehi tatheva saññaṃ adāsi. Khujjassa pana – “tvaññeva mama piyo, tavatthāya ahaṃ jīvissāmī”ti jivhāya saññaṃ adāsi. Te sabbepi pubbe kathitabhāvena [V 5.0423] tāya saññāya tamatthaṃ jāniṃsu. Tesu sesā attano dinnasaññāyeva jāniṃsu. Ajjunakumāro pana tassā hatthapādajivhāvikāre [P 5.0427] disvā – “yathā mayhaṃ, evaṃ sesānampi imāya saññā dinnā bhavissati, khujjena cāpi saddhiṃ etissāya santhavena bhavitabba”nti cintetvā bhātaro gahetvā bahi nikkhamitvā pucchi – “diṭṭhā vo pañcapatikā mama sīsavikāraṃ dassentī”ti? “Āma, diṭṭhā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Na jānāmā”ti. “Idaṃ nāmettha kāraṇaṃ, tumhākaṃ pana hatthapādehi dinnasaññāya kāraṇaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma, jānāmā”ti. “Amhākampi teneva kāraṇena adāsi, khujjassa jivhāvikārena saññādānassa kāraṇaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Na jānāmā”ti. Atha nesaṃ ācikkhitvā “imināpi saddhiṃ etāya pāpakammaṃ kata”nti vatvā tesu asaddahantesu khujjaṃ pakkositvā pucchi. So sabbaṃ pavattiṃ kathesi.

One day, she fell ill. They surrounded her; one sat massaging her head, while the others each massaged a hand or a foot. The hunchback, however, sat at her feet. To the eldest brother, Prince Ajjuna, who was massaging her head, she gave a sign with her head, saying, 'No one is dearer to me than you. While I live, I will live for you. After my father’s passing, I will have the kingdom given to you,' and thus she captivated him. She gave similar signs to the others with her hands and feet. To the hunchback, however, she gave a sign with her tongue, saying, 'You alone are my beloved. For your sake, I will live.' All of them, because of what she had said to them individually before, understood the meaning of her sign. Each of the others understood only the sign given to himself. But Prince Ajjuna, seeing the gestures of her hands, feet, and tongue, thought: 'Just as she has given me a sign, she must have given signs to the others. And there must be an intimacy between her and the hunchback.' Taking his brothers outside, he asked: 'Did you see the woman with five husbands showing me a gesture with her head?' 'Yes, we saw it.' 'Do you know the reason?' 'We do not know.' 'This is the reason. But do you know the reason for the sign she gave you with your hands and feet?' 'Yes, we know.' 'She gave it to us for that same reason. Do you know the reason for the sign given to the hunchback with her tongue?' 'We do not know.' Then, explaining it to them, he said: 'She has committed an evil deed with him too.' When they did not believe him, he called the hunchback and questioned him. He confessed the whole affair.

Te tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tassā vigatacchandarāgā hutvā – “aho mātugāmo nāma pāpo dussīlo, mādise nāma jātisampanne sobhaggappatte pahāya evarūpena jegucchapaṭikūlena khujjena saddhiṃ pāpakammaṃ karoti, ko nāma paṇḍitajātiko evaṃ nillajjāhi pāpadhammāhi itthīhi saddhiṃ ramissatī”ti anekapariyāyena mātugāmaṃ garahitvā “alaṃ no gharāvāsenā”ti pañca janā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā āyupariyosāne yathākammaṃ gatā. Kuṇālo pana sakuṇarājā tadā ajjunakumāro ahosi. Tasmā attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ dassento “diṭṭhā mayā”tiādimāha.

Hearing his words, they became free from desire and passion for her. 'Alas, how wicked and immoral is womankind! Having abandoned such noble-born and splendid men as us, she commits an evil deed with such a repulsive and disgusting hunchback. What man of a wise nature would ever take delight in such shameless and wicked women?' Thus, they rebuked womankind in many ways and, declaring, 'Enough of household life for us!', the five men entered the Himalayas, went forth, practiced kasiṇa meditation, and at the end of their lives, passed away according to their deeds. Kuṇāla, the king of birds, was Prince Ajjuna at that time. Therefore, to show the instance he himself had witnessed, he said, 'I have seen,' and so forth.

Tattha [M 5.0459] dvepitikāti kosalarañño ca kāsirañño ca vasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pañcapatikāyāti pañcapatikā, ya-kāro nipātamatto. Paṭibandhantiyāti paṭibandhamānā. Kabandheti tassa kira gīvā onamitvā uraṃ allīnā, tasmā chinnasīso viya khāyati. Pañca maticcāti ete pañca atikkamitvā. Khujjavāmanakenāti khujjena vāmanakena.

Here, 'dvepitikā' is said with reference to the king of Kosala and the king of Kasi. 'Pañcapatikāyāti' means 'pañcapatikā'; the 'ya' is merely a particle. 'Paṭibandhantiyāti' means 'paṭibandhamānā' (obstructing). 'Kabandheti': it is said that his neck was bent down and adhered to his chest, therefore he appeared as if headless. 'Pañca maticcāti' means 'having transgressed these five'. 'Khujjavāmanakenāti' means 'by a hunchbacked dwarf'.

Idaṃ vatvā aparānipi diṭṭhapubbāni dassento puna “diṭṭhā”tiādimāha. Tattha dutiyavatthusmiṃ tāva ayaṃ vibhāvanā – atīte kira bārāṇasiṃ nissāya saccatapāpī nāma setasamaṇī susāne paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā tattha vasamānā cattāri bhattāni atikkamitvā bhuñjati, sakalanagare cando viya sūriyo viya ca pākaṭā ahosi. Bārāṇasivāsino khipitvāpi khalitvāpi “namo saccatapāpiyā”ti vadanti. Athekasmiṃ chaṇakāle paṭhamadivase tāva suvaṇṇakārā gaṇabandhena ekasmiṃ padese maṇḍapaṃ katvā macchamaṃsasurāgandhamālādīni āharitvā [V 5.0424] surāpānaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Atheko suvaṇṇakāro surāpiṭṭhakaṃ chaḍḍento – “namo saccatapāpiyā”ti vatvā ekena paṇḍitena – “ambho andhabāla, calacittāya itthiyā namo karosi, aho bālo”ti vutte – “samma, mā evaṃ avaca, mā nirayasaṃvattanikaṃ kammaṃ karī”ti āha. Atha naṃ so “dubbuddhi tuṇhī hohi, sahassena abbhutaṃ karohi, ahaṃ te saccatapāpiṃ ito sattame divase alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nisinno surāpiṭṭhakaṃ gāhāpetvā suraṃ pivissāmi[P 5.0428], mātugāmo dhuvasīlo nāma natthī”ti āha. So “na sakkhissasī”ti vatvā tena saddhiṃ sahassena abbhutamakāsi. So taṃ aññesaṃ suvaṇṇakārānaṃ ārocetvā punadivase pātova tāpasavesena susānaṃ pavisitvā tassā vasanaṭṭhānassa avidūre sūriyaṃ namassanto aṭṭhāsi.

Having said this, showing other instances seen before, he further said, 'I have seen,' and so forth. Here, in the second story, this is the explanation: In the past, near Benares, there was a white-clad female ascetic named Saccatapāpī who had a leaf-hut built in a charnel ground and lived there. She would eat only after skipping four meals, and she became as famous throughout the city as the moon or the sun. The residents of Benares would say, 'Homage to Saccatapāpī,' even when sneezing or stumbling. Once, during a festival, on the first day, a group of goldsmiths built a pavilion in a certain place and, having brought fish, meat, liquor, perfumes, and garlands, began drinking. One goldsmith, while discarding a liquor-vessel, said, 'Homage to Saccatapāpī.' A wise man then said, 'Hey, you blind fool, you pay homage to a fickle-minded woman? How foolish!' When the goldsmith replied, 'Friend, do not speak like that; do not commit an act that leads to hell,' the wise man said to him: 'You fool, be silent. Wager a thousand! On the seventh day from now, I, seated right here in this pavilion, will have Saccatapāpī, adorned and prepared, carry a vessel of liquor, and I will drink it. There is no woman who is truly virtuous.' The goldsmith said, 'You will not be able to,' and made a wager of a thousand with him. The wise man informed the other goldsmiths and, the next day, early in the morning, disguised as an ascetic, he entered the charnel ground and stood not far from her dwelling, paying homage to the sun.

Sā bhikkhāya gacchamānā naṃ disvā – “mahiddhiko tāpaso bhavissati, ahaṃ tāva susānapasse vasāmi, ayaṃ majjhe susānassa vasati, bhavitabbamassabbhantare santadhammena, vandissāmi na”nti upasaṅkamitvā vandi. So neva olokesi na ālapi. Dutiyadivasepi tatheva akāsi. Tatiyadivase pana vanditakāle adhomukhova “gacchāhī”ti āha. Catutthadivase [M 5.0460] “kacci bhikkhāya na kilamasī”ti paṭisanthāramakāsi. Sā “paṭisanthāro me laddho”ti tuṭṭhā pakkāmi. Pañcamadivase bahutaraṃ paṭisanthāraṃ labhitvā thokaṃ nisīditvā gatā. Chaṭṭhe divase pana taṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ – “bhagini, kiṃ nu kho ajja bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāgītavāditasaddo”ti vatvā – “ayya, tumhe na jānātha, nagare chaṇo ghuṭṭho, tattha kīḷantānaṃ esa saddo”ti vutte – “ettha nāmeso saddo”ti ajānanto viya hutvā – “bhagini, kati bhattāni atikkamesī”ti pucchi. “Cattāri, ayya, tumhe pana kati atikkamethā”ti? “Satta bhaginī”ti. Idaṃ so musā abhāsi. Devasikaṃ hesa rattiṃ bhuñjati.
