So taṃ “kati te bhagini vassāni pabbajitāyā”ti pucchitvā tāya “dvādasa vassānī”ti vatvā “tumhākaṃ kati vassānī”ti vutto “idaṃ me chaṭṭhaṃ vassa”nti āha. Atha naṃ “atthi pana te bhagini santadhammādhigamo”ti pucchitvā “natthi, ayya, tumhākaṃ pana atthī”ti vutte “mayhampi natthī”ti vatvā – “bhagini, mayaṃ neva kāmasukhaṃ labhāma, na nekkhammasukhaṃ, kiṃ amhākaṃyeva uṇho nirayo, mahājanassa kiriyaṃ karoma, ahaṃ gihī bhavissāmi, atthi me mātu santakaṃ dhanaṃ, na sakkomi dukkhaṃ anubhavitu”nti āha. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā attano calacittatāya tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā hutvā – “ayya, ahampi ukkaṇṭhitā, sace pana maṃ na chaḍḍessatha, ahampi gihinī bhavissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ so “ehi taṃ na chaḍḍessāmi, bhariyā me bhavissasī”ti taṃ nagaraṃ pavesetvā saṃvasitvā surāpānamaṇḍapaṃ [V 5.0425] gantvā tāya surāpiṭṭhakaṃ gāhāpetvā suraṃ pivi. Itaro sahassaṃ jito. Sā taṃ paṭicca puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhi. Tadā kuṇālo surādhuttako ahosi. Tasmā attanā diṭṭhaṃ pakāsento “diṭṭhā mayā”tiādimāha.

While going for alms, she saw him and thought: 'This must be a powerful ascetic. I stay at the edge of the charnel ground, while he stays in its center. He must have attained the peaceful state within. I will pay homage to him.' She approached and paid homage. He neither looked at her nor spoke. He did the same on the second day. On the third day, however, when she paid homage, he said with his face cast down, 'Go away.' On the fourth day, he greeted her, asking, 'I hope you are not weary from the alms round?' Delighted, she thought, 'I have received a greeting,' and left. On the fifth day, she received more conversation, sat for a short while, and departed. On the sixth day, when she came, paid homage, and sat down, he asked: 'Sister, what is that great sound of music in Benares today?' She replied, 'Venerable sir, do you not know? A festival has been proclaimed in the city. That is the sound of those celebrating.' He, acting as if he did not know, said, 'So that is what the sound is.' Then he asked, 'Sister, how many meals do you skip?' 'Four, venerable sir. And how many do you skip?' 'Seven, sister,' he lied—for he actually ate every night. He then asked, 'Sister, how many years have you been ordained?' When she replied, 'Twelve years,' and asked, 'And how many for you?' he said, 'This is my sixth year.' Then he asked, 'Sister, have you attained any peaceful state?' She answered, 'No, venerable sir. Have you?' 'I have not either,' he said. 'Sister, we enjoy neither sensual pleasures nor the bliss of renunciation. Is hell hot only for us? Let us do as the people do. I will return to household life. I have wealth inherited from my parents—I cannot endure this suffering.' Hearing his words, her mind, being wavering, became attached to him. She said, 'Venerable sir, I too am discontent. If you will not abandon me, I will also return to lay life.' He replied, 'Come, I will not abandon you. You shall be my wife.' He led her into the city, cohabited with her, and went to the liquor-drinking pavilion. He had her carry the liquor-vessel and he drank the liquor. The other man lost the thousand. Relying on that drunkard, she prospered with sons and daughters. At that time, Kuṇāla was that drunkard. Therefore, revealing what he had seen, he said, 'I have seen...' and so on.

Tatiyavatthusmiṃ atītakathā catukkanipāte kākavatījātakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 3.4.kākavatījātakavaṇṇanā) vitthāritā. Tadā pana kuṇālo garuḷo ahosi. Tasmā attanā diṭṭhaṃ pakāsento “diṭṭhā mayā”tiādimāha.

In the third story, the past account is detailed in the commentary on the Kākavatī Jātaka in the Catukkanipāta. At that time, Kuṇāla was a garuḷa. Therefore, revealing what he himself had seen, he said, 'I have seen,' and so forth.

Catutthavatthusmiṃ atīte brahmadatto kosalarājānaṃ vadhitvā rajjaṃ gahetvā tassa aggamahesiṃ gabbhiniṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā tassā gabbhinibhāvaṃ jānantopi taṃ aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Sā paripakkagabbhā suvaṇṇarūpakasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyitvā – “vuddhippattampi naṃ bārāṇasirājā ‘esa [M 5.0461] me [P 5.0429] paccāmittassa putto, kiṃ iminā’ti mārāpessati, mā me putto parahatthe maratū”ti cintetvā dhātiṃ āha – “amma, imaṃ dārakaṃ pilotikaṃ attharitvā āmakasusāne nipajjāpetvā ehī”ti. Dhātī tathā katvā nhatvā paccāgami. Kosalarājāpi maritvā puttassa ārakkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tassānubhāvena ekassa eḷakapālakassa tasmiṃ padese eḷake cārentassa ekā eḷikā taṃ kumāraṃ disvā sinehaṃ uppādetvā khīraṃ pāyetvā thokaṃ caritvā puna gantvā dve tayo cattāro vāre pāyesi. Eḷakapālako tassā kiriyaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ dārakaṃ disvā puttasinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā netvā attano bhariyāya adāsi. Sā pana aputtikā, tenassā thaññaṃ natthi, atha naṃ eḷikakhīrameva pāyesi. Tato paṭṭhāya pana devasikaṃ dve tisso eḷikā maranti. Eḷakapālo – “imasmiṃ paṭijaggiyamāne sabbā eḷikā marissanti, kiṃ no iminā”ti taṃ ekasmiṃ mattikābhājane nipajjāpetvā aparena pidahitvā māsacuṇṇena mukhaṃ nibbivaraṃ vilimpitvā nadiyaṃ vissajjesi. Tamenaṃ vuyhamānaṃ heṭṭhātitthe rājanivesane jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkhārako eko caṇḍālo sapajāpatiko makaciṃ dhovanto disvāva vegena gantvā āharitvā tīre ṭhapetvā “kimetthā”ti vivaritvā olokento dārakaṃ passi. Bhariyāpissa aputtikā, tassā tasmiṃ puttasineho nibbatti, atha naṃ gehaṃ netvā paṭijaggi. Taṃ sattaṭṭhavassakālato paṭṭhāya mātāpitaro rājakulaṃ gacchantā ādāya gacchanti. Soḷasavassakālato pana paṭṭhāya sveva bahulaṃ gantvā jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karoti.

In the fourth story, in the past, Brahmadatta, the king of Bārāṇasī, killed the king of Kosala, seized his kingdom, and took his chief queen, who was pregnant, back to Bārāṇasī. Even though he knew of her pregnancy, he made her his chief queen. When her pregnancy came to term, she gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. Thinking, 'Even when he grows up, the king of Bārāṇasī will say, "This is the son of my enemy, what use is he to me?" and will have him killed. May my son not die at the hands of another,' she instructed her nurse, 'My dear, spread out a rag and lay this child in the charnel ground, then return.' The nurse did as she was told, bathed, and came back. The king of Kosala, having died, was reborn as a protective deity for his son. By the power of that deity, while a certain goatherd was tending goats in that area, a she-goat saw the boy and felt affection for him; she gave him milk and, after wandering a bit, returned and fed him two, three, or four times. The goatherd, observing her behavior, went to that spot, saw the child, and felt paternal affection arise; he took him and gave him to his wife. Since she was childless and had no milk, she fed the child only goat's milk. From then on, two or three she-goats died each day. The goatherd thought, 'If this child is cared for, all the she-goats will die. What use is he to us?' So he placed the child in an earthen pot, covered it with another vessel, sealed its mouth with bean flour so that there was no opening, and set it adrift in the river. As it was floating downstream, a certain caṇḍāla who repaired old things, along with his wife, saw it while washing a fiber-garment at the lower ford of the royal residence. They quickly went and fetched it, placed it on the bank, and upon opening it, saw the child. Since his wife was also childless, she felt maternal affection for him; they took him home and raised him. From the age of seven or eight, whenever his parents went to the royal palace, they took him along. From the age of sixteen onwards, he himself frequently went there to perform the repair work.

Rañño ca aggamahesiyā kuruṅgadevī nāma dhītā ahosi uttamarūpadharā. Sā tassa diṭṭhakālato [V 5.0426] paṭṭhāya tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā hutvā aññattha anabhiratā tassa kammakaraṇaṭṭhānameva āgacchati. Tesaṃ abhiṇhadassanena aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhacittānaṃ antorājakuleyeva paṭicchannokāse ajjhācāro pavatti. Gacchante kāle paricārikāyo ñatvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā kujjhitvā amacce sannipātetvā – “iminā caṇḍālaputtena idaṃ nāma kataṃ, imassa kattabbaṃ jānāthā”ti āha. Amaccā “mahāparādho esa, nānāvidhakammakāraṇā kāretvā pacchā māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kumārassa pitā ārakkhadevatā [M 5.0462] tasseva kumārassa mātu sarīre adhimucci. Sā devatānubhāvena rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “mahārāja, nāyaṃ kumāro caṇḍālo, esa kumāro mama kucchimhi nibbatto kosalarañño putto, ahaṃ ‘putto me mato’ti tumhākaṃ musā avacaṃ, ahametaṃ ‘tumhākaṃ paccāmittassa putto’ti dhātiyā datvā āmakasusāne chaḍḍāpesiṃ, atha naṃ eko eḷakapālako paṭijaggi, so attano eḷikāsu marantīsu nadiyā pavāhesi, atha naṃ vuyhamānaṃ tumhākaṃ gehe jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkhārako caṇḍālo disvā posesi, sace na saddahatha, te sabbe pakkosāpetvā pucchathā”ti.

The king and his chief queen had a daughter named Kuruṅgadevī, who was of surpassing beauty. From the moment she saw him, her heart became attached to him, and finding no pleasure elsewhere, she would come only to the place where he worked. Through their frequent meetings, their hearts became bound to each other, and an illicit affair took place in a secluded spot within the royal palace. As time passed, the attendants learned of this and informed the king. The king, enraged, assembled his ministers and said, 'This son of a caṇḍāla has done such a thing—decide what should be done to him.' The ministers replied, 'This is a grave offense. After subjecting him to various kinds of torture, he should be put to death.' At that very moment, the boy's father, who was the guardian deity, possessed the body of the boy’s mother. By the power of the deity, she approached the king and said, 'Great king, this boy is not a caṇḍāla. He is the son of the king of Kosala, born from my womb. I lied to you when I said my son was dead. Thinking, "He is the son of your enemy," I gave him to a nurse and had him abandoned in the charnel ground. Then a goatherd cared for him, and when his she-goats started dying, he set him adrift on the river. Then, as he floated along, a caṇḍāla in your household who repairs old things saw him and raised him. If you do not believe this, summon them all and question them.'

Rājā dhātiṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbe pakkosāpetvā pucchitvā tatheva taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “jātisampannoyaṃ kumāro”ti tuṭṭho taṃ nhāpetvā alaṅkārāpetvā tasseva dhītaraṃ adāsi. Tassa pana eḷikānaṃ māritattā [P 5.0430] “eḷikakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Athassa rājā sasenavāhanaṃ datvā – “gaccha attano pitu santakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhā”ti taṃ uyyojesi. Sopi kuruṅgadeviṃ ādāya gantvā rajje patiṭṭhāsi. Athassa bārāṇasirājā “anuggahitasippo aya”nti sippasikkhāpanatthaṃ chaḷaṅgakumāraṃ nāma ācariyaṃ pesesi. So tassa “ācariyo me”ti senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Aparabhāge kuruṅgadevī tena saddhiṃ anācāramakāsi. Senāpatinopi paricārako dhanantevāsī nāma atthi. So tassa hatthe kuruṅgadeviyā vatthālaṅkārādīni pesesi. Sā tenapi saddhiṃ pāpamakāsi. Kuṇālo taṃ kāraṇaṃ āharitvā dassento “diṭṭhā mayā”tiādimāha.

The king, having summoned the nurse and all the others and questioned them, heard the true account and, being pleased, declared, 'This prince is indeed of noble birth.' He then had him bathed and adorned, and gave him his own daughter, Kuruṅgadevī, in marriage. However, because of the death of the she-goats, they named him 'Eḷikakumāra.' Then the king gave him an army with its vehicles and sent him off, saying, 'Go and claim your father's property, the kingdom of Kosala.' Taking Kuruṅgadevī with him, he went and established himself in the kingship. Later, the king of Bārāṇasī, thinking, 'This prince is untrained in the arts,' sent a teacher named Chaḷaṅgakumāra to instruct him in the arts. The prince, thinking, 'This is my teacher,' gave him the position of commander of the army. In time, Kuruṅgadevī committed misconduct with him. The commander also had an attendant named Dhanantevāsī. By his hand, the commander would send clothes, ornaments, and so on to Kuruṅgadevī. She committed misconduct with him as well. Kuṇāla, bringing up this matter to point it out, said the verse beginning with 'Diṭṭhā mayā' (I have seen).

Tattha lomasuddarīti lomarājiyā maṇḍitaudarā. Chaḷaṅgakumāradhanantevāsināti eḷikakumārakaṃ patthayamānāpi chaḷaṅgakumārasenāpatinā ca tasseva paricārakena dhanantevāsinā ca saddhiṃ pāpamakāsi. Evaṃ anācārā itthiyo dussīlā pāpadhammā, tenāhaṃ tā nappasaṃsāmīti idaṃ mahāsatto atītaṃ āharitvā dassesi. So hi tadā chaḷaṅgakumāro ahosi, tasmā attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ āhari.

In that context, 'lomasuddarī' means 'one whose belly is adorned with a line of hair.' The phrase 'with Chaḷaṅgakumāra and Dhanantevāsī' means that although she was desirous of Prince Eḷikakumāra, she committed sin with the commander Chaḷaṅgakumāra and with his attendant Dhanantevāsī. Thus, women of bad conduct are immoral and of wicked nature; therefore, I do not praise them—the Great Being showed this by relating a past event. For at that time, he was Chaḷaṅgakumāra; therefore, he recounted the event he had seen himself.

Pañcamavatthusmimpi [V 5.0427] atīte kosalarājā bārāṇasirajjaṃ gahetvā bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiṃ gabbhinimpi aggamahesiṃ katvā sakanagarameva gato[M 5.0463]. Sā aparabhāge puttaṃ vijāyi. Rājā aputtakattā taṃ puttasinehena posetvā sabbasippāni sikkhāpetvā vayappattaṃ “attano pitu santakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhā”ti pesesi. So tattha gantvā rajjaṃ kāresi. Athassa mātā “puttaṃ passitukāmāmhī”ti kosalarājānaṃ āpucchitvā mahāparivārā bārāṇasiṃ gacchantī dvinnaṃ raṭṭhānaṃ antare ekasmiṃ nigame nivāsaṃ gaṇhi. Tattheveko pañcālacaṇḍo nāma brāhmaṇakumāro atthi abhirūpo. So tassā paṇṇākāraṃ upanāmesi. Sā taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā tena saddhiṃ pāpakammaṃ katvā katipāhaṃ tattheva vītināmetvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā puttaṃ disvā khippaṃ nivattitvā puna tasmiṃyeva nigame nivāsaṃ gahetvā katipāhaṃ tena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ caritvā kosalanagaraṃ gatā. Sā tato paṭṭhāya nacirasseva taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ vatvā “puttassa santikaṃ gacchāmī”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā gacchantī ca āgacchantī ca tasmiṃ nigame aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ tena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ cari. Samma puṇṇamukha, itthiyo nāmetā dussīlā musāvādiniyoti idampi atītaṃ dassento mahāsatto “evañheta”ntiādimāha.

In the fifth story as well, in the past, the King of Kosala, having seized the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, made the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī, even though she was pregnant, his own chief queen and returned to his own city. Later, she gave birth to a son. Since the King had no son of his own, he raised the boy with paternal affection, had him taught all the arts, and when he reached maturity, sent him away, saying, 'Go and take the kingdom that belonged to your father.' He went there and ruled as king. Then his mother, wishing to see her son, took leave of the King of Kosala and set out for Bārāṇasī with a large retinue. Between the two kingdoms, she took up residence in a certain market town. There was a handsome young brahmin there named Pañcālacaṇḍa. He presented her with a gift. Seeing him, she became infatuated and committed an evil deed with him. After spending a few days there, she went to Bārāṇasī, saw her son, quickly returned, and again took up residence in that same market town. For a few days, she engaged in misconduct with him, then went to the city of Kosala. From then on, before long, making various excuses, she would say, 'I am going to see my son,' take leave of the king, and on her way there and back, spend about half a month in that market town engaging in misconduct with him. 'Friend Puṇṇamukha, women are indeed immoral and deceitful'—thus, the Great Being, showing this past event, said, 'So it is,' and so forth.

Tattha brahmadattassa mātaranti bārāṇasirajjaṃ kārentassa brahmadattakumārassa mātaraṃ. Tadā kira kuṇālo pañcālacaṇḍo ahosi, tasmā taṃ attanā ñātakāraṇaṃ dassento evamāha.

There, 'Brahmadatta’s mother' refers to the mother of Prince Brahmadatta, who was ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. At that time, it is said, Kuṇāla was Pañcālacaṇḍa; therefore, showing the fact known to himself, he spoke thus.

Etā cāti, samma puṇṇamukha, etāva pañca itthiyo pāpamakaṃsu, na aññāti saññaṃ mā kari, atha kho etā ca aññā ca bahū pāpakammakārikāti. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhatvā loke aticārinīnaṃ vatthūni kathetabbāni. Jagatīti yathā jagatisaṅkhātā mahī samānarattā paṭighābhāvena sabbesu samānarattā hutvā sā vasundharā itarītarāpatiṭṭhā [P 5.0431] uttamānañca adhamānañca patiṭṭhā hoti, tathā itthiyopi kilesavasena sabbesampi uttamādhamānaṃ patiṭṭhā honti. Itthiyo hi okāsaṃ labhamānā kenaci saddhiṃ pāpakaṃ karonti nāma. Sabbasahāti yathā ca sā sabbameva sahati na phandati na kuppati na calati, tathā itthiyo sabbepi purise lokassādavasena sahanti. Sace tāsaṃ koci puriso citte patiṭṭhito hoti, tassa rakkhaṇatthaṃ na phandanti na calanti na kolāhalaṃ karonti[M 5.0464]. Yathā ca sā na kuppati na calati, evaṃ itthiyopi methunadhammena na kuppanti na calanti, na sakkā tena pūretuṃ.

“These and others,” means: 'Friend Puṇṇamukha, do not form the notion that only these five women have done evil, and no others; rather, both these and many others are doers of wicked deeds.' At this point, stories of unchaste women in the world should be told. 'The earth' (jagatī): just as the earth, known as 'jagatī,' is impartial because of its lack of aversion, being impartial toward all, that earth is the support for each and every thing, the support for both the noble and the base; so too, women, through the power of defilement, are the support for all men, both noble and base. For when women get an opportunity, they indeed commit evil with anyone. 'All-enduring' (sabbasahā): just as the earth endures everything, does not tremble, does not get angry, and does not move, so too women endure all men through the power of delighting in defilement. If any man is established in their minds, they do not tremble, move, or make an uproar to protect him. And just as the earth does not get angry or move, so too women are not satisfied or shaken by sexual intercourse; it is impossible to satisfy them with it.

Vāḷamigoti duṭṭhamigo. Pañcāvudhoti mukhassa ceva catunnañca caraṇānaṃ vasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Suruddhoti suluddho supharuso. Tathitthiyoti yathā hi sīhassa mukhañceva cattāro ca hatthapādāti [V 5.0428] pañcāvudhāni, tathā itthīnampi rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbāni pañcāvudhāni. Yathā so attano bhakkhaṃ gaṇhanto tehipi pañcahi gaṇhāti, tathā tāpi kilesabhakkhaṃ gaṇhamānā rūpādīhi āvudhehi paharitvā gaṇhanti. Yathā so kakkhaḷo pasayha khādati, evaṃ etāpi kakkhaḷā pasayha khādikā. Tathā hetā thirasīlepi purise attano balena pasayhakāraṃ katvā sīlavināsaṃ pāpenti. Yathā so parahiṃsane rato, evametāpi kilesavasena parahiṃsane ratā. Tāyoti tā evaṃ aguṇasammannāgatā na vissase naro.

'A fierce beast' (vāḷamigo) means a vicious animal. 'Five-weaponed' (pañcāvudho) is said with reference to the mouth and the four feet. 'Very fierce' (suruddho) means very cruel and very harsh. 'Just so with women' means: just as a lion has five weapons in its mouth and its four paws, so too women have five weapons in the form of sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Just as a lion seizes its prey with those five weapons, so too do they, seeking the prey of defilement, strike and seize with the weapons of sight and so on. Just as it is fierce and devours by force, so too are they fierce and devourers by force. For thus they, by their own power, using force even upon men of firm virtue, bring about the destruction of their virtue. Just as it delights in harming others, so too do they, through the power of defilement, delight in harming others. 'By those' (tāyo) means a man should not trust those who are thus endowed with bad qualities.

Gamaniyoti gaṇikāyo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma puṇṇamukha, yānetāni itthīnaṃ “vesiyo”tiādīni nāmāni, na etāni tāsaṃ sabhāvanāmāni. Na hetā vesiyo nāma gamaniyo nāma bandhakiyo nāma, sabhāvanāmato pana vadhikāyo nāma etāyo, yā etā vesiyo nāriyo gamaniyoti vuccanti. Vadhikāyoti sāmikaghātikāyo. Svāyamattho mahāhaṃsajātakena dīpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Courtesans' (gamaniyo) means prostitutes. This is what is said: 'Friend Puṇṇamukha, these names given to women, such as prostitutes (vesiyo) and so forth, are not their names according to their true nature. For they are not called prostitutes, courtesans, or harlots by nature; but according to their inherent nature, these who are called prostitutes, women, and courtesans are called murderesses (vadhikāyo).' 'Murderesses' means killers of their husbands. This meaning should be explained by the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka. For it is said:

“Māyā cetā marīcī ca, sokā rogā cupaddavā;

Kharā ca bandhanā cetā, maccupāsā guhāsayā;

Tāsu yo vissase poso, so naresu narādhamo”ti. (jā. 2.21.118);

“These women are illusion and mirage, sorrow, disease, and calamity; they are harsh and are the bonds of death; they are the snares of Death, dwelling in the cave of the body. Whatever man trusts in them, he is the lowest among men.”

Veṇikatāti kataveṇiyo. Yathā hi moḷiṃ bandhitvā aṭaviyaṃ ṭhitacoro dhanaṃ vilumpati, evametāpi kilesavasaṃ netvā dhanaṃ vilumpanti. Madirāva diddhāti visamissakā surā viya. Yathā sā vikāraṃ dasseti, evametāpi aññesu purisesu sārattā kiccākiccaṃ ajānantiyo aññasmiṃ kattabbe aññameva karontiyo vikāraṃ dassenti. Vācāsanthutiyoti yathā vāṇijo attano bhaṇḍassa vaṇṇameva bhaṇati, evametāpi [M 5.0465] attano aguṇaṃ paṭicchādetvā guṇameva pakāsenti. Viparivattāyoti yathā issamigassa siṅgaṃ parivattitvā ṭhitaṃ, evaṃ lahucittatāya viparivattāyova honti. Uragamivāti urago viya [P 5.0432] musāvāditāya dujivhā nāma. Sobbhamivāti yathā padarapaṭicchanno gūthakūpo, evaṃ vatthālaṅkārapaṭicchannā hutvā vicaranti. Yathā ca kacavarehi paṭicchanno āvāṭo akkanto pādadukkhaṃ janeti, evametāpi vissāsena upaseviyamānā. Pātālamivāti yathā mahāsamudde pātālaṃ duppūraṃ, evametāpi methunena vijāyanena alaṅkārenāti tīhi duppūrā. Tenevāha – “tiṇṇaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ atitto mātugāmo”tiādi.

Braided (veṇikatā) means those who have made braids. Just as a thief, having tied his top-knot, stands in the forest and plunders wealth, so too do these women, having brought men under the sway of defilements, plunder their wealth. Like liquor mixed with poison (madirāva diddhā) means like spirits mixed with poison. Just as that liquor causes distortion, so too do these women—being infatuated with other men, being unaware of what should or should not be done, and doing one thing when another should be done—display their distortion. Praising with speech (vācāsanthuti): just as a merchant praises only the quality of his own goods, so too do these women conceal their faults and proclaim only their virtues. Twisted (viparivattā): just as the horn of an issa-deer is twisted, so too are they, due to their fickle-mindedness, ever-changing. Like a snake (uragamiva): like a snake, because of their false speech, they are called 'double-tongued.' Like a pit (sobbhamiva): just as a cesspit is covered by a plank, so too do they wander about concealed by clothes and ornaments. And just as a pit covered with rubbish, when stepped upon, causes pain to the foot, so too do these women cause suffering when associated with through trust. Like the abyss (pātālamiva): just as the abyss in the great ocean is hard to fill, so too are these women insatiable in three ways: through sexual intercourse, childbirth, and adornment. Therefore, he said: 'Monks, a woman is insatiable in three things...' and so on.

Rakkhasī [V 5.0429] viyāti yathā rakkhasī nāma maṃsagiddhatāya dhanena na sakkā tosetuṃ, bahumpi dhanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā maṃsameva pattheti, evametāpi methunagiddhatāya bahunāpi dhanena na tussanti, dhanaṃ agaṇetvā methunameva patthenti. Yamovāti yathā yamo ekantaharo na kiñci pariharati, evametāpi jātisampannādīsu na kañci pariharanti, sabbaṃ kilesavasena sīlādivināsaṃ pāpetvā dutiyacittavāre nirayaṃ upanenti. Sikhīrivāti yathā sikhī sucimpi asucimpi sabbaṃ bhakkhayati, tathetāpi hīnuttame sabbe sevanti. Nadīupamāyampi eseva nayo. Yenakā maṃcarāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, yattha etāsaṃ kāmo hoti, tattheva dhāvanti. Nerūti himavati eko suvaṇṇapabbato, taṃ upagatā kākāpi suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva honti. Yathā so, evaṃ etāpi nibbisesakarā attānaṃ upagataṃ ekasadisaṃ katvā passanti.

Rakkhasī viya means 'like a female demon': just as a female demon, due to her craving for flesh, cannot be satisfied with wealth—rejecting much wealth, she desires only flesh—so too these women, due to their craving for sexual intercourse, are not satisfied even with much wealth. Disregarding wealth, they seek only sexual intercourse. Yama viya means 'like Yama': just as Yama takes everything and spares no one, so too these women spare no one among those endowed with good birth and so forth. Through the power of defilements, they bring about the destruction of virtue and the like, and in the next life lead one to hell. Sikhī viya means 'like fire': just as fire devours everything, whether pure or impure, so too these women associate with all, whether low or high. The same principle applies to the simile of the river. Yenakāmaṃcarā means 'they roam where they will': this is an instrumental case used in the sense of location. Wherever their lust arises, there they rush. Neru means: on the Himalayas, there is a golden mountain called Neru. Even crows that approach it take on a golden hue. Just as that mountain makes no distinction and treats all who approach it as the same, so too these women treat the men who approach them as all the same.

Visarukkhoti ambasadiso kiṃpakkarukkho. So niccameva phalati, vaṇṇādisampanno ca hoti, tena naṃ nirāsaṅkā paribhuñjitvā maranti, evameva tāpi rūpādivasena niccaphalitā ramaṇīyā viya khāyanti. Seviyamānā pana pamādaṃ uppādetvā apāyesu pātenti. Tena vuttaṃ –

A poisonous tree means the kiṃpakka tree, which resembles a mango tree. It always bears fruit and is endowed with beauty and other qualities. Therefore, people, unsuspecting, consume it and die. In the same way, these women, by way of their physical forms and so on, appear delightful as if always bearing fruit. Yet, when associated with, they give rise to heedlessness and cause one to fall into the four realms of misery. Thus it is said:

“Āyatiṃ dosaṃ naññāya, yo kāme paṭisevati;

Vipākante hananti naṃ, kiṃpakkamiva bhakkhita”nti. (jā. 1.1.85);

“Not understanding the future danger, whoever indulges in sensual pleasures; in the end, they destroy him, like an eaten kiṃpakka fruit.”

Yathā vā visarukkho niccaphalito sadā anatthāvaho hoti, evametāpi sīlādivināsanavasena. Yathā visarukkhassa mūlampi tacopi pattampi pupphampi [M 5.0466] phalampi visamevāti niccaphalo, tatheva tāsaṃ rūpampi…pe… phoṭṭhabbampi visamevāti visarukkho viya niccaphalitāyoti.

Or, just as a poisonous tree, constantly bearing fruit, is always harmful, so too are these women, by way of destroying virtue and so forth. Just as the root, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit of a poisonous tree are all poison—thus it is 'constantly fruit-bearing'—so too their form... and so on... and tangible objects are all poison. Thus they are 'like a poisonous tree, constantly bearing fruit'.

“Panuttaretthā”ti gāthābandhena tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ evamāha. Tattha ratanantakaritthiyoti sāmikehi dukkhasambhatānaṃ ratanānaṃ antarāyakarā itthiyo etāni paresaṃ datvā anācāraṃ caranti.

To make that meaning clear with the verse beginning 'Panuttaretthā,' he spoke thus. Therein, 'ratanantakaritthiyo' (women who destroy jewels) means women who cause the loss of jewels and wealth acquired by their husbands through hardship, giving these away to others and conducting themselves improperly.

Ito paraṃ nānappakārena attano dhammakathāvilāsaṃ dassento āha –

Thereafter, displaying the elegance of his Dhamma discourse in various ways, he said:

“Cattārimāni, samma puṇṇamukha, yāni vatthūni kicce jāte anatthacarāni bhavanti[V 5.0430], tāni parakule na vāsetabbāni, goṇaṃ dhenuṃ yānaṃ bhariyā. Cattāri etāni paṇḍito dhanāni gharā na vippavāsaye. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

“Friend Puṇṇamukha, there are these four things that, when a need arises, become unprofitable. They should not be kept in another's household: a bull, a milch-cow, a vehicle, and a wife. A wise man should not let these four treasures be away from his home. And in this regard, there is this further verse:

296.

296.

‘Goṇaṃ [P 5.0433] dhenuñca yānañca, bhariyaṃ ñātikule na vāsaye;

Bhañjanti rathaṃ ayānakā, ativāhena hananti puṅgavaṃ;

Dohena hananti vacchakaṃ, bhariyā ñātikule padussatī’”ti.

‘One should not keep a bull, a milch-cow, a vehicle, or a wife in a kinsman’s household; those without a vehicle break the chariot; by over-loading they kill the bull; by over-milking they kill the calf; and a wife in her kinsmen’s household is corrupted.’”

“Cha imāni, samma puṇṇamukha, yāni vatthūni kicce jāte anatthacarāni bhavanti –

“Friend Puṇṇamukha, there are these six things that, when a need arises, become unprofitable:

297.

297.

‘Aguṇaṃ dhanu ñātikule ca bhariyā, pāraṃ nāvā akkhabhaggañca yānaṃ;

Dūre mitto pāpasahāyako ca, kicce jāte anatthacarāni bhavantī’”ti.

‘A stringless bow, a wife in her kinsmen's household, a boat on the far shore, and a vehicle with a broken axle; a friend who is far away, and an evil companion—when a need arises, these become unprofitable.’”

“Aṭṭhahi khalu, samma puṇṇamukha ṭhānehi itthī sāmikaṃ avajānāti – daliddatā, āturatā, jiṇṇatā, surāsoṇḍatā, muddhatā, pamattatā, sabbakiccesu anuvattanatā, sabbadhanaanuppadānena. Imehi khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, aṭṭhahi ṭhānehi itthī sāmikaṃ avajānāti. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

“Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, a wife despises her husband on eight grounds: because of his poverty, sickness, old age, drunkenness, foolishness, heedlessness, his compliance with her in all affairs, and his giving her all his wealth. Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, a wife despises her husband on these eight grounds. And in this regard, there is this further verse:

298.

298.

“‘Daliddaṃ [M 5.0467] āturañcāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ surasoṇḍakaṃ;

Pamattaṃ muddhapattañca, sabbakiccesu hāpanaṃ;

Sabbakāmappadānena, avajānāti sāmika’”nti.

‘A poor man, a sick one, and an old one, a drunkard; a heedless one, one who is foolish, and one who yields in all affairs; even by the bestowing of all her desires, she despises her husband.’”

“Navahi khalu, samma puṇṇamukha ṭhānehi itthī padosamāharati – ārāmagamanasīlā ca hoti, uyyānagamanasīlā ca hoti, nadītitthagamanasīlā ca hoti, ñātikulagamanasīlā ca hoti, parakulagamanasīlā ca hoti, ādāsadussamaṇḍanānuyogamanuyuttasīlā ca hoti, majjapāyinī ca hoti, nillokanasīlā ca hoti, sadvāraṭṭhāyinī ca hoti. Imehi khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, navahi ṭhānehi itthī padosamāharati. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

“Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, a woman brings fault upon her husband on nine grounds: she is fond of going to parks, fond of going to gardens, fond of going to river-fords, fond of going to her kinsmen's homes, fond of going to others' homes, she is devoted to the practice of adorning herself with mirrors and fine cloth, she is a drinker of intoxicants, she is fond of looking out from windows, and she is fond of standing in the doorway. Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, a woman brings fault upon her husband on these nine grounds. And in this regard, there is this further verse:

299.

299.

‘Ārāmasīlā [V 5.0431] ca uyyānaṃ, nadī ñāti parakulaṃ;

Ādāsadussamaṇḍanamanuyuttā, yā citthī majjapāyinī.

‘The woman who is fond of parks and gardens, rivers, kinsmen, and others' households; who is devoted to adornment with mirrors and fine cloth, and who is a drinker of intoxicants;

300.

300.

“‘Yā ca nillokanasīlā, yā ca sadvāraṭhāyinī;

Navahetehi ṭhānehi, padosamāharanti itthiyo’”ti.

‘and who is fond of looking out, and who is fond of standing in her doorway—on these nine grounds, such women bring fault upon their husbands.’”

“Cattālīsāya khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, ṭhānehi itthī purisaṃ accācarati – vijambhati, vinamati, vilasati, vilajjati, nakhena nakhaṃ ghaṭṭeti, pādena pādaṃ akkamati, kaṭṭhena pathaviṃ vilikhati, dārakaṃ ullaṅghati ullaṅghāpeti[P 5.0434], kīḷati kīḷāpeti, cumbati cumbāpeti, bhuñjati bhuñjāpeti, dadāti, yācati, katamanukaroti, uccaṃ bhāsati, nīcaṃ bhāsati, aviccaṃ bhāsati, viviccaṃ bhāsati, naccena gītena vāditena rodanena vilasitena vibhūsitena jagghati, pekkhati, kaṭiṃ cāleti, guyhabhaṇḍakaṃ sañcāleti, ūruṃ vivarati, ūruṃ pidahati, thanaṃ dasseti, kacchaṃ dasseti, nābhiṃ dasseti, akkhiṃ nikhanati, bhamukaṃ ukkhipati, oṭṭhaṃ upalikhati, jivhaṃ nillāleti, dussaṃ muñcati, dussaṃ paṭibandhati, sirasaṃ muñcati, sirasaṃ bandhati. Imehi khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, cattālīsāya ṭhānehi itthī purisaṃ accācarati.

“Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, in forty ways a woman misbehaves against a man: she stretches her limbs; she bends down; she displays her charms; she feigns shyness; she scratches one nail with another; she steps on his foot; she scratches the ground with a stick; she lifts a child or has one lifted; she plays or has someone play; she kisses or has someone kiss; she eats or has someone eat; she gives; she begs; she imitates what is done; she speaks loudly; she speaks softly; she speaks clearly; she speaks secretly; with dancing, singing, music, weeping, coquetry, and finery, she laughs; she looks askance; she sways her hips; she moves her private parts; she uncovers her thigh; she covers her thigh; she shows her breast; she shows her armpit; she shows her navel; she winks; she raises her eyebrows; she licks her lips; she sticks out her tongue; she loosens her garment; she refastens her garment; she undoes her hair; she ties up her hair. Friend Puṇṇamukha, in these forty ways indeed, a woman misbehaves against a man.”

“Pañcavīsāya [M 5.0468] khalu, samma puṇṇamukha, ṭhānehi itthī paduṭṭhā veditabbā bhavati – sāmikassa pavāsaṃ vaṇṇeti, pavuṭṭhaṃ na sarati, āgataṃ nābhinandati, avaṇṇaṃ tassa bhaṇati, vaṇṇaṃ tassa na bhaṇati, anatthaṃ tassa carati, atthaṃ tassa na carati, akiccaṃ tassa karoti, kiccaṃ tassa na karoti, paridahitvā sayati, parammukhī nipajjati, parivattakajātā kho pana hoti kuṅkumiyajātā, dīghaṃ assasati, dukkhaṃ vedayati, uccārapassāvaṃ abhiṇhaṃ gacchati, vilomamācarati, parapurisasaddaṃ sutvā kaṇṇasotaṃ vivaramodahati, nihatabhogā kho pana hoti, paṭivissakehi santhavaṃ karoti, nikkhantapādā kho pana hoti visikhānucārinī, aticārinī kho pana hoti niccaṃ sāmike agāravā paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā, abhiṇhaṃ dvāre tiṭṭhati, kacchāni aṅgāni thanāni dasseti, disodisaṃ gantvā pekkhati. Imehi khalu samma puṇṇamukha, pañcavīsāya ṭhānehi itthī paduṭṭhā veditabbā bhavati. Bhavati ca panuttarettha vākyaṃ –

“Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, by twenty-five grounds a woman should be known as corrupt: she praises her husband's journey; when he is away, she does not miss him; when he returns, she does not rejoice; she speaks of his faults; she does not speak of his virtues; she acts for his harm; she does not act for his benefit; she does for him what should not be done; she does not do for him what should be done; she sleeps fully dressed; she lies facing away from him; she becomes restless, turning over and over; she makes a commotion and sighs deeply; she expresses her pain; she frequently goes to defecate and urinate; she acts perversely; hearing the voice of another man, she opens her ears and listens; she becomes a squanderer of wealth; she becomes intimate with neighbors; she is one whose feet are always out of the house, a wanderer of the streets; she is unfaithful, always disrespectful to her husband, with a corrupt mind and intent; she frequently stands in the doorway; she displays her armpits, limbs, and breasts; she goes about looking in all directions. Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, by these twenty-five grounds a woman should be known as corrupt. And in this regard, there is this verse:”

301.

301.

‘Pavāsaṃ [V 5.0432] tassa vaṇṇeti, gataṃ tassa na socati;

Disvāna patimāgataṃ nābhinandati, bhattāravaṇṇaṃ na kadāci bhāsati;

Ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“She praises his journey; she does not grieve for his absence. Seeing her husband returned, she does not rejoice. She never speaks of her husband’s virtues. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

302.

302.

‘Anatthaṃ tassa carati asaññatā, atthañca hāpeti akiccakārinī;

Paridahitvā sayati parammukhī, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“Unrestrained, she acts for his harm; doing what should not be done, she neglects his welfare. She sleeps fully dressed, lying facing away. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

303.

303.

‘Parivattajātā [P 5.0435] ca bhavati kuṅkumī, dīghañca assasati dukkhavedinī;

“She becomes restless, turning over and over, making a commotion; she sighs deeply, expressing her pain.”

Uccārapassāvamabhiṇhaṃ gacchati, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“She frequently goes to defecate and urinate. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

304.

304.

‘Vilomamācarati [M 5.0469] akiccakārinī, saddaṃ nisāmeti parassa bhāsato;

Nihatabhogā ca karoti santhavaṃ, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“She acts perversely, doing what should not be done; she listens to the voice of another man speaking. She squanders wealth and enters into intimacy. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

305.

305.

‘Kicchena laddhaṃ kasirābhataṃ dhanaṃ, vittaṃ vināseti dukkhena sambhataṃ;

Paṭivissakehi ca karoti santhavaṃ, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“Wealth obtained with difficulty, brought with hardship, she squanders the wealth accumulated with suffering. She enters into intimacy with neighbors. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

306.

306.

‘Nikkhantapādā visikhānucārinī, niccañca sāmimhi paduṭṭhamānasā;

Aticārinī hoti apetagāravā, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“She is one whose feet are always out, a wanderer in the streets, and always with a mind corrupted towards her husband. She is unfaithful and devoid of respect. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

307.

307.

‘Abhikkhaṇaṃ tiṭṭhati dvāramūle, thanāni kacchāni ca dassayantī;

Disodisaṃ pekkhati bhantacittā, ete paduṭṭhāya bhavanti lakkhaṇā.

“She frequently stands at the doorway, displaying her breasts and armpits. With a wavering mind, she looks in all directions. These are the marks of a corrupt woman.”

308.

308.

‘Sabbā nadī vaṅkagatī, sabbe kaṭṭhamayā vanā;

Sabbitthiyo kare pāpaṃ, labhamāne nivātake.

“All rivers have a winding course; all forests are made of wood. All women would do evil, if they found a secluded spot.”

309.

309.

‘Sace labhetha khaṇaṃ vā raho vā, nivātakaṃ vāpi labhetha tādisaṃ;

Sabbāva itthī kayiruṃ nu pāpaṃ, aññaṃ alattha pīṭhasappināpi saddhiṃ.

“If she should find an opportunity, or a secret place, or even such a secluded spot; all women would indeed do evil, and if they found no one else, even with a cripple.”

310.

310.

‘Narānamārāmakarāsu nārisu, anekacittāsu aniggahāsu ca;

Sabbattha nāpītikarāpi ce siyā, na vissase titthasamā hi nāriyo’”ti.

“Among women who find pleasure in men, who are fickle-minded and unrestrained, even if she were pleasing in every way, one should not trust her; for women are like river-fords.”

Tattha [V 5.0433] goṇaṃ dhenunti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Ñātikule padussatīti tattha sā nibbhayā hutvā taruṇakālato paṭṭhāya vissāsakehi dāsādīhipi [M 5.0470] saddhiṃ anācāraṃ carati, ñātakā ñatvāpi niggahaṃ na karonti, attano akittiṃ pariharamānā ajānantā viya honti. Anatthacarānīti acaritabbāni atthāni, akiccakārānīti attho. Aguṇanti jiyārahitaṃ. Pāpasahāyakoti dummitto.

“In that context, ‘goṇaṃ dhenu’ is stated with a reversal of gender. ‘She is corrupted in her kinsmen's house’ means that there, being fearless from her youth, she behaves improperly even with trusted servants and others; her relatives, though knowing, do not restrain her; pretending to be ignorant, they ward off their own disgrace. ‘Anatthacarānī’ means doing what should not be done, that is, one who does what is improper. ‘Aguṇa’ means without a bowstring. ‘Pāpasahāyaka’ means a bad friend.”

Daliddatāti daliddatāya. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha daliddo alaṅkārādīnaṃ abhāvato kilesena saṅgaṇhituṃ na sakkotīti taṃ avajānāti. Gilāno vatthukāmakilesakāmehi saṅgaṇhituṃ na sakkoti. Jarājiṇṇo kāyikavācasikakhiḍḍāratisamattho na hoti. Surāsoṇḍo [P 5.0436] tassā hatthapiḷandhanādīnipi surāgharaññeva paveseti. Muddho andhabālo ratikusalo na hoti. Pamatto dāsisoṇḍo hutvā gharadāsīhi saddhiṃ saṃvasati, bhariyaṃ pana akkosati paribhāsati, tena naṃ avajānāti. Sabbakiccesu anuvattantaṃ “ayaṃ nittejo, mameva anuvattatī”ti taṃ akkosati paribhāsati. Yo pana sabbaṃ dhanaṃ anuppadeti kuṭumbaṃ paṭicchāpeti, tassa bhariyā sabbaṃ dhanasāraṃ hatthe katvā taṃ dāsaṃ viya avajānāti, icchamānā “ko tayā attho”ti gharatopi naṃ nikkaḍḍhati. Muddhapattanti muddhabhāvappattaṃ.

‘Daliddatā’ means because of poverty. The same method applies to the remaining cases. There, because a poor man lacks ornaments and such, he cannot win her over with sensual passion; therefore, she scorns him. A sick man cannot win her over with material desires or sensual pleasures. An old man is not capable of physical or verbal play and enjoyment. A drunkard takes even her hand-ornaments and so on to the tavern. A fool, blind and ignorant, is not skilled in lovemaking. A negligent man, being addicted to female servants, lives with the household slaves, but scolds and abuses his wife; therefore, she scorns him. One who is compliant in all tasks—thinking, ‘This man is powerless, he just follows my lead’—she scolds and abuses him. But as for one who gives her all his wealth and hands over the household to her, his wife, having taken all the wealth into her hands, scorns him like a slave, and if she wishes, she drives him out of the house, saying, ‘What use is there for you?’ ‘Muddhapattā’ means having reached a state of foolishness.

Padosamāharatīti sāmike padosaṃ āharati dussati, pāpakammaṃ karotīti attho. Ārāmagamanasīlāti sāmikaṃ āpucchā vā anāpucchā vā abhiṇhaṃ pupphārāmādīsu aññataraṃ gantvā tattha anācāraṃ caritvā “ajja mayā ārāme rukkhadevatāya balikammaṃ kata”ntiādīni vatvā bālasāmikaṃ saññāpeti. Paṇḍito pana “addhā esā tattha anācāraṃ caratī”ti puna tassā gantuṃ na deti. Evaṃ sabbapadesupi attho veditabbo. Parakulanti sandiṭṭhasambhattādīnaṃ gehaṃ. Taṃ sā “asukakule me vaḍḍhi payojitā atthi, tāvakālikaṃ dinnakaṃ atthi, taṃ sādhemī”tiādīni vatvā gacchati. Nillokanasīlāti vātapānantarādīhi olokanasīlā. Sadvāraṭṭhāyinīti attano aṅgapaccaṅgāni dassentī sadvāre tiṭṭhati.

‘Padosamāharati’ means she harbors ill-will toward her husband and acts corruptly; the meaning is that she commits evil deeds. ‘Ārāmagamanasīlā’ means that, with or without her husband’s permission, she frequently goes to one of the flower gardens or similar places, behaves improperly there, and then convinces her foolish husband, saying, ‘Today I made an offering to the tree deity in the park,’ and so on. But a wise man, thinking, ‘Surely she is behaving improperly there,’ does not let her go again. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances. ‘Parakula’ means the house of acquaintances, friends, and so on. She goes there, saying, ‘I have some business to attend to in such-and-such a family, there is something I lent temporarily that I must collect,’ and so on. ‘Nillokanasīlā’ means she is in the habit of looking out through windows and so forth. ‘Sadvāraṭṭhāyinī’ means she stands at the doorway, displaying her limbs and minor parts.

Accācaratīti atikkamma carati, sāmikassa santike ṭhitāva aññassa nimittaṃ dassetīti attho. Vijambhatīti “ahaṃ taṃ disvā vijambhissāmi, tāya [M 5.0471] saññāya okāsassa atthibhāvaṃ vā natthibhāvaṃ vā jāneyyāsī”ti paṭhamameva katasaṅketā vā hutvā akatasaṅketā vāpi “evaṃ esa mayi bajjhissatī”ti sāmikassa passe ṭhitāva vijambhati vijambhanaṃ [V 5.0434] dasseti. Vinamatīti kiñcideva bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā taṃ ukkhipantī viya onamitvā piṭṭhiṃ dasseti. Vilasatīti gamanādīhi vā iriyāpathehi alaṅkārena vā vilāsaṃ dasseti. Vilajjatīti lajjantī viya vatthena sarīraṃ chādeti, kavāṭaṃ vā bhittiṃ vā allīyati. Nakhenāti pādanakhena pādanakhaṃ, hatthanakhena hatthanakhaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Kaṭṭhenāti daṇḍakena. Dārakanti attano vā puttaṃ aññassa vā puttaṃ gahetvā ukkhipati vā ukkhipāpeti vā. Kīḷatīti sayaṃ vā kīḷati, dārakaṃ vā kīḷāpeti. Cumbanādīsupi eseva nayo. Dadātīti tassa kiñcideva phalaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā deti. Yācatīti tameva paṭiyācati. Anukarotīti dārakena kataṃ kataṃ anukaroti. Uccanti mahāsaddavasena vā thomanavasena vā uccaṃ. Nīcanti mandasaddavasena vā amanāpavacanena vā paribhavavacanena vā nīcaṃ. Aviccanti bahujanamajjhe appaṭicchannaṃ. Viviccanti raho paṭicchannaṃ. Naccenāti etehi naccādīhi nimittaṃ karoti. Tattha roditena nimittakaraṇena rattiṃ deve vassante vātapānena hatthiṃ āropetvā seṭṭhiputtena nītāya purohitabrāhmaṇiyā vatthu kathetabbaṃ. Jagghatīti mahāhasitaṃ hasati, evampi nimittaṃ karoti[P 5.0437]. Kacchanti upakacchakaṃ. Upalikhatīti dantehi upalikhati. Sirasanti kesavaṭṭiṃ. Evaṃ kesānaṃ mocanabandhanehipi parapurisānaṃ nimittaṃ karoti, niyāmetvā vā aniyāmetvā vā kocideva sārajjissatītipi karotiyeva.

‘Accācarati’ means she transgresses; the meaning is that even while standing near her husband, she gives a sign to another man. ‘Vijambhati’ means she either has a prior signal—thinking, "I will stretch when I see him, and by that sign you will know whether there is an opportunity or not"—or even without a prior signal, thinking, "In this way he will be captivated by me," she stretches and displays the act of stretching while standing beside her husband. ‘Vinamati’ means she drops something on the ground and, as if picking it up, she bends down and shows her back. ‘Vilasati’ means she displays charm through her movements, postures, or ornaments. ‘Vilajjatīti’ means that, as if feeling shy, she covers her body with her garment or leans against a door or wall. ‘Nakhena’ means she rubs one toenail with another toenail, or one fingernail with another fingernail. ‘Kaṭṭhena’ means with a small stick. ‘Dārakaṃ’ means she picks up or has someone pick up either her own child or another’s child. ‘Kīḷati’ means she either plays herself or makes the child play. The same applies to kissing and so forth. ‘Dadāti’ means she gives him some fruit or a flower. ‘Yācati’ means she asks for the same from him. ‘Anukaroti’ means she mimics whatever the child does. ‘Uccaṃ’ means she speaks loudly, either with a great sound or in praise. ‘Nīcaṃ’ means she speaks softly, either with a low voice, or with unpleasant or disparaging words. ‘Aviccaṃ’ means openly in the midst of many people. ‘Viviccaṃ’ means secretly in private. ‘Naccena’ means she makes a sign through these acts of dancing and so forth. In that regard, regarding making a sign by weeping, the story of the chaplain’s wife should be told, who was taken away by a merchant’s son using an elephant at the window while it was raining at night. ‘Jagghatī’ means she laughs loudly; in this way too, she makes a sign. ‘Kacchaṃ’ means the armpit. ‘Upalikhati’ means she nibbles with her teeth. ‘Sirasā’ refers to the arrangement of her hair. In this way, by loosening or binding her hair, she makes signs to other men, thinking, "Perhaps someone will become infatuated," whether she does so intentionally or unintentionally.

Paduṭṭhā veditabbā bhavatīti ayaṃ mayi paduṭṭhā kuddhā, kujjhitvā ca pana micchācāraṃ caratīti paṇḍitena veditabbā bhavati. Pavāsanti “asukagāme payuttaṃ dhanaṃ nassati, gaccha taṃ sādhehi, vohāraṃ karohī”tiādīni vatvā tasmiṃ gate anācāraṃ caritukāmā pavāsaṃ vaṇṇeti. Anatthanti avaḍḍhiṃ. Akiccanti akattabbayuttakaṃ. Paridahitvāti gāḷhaṃ nivāsetvā. Parivattakajātāti ito cito ca parivattamānā. Kuṅkumiyajātāti kolāhalajātā pādamūle nipannā paricārikā uṭṭhāpeti, dīpaṃ jālāpeti, nānappakāraṃ kolāhalaṃ karoti, tassa kilesaratiṃ nāseti. Dukkhaṃ vedayatīti sīsaṃ me rujjatītiādīni vadati. Vilomamācaratīti āhāraṃ [M 5.0472] sītalaṃ icchantassa uṇhaṃ detītiādīnaṃ vasena paccanīkavutti hoti. Nihatabhogāti sāmikena dukkhasambhatānaṃ bhogānaṃ surālolatādīhi vināsikā. Santhavanti kilesavasena santhavaṃ karoti. Nikkhantapādāti jārassa upadhāraṇatthāya nikkhantapādā. Sāmiketi patimhi agāravena ca paduṭṭhamānasāya ca aticārinī hoti.

She should be understood as corrupt: a wise person should understand, 'This one is corrupt and angry with me, and being angry, she engages in misconduct.' She sends him away: saying things such as, 'The wealth invested in such-and-such a village is being lost; go and secure it, do business,' and after he has gone, desiring to engage in misconduct, she praises his absence. Unprofitable means decline. Improper means that which is unfitting to do. Having dressed means having dressed tightly. Given to shifting means constantly shifting from here to there. Given to commotion means causing a commotion: she makes the attendant, who is lying at his feet, get up; she lights a lamp; she makes various kinds of noise and destroys his delight in defilements. She feels pain: saying things such as, 'My head hurts.' She acts contrarily means she behaves in opposition, for example, giving hot food when he wants something cold. One who has ruined wealth means she who destroys the wealth acquired with difficulty by her husband through addiction to liquor and other vices. She consorts means she consorts driven by defilements. With feet gone forth means with feet gone forth to meet her lover. Towards her husband means she is disrespectful towards her husband and, with a corrupted mind, commits adultery.

Sabbitthiyoti ṭhapetvā vipassanāya tanukatakilesā sesā sabbā itthiyo pāpaṃ kareyyuṃ. Labhamāneti labbhamāne, saṃvijjamāneti attho. Nivātaketi rahomantanake paribhedake. Khaṇaṃ vā raho [V 5.0435] vāti pāpakaraṇatthāya okāsaṃ vā paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Kayiruṃ nūti ettha nū-ti nipātamattaṃ. Alatthāti aladdhā. Ayameva vā pāṭho, aññaṃ sampannapurisaṃ alabhitvā pīṭhasappināpi tato paṭikkūlatarenāpi pāpaṃ kareyyuṃ. Ārāmakarāsūti abhiratikārikāsu. Aniggahāsūti niggahena vinetuṃ asakkuṇeyyāsu. Titthasamāti yathā titthaṃ uttamādhamesu na kañci nhāyantaṃ vāreti, tathā etāpi raho vā khaṇe vā nivātake vā sati na kañci paṭikkhipanti.

'All women' means that, setting aside those whose defilements have been attenuated by insight, all other women might do evil. 'Being obtained' means when it is available or present. 'In a secluded place' means in a place for secret and divisive counsel. 'An opportunity or in secret' means an opportunity or a concealed place for doing evil. 'Would they do it?': here, 'nū' is merely a particle. 'Not obtaining' means having not obtained. Or this is the reading: not having obtained another suitable man, they might do evil even with a cripple who moves on a stool, or with someone even more repulsive than that. 'Those who delight in pleasure-grounds' means those who create delight. 'Unrestrained' means those who cannot be disciplined by restraint. 'Like a ford' means that just as a ford does not prevent anyone, high or low, from bathing, so too these women, when there is secrecy, an opportunity, or a secluded place, do not reject anyone.

Tathā hi atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ kaṇḍarī nāma rājā ahosi uttamarūpadharo. Tassa devasikaṃ amaccā gandhakaraṇḍakasahassaṃ āharanti. Tenassa nivesane paribhaṇḍaṃ katvā gandhakaraṇḍake phāletvā gandhadārūni katvā āhāraṃ pacanti. Bhariyāpissa abhirūpā ahosi nāmena kinnarā nāma. Purohitopissa samavayo pañcālacaṇḍo nāma buddhisampanno ahosi. Rañño pana pāsādaṃ nissāya antopākāre jamburukkho nibbatti, tassa sākhā pākāramatthake olambati. Tassa chāyāya jeguccho dussaṇṭhāno pīṭhasappī vasati. Athekadivasaṃ kinnarā devī vātapānena olokentī taṃ ditvā paṭibaddhacittā [P 5.0438] hutvā rattiṃ rājānaṃ ratiyā saṅgaṇhitvā tasmiṃ niddaṃ okkante saṇikaṃ uṭṭhāyāsanā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ suvaṇṇasarake pakkhipitvā ucchaṅge katvā sāṭakarajjuyā vātapānena otaritvā jambuṃ āruyha sākhāya oruyha pīṭhasappiṃ bhojetvā pāpaṃ katvā āgatamaggeneva pāsādaṃ āruyha gandhehi sarīraṃ [M 5.0473] ubbaṭṭetvā raññā saddhiṃ nipajji. Etenupāyena nibaddhaṃ tena saddhiṃ pāpaṃ karoti. Rājā pana na jānāti.

For in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Kaṇḍarī, who was of excellent appearance. Every day, his ministers brought him a thousand caskets of perfume. Having used these for the fragrant lining of his residence, they would split the caskets to make fragrant firewood and cook his food. His wife, named Kinnarā, was also beautiful. His chaplain, named Pañcālacaṇḍa, was of the same age and endowed with wisdom. Near the king's palace, within the inner wall, a rose-apple tree grew, its branches hanging over the top of the wall. In its shade lived a loathsome, misshapen cripple who moved on a stool. One day, Queen Kinnarā, looking out through a window, saw him and became infatuated. At night, having satisfied the king with sensual pleasure, when he had fallen asleep, she rose quietly from her place, put various foods of the finest flavors into a golden bowl, and carrying it in the fold of her garment, she descended from the window by a rope of cloth. She climbed the rose-apple tree, descended by a branch, fed the cripple, and committed misconduct with him. Then, returning by the way she had come, she ascended to the palace, rubbed her body with perfumes, and lay down with the king. In this way, she constantly committed misconduct with him. The king, however, did not know.

So ekadivasaṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nivesanaṃ pavesanto jambuchāyāya sayitaṃ paramakāruññappattaṃ pīṭhasappiṃ disvā purohitaṃ āha – “passetaṃ manussapeta”nti. “Āma, passāmi devā”ti. “Api nu kho, samma, evarūpaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ kāci itthī chandarāgavasena upagaccheyyā”ti. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā pīṭhasappī mānaṃ janetvā “ayaṃ rājā kiṃ katheti, attano deviyā mama santikaṃ āgamanaṃ na jānāti maññe”ti jamburukkhassa añjaliṃ paggahetvā “suṇa sāmi, jamburukkhe nibbattadevate, ṭhapetvā taṃ añño etaṃ kāraṇaṃ na jānātī”ti āha. Purohito tassa kiriyaṃ disvā cintesi – “addhā rañño aggamahesī jamburukkhena gantvā iminā saddhiṃ pāpaṃ karotī”ti. So rājānaṃ pucchi – “mahārāja, deviyā te rattibhāge sarīrasamphasso kīdiso hotī”ti? “Samma, aññaṃ na passāmi, majjhimayāme panassā sarīraṃ sītalaṃ hotī”ti. “Tena hi, deva, tiṭṭhatu aññā itthī, aggamahesī te kinnarādevī [V 5.0436] iminā saddhiṃ pāpaṃ karotī”ti. “Samma, kiṃ vadesi, evarūpā paramavilāsasampannā kiṃ iminā paramajegucchena saddhiṃ abhiramissatī”ti? “Tena hi naṃ, deva, pariggaṇhāhī”ti.

One day, while entering his residence after circumambulating the city, he saw the cripple who moved on a stool, who had reached a most pitiable state, lying in the shade of the rose-apple tree, and he said to the chaplain, 'Look at this human ghost.' 'Yes, I see, Your Majesty.' 'Tell me, my friend, could any woman approach such a repulsive being out of desire and lust?' Hearing this talk, the cripple became conceited and thought, 'What is this king saying? I suppose he does not know that his own queen comes to me.' Then, raising his hands in reverence to the rose-apple tree, he said, 'Listen, my lord, O deity dwelling in the rose-apple tree, no one else besides you knows of this matter.' The chaplain, seeing his action, thought, 'Surely the king’s chief queen goes by way of the rose-apple tree and commits misconduct with this man.' He asked the king, 'Great king, what is the touch of the queen's body like in the night?' 'My friend, I notice nothing else, but in the middle watch of the night her body becomes cold.' 'In that case, Your Majesty, let other women be; your chief queen, Queen Kinnarā, is committing misconduct with this man.' 'My friend, what are you saying? How could such a woman, endowed with supreme grace, take pleasure with this utterly loathsome man?' 'Then, Your Majesty, you must investigate her.'

So “sādhū”ti rattiṃ bhuttasāyamāso tāya saddhiṃ nippajjitvā “pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti pakatiyā niddupagamanavelāya niddupagato viya ahosi. Sāpi uṭṭhāya tatheva akāsi. Rājā tassā anupadaññeva gantvā jambuchāyaṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi. Pīṭhasappī deviyā kujjhitvā “tvaṃ ajja aticirāyitvā āgatā”ti hatthena kaṇṇasaṅkhalikaṃ pahari. Atha naṃ “mā maṃ kujjhi, sāmi, rañño niddupagamanaṃ olokesi”nti vatvā tassa gehe pādaparicārikā viya ahosi. Tena panassā pahārena sīhamukhakuṇḍalaṃ kaṇṇato gaḷitvā rañño pādamūle pati. Rājā “vaṭṭissati ettaka”nti taṃ gahetvā gato. Sāpi tena saddhiṃ aticaritvā purimaniyāmeneva gantvā raññā saddhiṃ nipajjituṃ ārabhi. Rājā paṭikkhipitvā punadivase “kinnarādevī mayā dinnaṃ sabbālaṅkāraṃ alaṅkaritvā etū”ti āṇāpesi. Sā “sīhamukhakuṇḍalaṃ me suvaṇṇakārassa santike”ti vatvā nāgami, puna pesite ca pana ekakuṇḍalāva āgamāsi[P 5.0439]. Rājā pucchi – “kahaṃ te kuṇḍala”nti? “Suvaṇṇakārassa santike”ti[M 5.0474]. Suvaṇṇakāraṃ pakkosāpetvā “kiṃkāraṇā imissā kuṇḍalaṃ na desī”ti āha. “Nāhaṃ gaṇhāmi devā”ti. Rājā tassā kujjhitvā “pāpe caṇḍāli mādisena te suvaṇṇakārena bhavitabba”nti vatvā taṃ kuṇḍalaṃ tassā puratho khipitvā purohitaṃ āha – “samma, saccaṃ tayā vuttaṃ, gaccha sīsamassā chedāpehī”ti. So taṃ rājageheyeva ekasmiṃ padese ṭhapetvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “deva, mā kinnarādeviyā kujjhittha, sabbā itthiyo evarūpāyeva. Sacepi itthīnaṃ dussīlabhāvaṃ ñātukāmosi, dassessāmi te etāsaṃ pāpakañceva bahumāyābhāvañca, ehi aññātakavesena janapadaṃ carāmā”ti āha.

“Very well,” he said. After eating his evening meal, he lay down with her that night, and thinking, “I will investigate her,” he pretended to be asleep at his usual bedtime. She too got up and acted in the same way. The king, following her closely, went and stood in the shade of the rose-apple tree. The cripple, becoming angry with the queen, said, “You have come very late today,” and struck her on the ear with his hand. Then she said, “Do not be angry with me, my lord, I was watching for the king to fall asleep,” and she acted like a devoted wife to him. But from that blow, the lion-faced earring fell from her ear and landed at the king’s feet. The king, thinking, “This much will be enough,” took it and departed. She too, having committed misconduct with him, went as before and began to lie down with the king. The king rejected her, and the next day commanded, “Let Queen Kinnarā adorn herself with all the ornaments I have given her and come.” She said, “My lion-faced earring is with the goldsmith,” and did not come. When sent for again, she came wearing only one earring. The king asked, “Where is your earring?” “With the goldsmith,” she replied. The king had the goldsmith summoned and asked, “Why have you not returned her earring?” “I did not take it, Your Majesty,” he said. The king, angry with her, said, “You wicked outcaste, must someone like me be your goldsmith!” and throwing the earring in front of her, said to the chaplain, “My friend, what you said is true. Go and have her head cut off.” The chaplain, having placed her in a certain part of the palace itself, approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, do not be angry with Queen Kinnarā. All women are like this. If you wish to know the immoral nature of women, I will show you their wickedness and great deceit. Come, let us travel the countryside in disguise.”

Rājā “sādhū”ti mātaraṃ rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā tena saddhiṃ cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Tesaṃ yojanaṃ maggaṃ gantvā mahāmagge nisinnānaṃyeva eko kuṭumbiko puttassatthāya maṅgalaṃ katvā ekaṃ kumārikaṃ paṭicchannayāne nisīdāpetvā mahantena parivārena gacchati. Taṃ disvā purohito rājānaṃ āha – “sace icchasi, imaṃ kumārikaṃ tayā saddhiṃ pāpaṃ kāretuṃ sakkā devā”ti. “Kiṃ kathesi, mahāparivārā esā, na sakkā sammā”ti? Purohito “tena hi passa, devā”ti purato gantvā maggato avidūre sāṇiyā parikkhipitvā rājānaṃ antosāṇiyaṃ katvā sayaṃ maggapasse rodanto nisīdi. Atha naṃ so kuṭumbiko disvā “tāta, kasmā rodasī”ti [V 5.0437] pucchi. “Bhariyā me garubhārā, taṃ kulagharaṃ netuṃ maggapaṭipannosmi, tassā antarāmaggeyeva gabbho cali, esā antosāṇiyaṃ kilamati, kācissā itthī santike natthi, mayāpi tattha gantuṃ na sakkā, na jānāmi ‘kiṃ bhavissatī’ti, ekaṃ itthiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Mā rodi, bahū me itthiyo, ekā gamissatī”ti. “Tena hi ayameva kumārikā gacchatu, etissāpi maṅgalaṃ bhavissatī”ti. So cintesi – “saccaṃ vadati, suṇisāyapi me maṅgalameva, iminā hi nimittena sā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissatī”ti tameva pesesi. Sā tattha pavisitvā rājānaṃ disvāva paṭibaddhacittā hutvā pāpamakāsi. Rājāpissā aṅgulimuddikaṃ adāsi. Atha naṃ katakiccaṃ nikkhamitvā āgataṃ pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ vijātā”ti? “Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ putta”nti. Kuṭumbiko taṃ ādāya pāyāsi[M 5.0475]. Purohitopi rañño santikaṃ gantvā “diṭṭhā te, deva, kumārikāpi evaṃ pāpā, kimaṅgaṃ pana aññā, api pana te kiñci dinna”nti pucchi. “Āma, aṅgulimuddikā dinnā”ti. “Nāssā taṃ dassāmī”ti vegena gantvā yānakaṃ gaṇhitvā “kimeta”nti vutte “ayaṃ me brāhmaṇiyā ussīsake ṭhapitaṃ muddikaṃ gahetvā āgatā, dehi, amma, muddika”nti āha. Sā taṃ dadamānā [P 5.0440] brāhmaṇaṃ hatthe nakhena vijjhitvā “gaṇha corā”ti adāsi.

The king said, “Very well,” and having entrusted the kingdom to his mother, he set out on a journey with the chaplain. After traveling a distance of one league, while they were seated by the main road, a householder, having performed a wedding ceremony for his son, was traveling with a large retinue, having seated a young maiden in a covered carriage. Seeing this, the chaplain said to the king, “If you wish, O king, I am able to make this maiden commit wrongdoing with you.” “What are you saying? She has a large retinue; it cannot be done,” replied the king. The chaplain said, “Then watch, O king.” He went ahead and, not far from the road, enclosed an area with a screen, placing the king inside the screen, while he himself sat by the roadside weeping. The householder, seeing him, asked, “Friend, why are you weeping?” “My wife is heavily pregnant. I was on my way to take her to her family home, but on the way, the fetus moved. She is suffering inside the screen, and there is no woman nearby her. I cannot go there myself. I do not know what will happen. It is necessary to find a woman.” “Do not weep. I have many women; one will go,” said the householder. “Then let this very maiden go. It will be an auspicious omen for her too,” replied the chaplain. The householder thought, “He speaks the truth. For my daughter-in-law, too, it will be an auspicious omen. By this sign, she will increase with sons and daughters,” and so he sent her. She entered there, and upon seeing the king, her heart was immediately attached, and she committed wrongdoing. The king also gave her a finger-ring. When she, having completed her business, came out, they asked her, “What was born?” “A son with the color of gold,” she replied. The householder took her and departed. The chaplain also went to the king and asked, “Have you seen, O king? Even a maiden is so wicked—what then of others? But did you give her anything?” “Yes, I gave her a finger-ring,” said the king. “I will not let her have it,” said the chaplain. He quickly went and stopped the carriage. When asked, “Who is this stopping the carriage?” he said, “This woman has come having taken a ring that my brahmin wife had placed at the head of her bed. Give it back, daughter, the ring.” As she was giving it, she scratched the brahmin’s hand with her nail and said, “Take it, you thief!”

Evaṃ brāhmaṇo nānāvidhehi upāyehi aññāpi bahū aticāriniyo rañño dassetvā “idha tāva ettakaṃ hotu, aññattha gamissāma, devā”ti āha. Rājā “sakalajambudīpe caritepi sabbā itthiyo evarūpāva bhavissanti, kiṃ no etāhi, nivattāmā”ti bārāṇasimeva paccāgantvā – “mahārāja, itthiyo nāma evaṃ pāpadhammā, pakati esā etāsaṃ, khamatha, deva, kinnarādeviyā”ti purohitena yācito khamitvā rājanivesanato naṃ nikkaḍḍhāpesi, ṭhānato pana taṃ apanetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Tañca pīṭhasappiṃ nikkaḍḍhāpetvā jambusākhaṃ chedāpesi. Tadā kuṇālo pañcālacaṇḍo ahosi. Iti attanā diṭṭhakāraṇameva āharitvā dassento gāthamāha –

Thus, the chaplain, having shown the king many other adulterous women through various means, said, “For now, let this much be enough; we shall go elsewhere, O king.” The king replied, “Even if we were to travel the whole of Jambudīpa, all women would be of this nature. What use have we for them? Let us turn back.” Returning to Bārāṇasī, the chaplain pleaded, “Great king, women are indeed of such wicked nature; this is their natural disposition. Forgive Kinnarādevī, O king.” Being thus requested by the chaplain, the king forgave her but had her expelled from the royal palace. He removed her from her position and appointed another as chief queen. He also had the cripple expelled and ordered the jambu branch to be cut down. At that time, the Kuṇāla bird king was Pañcālacaṇḍa. Thus, bringing forth the very reason he had witnessed, he spoke this verse:

311.

311.

“Yaṃ ve disvā kaṇḍarīkinnarānaṃ, sabbitthiyo na ramanti agāre;

Taṃ tādisaṃ maccaṃ cajitvā bhariyā, aññaṃ disvā purisaṃ pīṭhasappi”nti.

“Seeing what happened to Kaṇḍari and Kinnarā, one knows that all women find no delight in the home; for his wife, having abandoned such a man, seeing another man, a cripple, committed sin.”

Tassattho – yaṃ ve kaṇḍarissa rañño kinnarāya deviyā cāti imesaṃ kaṇḍarikinnarānaṃ virāgakāraṇaṃ ahosi, taṃ disvā jānitabbaṃ – sabbitthiyo attano sāmikānaṃ na ramanti agāre[V 5.0438]. Tathā hi aññaṃ pīṭhasappiṃ purisaṃ disvā taṃ rājānaṃ tādisaṃ ratikusalaṃ maccaṃ cajitvā bhariyā tena manussapetena saddhiṃ pāpamakāsīti.

The meaning is: Having seen that which was the cause of disillusionment between King Kaṇḍari and Queen Kinnarā, it should be understood that all women do not find pleasure in their husbands’ homes. Indeed, upon seeing another man, a cripple, the wife abandoned that king, a man so skilled in the arts of love, and committed evil with that wretched human.

Aparopi atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ bako nāma rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bārāṇasiyā pācīnadvāravāsino ekassa daliddassa pañcapāpī nāma dhītā ahosi. Sā kira pubbepi ekā daliddadhītā mattikaṃ madditvā gehe bhittiṃ vilimpati. Atheko paccekabuddho attano pabbhāraparibhaṇḍakaraṇatthaṃ [M 5.0476] “kahaṃ mattikaṃ labhissāmī”ti cintetvā “bārāṇasiyaṃ laddhuṃ sakkā”ti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattahattho nagaraṃ pavisitvā tassā avidūre aṭṭhāsi. Sā kujjhitvā ullokentī paduṭṭhena manasā “mattikampi bhikkhatī”ti avoca. Paccekabuddho niccalova ahosi. Atha sā paccekabuddhaṃ niccalitaṃ disvā puna cittaṃ pasādetvā, “samaṇa, mattikampi na labhasī”ti vatvā mahantaṃ mattikāpiṇḍaṃ āharitvā patte ṭhapesi. So tāya mattikāya pabbhāre paribhaṇḍamakāsi. Sā nacirasseva tato cavitvā tasmiṃyeva nagare bahidvāragāme duggatitthiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā dasamāsaccayena mātu kucchito nikkhami. Tassā mattikāpiṇḍaphalena [P 5.0441] sarīraṃ phassasampannaṃ ahosi, kujjhitvā ullokitattā pana hatthapādamukhaakkhināsāni pāpāni virūpāni ahesuṃ. Tena taṃ “pañcapāpī”tveva sañjāniṃsu.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, another king named Baka ruled righteously. At that time, a poor man living by the eastern gate of Bārāṇasī had a daughter named Pañcapāpī. In a previous life, she was the daughter of a poor man and was kneading clay to plaster the wall of her house. Then, a Paccekabuddha, wishing to plaster his cave dwelling, thought, “Where can I obtain clay?” and reflecting, “It can be obtained in Bārāṇasī,” he put on his robe, took his bowl, and entered the city, standing not far from the maiden. She, looking at him angrily with a corrupt mind, said, “He even begs for clay!” The Paccekabuddha remained unmoved. Seeing the Paccekabuddha standing still, she felt faith again and saying, “Ascetic, can you not even get clay?” she brought a large lump of clay and placed it in his bowl. With that clay, he plastered his cave dwelling. Not long after, she passed away from that existence and was reborn in the womb of a poor woman in a village outside the city gate. After ten months, she was born from her mother’s womb. As a result of the lump of clay, her body was endowed with an exquisite touch, but because she had looked at him angrily, her hands, feet, mouth, eyes, and nose were ugly and deformed. Therefore, she was known as ‘Pañcapāpī’ (Five-Sins).

Athekadivasaṃ bārāṇasirājā rattiṃ aññātakavesena nagaraṃ pariggaṇhanto taṃ padesaṃ gato. Sāpi gāmadārikāhi saddhiṃ kīḷantī ajānitvāva rājānaṃ hatthe gaṇhi. So tassā hatthasamphassena sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, dibbasamphassena phuṭṭho viya ahosi. So phassarāgaratto tathāvirūpampi taṃ hatthe gahetvā “kassa dhītāsī”ti pucchitvā “dvāravāsino”ti vutte assāmikabhāvaṃ pucchitvā “ahaṃ te sāmiko bhavissāmi, gaccha mātāpitaro anujānāpehī”ti āha. Sā mātāpitaro upagantvā “eko, amma, puriso maṃ icchatī”ti vatvā “sopi duggato bhavissati, sace tādisampi icchati, sādhū”ti vutte gantvā mātāpitūhi anuññātabhāvaṃ ārocesi. So tasmiṃyeva gehe tāya saddhiṃ vasitvā pātova rājanivesanaṃ pāvisi. Tato paṭṭhāyeva aññātakavesena nibaddhaṃ tattha gacchati, aññaṃ itthiṃ oloketumpi na icchati.

One day, the King of Bārāṇasī, while inspecting the city at night in disguise, went to that place. She, too, while playing with the village girls, unknowingly took the king’s hand. He was unable to maintain his composure due to the touch of her hand; he felt as if he were touched by a divine touch. Infatuated by the passion for that touch, even though she was so ill-favored, he held her hand and asked, 'Whose daughter are you?' When she replied, 'A gate-dweller's,' he asked if she was unmarried and said, 'I will be your husband; go and ask your parents for permission.' She went to her parents and said, 'Mother, a certain man desires me.' They replied, 'He must be a poor man too; if he desires such a one, it is well.' She went and informed him that her parents had given their consent. He stayed with her in that very house and entered the royal residence at dawn. From then on, he regularly went there in disguise, not even wishing to look at another woman.

Athekadivasaṃ tassā pitu lohitapakkhandikā uppajji. Asambhinnakhīrasappimadhusakkharayuttapāyāsova etassa bhesajjaṃ, taṃ te daliddatāya uppādetuṃ na sakkonti[V 5.0439]. Tato pañcapāpimātā dhītaraṃ āha – “kiṃ, amma, tava sāmiko pāyāsaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkhissatī”ti? “Amma, mama sāmikena amhehipi duggatatarena bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃ santepi pucchissāmi naṃ, mā [M 5.0477] cintayī”ti vatvā tassāgamanavelāyaṃ dummanā hutvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ rājā āgantvā “kiṃ dummanāsī”ti pucchi. Sā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā “bhadde idaṃ atirasabhesajjaṃ, kuto labhissāmī”ti vatvā cintesi – “na sakkā mayā niccakālaṃ evaṃ carituṃ, antarāmagge parissayopi daṭṭhabbo, sace kho pana etaṃ antepuraṃ nessāmi, etissā phassasampadaṃ ajānantā ‘amhākaṃ rājā yakkhiniṃ gahetvā āgato’ti keḷiṃ karissanti, sakalanagaravāsino etissā samphassaṃ jānāpetvā garahaṃ mocessāmī”ti. Atha naṃ rājā – “bhadde, mā cintayi, āharissāmi te pitu pāyāsa”nti vatvā tāya saddhiṃ abhiramitvā rājanivesanaṃ gantvā punadivase tādisaṃ pāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā paṇṇāni āharāpetvā dve puṭe katvā ekasmiṃ pāyāsaṃ pakkhipitvā ekasmiṃ cūḷāmaṇiṃ ṭhapetvā bandhitvā rattibhāge gantvā, “bhadde, mayaṃ daliddā, kicchena sampāditaṃ, tava pitaraṃ ‘ajja imamhā puṭā pāyāsaṃ bhuñja, sve imamhā’ti vadeyyāsī”ti āha. Sā tathā akāsi. Athassā pitā ojasampannattā pāyāsassa thokameva bhuñjitvā suhito jāto. Sesaṃ mātu datvā sayampi [P 5.0442] bhuñji. Tayopi suhitā ahesuṃ. Cūḷāmaṇipuṭaṃ pana punadivasatthāya ṭhapesuṃ.

One day, her father was afflicted with bloody dysentery. The remedy for this was a rice porridge made with fresh milk, ghee, honey, and sugar. But due to their poverty, they were unable to obtain it. Then Pañcapāpī’s mother said to her daughter, 'My dear, will your husband be able to provide the porridge?' 'Mother, my husband must be even poorer than we are. Even so, I will ask him; do not worry,' she replied. When the time came for his arrival, she sat down looking dejected. When the king arrived, he asked, 'Why are you dejected?' She told him the reason. Hearing this, the king said, 'Dear, this is a remedy of excellent taste, but where shall I obtain it?' Then he thought, 'I cannot always act in this manner. Dangers along the way must also be considered. But if I take her to the inner palace, those who do not know the excellence of her touch will mock me, saying, “Our king has brought a female demon.” I must make all the city-dwellers aware of her touch and thereby remove their censure.' Then the king said to her, 'Dear, do not worry. I will bring the porridge for your father.' After enjoying himself with her, he returned to the royal residence. The next day, he had such porridge prepared, had leaves brought, made two packets, placed the porridge in one and a crest jewel in the other, tied them up, and went at night. 'Dear, we are poor,' he said. 'This was obtained with difficulty. Tell your father, “Today eat from this packet, tomorrow from that one.”' She did so. Then her father, because the porridge was so nourishing, ate only a little and was satisfied. He gave the rest to her mother, and she also ate. All three were satisfied. They kept the packet with the crest jewel for the following day.

Rājā nivesanaṃ gantvā mukhaṃ dhovitvāva “cūḷāmaṇiṃ me āharathā”ti vatvā “na passāma, devā”ti vutte “sakalanagaraṃ vicinathā”ti āha. Te vicinitvāpi na passiṃsu. Tena hi bahinagare daliddagehesu bhattapaṇṇapuṭe upādāya vicinathāti. Vicinantā tasmiṃ ghaṭe cūḷāmaṇiṃ disvā tassā mātāpitaro “corā”ti bandhitvā nayiṃsu. Athassā pitā, “sāmi, na mayaṃ corā, aññenāyaṃ maṇi ābhato”ti vatvā “kenā”ti vutte “jāmātarā me”ti ācikkhitvā “kahaṃ so”ti pucchito “dhītā me jānātī”ti āha. Tato dhītāya saddhiṃ kathesi – “amma, sāmikaṃ te jānāsī”ti? “Na jānāmī”ti. “Evaṃ sante amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ natthī”ti. “Tāta, so andhakāre āgantvā andhakāre eva yāti, tenassa rūpaṃ na jānāmi, hatthasamphassena pana naṃ jānituṃ sakkomī”ti. So rājapurisānaṃ ārocesi. Tepi rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā [M 5.0478] ajānanto viya hutvā “tena hi taṃ itthiṃ rājaṅgaṇe antosāṇiyaṃ ṭhapetvā sāṇiyā hatthappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ katvā nagaravāsino sannipātetvā hatthasamphassena coraṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Rājapurisā tathā kātuṃ tassā santikaṃ gantvā rūpaṃ disvāva vippaṭisārino hutvā – “dhī, dhī pisācī”ti jigucchitvā phusituṃ na ussahiṃsu, ānetvā pana [V 5.0440] naṃ rājaṅgaṇe antosāṇiyaṃ ṭhapetvā sakalanagaravāsino sannipātesuṃ. Sā āgatāgatassa chiddena pasāritahatthaṃ gahetvāva “no eso”ti vadati. Purisā tassā dibbaphassasadise phasse bajjhitvā apagantuṃ na sakkhiṃsu, “sacāyaṃ daṇḍārahā, daṇḍaṃ datvāpi dāsakammakārabhāvaṃ upagantvāpi etaṃ ghare karissāmā”ti cintayiṃsu. Atha ne rājapurisā daṇḍehi koṭṭetvā palāpesuṃ. Uparājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbe ummattakā viya ahesuṃ.

The king went to his residence, washed his face, and said, 'Bring me the crest jewel.' When they replied, 'We do not see it, O king,' he ordered, 'Search the entire city.' They searched but still did not find it. 'In that case, search in the poor houses outside the city, starting from the food and leaf packets,' he said. While searching, they saw the crest jewel in that pot and, thinking her parents were thieves, bound them and led them away. Then her father said, 'Lord, we are not thieves; this gem was brought by someone else.' When asked, 'By whom?' he said, 'By my son-in-law.' Asked, 'Where is he?' he replied, 'My daughter knows.' Then he spoke with his daughter: 'My dear, do you know your husband?' 'I do not know.' 'If that is so, our lives are forfeit.' 'Father, he comes in the dark and leaves in the dark; therefore, I do not know his appearance, but I can recognize him by the touch of his hand.' He reported this to the king's men, and they informed the king. The king, acting as if he did not know, said, 'Then place that woman in the royal courtyard inside a screen, make a hand-sized hole in the screen, assemble the city-dwellers, and catch the thief by the touch of his hand.' The king's men went to her to do so, but upon seeing her appearance, they were filled with revulsion, saying, 'Fie, fie, you ogress!' and, being disgusted, did not dare to touch her. However, they brought her and placed her inside the screen in the royal courtyard, assembling all the city-dwellers. As each one came, she grasped the hand extended through the hole and said, 'This is not he.' The men, captivated by her divine-like touch, could not move away. They thought, 'If she is deserving of punishment, we would pay the fine, or even become her slaves and workers, just to keep her in our house.' Then the king's men beat them with sticks and drove them away. Starting with the viceroy, everyone became as if mad.

Atha rājā – “kacci ahaṃ bhaveyya”nti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Taṃ hatthe gahetvāva “coro me gahito”ti mahāsaddaṃ kari. Rājā tepi pucchi – “tumhe etāya hatthe gahitā kiṃ cintayitthā”ti. Te yathābhūtaṃ ārocesuṃ. Atha ne rājā āha – “ahaṃ etaṃ attano gehaṃ ānetuṃ evaṃ kāresiṃ ‘etissā phassaṃ ajānantā maṃ paribhaveyyu’nti cintetvā, tasmā mayā sabbe tumhe jānāpitā, vadatha, bho dāni, sā kassa gehe bhavituṃ yuttā”ti? “Tumhākaṃ, devā”ti. Atha naṃ abhisiñcitvā aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Mātāpitūnampissā [P 5.0443] issariyaṃ dāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca pana tāya sammatto neva vinicchayaṃ paṭṭhapesi, na aññaṃ itthiṃ olokesi. Tā tassā antaraṃ pariyesiṃsu. Sā ekadivasaṃ dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ aggamahesibhāvassa supine nimittaṃ disvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā supinapāṭhake pakkosāpetvā “evarūpe supine diṭṭhe kiṃ hotī”ti pucchi. Te itarāsaṃ itthīnaṃ santikā lañjaṃ gahetvā – “mahārāja, deviyā sabbasetassa hatthino khandhe nisinnabhāvo tumhākaṃ maraṇassa pubbanimittaṃ, hatthikhandhagatāya pana candaparāmasanaṃ tumhākaṃ paccāmittarājānayanassa pubbanimitta”nti vatvā “idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti vutte “deva imaṃ māretuṃ na sakkā, nāvāya pana naṃ ṭhapetvā nadiyaṃ vissajjetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā āhāravatthālaṅkārehi saddhiṃ rattibhāge naṃ nāvāya ṭhapetvā nadiyaṃ vissajjesi.

Then the king thought, “Could it be I?” and stretched out his hand. Taking him by the hand, she cried out loudly, “I have caught the thief!” The king asked those people, “What did you all think when you were taken by her hand?” They reported the matter as it truly was. Then the king said to them, “I did this to bring her to my own palace, thinking, ‘Lest those who do not know her touch might revile me.’ Therefore, I have made it known to all of you. Now speak, sirs, in whose house is it fitting for her to dwell?” “In yours, O King,” they replied. Then he had her consecrated and made her his chief queen. He also granted great wealth to her parents. From then on, being infatuated with her, he neither held court to settle disputes nor looked at another woman. The other women sought an opportunity to find fault with her. One day, she saw in a dream a sign of her being the chief queen of two kings and reported it to the king. The king summoned dream interpreters and asked, “What happens when such a dream is seen?” Taking bribes from the other women, they said, “Great King, the queen sitting on the back of an all-white elephant is a premonition of your death, and her touching the moon while on the elephant’s back is a premonition of you being carried away by enemy kings.” When asked, “What should be done now?” they replied, “O King, it is not possible to kill her, but it is proper to place her on a boat and set her adrift on the river.” So, during the night, the king placed her on a boat along with food, clothing, and ornaments, and set her adrift on the river.

Sā [M 5.0479] nadiyā vuyhamānā heṭṭhānadiyā nāvāya udakaṃ kīḷantassa bāvarikarañño abhimukhaṭṭhānaṃ pattā. Tassa senāpati nāvaṃ disvā “ayaṃ nāvā mayha”nti āha. Rājā “nāvāya bhaṇḍaṃ mayha”nti vatvā āgatāya nāvāya taṃ disvā “kā nāma tvaṃ pisācīsadisā”ti pucchi. Sā sitaṃ katvā bakassa rañño aggamahesibhāvaṃ kathetvā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ tassa kathesi. Sā pana pañcapāpīti sakalajambudīpe pākaṭā. Atha naṃ rājā hatthe gahetvā ukkhipi, saha gahaṇeneva phassarāgaratto aññāsu itthīsu itthisaññaṃ akatvā taṃ [V 5.0441] aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā tassa pāṇasamā ahosi. Bako taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “nāhaṃ tassa aggamahesiṃ kātuṃ dassāmī”ti senaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā tassa paṭititthe nivesanaṃ katvā paṇṇaṃ pesesi – “bhariyaṃ vā me detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti. So “yuddhaṃ dassāmi, na bhariya”nti vatvā yuddhasajjo ahosi. Ubhinnaṃ amaccā “mātugāmaṃ nissāya maraṇakiccaṃ natthi, purimasāmikattā esā bakassa pāpuṇāti, nāvāya laddhattā bāvarikassa, tasmā ekekassa gehe satta satta divasāni hotū”ti mantetvā dvepi rājāno saññāpesuṃ. Te ubhopi attamanā hutvā titthapaṭititthe nagarāni māpetvā vasiṃsu. Sā dvinnampi tesaṃ aggamahesittaṃ kāresi. Dvepi tassā sammattā ahesuṃ.
