Sā pana ekassa ghare sattāhaṃ vasitvā nāvāya itarassa gharaṃ gacchantī nāvaṃ pājetvā nentena ekena mahallakakhujjakevaṭṭena saddhiṃ nadīmajjhe pāpaṃ karoti. Tadā kuṇālo sakuṇarājā [P 5.0444] bako ahosi, tasmā idaṃ attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ āharitvā dassento gāthamāha –

As she was being carried by the river, she reached a place in front of King Bāvarika, who was playing in the water with a boat on the lower river. His general, seeing the boat, said, “This boat is mine.” The king said, “The treasure in the boat is mine.” Upon seeing her when the boat arrived, he asked, “Who are you, you who look like an ogress?” She smiled, told him of her status as King Baka’s chief queen, and related the whole matter to him. She was well known throughout all Jambudīpa as Pañcapāpī. Then the king took her by the hand and lifted her up. Immediately upon taking her hand, infatuated with the passion of touch, he disregarded other women and placed her in the position of chief queen. She became as dear to him as his own life. King Baka heard that news and said, “I will not allow him to make her his chief queen.” He gathered his army, set up a palace on the opposite bank, and sent a message: “Either give me my wife or give battle.” King Bāvarika said, “I will give battle, not my wife,” and prepared for war. The ministers of both conferred, saying, “There is no need to die on account of a woman. Since she had a former husband, she belongs to Baka; since she was found in the boat, she belongs to Bāvarika. Therefore, let her stay seven days in each of their palaces.” Having thus advised, they persuaded both kings. Both of them, being satisfied, built cities on opposite banks and lived there. She served as the chief queen for both of them, and both were infatuated with her. But while she, having stayed seven days in one house, was going by boat to the other’s house, she committed misconduct in the middle of the river with an old, hunchbacked fisherman who was rowing the boat. At that time, Kuṇāla, the king of birds, was King Baka. Therefore, recalling this incident which he himself had seen, he spoke this verse to illustrate it:

312.

312.

“Bakassa ca bāvarikassa ca rañño, accantakāmānugatassa bhariyā;

Avācarī paṭṭhavasānugassa, kaṃ vāpi itthī nāticare tadañña”nti.

The wife of King Baka and King Bāvarika, who were utterly devoted to her, committed misconduct with a servant who followed her will. What other man, then, would a woman not transgress against?

Tattha accantakāmānugatassāti accantaṃ kāmaṃ anugatassa. Avācarīti anācāraṃ cari. Paṭṭhavasānugassāti paṭṭhassa attano vasānugatassa, attano pesanakārassa santiketi attho. Karaṇatthe vā sāmivacanaṃ[M 5.0480], tena saddhiṃ pāpamakāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tadaññanti kataraṃ taṃ aññaṃ purisaṃ nāticareyyāti attho.

Here, ‘accantakāmānugatassa’ means ‘of those who followed her with extreme desire.’ ‘Avācarī’ means ‘she practiced misconduct.’ ‘Paṭṭhavasānugassāti’ means ‘with one who was at her beck and call,’ meaning in the presence of one who carries out her commands. Or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning ‘she committed a sin with him.’ ‘Tadañña’ means ‘what other man would she not transgress against?’—that is the meaning.

Aparāpi atīte brahmadattassa bhariyā piṅgiyānī nāma aggamahesī sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokentī maṅgalaassagopakaṃ disvā rañño niddupagamanakāle vātapānena oruyha tena saddhiṃ aticaritvā puna pāsādaṃ āruyha gandhehi sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭetvā raññā saddhiṃ nipajji. Athekadivasaṃ rājā “kiṃ nu kho deviyā aḍḍharattasamaye niccaṃ sarīraṃ sītaṃ hoti, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti ekadivasaṃ niddupagato viya hutvā taṃ uṭṭhāya gacchantiṃ anugantvā assabandhena saddhiṃ aticarantiṃ disvā nivattitvā sayanaṃ abhiruhi. Sāpi aticaritvā āgantvā cūḷasayanake nipajji. Punadivase rājā amaccagaṇamajjheyeva taṃ pakkosāpetvā taṃ kiccaṃ āvikatvā “sabbāva itthiyo pāpadhammā”ti tassā vadhabandhachejjabhejjārahaṃ dosaṃ khamitvā ṭhānā cāvetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Tadā kuṇālo rājā brahmadatto ahosi, tena taṃ attanā diṭṭhaṃ āharitvā dassento gāthamāha –

Moreover, in the past, King Brahmadatta’s chief queen named Piṅgiyānī, opening the lion-window and looking out, saw the royal horse-keeper. When the king was asleep, she descended through the window, committed adultery with him, then climbed back into the palace, perfumed her body, and lay down with the king. Then one day the king thought, ‘Why is the queen’s body always cold at midnight? I will investigate.’ Pretending to be asleep one day, he followed her as she rose and went out. Seeing her commit adultery with the horse-groom, he returned and climbed onto his bed. She too, after committing adultery, came back and lay down on her small couch. The next day, in the midst of his ministers, the king had her summoned, exposed her deed, and saying, ‘All women are of wicked nature,’ he forgave her fault which deserved execution, imprisonment, or mutilation, but deposed her from her position and appointed another chief queen. At that time, King Brahmadatta was Kuṇāla. Therefore, recalling what he himself had seen, he spoke this verse to illustrate it:

313.

313.

“Piṅgiyānī [V 5.0442] sabbalokissarassa, rañño piyā brahmadattassa bhariyā;

Avācarī paṭṭhavasānugassa, taṃ vāpi sā nājjhagā kāmakāminī”ti.

Piṅgiyānī, the beloved wife of King Brahmadatta, lord of the whole world, committed misconduct with a horse-groom who followed her will; desiring sensual pleasures, that woman, craving for lust, attained neither her lover nor her position.

Tattha taṃ vāti sā evaṃ aticarantī taṃ vā assabandhaṃ taṃ vā aggamahesiṭṭhānanti ubhayampi nājjhagā, ubhato bhaṭṭhā ahosi. Kāmakāminīti kāme patthayamānā.

In this context, ‘taṃ vā’ means that she, while thus transgressing, attained neither that horse-groom nor the position of chief queen; she was ruined in both respects. ‘Kāmakāminī’ means ‘desiring sensual pleasures’.

Evaṃ pāpadhammā itthiyoti atītavatthūhi [P 5.0445] itthīnaṃ dosaṃ kathetvā aparenapi pariyāyena tāsaṃ dosameva kathento āha –

Having thus shown the faults of women through these past stories, the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla, wishing to speak of their faults in another way, said:

314.

314.

“Luddhānaṃ lahucittānaṃ, akataññūna dubbhinaṃ;

Nādevasatto puriso, thīnaṃ saddhātumarahati.

A man not possessed by the god of passion should not trust women, who are greedy, fickle-minded, ungrateful, and treacherous to their friends.

315.

315.

“Na tā pajānanti kataṃ na kiccaṃ, na mātaraṃ pitaraṃ bhātaraṃ vā;

Anariyā samatikkantadhammā, sasseva cittassa vasaṃ vajanti.

They recognize neither the favor done for them nor their duties; they know neither mother, father, nor brother. Ignoble and transgressing righteousness, they follow the will of their own minds.

316.

316.

“Cirānuvuṭṭhampi [M 5.0481] piyaṃ manāpaṃ, anukampakaṃ pāṇasamampi bhattuṃ;

Āvāsu kiccesu ca naṃ jahanti, tasmāhamitthīnaṃ na vissasāmi.

Even a husband with whom they have long lived, who is dear, pleasing, compassionate, and like life itself, they abandon in times of danger and in various affairs. Therefore, I do not trust women.

317.

317.

“Thīnañhi cittaṃ yathā vānarassa, kannappakannaṃ yathā rukkhachāyā;

Calācalaṃ hadayamitthiyānaṃ, cakkassa nemi viya parivattati.

For the mind of a woman is like that of a monkey, shifting like the shadow of a tree. The heart of women is unsteady; it turns like the rim of a wheel.

318.

318.

“Yadā tā passanti samekkhamānā, ādeyyarūpaṃ purisassa vittaṃ;

Saṇhāhi vācāhi nayanti menaṃ, kambojakā jalajeneva assaṃ.

When, looking closely, they see a man’s desirable wealth, they lead him on with gentle words, just as the Kambojans lead a horse with water-moss.

319.

319.

“Yadā na passanti samekkhamānā, ādeyyarūpaṃ purisassa vittaṃ;

Samantato naṃ parivajjayanti, tiṇṇo nadīpāragatova kullaṃ.

When, looking closely, they see no desirable wealth in a man, they shun him on all sides, just as one who has crossed to the other bank of a river does not look back at the raft.

320.

320.

“Silesūpamā sikhiriva sabbabhakkhā, tikkhamāyā nadīriva sīghasotā;

Sevanti hetā piyamappiyañca, nāvā yathā orakulaṃ parañca.

They are like bird-lime and like fire consuming all; they have sharp deceit like a swift-flowing river. Indeed, they serve both the dear and the not-dear, just as a boat serves this shore and the other.

321.

321.

“Na [V 5.0443] tā ekassa na dvinnaṃ, āpaṇova pasārito;

Yo tā mayhanti maññeyya, vātaṃ jālena bādhaye.

They belong not to one, nor to two, but are like a shop spread open. Whoever might think, ‘She is my wife,’ would be trying to bind the wind with a net.

322.

322.

“Yathā [P 5.0446] nadī ca pantho ca, pānāgāraṃ sabhā papā;

Evaṃ lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati.

Just as a river, a road, a tavern, a meeting hall, and a public water-stall, so indeed are the women of the world; no boundary is found for them.

323.

323.

“Ghatāsanasamā etā, kaṇhasappasirūpamā;

Gāvo bahi tiṇasseva, omasanti varaṃ varaṃ.

These are like fire, similar to the head of a cobra. Like cows outside seeking grass, they graze upon one choice thing after another.

324.

324.

“Ghatāsanaṃ [M 5.0482] kuñjaraṃ kaṇhasappaṃ, muddhābhisittaṃ pamadā ca sabbā;

Ete naro niccayato bhajetha, tesaṃ have dubbidu sabbabhāvo.

Fire, an elephant, a cobra, an anointed king, and all women—a man should attend to these five with constant heedfulness, for indeed, their entire nature is hard to know.

325.

325.

“Naccantavaṇṇā na bahūna kantā, na dakkhiṇā pamadā sevitabbā;

Na parassa bhariyā na dhanassa hetu, etitthiyo pañca na sevitabbā”ti.

One who is exceedingly beautiful, one who is the beloved of many, and a woman skilled in arts are not to be associated with; nor another’s wife, nor one who consorts for the sake of wealth—these five kinds of women are not to be associated with.

Tattha luddhānanti lubbhānaṃ. Kaṇaverajātake (jā. 1.4.69-72) viya baddhacorepi sārajjanaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Lahucittānanti muhuttameva parivattanacittānaṃ. Cūḷadhanuggahajātakena (jā. 1.5.128 ādayo) etaṃ dīpetabbaṃ. Akataññutā pana etāsaṃ ekakanipāte takkāriyajātakena (jā. 1.13.104 ādayo) dīpetabbā. Nādevasattoti na adevasatto devena anāsatto ayakkhagahitako abhūtaviṭṭho puriso thīnaṃ sīlavantataṃ saddhātuṃ nārahati, bhūtaviṭṭho pana saddaheyya. Katanti attano kataṃ upakāraṃ. Kiccanti attanā kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ. Na mātaranti sabbepi ñātake chaḍḍetvā yasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā honti, taññeva anubandhanato ete mātādayo na jānanti nāma mahāpanthakamātā viya. Anariyāti nillajjā. Sassevāti sakassa. Āvāsūti āpadāsu. Kiccesūti tesu tesu karaṇīyesu.

Here, `luddhānaṃ` means 'of the greedy.' As in the Kaṇavera Jātaka, this is said with reference to becoming infatuated even with a bound thief. `Lahucittānaṃ` means 'of those whose minds change in a moment.' This should be illustrated by the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka. The ungratefulness of these women, moreover, should be explained by the Takkāriya Jātaka in the Ekakanipāta. `Nādevasatto` means: a man who is not possessed by a deva—that is, not attached by a deva, not seized by a yakkha, not possessed by a spirit—is not able to trust in the virtue of women; one who is possessed by a spirit, however, would trust. `Katanti` means a good deed done by oneself. `Kiccanti` means a duty to be done by oneself. `Na mātaran`ti means that, having abandoned all their relatives, they follow only him to whom their minds are attached; thus they do not recognize their mother and others, like the mother of Mahāpanthaka. `Anariyā`ti means shameless. `Sassevā`ti means of one's own. `Āvāsū`ti means in calamities. `Kiccesū`ti means in various duties.

Kannappakannanti otiṇṇotiṇṇaṃ. Yathā hi visame padese rukkhachāyā ninnampiorohati, thalampi abhiruhati, tathā etāsampi cittaṃ na kañci uttamādhamaṃ vajjeti. Calācalanti ekasmiṃyeva apatiṭṭhitaṃ. Nemi viyāti sakaṭassa gacchato cakkanemi viya. Ādeyyarūpanti gahetabbajātikaṃ. Vittanti dhanaṃ. Nayantīti attano vasaṃ nenti. Jalajenāti jalajātasevālena. Kambojaraṭṭhavāsino kira yadā aṭavito asse gaṇhitukāmā honti, tadā ekasmiṃ [V 5.0444] ṭhāne vatiṃ parikkhipitvā dvāraṃ yojetvā assānaṃ udakapānatitthe sevālaṃ madhunā makkhetvā sevālasambandhāni tīre tiṇāni ādiṃ katvā yāva parikkhepadvārā makkhenti, assā pānīyaṃ pivitvā [M 5.0483] rasagiddhena madhunā makkhitāni tāni tiṇāni khādantā anukkamena taṃ ṭhānaṃ pavisanti. Iti yathā te jalajena palobhetvā [P 5.0447] asse vasaṃ nenti, tathā etāpi dhanaṃ disvā tassa gahaṇatthāya saṇhāhi vācāhipi purisaṃ vasaṃ nentīti attho. Kullanti taraṇatthāya gahitaṃ yaṃ kiñci.

`Kannappakannan`ti means descending everywhere. For just as in an uneven place the shade of a tree descends into a hollow and ascends to high ground, so too their mind avoids no one, whether superior or inferior. `Calācalan`ti means unsteady, not established in one place. `Nemi viyā`ti means like the rim of the wheel of a moving cart. `Ādeyyarūpan`ti means of a nature to be taken. `Vittan`ti means wealth. `Nayantī`ti means they bring under their control. `Jalajenā`ti means by water-born moss. It is said that when the inhabitants of the Kamboja country wish to capture horses from the forest, they enclose a place with a fence, fix a gate, and at the horses' watering place, they smear the moss with honey. Then, beginning with the grass on the bank connected to the moss, they smear it all the way to the gate of the enclosure. The horses, after drinking water, greedy for the taste, eat that grass smeared with honey and gradually enter that place. Thus, just as they entice the horses with water-born moss and bring them under control, so too do these women, seeing wealth, bring a man under their control with gentle words in order to take it. This is the meaning. `Kullan`ti means anything taken for the purpose of crossing over.

Silesūpamāti purisānaṃ cittabandhanena silesasadisā. Tikkhamāyāti tikhiṇamāyā sīghamāyā. Nadīrivāti yathā pabbateyyā nadī sīghasotā, evaṃ sīghamāyāti attho. Āpaṇovāti yathā ca pasāritāpaṇo yesaṃ mūlaṃ atthi, tesaññeva upakāro, tatheva tāpi. Yo tāti yo puriso tā itthiyo. Bādhayeti so vātaṃ jālena bādheyya. Velā tāsaṃ na vijjatīti yathā etesaṃ nadīādīnaṃ “asukavelāyameva ettha gantabba”nti velā natthi, rattimpi divāpi icchiticchitakkhaṇe upagantabbāneva, asukenevātipi mariyādā natthi, atthikena upagantabbāneva, tathā tāsampīti attho.

`Silesūpamā`ti means like bird-lime, because they bind the minds of men. `Tikkhamāyā`ti means of sharp deceit, of swift deceit. `Nadīrivā`ti means just as a mountain river is swift-flowing, so too is their deceit swift; this is the meaning. `Āpaṇovā`ti means just as a spread-out shop is of use only to those who have capital, so too are they. `Yo tā`ti means 'whatever man... those women.' `Bādhaye`ti means he would bind the wind with a net. `Velā tāsaṃ na vijjatī`ti means no boundary is found for them. Just as for these rivers and so on there is no set time, such as 'one must go here only at such-and-such a time'—for they are to be approached day or night at any desired moment—and there is no restriction, such as 'only by so-and-so'—for they are to be approached by anyone in need—so it is for them too; this is the meaning.

Ghatāsanasamā etāti yathā aggi indhanena na tappati, evametāpi kilesaratiyā. Kaṇhasappasirūpamāti kodhanatāya upanāhitāya ghoravisatāya dujivhatāya mittadubbhitāyāti pañcahi kāraṇehi kaṇhasappasirasadisā. Tattha bahularāgatāya ghoravisatā, pisuṇatāya dujivhatā, aticāritāya mittadubbhitā veditabbā. Gāvo bahi tiṇassevāti yathā gāvo khāditaṭṭhānaṃ chaḍḍetvā bahi manāpamanāpassa tiṇassa varaṃ varaṃ omasanti khādanti, evametāpi niddhanaṃ chaḍḍetvā aññaṃ sadhanameva bhajantīti attho. Muddhābhisittanti rājānaṃ. Pamadā ca sabbāti sabbā ca itthiyo. Eteti ete pañca jane. Niccayatoti niccasaññato, upaṭṭhitassati appamattova hutvāti attho. Dubbidūti dujjāno. Sabbabhāvoti ajjhāsayo. Cirapariciṇṇopi hi aggi dahati, ciravissāsikopi kuñjaro ghāteti, ciraparicitopi sappo ḍaṃsati, ciravissāsikopi rājā anatthakaro hoti, evaṃ cirāciṇṇāpi itthiyo vikāraṃ dassentīti.

`Ghatāsanasamā etā`ti means these are like fire; just as a fire is not satisfied with fuel, so they are not satisfied with sensual pleasure. `Kaṇhasappasirūpamā`ti means they are like the head of a black snake for five reasons: anger, resentment, dreadful venom, being double-tongued, and treachery to friends. Therein, dreadful venom should be understood as due to great lust, being double-tongued as due to slander, and treachery to friends as due to misconduct. `Gāvo bahi tiṇassevā`ti means just as cows, having abandoned the place where they have eaten, graze on choice grasses outside, so too do these women, having abandoned a poor man, attend only to a wealthy one; this is the meaning. `Muddhābhisittan`ti means a king. `Pamadā ca sabbā`ti means and all women. `Ete`ti means these five kinds of beings. `Niccayato`ti means with constant mindfulness, that is, having become one with established mindfulness and diligence. `Dubbidū`ti means hard to know. `Sabbabhāvo`ti means disposition. For a long-tended fire still burns, a long-trusted elephant still kills, a long-familiar snake still bites, a long-trusted king still causes harm; so too, women, even when long associated with, show their changeability.

Naccantavaṇṇāti abhirūpavatī. Na bahūna kantāti aḍḍhakāsigaṇikā viya bahūnaṃ piyā manāpā. Na dakkhiṇāti naccagītakusalā. Tathārūpā hi [M 5.0484] bahupatthitā bahumittā honti, tasmā na [V 5.0445] sevitabbā. Na dhanassa hetūti yā dhanahetuyeva bhajati, sā apariggahāpi na sevitabbā. Sā hi dhanaṃ alabhamānā kujjhatīti.

`Accantavaṇṇā`ti means exceedingly beautiful. `Bahūnaṃ kantā`ti means dear and pleasing to many, like a half-kasi-coin courtesan. `Dakkhiṇā`ti means skilled in dance and song. For such a woman is much desired and has many lovers; therefore, she is not to be associated with. `Na dhanassa hetū`ti means she who consorts only for the sake of wealth; even if she is not possessed by another, she is not to be associated with. For if she does not obtain wealth, she becomes angry.

Evaṃ vutte mahājano mahāsattassa “aho sukathita”nti sādhukāramadāsi. Sopi ettakehi kāraṇehi itthīnaṃ aguṇaṃ kathetvā tuṇhī ahosi. Taṃ sutvā ānando gijjharājā, “samma kuṇāla, ahampi attano ñāṇabalena itthīnaṃ aguṇaṃ kathessāmī”ti vatvā aguṇakathaṃ ārabhi. Taṃ dassento satthā āha –

When this was said, the great crowd gave their approval to the Great Being, saying, “Aho! Well spoken!” And he, having spoken of the faults of women through these many reasons, became silent. Hearing this, Ānanda the vulture king said, “Friend Kuṇāla, I too will speak of the faults of women by the power of my own knowledge,” and began his talk on their faults. To show this, the Teacher said:

“Atha khalu, bho, ānando gijjharājā kuṇālassa ādimajjhakathāpariyosānaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then indeed, sirs, Ānanda the vulture king, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of Kuṇāla’s talk, at that time spoke these verses:

326.

326.

“Puṇṇampi [P 5.0448] cemaṃ pathaviṃ dhanena, dajjitthiyā puriso sammatāya;

Laddhā khaṇaṃ atimaññeyya tampi, tāsaṃ vasaṃ asatīnaṃ na gacche.

Even if a man were to fill this entire earth with wealth and give it to a cherished woman, given the opportunity, she would despise even him. One should not come under the power of such wicked women.

327.

327.

“Uṭṭhāhakaṃ cepi alīnavuttiṃ, komārabhattāraṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ;

Āvāsu kiccesu ca naṃ jahanti, tasmāhamitthīnaṃ na vissasāmi.

Even if he is energetic, of steady conduct, a dear and pleasing husband from her youth, they abandon him in times of danger and in various affairs; therefore, I do not trust women.

328.

328.

“Na vissase ‘icchati ma’nti poso, na vissase ‘rodati me sakāse’;

Sevanti hetā piyamappiyañca, nāvā yathā orakūlaṃ parañca.

A man should not trust her, thinking, ‘She desires me,’ nor should he trust her, thinking, ‘She weeps in my presence.’ For they serve both the dear and the not-dear, just as a boat serves this shore and the other.

329.

329.

“Na vissase sākhapurāṇasanthataṃ, na vissase mittapurāṇacoraṃ;

Na vissase rājānaṃ ‘sakhā mama’nti, na vissase itthi dasanna mātaraṃ.

Do not trust a bed spread with old branches; do not trust a former friend who is a thief; do not trust a king, thinking, ‘He is my friend’; do not trust a woman, even the mother of ten children.

330.

330.

“Na [M 5.0485] vissase rāmakarāsu nārisu, accantasīlāsu asaññatāsu;

Do not trust in women who delight in the ways of fools, who are habitually immoral and unrestrained.

Accantapemānugatassa bhariyā, na vissase titthasamā hi nāriyo.

Even if a wife is devoted with boundless love, one should not trust her; for women are indeed like common fords.

331.

331.

“Haneyyuṃ chindeyyuṃ chedāpeyyumpi, kaṇṭhepi chetvā rudhiraṃ piveyyuṃ;

Mā dīnakāmāsu asaññatāsu, bhāvaṃ kare gaṅgatitthūpamāsu.

They may kill, they may cut, they may even cause one to be cut; they may even cut the throat and drink the blood. Let one not form an attachment to women of base desires, who are unrestrained and like the fords of the Ganges.

332.

332.

“Musā [V 5.0446] tāsaṃ yathā saccaṃ, saccaṃ tāsaṃ yathā musā;

Gāvo bahi tiṇasseva, omasanti varaṃ varaṃ.

To them, falsehood is as truth, and truth as falsehood; like cows outside seeking grass, they search for the choicest, one after another.

333.

333.

“Gatenetā palobhenti, pekkhitena mhitena ca;

Athopi dunnivatthena, mañjunā bhaṇitena ca.

These women entice by their gait, by glances, and by smiles; also by improper dress and by sweet, charming speech.

334.

334.

“Coriyo kathinā hetā, vāḷā ca lapasakkharā;

Na tā kiñci na jānanti, yaṃ manussesu vañcanaṃ.

These women are thieves, hard-hearted, fierce, and sugar-tongued; their intentions cannot be known, nor can any of the deceit they practice among men be known.

335.

335.

“Asā lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati;

Sārattā ca pagabbhā ca, sikhī sabbaghaso yathā.

Worldly women are indeed wicked and untrustworthy; for them, no limit is found. They are passionate and impudent, like an all-devouring fire.

336.

336.

“Natthitthīnaṃ piyo nāma, appiyopi na vijjati;

Sevanti hetā piyamappiyañca, nāvā yathā orakūlaṃ parañca.

For women, there is no one truly dear, nor is there anyone truly unloved; they attend to both the dear and the unloved, like a boat that goes to this shore and the other.

337.

337.

“Natthitthīnaṃ [P 5.0449] piyo nāma, appiyopi na vijjati;

Dhanattā paṭivallanti, latāva dumanissitā.

For women, there is no one truly dear, nor is there anyone truly unloved; for the sake of wealth they cling to men, like a vine clinging to a tree.

338.

338.

“Hatthibandhaṃ assabandhaṃ, gopurisañca maṇḍalaṃ;

Chavaḍāhakaṃ pupphachaḍḍakaṃ, sadhanamanupatanti nāriyo.

Women follow after an elephant-trainer, a horse-trainer, a cowherd, a group of such men, a corpse-burner, and a scavenger, provided they have wealth.

339.

339.

“Kulaputtampi jahanti akiñcanaṃ, chavakasamasadisampi;

Anugacchanti anupatanti, dhanahetu hi nāriyo”ti.

They abandon even a son of good family if he is destitute; for the sake of wealth, they follow and pursue even one who is as low as a dog-eating outcaste. For women indeed act for the sake of riches.

Tattha [M 5.0486] ādimajjhakathāpariyosānanti kathāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ. Laddhā khaṇanti okāsaṃ labhitvā. Icchati manti maṃ esā icchatīti puriso itthiṃ na vissaseyya. Sākhapurāṇasanthatanti hiyyo vā pare vā santhataṃ purāṇasākhāsanthataṃ na vissase, apapphoṭetvā apaccavekkhitvā na paribhuñjeyya. Tatra hi dīghajātiko vā pavisitvā tiṭṭheyye, paccāmitto vā satthaṃ nikkhipeyya. Mittapurāṇacoranti panthadūhanaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ coraṃ “purāṇamitto me”ti na vissaseyya. Corā hi ye sañjānanti teyeva mārenti. Sakhā mamanti so hi khippameva [V 5.0447] kujjhati, tasmā rājānaṃ “sakhā me”ti na vissase. Dasannamātaranti “ayaṃ mahallikā idāni maṃ na aticarissati, attānaṃ rakkhissatī”ti na vissasetabbā. Rāmakarāsūti bālānaṃ ratikarāsu. Accantasīlāsūti atikkantasīlāsu. Accantapemānugatassāti sacepi accantaṃ anugatapemā assa, tathāpi taṃ na vissase. Kiṃkāraṇā? Titthasamā hi nāriyoti sambandho, titthaṃ viya sabbasādhāraṇāti attho.

Here, ādimajjhakathāpariyosānanti means the beginning, middle, and end of the talk. Laddhā khaṇanti means having obtained an opportunity. Icchati manti means a man should not trust a woman, thinking, 'She desires me.' Sākhapurāṇasanthatanti means one should not trust a bed spread with old branches, arranged yesterday or the day before, nor should one use it without shaking it out and inspecting it. For a snake might have entered and be staying there, or an enemy might have placed a weapon. Mittapurāṇacoranti means one should not trust a thief standing in a place where travelers are robbed, thinking, 'He is my old friend.' For thieves kill the very ones they recognize. Sakhā mamanti means for he may quickly become angry; therefore, one should not trust a king, thinking, 'He is my friend.' Dasannamātaranti means one should not trust an elderly woman, thinking, 'Now she will not transgress against me; she will protect herself.' Rāmakarāsūti means in those who give pleasure to fools. Accantasīlāsūti means in those who have transgressed virtue. Accantapemānugatassāti means even if she shows extreme affection, still, one should not trust her. Why? The connection is Titthasamā hi nāriyo, meaning that they are common to all, just like a bathing place.

Haneyyunti kuddhā vā aññapurisasārattā vā hutvā sabbametaṃ hananādiṃ kareyyuṃ. Mā dīnakāmāsūti hīnajjhāsayāsu saṃkiliṭṭhaāsayāsu. Bhāvanti evarūpāsu sinehaṃ mā kare. Gaṅgatitthūpamāsūti sabbasādhāraṇaṭṭhena gaṅgātitthasadisāsu. Musāti musāvādo tāsaṃ saccasadisova. Gatenātiādīsu pekkhitena palobhane ummādantījātakaṃ, (jā. 2.18.57 ādayo) dunnivatthena niḷinikājātakaṃ, (jā. 2.18.1 ādayo) mañjunā bhaṇitena “tuvaṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī”ti nandattherassa vatthu (udā. 22) kathetabbaṃ. Coriyoti sambhatassa dhanassa vināsanena coriyo. Kathināti thaddhahadayā. Vāḷāti duṭṭhā appakeneva kujjhanasīlā. Lapasakkharāti niratthakalapanena sakkharā viya madhurā. Asāti asatiyo lāmakā. Sārattāti sabbadā sārattā. Pagabbhāti kāyapāgabbhiyādīhi pagabbhā. Yathāti yathā sikhī sabbaghaso, evametāpi sabbaghasā. Paṭivallantīti parissajanti upagūhanti veṭhenti. Latāvāti yathā latā rukkhanissitā rukkhaṃ veṭhenti, evametā purisaṃ parissajanti nāma.

‘They might kill’ (Haneyyuṃ): Being angry or infatuated with another man, they might do all this, killing and so on. ‘To those of base desires’ (Mā dīnakāmāsu): To those of low and defiled intentions. ‘Attachment’ (Bhāvaṃ): Let one not have affection for such women. ‘Like fords in the Ganges’ (Gaṅgatitthūpamāsu): Like fords in the Ganges in the sense of being common to all. ‘Falsehood’ (Musā): Their falsehood is just like truth. Regarding ‘by their gait’ (gatena) and so on: for enticement by a glance, the Ummādantī Jātaka should be told; for improper dress, the Niḷinikā Jātaka; for charming speech, the story of the Elder Nanda—‘Come quickly, noble son!’—should be recounted. ‘Thieves’ (Coriyo): They are thieves through the destruction of accumulated wealth. ‘Cruel’ (Kathinā): Hard-hearted. ‘Fierce’ (Vāḷā): Vicious, prone to anger over a small thing. ‘Sweet-talkers’ (Lapasakkharā): Sweet like sugar with meaningless chatter. ‘Insatiable’ (Asā): They are wicked, base women. ‘Passionate’ (Sārattā): Always passionate. ‘Impudent’ (Pagabbhā): Impudent in body, and so on. ‘Like’ (Yathā): Just as fire is an all-devourer, so too are they all-devourers. ‘They cling’ (Paṭivallanti): They embrace, they hold close, they entwine. ‘Like a vine’ (Latāva): Just as a vine depending on a tree entwines the tree, so too do they embrace a man.

Hatthibandhantiādīsu [M 5.0487] gopuriso vuccati gopālako. Chavaḍāhakanti chavānaṃ ḍāhakaṃ, susānapālanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pupphachaḍḍakanti vaccaṭṭhānasodhakaṃ. Sadhananti etesupi sadhanaṃ anugacchantiyeva[P 5.0450]. Akiñcananti adhanaṃ. Chavakasamasadisanti sunakhamaṃsakhādacaṇḍālena samaṃ sadisaṃ, tena nibbisesampi purisaṃ gacchanti bhajanti. Kasmā? Yasmā anupatanti dhanahetu nāriyoti.

In the section beginning with Hatthibandha: gopuriso is called a cowherd. Chavaḍāhaka means a burner of corpses; it is said to mean a cemetery keeper. Pupphachaḍḍaka means a cleaner of toilets. Sadhanam means that even among these, they follow one who is wealthy. Akiñcana means without wealth. Chavakasamasadisa means equal or similar to a dog-flesh-eating outcaste; they go to and associate with a man who is no different from that. Why? Because women pursue for the sake of wealth.

Evaṃ attano ñāṇe ṭhatvā ānando gijjharājā itthīnaṃ aguṇaṃ kathetvā tuṇhī ahosi. Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā nāradopi attano ñāṇe ṭhatvā tāsaṃ aguṇaṃ kathesi. Taṃ dassento satthā āha –

Thus, standing in his own wisdom, Ānanda the vulture king spoke of the faults of women and then became silent. Having heard his words, Nārada also, standing in his own wisdom, spoke of their faults. To illustrate this, the Teacher said:

“Atha khalu, bho, nārado devabrāhmaṇo ānandassa gijjharājassa ādimajjhakathāpariyosānaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then indeed, good sir, the divine brahmin Nārada, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the discourse of Ānanda the vulture king, at that time spoke these verses:

340.

340.

“‘Cattārome [V 5.0448] na pūrenti, te me suṇātha bhāsato;

Samuddo brāhmaṇo rājā, itthī cāpi dijampati.

‘These four are never filled; listen to me as I speak of them: the ocean, a brahmin, a king, and a woman, O king of birds.

341.

341.

“Saritā sāgaraṃ yanti, yā kāci pathavissitā;

Tā samuddaṃ na pūrenti, ūnattā hi na pūrati.

Whatever rivers flow, dependent on the earth, go to the ocean; yet they do not fill the ocean, for due to its deficiency, it is not filled.

342.

342.

“Brāhmaṇo ca adhīyāna, vedamakkhānapañcamaṃ;

Bhiyyopi sutamiccheyya, ūnattā hi na pūrati.

And a brahmin, having studied the four Vedas with the legends as the fifth, would still desire to hear more; for due to his deficiency, he is not filled.

343.

343.

“Rājā ca pathaviṃ sabbaṃ, sasamuddaṃ sapabbataṃ;

Ajjhāvasaṃ vijinitvā, anantaratanocitaṃ;

Pāraṃ samuddaṃ pattheti ūnattā hi na pūrati.

And a king, having conquered and dwelt upon the whole earth with its oceans and mountains, though it be filled with diverse and endless treasures, still desires the far shore of the ocean; for due to his deficiency, he is not filled.

344.

344.

“Ekamekāya itthiyā, aṭṭhaṭṭha patino siyā;

Sūrā ca balavanto ca, sabbakāmarasāharā;

Kareyya navame chandaṃ, ūnattā hi na pūrati.

For a single woman, if there were eight husbands, brave, strong, and capable of bringing every sensual delight, she would still form a desire for a ninth; for due to her deficiency, she is not filled.

345.

345.

“Sabbitthiyo sikhīriva sabbabhakkhā, sabbitthiyo nadīriva sabbavāhī;

Sabbitthiyo kaṇṭakānaṃva sākhā, sabbitthiyo dhanahetu vajanti.

All women are like fire, devouring everything; all women are like a river, carrying everything away; all women are like a branch of thorns; all women go to another for the sake of wealth.

346.

346.

“Vātañca [M 5.0488] jālena naro parāmase, osiñcaye sāgaramekapāṇinā;

Sakena hatthena kareyya ghosaṃ, yo sabbabhāvaṃ pamadāsu ossaje.

He who would abandon his whole heart to women might as well try to grasp the wind with a net, bail out the ocean with a single hand, or make a sound by clapping his own hands.

347.

347.

“Corīnaṃ bahubuddhīnaṃ, yāsu saccaṃ sudullabhaṃ;

Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno, macchassevodake gataṃ.

Among thievish women of many wiles, in whom truth is very hard to find, the nature of women is as hard to know as the path of a fish in water.

348.

348.

“Analā [P 5.0451] mudusambhāsā, duppūrā tā nadīsamā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

Insatiable, yet soft-spoken, they are hard to fill like a river; knowing that they sink into the four woeful states, one should avoid them from afar.

349.

349.

“Āvaṭṭanī [V 5.0449] mahāmāyā, brahmacariyavikopanā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

Like a whirlpool, full of great illusions, destroyers of the holy life, they sink into the four woeful states; knowing this, one should avoid them from afar.

350.

350.

“Yaṃ etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti na’”nti.

Whomever these women associate with, whether out of desire or for wealth, they quickly burn him up, just as fire burns its own foundation.

Tattha dijampatīti dijajeṭṭhakaṃ kuṇālaṃ ālapati. “Saritā”tiādi ṭhapitamātikāya bhājanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ūnattāti udakapatiṭṭhānassa mahantatāya ūnā eva. Adhīyānāti sajjhāyitvā. Vedamakkhānapañcamanti itihāsapañcamaṃ vedacatukkaṃ. Ūnattāti so hi ajjhāsayamahantatāya sikkhitabbassa na pūrati. Anantaratanocitanti nānāratanehi ocitaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ. Ūnattāti so hi taṇhāmahantatāya na pūrati. Siyāti siyuṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sabbakāmarasāharāti sabbesaṃ kāmarasānaṃ āharakā. “Navame”ti aṭṭhahi atittabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sā pana dasamepi vīsatimepi tato uttaritarepi chandaṃ karoteva. Ūnattāti sā hi kāmataṇhāya mahantatāya na pūrati. Kaṇḍakānaṃva sākhāti sambādhamagge kaṇṭakasākhasadisā. Yathā hi sākhā laggitvā ākaḍḍhati, evaṃ etāpi rūpādīhi kaḍḍhanti. Yathā sākhā hatthādīsu vijjhitvā dukkhaṃ uppādeti, evaṃ etāpi phuṭṭhamattā sarīrasamphassena vijjhitvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpenti. Vajantīti parapurisaṃ vajanti.

Here, ‘dijampatī’ refers to addressing Kuṇāla, the chief of birds. ‘Saritā’ and so on are said for the purpose of the analysis of the established matrix. ‘Ūnattā’ (not filled): It means that due to the vastness of the water’s resting place, it is indeed insufficient. ‘Adhīyāna’ (having studied): It means having recited. ‘Vedamakkhānapañcamaṃ’ (the Vedas with the fifth Itihāsa): It means the four Vedas with Itihāsa as the fifth. ‘Ūnattā’ (not filled): For he is not filled by what should be learned, due to the vastness of his aspiration. ‘Anantaratanocitaṃ’ (adorned with endless treasures): It means filled and complete with various jewels. ‘Ūnattā’ (not filled): For he is not filled due to the vastness of his craving. ‘Siyā’ (might be): It means ‘siyuṃ’ (they might be); or this is indeed the reading. ‘Sabbakāmarasāharā’ (bringing all sensual pleasures): It means bringing all sensual pleasures. ‘Navame’ (a ninth): This is said to show the state of insatiability after eight. But she would indeed desire even a tenth, a twentieth, and even more beyond that. ‘Ūnattā’ (not filled): For she is not filled due to the vastness of sensual craving. ‘Kaṇḍakānaṃva sākhā’ (like branches of thorns): It means they are like thorny branches in a narrow path. Just as a branch catches and pulls, so too do these women pull one through forms and so on. Just as a branch pierces hands and so on, causing pain, so too do these women, when merely touched, pierce through bodily contact and lead to great ruin. ‘Vajanti’ (they go): It means they go to another man.

Parāmaseti gaṇheyya. Osiñcayeti nhāyituṃ otiṇṇo ekena pāṇinā sakalasamuddaudakaṃ osiñceyya gahetvā chaḍḍeyya. Sakenāti ekena [M 5.0489] attano hatthena tameva hatthaṃ haritvā ghosaṃ uppādeyya. Sabbabhāvanti “tvameva iṭṭho kanto piyo manāpo”ti vuccamāno yo puriso “evameta”nti saddahanto sabbaṃ attano ajjhāsayaṃ pamadāsu ossajeyya, so jālādīhi vātaggahaṇādīni kareyyāti attho. Gatanti gamanaṃ. Analāti tīhi dhammehi alanti vacanavirahitā. Duppurā tāti yathā mahānadī udakena, evaṃ kilesaratiyā tā duppūrā. Sīdanti naṃ viditvānāti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ, itthiyo allīnā catūsu apāyesu sīdantīti viditvā. Āvaṭṭanīti yathā āvaṭṭanī mahājanassa hadayaṃ mohetvā attano vase vatteti, evametāpīti attho. Vikopanāti nāsanatthena ca garahatthena ca brahmacariyassa kopikā. Chandasā vāti piyasaṃvāsena vā. Dhanena vāti dhanahetu vā. Saṃṭhānanti yathā jātavedo attano ṭhānaṃ yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ allīyati, taṃ taṃ dahati, tathā etāpi yaṃ yaṃ purisaṃ kilesavasena allīyanti, taṃ taṃ anudahanti mahāvināsaṃ pāpenti.

‘Parāmase’ (might grasp): It means one might grasp. ‘Osiñcaye’ (might bail out): It means one who has entered to bathe might bail out all the ocean’s water with one hand, taking it and throwing it away. ‘Sakena’ (with his own): It means with one’s own single hand, by moving that very hand, one might produce a sound. ‘Sabbabhāvaṃ’ (all his being): The meaning is that a man who, when told ‘You alone are liked, beloved, pleasing, and agreeable,’ believes it to be so and abandons all his inclination to women, would be able to do such things as catching the wind with a net and so on. ‘Gata’ (path): It means going. ‘Analā’ (insatiable): It means devoid of the word ‘enough’ in three respects. ‘Duppurā tā’ (hard to fill): Just as a great river is not filled with water, so too are they not filled with the delight of defilements. ‘Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna’ (knowing they sink): Here, ‘naṃ’ is merely a particle; it means knowing that women, clinging, sink in the four states of misery. ‘Āvaṭṭanī’ (a whirlpool): The meaning is that just as a whirlpool deludes the hearts of many and keeps them under its sway, so too do these women. ‘Vikopanā’ (agitator): It means an agitator of the holy life, in the sense of destruction and in the sense of blame. ‘Chandasā vā’ (through desire): It means either through affectionate cohabitation. ‘Dhanena vā’ (or wealth): It means or for the sake of wealth. ‘Saṃṭhānaṃ’ (its dwelling place): Just as fire clings to any place it touches and burns it, so too do these women, clinging to any man through defilements, consume him and bring great ruin.

Evaṃ [V 5.0450] nāradena itthīnaṃ aguṇe pakāsite puna mahāsatto visesetvā tāsaṃ aguṇaṃ pakāseti. Taṃ [P 5.0452] dassetuṃ satthā āha –

Thus, when Nārada had revealed the faults of women, the Great Being further detailed their faults. To illustrate this, the Teacher said:

“Atha khalu, bho, kuṇālo sakuṇo nāradassa devabrāhmaṇassa ādimajjhakathāpariyosānaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imā gāthāyo ajjhabhāsi –

“Then indeed, good sirs, the bird Kuṇāla, knowing the beginning, middle, and end of the divine brahmin Nārada’s discourse, at that time recited these verses:

351.

351.

“‘Sallape nisitakhaggapāṇinā, paṇḍito api pisācadosinā;

Uggatejamuragampi āside, eko ekāya pamadāya nālape.

“A wise man might converse even with one holding a sharpened sword, or with a malicious demon; one might even approach a serpent of fierce energy; but one should never speak alone with a woman in a secluded place.”

352.

352.

“Lokacittamathanā hi nāriyo, naccagītabhaṇitamhitāvudhā;

Bādhayanti anupaṭṭhitassatiṃ, dīpe rakkhasigaṇova vāṇije.

“Women are indeed disturbers of worldly minds, with weapons of dance, song, speech, and smiles. They harass a man whose mindfulness is unestablished, just as a pack of ogresses devours merchants on an island.”

353.

353.

“Natthi [M 5.0490] tāsaṃ vinayo na saṃvaro, majjamaṃsaniratā asaññatā;

Tā gilanti purisassa pābhataṃ, sāgareva makaraṃ timiṅgalo.

“They have neither discipline nor restraint; they delight in liquor and meat, being uncontrolled. They swallow the wealth a man has earned with hardship, as the Timiṅgala fish swallows a makara in the ocean.”

354.

354.

“Pañcakāmaguṇasātagocarā, uddhatā aniyatā asaññatā;

Osaranti pamadā pamādinaṃ, loṇatoyavatiyaṃva āpakā.

“Whose pasture is the delight of the five strands of sensual pleasure, arrogant, unstable, and unrestrained—women descend upon the heedless, like rivers flowing into a salty ocean.”

355.

355.

“Yaṃ naraṃ upalapenti nāriyo, chandasā vā ratiyā dhanena vā;

Jātavedasadisampi tādisaṃ, rāgadosavadhiyo dahanti naṃ.

“Whomever women entice, whether through desire, lust, or wealth—such a man they burn, like fire, for they are slayers through lust and hatred.”

356.

356.

“Aḍḍhaṃ ñatvā purisaṃ mahaddhanaṃ, osaranti sadhanaṃ sahattanā;

Rattacittamativeṭhayanti naṃ, sāla māluvalatāva kānane.

“Knowing a man to be prosperous and very wealthy, they give their own wealth and their very selves to approach him; they excessively entwine that man of impassioned mind, as a māluva creeper entwines a sal tree in the forest.”

357.

357.

“Tā upenti vividhena chandasā, citrabimbamukhiyo alaṅkatā;

Uhasanti pahasanti nāriyo, sambarova satamāyakovidā.

“Adorned, with faces like painted images, they approach with various wiles. Women laugh and mock, like the magician Sambara, skilled in a hundred deceptions.”

358.

358.

“Jātarūpamaṇimuttabhūsitā, sakkatā patikulesu nāriyo;

Rakkhitā [P 5.0453] aticaranti sāmikaṃ, dānavaṃva hadayantarassitā.

“Adorned with gold, jewels, and pearls, and honored in their husbands' families, women, even when guarded, transgress against their lord, just as the woman kept within the heart of a dānava demon transgressed against him.”

359.

359.

“Tejavāpi [V 5.0451] hi naro vicakkhaṇo, sakkato bahujanassa pūjito;

Nārinaṃ vasagato na bhāsati, rāhunā upahatova candimā.

“Even a man of splendor, discerning, honored, and revered by many, when he falls under the sway of women, does not shine, like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.”

360.

360.

“Yaṃ [M 5.0491] kareyya kupito diso disaṃ, duṭṭhacitto vasamāgataṃ ariṃ;

Tena bhiyyo byasanaṃ nigacchati, nārinaṃ vasagato apekkhavā.

“Whatever ruin an angry enemy with a corrupt mind might inflict on an adversary who has come under his power, greater ruin does he incur who falls under the sway of women, being full of longing.”

361.

361.

“Kesalūnanakhachinnatajjitā, pādapāṇikasadaṇḍatāḷitā;

Hīnamevupagatā hi nāriyo, tā ramanti kuṇapeva makkhikā.

“Though threatened with hair-plucking and scratching by nails, and beaten with feet, hands, elbows, ropes, and clubs, women still resort to the base; they delight only in the low, just as flies delight in a corpse.”

362.

362.

“Tā kulesu visikhantaresu vā, rājadhāninigamesu vā puna;

Oḍḍitaṃ namucipāsavākaraṃ, cakkhumā parivajje sukhatthiko.

“In families, on streets, or in royal cities and towns, they set out the snare and trap of Namuci; the discerning one, seeking happiness, should avoid them.”

363.

363.

“Ossajitva kusalaṃ tapoguṇaṃ, yo anariyacaritāni mācari;

Devatāhi nirayaṃ nimissati, chedagāmimaṇiyaṃva vāṇijo.

“Having abandoned the wholesome virtue of asceticism, whoever practices ignoble conduct will be led by the deities to hell, like a merchant who, giving a hundred thousand, takes a defective gem that leads to loss.”

364.

364.

“So idha garahito parattha ca, dummatī upahato sakammunā;

“Here he is blamed, and in the next world too; the fool is afflicted by his own deeds.”

Gacchatī aniyato gaḷāgaḷaṃ, duṭṭhagadrabharathova uppathe.

“Unrestrained, he goes tumbling down to ruin, like a wicked donkey-cart on a wrong path.”

365.

365.

“So upeti nirayaṃ patāpanaṃ, sattisimbalivanañca āyasaṃ;

Āvasitvā tiracchānayoniyaṃ, petarājavisayaṃ na muñcati.

“He goes to the Patāpana hell, and the iron Simbali forest with spear-like thorns; having dwelt in the animal realm, he is not freed from the realm of the king of the petas.”

366.

366.

“Dibyakhiḍḍaratiyo ca nandane, cakkavatticaritañca mānuse;

Nāsayanti pamadā pamādinaṃ, duggatiñca paṭipādayanti naṃ.

“Divine pleasures and delights in Nandana, and the life of a wheel-turning monarch among humans—women destroy these for the heedless, and lead him to a bad destination.”

367.

367.

“Dibyakhiḍḍaratiyo [M 5.0492][P 5.0454] na dullabhā, cakkavatticaritañca mānuse;

Soṇṇabyamhanilayā ca accharā, ye caranti pamadāhanatthikā.

“Divine pleasures and delights are not hard to find, nor the life of a wheel-turning monarch among humans, nor celestial nymphs dwelling in golden aerial mansions, for those who practice, having no need for women.”

368.

368.

“Kāmadhātusamatikkamā gati, rūpadhātuyā bhāvo na dullabho;

Vītarāgavisayūpapatti yā, ye caranti pamadāhanatthikā.

“Transcending the realm of sensual desire is the destination, existence in the realm of form is not difficult, and rebirth in the sphere free from passion, for those who practice, having no need for women.”

369.

369.

“Sabbadukkhasamattikkamaṃ [V 5.0452] sivaṃ, accantamacalitaṃ asaṅkhataṃ;

Nibbutehi sucihī na dullabhaṃ, ye caranti pamadāhanatthikā’”ti.

“The transcending of all suffering, the auspicious, the ultimate, the unmoving, the unconditioned—not difficult for the extinguished and the pure, for those who practice, having no need for women.”

Tattha sallapeti “sace mayā saddhiṃ sallapessasi, sīsaṃ te pātessāmī”ti vatvā khaggaṃ ādāya ṭhitenāpi, “sallapitamatteyeva taṃ khāditvā jīvitavināsaṃ pāpessāmī”ti dosinā hutvā ṭhitenāpi pisācena saddhiṃ sallape. “Upagataṃ ḍaṃsitvā nāsessāmī”ti ṭhitaṃ uggatejaṃ uragampi āside. Eko pana hutvā raho ekāya pamadāya na hi ālape. Lokacittamathanāti lokassa cittaghātikā. Dīpe rakkhasigaṇoti yathā dīpe rakkhasigaṇo manussavesena vāṇije upalāpetvā attano vase gate katvā khādati, evaṃ imāpi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attano vase katvā satte mahāvināsaṃ pāpentīti attho. Vinayoti ācāro. Saṃvaroti mariyādo. Purisassa pābhatanti dukkhasambhataṃ dhanaṃ gilanti nāsenti.

There, ‘sallape’ means one might converse even with one who stands with a drawn sword, saying, “If you speak with me, I will cut off your head,” and even with a demon who stands full of hate, thinking, “Just by your speaking, I will devour you and bring you to the destruction of life.” One might approach even a fiercely powerful serpent standing ready, thinking, “I will bite and destroy anyone who approaches.” But being alone in secret with a woman, one should not speak. ‘Crushing the world's mind’ means they are the destroyers of people's hearts. ‘On the island, a horde of ogresses’—the meaning is that just as on an island, a horde of ogresses deceives merchants by disguising themselves as humans, brings them under their control, and then devours them, so too do these women, by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure, bring beings under their control and lead them to great ruin. ‘Discipline’ refers to conduct. ‘Restraint’ refers to boundaries. ‘A man's provisions’ means they swallow and destroy wealth amassed through suffering.

Aniyatāti aniyatacittā. Loṇatoyavatiyanti loṇatoyavantaṃ samuddanti attho. Āpakāti āpagā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Yathā samuddaṃ nadiyo osaranti, evaṃ pamādinaṃ pamadāti attho. Chandasāti pemena. Ratiyāti pañcakāmaguṇaratiyā. Dhanena vāti dhanahetu vā. Jātavedasadisanti guṇasampattiyā aggimiva jalitampi. Rāgadosavadhiyoti [M 5.0493] kāmarāgadosehi vadhikā. Rāgadosagatiyotipi pāṭho. Osarantīti dhanagahaṇatthāya madhuravacanena taṃ bandhantiyo upagacchanti. Sadhananti sadhanā. Ayameva vā pāṭho, vatthālaṅkāratthāya kiñci attano dhanaṃ datvāpi osarantīti attho. Sahattanāti attabhāvena saddhiṃ attabhāvampi tasseva pariccajantiyo viya honti. Ativeṭhayantīti dhanagahaṇatthāya ativiya veṭhenti pīḷenti.

"Uncertain" means having an uncertain mind. "Loṇatoyavatiyanti" means the ocean with salty water—this is the meaning. "Āpakāti" means rivers, or this is another reading. Just as rivers flow into the ocean, so do women flow to the heedless—this is the meaning. "Chandasāti" means with affection. "Ratiyāti" means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Dhanena vāti" means for the sake of wealth. "Jātavedasadisanti" means, due to the abundance of qualities, blazing like fire. "Rāgadosavadhiyoti" means killers by lust and hatred. Another reading is "Rāgadosagatiyotipi." "Osarantīti" means they approach, binding him with sweet words for the sake of taking his wealth. "Sadhananti" means with wealth. Or this is another reading: giving some of their own wealth for the sake of clothing and ornaments, they approach—this is the meaning. "Sahattanāti" means, along with their own person, they are as if abandoning their very being to him. "Ativeṭhayantīti" means they excessively wrap around and oppress for the sake of taking wealth.

Vividhena chandasāti nānāvidhena ākārena. Citrabimbamukhiyoti alaṅkāravasena citrasarīrā citramukhiyo hutvā. Uhasantīti mahāhasitaṃ hasanti. Pahasantīti mandahasitaṃ hasanti. Sambarovāti māyākārapuriso viya asurindo viya ca[P 5.0455]. Dānavaṃva hadayantarassitāti yathā “kuto nu āgacchatha, bho, tayo janā”ti karaṇḍakajātake (jā. 1.9.87 ādayo) hadayantaranissitā antoudaragatāpi dānavaṃ aticari, evaṃ aticaranti. Arakkhitā hetāti dīpeti. Na bhāsatīti na virocati haritacalomasakassapakusarājāno viya. Tenāti tamhā amittena katā byasanā atirekataraṃ byasananti attho. Apekkhavāti sataṇho.

"By various ways" means in many different ways. "With faces like painted images" means adorned with ornaments, their bodies painted, their faces like paintings. "Laughing loudly" means laughing with great laughter. "Smiling gently" means laughing with a soft laugh. "Like Sambara" means like a magician or like the lord of demons. "Like a demon lurking in the heart" means, just as in the Karaṇḍaka Jātaka (Jā. 1.9.87 ff.) the demon was outwitted even while one was situated deep within its belly, so they outwit. "Unprotected" is explained. "Does not shine" means it does not shine, like the green-haired Kassapa and King Kusa. "Therefore" means a calamity far greater than that caused by an enemy—this is the meaning. "Longing" means with craving.

Kesalūnanakhachinnatajjitāti ākaḍḍhitvā lūnakesā nakhehi chinnagattā tajjitā pādādīhi ca [V 5.0453] tāḷitāva hutvā. Yo kilesavasena etepi vippakāre karoti, tādisaṃ hīnameva upagatā nāriyo ramanti, na ete vippakāre pariharanti, madhurasamācāre kiṃkāraṇā tā na ramanti. Kuṇapeva makkhikāti yasmā jegucchahatthikuṇapādimhi makkhikā viya tā hīneyeva ramantīti attho. Oḍḍitanti na etā itthiyo nāma, atha kho imesu ṭhānesu namucino kilesamārassa migapakkhigahaṇatthaṃ luddakehi oḍḍitaṃ pāsañca vākarañcāti maññamāno paññācakkhumā puriso dibbamānusikena sukhena atthiko parivajjeyya.

"With hair plucked out, nails cut, and threatened" means having their hair dragged and cut, their bodies cut by nails, and threatened, and beaten with feet and the like. It means that women who have fallen into such lowliness delight even in these abuses which one inflicts due to defilements. They do not avoid these abuses. Why do they not delight in gentle conduct? "Like flies on a corpse"—just as flies delight in disgusting elephant corpses and the like, so too do these women delight in lowly things. "Entrapped" means these are not women. Rather, in such situations, they are the snare and trap of Namuci, the Māra of defilements, set to catch beasts and birds—so should a wise person, seeing with the eye of wisdom, desiring heavenly and human happiness, avoid them.

Ossajitvāti devamanussesu mahāsampattidāyakaṃ tapoguṇaṃ chaḍḍetvā. Yoti yo puriso anariyesu aparisuddhesu kāmaguṇesu kāmaraticaritāni ācarati. Devatāhi nirayaṃ nimissatīti so devalokena parivattitvā nirayaṃ gaṇhissati. Chedagāmimaṇiyaṃva vāṇijoti [M 5.0494] yathā bālavāṇijo satasahassagghabhaṇḍaṃ datvā chedagāmimaṇikaṃ gaṇhāti, tathārūpo ayaṃ hotīti attho. Soti so itthīnaṃ vasaṃ gato. Aniyatoti ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ apāyesu paccissatīti aniyato. Gaḷāgaḷanti devalokā vā manussalokā vā gaḷitvā apāyameva gacchatīti attho. Yathā kiṃ? Duṭṭhagadrabharathova uppatheti, yathā kūṭagadrabhayuttaratho maggā okkamitvā uppatheyeva gacchati, tathā. Sattisimbalivananti sattisadisehi kaṇṭakehi yuttaṃ āyasaṃ simbalivanaṃ. Petarājavisayanti petavisayañca kālakañcikaasuravisayañca.

"Having abandoned" means giving up the virtue of asceticism, which is a giver of great wealth among gods and humans. "Who" refers to the man who practices conduct consisting of sensual pleasures that are ignoble and impure. "The gods will cast him into hell" means he will exchange the world of the gods for hell. "Like a merchant who trades a gem for a shard" means just as a foolish merchant gives up goods worth a hundred thousand for a fragment of a chedagāma gem, so too is this man. "He" means he has fallen under the sway of women. "Uncertain" means it is uncertain how long he will be cooked in the lower realms. "Falling headlong" means from the heavenly world or the human world, he has fallen away and goes to the lower realms—this is the meaning. Like what? Like a wicked donkey-cart that goes astray—just as a cart yoked to a wicked donkey leaves the path and goes astray, so too. "A forest of simbali trees with spikes" means an iron simbali forest filled with thorns like spears. "The realm of the king of the dead" means the realm of ghosts and also the realm of the kālakañcika asuras.

Pamādinanti pamattānaṃ. Te hi pamadāsu pamattā tāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ kusalaṃ na karonti, iti tesaṃ pamadā sabbā tā nāsenti nāma. Paṭipādayantīti tathāvidhaṃ purisaṃ tā pamādavaseneva akusalaṃ kāretvā duggatiṃ paṭipādenti nāma. Soṇṇabyamhanilayāti suvaṇṇamayavimānavāsiniyo. Pamadāhanatthikāti ye purisā pamadāhi anatthikā hutvā brahmacariyaṃ caranti. Kāmadhātusamatikkamāti kāmadhātusamatikkamā yā gati. Rūpadhātuyā bhāvoti yo kāmadhātusamatikkamagatisaṅkhāto rūpadhātuyā bhāvo, so tesaṃ na dullabho. Vītarāgavisayūpapatti yāti yā vītarāgavisaye suddhāvāsaloke upapatti, sāpi tesaṃ na dullabhāti attho. Accantanti antātītaṃ avināsadhammaṃ. Acalitanti kilesehi akampitaṃ. Nibbutehīti nibbutakilesehi. Sucihīti sucīhi parisuddhehi evarūpaṃ nibbānaṃ na dullabhanti.

"Pamādinanti" means for the heedless. For they, being heedless regarding women, do not perform the wholesome deeds that are the root of their attainments; thus, all those women destroy them indeed. "Paṭipādayanti" means that those women lead such a person to a bad destination indeed, by making him do unwholesome deeds through heedlessness. "Soṇṇabyamhanilayāti" refers to those who dwell in golden aerial mansions. "Pamadāhanatthikāti" means those men who, having no need for women, lead the holy life. "Kāmadhātusamatikkamāti" refers to the transcending of the realm of sensual desire. "Rūpadhātuyā bhāvoti" means the state of the form realm, which is described as a state of transcending the realm of sensual desire; that is not hard for them to attain. "Vītarāgavisayūpapatti yāti" means rebirth in the realm of the passionless, in the pure abodes; that too is not hard for them to attain, this is the meaning. "Accantanti" means beyond end, of indestructible nature. "Acalitanti" means unshaken by defilements. "Nibbutehīti" means by those whose defilements are extinguished. "Sucihīti" means by the pure and utterly cleansed; such Nibbāna is not hard to attain.

Evaṃ [P 5.0456] mahāsatto amatamahānibbānaṃ pāpetvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Himavante kinnaramahoragādayo ākāse ṭhitā devatā ca “aho buddhalīlāya kathitā”ti sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu[V 5.0454]. Ānando gijjharājā nārado devabrāhmaṇo puṇṇamukho ca phussakokilo attano attano parisaṃ ādāya yathāṭhānameva gamiṃsu. Mahāsattopi sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Itare pana antarantarā gantvā mahāsattassa santike ovādaṃ gahetvā tasmiṃ ovāde ṭhatvā saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Thus, the Great Being, having led beings to the deathless great Nibbāna, concluded the discourse. Kinnaras, Mahoragas, and other beings of the Himalayas, and the deities standing in the sky, gave their approval, saying, "Ah, how wonderfully it was spoken with the Buddha's grace!" Ānanda the vulture king, Nārada the divine brahmin, Puṇṇamukha, and Phussakokila, each taking their own retinues, departed to their respective places. The Great Being also went to his own place. But the others, going from time to time, received instruction from the Great Being, and abiding by that instruction, became destined for heaven.

Satthā [M 5.0495] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānento osānagāthā abhāsi –

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, connecting the Jātaka, recited the concluding verses:

370.

370.

“Kuṇālohaṃ tadā āsiṃ, udāyī phussakokilo;

Ānando gijjharājāsi, sāriputto ca nārado;

Parisā buddhaparisā, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti.

“Then I was Kuṇāla, Udāyī was Phussakokila, Ānanda was the king of vultures, and Sāriputta was Nārada. The assembly was the Buddha's assembly—thus remember this birth story.”

Te pana bhikkhū gamanakāle satthānubhāvena gantvā āgamanakāle attano attanova ānubhāvena āgatā. Tesaṃ satthā mahāvaneyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Sabbepi te taṃ divasameva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Mahādevatāsamāgamo ahosi. Athassa bhagavā mahāsamayasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 2.331 ādayo) kathesi.

Then those monks, when going, went by the Teacher's power; when returning, they came by their own power. The Teacher taught them the meditation subject in the Great Forest itself. All of them attained arahantship that very day. There was a great assembly of deities. Then the Blessed One taught them the Mahāsamaya Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.331 ff.).

Kuṇālajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Kuṇāla Jātaka, the Fourth.

[537] 5. Mahāsutasomajātakavaṇṇanā

[537] 5. The Commentary on the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka

Kasmā tuvaṃ rasaka edisānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aṅgulimālattheradamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa uppatti ca pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca aṅgulimālasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.34 ādayo) vuttanayena vitthārato veditabbā. So pana saccakiriyāya mūḷhagabbhāya itthiyā sotthibhāvaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya sulabhapiṇḍo hutvā vivekamanubrūhanto aparabhāge arahattaṃ patvā abhiññātova asītiyā mahātherānaṃ abbhantaro ahosi. Tasmiṃ kāle dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, aho vata bhagavatā tathārūpaṃ luddaṃ lohitapāṇiṃ mahācoraṃ aṅgulimālaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dametvā nibbisevanaṃ karontena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, aho buddhā nāma dukkarakārino”ti. Satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ ṭhitova dibbasotena taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “ajja mama gamanaṃ bahupakāraṃ bhavissati, mahādhammadesanā pavattissatī”ti ñatvā anopamāya buddhalīlāya dhammasabhaṃ gantvā varapaññattāsane nisīditvā “kāya [V 5.0455] nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, idāneva paramābhisambodhiṃ [P 5.0457] pattena mayā etassa damanaṃ, svāhaṃ pubbacariyaṃ [M 5.0496] caranto padesañāṇe ṭhitopi etaṃ damesi”nti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"Why are you like this, Rasaka?" This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the taming of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla. His birth, going forth, and higher ordination should be understood in detail as explained in the commentary to the Aṅgulimāla Sutta (MN.A. 2.34 ff.). But he, having brought safety to a woman with an obstructed birth by an act of truth, from that time onward became one who easily obtained alms. Cultivating seclusion, in due course he attained arahantship and became well-known, being counted among the eighty great elders. At that time, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, indeed, the Blessed One accomplished a difficult task by taming such a fierce, blood-stained, great robber as Aṅgulimāla without rod or weapon, making him harmless. Truly, Buddhas are doers of difficult deeds." The Teacher, standing in the perfumed chamber, heard this discussion with his divine ear. Knowing, "Today my going will be of great benefit, a great Dhamma discourse will take place," he went to the Dhamma hall with incomparable Buddha-grace. Seated on the excellent prepared seat, he asked, "Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?" When they replied, "This one," he said, "It is no wonder, monks, that now, having attained supreme enlightenment, I tamed him. Even when I was practicing the conduct of a bodhisatta in the past, established in partial knowledge, I tamed him." Then, being requested by them, he related the past.

Atīte kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare korabyo nāma rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Dasamāse atikkante suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi, sutavittatāya pana naṃ “sutasomo”ti sañjāniṃsu. Tamenaṃ rājā vayappattaṃ nikkhasahassaṃ datvā disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sippuggahaṇatthāya takkasilaṃ pesesi. So ācariyabhāgaṃ ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ kāsirañño putto brahmadattakumāropi tatheva vatvā pitarā pesito nagarā nikkhamitvā tameva maggaṃ paṭipajji. Atha sutasomo maggaṃ gantvā nagaradvāre sālāya phalake vissamatthāya nisīdi. Brahmadattakumāropi gantvā tena saddhiṃ ekaphalake nisīdi. Atha naṃ sutasomo paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “samma, maggakilantosi, kuto āgacchasī”ti pucchitvā “bārāṇasito”ti vutte “kassa puttosī”ti vatvā “kāsirañño puttomhī”ti vutte “ko nāmosī”ti vatvā “ahaṃ brahmadattakumāro nāmā”ti vutte “kena kāraṇena idhāgatosī”ti pucchi. So “sippuggahaṇatthāyā”ti vatvā “tvampi maggakilantosi, kuto āgacchasī”ti teneva nayena itaraṃ pucchi. Sopi tassa sabbaṃ ācikkhi. Te ubhopi “mayaṃ khattiyā, ekācariyasseva santike sippuggahaṇatthāya gacchāmā”ti aññamaññaṃ mittabhāvaṃ katvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā ācariyakulaṃ gantvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā attano jātiādiṃ kathetvā sippuggahaṇatthāya āgatabhāvaṃ kathesuṃ. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Te ācariyabhāgaṃ datvā sippaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ.

In the past, in the city of Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, a king named Korabya ruled righteously. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When ten months had passed, she gave birth to a golden-hued son, and because of his wealth of learning, they named him 'Sutasoma.' When he came of age, the king gave him a thousand nikkhas and sent him to Takkasilā to learn the arts under a world-renowned teacher. Taking the teacher’s fee, he left the city and set out on the road. At that time, Prince Brahmadatta, the son of the king of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī, was also sent by his father in the same manner. Leaving the city, he took the same road. As Sutasoma traveled, he sat down on a bench in a hall at the city gate to rest. Prince Brahmadatta also arrived and sat with him on the same bench. Then Sutasoma, making a friendly greeting, asked, 'Friend, you seem weary from the journey. Where have you come from?' When the prince replied, 'From Bārāṇasī,' Sutasoma asked, 'Whose son are you?' The prince answered, 'I am the son of the king of Kāsi.' Sutasoma then asked, 'What is your name?' The prince replied, 'My name is Prince Brahmadatta.' Sutasoma inquired further, 'For what reason have you come here?' The prince explained, 'To learn the arts.' Then, in the same manner, the prince asked Sutasoma, 'You too seem weary from the journey. Where have you come from?' Sutasoma told him everything. Both of them, thinking, 'We are khattiyas, and we are going to learn the arts under the same teacher,' established a friendship with each other. They entered the city, went to the teacher’s house, paid their respects to the teacher, and, after stating their lineage and other details, told him they had come to learn the arts. He accepted them, saying, 'Very well.' They paid their teacher’s fee and began their studies.

Na kevalañca te dveva, aññepi tadā jambudīpe ekasatamattā rājaputtā tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanti. Sutasomo tesaṃ jeṭṭhantevāsiko hutvā sippaṃ upadisanto nacirasseva nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. So aññassa santikaṃ agantvā “sahāyo [P 5.0458] me”ti brahmadattassa kumārasseva santikaṃ gantvā tassa piṭṭhiācariyo hutvā sippaṃ sikkhāpesi. Itaresampi anukkamena sippaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ. Te anuyogaṃ datvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā sutasomaṃ parivāretvā nikkhamiṃsu. Atha ne sutasomo maggantare ṭhatvā uyyojento “tumhe attano attano pitūnaṃ sippaṃ dassetvā rajjesu [M 5.0497] patiṭṭhahissatha, patiṭṭhitā ca pana mamovādaṃ kareyyāthā”ti āha. “Kiṃ[V 5.0456], ācariyā”ti? “Pakkhadivasesu uposathikā hutvā mā ghātaṃ kareyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. Bodhisattopi aṅgavijjāpāṭhakattā “anāgate bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadattakumāraṃ nissāya mahābhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti ñatvā te evaṃ ovaditvā uyyojesi. Te sabbepi attano attano janapadaṃ gantvā pitūnaṃ sippaṃ dassetvā rajjesu patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhitabhāvañceva ovāde vattanabhāvañca jānāpetuṃ paṇṇākārena saddhiṃ paṇṇāni pahiṇiṃsu. Mahāsatto taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “appamattāva hothā”ti paṇṇāni paṭipesesi.

Not only those two, but at that time in Jambudīpa, about one hundred and one princes were learning the arts under him. Sutasoma, becoming their senior student and instructing them in the arts, soon achieved mastery. He did not go to anyone else but, thinking 'He is my friend,' went to Prince Brahmadatta, becoming his assistant teacher and teaching him the arts. In due course, the others also completed their training. Having completed their studies, they paid respects to their teacher and, surrounding Sutasoma, departed. Then Sutasoma stood in the middle of the road and, as he sent them off, said, 'After demonstrating your skills to your fathers, you will each be established in your kingdoms. Once established, you should follow my advice.' 'What is it, teacher?' 'On the days of the lunar fortnight, having undertaken the Uposatha, you should not kill.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The Bodhisatta, being an expert in reading body marks, knew that 'In the future, a great danger will arise in Bārāṇasī on account of Prince Brahmadatta,' and having thus advised them, he sent them off. All of them returned to their own countries, demonstrated their skills to their fathers, and were established in their kingdoms. To inform him of their establishment and their adherence to his advice, they sent letters along with gifts. The Great Being, hearing this news, sent back letters saying, 'Be diligent!'

Tesu bārāṇasirājā vinā maṃsena bhattaṃ na bhuñjati. Uposathadivasatthāyapissa maṃsaṃ gahetvā ṭhapesi. Athekadivasaṃ evaṃ ṭhapitamaṃsaṃ bhattakārakassa pamādena rājagehe koleyyakasunakhā khādiṃsu. Bhattakārako taṃ maṃsaṃ aditvā kahāpaṇamuṭṭhiṃ ādāya carantopi maṃsaṃ uppādetuṃ asakkonto “sace amaṃsakabhattaṃ upanāmessāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthi, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti cintetvā “attheso upāyo”ti vikāle āmakasusānaṃ gantvā muhuttamatassa purisassa ūrumaṃsaṃ āharitvā supakkaṃ pacitvā bhattaṃ upanāmesi. Rañño maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ jivhagge ṭhapitamattameva satta rasaharaṇisahassāni phari, sakalasarīraṃ khobhetvā aṭṭhāsi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Pubbe cassa sevanatāya. So kira atītānantare attabhāve yakkho hutvā bahuṃ manussamaṃsaṃ khāditapubbo, tenassa taṃ piyaṃ ahosi[P 5.0459]. So “sacāhaṃ tuṇhīyeva bhuñjissāmi, na me ayaṃ imaṃ maṃsaṃ kathessatī”ti cintetvā saha kheḷena bhūmiyaṃ pātesi. “Niddosaṃ, deva, khādāhī”ti vutte manusse paṭikkamāpetvā “ahametassa niddosabhāvaṃ jānāmi, kiṃ nāmetaṃ maṃsa”nti pucchi. “Purimadivasesu paribhogamaṃsameva, devā”ti. “Nanu aññasmiṃ kāle ayaṃ raso natthī”ti? “Ajja supakkaṃ, devā”ti. “Nanu pubbepi evameva pacasī”ti. Atha naṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ ñatvā “sabhāvaṃ kathehi, no ce kathesi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti āha. So abhayaṃ yācitvā yathābhūtaṃ kathesi. Rājā “mā saddamakāsi, pakatiyā pacanakamaṃsaṃ tvaṃ khāditvā mayhaṃ manussamaṃsameva pacāhī”ti āha. “Nanu dukkaraṃ, devā”ti? “Mā bhāyi, na dukkara”nti. “Nibaddhaṃ kuto labhissāmi, devā”ti? “Nanu bandhanāgāre bahū manussā”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya tathā akāsi.

Among them, the king of Bārāṇasī would not eat a meal without meat. For the sake of the Uposatha day, his meat was set aside. One day, however, due to the cook’s negligence, the meat thus set aside was eaten by the dogs bred in the palace. The cook, not finding the meat and being unable to procure any even after searching with a handful of coins, thought: 'If I serve a meatless meal, I will lose my life. What should I do?' Then, thinking 'This is the way,' he went to a charnel ground at an improper hour, took the thigh-meat of a man who had just died, cooked it well, and served the meal. As soon as the king placed the piece of meat on the tip of his tongue, it pervaded the seven thousand taste-conducting nerves, and his whole body was shaken. Why? Because of his habit in the past. It is said that in his immediately preceding existence, he had been a yakkha and had eaten much human flesh; therefore, it was dear to him. Thinking, 'If I eat this in silence, he will not tell me about this meat,' the king spat it on the ground along with his saliva. When told, 'It is blameless, lord, please eat,' he had the people dismissed and asked, 'I know its blamelessness; what kind of meat is this?' 'It is the same meat consumed on previous days, lord.' 'But at other times, there was no such flavor.' 'Today it was well cooked, lord.' 'Was it not cooked the same way before?' Then, knowing the cook was silent, the king said, 'Tell the truth; if you do not, your life is over.' The cook, begging for pardon, told the truth. The king said, 'Do not make a sound; keep quiet. You eat the meat cooked normally, and for me, cook only human flesh.' 'But lord, is it not hard to get?' 'Do not fear, it is not hard.' 'Where will I get it constantly, lord?' 'Are there not many people in the prison?' From then on, he did as the king said.

Aparabhāge [M 5.0498] bandhanāgāre manussesu khīṇesu “idāni kiṃ karissāmi, devā”ti āha. “Antarāmagge sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ khipitvā yo taṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ ‘coro’ti gahetvā mārehī”ti āha. So tathā akāsi. Aparabhāge rājabhayena sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ olokentampi adisvā “idāni kiṃ karissāmī”ti āha. “Yadā bherivelāya nagaraṃ ākulaṃ hoti, tadā tvaṃ pana ekasmiṃ [V 5.0457] gharasandhimhi vā vīthiyaṃ vā catukke vā ṭhatvā manusse māretvā maṃsaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya tathā katvā thūlamaṃsaṃ ādāya gacchati. Tesu tesu ṭhānesu kaḷevarāni dissanti. Mama mātā na paññāyati, mama pitā na paññāyati, mama bhātā bhaginī ca na paññāyati, manussānaṃ paridevanasaddo sūyati. Nāgarā bhītatasitā “ime manusse sīho nu kho khādati, byaggho nu kho khādati, yakkho nu kho khādatī”ti olokentā pahāramukhaṃ disvā “eko manussakhādako coro ime khādatī”ti maññanti. Mahājanā rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā upakkosiṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. “Deva imasmiṃ nagare manussakhādako coro atthi, taṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ kathaṃ taṃ jānissāmi, kiṃ ahaṃ nagaraṃ rakkhantopi carāmī”ti.

Later, when the people in the prison were exhausted, he said, 'What shall I do now, lord?' The king said, 'Drop a bundle of a thousand coins in the middle of the road, and whoever picks it up, seize him as a "thief," kill him, and cook him.' He did so. Later, when he did not see even one person looking at the bundle of a thousand coins due to fear of the king, he asked again, 'What shall I do now?' The king said, 'When the city is in turmoil at the hour of the night-drum, then you, standing at a house-junction, or in a street, or at a crossroads, kill people and take their meat.' From then on, the cook did as the king said, taking choice meat and going away. In various places, corpses were seen. The sound of people's lamentation was heard: 'My mother is not found, my father is not found, my brother or sister is not found.' The citizens, terrified and trembling, wondered, 'Is it a lion eating these people, a tiger, or a yakkha?' Seeing the wounds, they realized, 'A single man-eating thief is eating them.' A great crowd gathered in the royal courtyard and cried out. The king asked, 'What is it, friends?' They said, 'Lord, there is a man-eating thief in this city; have him caught.' 'How can I know him? Do I go about guarding the city myself?'

Mahājanā “rājā nagarena [P 5.0460] anatthiko, kāḷahatthisenāpatissa ācikkhissāmā”ti gantvā tassa taṃ kathetvā “coraṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadiṃsu. So “sādhu sattāhaṃ āgametha, pariyesitvā coraṃ dassāmī”ti mahājane uyyojetvā purise āṇāpesi, “tātā, nagare kira manussakhādako coro atthi, tumhe tesu tesu ṭhānesu nilīyitvā taṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya nagaraṃ pariggaṇhanti. Bhattakārakopi ekasmiṃ gharasandhimhi sampaṭicchanno hutvā ekaṃ itthiṃ māretvā ghanaghanamaṃsaṃ ādāya pacchiyaṃ pūretuṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ te purisā gahetvā pothetvā pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā “gahito manussakhādako coro”ti mahāsaddaṃ kariṃsu. Mahājano taṃ parivāresi. Atha naṃ suṭṭhu bandhitvā maṃsapacchiṃ gīvāya bandhitvā ādāya senāpatissa dassesuṃ. Senāpati taṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho esa imaṃ maṃsaṃ khādati, udāhu aññena maṃsena missetvā vikkiṇāti, udāhu [M 5.0499] aññassa vacanena māretī”ti cintetvā tamatthaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The people said, 'This king has no concern for the country; we will inform the general named Kāḷahatthi.' They went and told him the matter, saying, 'It is right to search for the thief.' He said, 'Very well, wait for seven days; I will search for and give you the thief.' Dismissing the crowd, he ordered his men, 'Friends, it is said there is a man-eating thief in the city; you hide in various places and capture him.' They agreed, and from then on, they patrolled the city. The cook also, having hidden in a gap between houses, killed a woman and began taking the solid flesh to fill his basket. Then the men caught him, beat him, bound his hands behind his back, and made a great noise, 'The man-eating thief is caught!' The crowd surrounded him. Then, having bound him tightly and tied the meat-basket to his neck, they took him and showed him to the general. Seeing the cook, the general thought, 'Does he eat this human flesh himself, or does he mix it with other meat and sell it, or does he kill on another’s order?' Wishing to ask him about the matter, he spoke this first verse:

371.

371.

“Kasmā tuvaṃ rasaka edisāni, karosi kammāni sudāruṇāni;

Hanāsi itthī purise ca mūḷho, maṃsassa hetu adu dhanassa kāraṇā”ti.

371. 'Why, cook, do you perform such extremely cruel deeds? Deluded, you kill women and men; is it for the sake of meat or for the sake of wealth?'

Tattha rasakāti bhattakāraṇaṃ ālapati.

Therein, 'rasaka' is the address to the cook.

Ito paraṃ uttānasambandhāni vacanapaṭivacanāni pāḷivaseneva veditabbāni –

Henceforth, the questions and answers, being clear in their connection, should be understood according to the Pali text itself.

372.

372.

“Na [V 5.0458] attahetū na dhanassa kāraṇā, na puttadārassa sahāyañātinaṃ;

Bhattā ca me bhagavā bhūmipālo, so khādati maṃsaṃ bhadantedisaṃ.

372. 'Not for my own sake, nor for the sake of wealth, nor for my children, wife, friends, or kin; my master, the lordly ruler of the earth—it is he who eats such meat, O venerable sir.'

373.

373.

“Sace tuvaṃ bhatturatthe payutto, karosi kammāni sudāruṇāni;

Pātova [P 5.0461] antepuraṃ pāpuṇitvā, lapeyyāsi me rājino sammukhe taṃ.

373. 'If you are employed for your master’s sake and perform such extremely cruel deeds, then, having reached the inner palace early in the morning, you should speak this before the king in my presence.'

374.

374.

“Tathā karissāmi ahaṃ bhadante, yathā tuvaṃ bhāsasi kāḷahatthi;

Pātova antepuraṃ pāpuṇitvā, vakkhāmi te rājino sammukhe ta”nti.

"I will do just as you say, sir, Kāḷahatthi. Having reached the inner palace early in the morning, I will speak this to you in the presence of the king."

Tattha bhagavāti gāravādhivacanaṃ. Sace tuvanti “saccaṃ nu kho bhaṇati, udāhu maraṇabhayena musā bhaṇatī”ti vīmaṃsanto evamāha. Tattha sudāruṇānīti manussaghātakammāni. Sammukhe tanti sammukhe ṭhatvā evaṃ vadeyyāsīti. So sampaṭicchanto gāthamāha.

In that context, 'bhagavā' is a term of reverence. 'Sace tuvaṃ' (If you)—he said this while investigating, thinking, 'Is he telling the truth, or is he lying out of fear of death?' There, 'sudāruṇāni' refers to the deeds of killing humans. 'Sammukhe taṃ' means 'you should stand in his presence and speak thus.' He, in agreement, spoke the verse.

Atha naṃ senāpati gāḷhabandhanameva sayāpetvā vibhātāya rattiyā amaccehi ca nāgarehi ca saddhiṃ mantetvā sabbesu ekacchandesu jātesu sabbaṭṭhānesu ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā nagaraṃ hatthagataṃ katvā rasakassa gīvāyaṃ maṃsapacchiṃ [M 5.0500] bandhitvā ādāya rājanivesanaṃ pāyāsi. Sakalanagaraṃ viravi. Rājā hiyyo bhuttapātarāso sāyamāsampi alabhitvā “rasako idāni āgacchissati, idāni āgacchassatī”ti nisinnova taṃ rattiṃ vītināmetvā “ajjapi rasako nāgacchati, nāgarānañca mahāsaddo sūyati, kiṃ nū kho eta”nti vātapānena olokento taṃ tathā ānīyamānaṃ disvā “pākaṭaṃ idaṃ kāraṇaṃ jāta”nti cintetvā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā pallaṅkeyeva nisīdi. Kāḷahatthipi naṃ upasaṅkamitvā anuyuñji, sopissa kathesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then the general had him kept tightly bound. At the break of dawn, having consulted with the ministers and the citizens, and when all were of one mind, he set guards in every place, took control of the city, and having tied a basket of meat to the cook’s neck, took him and set off for the king’s palace. The whole city was in an uproar. The king, having eaten his breakfast the day before but not receiving his evening meal, had passed the night sitting and thinking, 'The cook will come now, he will come now.' The next day, when the cook still had not come and a great noise from the citizens was heard, the king wondered, 'What could this be?' Looking through the window, he saw him being brought in that manner and thought, 'The reason for this has become clear.' Establishing mindfulness, he remained seated on his throne. Kāḷahatthi approached and questioned him, and the king told him the matter. Revealing this fact, the Teacher said:

375.

375.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Kāḷo rasakamādāya, rājānaṃ upasaṅkami;

Upasaṅkamma rājānaṃ, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

"Then, at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, Kāḷa took the cook and approached the king. Having approached the king, he spoke these words:

376.

376.

“Saccaṃ kira mahārāja, rasako pesito tayā.

"Is it true, great king, that the cook was sent by you?

Hanati itthipurise, tuvaṃ maṃsāni khādasi.

He kills men and women, and you eat the flesh."

377.

377.

“Evameva [V 5.0459][P 5.0462] tathā kāḷa, rasako pesito mayā;

Mama atthaṃ karontassa, kimetaṃ paribhāsasī”ti.

"It is just so, Kāḷa; the cook was sent by me. While he was acting for my benefit, why do you rebuke him?"

Tattha kāḷāti kāḷahatthi. Evamevāti tena senāpatinā tejavantena anuyutto rājā musā vattuṃ asakkonto evamāha. Tattha tathāti idaṃ purimassa vevacanaṃ. Mama atthanti mama vuḍḍhiṃ. Karontassāti karontaṃ. Kimetanti kasmā etaṃ. Paribhāsasīti aho dukkaraṃ karosi, kāḷahatthi tvaṃ nāma aññaṃ coraṃ aggahetvā mama pesanakārakaṃ gaṇhāsīti tassa bhayaṃ janento kathesi.

Therein, 'Kāḷa' refers to Kāḷahatthi. 'Evameva' (Just so)—the king, being questioned by the powerful general and unable to tell a lie, spoke thus. There, 'tathā' is a synonym for the former. 'Mama atthaṃ' means my welfare. 'Karontassa' refers to the one who is performing it. 'Kimetaṃ' means why this? 'Paribhāsasī' (you rebuke)—he spoke this to instill fear in him, saying, 'Alas, you are doing a difficult thing, Kāḷahatthi! You seize my messenger instead of catching some other thief!'

Taṃ sutvā senāpati “ayaṃ sakeneva mukhena paṭijānāti, aho sāhasiko, ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ ime manussā etena khāditā, vāressāmi na”nti cintetvā āha – “mahārāja, mā evaṃ kari, mā manussamaṃsaṃ khādasī”ti. “Kāḷahatthi kiṃ kathesi, nāhaṃ viramituṃ sakkomī”ti. “Mahārāja, sace na viramissasi, attānañca raṭṭhañca nāsessasī”ti. “Evaṃ nassantepi ahaṃ neva tato viramituṃ sakkomī”ti. Tato senāpati tassa saññāpanatthāya vatthuṃ āharitvā dasseti – atītasmiñhi kāle mahāsamudde cha mahāmacchā ahesuṃ. Tesu ānando timinando ajjhārohoti [M 5.0501] ime tayo macchā pañcayojanasatikā, timiṅgalo timirapiṅgalo mahātimirapiṅgaloti ime tayo macchā sahassayojanikā honti. Te sabbepi pāsāṇasevālabhakkhā ahesuṃ. Tesu ānando mahāsamuddassa ekapasse vasati. Taṃ bahū macchā dassanāya upasaṅkamanti, ekadivasaṃ “sabbesaṃ dvipadacatuppadānaṃ sattānaṃ rājā paññāyati, amhākaṃ rājā natthi, mayampetaṃ rājānaṃ karissāmā”ti cintetvā sabbe ekacchandā hutvā ānandaṃ rājānaṃ kariṃsu. Te macchā tato paṭṭhāya tassa sāyaṃ pātova upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti.

Hearing this, the general thought, 'This king admits it with his own mouth! How reckless! For so long a time, these people have been eaten by him. I will stop him!' Thinking this, he said, 'Great king, do not do such a thing; do not eat human flesh.' 'Kāḷahatthi, what are you saying? I am unable to stop.' 'Great king, if you do not stop, you will destroy yourself and the kingdom.' 'Even if there is such destruction, I cannot stop it.' Then the general, to convince him, brought forward a story: In the past, there were six great fish in the ocean. Among them, Ānanda, Timinanda, and Ajjhāroha were five hundred yojanas in length. Timiṅgala, Timirapiṅgala, and Mahātimirapiṅgala were a thousand yojanas in length. All of them fed on rock-moss and algae. Among them, Ānanda lived on one side of the great ocean.
