Many fish would come to visit him. One day, they thought, 'A king is known among all two-footed and four-footed creatures, but we have no king. Let us make him our king.' Having reached a unanimous decision, they made Ānanda their king. From then on, those fish went to attend upon him every evening and morning.

Athekadivasaṃ ānando ekasmiṃ pabbate pāsāṇasevālaṃ khādanto ajānitvā “sevālo”ti saññāya ekaṃ macchaṃ [P 5.0463] khādi. Tassa taṃ maṃsaṃ khādantassa sakalasarīraṃ saṅkhobhesi. So “kiṃ nu kho idaṃ ativiya madhura”nti nīharitvā olokento macchamaṃsakhaṇḍaṃ disvā “ettakaṃ kālaṃ ajānitvā na khādāmī”ti cintetvā “sāyaṃ pātopi macchānaṃ āgantvā gamanakāle ekaṃ dve macche khādissāmi, pākaṭaṃ katvā khādiyamāne ekopi maṃ na upasaṅkamissati, sabbe palāyissanti, paṭicchanno hutvā pacchā osakkitosakkitaṃ paharitvā khādissāmī”ti tathā katvā khādi. Macchā parikkhayaṃ gacchantā cintayiṃsu. “Kuto nu kho ñātīnaṃ bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti. Atheko paṇḍito maccho “mayhaṃ ānandassa kiriyā [V 5.0460] na ruccati, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti macchesu upaṭṭhānaṃ gatesu ānandassa kaṇṇapatte paṭicchanno aṭṭhāsi. Ānando macche uyyojetvā sabbapacchato gacchantaṃ macchaṃ khādi. So paṇḍitamaccho tassa kiriyaṃ disvā itaresaṃ ārocesi. Te sabbepi bhītatasitā palāyiṃsu.

Then one day, Ānanda, while eating algae from a rock on a mountain, unknowingly, perceiving it as algae, ate a fish. As he ate that flesh, his entire body was thrilled. Thinking, 'What is this that is so exceedingly delicious?' he took it out and looked, and seeing a piece of fish meat, he thought, 'For all this time, being unaware, I have not eaten this.' He then resolved, 'In the evening and in the morning, when the fish come and go, I will eat one or two fish. If I eat them openly, not even one will approach me—they will all flee. I will hide and, lagging behind as they leave, I will strike and eat them.' And so he did. As the fish were being depleted, they wondered, 'From where can danger to our kin have arisen?' Then a wise fish thought, 'I do not approve of Ānanda's behavior; I will investigate him.' When the fish went to attend upon him, he hid behind Ānanda’s gill-cover. Ānanda, having sent the fish away, ate the one that went last. The wise fish, seeing his behavior, informed the others. They all, terrified, fled.

Ānando tato paṭṭhāya macchamaṃsagiddhena aññaṃ gocaraṃ na gaṇhi. So jighacchāya pīḷito kilanto “kahaṃ nu kho ime gatā”ti te macche pariyesanto ekaṃ pabbataṃ disvā “mama bhayena imaṃ pabbataṃ nissāya vasanti maññe, pabbataṃ parikkhipitvā upadhāressāmī”ti naṅguṭṭhena ca sīsena ca ubho passe parikkhipitvā gaṇhi. Tato “sace idha vasanti, palāyissantī”ti pabbataṃ parikkhipantaṃ attano naṅguṭṭhaṃ disvā “ayaṃ maccho maṃ vañcetvā pabbataṃ nissāya vasatī”ti kuddho paṇṇāsayojanamattaṃ sakanaṅguṭṭhakhaṇḍaṃ aññamacchasaññāya daḷhaṃ gahetvā murumurāyanto [M 5.0502] khādi, dukkhavedanā uppajji. Lohitagandhena macchā sannipatitvā luñjitvā khādantā yāva sīsā āgamaṃsu. Mahāsarīratāya [P 5.0464] parivattetuṃ asakkonto tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi, pabbatarāsi viya aṭṭhirāsi ahosi. Ākāsacārino tāpasaparibbājakā manussānaṃ kathayiṃsu. Sakalajambudīpe manussā jāniṃsu. Taṃ vatthuṃ āharitvā dassento kāḷahatthi āha –

From that time onward, Ānanda, greedy for fish-flesh, took no other food. Tormented by hunger and weary, while searching for those fish, he thought, "Where can they have gone?" Seeing a mountain, he thought, "They must be living near this mountain out of fear of me. I will encircle the mountain and investigate." With his tail and head, he encircled both sides and took hold. Then, while encircling the mountain, thinking, "If they are living here, they will flee," he saw his own tail. Angrily, he thought, "This fish has deceived me and is living near the mountain!" Mistaking a fifty-yojana-long piece of his own tail for another fish, he seized it firmly and chewed it with a crunching sound. A painful feeling arose. Drawn by the scent of blood, the other fish gathered and, tearing at him, ate their way up to his head. Unable to turn over due to his great size, he met his end right there. His bones became a heap like a mountain. Ascetics and wanderers who travel through the air told this to the humans, and all the people in Jambudīpa came to know of it. Presenting this story as an example, Kāḷahatthi said:

378.

378.

“Ānando sabbamacchānaṃ, khāditvā rasagiddhimā;

Parikkhīṇāya parisāya, attānaṃ khādiyā mato.

"Ānanda, greedy for flavors, having eaten all the fish, when his retinue was depleted, devoured himself and died.

379.

379.

“Evaṃ pamatto rasagārave ratto, bālo yadī āyati nāvabujjhati;

Vidhamma putte caji ñātake ca, parivattiya attānaññeva khādati.

"Thus, heedless, delighting in attachment to flavor, the fool does not understand the future. Destroying his children and abandoning his relatives, he turns and consumes himself alone.

380.

380.

“Idaṃ te sutvāna vigetu chando, mā bhakkhayī rāja manussamaṃsaṃ;

Mā tvaṃ imaṃ kevalaṃ vārijova, dvipadādhipa suññamakāsi raṭṭha”nti.

"Having heard this, may your desire depart. Do not, O king, eat human flesh. O lord of two-footed beings, do not, like that fish, render this entire kingdom empty."

Tattha ānandoti, mahārāja, atītasmiṃ kāle mahāsamudde pañcasatayojaniko ānando nāma mahāmaccho sabbesaṃ macchānaṃ rājā mahāsamuddassa ekapasse ṭhito. Khāditvāti sakajātikānaṃ macchānaṃ rasagiddhimā macche khāditvā. Parikkhīṇāyāti macchaparisāya khayappattāya. Attānanti aññaṃ gocaraṃ aggahetvā pabbataṃ parikkhipanto paṇṇāsayojanamattaṃ attano naṅguṭṭhakhaṇḍaṃ aññamacchasaññāya khāditvā mato maraṇappatto hutvā idāni mahāsamudde pabbatamatto [V 5.0461] aṭṭhirāsi ahosi. Evaṃ pamattoti yathā mahāmaccho ānando, evampi tathā tvaṃ taṇhārasagiddhiko hutvā pamatto pamādabhāvappatto.

Here, 'Ānanda,' O great king, refers to the great fish named Ānanda, five hundred yojanas in size, who was the king of all fish in the great ocean in a past age. 'Having eaten' means that, greedy for the taste of his own kind, he devoured the fish. 'When his retinue was exhausted' means when the assembly of fish had reached depletion. 'Himself' means that, not taking other food, while encircling the mountain, he mistook a fifty-yojana-long piece of his own tail for another fish, ate it, and died; now there remains a heap of bones as large as a mountain in the great ocean. 'Thus heedless' means just as the great fish Ānanda was, so too are you, having become greedy for the taste of craving, heedless and fallen into negligence.

Rasagārave rattoti manussamaṃsassa rasagārave ratto atirattacitto hoti. Bāloti yadi bālo duppañño āyatiṃ anāgate kāle uppajjanakadukkhaṃ nāvabujjhati na jānāti. Vidhammāti vidhametvā vināsetvā[M 5.0503]. Putteti puttadhītaro ca. Ñātake cāti sesañātake ca sahāye ca, vidhamma putte ca cajitvā ñātake cāti attho. Parivattiyāti aññaṃ āhāraṃ alabhitvā jighacchāya pīḷito sakalanagaraṃ parivattiya vicaritvā manussamaṃsaṃ alabhitvā attānaṃ khādanto ānando maccho viya attānaññeva khādati.

'Attached to the esteem for taste' means being deeply infatuated with the flavor of human flesh, with an excessively attached mind. 'The fool' means if the unwise one does not understand or know the suffering that will arise in the future. 'Having destroyed' means having ruined or annihilated. 'Children' means sons and daughters. 'And relatives' means the remaining kin and companions; the meaning is having ruined his children and abandoned his relatives. 'Turning around' means, failing to find other food and tormented by hunger, he wanders around the entire city and, not obtaining human flesh, he devours himself, just as the fish Ānanda devoured only himself.

Idaṃ te sutvānāti, mahārāja, te tuyhaṃ mayā ānītaṃ idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ sutvā chando manussamaṃsakhādanacchando vigetu vigacchatu viramatu. Mā bhakkhayīti rāja manussamaṃsaṃ mā bhakkhayi mā khādi. Mā tvaṃ imaṃ kevalanti mahāsamuddaṃ suññaṃ karonto vārijo ānando maccho iva, bho dvipadādhipa, dvipadānaṃ manussānaṃ, issara mahārāja, tvaṃ kevalaṃ saccato imaṃ tava kāsiraṭṭhaṃ nagaraṃ suññaṃ mā akāsīti attho.

'Having heard this of yours' means: O great king, having heard this example brought to you by me, may your desire—the desire to eat human flesh—depart, cease, and desist. 'Do not consume' means: O king, do not eat human flesh. 'Do not make this entirely [empty]' means: O lord of bipeds, ruler of humans, great king, do not, like the fish Ānanda who made the great ocean empty, truly make this your kingdom of Kāsi and its city empty. That is the meaning.

Taṃ [P 5.0465] sutvā rājā, “bho kāḷahatthi, na tvameva upamaṃ jānāsi, ahampi jānāmī”ti manussamaṃsagiddhatāya porāṇakavatthuṃ āharitvā dassento āha –

Hearing this, the king said, "O Kāḷahatthi, you are not the only one who knows a comparison; I too know one." Then, driven by his craving for human flesh, he spoke, presenting an ancient story:

381.

381.

“Sujāto nāma nāmena, oraso tassa atrajo;

Jambupesimaladdhāna, mato so tassa saṅkhaye.

"There was a householder named Sujāta, whose own legitimate son, not obtaining a slice of rose-apple, died when it was gone."

382.

382.

“Evameva ahaṃ kāḷa, bhutvā bhakkhaṃ rasuttamaṃ;

Aladdhā mānusaṃ maṃsaṃ, maññe hissāmi jīvita”nti.

"Just so, Kāla, having eaten the finest of foods, if I do not obtain human flesh, I think I will give up my life."

Tattha sujāto nāmāti kāḷahatthi kuṭumbiko nāmena sujāto nāma, tassa atrajo putto oraso jambupesiṃ aladdhāna alabhitvāna. Matoti yathā tassā jambupesiyā saṅkhaye so kuṭumbikaputto mato, evameva ahaṃ rasuttamaṃ aññarasānaṃ uttamaṃ manussānaṃ maṃsaṃ bhutvā bhuñjitvā aladdhā manussamaṃsaṃ jīvitaṃ hissāmīti maññe maññāmi.

In that context, 'named Sujāta' refers to a householder named Sujāta, O Kāḷahatthi. 'His own legitimate son, not obtaining the rose-apple piece' means not receiving it. 'Died' means just as that householder's son died when that rose-apple piece was gone, so too I, having eaten the supreme among all tastes—human flesh—think I will give up my life if I do not obtain it.

Atīte [M 5.0504][V 5.0462] kira bārāṇasiyaṃ sujāto nāma kuṭumbiko loṇambilasevanatthāya himavantato āgatāni pañca isisatāni attano uyyāne vasāpetvā upaṭṭhāsi. Ghare cassa nibaddhaṃ pañcasatamattā bhikkhā ahosi. Te pana tāpasā kadāci janapadepi bhikkhāya caranti, kadāci mahājambupesiṃ āharitvā khādanti. Tesaṃ jambupesiṃ āharitvā khādanakāle sujāto cintesi – “ajja bhaddantānaṃ tayo cattāro divasā anāgacchantānaṃ, kahaṃ nu kho gatā”ti. So attano puttakaṃ aṅguliyaṃ gāhāpetvā tesaṃ bhattakiccakāle tattha agamāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye mahallakānaṃ mukhavikkhālanakāle udakaṃ datvā sabbanavako jambupesiṃ khādati. Sujāto tāpase vanditvā nisinno – “kiṃ, bhante, khādathā”ti pucchi. “Mahājambupesiṃ, āvuso”ti. Taṃ sutvā kumāro pipāsaṃ uppādesi. Athassa gaṇajeṭṭhako tāpaso thokaṃ dāpesi. So taṃ khāditvā madhurarase bajjhitvā – “jambupesiṃ me dethā”ti punappunaṃ yāci. Kuṭumbiko dhammaṃ suṇanto, “puttaka, mā viravi, gehaṃ gantvā khādissasī”ti taṃ vañcetvā “imaṃ nissāya bhadantā ukkaṇṭheyyu”nti taṃ samassāsento isigaṇaṃ anāpucchitvā gehaṃ gato. Gatakālato paṭṭhāya cassa putto “jambupesiṃ me dethā”ti paridevi. Sujāto “isayopi ācikkhissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gato. Te isayopi “idha ciraṃ vasimhā”ti himavantameva gatā. Ārāme isayo apassanto tassa jambuambapanasamocādīnaṃ pesiyo madhusakkharacuṇṇasaṃyuttā adāsi. Tā tassa jivhagge ṭhapitamattā halāhalavisasadisā honti. So sattāhaṃ nirāhāro hutvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā idaṃ kāraṇaṃ [P 5.0466] āharitvā dassento evamāha.

In the past, it is said, in Bārāṇasī, a householder named Sujāta, for the sake of obtaining salt and sour relishes, had five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himalayas stay in his park and attended to them. In his house, there was a regular alms-offering for about five hundred. Those ascetics sometimes went for alms in the countryside, and sometimes they brought large rose-apple slices and ate them. When they brought the rose-apple slices and were eating them, Sujāta thought: 'The venerable ones have not come for three or four days now; where could they have gone?' Taking his little son by the finger, he went there during their mealtime. At that time, while the elders were being given water to rinse their mouths, the youngest of all was eating a rose-apple slice. Sujāta, having paid homage to the ascetics and sat down, asked: 'Venerable sirs, what are you eating?' 'A large rose-apple slice, friend.' Hearing this, the boy developed a craving. Then the leader of the group of ascetics had a little given to him. Having eaten it and being captivated by the sweet taste, he repeatedly begged: 'Give me a rose-apple slice!' The householder, listening to the Dhamma, comforted him, deceiving him by saying: 'Son, do not cry, you will eat it when we get home.' Thinking: 'The venerable ones might become dissatisfied because of this child,' he left for home without taking leave of the group of sages. From the time he returned, his son lamented: 'Give me a rose-apple slice!' Sujāta went to the park, thinking: 'I will tell the sages too.' But the sages, thinking: 'We have lived here a long time,' had already gone back to the Himalayas. Not seeing the sages in the park, he gave him slices of rose-apple, mango, jackfruit, banana, and the like, mixed with honey and sugar powder. As soon as they were placed on the tip of his tongue, they were like deadly halāhala poison. He, being without food for seven days, reached the end of his life. The king, bringing forth this reason to show it, spoke thus.

Tato kāḷahatthi “ayaṃ rājā ativiya rasagiddho, aparānipissa udāharaṇāni āharissāmī”ti cintetvā, “mahārāja, viramāhī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ viramituṃ na sakkomī”ti. Deva, sace na viramissasi, tuvaṃ ñātimaṇḍalato ceva rajjasirito ca parihāyissasi. Atītasmiñhi, mahārāja, idheva bārāṇasiyaṃ pañcasīlarakkhakaṃ sotthiyakulaṃ ahosi[M 5.0505]. Tassa kulassa ekaputtako ahosi. So mātāpitūnaṃ piyo manāpo ahosi paṇḍito byatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū. So samavayehi taruṇehi saddhiṃ gaṇabandhanena vicari. Sesā gaṇabandhā macchamaṃsādīni khādantā suraṃ pivanti. Māṇavo maṃsādīni na khādati, suraṃ na pivati. Te mantayiṃsu – “ayaṃ surāya apivanato amhākaṃ mūlaṃ na deti, upāyena naṃ suraṃ pāyessāmā”ti. Te sannipatitvā, “samma, chaṇakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Samma, tumhe suraṃ pivatha, ahaṃ suraṃ na pivāmi, tumheva gacchathā”ti. “Samma, tava pivanatthāya khīraṃ gaṇhāpessāmā”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Dhuttā uyyānaṃ gantvā paduminipattesu tikhiṇasuraṃ [V 5.0463] bandhāpetvā ṭhapayiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ pānakāle māṇavassa khīraṃ upanayiṃsu. Atha eko dhutto “pokkharamadhuṃ, bho, āharā”ti āharāpetvā paduminipattapuṭaṃ heṭṭhā chiddaṃ katvā aṅgulīhi mukhe ṭhapetvā ākaḍḍhi. Evaṃ itarepi āharāpetvā piviṃsu. Māṇavo “kiṃ nāmeta”nti pucchi. “Pokkharamadhunāmā”ti. “Ahampi thokaṃ labhissāmi, detha bhonto”ti. Tassapi dāpayiṃsu. So pokkharamadhusaññāya suraṃ pivi. Athassa aṅgārapakkamaṃsaṃ adaṃsu, tampi khādi.

Then Kāḷahatthi, thinking: 'This king is excessively greedy for tastes; I will bring him other examples,' said: 'Great king, desist!' 'I cannot desist.' 'Your Majesty, if you do not desist, you will fall away from the circle of your kinsmen and from the glory of your kingdom. For in the past, great king, right here in Bārāṇasī, there was a Sottiya family that observed the five precepts. That family had an only son, dear and pleasing to his parents, wise, clever, and a master of the three Vedas. He wandered in a group with youths of the same age. The rest of the group ate fish, meat, and so on, and drank liquor. The young man did not eat meat or drink liquor. They conspired: 'This one, because he doesn't drink liquor, doesn't give us money; we will make him drink liquor by some means.' They gathered and said: 'Friend, let's celebrate a festival.' 'Friends, you drink liquor, but I do not drink; you go yourselves.' 'Friend, we will have milk brought for you to drink.' He agreed: 'Very well.' The scoundrels went to the park and had strong liquor tied up in lotus leaves. Then, at the time of drinking, they brought milk to the young man. Then one scoundrel said: 'Sirs, bring the lotus honey!' and had it brought. He made a hole in the bottom of a lotus-leaf bundle, and placing it to his mouth with his fingers, sucked it in. In this way, the others also had it brought and drank. The young man asked: 'What is this called?' 'It is called lotus honey.' 'I too would like a little, sirs, give it to me.' They had it given to him. Thinking it was lotus honey, he drank the liquor. Then they gave him meat cooked on coals, and he ate that too.

Evamassa punappunaṃ pivantassa mattakāle “na etaṃ pokkharamadhu, surā esā”ti vadiṃsu. So “ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ madhurarasaṃ na jāniṃ, āharatha, bho, sura”nti āha. Te āharitvā punapi adaṃsu. Pipāsā mahatī ahosi. Athassa [P 5.0467] punapi yācantassa “khīṇā”ti vadiṃsu. So “handa taṃ, bho, āharāpethā”ti aṅgulimuddikaṃ adāsi, so sakaladivasaṃ tehi saddhiṃ pivitvā matto rattakkho kampanto vilapanto gehaṃ gantvā nipajji. Athassa pitā surāya pivitabhāvaṃ ñatvā vigate matte, “tāta, ayuttaṃ te kataṃ sottiyakule jātena suraṃ pivantena, mā puna evaṃ akāsī”ti āha. “Tāta, ko mayhaṃ doso”ti. “Surāya pivitabhāvo”ti. “Tāta, kiṃ kathesi, mayā evarūpaṃ madhurarasaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ aladdhapubba”nti. Brāhmaṇo punappunaṃ yāci. Sopi “na sakkomi viramitu”nti āha. Atha brāhmaṇo “evaṃ sante amhākaṃ kulavaṃso ca ucchijjissati, dhanañca vinassissatī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Thus, as he drank repeatedly, when he was intoxicated, they said: 'This is not lotus honey; this is liquor.' He said: 'All this time I did not know such a sweet taste; sirs, bring the liquor!' They brought it and gave it to him again. His craving became great. Then, as he asked again, they said: 'It's all gone.' He said: 'Well then, sirs, have it brought!' and gave his signet ring. He drank with them the whole day, and being intoxicated, with red eyes, trembling and lamenting, he went home and lay down. Then his father, knowing he had drunk liquor, when the intoxication had passed, said: 'Son, you have done what is improper by drinking liquor, being born in a Sottiya family. Do not do so again.' 'Father, what is my fault?' 'The fact that you drank liquor.' 'Father, what are you saying? Never before in all this time have I obtained such a sweet taste as this.' The Brahmin pleaded with him repeatedly. But he said: 'I cannot desist.' Then the Brahmin, thinking: 'If it is so, our family lineage will be cut off and our wealth will be destroyed,' spoke this verse:

383.

383.

“Māṇava abhirūposi, kule jātosi sotthiye;

Na tvaṃ arahasi tāta, abhakkhaṃ bhakkhayetave”ti.

“Young man, you are handsome, and you are born in a Sottiya family; you should not, dear son, consume what is unfit to be consumed.”

Tattha[M 5.0506], māṇavāti, māṇava, tvaṃ abhirūpo asi, sotthiye kule jātopi asi. Abhakkhaṃ bhakkhayetaveti, tāta, tvaṃ abhakkhitabbayuttakaṃ bhakkhayituṃ na arahasi.

In this verse, 'māṇava' means: 'Young man, you are handsome and also born in a Sottiya family.' 'To consume what is unfit to be consumed' means: 'Dear son, you should not consume what is improper to be consumed.'

Evañca pana vatvā, “tāta, virama, sace na viramasi, ahaṃ taṃ ito gehā nikkhāmessāmi, tava raṭṭhā pabbājanīyakammaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Māṇavo “evaṃ santepi ahaṃ suraṃ jahituṃ na sakkomī”ti vatvā gāthādvayamāha –

Having said this, he continued, “Son, desist! If you do not desist, I will expel you from this house and carry out the act of banishment against you from the kingdom.” The young man said, “Even so, I am unable to give up liquor,” and spoke these two verses:

384.

384.

“Rasānaṃ [V 5.0464] aññataraṃ etaṃ, kasmā maṃ tvaṃ nivāraye;

Sohaṃ tattha gamissāmi, yattha lacchāmi edisaṃ.

“This is one among the tastes; why do you restrain me? I will go to that place where I can obtain such a taste.”

385.

385.

“Sovāhaṃ nippatissāmi, nate vacchāmi santike;

Yassa me dassanena tvaṃ, nābhinandasi brāhmaṇā”ti.

“Therefore, I will depart; I will not stay in your presence, O Brahmin, since you do not rejoice at the sight of me.”

Tattha rasānanti loṇambilatittakakaṭukakhārikamadhurakasāvasaṅkhātānaṃ sattannaṃ rasānaṃ aññataraṃ uttamarasametaṃ majjaṃ nāma. Sovāhanti so ahaṃ eva. Nippatissāmīti nikkhamissāmi.

Here, “of the tastes” means that this thing called liquor is one of the seven tastes—namely salty, sour, bitter, pungent, alkaline, sweet, and astringent—and is the best of tastes. “Sovāhaṃ” means “that I myself.” “Nippatissāmi” means “I will depart.”

Evañca pana vatvā “nāhaṃ surāpānā viramissāmi, yaṃ te ruccati, taṃ karohī”ti āha. Atha brāhmaṇo “tayi amhe pariccajante mayampi taṃ pariccajissāmā”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Having said this, he declared, “I will not abstain from drinking liquor. Do as you please.” Then the Brahmin said, “If you abandon us, we too will abandon you,” and uttered this verse:

386.

386.

“Addhā [P 5.0468] aññepi dāyāde, putte lacchāma māṇava;

Tvañca jamma vinassasu, yattha pattaṃ na taṃ suṇe”ti.

“Surely, young man, we may obtain other heirs, other sons. But you, wretch, perish where no news of you is heard.”

Tattha yattha pattanti yattha gataṃ taṃ “asukaṭṭhāne nāma vasatī”ti na suṇoma, tattha gacchāhīti attho.

Here, “where no news of you is heard” means: go to a place where we do not hear that ‘he is living in such and such a place’.

Atha naṃ vinicchayaṃ netvā aputtabhāvaṃ katvā nīharāpesi. So aparabhāge nippaccayo kapaṇo jiṇṇapilotikaṃ nivāsetvā kapālahattho piṇḍāya caranto aññataraṃ kuṭṭaṃ nissāya kālamakāsi. Idaṃ kāraṇaṃ āharitvā kāḷahatthi rañño dassetvā, “mahārāja, sace tvaṃ amhākaṃ vacanaṃ na karissasi, pabbājanīyakammaṃ te karissantī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then, having brought him to a tribunal, declaring him disinherited, he had him expelled. Later, without support, destitute, clad in worn-out rags, carrying a bowl, he wandered for alms until he died leaning against a certain wall. Presenting this case, Kāḷahatthi showed it to the king and, saying, “Great King, if you do not follow our words, they will carry out the act of banishment against you,” spoke this verse:

387.

387.

“Evameva [M 5.0507] tuvaṃ rāja, dvipadinda suṇohi me;

Pabbājessanti taṃ raṭṭhā, soṇḍaṃ māṇavakaṃ yathā”ti.

“Even so, O king, lord of bipeds, listen to me; they will banish you from the kingdom, just like the young drunkard.”

Tattha dvipadindāti dvipadānaṃ inda, bho mahārāja, me mama vacanaṃ suṇohi tuvaṃ, evameva soṇḍaṃ māṇavakaṃ yathā taṃ bhavantaṃ raṭṭhato pabbājessanti.

Here, “lord of bipeds” means “king of bipeds”. The verse means: O great king, listen to my words; just as they banished the young drunkard, even so will they banish you from the kingdom.

Evaṃ [V 5.0465] kāḷahatthinā upamāya āhaṭāyapi rājā tato viramituṃ asakkonto aparampi udāharaṇaṃ dassetuṃ āha –

Even though Kāḷahatthi presented this simile, the king, being unable to desist from that, spoke in order to present another example:

388.

388.

“Sujāto nāma nāmena, bhāvitattāna sāvako;

“Sujāta by name, a disciple of those with developed minds;

Accharaṃ kāmayantova, na so bhuñji na so pivi.

longing for a celestial nymph, he neither ate nor drank.”

389.

389.

“Kusaggenudakamādāya, samudde udakaṃ mine;

Evaṃ mānusakā kāmā, dibbakāmāna santike.

“Taking water on the tip of a kusa grass, one might measure the water in the ocean; so too are human sensual pleasures in the presence of divine ones.”

390.

390.

“Evameva ahaṃ kāḷa, bhutvā bhakkhaṃ rasuttamaṃ;

Aladdhā mānusaṃ maṃsaṃ, maññe hissāmi jīvita”nti.

“Just so, Kāḷa, having experienced this supreme flavor of food, if I do not obtain human flesh, I think I will lose my life.”

Vatthu heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva.

The story is just as was told before.

Tattha bhāvitattānāti bhāvitacittānaṃ tesaṃ pañcannaṃ isisatānaṃ. Accharaṃ kāmayantovāti so kira tesaṃ isīnaṃ mahājambupesiyā khādanakāle anāgamanaṃ viditvā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇā na āgacchanti, sace katthaci gatā, jānissāmi, no ce, atha nesaṃ santike dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā isigaṇe vanditvā gaṇajeṭṭhakassa santike dhammaṃ suṇanto nisinnova sūriye atthaṅgate uyyojiyamānopi “ajja idheva vasissāmī”ti vatvā isigaṇaṃ vanditvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nipajji. Rattibhāge sakko devarājā devaccharāsaṅghaparivuto saddhiṃ attano paricārikāhi isigaṇaṃ vandituṃ āgato, sakalārāmo ekobhāso ahosi. Sujāto “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti uṭṭhāya paṇṇasālachiddena olokento sakkaṃ isigaṇaṃ vandituṃ āgataṃ devaccharāparivutaṃ [P 5.0469] disvā accharānaṃ saha dassanena rāgaratto ahosi. Sakko nisīditvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Kuṭumbikopi punadivase isigaṇaṃ vanditvā [M 5.0508] pucchi – “bhante, ko nāmesa rattibhāge tumhākaṃ vandanatthāya āgato”ti? “Sakko, āvuso”ti. “Taṃ parivāretvā nisinnā kā nāmetā”ti? “Devaccharā nāmetā”ti. So isigaṇaṃ vanditvā gehaṃ gantvā gatakālato paṭṭhāya “accharaṃ me detha, accharaṃ me dethā”ti vilapi. Ñātakā parivāretvā “bhūtāviṭṭho nu kho”ti accharaṃ pahariṃsu. So “nāhaṃ etaṃ accharaṃ kathemi, devaccharaṃ kathemī”ti vatvā “ayaṃ accharā”ti alaṅkaritvā ānītaṃ bhariyampi [V 5.0466] gaṇikampi olokento “nāyaṃ accharā, yakkhinī esā, devaccharaṃ me dethā”ti vilapanto nirāhāro hutvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Here, 'of those with developed minds' refers to the cultivated minds of those five hundred sages. 'Longing for a celestial nymph'—it is said that when those sages did not come at the time for eating a portion of the great rose-apple, he, noticing their absence, thought, 'Why do they not come? If they have gone somewhere, I will find out. If not, then I will listen to the Dhamma in their presence.' He went to the park, paid homage to the group of sages, and while listening to the Dhamma near the leader of the group, the sun set. Even though he was being dismissed, he said, 'Today I will stay right here.' He paid homage to the group of sages, entered a leaf hut, and lay down. During the night, Sakka, king of the gods, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs and accompanied by his own attendants, came to pay homage to the group of sages. The entire monastery became a single mass of light. Sujāta, wondering 'What is this?', rose and, looking through a crack in the leaf hut, saw Sakka, who had come to pay homage to the group of sages, surrounded by celestial nymphs. At the very sight of the nymphs, he became inflamed with passion. Sakka sat down, listened to a Dhamma talk, and then returned to his own place. The householder also, the next day, paid homage to the group of sages and asked, 'Venerable sirs, who was it that came to pay homage to you during the night?' 'It was Sakka, friend.' 'Who were those seated surrounding him?' 'They were celestial nymphs.' He paid homage to the group of sages, returned home, and from the moment he arrived, he wailed, 'Give me a celestial nymph! Give me a celestial nymph!' His relatives gathered around him and, thinking 'Is he possessed by a spirit?', they snapped their fingers. He said, 'I am not speaking of that finger-snap (acchara), I am speaking of a celestial nymph (devacchara)!' Looking at his wife and even a courtesan, who were adorned and brought to him with the words, 'This is a celestial nymph,' he said, 'This is not a celestial nymph, this is a demoness! Give me a celestial nymph!' Wailing thus, he went without food and right there died. Therefore, it is said:

“Accharaṃ kāmayantova, na so bhuñji na so pivī”ti.

“Longing for a celestial nymph, he neither ate nor drank.”

Kusaggenudakamādāya, samudde udakaṃ mineti, samma kāḷahatthi, yo kusaggeneva udakaṃ gahetvā “ettakaṃ siyā mahāsamudde udaka”nti tena saddhiṃ upamāya mineyya, so kevalaṃ mineyyeva, kusagge pana udakaṃ atiparittakameva. Yathā taṃ, evaṃ mānusakā kāmā dibbakāmānaṃ santike, tasmā so sujāto aññaṃ itthiṃ na olokesi, accharameva patthento mato. Evamevāti yathā so dibbakāmaṃ alabhanto jīvitaṃ jahi, evaṃ ahampi uttamarasaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ alabhanto jīvitaṃ jahissāmīti vadati.

Taking water on the tip of a blade of grass, one measures the water of the ocean. Indeed, Kāḷahatthi, whoever takes water on the tip of a blade of grass and would measure it by way of comparison, thinking, 'This much water there would be in the great ocean,' he would merely measure; but the water on the tip of the blade of grass is exceedingly little indeed. Just so are human sensual pleasures in comparison to divine sensual pleasures. Therefore, Sujāta did not look at another woman; desiring only a celestial nymph, he died. 'Even so, just as he, not obtaining divine sensual pleasure, gave up his life, so too I, not obtaining the supreme taste of human flesh, will give up my life,' thus he says.

Taṃ sutvā kāḷahatthi “ayaṃ rājā ativiya rasagiddho, saññāpessāmi na”nti sakajātikānaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā ākāsacarā suvaṇṇahaṃsāpi tāva vinaṭṭhāti dassetuṃ gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, Kāḷahatthi thought, 'This king is excessively greedy for taste; I will make him understand.' To show that even the golden swans, sky-roaming, were ruined by eating the flesh of their own kind, he spoke these two verses:

391.

391.

“Yathāpi te dhataraṭṭhā, haṃsā vehāyasaṅgamā;

Abhuttaparibhogena, sabbe abbhatthataṃ gatā.

Just as those Dhataraṭṭha geese, who fly through the sky, all met with destruction by consuming what should not be consumed.

392.

392.

“Evameva tuvaṃ rāja, dvipadinda suṇohi me;

Abhakkhaṃ rāja bhakkhesi, tasmā pabbājayanti ta”nti.

Even so, O King, lord of bipeds, listen to me: You have eaten what should not be eaten, O King; therefore they banish you.

Tattha abhuttaparibhogenāti attano samānajātikānaṃ paribhogena. Abbhatthataṃ gatāti sabbe maraṇameva pattā. Atīte kira cittakūṭe suvaṇṇaguhāyaṃ navuti haṃsasahassāni vasanti. Te vassike cattāro māse na nikkhamanti, sace nikkhameyyuṃ, udakapuṇṇehi pattehi uppatituṃ asakkontā [M 5.0509] mahāsamuddeyeva pateyyuṃ, tasmā na ca nikkhamanti. Upakaṭṭhe pana vassakāle jātassarato sayaṃjātasāliyo āharitvā guhaṃ pūretvā sāliṃ khādantā vasanti. Tesaṃ pana guhaṃ paviṭṭhakāle guhadvāre eko rathacakkappamāṇo uṇṇanābhi nāma makkaṭako ekekasmiṃ māse ekekaṃ jālaṃ vinandhati. Tassa ekekaṃ suttaṃ gorajjuppamāṇaṃ hoti. Haṃsā “taṃ jālaṃ bhindissatī”ti ekassa taruṇahaṃsassa dve koṭṭhāse [P 5.0470] denti. So vigate deve purato gantvā taṃ [V 5.0467] jālaṃ bhindati. Tena maggena sesā gacchanti. Athekasmiṃ kāle pañca māse vasso vuṭṭho ahosi. Haṃsā khīṇagocarā “kiṃ nu kho kattabba”nti mantetvā “mayaṃ jīvantā aṇḍāni labhissāmā”ti paṭhamaṃ aṇḍāni khādiṃsu, tato potake, tato jiṇṇahaṃse. Pañcamāsaccayena vassaṃ apagataṃ. Makkaṭako pañca jālāni vinandhi. Haṃsā sakajātikānaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā appathāmā jātā. Dviguṇakoṭṭhāsalābhī haṃsataruṇo jāle paharitvā cattāri bhindi, pañcamaṃ chindituṃ nāsakkhi, tattheva laggi. Athassa sīsaṃ vijjhitvā makkaṭako lohitaṃ pivi. Aññopi āgantvā jālaṃ pahari, sopi tattheva laggīti evaṃ sabbesaṃ makkaṭako lohitaṃ pivi. Tadā dhataraṭṭhakulaṃ ucchinnanti vadanti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe abbhatthataṃgatā”ti.

Therein, 'by consuming what was not to be consumed' means by consuming those of their own kind. 'All met with destruction' means all met their death. It is said that in the past, ninety thousand geese lived in the Golden Cave on Mount Cittakūṭa. They did not leave for the four months of the rainy season. If they had left, unable to fly with water-laden wings, they would have fallen into the great ocean—hence, they did not leave. But as the rainy season approached, they would gather wild-grown rice from a natural lake and fill the cave, living by eating the rice. When they had entered the cave, a spider named Uṇṇanābhi, the size of a chariot wheel, would spin a web each month at the cave's entrance. Each thread of its web was as thick as a cow's rope. The geese, thinking, 'He will break that web,' would give two portions of food to one young goose. When the rains ceased, he would go ahead and break that web. The rest would then follow that path. But on one occasion, it rained for five months. The geese, their food exhausted, deliberated, 'What indeed should be done?' Deciding, 'If we live, we shall obtain eggs,' they first ate the eggs, then the goslings, then the old geese. After five months, the rains ceased. The spider had spun five webs. The geese, having eaten the flesh of their own kind, became weak. The young goose, who had received double portions, struck the webs and broke four, but could not cut through the fifth; he got stuck there. Then the spider pierced his head and drank his blood. Others also came and struck the web, and they too got stuck there. Thus, the spider drank the blood of all of them. It is said that at that time the Dhataraṭṭha lineage was destroyed. Therefore it was said, 'All met with destruction.'

Evameva tuvanti yathā ete haṃsā abhakkhaṃ sakajātikamaṃsaṃ khādiṃsu, tathā tvampi khādasi, sakalanagaraṃ bhayappattaṃ, virama, mahārājāti. Tasmā pabbājayanti tanti yasmā abhakkhaṃ sakajātikamaṃsaṃ bhakkhesi, tasmā ime nagaravāsino taṃ raṭṭhā pabbājayanti.

The words 'Even so, you' mean: just as these geese devoured the forbidden flesh of their own kind, so too do you devour. The entire city is stricken with fear. Desist, O great king! The words 'therefore they banish you' mean: because you have consumed the forbidden flesh of your own kind, therefore these city dwellers banish you from the kingdom.

Rājā aññampi upamaṃ vattukāmo ahosi. Nāgarā pana uṭṭhāya, “sāmi senāpati, kiṃ karosi, kiṃ manussamaṃsakhādakaṃ coraṃ gahetvā vicarasi, sace na viramissati, raṭṭhato naṃ pabbājehī”ti vatvā nāssa kathetuṃ adaṃsu. Rājā bahūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā bhīto puna vattuṃ nāsakkhi. Punapi naṃ senāpati “kiṃ mahārāja viramituṃ sakkhissasi, udāhu na sakkhissasī”ti vatvā “na sakkomī”ti vutte sabbaṃ orodhagaṇañca puttadhītaro ca sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍite passe ṭhapetvā, “mahārāja, ime ñātimaṇḍale ceva amaccagaṇañca rajjasiriñca olokehi, mā vinassi, virama manussamaṃsato”ti āha. Rājā “na [M 5.0510] mayhaṃ ete manussamaṃsato piyatarā”ti vatvā “tena hi, mahārāja, imamhā nagarā ca raṭṭhā ca nikkhamathā”ti vutte, “kāḷahatthi, na me rajjenattho, nagarā nikkhamāmi, ekaṃ pana me khaggañca rasakañca bhājanañca dehī”ti āha. Athassa khaggañca maṃsapacanabhājanañca pacchiñca ukkhipāpetvā rasakañca datvā raṭṭhā pabbājanīyakammaṃ kariṃsu.

The king wished to speak another simile. But the citizens rose up and said, 'Lord commander, what are you doing? Why do you go about with this man-eating thief whom you have seized? If he does not desist, banish him from the kingdom!' Having said this, they did not allow him to speak. The king, hearing the words of many, became frightened and could not speak again. Again the commander said to him, 'O great king, will you be able to desist, or will you not be able?' When he said, 'I cannot,' the commander had the entire royal household, his sons and daughters, adorned with all their ornaments, placed before him, and said, 'O great king, behold this circle of relatives, this assembly of ministers, and the splendor of kingship. Do not let it perish—desist from human flesh!' The king replied, 'These are not dearer to me than human flesh.' When it was said, 'In that case, O great king, depart from this city and the kingdom,' he replied, 'Kāḷahatthi, I have no use for the kingdom. I will leave the city, but give me a sword, the cook Rasaka, and a vessel.' Then, having given him a sword, a meat-cooking vessel, a basket, and the cook, they performed the act of banishment from the kingdom.

So khaggañca rasakañca [P 5.0471] ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā ekasmiṃ nigrodhamūle vasanaṭṭhānaṃ katvā tattha vasanto aṭavimagge ṭhatvā manusse māretvā āharitvā rasakassa deti. Sopissa maṃsaṃ pacitvā upanāmeti. Evaṃ ubhopi jīvanti. Manussagahaṇakāle “ahaṃ are manussacoro porisādo”ti vatvā tasmiṃ pakkhante koci sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, sabbe bhūmiyaṃ patanti. Tesu yaṃ icchati, taṃ uddhaṃpādaṃ adhosīsaṃ [V 5.0468] katvā āharitvā rasakassa deti. So ekadivasaṃ araññe kañci manussaṃ alabhitvā āgato rasakena “kiṃ devā”ti vutte “uddhane ukkhaliṃ āropehī”ti āha. “Maṃsaṃ kahaṃ, devā”ti? “Labhissāmahaṃ maṃsa”nti. So “natthi me dāni jīvita”nti kampamāno uddhane aggiṃ katvā ukkhaliṃ āropesi. Atha naṃ porisādo asinā māretvā maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādi. Tato paṭṭhāya ekakova jāto sayameva pacitvā khādati. “Porisādo magge maggapaṭipanne hanatī”ti sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi.

He took the sword and the cook Rasaka, left the city, entered the forest, and making a dwelling place at the foot of a banyan tree, he lived there. Standing on the forest path, he would kill people, bring them back, and give them to the cook. And the cook would cook the meat and serve it to him. Thus, both lived. When capturing people, he would shout, 'Ho, I am the man-thief Porisāda!' When he charged forth, no one could stand firm; all fell to the ground. Among them, whomever he wished, he would take up by the feet with head hanging down, bring them back, and give them to the cook. One day, having found no one in the forest, he returned. When the cook asked, 'What is it, lord?' he replied, 'Put the pot on the hearth.' 'Where is the meat, lord?' 'I shall obtain meat,' he said. The cook, trembling and thinking, 'Now my life is over,' made a fire on the hearth and placed the pot on it. Then Porisāda killed him with his sword, cooked the meat, and ate it. From then on, he was all alone, cooking and eating by himself. It became known throughout all of Jambudīpa that 'Porisāda kills travelers on the road.'

Tadā eko sampannavibhavo brāhmaṇo pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vohāraṃ karonto pubbantato aparantaṃ sañcarati. So cintesi – “porisādo nāma kira coro antarāmagge manusse māresi, dhanaṃ datvā taṃ aṭaviṃ atikkamissāmī”ti. So aṭavimukhavāsīnaṃ manussānaṃ “tumhe maṃ aṭavito atikkāmethā”ti sahassaṃ datvā tehi saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Gacchanto ca brāhmaṇo sabbasatthaṃ purato katvā sayaṃ nhātānulitto sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito setagoṇayutte sukhayānake nisinno tehi aṭavivāsikapurisehi parivuto sabbapacchato agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe porisādo rukkhaṃ āruyha purise upadhārento sesamanussesu “kiṃ imesu mayā khāditabbaṃ atthī”ti vigatacchando hutvā brāhmaṇaṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya taṃ khāditukāmatāya paggharitakheḷo ahosi. So tasmiṃ attano santikaṃ āgate rukkhato [M 5.0511] oruyha “ahaṃ [P 5.0472] are porisādo”ti nāmaṃ tikkhattuṃ sāvetvā khaggaṃ parivattento vālukāya tesaṃ akkhīni pūrento viya pakkhandi. Ekopi ṭhātuṃ samattho nāma natthi, sabbe bhūmiyaṃ urena nipajjiṃsu. So sukhayānake nisinnaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pāde gahetvā piṭṭhiyaṃ adhosīsakaṃ olambetvā sīsaṃ gopphakehi paharanto ukkhipitvā pāyāsi.

At that time, a brahmin of abundant wealth, conducting trade with five hundred carts, traveled from the eastern border to the western border. He thought, 'It is said that a thief named Porisāda kills people on the road; I shall cross that forest by giving wealth.' So he gave a thousand coins to the people living at the entrance of the forest, saying, 'You must help me cross the forest,' and set out on the road with them. As he traveled, the brahmin sent the entire caravan ahead, while he himself, bathed and anointed, adorned with all ornaments, seated in a comfortable carriage drawn by white oxen and surrounded by those forest-dwellers, followed at the very rear of all the people. At that moment, Porisāda climbed a tree and observed the men. Having lost interest in the other men, thinking, 'What is there to eat among these?' from the moment he saw the brahmin, his mouth watered with the desire to devour him. When the brahmin came near him, he descended from the tree, announced his name three times, 'Hey, sirs, I am Porisāda!' and swinging his sword, he charged as if to fill their eyes with sand. Not a single one was able to stand; all lay prostrate with their chests to the ground. Seizing the brahmin, who was seated in the comfortable carriage, by the feet, Porisāda hung him upside down on his back with his head hanging down, and striking the brahmin's head against his own ankles, he lifted him up and departed.

Tadā te purisā uṭṭhāya, “bho, purisā mayaṃ brāhmaṇassa hatthato kahāpaṇasahassaṃ gaṇhimhā, ko nāma amhākaṃ purisakāro, sakkontā vā asakkontā vā thokaṃ anubandhāmā”ti vatvā anubandhiṃsu. Porisādopi nivattitvā olokento kañci aditvā saṇikaṃ pāyāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thāmasampanno eko sūrapuriso vegena taṃ pāpuṇi. So taṃ disvā ekaṃ vatiṃ laṅghanto khadirakhāṇukaṃ akkami, khāṇuko piṭṭhipādena nikkhami. Lohitena paggharantena laṅghamāno yāti. Atha naṃ so disvā, “bho, mayā esa viddho, kevalaṃ tumhe pacchato etha, gaṇhissāmi na”nti āha. Te dubbalabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ anubandhiṃsu. So tehi anubaddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā brāhmaṇaṃ vissajjetvā attānaṃ sotthimakāsi. Atha aṭavivāsikapurisā brāhmaṇassa laddhakālato paṭṭhāya “kiṃ amhākaṃ corenā”ti tato nivattiṃsu.

Then those men rose up and said, 'Friends, we have taken a thousand kahāpaṇas from the brahmin's hand. What of our manliness? Whether we are able or not, let us pursue him for a little while.' Having said this, they pursued him. Porisāda, turning back and looking, saw no one and proceeded slowly. At that moment, a certain courageous man full of strength quickly caught up to him. Seeing him, as Porisāda was leaping over a hedge, he stepped on a khadira stump; the stump pierced through from the sole and came out the top of his foot. With blood gushing, he continued on, leaping. Then the courageous man, seeing him, said, 'Friends, I have pierced him! You just follow behind; I will capture him.' Knowing Porisāda's weakened state, they pursued him. Realizing that he was being pursued, Porisāda released the brahmin and made himself safe. Then the forest-dwelling men, from the time they recovered the brahmin, thought, 'What business have we with the thief?' and turned back from there.

Porisādopi [V 5.0469] attano nigrodhamūlaṃ gantvā pārohantaraṃ pavisitvā nipanno, “ayye rukkhadevate, sace me sattāhabbhantareyeva vaṇaṃ phāsukaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasi, sakalajambudīpe ekasatakhattiyānaṃ galalohitena tava khandhaṃ dhovitvā antehi parikkhipitvā pañcamadhuramaṃsena balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti āyācanaṃ kari. Tassa annapānamaṃsaṃ alabhantassa sarīraṃ sussitvā antosattāheyeva vaṇo phāsuko ahosi. So devatānubhāvena tassa phāsukabhāvaṃ sallakkhesi. So katipāhaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā balaṃ gahetvā cintesi – “bahupakārā me devatā, āyācanā assā muccissāmī”ti. So khaggaṃ ādāya rukkhamūlato nikkhamitvā [P 5.0473] “rājāno ānessāmī”ti pāyāsi. Atha naṃ purimabhave yakkhakāle ekato manussamaṃsakhādako sahāyakayakkho anuvicarantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mama atītabhave sahāyo”ti ñatvā, “samma, maṃ sañjānāsī”ti pucchi. “Na sañjānāmī”ti. Athassa purimabhave katakāraṇaṃ [M 5.0512] kathesi. So taṃ sañjānitvā paṭisanthāramakāsi. “Kahaṃ nibbattosī”ti puṭṭho nibbattaṭṭhānañca raṭṭhā pabbājitakāraṇañca idāni vasanaṭṭhānañca khāṇunā viddhakāraṇañca devatāya āyācanāmocanatthaṃ gamanakāraṇañca sabbaṃ ārocetvā “tayāpi mametaṃ kiccaṃ nittharitabbaṃ, ubhopi gacchāma, sammā”ti āha. “Samma na gaccheyyāhaṃ, ekaṃ pana me kammaṃ atthi, ahaṃ kho pana anagghaṃ padalakkhaṇaṃ nāma ekaṃ mantaṃ jānāmi, so balañca javañca saddañca karoti, taṃ mantaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Yakkhopissa taṃ datvā pakkāmi.

Porisāda went to his own banyan tree, entered between the aerial roots, and lay down, making a prayer: 'Noble tree deity, if you can heal my wound within seven days, I will wash your trunk with the throat-blood of one hundred and one kings from all of Jambudīpa, surround it with their entrails, and perform a sacrificial offering with meat of the five sweet flavors.' As he did not obtain food, drink, or meat, his body withered, and within only seven days the wound healed. He perceived that it had healed through the power of the deity. After eating human flesh for a few days and regaining his strength, he thought, 'The deity has been of great help to me; I shall be freed from my vow to her.' Taking his sword, he left the base of the tree and set out, thinking, 'I will bring the one hundred and one kings.' Then a yakkha, who had been his companion and fellow eater of human flesh in a former life when Porisāda was a yakkha, saw him wandering about and recognized him, thinking, 'This was my companion in a past life.' He asked, 'Friend, do you recognize me?' 'I do not recognize you,' he replied. Then the yakkha told him of the events of their former life. Recognizing him, Porisāda engaged in friendly conversation. When asked, 'Where were you reborn?' he told him everything: his place of birth, the reason for his exile from the kingdom, his current dwelling, how he was pierced by the stump, and the reason for his journey to be freed from his vow to the deity. He then said, 'You too should help me complete this task; let us both go together, friend.' The yakkha replied, 'Friend, I will not go, but I have a certain duty. I know a priceless mantra called Padalakkhaṇa, which provides strength, speed, glory, and voice. Take this mantra.' Porisāda accepted, saying, 'Very well.' The yakkha gave him the mantra and departed.

Porisādo mantaṃ uggahetvā tato paṭṭhāya vātajavo atisūro ahosi. So sattāhabbhantareyeva ekasatarājāno uyyānādīni gacchante disvā vātavegena pakkhanditvā “ahaṃ are manussacoro porisādo”ti nāmaṃ sāvetvā vagganto nadanto bhayappatte katvā pāde gahetvā adhosīsake katvā paṇhiyā sīsaṃ paharanto vātavegena netvā hatthatalesu chiddāni katvā rajjuyā āvunitvā nigrodharukkhe olambesi aggapādaṅgulīhi bhūmiyaṃ phusamānāhi. Te sabbe rājāno vāte paharante milātakuraṇḍakadāmāni viya parivattantā olambiṃsu. “Sutasomo pana me piṭṭhiācariyo hoti, sace gaṇhissāmi, sakalajambudīpo tuccho bhavissatī”ti taṃ na nesi. So “balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti aggiṃ katvā sūle tacchanto nisīdi. Rukkhadevatā taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā “mayhaṃ kiresa balikammaṃ karoti, vaṇampissa mayā kiñci phāsukaṃ kataṃ natthi, idāni imesaṃ mahāvināsaṃ [P 5.0474] karissati, kiṃ nu kho kattabba”nti cintetvā “ahaṃ etaṃ vāretuṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti cātumahārājikānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ kathetvā “nivāretha na”nti āha. Tehipi “na mayaṃ porisādassa kammaṃ nivāretuṃ sakkhissāmā”ti vutte “ko sakkhissatī”ti pucchitvā “sakko, devarājā”ti sutvā [V 5.0470] sakkaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ kathetvā “nivāretha na”nti āha. Sopi “nāhaṃ sakkomi nivāretuṃ, samatthaṃ pana ācikkhissāmī”ti vatvā “konāmo”ti vutte “sadevake loke añño natthi, kururaṭṭhe pana indapatthanagare korabyarājaputto sutasomo nāma taṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā damessati, rājūnañca jīvitaṃ dassati, tañca manussamaṃsā oramāpessati, sakalajambudīpe amataṃ viya dhammaṃ abhisiñcissati, sacepi rājūnaṃ [M 5.0513] jīvitaṃ dātukāmo, ‘sutasomaṃ ānetvā balikammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti vadehī”ti āha.

Having learned the mantra, Porisāda became from that time onward as swift as the wind and exceedingly brave. Within seven days, seeing one hundred and one kings going to parks and other such places, he rushed upon them with the speed of the wind, announcing his name, 'Ho, I am Porisāda, the man-thief!' Leaping and roaring, he terrified them, seized them by the feet, turned them upside down, and struck their heads with his heels. Carrying them away with the speed of the wind, he pierced holes in the palms of their hands, strung them up with a rope, and hung them from a banyan tree, with the tips of their toes just touching the ground. All those kings, buffeted by the wind, dangled and swayed like garlands of withered milātaka and kuraṇḍaka flowers. Thinking, 'But Sutasoma is my teacher; if I seize him, all of Jambudīpa will become empty,' he did not take him. Deciding, 'I will perform the sacrifice for the deity,' he made a fire and sat down, sharpening a stake. The tree-deity, seeing this action, thought, 'He is performing this sacrifice for me, yet I did nothing to heal his wound. Now he will cause a great destruction of these kings. What is to be done?' Realizing, 'I cannot stop him,' she went to the Four Great Kings, explained the matter, and said, 'You must stop him.' When they too said, 'We cannot stop Porisāda’s deed,' she asked, 'Who can?' Hearing them say, 'Sakka, the king of the gods, will be able to,' she approached Sakka, explained the matter, and said, 'You must stop him.' He too said, 'I cannot stop him, but I will point out one who is able. In all the world with its gods, there is no other; but in the Kuru kingdom, in the city of Indapatta, there is a son of the Korabya king named Sutasoma. He will render him harmless and tame him. He will grant the kings their lives, make him cease from eating human flesh, and sprinkle the nectar-like Dhamma over all of Jambudīpa. If you wish to give life to the kings, you should say to him, "It is fitting to bring King Sutasoma and perform the sacrifice."'

Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā khippaṃ āgantvā pabbajitavesena tassa avidūre pāyāsi. So padasaddena “rājā nu kho koci palāto bhavissatī”ti olokento taṃ disvā “pabbajitā nāma khattiyāva, imaṃ gahetvā ekasataṃ pūretvā balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti uṭṭhāya asihattho anubandhi, tiyojanaṃ anubandhitvāpi taṃ pāpuṇituṃ nāsakkhi, gattehi sedā mucciṃsu. So cintesi – “ahaṃ pubbe hatthimpi assampi rathampi dhāvantaṃ anubandhitvā gaṇhāmi, ajja imaṃ pabbajitaṃ sakāya gatiyā gacchantaṃ sabbathāmena dhāvantopi gaṇhituṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti. Tato so “pabbajitā nāma vacanakarā honti, ‘tiṭṭhā’ti naṃ vatvā ṭhitaṃ gahessāmī”ti cintetvā “tiṭṭha, samaṇā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ tāva ṭhito, tvaṃ pana dhāvituṃ vāyāmamakāsī”ti. Atha naṃ, “bho, pabbajitā nāma jīvitahetupi alikaṃ na bhaṇanti, tvaṃ pana musāvādaṃ kathesī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

The deity, having accepted with 'Very well,' quickly came and proceeded not far from him in the guise of a renunciant. Porisāda, hearing the sound of footsteps and wondering, 'Could this be some king who has escaped?' saw her and thought, 'Indeed, renunciants are of royal stock. I will capture this one, complete the one hundred and one, and perform the sacrifice.' Rising up, armed with a sword, he pursued her. Though he chased her for three leagues, he could not catch her, and sweat poured from his body. He reflected, 'Before, I could chase and capture even running elephants, horses, and chariots. Yet today, though I run with all my might, I cannot catch this renunciant moving at an ordinary pace. What could be the reason?' Then he thought, 'Renunciants are obedient to words. I will tell her to stop and then capture her.' Having resolved this, he called out, 'Stop, ascetic!' She replied, 'I have stopped; you, however, are still running.' Then he said to her, 'Sir, renunciants do not lie even to save their lives, yet you speak a falsehood,' and to make it known to her, he spoke this verse:

393.

393.

“Tiṭṭhāhīti [P 5.0475] mayā vutto, so tvaṃ gacchasi pammukho;

Aṭṭhito tvaṃ ṭhitomhīti, lapasi brahmacārini;

Idaṃ te samaṇāyuttaṃ, asiñca me maññasi kaṅkapatta”nti.

“Though told by me, ‘Stand still!’, you go on ahead. Though not standing still, you say, ‘I am standing still,’ O practitioner of the holy life. This is not fitting for an ascetic; or do you think my sword is but a heron's feather?”

Tassattho – samaṇa, tiṭṭhāhi iti vacanaṃ mayā vutto so tvaṃ pammukho parammukho hutvā gacchasi, brahmacārini aṭṭhito samāno tvaṃ ṭhito amhi iti lapasi, asiñca me kaṅkapattaṃ maññasīti.

The meaning is: O ascetic, though told by me the words, 'Stand still!', you go on ahead, being turned away. O practitioner of the holy life, though not standing still, you babble, 'I am standing.' Do you consider my sword to be like a heron's feather?

Tato devatā gāthādvayamāha –

Then the deity, wishing to explain the matter to him, spoke these two verses:

394.

394.

“Ṭhitohamasmī sadhammesu rāja, na nāmagottaṃ parivattayāmi;

Corañca loke aṭhitaṃ vadanti;

Āpāyikaṃ nerayikaṃ ito cutaṃ.

“I am established in the ten wholesome paths of Dhamma, O king; I do not change my name or clan. In the world, they call a thief 'unestablished,' one who is bound for the lower realms and hell when fallen from here.”

395.

395.

“Sace [V 5.0471] tvaṃ saddahasi rāja, sutaṃ gaṇhāhi khattiya;

Tena yaññaṃ yajitvāna, evaṃ saggaṃ gamissasī”ti.

“If you have faith, O king, seize Sutasoma, O khattiya. Having performed the sacrifice with him, you will thus go to heaven.”

Tattha [M 5.0514] sadhammesūti, mahārāja, ahaṃ sakesu dasasu kusalakammapathadhammesu ṭhito asmi bhavāmi. Na nāmagottanti tvaṃ pubbe daharakāle brahmadatto hutvā pitari kālakate bārāṇasiṃ rajjaṃ labhitvā bārāṇasirājā jāto, taṃ nāmaṃ jahitvā porisādo hutvā idāni kammāsapādo jāto, khattiyakule jātopi abhakkhaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ yasmā bhakkhesi, tasmā attano nāmagottaṃ yathā parivattesi, tathā ahaṃ attano nāmagottaṃ na parivattayāmi. Corañcāti loke corañca dasakusalakammapathesu aṭhitaṃ nāma vadanti. Ito cutanti ito cutaṃ hutvā apāye niraye patiṭṭhitaṃ. Khattiya, bhūmipāla mahārāja, tvaṃ mama vacanaṃ sace saddahasi, sutasomaṃ gaṇhāhi, tena sutasomena yaññaṃ yajitvāna evaṃ saggaṃ gamissasi. Bho, porisāda musāvādi tayā mayhaṃ “sakalajambudīpe rājāno ānetvā bahikammaṃ karissāmī”ti paṭissutaṃ, idāni ye vā te vā dubbalarājāno ānesi, jambudīpatale jeṭṭhakaṃ sutasomarājānaṃ sace tvaṃ na ānessasi, vacanaṃ te musā nāma hoti, tasmā sutasomaṃ gaṇhāhīti.

Herein, ‘in the true Dhamma’ means: O great king, I am established in my own ten wholesome paths of action. As for ‘name and clan’—you, in your early youth, were Brahmadatta; after your father passed away, you obtained the kingdom of Bārāṇasī and became the king of Bārāṇasī. But you abandoned that name, became a man-eater, and now have become Kammāsapāda. Though born in a khattiya clan, because you ate human flesh, which is not to be eaten, you changed your own name and clan. In that way, I do not change my name and clan. As for ‘and a thief’—in the world, they call a thief one who is not established in the ten wholesome paths of action. ‘Fallen from here’ means having fallen from here, one is established in the plane of misery, in hell. O khattiya, O great king, ruler of the land, if you have faith in my words, seize Sutasoma. Having performed a sacrifice with that Sutasoma, you will thus go to heaven. O man-eater, you liar! You promised me, ‘I will bring the kings from all over Jambudīpa and perform the sacrificial offering.’ But now you have brought only some weak kings. If you do not bring Sutasoma, the foremost king in all of Jambudīpa, your word will become a lie. Therefore, seize Sutasoma!

Evañca pana vatvā devatā pabbajitavesaṃ antaradhāpetvā sakena vaṇṇena ākāse taruṇasūriyo viya jalamānā aṭṭhāsi. So tassā kathaṃ sutvā rūpañca oloketvā “kāsi tva”nti āha. Imasmiṃ “rukkhe nibbattadevatā”ti. So “diṭṭhā me attano, devatā”ti tussitvā, “sāmi devarāja, mā sutasomassa kāraṇā cintayi, attano rukkhaṃ [P 5.0476] pavisā”ti āha. Devatā tassa passantasseva rukkhaṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sūriyo atthaṅgato, cando uggato. Porisādo vedaṅgakusalo nakkhattacāraṃ jānāti. So nabhaṃ oloketvā “sve phussanakkhattaṃ bhavissati, sutasomo nhāyituṃ uyyānaṃ gamissati, tattha gaṇhissāmi, ārakkho panassa mahā bhavissati, samantā tiyojanaṃ sakalanagaravāsino rakkhantā carissanti, asaṃvihite ārakkhe paṭhamayāmeyeva [M 5.0515] migājinaṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā maṅgalapokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā ṭhassāmī”ti cintetvā tattha gantvā pokkharaṇiṃ oruyha padumapattena sīsaṃ paṭicchādetvā aṭṭhāsi. Tassa tejena macchakacchapādayo osakkitvā udakapariyante vaggavaggā hutvā vicariṃsu.

Having spoken thus, the deity made her ascetic disguise disappear and stood in the sky in her own form, radiant like the rising sun. Hearing her words and beholding her form, he asked, “Who are you?” She replied, “I am the deity born in this banyan tree.” Pleased, he said, “I have seen my own deity. Lord, O king of devas, do not worry on account of Sutasoma. Enter your own tree.” Even as he watched, the deity entered the tree. At that moment, the sun set and the moon rose. Porisāda, skilled in the Vedas and knowing the course of the constellations, looked up at the sky and thought, “Tomorrow the moon will be in the Phussa constellation. Sutasoma will go to the park to bathe. There I will seize him. But his guard will be great—all the city dwellers for three leagues around will be on guard. Before the guard is deployed, in the first watch of the night, I will go to the Migājina Grove, descend into the Maṅgala Pond, and wait there.” Having resolved this, he went to that garden, descended into the pond, and stood with his head covered by a lotus leaf. Due to his power, the fish, turtles, and other creatures retreated and moved about in groups along the edges of the water.

Kuto pana laddhoyaṃ tejoti? Pubbayogavasena. So hi kasapadasabalassa kāle khīrasalākabhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi, tena mahāthāmo ahosi. Aggisālañca kāretvā bhikkhusaṅghassa sītavinodanatthaṃ [V 5.0472] aggiñca dārūni ca dārucchedanavāsiñca pharasuñca adāsi, tena tejavā ahosi.

But from where was this power acquired? Through the power of past practice. For in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers, he established a ticket-meal of milk-rice; through that, he came to have great physical strength. Having also built a fire-hall, he gave fire, firewood, an adze for cutting wood, and an axe for the purpose of dispelling the cold for the Sangha of monks; because of that, he became powerful.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ antouyyānaṃ gateyeva balavapaccūsasamaye samantā tiyojanaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Rājāpi pātova bhuttapātarāso alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato caturaṅginiyā senāya parivuto nagarato nikkhami. Tadā takkasilato nando nāma brāhmaṇo catasso satārahā gāthāyo ādāya vīsatiyonajasataṃ maggaṃ atikkamitvā taṃ nagaraṃ patvā dvāragāme vasitvā sūriye uggate nagaraṃ pavisanto rājānaṃ pācīnadvārena nikkhantaṃ disvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā jayāpesi. Rājā disācakkhuko hutvā gacchanto unnatappadese ṭhitassa brāhmaṇassa pasāritahatthaṃ disvā hatthinā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi –

Thus, as soon as he had entered the inner park, at the peak of dawn, they took up a guard for three leagues all around. The king, too, having eaten his breakfast early in the morning, mounted a splendid, adorned elephant and left the city surrounded by his fourfold army. At that time, a brahmin named Nanda from Takkasilā, carrying four verses worth a hundred each, having traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty leagues, reached that city. Staying in a village at the gate, as the sun rose, he entered the city and saw the king leaving through the eastern gate; he stretched out his hand and hailed him with victory. The king, having an eye for his surroundings, as he went, noticed the brahmin standing on high ground with his hand outstretched. Approaching him on his elephant, he asked:

396.

396.

“Kismiṃ nu raṭṭhe tava jātibhūmi, atha kena atthena idhānupatto;

Akkhāhi [P 5.0477] me brāhmaṇa etamatthaṃ, kimicchasī demi tayajja patthita”nti.

“In what country is your birthplace, and for what purpose have you come here? Tell me this matter, brahmin. What do you desire? I shall give you today what you have wished for.”

Tassattho – bho brāhmaṇa, tava jātibhūmi kismiṃ raṭṭhe atthi nu, kena atthena payojanena hetubhūtena ida imasmiṃ nagare anuppatto, bho brāhmaṇa, mayā pucchito so tvaṃ etamatthaṃ etaṃ payojanaṃ me mayhaṃ akkhāhi kathehi, tayā patthitavatthuṃ te tuyhaṃ ajja idāni dadāmi, kiṃ vatthuṃ icchasīti.

The meaning is: O brahmin, in which country is your birthplace? For what purpose, for what use, and for what cause have you arrived here in this city? O brahmin, being questioned by me, tell me this matter, this purpose. Whatever object you have wished for, I shall give to you today, right now. What object do you desire?

Atha [M 5.0516] naṃ so gāthamāha –

Then he spoke a verse to him:

397.

397.

“Gāthā catasso dharaṇīmahissara, sugambhīratthā varasāgarūpamā;

Taveva atthāya idhāgatosmi, suṇohi gāthā paramatthasaṃhitā”ti.

“There are four verses, O great lord of the earth, of very profound meaning, like the noble ocean. For your sake alone have I come here. Listen to these verses, which are connected with the highest good.”

Tattha dharaṇīmahissarāti bhūmipāla catasso gāthā kiṃ bhūtā?. Sugambhīratthā varasāgarūpamā, taveva tava eva atthāya idha ṭhānaṃ anuppatto asmi bhavāmi. Suṇohīti kassapadasabalena desitā paramatthasaṃhitā imā satārahā gāthāyo suṇohīti attho.

In that verse, “great lord of the earth” means ruler of the land. What are the four verses like? Of very profound meaning and like the noble ocean. “For your sake alone have I reached this place, I have come.” “Listen” means: listen to these verses worth a hundred, taught by Kassapa of the Ten Powers, which are connected with the highest good.

Iti vatvā, “mahārāja, imā kassapadasabalena desitā catasso satārahā gāthāyo “tumhe sutavittakā’ti sutvā tumhākaṃ desetuṃ āgatomhī”ti āha. Rājā tuṭṭhamānaso hutvā, “ācariya[V 5.0473], suṭṭhu te āgataṃ, mayā pana nivattituṃ na sakkā, ajja phussanakkhattayogena sīsaṃ nhāyituṃ āgatomhi, ahaṃ punadivase āgantvā sossāmi, tvaṃ mā ukkaṇṭhī”ti vatvā “gacchatha brāhmaṇassa asukagehe sayanaṃ paññāpetvā ghāsacchādanaṃ saṃvidahathā”ti amacce āṇāpetvā uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Taṃ aṭṭhārasahatthena pākārena parikkhittaṃ ahosi. Taṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭentā samantā hatthino parikkhipiṃsu, tato assā, tato rathā, tato dhanuggahā, tato pattīti, saṅkhubhitamahāsamuddo viya unnādento balakāyo ahosi. Atha rājā oḷārikāni ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā massukammaṃ kāretvā ubbaṭṭitasarīro pokkharaṇiyā anto rājavibhavena nhatvā paccuttaritvā udakaggahaṇasāṭakena nivāsetvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassa dussagandhamālālaṅkāre upanayiṃsu. Porisādo cintesi – “rājā alaṅkatakāle bhāriko bhavissati, sallahukakāleyeva naṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. So [P 5.0478] nadanto vagganto udake macchaṃ āluḷento vijjulatā viya matthake khaggaṃ paribbhamento “ahaṃ are manussacoro porisādo”ti nāmaṃ sāvetvā aṅguliṃ nalāṭe ṭhapetvā udakā uttari. Tassa saddaṃ sutvāva hatthārohā hatthīhi, assārohā [M 5.0517] assehi, rathārohā rathehi bhassiṃsu. Balakāyo gahitagahitāni āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā urena bhūmiyaṃ nipajji.

Having said this, he said: 'Great king, these four verses worth a hundred were taught by Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers. Having heard that you delight in what you have heard, I have come to teach them to you.' The king, with a pleased mind, said: 'Teacher, your coming is good. However, I cannot turn back; today I have come to bathe my head in conjunction with the Phussa constellation. I will come and listen tomorrow; do not be disheartened.' Then, after commanding his ministers, 'Go, prepare a bed for the brahmin teacher in such-and-such a house and provide him with food and clothing,' he entered the park. It was surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high. Elephants, pressing against one another, surrounded it on all sides, then horses, then chariots, then archers, then foot soldiers; the army was like a churning great ocean making a loud noise. Then the king, having removed his heavy ornaments, having had his beard trimmed, and having his body rubbed with powder, bathed with royal majesty in the lotus pond. Emerging from the water, he stood dressed in a bathing garment. Then they brought him cloths, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Porisāda thought: 'The king will be heavy when he is adorned; I will seize him only when he is light.' So, roaring and leaping, agitating the fish in the water, brandishing his sword above his head like a flash of lightning, he announced his name, 'Hey! I am the man-thief Porisāda!' and placing a finger on his forehead, he rose from the water. Upon hearing his voice, elephant riders fell from their elephants, horse riders from their horses, and chariot riders from their chariots. The army, dropping the weapons they were holding, fell on their chests to the ground.

Porisādo sutasomaṃ ukkhipitvā gaṇhi, sesarājāno pāde gahetvā adhosīsake katvā paṇhiyā sīsaṃ paharanto gacchati. Bodhisattaṃ pana upagantvā onato ukkhipitvā khandhe nisīdāpesi. So “dvārena gamanaṃ papañco bhavissatī”ti sammukhaṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ pākāraṃ laṅghitvā purato galitamadamattavāraṇakumbhe akkamitvā pabbatakūṭāni pātento viya vātajavānaṃ assatarānaṃ piṭṭhe akkamanto pātetvā rathadhurarathasīsesu akkamitvā bhamikaṃ bhamanto viya nīlaphalakāni nigrodhapattāni maddanto viya ekavegeneva tiyojanamattaṃ maggaṃ gantvā “atthi nu kho koci sutasomassatthāya pacchato āgacchanto”ti oloketvā kañci aditvā saṇikaṃ gacchanto sutasomassa kesehi udakabindūni attano ure patitāni disvā “maraṇassa abhāyanto nāma natthi, sutasomopi maraṇabhayena rodati maññe”ti cintetvā āha –

Porisāda lifted and seized Sutasoma. He took the other kings by the feet, held them upside down, and went along striking their heads with his heels. But approaching the Bodhisatta, he bent down, lifted him up, and seated him on his shoulders. Thinking, 'Going through the gate will be a delay,' he leaped over the eighteen-cubit wall right where he stood. He stepped on the frontal globes of the rutting elephants in front, as if toppling mountain peaks, and trampling on the backs of wind-swift mules, he knocked them down. He stepped on the poles and heads of the chariots, making them spin as if spinning a potter's wheel, and as if crushing blue slabs and banyan leaves, he trampled many armed men. In a single rush, he traveled a distance of three leagues. Then he looked back, thinking, 'Is there anyone coming after Sutasoma?' Seeing no one, as he was going slowly, he noticed droplets of water from Sutasoma’s hair falling on his own chest. Thinking, 'There is no one who does not fear death; I suppose even Sutasoma is weeping for fear of death,' he said:

398.

398.

“Na ve rudanti matimanto sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Dīpañhi etaṃ paramaṃ narānaṃ, yaṃ paṇḍitā sokanudā bhavanti.

“Truly, the intelligent and wise do not weep, nor those who are learned and who reflect on many situations. For this is the supreme lamp for men: that the wise are the dispellers of sorrow.”

399.

399.

“Attānaṃ [V 5.0474] ñātī udāhu puttadāraṃ, dhaññaṃ dhanaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ;

Kimeva [P 5.0479] tvaṃ sutasomānutappe, korabyaseṭṭha vacanaṃ suṇoma teta”nti.

“Is it for yourself, your kinsmen, or your children and wife? For grain, wealth, silver, or gold? For what exactly do you lament, Sutasoma? O best of the Korabyas, let us hear your word on this.”

Tattha, bho sutasoma mahārāja, ye paṇḍitā kiṃ bhūtā? Matimanto atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ jānanapaññāya samannāgatā, sappaññā vicaraṇapaññāya samannāgatā, bahussutā bahussutadharā bahuṭṭhānacintino bahukāraṇacintanasīlā, te paṇḍitā maraṇabhaye uppanne sati bhītā hutvā ve ekantena na rudanti na paridevanti. Dīpaṃ hīti, bho sutasoma [M 5.0518] mahārāja hi kasmā pana vadāmi, mahāsamudde bhinnanāvānaṃ vāṇijakānaṃ janānaṃ patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ mahādīpaṃ iva, evampi tathā etaṃ paṇḍitaṃ appaṭisaraṇānaṃ narānaṃ paramaṃ. Yaṃ yena kāraṇena ye paṇḍitā sokīnaṃ janānaṃ sokanudā bhavanti, bho sutasoma mahārāja, tvaṃ maraṇabhayena paridevīti maññe maññāmi. Attānanti, bho sutasoma mahārāja, attahetu udāhu ñātihetu puttadārahetu udāhu dhaññadhanarajatajātarūpahetu kimeva tvaṃ kimeva dhammajātaṃ tvaṃ anutappe anutappeyyāsi. Korabyaseṭṭha kururaṭṭhavāsīnaṃ seṭṭha uttama, bho mahārāja, etaṃ tava vacanaṃ suṇomāti.

Here, O great king Sutasoma, who are the wise? They are intelligent, endowed with the wisdom that knows what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not a cause; discerning, endowed with discriminative wisdom; learned, upholders of much learning, thinkers on many grounds, those accustomed to contemplating many reasons. These wise ones, when the fear of death arises, though they may be afraid, do not utterly weep or lament. As for the phrase 'For this is the supreme refuge,' O great king Sutasoma, why do I say this? Just as a great island is a place of refuge for merchants whose ships are wrecked in the great ocean, so too is this wise person the supreme refuge for people without protection. The phrase 'that the wise become dispellers of sorrow' means that for this reason the wise dispel the sorrow of sorrowful people. O great king Sutasoma, I think you lament from fear of death. As for 'yourself,' O great king Sutasoma, is it for your own sake, or for the sake of relatives, or for the sake of children and wife, or for the sake of grain, wealth, silver, and gold? Over what sort of thing do you grieve? O best of the Korabyas, foremost and supreme among the inhabitants of the Kuru country, O great king, let us hear that word of yours.

Sutasomo āha –

Sutasoma said:

400.

400.

“Nevāhamattānamanutthunāmi, na puttadāraṃ na dhanaṃ na raṭṭhaṃ;

Satañca dhammo carito purāṇo, taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassānutappe.

"I do not grieve for myself, nor for children and wife, nor for wealth or kingdom; but for the ancient principle practiced by the good—that pledge to the brahmin, I lament."

401.

401.

“Kato mayā saṅgaro brāhmaṇena, raṭṭhe sake issariye ṭhitena;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇasappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti.

"A pledge was made by me with a brahmin, while I was established in sovereignty over my own kingdom. To fulfill that pledge to the brahmin, I, a guardian of truth, will return again."

Tattha nevāhamattānamanutthunāmīti ahaṃ tāva attatthāya neva rodāmi na socāmi, imesampi puttādīnaṃ atthāya na rodāmi na socāmi, apica kho pana sataṃ paṇḍitānaṃ carito purāṇadhammo atthi, yaṃ saṅgaraṃ katvā pacchā anutappanaṃ nāma, taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassa ahaṃ anusocāmīti attho[M 5.0519]. Saccānurakkhīti saccaṃ anurakkhanto. So hi brāhmaṇo takkasilato kassapadasabalena desitā catasso satārahā gāthāyo ādāya āgato, tassāhaṃ āgantukavattaṃ kāretvā “nhatvā āgato suṇissāmi, yāva mamāgamanā āgamehī”ti saṅgaraṃ katvā āgato, tvaṃ tā gāthāyo sotuṃ adatvāva maṃ gaṇhi. Sace maṃ vissajjesi, taṃ dhammaṃ sutvā saccānurakkhī punarāvajissāmīti vadati.

Here, 'I do not grieve for myself' means: I do not weep or grieve for my own sake, nor do I weep or grieve for the sake of these children and others. However, there is an ancient principle, a practice of the wise, regarding a pledge made: that one should not have to feel regret later. The meaning is: 'I lament that pledge made to the brahmin.' 'A guardian of truth' means one who protects the truth. For that brahmin came from Takkasilā, bringing four verses, each worth a hundred, taught by Buddha Kassapa of the Ten Powers. I performed the guest-duties for him and, having made a pledge, saying, 'When I have bathed and returned, I will listen; wait until my arrival,' I came here. But you seized me without letting me hear those verses. If you release me, then having heard that teaching and being a guardian of truth, I will return.

Atha [V 5.0475] naṃ porisādo āha –

Then the man-eater said to him:

401.

401.

“Nevāhametaṃ abhisaddahāmi, sukhī naro maccumukhā pamutto;

Amittahatthaṃ punarāvajeyya, korabyaseṭṭha na hi maṃ upesi.

"I do not believe this: that a man, happy, freed from the jaws of death, would return to the hand of an enemy. O best of the Korabyas, you will surely not come to me."

403.

403.

“Mutto [P 5.0480] tuvaṃ porisādassa hatthā, gantvā sakaṃ mandiraṃ kāmakāmī;

Madhuraṃ piyaṃ jīvitaṃ laddha rāja, kuto tuvaṃ ehisi me sakāsa”nti.

"Freed from the hand of the man-eater, having gone to your own palace as one who desires sensual pleasures, and having regained your sweet, dear life, O king, for what reason will you come into my presence?"

Tattha sukhīti sukhappatto hutvā. Maccumukhā pamuttoti mādisassa corassa hatthato muttatāya maraṇamukhā mutto nāma hutvā amittahatthaṃ punarāvajeyya āgaccheyya, ahaṃ etaṃ vacanaṃ neva abhisaddahāmi, korabyaseṭṭha tvaṃ mama santikaṃ na hi upesi. Muttoti sutasoma tuvaṃ porisādassa hatthato mutto. Sakaṃ mandiranti rājadhānigehaṃ gantvā. Kāmakāmīti kāmaṃ kāmayamāno. Laddhāti ativiya piyaṃ jīvitaṃ labhitvā tuvaṃ me mama santike kuto kena nāma kāraṇena ehisi.

In this context, 'happy' means having attained happiness. 'Freed from the jaws of death' means that by being freed from the hand of a thief like me, one is said to be freed from the mouth of death. That such a person 'would return to the hand of an enemy'—that is, he would come back—this statement I do not believe. 'O best of the Korabyas, you will surely not come into my presence.' 'Freed' means: Sutasoma, you are freed from the hand of the man-eater. 'To your own palace' means having gone to your royal city home. 'Desiring sensual pleasures' means one who desires sensual pleasures. 'Having regained' means having obtained your exceedingly dear life. 'For what reason' then would you come to me, into my presence?

Taṃ [M 5.0520] sutvā mahāsatto sīho viya asambhito āha –

Hearing this, the Great Being, fearless like a lion, said:

404.

404.

“Mataṃ vareyya parisuddhasīlo, na jīvitaṃ garahito pāpadhammo;

Na hi taṃ naraṃ tāyati duggatīhi, yassāpi hetu alikaṃ bhaṇeyya.

"A person of pure virtue would choose death, and not a blameworthy life of evil conduct; for that for the sake of which one would tell a lie does not protect a person from woeful states."

405.

405.

“Sacepi vāto girimāvaheyya, cando ca sūriyo ca chamā pateyyuṃ;

Sabbā ca najjo paṭisotaṃ vajeyyuṃ, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyyaṃ.

"Even if the wind should carry away a mountain, if the moon and sun should fall to the earth, if all the rivers should flow upstream, still, O king, I would never speak falsely."

406.

406.

“Nabhaṃ phaleyya udadhīpi susse, saṃvattaye bhūtadharā vasundharā;

Siluccayo meru samūlamuppate, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyya”nti.

"Even if the sky were to burst open, the ocean dry up, the earth which supports beings were to be overturned, or rocky Mount Meru were uprooted from its base, O king, I would not speak falsely."

Tattha mataṃ vareyyāti porisāda yo naro parisuddhasīlo jīvitahetu aṇumattampi pāpaṃ na karoti, sīlasampanno hutvā vareyya taṃ maraṇaṃ iccheyya, garahito pāpadhammo taṃ jīvitaṃ na seyyo, dussīlo puggalo yassāpi hetu attādinopi hetu alikaṃ vacanaṃ bhaṇeyya, taṃ naraṃ evarūpaṃ duggatīhi taṃ alikaṃ na tāyate. Sacepi vāto girimāvaheyyāti, samma porisāda, tayā saddhiṃ ekācariyakule [V 5.0476] sikkhito evarūpo sahāyako hutvā ahaṃ jīvitahetu musā na kathemi, kiṃ na saddahasi. Sace puratthimādibhedo vāto uṭṭhāya mahantaṃ giriṃ tūlapicuṃ viya ākāse āvaheyya, cando ca sūriyo ca attano attano vimānena saddhiṃ chamā pathaviyaṃ pateyyuṃ, sabbāpi najjo patisotaṃ vajeyyuṃ, bho porisāda[M 5.0521], evarūpaṃ vacanaṃ sace bhaṇeyya, taṃ saddahitabbaṃ, ahaṃ musā bhaṇeyyaṃ iti vacanaṃ tuyhaṃ janehi vuttaṃ, na tveva taṃ saddahitabbaṃ.

In this context, ‘one should choose death’ means: Friend Porisāda, a person of pure conduct who, for the sake of life, does not commit even the slightest evil, being endowed with virtue, would choose and desire that death. For a blameworthy and evil person, that life is not better. An immoral person might speak a lie for whatever reason, or for the sake of themselves and others; such a lie does not protect that person from the states of misery. As for ‘Even if the wind were to blow away a mountain’: Friend Porisāda, having been such a companion trained with you in the same teacher’s household, I do not speak falsely for the sake of life; why do you not believe me? Even if a wind, arising from the east and other directions, were to carry a great mountain through the sky like a tuft of cotton; and the moon and the sun, along with their respective mansions, were to fall to the earth; and all the rivers were to flow upstream—O Porisāda, if such things were said, they should be believed. But the statement ‘I would speak falsely,’ which was told to you by your people, should certainly not be believed.

Evaṃ vuttepi so na saddahiyeva. Atha bodhisatto “ayaṃ mayhaṃ na saddahati, sapathenapi naṃ saddahāpessāmī”ti cintetvā, “samma porisāda, khandhato tāva maṃ otārehi, sapathaṃ katvā taṃ saddahāpessāmī”ti vutte tena otāretvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapito sapathaṃ karonto āha –

Even when spoken to thus, he still did not believe. Then the Bodhisatta thought, "This man does not believe me; I will make him believe by taking an oath." So he said, "Friend Porisāda, first lower me from your shoulder, and I will make you believe by taking an oath." When he was lowered and placed on the ground, the Bodhisatta, wishing to take the oath, said:

407.

407.

“Asiñca [P 5.0481] sattiñca parāmasāmi, sapathampi te samma ahaṃ karomi;

Tayā pamutto anaṇo bhavitvā, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti.

I touch the sword and the spear, good man, and I make this oath to you: Released by you, being free from debt and protecting the truth, I shall return.

Tassattho – samma porisāda, sace icchasi, evarūpehi āvudhehi saṃvihitārakkhe khattiyakule me nibbatti nāma mā hotūti asiñca sattiñca parāmasāmi. Sace aññehi rājūhi akattabbaṃ aññaṃ vā yaṃ icchasi, taṃ sapathampi te, samma, ahaṃ karomi. Yathāhaṃ tayā pamutto gantvā brāhmaṇassa anaṇo hutvā saccamanurakkhanto punarāgamissāmīti.

The meaning is: Good man Porisāda, if you wish, let me not be reborn in a royal warrior family where one is protected by such weapons as these; thus I touch the sword and the spear. If you wish for any other oath that other kings would not make, I will make that oath to you, friend. Once I am released by you, having become debt-free to the brahmin and protecting the truth, I will return.

Tato porisādo “ayaṃ sutasomo khattiyehi akattabbaṃ sapathaṃ karoti, kiṃ me iminā, esa etu vā mā vā, ahampi khattiyarājā, mameva bāhulohitaṃ gahetvā devatāya balikammaṃ karissāmi, ayaṃ ativiya kilamatī”ti cintetvā –

Then the man-eater thought, "This Sutasoma makes an oath that other kings would not make. What use is this Sutasoma to me? Whether he comes or not, I too am a king who rules the land. I will simply take the blood from my own arm and perform the sacrifice to the deity. This Sutasoma is suffering exceedingly." Thinking thus, wishing to release the Bodhisatta, he said:

408.

408.

“Yo te kato saṅgaro brāhmaṇena, raṭṭhe sake issariye ṭhitena;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇasappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajassū”ti.

The pledge that was made by you to the brahmin, while you were established in power in your own kingdom; having fulfilled that pledge for the brahmin, you, a protector of truth, should return.

Tattha punarāvajassūti puna āgaccheyyāsi.

There, 'punarāvajassū' means: you should come back again.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto, “samma, mā cintayi, catasso satārahā gāthā sutvā dhammakathikassa pūjaṃ katvā pātovāgamissāmī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being said to him, "Friend, do not worry. After hearing the four verses worthy of a hundred and making an offering to the one who preaches the Dhamma, I will come back early in the morning." Having said this, to express this reason, he spoke the verse:

409.

409.

“Yo [M 5.0522][V 5.0477] me kato saṅgaro brāhmaṇena, raṭṭhe sake issariye ṭhitena;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇasappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti.

The pledge that was made by me to the brahmin, while I was established in power in my own kingdom; having fulfilled that pledge for the brahmin, I, a protector of truth, shall return.

Atha naṃ porisādo, “mahārāja, tumhe khattiyehi akattabbaṃ sapathaṃ karittha, taṃ anussareyyāthā”ti vatvā, “samma porisāda, tvaṃ maṃ daharakālato paṭṭhāya jānāsi, hāsenapi me musā na kathitapubbā, sohaṃ idāni rajje patiṭṭhito dhammādhammaṃ jānanto kiṃ musā kathessāmi, saddahasi mayhaṃ[P 5.0482], ahaṃ te sve balikammaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti saddahāpito “tena hi gaccha, mahārāja, tumhesu anāgatesu balikammaṃ na bhavissati, devatāpi tumhehi vinā na sampaṭicchati, mā me balikammassa antarāyaṃ karitthā”ti mahāsattaṃ uyyojesi. So rāhumukhā muttacando viya nāgabalo thāmasampanno khippameva nagaraṃ sampāpuṇi. Senāpissa “sutasomo rājā paṇḍito madhuradhammakathiko ekaṃ dve kathā kathetuṃ labhanto porisādaṃ dametvā sīhamukhā muttamattavāraṇo viya āgamissati, ‘ime rājānaṃ porisādassa datvā āgatā’ti mahājano garahissatī”ti cintetvā bahinagareyeva khandhāvāraṃ katvā ṭhitā taṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā paccuggantvā vanditvā “kacci, mahārāja, porisādena kilamito”ti paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “porisādena mayhaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkaraṃ kataṃ, tathārūpo nāma caṇḍo sāhasiko porisādo mama dhammakathaṃ sutvā maṃ vissajjesī”ti vutte rājānaṃ alaṅkaritvā hatthikkhandhaṃ āropetvā parivāretvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Taṃ disvā sabbe nāgarā tussiṃsu.

Then the man-eater said to him, "Great king, you have made an oath that kings do not usually make; remember that oath."
