The king convinced him, replying, "Friend Porisāda, you have known me since I was a child. Even in jest I have never spoken a lie. Now that I am established in the kingship and know right from wrong, why would I speak falsely? Believe me; I will return in time for your sacrifice tomorrow." Having made him believe, the man-eater said, "If that is so, then go, great king. If you do not return, the sacrifice to the deity will fail. The deity will not accept the offering without you. Do not obstruct my sacrifice." Thus he dismissed the Great Being. Like the moon freed from Rahu's mouth, the Bodhisatta, endowed with the strength of an elephant, quickly reached the city. His army, thinking, "King Sutasoma is wise and a sweet preacher of Dhamma. If he gets the chance to speak even one or two verses, he will tame Porisāda and return like a rutting elephant freed from a lion's mouth; but if we return alone, the people will blame us, saying we gave the king to the man-eater," had set up camp outside the city to wait. Seeing him approaching from afar, they went to meet him, paid homage, and asked, "Great king, did the man-eater weary you?" The king replied, "The man-eater has done for me what even parents could hardly do. Though he is so fierce and violent, after hearing my Dhamma talk, he let me go." Then they adorned the king, had him mount an elephant, and escorted him into the city. Seeing him, all the citizens rejoiced.

Sopi dhammagarutāya dhammasoṇḍatāya mātāpitaro adisvāva “pacchāpi ne passissāmī”ti rājanivesanaṃ pavisitvā rājāsane nisīditvā brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā massukammādīnissa āṇāpetvā taṃ kappitakesamassuṃ nhātānulittaṃ vatthālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā ānetvā dassitakāle sayaṃ pacchā nhatvā tassa attano bhojanaṃ dāpetvā tasmiṃ bhutte sayaṃ bhuñjitvā taṃ mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā dhammagarukatāya assa gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ katvā sayaṃ nīce āsane nisīditvā [M 5.0523] “tumhehi mayhaṃ ābhatā satārahā gāthā suṇoma ācariyā”ti yāci. Tamatthaṃ dīpento satthā gāthamāha –

Due to his great reverence and thirst for the Dhamma, the king did not even see his parents first, thinking, "I will see them later." He entered the palace, sat on the royal throne, and summoned the brahmin Nanda. He ordered the brahmin's hair and beard to be trimmed, and after the brahmin had bathed, been anointed, and dressed in fine garments, he was brought before him. Then the king himself bathed and anointed himself, had his own royal food served to the brahmin, and after the brahmin had finished, the king ate. He then seated the brahmin on a magnificent throne and, out of reverence for the Dhamma, honored him with perfumes and garlands. Sitting himself on a low seat, he requested, "Teacher, let me hear the verses worthy of a hundred that you have brought for me." To clarify this, the Teacher spoke the verse:

410.

410.

“Mutto ca so porisādassa hatthā, gantvāna taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca;

Suṇomi [P 5.0483] gāthāyo satārahāyo, yā me sutā assu hitāya brahme”ti.

Freed from the man-eater's hand, he went and said to that brahmin: "I shall listen to the verses worthy of a hundred, which, having been heard by me, may be for my benefit, O Brahmin."

Tattha etadavocāti etaṃ avoca.

There, 'etadavoca' means 'he said this'.

Atha [V 5.0478] brāhmaṇo bodhisattena yācitakāle gandhehi hatthe ubbaṭṭetvā pasibbakā manoramaṃ potthakaṃ nīharitvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā “tena hi, mahārāja, kassapadasabalena desitā rāgamadādinimmadanā amatamahānibbānasampāpikā catasso satārahā gāthāyo suṇohī”ti vatvā potthakaṃ olokento āha –

Then the brahmin, when requested by the Bodhisatta, rubbed his hands with perfumes, took out a delightful manuscript from his bag, and holding it with both hands, said, "Well then, great king, listen to these four verses worthy of a hundred, taught by Kassapa the Ten-Powered One, which crush lust and intoxication and lead to the deathless great Nibbāna." Looking at the manuscript, he spoke:

411.

411.

“Sakideva sutasoma, sabbhi hoti samāgamo;

Sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti, nāsabbhi bahu saṅgamo.

Even a single association with the virtuous, O Sutasoma, is beneficial; that association protects one, but many associations with the wicked do not.

412.

412.

“Sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Sataṃ saddhammamaññāya, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.

Associate only with the virtuous, cultivate friendship with the virtuous; knowing the true Dhamma of the virtuous, one becomes better, not worse.

413.

413.

“Jīranti ve rājarathā sucittā, atho sarīrampi jaraṃ upeti;

Satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upeti, santo have sabbhi pavedayanti.

Indeed, well-adorned royal chariots wear out, and the body also yields to old age; but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay; the virtuous indeed proclaim this to the virtuous.

414.

414.

“Nabhañca dūre pathavī ca dūre, pāraṃ samuddassa tadāhu dūre;

Tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, satañca dhammo asatañca rājā”ti.

The sky is far, and the earth is far; the far shore of the sea they call far. But farther than that, indeed, they say, is the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the unvirtuous, O king.

Tattha sakidevāti ekavārameva. Sabbhīti sappurisehi. Sā nanti sā sabbhi sappurisehi saṅgati samāgamo ekavāraṃ pavattopi taṃ [M 5.0524] puggalaṃ pāleti rakkhati. Nāsabbhīti asappurisehi pana bahu sucirampi kato saṅgamo ekaṭṭhāne nivāso na pāleti, na thāvaro hotīti attho. Samāsethāti saddhiṃ nisīdeyya, sabbepi iriyāpathe paṇḍiteheva saddhiṃ pavatteyyāti attho. Santhavanti mittasanthavaṃ. Sataṃ saddhammanti paṇḍitānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhātaṃ saddhammaṃ. Seyyoti etaṃ dhammaṃ ñatvā vaḍḍhiyeva hoti, hāni nāma natthīti attho. Rājarathāti rājūnaṃ [P 5.0484] ārohanīyarathā. Sucittāti suparikammakatā. Sabbhi pavedayantīti buddhādayo santo “sabbhī”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ sobhanaṃ uttamaṃ nibbānaṃ pavedenti thomenti, so nibbānasaṅkhāto sataṃ dhammo jaraṃ na upeti na jīrati. Nabhanti ākāso. Dūreti pathavī hi sappatiṭṭhā sagahaṇā, ākāso nirālambo appatiṭṭho, iti ubho ete ekābaddhāpi visaṃyogaṭṭhena anupalittaṭṭhena ca dūre nāma honti. Pāranti orimatīrato paratīraṃ. Tadāhūti taṃ āhu.

In this context, 'sakideva' means just once. 'Sabbhī' means with good people. 'Sā naṃ' means that association or meeting with good people, even if it happens just once, protects and guards that person. 'Nāsabbhi' means that association with bad people, even if done many times or living together for a long time, does not protect and is not stable—this is the meaning. 'Samāsetha' means one should sit with them; one should conduct oneself in all postures only with the wise—this is the meaning. 'Santhavaṃ' means intimate friendship. 'Sataṃ saddhammaṃ' refers to the true Dhamma of the wise, such as the Buddhas, consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. 'Seyyo' means that by knowing this Dhamma, there is only growth and no decline—this is the meaning. 'Rājarathā' means the chariots for kings to ride. 'Sucittā' means well-adorned. 'Sabbhi pavedayanti' means the noble ones, such as the Buddhas, proclaim and praise Nibbāna, which is known as 'sabbhī' and is excellent and supreme; that Dhamma of the virtuous, namely Nibbāna, does not age or decay. 'Nabhaṃ' means the sky. 'Dūre' means far; the earth is fixed and graspable, whereas the sky is without support and unestablished; thus, though they are linked, they are called 'far' because they are disjoined and unsullied. 'Pāraṃ' means the far shore from the near shore. 'Tadāhu' means they call it that.

Iti brāhmaṇo catasso satārahā gāthā kassapadasabalena desitaniyāmena desetvā tuṇhī ahosi[V 5.0479]. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “sapphalaṃ vata me āgamana”nti tuṭṭhacitto hutvā “imā gāthā neva sāvakabhāsitā, na isibhāsitā, na kenaci bhāsitā, sabbaññunāva bhāsitā, kiṃ nu kho agghantī”ti cintetvā “imāsaṃ sakalampi cakkavāḷaṃ yāva brahmalokā sattaratanapuṇṇaṃ katvā dadamānopi neva anucchavikaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, ahaṃ kho panassa tiyojanasate kururaṭṭhe sattayojanike indapatthanagare rajjaṃ dātuṃ pahomi, atthi nu khvassa rajjaṃ kāretuṃ bhāgya”nti aṅgavijjānubhāvena olokento nāddasa. Tato senāpatiṭṭhānādīni olokento ekagāmabhojakamattassapi bhāgyaṃ adisvā dhanalābhassa olokento koṭidhanato paṭṭhāya oloketvā catunnaṃyeva kahāpaṇasahassānaṃ bhāgyaṃ disvā “ettakena naṃ pūjessāmī”ti catasso sahassatthavikā dāpetvā, “ācariya, tumhe aññesaṃ khattiyānaṃ imā gāthā desetvā kittakaṃ dhanaṃ labhathā”ti pucchati. “Ekekāya gāthāya sataṃ sataṃ, mahārāja, teneva tā satārahā nāma jātā”ti. Atha naṃ mahāsatto, “ācariya, tvaṃ attanā gahetvā vikkeyyabhaṇḍassa agghampi na jānāsi[M 5.0525], ito paṭṭhāya ekekā gāthā sahassārahā nāma hontū”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Thus the brahmin, having taught the four verses worthy of a hundred according to the method taught by Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, became silent. Hearing them, the Great Being, with a joyful heart, thought, "My coming here has indeed been fruitful." He reflected, "These verses were not spoken by disciples, nor by seers, nor by anyone else; they were spoken only by the Omniscient One. How much are they worth? Even if one were to fill the entire world-system up to the Brahma realm with the seven treasures and give it, it would not be a fitting price. I, however, am able to give him kingship over the Kuru country, three hundred leagues in extent, and the city of Indapatta, seven leagues in extent. But does he have the merit to rule a kingdom?" Using the power of physiognomy, he looked but did not see such merit. Then, examining positions such as commander-in-chief, he saw no merit even for a village headman. Looking into his merit for wealth, he examined starting from a crore and saw merit for only four thousand kahāpaṇas. Thinking, "I will honor him with this much," he had four bags of a thousand given and asked, "Teacher, when you teach these verses to other kings, how much wealth do you receive?" "A hundred for each verse, great king; for that reason they are called verses worthy of a hundred." Then the Great Being said, "Teacher, you do not know the value of the goods you have taken and sold. From today onwards, let each verse be worthy of a thousand," and spoke this verse:

415.

415.

“Sahassiyā imā gāthā, nahimā gāthā satārahā;

Cattāri tvaṃ sahassāni, khippaṃ gaṇhāhi brāhmaṇā”ti.

These verses are worthy of a thousand; these verses are not worthy of a hundred. Quickly take four thousand, O brahmin.

Tassattho – brāhmaṇa, imā gāthā sahassiyā sahassārahā, imā gāthā satārahā na hi hontu, brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ cattāri sahassāni khippaṃ gaṇhāti.

The meaning is this: O brahmin, these verses are worthy of a thousand; let them not be verses worthy of a hundred. O brahmin, you quickly take four thousand.

Athassa ekaṃ sukhayānakaṃ datvā “brāhmaṇaṃ sotthinā gehaṃ [P 5.0485] sampāpethā”ti purise āṇāpetvā taṃ uyyojesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe “sutasomaraññā satārahā gāthā sahassārahā katvā pūjitā sādhu sādhū”ti mahāsādhukārasaddo ahosi. Tassa mātāpitaro taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ saddo nāmesā”ti pucchitvā yathābhūtaṃ sutvā attano dhanalobhatāya mahāsattassa kujjhiṃsu. Sopi brāhmaṇaṃ uyyojetvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassa pitā “kathaṃ, tāta, evarūpassa sāhasikassa corassa hatthato muttosī”ti paṭisanthāramattampi akatvā attano dhanalobhatāya “saccaṃ kira, tāta, tayā catasso gāthā sutvā cattāri sahassāni dinnānī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte gāthamāha –

Then, giving him a comfortable carriage, he ordered his men, "Escort the brahmin Nanda safely home," and sent him away. At that moment, a great shout of applause arose: "King Sutasoma has honored the verses worthy of a hundred by making them worthy of a thousand—well done, well done!" His parents, hearing that shout, asked, "What is that noise?" and upon hearing the truth, they became angry with the Great Being, Prince Mahasutasoma, due to their own greed for wealth. After sending the brahmin away, he went to his parents, paid his respects, and stood there. Then his father, without even a polite greeting, but out of greed for wealth, asked, "How, dear son, were you released from the hands of such a violent robber?" and added, "Is it true, dear son, that you gave four thousand after hearing four verses?" When he said, "It is true," his father spoke this verse to reproach him:

416.

416.

“Āsītiyā nāvutiyā ca gāthā, satārahā cāpi bhaveyya gāthā;

A verse might be worthy of eighty or ninety, and a verse might even be worthy of a hundred;

Paccattameva sutasoma jānahi, sahassiyā nāma kā atthi gāthā”ti.

But know for yourself, Sutasoma, what verse is there that is called 'worthy of a thousand'?

Tassattho [V 5.0480] – gāthā nāma, tāta, āsītiyā ca nāvutiyā ca satārahā cāpi bhaveyya, paccattameva attanāva jānāhi, sahassārahā nāma gāthā kā kassa santike atthīti.

The meaning is this: Dear son, a verse might be worthy of eighty, ninety, or even a hundred. Know for yourself: what verse called 'worthy of a thousand' exists, and with whom?

Atha naṃ mahāsatto “nāhaṃ, tāta, dhanena vuddhiṃ icchāmi, sutena pana icchāmī”ti saññāpento āha –

Then the Great Being, explaining to his father, said: "Father, I do not desire growth through wealth, but I desire only growth through learning."

417.

417.

“Icchāmi [M 5.0526] vohaṃ sutavuddhimattano, santoti maṃ sappurisā bhajeyyuṃ;

Ahaṃ savantīhi mahodadhīva, na hi tāta tappāmi subhāsitena.

I desire the growth of my own learning, so that good people might associate with me as one who is peaceful. Like the great ocean that is never sated with its flowing rivers, I am never satisfied with well-spoken words, father.

418.

418.

“Aggi yathā tiṇakaṭṭhaṃ dahanto, na kappatī sāgarova nadībhi;

Evampi te paṇḍitā rājaseṭṭha, sutvā na tappanti subhāsitena.

Just as fire burning grass and wood is not sated, nor the ocean by rivers; so too, indeed, O best of kings, the wise are not satisfied by well-spoken words, even after hearing them.

419.

419.

“Sakassa dāsassa yadā suṇomi, gāthaṃ ahaṃ atthavatiṃ janinda;

Tameva [P 5.0486] sakkacca nisāmayāmi, na hi tāta dhammesu mamatthi tittī”ti.

When I hear a meaningful verse, O lord of men, even from my own slave, I listen to it attentively; for indeed, father, I have no satiety in the teachings.

Tattha voti nipātamattaṃ. “Santo”ti ete ca maṃ bhajeyyuṃ iti icchāmi. Savantīhīti nadīhi. Sakassāti tiṭṭhatu, nanda, brāhmaṇo, yadā ahaṃ attano dāsassapi santike suṇomi, tāta, dhammesu mama titti na hi atthīti.

Therein, 'vo' is merely a particle. The meaning of 'santo' is: 'I wish that these good people would associate with me.' 'Savantīhi' means 'by rivers.' As for 'Sakassa', it means: 'Never mind the brahmin, Nanda; when I hear even from my own slave, father, I have no satiety in the teachings.'

Evañca pana vatvā “mā maṃ, tāta, dhanahetu paribhāsasi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā āgamissāmī”ti sapathaṃ katvā āgato, idānāhaṃ porisādassa santikaṃ gamissāmi, idaṃ te rajjaṃ gaṇhathā”ti rajjaṃ niyyādento gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, he said, 'Father, do not reproach me for the sake of wealth. I have returned, having made an oath that I would come back after hearing the Dhamma. Now I shall go to the presence of Porisāda. Take this kingdom of yours.' Thus handing over the kingdom, he uttered this verse:

420.

420.

“Idaṃ te raṭṭhaṃ sadhanaṃ sayoggaṃ, sakāyuraṃ sabbakāmūpapannaṃ;

Kiṃ kāmahetu paribhāsasi maṃ, gacchāmahaṃ porisādassa ñatte”ti.

“This kingdom is yours, with its wealth, its vehicles, and its royal regalia, endowed with all sensual pleasures. Why do you scold me for the sake of desires? I shall go to the presence of Porisāda.”

Tattha ñatteti santike.

Therein, 'ñatte' means 'in the presence of'.

Tasmiṃ samaye piturañño hadayaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. So, “tāta sutasoma, kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathesi, mayaṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya coraṃ gahessāmā”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

At that time, the heart of the king, his father, grew hot. He said, 'Dear Sutasoma, what is this you say? We shall capture the robber with a fourfold army,' and then spoke this verse:

421.

421.

“Attānurakkhāya [M 5.0527][V 5.0481] bhavanti hete, hatthārohā rathikā pattikā ca;

Assārohā ye ca dhanuggahāse, senaṃ payuñjāma hanāma sattu”nti.

“For one's own protection indeed are these: elephant riders, charioteers, and foot soldiers, horsemen and those who are archers. Let us deploy the army and slay the enemy!”

Tattha hanāmāti sace evaṃ payojitā senā taṃ gahetuṃ na sakkonti, atha naṃ sakalaraṭṭhavāsino gahetvā gantvā hanāma sattuṃ, mārema taṃ amhākaṃ paccāmittanti attho.

Here, 'hanāma' means: if the army thus deployed cannot capture him, then all the people of the kingdom will seize him, and having gone, let us slay the foe—that is, let us kill him, our enemy.

Atha naṃ mātāpitaro assupuṇṇamukhā rodamānā vilapantā, “tāta, mā gaccha, gantuṃ na labbhā”ti yāciṃsu. Soḷasasahassā nāṭakitthiyopi sesaparijanopi “amhe anāthe katvā kuhiṃ gacchasi, devā”ti parideviṃsu. Sakalanagare koci sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonto “sutasomo porisādassa kira paṭiññaṃ datvā āgato, idāni catasso [P 5.0487] satārahā gāthā sutvā dhammakathikassa sakkāraṃ katvā mātāpitaro vanditvā punapi kira corassa santikaṃ gamissatī”ti sakalanagaraṃ ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Sopi mātāpitūnaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā gāthamāha –

Then his parents, with tearful faces, weeping and lamenting, pleaded, 'Dear son, do not go; you cannot go.' Sixteen thousand dancing women and the rest of the retinue also lamented, 'Having made us helpless, where are you going, O lord?' Throughout the entire city, no one was able to remain calm, saying, 'It seems that Sutasoma, having given his word to Porisāda, has returned; and now, after hearing the four verses worthy of a hundred, honoring the Dhamma preacher, and paying respects to his parents, he will again go to the robber’s presence!' The entire city became one great uproar. Having heard his parents’ words, he spoke this verse:

422.

422.

“Sudukkaraṃ porisādo akāsi, jīvaṃ gahetvāna avassajī maṃ;

Taṃ tādisaṃ pubbakiccaṃ saranto, dubbhe ahaṃ tassa kathaṃ janindā”ti.

“Porisāda has done what is extremely difficult to do; having taken me alive, he released me. Remembering such a former service, how could I betray him, O king?”

Tattha jīvaṃ gahetvānāti jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā. Taṃ tādisanti taṃ tena kataṃ tathārūpaṃ. Pubbakiccanti purimaṃ upakāraṃ. Janindāti pitaraṃ ālapati.

Here, 'jīvaṃ gahetvāna' means 'having taken a living being captive.' 'Taṃ tādisaṃ' refers to something done by him, of that nature. 'Pubbakiccaṃ' means a previous service. 'Janinda' addresses his father.

So mātāpitaro assāsetvā, “amma tātā, tumhe mayhaṃ mā cintayittha, katakalyāṇo ahaṃ, mama chakāmassaggissariyaṃ na dullabha”nti mātāpitaro vanditvā āpucchitvā sesajanaṃ anusāsitvā pakkāmi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having reassured his parents, saying, 'Mother, father, do not worry about me. I have performed good deeds; for me, the sovereignty of the six sensual heavens is not difficult to attain,' he paid respects to his parents, took leave, instructed the remaining people, and departed. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

423.

423.

“Vanditvā [M 5.0528] so pitaraṃ mātarañca, anusāsitvā negamañca balañca;

Saccavādī saccānurakkhamāno, agamāsi so yattha porisādo”ti.

“Having paid homage to his father and mother, and having instructed the townsfolk and the army, the speaker of truth, guarding the truth, went to where Porisāda was.”

Tattha saccānurakkhamānoti saccaṃ anurakkhamāno. Agamāsīti taṃ rattiṃ nivesaneyeva vasitvā punadivase aruṇuggamanavelāya mātāpitaro vanditvā āpucchitvā sesajanaṃ anusāsitvā assumukhena nānappakāraṃ paridevantena itthāgārādinā mahājanena anugato nagarā nikkhamma [V 5.0482] taṃ janaṃ nivattetuṃ asakkonto mahāmagge daṇḍakena tiriyaṃ lekhaṃ kaḍḍhitvā “sace mayi sineho atthi, imaṃ mā atikkamiṃsū”ti āha. Mahājano sīlavato tejavantassa āṇaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto mahāsaddena paridevamāno taṃ sīhavijambhitena gacchantaṃ oloketvā tasmiṃ dassanūpacāraṃ atikkante ekaravaṃ ravanto nagaraṃ pāvisi. Sopi āgatamaggeneva tassa santikaṃ gato. Tena vuttaṃ “agamāsi so yattha porisādo”ti.

Here, 'saccānurakkhamāno' means guarding the truth. As for 'agamāsi' (he went), after staying that very night in the palace, at dawn the next day, he paid respects to his parents, took leave, instructed the remaining people, and then, followed by a great crowd of people—including the ladies of the court—weeping with tearful faces and lamenting in various ways, he left the city. Unable to turn the people back, he drew a line across the main road with a stick and said, 'If you have any affection for me, do not cross this line.' The people, unable to disobey the command of the virtuous and powerful one, lamented loudly. Watching him go with the gait of a lion, they entered the city with a single cry when he had passed out of sight. He went to the other's presence by the same path he had come. Therefore, it is said, 'He went where Porisāda was.'

Tato porisādo cintesi – “sace mama sahāyo sutasomo āgantukāmo, āgacchatu, anāgantukāmo, anāgacchatu, rukkhadevatā yaṃ mayhaṃ icchati[P 5.0488], taṃ karotu, ime rājāno māretvā pañcamadhuramaṃsena balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti citakaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā “aṅgārarāsi tāva hotū”ti tassa sūle tacchantassa nisinnakāle sutasomo āgato. Atha naṃ porisādo disvā tuṭṭhacitto, “samma, gantvā kattabbakiccaṃ te kata”nti pucchi. Mahāsatto, “āma mahārāja, kassapadasabalena desitā gāthā me sutā, dhammakathikassa ca sakkāro kato, tasmā gantvā kattabbakiccaṃ kataṃ nāma hotī”ti dassetuṃ gāthamāha –

Then Porisāda thought: 'If my friend Sutasoma wishes to come, let him come; if he does not wish to come, let him not come; let the tree deity do what she wants with me. I will kill these kings and perform the sacrifice with the five choice meats.' Having prepared the pyre and lit the fire, thinking, 'Let there be a heap of embers first,' he sat down sharpening his stakes. At that moment, Sutasoma arrived. Seeing him, Porisāda was delighted and asked, 'Friend, have you gone and done what needed to be done?' The Great Being replied, 'Yes, Great King, I have heard the verses taught by Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, and have honored the Dhamma preacher. Therefore, it is said that what needed to be done has been done.' To show this, he spoke the verse:

424.

424.

“Kato mayā saṅgaro brāhmaṇena, raṭṭhe sake issariye ṭhitena;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇasappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāgatosmi;

Yajassu yaññaṃ khāda maṃ porisādā”ti.

“I have fulfilled the agreement with the brahmin, while established in sovereignty in my own kingdom. Having satisfied that agreement for the brahmin, I have returned, guarding the truth. Perform the sacrifice, eat me, O Porisāda!”

Tattha [M 5.0529] yajassūti maṃ māretvā devatāya vā yaññaṃ yajassu, maṃsaṃ vā me khādāhīti attho.

In this context, 'yajassu' means: 'having killed me, perform the sacrifice to the deity, or eat my flesh.'

Taṃ sutvā porisādo “ayaṃ rājā na bhāyati, vigatamaraṇabhayo hutvā katheti, kissa nu kho esa ānubhāvo”ti cintetvā “aññaṃ natthi, ayaṃ ‘kassapadasabalena desitā gāthā me sutā’ti vadati, tāsaṃ etena āsubhāvena bhavitabbaṃ, ahampi taṃ kathāpetvā tā gāthāyo sossāmi, evaṃ ahampi nibbhayo bhavissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Porisāda thought, 'This king does not fear; he speaks without any fear of death. What is the power behind this?' Then he concluded, 'There is nothing else; he says, "I have heard the verses taught by Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One." It must be the power of those verses. I too will have him recite them and listen to those verses. In this way, I too will become fearless.' Having made this resolution, he spoke a verse:

425.

425.

“Na hāyate khāditaṃ mayhaṃ pacchā, citakā ayaṃ tāva sadhūmikāva;

Niddhūmake pacitaṃ sādhupakkaṃ, suṇomi gāthāyo satārahāyo”ti.

“My eating will not be lost by waiting; this pyre is still smoking. When cooked over smokeless coals, it will be well-cooked. I will listen to the verses worthy of a hundred.”

Tattha khāditanti khādanaṃ. Taṃ khādanaṃ mayhaṃ pacchā vā pure vā na parihāyati, pacchāpi hi [V 5.0483] tvaṃ mayā khāditabbova. Niddhūmake pacitanti niddhūme nijjhāle aggimhi pakkamaṃsaṃ sādhupakkaṃ nāma hoti.

Here, 'khāditaṃ' means eating. That eating is not lost for me, whether later or earlier, for even later you are certainly to be eaten by me. 'Niddhūmake pacitanti' means that meat cooked on a fire without smoke and without flame is called well-cooked.

Taṃ [P 5.0489] sutvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ porisādo pāpadhammo, imaṃ thokaṃ niggahetvā lajjāpetvā kathessāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

Hearing this, the Great Being, thinking, 'This Porisāda is of wicked character; I will speak after censuring him a little and making him feel ashamed,' said:

426.

426.

“Adhammiko tvaṃ porisādakāsi, raṭṭhā ca bhaṭṭho udarassa hetu;

Dhammañcimā abhivadanti gāthā, dhammo ca adhammo ca kuhiṃ sameti.

“You have become an unrighteous man-eater, fallen from your kingdom for the sake of your belly. These verses proclaim the Dhamma; where do Dhamma and non-Dhamma ever meet?”

427.

427.

“Adhammikassa luddassa, niccaṃ lohitapāṇino;

Natthi saccaṃ kuto dhammo, kiṃ sutena karissasī”ti.

“For the unrighteous and cruel one, whose hands are ever bloodstained, there is no truth. Whence could there be Dhamma? What will you do with what you have heard?”

Tattha dhammañcimāti imā ca gāthā navalokuttaradhammaṃ abhivadanti. Kuhiṃ sametīti kattha samāgacchati. Dhammo hi sugatiṃ pāpeti nibbānaṃ vā, adhammo duggatiṃ. Kuto dhammoti vacīsaccamattampi natthi, kuto dhammo. Kiṃ sutenāti tvaṃ etena sutena kiṃ karissasi, mattikābhājanaṃ viya hi sīhavasāya abhājanaṃ tvaṃ dhammassa.

Here, ‘dhammañcimā’ means these verses speak of the nine supramundane Dhammas. ‘Kuhiṃ sameti’ means where do they meet? For Dhamma leads to a happy destination or Nibbāna, while non-Dhamma leads to a woeful state. ‘Kuto dhammo’ means there is not even the slight truth of speech—whence could there be Dhamma? ‘Kiṃ sutena’ means what will you do with this learning? For you are an unfit vessel for the Dhamma, just as a clay pot is an unfit vessel for lion's fat.

So [M 5.0530] evaṃ kathitepi neva kujjhi. Kasmā? Mahāsattassa mettābhāvanāya mahattena. Atha naṃ “kiṃ pana samma sutasoma ahameva adhammiko”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Even when spoken to thus, he did not get angry. Why? Because of the greatness of the Great Being’s development of loving-kindness. Then he said to him, “But, friend Sutasoma, am I the only one who is unrighteous?” and to inform the Great Being of that reason, he spoke this verse:

428.

428.

“Yo maṃsahetu migavaṃ careyya, yo vā hane purisamattahetu;

Ubhopi te pecca samā bhavanti, kasmā no adhammikaṃ brūsi maṃ tva”nti.

“One who would hunt game for the sake of meat, or who would kill a person for his own sake; both of them are equal after death. Why do you call only me unrighteous?”

Tattha kasmā noti ye jambudīpatale rājāno alaṅkatapaṭiyattā mahābalaparivārā rathavaragatā migavaṃ carantā tikhiṇehi sarehi mige vijjhitvā mārenti, te avatvā kasmā tvaṃ maññeva adhammikanti vadati. Yadi te niddosā, ahampi niddoso evāti dīpeti.

Therein, ‘kasmā no’ means: why, when kings on the surface of the continent of Jambudīpa, adorned and well-prepared, surrounded by great forces and riding in excellent chariots, go hunting game and kill animals by piercing them with sharp arrows—why, without speaking of them, do you call only me unrighteous? He shows that if they are faultless, then I too am faultless.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto tassa laddhiṃ bhindanto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being, desiring to refute his view, spoke this verse:

429.

429.

“Pañca [V 5.0484] pañca na khā bhakkhā, khattiyena pajānatā;

Abhakkhaṃ rāja bhakkhesi, tasmā adhammiko tuva”nti.

“Five and five animals are not to be eaten by a discerning warrior. You, O king, have eaten what is unfit to be eaten; therefore, you are unrighteous.”

Tassattho – samma porisāda, khattiyena nāma khattiyadhammaṃ jānantena pañca pañca hatthiādayo daseva sattā maṃsavasena na khā bhakkhā na kho khāditabbayuttakā. “Na kho”tveva vā pāṭho. Aparo nayo khattiyena khattiyadhammaṃ jānantena pañcanakhesu sattesu sasako, sallako, godhā, kapi kummoti [P 5.0490] ime pañceva sattā bhakkhitabbayuttakā, na aññe, tvaṃ pana abhakkhaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ bhakkhesi, tena adhammikoti.

The meaning is: Friend man-eater, by a warrior who knows the warrior’s duty, five and five—ten beings such as elephants—are not to be eaten as meat; they are not fit for eating. Or, alternatively, the reading is “na kho”. Another interpretation: by a warrior who knows the warrior’s duty, among five-clawed animals, only these five—the rabbit, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the monkey, and the turtle—are fit to be eaten, and no others. But you eat human flesh, which is forbidden; therefore, you have become unrighteous.

Iti so niggahaṃ patvā aññaṃ nissaraṇaṃ adisvā attano pāpaṃ paṭicchādento gāthamāha –

Thus, having met with rebuke and seeing no other refuge, desiring to conceal his own evil, he spoke this verse:

430.

430.

“Mutto tuvaṃ porisādassa hatthā, gantvā sakaṃ mandiraṃ kāmakāmī;

Amittahatthaṃ punarāgatosi, na khattadhamme kusalosi rājā”ti.

“You were freed from the grasp of the man-eater and went to your own palace, O lover of pleasures; yet you have returned to the enemy’s hand. You are not skilled in the warrior’s duty, O king.”

Tattha [M 5.0531] na khattadhammeti tvaṃ khattiyadhammasaṅkhāte nītisatthe na kusalosi, attano atthānatthaṃ na jānāsi, akāraṇeneva te loke paṇḍitoti kitti patthaṭā, ahaṃ pana te paṇḍitabhāvaṃ na passāmi na jānāmi, atibālosīhi vadati.

Therein, ‘not skilled in the warrior’s duty’ means you are not skilled in the science of statecraft known as the warrior’s duty; you do not know your own benefit or harm. Without any cause, your reputation as a wise person has spread in the world; but I do not see or recognize your wisdom. You are extremely foolish, he says.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto, “samma, khattiyadhamme kusalena nāma mādiseneva bhavitabbaṃ. Ahañhi taṃ jānāmi, na pana tadatthāya paṭipajjāmī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being said to him, “Friend, one who is skilled in the warrior’s duty should indeed be like me. For I know that statecraft, but I do not practice it for that purpose.” And to inform the man-eater of that reason, he spoke this verse:

431.

431.

“Ye khattadhamme kusalā bhavanti, pāyena te nerayikā bhavanti;

Tasmā ahaṃ khattadhammaṃ pahāya, saccānurakkhī punarāgatosmi;

Yajassu yaññaṃ khāda maṃ porisādā”ti.

“Those who are skilled in the warrior’s duty mostly become inhabitants of hell. Therefore, I have abandoned the warrior’s duty and returned as a protector of truth. Perform your sacrifice or eat me, O man-eater!”

Tattha kusalāti tadatthāya paṭipajjanakusalā. Pāyenāti yebhuyyena nerayikā. Ye pana tattha na nibbattanti, te sesāpāyesu nibbattanti.

Therein, ‘skilled’ means skilled in practicing for that purpose. ‘Mostly’ means for the most part they become inhabitants of hell. As for those who are not reborn there, they are reborn in the other woeful states.

Porisādo āha –

The man-eater said:

432.

432.

“Pāsādavāsā [V 5.0485] pathavīgavāssā, kāmitthiyo kāsikacandanañca;

Sabbaṃ tahiṃ labhasi sāmitāya, saccena kiṃ passasi ānisaṃsa”nti.

“Palace dwellings, land, cattle, and horses, desired women, and Kāsī cloth and sandalwood; all this you obtain there through lordship. What benefit do you see in truth?”

Tattha pāsādavāsāti, samma sutasoma, tava tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavikā dibbavimānakappā tayo nivāsapāsādā. Pathavīgavāssāti pathavī ca gāvo ca assā ca bahū. Kāmitthiyoti kāmavatthubhūtā itthiyo. Kāsikacandanañcāti [P 5.0491] kāsikavatthañca lohitacandanañca. Sabbaṃ tahinti etañca aññañca upabhogaparibhogaṃ sabbaṃ tvaṃ tahiṃ attano nagare sāmitāya labhasi, sāmī hutvā yathā icchasi, tathā paribhuñjituṃ labhati, so tvaṃ sabbametaṃ pahāya saccānurakkhī idhāgacchanto saccena kiṃ ānisaṃsaṃ passasīti.

Therein, ‘palace dwellings’ means, friend Sutasoma, your three residential palaces suitable for the three seasons, like divine abodes. ‘Land, cattle, and horses’ means much land, cows, and horses. ‘Desired women’ means women who are the objects of desire. ‘Kāsī cloth and sandalwood’ means Kāsī cloth and red sandalwood. ‘All this you obtain there’ means all this and other items of use and enjoyment, you obtain in your own city through lordship; being the lord, you are able to enjoy them as you wish. You, having abandoned all this and returning here to protect the truth—what benefit do you see in truth?

Bodhisatto [M 5.0532] āha –

The Bodhisatta said:

433.

433.

“Ye kecime atthi rasā pathabyā, saccaṃ tesaṃ sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ;

“Whatever flavors exist here on earth, truth is the sweetest of those flavors.

Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca, taranti jātimaraṇassa pāra”nti.

Established in truth, ascetics and brahmins cross to the far shore of birth and death.”

Tattha sādutaranti yasmā sabbepi rasā sattānaṃ saccakāleyeva paṇītā madhurā honti, tasmā saccaṃ tesaṃ sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ, yasmā vā viratisaccavacīsacce ṭhitā jātimaraṇasaṅkhātassa tebhūmakavaṭṭassa pāraṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ taranti pāpuṇanti, tasmāpi taṃ sādutaranti.

Therein, ‘sweeter’ means that because all flavors are exquisite and sweet to beings only when truth prevails, truth is therefore the sweetest of those flavors. Alternatively, because those established in the truth of abstinence and the truth of speech cross over and reach the far shore of the cycle of the three planes, known as birth and death—the great deathless Nibbāna—it is therefore also called sweeter.

Evamassa mahāsatto sacce ānisaṃsaṃ kathesi. Tato porisādo vikasitapadumapuṇṇacandasassirikamevassa mukhaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ sutasomo aṅgāracitakaṃ mañca sūlaṃ tacchantaṃ passati, cittutrāsamattampissa natthi, kiṃ nu kho esa satārahagāthānaṃ ānubhāvo, udāhu saccassa, aññasseva vā kassacī”ti cintetvā “pucchissāmi tāva na”nti pucchanto gāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being preached the benefit of truth to him. Then the man-eater, gazing upon his face which was glorious like a blooming lotus or the full moon, thought: “This Sutasoma sees the charcoal pyre and the impaling stake being sharpened, yet there is not even a trace of mental terror in him. What can this be? Is it the power of the verses worth a hundred each, or of truth, or of something else?” Deciding, “I shall first ask him,” he questioned him with this verse:

434.

434.

“Mutto tuvaṃ porisādassa hatthā, gantvā sakaṃ mandiraṃ kāmakāmī;

Amittahatthaṃ punarāgatosi, na hi nūna te maraṇabhayaṃ janinda;

Alīnacitto asi saccavādī”ti.

“Freed from the man-eater’s grasp, you went to your own palace, O lover of desires; yet you have returned to the enemy’s hand. Surely, O lord of people, you have no fear of death! With unwavering mind, you are a speaker of truth.”

Mahāsattopissa ācikkhanto āha –

The Great Being, informing him of the reason, said:

435.

435.

“Katā [V 5.0486] me kalyāṇā anekarūpā, yaññā yiṭṭhā ye vipulā pasatthā;

Visodhito paralokassa maggo, dhamme ṭhito ko maraṇassa bhāye.

“Many kinds of wholesome deeds have I done; sacrifices both great and praised have I offered. The path to the world beyond is purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?”

436.

436.

“Katā [M 5.0533] me kalyāṇā anekarūpā, yaññā yiṭṭhā ye vipulā pasatthā;

Anānutappaṃ [P 5.0492] paralokaṃ gamissaṃ, yajassu yaññaṃ ada maṃ porisāda.

“Many kinds of wholesome deeds have I done; sacrifices both great and praised have I offered. I shall go to the world beyond without remorse. Perform your sacrifice! Eat me, O man-eater!”

437.

437.

“Pitā ca mātā ca upaṭṭhitā me, dhammena me issariyaṃ pasatthaṃ;

Visodhito paralokassa maggo, dhamme ṭhito ko maraṇassa bhāye.

“I have attended to my father and mother; my dominion is praised for its righteousness. The path to the world beyond is purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?”

438.

438.

“Pitā ca mātā ca upaṭṭhitā me, dhammena me issariyaṃ pasatthaṃ;

Anānutappaṃ paralokaṃ gamissaṃ, yajassu yaññaṃ ada maṃ porisāda.

“I have attended to my father and mother; my dominion is praised for its righteousness. I shall go to the world beyond without remorse. Perform your sacrifice! Eat me, O man-eater!”

439.

439.

“Ñātīsu mittesu katā me kārā, dhammena me issariyaṃ pasatthaṃ;

Visodhito paralokassa maggo, dhamme ṭhito ko maraṇassa bhāye.

“I have performed my duties to relatives and friends; my dominion is praised for its righteousness. The path to the world beyond is purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?”

440.

440.

“Ñātīsu mittesu katā me kārā, dhammena me issariyaṃ pasatthaṃ;

Anānutappaṃ paralokaṃ gamissaṃ, yajassu yaññaṃ ada maṃ porisāda.

“I have performed my duties to relatives and friends; my dominion is praised for its righteousness. I shall go to the world beyond without remorse. Perform your sacrifice! Eat me, O man-eater!”

441.

441.

“Dinnaṃ me dānaṃ bahudhā bahūnaṃ, santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca;

Visodhito paralokassa maggo, dhamme ṭhito ko maraṇassa bhāye.

“I have given gifts in many ways to many, and ascetics and brahmins have been satisfied. The path to the world beyond is purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?”

442.

442.

“Dinnaṃ me dānaṃ bahudhā bahūnaṃ, santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca;

Anānutappaṃ paralokaṃ gamissaṃ, yajassu yaññaṃ ada maṃ porisādā”ti.

“I have given gifts in many ways to many, and ascetics and brahmins have been satisfied. I shall go to the world beyond without remorse. Perform your sacrifice! Eat me, O man-eater!”

Tattha [M 5.0534] kalyāṇāti kalyāṇakammā. Anekarūpāti dānādivasena anekavidhā. Yaññāti dasavidhadānavatthupariccāgavasena ativipulā paṇḍitehi pasatthā yaññāpi yiṭṭhā pavattitā. Dhamme ṭhitoti evaṃ dhamme patiṭṭhito mādiso ko nāma maraṇassa bhāyeyya. Anānutappanti anānutappamāno. Dhammena me issariyaṃ pasatthanti dasavidhaṃ rājadhammaṃ akopetvā dhammeneva mayā rajjaṃ pasāsitaṃ. Kārāti ñātīsu ñātikiccāni, mittesu ca mittakiccāni. Dānanti savatthukacetanā. Bahudhāti bahūhi ākārehi. Bahūnanti na pañcannaṃ, na dasannaṃ, satassapi sahassassapi [V 5.0487] satasahassassapi dinnameva. Santappitāti gahitagahitabhājanāni pūretvā suṭṭhu tappitā.

Therein, ‘wholesome deeds’ means wholesome actions. ‘Many kinds’ means diverse, in ways such as giving and so forth. ‘Sacrifices’ means that extensive sacrifices praised by the wise have also been performed through the relinquishment of the ten kinds of objects of giving. ‘Established in the Dhamma’ means one like me, established in such Dhamma—who would fear death? ‘Without remorse’ means not regretting. ‘My dominion is praised for its righteousness’ means the kingdom was governed by me according to the Dhamma, without violating the ten royal virtues. ‘Duties’ means the duties to relatives and the duties to friends. ‘Given’ means the intention together with the object. ‘In many ways’ means in many forms. ‘To many’ means having given not to five, not to ten, but even to a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand. ‘Satisfied’ means having filled the bowls as they were taken, they were well satisfied.

Taṃ [P 5.0493] sutvā porisādo “ayaṃ sutasomamahārājā sappuriso ñāṇasampanno madhuradhammakathiko, sacāhaṃ etaṃ khādeyyaṃ, muddhā me sattadhā phaleyya, pathavī vā pana me vivaraṃ dadeyyā”ti bhītatasito hutvā, “samma, na tvaṃ mayā khāditabbarūpo”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the man-eater became terrified and trembling, and thought: “This great king Sutasoma is a virtuous man, endowed with wisdom, and a sweet speaker of the Dhamma. If I were to eat him, my head would split into seven pieces, or the earth would give me an opening.” So he said, “Friend, you are not the kind to be eaten by me,” and spoke this verse:

443.

443.

“Visaṃ pajānaṃ puriso adeyya, āsīvisaṃ jalitamuggatejaṃ;

Muddhāpi tassa viphaleyya sattadhā, yo tādisaṃ saccavādiṃ adeyyā”ti.

“A man might knowingly eat poison, or a venomous viper blazing with fierce power; yet for one who would eat such a speaker of truth, even their head would split into seven pieces.”

Tattha visanti tattheva māraṇasamatthaṃ halāhalavisaṃ. Jalitanti attano visatejena jalitaṃ teneva uggatejaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ viya carantaṃ āsīvisaṃ vā pana so gīvāya gaṇheyya.

Therein, ‘poison’ means deadly venom like halāhala poison. ‘Blazing’ means blazing with its own venomous power; by that same power, it is a viper of fierce energy, moving about like a mass of fire. Or, he might seize it by the neck.

Iti so mahāsattaṃ “halāhalavisasadiso tvaṃ, ko taṃ khādissatī”ti vatvā gāthā sotukāmo taṃ yācitvā tena dhammagāravajananatthaṃ “evarūpānaṃ anavajjagāthānaṃ tvaṃ abhājana”nti paṭikkhittopi “sakalajambudīpe iminā sadiso paṇḍito natthi, ayaṃ mama hatthā muccitvā gantvā tā gāthā sutvā dhammakathikassa sakkāraṃ katvā nalāṭena maccuṃ ādāya punāgato, ativiya sādhurūpā gāthā bhavissantī”ti suṭṭhutaraṃ sañjātadhammassavanādaro hutvā taṃ yācanto gāthamāha –

Thus, he said to the Great Being, “You are like halāhala poison—who would eat you?” Though the man-eater was eager to hear the verses and begged for them, he was refused by him—for the purpose of generating respect for the Dhamma—with the words, “You are unworthy of such blameless verses.” Yet, thinking, “In all of Jambudīpa, there is no one as wise as this man. He was released from my hand, went and heard those verses, honored the Dhamma teacher, and has returned, carrying his own death upon his forehead—those verses must be exceedingly fine,” his reverence for hearing the Dhamma grew even stronger, and begging him, he recited this verse:

444.

444.

“Sutvā [M 5.0535] dhammaṃ vijānanti, narā kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Api gāthā suṇitvāna, dhamme me ramate mano”ti.

“Having heard the Dhamma, people discern what is wholesome and unwholesome; perhaps, having heard these verses, my mind may come to delight in the Dhamma.”

Tassattho – “samma sutasoma, narā nāma dhammaṃ sutvā kalyāṇampi pāpakampi jānanti, appeva nāma tā gāthā sutvā mamapi kusalakammapathadhamme mano rameyyā”ti.

Its meaning is: “Friend Sutasoma, people, having heard the Dhamma, come to know both what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. Perhaps after hearing those verses, my mind too might delight in the Dhamma of the wholesome paths of action.”

Atha mahāsatto “sotukāmo dāni porisādo, kathessāmī”ti cintetvā “tena hi, samma, sādhukaṃ suṇāhī”ti taṃ ohitasotaṃ katvā nandabrāhmaṇena kathitaniyāmeneva gāthānaṃ thutiṃ katvā chasu kāmāvacaradevesu ekakolāhalaṃ katvā [P 5.0494] devatāsu sādhukāraṃ dadamānāsu porisādassa dhammaṃ kathesi –

Then the Great Being, thinking, “Now the man-eater desires to listen, I shall speak,” said to him, “Well then, friend, listen carefully.” Having made him an attentive listener, he praised the verses in the very manner taught by the brahmin Nanda, causing a single great uproar among the six desire-realm heavens; and while the deities were acclaiming him, he taught the Dhamma to the man-eater:

445.

445.

“Sakideva [V 5.0488] mahārāja, sabbhi hoti samāgamo;

Sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti, nāsabbhi bahu saṅgamo.

“O great king, association with the good, even if only once, is enough; that association protects one, not much association with the wicked.”

446.

446.

“Sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Sataṃ sandhammamaññāya, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.

“One should associate only with the good, one should make friends only with the good; knowing the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.”

447.

447.

“Jīranti ve rājarathā sucittā, atho sarīrampi jaraṃ upeti;

Satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upeti, santo have sabbhi pavedayanti.

“Indeed, beautifully adorned royal chariots wear out, and the body also comes to old age; but the Dhamma of the good does not come to old age; the good, indeed, proclaim this to the good.”

448.

448.

“Nabhañca dūre pathavī ca dūre, pāraṃ samuddassa tadāhu dūre;

Tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, satañca dhammo asatañca rājā”ti.

“The sky is far, and the earth is far; the far shore of the sea, they say, is far. But farther still than that, they say, is the Dhamma of the good and that of the wicked, O king.”

Tassa tena sukathitattā ceva attano paṇḍitabhāvena ca tā gāthā sabbaññubuddhakathitā viyāti cintentassa sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā paripūri, bodhisatte muducittaṃ ahosi, setacchattadāyakaṃ pitaraṃ viya naṃ amaññi. So “ahaṃ sutasomassa dātabbaṃ kiñci hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ na passāmi, ekekāya panassa gāthāya ekekaṃ varaṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Because the verses were so well-spoken by him, and because of his own wisdom, as he reflected that those verses seemed as if spoken by an All-Knowing Buddha, his entire body was filled with five-hued rapture. His heart softened towards the Bodhisatta, and he regarded him as he would a father bestowing a white parasol. Thinking, “I see no gold or silver to give to Sutasoma, but for each verse I shall grant him a boon,” he spoke this verse:

449.

449.

“Gāthā [M 5.0536] imā atthavatī subyañjanā, subhāsitā tuyha janinda sutvā;

Ānandi vitto sumano patīto, cattāri te samma vare dadāmī”ti.

“Having heard these verses, meaningful and well-phrased, so well-spoken by you, O lord of men, I am joyful, delighted, glad-hearted, and pleased. I grant you four boons, my friend.”

Tattha ānandīti ānandajāto. Sesāni tasseva vevacanāni. Cattāropi hete tuṭṭhākārā eva.

Herein, ‘joyful’ means joy has arisen. The other words are synonyms for it. All four are simply aspects of satisfaction.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto “kiṃ nāma tvaṃ varaṃ dassasī”ti apasādento gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, disparaging him with the words, “What sort of boon can you give?” spoke a verse:

450.

450.

“Yo [P 5.0495] nattano maraṇaṃ bujjhasi tuvaṃ, hitāhitaṃ vinipātañca saggaṃ;

Giddho rase duccarite niviṭṭho, kiṃ tvaṃ varaṃ dassasi pāpadhamma.

“You who do not understand your own death, nor what is beneficial or harmful, nor ruin and heaven; greedy for tastes, entrenched in misconduct—what boon can you give, O you of wicked ways?”

451.

451.

“Ahañca taṃ ‘dehi vara’nti vajjaṃ, tvaṃ cāpi datvā na avākareyya;

Sandiṭṭhikaṃ kalahamimaṃ vivādaṃ, ko paṇḍito jānamupabbajeyyā”ti.

“And if I were to say to you, ‘Give a boon,’ and you, having promised, were then not to fulfill it—what wise person, knowingly, would enter into this immediate quarrel and dispute?”

Tattha [V 5.0489] yoti yo tvaṃ “maraṇadhammohamasmī”ti attanopi maraṇaṃ na bujjhasi na jānāsi, pāpakammameva karosi. Hitāhitanti “idaṃ me kammaṃ hitaṃ, idaṃ ahitaṃ, idaṃ vinipātaṃ nessati, idaṃ sagga”nti na jānāsi. Raseti manussamaṃsarase. Vajjanti vadeyyaṃ. Na avākareyyāti vācāya datvā “dehi me vara”nti vuccamāno na avākareyyāsi na dadeyyāsi. Upabbajeyyāti ko imaṃ kalahaṃ paṇḍito upagaccheyya.

Herein, ‘yo’ means: you who do not understand even your own death, that is, you do not know ‘I am subject to death,’ and you perform only evil deeds. ‘Hitāhitaṃ’ means: you do not know, ‘This action is beneficial for me, this is harmful; this will lead to ruin, this to heaven.’ ‘Rase’ means: in the taste of human flesh. ‘Vajjaṃ’ means: ‘I should say.’ ‘Na avākareyya’ means: having given your word, when told, ‘Give me the boon,’ you might not fulfill it, you might not give it. ‘Upabbajeyyā’ means: what wise person would enter into this quarrel?

Tato porisādo “nāyaṃ mayhaṃ saddahati, saddahāpessāmi na”nti gāthamāha –

Then the man-eater, thinking, “This man does not trust me; I must make him trust me,” spoke this verse:

452.

452.

“Na taṃ varaṃ arahati jantu dātuṃ, yaṃ vāpi datvā na avākareyya;

Varassu samma avikampamāno, pāṇaṃ cajitvānapi dassamevā”ti.

“A person is not worthy to grant a boon who, having promised it, would then fail to fulfill it. Choose, friend, without hesitation; I will give it, even if it means sacrificing my life.”

Tattha avikampamānoti anolīyamāno.

Herein, ‘avikampamāno’ means not hesitating.

Atha [M 5.0537] mahāsatto “ayaṃ ativiya sūro hutvā katheti, karissati me vacanaṃ, varaṃ gaṇhissāmi, sace pana “manussamaṃsaṃ na khāditabba’nti paṭhamameva varaṃ vārayissaṃ, ativiya kilamissati, paṭhamaṃ aññe tayo vare gahetvā pacchā etaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

Then the Great Being thought: “This one speaks as if he is very brave; he will do as I say. I will accept a boon. But if I were to ask for the boon ‘human flesh is not to be eaten’ as the very first one, he would be greatly burdened. First, I shall take the other three boons, and afterwards, I shall take this one.” Thinking thus, he said:

453.

453.

“Ariyassa ariyena sameti sakhyaṃ, paññassa paññāṇavatā sameti;

Passeyya taṃ vassasataṃ arogaṃ, etaṃ varānaṃ paṭhamaṃ varāmī”ti.

“The friendship of a noble one matches with a noble one; the wise one matches with the one possessing wisdom. May I see you for a hundred years in good health—this I choose as the first of the boons.”

Tattha [P 5.0496] ariyassāti ācāraariyassa. Sakhyanti sakhidhammo mittadhammo. Paññāṇavatāti ñāṇasampannena. Sametīti gaṅgodakaṃ viya yamunodakena saṃsandati. Dhātuso hi sattā saṃsandanti. Passeyya tanti sutasomo porisādassa ciraṃ jīvitaṃ icchanto viya paṭhamaṃ attano jīvitavaraṃ yācati. Paṇḍitassa hi “mama jīvitaṃ dehī”ti vattuṃ ayuttaṃ, apica so ‘mayhameva esa ārogyaṃ icchatī’ti cintetvā tussissatīti evamāha.

Herein, ‘ariyassa’ means of one with noble conduct. ‘Sakhyaṃ’ means friendship, the nature of a friend. ‘Paññāṇavatā’ means with one endowed with wisdom. ‘Sameti’ means it accords, it mingles—like the water of the Ganges mingling with the water of the Yamuna. For beings associate according to their nature. As for ‘Passeyya taṃ,’ Sutasoma, as if desiring long life for the man-eater, first asks for the boon of his own life. For it is not fitting for a wise one to say, ‘Give me my life’; rather, he spoke in this way so that the other would think, ‘He desires good health for me,’ and be pleased.

Sopi taṃ sutvāva “ayaṃ issariyā dhaṃsetvā idāni maṃsaṃ khāditukāmassa evaṃ mahāanatthakarassa mahācorassa mayhameva jīvitaṃ icchati, aho mama hitakāmo”ti tuṭṭhamānaso vañcetvā varassa gahitabhāvaṃ ajānitvā taṃ varaṃ dadamāno gāthamāha –

Hearing this, he too thought: ‘This King Sutasoma desires my life—mine, who has destroyed prosperity and now desires to eat human flesh, who am such a great bringer of harm, a great thief! How wonderful, he wishes for my welfare!’ With a delighted mind, not realizing that the boon had been strategically taken, and wishing to grant it to King Sutasoma, he spoke this verse:

454.

454.

“Ariyassa [V 5.0490] ariyena sameti sakhyaṃ, paññassa paññāṇavatā sameti;

Passāsi maṃ vassasataṃ arogaṃ, etaṃ varānaṃ paṭhamaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“The friendship of a noble one matches with a noble one; the wise one matches with the one possessing wisdom. You shall see me for a hundred years in good health—this I grant as the first of the boons.”

Tattha varānanti catunnaṃ varānaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Herein, ‘varānaṃ’ means the first of the four boons.

Tato bodhisatto āha –

Then King Sutasoma, wishing to take another boon, said:

455.

455.

“Ye khattiyāse idha bhūmipālā, muddhābhisittā katanāmadheyyā;

Na tādise bhūmipatī adesi, etaṃ varānaṃ dutiyaṃ varāmī”ti.

“Those kshatriyas here, lords of the earth, who are head-anointed and have been given names—do not eat such lords of the land. This I choose as the second of the boons.”

Tattha [M 5.0538] katanāmadheyyāti muddhani abhisittattāva “muddhābhisittā”ti katanāmadheyyā. Na tādiseti tādise khattiye na adesi mā khādi.

Herein, ‘katanāmadheyyā’ means that because they are anointed on the head, they are given the designation ‘head-anointed.’ ‘Na tādise’ means: do not eat, do not devour, such kshatriyas.

Iti so dutiyaṃ varaṃ gaṇhanto parosatānaṃ khattiyānaṃ jīvitavaraṃ gaṇhi. Porisādopissa dadamāno āha –

Thus, in choosing the second boon, King Sutasoma took the boon of life for a great many kings. Porisāda, wishing to grant the boon, said:

456.

456.

“Ye khattiyāse idha bhūmipālā, muddhābhisittā katanāmadheyyā;

Na tādise bhūmipatī ademi, etaṃ varānaṃ dutiyaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“Those kshatriyas here, lords of the earth, who are head-anointed and have been given names—such lords of the land I shall not eat. This I grant as the second of the boons.”

Kiṃ [P 5.0497] pana te tesaṃ saddaṃ suṇanti, na suṇantīti? Na sabbaṃ suṇanti. Porisādena hi rukkhassa dhūmajālaupaddavabhayena paṭikkamitvā aggi kato, aggino ca rukkhassa ca antare nisīditvā mahāsatto tena saddhiṃ kathesi, tasmā sabbaṃ asutvā upaḍḍhupaḍḍhaṃ suṇiṃsu. Te “idāni sutasomo porisādaṃ damessati, mā bhāyathā”ti aññamaññaṃ samassāsesuṃ. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Did those many kings hear the sound of the conversation between King Sutasoma and Porisāda? They did not hear everything. This is the truth: Porisāda, fearing that the smoke might harm the banyan tree, moved away and lit a fire. King Sutasoma spoke with Porisāda while sitting between the fire and the tree; therefore, not hearing everything, they heard only fragments. Those kings reassured one another, saying, 'Now the noble King Sutasoma will tame Porisāda; do not fear.' At that moment, King Sutasoma, wishing to take another boon, said:

457.

457.

“Parosataṃ khattiyā te gahītā, talāvutā assumukhā rudantā;

Sake te raṭṭhe paṭipādayāhi, etaṃ varānaṃ tatiyaṃ varāmī”ti.

“Over a hundred kshatriyas have been seized by you, their palms pierced and strung together, weeping with tearful faces. Restore them to their own kingdoms—this I choose as the third of the boons.”

Tattha parosatanti atirekasataṃ. Te gahītāti tayā gahitā. Talāvutāti hatthatalesu āvutā.

Herein, 'parosataṃ' means more than a hundred. 'Te gahītā' means seized by you. 'Talāvutā' means covered by the palms of their hands.

Iti [V 5.0491] mahāsatto tatiyaṃ varaṃ gaṇhanto tesaṃ khattiyānaṃ sakaraṭṭhaniyyātanavaraṃ gaṇhi. Kiṃkāraṇā? So akhādantopi verabhayena sabbe te dāse katvā araññeyeva vāseyya, māretvā vā chaḍḍeyya, paccantaṃ netvā vā vikkiṇeyya, tasmā tesaṃ sakaraṭṭhaniyyātanavaraṃ gaṇhi. Itaropissa dadamāno imaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, in choosing the third boon, King Sutasoma took the boon of returning those kings to their own countries. Why did he choose this? Because even if Porisāda did not eat them, out of fear of their enmity, he might enslave them all and keep them in the forest, or kill and abandon them, or take them to the frontier and sell them. Therefore, he chose the boon for them to be sent back to their own kingdoms. Porisāda, wishing to grant the boon to King Sutasoma, said:

458.

458.

“Parosataṃ khattiyā me gahītā, talāvutā assumukhā rudantā;

Sake te raṭṭhe paṭipādayāmi, etaṃ varānaṃ tatiyaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“Over a hundred kshatriyas have been seized by me, their palms pierced and strung together, weeping with tearful faces. I shall restore them to their own kingdoms—this I grant as the third of the boons.”

Catutthaṃ [M 5.0539] pana varaṃ gaṇhanto bodhisatto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then King Sutasoma, wishing to take the fourth boon, said:

459.

459.

“Chiddaṃ te raṭṭhaṃ byathitā bhayā hi, puthū narā leṇamanuppaviṭṭhā;

Manussamaṃsaṃ viramehi rāja, etaṃ varānaṃ catutthaṃ varāmī”ti.

“Your kingdom is gaping, distressed by fear; many people have entered hiding places. Abstain from human flesh, O King; this I choose as the fourth of the boons.”

Tattha [P 5.0498] chiddanti na ghanavāsaṃ tattha tattha gāmādīnaṃ uṭṭhitattā savivaraṃ. Byathitā bhayāhīti “porisādo idāni āgamissatī”ti tava bhayena kampitā. Leṇamanuppaviṭṭhāti dārake hatthesu gahetvā tiṇagahanādinilīyanaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Manussamaṃsanti duggandhaṃ jegucchaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ pajaha. Nissakkatthe vā upayogaṃ, manussamaṃsato viramāhīti attho.

In this context, 'chiddaṃ' means not densely inhabited because villages and such have been deserted here and there, leaving gaps. 'Byathitā bhayā hi' means shaken by fear of you, thinking, 'The man-eater will come now.' 'Leṇamanuppaviṭṭhā' means they have entered hiding places like thickets, taking their children by the hand. 'Manussamaṃsaṃ' means abandon foul, disgusting, repulsive human flesh. The sense is 'refrain from human flesh'.

Evaṃ vutte porisādo pāṇiṃ paharitvā hasanto “samma sutasoma kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathesi, kathāhaṃ tumhākaṃ etaṃ varaṃ dassāmi, sace gaṇhitukāmo, aññaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

When King Sutasoma said this, Porisāda struck his hands together and laughed mockingly, saying, 'Friend Sutasoma, why do you say such a thing? How can I grant you this boon? If you wish to take a boon, choose another.' Thus, wishing to reject that boon, he said:

460.

460.

“Addhā hi so bhakkho mama manāpo, etassa hetumhi vanaṃ paviṭṭho;

Sohaṃ kathaṃ etto upārameyyaṃ, aññaṃ varānaṃ catutthaṃ varassū”ti.

“Indeed, that food is pleasing to me; for its sake I entered the forest. How could I abstain from it? Choose another fourth boon!”

Tattha vananti rajjaṃ pahāya imaṃ vanaṃ paviṭṭho.

In this context, 'vanaṃ' means having abandoned the kingdom and entered this forest.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto “tvaṃ ‘manussamaṃsassa piyatarattā tato viramituṃ na sakkomī”ti vadasi. Yo hi piyaṃ nissāya pāpaṃ karoti, ayaṃ bālo”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then King Sutasoma said to Porisāda: 'Friend Porisāda, you say you cannot refrain from human flesh because you love it. That is true; but whoever does evil for the sake of what is dear is called a fool.' Wishing to explain this reason to Porisāda, he said:

461.

461.

“Na [V 5.0492] ve ‘piyaṃ me’ti janinda tādiso, attaṃ niraṃkacca piyāni sevati;

Attāva seyyo paramā ca seyyo, labbhā piyā ocitatthena pacchā”ti.

“Indeed, O King, a man like you should not pursue dear things while disregarding the self, thinking 'this is dear to me.' The self is indeed better, even better than the most excellent thing. Dear things can be obtained later by one who has developed his self.”

Tattha [M 5.0540] tādisoti janinda tādiso yuvā abhirūpo mahāyaso “idaṃ nāma me piya”nti piyavatthulobhena tattha attānaṃ niraṃkatvā sabbasugatīhi ceva sukhavisesehi ca cavitvā niraye pātetvā na ve piyāni sevati. Paramā ca seyyoti purisassa hi paramā piyavatthumhā attāva varataro. Kiṃkāraṇā? Labbhā piyāti, piyā nāma visayavasena ceva puññena ca ocitatthena vaḍḍhitatthena diṭṭhadhamme ceva parattha ca devamanussasampattiṃ patvā sakkā laddhuṃ.

In this context, 'tādiso' refers to a person like you—young, handsome, and of great fame—who, thinking 'this is dear to me' out of greed for beloved objects, disregards himself and, falling from all happy states and special pleasures, is cast into hell; such a one does not truly pursue what is dear. 'Paramā ca seyyo' means that for a person, the self is more excellent than the dearest of objects. Why? 'Labbhā piyā' means that beloved things, through the power of sense objects and merit, can be obtained later by one who has cultivated his body and mind, after attaining the prosperity of gods and humans in this life and the next.

Evaṃ vutte porisādo bhayappatto hutvā “ahaṃ sutasomena gahitaṃ varaṃ vissajjāpetumpi manussamaṃsato viramitumpi [P 5.0499] na sakkomi, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti assupuṇṇehi nettehi gāthamāha –

When King Sutasoma said this, Porisāda became filled with fear. Thinking, 'I can neither make King Sutasoma give up the boon he has chosen, nor can I refrain from human flesh; what shall I do?' He wept with eyes full of tears and, wishing Sutasoma to take another boon, said:

462.

462.

“Piyaṃ me mānusaṃ maṃsaṃ, sutasoma vijānahi;

Namhi sakkā nivāretuṃ, aññaṃ varaṃ samma varassū”ti.

“Human flesh is dear to me, Sutasoma, know this; I cannot be restrained from it; choose another boon, friend.”

Tattha vijānahīti tvampi jānāhi.

In this context, 'vijānahi' means 'you too should know'.

Tato bodhisatto āha –

Then King Sutasoma, wishing to teach the Dhamma by showing the danger of doing evil, said to Porisāda:

463.

463.

“Yo ve ‘piyaṃ me’ti piyānurakkhī, attaṃ niraṃkacca piyāni sevati;

Soṇḍova pitvā visamissapānaṃ, teneva so hoti dukkhī parattha.

One who, thinking ‘This is dear to me,’ protects what is dear, and neglecting himself, pursues dear things; like a drunkard having drunk a poisoned drink, he becomes miserable in the hereafter by that very act.

464.

464.

“Yo cīdha saṅkhāya piyāni hitvā, kicchenapi sevati ariyadhamme;

Dukkhitova pitvāna yathosadhāni, teneva so hoti sukhī paratthā”ti.

But one who here, having reflected and abandoned dear things, follows the noble Dhamma even with hardship; like a sick person drinking medicines, he becomes happy in the hereafter by that very act.

Tattha yo veti, samma porisāda, yo puriso “idaṃ me piya”nti pāpakiriyāya attānaṃ niraṃkatvā piyāni vatthūni sevati, so surāpemena visamissaṃ suraṃ pitvā soṇḍo viya [V 5.0493] tena pāpakammena parattha nirayādīsu dukkhī hoti. Saṅkhāyāti jānitvā tuletvā. Piyāni hitvāti adhammapaṭisaṃyuttāni piyāni chaḍḍetvā.

Herein, 'one who,' O friend Porisāda, refers to a person who, thinking 'this is dear to me,' disregarding himself through evil actions, indulges in dear things; like a drunkard who, out of love for liquor, drinks liquor mixed with poison, by that evil deed he suffers in hell and other realms hereafter. 'Having reflected' means knowing and weighing. 'Abandoned dear things' means giving up dear things associated with unrighteousness.

Evaṃ [M 5.0541] vutte porisādo kalūnaṃ paridevanto gāthamāha –

When this was said, Porisāda, wishing to lament piteously, spoke this verse:

465.

465.

“Ohāyahaṃ pitaraṃ mātarañca, manāpiye kāmaguṇe ca pañca;

Etassa hetumhi vanaṃ paviṭṭho, taṃ te varaṃ kinti mahaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“Having abandoned my father and mother, and the five pleasing strands of sensual pleasure, I entered the forest for the sake of this human flesh. How can I give you that boon?”

Tattha etassāti manussamaṃsassa. Kinti mahanti kinti katvā ahaṃ taṃ varaṃ demi.

Herein, ‘etassa’ means for the sake of human flesh. ‘Kinti mahaṃ’ means ‘In what way can I give that boon?’

Tato mahāsatto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, wishing to rebuke Porisāda’s words, spoke this verse:

466.

466.

“Na paṇḍitā diguṇamāhu vākyaṃ, saccappaṭiññāva bhavanti santo;

‘Varassu [P 5.0500] samma’ iti maṃ avoca, iccabravī tvaṃ na hi te sametī”ti.

“The wise do not speak a twofold word; the virtuous are of truthful promise. ‘Choose a boon, friend,’ you said to me. Thus you spoke, but it does not agree with your current words.”

Tattha diguṇanti, samma porisāda, paṇḍitā nāma ekaṃ vatvā puna taṃ visaṃvādentā dutiyaṃ vacanaṃ na kathenti. Iti maṃ avocāti, “samma sutasoma varassu vara”nti evaṃ maṃ abhāsasi. Iccabravīti tasmā yaṃ tvaṃ iti abravi, taṃ te idāni na sameti.

Herein, ‘diguṇaṃ’ means, friend Porisāda, the wise, having said one thing, do not speak a second word that contradicts it. ‘Iti maṃ avoca’ means, ‘Friend Sutasoma, choose a boon,’ thus you addressed me. ‘Iccabravi’ means because of what you spoke thus, it does not now agree with your words.

So puna rodanto eva gāthamāha –

Then, weeping again, Porisāda spoke this verse wishing to grant the boon:

467.

467.

“Apuññalābhaṃ ayasaṃ akittiṃ, pāpaṃ bahuṃ duccaritaṃ kilesaṃ;

Manussamaṃsassa kate upāgā, taṃ te varaṃ kinti mahaṃ dadeyya”nti.

“I have incurred the gain of demerit, disgrace, ill-fame, much evil, misconduct, and defilement for the sake of human flesh. How can I give you that boon?”

Tattha pāpanti kammapathaṃ appattaṃ. Duccaritanti kammapathappattaṃ. Kilesanti dukkhaṃ. Manussamaṃsassa kateti manussamaṃsassa hetu. Upāgāti upagatomhi. Taṃ teti taṃ tuyhaṃ kathāhaṃ varaṃ demi, mā maṃ vārayi, anukampaṃ kāruññaṃ mayi karohi, aññaṃ varaṃ gaṇhāhīti āha.

Herein, ‘pāpa’ refers to what has not reached the course of action. ‘Duccarita’ refers to what has reached the course of action. ‘Kilesa’ means suffering. ‘Manussamaṃsassa kate’ means for the reason of human flesh. ‘Upāgā’ means ‘I have incurred.’ ‘Taṃ te’ means ‘How can I give you that boon? Do not hinder me, show compassion and pity to me, choose another boon,’ he said.

Atha [M 5.0542] mahāsatto āha –

Then the Great Being, wishing to point out the boon previously granted by Porisāda, said:

468.

468.

“Na [V 5.0494] taṃ varaṃ arahati jantu dātuṃ, yaṃ vāpi datvā na avākareyya;

Varassu samma avikampamāno, pāṇaṃ cajitvānapi dassamevā”ti.

“A person should not give a boon that one would not fulfill after giving. Choose a boon, friend, without wavering; you said, ‘Even giving up my life, I will surely give it.’ Thus what you spoke before does not agree with what you say now.”

Evaṃ tena paṭhamaṃ vuttagāthaṃ āharitvā dassetvā varadāne ussāhento gāthā āha –

Thus, having pointed out the verse previously spoken by Porisāda, and while encouraging him to grant the boon, he spoke these verses:

469.

469.

“Pāṇaṃ cajanti santo nāpi dhammaṃ, saccappaṭiññāva bhavanti santo;

Datvā varaṃ khippamavākarohi, etena sampajja surājaseṭṭha.

“The virtuous give up life, but not the Dhamma; the virtuous are of truthful promise. Having given a boon, quickly fulfill it; be endowed with this truth, O best of good kings.”

470.

470.

“Caje dhanaṃ aṅgavarassa hetu, aṅgaṃ caje jīvitaṃ rakkhamāno;

Aṅgaṃ [P 5.0501] dhanaṃ jīvitañcāpi sabbaṃ, caje naro dhammamanussaranto”ti.

“One should give up wealth for the sake of a noble limb; one should give up a limb to protect life. A person, recollecting the Dhamma, should give up limb, wealth, and even all of life itself.”

Tattha pāṇanti jīvitaṃ. Santo nāma api jīvitaṃ cajanti, na dhammaṃ. Khippamavākarohīti idha khippaṃ mayhaṃ dehīti attho. Etenāti etena dhammena ceva saccena ca sampajja sampanno upapanno hohi. Surājaseṭṭhāti taṃ paggaṇhanto ālapati. Caje dhananti, samma porisāda, paṇḍito puriso hatthapādādimhi aṅge chijjamāne tassa rakkhaṇatthāya bahumpi dhanaṃ cajeyya. Dhammamanussarantoti aṅgadhanajīvitāni pariccajantopi “sataṃ dhammaṃ na vītikkamissāmī”ti evaṃ dhammaṃ anussaranto.

Therein, 'pāṇa' means life. The virtuous, indeed, give up even life, but not the Dhamma. 'Khippaṃ avākarohi' here means 'give it to me quickly.' 'Etena' means: by this Dhamma and by this truth, may you succeed, be accomplished, and be endowed. 'Surājaseṭṭha' is an address of honor to him. 'Caje dhanaṃ' means: friend Porisāda, a wise person would give up even much wealth for the sake of protecting a limb, such as a hand or foot, when it is being cut off. 'Dhammamanussaranto' means: even while relinquishing limbs, wealth, and life, one recollects the Dhamma thus: 'I will not transgress the Dhamma of the virtuous.'

Evaṃ mahāsatto imehi kāraṇehi taṃ sacce patiṭṭhāpetvā idāni attano gurubhāvaṃ dassetuṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being, having established Porisāda in truth by these reasons, now spoke a verse to show his status as a teacher:

471.

471.

“Yasmā hi dhammaṃ puriso vijaññā, ye cassa kaṅkhaṃ vinayanti santo;

Taṃ hissa dīpañca parāyaṇañca, na tena mittiṃ jirayetha pañño”ti.

“The person from whom one might understand the Dhamma, and the virtuous ones who dispel one's doubt—he is one's island and refuge; a wise man should not allow friendship with him to decay.”

Tattha [M 5.0543] yasmāti yamhā purisā. Dhammanti kusalākusalajotakaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Vijaññāti vijāneyya. Taṃ hissāti taṃ ācariyakulaṃ etassa puggalassa patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena dīpaṃ, uppanne bhaye gantabbaṭṭhānaṭṭhena parāyaṇañca. Na tena mittinti tena ācariyapuggalena saha so paṇḍito kenacipi kāraṇena mittiṃ na jīrayetha na vināseyya.

Therein, ‘yasmā’ means from which person. ‘Dhamma’ means the reason that illuminates the wholesome and unwholesome. ‘Vijaññā’ means one should understand. ‘Taṃ hissa’ means that teacher is an island for this person in the sense of being a support, and a refuge in the sense of being a place to go when fear has arisen. ‘Na tena mittiṃ’ means the wise person should not, for any reason, allow friendship with that teacher to decay or be destroyed.

Evañca pana vatvā, “samma porisāda, guṇavantassa ācariyassa vacanaṃ nāma bhindituṃ na [V 5.0495] vaṭṭati, ahañca taruṇakālepi tava piṭṭhiācariyo hutvā bahuṃ sikkhaṃ sikkhāpesiṃ, idānipi buddhalīlāya satārahā gāthā te kathesiṃ, tena me vacanaṃ kātuṃ arahasī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā porisādo “ayaṃ sutasomo mayhaṃ ācariyo ceva paṇḍito ca, varo cassa mayā dinno, kiṃ sakkā kātuṃ, ekasmiṃ attabhāve maraṇaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ, manussamaṃsaṃ na khādissāmi, dassāmissa vara”nti assudhārāhi pavattamānāhi uṭṭhāya sutasomanarindassa pādesu patitvā varaṃ dadamāno imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, Sutasoma said, ‘Friend Porisāda, it is not proper to break the word of a virtuous teacher. Even in your youth, I was your teacher and taught you much. Now, with the grace of a Buddha, I have spoken to you these verses worth a hundred. Therefore, you ought to do my bidding.’ Hearing this, Porisāda thought, ‘This Sutasoma is my teacher and a wise man, and a boon has been given to him by me. What can be done? Death in a single existence is certain. I will not eat human flesh; I will grant him the boon.’ With streams of tears flowing, he rose, fell at the feet of King Sutasoma, and while granting the boon, spoke this verse:

472.

472.

“Addhā [P 5.0502] hi so bhakkho mama manāpo, etassa hetumhi vanaṃ paviṭṭho;

Sace ca maṃ yācasi etamatthaṃ, etampi te samma varaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“Truly, that food is pleasing to me; for its sake I entered the forest. If you ask me for this thing, friend, I give even this to you as a boon.”

Atha naṃ mahāsatto evamāha – “samma, sīle ṭhitassa maraṇampi varaṃ, gaṇhāmi, mahārāja, tayā dinnaṃ varaṃ, ajja paṭṭhāya ariyapathe patiṭṭhitosi, evaṃ santepi taṃ yācāmi, sace te mayi sineho atthi, pañca sīlāni gaṇha, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, samma, dehi me sīlānī”ti. “Gaṇha mahārājā”ti. So mahāsattaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Mahāsattopi naṃ pañcasīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tattha sannipatitā bhummā devā mahāsatte pītiṃ janetvā “avīcito yāva bhavaggā añño porisādaṃ manussamaṃsato nivāretuṃ samattho nāma natthi, aho sutasomena dukkarataraṃ kata”nti mahantena saddena vanaṃ unnādentā sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu. Tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā cātumahārājikāti evaṃ yāva [M 5.0544] brahmalokā ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Rukkhe laggitarājānopi taṃ devatānaṃ sādhukārasaddaṃ suṇiṃsu. Rukkhadevatāpi sakavimāne ṭhitāva sādhukāramadāsi. Iti devatānaṃ saddova sūyati, rūpaṃ na dissati. Devatānaṃ sādhukārasaddaṃ sutvā rājāno cintayiṃsu – “sutasomaṃ nissāya no jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, dukkaraṃ kataṃ sutasomena porisādaṃ damentenā”ti bodhisattassa thutiṃ kariṃsu. Porisādo mahāsattassa pāde vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto – “samma, khattiye mocehī”ti āha. So cintesi “ahaṃ etesaṃ paccāmitto, ete mayā mocitā ‘gaṇhatha no paccāmitta’nti maṃ hiṃseyyuṃ, mayā jīvitaṃ cajantenapi na sakkā sutasomassa santikā gahitaṃ sīlaṃ bhindituṃ, iminā saddhiyeva gantvā mocessāmi, evaṃ me bhayaṃ na bhavissatī”ti. Atha bodhisattaṃ vanditvā, “sutasoma, ubhopi gantvā khattiye mocessāmā”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being said to him: "Friend, for one established in virtue, even death is preferable. I accept, great king, the boon you have given. From this day forward, you are established on the noble path. Even so, I ask this of you—if you have any affection for me, great king, take the five precepts." "Very well, friend, give me the precepts." "Take them, great king." He paid homage to the Great Being with the five-point prostration and sat to one side. The Great Being then established him in the five precepts. At that moment, the earth-dwelling deities who had gathered there, arousing joy in the Great Being, made the forest resound with a great noise as they gave their approval, saying: "From the Avģci hell up to the highest state of existence, there is no one else capable of restraining Porisāda from eating human flesh. Ah! Sutasoma has done what is exceedingly difficult!" Hearing their sound, from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Brahmā world, there was a single uproar. Even the kings hanging from the trees heard the approving sound of the deities. The tree deities, standing in their own celestial mansions, also gave their approval. Thus, only the sound of the deities was heard; their forms were not seen. Hearing the deities' approving sound, the kings reflected: "Through Sutasoma our lives have been saved. A difficult thing has been done by Sutasoma in taming Porisāda!" And they praised the Bodhisatta. Porisāda paid homage at the Great Being's feet and stood to one side. Then the Bodhisatta said to him: "Friend, release the khattiyas." He thought: "I am their enemy. If I release them, they might harm me, saying, 'Seize our enemy!' Even if it means giving up my life, I cannot break the precepts I have taken from Sutasoma. I will go with him and release them; in that way, I will have no fear." Then, paying homage to the Bodhisatta, he said: "Sutasoma, let us both go and release the khattiyas," and he spoke this verse:

473.

473.

“Satthā [V 5.0496][P 5.0503] ca me hosi sakhā ca mesi, vacanampi te samma ahaṃ akāsiṃ;

Tuvampi me samma karohi vākyaṃ, ubhopi gantvāna pamocayāmā”ti.

"You were my teacher and you were my friend; I did your bidding, friend. You too, friend, do my bidding; let us both go and release them."

Tattha satthāti saggamaggassa desitattā satthā ca, taruṇakālato paṭṭhāya sakhā ca.

Therein, 'satthā' means teacher because he taught the path to heaven, and 'sakhā' means friend from a young age onwards.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha –

Then the Bodhisatta said to him:

474.

474.

“Satthā ca te homi sakhā ca tyamhi, vacanampi me samma tuvaṃ akāsi;

Ahampi te samma karomi vākyaṃ, ubhopi gantvāna pamocayāmā”ti.

"I am your teacher and I am your friend; you did my bidding, friend. I too, friend, will do your bidding; let us both go and release them."

Evaṃ vatvā te upasaṅkamitvā āha –

Having said this, he approached them and said:

475.

475.

“Kammāsapādena viheṭhitattha, talāvutā assumukhā rudantā;

Na jātu dubbhetha imassa rañño, saccappaṭiññaṃ me paṭissuṇāthā”ti.

"You have been harassed by Kammāsapāda, with palms pierced, weeping with tearful faces; never be malicious to this king. Accept my pledge of truth."

Tattha [M 5.0545] kammāsapādenāti idaṃ mahāsatto “ubhopi gantvāna pamocayāmā”ti sampaṭicchitvā “khattiyā nāma mānathaddhā honti, muttamattāva ‘iminā mayaṃ viheṭhitamhā’ti porisādaṃ potheyyumpi haneyyumpi, na kho panesa tesu dubbhissati, ahaṃ ekakova gantvā paṭiññaṃ tāva nesaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā tattha gantvā te hatthatale āvunitvā aggapādaṅgulīhi bhūmiṃ phusamānāhi rukkhasākhāsu olaggite vātappaharaṇakāle nāgadantesu olaggitakuraṇḍakadāmāni viya samparivattante addasa. Tepi taṃ disvā “idānimhā mayaṃ arogā”ti ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ raviṃsu. Atha ne mahāsatto “mā bhāyitthā”ti assāsetvā “mayā porisādo damito, tumhākaṃ abhayaṃ gahitaṃ, tumhe pana me vacanaṃ karothā”ti vatvā evamāha. Tattha na jātūti ekaṃseneva na dubbhetha.

Therein, regarding 'by Kammāsapāda': the Great Being, having agreed, 'Let us both go and release them,' thought to himself, 'Khattiyas are proud and stubborn. As soon as they are freed, they might strike or even kill Porisāda, saying, "We have been harassed by this one." But he will not be malicious towards them. I will go alone and first obtain a promise from them.' Having thought thus, he went there and saw them with their palms pierced, their toes just touching the ground, hanging from the branches of trees, turning round and round like dry garlands of kuraᅇᄉaka flowers hanging from ivory hooks when struck by the wind. They, seeing him, cried out loudly all at once, saying, 'Now we are safe!' Then the Great Being reassured them, saying, 'Do not be afraid, O kings. Porisāda has been tamed by me and safety has been secured for you; therefore, do as I say,' and he spoke thus. Therein, 'na jātu' means that on no account should you be malicious.

Te āhaṃsu –

They said:

476.

476.

“Kammāsapādena viheṭhitamhā, talāvutā assumukhā rudantā;

Na jātu dubbhema imassa rañño, saccappaṭiññaṃ te paṭissuṇāmā”ti.

"We have been harassed by Kammāsapāda, with palms pierced, weeping with tearful faces; never would we be malicious to this king. We accept your truthful pledge."

Tattha [V 5.0497][P 5.0504] paṭissuṇāmāti “evaṃ paṭiññaṃ adhivāsema sampaṭicchāma, apica kho pana mayaṃ kilantā kathetuṃ na sakkoma, tumhe sabbasattānaṃ saraṇaṃ, tumheva kathetha, mayaṃ vo vacanaṃ sutvā paṭiññaṃ dassāmā”ti.

Therein, 'we accept' means: 'We agree to such a promise and accept it. However, we are too exhausted to speak. You are the refuge of all beings; you yourself speak, and having heard your words, we will give our promise.'

Atha ne bodhisatto “tena hi paṭiññaṃ dethā”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, saying, 'In that case, give your promise,' spoke this verse:

477.

477.

“Yathā pitā vā atha vāpi mātā, anukampakā atthakāmā pajānaṃ,.

"Just as a father or even a mother, compassionate and desiring the welfare of their children,"

Evameva vo hotu ayañca rājā, tumhe ca vo hotha yatheva puttā”ti.

"Even so may this king be to you, and may you be to him just like sons."

Atha [M 5.0546] naṃ tepi sampaṭicchamānā imaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then they, accepting this, spoke this verse:

478.

478.

“Yathā pitā vā atha vāpi mātā, anukampakā atthakāmā pajānaṃ;

Evameva no hotu ayañca rājā, mayampi hessāma yatheva puttā”ti.

"Just as a father or even a mother, compassionate and desiring the welfare of their children; even so may this king be to us, and we too shall be to him just like sons."

Tattha tumhe ca voti vo-kāro nipātamattaṃ.

Here, the ‘vo’ in ‘tumhe ca vo’ is merely a particle.

Iti mahāsatto tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā porisādaṃ pakkositvā “ehi, samma, khattiye mocehī”ti āha. So khaggaṃ gahetvā ekassa rañño bandhanaṃ chindi. Rājā sattāhaṃ nirāhāro vedanappatto saha bandhanachedā mucchito bhūmiyaṃ pati. Taṃ disvā mahāsatto kāruññaṃ katvā, “samma porisāda, mā evaṃ chindī”ti ekaṃ rājānaṃ ubhohi hatthehi daḷhaṃ gahetvā ure katvā “idāni bandhanaṃ chindāhī”ti āha. Porisādo khaggena chindi. Mahāsatto thāmasampannatāya naṃ ure nipajjāpetvā orasaputtaṃ viya muducittena otāretvā bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpesi. Evaṃ sabbepi te bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā vaṇe dhovitvā dārakānaṃ kaṇṇato suttakaṃ viya saṇikaṃ rajjuyo nikkaḍḍhitvā pubbalohitaṃ dhovitvā vaṇe niddose katvā, “samma porisāda, ekaṃ rukkhatacaṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā āharā”ti āharāpetvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā tesaṃ hatthatalāni makkhesi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva vaṇo phāsukaṃ ahosi. Porisādo taṇḍulaṃ gahetvā taralaṃ paci[P 5.0505], ubho janā parosataṃ khattiye pāyesuṃ. Iti te sabbeva santappitā, sūriyo atthaṅgato. Punadivase pāto ca majjhanhike ca sāyañca taralameva pāyetvā tatiyadivase sasitthakayāguṃ pāyesuṃ, tāvatā te arogā ahesuṃ.

Then the Great Being, having accepted their pledge, called the man-eater and said, “Come, friend, release the kings.” Taking a sword, he cut the bonds of one king. The king, having been without food for seven days and overcome with pain, fainted and fell to the ground as soon as his bonds were cut. Seeing this, the Great Being, filled with compassion, said, “Friend man-eater, do not cut them in this way.” He firmly grasped one king with both hands, held him against his chest, and said, “Now cut the bonds.” The man-eater cut them with the sword. Due to his great strength, the Great Being laid the king on his chest and, with a tender heart, gently lowered him as if he were his own son, placing him on the ground. In this way, he laid all of them on the ground, washed their wounds, and slowly pulled out the ropes from their ears as gently as pulling a thread from a child's freshly pierced ear. He washed away the pus and blood, cleansed the wounds, and said, “Friend man-eater, grind a piece of tree bark on a stone and bring it.” Having had it brought, he performed an act of truth and smeared it on the palms of their hands. Instantly, the wounds were healed. The man-eater took rice and cooked a strained gruel, and both of them fed it to the more than one hundred kings. Thus, they were all refreshed, and the sun set. The next day, in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, they fed them only strained gruel. On the third day, they fed them gruel with rice grains. By then, they were restored to health.

Atha [V 5.0498] ne mahāsatto “gantuṃ sakkhissathā”ti pucchitvā “gacchāmā”ti vutte “ehi, samma porisāda, sakaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gacchāmā”ti āha.
