So rodamāno tassa pādesu patitvā “tvaṃ, samma, rājāno gahetvā gaccha, ahaṃ idheva vanamūlaphalāni khādanto vasissāmī”ti āha. “Samma, idha kiṃ karissasi, ramaṇīyaṃ te raṭṭhaṃ, bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kārehī”ti. “Samma kiṃ kathesi, na sakkā mayā tattha gantuṃ, sakalanagaravāsino hi [M 5.0547] me verino, te ‘iminā mayhaṃ mātā khāditā, mayhaṃ pitā, mayhaṃ bhātā’ti maṃ paribhāsissanti, ‘gaṇhatha imaṃ cora’nti ekekadaṇḍena vā ekekaleḍḍunā vā maṃ jīvitā voropessanti, ahañca tumhākaṃ santike sīlesu patiṭṭhito, jīvitahetupi na sakkā mayā paraṃ māretuṃ, tasmā nāhaṃ gacchāmi, ahaṃ manussamaṃsato viratattā kittakaṃ jīvissāmi, idāni mama tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ natthī”ti roditvā “gacchatha tumhe”ti āha. Atha mahāsatto tassa piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā, “samma porisāda, mā cintayi, sutasomo nāmāhaṃ, mayā tādiso kakkhaḷo pharuso vinīto, bārāṇasivāsikesu kiṃ vattabbaṃ atthi, ahaṃ taṃ tattha patiṭṭhāpessāmi, asakkonto attano rajjaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā dassāmī”ti vatvā “tumhākampi nagare mama verino atthiyevā”ti vutte “iminā mama vacanaṃ karontena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, yena kenaci upāyena porāṇakayase patiṭṭhapetabbo esa mayā”ti cintetvā tassa palobhanatthāya nagarasampattiṃ vaṇṇento āha –

Then the Great Being, having asked them, “Will you be able to go?” and being told, “We will be able to go,” said, “Come, friend man-eater, let us go to your own kingdom.” Weeping, he fell at the Great Being's feet and said, “You, friend, take the kings and go. I will stay right here in the forest, eating roots and fruits.” “Friend, what will you do here? Your kingdom is delightful; rule in Bārāṇasī.” “Friend, what are you saying? I cannot go there; all the city dwellers are my enemies. They will revile me, saying, ‘By him my mother was eaten, my father, my brother.’ They will seize me, shouting, ‘Catch this thief!’ and with a single stick or a single stone, they will take my life. And I, established in virtue in your presence, cannot kill another even to save my own life. Therefore, I will not go. Having abstained from human flesh, how long will I live? Now I shall see you no more.” Weeping, he said, “You go.” Then the Great Being stroked his back and said, “Friend man-eater, do not worry. I am Sutasoma; I have tamed one as harsh and cruel as you. What need is there to speak of the residents of Bārāṇasī? I will establish you there. If I am unable, I will divide my own kingdom in two and give half to you.” When he replied, “Even in your city, my enemies exist,” the Great Being thought, “By acting on my word, he has done a difficult deed. By some means, I must establish him in his former glory.” To entice him, he praised the city’s prosperity, saying:

479.

479.

“Catuppadaṃ sakuṇañcāpi maṃsaṃ, sūdehi randhaṃ sukataṃ suniṭṭhitaṃ;

Sudhaṃva indo paribhuñjiyāna, hitvā katheko ramasī araññe.

“Meat of quadrupeds and also of birds, well-cooked and well-prepared by cooks; having partaken of it as Indra does of nectar, how can you, having abandoned it, delight alone in the forest?

480.

480.

“Tā [P 5.0506] khattiyā vellivilākamajjhā, alaṅkatā samparivārayitvā;

Indaṃva devesu pamodayiṃsu, hitvā katheko ramasī araññe.

“Those Khattiya women, slender-waisted, adorned, having surrounded you, delighted you as celestial maidens do Indra among the gods. Having abandoned them, how can you, alone, delight in the forest?

481.

481.

“Tambūpadhāne bahugoṇakamhi, subhamhi sabbassayanamhi saṅge;

Seyyassa majjhamhi sukhaṃ sayitvā

Hitvā katheko ramasī araññe.

“On a bed with red cushions, richly carpeted, in a beautiful chamber of a tiered palace; having slept happily in the middle of such a bed, how can you, having abandoned it, delight alone in the forest?

482.

482.

“Pāṇissaraṃ kumbhathūṇaṃ nisīthe, athopi ve nippurisampi tūriyaṃ;

Bahuṃ sugītañca suvāditañca, hitvā katheko ramasī araññe.

“The sound of hand-drums and pot-drums in the night, and even music played by a female orchestra, with many songs beautifully sung and played; having abandoned such prosperity, how can you, alone, delight in the forest?

483.

483.

“Uyyānasampannaṃ [M 5.0548] pahūtamālyaṃ, migājinūpetaṃ puraṃ surammaṃ;

Hayehi nāgehi rathehupetaṃ, hitvā katheko ramasī araññe”ti.

“Your delightful city, endowed with parks, abundant with flowers, filled with deer and antelope; your city, equipped with horses, elephants, and chariots—having abandoned it, how can you, alone, delight in the forest?”

Tattha [V 5.0499] sukatanti nānappakārehi suṭṭhu kataṃ. Suniṭṭhitanti nānāsambhārayojanena suṭṭhu niṭṭhitaṃ. Kathekoti kathaṃ eko. Ramasīti mūlaphalādīni khādanto kathaṃ ramissasi, “ehi, mahārāja, gamissāmā”ti. Vellivilākamajjhāti ettha vellīti rāsi, vilākamajjhāti vilaggamajjhā. Uttattaghanasuvaṇṇarāsipabhā ceva tanudīghamajjhā cāti dasseti. Devesūti devalokesu accharā indaṃ viya ramaṇīye bārāṇasinagare pubbe taṃ pamodayiṃsu, tā hitvā idha kiṃ karissasi, “ehi, samma, gacchāmā”ti. Tambūpadhāneti rattūpadhāne. Sabbassayanamhīti sabbattharaṇatthate sayane. Saṅgeti anekabhūmike dassetvā addharattaaṅgayutte tattha tvaṃ pubbe sayīti attho. Sukhanti tādisassa sayanassa majjhamhi sukhaṃ sayitvāna idāni kathaṃ araññe ramissasi, “ehi gacchāma, sammā”ti. Nisītheti rattibhāge. Hitvāti evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ chaḍḍetvā. Uyyānasampannaṃ pahūtamālyanti, mahārāja, tava uyyānasampannaṃ nānāvidhapupphaṃ. Migājinūpetaṃ puraṃ surammanti [P 5.0507] taṃ uyyānaṃ migājinaṃ nāma nāmena, tena upetaṃ purampi te suṭṭhu rammaṃ. Hitvāti evarūpaṃ manoramaṃ nagaraṃ chaḍḍetvā.

There, ‘sukataṃ’ (well-made) means ‘excellently crafted in various ways’. ‘Suniṭṭhitaṃ’ (well-finished) means ‘excellently completed with various materials’. ‘Kathekoti’ (how alone) means ‘how alone’. ‘Ramasīti’ (you delight) means ‘how will you delight eating roots and fruits?’ (and implies the speaker's thought) ‘Come, great king, let us go!’ ‘Vellivilākamajjhā’—here, ‘vellī’ means a heap, and ‘vilākamajjhā’ means slender-waisted. This shows both the radiance of a heap of refined molten gold and a slender, elongated waist. ‘Devesu’ (among the gods)—in the heavenly realms, celestial nymphs delighted you as they once did Indra in the charming city of Bārāṇasī. Having abandoned them, what will you do here? (and implies the speaker's thought) ‘Come, friend, let us go!’ ‘Tambūpadhāne’ (with a red cushion) means ‘with a red pillow’. ‘Sabbassayanamhī’ (in all bedding) means ‘in a bed spread with all coverings’. ‘Saṅge’ (in the midst of): this refers to a many-tiered palace with apartments for midnight dalliance; the meaning is that you once slept there. ‘Sukhaṃ’ (happily) means, ‘having slept happily in the middle of such a bed, how will you now find joy in the forest?’ (and implies the speaker's thought) ‘Come, let us go, friend!’ ‘Nisīthe’ (at night) means ‘during the nighttime’. ‘Hitvā’ (having abandoned) means ‘having discarded such prosperity’. ‘Uyyānasampannaṃ pahūtamālyaṃ’ (endowed with parks, abundant with flowers) means, ‘Great king, your city is endowed with parks having various kinds of flowers’. ‘Migājinūpetaṃ puraṃ surammaṃ’ (a beautiful city associated with Migājina) means, ‘that park is known by the name Migājina, and thus your city too is exceedingly charming’. ‘Hitvā’ (having abandoned) means ‘having forsaken such a delightful city’.

Iti mahāsatto “appeva nāmesa pubbe upabhuttaparibhogarasaṃ saritvā gantukāmo bhaveyyā”ti paṭhamaṃ bhojanena palobhesi, dutiyaṃ kilesena, tatiyaṃ sayanena, catutthaṃ naccagītavāditena, pañcamaṃ uyyānena ceva nagarena cāti imehi ettakehi palobhetvā “ehi, mahārāja, ahaṃ taṃ ādāya gantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā pacchā sakaraṭṭhaṃ gamissāmi, sace bārāṇasirajjaṃ na labhissasi, upaḍḍharajjaṃ te dassāmi, kiṃ te araññavāsena, mama vacanaṃ karohī”ti āha. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā gantukāmo hutvā “sutasomo mayhaṃ atthakāmo anukampako, paṭhamaṃ maṃ kalyāṇe patiṭṭhāpetvā ‘idāni porāṇakayaseva patiṭṭhāpessāmī’ti vadati, sakkhissati cesa patiṭṭhāpetuṃ, iminā saddhiṃyeva gantuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ me araññavāsenā”ti cintetvā [M 5.0549] tuṭṭhacitto tassa guṇaṃ nissāya vaṇṇaṃ kathetukāmo “samma, sutasoma, kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggato sādhutaraṃ, pāpamittasaṃsaggato vā pāpataraṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā āha –

Thus, the Great Being thought, ‘Perhaps, remembering the taste of delights formerly enjoyed, he may wish to go.’ First, he tempted him with food, second with sensual pleasures, third with a bed, fourth with music and song, and fifth with parks and the city. Having tempted him with these five means, he said, ‘Come, great king, I will take you and establish you in the kingship of Bārāṇasī, and afterward go to my own kingdom. If you do not obtain the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, I will give you half of my kingdom. What use is this forest life to you? Heed my words.’ Hearing his words, the man-eater became desirous of going and thought, ‘Sutasoma desires my welfare and is compassionate. Having first established me in virtue, he now says, “I will establish you in your former glory.” And he will be able to establish me. It is fitting to go with him alone. What use is this forest life to me?’ With a joyful mind, wishing to speak in praise of the Great Being’s virtues, he said, ‘Friend Sutasoma, there is nothing better than association with a good friend, and nothing worse than association with a wicked friend.’ Then he spoke:

484.

484.

“Kāḷapakkhe yathā cando, hāyateva suve suve;

Kāḷapakkhūpamo rāja, asataṃ hoti samāgamo.

“Just as the moon in the dark fortnight wanes day by day, O king, so too is association with the wicked like the dark fortnight.”

485.

485.

“Yathāhaṃ rasakamāgamma, sūdaṃ kāpurisādhamaṃ;

Akāsiṃ pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, yena gacchāmi duggatiṃ.

Because of relying on Rasaka the cook, that most wretched of men, I committed that evil deed by which I shall go to a state of woe.

486.

486.

“Sukkapakkhe [V 5.0500] yathā cando, vaḍḍhateva suve suve;

Sukkapakkhūpamo rāja, sataṃ hoti samāgamo.

Just as the moon in the bright fortnight grows day by day, O king, so too the association with the virtuous is like the bright fortnight.

487.

487.

“Yathāhaṃ tuvamāgamma, sutasoma vijānahi;

Kāhāmi kusalaṃ kammaṃ, yena gacchāmi suggatiṃ.

Because of you, O Sutasoma, know this: I will perform wholesome deeds by which I shall go to a happy destination.

488.

488.

“Thale yathā vāri janinda vuṭṭhaṃ, anaddhaneyyaṃ na ciraṭṭhitīkaṃ;

Evampi [P 5.0508] hoti asataṃ samāgamo, anaddhaneyyo udakaṃ thaleva.

Just as rain fallen on dry land, O lord of men, is not long-lasting and does not endure for long; even so is association with the wicked short-lived, like water on dry land.

489.

489.

“Sare yathā vāri janinda vuṭṭhaṃ, ciraṭṭhitīkaṃ naravīraseṭṭha;

Evampi ve hoti sataṃ samāgamo, ciraṭṭhitīko udakaṃ sareva.

Just as rain fallen into a lake, O lord of men, O best of heroes, endures for a long time; even so indeed is association with the virtuous long-lasting, like water in a lake.

490.

490.

“Abyāyiko hoti sataṃ samāgamo, yāvampi tiṭṭheyya tatheva hoti;

Khippañhi veti asataṃ samāgamo, tasmā sataṃ dhammo asabbhi ārakā”ti.

Association with the virtuous is imperishable; however long it lasts, it remains just the same. For association with the wicked quickly vanishes; therefore, the nature of the virtuous is far from that of the ignoble.

Tattha suve suveti divase divase. Anaddhaneyyanti na addhānakkhamaṃ. Sareti samudde. Naravīraseṭṭhāti naresu vīriyena seṭṭha. Udakaṃ sarevāti samudde vuṭṭhaudakaṃ viya. Abyāyikoti avigacchanako. Yāvampi [M 5.0550] tiṭṭheyyāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ jīvitaṃ tiṭṭheyya, tattakaṃ kālaṃ tatheva hoti, na jīrati sappurisehi mittabhāvoti.

Here, 'suve suve' means 'day by day'. 'Anaddhaneyyaṃ' means 'not able to endure for long'. 'Sare' refers to the ocean. 'Naravīraseṭṭha' means 'the foremost in energy among men'. 'Udakaṃ sareva' means 'like water that has fallen into the ocean'. 'Abyāyiko' means 'not passing away'. 'Yāvampi tiṭṭheyya' means 'for as long as life lasts, for that long it is just so; the friendship with good people does not decay'.

Iti porisādo sattahi gāthāhi mahāsattasseva vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Mahāsattopi porisādañca te ca rājāno gahetvā attano paccantagāmaṃ agamāsi. Paccantagāmavāsino mahāsattaṃ disvā nagaraṃ gantvā amaccānaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Amaccā balakāyaṃ ādāya gantvā parivārayiṃsu. Mahāsatto tena parivārena bārāṇasirajjaṃ agamāsi. Antarāmagge janapadavāsino bodhisattassa paṇṇākāraṃ datvā anugacchiṃsu, mahanto parivāro ahosi, tena saddhiṃ bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā porisādassa putto rājā hoti, senāpati kāḷahatthiyeva. Nāgarā rañño ārocayiṃsu – “mahārāja, sutasomo kira porisādaṃ dametvā ādāya idhāgacchati, nagaramassa pavisituṃ na dassāmā”ti sīghaṃ nagaradvārāni pidahitvā āvudhahatthā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahāsatto dvārānaṃ pihitabhāvaṃ ñatvā porisādañca parosatañca rājāno ohāya katipayehi amaccehi saddhiṃ āgantvā “ahaṃ sutasomarājā, dvāraṃ vivarathā”ti āha. Purisā gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ. So “khippaṃ [V 5.0501] vivarathā”ti vivarāpesi. Mahāsatto nagaraṃ pāvisi. Rājā ca kāḷahatthi cassa paccuggamanaṃ [P 5.0509] katvā ādāya pāsādaṃ āropayiṃsu.

Thus, the man-eater praised the Great Being with these seven verses. The Great Being then took the man-eater and the kings and went to his border village. When the inhabitants of the border village saw the Great Being, they went to the city and informed the ministers. The ministers, taking their forces, went and surrounded him. Accompanied by that retinue, the Great Being proceeded to the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. Along the way, the inhabitants of the districts gave gifts to the Bodhisatta and followed him, so that there was a great entourage; with them, he reached Bārāṇasī. At that time, the man-eater’s son was the king, and Kāḷahatthi was the general. The citizens reported to the king: 'Great King, it is said that Sutasoma has tamed the man-eater and is bringing him here; we will not allow him to enter the city.' They quickly closed the city gates and stood with weapons in hand. The Great Being, realizing the gates were closed, left the man-eater and the more than one hundred kings and approached with a few ministers, saying, 'I am King Sutasoma, open the gate!' The men went and told the king. He ordered, 'Open it quickly!' and had it opened. The Great Being entered the city. The king and Kāḷahatthi came out to meet him and, taking him, led him up to the palace.

So rājapallaṅke nisīditvā porisādassa aggamahesiṃ sesāmacce ca pakkosāpetvā kāḷahatthiṃ āha – “kāḷahatthi, kasmā rañño nagaraṃ pavisituṃ na dethā”ti? “So rajjaṃ kārento imasmiṃ nagare bahū manusse khādi, khattiyehi akattabbaṃ kari, sakalajambudīpaṃ chiddamakāsi, evarūpo pāpadhammo, tena kāraṇenā”ti. “Idāni ‘so evarūpaṃ karissatī’ti mā cintayittha, ahaṃ taṃ dametvā sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesiṃ, jīvitahetupi kañci na viheṭhessati, natthi vo tato bhayaṃ, evaṃ mā karittha, puttehi nāma mātāpitaro paṭijaggitabbā, mātāpituposakā hi saggaṃ gacchanti, itare niraya”nti evaṃ so nicāsane nisinnassa puttarājassa ovādaṃ datvā, “kāḷahatthi, tvaṃ rañño sahāyo ceva sevako ca, raññāpi mahante issariye patiṭṭhāpito, tayāpi rañño atthaṃ carituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti senāpatimpi anusāsitvā, “devi, tvampi kulagehā āgantvā tassa santike aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ patvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhippattā, tayāpi tassa atthaṃ carituṃ [M 5.0551] vaṭṭatī”ti deviyāpi ovādaṃ datvā tamevatthaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ dhammaṃ desento gāthā āha –

Seated on the royal throne, he summoned the man-eater’s chief queen and the other ministers, and said to Kāḷahatthi, 'Kāḷahatthi, why do you not allow the king to enter the city?' 'While ruling, he devoured many people in this city, did what should not be done by kings, and made all of Jambudīpa full of gaps; he is of such wicked nature—that is why.' 'Do not think now that he will do such things. I have tamed him and established him in the precepts; he will not harm anyone even for the sake of his life. You have nothing to fear from him. Do not act in this way. Children should look after their parents; for those who support their parents go to heaven, the others to hell.' In this way, he gave advice to the prince who was seated on a low seat, and then exhorted the general, 'Kāḷahatthi, you are both the king’s friend and servant, and you have been established in great power by the king; it is also right for you to act for the king’s benefit.' He also gave advice to the queen, saying, 'O Queen, you too, having come from your parental home and attained the rank of chief queen in his presence, have prospered with sons and daughters; it is also right for you to act for his benefit.' And to bring that matter to a conclusion, teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

491.

491.

“Na so rājā yo ajeyyaṃ jināti, na so sakhā yo sakhāraṃ jināti;

Na sā bhariyā yā patino na vibheti, na te puttā ye na bharanti jiṇṇaṃ.

He is no king who overcomes those who should not be overcome; he is no friend who overcomes his friend; she is no wife who does not fear her husband; they are no sons who do not support their aged parents.

492.

492.

“Na sā sabhā yattha na santi santo, na te santo ye na bhaṇanti dhammaṃ;

Rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ, dhammaṃ bhaṇantāva bhavanti santo.

That is no assembly where the virtuous are not present; they are not virtuous who do not speak the Dhamma. Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, only those who speak the Dhamma are indeed virtuous.

493.

493.

“Nābhāsamānaṃ jānanti, missaṃ bālehi paṇḍitaṃ;

Bhāsamānañca jānanti, desentaṃ amataṃ padaṃ.

They do not recognize a wise man when he is mixed with fools if he does not speak; but they do recognize him when he speaks, teaching the state of the deathless.

494.

494.

“Bhāsaye jotaye dhammaṃ, paggaṇhe isinaṃ dhajaṃ;

Subhāsitaddhajā isayo, dhammo hi isinaṃ dhajo”ti.

One should speak and illuminate the Dhamma; one should uphold the banner of the sages. Sages have well-spoken words as their banner, for the Dhamma is indeed the banner of the sages.

Tattha [P 5.0510] ajeyyanti ajeyyā nāma mātāpitaro, te jinanto rājā nāma na hoti. Sace tvampi pitu santakaṃ rajjaṃ labhitvā tassa paṭisattu hosi, akiccakārī nāma bhavissasi[V 5.0502]. Sakhāraṃ jinātīti kūṭaḍḍena jināti. Sace tvaṃ, kāḷahatthi, raññā saddhiṃ mittadhammaṃ na pūresi, adhammaṭṭho hutvā niraye nibbattissasi. Na vibhetīti na bhāyati. Sace tvaṃ rañño na bhāyasi, bhariyādhamme ṭhitā nāma na hosi, akiccakārī nāma bhavissasi. Jiṇṇanti mahallakaṃ. Tasmiñhi kāle abharantā puttā puttā nāma na honti.

Here, 'those who should not be overcome' refers to parents; a king who overcomes them is no true king. If you, having obtained your father's kingdom, become his enemy, you will be a wrongdoer. 'Overcomes his friend' means he overcomes him by cheating. If you, Kāḷahatthi, do not fulfill the duties of friendship with the king, you will be unrighteous and be reborn in hell. 'Does not fear' means she is not afraid. If you are not afraid of the king, you are not established in the duties of a wife and will be a wrongdoer. 'Aged' means the elderly. For at that time, sons who do not support them are not true sons.

Santoti paṇḍitā. Ye na bhaṇanti dhammanti ye pucchitā saccasabhāvaṃ na vadanti, na te paṇḍitā nāma. Dhammaṃ bhaṇantāvāti ete rāgādayo pahāya parassa hitānukampakā hutvā sabhāvaṃ bhaṇantāva paṇḍitā nāma honti. Nābhāsamānanti na abhāsamānaṃ. Amataṃ padanti amatamahānibbānaṃ desentaṃ “paṇḍito”ti jānanti, teneva porisādo maṃ ñatvā pasannacitto cattāro vare datvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhito. Bhāsayeti [M 5.0552] paṇḍito puriso dhammaṃ bhāseyya joteyya, buddhādayo isayo yasmā dhammo etesaṃ dhajo, tasmā subhāsitaddhajā nāma subhāsitaṃ paggaṇhanti, bālā pana subhāsitaṃ paggaṇhantā nāma natthīti.

'The good' (santo) means the wise. Those who, when asked about the true nature of things, do not speak the truth, are not called wise. 'Those who speak the Dhamma' means those who, having abandoned lust and the like, and being compassionate for the welfare of others, speak according to the truth—they are called the wise. 'Nābhāsamānaṃ' means not speaking. 'The deathless state' means the great Nibbāna. They recognize as 'wise' one who teaches it; thus, knowing me, with a serene mind, Porisāda gave four boons and was established in the five precepts. 'Let the wise proclaim' means a wise person should speak and illuminate the Dhamma. Since the Dhamma is the banner of the seers—the Buddhas and others—they are called 'those whose banner is well-spoken words' and they uphold what is well-spoken, but fools do not uphold well-spoken words.

Imassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā rājā ca senāpati ca devī ca tuṭṭhā “gacchāma, mahārāja, ānemā”ti vatvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā nāgare sannipātetvā “tumhe mā bhāyittha, rājā kira dhamme patiṭṭhito, etha naṃ ānemā”ti mahājanaṃ ādāya mahāsattaṃ purato katvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā kappake upaṭṭhāpetvā kappitakesamassuṃ nhātānulittapasādhitaṃ rājānaṃ ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisiñcitvā nagaraṃ pavesesuṃ. Porisādo rājā hutvā parosatānaṃ khattiyānaṃ mahāsattassa ca mahāsakkāraṃ kāresi. “Sutasomanarindena kira porisādaṃ dametvā rajje patiṭṭhāpito”ti sakalajambudīpe mahākolāhalaṃ udapādi. Indapatthanagaravāsinopi “rājā no āgacchatū”ti dūtaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. So tattha māsamattaṃ vasitvā, “samma, gacchāmahaṃ, tvaṃ appamatto hohi, nagaradvāresu ca majjhe cāti pañca dānasālāyo kārehi, dasa rājadhamme akopetvā agatigamanaṃ pariharā”ti porisādaṃ ovadi. Parosatāhi rājadhānīhi balakāyo yebhuyyena sannipati[P 5.0511]. So tena balakāyena parivuto bārāṇasito nikkhami. Porisādopi nikkhamitvā upaḍḍhapathā nivatti. Mahāsatto avāhanānaṃ rājūnaṃ vāhanāni datvā uyyojesi. Tepi rājāno tena saddhiṃ sammoditvā mahāsattaṃ vandanādīni katvā attano attano janapadaṃ agamiṃsu.

Having heard this Dhamma talk, the king, the commander-in-chief, and the queen were delighted and said, "Let us go, great king, and bring him back." They had drums beaten throughout the city, assembled the citizens, and reassured them, saying, "Do not be afraid. The king, it is said, is established in the Dhamma. Come, let us bring him back." Taking a large crowd with them and placing the Great Being at the forefront, they went to the king, paid homage to him, and had barbers attend to him. After the king was bathed, anointed, and adorned, with his hair and beard trimmed, they placed him upon a heap of jewels, consecrated him, and led him into the city. Having become king, Porisāda showed great honor to the hundreds of kshatriyas and to the Great Being. The news spread throughout all of Jambudīpa: "It is said that King Sutasoma tamed Porisāda and established him on the throne." The inhabitants of Indapatta city also sent a messenger, saying, "Let our king return." After staying there for about a month, the Great Being advised Porisāda, "Friend, I shall go now. Be diligent. Establish five alms halls at the four city gates and at the palace gate. Uphold the ten royal virtues without failing and avoid the wrong paths of prejudice." From hundreds of royal cities, a large army gathered. Surrounded by this army, the Great Being departed from Bārāṇasī. Porisāda also set out but turned back halfway. The Great Being provided vehicles for the kings who had none and sent them off. Those kings, after exchanging pleasantries and paying homage to the Great Being, each returned to their own kingdoms.

Mahāsattopi nagaraṃ patvā indapatthanagaravāsīhi devanagaraṃ viya alaṅkatanagaraṃ pavisitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā mahātalaṃ abhiruhi. So dhammena rajjaṃ kārento cintesi [V 5.0503] – “rukkhadevatā mayhaṃ bahūpakārā, balikammalābhamassā karissāmī”ti. So tassa nigrodhassa avidūre mahantaṃ taḷākaṃ kāretvā bahūni kulāni pesetvā [M 5.0553] gāmaṃ nivesesi. Gāmo mahā ahosi asītimattaāpaṇasahassapaṭimaṇḍito. Tampi rukkhamūlaṃ sākhantato paṭṭhāya samatalaṃ kāretvā parikkhittavedikatoraṇadvārayuttaṃ akāsi, devatā abhippasīdi. Kammāsapādassa damitaṭṭhāne nivuṭṭhattā pana so gāmo kammāsadammanigamo nāma jāto. Tepi sabbe rājāno mahāsattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā āyupariyosāne saggaṃ pūrayiṃsu.

The Great Being, having arrived at the city, entered Indapatta, which had been adorned like a divine city. After paying respects to his parents and engaging in pleasant conversation, he ascended the great terrace. Ruling righteously, he thought, "The tree deity has been very helpful to me; I shall make an offering to her." Not far from that banyan tree, he had a large reservoir constructed and settled many families there, establishing a village. The village became great, adorned with eighty thousand shops. Because it was established in the place where the dappled-footed Porisāda had been tamed, the village came to be known as Kammāsadammanigama. He also had the ground at the base of the banyan tree, from the edge of its branches inwards, leveled and surrounded it with railings, and provided it with arches and gates. The deity was greatly pleased. All those kings, abiding by the advice of the Great Being, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the heavens at the end of their lives.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā “na, bhikkhave, idānevāhaṃ aṅgulimālaṃ damemi, pubbepesa mayā damitoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā porisādo rājā aṅgulimālo ahosi, kāḷahatthi sāriputto, nandabrāhmaṇo ānando, rukkhadevatā kassapo, sakko anuruddho, sesarājāno buddhaparisā, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, sutasomarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have tamed Aṅgulimāla; in the past too, he was tamed by me." Then he connected the Jātaka: "At that time, King Porisāda was Aṅgulimāla, Kāḷahatthi was Sāriputta, the brahmin Nanda was Ānanda, the tree-deity was Kassapa, Sakka was Anuruddha, the remaining kings were the Buddha's assembly, the parents of the great royal family were the current royal parents, and King Sutasoma was indeed myself."

Mahāsutasomajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth part of the Commentary on the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka is finished.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Summary of the Jātakas:

Sumukho pana haṃsavaro ca mahā, sudhabhojaniko ca paro pavaro;

Sakuṇāladijādhipativhayano, sutasomavaruttamasavhayanoti.

Sumukha, the great and excellent goose; and Sudhābhojanika, another supreme one; the one named Lord of the Sakuṇāla birds; and the one named Sutasoma, excellent and supreme.

Asītinipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Eighty is concluded.

Pañcamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The fifth section is completed.
